This intermediate is subsequently cleaved by cystathionine γ-lyase (CSE), yielding α-ketobutyrate (αKB) and cysteine [25]. The generated cysteine then enters distinct metabolic branches: serving as a precursor for protein synthesis; participating in GSH biosynthesis through sequential conjugation with glutamate and glycine, catalyzed by γ-glutamyl cysteine synthetase (γ-GCS) and glutathione synthetase (GS); or being converted to other biologically significant sulfur-containing molecules, including hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and taurine [26]. This metabolic versatility underscores the central role of cysteine in cellular homeostasis, functioning not only as a proteinogenic amino acid but also as a critical component in antioxidant defense systems and cellular signaling pathways. Consequently, dysregulation of sulfur-containing amino acid metabolism has been linked to perturbations in cellular redox homeostasis and is proposed to impair DNA repair fidelity. Specifically, insufficient cysteine availability restricts GSH synthesis, compromising antioxidant capacity and leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and oxidative DNA damage. Moreover, the activity of key DNA repair enzymes is modulated by cellular redox status, and their dysfunction further exacerbates genomic instability. Ultimately, these processes are thought to contribute to oncogenic transformation through the accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions and genetic mutations.Beyond the direct consequences of oxidative stress, a critical yet often underappreciated impact of enhanced trans-sulphuration flux is its competitive pressure on methyl group availability. Homocysteine occupies a central metabolic node where it can either be remethylated to regenerate methionine and sustain SAM-dependent methylation reactions or be irreversibly diverted into the trans-sulphuration pathway for cysteine and GSH synthesis. Under conditions of metabolic stress or nutrient limitation such as folate or vitamin B deficiency, serine/glycine restriction, or increased oxidative burden in which cells preferentially channel homocysteine toward trans-sulphuration to reinforce antioxidant defenses.While this metabolic adaptation supports redox homeostasis, it may come at the expense of methyl donor availability. Reduced remethylation flux limits methionine regeneration and consequently decreases intracellular SAM levels, thereby lowering the SAM/SAH ratio, a key determinant of cellular methylation potential. This shift can impair DNA and histone methylation, leading to epigenetic dysregulation, altered chromatin accessibility, and aberrant gene expression. In the stressed tumor microenvironment, this prioritization of trans-sulphuration creates a metabolic trade-off: cells survive by enhancing their antioxidant capacity but simultaneously exacerbate epigenetic instability, further fueling cancer development.From an evolutionary perspective, the directionality of this pathway exhibits significant variation across species. While prokaryotes, fungi and plants possess the metabolic flexibility to reversibly convert cysteine to methionine, mammals have evolved an irreversible trans-sulphuration pathway [27]. This evolutionary adaptation reflects the specialized metabolic requirements of mammalian systems, where the unidirectional nature of the pathway ensures efficient sulfur redistribution and antioxidant production. To avoid confusion, the trans-sulphuration pathway in the context of this review referred to an irreversible process in mammals, distinguishing it from the bidirectional pathways observed in other organisms.The role of intracellular amino acid homeostasis in regulating 1C metabolismGiven that multiple amino acids serve as primary donors and regulators within 1C metabolism, the maintenance of intracellular amino acid homeostasis plays an essential role in sustaining 1C metabolic flux. Since amino acids exceeding the immediate demands of protein synthesis are generally redirected toward catabolic or biosynthetic pathways, their intracellular availability must be tightly coordinated through sensing and feedback mechanisms. These regulatory systems ensure a balanced amino acid pool that can dynamically support nucleotide biosynthesis, methylation reactions, and the maintenance of genomic integrity.Amino acid availability and sensing mechanismsUnder physiological conditions, intracellular amino acid levels, including their uptake, synthesis, and utilization, are tightly regulated by integrated nutrient-sensing pathways. Two major systems, general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) and mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), play complementary roles in maintaining this balance [28]. GCN2 functions as a sensor of amino acid deprivation by detecting the accumulation of uncharged transfer RNAs (tRNAs). Upon activation, GCN2 phosphorylates eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α), leading to a global attenuation of protein translation and a consequent reduction in amino acid consumption [29]. At the same time, this signaling selectively enhances the translation of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), which transcriptionally upregulates genes involved in amino acid transport and biosynthesis, including members of the solute carrier (SLC) family. This adaptive response increases amino acid uptake and promotes the synthesis of key metabolites, particularly serine and glycine. However, the role of the GCN2-eIF2α-ATF4 axis is not universally cytoprotective; its impact appears context-dependent. While acute activation supports 1C metabolic flux, chronic or excessive GCN2 signaling can paradoxically trigger apoptosis through the induction of CHOP, suggesting a fine-tuned threshold between metabolic adaptation and cell death that is often overlooked in descriptive models [30]. Furthermore, most mechanistic insights into these sensing pathways have been derived from in vitro studies using nutrient-defined media, which may not accurately reflect the complex, fluctuating amino acid gradients present in physiological tissues [31]. In contrast, mTORC1 serves as a central sensor of amino acid sufficiency, coordinating anabolic growth programs. When amino acids are abundant, mTORC1 is activated through Rag GTPase-dependent recruitment to the lysosomal surface, a process regulated by upstream amino acid sensors acting via the GATOR1-GATOR2 complex. Activated mTORC1 promotes protein synthesis and cell growth by phosphorylating downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) and eukaryotic initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1) [28]. In parallel, mTORC1 enhances metabolic pathways that support biosynthesis, thereby linking amino acid availability to cellular proliferation. Notably, recent evidence highlights a complex crosstalk where mTORC1 can suppress GCN2 activity, yet both pathways may be simultaneously active in different sub-regions of the same tissue, a spatial heterogeneity that challenges the traditional binary switch model of nutrient sensing.Rewiring of amino acid sensing in cancerIn the context of malignancy, the balance between amino acid availability and metabolic demand is frequently disrupted. Oncogenic signaling often results in sustained activation of mTORC1, partially uncoupling anabolic processes from nutrient availability. Mechanistically, mTORC1 promotes the mitochondrial tetrahydrofolate (mTHF) cycle through ATF4-dependent upregulation of methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase 2 (MTHFD2), thereby enhancing mitochondrial one-carbon flux. These 1C units are preferentially directed toward purine nucleotide biosynthesis, supporting the increased anabolic requirements of rapidly proliferating cancer cells [32]. As a result, activation of the mTHF pathway contributes to maintaining elevated 1C flux and facilitates tumor growth. Meanwhile, tumor cells frequently exploit the GCN2-ATF4 axis as an adaptive mechanism to cope with nutrient stress within the tumor microenvironment. This pathway is often upregulated under conditions of limited nutrient supply, promoting de novo amino acid synthesis and enhancing amino acid transport. Such metabolic reprogramming helps sustain one-carbon metabolism and alleviates replication stress, thereby supporting tumor cell survival under adverse conditions.Importantly, not all tumor types exhibit uniform dependence on these pathways. Emerging evidence indicates that certain cancers display limited reliance on GCN2 signaling or can bypass amino acid stress responses through alternative metabolic routes, such as increased nutrient scavenging or stromal support [33]. In addition, the majority of current evidence linking GCN2/mTORC1 signaling to 1C metabolism is based on cell culture or animal models, whereas clinical data remain relatively sparse and sometimes inconsistent [34]. These limitations underscore the need for integrative studies that combine metabolic flux analysis, genetic models, and patient-derived data to clarify the physiological and pathological relevance of these pathways.Methionine sensing and SAM-dependent regulation of 1C metabolismAmong amino acids, methionine plays a particularly important role in linking amino acid availability to one-carbon metabolism through its conversion to SAM, the universal methyl donor. Cellular SAM levels are sensed by SAMTOR, a key regulator of mTORC1 signaling [35]. Under conditions of sufficient methionine, SAM directly binds to SAMTOR, disrupting the SAMTOR-GATOR1 interaction and leading to activation of mTORC1 [36]. Through this mechanism, methionine availability is tightly coupled to anabolic signaling and methylation capacity. This methionine-SAM-mTORC1 axis not only regulates protein synthesis but also modulates SAM-dependent methylation reactions, including DNA and histone methylation. Dysregulation of this sensing pathway is commonly associated with methionine dependence in cancer cells, which exhibit an increased requirement for SAM to sustain aberrant epigenetic modifications. Consequently, enhanced methionine metabolism supports both nucleotide synthesis and epigenetic reprogramming, contributing to tumor progression and genomic instability.1C metabolism provides the constructive building blocks for gene mediated cell proliferationTurnover of specific amino acid components into 1C metabolism that are processed through the three reactive cycles, may output diverse constructive building blocks with informative biological functions. Here, we emphatically outline some building blocks conducted at gene levels for tumor cell proliferation, such as basic groups to assemble nucleotides, biosynthetic amino acid to trigger metabolic rewiring and biomacromolecules to maintain genomic integrity [37]. Importantly, dysregulation of these components contributes not only to proliferative capacity but also to tumor initiation. Specifically, perturbations in 1C metabolism disrupt nucleotide biosynthesis, leading to imbalanced nucleotide pools, replication stress, and increased rates of DNA misincorporation and DSBs, hallmarks of genomic instability. Such instability provides a substrate for oncogenic transformation. In many cancers, these pathways are aberrantly upregulated through multiple mechanisms, including direct transcriptional activation by oncogenic mutations, indirect modulation via altered translation of upstream or downstream regulators, and signaling pathway–driven expression of bioactive mediators. By delivering activated one-carbon units in distinct oxidative states, this cycle orchestrates the precise assembly of the genetic building blocks essential for DNA and RNA synthesis [15].Downstream impact on purine and thymidylate poolsThe metabolic outputs of the folate pool, specifically 10-formyl-THF and 5,10-me-THF, are indispensable for maintaining the structural integrity of the genome. Purine nucleotide bases, which are divided into adenine (A) and guanine (G), are generated from the folate pool through the intermediate 10-formyl-THF, which donates 1C units to carbon atoms 2 and 8 of the purine backbone [38]. The 1C units of 10-formyl-THF are originally from serine and glycine and glycine is required for purine synthesis because it can donate nitrogen atom 7 and carbon atoms 4 and 5 for purine ring [39]. And the de novo thymidylate synthesis is a pathway which involves the folate-dependent enzymes SHMT, thymidylate synthase (TYMS) and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) [42]. The efficiency of these reactions directly determines the fidelity of DNA replication and gene expression [43].Consequences of metabolic dysfunction for genomic stabilityGenome maintenance requires the precise balance of these nucleotide precursors, a process often jeopardized in cancers [44]. When folate-mediated 1C-flux is disrupted, an imbalance between dUMP and thymidylate occurs. As a result, uracil is incorporated into DNA by mistake, contributing to double-strand breaks (DSBs), chromosomal abnormalities, and genetic instability [45]. Furthermore, in scenarios of metabolic stress, such as SHMT depletion, the cell may prioritize the methionine cycle at the expense of thymidylate synthesis. This is because hypusine is necessary for the association of eukaryotic initiation factor 5 A (eIF5A) with ribosomes [48] (Fig. 4). Normal cells maintain low basal ROS levels with tightly controlled antioxidant responses, ensuring genomic integrity and signaling fidelity. In contrast, cancer cells operate under a state of chronic oxidative stress due to oncogene activation, metabolic rewiring, and hypoxic microenvironments. To survive under these conditions, malignant cells upregulate antioxidant systems, particularly NADPH and GSH production through 1C metabolism, creating a new redox equilibrium characterized by elevated ROS alongside enhanced buffering capacity. This altered redox state provides selective advantages for tumor progression, including increased mutation rates and adaptive signaling, while simultaneously rendering cancer cells more dependent on redox homeostasis mechanisms and thus more susceptible to therapeutic disruption.Effect of redox imbalance on biomacromolecules and cellular structuresStructural perturbations in key amino acids disrupt 1C metabolism, compromises the production of antioxidant intermediates required to counteract ROS. The resultant cumulative ROS accumulation surpasses cellular detoxification capacity, precipitating a state of oxidative stress and redox imbalance [58]. ROS exhibits inherent chemical reactivity that drives indiscriminate modifications of biomolecules, inducing structural alterations, aberrant localization, disrupted intermolecular interactions and functional impairment. Given the pervasive involvement of redox imbalance across diverse metabolic pathways, a comprehensive enumeration of all affected biological macromolecules and cellular compartments exceeds the scope of this discussion. Consequently, we concentrate on oxidative damage mechanisms targeting nucleic acids integrity and mitochondrial structural alterations.Impact on genomic integrity and cancer-specific 1C alterationsThe maintenance of genomic integrity is tethered to a dynamic redox equilibrium governed by mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and 1C metabolic pathway. 1C metabolism serves as the critical determinant of cellular redox buffering capacity, primarily through the generation of NADPH, which is essential for the regeneration of reduced GSH and the functional integrity of the thioredoxin system.When ROS production exceeds the kinetic saturation of 1C-supported antioxidant systems, oxidative damage manifests as 8-oxodG and DSBs [59]. This process is not merely a bystander effect of metabolic stress but a causal driver of mutagenesis. We posit a self-reinforcing loop: 1C-deficiency-induced ROS causes initial DNA lesions, which impair the transcription of mitochondrial repair enzymes, leading to mitochondrial ETC dysfunction, further ROS leakage, and systemic genomic collapse [60].The dysregulation of specific 1C metabolic intermediates significantly modulates this damage landscape across various malignancies. Crucially, the redox response of malignant cells undergo a fundamental redox resetting, characterized by chronically elevated ROS levels and a compensatory, albeit fragile, reliance on 1C-dependent antioxidant machinery (e.g., PHGDH or MTHFD2 overexpression). This adaptation creates a narrow therapeutic window: while cancer cells leverage these metabolic adjustments to support rapid proliferation, their proximity to the lethal threshold of oxidative stress makes them hypersensitive to interventions that disrupt NADPH/GSH synthesis.For instance, in phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase-amplified breast cancer and melanoma, the redirection of glycolytic flux toward serine synthesis is markedly upregulated [61]. This elevation in intracellular serine not only fuels nucleotide biosynthesis but also ensures a robust supply of glycine and cysteine for GSH production, allowing these cells to tolerate high ROS loads while maintaining genomic stability. Conversely, in MYC-driven lung adenocarcinoma, an overflow of formate, a key 1C intermediate is often observed; this formate surplus accelerates purine synthesis to support rapid proliferation, yet simultaneously alters the NADPH/NADP+ ratio, potentially sensitizing the genome to oxidative lesions if the antioxidant buffer is breached [62]. Furthermore, in hepatocellular carcinoma, depletion of SAM often leads to global DNA hypomethylation, which synergizes with ROS-mediated damage to promote chromosomal instability and the activation of oncogenic drivers [63].These metabolic-redox-genomic axes illustrate that 1C metabolic defects do not merely permit DNA damage but actively shape the mutational signature of specific cancers by limiting the production of NADPH (essential for GSH recycling) or altering the availability of methyl donors. This interplay determines cell fate: depending on the magnitude of damage, cells may undergo ATM/ATR-mediated cell cycle arrest to allow for repair, or trigger p53-dependent apoptosis via Bax or p21 pathways to eliminate compromised cell [64]. However, surviving clones often leverage 1C metabolic flexibility to evolve resistance against persistent oxidative stress. This adaptability, which involves switching between mitochondrial and cytosolic 1C pathways, contributes to clonal evolution and malignancy.The convergence of metabolic dysfunction, redox imbalance and genomic instability forms a critical axis that not only underlies tissue-specific pathologies in response to abnormal 1C metabolic intermediates but also offers a compelling framework for understanding the shared etiology of cancer initiation. This triad creates a self-reinforcing cycle for tumor oxidative microenvironment, in which mitochondrial ROS damages nuclear DNA and impairs transcription of metabolic genes, then further exacerbates oxidative stress. Ultimately, deciphering this metabolic-redox-genomic network may unlock novel strategies to safeguard genomic health and mitigate mutation-related disease through targeted modulation of 1C metabolism or selective activation of damage clearance pathways.Redox imbalance disrupts mitochondrial function and metabolic homeostasisUnder sustained environmental stress, prolonged overproduction of ROS causes cumulative damage to cellular structures and functions, potentially leading to somatic mutations and neoplastic transformation. Concurrently, the oxidative TME created by invasive tumors can itself be a source of oxidative stress, impairing major organelles such as mitochondria. In this context, 1C metabolism is co-opted to help neutralize the resulting oxidative burden. As central hubs of intracellular energy metabolism, mitochondria orchestrate nutrient catabolism for ATP production while simultaneously generating biosynthetic precursors. Thus, mitochondria must dynamically upregulate their antioxidant defense system to counteract redox imbalance. Critically, excessive ROS accumulation triggers a self-perpetuating cycle: mitochondrial dysfunction induces metabolic stress that paradoxically amplifies ROS generation through electron transport chain leakage, resulting in biomolecular damage and programmed cell death. Significantly, mitochondria-derived ROS exert dual oncogenic roles: directly inducing mtDNA mutations while simultaneously activating pro-tumorigenic signaling pathways through oxidative modification of nuclear transcription factors. Recent mechanistic studies reveal that serine catabolism through 1C metabolism serve as a redox rheostat within the mitochondrial matrix, maintaining NADPH/GSH pools with antioxidant responses [65]. This metabolic adaptation highlights mitochondrial essential role as both biosynthetic centers and gatekeepers against oxidative cascades that could otherwise initiate malignant transformation. Therefore, maintaining redox homeostasis through 1C metabolic adaptations enables mitochondria to effectively serve as central hubs for metabolic waste processing while safeguarding genomic integrity and cellular viability.Importantly, cell fate decisions are strongly influenced by ROS thresholds: moderate increases promote adaptive responses and proliferation, whereas excessive ROS accumulation beyond repair capacity triggers irreversible damage, leading to apoptosis or other forms of cell death.Remodeling immunosuppressive TMEThe TME constitutes a sophisticated biological niche characterized by dynamic interactions between malignant cells, resident immune populations, stromal constituents and extracellular matrix components [66]. A pathological hallmark of the TME is its profound immunosuppressive nature, which orchestrates tumor immune escape mechanisms and fosters neoplastic advancement through multiple signaling pathways. Notably, ROS demonstrate a concentration-dependent duality in their biological impacts: at physiological levels, they mediate crucial cellular signaling for immune activation, while excessive accumulation may promote oxidative stress and immunosuppression [67]. Given this context, the strategic modulation of 1C metabolism-derived intermediates to maintain redox homeostasis, coupled with the reprogramming of the immunosuppressive TME, has emerged as a critical therapeutic approach to enhance anti-tumor immunity and improve the effectiveness of cancer treatments (Fig. 5).ROS acts as promoter for immune activationROS function as critical secondary messengers and promoter in immune activation, orchestrating both innate and adaptive immune responses through redox-sensitive signaling pathways. At physiological concentrations, ROS sustain T cell activation by amplifying T cell receptor (TCR) signaling cascades. Mechanistically, ROS-mediated TCR potentiation drives the nuclear translocation of key transcription factors, including nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT), activator protein-1 (AP-1) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), thereby coordinating T cell proliferation and effector functions [68]. Concurrently, ROS modulate macrophage plasticity by polarizing these cells toward a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype, which mediates antitumor responses via enhanced phagocytic clearance, immunostimulatory cytokine secretion (e.g., TNF-α, IL-12) and tumor-associated antigen presentation. This dual regulatory role underscores the importance of maintaining ROS within a tightly controlled physiological range, as optimal redox balance ensures proper immunometabolic reprogramming, biosynthetic activity and functional coordination of immune effectors [69].Excess redox leads to immunosuppressionMaintaining redox equilibrium becomes particularly challenging when dysregulation occurs in 1C metabolism, a process critically dependent on key amino acids such as serine and glycine. Disruption of 1C metabolic pathways disrupts GSH homeostasis, culminating in excessive ROS accumulation. This redox imbalance disrupts antitumor immunity by crippling dendritic cell (DC) functionality, specifically impairing antigen cross-presentation to CD8+T cells, a process essential for priming adaptive antitumor responses [70]. Paradoxically, elevated ROS levels create a permissive niche for immunosuppressive cell populations, including M2-polarized macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and regulatory T cells (Treg cell) [71]. These immunosuppressive cells not only survive in high-ROS environments but also further amplify ROS production. This self-reinforcing cycle sustains immunosuppression through the secretion of immunosuppressive cytokines (e.g., IL-10, TGF-β) and upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules (e.g., PD-L1, CTLA-4). These mechanisms synergize with tumor-promoting matrix remodeling and angiogenesis, collectively driving malignant progression. Specifically, TGF-β not only inhibits T cell function but also induces PD-L1 expression on tumor cells, while simultaneously activating cancer-associated fibroblasts to deposit a pro-angiogenic extracellular matrix [72]. Such interactions establish a feedforward loop wherein tumor growth reinforces immunosuppression and vice versa.Severe ROS overload initiates a self-amplifying cytotoxic cascade, wherein oxidative damage to nuclear and mitochondrial DNA synergizes with metabolic collapse to propagate further ROS generation. This vicious cycle arises from mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by impaired ETC activity and increased mitochondrial membrane permeability. This permeability facilitates the release of mtDNA into the cytosol, where it activates the cGAS-STING pathway to initiate innate immune signaling thus causing nuclear DNA damage responses [73]. Concurrently, DSBs and base modifications activate poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)-mediated repair pathways, depleting NAD+ reserves and exacerbating metabolic stress [74]. The resulting NAD+/ATP crisis destabilizes redox-sensitive signaling networks, as evidenced by oxidation-induced inactivation of AKT and AMPK-driven mTOR suppression, culminating in irreversible biomolecular damage through lipid peroxidation, protein carbonylation and RNA oxidation [75]. Non-malignant cells, particularly SOD2-low lymphocytes, undergo apoptosis or functional exhaustion under sustained oxidative pressure. In contrast, cancer cells adapt via dual stress-response mechanisms: HIF-1α-driven glycolytic reprogramming to bypass mitochondrial ROS and Nrf2-mediated upregulation of GPx4 to resist ferroptosis [76]. This dichotomy underscores the therapeutic imperative to precisely modulate redox homeostasis, suppressing tumor-promoting oxidative stress while preserving ROS-dependent immune activation through strategies such as antioxidant-boosted immunotherapy.Dysregulation of methylation donors drives epigenetic chaosSAM, the principal methyl donor in mammalian methylation processes, is generated through the methionine cycle and serves as a cornerstone for epigenetic and epitranscriptomic regulation [77]. Beyond its canonical role in mediating DNA and histone methylation, SAM has emerged as a critical modulator of genetic stability, bridging metabolic dynamics with mutagenic and adaptive mechanisms. Tumorigenesis is frequently characterized by elevated mutational stress, in terms of epigenetics, attributing to early microenvironmental stressors such as hypoxia, overnutrition, or redox imbalance that disrupt SAM homeostasis [78]. These stressors promote a state of epigenetic chaos driven by the dysregulation of methylation donors, as summarized in Table 2. This manifests via compromised DNA repair fidelity (e.g., through erroneous repair pathway choice or impaired damage sensing) and lead to chromosomal segregation errors, thereby accelerating mutation accumulation and fostering the evolution of cell populations toward increasingly aggressive phenotypes. Crucially, hypermethylation or the redistribution of methylation marks under these conditions disrupts the epigenetic landscape, thereby creating a permissive ‘breeding ground’ for the accumulation of mutations and oncogenic reprogramming. To unravel this nexus, we systematically dissect the tripartite roles of SAM-dependent methylation in DNA, histones and RNA, highlighting their convergent impacts on genomic integrity and tumor suppression. Elucidating these mechanisms not only advances our understanding of carcinogenesis but also unveils therapeutic opportunities to restore methylation equilibrium and intercept tumor progression. Molecular and genetic studies have demonstrated that this methylation leads to gene silencing through two primary mechanisms: direct steric hindrance that prevents transcription factors from binding to their regulatory elements, and the recruitment of methyl-CpG-binding domain proteins (MBDs) and associated repressor complexes to methylated regions. This epigenetic imbalance disrupts the transcriptional programs that govern cell identity and genetic stability, thereby creating a permissive environment for tumorigenesis (Fig. 7). The following sections dissect how aberrant histone methylation, through both the loss of repression and gain of activation, drives oncogenic transformation. Fig. 7Histone methylation associates with the alteration of genetic stability. The nuclear chromatin landscape is dynamically regulated between two principal states: euchromatin and heterochromatin, which are defined by distinct histone PTMs that modulate nucleosome packing density and transcriptional activity. In euchromatin, histones are loosely packed, allowing TFs and RNA polymerase (RNA Pol) to access DNA. This open chromatin state is enriched with transcription-activating histone marks, most notably H3K4me3, which accumulates at promoters of actively transcribed genes, peaking near the TSS. Collectively, such modifications are represented by H3K4me3 can coordinate splicing, maintain transcriptional stability, regulate cryptic transcription and sense-antisense transcriptions, as well as confer transcriptional memory, which are all associated with their promotion of transcription. This condensed state is marked by repressive histone methylations, including H3K9me3 and H3K27me3. In addition, H3K9me3 heterochromatin is required for the formation of NPCs, which are channels that facilitate the continuous flow of molecules and macromolecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm. NPCs improve the transport efficiency of a kind of protein associated with gene regulation into the nucleus and ultimately help maintain the heterochromatin. Unlike DNA methylation, which predominantly represses transcription, the function outcome of histone methylation depends on the modified residue and its methylation state, leading to either transcriptional activation or repression [85]. This fidelity of histone methylation is critically dependent on SAM availability from 1C metabolism. H3K9me is primarily linked to the formation of heterochromatin, a tightly packed chromatin state that silences gene expression. Conversely, when H3K36me is located in promoter regions, it can repress transcription. Among these, histones PTMs play a pivotal role by modulating histone-DNA interactions, leading to the formation of tightly packed heterochromatin. Its dysregulation contributes to the epigenetic silencing of TSGs. Consequently, therapeutic strategies are being developed to target this cycle, primarily by depleting the universal methyl donor SAM, thereby reversing aberrant hypermethylation and restoring gene expression.A hallmark of many cancers is methionine addiction, a dependency on exogenous methionine despite a functionally intact intrinsic synthesis pathway. The duration of methionine restriction is a crucial: short-term deprivation or intermittent dietary methionine restriction can induce ferroptosis in these cells by upregulating the transcription of cation transport regulator homolog 1 (CHAC1) [115]. Beyond methionine, the dietary restriction of other intermediate metabolites from methionine cycle, such as Cys and GSH, represents promising strategies for cancer therapy.The efficacy of direct epigenetic drugs can be potentiated by simultaneously targeting the methionine cycle. Nucleoside analogs like decitabine and azacitidine incorporate into DNA and trap DNMTs, leading to their degradation. Pre-treatment or co-treatment with methionine restriction depletes the SAM pool, synergistically enhancing DNA hypomethylation.Consistently, DNMT inhibitors have been extensively evaluated in ClinicalTrials.gov-registered studies, and their combination with metabolic interventions is gaining increasing clinical interest (Table 3).This combination strategy promotes more robust and sustained reactivation of TSGs, potentially enabling the use of lower, less toxic doses of DNMT inhibitors. This approach has entered preclinical verification in leukemia and lymphoma models [116].Therefore, targeting the methionine cycle is proposed to undermine the foundational machinery and sustains DNA hypermethylation to disrupt the adaptive flexibility of tumor cells. By depleting SAM, increasing the level of its inhibitory derivative SAH, or creating specific metabolic vulnerabilities, these interventions shift the epigenetic landscape away from a transcriptionally repressed state. The subsequent reactivation of critical TSGs is suggested to restore their anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic functions, ultimately potentially inhibiting tumor growth and survival.Challenges and limitations in targeting 1C metabolism in cancerDespite the increasing recognition of 1C metabolism as a central regulator of tumor proliferation and genomic integrity, several formidable challenges impede its effective therapeutic exploitation. A primary obstacle lies in the profound metabolic plasticity of cancer cells, which enables a dynamic rewiring of 1C flux across interconnected subnetworks, including the folate cycle, methionine cycle, and trans-sulphuration pathway. This inherent flexibility allows tumor cells to circumvent the pharmacological blockade of a single enzymatic node by engaging alternative nutrient sources or compensatory biochemical routes. For instance, the inhibition of mitochondrial 1C enzymes such as SHMT2 or MTHFD2 may be effectively bypassed through the upregulation of cytosolic serine catabolism or the enhanced scavenging of exogenous metabolites like formate [117]. Consequently, such adaptive reprogramming markedly attenuates the clinical efficacy of single-pathway inhibition strategies, suggesting that only multi-node targeting can achieve sustained suppression.Furthermore, accumulating evidence underscores the context-dependent and, at times, ostensibly contradictory roles of 1C metabolism in tumorigenesis. While elevated 1C flux typically facilitates nucleotide biosynthesis and redox homeostasis, there are notable contexts where it may confer a metabolic liability rather than an advantage. These discrepancies are heavily dictated by the tumor lineage, the underlying genetic landscape (such as MYC amplification or p53 status), and the specific microenvironmental niche, all of which influence a tumor’s dependency on 1C-derived metabolites [88, 118]. This heterogeneity is further complicated by the narrow therapeutic window inherent to 1C-targeted agents; since this pathway is equally vital for the homeostasis of rapidly dividing healthy cells, such as hematopoietic progenitors and intestinal epithelium, potent inhibition often leads to significant systemic toxicity. Thus, identifying collateral lethality or tumor-specific vulnerabilities remains a prerequisite for minimizing off-target effects.Finally, substantial barriers persist in translating mechanistic insights derived from experimental models to the complexity of human disease. Much of our current understanding originates from in vitro cultures or murine models, which frequently fail to recapitulate the nutrient architecture of the human TME. Notably, standard culture media are often replete with supraphysiological concentrations of folate and serine, which may artificially inflate the apparent dependence of cancer cells on specific pathways while masking others. Moreover, critical interspecies differences exist between murine and human physiology, particularly regarding systemic nutrient flux and folate transport kinetics that may obscure potential therapeutic liabilities. These discrepancies likely contribute to the frequent disconnect between promising preclinical observations and the modest clinical performance of several 1C-targeted therapies. Collectively, these challenges underscore the imperative for more nuanced therapeutic paradigms, necessitating combinatorial strategies and the development of robust biomarkers for patient stratification.Collectively, this review highlights that the precise regulation of 1C metabolism, tightly dependent on key amino acids, serves as a critical cellular safeguard for oncogenesis. Disruption of this network can initiate a self-perpetuating cascade of genomic instability, driven by epigenetic alteration and the accumulation of mutational burden. Notably, cancer cells actively exploit the oncogenic potential of 1C metabolism by exploiting its role in maintaining genetic stability, thereby converting it into a driver of tumor development.Through the integrated disturbance of nucleotide synthesis, methylation dynamics, and redox balance, aberrant 1C metabolism linking epigenetic reprogramming, genomic instability and oxidative stress, ultimately promoting malignant progression. In this context, targeting dysregulated 1C metabolic pathways represents a promising therapeutic avenue. This review synthesized current genetic and metabolic evidence across cancer types to support this perspective. The critical next step lies in translating this knowledge into clinical breakthroughs through the continued development of more effective and highly specific compounds.

title: Protein phosphatase 2 phosphatase activator (PTPA) promotes oncogene-induced senescence and carboplatin response in human malignant pleural mesothelioma cells
abstract: PurposeMalignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is a rare cancer of the pleura, frequently related to asbestos exposure. It is characterized by a grim prognosis, as few therapeutic options are available. Typically, MPM exhibits high molecular heterogeneity, providing opportunities for exploiting therapeutic vulnerabilities in well-defined subgroups of patients. Nevertheless, these options have been insufficiently explored.Methods & We found that inactivation of Protein Phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a recurrent event in MPM, affecting the cancer cell phenotype and chemotherapy response. Specifically, in silico analysis showed that heterozygous loss of PTPA (PPP2R4), encoding the PP2A activator PTPA, occurred in 26% of MPM patients (TCGA, n = 87), correlating with significantly decreased overall survival. Re-expression of PTPA in PTPA-low human MPM cells decreased 2D colony formation and anchorage-independent cell growth, without affecting cell migration. At enzyme level, PTPA restoration increased PP2A catalytic subunit expression and activity (methylation), without favoring specific PP2A holoenzymes. Comparative RNAseq and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis revealed increased RAS pathway activation, activated p53 signaling and induction of senescence (SA-β-Galactosidase, SASP, NF-κB activation) upon PTPA restoration, presumably by increased PP2A-dependent dephosphorylation of Kinase Suppressor of Ras 1. Suppressing Ras signaling by Trametinib (MEK-inhibitor) prevented senescence induction, and pretreatment with senolytic agents restored impaired growth. ATUX-792, a pharmacologic PP2A activator, did not phenocopy senescence induction. Finally, PTPA restoration sensitized MPM cells to carboplatin as the likely consequence of lethal stress induction.sPTPA promotes oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) in MPM. By preventing OIS, heterozygous PTPA loss may contribute to mesothelial transformation and carboplatin resistance.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at
full_text: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare cancer with a unique biology that originates in the mesothelium, a protective cell layer covering body cavities, such as the pleura, the peritoneum, the pericardium, and the tunica vaginalis [1]. Among its different subtypes, malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is the most common, accounting for 90% of cases [2]. The main risk factor for MPM is asbestos fibre inhalation, with a long latency period of 20–40 years between initial exposure and disease presentation [2, 3]. Despite asbestos being banned in more than 55 countries, global MPM incidence is still increasing, with approximately 2400 new cases reported each year [3, 4]. According to molecular genomics studies, MPM is a highly heterogeneous cancer that is largely defined by loss-of-function mutations in tumor suppressor genes, most frequently in CDKN2A, BAP1, NF2, LATS2, and TP53 [5, 6]. Hence, besides aberrant cell cycle checkpoint regulation, inactivated Hippo signaling, characterized by increased oncogenic YAP activity, is one of the major molecularly altered pathways [1]. Rarely, activating oncogenic driver mutations have been found (e.g. in KRAS, EGFR, HGFR and FGFR) [7–9] and signaling pathways such as mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) or Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) are only sporadically activated [1]. Despite this comprehensive molecular profiling, limited and ineffective treatment options exist for MPM. For decades, chemotherapy based on cisplatin (or carboplatin) and pemetrexed has been the standard of care; targeted treatments, although tested to some extent in clinical trials, have not shown any improved outcomes. Recently, the emergence of immune checkpoint inhibitors has shown promising results, though only in a small group of responder patients [2, 10]. Consequently, MPM prognosis remains poor, with an overall survival rate of +1 (Suppl. Fig. S2), and these values were also correlated with overall survival. Overall survival analyses were performed in cBioPortal (Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank tests) comparing PTPA hetloss and PTPA unaltered groups, and independently, using Cox proportional hazards models, including both univariate and multivariate analyses to identify independent prognostic factors. Statistical analyses and visualization were conducted in R using the packages survival, broom, dplyr, and ggplot2. Further analyses were performed in cBioPortal to compare differences in distribution of specific histological subtypes, tumor stages, genomic instability scores, age at diagnosis and treatment (only radiation therapy data were available) between the PP2A altered and unaltered patient groups, and to determine co-occurrence or mutual-exclusivity of defined PP2A alterations with each other, or with established MPM marker genes (BAP1, TP53, CDKN2A, CDKN2B, LATS2 and NF2).Cell linesA panel of cell lines representative of different histological MPM subtypes was used, including IST-MES1, IST-MES2, NCI-H2052, MSTO-211H, NCI-H2452, ZL34, and NCI-H226, along with an untransformed pleural mesothelial cell line MeT-5A. All cell lines were cultured at 37 °C and 5% CO₂ in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco, #A1049101) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Biowest, #S1600) and penicillin/streptomycin (100 units/mL and 10 mg/mL, respectively; Sigma, #P0781). All cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC), except for ZL34, which was a generous gift of Prof. L. Willems (ULg, Liège, Belgium) and NCI-H226, which was kindly provided by Prof. G. Halder (KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium) (Table 1). IST-MES1 and IST-MES2 were purchased from IRCCS Ospedale Policlinico San Martino. Mycoplasma-free status was regularly tested with Venor™ GeM (Minerva Biolabs, #11–1050). Table 1MPM gene marker alterations in the three MPM cell lines used for phenotypic studiesZL34NCI-H226NCI-H2452BAP1/Hom del [42]Het loss [42] CDKN2A Hom del (this study)Hom del (CVCL_1544)Hom del (CVCL_1553) NF2 Hom del (this study)Hetloss [43]WT [43] TP53 WT (this study, [44])WT [45]Truncation [45] Lentiviral transductionHEK293T cells (ATCC) were cultured in DMEM (Sigma, #D6546) supplemented with 10% FBS, 2 mM L-glutamine (Sigma, #G7513), and penicillin/streptomycin (100 units/mL and 10 mg/mL, respectively). For lentivirus production, cells in a 6-well plate were co-transfected with 0.9 µg of pCMV-deltaR8.9, 0.1 µg of pMD.G-VSVG, and 1 µg of either a pLenti6.4(3xFLAG)- or pLKO-based expression plasmid using TurboFect™ (Thermo Fisher, #R0531). To generate EGFP pLenti6.4(3xFLAG) and PTPA pLenti6.4(3xFLAG), the EGFP and PTPA coding regions were cloned into pLenti6.4(3×FLAG) without removing the start codons, resulting in expression of both tagged and untagged GFP or PTPA. For stable knockdown experiments, two independent PTPA-targeting short hairpins (shPTPA1 and shPTPA2) and one short hairpin targeting EGFP (shGPP) were cloned into pLKO (sequences in Suppl. Table S1). The viral supernatant was collected 72 h post-transfection, passed through a 0.45 μm filter, and quantified using the Lentivirus qPCR Quantification Kit (Abm, #LV900). Subsequently, MPM or MeT-5A cells were seeded in a 24-well plate and transduced with a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 10 for 24 h in the presence of Polybrene (Sigma, #TR-1003-G), and then selected with Blasticidin (Gibco, #A1113903) (pLenti6.4) or puromycin (Gibco, #A1113803) (pLKO). Protein lysates were prepared, and immunoblotting for PTPA was performed to confirm overexpression or knockdown. All subsequent experiments were executed with polyclonal populations of each transduced cell line.Protein extraction, nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation, and western blottingCells were collected and washed twice with ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (Sigma, #D8537) before being lysed in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher, # ) supplemented with cOmplete™ protease inhibitors (Roche, # ) and PhosSTOP™ phosphatase inhibitors (Roche, # ) to obtain total cell lysates. Protein concentration of the lysates was determined using Pierce™ BCA (Invitrogen, # ) to ensure equal loading. To obtain nuclear and cytoplasmic extracts, subcellular fractionation was performed with the NE-PER Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction kit (Thermo Fisher, #7833), according to manufacturer’s instructions.For Western blotting, lysates or IPs were diluted in sample buffer (4X NuPAGE™ LBS,#NP0008 and Invitrogen, #NP007) and boiled (10 min, 96 °C). Total lysates (15–20 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE on NuPAGE™ 4–12% Bis–Tris Midi Protein Gels (Invitrogen,#WG1402) at 150 V for 90 min. Proteins were transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane (Cytiva, # ) by wet blotting (60 min, 100 V). Membranes were stained with Ponceau (Thermo Fisher, #BP103) and blocked for 1 h at room temperature using either 5% non-fat dry milk (PanReac AppliChem,#A0830) or 0.1% bovine serum albumin (BSA, PanReac AppliChem, #A6588) in Tris-buffered saline (TBS)-Tween®20 (TBS-T). Membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies (Suppl. Table S2), followed by incubation with the corresponding HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Suppl. Table S2) for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized with WesternBright® HRP ECL substrate (Advansta, #K- -D50) using Amersham™ ImageQuant™ 800 imager (Cytiva). Signals were quantified using Image Studio Lite (5.2) and ImageQuantTL (v10.2–499). Quantification of phospho-specific and total protein signals was performed on different blots by normalization to the vinculin signal (loading control), followed by calculation of the ratios between the normalized phospho-specific and normalized total protein signals.PP2A C subunit immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS)ZL34 cells were seeded in 10 cm dishes at a density of 7.5-8 × 105 cells/dish. Following protein extraction, equal amounts of lysates of parental and PTPA-overexpressing cells were incubated with a GFP-tagged PP2A C nanobody (10 µg nanobody per 1 mg of lysate protein) for 1 h at 4 °C, followed by incubation with 20 µl of GFP-trapping beads (ChromoTek) pre-washed in NENT 100 buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% NP-40, 25% glycerol, and 100 mM NaCl) containing 1 mg/mL BSA, for an additional hour at 4 °C. Beads were then extensively washed: twice with 500 µL NENT 150 (NENT 100 with 150 mM NaCl instead); twice with NENT 100; twice with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), twice with Tris-HCl (pH 8.5) containing 0.0025% ProteaseMAX (Promega, #V2072), and subjected to overnight on-bead digestion in the presence of 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 0.01% ProteaseMAX and 0.5 µg trypsin (Thermo Fisher, # ). After digestion, 100 µl of water was added to the beads. The supernatant was brought to 0.5% TFA and allowed to stand at room temperature for 15 min to degrade the ProteaseMAX. After centrifugation, the supernatant was desalted on Pierce C18 Spin Columns (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The eluate was vacuum-dried and resuspended in 20 µl of 5% CH3CN, 0.1% formic acid of which 5 µl was injected on a Xevo G3 QTOF (Waters) LC-MS/MS instrument operated in MSe mode. Data analysis was executed using PLGS™ software (Waters) using Uniprot Homo sapiens (reviewed) to which the GFP protein was added as a database. Oxidation (M) was included as a variable modification. Two missed trypsin cleavages were allowed. Semi-quantification of proteins was executed using the Hi3 method essentially as described in Silva et al. [46] Only ‘pass2’ peptides were taken into account. Samples were normalized based on the GFP tag of the nanobody. Missing values were imputed (average). Peptide abundances that were common to different PP2A isoforms were attributed to the individual isoforms pro rata of their Hi3 values only taking unique peptides into account.2D colony formationMPM or MeT-5A cells were seeded at a density of 3000–5000 cells/dish in 10 cm dishes. After 5 days of incubation, the medium was carefully removed and replaced with fresh complete medium. After 12–14 days of growth, cell colonies were washed with PBS and stained with crystal violet (2 g/L in H2O; Sigma, #V5265) prepared in 2.5% glutaraldehyde solution (Sigma, # ). Colony number was quantified using the GelCount software.3D colony formation in soft agar24-well plates were coated with culture medium containing 0.8-1% low-gelling temperature agarose (Sigma-Aldrich, #A9045). MPM cell lines were seeded at a density of 1–3 × 103 cells per well. Cells were resuspended in RPMI containing 20% FBS and 0.4–0.5% agarose. After solidification, medium was added on top, and plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2. After 21 days, cells were stained with Thiazolyl Blue Tetrazolium bromide (MTT, 3 mg/mL in PBS; Thermo Fisher, #L11939.06) at 37 °C for 4 h. Images were acquired using HP Scanjet G2710 Photo Scanner, and colonies were quantified using Fiji (ImageJ).Wound healing assayZL34 cells were seeded at a density of 4 × 104 cells/well in a 96-well plate (Sartorius ImageLock, #4856) and incubated overnight. The wound was made using the WoundMaker™ pin block, followed by two washes with PBS. Cells were cultured in RPMI containing 2% FBS to prevent growth. Cell migration was monitored and imaged using an IncuCyte® S3 device (Sartorius) for 24 h. Relative wound density (%) was quantified using the IncuCyte 2024 B Software, defined as the ratio of the cell-occupied area of the initial wound area to the total wound area.Confluency assay in real-timeMeT-5A cells were seeded at a concentration of 3000 cells per well in a 96-well plate. After 24 h, the cells were transfected with one of three predesigned DsiRNAs targeting human PTPA or a negative DsiRNA control (TriFECTa® DsiRNA kit (IDT), sequences in Suppl. Table S1) at a final concentration of 10 nM, using Lipofectamine™ RNAiMAX (Invitrogen, # ). Live-cell imaging was performed for 96 h in the Incucyte (Sartorius). Confluency was determined by using the AI confluency mask provided by the Incucyte software. The same setup was used for stably transduced shGFP and shPTPA MeT-5A cells. Cells were seeded at 3000 cells per well (96-well-plate) and imaged for 96 h in the Incucyte device.Bulk RNA-sequencingZL34 cells with or without stable PTPA overexpression were seeded in a 6-well plate at a density of 2 × 105 cells/well. After 48 h, RNA extraction was performed using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, # ). The samples were subjected to DNase (Qiagen, # ) digestion to remove any residual DNA. Samples with a 260 nm/280 nm ratio between 1.8 and 2.1 were further processed for RNAseq, which was outsourced to Novagen. Raw FASTQ reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38) using STAR (v2.7.3a) with GENCODE v42 annotation. Gene-level counts were generated with featureCounts based on the same annotation. Differential expression analysis was performed in R using DESeq2 following standard procedures. All protein-coding genes were ranked by Log2FoldChange and used to perform pre-ranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) to identify enriched pathways. Raw and processed data are available in Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) through accession number GSE312009.Compound treatmentsCarboplatin (Sanbio, #HY- ), Trametinib (MedChemExpress, #HY- ), Dasatinib (Merck, #SML2589) and Quercetin (MedChemExpress, #HY- ) were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions. ATUX-792 (Atux Iskay LLC) was prepared and stored as described previously [47]. To obtain dose-response curves, MPM cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 3,000 cells per well and treated with increasing concentrations of ATUX-792 (0.39, 0.78, 1.56, 3.13, 6.25, 12.5, 25 and 50 µM) or carboplatin (2.5, 5, 15, 50, 100, 120, 180, 200 and 300 µM) for 72 h. Cell viability was assessed using Thiazolyl Blue Tetrazolium bromide (MTT) (Alfa Aesar, #L11939.06). Briefly, 20 µL of MTT solution (2 mg/mL) was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 4 h. Following incubation, the medium was removed, and formazan crystals were solubilized in 200 µL DMSO. Absorbance was measured at 550 nm, and EC50 values were calculated using logistic regression in GraphPad Prism 8.0.1 (GraphPad Software; RRID: SCR_002798). For short-term treatment assays, MPM cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 80,000 cells per well. After 24 h, cells were treated with Trametinib at 25 µM (NCI-H2452) or 15 µM (ZL34 cells), or with ATUX-792 at 6 µM (ZL34) or 8 µM (NCI-H2452). These concentrations were pre-determined in MTT assays. After 48 h of treatment, protein extraction was performed. The same experimental setup was used for 48 h of treatment with dasatinib (10 nM) and quercetin (1 µM), after which the surviving cells were re-seeded at 10,000 cells per well in 24-well plates and allowed to grow for one week. At the end of the experiment, cells were stained with crystal violet, and images were acquired using an HP Scanjet G2710 Photo Scanner. Cell confluence was quantified using Fiji (ImageJ). For long-term treatment, ZL34 cells were seeded in 6-well and 24-well plates at a density of 100,000 and 7500 cells per well, respectively. After 24 h, cells were treated with the indicated concentration of carboplatin for a duration of 12 days (25, 50, 75 µM). The treatment medium was refreshed every three days. At the end point, cells were fixed using crystal violet (2 g/L in H2O) prepared in 2.5% glutaraldehyde solution. Images were acquired using HP Scanjet G2710 Photo Scanner, and confluence was quantified using Fiji (ImageJ). The same experimental setup was used for ZL34 cells pretreated with dasatinib/quercetin for 48 h, and which were then further treated with a single concentration of carboplatin (50 µM) for 12 days.Flowcytometric cell cycle analysisZL34 cells were treated with 50 µM carboplatin for 12 days, as described above. Following treatment, cells were fixed in 70% ethanol (ThermoFisher Scientific, # ) and stained with 10 µg/mL propidium iodide (PI) (Sigma-Aldrich, #P4170) supplemented with 100 µg/mL RNase A (Invitrogen, # ). Cell cycle profiles were analyzed by flow cytometry using a FACSVerse instrument (BD Biosciences).Senescence associated (SA)-β-galactosidase activity assaysFor colorimetric SA-β-Gal activity quantification, GFP- or PTPA-overexpressing ZL34 cells were seeded in a 6-well plate at a density of 15,000 cells per well and cultured for 5 days. Cellular senescence was assessed using the Senescence β-Galactosidase Staining Kit (Cell Signaling Technology, #9860) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, cells were fixed and incubated with β-galactosidase staining solution containing X-gal at pH 6. Plates were then incubated overnight at 37 °C in the absence of CO₂. Image analysis was performed using QuPath v0.6.0 [48] with the QuPath extension Cellpose0.11.3 [49] installed. Regions corresponding to 50–70% confluent cell areas were manually annotated, and cell detection was carried out using Cellpose-SAM [50] on the optical density sum of the images. Subsequently, a training dataset was generated from representative images to train an object classifier distinguishing senescent from non-senescent cells, enabling quantification of the relative percentage of senescent cells per condition (all channels were included except DAB).For flow cytometric SA-β-Gal activity quantification, parental and PTPA OE cells were seeded in 10 cm culture dishes at a density of 1.5 × 10⁵ cells per dish and cultured for 5 days, after which they were harvested and fixed in 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 10 min. SA-β-Gal activity was then assessed by flow cytometry using the CellEvent™ Senescence Green Flow Cytometry Assay Kit (Invitrogen, #C10850) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were analysed in a BD FACSymphony™ A1 Cell Analyzer (Waters Biosciences). FlowjoTM 10.10.0 software (Waters Biosciences) was used for data analysis.In silico analysis of PP2A alterations in MPM patient datasetTo obtain a comprehensive image of potential PP2A alterations in MPM, we analyzed a publicly available Pleural Mesothelioma dataset (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas, 87 patients) in silico, using cBioPortal [39–41]. We evaluated genomic alterations in PP2A-related genes (canonical PP2A subunits and several PP2A regulators) by determining the frequency of gene amplification/gain, homozygous or heterozygous loss, and mutations (Suppl. Fig. S1). Additionally, RNA expression levels of these genes were analyzed (Suppl. Fig. S2). All identified alterations were then correlated with overall survival (OS) to identify potential clinical relevance. In accordance with findings in most other cancer types [18], PP2A gene mutations were overall rare ( 1, and padj 1, padj 0.05. (B) Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) bubble plot showing significantly enriched signaling pathways in PTPA-overexpressing versus GFP control ZL34 cells, based on RNAseq analysis of both stable cell lines (n = 3). (C) GSEA plot showing enrichment of the ‘HALLMARK KRAS SIGNALING UP’ pathway, with normalized enrichment score (NES) and false discovery rate (FDR) indicated. (D) Increased KRAS signaling in PTPA OE cells, underscored by decreased phospho-KSR1(Ser392)/total KSR1, increased phospho-MEK1/2(Ser217/221)/total MEK1/2, and increased phospho-ERK1/2(Thr202/Tyr204)/total ERK1/2, as determined by immunoblotting with indicated antibodies, followed by quantification of the bands. Statistical analysis was performed using an unpaired t-test (n = 3, *p < 0.05) As activated Ras signaling coincided with decreased growth (Fig. 2), we hypothesized PTPA re-expression might actually be promoting oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), a cellular response to oncogene-induced replicative, oxidative or metabolic stress that prevents the active proliferation of genomically unstable cells. In support of this hypothesis, GSEA analysis revealed increased p53 pathway activation (Figs. 4B and 5A), further validated by increased p21 expression (CDKN1A: p53 target gene) at the protein level (Fig. 5B) and increased markers of DNA-damage (phospho-ATR/total ATR and γH2AX) (Fig. 5B). Consistent with the results observed in ZL34, a pronounced increase in p21 expression was also detected in PTPA re-expressing NCI-H226 and NCI-H2452 cells (Suppl. Fig. S12). Activation of p53, either by the DNA Damage Response (DDR) pathway or DDR-independent mechanism [58, 59], is indeed recognized as the major driver of OIS in response to activated Ras signaling [60–62]. In accordance, GSEA analysis using the SenMayo gene set revealed significant positive enrichment in PTPA OE cells (Fig. 5C), a finding that was further corroborated by increased SA-β-Galactosidase activity (Fig. 5D–E , Suppl. Fig. S13) and the upregulation of genes associated with the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP), including IL6, MMP1, MMP3, and IL1A (Fig. 5F). Finally, our RNAseq data revealed enrichment of TNFα signaling via the NF-κB gene set (Figs. 4B and 5G): NF-κB activation is also associated with cellular senescence as the master regulator of gene transcription of SASP [63, 64]. Consistently, subcellular fractionation followed by immunoblotting revealed elevated levels of NF-κB p65 in the nuclear compartment of PTPA OE cells (Fig. 5H), supporting activation of NF-κB-mediated transcription. Thus, we concluded that PTPA re-expression in PTPA-low ZL34 cells promotes RAS pathway activation and oncogene-induced senescence, thereby likely explaining the observed decrease in MPM cell growth (Fig. 2). (B) Increased DNA-damage marker (phospho-ATR/total ATR and γH2AX) and CDKN1A (p53 target gene, encoding p21 CIP/KIP) expression in PTPA OE cells was confirmed by immunoblot analysis. Quantification of p21 and γH2AX signal intensity was normalized to vinculin (loading control), with GFP control condition set to 1 (unpaired t-test, n = 3–4, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01). Phospho-ATR signals were normalized to total ATR protein, and set to 1 in the GFP control condition (unpaired t-test, n = 3). (C) GSEA enrichment plot for the ‘SenMayo’ gene set, underscoring increased senescence in PTPA OE cells. (D) Colorimetric SA-β-Gal activity assay. Quantification of blue, senescent cells in GFP control versus PTPA OE ZL34 cells was executed in QuPath (n = 6, unpaired t-test, **p < 0.01). Representative pictures can be found in Suppl. Fig. S13. On the right, quantification of NF-κB levels in the nuclear compartment is shown (n = 2), normalized to Sp1 Activated Ras signaling, increased p21 expression and induced senescence cause the observed growth decrease in PTPA overexpressing MPM cellsTo determine whether increased Ras signaling is indeed the cause of senescence induction in PTPA re-expressing cells, we used the MEK inhibitor Trametinib to suppress RAF/MEK/ERK signaling. Trametinib treatment abolished ERK activation (phospho-ERK/total ERK) as expected, while also completely reversing induced p21 expression in PTPA overexpressing ZL34 (Fig. 6A) and NCI-2452 cells (Fig. 6B). Further, pretreatment of ZL34 cells with senolytic agents dasatinib/quercetin for 48 h, enabled a full rescue of the observed growth defect of the surviving cells in a confluency assay (Fig. 6C), underscoring that PTPA re-expression-induced growth inhibition is indeed caused by oncogene-induced senescence. (A-B) ZL34 and NCI-H2452 control and PTPA-overexpressing cells were treated for 48 h with 15 µM and 25 µM Trametinib, respectively, and harvested for protein extraction. Immunoblot analysis of the lysates demonstrated decreased ERK phosphorylation (phospho-ERK/total ERK), alongside decreased p21 levels (senescent marker) in ZL34 (A) and NCI-H2452 cells (B) (n = 3 (ZL34) and n = 4 (NCI-H2452); two-way ANOVA, *p < 0.05, ***p < 0.001). After 7 days of growth, cells were stained with crystal violet and quantified to assess confluency (n = 3; unpaired t-test, *p < 0.05). Dasatinib/quercetin-untreated cells (No pre-T) were used as a control The pharmacologic PP2A activator ATUX-792 does not phenocopy the effects of PTPA restoration in MPM cellsLately, there has been much excitement about the development of pharmacologic PP2A activators (SMAPs, Small Molecule Activators of PP2A) and their potential application in cancer treatment [65, 66]. To test whether the effects of PTPA restoration in PTPA-low MPM cells could be phenocopied by such a SMAP, we used the ATUX-792 compound [47] to evaluate its putative senescence-inducing potential in our cell models (Fig. 7A–D). Although ATUX-792 clearly exerted a therapeutic effect, decreasing cell viability in both control and PTPA OE cells in two independent MPM cell lines (Fig. 7C and D), immunoblot analysis of p21 expression demonstrated this did not correlate with senescence induction (Fig. 7A and B). In fact, ATUX-792 even reduced increased p21 levels in PTPA OE cells (Fig. 7A and B). This unexpected, seemingly senolytic effect of ATUX-792 might explain why PTPA OE NCI-H2452 cells appeared more sensitive to this compound than the control cells (Fig. 7C), although this was not well reproduced in the other MPM cell line, ZL34 (Fig. 7D). Overall, these data suggest that the therapeutic effect of ATUX-792 in MPM cells does not involve induction of senescence, but is likely caused by other growth-inhibiting or cell-killing mechanisms, one of which could be the promotion of senolytic death. Immunoblot analysis of the lysates was performed for the senescence marker p21 (n = 3, two-way ANOVA, *p < 0.05, ***p < 0.001). Cells were plated, treated and viability assessed by MTT at 72 h (n = 1, each datapoint is the average of three technical replicates). Curves were fitted by nonlinear regression, and EC50 values were calculatedPTPA overexpression sensitizes MPM cells to carboplatinAs induction of senescence is often associated with chemosensitization as a result of lethal cell stress [63, 64], we next hypothesized that MPM cells with high vs. low PTPA expression might respond differently to anti-cancer drugs. This was tested for chemotherapeutics carboplatin and pemetrexed, which are both in clinical use for MPM treatment [1, 2]. While no PTPA-dependent effects were observed for pemetrexed treatment, PTPA re-expression sensitized MPM cells for carboplatin following short-term (72 h) treatment in two independent cell lines (Fig. 8A and B). Since the effect was rather modest in ZL34 cells (Fig. 8A), we further subjected these cells to a long-term treatment of 12 days and found a clearly reduced total colony area compared to GFP control cells at a dose of 50 µM (Fig. 8C). Notably, pretreatment with senolytic agents (combo dasatinib/quercetin) abolished the difference in carboplatin sensitivity between control and PTPA OE cells in this assay (Fig. 8C). Assessment of p21 expression further suggested that carboplatin exerts its therapeutic effect, at least in by inducing (DNA-damage-induced) senescence, as p21 levels were significantly further increased in both PTPA-high and PTPA-low cells (Fig. 8D). Since the difference in carboplatin sensitivity between control and PTPA OE cells was abolished by pre-removal of the senescent cells in the PTPA OE condition, we concluded that their difference in carboplatin sensitivity is likely to be explained by a lethal combination of PTPA-dependent oncogene-induced senescence and carboplatin-dependent DNA-damage-induced senescence. This is supported by flow cytometry-based cell cycle analysis following 12 days of treatment, showing a trend toward increased cell death in PTPA-overexpressing ZL34 cells (Fig. 8E, Suppl. Fig. S14). Increased carboplatin sensitivity was further accompanied by trends for increased γH2AX (a marker of DNA damage) and increased ATR phosphorylation following 12 days of treatment (Fig. 8F). Overall, these results underscore the clinical survival data (Fig. 1C), hinting towards heterozygous loss of PTPA as a potential predictive marker for adverse carboplatin outcome, and hence, associated with a worse prognosis.
