Collectively, all these results suggest that Mito-TEMPO is associated with enhanced PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy via up-regulating SOD2 expression, which may partly underlie its therapeutic effect on U18666A-induced HepG2 cells.Zebrafish has a single npc1 gene (NCBI Gene ID: ) located on chromosome 2 (43). The amino acid sequence of zebrafish npc1 shares 60% identity and 66% similarity with the human NPC1 ortholog (44), making zebrafish an ideal model organism for NPC disease research. In our previous work, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing targeting exon 2 of NPC1 was used to generate an NPC1-KO zebrafish model (31). The mutation site was located in the cysteine-rich loop of the lumen A region (amino acid residue position C27), corresponding to the conserved NPC1-specific cysteine-rich domain (45, 46). The NPC1-KO zebrafish displayed phenotypes resembling human NPC disease and exhibited typical characteristics of liver disease or other digestive tract impairments in early stage, including jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, emaciation, and abdominal lipid accumulation. Most NPC1-KO zebrafish died within 1 month, paralleling clinical observations in patients with the p.C31Wfs*26 mutation, who typically succumb during early infancy (47, 48). Thus, improving early-stage survival is a critical therapeutic objective. Because of the rarity of NPC disease and the limitations of mammalian models, effective early-life therapies such as β-CD remain under Phase 1 and Phase 2 clinical trials (35). Building on our established NPC1-KO zebrafish model, this study aimed to explore alternative treatments capable of enhancing early survival in NPC disease.Loss of NPC1 function leads to lipid accumulation (including cholesterol and sphingolipids) in late endosomal/lysosomal compartments (49). Abnormal cholesterol storage disrupts lysosomal function and affects other organelles such as the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi apparatus, and mitochondria, resulting in OS and impaired autophagic flux (50–52). OS contributes to excessive lipid and cholesterol synthesis (lipid peroxidation) and autophagy dysregulation (53–55). Moreover, abnormal autophagy induces ER stress, triggers the unfolded protein response, and hinders degradation of damaged organelles through processes such as mitophagy, ER-phagy, and pexophagy, leading to amyloid accumulation and cellular injury in NPC1 disease (15, 51, 52). Consistent with this, our NPC1-KO zebrafish exhibited elevated OS, blocked autophagic flux, and shortened lifespan compared with WT controls. Accumulating evidence has demonstrated that hepatocytes degrade lipid droplets via macrolipophagy or microlipophagy, thereby alleviating hepatic steatosis (56–58). Thus, autophagy induction could represent a rational therapeutic approach for NPC disease. However, several studies suggest that autophagy activation alone cannot rescue cholesterol accumulation in NPC1-deficient cells (59), mitophagy impairment and cholesterol accumulation seem to be two parallel pathological mechanisms in NPC disease. Rather, combining autophagy activators with cholesterol-lowering agents may synergistically restore cellular homeostasis (23, 26, 59). In addition, β-CD–threaded polyrotaxanes have been shown to both reduce cholesterol accumulation and enhance autophagy in NPC1 fibroblasts (60). Considering these findings and our zebrafish results, effective NPC therapies may require multitarget agents that simultaneously reduce OS and restore autophagy.The SOD family plays a vital role in OS regulation (61). In this study, proteomic analysis of NPC1-KO zebrafish identified significantly decreased SOD2 expression, whereas SOD1 and SOD3 remained unchanged. Reduced SOD2 expression can lead to excessive ROS accumulation (62). A similar reduction has been reported in NPC1I1061T cells, where N-acetylcysteine or histone deacetylase inhibitors alleviated OS by up-regulating SOD2 and preventing apoptosis (5, 17). Zinc ions have also been shown to facilitate metabolic and bioenergetic recovery following spinal cord injury by activating microglial mitophagy via the FOXO3a-SOD2 pathway (63). Nevertheless, no prior in vivo studies have investigated whether SOD2 enhancement can directly ameliorate NPC disease. We found that Mito-TEMPO, a mitochondrial antioxidant acting through SOD promotion (64), might serve as a potential therapeutic candidate. Mito-TEMPO has exhibited significant therapeutic efficacy in neurodegenerative disease and metabolic disorder models: 50 to 100 μM Mito-TEMPO improves neuronal survival in Alzheimer’s disease models by increasing SOD activity (65, 66). Similarly, 70 μM Mito-TEMPO has a therapeutic effect on ferroptosis in pancreatic β cells through the mitochondrial ROS autophagy-lysosomal pathway (67). However, the therapeutic effects of Mito-TEMPO on NPC disease have not been reported in either in vitro or in vivo models. On the basis of the previously reported effective doses of Mito-TEMPO and our zebrafish developmental toxicity and cytotoxicity assays, we selected 100 μM as the treatment concentration for zebrafish in vitro models and 12.5, 25, and 50 μM as the concentration gradients for in vitro cell culture models in this study. Mito-TEMPO treatment significantly improved early-stage survival in NPC1-KO zebrafish, reduced hepatic cholesterol and lipid accumulation, and mitigated liver function impairment, with effects comparable to β-CD. Furthermore, Mito-TEMPO reduced OS and restored dysregulated autophagy levels in NPC1 model.Proteomic and ultrastructural analyses also revealed mitochondrial structural damage and down-regulation of PINK1 and Parkin(key mitophagy-related proteins) in NPC1-KO zebrafish, implying suppression of mitophagy. Mitophagy can proceed through Parkin-dependent or Parkin-independent mechanisms, with the PINK1/Parkin pathway being the most characterized (68, 69). In this pathway, PINK1 accumulation recruits and activates Parkin, initiating mitophagy to preserve cellular homeostasis (70). A previous study has shown that cadmium induces PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy to protect cortical neurons from apoptosis (71), whereas taurine activates the same pathway to reduce OS and mitigate intervertebral disc degeneration (72). However, few studies have linked mitophagy modulation to NPC1 pathology. Our results indicate that Mito-TEMPO restored mitochondrial integrity, enhanced mitophagic flux, and up-regulated PINK1/Parkin signaling, consistent with the idea that its therapeutic efficacy in NPC disease involves the enhancement of Parkin-dependent mitophagy and attenuation of apoptosis.Generally, Mito-TEMPO is a mitochondrion-targeted SOD mimetic especially for SOD2 (65, 73), which may underpin its ability to reverse the SOD2 down-regulation and degradation induced by NPC disease. However, our preliminary molecular docking analysis revealed strong binding affinities between Mito-TEMPO and SOD2 in both zebrafish and human models, despite minor structural variations in SOD2 orthologs between these two species. These findings are consistent with the possibility that Mito-TEMPO might interact with SOD2 to stabilize the protein, potentially contributing to the up-regulation of SOD2 expression and activity. Notably, SOD2 knockdown in our NPC1 models partially attenuated the therapeutic efficacy (including reduced cholesterol and ROS levels and ameliorated mitochondrial membrane potential) and reduced PINK1/Parkin signaling triggered by Mito-TEMPO, indicating that its therapeutic effects were partially suppressed in association with the lack of sufficient SOD2 binding partners. Consistently, our data suggest that Mito-TEMPO reduced cholesterol accumulation in the NPC1 model by alleviating OS and restoring autophagic flux by enhancing SOD2. We observed that SOD2 OE also improved cholesterol homeostasis in the in vitro NPC1 model, which supports the potential feasibility of SOD2-targeted therapy for NPC disease in vivo.There still exist several limitations in this study. First, the random nature of point mutations within NPC1-KO sites, combined with current genetic engineering limitations, precludes the reliable establishment of stable NPC1-KO cell lines that accurately replicate the specific loss-of-function mutations found in NPC1-KO zebrafish. Therefore, an in vitro NPC1 dysfunction model was established using U18666A, a potent inhibitor of late endosomal trafficking, to investigate the disease’s underlying mechanisms. Besides, NPC disease is also characterized by neurodegenerative symptoms such as ataxia and muscular tremors. Nevertheless, this study primarily focused on therapeutic interventions aimed at improving survival and cholesterol homeostasis rather than addressing neurological pathology as neurodegenerative symptoms typically occur later than lipid accumulation. Accordingly, hepatic and intestinal tissues were selected as the primary target organs, given their central roles in lipid metabolism. Last, although Mito-TEMPO exhibited activity through docking with SOD2 and showed potential therapeutic effects in the NPC1 models, Mito-TEMPO may also exert its therapeutic effects via alternative molecular pathways or targets. Similarly, enhancing SOD2 expression alleviated cholesterol accumulation in the in vitro NPC1 model, and the study could not conclusively determine whether direct targeting of SOD2 alone would yield comparable outcomes in vivo. Future studies will focus on elucidating the precise molecular mechanisms (Parkin or PINK1 KO models) and evaluating nervous system development (spinal cord and brain) of the NPC disease model to further clarify the therapeutic potential of Mito-TEMPO. In addition, we will assess the merits of combination therapy involving Mito-TEMPO and other promising compounds (e.g., β-CD), as well as the therapeutic value of SOD2-targeted interventions in vivo for NPC disease.Collectively, using the NPC1-KO zebrafish model, our findings support that Mito-TEMPO effectively improves survival, reduces cholesterol accumulation, and restores liver function in NPC1-KO zebrafish. Its mechanism is likely consistent with the suppression of OS and the promotion of Parkin-dependent mitophagy via Sod2 activity enhancement (Fig. 8). A 2% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Sigma-Aldrich, D5879) was used as the positive control.For staining and flow cytometry assays, cells were pretreated with 3 μM U18666A (Sigma-Aldrich, HY- ) for 24 hours to induce the NPC1 model, followed by PBS or Mito-TEMPO (12.5, 25, 50, and 100 μM). A 2-hour starvation period was included to induce mitophagy (Fig. 4A).Survival assaysZebrafish survival was monitored every other day for 60 days. Mortality was recorded as 1, and accidental loss or survival as 0, for survival curve analysis.Liver enzyme assaysLiver function was evaluated by measuring AST (Beyotime Biotechnology, P2715S) and ALT (Beyotime Biotechnology, P2711S) levels using assay kits according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Fluorescence intensity was measured with a microplate reader (SpectraMax i3x, Molecular Devices, China) at 560/590 nm.Transmission electron microscopy assaysWhole zebrafish tissues were fixed in electron microscopy fixation solution under light-protected conditions at 4°C, cut into 1-mm3 sections, rinsed in 0.1 M PBS, and postfixed in 1% osmium tetroxide (Ted Pella, ) for 2 hours. Samples were dehydrated through a graded acetone series, infiltrated with epoxy resin for 2 to 3 hours, embedded, and polymerized at 70°C for 30 min using Epon 812 epoxy resin (SPI-CHEM, -77-4) in predried molds. Resin blocks were then cured at 40°C for 12 hours and 60°C for 48 hours to form hard plastic. After trimming, ultrathin sections (60 to 80 nm) were prepared, mounted on copper grids, and stained with lead citrate and uranyl acetate (SPI-CHEM, -AB). Sections were examined and imaged using a transmission electron microscope (HT7800, Hitachi, Japan).OS assaysFor the cellular ROS assay, cells were incubated with 10 μM dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA; Beyotime Biotechnology, S0033S) for 20 min at 37°C in the dark following drug treatment. Cells were then washed with cold PBS. Fluorescence images were captured using a fluorescence microscope (Ti-E, Nikon, Japan), and quantitative data were obtained with a microplate reader (SpectraMax i3x, Molecular Devices, China) at 488/525 nm.For zebrafish ROS assays, frozen tissue sections were incubated with 10 μM dihydroethidium (DHE; Servicebio, G1746) for 30 min at 37°C in the dark, followed by fluorescence microscopy examination.For zebrafish MDA detection (Beyotime Biotechnology, S0131S), whole-tissue homogenates were prepared on ice, centrifuged at 1000g for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected for measurement. Cholesterol levels were determined using the Amplex Red cholesterol assay (Beyotime Biotechnology, S0211S) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Reactions were conducted with and without cholesterol esterase to quantify total cholesterol (TC) and free cholesterol (FC). Cholesteryl esters (CEs) were calculated as TC−FC, and the CE/FC ratio was determined. Fluorescence intensity was measured at 560/590 nm using a microplate reader.Western blotting assaysWhole zebrafish tissues were lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA; Beyotime Biotechnology, P0038) buffer on ice for 30 min. Supernatants were collected after centrifugation at 12,000g for 15 min. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, P0010). Equal amounts of protein (20 to 40 μg) were resolved by SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. Membranes were blocked in 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA; BioFroxx, 4240GR025) for 1 hour at RT and then incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies: SOD2 (1:200; GeneTex, GTX124294), LC3 (1:200; ABclonal, A15591), PARK2 (1:200; ABclonal, A0968), and β-actin (1:1000; Proteintech, -1-RR), followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–conjugated secondary antibodies (Kirkegaard & Perry Laboratories, 074-1506) for 1 hour at RT. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL; Beyotime Biotechnology, P0018M) and imaged with a ChemiDoc system (5200, Tanon, China). Densitometric analysis was performed using the ImageJ software.Cell viability assaysCell viability was measured using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Beyotime Biotechnology, C0038). After drug treatment, CCK-8 reagent was added to each well, and cells were incubated for 2 hours at 37°C. Optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader.Mitochondrial transmembrane potential assaysCells were seeded in 96-well plates and subjected to drug treatment, followed by staining with JC-1 dye according to the JC-1 Mitochondrial Membrane Potential Assay Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, C2006) protocol. Fluorescence was recorded using a microplate reader at 490/530 nm or 525/590 nm,Immunofluorescence microscopyFor zebrafish immunofluorescence staining, tissue sections underwent antigen retrieval using citric acid buffer at 95°C, followed by blocking with H2O2 for 25 min at RT, permeabilization with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 10 min, and blocking with 5% BSA in PBS for 1 hour at RT. Sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (1:25) diluted in 0.1% Triton X-100 and 2% BSA in PBS. After washing, sections were incubated with Cy3-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:100; Beyotime Biotechnology, A0516) for 1 hour at RT. Antigen retrieval and immune elution were performed for 30 min before incubation with a second antibody, followed by fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)–conjugated secondary antibody (1:100; Beyotime Biotechnology, A0562) for 1 hour at RT. After 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining (Beyotime Biotechnology, R0306S-6) for 5 min, images were acquired using a fluorescence or confocal microscope (TCS SP8, Leica, Germany).For cell immunofluorescence staining, treated cells were washed with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min at RT, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 10 min, and blocked with 5% BSA in PBS for 1 hour. Cells were incubated with primary antibodies (1:100) overnight at 4°C, followed by appropriate fluorescent secondary antibodies for 1 hour and DAPI counterstaining for 5 min at RT. Images were captured using a confocal microscope.For mitophagy flux analysis, cells transfected with tandem fluorescence reporters were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at RT after treatment, and fluorescence images were captured using a confocal microscope.Flow cytometryFor apoptosis analysis, cell apoptosis was evaluated using the Annexin V Apoptosis Detection Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, C1062M) following the manufacturer’s instructions. A total of 5 × 105 cells were washed with PBS and resuspended in 100 μl of binding buffer containing 5 μl of annexin V–FITC and 10 μl of propidium iodide (PI). After incubation for 15 min at RT in the dark, 400 μl of binding buffer was added, and samples were immediately analyzed on a flow cytometer (CytoFLEX S, Beckman, USA). The data were analyzed by FlowJo V (FlowJo LLC, USA).For intracellular staining of LC3B, SQSTM1/p62, PINK1, PARK2, TOMM20, COX-IV, and SOD2, cells were fixed and permeabilized (Multisciences, GAS005) and then blocked for 1 hour at RT with PBS containing 5% BSA. Cells were incubated with rabbit anti-mouse primary antibodies against LC3B (1:100, ABclonal, A11923), SQSTM1/p62 (1:100, ABclonal, A11483), PINK1 (1:100, ABclonal, A7131), PARK2 (1:100, ABclonal, A0968), TOMM20 (1:100, ABclonal, A6774), COX-IV (1:100, ABclonal, HB, A6564), or SOD2 (1:100, GeneTex, GTX124294) for 4 hours, followed by FITC-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1:100, Thermo Fisher Scientific, F-2765) for 1 hour at RT. After washing, fluorescence intensity was detected using a flow cytometer and the data were analyzed by FlowJo V.Proteomic analysisWT and NPC1-KO zebrafish at 1 mpf were collected for proteomic profiling. Three biological replicates were analyzed per group. Samples were rinsed with ultrapure water, and protein extraction and trypsin digestion were performed. Frozen samples were ground into powder using liquid nitrogen, transferred to 1.5-ml centrifuge tubes, and lysed with buffer containing 8 M urea, 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (Sinopharm, XW020003), and 2 mM EDTA (Sinopharm, ). Ultrasonic lysis was conducted for 5 min on ice, followed by centrifugation at 15,000g and 4°C for 10 min to collect the supernatant.A total of 100 μg of protein per sample was diluted to 200 μl with 8 M urea, reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT; Solarbio, D8220) at 37°C for 45 min, and alkylated with 11 mM iodoacetamide (Aladdin, I131590) for 15 min in the dark at RT. The reaction was diluted with 800 μl of 25 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and digestion was initiated with 2 μg of trypsin overnight at 37°C. The pH of the digested peptides was adjusted to 2 to 3 using 20% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), and samples were desalted with C18 columns.Peptide separation was performed using a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system. The mobile phase A consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water, and mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. A trap-and-elute dual-column setup was used, with a PepMap Neo Trap Cartridge (300 μm by 5 mm, 5 μm) as the trapping column and an Easy-Spray PepMap Neo UHPLC column (150 μm by 15 cm, 2 μm) as the analytical column. The column temperature was maintained at 55°C, injection volume at 200 ng, flow rate at 2.5 μl/min, gradient time at 6.9 min, and total run time at 8 min.Chromatographically separated peptides were analyzed using the Orbitrap Astral high-resolution mass spectrometer (Orbitrap Astral, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) operating in positive ion mode under data-independent acquisition (DIA). The precursor ion scan range was 380 to 980 mass/charge ratio (m/z), with an MS1 resolution of 240,000 (at 200 m/z), normalized automatic gain control (AGC) target of 500%, and maximum injection time (IT) of 5 ms. MS2 analysis was performed using DIA mode with 299 scan windows, an isolation window of 2 Th, higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) collision energy of 25%, normalized AGC target of 500%, and maximum IT of 3 ms. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified and annotated using Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and subcellular localization analyses.Quantification and statistical analysisRaw mass spectrometry (MS) data were processed using DIA-NN (v1.8.1) in library-free mode. The UniProtKB database (uniprotkb_proteome_UP000000437_banmayu_2024_08_06. fasta; 46 559 sequences) was used to generate a spectral library through neural network–based deep learning algorithms. The “match between runs” (MBR) option was applied to create a DIA-based spectral library, followed by reanalysis with this library. The false discovery rate (FDR) for both protein and precursor ion identification was controlled below 1%.All quantitative data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software, USA). Statistical comparisons between two groups were conducted using Student’s t test or the Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test where appropriate. Unless otherwise indicated, results are expressed as means ± SEM. Significance levels were denoted as *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001; nonsignificant (n.s.), P ≥ 0.05.

title: Oral Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma and Its Management: A Rare Enigmatic Pediatric Case Report with Immunohistochemistry
abstract: Aim and Malignant tumors are rarely seen in children, of which lymphomas and sarcomas like rhabdomyosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma prevail. Histopathologically, these lesions show numerous round cells, which make it difficult to differentiate between one another. Molecular analysis such as immunohistochemistry has proved to be beneficial and cost-effective. The current report aims to highlight an enigmatic case of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), emphasizing the role of immunohistochemistry.Case descriptionA 3-year-old female patient presented to the dental outpatient department with a chief complaint of a progressively enlarging, diffuse swelling over the left cheek region, persisting for the past 2 weeks. Radiographic examination revealed a poorly defined radiopacity involving the maxillary sinus, leading to a provisional diagnosis of odontogenic myxoma. However, tru-cut biopsy from the lesion demonstrated undifferentiated small round to oval cells with occasional strap-like cells and an absence of odontogenic islands, contradicting the initial impression. Subsequent immunohistochemical analysis revealed cytoplasmic desmin positivity, a high Ki-67 labeling index, and negativity for S-100 and CK-19. Based on the immunohistochemical findings, a definitive diagnosis of ERMS was rendered. The patient underwent chemotherapy, and posttreatment evaluation with positron emission tomography and computed tomography (PET-CT) demonstrated marked tumor regression.This case report highlights the crucial importance of using tru-cut biopsy along with immunohistochemical analysis to obtain an accurate and timely diagnosis of ERMS, which facilitates the early start of appropriate targeted treatment.Clinical significanceThe resolution of diagnostic challenges in ERMS hinges on the use of meticulous biopsy technique coupled with advanced immunohistochemical analysis.
full_text: Head and neck cancers (HNC), though relatively rare, comprise 2–15% of all pediatric malignancies. Despite their rarity, cancer persists as a major contributor to mortality among children and adolescents on a global scale.1 Pediatric head and neck cancers (PHNC) encompass a diverse array of malignancies, with the principal entities including non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL), Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL), rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), thyroid carcinoma (TC), neuroblastoma, and salivary gland carcinoma, each representing a critical facet of this oncological subset.2 Among them, RMS is an infrequent malignancy in the oral cavity, comprising merely 10–12% of all head and neck cases.3 Among intraoral sites, the tongue is the predominant location, followed by the palate and buccal mucosa, whereas gingival involvement is exceedingly rare.4 The embryonal variant represents the predominant histological subtype of RMS, accounting for approximately 49% of all cases. While it predominantly arises in children under the age of 10, its occurrence is also documented in adolescents and young adults.5 Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) in the oral cavity may mimic infectious or inflammatory swellings, leading to diagnostic ambiguity and potential delays in timely therapeutic intervention. Early and precise diagnosis is crucial for maximizing survival outcomes, as it facilitates timely intervention and enhances prognostic efficacy. Histopathological analysis is paramount in the accurate diagnosis of ERMS of the jaw, facilitating a definitive characterization of the tumor's cellular architecture and histological composition, thereby distinguishing it from other pathologies.6 In pediatric patients, selecting an appropriate biopsy technique is fundamental, not only for ensuring an accurate and definitive diagnosis but also for mitigating procedural trauma and enhancing patient comfort. Tru-cut biopsy, by virtue of its minimally invasive nature, significantly attenuates patient morbidity in comparison to open surgical biopsies. This is particularly crucial for pediatric patients, who possess an increased vulnerability to the complications that often accompany more invasive surgical procedures.7 The diagnosis of RMS using conventional hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining is fraught with difficulty, owing to the substantial overlap in its histopathological features with a range of other neoplastic lesions exhibiting round and spindle-shaped cellular morphology.8 Immunohistochemistry is an indispensable tool in the diagnostic arsenal for ERMS. It not only confirms the myogenic origin of the tumor but also facilitates accurate differentiation from other malignancies, enabling precise diagnosis and guiding effective therapeutic interventions. ERMS exhibits a well-documented male predominance; however, the current case involved a pediatric female patient, thereby representing an uncommon demographic presentation for this malignancy.This case report aims to underscore the critical importance of tru-cut biopsy and immunohistochemistry in navigating the intricate diagnostic challenges associated with ERMS in a pediatric patient.Case DescriptionA 3-year-old female patient reported to the OPD of the Faculty of Dental Sciences, MS Ramaiah University of Applied Sciences, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India, with a chief complaint of diffuse extraoral swelling in the left cheek region for the past 2 weeks. An extraoral examination revealed a firm, nonindurated soft tissue swelling measuring approximately 5 × 6 cm. The swelling extended superoinferiorly from the infraorbital region to the lower border of the mandible and anteroposteriorly from the alar cartilage to the tragus of the ear. Intraoral examination demonstrated a diffuse swelling that resulted in obliteration of the vestibular space (Figs 1A to D).Figs 1A to D(A) Extraoral view showing a nonindurated soft tissue swelling; (B) Lateral view showing the extent of the swelling; (C) Intraoral examination demonstrating a diffuse swelling; (D) The swelling exhibiting obliteration of the vestibular spaceA tru-cut biopsy was executed for comprehensive histopathological evaluation. A provisional diagnosis of odontogenic myxoma was deduced through meticulous gross examination of the tissue specimen. Microscopic examination following staining by H&E revealed undifferentiated small round to oval cells with pleomorphism arranged in sheets. The majority of the cells showed hyperchromatic nuclei, and a few were vesicular in appearance. Some cells showed abundant cytoplasm with eccentrically placed nuclei, suggestive of strap cells or rhabdomyoblasts. The stroma showed varying-sized endothelial-lined blood vessels and loose myxoid stroma. A focal area showed normal skeletal muscle and bone (Figs 2A to D).Figs 2A to DPhotomicrographs of ERMS; (A) Sheets of round to oval-shaped tumor cells (H&E; ×40); (B) Loose, myxoid stroma showing bizarre tumor cells with pleomorphism and hyperchromatic nuclei (H&E; ×400); (C) PAS-positive strap cells or rhabdomyoblasts showing abundant cytoplasm and eccentrically placed nuclei (PAS; ×100); (D) Pleomorphic tumor cells with strap cells demonstrating glycogen (PAS; ×400)The following differential diagnoses were considered: non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, malignant schwannoma, neuroblastoma, and ERMS. To achieve a conclusive diagnosis, a comprehensive immunohistochemical analysis was carried out. A panel was performed utilizing markers including desmin, vimentin, Ki-67, CK-19, and S-100 to enable a thorough diagnostic evaluation. The tumor cells demonstrated strong immunopositivity for desmin, vimentin, and Ki-67, alongside an absence of immunoreactivity for CK-19 and S-100.The tumor cells exhibited strong cytoplasmic immunopositivity for desmin, indicative of myogenic differentiation, coupled with faint cytoplasmic reactivity for vimentin, reinforcing their mesenchymal lineage. The tumor cells revealed pronounced nuclear immunoreactivity for Ki-67, with a labeling index of 80%, underscoring a highly proliferative cellular phenotype. The assessment of positive cell count was carried out in strict accordance with the methodology established by Iamaroon et al. (2004).9 The tumor cells exhibited an absence of CK-19 expression, suggesting a nonodontogenic etiology, while the lack of S-100 immunoreactivity further corroborated a nonneurogenic origin (Figs 3A to J).Figs 3A to JPhotomicrographs of immunostained sections of ERMS; (A) Control tissue of lymph node showing nuclear positivity for Ki-67 (IHC; ×400); (B) Tumor cells of ERMS showing nuclear positivity for Ki-67 with 80% labeling index (IHC; ×400); (C) Control tissue of colon showing strong cytoplasmic and membrane positivity for CK19 (IHC; ×100); (D) Tumor cells of ERMS tissue showing negative staining for CK19; (E) Melanoma tissue used as control for S100 shows strong immunopositivity (IHC; ×400); (F) Tumor cells of ERMS showing negative immunostaining for S100 (IHC; ×400); (G) Colon tissue as control showing positive immunostaining for vimentin (IHC; ×100); (H) Cytoplasm of ERMS tumor cells showing immunopositivity for vimentin (IHC; ×400); (I) Leiomyosarcoma used as control showing strong positivity for desmin immunostain (IHC; ×100); (J) ERMS tumor tissue showing strong cytoplasmic immunopositivity for desmin (IHC; ×400)The application of an immunohistochemical panel was essential for distinguishing between differential diagnoses, particularly in ruling out odontogenic myxoma, neuroblastoma, and malignant schwannoma. This thorough diagnostic process ultimately culminated in the definitive diagnosis of ERMS.Positron emission tomography and computed tomography (PET-CT) revealed a metabolically active soft tissue mass measuring 6.3 × 5.6 × 5.4 cm in the left infratemporal fossa, accompanied by scalloping and thinning of adjacent bony structures, as well as adenotonsillar enlargement. Additionally, the scan demonstrated multiple enlarged or prominent lymph nodes in the bilateral submandibular and upper jugular regions. The lesion exhibited scalloping and destruction of the left mandibular ramus, including the coronoid process, condylar process, and mandibular head, along with thinning of the adjacent skull base. Furthermore, there was scalloping of the maxillary alveolus, zygomatic arch, and pterygoid plate, with extension into the superior gingivobuccal sulcus and cheek. The mass collectively measured 6.3 × 5.6 × 5.4 cm and caused effacement and posteromedial displacement of the parapharyngeal fat pad. The CT scan further revealed marked adenotonsillar hypertrophy, left-sided serous otitis media, and multiple enlarged or prominent lymph nodes within the bilateral submandibular and upper jugular regions, with the largest node measuring about 2.1 × 1.0 cm (Fig. 4A).Figs 4A and B(A) PET-CT revealed a metabolically active soft tissue mass accompanied by scalloping and thinning of adjacent bony structures; (B) Posttreatment assessment with PET-CT demonstrated pronounced attenuation in the tumor's sizeAs a therapeutic intervention, the patient was administered a two-cycle chemotherapy protocol comprising intravenous vincristine (0.48 mg), cyclophosphamide (700 mg in 250 mL of normal saline), mesna (140 mg), dexamethasone (2 mg), and dactinomycin (0.45 mg). Posttreatment assessment with PET-CT demonstrated a pronounced reduction in tumor size (Fig. 4B), indicative of a robust therapeutic response (Figs 5A and B). The patient was subsequently placed under structured clinical surveillance to monitor for disease progression or recurrence.Figs 5A and B(A) Posttreatment assessment showing reduction in size extraorally; (B) Posttreatment assessment showing reduction in size intraorallyDiscussionRhabdomyosarcomas stand as the most prevalent malignant neoplasms of mesenchymal origin affecting the musculoskeletal system in the pediatric and adolescent demographic. The prognosis of RMS is generally less favorable than that of other malignant lesions affecting the oral soft tissues. The most recent WHO classification delineates four principal subtypes: ERMS, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS), pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma (PMRMS), and spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SpRMS),10 supplemented by descriptions of several newly identified variants.The various histological subtypes of rhabdomyosarcoma, along with their associated prognostic outcomes, age of onset, and underlying genetic alterations, are comprehensively detailed in Table 1. Among the diverse histopathological variants, ERMS is the most frequently encountered subtype within the oral cavity, accounting for approximately 70–80% of documented cases.11 According to the literature, clinically ERMS manifests along a wide pathological continuum, from a discrete submucosal nodule to an aggressively expanding facial mass. While it may remain asymptomatic, certain cases present with associated symptoms such as pain, trismus, paresthesia, facial palsy, and nasal discharge, reflecting the tumor's potential for perineural invasion and regional extension.12Table 1A comparative evaluation of the diverse histopathologic subtypes of rhabdomyosarcoma Parameters ERMS ARMS SCRMS PMRMS Age at presentationChildren younger than 10 years10–25 yearsBroad age spectrum with a bimodal distribution, manifesting in both pediatric and geriatric populationsOlder adults, >40 yearsHistopathological featuresProliferation of undifferentiated small round blue cells, interspersed with occasional rhabdomyoblasts, and demonstrating a prominent botryoid growth patternProminent alveolar architecture, composed of sheets of medium-sized cells, interspersed with scattered multinucleated giant cellsSpindle cells arranged in fascicles, exhibiting a sclerosing architecture with a distinctive pseudovascular patternPleomorphic rhabdomyoblasts, characterized by pronounced cytological atypia, striking nuclear hyperchromasia, and considerable variation in cellular and nuclear morphologyGenetic variationsAneuploidy with distinct chromosomal gains and losses, alongside molecular alterations involving key oncogenic pathways, including mutations in the RAS gene family (HRAS, NRAS, KRAS), FGFR4, PIK3CA, NF1, and FBXW7PAX3−FOXO1 and PAX7−FOXO1 gene fusionsThe presence of VGLL2/NCOA2 gene fusions, typically observed in infantile forms, alongside mutations in the MYOD1 geneMultifaceted genetic alterations5-year overall survival rate81%53%86% (absence of MYOD1 mutation) and 30% (in cases of MYOD1 mutation)26.6%PrognosisFavorablePoorInfantile cases are generally associated with a more favorable prognosis, whereas mutations in MYOD1 are indicative of a poorer clinical outcomePoorARMS, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma; ERMS, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma; PMRMS, pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma; SCRMS, spindle cell rhabdomyosarcomaIn the present case, a diffuse extraoral swelling was observed in the left cheek region, persisting for the past 2 weeks. A slight male predominance is observed in the occurrence of this malignancy. In this case, a 3-year-old female patient presented with a diffuse swelling localized to the left cheek region. A tru-cut biopsy was carried out to facilitate a comprehensive histopathological evaluation. Tru-cut biopsy is an invaluable diagnostic tool in pediatric populations, offering significant advantages due to its minimally invasive nature. By reducing the risks of complications, postoperative pain, and recovery time, it provides a safer alternative to traditional surgical biopsies. The technique ensures high diagnostic precision by obtaining a representative tissue sample for histopathological analysis, which is essential for diagnosis.13According to the literature, microscopic analysis revealed the presence of primitive cells characterized by amphophilic cytoplasm and centrally located angular or oval nuclei. A few stellate cells were interspersed throughout the tissue. Notably, distinctive tadpole-shaped, strap-like, and spider cells were prominently discernible.14 Histopathologic analysis of this case revealed undifferentiated small round to oval cells exhibiting pleomorphism, predominantly organized in sheet-like patterns. The majority of cells displayed hyperchromatic nuclei, while a few exhibited vesicular nuclei. Some cells presented abundant cytoplasm with eccentrically located nuclei, indicative of strap cells or rhabdomyoblasts. The provisional differential diagnoses encompassed ERMS, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, malignant schwannoma, and neuroblastoma.To achieve diagnostic certainty, a meticulous and comprehensive immunohistochemical analysis was performed. For diagnostic confirmation, an extensive panel of immunohistochemical markers was employed, including desmin, vimentin, Ki-67, CK-19, and S-100. Desmin is an intermediate filament protein residing in the cytoplasm, where it plays a vital role in preserving the structural integrity and proper alignment of the contractile apparatus within muscle cells. Desmin is regarded as one of the most sensitive markers for rhabdomyosarcoma, including its poorly differentiated forms. Research demonstrated that in desmin-positive cases, over 95% of tumor cells exhibit immunoreactivity, strongly supporting a diagnosis of RMS and indicating its muscle-derived origin.15Vimentin, an intermediate filament protein predominantly localized in the cytoplasm of mesenchymal cells, is integral to maintaining cellular structural integrity and organizing the cytoskeletal framework. In cancer diagnostics, vimentin serves as a valuable immunohistochemical marker for identifying mesenchymal-origin tumors, including rhabdomyosarcoma, due to its characteristic expression in the cytoplasm of malignant mesenchymal cells.16Ki-67, a nuclear protein, is extensively utilized to evaluate the proliferative activity of tumor cells. An elevated Ki-67 index reflects a higher proportion of actively proliferating cells, which is frequently associated with enhanced tumor aggressiveness and poorer prognostic implications.17 In this case, the labeling index was assessed at 80%, suggesting a highly aggressive proliferative cellular phenotype.S-100 is a family of proteins typically expressed in the cytoplasm and nucleus of cells, particularly in neural and melanocytic cells. In the context of immunohistochemistry, S-100 is often used to identify neural differentiation.18 In this report, immunohistochemical profiling demonstrated the lack of S-100 expression, implying a nonneural origin for the tumor and excluding the possibility of malignant schwannoma and neuroblastoma.CK-19 is a cytoplasmic marker commonly employed to delineate odontogenic epithelium, aiding in the identification of odontogenic lesions and tumors.19 In this case, the absence of CK-19 expression unequivocally eliminated the possibility of an odontogenic tumor.Datta et al. (2016)5 reported a case of a 17-year-old female presenting with a mass on the left side of her mouth that had persisted for 1.5 months. Immunohistochemical evaluation was conducted using a comprehensive panel, including desmin, MYOD1, myogenin, muscle-specific actin, cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, Mic-2, synaptophysin, CD31, CD34, and leukocyte common antigen. The results showed positive staining for desmin, MYOD1, myogenin, and muscle-specific actin, while cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, Mic-2, synaptophysin, CD31, CD34, and leukocyte common antigen were negative. These findings culminated in a definitive diagnosis of ERMS.The management of oral rhabdomyosarcoma generally involves radical surgical excision, complemented by a multi-agent chemotherapy regimen, typically consisting of vincristine, dactinomycin, and cyclophosphamide. In instances where complete resection is not feasible, adjuvant postoperative radiotherapy may be employed to enhance treatment efficacy.20 In this case, the patient received a two-cycle chemotherapy regimen consisting of intravenous vincristine (0.48 mg), cyclophosphamide (700 mg in 250 mL of normal saline), mesna (140 mg), dexamethasone (2 mg), and dactinomycin (0.45 mg). Posttreatment evaluation using PET-CT demonstrated a substantial reduction in tumor metabolic activity, signifying an effective response to therapy, and the patient remained under regular clinical follow-up thereafter.This case report underscored the indispensable role of tru-cut biopsy in conjunction with immunohistochemical profiling in achieving a precise and expedient diagnosis of ERMS, thereby enabling the prompt initiation of targeted therapy.Clinical SignificanceThe involvement of a pediatric female patient marked a distinctly uncommon demographic presentation for this neoplasm, accentuating its atypical clinical manifestation. The patient's favorable chemotherapeutic response further highlighted the critical importance of an integrated, multidisciplinary framework for optimizing therapeutic outcomes and ensuring robust long-term surveillance.AcknowledgmentNil.AI DisclosureNo AI was used.Author ContributionsConcepts, definition of intellectual content, literature search, manuscript review: Dominic Augustine, Sowmya SV, Rajanikanth B Rajaram, Kavitha Prasad, Kuntala Mondal, Harini Palanivelu.Experimental studies: Dominic Augustine, Sowmya SV, Kuntala Mondal.Manuscript preparation, manuscript editing: Dominic Augustine, Sowmya SV, Rajanikanth B Rajaram, Kuntala Mondal.

title: Histone modifications across cancers: mechanisms, therapy and clinical translation
abstract: Cancer continues to be a major cause of death across the globe, and epigenetic dysregulation, including histone modifications, has been recognized as a major hallmark of cancer development, heterogeneity, and drug resistance. This review seeks to offer an overview of histone modifications in cancer, including the more studied histone modifications such as acetylation and methylation, as well as the less explored histone modifications such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and glycosylation. It also examines the role of histone modifications in the dysregulation of the three categories of enzymes: the writers, the erasers, and the readers, in the development of cancer, including solid tumors and hematological malignancies. This review also further explores the complex crosstalk between histone modifications, DNA methylation, non-coding RNA, and metabolic reprogramming, focusing on the complex epigenetic networks that maintain oncogenic states and confer plasticity to cancer. In terms of the development of new therapeutic agents, recent advances in epigenetic drugs such as HDAC inhibitors, EZH2 inhibitors, and BET inhibitors are also reviewed, as are new therapeutic avenues such as PROTACs, dual inhibitors, and natural epigenetic modulators. It also emphasizes the fact that the expression of histone modifying enzymes is a key change underlying oncogenic transcriptional states in all cancers. Some of the new aspects of epigenetics revealed in the review include the context-dependent role of H3K27me3 and H2BK120ub modifications, the therapeutic potential of epigenetic targets such as EZH2 and BRD4, and the therapeutic potential of combining epigenetic therapy with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
full_text: Cancer is still one of the major health issues worldwide. In the year 2022, there were nearly 20 million new cases and 9.7 million deaths recorded globally [1]. Asia contributed half of the cases (49.2%), as well as most of the cancer deaths (56.1%), while Europe contributed a quarter of the cases [2]. The projections suggest that by the year 2050, new cases of cancer could reach up to 30.5 million annually, with mortality rates expected to increase by 74.5% compared to the estimates for the year 2024 [3]. The survival rates for cancer patients show significant variability depending on the type and geographical location. Although the relative survival rates for all cancers in the US have shown an improvement from 49% in the 1970s to 69% from 2014 to 2020, disparities still exist for some cancers. For example, pancreatic (13%), liver (22%), and lung cancers have poor survival rates, whereas thyroid (98%), prostate (97%), and testicular cancers (95%) have better survival rates. These disparities are even higher in low- and middle-income countries, where survival rates are significantly low owing to the lack of access to early detection and treatment modalities [4]. Even within the continent of Europe, Eastern European countries have lower survival rates than Western countries due to unequal access to healthcare facilities [5]. In Asia, Japan and South Korea have high survival rates for breast and prostate cancers, exceeding 86% and 89%, respectively; however, lung cancer survival remains dishearteningly low at 32.9% and 25.1%, respectively [6, 7]. The current cancer treatment modalities such as surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy face the same challenges as before. Genomic instability, epigenetic changes, and heterogeneity are all factors that can induce drug resistance, a major problem. Immunotherapy agents such as immune checkpoint inhibitors produce durable responses in only 15–30% of the total patient pool due to the lack of patient selection biomarkers and immunosuppressive microenvironment [8]. Tumor heterogeneity, both intratumoral and intertumoral, makes it difficult to develop effective treatment strategies, leading to resistance and recurrence. To address these issues, new strategies must be developed. One of these new strategies could be epigenetic therapy, specifically targeting histone modifications, which can overcome resistance and restore responses.Histone modifications are chemical changes that happen to histone proteins after they have been translated. Histone proteins are important parts of nucleosomes, which are the basic repeating units of chromatin. These changes, which mainly happen on the N-terminal tails of histones (e.g., H3, H4), include acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and others [9]. They are essential for chromatin dynamics and gene regulation because they modify how easily DNA can be accessed by transcriptional machinery. For example, histone acetylation usually neutralizes the positive charge of histones, which lowers the DNA-histone affinity and encourages a “open” chromatin state that is beneficial for transcription. On the other hand, some methylation marks, like H3K27me3, are linked to chromatin that is tightly packed and stops transcription. The fact that these changes can be combined, often called the “histone code”, means that they can act as a flexible signaling system that controls gene expression, DNA repair, and other chromatin-templated processes without changing the DNA sequence itself [10].The malfunction of histone modifications is increasingly acknowledged as a characteristic of cancer pathogenesis, as it may result in the inappropriate activation of oncogenes or the repression of tumor suppressor genes. This dysregulation often arises from recurrent mutations, amplifications, or deletions in genes that encode histone-modifying enzymes, categorized as “writers” (e.g., methyltransferases), “erasers” (e.g., demethylases), and “readers” (e.g., bromodomain proteins). For instance, gain-of-function mutations or overexpression of EZH2, the catalytic subunit of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) that facilitates H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), are present in lymphomas, breast cancer, and many more malignancies [11]. EZH2 hyperactivation stimulates the silencing of tumor suppressors, which allows cells to grow and spread without control. KDM6A (UTX), a histone demethylase that removes restrictive H3K27me3 marks that normally serves as a tumor suppressor, is often deactivated by mutations in malignancies including breast cancer, bladder cancer, and leukemia [12]. These modifications disturb conventional gene expression patterns, facilitating neoplastic transformation.Recurrent mutations in histone modifiers are common in a variety of cancers, which shows how essential they are in the development of tumors. In lung cancer, histone acetylation (like the global loss of H4K16ac) and methylation (like the overexpression of EZH2) are frequently dysregulated, and these changes are often linked to harmful prognosis and resistance to treatment [13, 14]. In breast cancer, abnormal histone methylation, like EZH2-mediated silencing of hormone receptors, causes tumors to be different from each other and spread to other parts of the body, especially in triple-negative subtypes [15]. Colorectal cancer also shows a lot of epigenetic changes, like mutations in histone methyltransferases (like SETD2) and demethylases, which help tumors grow through pathways like Wnt signaling [16]. The fact that these mutations happen a lot in several distinct kinds of cancer shows that disrupting chromatin homeostasis is a key way that cancer cells grow, which is why histone modifiers are an appealing target for treatment.It is now well known that epigenetic dysregulation, especially alterations in histones, plays a key role in the development of tumors (Fig. 1). Moreover, comprehensive studies have elucidated how recurrent mutations in enzymes like EZH2 and KDM6A perturb the epigenetic landscape, resulting in dysregulated gene expression programs that drive cancer hallmarks [17]. Histone modifications are acknowledged as significant contributors to various cancers; however, their subtype-specific functions, therapeutic targeting difficulties, and complex interactions with genetic alterations and other cancer hallmarks are still inadequately investigated. For example, the functional importance of less-explored modifications such as histone phosphorylation (e.g., H3Y41ph) in signal transduction and ubiquitination (e.g., H2BK120ub) in transcriptional regulation across various cancer subtypes remains inadequately researched [18, 19]. Moreover, the clinical application of epigenetic therapies is frequently obstructed by challenges related to drug resistance, selectivity, and an inadequate comprehension of the mechanisms by which tumor cells reorganize their epigenome in response to targeted therapies. This review aims to fill these gaps by looking at histone modifications in a broad way, comparing how they work and what they do across different types of cancer, from lung and breast cancer to colorectal tumors and blood cancers. We will examine how the tumor’s histone modification landscape affects the tumor-immune microenvironment, affecting how immune cells are recruited and how they respond to immunotherapies. Finally, some potential natural products with the function of affecting histone modifications will be discussed. These covalent post-translational modifications (PTMs) primarily occur on the N-terminal tails of core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) and encompass well-characterized marks such as acetylation and methylation, alongside less-explored modifications including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and glycosylation. Specific enzymes called “writers” and “erasers” add and remove them dynamically, and “reader” proteins interpret them and bring in downstream effector complexes to change transcriptional states, DNA repair, replication, and the cell cycle [20]. In cancer, mutations, overexpression, or deletion of the modifying enzymes often throw off the exact balance of these changes, which leads to the activation of oncogenes or the silencing of tumor suppressor genes, which drives tumorigenesis and metastasis [21]. Although acetylation and methylation have been extensively studied in the field of oncology in the past decades, recent studies have emphasized the relevance of other modifications in the field of cancer research, such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, glycosylation, sumoylation, ADP-ribosylation, lactylation, β-hydroxybutyrylation, crotonylation, and citrullination (Table 1). Histone phosphorylation, as demonstrated by H3S10ph, serves a dual function in transcriptional activation and chromosome condensation during mitosis [22]. H3S10ph is often upregulated in cancer and is linked to a worse prognosis in cancers like breast cancer and glioblastoma. It plays a role in keeping the genome stable by marking DNA-RNA hybrids (R-loops). If these are not working properly, they can cause DNA damage and chromosomal instability, which is an indication of cancer. Aurora B, MSK1/2, and PIM1 are some of the kinases that add this mark. These kinases are frequently dysregulated in tumors. A significant mechanism is the “phospho-methyl switch,” in which H3S10ph stops repressive proteins like HP1 from binding to nearby H3K9me2/3. This stops heterochromatin from spreading and can even turn on oncogenes [23].Histone ubiquitination, especially the mono-ubiquitination of H2BK120 (H2BK120ub), is another important change that plays a complicated role in cancer. H2BK120ub, mainly caused by the RNF20/40 E3 ligase complex, is usually linked to transcriptional activation and can act as a tumor suppressor [24]. For example, in triple-negative breast cancer, UBR7 promotes H2BK120ub, which stops tumors from growing and spreading. H2BK120ub helps bring repair elements to double-strand breaks in the DNA damage response. On the other hand, the deubiquitinase USP22, which is part of the SAGA complex, removes H2BK120ub [25]. Blocking USP22 increases H2BK120ub levels and makes it harder for γH2AX to form, which is a hallmark of DNA damage. This makes DNA repair harder and makes cancer cells more unstable [26].Histone glycosylation, particularly O-GlcNAcylation, has been identified as a nutrient-responsive post-translational modification that connects cellular metabolism with epigenetic regulation. O-GlcNAcylation is the process by which O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) adds O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) to serine or threonine residues on histones. O-GlcNAcase (OGA) then processes it away [27]. The shift is often higher in cancers like breast, prostate, and colon cancer, and it helps tumors grow by controlling important processes. For instance, O-GlcNAcylation of H2B at serine 112 (H2BS112GlcNAc) makes it easier for a single ubiquitin molecule to be added to lysine 120 (K120) on H2B, which helps gene transcription [28]. O-GlcNAcylation can compete with phosphorylation at the same residue, as seen at H3S10, where higher levels of O-GlcNAcylation are linked to lower levels of phosphorylation, which affects how chromatin condenses during mitosis [29]. O-GlcNAcylation acts as a sensor for the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, linking the availability of nutrients such as glucose, glutamine, and ATP to chromatin dynamics. This represents a mechanistic connection between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic changes in cancer [30].In histone sumoylation, small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) proteins are covalently attached to lysine residues on histones H4, H2A, H2B, and H3. Unlike ubiquitination, in which the target protein is often marked for degradation, protein-protein interactions and subcellular localization are the major targets of sumoylation. With respect to chromatin, histone sumoylation is generally associated with transcriptional repression. It does so by facilitating the recruitment of repressive complexes such as histone deacetylases (HDACs) and heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) or by counteracting activation marks [31, 32]. This process is regulated by a series of enzymes including E1, E2 (Ubc9), and E3 enzymes such as the PIAS family. The reverse reaction is mediated by sentrin-specific proteases, also known as SENPs. The role of histone sumoylation in cancer development is complex and dependent on the context. For example, the sumoylation of histone H4 occurs at multiple lysine residues, including K5, K8, K12, K16, and K20, which has been implicated as a key factor in the maintenance of heterochromatin stability, and its deregulation has been implicated in genomic instability, a hallmark of cancer development [33]. Additionally, the overexpression of the sumoylation machinery has been implicated in cancer development. For instance, Ubc9 is overexpressed in a number of cancers and is associated with poor prognosis, thus offering a new avenue for the development of cancer therapy [34].ADP-ribosylation is a distinctive and dynamic post-translational modification wherein ADP-ribose moieties are transferred from NAD+ onto protein targets. This can happen as mono(ADP-ribosylation) (MARylation) or poly(ADP-ribosylation) (PARylation). On histones, especially H2B and H3, this post-translational modification is mainly mediated by members of the PARP protein family, including PARP1, which ADP-ribosylates specific residues such as H2BK30, H3K27, and H3K37 [35]. The incorporation of these bulky, negatively charged ADP-ribose polymers is known to profoundly alter chromatin architecture, leading to an open, relaxed structure that is favorable for DNA repair, replication, and transcription [36]. This modification is undone by erasers such as PARG. The significance of ADP-ribosylation in cancer is substantial, especially given the central role of PARP1 in DNA damage response pathways. Histone PARylation is among the first responders to DNA damage, given its role in marking sites of DNA breaks for repair [37]. This is particularly relevant in cancers that have deficiencies in homologous recombination repair, such as BRCA1/2, for which PARP inhibitors (PARPi) have emerged as therapeutic agents that trigger synthetic lethality [38]. In addition to DNA damage response, aberrant PARPs have also been implicated in inflammation and transcription of oncogenes, thus securing their place as key players in cancer that is critical for therapeutic intervention.Histone lactylation, a newly discovered epigenetic modification, was derived from the metabolic byproduct lactate, thus creating a direct link between the metabolic state, as determined by the Warburg effect or aerobic glycolysis, and gene expression. Lactylation was first discovered on lysine residues of histones, including H4K5la, H4K8la, and H3K18la, and is catalyzed by writers such as p300 [39]. Lactylation, like acetylation, was shown to activate genes, but, in contrast to acetylation, which is derived from the metabolic byproduct acetyl-CoA, lactylation was directly linked to the cellular metabolic state and specifically to high rates of lactate production. Lactylation was shown to play a critical role in modulating M1/M2 macrophages polarization. In later stages of the inflammatory response, continuous glycolytic pathway activation results in intracellular lactate accumulation, thereby promoting histone lactylation, especially of H3K18 at the promoters of genes involved in wound healing and immunosuppression, such as Arg1, Vegf, Il10, Tgfb1, and Mrc1/CD206 [40]. Within the tumor microenvironment (TME), the lactate-mediated histone lactylation process is hijacked by tumor-associated macrophages to promote the establishment of a pro-oncogenic M2-like phenotype, resulting in immune evasion, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Furthermore, in cancer, elevated lactate, which is a result of the Warburg effect, has been implicated in the regulation of histone lactylation, which may, in turn, lead to the expression of genes that regulate cell proliferation and angiogenesis [41]. For example, histone lactylation has been implicated in the regulation of tumor growth and immune surveillance in ocular melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer through the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages [42, 43].β-hydroxybutyrylation (Kbhb) is a histone modification that is derived from the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), which is produced in large quantities during metabolic stress conditions such as caloric restriction and fasting. This histone modification has been found on histones such as H3K9bhb and H3K14bhb and has been linked to an open chromatin configuration and transcription, which counteracts the repressive effects of histone deacetylases [44]. The larger and hydrophobic nature of the β-hydroxybutyryl group, compared to the acetyl group, is believed to better repel the histones from the DNA, allowing for the transcription factor to have greater access. In the context of cancer, the function of Kbhb is an emerging field of study. Although BHB has been shown to have anti-tumor effects, this is generally through the function of providing a metabolic fuel and/or signal. However, the direct function of providing an epigenetic mark suggests a more complex function. For example, in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, which is known for having significant metabolic reprogramming, decreased levels of Kbhb at the promoters of tumor suppressor genes have been observed implying that Kbhb may function as a tumor-suppressive mark in this context. In this way, lowering its expression would help silence these genes and increase lipolysis leading to tumor development [45].Histone crotonylation, abbreviated as Kcr, is a short-chain lysine acylation mark that is both structurally and functionally distinct from acetylation. Kcr is derived from crotonyl-CoA, an intermediate of fatty acid oxidation and amino acid degradation. Histone crotonylation, such as H3K18cr and H4K8cr, is found at active gene promoters and enhancers and is enriched on genes that are involved in crucial cellular processes including cell cycle regulation, metabolic reprogramming, and signal transduction pathways [46]. Although the writers and erasers of both acetylation and crotonylation are the same, such as p300/CBP and HDACs, SIRT1-3, respectively, crotonylation has been found to be more potent at activating genes compared to acetylation because of its bulkier and more hydrophobic size, thus facilitating greater decompaction of chromatin [47, 48]. Moreover, the alteration of histone crotonylation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of cancer. For example, the reduction of global levels of histone crotonylation has been observed in hepatocellular carcinoma and other cancers, which correlates with poor clinical outcome and metastasis [49, 50]. Such reduction could lead to the repression of tumor suppressor genes, implying that the proper regulation of histone crotonylation is crucial for the suppression of tumorigenic phenotypes. The crosstalk between acetylation and crotonylation at the same lysine residue introduces another dimension to the “histone code” in cancer.Citrullination is a special post-translational modification, where the amino acid arginine, which is one of the most common residues found on histone tails, is converted into citrulline. This is not an addition of a chemical group, but rather a deimination reaction, and it is carried out by the peptidylarginine deiminase family of enzymes, most specifically PAD4 [51]. By converting the positively charged amino acid into a neutral amino acid, this modification has the effect of dramatically altering the positive charge of the histones, and hence the interaction between the histones and the negatively charged DNA backbone. This has the effect of directly leading to the decondensation of the chromosomes, and it also antagonizes the modification of arginine methylation, which is found at active genes, by removing the target for the methyltransferases. This is an important modification for processes such as neutrophil extracellular trap formation, NETosis, but it has profound effects if it is dysregulated, such as in the case of cancer [52]. PAD4 overexpression has been observed in various cancers, including breast, lung, and colon cancers. Overexpression of PAD4 results in the inhibition of histone arginine methylation and the decompaction of chromatin structures at promoters of genes involved in the processes of cell proliferation and invasion, resulting in the activation of the transcription of these genes [53]. Moreover, citrullination of histone H3 at arginine 8 (H3R8Cit) and histone H4 at arginine 3 (H4R3Cit) blocks the methylation of the sites in these histones, which has been associated with the epigenetic inactivation of the tumor suppressors, including p21. In the TME, this mechanism might result in the tumor-promoting and metastasis-promoting activities of NETs. It has been reported that citrullination of histones in NETs induces the proliferation and migration of cancer cells, increasing their resistance to the host’s immune system [54, 55].In the following sections, this review aims to discuss the implications of these findings with respect to cancer. Due to the nascent nature of this field of study, as well as the limited number of potential drug candidates, this review will specifically discuss two of the more well-characterized processes, namely methylation and acetylation.Functional implications in cancerHistone modifications are not just epigenetic spectators; they actively drive tumorigenesis by disrupting fundamental cancer hallmarks, leading to significant functional consequences. These changes have a direct effect on how important oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes are expressed, which in turn shifts important cellular processes. For example, PRC2 and its catalytic subunit EZH2 put down repressive marks like H3K27me3, which are often found at the promoters of tumor suppressor genes like p16INK4a and RB. This stops the genes from functioning and lets the cell cycle go on without control [56]. On the other hand, triggering motifs like H3K4me3 and histone acetylation (e.g., H3K27ac) frequently occur at the enhancers and promoters of strong oncogenes like MYC and KRAS, which makes their pro-tumorigenic signals more powerful [57, 58]. The mutant histone H3K27M, which is found in some pediatric gliomas, works as a dominant-negative inhibitor of PRC2. This causes an overall decrease in H3K27me3, but it also causes gene-specific hypermethylation and activation of oncogenic pathways [59]. Moreover, histone modification enzymes can directly engage with transcription factors to refine gene expression programs critical for cancer advancement. Abbreviations: HAT, histone acetyltransferase; MLL, mixed lineage leukemia; PRC2, Polycomb Repressive Complex 2; EZH2, enhancer of zeste homolog 2; ACLY, ATP-citrate lyase; EMT, epithelial-mesenchymal transition; PD-L1, programmed death-ligand 1 The interaction between cellular metabolism and histone modifications, especially acetylation, constitutes a critical axis of epigenetic interaction in cancer. The accessibility of acetyl-CoA, a necessary co-factor for HATs, is closely related to the cell’s metabolic state. A lot of cancer cells change to aerobic glycolysis and make more lipids, both of which can raise the amount of acetyl-CoA in the nucleus [60]. For instance, ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY) changes citrate that comes from glucose into acetyl-CoA in the nucleus. This directly connects the flow of glycolysis to the acetylation of histones. This higher level of acetyl-CoA can cause histones to become hyperacetylated at the promoters and enhancers of genes that help cells grow and divide [61]. Conversely, in nutrient-deprived environments or via pharmacological blockade with specific metabolic pathways, diminished acetyl-CoA concentrations can result in widespread histone hypoacetylation and the repression of tumorigenic transcripts. This metabolic-epigenetic axis is apparent in multiple cancer types; in hepatocellular carcinoma, increased acetyl-CoA production from various fuel sources facilitates histone acetylation and tumor proliferation, whereas in breast cancer, oncogenic signaling may augment acetyl-CoA production to maintain an oncogenic transcriptome [62].Based on this mechanistic understanding, several strategies targeting metabolism have been used therapeutically. Ketogenic diet-based metabolic approaches that induce an elevation in the plasma concentration of BHB were found to enhance the histone Kbhb at the promoters of tumor-suppressive genes such as TP53 and FOXO3a, thus increasing the transcription of these genes and inhibiting the progression of colorectal cancer xenografts [63]. Calorie restriction and fasting, which limit the systemic concentrations of glucose and insulin, cause depletion of nuclear acetyl-CoA, resulting in inhibition of histone acetylation and consequent decreased tumor growth in breast cancer and glioblastoma models [64, 65]. Pharmacologically, inhibitors of ACLY, including BMS-303,141 and bempedoic acid, decrease glucose-dependent acetyl-CoA synthesis, leading to decreased levels of histone H3K27ac and H3K9ac at oncogenic genes, causing cell proliferation inhibition in prostatic cancer models [66, 67]. Likewise, inhibitors of glutaminase such as CB-839 (telaglenastat) inhibit glutamine-derived α-ketoglutarate, which is essential for the activity of ten-eleven translocation family DNA demethylases and Jumonji C domain histone demethylases, resulting in locus-specific methylation of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, affecting gene expression pathways and inhibiting the growth of triple-negative breast cancer [68, 69]. These examples illustrate the therapeutic potential of targeting the metabolic-epigenetic axis in cancer.Histone modifications and the tumor immune microenvironmentHistone modifications have recently been identified as important factors that contribute to the immunogenic nature of cancer cells as well as the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). The repressive histone modification H3K27me3, catalyzed by EZH2 in its role as the catalytic unit of PRC2, directly inhibits the transcription of T-helper 1 (Th1)-type chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10, which play a key role in attracting effector CD8 + T cells into tumors [70]. Moreover, the recruitment of EZH2 to the promoter regions of genes coding MHC-I antigens and TAP1/2 facilitates the repression of antigen presentation in tumor cells, thus facilitating their immune escape [71]. This epigenetically based silencing mechanism causes the TME to be “cold,” with minimal T cell penetration and immunogenicity. Thus, the pharmacologic inhibition of EZH2 through tazemetostat promotes reexpression of these chemokines and restoration of MHC-I presentation at the surface of cells, resulting in greater CD8 + T cell infiltration and response to immune checkpoint blockade therapy in experimental models of ovarian, small cell lung, and melanoma cancers [72].However, the H3K4me3 tag, which is installed by COMPASS-related histone methyltransferases such as the MLL complex, is found at the promoters of several other genes in various cancers, including the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 (CD274) and the immunosuppressive enzyme indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 [73]. This modification leads to elevated expression levels of immunosuppressive ligands and hence T cell exhaustion and immune escape. The inhibition of the MLL protein complex by inhibitors like MI-463 and MI-503 leads to a reduction of H3K4me3 marks in the PD-L1 promoter region and thus transcriptional downregulation of PD-L1, and inhibition of LSD1 by inhibitors such as bomedemstat leads to reduced PD-L1 expression levels [74]. In addition to that, the repressive mark of H3K9me3, placed by SETDB1 and read by HP1, acts to transcriptionally silence retroviruses. The pharmacologic or genetic suppression of SETDB1 results in viral mimicry, which is defined as an induction of double-stranded RNA, activation of the Type I interferon pathway via the MDA5/MAVS axis, and the establishment of anti-tumor immunity [75, 76].Key proteins and signaling pathwaysIn addition to the inherent mutational landscape of epigenetic enzymes, canonical oncogenic drivers continually restructure the epigenetic landscape to promote neoplastic programs. An example of this is mutant KRAS, which causes major changes in transcription by bringing in and changing histone modifiers. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and colorectal cancer, oncogenic KRAS signaling has been demonstrated to enhance the expression of the histone methyltransferase EZH2. The MAPK pathway leads to this, which raises global H3K27me3 levels and turns off important tumor-suppressive and differentiation pathways [77]. Moreover, mutant KRAS participates in a positive feedback loop with the epigenome. It can help histone demethylases like KDM5A work better, which keeps cells in a dedifferentiated, therapy-resistant state [78]. Importantly, KRAS-driven tumors frequently demonstrate increased histone acetylation at the promoters and enhancers of pro-proliferative genes. This is made easier by the fact that acetyl-CoA, an important metabolite and substrate for HATs, is facilitated more, which connects the KRAS-driven metabolic reprogramming directly to the epigenetic state [79]. The reliance of mutant KRAS tumors on particular epigenetic regulators, including EZH2 and BRD4, indicates essential co-dependency and presents a logical therapeutic strategy for targeting these otherwise “undruggable” oncogenes via their epigenetic co-factors [80]. The functions of histone-modifying enzymes are often contingent on specific contexts, exhibiting considerable variation across different cancer types and molecular subtypes, thereby highlighting the intricacy of the cancer epigenome. They work with other regulatory mechanisms, like DNA methylation and non-coding RNAs, to keep oncogenic gene expression states stable. A quintessential illustration of this synergy is the collaborative repression of the tumor suppressor gene CDKN2A (p16INK4a). In many types of cancer, such as glioblastoma and lung cancer, this locus often shows both promoter DNA hypermethylation and repressive histone methylation (H3K27me3 and H3K9me2/3) at the same time [88]. The interaction is two-way: DNA methylation can help bring in proteins that promote a repressive histone state, and on the other hand, some repressive histone marks can direct DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) to specific genomic sites [89]. This sets off a cycle of epigenetic silencing that is stronger and less likely to be undone than either change on its own. Also, the MBD family of proteins, which bind to methylated DNA, often bring in complexes that contain histone deacetylases (HDACs), which causes local histone deacetylation and more chromatin compaction [90, 91]. This combined axis of DNA methylation and histone deacetylation is a strong way to keep important cancer-related genes from being expressed for a long time.In addition to DNA methylation, histone modifications extensively interact with non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) can function as modular scaffolds that physically attract and direct histone-modifying complexes to particular genomic loci. The most well-studied interaction is between the lncRNA XIST, which is necessary for X-chromosome inactivation, and the PRC2. XIST binds to PRC2 and informs it where to put H3K27me3 on the inactive X chromosome. For example, the lncRNA HOTAIR, which is overexpressed in breast, liver, and gastrointestinal cancers, serves as a link between PRC2 (which catalyzes H3K27me3) and the LSD1/CoREST/REST complex (which demethylates H3K4me). This creates a double repressive marker on genes that stop metastasis [92]. lncRNA ANRIL, which comes from the CDKN2A/B locus, also directly attracts PRC2 to silence this locus. This creates an autoregulatory feedback loop that encourages cell growth [93].Therapeutic targeting and emerging strategiesEpigenetic drugs in cancerThe reversible character of epigenetic modifications has rendered them appealing therapeutic targets, resulting in the creation of epigenetic drugs (epi-drugs) aimed at restoring regular gene expression patterns in cancer cells [94]. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved various epi-drugs, mostly for blood cancers. These include DNA methyltransferase inhibitors (DNMTi) like azacitidine and decitabine for myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) like vorinostat and romidepsin for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. More recently, methyltransferase inhibitor (HMTi) tazemetostat, which inhibits EZH2, has been approved for follicular lymphoma and epithelioid sarcoma [95]. These agents operate via different mechanisms: DNMT inhibitors integrate into DNA and covalently sequester DNMT enzymes, resulting in DNA demethylation and the reactivation of silenced tumor suppressor genes, whereas HDAC inhibitors impede the removal of acetyl groups, fostering a more accessible chromatin state and the transcription of genes associated with differentiation and apoptosis [96]. Even though they have worked well in the clinic, there are still limitations, such as toxicity (especially with the nucleoside analogue DNMTi), limited effectiveness as monotherapies in solid tumors, and an increase of drug resistance [97]. The continual improvement of next-generation epi-drugs, such as non-nucleoside DNMTi and lysine acetyltransferase inhibitors (KATi), aims to address these limitations and enhance the repertoire of epigenetic therapeutics.
