Tip60 is involved in DNA damage response and metastasisPreclinicalSignificant in vivo activity against breast cancer models in preclinical studiesBalancing efficacy with potential systemic toxicity due to broad roles of KATs[103]BET inhibitors are one of the most studied types of new epi-drugs, but their application in real life has shown that they have both promise and problems. Mechanistically, BET inhibitors operate by competing with BET proteins, mostly BRD4, for the acetyl-lysine recognition pockets, which pushes them out of chromatin [104]. This stops the positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) and other co-activators from coming together, which quickly and preferentially turns off important oncogenes, especially MYC, in different types of blood cancers and NUT midline carcinoma [105]. A defining feature of BETi action is their selective targeting of super-enhancers—large groups of enhancers that control the expression of genes that determine cell identity, including many oncogenes. This may explain why they work as medicines [106].Even though there is strong preclinical evidence, clinical trials with BETi monotherapy have produced mixed results and limited effectiveness. Some hematologic malignancies have demonstrated responses; however, outcomes in solid tumors have been predominantly unsatisfactory. There are a number of reasons for this. Dose-limiting toxicities, especially thrombocytopenia, gastrointestinal issues, and fatigue, have made it impossible to give doses high enough to completely block the target [107]. Additionally, swift development of resistance and the failure to maintain MYC suppression in various contexts have been noted. Kinome reprogramming is one of the crucial ways that cells can resist BET inhibition; the cells will activate the receptor tyrosine kinases and MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways that promote oncogenic transcription independently of BRD4 [108]. Surprisingly, opposing effects on broad transcription have also been reported: while BETi inhibit many protein-coding genes like MYC, they may also cause a global increase in total RNA synthesis by increasing highly transcribed non-polyadenylated RNAs (e.g., histone genes), which may result in transcription-replication conflicts and replication stress [109]. This dual transcriptional effect highlights the intricacy of BET protein biology.BET proteins have biological functions that include both promoting cancer and causing inflammation. This makes their inhibitors work in a more complicated way. BET proteins are essential for the expression of pro-oncogenic drivers. Conversely, they serve as principal regulators of the inflammatory response. BET proteins, particularly BRD4, are essential for the expression of NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines [110]. In myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), constitutive JAK2 signaling alters the enhancer landscape, resulting in BRD4-dependent activation of NF-κB signaling in both malignant and non-malignant cells, thereby sustaining a chronic inflammatory state and promoting bone marrow fibrosis [111]. In this context, BET inhibition diminishes NF-κB signaling and decreases cytokine production in vivo. This anti-inflammatory effect can be therapeutically advantageous, as evidenced by the enhanced efficacy of combining BET inhibitors with JAK inhibitors (e.g., pelabresib with ruxolitinib) in MPN, resulting in diminished symptom burden and reversal of fibrosis. Nonetheless, this identical mechanism may also be responsible for immunosuppressive side effects or context-dependent alterations of the TIME. So, the future of BET inhibitors probably depends on smart ways to combine them. Synergy has been noted with other targeted agents (e.g., enzalutamide in prostate cancer), immunotherapy, and particularly with other epigenetic drugs such as HDAC inhibitors, frequently enabling reduced, less toxic doses of each agent while augmenting antitumor efficacy [112].Functional classification of therapeuticsPROTACs targeting histone modifiersIn addition to traditional enzyme inhibitors, novel treatments have been developed to target the epigenetic system in cancer. These strategies offer better specificity, effectiveness, and the ability to get around drug resistance. Some of these methods are proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) that break down histone-modifying enzymes, dual-inhibitors that target more than one epigenetic pathway at the same time, and allosteric modulators that use new regulatory sites. These modalities signify a functional advancement in epigenetic drug development, progressing from occupancy-based inhibition to catalytic degradation and multi-target modulation. PROTACs are heterobifunctional molecules that bring an E3 ubiquitin ligase to a specific protein of interest. This causes the protein to be ubiquitinated and then broken down by the proteasome [113]. This event-driven mechanism has many benefits over conventional small-molecule inhibitors. For example, it can target “undruggable” proteins like transcription factors or scaffolding proteins, get around resistance caused by protein overexpression, and maintain the pharmacological effects going through catalytic degradation [114]. The creation of the first BRD4-targeting PROTAC was a major step forward in this field. It showed that this bromodomain-containing protein could be broken down quickly and selectively [115]. Since then, PROTACs have been effectively developed and tested against different histone-modifying enzymes and readers. For example, EZH2-directed PROTACs have been effective in reducing EZH2 and lowering H3K27me3 levels in lymphomas as well as other cancers, possibly providing benefits over chemical inhibitors in specific situations [116]. In the same manner, PROTACs that target BET family proteins (like BRD2/3/4) and HDACs have been shown in preclinical models to cause stronger and longer-lasting anti-tumor responses than their inhibitory equivalents [117]. The most advanced PROTACs, especially those that recruit the Cereblon E3 ligase, have begun clinical trials (Phase I-III) for hematological and solid tumors. This is a big step forward in the use of epigenetic degradation strategies [118].Although there is immense potential in proteolysis-targeting chimeras, mechanisms of resistance have begun to develop that should be considered. Major mechanisms of PROTAC resistance can be categorized as the loss or mutation of the E3 ligase subunit, the inability to form the ternary complex, increased drug efflux and metabolism, and the reexpression or stabilization of the target protein. Loss or inactivating mutations in Cereblon (CRBN), which has become the most frequent E3 ligase to recruit, will lead to the inability to degrade the target. This mechanism of resistance was first discovered in association with resistance to immunomodulators, such as lenalidomide and pomalidomide, in patients suffering from multiple myeloma [119]. A mutation at the interface between the target protein and PROTAC, or PROTAC and E3 ubiquitin ligase, will destabilize the three-component complex formation. The consequence will be decreased ubiquitination efficiency without influencing the natural role of the targeted protein. The activation of ATP-binding cassette transporters like P-glycoprotein decreases the intracellular levels of PROTACs due to the molecule’s relatively higher molecular weight [120].Designs of next-generation degraders are emerging to counteract such resistance mechanisms using several methods. The use of E3 ligase switching strategies allows for developing degraders that utilize E3 ligases other than CRBN or von Hippel-Lindau, such as MDM2, IAPs, DCAF16, and KEAP1. Pan-E3 ligand strategies have also been envisaged in which E3 ligands are used to engage several ligases at once to avoid resistance [121]. Trivalent PROTACs involving dual binding of E3 ligases or dual epitope targeting on the target protein increase ternary complex stability and efficiency while making it less likely for resistance-conferring mutations to occur [122]. The use of covalent PROTACs involves electrophilic warheads that create irreversible or reversible covalent modifications of the cysteine or lysine residue of the target protein or E3 ligase, promoting target engagement and degradation despite mutations that may impair non-covalent interactions [123]. The antibody-PROTAC conjugates and folate receptor-PROTAC conjugates enhance tumor selectivity, limiting systemic exposure and thus the selective pressure to develop resistance mechanisms [124]. Finally, molecular glue refers to the thalidomide analogues and aryl sulfonamides that create new protein interactions between a target protein and E3 ligase, regardless of any ligandable pocket within the target protein. Molecular glues help degrade targets once considered undruggable and prevent resistant mutations from interfering with PROTAC binding [125].Dual inhibitorsThe intricate and compensating characteristics of epigenetic systems have catalyzed the creation of dual inhibitors that simultaneously regulate two separate epigenetic targets. This approach can make treatments more effective, lower the chances of resistance, and deal with the many different causes of cancer. A notable example is the development of dual inhibitors aimed at histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) and other proteins pertinent to disease. One reported compound was designed for Alzheimer’s disease, targeting HDAC6 and butyrylcholinesterase; the same conceptual structure is currently being utilized in oncology [126]. Some of these dual targeting HDAC inhibitors, like EDO-S101, which inhibits HDAC and alkylates DNA; the dual HDAC/PI3K inhibitor CUDC-907; 4SC-202, which inhibits both HDAC and LSD1; and the dual HDAC/EGFR inhibitor CUDC-101, have already begun clinical trials, respectively [127]. These agents can cause synergistic reactivation of silenced tumor suppressors or apoptosis by inhibiting various nodes in the epigenetic circuitry at the same time, such as a histone-modifying enzyme and a cooperating transcription factor or metabolic enzyme.Allosteric modulatorsTargeting allosteric sites that are unique to an enzyme’s active site could offer an attractive therapeutic approach in the development of highly specific epigenetic drugs. Allosteric modulators can offer enhanced specificity in this regard because they can exploit unique regulatory regions that are not conserved across enzyme families and can offer more nuanced control over protein function [128]. Recent research into cancer-associated histone missense mutations identified that the oncogenic activity of these mutations can be mediated through allosteric regulation. Mutations such as H2BS64Y and H2BS64F were identified to exhibit long-range allosteric activity that disrupted the normal function of the histone complex, altered H2BK120 ubiquitination levels, and disrupted genome stability [129]. Consequently, this mechanism highlights the importance of allosteric regulation in nucleosomes and that this mechanism could potentially be targeted using synthetic compounds that can modulate these allosteric sites in histone-modifying complexes or reader complexes. Although the development of synthetic allosteric modulators for epigenetic targets is still in its relative infancy compared to the development of PROTACs, this therapeutic approach could potentially offer attractive therapeutic opportunities in the development of drugs that can target historically difficult targets with minimal off-target effects.Combination therapiesThe limited effectiveness of epigenetic monotherapies, especially in solid tumors, has generated considerable interest in practical combination strategies [130]. The main rationale for using epigenetic drugs is their ability to reprogram the tumor cell and its microenvironment to overcome resistance mechanisms and increase the effectiveness of conventional and targeted therapies. By reversing epigenetic silencing, modulating the immune system, and inducing replicative stress, these drugs can put the cancer cell in a “sensitized” state, unlocking the synergistic antitumor activity. A thorough screening of a chemical library containing 2,697 compounds revealed that anti-microtubule agents, including vincristine, demonstrated the most potent synergistic anticancer effects when paired with the BET bromodomain inhibitor JQ1 in neuroblastoma models [144]. The mechanistic foundation of this synergy entails BET inhibition inducing cell cycle arrest at the G2/M phase, thereby augmenting the cytotoxic effects of microtubule-targeting agents. Also, quinone-containing compounds, like some anthracycline chemotherapies, worked very well with BET inhibitors by blocking the Nrf2-antioxidant signaling pathway. Cancer cells usually turn this pathway on to protect themselves from oxidative stress caused by chemotherapy. As a BET inhibitor, JQ1 also stopped human gastric cancer cells from growing and spreading by turning off the RUNX2/NID1 signaling pathway. It induced global site-specific chromatin remodeling in the genome of GC cells, resulting in increased site inaccessibility [145]. A lot of clinical trial data backs up the clinical translation of these findings. For example, vorinostat with carboplatin/paclitaxel for ovarian cancer, panobinostat with decitabine/temozolomide for melanoma, and valproic acid with different chemotherapy regimens for different types of cancer. The most clinically advanced of these combinations involves the simultaneous use of DNMTi and HDAC inhibitors, which target different ways of silencing genes. Preclinical studies have shown that DNMT inhibitors may lead to hypermethylated tumor suppressor genes to be expressed again. HDAC inhibitors make this effect stronger by relaxing chromatin at these loci [146]. Although there is substantial experimental evidence supporting the use of DNA methyltransferase inhibitors and histone deacetylase inhibitors together, therapeutic resistance is a major barrier. Mechanisms leading to resistance involve activation of alternate epigenetic silencing systems, including increased deposition of H3K27me3 by EZH2 or H3K9me3 by SETDB1 in the absence of global DNA hypomethylation and histone hyperacetylation, metabolic adjustments to ensure adequate production of the universal methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine and acetyl-CoA, and triggering an epithelial-mesenchymal transition to become tolerant to drugs [147, 148]. Resistance can be overcome through triple epigenetic combination approaches that target DNA methylation, histone deacetylation, and histone methylation to avoid repressive marks as compensation; triple combination approaches with an EZH2 or LSD1 inhibitor in preclinical models of acute myeloid leukemia and ovarian cancers have shown to effectively block silencing in reactivated tumor suppressor genes [149–151]. Interruption therapies based on the relatively slow dynamics of epigenetic remodeling are possible since they permit normal tissue restoration while still applying drug pressure to cancer cells. Moreover, incorporating metabolic blockers such as methionine restriction through diet or methionine adenosyltransferase 2 A inhibition via drugs such as AG-270 can lead to depletion of S-adenosylmethionine, which is necessary for resistance [152].A combination of methods should be recommended to experimentally test the mechanisms behind the resistance. For instance, whole-genome epigenomic analysis based on sequencing of ChIP for H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3, and H3K27ac, WGBS for DNA methylation, and ATAC-seq for chromatin accessibility, needs to be conducted at baseline, at the maximal response stage, and at the resistance stage. Lineage tracking by using lentivirus barcode tagging along with single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq may help differentiate pre-existing resistant clones from de novo epigenetic changes acquired resistance [153]. Genes that induce resistance when inhibited or induced by pooled CRISPR inhibition and CRISPR activation epigenome screens for all epigenetic modifiers can be identified [154]. The metabolic activity using carbon-13 glucose, glutamine, and serine can trace methylation and acetylation processes in drug sensitive and resistant cells [155]. Finally, patient derived xenografts or organoids in drug treatment can provide clinically important insights into mechanisms of resistance.In addition to combinations of DNA methylation and histone modification, new strategies are targeting several histone modifications at once. For instance, the combination of EZH2 inhibitors and BET bromodomain inhibitors has shown synergistic effects in preclinical cancer models [156, 157]. Researchers found that BET and EZH2 inhibitors stopped MYC from being activated, which led to a synergistic effect on stopping the growth and cloning of metastatic prostate cancer cells [158]. The combination of various classes of histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors—such as HAT inhibitors with HDAC inhibitors—remains to be investigated as a strategy to more accurately regulate the epigenetic state of cancer cells [159]. Such multi-epigenetic strategies are a reflection of the realization that cancer epigenomes are maintained by complex and redundant regulatory systems that may need to be targeted simultaneously.Translational perspectives and cross-disciplinary insightsClinical trials and challengesBarriers to clinical translationThe translation of epigenetic therapies from promising preclinical models to the clinic has been a journey of both encouraging successes and sobering challenges. Although epi-drugs have established a firm foothold in hematological malignancies, their use in solid malignancies has been more restricted, thereby emphasizing the need to understand and overcome the barriers to their efficacy [160]. A significant obstacle is extensive tumor heterogeneity, which manifests at various levels. Intratumor heterogeneity denotes subpopulations of neoplastic cells exhibiting unique molecular characteristics within a singular tumor [161]. This diversity is a significant cause of treatment failure, as epi-drugs may only effectively target a vulnerable subset, allowing resistant clones to multiply and cause relapse [162]. Moreover, bulk-tissue molecular profiling, which assesses an average across all cell types in a sample, may conceal significant cell-type-specific epigenetic modifications that facilitate cancer progression [163]. A new computational method called cell-type-specific combinatorial clustering (CELTYC) has shown that breaking down the epigenetic landscape by cell type can help doctors better predict how well a patient will do with liver or kidney cancer. This means that future clinical trials may need to take this complexity into account to find patient groups that really respond to treatment [163].Another major problem is that there aren’t enough validated predictive biomarkers. Some epi-drugs have clear biomarkers, like EZH2 mutations for tazemetostat and MTAP deletion for PRMT1 and PRMT5 inhibitors. However, these are the only ones [164, 165]. It is still not clear which patients will benefit the most from most epi-drugs, especially when they are used with other drugs. The advancement of epigenetic biomarkers, such as distinct DNA methylation patterns (e.g., MGMT promoter methylation correlating with temozolomide response in glioblastoma) or histone modification signatures, shows potential for patient stratification [166]. The amalgamation of multi-omics technologies is essential for discerning these fundamental drivers from intricate epigenetic networks and for creating blood-based liquid biopsies for non-invasive monitoring [167].To address the critical need for predictive biomarkers, several strategies have emerged to create a composite epigenetic biomarker that utilizes the histone modification profile, the DNA methylation pattern, and the chromatin accessibility landscape. The method employed in practice involves the co-profiling of histone modifications, DNA methylation, and chromatin accessibility on one single tumor sample. Histone modification profiles, such as H3K27me3, H3K27ac, and H3K4me3, are characterized using ChIP-seq technology, but recently the CUT&RUN (Cleavage Under Targets and Release Using Nuclease) and CUT&Tag (Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation) technologies are also being employed [168]. Genome-wide analysis of DNA methylation levels is performed by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing or the use of reduced representation bisulfite sequencing or Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip in clinical samples with low DNA availability [169]. Chromatin accessibility maps are generated by ATAC-seq that can be carried out even in cell counts as low as 500 cells [170]. In clinical samples where heterogeneity within the tumor is a major confounding variable, single-cell multi-omics approaches, which include the use of scCUT&Tag with scBS-seq or scATAC-seq, as well as the 10x Genomics Chromium system that allows for simultaneous profiling of the transcriptome and chromatin accessibility in the same cell, make this possible [171].The computational approach used in the development of composite biomarkers involves a number of different steps. The first step is multi-omics data integration, where techniques like Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA), which detects latent factors that capture the primary sources of variance in the data sets [172]; iClusterPlus, which uses multiple data sets to detect integrated clusters [173]; and Similarity Network Fusion, which creates patient similarity networks for individual data sets before fusing them together [174]. After integration, the selection of features is done using machine learning approaches like LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression, random forests, or gradient boosting, in order to find the smallest number of epigenetic features that carry maximum prediction value for response to treatment [175]. The selected features are then merged to form composite scores using approaches like the Machine Learning-derived Epigenetic Model (MLEM) for breast cancer, whereby DNA methylation and histone modification data are integrated into one score that can later be assessed using targeted deep sequencing/qPCR analysis on patient samples [176]. Such composite scores need validation in independent patient populations as well.Building predictive biomarkersThese challenges can be met by the move toward the development of a novel approach to epigenetic stratification through the identification of specific subtypes based on genomic and epigenomic markers rather than the organ from which the tumor originates. Mutation-driven epigenetic therapy takes advantage of the presence of certain genetic changes within the tumor that render it sensitive to epigenetic inhibition. Tumors carrying gain-of-function EZH2 mutations, including hotspots such as Y641, A677, and A687 mutations in germinal center B cell-like diffuse large B cell lymphomas and follicular lymphomas, are highly sensitive to EZH2 inhibition through drugs like tazemetostat [177]. Similarly, MTAP homozygous deletions, found in up to 15% of all tumors, in particular, glioblastoma, pancreatic adenocarcinomas, and mesotheliomas, induce PRMT5 inhibition sensitivity due to synthetic lethality based on methylthioadenosine metabolite accumulation [178]. Mutations in the ARID1A gene, leading to a shortage of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers, suggest the sensitivity of EZH2 inhibitors in ovarian clear cell carcinomas, gastric cancers, and endometrial carcinomas, based on a recognized antagonistic effect of the two complexes and tumor dependence on EZH2 for transcriptional suppression [179].Beyond mutations in individual genes, epigenomic marker-based stratification identifies cancers on the basis of a more extensive epigenetic pattern. The CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), defined by coordinated methylation of a large number of CpG islands first identified in colorectal cancer, identifies different responses to DNMT inhibitors and is being evaluated prospectively in clinical trials [180]. Histone modification-based patterns such as comparison of H3K27me3 versus H3K27ac identified using ChIP-seq may predict dependence on PRC2 activity, hence sensitivity to EZH2 inhibition, and/or on super enhancers, hence sensitivity to BET inhibition [181]. Additionally, the relative abundance of H3K27me3/H3K27ac at the promoter region of established PRC2-targeted genes evaluated using ChIP-seq or targeted CUT&Tag assays of selected PRC2-targeted tumor suppressor genes, like the Hoxa cluster gene, is useful in identifying highly PRC2-dependent cancers and those that are sensitive to EZH2 inhibitors [182]. Furthermore, the H3K27me3 domains distribution pattern can be used as a marker, where the presence of wide H3K27me3 domains, meaning the spreading of the mark beyond the CpG islands rather than the focal deposition at CpG islands, denotes an EZH2-dependent and inhibitor-sensitive cancer phenotype [183].Locus-specific validation for clinical applicationSeveral methods for locus-specific validation of epigenetic biomarker candidates identified using genome-wide approaches can be adopted. ChIP-qPCR allows researchers to explore genomic loci for enrichment of specific histone modifications and is possible with just 10,000 to 50,000 cells. Alternatively, CUT&RUN-qPCR and CUT&Tag-qPCR have been developed as more efficient techniques for clinical studies as they involve minimal number of cells (about 500 to 5,000 cells) and provide a much higher signal-to-noise ratio because of no cross-linking and sonication steps involved [184, 185]. Regarding DNA methylation, methylation-sensitive PCR and pyrosequencing are the locus-specific, quantitative methods that have the further advantage of being able to evaluate several CpG sites at once within one specific area in the bisulfite-modified DNA, which is stable in FFPE tissue [186].Nonetheless, major challenges exist in the clinical application of such locus-specific approaches. One is the issue of heterogeneous tissue samples, whereby the averaging effect on epigenetic information obtained from tumor, stromal, and immune cells can obscure important changes within different cellular types [187]. Issues such as sample integrity and volume due to the small amount of material obtainable from core needle biopsy or FFPE block samples pose a challenge to the reliability of results since DNA degradation and protein crosslinking can significantly influence the outcome. Additionally, since epigenetic modification exhibits flexibility, a single snapshot measurement from a biopsy sample collected prior to treatment may fail to capture the dynamic nature of tumor epigenetics [188]. Moreover, inconsistent protocols and the absence of standard references used between laboratories prevent reproducibility and translation into clinic. Deconvolution methods like EpiDISH and CELTYC, along with the development of single-cell epigenomics, are some strategies that have been adopted to tackle these problems; however, their application into the clinic is still a distant goal [163, 189].Designing biomarker-driven trialsA well-designed translational trial for the combination of an EZH2 inhibitor (tazemetostat) and an immune checkpoint inhibitor (pembrolizumab) should consider four interrelated aspects: biomarker-based patient selection, tumor type selection, lead-in design, and response evaluation beyond standard radiographic assessments.A biomarker-driven enrichment strategy aims to select a cohort of patients with tumors that are dependent on EZH2, which helps in achieving a greater chance of success. The literature provides examples where synthetic lethality with EZH2 has been achieved by using EZH2 gain-of-function mutations (Y641, A677, A687) in follicular lymphoma and ARID1A mutations in ovarian clear cell carcinoma and gastric cancers [177, 179, 190]. However, relying solely on mutational status has limitations: the prevalence of EZH2 mutations in solid tumors is low (typically 2–5%), and some EZH2-wild-type tumors exhibit high PRC2 activity driven by upstream oncogenic signaling, such as mutant KRAS or MYC amplification [77, 79]. Consequently, functional epigenomic biomarkers including global H3K27me3 levels, the H3K27me3/H3K27ac ratio at PRC2 target genes, or broad H3K27me3 domain patterns may offer complementary predictive value [181–183]. A pragmatic approach is to enroll patients based on either mutational status (e.g., EZH2 or ARID1A mutations) or elevated H3K27me3 expression by immunohistochemistry, with pre-specified subgroup analyses to compare response rates across enrichment criteria.It is mechanistically sound to choose specific cancer types, such as small cell lung cancer, ovarian clear cell carcinoma, triple-negative breast cancer, and ARID1A mutant endometrial and gastric cancers, due to the presence of preclinical data. The first type of cancer has increased EZH2 and H3K27me3 levels, and EZH2 inhibition improves chemotherapeutic response by derepression of SLFN11 [191]. EZH2 dependency in ovarian clear cell carcinoma and ARID1A-mutated gastric cancers arises due to the loss of function of the SWI/SNF complex [190, 192]. Overexpression of EZH2 occurs in triple-negative breast cancer, which results in gene silencing and induction of stemness; furthermore, inhibition of EZH2 promotes immune response against tumor cells [132, 133]. However, one important consideration is that most of this evidence is derived from preclinical xenograft models, which might not accurately represent the immune microenvironment of human tumors. Additionally, there is notable diversity in the immune contexture of different types of tumors; for instance, small cell lung cancer is usually an immune “cold” tumor due to the lack of T cell infiltration, while some ARID1A-mutant gastric cancers are characterized by high mutational load and existing immune infiltration.Regarding the timing of the trials, the rationale for a 14 to 21 day lead-in treatment period with tazemetostat monotherapy prior to the first pembrolizumab dose is based on the mechanism of action. For EZH2 inhibition to be effective, it will take time to deplete pre-existing H3K27me3 marks (half-life of 48 to 72 h), re-express Th1-related chemokines, CXCL9 and CXCL10, and attract CD8 + T cells [193]. A similar type of lead-in design is also being used in current trials for EZH2 inhibitors combined with ICIs (NCT04624113, NCT04846478). The continuous dosing regimen of tazemetostat at 800 mg BID (the FDA approved dose) is preferred over the intermittent dosing regimen because of the slow turnover of histone methylation [101]. Immune-mediated adverse event management should be guided by the standard ICI toxicity guidelines that recommend the administration of corticosteroids for all events of grade 2 and above. However, prophylaxis is not generally recommended since it could reduce the effectiveness of the anti-tumor immune response.The choice of endpoints for response assessment requires careful consideration. Despite being the accepted primary endpoint in phase II studies, objective response rate based on RECIST v1.1 could fail to recognize atypical responses such as pseudoprogression, due to immune infiltration, which could be incorrectly classified by the criteria. Therefore, immune-related response criteria (iRECIST) need to be used as a secondary endpoint. More importantly, pharmacodynamic markers would include the degree of decrease in H3K27me3 modification, determined by CUT&Tag-qPCR using on-treatment tumor biopsies, and the fold increase in the expression of CXCL9, CXCL10, and CCL5 by RNAscope. These need to be included as co-primary or key secondary endpoints to prove the mechanism. Changes in promoter DNA methylation of PRC2 targets in circulating tumor DNA, determined by targeted bisulfite sequencing, could be considered an exploratory surrogate endpoint [167]. It would be important to validate the mechanistic hypothesis and inform future phase III trial design by proving the correlation between pharmacodynamic markers and objective response rate.Natural products as epigenetic modulatorsNatural products, which are obtained from plants, fungi, and marine organisms, are a promising and very rich source of epigenetic modulators for cancer prevention and treatment [194]. The attraction towards these compounds is based on their varied chemical structures and their potential to target various aspects of the epigenetic system, such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA expression [195]. The fact that epigenetic modifications are reversible makes them a highly attractive target for therapeutic intervention, and natural compounds have shown great promise in resetting dysfunctional epigenetic marks in cancer cells [196]. These bioactive compounds have the ability to reverse the epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes, suppress the proliferation of cancer cells, trigger apoptosis, and reverse chemoresistance, as shown in various preclinical studies [197].Some major categories of natural products have been extensively explored in the context of their ability to modulate epigenetic functions. The most prominent of these are the polyphenolic compounds, including curcumin derived from turmeric and resveratrol derived from grapes and berries. Curcumin is an all-around epigenetic modulator that can inhibit both HATs and HDACs while also modulating the activity of enzymes that regulate both histone methylation and demethylation processes [198]. In the same way that curcumin does, another compound derived from grapes and berries, named resveratrol, is also known to activate sirtuins, a class of NAD+-dependent HDACs; downregulate the expression of epigenetic writers like EZH2 and PRMT5; and inhibit Class I/III HDACs, leading to the reactivation of tumor suppressors like p53 through changes in both histone H3 acetylation and methylation marks [199]. Other notable compounds include EGCG derived from green tea, which can directly inhibit DNMTs, while compounds like anacardic acid and garcinol are potent inhibitors of HATs [200]. The epigenetic targets, mechanisms, and status of development of these and other major natural compounds are listed in Table 5. These compounds include green tea polyphenols, flavonoids, curcuminoids, and isothiocyanates, all of which can regulate the activity of key enzymes that play a role in the methylation or demethylation of lysine or arginine residues of histones [225]. The key enzymes that have been the focus of this research include EZH2, an enzyme that catalyzes the formation of the repressive H3K27me3 modification, and LSD1, an enzyme that catalyzes the removal of the activating H3K4me3 modification [226]. The inhibition of these enzymes can result in the regulation of gene expression in cancer cells, thereby leading to reduced cell proliferation, migration, and increased apoptosis in cancer cells [227].However, despite their promising preclinical antitumor activities, the clinical application of natural epigenetic modulators is hindered by a number of challenges. First, natural epigenetic modulators have poor bioavailability. Many natural agents, such as curcumin and resveratrol, exhibit poor solubility in water, instability in the gastrointestinal environment, and undergo first-pass metabolism, resulting in extremely poor circulation of the active compound in the body [228]. In addition, natural agents are known to be pleiotropic agents, which, although beneficial in a synergistic manner, make it difficult to establish the exact mechanism of action. To address these challenges, new and advanced strategies are being explored. Nanotechnology, in new drug delivery systems, is a promising tool for improving the antitumor activities of natural epigenetic modulators [229]. Nanoparticles, such as liposomes and polymeric nanoparticles, can be used to deliver natural agents, and this is advantageous because it improves solubility, stability, and antitumor activity through enhanced targeting and controlled release of the compound, which is a significant improvement over conventional delivery [230]. In addition, the synthesis of semi-synthetic analogs, such as dimethoxycurcumin, is a new and promising strategy to improve stability and potency, and retain epigenetic modulating activities [231].In summary, natural products are invaluable resources for histone-modifying enzyme modulators and epigenetic regulators. Although there are still issues regarding bioavailability and understanding of mechanisms, approaches such as structural optimization, advanced delivery systems, and combination therapies are promising ways to overcome these challenges and unlock their potential for the benefit of cancer patients.Integrative epigenetic frameworksThis intricacy of cancer epigenetics is not limited to specific epigenetic modifications but extends to a complex interplay between epigenetic layers, where histone modifications, DNA methylation, non-coding RNAs, and chromatin remodeling factors communicate and coordinate to modulate and regulate gene expression. This integrative epigenetic landscape, which describes the main axes of epigenetic crosstalk, is depicted in Fig. 4. This crosstalk between epigenetic modifications is perhaps most vividly exemplified by the cooperative regulation of tumor suppressor gene silencing, where histone modifications, e.g., H3K27me3, which is catalyzed by PRC2, provide a binding site for DNMTs that catalyze hypermethylation of tumor suppressor gene promoters, thereby stably and heritably silencing genes [232]. Conversely, DNA methylation can modulate and regulate histone modifications, e.g., by binding methyl-binding proteins such as MeCP2, which can subsequently recruit HDACs and other chromatin remodeling factors that catalyze epigenetic gene expression regulation [233]. Fig. 4A Unified Model of Epigenetic Crosstalk Driving Cancer Plasticity. A Core integrative framework and crosstalk mechanisms. Major epigenetic interactions are depicted: (1) DNA methylation-histone crosstalk: PRC2 deposits H3K27me3, recruiting DNMTs for synergistic gene silencing. Simultaneously, MeCP2 binds methylated DNA to recruit HDACs. (2) Non-coding RNA regulation: Long non-coding RNAs (e.g., XIST) and microRNAs modulate the expression and activity of epigenetic complexes, while RNA modifications (e.g., m6A) regulate their stability. B Functional consequence: Tumor heterogeneity and plasticity. The integrated epigenetic system allows for dynamic, reversible transitions between different cell states (e.g., proliferative, invasive, drug-tolerant persister). This plasticity is the hallmark of CSC maintenance, which is regulated by PRC2/BMI1. Abbreviations: PRC2, Polycomb Repressive Complex 2; EZH2, enhancer of zeste homolog 2; DNMT, DNA methyltransferase; MeCP2, methyl-CpG-binding protein 2; HDAC, histone deacetylase; lncRNA, long non-coding RNA; miRNA, microRNA; m⁶A, N⁶-methyladenosine; CSC, cancer stem cell; EMT, epithelial-mesenchymal transition In addition to the traditional interplay between DNA and histone modifications, ncRNAs play a pivotal role as integrators and master regulators in this regulatory circuit. LncRNAs have been shown to act as modular scaffolds that physically bring histone-modifying enzymes together with specific genomic loci. For example, the lncRNA HOTAIR acts as a scaffold that brings the PRC2 complex to target genes, leading to the deposition of H3K27me3 and silencing of metastasis suppressors [234]. Similarly, microRNAs (miRNAs) also play a role in epigenetic regulation by modulating the levels of epigenetic enzymes. For example, miRNAs targeting DNMT3B or HDAC4 can indirectly modulate global methylation and acetylation levels, providing another layer of post-transcriptional regulation of the epigenome [235]. The relatively recent discovery of the epitranscriptome, or post-transcriptional modifications of RNA, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A), provides a new layer of complexity to this regulatory framework. The m6A modification of ncRNAs has been shown to modulate their stability and function. For example, m6A modification of the lncRNA XIST is essential for its function in X-chromosome inactivation [236]. On the other hand, epigenetic modifications can regulate the transcription of ncRNA genes, illustrating the complex reciprocity of this regulatory framework [237].The functional outcome of this integrated epigenetic system is the creation of a deep heterogeneity and plasticity of tumor cells. This system enables the dynamic and reversible transition between different cell states, like from a proliferative state to an invasive or drug-tolerant persister state, without the need for genetic mutations [238]. Cancer stem cells (CSCs), a subset of cancer cells that initiate tumor formation and are also responsible for therapeutic resistance, are a major reflection of this plasticity. The maintenance of these CSCs is extremely epigenetics-dependent, often mediated by a particular epigenetic program, which is frequently controlled by complexes such as PRC2 and BMI1, suppressing differentiation genes [239]. Moreover, the interplay between DNA repair mechanisms and the epigenetic system also plays a role in this dynamic system. DNA damage can trigger a specific chromatin modification, and vice versa, the existing epigenetic status of a region determines the pathway of DNA repair, as observed in CSCs, where a particular chromatin structure can improve the efficiency of DNA repair and generate resistance [240].Multi-omics approaches for single cells have recently been developed as useful techniques to discover and analyze DTPs (drug-tolerant persisters), which are rare subclones characterized by their epigenetic state and drug insensitivity that can reverse and develop acquired drug resistance [241]. To discover DTP cells, the protocol includes the simultaneous analysis of the transcriptional profile, chromatin accessibilities, and histone modification profiles of the same individual cells with the help of combinatorial barcodes or split-pool strategies. Technology platforms like the 10x Genomics Multiome platform allow for the simultaneous acquisition of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data, whereas CUT&Tag methods could be modified to analyze two or three histone marks in single cells at the same time. This includes the identification of both the repressive H3K27me3 and the active H3K27ac modifications [242].The hallmark features of DTPs are determined using computational approaches based on the following characteristics: cell cycle arrest through the downregulation of proliferation genes like MKI67 and PCNA; upregulation of genes associated with stemness and lineage plasticity, including high levels of SOX2, NANOG, and CD44; specific chromatin accessibility maps in enhancer and promoter regions of genes associated with drug resistance and survival; and histone modifications, especially the increased presence of H3K27me3 marks at pro-apoptotic gene promoters and H3K4me3 marks at stemness gene promoters. The use of computational approaches like Monocle 3, Slingshot, or RNA velocity to analyze the gene expression and chromatin accessibility data allows the reconstruction of the epigenetic pathway in the process of tumor cell transformation from naïve states through the DTP phase to resistance state [243, 244]. With the integration of endogenous mtDNA mutations used as lineage barcodes or exogenous lentivirus-based lineage tracing, clonal relationships between DTP cells and subsequent resistant lineages can be determined [245]. For example, studies on non-small cell lung cancer resistant to EGFR inhibitors have used scATAC-seq to profile a DTP cell subpopulation exhibiting an open chromatin state of enhancers for the transcription factor HOPX, which drives neuroendocrine differentiation into small cell carcinoma [246].s and sOne of the important concepts of the review is the difference between particular histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors (e.g., EZH2 in lymphomas), which allow a “precision medicine” approach to cancer therapy, and broad-spectrum histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors (e.g., pan-HDAC inhibitors), which have more toxic side effects. It also demonstrated the value of a “pan-cancer” approach to histone modifications in cancer development: although certain mechanisms, such as PRC2 dysregulation, are common in cancer development, they cannot be disentangled from cellular context. The strengths in the histone modifications in cancer development are in the mechanistic understanding from a broad concept to a more precise concept of how histone modifications interact with DNA methylation, non-coding RNAs, and chromatin remodelers in sustaining cancer development. Concurrently, the therapeutic armamentarium has moved from the initial DNMTs and HDAC inhibitors to include agents targeting BET, DOT1L, and LSD1 proteins, in addition to new modalities like PROTACs and dual inhibitors. These developments notwithstanding, there are also considerable hurdles in terms of translation. Achievement of clinical success, especially in the context of solid tumors, remains suboptimal. These can be explained by several key factors: dose-limiting toxicities, tumor cell plasticity that facilitates adaptive resistance mechanisms, and an alarming paucity of reliable biomarkers. The biggest paradox in this context is that while epigenetic profiles are constantly evolving in tumors, these interventions do not result in sustained remissions due to the ability of tumor cells to utilize alternative mechanisms for sustaining malignancy. To fully exploit the clinical potential of epigenomic targeting in cancer, subsequent studies must prioritize a series of strategic objectives. First, it will be important to find strong predictive biomarkers, such as global histone marks, specific DNA methylation profiles, or mutations in epigenetic regulators, in order to group patients. Second, it will be necessary to use combination therapies. Combinations with immunotherapy will not only focus on the TME but may also enhance immune recognition. Conversely, combinations with metabolic inhibitors will specifically target the metabolite pools necessary for chromatin regulation. Third, we will need to use the latest technologies, like single-cell multi-omics, to figure out how different types of cells are in tumors and how flexible persister cell populations are in terms of their epigenetics. Finally, therapeutic windows will need to be improved by using new delivery systems, like nanoparticles, to make targeting more precise and cut down on off-target effects.In conclusion, histone modifications, including histone acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, and newly identified modifications such as lactylation and crotonylation, play important roles as histone modification dysregulation is associated with tumorigenesis in various forms of cancer. Although there have been notable successes in the therapeutic targeting of histone modification dysregulation in cancer, including in hematological malignancies, there are still many hurdles to be overcome, including drug resistance, heterogeneity, and efficacy in solid tumors. However, by applying precision medicine approaches, rational drug combinations, and new technologies such as PROTACs, the full therapeutic potential of the cancer epigenome will be realized.

title: Mesembryanthemum crystallinum -guided green synthesis of ZnO nanoparticles with selective anticancer activity via ROS-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction
abstract: Green synthesis of zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) using Mesembryanthemum crystallinum L. (M. crystallinum), a halophytic plant adapted to saline environments of North Sinai, Egypt, offers a sustainable nanofabrication strategy with inherent therapeutic potential. High-resolution LC-ESI-QTOF-MS metabolomic profiling identified 13 major phytochemicals in the ethanolic leaf extract, dominated by citramalate (peak area 31,601), L-phenylalanine (30,377), and stress-responsive organic acids, reflecting the plant’s halophytic adaptation. These redox-active compounds templated the biosynthesis of crystalline ZnO-NPs under ambient aqueous conditions, yielding spherical to quasi-spherical nanoparticles (4.4–12.2 nm primary size; 40–150 nm aggregates) with a hexagonal wurtzite structure, as confirmed by XRD and SAED. FTIR and EDX analyses verified surface functionalization by phytochemical capping agents (polyphenols, organic acids), while SEM revealed characteristic aggregation with rough surface morphology indicative of biomolecular adsorption. Biosynthesized ZnO-NPs exhibited selective cytotoxicity against human malignant melanoma A375 cells (IC₅₀ = 100.55 ± 8.6 µg/mL) with four-fold lower toxicity toward normal human skin fibroblasts (IC₅₀ = 406.01 ± 35.2 µg/mL; selectivity index ≈ 4.0). Mechanistic investigations demonstrated that nanoparticle internalization triggered robust ROS generation (~ 3.8 × 10⁴ fluorescence units), mitochondrial membrane depolarization, and mixed apoptotic/necrotic cell death (40% total death; 25% late apoptosis, 15% necrosis). Cell cycle analysis revealed cancer-selective G2/M arrest in A375 cells (20.87% vs. 8.59% control; p < 0.001) versus protective G1 arrest in fibroblasts (69.14% vs. 56.01% control; p < 0.001). Paradoxically, qPCR showed BAX downregulation in cancer cells but upregulation in normal cells, suggesting non-transcriptional execution of apoptosis in malignancies. These findings establish M. crystallinum as an ecologically sustainable nanofactory whose stress-adapted metabolome directs the formation of selectively cytotoxic ZnO-NPs acting through ROS-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction, a paradigm for designing plant-guided nanotherapeutics with defined molecular mechanisms.Graphical abstract
full_text: Cancer remains a leading cause of global mortality, with conventional therapeutic modalities frequently limited by systemic toxicity, lack of tumor specificity, and the emergence of multidrug resistance (Zafar et al. 2025). These challenges have accelerated the development of nanotechnology-based platforms that offer enhanced targeting capabilities, improved pharmacokinetics, and the potential to circumvent resistance mechanisms inherent to traditional chemotherapy (Salem 2023, Deivayanai et al. 2025, Sivalingam 2026, Salem and Fouda 2021, Selim et al. 2026, Alruhaili et al. 2025). Among nanomaterials investigated for oncological applications, zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) have garnered considerable attention owing to their unique physicochemical properties, biocompatibility, and demonstrated capacity to selectively induce cytotoxicity in malignant cells while sparing normal tissues (Almuhayawi et al. 2024, El-Saadony et al. 2024, Selim et al. 2025).The anti-cancer potential of ZnO-NPs is primarily attributed to their ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) within tumor microenvironments, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, cell cycle arrest, and activation of intrinsic apoptotic pathways (Mohammed et al. 2025). Unlike conventional chemotherapeutics, which often fail to discriminate between proliferating cancerous and healthy cells, ZnO-NPs exploit the heightened baseline oxidative stress and altered redox homeostasis characteristic of many cancer phenotypes, thereby achieving selective toxicity (Chen et al. 2025). Furthermore, their capacity to bypass P-glycoprotein-mediated efflux mechanisms and modulate key signaling cascades, including PI3K/Akt/mTOR and NF-κB, positions ZnO-NPs as promising candidates for overcoming multidrug resistance (Mu et al. 2025).Conventional synthesis routes for ZnO-NPs, however, typically rely on physical or chemical methods that involve high-energy inputs, toxic reducing agents, and organic solvents, which compromise biocompatibility and generate hazardous waste (Gong et al. 2026). These limitations have catalyzed interest in green synthesis approaches that harness biological entities, particularly plant extracts, as sustainable alternatives for nanoparticle fabrication (Abdullah et al. 2021, Sivalingam 2025, Soliman and Salem 2025). Plant-mediated synthesis leverages endogenous phytochemicals (polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and proteins) to simultaneously reduce metal ions and cap the resulting nanoparticles, yielding stable, biocompatible nanomaterials with enhanced therapeutic potential (Sivalingam 2024, Sivalingam and Pandian 2024, Sivalingam and Pandian 2025, Sivalingam 2025, Soliman and Salem 2025). This strategy aligns with green chemistry principles by eliminating toxic reagents, reducing energy consumption, and minimizing environmental footprint (Okaiyeto et al. 2024).Mesembryanthemum crystallinum L. (Aizoaceae; M. crystallinum), commonly known as ice plant, represents an underexplored yet highly promising candidate for green nanoparticle synthesis. This halophytic succulent has evolved sophisticated physiological adaptations to thrive in saline, arid environments, including facultative Crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) photosynthesis and specialized epidermal bladder cells that sequester sodium ions at concentrations up to 1 M (Rincón-Cervera et al. 2024). These adaptations correlate with a rich phytochemical repertoire; recent LC-QTOF/MS profiling identified 178 distinct compounds in M. crystallinum, with lipids and lipid-like molecules constituting 69.8% of its composition, alongside phenolic derivatives (e.g., ferulic acid, 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzamide), nucleosides, and amino acids (Yadav et al. 2020). The plant’s documented antioxidant capacity, mediated by enzymatic systems (superoxide dismutase, catalase, ascorbate peroxidase) and non-enzymatic scavengers (polyphenols, flavonoids), suggests inherent redox activity suitable for metal ion reduction (Maury et al. 2020, Bas 2026).Critically, M. crystallinum extracts have demonstrated direct antitumor effects. Seo and Ju reported dose-dependent growth inhibition and apoptosis induction in HCT116 human colon cancer cells, with the butanol fraction exhibiting superior activity compared to crude ethanol extracts (Seo and Ju 2019). More recently, Rincón-Cervera et al. documented concentration- and time-dependent antiproliferative effects against HT-29 colorectal adenocarcinoma cells, with moderate selectivity toward malignant versus normal cells (selectivity index 1.2–1.7) (Rincón-Cervera et al. 2024). These findings implicate phenolic compounds, carotenoids, and other bioactive constituents in the plant’s cytotoxic mechanisms, likely acting synergistically to disrupt cancer cell viability.Despite these promising attributes, a significant research gap persists: no published studies have explored M. crystallinum L. as a phyto-reductant for ZnO-NP biosynthesis, nor have the molecular mechanisms underlying the cytotoxic effects of such biosynthesized nanoparticles been systematically investigated. Existing literature on plant-mediated ZnO-NPs predominantly features common medicinal species (e.g., Aloe vera, Ocimum basilicum), overlooking halophytes with unique stress-adaptive metabolomes that may confer distinctive nanoparticle properties (Yahya et al. 2022). Moreover, most green-synthesized ZnO-NP studies limit assessment to basic cytotoxicity screening without probing downstream molecular events, such as mitochondrial membrane depolarization, caspase activation, Bax/Bcl-2 modulation, or ROS-mediated DNA damage, that define mechanistic anti-cancer efficacy (Wang et al. 2024).This study, therefore, aimed to biosynthesize ZnO-NPs using M. crystallinum L. leaf extract via an eco-friendly green approach and conduct a comprehensive in vitro cytotoxic and molecular assessment against human cancer cell lines. We hypothesized that phytochemicals inherent to this halophyte would yield ZnO-NPs with enhanced stability and anti-cancer potency, acting through ROS-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis. Specific objectives included: physicochemical characterization of biosynthesized nanoparticles using XRD, FTIR, TEM, and SEM/EDX; evaluation of dose-dependent cytotoxicity against selected carcinoma cell lines; molecular dissection of cell death mechanisms through assessment of ROS generation, mitochondrial membrane potential disruption, and expression modulation of key apoptotic regulators (Bax and Bcl-2). By bridging green nanotechnology with halophyte phytochemistry, this work addresses an unmet need for sustainable nanotherapeutics with defined molecular mechanisms of action.Materials and Chemicals and reagentsAll chemicals and reagents were of analytical grade or higher purity. All analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism v10.4.1 (GraphPad Software, USA).Results and Phytochemical profiling of M. crystallinum L. extract reveals a stress-adapted metabolome rich in redox-active compoundsHigh-resolution LC-ESI-QTOF-MS analysis in negative ionization mode identified 13 major metabolites in the ethanolic leaf extract of M. crystallinum, with citramalate emerging as the most abundant compound (peak area 31,601) (Table 1; Fig. 1) (Sugimoto et al. 2021, Islamova et al. 2023). This branched-chain α-keto acid, a key intermediate in isoleucine biosynthesis, has been implicated in microbial stress adaptation but remains underexplored in higher plants. Its prominence in M. crystallinum, collected from the saline coastal environment of Arish, North Sinai, suggests a potential role in osmotic adjustment and carbon-nitrogen balance under salinity stress (Guan et al. 2020). This hypothesis is reinforced by the co-occurrence of multiple organic acids (citraconic, maleic, methylsuccinic, lactic), indicating active primary metabolism geared toward pH homeostasis and redox regulation in harsh environments.L(–)-Phenylalanine (peak area 30,377), a precursor to the phenylpropanoid pathway, was detected alongside 3-(4-hydroxyphenyl) prop-2-enoic acid, a structural analog of p-coumaric acid (Yadav et al. 2020). These findings confirm the plant’s capacity to synthesize phenolic compounds with established roles in UV protection and anti-microbial defense, critical adaptations for a halophyte exposed to intense solar radiation and microbial challenges in saline habitats (Kavaliauskas et al. 2024). The dark brown coloration of the crude extract visually corroborates this high phenolic content, a trait commonly associated with halophytic stress resilience (Cebani et al. 2024).Notably, L-5-oxoproline, a cyclic derivative of glutamate and intermediate in the γ-glutamyl cycle of glutathione metabolism, was identified with substantial abundance (peak area 15,405). Elevated oxoproline levels often correlate with oxidative stress or enhanced glutathione turnover, aligning with M. crystallinum’s documented capacity to accumulate antioxidants under high salinity (Singh et al. 2025). This observation reinforces the critical role of sulfur-containing metabolites in the plant’s stress defense architecture (Abooshahab et al. 2025). Similarly, trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline, enriched in hydroxyproline-rich glycoproteins such as extensins, suggests active cell wall remodeling to maintain structural integrity under osmotic stress, a recognized hallmark of halophytic adaptation (Castilleux et al. 2021).The detection of nucleotide derivatives (uridine 5’-monophosphate, inosine 5’-diphosphate, xanthosine 5’-monophosphate) and gamma-linolenic acid, an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid precursor to jasmonate signaling molecules, further illustrates a metabolome finely tuned for environmental resilience (Rinne et al. 2024, Xiao et al. 2024). While several compounds (phenylalanine, gamma-linolenic acid, hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives) have been previously reported in M. crystallinum (Oh et al. 2024, Wasternack and Song 2016), our study significantly expands the known metabolome by highlighting citramalate, citraconic acid, and methylsuccinic acid as major constituents. These compounds have not been emphasized in prior LC-MS analyses, suggesting that our extraction protocol (74% ethanol) and chromatographic conditions (high-pH mobile phase, pH 8) enhanced detection of stress-induced organic acids (Bergmann et al. 2024). Green synthesis and physicochemical characterization of ZnO-NPsMorphology and elemental compositionScanning electron microscopy revealed that biosynthesized ZnO-NPs formed dense aggregates ranging from 40 to 150 nm, with predominantly spherical to irregular morphology (Fig. 2). This aggregation behavior is characteristic of plant-mediated synthesis and arises from high surface energy, incomplete surface passivation, or van der Waals interactions between particles. Critically, the rough surface texture visible at 60,000× magnification strongly suggests adsorption of organic biomolecules from the plant extract, likely polyphenols, flavonoids, or proteins, acting as natural capping agents that limit uncontrolled growth while enhancing colloidal stability (Österberg et al. 2023, Arcot et al. 2024, Khan et al. 2025, El-Saadony et al. 2025). Fig. 2Scanning electron micrographs at a 30,000× and b 60,000× magnification reveal dense aggregates of spherical to irregular nanoparticles (40–150 nm). Higher magnification resolves primary particles with rough, textured surfaces indicative of phytochemical capping Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy confirmed the chemical identity of the nanoparticles, displaying prominent zinc (43–53 wt%) and oxygen (26–38 wt%) peaks consistent with ZnO stoichiometry (Fig. 3). The high atomic percentage of oxygen (38–51%) closely matches the theoretical ZnO composition (50% oxygen), confirming phase purity (Hazrati Saadabadi et al. 2024, Chanthapong et al. 2025). A significant carbon signal (13–22 wt%) indicated persistent adsorption of phytochemical residues from the extract, with functional groups serving dual roles as reducing agents during Zn²⁺ conversion and as stabilizing ligands post-synthesis (Pei et al. 2024). Trace elements (Ca, Cl, K, Cu 450 µg/mL in A375; no detectable toxicity in hFB at 500 µg/mL), confirming that observed anti-cancer effects derive primarily from nanoparticle formation rather than residual phytochemicals (Cabrera-Serrano et al. 2025).This selectivity may arise from three interconnected mechanisms. First, cancer cells often exhibit enhanced endocytic activity due to upregulated membrane dynamics and nutrient scavenging pathways, facilitating greater nanoparticle internalization (Sousa de Almeida et al. 2021). Second, melanoma cells maintain elevated basal ROS levels and possess compromised antioxidant defenses compared to normal cells, a redox imbalance that renders them vulnerable to additional oxidative insults (Stojanovic et al. 2025). Third, the phytochemical corona surrounding biosynthesized ZnO-NPs may modulate cellular interactions in a cell-type-specific manner, potentially exploiting differential expression of surface receptors between malignant and normal cells (Guo and Morshedi 2025). These findings align with recent reports demonstrating the selective toxicity of green-synthesized ZnO-NPs against various carcinoma lines while preserving normal cell viability (Maheswaran et al. 2024), and position M. crystallinum-mediated ZnO-NPs as promising candidates for melanoma-targeted therapy. Data represent mean ± SD of triplicate experiments ROS-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction as a central mechanism of actionIntracellular ROS quantification revealed that biosynthesized ZnO-NPs induced the highest oxidative stress among all test agents in A375 cells (fluorescence intensity ~ 3.8 × 10⁴), significantly exceeding untreated controls and surpassing even Doxorubicin (Fig. 8). This robust ROS generation likely stems from multiple nanoparticle-specific mechanisms: (i) surface-catalyzed redox reactions involving Zn²⁺ dissolution and Fenton-like chemistry; (ii) disruption of mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes; and (iii) depletion of cellular antioxidants such as glutathione (Parthasarathy et al. 2022, Liao et al. 2020, Gruin et al. 2026, Sharma et al. 2025, Becker and Indra 2023). Critically, while ROS elevation occurred in both cell lines, the magnitude was greater in A375 cells, a finding consistent with the “redox vulnerability” hypothesis wherein cancer cells, already operating near oxidative stress thresholds, succumb to additional ROS burdens that normal cells can tolerate through intact antioxidant systems (Nakamura and Takada 2021). Mitochondrial depolarization represents a point-of-no-return in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, triggering cytochrome c release, apoptosome formation, and possible caspase-9/-3 activation (Petit 2025). The sequence follows a coherent cascade: preferential nanoparticle uptake, Zn²⁺-mediated ROS burst, oxidative damage to cardiolipin and mitochondrial permeability transition pore components, ΔΨm dissipation, and apoptotic execution (Pan et al. 2021). Notably, commercial ZnO-NPs and plant extract alone failed to significantly disrupt ΔΨm in either cell line, underscoring that the unique surface chemistry conferred by M. crystallinum phytochemicals is essential for mitochondrial targeting, a finding with important implications for rational nanotherapeutic design (Udayagiri et al. 2024). In A375 cells, biosynthesized ZnO-NPs induced 25% late apoptosis and 15% necrosis, exceeding Doxorubicin in late apoptotic induction (30%) while generating comparable total cell death (40 vs. 43%). This mixed death modality may reflect dose-dependent progression from programmed apoptosis to secondary necrosis as cellular energy reserves deplete (Qian et al. 2024). Importantly, necrotic cell death releases DAMPs: HMGB1 and ATP that can stimulate antitumor immune responses, a potential advantage over purely apoptotic inducers in immunocompetent hosts (Arimoto et al. 2024).In hFB fibroblasts, biosynthesized ZnO-NPs induced moderate late apoptosis (18%) and necrosis (15%), yet the viable fraction remained higher than in A375 cells (55% vs. 48%), consistent with reduced cytotoxicity (Fig. 10b). This differential response likely stems from fundamental disparities in redox homeostasis: normal fibroblasts maintain robust glutathione pools and functional thioredoxin systems that buffer oxidative insults, whereas melanoma cells exhibit chronic oxidative stress with limited reserve capacity (Pourzand et al. 2022). The plant extract alone caused only mild apoptosis in both lines (10–12% late apoptosis), reinforcing that nanoparticle formation, not residual phytochemicals, drives potent cell death. These morphological findings integrate seamlessly with ROS and ΔΨm data, confirming that biosynthesized ZnO-NPs trigger a coordinated death program initiated by oxidative stress and executed through mitochondrial dysfunction (Chen et al. 2025). Right panels display the quantitative distribution of death modalities based on 1,000-cell counts per treatment Cell cycle arrest patterns differ between cancer and normal cellsFlow cytometric analysis revealed a striking cell-type-specific response to biosynthesized ZnO-NPs (Fig. 11). In A375 melanoma cells, nanoparticles induced significant G2/M phase arrest (20.87% vs. 8.59% control; p < 0.001), with concomitant reduction in G1 fraction (58.12% vs. 67.71%). G2/M arrest typically reflects DNA damage checkpoint activation, consistent with ZnO-NP-induced ROS causing double-strand breaks that activate ATM/ATR-Chk1/2 signaling and prevent mitotic entry (Gao et al. 2016). Cancer cells with defective G1/S checkpoints (common in melanoma due to p16INK4a loss or CDK4 amplification) become particularly vulnerable to G2/M arrest, which often culminates in apoptosis rather than repair (Pellarin et al. 2025).Conversely, in hFB fibroblasts, biosynthesized ZnO-NPs triggered G1 phase arrest (69.14% vs. 56.01% control; p < 0.001) with reduced S-phase entry (19.17% vs. 23.70%). This G1 arrest likely represents a protective response wherein normal cells activate p53-p21CIP1/WAF1 signaling to halt cycle progression, repair damage, and resume proliferation once stress resolves (Pati et al. 2016, Zarrinnahad et al. 2024). The divergent arrest patterns, G2/M in cancer versus G1 in normal cells, highlight a fundamental therapeutic window: nanoparticles exploit cancer-specific cell cycle vulnerabilities while permitting normal cells to activate protective checkpoints. Commercial ZnO-NPs induced only mild G2/M elevation in A375 cells (16.42%) without significant effects in hFB cells, suggesting that the phytochemical corona of biosynthesized nanoparticles uniquely modulates cell cycle checkpoint engagement. In A375 cells, biosynthesized ZnO-NPs significantly suppressed BAX mRNA (fold change ~ 0.25; p < 0.05) alongside commercial NPs (~ 0.35) and Doxorubicin (~ 0.60). All treatments also decreased BCL2 expression (~ 0.01–0.08 fold), but without inter-group differences. This transcriptional downregulation contrasts with expected pro-apoptotic BAX upregulation yet aligns with rapid, non-transcriptional apoptosis execution, likely direct mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization via ROS-induced Bax oligomerization independent of new gene expression. Such post-translational activation bypasses transcriptional regulation, explaining the disconnect between protein activity and mRNA levels (Tsamandas et al. 2003).In hFB cells, biosynthesized ZnO-NPs uniquely induced statistically significant BAX-upregulation (fold change ~ 3.2; p < 0.05) without altering BCL2, a pattern typically associated with apoptosis initiation. However, minimal cell death occurred (45% viability), suggesting compensatory survival mechanisms such as enhanced autophagy, heat shock protein induction, or NF-κB-mediated anti-apoptotic signaling (Jaime-Martinez et al. 2022). The plant extract alone significantly upregulated BCL2 (~ 16-fold), potentially explaining its cytoprotective effects in normal cells. These divergent transcriptional responses, BAX suppression in cancer versus induction in normal cells, further underscore the selective nature of biosynthesized ZnO-NP toxicity and highlight context-dependent apoptotic regulation that cannot be predicted from gene expression alone (Mohamed et al. 2024).
