Amino acid changes are annotated based on the ENST00000373988 transcript. Functional domains of ZMYM3 protein are represented in blue (9 zinc-finger MYM type) and orange (domain of unknown function 3504). (C) Mutational frequencies and associations within the CLL cohort according to the presence of ZMYM3 mutations. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗P 1; FDR 2) in ZMYM3MUT (left) and ZMYM3MUTNOTCH1MUT cells (right) compared with WT cells. (C-E) GSEA highlighting the top significantly upregulated (red) or downregulated (blue) Reactome pathways (P 2; P 1; P < .01) that were exclusive to WT cells, whereas 1 and 9 peaks were detected solely in ZMYM3MUT or ZMYM3MUT NOTCH1MUT cells, respectively (Figure 4E; supplemental Table 8), suggesting that ZMYM3 mutations reduce chromatin accessibility. Interestingly, 83 regions that gained chromatin accessibility, shared between ZMYM3MUT and ZMYM3MUT NOTCH1MUT cells, were enriched for IRF transcription factor binding sites (Figure 4F; supplemental Figure 8B). Subsequently, we integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data to explore the interplay between chromatin accessibility and gene expression. Among the 381 regions with increased accessibility in WT cells, 125 genes were downregulated and 51 were upregulated in ZMYM3MUT NOTCH1MUT cells, whereas 205 peaks showed no significant gene expression changes. The 125 downregulated genes were predominantly involved in cell cycle regulation (CCNA1, CDC14A), MAPK signaling, or caspase pathway (LMNA, MGMT) (Figure 4G; supplemental Figure 8C; supplemental Table 9). These findings may underscore a ZMYM3-dependent intricate relationship between chromatin accessibility dynamics, histone acetylation, and transcriptional regulation.Co-occurrence of ZMYM3 and NOTCH1 mutations promotes apoptosis evasion and potentiates growth capacity of CLL cellsGiven that transcriptomic analyses identified apoptosis-related pathways among the most significantly dysregulated processes in ZMYM3MUT cells, we next assessed the impact of ZMYM3 mutations and their co-occurrence with NOTCH1 mutations on programmed cell death. ZMYM3MUT cells showed reduced annexin V+/PI+ events compared with WT cells (Figure 5A; supplemental Figure 9A), with an even more pronounced effect in ZMYM3MUT NOTCH1MUT cells, suggesting cooperative apoptosis evasion. These cells also showed enhanced growth rates (Figure 5B), likely because of reduced apoptosis, as carboxyfluorescein diacetate succinimidyl ester staining indicated no effect on proliferation (supplemental Figure 9B).Figure 5.Impact of ZMYM3 mutations on apoptosis and growth of CLL cells. (A) Apoptosis levels determined by annexin V/PI staining in CRISPR/Cas9-edited HG3, including WT, ZMYM3MUT, NOTCH1MUT, and ZMYM3MUTNOTCH1MUT cells. Analysis was performed on 3 clones per condition analyzed in 4 independent experiments. Results are shown as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Data represent 3 independent experiments, with each clone depicted by a different symbol. Statistical significance are denoted as ∗P < .05 and ∗∗∗P < .001. (B) Cell viability analysis of WT, ZMYM3MUT, NOTCH1MUT, and ZMYM3MUTNOTCH1MUT cells over 72 hours, measured by methyl thiazolyl tetrazolium (MTT) assay. Absorbance values were normalized to day 0. Analysis included 3 clones per condition analyzed in 3 independent experiments. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗P < .05. (C) Western blot analysis of caspase-8, -7, and -3; and PARP as apoptosis marker in WT and ZMYM3MUT CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells (left). Cells were cultured under standard conditions, without any apoptosis-inducer treatment. β-tubulin was used as a loading control. Quantification of caspases was performed in 4 clones per condition across 2 independent experiments, with tubulin used as loading control for the calculation of relative protein levels (right). (D) Quantification of caspase-8 (left) and caspase-7 (right) gene expression in WT (n = 8) and ZMYM3MUT (n = 8) primary CLL samples from the Hospital of Salamanca cohort using droplet digital PCR. Relative values are calculated between positive droplets of caspases and ABL1 as a reference gene. Error bars represent SD. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗P < .05. (E) Caspase-7 mRNA expression levels in patients with CLL from the CLLmap cohort, stratified by ZMYM3 mutational status. Expression values are presented as log-transformed TPM. Statistical significance was assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗∗P < .01. (F) Western blot analyses illustrating the expression of antiapoptotic proteins in WT and ZMYM3MUT HG3 cells (left). Quantification of antiapoptotic proteins was performed in 4 clones per condition across 2 independent experiments, with GAPDH used as loading control for the calculation of relative protein levels (right). CASP7, caspase-7; GADPH, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase; TPM, transcripts per million.Mechanistically, western blot analysis revealed decreased levels of extrinsic apoptotic proteins, including caspase-8, -3, and -7, and cleaved poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase in ZMYM3MUT cells (Figure 5C). Consistently, digital droplet PCR confirmed downregulation of caspase-7 and -8 in primary ZMYM3MUT CLL cells (Figure 5D), whereas RNA-seq showed downregulation of caspase-7 in ZMYM3MUT samples from the CLLmap cohort participants (Figure 5E). In addition, ZMYM3MUT cells exhibited moderately higher levels of the antiapoptotic proteins BCL2 and, to a lesser extent, BCL-XL and MCL1 (Figure 5F), whereas no significant changes were observed in proapoptotic proteins BIM, BAK, BAX, BAD, or NOXA (supplemental Figure 9C). Collectively, this imbalanced expression of apoptotic regulatory factors could potentially contribute to the antiapoptotic phenotype observed in ZMYM3MUT cells.ZMYM3 mutations sensitize primary CLL cells to BCL-XL inhibition and ibrutinibTo define the drug response profile of patients with ZMYM3MUT CLL, we conducted a drug screen using clinically approved therapies on 100 untreated CLL primary samples (n = 91, control; n = 9, ZMYM3MUT; supplemental Table 5). The panel included the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax, BTK inhibitors ibrutinib and acalabrutinib, PI3K inhibitors idelalisib and duvelisib, and the chemotherapeutic agent fludarabine, each tested at 3 optimized doses. In addition, a subset of samples (n = 11) was evaluated with the BCL-XL inhibitor A- . Drug responses were assessed after 48 hours in both monoculture and coculture settings with stromal stimulation, using HS-5 cells, CpG, and interleukin-219,30 (Figure 6A; supplemental Figure 10). In monoculture, primary ZMYM3MUT cells exhibited significant resistance to venetoclax in the entire cohort and within IGHV-UM subgroup (supplemental Figure 11). Moreover, ZMYM3MUT samples lacking NOTCH pathway alterations were more resistant to venetoclax. ZMYM3 mutations also increased venetoclax resistance among NOTCH1MUT samples, whereas ZMYM3 variants did not influence the response of TP53-mutated samples.Figure 6.Effects of ZMYM3 mutations in response to targeted therapies in primary CLL cells. (A) Primary CLL cells were cultured either in monoculture (unstimulated) or in the presence of HS-5 bone marrow stromal cells, CpG (1.5 μg/mL), and interleukin-2 (50 ng/mL). Cells were treated for 48 hours with indicated doses of venetoclax, ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, idelalisib, duvelisib, and fludarabine. Normalized surviving fraction is expressed relative to untreated cells. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗P < .05. (B) Dose-response curves of WT and ZMYM3MUT CRISPR/Cas9-edited cells treated with the indicated concentrations of the BCL-XL inhibitor A- (left). Cell viability was determined by MTT assay after 72 hours. Live cells were quantified with respect to dimethyl sulfoxide control (DMSO). Data are summarized as mean ± SD. Response of primary CLL cells to BCL-XL inhibition with A- in monoculture and coculture for 48 hours (right). Normalized surviving fraction is expressed relative to untreated cells. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗P < .05.Although ZMYM3 mutations did not impact responses to acalabrutinib, idelalisib, duvelisib, and fludarabine, ZMYM3MUT CLL samples displayed increased sensitivity to ibrutinib in coculture (Figure 6A). Further exploration using CRISPR/Cas9-edited cells showed that ZMYM3MUT cells were more sensitive to the BCL-XL inhibitor A- , a finding subsequently validated in primary ZMYM3MUT CLL cells under stromal stimulation (Figure 6B). These results suggest that ZMYM3MUT cells are more dependent on BCL-XL for survival, highlighting the potential clinical relevance of BCL-XL inhibition in the context of ZMYM3 mutations.ZMYM3 has emerged as a putative genetic driver of CLL in independent NGS studies.4, 5, 6 This work presents novel insights into the clinical significance of ZMYM3 variants, demonstrating their association with NOTCH1 mutations and their potential prognostic value in CLL. Using CRISPR/Cas9 models along with primary patient samples, this study highlights the function of ZMYM3 in regulating histone acetylation and gene expression. Moreover, ZMYM3 mutations compromise DNA damage response and promote apoptosis evasion, providing mechanistic insight into their role in CLL pathogenesis and offering potential therapeutic vulnerabilities.This study characterizes ZMYM3 variants in CLL, revealing that 75% of variants were truncating (frameshift and nonsense), whereas missense variants clustered within functional domains, thus proposing a tumor suppressor role for ZMYM3. These mutations do not affect transcript levels, indicating that protein dysfunction underlies their pathogenic effect. The recurrent frameshift mutation p.P48fs, previously reported in CLL4,31 and other cancer types,32, 33, 34, 35 suggests its potential as a mutational hot spot. In addition, patients with ZMYM3MUT CLL exhibit a distinct mutational profile enriched for NOTCH1 mutations, consistent with previous observations.11 Notably, paired VAF analyses identified ZMYM3 mutations within dominant or codominant clones, suggesting that ZMYM3 alterations are not merely late passenger events.By integrating molecular insights with clinical outcomes, we observed that ZMYM3 variants were independently associated with shorter TTFT in multivariable analyses across the overall cohort, including Binet A and IGHV-UM patients. These results highlight ZMYM3 mutations as a biomarker to refine risk stratification by identifying patients with an earlier treatment requirement. Importantly, ZMYM3 mutations did not impact OS, suggesting that ZMYM3MUT patients require earlier treatment but respond comparably to nonmutated patients. This observation was consistent with our ex vivo data. Validation of these findings in independent cohorts is warranted.Although a previous study had suggested that ZMYM3 may function in chromatin regulation,13 its precise role in CLL remains elusive. Functional studies using CRISPR/Cas9-edited cells, complemented with ex vivo assays and transcriptome analysis from 2 independent cohorts to overcome limitations of Epstein-Barr virus-transformed cell lines,36 revealed that ZMYM3 mutations dysregulate histone acetylation. To our knowledge, this study provides the first proteomic evidence in CLL supporting the association of ZMYM3 with histone-deacetylases complexes. Because histone acetylation is essential for gene expression through promoting open chromatin,37, 38, 39, 40 the involvement of ZMYM3 in this corepressor network provides mechanistic explanation for how ZMYM3 mutations drive a global histone H4 hypoacetylation and enforce a compacted chromatin conformation that results in transcriptional repression, with cooperative effects when ZMYM3 and NOTCH1 mutations co-occur.Previous studies have reported that CLL cells display histone hypoacetylation and upregulation of histone-deacetylase–complexes compared with normal B cells, which are features associated with adverse clinical outcomes.41, 42, 43, 44, 45 Our results demonstrate how a CLL-driver mutation impacts histone acetylation, expanding our understanding of functional consequences resulting from chromatin remodeling alterations,4, 5, 6 and highlighting histone acetylation as particularly relevant in CLL. Moreover, ZMYM3 mutations may also display regulatory potential, as ZMYM3MUT and ZMYM3MUT NOTCH1MUT cells are enriched in IRF transcription factor motifs, a family associated with the IGHV-UM subtype.46ZMYM3 was identified as a chromatin-interacting protein involved in maintaining genome integrity by binding to double-stranded DNA, H2A/H2AX, and BRCA1 complex recruitment during homologous recombination repair.12,47 In our study, this described role was reflected at the transcriptomic level in both cellular models and patients with CLL, establishing an impact of ZMYM3 disruption in DNA damage-related pathways. Our findings extend these observations by identifying apoptosis evasion as a biologically relevant consequence of ZMYM3 mutations in CLL, with caspase downregulation emerging as a potential molecular basis for the reduced basal apoptosis observed in ZMYM3MUT cells. Therapeutically, ex vivo experiments indicated that primary ZMYM3MUT CLL cells are more dependent on BCL-XL than BCL2 which, together with the co-occurrence with NOTCH1 mutations48,49 and overexpression of antiapoptotic proteins,50, 51, 52, 53, 54 may contribute to the observed venetoclax resistance. Mechanistically, this apoptotic shift suggests BCL-XL targeting as a strategy to overcome venetoclax resistance, positioning BCL-XL–targeting approaches and BTK inhibition as promising therapeutic strategies for patients with ZMYM3MUT CLL. Further studies are required to explore the broader implications of these results.In conclusion, our work provides insights into the clinical and biological implications of ZMYM3 mutations in CLL through the integration of clinical data from patients with CLL and in vitro and ex vivo models. We show that ZMYM3 mutational status may refine outcomes of early-stage CLL patients. In addition, we uncovered that ZMYM3 mutations associate and cooperate with NOTCH1 alterations, leading to transcriptional dysregulation. Our study demonstrates that ZMYM3 variants reduce histone acetylation and modulate chromatin accessibility, resulting in the downregulation of key processes involved in CLL pathobiology such as apoptosis, underscoring the relevance of chromatin remodeling and histone acetylation in CLL development. Collectively, this study enhances our understanding of the heterogeneous genetic landscape of CLL and may contribute to the development of personalized medicine, facilitating the optimization of treatment strategies.Conflict-of-interest disclosure: The authors declare no competing financial interests.

title: Single cell and spatial atlas of macrophage and astrocyte interactions in glioblastoma
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits pronounced intratumoral heterogeneity, yet the interactions between macrophages and astrocyte-like (AC-like) cells remain incompletely understood.We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from 10 GBM patients, performing clustering with Seurat and Harmony, copy number variation to distinguish malignant cells, and trajectory inference to map lineage relationships. CellChat was applied to predict intercellular signaling, while CellTrek reconstructed spatial co-localization. Prognostic significance of identified key subpopulations was evaluated using Cox regression analysis.Thirteen cell subtypes were identified in GBM, including four macrophage clusters (e.g., Macro_CCL3, Macro_C1QL1) and eight AC-like clusters (e.g., AClike_RGCC, AClike_SLC7A5). Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC7A5 were enriched in malignant regions and correlated with poor prognosis. Intercellular communication analysis indicated that Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC7A5 cells engage in strengthened APP–CD74 signaling, emphasizing the involvement of tumor-specific CypA and APP pathways. Spatial mapping confirmed their co-localization in tumor-dense areas, supporting niche-specific interactions.This study provides an integrated single-cell and spatial characterization of macrophage and AC-like cell crosstalk in GBM, identifying key signaling networks and potential therapeutic targets.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at
full_text: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive and lethal primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by rapid progression, high recurrence, and poor prognosis despite multimodal therapies [1]. The median survival remains less than 15 months [2]. Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have revolutionized the understanding of GBM heterogeneity [3]. For instance, Patel et al. [4] first revealed extensive transcriptional diversity within individual GBM tumors, identifying multiple coexisting cellular states. These findings underscore the utility of scRNA-seq in delineating the intricate tumor ecosystem of GBM.Among the diverse cell populations identified by single-cell studies, tumor-associated macrophages [5] (TAMs) and astrocyte-like (AC-like) [6] malignant cells play pivotal roles in GBM biology. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis have revealed distinct macrophage subsets of both microglial and bone marrow origin, with immunosuppressive phenotypes contributing to tumor progression and therapy resistance [7]. Meanwhile, AC-like tumor cells, first defined by Neftel et al. [8], represent one of the major transcriptional states of GBM, displaying astrocytic gene signatures and being closely linked to mesenchymal transition and invasion. Single-cell transcriptomics reveals cellular heterogeneity but not functional interactions, while cell–cell communication analysis predicts signaling networks but requires precise cell subtyping. Integrating both approaches enables us to characterize GBM composition and dissect how specific macrophage and tumor subpopulations communicate to drive tumor progression, a necessity given the context-dependent and paracrine nature of these interactions that neither method alone can fully address.Although both macrophages and AC-like tumor cells have been well characterized separately, their functional interactions within the GBM microenvironment remain largely unexplored. Previous studies have shown that TAMs can induce malignant cells to adopt an AC-like phenotype, and conversely, AC-like malignant cells can recruit and reprogram macrophages through secreted factors [9, 10]. However, these two cell subsets are still lacking in the single-cell interaction landscape of GBM. In particular, no study has systematically analyzed the spatial organization or communication between these two key cell types using integrated spatial transcriptomic approaches. This lack of spatial context limits our understanding of how macrophage–AC-like crosstalk shapes tumor evolution. Therefore, we performed a combined single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analysis to comprehensively map macrophage–AC-like interactions in GBM.Materials and Data acquisitionSingle-cell RNA sequencing datasets were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession numbers GSE242044 [11] (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgiacc=GSE242044) and GSE103224 [12] (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi? acc=GSE103224). The combined dataset comprised 17 specimens from 15 patients, including 10 tumor tissue samples and 7 normal tissue samples. These two datasets were selected because they contain GBM transcriptomic profiles and include both tumor and adjacent non‑tumor tissues, whereas many other datasets lack normal controls or have very small sample sizes. In addition, the spatial transcriptomic data were obtained from GSE235672 [13]. The sequencing platform used in this dataset is 10x Visium, and we analyzed two tumor tissue samples. This dataset is derived from different samples than the single-cell RNA sequencing cohort.Processing and computational analysis of single-cell dataQuality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering of scRNA-seq data were performed using Seurat (v4.3.0.1) [14]. The Harmony algorithm (v0.1.1) [15] was applied to correct for technical artifacts and batch effects arising from multi-sample integration. Cell clusters were identified through principal component analysis (PCA) and visualized in two-dimensional space using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) [16]. To account for matching and batch effects, we included two matched tumor-normal samples and performed PCA before and after batch correction, confirming that batch effects were mitigated without losing biological differences. We used the FindAllMarkers function to calculate marker genes for cell subclusters (p < 0.05, logfc.threshold = 0.5).Lineage trajectory reconstructionDevelopmental trajectories and cellular differentiation states were inferred using pseudotemporal ordering. CytoTRACE2 (v1.0.0) [17] was employed to estimate differentiation potential, while Slingshot (v2.8.0) [18] was used to reconstruct branching lineage paths.Inference of somatic copy number alterationsThe inferCNV package [19] was utilized to predict large-scale chromosomal copy number variations from gene expression data. Cells were classified as malignant or non-malignant based on the magnitude and pattern of inferred CNV profiles. We used T cells and B cells as reference cells. A cell was classified as malignant if its inferCNV score (mean absolute CNV signal) exceeded the 95th percentile of the distribution of scores from the reference cells. Denoising was performed using the “denoise” function with the Hidden Markov Model method. The denoise cutoff was set to 0.15 for amplification and deletion events, respectively, and the window length was set to 100 (the actual value was slightly adjusted based on the number of genes on each chromosome).Functional annotation and pathway analysisDifferentially expressed genes for each cell cluster were analyzed for functional enrichment using clusterProfiler [20]. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses revealed biological processes and signaling pathways characteristic of distinct cellular subpopulations.Survival analysisWe performed survival analysis using the TCGA-GBM dataset (n = 173). The gsva() function was used to calculate GSVA scores for Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC7A5 for each patient. Patients were divided into high and low groups using thresholds of 5.5549 and 0.065, respectively. The log-rank test was used to assess whether there was a significant difference in survival between the two groups.Intercellular signaling network analysisCell–cell communication was systematically investigated with CellChat (v2.1.2) [21]. By identifying significant ligand–receptor interactions across cell types, signaling networks within the tumor microenvironment were comprehensively characterized. Ligand–receptor pairs were prioritized based on a combination of statistical significance (p < 0.001) and communication probability, with emphasis placed on interactions that ranked highest across these metrics. At the signaling pathway level, networks were further ranked according to their overall communication strength and statistical significance (adjusted p < 0.01), and those with the highest ranking were selected for detailed downstream analysis.Spatial transcriptomic mappingCellTrek (v0.0.94) [22] was applied to deconvolute spatial transcriptomics data using scRNA-seq references, enabling the reconstruction of spatial localizations and co-localization patterns of distinct cell types in GBM and adjacent parenchyma. We used the dist_thresh = 0.55 parameter to define the distance threshold; only when the distance between a single cell and a spatial spot is less than this threshold is it considered mappable. The top_spot = 5 parameter limits each cell to mapping to at most the top 5 most similar spatial spots. The repel_r = 20 parameter defines the repulsion radius (units are typically pixels or micrometers in spatial coordinates). When multiple cells map to the same spatial location, a minimum distance constraint is imposed to avoid excessive overlap; a value of 20 indicates that two mapping points must maintain a distance of 20 units from each other.The single-cell landscape of glioblastomaTo explore cellular heterogeneity in GBM, we examined scRNA-seq data from 17 specimens from 15 patients, including 10 tumor tissue samples and 7 normal tissue samples. Following stringent quality control, dimensionality reduction, and batch-effect correction, we identified 13 major cell populations, visualized via UMAP (Fig. 1A). Based on canonical marker gene expression, these clusters were annotated as AC-like cell, OPC-like cell, MES-like cell, oligodendrocyte, microglia, T cell, B cell, fibroblast, endothelial cell, macrophage, NPC-like cell, mast cell, and plasma cell. Tumor tissues exhibited substantial enrichment of AC-like, MES-like, endothelial, and fibroblast populations, along with multiple immune subsets such as T cells, B cells, mast cells, and macrophages (Fig. 1B). Fig. 1Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals cellular heterogeneity in glioblastoma and adjacent normal tissues. A UMAP projection illustrating the composition and distribution of 13 distinct cell clusters (FindAllMarkers function: p < 0.05, logfc.threshold = 0.5). B Comparative analysis of cell cluster abundances between tumor and normal tissue conditions. C Bubble plot displaying canonical marker genes across the 13 major cell types. D Proportion of the 13 cell types between tumor and normal tissue groups. E Feature plots showing expression of representative marker genes for each cell type on UMAP (FindAllMarkers function: p < 0.05, logfc.threshold = 0.5) To validate cluster identities, we assessed the expression of established marker genes. Bubble plots illustrated representative markers for each population, confirming their annotation (Fig. 1C). The tumor tissues exhibited greater cellular subpopulation diversity than normal tissues, with AC-like cells being the predominant subset among all subpopulations (Fig. 1D). In normal tissues, although the proportions of AC-like, MES-like, and OPS-like subsets were lower than those in tumor tissues (Figure S1A), these three subgroups rank among the top three in the cell subpopulations of normal tissues (Fig. 1D). Spatial feature mapping within the UMAP further highlighted distinct transcriptional profiles across lineages, reinforcing subtype-specific gene expression patterns (Fig. 1E). Together, these results establish a high-resolution single-cell atlas of GBM and matched normal brain tissues.The heterogeneity and lineage potential of macrophageBased on the above analysis, we observed that macrophages were the most abundant immune cell population and showed significant differences between tumor and normal tissues. Previous studies have reported that macrophages play important roles in GBM, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear [23, 24]. Therefore, we further characterized their heterogeneity by performing subclustering analysis. High-resolution clustering of macrophages identified 4 distinct subpopulations, designated Macro_SCGB1D2, Macro_PIGC, Macro_CCL3, and Macro_C1QL1, which were which were annotated by identifying marker genes for each subpopulation using the FindAllMarkers function and visualized using UMAP (Fig. 2A). Tumor tissues showed pronounced enrichment of the Macro_SCGB1D2 subset, while Macro_CCL3 was predominantly detected in normal tissues (Fig. 2B). The enrichment of the Macro_SCGB1D2 subset in tumor tissues suggests that this subset may be associated with the pro-tumor phenotype of TAMs. SCGB1D2, a member of the secretoglobin family, has been reported in previous studies to be involved in immune regulation and tissue remodeling [25, 26]. Its enrichment in tumors may indicate that this subset promotes the formation of an immunosuppressive microenvironment through the secretion of related factors, or interacts with tumor cells to support tumor progression. In contrast, the Macro_CCL3 subset is predominantly distributed in normal tissues. The preferential distribution of this subset in normal tissues suggests that it may be involved in maintaining tissue homeostasis and immune surveillance [27]. The cell type annotations are consistent with those shown in Fig. 1A. E–H Correlation analysis of four macrophage subsets with effector CD8 + T cells. I Functional enrichment analysis of Macro_C1QL1. J Relationship between Macro_C1QL1 and patient overall survival (log-rank p = 0.029) Bubble plots illustrated representative marker expression patterns, supporting the classification of each macrophage subset (Fig. 2C). Pseudotemporal trajectory analysis revealed two branching differentiation paths, suggesting developmental plasticity among macrophage populations during tumor progression, suggesting that they possess high developmental plasticity and potential for state transitions (Fig. 2D). Given that CD8 + T effector cells are central to anti-tumor immunity and have been linked to TAMs-related dysfunction [28], we next examined the correlation between each macrophage subpopulation and CD8 + T effector gene signatures. Correlation analysis further indicated that Macro_C1QL1 marker levels were inversely associated with CD8⁺ T effector gene signatures (Fig. 2E) (PMID: ), Combined with its complement activation-related functions, this suggests that this subset may inhibit T cell anti-tumor immune responses through complement-mediated immunoregulatory mechanisms. In contrast, the markers of Macro_CCL3, Macro_PIGC, and Macro_SCGB1D2 showed positive correlations with CD8⁺ T effector activity, suggesting that these subsets may have a synergistic relationship with the anti-tumor immune response (Figs. 2F–H).Gene Ontology analysis highlighted enrichment of the Macro_C1QL1 subset in processes related to cell growth, regulation of protein stability, and positive control of the cell cycle (Fig. 2I). Clinically, high Macro_C1QL1 signature scores were significantly associated with poor patient prognosis, with elevated scores predicting reduced overall survival (log-rank p = 0.029; Fig. 2J), suggesting that this subset not only possesses immunosuppressive potential but may also serve as an independent risk marker for poor prognosis in patients with glioblastoma. Based on these findings, Macro_C1QL1 emerges as a tumor-enriched, immunosuppressive macrophage subset associated with poor prognosis.The heterogeneity of AC-like cell in the tumor microenvironmentThe multi-omics study conducted by Xiong et al. [6] classified GBM into four subtypes: MES-like, AC-like, OPC-like and NPC-like, each reflecting distinct cellular states along the glioma differentiation hierarchy. The CNV analysis revealed pronounced genomic instability in NPC-like and AC-like cells, which exhibited elevated CNV burdens relative to other subtypes (Fig. 3A), suggesting that these populations may have undergone greater genomic divergence, potentially driven by accumulated oncogenic insults and contributing to intratumoral heterogeneity. We then performed survival analysis and found that AC-like cells with high CNV scores were significantly associated with poor prognosis in GBM patients (log-rank p = 0.04; Figure S1B), whereas OPC-like cells showed no significant association with prognosis (log-rank p = 0.14; Figure S1C). Based on genetic characteristics and clinical significance, we focused on the analysis of the AC-like cell subpopulation. Pseudotemporal trajectory reconstruction delineated a branched differentiation continuum across these four subtypes, with AC-like cells occupying the terminal position, suggesting a mature or end-state phenotype in GBM evolution (Fig. 3B), implying that they represent a more differentiated, possibly end-state phenotype in GBM evolution. Unsupervised subclustering of AC-like cell identified eight distinct subpopulations—AClike_RGCC, AClike_SLC7A5, AClike_ERMN, AClike_HLADRB5, AClike_IL1R1, AClike_CD52, AClike_MGP, and AClike_IGLJ3—each demonstrating differential spatial distributions between tumor and normal tissues (Fig. 3C). Tumor samples showed significant enrichment of the AClike_SLC7A5 subset, whereas AClike_RGCC was predominantly localized in normal tissue (Fig. 3D). These AC-like cell subpopulations were validated by their unique marker gene expression profiles (Fig. 3E). Fig. 3Dissection of AC-like cell heterogeneity and functional states in glioblastoma. C UMAP plot showing clustering of AC-like cells into eight distinct subsets (FindAllMarkers function: p < 0.05, logfc.threshold = 0.5). Clinically, high abundance of AClike_SLC7A5 was correlated with significantly worse overall survival in GBM patients (log-rank p = 0. ), underscoring its prognostic relevance and potential role in disease progression (Fig. 3G). Collectively, these findings elucidate the cellular and functional heterogeneity of AC-like cell and identify SLC7A5-enriched AC-like subpopulation as a clinically significant subgroup in GBM.Collectively, these findings not only reveal the functional heterogeneity of AC-like cells but also identify the SLC7A5-enriched subpopulation as a clinically significant subgroup in GBM. Its association with metabolic reprogramming and poor prognosis positions it as a potential therapeutic target and a candidate biomarker for risk stratification.Tumor-specific macrophage and AC-like cell interactionProfiling of intercellular communication revealed pronounced remodeling of signaling networks between tumor and normal tissues. Tumor samples displayed markedly increased activity in pathways such as JAM, APP, and GRN (Fig. 4A), while normal tissues were primarily characterized by stronger engagement of JAM, GRN, and APP signaling. Although the above pathways are significantly enriched in both tumor and normal tissues, their distribution across different cell subpopulations may differ significantly (Fig. 4B). In the normal state, only the Macro_CCL3 macrophage was found to interact with all other AC-like subpopulations except AClike_IGLJ3 (Fig. 4C). This restricted interaction pattern suggests a tightly regulated communication network in the normal state, possibly reflecting homeostatic surveillance and maintenance of tissue integrity. In contrast, tumor tissues exhibited a broader interaction landscape, where all four macrophage subsets communicated with all eight AC-like subtypes (Fig. 4D). This expansion of cellular crosstalk implies a loss of regulatory constraints in the tumor microenvironment and points to a globally activated signaling state that may drive diverse tumor-supportive functions, including immune suppression, metabolic cooperation, and stromal remodeling. Fig. 4Tumor-specific macrophage and AC-like cell communication landscape in glioblastoma. A, B Number of predicted cell-cell interactions between macrophage and AC-like cell subsets in tumor and normal tissues. C, D Circle plot showing the interaction between AC-like cell and macrophage subpopulations in tumor and normal tissues. E Bubble plot showing cell interactions between Macro_C1QL1 subtypes and AClike_SLC7A5. F, G Differences in ligand-receptor distribution of CypA and APP signaling pathway network in tumor and normal conditions Ligand–receptor analysis further identified a tumor-specific communication axis between macrophages and AC-like cells, predominantly mediated by interactions between Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC7A5 clusters through pairs such as PPIA-BSG and APP-CD74 which have the highest statistical significance (p < 0.001) and the greatest communication probability (Fig. 4E). Furthermore, prior studies have shown that APP–CD74 is involved in neuroinflammatory pathways, supporting its biological relevance [29, 30]. Consistently, CypA and APP signaling pathways ranked among the most significantly altered (adjusted p < 0.01) and exhibited the highest interaction scores across all predicted networks, while both CypA and APP have been implicated in immune regulation [29, 31], supporting their prioritization for further analysis. Based on the above analysis, we suggest that the CypA and APP signaling pathways may play important roles in mediating the tumor-promoting effects of Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC7A5. Detailed examination of CypA (Fig. 4F) and APP (Fig. 4G) signaling networks revealed distinct ligand-receptor distribution patterns distinguishing tumor from normal tissues. Notably, the Macro_C1QL1 to AClike_SLC7A5 connection represented the strongest tumor-specific interaction, but absent in normal tissues. Collectively, these findings demonstrate an extensively reprogrammed communication landscape in GBM, driven by macrophage and AC-like crosstalk and context-dependent pathway activation.Collectively, these findings demonstrate an extensively reprogrammed communication landscape in GBM, driven by context-dependent pathway activation and the emergence of specialized crosstalk between macrophage subsets and AC-like malignant cells. This reprogramming likely contributes to the establishment of an immunosuppressive and tumor-permissive microenvironment, and the identified tumor-specific ligand-receptor pairs, particularly the Macro_C1QL1-AClike_SLC7A5 axis, may represent promising therapeutic targets for disrupting pathogenic cellular communication in GBM.Spatial transcriptome characteristics of macrophage and AC-like cell subsetsSpatial transcriptomic analysis of GBM specimens revealed distinct topological reorganization within the tumor microenvironment. UMAP visualization illustrated clear regional segregation between histologically distinct malignant areas across two representative GBM cases (Figs. 5A, B), indicating that distinct transcriptional programs are spatially compartmentalized, a feature likely driven by local microenvironmental cues and contributing to functional heterogeneity within the tumor. Integration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets enabled high-resolution mapping of cellular distributions, uncovering region-specific localization patterns of major cell classes (Figs. 5C, D). This spatial segregation suggests that different cell types occupy specialized niches, where local signaling gradients and physical interactions may orchestrate context-dependent functional states. A, B Dimensionality reduction and clustering of spatial transcriptomics in tumor tissues from two glioblastoma patients. C, D Distribution of single cells and spatial spots in tumor tissues from two glioblastoma patients. E, F Spatial deconvolution of macrophage and AC-like cell in two glioblastoma patients. Red circles highlight representative regions of Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC75A co-localization observed in glioblastoma patients, illustrating the spatial reorganization of these cell populations in the tumor microenvironment. G, H Network diagram showing spatial co-localization of macrophage and AC-like cell subpopulations in tumor tissues. I, J Heatmap showing spatial neighborhoods of macrophage and AC-like cell subpopulations in tumor and normal tissues Spatial deconvolution further resolved the topographic organization of macrophage and AC-like cellular subsets, demonstrating fundamentally different spatial patterning between tumor and normal tissue contexts (Figs. 5E, F). Network analysis of cellular co-localization revealed extensive rewiring of macrophage–AC-like cell interactions in tumor regions, with emergence of specialized spatial neighborhoods unique to the malignant state (Figs. 5G, H). This reorganization implies that tumor progression drives the formation of spatially confined functional units, in which macrophage and malignant cell subsets co-localize to establish local microenvironments that may facilitate immune modulation, metabolic exchange, and pro-tumorigenic signaling. Quantitative evaluation of spatial adjacency through heatmap visualization confirmed ecosystem-level remodeling in GBM, characterized by systematic alteration of spatial relationships between macrophage and AC-like subpopulations compared to normal tissue counterparts (Figs. 5I, J).Spatial transcriptomic analysis reveals that GBM progression drives a marked reorganization of the tumor microenvironment, characterized by the spatial segregation of macrophage and AC-like cell subsets into distinct, functionally specialized niches that remodel cell-cell interactions compared with normal tissue.In this study, we performed an integrative single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analysis to comprehensively characterize the cellular heterogeneity and intercellular communication landscape of GBM. By delineating 13 major cell populations and focusing on macrophages and AC-like malignant cells, we uncovered profound transcriptional and spatial diversity within the tumor ecosystem. Among macrophage subsets, we identified a tumor-enriched Macro_C1QL1 population characterized by complement activation and cell growth signatures, whereas among AC-like cells, the AClike_SLC7A5 subgroup exhibited metabolic activation and poor prognostic implications. Notably, our integrative analysis revealed a tumor-specific interaction axis between Macro_C1QL1 and AClike_SLC7A5 mediated by PPIA-BSG and APP-CD74 signaling, suggesting a previously unrecognized immunometabolism crosstalk contributing to tumor progression. The combined single-cell and spatial approach thus provide a high-resolution view of GBM cellular ecosystems and their spatial organization, advancing the current understanding of tumor–immune communication in the brain tumor microenvironment.Recent single-cell studies have emphasized that TAMs in GBM exhibit marked heterogeneity and context-dependent immunoregulatory functions. For instance, Liu et al. [32] identified VSIG4S100A10TAM that drive M2 polarization and impair anti-PD-1 responses, while Chen et al. [33] described an EZH + TAM subset linked to cell-cycle activation and poor prognosis. Our data extend these findings by revealing four distinct TAM subsets, especially Macro_C1QL1, characterized by complement activation and protein stability pathways. Unlike the classically defined M2-like or metabolic TAMs such as ABCA1⁺ cells [34], Macro_C1QL1 displayed proliferative signatures and a strong inverse correlation with CD8⁺ T-cell effector genes, suggesting a non-canonical immunosuppressive phenotype. C1QL1 is a member of the C1q family, and previous studies have suggested that this family of proteins is involved in synaptic pruning and immune regulation [35, 36]. We speculate that the Macro_C1QL1 subpopulation may inhibit CD8 + T cell activation or effector function, for example, by interfering with T cell receptor signaling or inducing T cell exhaustion, through the secretion of C1QL1 or other synergistic molecules. Moreover, studies have reported that C1q family molecules can regulate the immunosuppressive phenotype of macrophages and indirectly suppress T cell responses [37, 38]. Thus, this inverse correlation may provide new insights into macrophage-mediated immune evasion. Functionally, its high abundance predicted unfavorable outcome, supporting the emerging concept that specific transcriptional programs—rather than simple M1/M2 polarization—govern TAM-mediated immune evasion in GBM. Additionally, recent studies have shown that tumor-specific CD4 + T cells expressing CXCL13 are associated with the transcriptional states of macrophage [39], suggesting that future investigations into different immune cell populations may further elucidate the complex immune landscape of GBM.GBM exhibits substantial intratumoral heterogeneity, with tumor cells classified into MES-like, AC-like, OPC-like, and NPC-like state [6, 40]. Previous studies indicate that AC-like cells occupy metabolically active region [10], which is consistent with our research. Unlike the previous single AC-like subtype, our study further delineated eight AC-like subpopulations, in particular identifying the AClike_SLC7A5 subset as specifically enriched in tumor tissue, exhibiting high oxidative phosphorylation, ATP metabolism, and epithelial-associated programs. Clinically, high abundance of AClike_SLC7A5 correlated with worse overall survival, highlighting its prognostic significance and potential role in GBM progression. Moreover, environmental carcinogens such as benzo[a]pyrene may further influence GBM progression via TP53 modulation in MES-like and AC-like cells and in CD8⁺ exhausted T cells [41]. Together, these results integrate cellular heterogeneity, metabolic reprogramming, and extrinsic factors, providing a comprehensive view of GBM plasticity and potential targets for immunotherapeutic interventions.Previous studies have shown that various cell types within GBM, including macrophages, microglia [24], oligodendrocyte [42], and other cell subpopulations [43, 44], interact extensively with each other within the tumor microenvironment (TME). These interactions have been reported to influence tumor progression, therapeutic resistance, and immune evasion. For example, TAMs and microglia are critical for GBM progression, and recent work demonstrates that lysis oxidase (LOX) and olfactomedin like-3 (OLFML3) mediate reciprocal regulation between macrophages and microglia, influencing immune infiltration and therapeutic response [45]. In addition, previous studies have demonstrated that combining VEGF pathway inhibitors with imipramine can remodel the tumor vasculature and reprogram immunosuppressive TAMs into immunostimulatory cells [46]. Inhibiting BACE1 has been shown to reprogram tumor-promoting macrophages into tumor-suppressive macrophages and enhance their phagocytosis of glioma cells [47]. These findings provide a strong rationale for investigating the crosstalk between TAMs and specific malignant cell subsets in our study. However, the specific interactions between macrophages and AC-like cells remain unexplored. In our study, we identified the AClike_SLC7A5 subpopulation, which is enriched in tumor regions and exhibits high oxidative phosphorylation and epithelial-like programs. Spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed its co-localization with macrophage-rich areas, suggesting that interactions between macrophages and AClike_SLC7A5 cells may contribute to local immunosuppression and tumor progression. These findings provide novel insights into the cellular heterogeneity and tumor microenvironment dynamics in GBM. Importantly, the identified AClike_SLC7A5 subpopulation and its crosstalk with macrophages via CypA/APP signaling pathways may serve as potential biomarkers for patient prognosis or therapeutic targets. Future translational studies, including the development of inhibitors targeting these signaling axes or the use of spatial signatures for patient stratification, could pave the way for more personalized immunotherapeutic strategies in GBM.This study has several noteworthy limitations. The cohort’s limited ethnic diversity and the underrepresentation of certain brain tumor subtypes may restrict the broader applicability of our results. Although our analysis concentrated on GBM, future studies should encompass additional brain malignancies, including neuroblastoma and oligodendroglioma. Moreover, while multi-omics integration allowed us to uncover previously unrecognized macrophage and AC-like subpopulations, their precise functional contributions to tumor progression remain to be experimentally validated, for instance, through organoid co-culture or targeted genetic perturbation. These constraints underscore the need for larger, multi-center cohorts and mechanistic investigations to facilitate the clinical translation of therapies targeting these newly defined cell populations.In summary, our study constructs a detailed single-cell and spatial atlas of macrophage and AC-like subset interactions in GBM, uncovering key communication networks and distinct cellular niches that may contribute to immunosuppression and tumor progression. These insights offer a valuable framework for future mechanistic studies and lay the groundwork for the development of therapeutic strategies that focus on specific cellular crosstalk within GBM.Supplementary InformationBelow is the link to the electronic supplementary material. title: Proteogenomic characterization of pulmonary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma identifies molecular features and therapeutic strategy
abstract: Pulmonary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is a rare yet highly aggressive subtype of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) with limited therapeutic options. We conduct a comprehensive proteogenomic analysis of LCNEC using tumors and paired normal adjacent tissues from 107 patients (81 pure LCNEC and 26 combined LCNEC). APOBEC mutational signatures strongly correlate processes of tumor initiation and immune suppression, and KEAP1 mutations correlate with metabolic reprogramming in LCNEC combined with NSCLC. A conflicting relationship is observed between neuroendocrine and immune phenotypes. We identify three LCNEC subtypes with unique prognosis features, microenvironment dysregulation, genetic alterations, and potential therapeutic targets. Interleukin-33 (IL-33) emerges as a critical therapeutic biomarker associated with enhanced T cell infiltration and antitumor activity. We further optimize recombinant IL-33 (rIL33) with site-directed mutagenesis and develop PEGylated rIL33, demonstrating its prolonged circulation time in cynomolgus monkeys and superior immune agonist activity in mouse models. Overall, this study offers insights into LCNEC biology and provides promising innovative immunoagonist therapy strategies for lung cancer.
full_text: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related death globally (1). Pulmonary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) represents a rare yet highly aggressive lung tumor, accounting for 2 to 3% of all resected lung cancers (2, 3). Annual incident cases of LCNECs are estimated to range from 44,000 to 66,000, with its incidence rising from 0.26 per 100,000 individuals in 2004 to 0.39 per 100,000 individuals in 2015 (4, 5). LCNEC, along with typical carcinoid (TC), atypical carcinoid (AC), and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), falls under the category of neuroendocrine lung tumors (2, 3). Unlike TC and AC, LCNEC exhibits a clinically aggressive phenotype, characterized by widely extensive metastases and a poor prognosis, with 5-year survival rates ranging from 15 to 25% (2, 3, 6, 7). The main therapeutic approaches for LCNEC include surgery and chemotherapy; however, the efficacy of chemotherapy remains limited, and no established standard treatment regimen has been established for this tumor type (8).Besides pure LCNEC, LCNEC frequently coexists with non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) and occasionally with SCLC components in clinical practice, which are referred to as combined large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomas with NSCLC (C-LCNEC with NSCLC) and combined large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomas with SCLC (C-LCNEC with SCLC), respectively (9). These combined large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomas (C-LCNEC) constitute approximately 20 to 25% of pulmonary LCNEC cases (10). Despite this prevalence, there is limited knowledge regarding the molecular differences between pure LCNEC and C-LCNEC. The insufficient knowledge of the molecular underpinnings of LCNEC poses a major barrier to the development of targeted therapies for this distinctive and aggressive subtype of lung cancer.Recent advances in genomic and transcriptomic sequencing analyses have begun to elucidate the molecular landscape of LCNEC (9–12). Despite these initial insights, our comprehension of the molecular landscape and heterogeneity in LCNEC, particularly for the development of targeted therapies, remains incomplete. A major challenge in LCNEC research is the scarcity of high-quality tumor specimens, which hampers both clinical and basic research efforts, due to the rarity of this disease. Comprehensive “omics” strategies, encompassing proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling in conjunction with genomic analysis, have identified previously unrecognized disease subtypes, signaling pathways, and potential therapeutic targets in NSCLC (13–16). Nonetheless, a systematic proteomic study of LCNEC has yet to be conducted, despite the pivotal role of proteins in determining tumor phenotype.In this study, we conducted an integrated proteogenomic characterization of 107 LCNEC tumors and paired normal adjacent tissues (NATs) by leveraging mass spectrometry (MS)–based quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics, along with genomic and transcriptomic sequencing. This comprehensive proteogenomic analysis provided critical insights into genomic aberrations, LCNEC-associated molecular characteristics, and therapeutic biomarkers, thereby improving our understanding of patient stratification for targeted treatment strategies. We also proposed that interleukin-33 (IL-33) and engineered polyethylene glycol–conjugated interleukin-33 (PEG–IL33) emerge as promising therapeutic strategies with immune-enhancing properties. Furthermore, the resulting dataset also serves as a valuable resource for ongoing and future researches in the field of LCNEC.The proteogenomic landscape of LCNECTo characterize the proteogenomic landscape of LCNEC in China, we collected tumor and paired NAT samples from 107 patients with surgically resected LCNEC [Tongji University (TU)-LCNEC cohort] (fig. S1A). All samples were cryo-pulverized and aliquoted for molecular profiling using whole-exome sequencing (WES), RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), and isobaric tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling–based global proteomics and phosphoproteomics (Fig. 1, A and B). Clinical information, including gender, age at diagnosis, tumor stage, survival, histology, etc., is summarized in table S1 (Fig. 1C). Four molecular profiling strategies were used to characterize the TU-LCNEC cohort (Fig. 1A and fig. S1A). The liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) identified 9580 proteins, with 5683 quantified in 103 sample pairs and 8142 detected in more than 50% of the 103 paired samples. TMT-based phosphoproteomics identified 30,009 highly reliable phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) from 7476 phosphoproteins, among which 8932 phosphosites from 3137 phosphoproteins were quantified in more than 50% of the 103 paired samples (table S1, Supplementary Materials). The TMT-based proteomics and phosphoproteomics data were of high quality as evaluated (fig. S1, B to E). Principal components analysis (PCA) showed no overall apparent batch effect in the global proteome and phosphoproteome data (fig. S1F). On the basis of transcriptomic and proteomic data from matched samples, 5393 mRNA-protein pairs were identified, with 88.5% exhibiting significant positive correlation [false discovery rate (FDR) A mutations (blue) and C>T mutations (red), respectively. (J) Boxplot showing the APOBEC signature differences between KEAP1 mutated and KEAP1 wild patients (Wilcoxon ranked-sum test). (K) Boxplot showing the APOBEC signature differences between PIK3CA mutated and PIK3CA wild patients (Wilcoxon ranked-sum test).Using WES data with a mean depth of more than 100× (fig. S1G), we detected 29,439 mutations, including 27,885 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and 1554 small insertion-deletions (indels) (table S1, Supplementary Materials). The genomic landscape reaffirmed previously reported somatic alterations in LCNEC (10, 12) (Fig. 1D). We identified six genes exhibiting significant recurrent somatic mutation (q 1), with 246 proteins up-regulated and 728 proteins down-regulated in LCNEC tumors compared with NATs (fig. S3B and table S3). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis revealed that DNA replication, cell cycle, and multiple DNA repair–related pathways were up-regulated in tumors, while complement and coagulation cascades, ECM-receptor interaction, and focal adhesion–related pathways were down-regulated (fig. S3C). After applying more stringent criteria for differential expression and adjusting for stromal and immune content, we further singled out 40 up-regulated proteins in tumors, which we termed LCNEC-associated proteins (fig. S3D). The potential clinical utility of these proteins was annotated using the Human Protein Atlas, revealing 21 plasma proteins, 22 enzymes, 13 known cancer-related genes, and 10 approved drug targets among them (fig. S3D). PLIN2 was the only LCNEC-associated protein with opposite mRNA and protein differential expression (fig. S3E), which is a ubiquitously expressed protein that regulates lipid droplets, particularly in nonadipose tissues such as the liver (31). Two LCNEC-associated proteins, RAB3B and MTHFD2 (32), were associated with poor survival (fig. S3, F and G).We obtained 1892 differentially expressed phosphosites between LCNECs tumor and NAT (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, FDR 1; Fig. 3H and table S3). In general, the differential expression pattern was largely concordant between phosphosites and cognate proteins (fig. S3I and table S3; Pearson correlation, R = 0.77, P 2-fold) than corresponding proteins in tumors (fig. S3I). For instance, PDHA1, whose dysregulation promotes tumor glycolysis by down-regulating the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity, exhibited markedly greater increases in phosphorylation than in protein abundance (fig. S4A) (33). Specifically, three phosphorylation sites on PDHA1 (Ser232, Ser293, and Ser300) showed increases exceeding twofold, whereas the change in protein abundance of PDHA1 was comparatively modest (fig. S4A). Quantitative analysis of immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of PDHA1 and phosphor-PDHA1 (Ser293) further confirmed a significant elevation of phosphorylation of PDHA1 at Ser293 in tumors relative to paired NATs (fig. S4, B and C). Although phosphosites and proteins exhibited comparable prognostic values (fig. S4D and table S3), specific phosphorylation sites exhibited more pronounced prognostic values than their corresponding proteins. For example, LCNECs with high phosphorylation at Ser293 on PDHA1 instead of PDHA1 protein abundance showed significantly worse OS (fig. S4, E and F). Total RNA-seq library construction was performed from the RNA samples using the NEBNext UltraTM RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB) following the manufacturer’s recommendations and index codes were added to attribute sequences to each sample. Then, paired-end libraries were sequenced on an Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform and 150-bp paired-end reads were generated.Peptides preparation for MS analysis Protein extraction and digestion For the TMT 11-plex proteomic and phosphoproteomic experiments, cryopulverized human LCNEC and corresponding NAT samples were homogenized in lysis buffer. This lysis buffer consisted of 1% SDS, 10 mM Hepes (pH 7.0), 2 mM MgCl2, Benzonase (diluted at a ratio of 1:1000), and Roche PhosSTOP (diluted at a ratio of 1:50). Following homogenization, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min to separate the supernatant, and the protein concentrations in the supernatant were quantified using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay. Subsequently, each sample (4.5 mg) was reduced with 2 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) (Sigma-Aldrich, D9163) for 20 min and then alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich, I1149) in the dark at room temperature for 20 min. Protein precipitation was performed using the methanol-chloroform method (1 part lysate:4 parts methanol:1 part chloroform:3 parts H2O). After precipitation, the protein pellet was washed with 1 ml of methanol. The resulting precipitated protein was then reconstituted in an 8 M urea solution, which contained 20 mM tris-HCl and 10 mM EDTA, pH 7.5.The protein digestion was performed in 8 M urea buffer using Lys-C enzyme (Promega, no. VA1170) at a ratio of 1:200 (enzyme:protein) for 3 hours. Subsequently, trypsin enzyme (Promega, no. V5280) was used at a ratio of 1:100 (enzyme:protein) in a 2 M urea diluted solution for overnight digestion at 37°C. The digested samples were acidified with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to achieve the desired pH range of 2 to 3. The resulting digested peptides were subjected to desalting, which was performed using C18 SepPak cartridges (60 mg, Waters Oasis HLB, WAT094226). Ten percent of each eluate was dried using Speedvac vacuum concentrators, and then the concentration of peptides for global proteomic analysis was measured using a BCA assay. The remaining eluate samples were supplemented with 2 M lactic acid for subsequent phosphopeptides enrichment. The reference samples used in the TMT-11 experiments were prepared by pooling 10 pairs of tumor and adjacent nontumor lung samples, which were randomly selected and mixed to yield equal amounts of protein. Aliquots of this reference mixture (4.5 mg) were frozen and used consistently for each multiplex experiment, beginning at the protein extraction and digestion stage. Phosphopeptide enrichment Phosphopeptide enrichment was carried out with titanium dioxide (TiO2) beads. The TiO2 beads underwent two washes with washing/binding buffer (comprising 50% acetonitrile, 0.1% TFA, and 2 M lactic acid) and were subsequently resuspended in the same buffer. Each digested sample was incubated with TiO2 beads at a ratio of 1:14 (peptide to beads) overnight, with end-over-end rotation at room temperature. Following incubation, the supernatant was removed through centrifugation, and the beads were subjected to three additional washes using the washing/binding buffer. The peptides captured on the beads were eluted twice with 600 μl of K2HPO4 (100 mM, pH 9.2). These eluates were combined, acidified to a pH of 3.0 using TFA, and desalted using 10-mg C18 SepPak cartridges (Waters Oasis HLB, ). Last, the eluates were dried using a vacuum centrifuge concentrator. TMT 11-plex labeling TMT 11-plex labeling was performed for the analysis of 103 unique tumor samples along with their paired NAT samples, distributed across 21 TMT 11-plex experiments. In this process, individual channels within the 11-plex were used for labeling, with one channel assigned to the reference sample and the remaining 10 channels used for labeling individual samples. For the proteome analysis, desalted peptides were reconstituted in a 200 mM Hepes (pH 8.0) solution into a final concentration of 1 mg/ml. Each 50-μg aliquot of peptides from an individual sample was labeled using 150 μg of TMT 11-plex reagents. In the case of phosphoproteome analysis, dried phosphopeptides were reconstituted in a 200 mM Hepes (pH 8.0) solution into a concentration of 0.5 mg/ml. Subsequently, 25 μg of phosphopeptides was labeled with 120 μg of TMT 11-plex reagents, resulting in a final acetonitrile concentration of 40%. After 1-hour incubation at room temperature, the reaction was quenched using hydroxylamine for an additional 30 min. The labeled peptides were then pooled, acidified with 20 μl of 20% TFA, then lyophilized and subjected to desalting using a 10-mg C18 SepPak column (Waters Oasis HLB, ). Offline HPLC fractionation To enhance protein identification depth and reduce sample complexity, peptide fractionation was performed using basic high pH reverse-phase high-pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC). The fractionation process used solvent A (10 mM ammonium formate, pH 9.9) and solvent B [10 mM ammonium formic acid (FA) in 80% acetonitrile, pH 9.9] as the mobile phases. TMT-labeled peptides were initially solubilized in solvent A and centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 10 min to remove insoluble peptides. The resulting soluble peptides were then loaded onto a ZORBAX 300 Extend-C18 column (2.1 mm by 150 mm, 3.5 μm particle, Agilent). Subsequent peptide separation was achieved through basic reverse-phase chromatography using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Ultimate 3000 HPLC instrument.For the proteome analysis, we used a 126-min separation gradient with a flow rate of 0.15 ml/min, using the following gradient settings: (min: %B) 0:4; 101:65; 106:100; 124:100; and 126:0. Eluents were collected to a total of 96 fractions spanning from 5 to 100 min. To reduce the number of fractions, a concatenation strategy was used, where these 96 fractions were grouped into 24 pooled fractions. Subsequently, these pooled fractions were acidified with TFA.For phosphoproteome analysis, a 100-min separation gradient was applied with the following settings: (min: %B) 0:4; 75.5:65; 80:100; 98:100; and 100:0. Eluents were collected and combined into 12 fractions ranging from 5 to 75.5 min. Similar to the proteome analysis, these fractions were acidified with TFA. Both the fractionated peptides and phosphopeptides were dried using a Speedvac and subsequently desalted using stage tip columns. The dried peptides and phosphopeptides were then resuspended in 15 μl of 4% can/0.1% FA for nanoLC-MS/MS analysis, with 4-μl injection volume per run. LC-MS/MS for proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis The LC-MS/MS analysis for both proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis was conducted using an EASY-nLC 1200 UHPLC system from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Fractionated peptides were loaded onto an in-house packed capillary nanospray column (15 cm × 75 μm; 1.9 μm particle size; 10 μm tip opening). The mobile phase consisted of two components: 0.1% FA (mobile phase A) and 90% acetonitrile with 0.1% FA (mobile phase B), with a flow rate of 250 nl/min. For proteome analysis, the LC-MS/MS method encompassed 110 min and included a 10-min column equilibration step, a 20-min sample loading step, and the subsequent gradient profile: (min: %B) 0:8; 95:28; 100:100; and 110:100. For phosphoproteome analysis, the same LC system and column configuration were used. For better separation of phosphopeptides, the gradient was extended to 180 min to get better separation, using the following profile: (min: %B) 0:5; 165:27; 170:100; and 180:100.Global proteome analyses and phosphoproteome analyses were conducted on the Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the MS3-based TMT centric mass spectrometer method (73). Data-dependent acquisition was performed in positive ion mode using Xcalibur v4.1 software. The spray voltage was set at 2.2 kV, and the ion transfer tube temperature was maintained at 275°C. MS1 data were acquired in the Orbitrap analyzer, featuring a resolution of 120,000, an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 4 × 105, and a mass/charge ratio (m/z) range from 400 to 1400. The maximum ion injection time was set to 50 ms. Charge states between 2 and 6 were selected, and a 60-s exclusion duration with isotopes excluded was applied. For MS2 analysis, ion trap detection was used, using a rapid scan rate. Quadrupole isolation was performed with a collision-induced dissociation (CID) collision energy set at 35% for 10 ms. The m/z window for precursor selection during sequencing was set to 400 to 1200, incorporating a low mass exclusion width of 18 and a high mass exclusion width of 5. MS3 quantification scans were carried out using SPS (synchronous precursor selection), where 10 precursor fragment ions from the MS2 spectrum were selected. These selected precursor ions underwent fragmentation by HCD (higher-energy collision dissociation) with a collision energy of 65% and were detected in the Orbitrap analyzer. The MS3 scans were conducted at a resolution of 50,000, with an AGC target of 5 × 104 and a maximum ion injection time of 86 ms. The MS isolation window was set to 1.2 m/z, and the MS2 was set to 2.0 m/z.Genomic and transcriptomic data analysis Somatic mutation detection and filtering After excluding low-quality reads, the exome sequencing data were first aligned to GRCh38/hg38 sequence reference using BWA MEM (version 0.7.10) (http://bio-bwa.sourceforge.net/). The resulting BAM files were further processed including marking duplicates with Picard (version 2.22.8) (https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) and base quality recalibration with BaseRecalibrator from GATK (version 4.1.7.0) (https://gatk.broadinstitute.org/hc/en-us). SNVs and indels were detected using Strelka2 (74) (version 2.9.x) from paired LCNEC samples with default parameters, then filtered out short tandem repeat region downloaded from the UCSC table browser (https://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgTables), and lastly annotated using Funcotator from GATK (version 4.1.7.0). Deciphering of mutational signatures in LCNEC The r package “Sigminer” (version 2.2.2) (75) was used to extract mutational signatures from the WES data. The Bayesian variant of non-NMF algorithm was used to decipher mutational signatures in cancer somatic mutations stratified by 96 base substitutions in trinucleotide sequence contexts, and the optimal factorization of k value is selected when the magnitude of the cophenetic correlation coefficient begins to decrease apparently. The gradient boosting machine learning technique yields an individual score for each mutational signature, combining likelihood with cosine similarity and exposure of signatures using the non-negative least squares (NNLS) algorithm. After decomposing into four signatures, signatures were compared against validated single base substitution mutational catalogs retrieved from COSMIC (https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/signatures/), and cosine similarity was calculated to identify the best match. Analysis of significantly mutated genes The significance of mutated genes was evaluated in tumors by MutSigCV (version 1.4) (76) in GenePattern, and mutated genes were deemed significant above the background mutation rate if FDR for the genes was less than 0.1. Comparison of significant mutation frequency in LCNEC with previous studies Combining previously reported WES or targeted sequencing cohorts (10, 12, 19, 20), we found differences in the distribution of the three significantly mutated genes (RB1, KEAP1, and STK11) across the cohorts. TMB and cancer-associated driver mutations TMB was calculated via the R package “maftools” (version 2.16.0). Cancer-associated driver mutations were acquired from DriverDBv3 (21). Estimation of APOBEC enrichment score Deaminase effects of APOBEC were preferentially found in TCW motif, especially resulting in C-to-G or C-to-A substitution. On the basis of these characteristics, APOBEC enrichment score was calculated using the method reported by Roberts et al. (77). Briefly, for each sample, the APOBEC enrichment score was calculated as the ratio of the proportion of C>T and C>G substitutions occurring within TCW motifs to the background frequency of TCW motifs in the 20-bp regions surrounding the mutated bases. Reverse-strand effects were also taken into account in the score estimation. Copy number variation calling Somatic copy number variation (CNV) with discrete copy number segments was determined using the copy number calling pipeline of CNVkit (version 0.9.6) (78). These were further examined using GISTIC (version 2.0.23) (79) to identify gained or lost focal-level and arm-level events as well as CNV at the gene level. Q value less than 0.25 was considered significant. To exclude more false positives, a log2 ratio greater than 0.4 or less than −0.4 was deemed as the threshold for gain or loss, respectively. Default value was used for other parameters. RNA quantification After the removal of adaptors and low-quality reads, RNA-seq cleaned sequence data were aligned to human reference sequence hg38 using STAR (version 2.7.6a) (80). The resulting BAM files were analyzed for gene expression using Salmon (version 1.3.0) (81) against a transcriptomic reference GENCODE (version 22, https://gencodegenes.org). Then, the resulting gene-level counts for protein-coding genes were normalized and transformed into transcripts per million values, followed by applying log2 transformation. Data rows of redundant gene symbols were aggregated by calculating the average expression values. Batch effects were adjusted using the “combat” function in the R package “sva” (version 3.48.0).Proteomic and phosphoproteomic data analysis MS database searching MS raw files generated by LC-MS/MS were searched against the UniProt human proteome database (version , 20,404 sequences) using MaxQuant (version 1.6.5.0) software enabled with Andromeda search engine. TMT 11-plex–based MS3 reporter ion quantification was chosen with reporter mass tolerance set at 0.003 Da. The precursor intensity fraction (PIF) filter value was set at 0.5 to reduce the interference of precursor cofragmentation. Carbamidomethyl (C) was considered as a fixed modification. In proteomic data analysis, variable modifications were oxidized methionine (M), acetylation (protein N-term), and asparagine and glutamine (NQ) deamidation. In phosphoproteomic data analysis, oxidized methionine (M), acetylation (protein N-term), asparagine and glutamine (NQ) deamidation, and phospho (S/T/Y) were set as variable modifications. The cutoff of FDR by using a target-decoy strategy was 1% for peptides, proteins, and phosphorylation sites. A maximum number of five modifications per peptide were allowed for each peptide. Enzyme specificity was set as trypsin. The maximum missing cleavage site was set as 2. The tolerances of the first search and main search for peptides were set at 20 and 4.5 parts per million (ppm), respectively. The minimal peptide length was set at 7. The leading PCs of the global proteomic and phosphoproteomic data clearly separated the tumor from normal samples, and no obvious batch effect was observed among the 21 TMT batches. Data normalization We corrected sample loading differences by normalizing data using a median centering method across total proteins or phosphorylation sites. The log2 TMT ratio for these proteins or phosphorylation sites should be zero in normalized samples. Normalized proteins/phosphorylation sites with SwissProt ID were converted to Human Genome Nomenclature Committee’s HUGO symbols provided by HGNC (https://genenames.org). Identification of high-potential candidate samples for targeted therapies For each of the three targeted therapies, i.e., RTK inhibitors, HDAC inhibitors, and complex Ii, we proposed samples to be high-potential candidates for response to these three therapeutic strategies if they have both a high level of pathway activity targetable by the drug and a high level of candidates reflecting the pathway activity. For RTK inhibitors, the pathway and candidates are AXL, PDGFRA, and PDGFRB. For HDAC inhibitors, the pathway and candidates are HDAC sensitivity score and HDAC1 to 6 protein expression, respectively. For complex Ii, the pathway and molecular signature is the PI3K-NEU score in the protein level. We required that the level of both pathways and molecular signatures from high-potential samples be significantly higher than the rest of tumor samples (i.e., low-potential candidates). For each feature in the molecular signatures and pathways mentioned above, we performed univariate k-means clustering to cluster samples into low or high groups (k = 2 for HDACi, k = 4 for RTKi, and k = 3 for complex Ii) using the “Ckmeans.1d.dp” R package (102). Samples were assigned to the “high potential” group if they belonged to the “high” group based on the pathway clustering and simultaneously belonged to the “high” group based on the clustering of at least one of the molecule signatures.
