The methodology established by Møller (2020) was used to purify, amplify, and sequence eccDNA from Untransformed MRC5, MRC5E6E7, and glioma patient tissue samples (Supplemental Fig. S3). Approximately 7.5 × 105 cells or 4 mm glioma tissue biopsies were harvested and processed for circular DNA extraction using the plasmid mini AX DNA kit (A&A Biotechnology). Digestion with Proteinase K was for 48 h at 700 RPM and 50°C; reduction of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) with MssI (PmeI) was for 1 h at 37°C; and elimination of linear genomic DNA involved five sequential doses of 25 U/sample plasmid-safe DNase (Biosearch Technologies) over 36 h at 37°C. Purified eccDNA were amplified by rolling circle amplification (RCA) with φ29 polymerase (Qiagen REPLI-g mini kit) over 60 h and were visualized by SYBR gold staining of electrophoresed products. Amplified eccDNA were sheared to 300–500 bp by ultrasonication with the Covaris M220 for Illumina 150 bp paired-end sequencing. Libraries from 500 ng sheared eccDNA were prepared utilizing the NEBNext Ultra II DNA library prep kit for Illumina and indices supplied in the NEBNext multiplex oligos for Illumina (primer sets 1–3). Agilent TapeStation analyses were performed at multiple stages to verify yields and size profiles. Samples were multiplexed and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq.Parallel Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) long-read sequencing experiments were also performed for Untransformed MRC5 and Early- and Deep-crisis MRC5E6E7 cells, as well as a single glioma tumor sample in pre- and post-RCA formats. To preserve long-read integrity, eccDNA samples were debranched with T7 endonuclease I for 1 h at 37°C, purified using Agencourt AMPure XP magnetic beads at a 1:1 ratio, and visualized by SYBR gold staining of electrophoresed products. Multiplexed amplicon libraries were prepared using the SMRTbell prep kit 3.0 (102-182-700) in conjunction with the SMRTbell barcoded adapter plate 3.0 (102-009-200). Verification and sizing of amplicons were conducted using an Agilent fragment analyzer system and Qubit 4 Fluorometer. One hundred nanograms of each adapted amplicon was pooled for PacBio sequencing using the Sequel II sequencing kit 2.0 (102-194-400) and SMRT cell 8m single-use tray (102-281-700). Sequencing was over 30 h, resulting in 15 Gb HiFi reads.Targeted capture sequencing experimentsFor a focused investigation of genomic instability during replicative crisis, a custom targeted capture panel was designed incorporating 68 genes recurrently identified in our SV data sets; three with full-length probe coverage, 64 with exon-only (coding and UTR with 50 bp flanks) coverage, and one intronic MSI locus. The panel additionally contained probes for capturing potentially unstable repeat elements, including selected LINE, centromeric satellites, subtelomere sequences, tRNA and rRNA clusters, G-quadruplex binding motifs, and an MSI locus (details available on request). The custom panel was synthesized and quality validated by Twist Bioscience.The Twist Bioscience cfDNA library preparation kit was used to prepare sequencing libraries from 50 ng each of MRC5 Untransformed and MRC5E6e7 Early-crisis (PD23), Deep-crisis (PD47), and Late-crisis (PD57) genomic DNA that had been sheared (Covaris) to a mean fragment size of 350 bp. Amplified libraries were subjected to a 16 h hybridization with the custom probe panel at 70°C in a thermocycler. Following targeted enrichment, multiplexed libraries were sequenced using Illumina NextSeq 550 high-output 300 cycle (2 × 150 bp) flow cell and reagents to achieve approximately 1500× coverage of the 8 Mb panel.Code availabilityNew computer code developed in this research is available at GitHub (https://github.com/e-coral) and as Supplemental Code.Data accessAll raw and curated sequencing data generated in this study have been submitted to the NCBI BioProject database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/) under the accession number PRJNA1181623.Supplemental upplement 1Supplement 2

title: Systemic management of adrenal malignancies: adrenocortical carcinoma and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma
abstract: Adrenal malignancies include adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL), rare endocrine tumors that share an adrenal or extra-adrenal location but differ substantially in origin, hormonal activity, molecular alterations, metastatic potential, and systemic treatment. In ACC, management is guided by stage, resectability, Ki-67, hormone secretion, tumor and pace of progression. Mitotane remains the central ACC-specific therapy, used according to recurrence risk after surgery and as monotherapy in selected patients with advanced, low-volume disease. When rapid tumor control is needed, etoposide, doxorubicin, cisplatin, and mitotane remain the standard first-line regimen. Immune checkpoint inhibitors and multikinase inhibitors have shown activity in some patients, but validated predictive biomarkers are lacking, and access across Europe is limited by reimbursement differences. In later lines, chemotherapy may still be appropriate, including platinum rechallenge in selected cases. PPGL care is increasingly driven by genetics, biochemistry, and functional imaging. Germline testing, biochemical phenotype, and imaging findings are essential for risk assessment and treatment choice. Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and dacarbazine may be considered for aggressive disease, rapid growth, or high tumor burden. Targeted and radiopharmaceutical approaches have expanded options, including high-specific-activity 131I-iobenguane for MIBG-avid tumors, 177Lu-DOTATATE for somatostatin receptor-positive disease, antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and HIF-2α inhibition with belzutifan in selected molecular contexts. For both ACC and PPGL, controlling steroid or catecholamine excess is crucial because endocrine complications affect treatment tolerance and outcomes. Future progress requires robust biomarkers, rational treatment sequencing, and trials using disease-specific endpoints beyond radiographic response and integrating patient-centered endocrine, molecular, and overall clinical measures of benefit.
full_text: Adrenal malignancies fall into two biologically and clinically distinct groups: adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) and paragangliomas, including intra-adrenal paragangliomas historically termed pheochromocytomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas (1). Because most systemic-therapy studies and clinical guidelines still use the abbreviation PPGL, we use PPGL as a pragmatic clinical term throughout this review. ACC and PPGL share an anatomic neighborhood but differ in cell of origin, endocrine phenotype, metastatic biology, and systemic treatment selection drivers. This review summarizes current evidence on systemic management of ACC and PPGL, with emphasis on biomarker-guided therapy, endocrine co-management, and emerging treatment sequencing strategies.Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) commonly presents in one of three clinical settings: endocrine syndromes secondary to steroid excess, symptoms related to local tumor mass effect, or incidental detection on imaging studies. Approximately 50–60% of patients have clinically overt hormone excess at diagnosis, most commonly hypercortisolism alone or combined cortisol–androgen secretion; isolated virilization is less frequent, while estrogenic or mineralocorticoid excess is uncommon. Mass-effect symptoms occur in roughly 30–40% of cases and may include abdominal or flank pain, abdominal fullness, nausea, vomiting, or early satiety. These endocrine phenotypes are clinically important not only for diagnosis but also for management, because severe cortisol excess can worsen hypertension, hypokalemia, diabetes, proximal myopathy, infection risk, and wound-healing complications. ACC is also associated with a meaningful postoperative venous thromboembolic risk (2, 3).PPGL classically manifests through catecholamine excess, with paroxysmal or sustained hypertension and spells of headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and anxiety (4); however, the clinical phenotype varies with catecholamine secretory pattern and tumor location (5). Diagnostic-accuracy studies established plasma free metanephrines and urinary fractionated metanephrines as the key biochemical confirmation tests before localization or intervention (6, 7). Preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade remains the conventional preparation for resection because tumor manipulation can trigger major hemodynamic instability (8). This is particularly relevant because invasive manipulation of an unrecognized catecholamine-secreting tumor, including adrenal biopsy, has precipitated hypertensive crises in primary reports; accordingly, adrenal biopsy should only be considered after pheochromocytoma has been biochemically excluded (9, 10). In contrast, head and neck paragangliomas are usually nonfunctional and commonly present with a neck mass, pulsatile tinnitus, hearing loss, hoarseness, or dysphagia (11, 12).Staging and prognostic factorsAdrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is conventionally staged with the ENSAT system. In practical terms, stage I denotes a tumor confined to the adrenal gland and measuring ≤5 cm (T1N0M0), stage II a tumor confined to the adrenal gland but >5 cm (T2N0M0), stage III locoregional extension and/or nodal involvement, and stage IV distant metastatic disease (13). Prognosis is driven primarily by stage, completeness of resection (14, 15), and tumor proliferative activity, with Ki-67 remaining one of the most informative routine markers (16); endocrine factors, especially autonomous cortisol secretion, also add prognostic information (17). Because these risk dimensions are not fully captured by stage alone, the S-GRAS score was developed to integrate Stage, Grade (Ki-67 grouped as 0–9%, 10–19%, and ≥20%), Resection status, Age, and tumor-related Symptoms (18). In the original multicenter ENSAT study, S-GRAS outperformed ENSAT stage or Ki-67 alone for progression-free and disease-specific survival and was proposed as a framework to personalize radiologic surveillance and adjuvant treatment decisions. A more recent external validation study supported its calibration and discriminatory capacity and suggested that higher S-GRAS categories may identify patients more likely to benefit from adjuvant mitotane (19), although prospective refinement with molecular biomarkers is still needed. Within this framework, high risk of recurrence after radical surgery is defined as ENSAT stage III, R1 resection, or Ki-67 > 10%, supporting consideration of adjuvant mitotane (20). Conversely, the ADIUVO randomized trial did not support routine adjuvant mitotane in completely resected low-/intermediate-risk disease (R0, stage I–III, Ki-67 ≤ 10%) (21).For paragangliomas, including intra-adrenal paragangliomas historically termed pheochromocytomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas, contemporary pathology no longer accepts a simple benign-versus-malignant dichotomy based on histology alone. The 2022 WHO classification emphasizes the paraganglioma family of tumors and recognizes intra-adrenal and extra-adrenal lesions within this spectrum (1). For clinical readability and consistency with systemic-therapy literature, the abbreviation PPGL is retained throughout this review. The same WHO classification emphasizes that any PPGL can have metastatic potential and that no single histologic feature reliably predicts metastatic behavior; accordingly, existing histologic scoring systems may be used as adjunctive risk tools, but they are not WHO-endorsed substitutes for clinical outcome. The same WHO framework incorporated AJCC staging specifically for pheochromocytoma and extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglioma, rather than for the entire PPGL spectrum. Subsequent cohort analyses suggest that AJCC TNM staging does correlate with overall survival (OS) (22), but the prognostic separation is driven mainly by the distinctly worse outcomes of stage IV disease, while discrimination among lower stages is more modest (23, 24). This has practical implications: risk assessment in PPGL should be multimodal, combining site, tumor size, catecholamine phenotype, genotype, metastatic status, and imaging behavior (25, 26) rather than relying on microscopic appearance alone.Diagnostic workupThe evaluation of suspected ACC should combine dedicated adrenal imaging, comprehensive steroid biochemical phenotyping, and expert pathology review (16, 20). A careful assessment for signs of hormone excess, a detailed hormonal workup to detect glucocorticoid, sex steroid, mineralocorticoid, and steroid precursor excess, and adrenal-focused imaging in all suspected cases, with chest CT added when suspicion is high for staging purposes, is needed (17, 20). Histopathology remains mandatory for definitive diagnosis and should report, at minimum, the Weiss score, exact Ki-67 index, resection status, and pathological stage, including capsular/surrounding tissue invasion and nodal status (20, 27). The 2022 WHO classification further underscores the diagnostic and prognostic relevance of vascular invasion (angioinvasion) and standardized Ki-67 assessment. Urine steroid metabolomics is best regarded as an emerging adjunct rather than universal standard of care, but the evidence base is substantial: in the EURINE-ACT prospective validation study, combining tumor size, unenhanced CT attenuation >20 HU, and urine steroid metabolomics markedly improved diagnostic stratification of adrenal masses (28), and postoperative longitudinal studies suggest that steroid fingerprinting can identify some ACC recurrences earlier than conventional imaging.PPGL diagnosis begins with biochemistry and proceeds to localization, staging, and hereditary risk assessment (6, 7, 29). Plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines are recommended as first-line biochemical tests, since they are more sensitive than direct catecholamine measurements for catecholamine-producing tumors (6, 7). Once biochemical evidence is obtained, anatomic imaging with CT or MRI is used for localization; CT is often first line for abdominal disease and operative planning, whereas MRI is especially useful for head and neck lesions, recurrent/metastatic disease, pediatric patients, and situations in which radiation exposure should be minimized (20). Functional imaging is then selected according to tumor location, genotype, metastatic risk, and therapeutic intent. Available modalities include 123I-MIBG, 18F-FDG, 18F-FDOPA, and 68Ga-labeled somatostatin receptor imaging (29); these studies are particularly valuable in metastatic, multifocal, extra-adrenal, SDHx-associated, or head-and-neck disease and can directly influence treatment selection, including whether a patient is a better theranostic candidate for 131I-MIBG- versus 177Lu-DOTATATE-based strategies. Because hereditary susceptibility is common (30, 31), germline genetic evaluation for all patients is supported after appropriate counseling.Disease biology: molecular drivers and prognostic factors in ACCACC is molecularly heterogeneous and is defined by recurrent lesions in tumor suppressors, developmental signaling pathways, and telomere-maintenance programs rather than by recurrent, readily targetable oncogenic addictions (32, 33, 34).Integrated genomic studies, including the TCGA cohort of 91 tumors, identified extensive chromosomal instability and copy-number disruption together with recurrent events affecting TP53 (21%), ZNRF3 (19%), CTNNB1 (16%), CDKN2A (15%), TERT (14%), and PRKAR1A (11%) (33). At the pathway level, these lesions converge on Wnt/β-catenin signaling (41%) and the p53/Rb/cell-cycle axis (44.9%), supporting a model in which pathway-defining alterations coexist with broad structural genomic damage (32, 33).IGF2 overexpression remains a hallmark transcriptomic feature, occurring in 86% of TCGA ACCs (33). However, the biological prominence of the IGF axis has not translated into broad clinical benefit in unselected patients; in a phase III trial, linsitinib failed to improve overall or progression-free survival (PFS) in advanced ACC (35). Telomere biology also has prognostic relevance: TCGA-identified TERT amplification in 14–15% of tumors (33), and a later combined analysis of 167 ACCs found TERT gains/amplifications in 22.2% of cases, with a higher frequency of metastatic behavior among TERT-altered tumors (70 vs 51.2% in tumors without TERT alterations) (36).ACC generally exhibits a low somatic mutation burden. In TCGA, the median mutation density was 0.9 mutations/Mb, although rare hypermutated or ultramutated outliers were observed, several with mismatch-repair defects (33). Consistent with this background, immune checkpoint inhibition in unselected ACC has shown variable but overall limited activity (37). Recent data further indicate that dMMR occurs in only a minority of ACCs (38), interestingly does not completely overlap with cases of microsatellite instability (MSI), and is not yet an established predictor of immunotherapy benefit in this disease, although its detection remains clinically relevant for hereditary cancer assessment.Epigenetic and transcriptomic subtypes with prognostic implicationsEpigenetic and transcriptomic stratification provides additional prognostic resolution. Genome-wide methylation studies identified a CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), and hypermethylated ACCs – subdivided into CIMP-low and CIMP-high groups – were associated with worse survival (39). TCGA subsequently integrated copy-number, DNA methylation, mRNA, and miRNA data into three cluster-of-clusters subtypes with markedly different outcomes, with disease progression rates of 7, 56, and 96%, respectively (30). These data underscore the prognostic value of multi-omic subclassification.PPGL biologyGenotype-defined disease and molecular architecturePPGL is best understood as a genotype-defined neoplasia rather than a tumor class whose biology can be inferred primarily from anatomic site or conventional histology. In the TCGA integrated analysis of 173 tumors, most cases could be assigned to a molecularly coherent driver framework based on pathogenic germline variants, recurrent somatic mutations, fusions, or copy-number events. TCGA organized PPGL into four principal molecular groups: pseudohypoxia, kinase signaling, Wnt-altered, and cortical admixture (30). The same study showed that MAML3 fusion-positive tumors were enriched among aggressive cases and emerged as a correlate of metastatic behavior. More recent single-nucleus and bulk-transcriptomic work refined this architecture further, resolving seven gene expression subtypes with distinct genotype, microenvironmental, and clinical associations (40). In practical terms, these data support the view that PPGL behavior is more tightly linked to its underlying molecular program than to its anatomic label alone.Pseudohypoxia and HIF-2α as a therapeutic axisAmong these programs, pseudohypoxia is the most therapeutically mature. It is particularly characteristic of tumors with VHL, SDHx, and related pathway alterations, although the downstream biology is not identical across genotypes. In a classic translational study, VHL-associated PPGLs showed relatively greater HIF-2α overexpression and higher expression of HIF-2 target genes, including VEGF and CCND1, whereas SDHB/SDHD-associated tumors more often showed nuclear HIF-1α staining (41, 42). More recent transcriptomic analysis has nevertheless shown that VHL-, SDHx-, and MAML3-fusion tumors converge on signatures of HIF signaling and neoangiogenesis (40), supporting pseudohypoxia as a shared actionable state even when the upstream lesion differs. This biology provided the rationale for HIF-2α inhibition with belzutifan (43).Tumor microenvironment and angiogenesisThe PPGL microenvironment also supports a vascularly targeted treatment paradigm, particularly in pseudohypoxic disease. Single-nucleus and bulk transcriptomics showed that PPGLs generally contain few infiltrating lymphocytes but abundant macrophages and that VHL, SDHx-, and MAML3-driven tumors are enriched for neoangiogenic programs (40). Earlier primary work likewise showed that cluster 1 tumors display increased vascularization and overexpression of major angiogenic mediators, including VEGF, VEGF receptors, HIF-2α, and angiopoietin-2 (44). Even before modern molecular clustering, pathology studies had already linked angiogenesis to aggressive behavior: metastatic pheochromocytomas showed higher VEGF expression and microvessel density than nonmetastatic tumors, and anti-VEGF antibodies suppressed angiogenesis in experimental pheochromocytoma xenografts (45, 46). Taken together, these data make abnormal angiogenesis not just a correlative feature but also a biologically plausible therapeutic dependency in at least a subset of PPGLs.This antiangiogenic rationale is now supported by prospective clinical trials. In FIRSTMAPPP (47), the first randomized trial in metastatic progressive PPGL, sunitinib met its primary endpoint, with 12-month PFS of 36 versus 19% with placebo. In the single-arm phase 2 Natalie trial (48), cabozantinib produced an objective response rate (ORR) of 25% in evaluable patients, with manageable toxicity and no grade 4 adverse events. Lenvatinib and axitinib have shown encouraging activity (49), yet the evidence base remains much less robust than that for sunitinib or cabozantinib.Biochemical and functional biomarkersUnlike most solid tumors, PPGL provides direct biochemical readouts of tumor activity, principally catecholamines and their O-methylated metabolites, with chromogranin A (CgA) serving as a complementary marker in selected settings, especially in some nonfunctional tumors and during follow-up. In a retrospective cohort of 61 patients with measured CgA at diagnosis, CgA was elevated in 86.9% overall, including 61.5% of nonfunctional PPGLs, supporting its role as an adjunct rather than a replacement for catecholamine-/metanephrine-based monitoring (50).Biochemical response and morphologic response, however, are not interchangeable endpoints. In a multicenter phase II trial of single-dose 131I-MIBG for refractory PPGL, the primary biochemical response rate, defined as a ≥50% reduction in urinary catecholamines, was 23.5%, whereas the RECIST CT/MRI response rate was only 5.9%. In a separate biomarker analysis from the pivotal phase II trial of high-specific-activity (HSA) 131I-MIBG, biochemical tumor marker response correlated only modestly with objective response (r = 0.36) and with durable reduction in antihypertensive medication use (r = 0.35) (51, 52). These data argue against treating biochemical improvement as a mere surrogate for radiographic shrinkage; instead, biochemical control should be followed as a parallel clinical endpoint, particularly in hormonally active disease where symptom burden and cardiovascular risk may improve even without major RECIST response.Functional imaging biomarkers are equally central and are best understood as theranostic biomarkers, because they reflect the underlying molecular machinery required for radionuclide uptake. 123I-MIBG targets the chromaffin catecholamine-handling complex, mainly plasma membrane norepinephrine transporter (NET) and vesicular monoamine transport systems; and its uptake has been linked to genotype-dependent transporter expression patterns in PPGL (51, 53).In parallel, SSTR2 expression identifies a biologically distinct subgroup: in a 202-patient cohort, SSTR2 positivity was independently associated with SDHB/SDHx-related disease and with metastatic PPGL, and among metastatic cases the disease control rate (DCR) with first-line SSTR-based radionuclide therapy was 67% (54). These findings mean that MIBG avidity and SSTR expression help determine whether a given tumor is biologically better suited to 131I-MIBG-based treatment or to SSTR-directed radiopharmaceutical strategies, such as 177Lu-DOTATATE.A practical implication is that biomarker assessment in PPGL should be multidimensional: secretory markers capture endocrine activity, whereas MIBG- and SSTR-based imaging captures target biology relevant to treatment selection. In metastatic or SDHx-related disease, the strong performance of 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT (29) relative to other imaging modalities reinforces the value of receptor-based imaging not only for staging but also for radionuclide eligibility assessment.Indications for systemic therapy and decision-makingIn both adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL), the decision to initiate systemic therapy should not be based on metastatic status alone, but on whether disease is unresectable, symptomatic, progressive, or no longer amenable to potentially meaningful local treatment. In ACC, retrospective studies of recurrent and metastatic disease showed that selected patients can derive prolonged survival and endocrine palliation from resection of recurrence, cytoreductive surgery, or other local metastasis-directed strategies, particularly when disease-free interval is longer and tumor biology is less aggressive (55, 56, 57). These data support integrating tumor burden, resectability, endocrine activity, Ki-67/tumor biology, and disease tempo into the decision, rather than reflexively defaulting to systemic therapy at first evidence of metastatic spread.In PPGL, treatment selection is similarly governed by clinical behavior rather than anatomy alone. Long-term cohort data show that the course of PPGL can be relatively indolent in some patients (58), whereas specialized-center treatment cohorts indicate that systemic therapy is most often deployed in patients with documented progression at baseline, high disease burden, or clinically relevant symptoms (59). This supports a pragmatic distinction between patients who may be followed with active surveillance and those who require escalation because of progression, symptomatic disease, or higher-risk biology.For PPGL specifically, radionuclide versus non-radionuclide therapy is informed in part by functional-imaging phenotype (54). In specialized multicenter cohorts of metastatic PPGL, first-line disease control has been observed with both 131I-MIBG (51) and somatostatin receptor-based radionuclide therapy (PRRT) (60), while molecular imaging studies show that MIBG uptake correlates with catecholamine transporter biology and that SSTR2 expression/SSTR imaging is enriched in SDHx-related and metastatic disease (54). This does not yet amount to prospective sequencing evidence, but it does provide a biologic basis for choosing MIBG-directed versus SSTR-directed theranostic strategies in individual patients.Endocrine morbidity is a parallel indication for escalation. In ACC, retrospective surgical series of recurrent disease showed that local treatment could palliate hypercortisolism, and modern metastatic analyses identify hormone excess as an adverse prognostic feature (57). In PPGL, this principle is directly embedded in prospective trial design: in the phase 2 study of HSA 131I-MIBG, the primary endpoint was a durable ≥50% reduction in baseline antihypertensive medication, achieved in 25% of treated patients (51); in LITESPARK-015, belzutifan produced a sustained ≥50% reduction in at least one antihypertensive medication in 32% of patients who were receiving antihypertensives at baseline (43). These studies support treating biochemical and cardiovascular/endocrine morbidity as clinically meaningful targets in their own right, even when radiographic change is modest.Finally, management in expert multidisciplinary boards is recommended. In ACC, surgery at high-volume centers has been associated with lower recurrence and longer time to recurrence (61), plausibly reflecting both technical expertise and more coordinated multidisciplinary care.Systemic therapy in ACCTable 1 summarizes the principal systemic therapies used in advanced ACC, highlighting the study source underlying each efficacy signal and the clinical setting in which each regimen has been evaluated.Table 1Selected systemic therapies in advanced ACC.TherapyClinical study (design; ORR, objective response rate; OS, overall survival; PFS, progression-free survival; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease.MitotaneMitotane remains the defining ACC-specific systemic drug and, according to the current US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) prescribing information, the only agent specifically indicated for inoperable, functional, or nonfunctional adrenocortical carcinoma. Its clinical utility is nevertheless highly context-dependent. In advanced ACC, mitotane monotherapy is best viewed as a relatively slow-acting treatment for selected patients with more indolent biology and lower tumor burden, whereas patients with rapidly progressive or high-burden disease are generally better served by more active combination strategies, such as EDP-M (etoposide, doxorubicin, cisplatin plus mitotane), as established in FIRM-ACT (62, 63).In advanced disease, the strongest contemporary efficacy dataset for mitotane monotherapy is the multicenter German series of 127 patients, in which the ORR was 20.5%, including 3 complete remissions, with median PFS 4.1 months and median OS 18.5 months. Benefit was not uniform: low tumor burden ( 14 mg/L was associated with longer OS (HR: 0.42; P = 0.003) (63). These data support mitotane monotherapy mainly in lower- less aggressive ACC, rather than as the default approach for all advanced cases.By contrast, in the adjuvant setting, the evidence is clearly risk-adapted rather than universal. Early multicenter retrospective studies suggested that adjuvant mitotane for 2 years could prolong recurrence-free survival after radical surgery, with the original 2007 case–control study showing markedly longer median recurrence-free survival in treated patients and the later long-term follow-up confirming a persistent recurrence-free survival advantage (64). However, the randomized ADIUVO trial showed that, in low-grade, localized, completely resected ACC, there was no significant benefit of routine adjuvant mitotane over surveillance: the 5-year recurrence-free survival was 79 versus 75% (HR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.30–1.85) and the 5-year OS was 95 versus 86%; all treated patients had adverse events and 19% discontinued therapy (21). An interpretation, therefore, is that postoperative mitotane is best reserved for patients with clinicopathologic features consistently associated with higher recurrence risk – particularly ENSAT stage III, microscopically positive margins, or Ki-67 > 10% – rather than used routinely after every resection.Therapeutic drug monitoring is central to mitotane use. The current FDA label recommends a starting dose of 2,000–6,000 mg/day in 3–4 divided doses with food, with titration to a plasma concentration of 14–20 mg/L and monitoring every 2 weeks after initiation and dose adjustment; the label also notes that the therapeutic range is usually reached only after 3–5 months, which helps explain why mitotane alone is frequently inadequate for rapidly progressive disease. Primary adjuvant studies support the biological relevance of that exposure target: in a six-center European series, reaching and maintaining ≥14 mg/L was associated with a lower recurrence risk (HR: 0.418, 95% CI: 0.22–0.79; P = 0.007), and in a later multicenter Italian cohort, both time to reach target range and time spent in target range independently correlated with lower recurrence risk (65, 66). Together, these studies argue that the therapeutic window should be treated as a dynamic exposure goal, not merely as a single static laboratory threshold.Mechanistically, mitotane still occupies an unusual position: the FDA label continues to describe its mechanism of action as unknown, but translational work has shown that mitotane inhibits SOAT1, causing accumulation of free cholesterol and other toxic lipids, induction of endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and adrenal-selective apoptosis in ACC cells. That mechanistic insight has not translated into a usable predictive biomarker (67). In the ENSAT multicenter validation study, SOAT1 protein expression did not predict recurrence-free survival, PFS, disease-specific survival, or response to mitotane monotherapy in either adjuvant or advanced settings (18, 68). Thus, SOAT1 is best described as a plausible mechanistic target, not as a validated tool for treatment selection.Cytotoxic chemotherapyFor advanced ACC requiring rapid tumor control, particularly in patients with symptomatic, bulky, or rapidly progressive disease, EDP-M remains the best validated first-line cytotoxic regimen, because it is supported by the only randomized phase III trial conducted specifically in advanced ACC. In FIRM-ACT, 304 patients were randomized to EDP-M or streptozotocin–mitotane; EDP-M achieved a higher ORR (23.2 vs 9.2%) and longer median PFS (5.0 vs 2.1 months), whereas OS was not significantly different (14.8 vs 12.0 months; HR: 0.79, 95% CI: 0.61–1.02; P = 0.07) (62). Because crossover to the alternate regimen after progression was mandated by protocol, the overall survival comparison is difficult to interpret as a pure first-line effect. Centralizing patients in referral centers allows optimal utilization of this type of treatment, preventing early discontinuation, reducing toxicity, and facilitating the integration of local therapeutic strategies (69, 70). Accordingly, EDP-M is best viewed as the regimen for patients whose disease tempo requires a more immediately active strategy, whereas mitotane monotherapy is more defensible in lower- slower-evolving disease; in the largest contemporary mitotane monotherapy series, low tumor burden ( 56.4 monthsSomatostatin analogs (octreotide LAR/lanreotide)Retrospective multicenter cohort; n = 202 overall, with 6 metastatic PPGL treated first-line with ‘cold’ SSAMetastatic SSTR2-positive PPGLDCR 100% in first-line treated cases (n = 6)CR, complete response; MIBG, meta-iodobenzylguanidine; ORR, objective response rate; OS, overall survival; PFS, progression-free survival; PPGL, pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma; PR, partial response; PRRT, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy; SSTR, somatostatin receptor; DCR, disease control rate; HSA, high-specific-activity.Radioligand therapiesAmong radiopharmaceuticals, HSA 131I-iobenguane provided important proof that radionuclide therapy can deliver both antitumor and functional benefit in MIBG-avid disease. In the pivotal phase II study, 25% of treated patients achieved a ≥50% reduction in baseline antihypertensive medication maintained for at least 6 months; the FDA review reported an overall RECIST response rate of 22%, 92% of evaluable patients had partial response or stable disease as best response within 12 months, and the median OS was 36.7 months (51). In practice, however, HSA 131I-iobenguane is no longer commercially available and is not a routinely prescribable option in current practice, because commercial production was halted after early 2024.For SSTR-positive disease, 177Lu-DOTATATE PRRT has moved beyond anecdotal use into a more substantive evidence base. In the recent prospective phase II study of progressive metastatic PPGL, the 6-month PFS rate was 86.1%, the median PFS was 19.9 months, the median OS was 51.7 months, and grade ≥ 3 catecholamine release syndrome occurred in 17% (60), emphasizing the need for careful adrenergic preparation and, in selected patients, intensive monitoring. A recent single-institution cohort also reported encouraging outcomes, with ORR 27%, DCR 73%, median PFS 26.9 months, and median OS 54.8 months (84). Taken together, these data support an imaging-matched radionuclide strategy in which MIBG-avid tumors are considered for iobenguane-based therapy, whereas SSTR-positive tumors are preferentially considered for PRRT.Cytotoxic chemotherapyCytotoxic chemotherapy remains important when rapid cytoreduction or urgent hormonal control is required. Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and dacarbazine (CVD) is still the main regimen in this setting. In the seminal prospective single-arm study, CVD produced complete or partial radiographic responses in 57% of patients and complete or partial biochemical responses in 79%, with parallel improvements in blood pressure and performance status among responders (85). Longer follow-up of this trial confirmed that CVD can produce meaningful tumor and symptomatic control, although cure is not expected and the evidence base remains limited by small, heterogeneous cohorts (86).Temozolomide has become the most biologically compelling cytotoxic alternative, particularly in SDHB-mutated disease (59, 87). In the original 15-patient French series, temozolomide achieved partial responses in 33%, stable disease in 47%, and a median PFS of 13.3 months (87). Importantly, all objective responses occurred in SDHB-mutant tumors, and responders showed MGMT promoter hypermethylation and low MGMT expression, making this the clearest existing example of genotype-informed chemotherapy selection in PPGL. A later Dana-Farber series also supported temozolomide activity, with RECIST partial responses in 40% of evaluable patients, although the biomarker–response relationship remains strongest for the SDHB/MGMT axis rather than for temozolomide use in unselected PPGL (88).Targeted therapiesAmong targeted therapies, antiangiogenic TKIs remain the best established non-radionuclide option for radiographically progressive disease. FIRSTMAPPP provided the first randomized evidence in PPGL and established sunitinib as the TKI with the highest level of evidence in this setting: the trial met its prespecified primary endpoint with a 12-month PFS of 36 versus 19% for placebo and a median PFS of 8.9 versus 3.6 months (47). Objective responses are described in approximately one-third of sunitinib-treated patients, with exploratory signals of higher activity in SDHB-related disease, although those subgroup findings remain hypothesis-generating.Cabozantinib is the strongest alternative, with the phase II NATALIE trial showing ORR 25%, median PFS 16.6 months, and median OS 24.9 months (48). Anlotinib has also shown notable activity in retrospective real-world data, with ORR 44.4%, disease control 96.3%, and median PFS 25.2 months, but those results still require prospective validation (89). Axitinib, a more selective VEGFR inhibitor, has been explored in a small phase II trial, and outcomes suggest partial responses in 36% and stable disease in 54% (49). Across the TKI class, hypertension, fatigue, mucosal toxicity, and frequent dose modification are common, which makes pretreatment catecholamine optimization and close hemodynamic monitoring essential.HIF-2α and rare genotype-selective targeted therapyBelzutifan has now defined a separate targeted axis in PPGL by directly exploiting HIF-2α-driven pseudohypoxic biology (30). In the phase II LITESPARK-015 PPGL cohort (n = 72), confirmed ORR was 26%, disease control 85%, median duration of response 20.4 months, median PFS 22.3 months, and 24-month OS 76% (43). Importantly, benefit extended beyond radiographic response: among patients receiving antihypertensive therapy at baseline, 32% achieved a sustained ≥50% reduction in at least one antihypertensive medication, reinforcing a PPGL-specific definition of efficacy that includes control of catecholamine-driven hypertension. Based on this trial, belzutifan received FDA approval for adult and pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic PPGL; however, at the time of this revision, this PPGL indication should be regarded as FDA-approved rather than globally approved, and access outside the United States remains jurisdiction-specific.By contrast, genotype-selective kinase inhibition currently applies only to rare subsets. In the first LIBRETTO-001 report of RET-mutant pheochromocytoma, four of six patients achieved a partial or complete response and the remaining two had stable disease, with some patients remaining on therapy for years and with biochemical improvement documented in selected cases; this argues for broad molecular profiling in metastatic PPGL when clinical behavior is aggressive or standard options are limited (90).Finally, non-radiolabeled somatostatin analogs should be viewed as low-toxicity options for indolent SSTR-expressing disease, or as part of a broader SSTR-targeted strategy that may later include PRRT, rather than as established antitumor standards. In the largest SSTR2 expression series, first-line ‘cold’ somatostatin analogs achieved disease control in six out of six metastatic cases, but the evidence base remains too small and largely extrapolative (54). More definitive data are awaited from the ongoing LAMPARA study (NCT03946527).Endocrine-specific management during systemic therapyOptimal endocrine co-management is essential for the safe and effective delivery of systemic therapy in adrenal malignancies. In ACC, uncontrolled steroid excess is not a minor comorbidity: cortisol-secreting tumors are associated with higher postoperative morbidity, adrenal insufficiency, and shorter recurrence-free survival, and ACC surgery itself carries a substantial postoperative venous thromboembolic burden (3, 15, 20). In parallel, glucocorticoid excess in ACC is linked to reduced tumor-infiltrating T-cell density and particularly poor outcomes, supporting the idea that endocrine control is relevant not only for metabolic stabilization but also for tumor-immune biology (91, 92). In PPGL, inadequate catecholamine control can turn surgery, invasive procedures, or even cancer-directed treatment into major hemodynamic events, which is why endocrine optimization should be treated as a co-primary therapeutic objective, not as ancillary supportive care (93, 94).In cortisol-secreting ACC, endocrine stabilization should ideally precede intensive oncologic therapy whenever clinically feasible. Several practical strategies deserve emphasis. First, severe hypercortisolism should be lowered rapidly with steroidogenesis inhibitors rather than waiting for mitotane alone, whose antisecretory effect is delayed. Metyrapone is often preferred when prompt control is required and may be combined with mitotane and cytotoxic therapy; when monotherapy is insufficient, combination metyrapone–ketoconazole can produce rapid biochemical improvement, including in ACC (95). Osilodrostat is another potent steroidogenesis inhibitor that may be considered when available, with careful monitoring for adrenal insufficiency, hypokalemia, hypertension, and accumulation of steroid precursors (96, 97). Mifepristone may be useful for clinical control of hypercortisolism in selected patients, particularly when rapid glucocorticoid receptor antagonism is needed, although biochemical cortisol levels cannot be used to monitor response (98). Ketoconazole or levoketoconazole may lower cortisol, but concomitant use with mitotane should generally be avoided or approached with extreme caution because of overlapping hepatotoxicity and complex drug–drug interactions (99, 100). Intravenous etomidate remains an accepted rescue option in critically ill patients or when oral therapy is not possible (101). Second, cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid effects should be corrected aggressively with potassium supplementation plus spironolactone (102); eplerenone is a reasonable alternative when antiandrogenic adverse effects or tolerability are concerns. In refractory cases, amiloride may also be considered (97). Serum electrolytes often need to be checked several times weekly early in treatment. Third, because overt hypercortisolism confers major infectious and thrombotic risk, guidelines recommend anticoagulation and Pneumocystis-directed prophylaxis until cortisol is safely controlled. More recent consensus work in endogenous Cushing’s syndrome further supports considering low-molecular-weight heparin from diagnosis through approximately 3 months after biochemical remission (103), although this duration is extrapolated from the broader Cushing literature rather than from ACC-specific trials.Mitotane adds a second layer of endocrine management that should be approached proactively. Glucocorticoid replacement should be initiated in all mitotane-treated patients without persistent cortisol excess; because mitotane induces CYP3A4 and increases cortisol-binding globulin (104), at least double the usual replacement dose is typically required. More physiological glucocorticoids, such as hydrocortisone, cortisone acetate, or prednisone, are generally preferred, and many centers start hydrocortisone at 40–50 mg/day in two or three divided doses, with some patients requiring up to 100 mg/day.Monitoring should be clinical and biochemical, including symptoms, postural blood pressure, electrolytes, ACTH when informative, and mitotane levels every 3–4 weeks until stable and then every 2–3 months thereafter; most groups continue to target concentrations >14 mg/L, while neurologic toxicity becomes more common above 20 mg/L (20). After resection of a cortisol-producing ACC, perioperative stress-dose hydrocortisone is mandatory, and if immune checkpoint blockade is being considered, minimizing endogenous and exogenous glucocorticoid exposure as much as safely possible is biologically sensible, given the association between glucocorticoid excess, lower T-cell infiltration, and worse outcome in ACC (105).In PPGL, the most practical endocrine targets remain physiologic rather than radiographic (93, 94). Current practice standards recommend α-adrenergic blockade for at least 7–14 days before surgery or another major intervention, with volume re-expansion using liberal salt and fluid intake. Proposed targets are sitting blood pressure 10 days, and depot antipsychotics for about 1 month, when clinically safe (107). For PRRT, the NANETS/SNMMI procedure standard recommends confirming hemoglobin > 8 g/dL, WBC > 2 k/mm3, platelets >70 k/mm3, eGFR >50 mL/min, bilirubin ≤3 × ULN, and albumin >3.0 g/dL, together with prophylactic lysine/arginine amino acid nephroprotection and structured hematologic, renal, and hepatic follow-up after treatment (108).Across both ACC and PPGL, adrenal insufficiency should be anticipated after bilateral adrenalectomy, after withdrawal from chronic cortisol excess, during mitotane therapy, and after treatment-related hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal suppression. Standard sick-day rules, therefore, need to be embedded in the cancer pathway. In primary adrenal insufficiency, oral hydrocortisone is typically doubled for fever >38°C and tripled for fever >39°C until recovery; if oral intake is compromised, 100 mg intramuscular or subcutaneous hydrocortisone should be given urgently. Suspected adrenal crisis requires immediate 100 mg intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone, rapid isotonic saline resuscitation, and continuation of hydrocortisone at 200 mg over 24 h (continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 h). In patients with proven mineralocorticoid deficiency, such as after bilateral adrenalectomy, fludrocortisone 50–100 μg/day is a standard starting replacement and should be titrated to symptoms, blood pressure, electrolytes, and renin. Steroid emergency cards, written sick-day instructions, and access to emergency injectable hydrocortisone should be considered mandatory.Future directions, key ongoing trials, and research gapsIn ACC, the most consequential unanswered questions are now treatment selection questions rather than purely descriptive ones: which patients truly require upfront intensification, whether post-EDP maintenance can delay progression, and which biomarkers can be developed into decision-grade tools for adjuvant and second-line management (109, 110). A central finding from the largest molecular classification study is that targeted multi-omic classifiers are most informative in localized stage I–III disease after complete resection, where they independently refine recurrence risk, whereas their discriminative value is clearly weaker in stage IV ACC (110). In parallel, minimally invasive biomarkers are becoming more credible but are not yet ready for routine treatment assignment: circulating cell-free DNA has shown prognostic and disease-monitoring potential in a prospective translational cohort (109), and a prospective serum steroid profiling study suggests that blood-based steroid signatures may provide a more deployable alternative to urine steroid profiling for noninvasive ACC characterization (111). Taken together, these studies suggest that the translational priority in ACC is the prospective validation of biomarker-guided risk stratification and treatment allocation.The current ACC trial pipeline (see Table 3) reflects that shift. ADIUVO-2 (NCT03583710) is the most important ongoing phase III study because it tests risk-adapted adjuvant intensification, randomizing high-risk resected ACC to mitotane alone versus mitotane plus cisplatin/etoposide; the registry also specifies embedded exploratory biomarker work, including steroid hormones/precursors, circulating tumor cells, and microRNAs. PESETA (NCT05913427) is a randomized, double-blind phase II study asking whether first-line EDP-M can be intensified pharmacologically with megestrol acetate. INTERVAL (NCT07085572) addresses a different but equally practical question: whether cemiplimab maintenance after response or stabilization on first-line chemotherapy can prolong disease control. In advanced disease, combination strategies are now being tested more explicitly than monotherapies: NCT06900595 randomizes patients to cabozantinib plus cemiplimab versus cabozantinib alone, NCT06006013 evaluates cabozantinib plus pembrolizumab, and NCT06066333 studies ablative radiotherapy followed by pembrolizumab in metastatic ACC. The common theme across these studies is that the next ACC advances are more likely to come from adjuvant refinement, maintenance therapy, and pharmacology-aware TKI/ICI combinations than from a new single-agent empiric therapy.Table 3Selected ongoing or recent key clinical trials in adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC).TrialSetting/populationDesign/interventionPhaseIdentifierLatest public status/key noteADIUVO-2High-risk localized ACC after curative-intent surgeryMitotane vs mitotane + cisplatin/etoposideIIINCT03583710Ongoing multicenter randomized trialCaboACCAdvanced unresectable/metastatic ACC, generally after prior standard therapyCabozantinib monotherapyIINCT03612232Active, not recruiting; last update posted August 19, 2024PEMBR-01Advanced ACC with progression within 6 months after EDP or EDP-MPembrolizumabIINCT05563467Multicenter phase II trial; the latest registry update (April 2, 2025) lists as recruitingRelacorilant + pembrolizumabCortisol-producing/glucocorticoid-excess ACCRelacorilant + pembrolizumabIbNCT04373265Completed study; results pendingPembrolizumab + mitotaneAdvanced ACCPembrolizumab + mitotaneIINCT05634577Terminated because of slow accrual; actual enrollment was three patientsACC, adrenocortical carcinoma; EDP-M, etoposide, doxorubicin, cisplatin plus mitotane.In PPGL, the central research gap is no longer proof that active systemic options exist, but the absence of a prospective sequencing framework. Belzutifan and sunitinib now provide prospective evidence for targeted systemic therapy, while 177Lu-DOTATATE PRRT, 131I-MIBG, temozolomide, and CVD remain validated options in selected patients. The unresolved question is how best to choose and order these modalities according to disease tempo, functional imaging phenotype, catecholamine burden, genotype, and prior radiopharmaceutical exposure. Retrospective multicenter data show that several available treatments can achieve disease control, but cross-modality comparisons remain heavily confounded by baseline progression status, disease burden, and prior therapy.The most relevant ongoing/recent PPGL studies now cluster around three themes (see Table 4): first, DNA damage exploitation: A021804/NCT04394858 evaluates temozolomide with or without olaparib, representing the clearest current attempt to move alkylator therapy toward a biomarker-rational framework; In PPGL, RECIST response, biochemical control, antihypertensive medication reduction, and symptom improvement often diverge, so future sequencing trials should not rely on imaging alone.ACC and PPGL should not be approached as a single therapeutic entity. Although both arise in the adrenal region, their biology, endocrine complications, and treatment selection drivers are fundamentally different. In ACC, clinical decision-making remains anchored in resectability, Ki-67, hormone excess, and growth kinetics, with mitotane-based strategies and EDP-M continuing to define the therapeutic backbone. Targeted therapy and immunotherapy have expanded the salvage landscape, but their use remains limited by modest activity in unselected populations and by the absence of validated predictive biomarkers. In contrast, PPGL has moved further toward precision oncology, where genotype, pseudohypoxic biology, catecholamine burden, and functional imaging phenotype can directly inform treatment choice. HIF-2α inhibition, antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and imaging-matched radionuclide therapies have meaningfully broadened the options for progressive or metastatic disease, although regulatory approval and real-world availability vary substantially.Across both malignancies, endocrine optimization is not merely supportive care but also a determinant of treatment safety and outcome. The next major advance in adrenal oncology will likely come less from a single new drug than from better biomarker integration, more rational sequencing of systemic and radiopharmaceutical therapies, and prospective trials using clinically meaningful endpoints that capture hormonal control, symptom improvement, and durable disease stabilization in addition to radiographic response. Until these tools mature, management should remain centralized in expert multidisciplinary teams with experience in endocrine oncology, nuclear medicine, and complex supportive care.Declaration of interestThe authors declare that there is no conflict of interest that could be perceived as prejudicing the impartiality of the work reported.This work did not receive any specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sector.Author contribution statementJDR conceptualized and supervised the study. title: The WHO Classification of Genetic Tumour Syndromes: Considerations for Genetics
abstract: The WHO Classification of Tumours is used widely by histopathologists and other disciplines as it provides an internationally agreed taxonomy of neoplastic disorders. Now published online and in print, it has often included genetic tumour syndromes (GTS) relevant to particular organs, as suggested by the editorial board. This highlighted the lack of a systematic classification of GTS, providing international standards for their diagnosis and a basis for research. The need for this was established by a series of meetings, leading to the adoption of a hierarchical classification of GTS based on the cellular mechanism affected, the molecular pathway involved, the clinical syndrome and the gene defects present. The major cellular mechanisms affected were identified as: growth factor receptors and related pathways; oxidative stress response and metabolism; cell cycle and apoptosis; DNA repair and genomic stability; telomere maintenance; epigenetic drivers and chromatin; RNA regulation and protein regulation. Assembly of the classification emphasised current gaps in knowledge, together with the need for further research. The new classification highlights the relationships between some genetic syndromes and provides an internationally agreed framework for the incorporation of new information as it becomes available.
full_text: 1IntroductionThe diagnosis of patients and their families with genetic tumour predisposition syndromes has assumed increasing clinical importance, as it germline findings now directly influence surveillance, therapeutic decision‐making and risk assessment across multiple organ systems. The World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Tumours, provides the internationally accepted framework for tumour taxonomy, underpinning diagnostic practice worldwide and evolving through successive evidence‐based editions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] on a 5‐to‐6‐year cycle between editions, now completing the fifth edition WHO Classification of Tumours (WCT5) [2, 3, 4, 5].Despite this progress, genetic tumour syndromes (GTS) have historically been incorporated in a fragmented manner, typically as appendices to WHO organ‐specific classifications. This approach obscures biological relationships, limits cross‐disciplinary integration given that many disorders impact multiple tumour types and fails to reflect the mechanistic basis of tumour predisposition. At the same time, gene‐centric catalogues, while valuable, do not adequately capture the shared pathways and cellular processes through which diverse variants converge to drive neoplasia.To address this gap, we developed a hierarchical classification of GTS based on four linked levels: cellular mechanism, molecular pathway, clinical syndrome and genetic change (Figure 1). This structure reflects the biological architecture of tumour predisposition, allowing syndromes to be grouped by shared mechanisms while preserving clinical and genetic specificity. The resulting framework provides a simplified but extensible ontology that supports both diagnostic application and the systematic incorporation of emerging knowledge.FIGURE 1An example of the hierarchical classification for GTS for RAD51‐related cancer predisposition showing the cellular mechanism, pathway, syndrome and genes involved.A diagram depicts 4 left to right pointed banner boxes detailing classification categories, cellular mechanisms categories, pathways families, syndromes, and genes, each listing bullet points of specific biological terms.This new (WHO) Classification of GTS, the last volume of the fifth edition, was developed through multidisciplinary collaboration, drawing on expertise in pathology, clinical genetics, oncology and molecular biology, and informed by bibliometric analysis and international consensus s. It represents a first step towards a unified, mechanism‐based taxonomy of GTS within the WHO system.2TerminologyAfter some discussion we agreed that the name, ‘genetic tumour syndrome’ as a short form for genetic tumour predisposition syndrome was the best description of these disorders. The collective term ‘genetic’ was preferred over ‘familial’ or ‘hereditary’, so that the classification could encompass those syndromes which often have a post‐zygotic causation. There was considerable debate over the use of the term ‘germline’ or ‘constitutional’, with the decision going to the former term as translation of ‘constitutional’ can have problems in countries where it can be confused with consanguinity. As ‘germline’ is also more commonly used within the published literature, this was therefore preferred. Table 1 outlines common terms and definitions used throughout the volume.TABLE 1Glossary of terms commonly used in the description of genetic tumour predisposition syndromes.TermDefinitionAlleleDifferent versions of the same gene or variant.ConstitutionalA sequence variant present in all the body's cells, including the germ cells, that can therefore be passed on to offspring.GeneThe basic unit of inheritance, containing the information encoding specific peptides/proteins or RNAs.GermlineIn this context, used as synonym for ‘constitutional’, though usually regarded as defining the germ cells—sperm and oocytes that pass on genetic material to offspring.Mosaic(ism)A genetic change present in some but not all cells in the body, caused by post‐zygotic mutation and resulting in mutiple genotypes within the individual affected.PenetranceThe age‐dependent cumulative incidence of a trait (phenotype) that is associated with the variant (or allele) of a gene (the genotype).PathogenicA genomic variant is called pathogenic if there is a direct and strong link between the change and a particular condition or syndrome.Post‐zygoticA change in the genome that is acquired during the lifespan of an individual, instead of being inherited (see mosaicism).SequenceThe sequence of nucleotides in DNA or RNA, or amino acids in protein.SomaticThe cells in the body other than sperm and oocytes (germ cells) and their gonadal progenitors.SyndromeA set of medical signs and symptoms (and pathological abnormalities) which are correlated with each other and often associated with a particular disease or disorder.TaxonomyAn ordered arrangement of groups or categories, used to indicate relationships.VariantA genetic variant is a permanent change in the DNA sequence. Not all variants are pathogenic.There are few issues around the accurate and standardised description of genes and DNA sequence variance, which has been expertly curated by the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) [6, 7] and the Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) for many years [8, 9, 10, 11]. However, there are several instances where colloquial shorthand is often used in medical practice rather than the more accurate (and often longer) correct scientific notation. The classification uses the scientific terms, and includes the colloquial terms where these will benefit understanding. One example is in the reporting of sequence variants in the histone H3.3 genes [12], in which the numbering based on immunohistochemistry (the more frequent use in practice) and on the DNA sequence differs, leading to possible confusion.Syndromes, by contrast, are given names according to their published names and common usage. We have listed these by chromosomal location and gene in Table 2. There is a move towards a dyadic disease nomenclature including the gene symbol for GTS, but this is by no means ubiquitous (Table 2) [13]. The syndrome we call hereditary gastric and breast cancer syndrome (HGBCS) in the classification is an autosomal dominant GTS with inactivating constitutional CDH1 or CTNNA1 sequence variants, which has also been called hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (HDGC) syndrome; hereditary lobular breast cancer (HLBC); diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer syndrome; diffuse gastric cancer syndrome/lobular breast cancer syndrome (DGCS/LBCS); CDH1‐related tumour susceptibility syndrome or cadherin‐related tumour susceptibility syndrome. This is largely historical, but a clear cause of confusion. In line with our practice in naming tumours, we have listed alternative terminology as ‘acceptable’, or ‘not recommended’, which we hope will go some way to solving these issues.TABLE 2Tumour 1Dyskeratosis congenita3ClassificationThe hierarchical classification for GTS is based on four linked levels: the cellular mechanism (known as the category), the molecular pathway (family), the clinical syndrome and the gene(s) affected with a text description of the most common disease associated changes (Figure 1). The pathway‐based approach adopted addresses the imperfect relationship between genes and tumour predisposition syndromes and emphasises that disruption of specific biological processes underlies neoplasia, with certain pathways or nodes within them recurrently associated with tumour development. Eight broad cellular mechanisms define the highest level categories: growth factor receptors and related pathways; oxidative stress response and metabolism; cell cycle and apoptosis pathways; DNA repair and genomic stability; telomere maintenance; epigenetic drivers and chromatin; RNA regulation and protein regulation.This can be best illustrated by a representative example.Within the category of DNA repair and genomic stability, homologous recombination defines one of the pathways responsible for repair of double‐strand DNA breaks. Pathogenic germline variants in genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51C and RAD51D are grouped within this pathway on the basis of shared biological function. Clinically, these variants define a spectrum of related tumour predisposition syndromes, most prominently hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, with increased risk across multiple tumour types. Although individual genes differ in penetrance and tumour spectrum, their classification within a common pathway reflects shared mechanism and supports convergent clinical strategies, including targeted surveillance and sensitivity to poly ADP‐ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibition.This hierarchical structure unifies multiple genes within a single mechanistic framework while preserving gene‐level specificity. It accommodates overlapping phenotypes and enables incorporation of newly identified genes without redefining the classification.This first edition of the classification of GTS has some limitations that precluded the inclusion of all possible syndromes (Table 2). In some cases, this was because they were extremely rare, while others were not yet sufficiently documented for inclusion. Those syndromes associated with haematolymphoid neoplasms caused considerable discussion. In the end, we opted to include the more common examples and a special introduction to haematolymphoid genetic disorders which will set the scene for future developments. Indeed, it is expected that the classification will evolve (and expand) with future editions.Of those GTS included in this edition, the largest categories were growth factor receptors and their related pathways (38 syndromes), and DNA repair and genomic stability (23 syndromes), while only one protein regulation syndrome was noted—BAP1‐related tumour predisposition syndrome. The classification emphasises certain points, such as the importance of alteration of growth factor receptors and their pathways in predisposition syndromes, while growth factors themselves are not represented. Equally, all DNA repair pathways are represented, with the common syndromes associated with homologous recombination (e.g., BRCA1 and BRCA2) and mismatch repair defects covered in depth.Pathways interact, and the effects of individual gene products on downstream signalling can be complex, producing distinct clinical syndromes despite a shared gene context. For example, variants in APC may result in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) or gastric adenocarcinoma and proximal polyposis of stomach (GAPPS) disorders, reflecting differences in the nature and location of the underlying alteration with GAPPS associated with specific promoter variants whereas FAP resulting from loss of function variants throughout the coding region. Conversely, variants within different genes may converge on a common tumour type, as seen in schwannomatosis associated with NF2, SMARCB1 and LZTR1. These relationships illustrate the complexity of genotype–phenotype associations and underscore the value of a pathway‐based framework for organising this diversity.4ConclusionThe WHO Classification of GTS establishes a unified framework that aligns tumour predisposition with its underlying biological mechanisms. By organising syndromes across linked levels of mechanism, pathway, phenotype and gene, this classification enables integration across disciplines and provides a structure within which new discoveries can be systematically incorporated.The framework also exposes areas of incomplete knowledge, highlighting pathways and syndromes that remain under‐characterised and directing attention towards priorities for future investigation. In doing so, it shifts the classification of tumour predisposition from a descriptive catalogue toward a biologically coherent system.This is not a static taxonomy. It is an infrastructure. As genomic data expand and mechanistic understanding deepens, the value of classification will lie not only in naming disease, but in organising knowledge in a way that predicts, connects and evolves. A mechanism‐based approach is essential to that task, and future iterations will depend on its continued refinement. Classification, in this context, is not an endpoint. It is the foundation on which the next generation of discovery will be built.Author ContributionsAll authors have accepted responsibility for the entire content of this manuscript and approved its submission.E.A.B. is currently funded by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) grant U24HG003345. title: Paediatric Therapeutic Development Workshop on rhabdomyosarcoma
abstract: The third in a series of Paediatric Therapeutic Development Workshops focused on rhabdomyosarcoma. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children, with 90% survival for those with the lowest risk disease, but just 20–30% in children with metastatic disease. An urgent unmet need exists to develop targeted therapeutics for high-risk disease and to reduce the toxicity of treatment. The results of trials of CAR T-cells and ADCs against FGFR4 are awaited with great interest, and developing a FGFR4 degrader is a priority. Directly targeting PAX3::FOXO1 and PAX7::FOXO1 fusion proteins is a high priority. An in vivo study of a MYOD1 degrader approach is required prior to clinical development. Degraders of P300/CBP should be evaluated preclinically with a view to clinical investigation. ROR2 is an interesting target for the L122R mutant MYOD1 rhabdomyosarcoma. Development of a TEAD degrader is a high priority, and this should be evaluated in combination with a Notch inhibitor. Considering targets with existing clinical agents, antibody-drug conjugates targeting cell-surface antigen B7-H3/CD276 are showing preclinical promise in other paediatric cancers and are also deemed a high priority for evaluation in rhabdomyosarcoma. Based on currently available evidence, MEK inhibitors should be evaluated, potentially with BRAF or PI3K inhibitors, in combination with chemotherapy in the maintenance setting. Understanding the mechanism of action underpinning drug combinations, gaining access to therapeutics and optimising clinical trial design will be essential to enable combinatorial testing in patients.
full_text: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a high-grade sarcoma resembling developing or embryonic skeletal muscle cells and is the most common form of soft tissue sarcoma in childhood, with 4.5 cases per 1 million people aged 0–20 years [1]. Current treatment for rhabdomyosarcoma is chemotherapy and local therapy (surgery and/or radiotherapy) with the exact regimens being guided by clinical risk groups [1]. Children in the lowest risk group have a good prognosis of >90% overall survival, but the prognosis for the highest risk group with metastatic disease is only 20–30% [2–9]. Despite advances from large, co-operative clinical trials, the outlook for children with metastatic or recurrent disease remains very poor. Moreover, current treatments for rhabdomyosarcoma are associated with severe short and long-term side effects, often due to extensive surgery and intensive radiotherapy and chemotherapy regimens, which seriously impact survivors’ quality of life [1].The third Paediatric Therapeutic Development Workshop focussed on rhabdomyosarcoma, aiming to understand unmet treatment needs in rhabdomyosarcoma and identify priorities for therapeutic development. The workshop was organised by LifeArc (a self-funded not-for-profit charity), Innovative Therapies for Children and Adolescents with Cancer (ITCC), Cancer Research UK and the Cancer Grand Challenge PROTECT team. The outputs of the workshop will be used to inform future strategies of academia, industry, regulators and charities working in rhabdomyosarcoma. This article summarises the prioritisation decisions and overarching recommendations of the workshop.Rhabdomyosarcoma has been divided by the WHO into four subtypes based on its histological features: embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS), spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SCRMS) and pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma (PRMS) [10]. ERMS has morphological and immunophenotypic features of embryonic skeletal muscle and is the most common rhabdomyosarcoma subtype, accounting for 60% of cases in children [11, 12]. For intermediate- and highest-risk disease, systemic therapy is based on a foundation of intensive, multiagent chemotherapy administered at intervals over 6-9 months [2, 6]. In North America, the combination of vincristine, actinomycin-D and cyclophosphamide (VAC) is the backbone for most rhabdomyosarcoma treatments [2, 6], whilst in Europe, the combination of ifosfamide, vincristine and actinomycin-D (IVA) is the reference regimen. Recently, the EpSSG has added maintenance chemotherapy with low-dose cyclophosphamide and weekly vinorelbine to the treatment of high-risk patients [9]. Patients with metastatic disease continue to have a poor outcome in spite of intensive therapy [3–5].For patients and parents, quality of life is a crucial aspect of rhabdomyosarcoma therapy. Many long-term survivors of rhabdomyosarcoma have chronic health issues, which may include lifelong severe late effects such as infertility, restricted bone and soft tissue growth, visual and auditory defects, learning difficulties and increased future cancer risk [40–42]. Local control measures, especially radiation, are a major source of long-term sequelae. A parent at the workshop stated that ‘survivors are alive but not living a life’. Moreover, frontline therapy has remained approximately the same over the past 40 years. New and innovative therapeutics for rhabdomyosarcoma are therefore desperately required to both save and improve the quality of patients’ lives.Biology of rhabdomyosarcomaThe aetiology of rhabdomyosarcoma is only partially understood, but rhabdomyosarcoma tumours are believed to arise when mesenchymal cells committed to the skeletal muscle lineage fail to fully differentiate into mature myocytes and are arrested at a proliferative rhabdomyoblastic stage [43]. Studies in mouse models suggest that rhabdomyosarcoma tumours can develop from multiple cell lineages, including muscle and non-muscle, but in humans, the precise developmental origins and tumorigenic processes remain unclear [43–48].Rhabdomyosarcoma is generally driven by a combination of genomic aberrations which function together to block rhabdomyoblast differentiation and promote tumour progression. The fusion genes are major disease-driving aberrations through their encoded transcriptional activity, as discussed below. The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is activated in ~80% of rhabdomyosarcoma tumours overall, including both PAX3/7::FOXO1 positive and negative cases [43]. Mutations in the RAS pathway frequently occur in PAX3/7::FOXO1-negative tumours, whereas PAX3/7::FOXO1-positive tumours have a lower mutational burden [39, 48]. Three key molecular features of SCRMS are used to subclassify this group into subgroups: MYOD1 mutations, TFCP fusions and VGLL2::NCOA2 fusions. This includes widely available ERMS and ARMS human cell lines, which vary in origin and treatment history (primary tumour vs metastasis; newly diagnosed vs previously treated), location, patient age, treatment history and PAX3/7::FOXO1 status [72]. Several publicly available model repositories and data resources on rhabdomyosarcoma exist, including. St Jude Children’s Research Hospital’s Childhood Solid Tumour Network with access to >45 rhabdomyosarcoma O-PDX models [73] and an Integrated Rhabdomyosarcoma Database comprising genomic, epigenetic, proteomic and drug sensitivity data [74]. The Innovative Therapies for Children with Cancer Paediatric Preclinical Proof-of-concept Platform (ITCC-P4) [75], National Cancer Institute Childhood Cancer Data Initiative (CCDI) Hub [76] and MAPPYACTS Biobank [77] provide repertoires of patient-derived models of paediatric tumours, supported by comprehensive datasets of corresponding molecular and pharmacological characterisation. These models reflect patient-specific rhabdomyosarcoma drug sensitivities and can be genetically modified using CRISPR/Cas9, although they also lack functional human immune systems. Sarcoma_CellMinerCDB is a publicly available interactive database and tool which merges publicly available sarcoma cell line data and newly generated omics data to create a comprehensive database of genomic, transcriptomic, methylomic, proteomic, metabolic, and pharmacologic data [78].The most commonly used mouse models for rhabdomyosarcoma are cell-line-derived xenografts (CDX), followed by patient-derived xenografts and syngeneic mouse models. However, CDX models do not always fully mimic human rhabdomyosarcoma phenotypes. Neither CDX nor PDX models have functional human immune systems [71]. There is, however, one humanised mouse model made with rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines [79]. An alternative resource is a collection of >30 mesenchymal tumour organoid/tumoroid models covering all major rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes developed by researchers in the Netherlands, which reflect rhabdomyosarcoma drug sensitivities in patients and can be modified by CRISPR/Cas9 [80].The Rhabdomyosarcoma Paediatric Therapeutic Development WorkshopTo identify unmet needs and research priorities in rhabdomyosarcoma, a detailed diligence review of rhabdomyosarcoma epidemiology, biology, preclinical tools, potential targets and existing commercial developments was prepared by LifeArc and circulated to experts ahead of the workshop. This included a list of therapeutic targets produced from the GlobalData Drugs Database, supplemented with literature searches, to identify preclinical and clinical evidence for each target’s association with rhabdomyosarcoma (Supplementary Table 1) and the list of drugs in development (Supplementary Table 2). This review was followed by a workshop comprising experts in the biology and therapy of rhabdomyosarcoma and patient advocates. The L122R mutant MYOD1 has MYC-like properties [99] and is present in 40% of SCRMS [17]. RAS and PI3K mutations frequently, as well as other aberrations, co-occur with MYOD1 mutations, and these are believed to function with mutant MYOD1 to drive tumour progression synergistically [14, 99]. As CBP and P300 are both ubiquitously expressed at RNA and protein levels, therapeutic approaches should consider possible off-target toxicities in healthy tissue, although CRISPR knockout of either P300 or CBP appears to be well tolerated across cancer cell lines [132]. PAX3::FOXO1 is more common [51] and has been the subject of extensive target validation studies using antisense oligonucleotides [134], siRNA, shRNA [135, 136], small molecules [137–139], CRISPR [126, 140] and degradation [141] in cell lines and mouse xenografts. However, PAX3/7::FOXO1 is amenable to targeting by other modalities. PAX3::FOXO1 degraders are in active preclinical development, for example, by the KOODAC Cancer Grand Challenge and the NIH FusOnC2 and TFCC Consortia. Other approaches discussed included molecular glues, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and T cell receptor (TCR) T-cells. Across different cancers, gain or loss of function mutations in YAP/TAZ are rare, and amplifications predominate [152, 153].
