Of note, age does influence upfront approach due to concerns for a non-WT diagnosis such that children under the age of 6 months and adolescents/young adults are stratified toward upfront biopsy and/or surgery rather than neoadjuvant therapy without biopsy, based on diagnostic variability at the extremes of the pediatric age group; age is not otherwise included in risk stratification in SIOP-RTSG.3,4The COG-RTC has incorporated similar prognostic factors in risk stratification: age, stage, histology, and lung nodule response. Considering histological classification, COG distinguishes between favorable histology (FH) and unfavorable histology (UH) including focal and diffuse anaplasia.54 In addition, COG-RTC protocols include molecular genetic markers such as combined loss of heterozygosity (LOH) of chromosome 1p and 16q currently, with plans for incorporation of LOH of 11p15 (in case of very low risk WT only6) and gain of chromosome 1q in the next generation of clinical trials (Table 2).7-9Present risk stratification of relapsed WTBoth SIOP-RTSG and COG-RTC stratify risk at relapse primarily based on the number of drugs received in the upfront setting, which is reflective of risk variables present in the upfront setting. The current SIOP-RTSG-2016 UMBRELLA protocol defines standard-risk patients (risk group AA according to SIOP relapsed WT risk classification) as those who relapsed after initial treatment with vincristine and/or dactinomycin (VA) only and without radiotherapy (RT) during first-line therapy.10 Relapse after more intensive therapy (usually vincristine, dactinomycin, and doxorubicin (VAD)) with or without RT, in the absence of diffuse anaplasia (DA) and/or blastemal-type (BT) histology after preoperative chemotherapy, is considered a high-risk (risk group BB) relapsed subgroup. Patients with upfront stage II-IV and DA and/or BT histology after chemotherapy at primary diagnosis are considered very high-risk (risk group CC), and have generally received 4 drugs (cyclophosphamide, carboplatin, etoposide and doxorubicin) with RT as first-line treatment.11The COG-RTC also uses a relapse WT classification including standard, high- and very high-risk groups.12,13 Patients with standard-risk relapsed FHWT (SRrFHWT) are those who relapse after receiving treatment with two chemotherapy agents (vincristine and dactinomycin without RT). Patients with high-risk relapsed FHWT (HRrFHWT) are those who relapse after treatment with three chemotherapy agents (vincristine, dactinomycin, and doxorubicin) and RT. Patients with very high-risk relapsed FHWT (VHRrFHWT) are those who relapse after receiving treatment with four or more chemotherapy agents and RT. There are no protocols within COG specifically for relapse DAWT.Notable controversies and knowledge gaps include the development of improved prognostic markers to enable more predictive risk stratification at the time of relapse. While many factors have been evaluated in smaller series including time to relapse, histology at relapse, biomarkers at relapse, and unifocal versus multi-focal relapse, their effects on treatment outcomes should be explored via large cooperative group investigations prior to incorporation into risk stratification schema.Chemotherapy for relapsed WTThe SIOP-RTSG 2016 UMBRELLA protocol is the first SIOP-RTSG protocol with a detailed and stratified relapsed WT guideline.2 AA group patients are treated with alternating courses of cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin and carboplatin/etoposide (CDCE) with RT and surgery when feasible.14 Interestingly, a retrospective study of the outcome of patients with characteristics similar to current AA classification, suggests a yet to be defined subset of patients can be potentially treated with less intensive VAD.14 Age and molecular genetic markers currently under investigation may help to further stratify this group of standard-risk relapse patients. Patients of the BB group are treated with alternating courses of cyclophosphamide/carboplatin/etoposide (CyCE) and ifosfamide/carboplatin/etoposide (ICE) combined with RT, where feasible and/or surgery. At the discretion of the treating physician, these patients may additionally be treated with high-dose single agent melphalan and autologous stem cell rescue, although the added value of high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell rescue remains undefined.15-16 Finally, treatment options for very high-risk relapse (CC group) patients are scarce as most conventional therapeutics have already been used in frontline treatment. UMBRELLA therefore recommends treatment with camptothecins, including vincristine/irinotecan (/temozolomide) (VI(T)) or topotecan/temozolomide (TOTEM),17 and ultimately relevant early phase trials. In this vein, a trial with VIT-Bevacizumab is being prepared by the SIOP-RTSG. The trial proposal was brought forth by a literature review wherein objective response or stable disease was observed in 8 out of 9 patients reported who were treated with VI(T)-Bevacizumab, while also showing good therapy tolerability.18The National Wilms Tumor Study-5 (NWTS-5) investigated the treatment of relapsed FHWT for two groups: 1) stage I and II FHWT that relapsed after initial treatment with Regimen EE-4A (vincristine/dactinomycin) were treated with surgical excision when feasible, RT, and alternating courses of vincristine/doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide and etoposide/cyclophosphamide per stratum B; 2) stage III and IV FHWT that relapsed after initial treatment with Regimen DD-4A (vincristine/dactinomycin/doxorubicin) were treated with surgical excision when feasible, RT, and alternating cycles of cyclophosphamide/etoposide and carboplatin/etoposide on stratum C. Stratum B evaluated 58 patients and noted a 4-year event free survival (EFS) after relapse of 71% and overall survival (OS) of 81% for all patients and 68% and 81%, respectively, in those 31 patients with lung-only relapse.19 Stratum C evaluated 60 patients and noted a 4-year EFS after relapse of 42% and OS of 48% for all patients and 49% and 53%, respectively, in those 33 patients with lung-only relapse.20 Complete delivery of the lengthy stratum C was not feasible in the majority of patients treated.The current open clinical trial AREN1921 (NCT04322318), is investigating treatment of patients with relapsed FHWT. Those with SRrFHWT are receiving treatment with Regimen UH-3 [vincristine/doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (VDCy) alternating with cyclophosphamide/carboplatin/etoposide (CCE) and vincristine/irinotecan (VI)]. HRrFHWT and VHRrFHWT patients are being treated with Regimen ICE/Cyclo/Topo (Ifosfamide/carboplatin/etoposide alternating with cyclophosphamide/topotecan). Patients will receive RT to all relapse sites, when feasible in addition to surgery. The primary aim of the FHWT strata of this trial is to evaluate if the addition of VI to VDCy alternating with CCE improves the EFS of patients with SRrFHWT as compared to historical controls, with a secondary aim to establish the EFS and OS for HRrFHWT and VHRrFHWT treated with Regimen ICE/Cyclo/Topo. Current chemotherapeutic approaches for both SIOP and COG are included in Table 3.Notable controversies and areas of ongoing research in the chemotherapy treatment of relapsed patients include the following: optimal treatment regimen at the time of relapse and long-term outcomes/late effects associated with relapse therapies.Surgery for abdominal or local (tumor bed) relapseSurgical or percutaneous biopsy may be required to definitively diagnose locoregional relapse of WT. However, the role of surgery as a local control modality for WT locoregional relapse has not yet been defined or evaluated in a prospective manner. An exploratory aim of the ongoing COG AREN1921 study is to better understand the role of complete resection in relapsed FHWT, either at time of relapse diagnosis or after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Furthermore, the prospective, ongoing SIOP-RTSG Umbrella Protocol Study (SIOP-RTSG 2016) also aims to improve understanding of the role of surgery for WT relapse.2 The Umbrella protocol advises consideration of surgical resection after proven reduction of recurrent disease post-chemotherapy, independent of the relapse risk group, when radical surgery is possible.Retrospective studies have suggested that complete surgical resection plays an important role in the multimodal approach to relapsed locoregional WT. In a single-institution, retrospective series of 54 patients treated for relapsed WT, 20 patients who had complete surgical resection of recurrent WT had improved survival when compared to the remaining 34 who had incomplete resection or no surgery (5-year OS 60.0% [standard error (SE) ± 12.6%] vs 19.6% (SE ±7.9%); relative risk (RR) 3.3 (95%CI=1.5-7.3); p=0.001).21 However, it is possible that patients with WT relapse who had complete resection had less aggressive tumors than those who did not, therefore reflecting a surgery selection bias.In general, surgery is advised at the time of initial locoregional relapse only if complete resection can be anticipated. If complete resection is not possible at the time of initial relapse, consideration for surgery should be made after each imaging cycle or at completion of relapse therapy. In contrast to primary WT, which typically displaces vascular structures rather than encasing them and does not usually exhibit intimate adherence to or invasion of adjacent abdominal organs, experience suggests relapsed WT has a higher propensity for encasement or dense adherence to adjacent structures making margin-negative surgical resection rarer at the time of relapse. However, this perceived increased adherence may be due to obliteration of normal tissue planes caused by prior surgery or radiotherapy in the re-operative field rather than relapsed tumor biology itself. As such, gross residual disease may need to be left behind to preserve form or function; marking of gross residual disease with surgical clips to guide radiotherapy fields is advised at the time of surgery for locoregional relapsed WT.Surgery for relapse at a distant site (lung/liver) metastatic Wilms tumor relapseMetastatic WT relapses occur most commonly in the lungs followed by liver, representing systemic disease. The general approach is to administer systemic chemotherapy first with subsequent local control surgery only if there is a response to treatment or if the initial relapse is small and readily manageable with surgery. An exception to this sequence of systemic treatment followed by surgery might be the case of a very late single metastasis (after several years, for example) which is often addressed first by surgery because it could represent a secondary malignancy or because a straightforward surgery could render the patient disease free. However, there are no clear or accepted guidelines for surgical management.In the lungs, the most frequent surgical procedure performed is wedge excision. For a limited burden of relapsed metastatic disease, this can usually be performed thoracoscopically. Superficial pulmonary metastases can be readily identified intraoperatively. Wedge excision of deeper pulmonary nodules may be facilitated using mechanical localization techniques including CT-guided hook-wire or coil localization or possible via novel approaches such as fluorescence-guided approaches with indocyanine green (ICG).22In the liver, relapsed metastatic WT can be surgically resected using non-anatomic wedge resection, or, when necessary, a variety of anatomic approaches. A recent systematic review and meta-regression analysis concluded that surgery potentially improved survival for patients with metachronous WT liver relapse.23 Intraoperative ultrasound is a standard approach for localization of liver lesions and energy devices such as the cavitron ultrasound aspirator (CUSA) can be used to divide the hepatic parenchyma.24 Three-dimensional reconstructed images including virtual and augmented reality are emerging technologies that may facilitate surgical planning and intraoperative localization of liver lesions.25While surgery is an often-employed treatment modality for solitary metastatic WT relapses or oligometastatic disease, when a greater number of metastatic nodules exist, local control may not always be appropriate even if the size of those nodules decreases under chemotherapy. In fact, a report of 211 combined patients from the older studies NWTS-1, 2, and 3 with relapse limited to the lungs demonstrated that there was no difference in 4-year OS when comparing children who underwent therapeutic pulmonary metastasectomy to those who did not (4-year OS 77% vs 76%, respectively).26 Data from AREN1921 will hopefully determine whether this is true in the context of contemporary relapse treatment regimens. Additionally, a report from NWTS-5 demonstrated the importance of surgery for directing therapy in patients with WT pulmonary disease because lesions detected on computed tomography (CT) scan are not always tumor.27 If complete resection is not deemed feasible, a biopsy of one or two metastatic nodules may provide histopathology of the relapsed disease and its response to treatment. Biopsy could also allow for biological and molecular examination of new features which could guide targeted treatment. How to best incorporate biopsy and the subsequent information gleaned is an area for future investigation.Radiofrequency ablation, other ablative techniques, or cryotherapy may be an option for local control of relapsed metastatic WT with relative indications including several previous surgical attempts, limited size, difficult location and an adequate distance from major vessels. It must be noted that no robust evidence-based data on the outcomes of these ablative techniques exist in children.28Controversies related to surgery at the time of relapse include the following: optimal timing of resection, the role of biopsy and histologic evaluation on planning for relapse therapy, the effect on outcomes of resection of relapsed disease, and the additional options for local control of relapse sites including combined modalities and ablative techniques (Table 4).Radiation OncologyIn line with the other modalities, key factors for radiotherapeutic options at the time of relapse depend on previous treatment intensity (Table 5). As little is known about the use and benefit of radiotherapy for WT at the time of recurrence, the added value to prevent subsequent local and pulmonary relapse must currently be extrapolated from what is known in the upfront setting.29, 30 Current and planned future relapse trials will further investigate the radiation response at relapse.For patients with relapses in areas not previously irradiated, radiotherapy doses are typically delivered as used for upfront treatment, which varies slightly between the COG and SIOP-RTSG approach (Table 2). For a local or regional recurrence 12 months from diagnosis may allow for consideration of targeting only the site of recurrence (Table 2), although this requires further validation in ongoing and upcoming trials. Whole lung irradiation is recommended for patients presenting with one or more metastases in the lung. Since evidence for this is lacking, it remains a point of debate whether a response adapted approach similar to the current stage IV strategy for patients who had received only very little treatment is justified too.Recurrences in areas previously irradiated are more challenging and require consideration of the initial dose, and the tolerance dose for each organ/structure at risk (in particular for the unique kidney, liver, bowel, and lungs), acknowledging some repair capacity after an interval since first RT. The upfront use of highly conformal flank target volumes and cardiac-sparing whole lung radiotherapy should provide more options for re-irradiation.31, 32 The different scenarios, including doses and volumes, for re-irradiation are summarized in Table 2. In general, a higher radiotherapy dose for patients with an infield recurrence is typical, except re-irradiation of the whole lungs is not considered to be a safe option. Stereotactic radiotherapy may be considered for a small number of relapsed lung nodules after prior whole lung RT. The indication of whole abdomen re-irradiation after initial treatment for COG UH-disease, or a SIOP-RTSG high-risk regimen, may be considered but must account for initial critical organ doses and resultant dysfunction.Controversies and areas for future research for radiation at the time of relapse include timing and dose of radiation in relapse in relation to both chemotherapy and surgery, the potential (or lack thereof) for omission of RT in certain low-risk relapse patients, safety of re-irradiation at various sites, and long-term outcomes/late effects for relapsed patients receiving high doses of RT.Genomics and New AgentsA major gap in the management of children with relapsed WT is the lack of biologically informed targeted agents. Thus, sadly the overall strategy is frequently just to increase treatment intensity with traditional drugs. The most commonly altered molecular pathways (wnt signaling, microRNA processing, IGF2 overexpression) have not yet been successfully targeted. Other pre-clinically defined potential targets emerging from drug screening specifically in WT models (patient derived xenografts) such as alternative anti-mitotic agents (Ispinesib, Ixabepilone), VEGF multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (mTKIs; sorafenib), CD56 antibody-drug-conjugate based therapy (IMGN901/Lorvotuzumab), for example, have not yet yielded corresponding clinical benefit in WT patients in phase 2 investigation.33-35 Aurora-kinase-A targeting yielded only one partial response in 10 patients.36 Investigation of beta-catenin inhibition and XPO1 inhibition are ongoing (NCT05985161 and NCT04851119; Table 6).A complimentary approach is precision medicine wherein genomic and/or functional data are developed for each patient to identify potentially efficacious treatments agnostic of tumor type. Although each individual alteration (gene specific and/or molecular pathway) is likely too low in frequency in WTs to justify a trial, it could still be targeted for the patient who harbors it. As examples, although extremely rare, some WTs have high mutational burdens that may render them sensitive to immunotherapy while others have variants in genes that have been successfully targeted by small molecule inhibitors in other disease types.Precision medicine approaches may also benefit patients with relapsed WTs by providing diagnostic clarity in cases where histologic diagnosis is difficult, and by potentially aiding in risk stratification, e.g. through identification of TP53 pathogenic variants with a particular poor outcome. A unique scenario for patients with WTs is the risk of metachronous bilateral or multifocal disease wherein a second renal tumor is a new primary rather than a relapse of the original disease. In these cases, patients would benefit from less toxic regimens designed for upfront therapy rather than relapse. Precision medicine approaches can define the molecular profiles of each tumor to differentiate relapse from a second primary with significant therapeutic implications.Precision medicine programs are accessible in most North American, European, and Australian jurisdictions and are being developed elsewhere. Each program has its own approach utilizing various mostly genomic-based platform tumor investigations making it difficult to compare between studies. However, many of the initial findings from these trials have been published and in total >120 patients with WTs have been reported. Approximately 35% of these have had a variant considered to be “actionable” in that it clarified diagnosis or potentially changed the approach to treatment. It is important to note however that the exact definition of “actionable” varies between programs.It is not possible to state from the published literature whether precision medicine trials have improved survival in children with relapsed WTs.37, 38 Some experienced clinicians have anecdotally observed a WT child with dramatic response on targeted treatment, but due to its rarity it is possibly not captured in overall statistical analyses.Unfortunately, it is likely that the majority of patients with relapsed WT do not derive direct benefit from precision medicine-based approaches as often no targets are identified in the tumor, a target is identified but no targeting agent is available for clinical use, or the putative target and/or agent proves ineffective. Nonetheless, the inevitable expansion of precision medicine approaches and programs should enhance our understanding of how to target genetic alterations and utilize these data for risk stratification. Concurrent with such advance, there remains a pressing need for continued expansion in understanding the specific biological mechanisms driving WT oncogenesis, progression, and treatment resistance. Global collaborative efforts between researchers, clinicians, patients and family stakeholders, and pharmaceutical companies are essential to accelerate the discovery and implementation of newer targeted therapy.On-going areas of research include improving the number of available early phase clinical trials for relapse patients including those with rare tumor histologies such as DAWT, continued pre-clinical work to develop relevant new agents, and international collaborations to improve outcomes.In conclusion, this international collaboration identified multiple questions and knowledge gaps and revealed that management of patients with relapsed WT continues to require additional research and investigation. Forthcoming priorities include identification of valid prognostic risk stratification factors that can be used to both augment and lessen therapy, the optimal chemotherapy backbones to be utilized at the time of relapse, the timing and application of surgery and radiation therapy in the management of relapsed disease, and the development of newer targeted therapies to improve outcomes in this patient population.Despite the challenges, the majority of children with WT suffering from a relapse are still curable. As risk stratification at initial diagnosis becomes increasingly nuanced, there are both growing cohorts of patients receiving more limited (no chemotherapy or 2-drug) upfront therapy along with cohorts receiving more intensive therapy (4+-drug therapy). Research goals must include strategies to lessen relapse therapy for the selected cohort of children with a more favorable prognosis at relapse in order to spare severe late morbidities, while developing novel strategies for high-risk patients who have already received aggressive multimodal therapy. Importantly, advancements in risk stratification and the cure of patients with relapsed Wilms tumor should not be limited to sites able to participate in large cooperative group initiatives; efforts should also be made to understand how to best offer curative relapse therapies for patients residing in low- and middle- income countries. Advances will require continued collaboration between the international community of researchers, clinicians, and drug developers to improve outcomes and decrease toxicity in this patient population as well as strict prioritizing among relevant early phase trials.

title: Cancer-associated alterations in O-GalNAc glycosylation
abstract: Aberrant O-GalNAc glycans such as Tn, STn, and T are among the most consistent tumor-associated carbohydrate antigens, broadly expressed on carcinomas but largely absent from healthy epithelia. In parallel, O-glycans can also be modified to carry functional motifs, such as Lewis antigens. Rather than a simple shift from elongated to truncated structures, cancer-associated O-glycans form a heterogeneous repertoire of truncated and elongated glycoforms that coexist across the tumor glycocalyx. Collectively, both short and elongated cancer-associated O-glycans co-drive tumor formation through their simultaneous influence on multiple cancer hallmarks, including adhesion, receptor signaling, dissemination, and immune evasion. The latter occurs through interactions with glycan-binding proteins including Selectins, Siglecs, macrophage galactose-type lectin (MGL), and galectins. The stable expression of especially truncated O-glycans across cancer stages, as well as their driving influence on cancer progression, make short, truncated O-glycans attractive therapeutic targets. While early vaccine approaches had limited efficacy, strategies that couple O-glycan recognition with potent effector mechanisms have shown promise. This includes O-glycan-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CARTs), T-cell bispecifics (TCBs), and particularly antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), which have demonstrated strong preclinical activity. Looking forward, multi-specific antibodies, bio-orthogonal chemistry, and artificial intelligence–driven engineering are expected to enhance safety, selectivity, and improve patient stratification, helping to further exploit O-GalNAc glycans in precision oncology.
full_text: Human malignancies arise when an initial driver generate self-proliferating clones that outgrow non-transformed counterparts while evading immune elimination (Hanahan and Weinberg 2011). Among the strategies that malignant cells use to outcompete the checks and balances of tissue homeostasis and hide from the immune system is remodeling of the cell-surface glycocalyx; a dense meshwork of glycans that decorate membrane proteins and lipids involved in cell adherence and cellular communication (Pinho and Reis 2015; Stowell et al. 2015; Britain et al. 2018; Smith and Bertozzi 2021; Heimburg-Molinaro et al. 2024; Aasted 2026). Glycosylation, which is one of the most abundant and diverse post-translational modifications, covalently attaches carbohydrate structures to proteins and lipids to generate glycoconjugates. Protein glycosylation is commonly classified as N-, C- and O-linked, denoted by the accepting atom within the peptide backbone (Schjoldager et al. 2020; de Haan et al. 2024) (Fig. 1). Among these, O-GalNAc (mucin-type) glycosylation (hereafter just O-glycans) undergoes prominent changes in human cancer that impact fundamental cellular and physiological processes. Malignant transformation perturbs the pattern of O-glycans in healthy epithelia, often changing them from extended and branched to truncated motifs, such as Tn, STn and TF that on mucins and proteins with mucin like domains forms clusters that may mediate avidity driven effects through interactions with glycan binding proteins (Springer 1983; Springer 1984; Thor et al. 1986; Kudelka et al. 2015; Stowell et al. 2015; Romer et al. 2021). In parallel, elongated O-glycan chains can also be changed into Lewis antigens (sLea/x/y) (Stowell et al. 2015). The two programs exist alongside each other, often giving rise to a heterogeneous repertoire of cancer-associated O-glycans, including both truncated structures unique to mucin-type O-glycosylation as well as more elongated glycoforms shared with other glycoconjugates that serve as ligands for glycan-binding proteins. Together, these altered glycans affect cellular signaling and enable metastasis and induction of immune tolerance through engagement of glycan-binding proteins, including Selectins, Siglecs, MGL and galectins (Liu and Rabinovich 2005; de Haan et al. 2024). Here, we review the current understanding of cancer-associated O-glycan changes, from changes in pathways to functional impact, and discuss how these signatures can be exploited for new diagnostics and therapeutics. The discussion is framed around a series of questions: i) What is the structural landscape of O-GalNAc glycans in healthy versus malignant epithelia? ii) How do cancer associated O-glycans emerge? iii) How do cancer associated O-GalNAc-glycans drive cancer formation and progression? iv) How can such signatures be exploited for safe, effective therapeutics? Our goal is to provide a mechanistic framework that outlines a path for converting cancer-restricted glycan signatures into precise, effective, and safe cancer treatments. While cancer-associated glycans linked to N-glycans, glycosphingolipids, and glycosaminoglycans are also highly important, these are beyond the scope of this review, and we refer to excellent reviews covering these areas (Pinho and Reis 2015; Varki 2017; Cummings 2019).Figure 1Overview of major glycosylation pathways and cancer-associated glycans. The biosynthesis of O-GalNAc glycans begins at the transcriptional level in the nucleus, where the enzymes responsible for glycosylation and sugar nucleotide metabolites are produced. Proteins destined for secretion or for the plasma membrane are translocated into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where folding and quality control take place. As these proteins are transported into the Golgi, the first O-GalNAc residues are attached to serine or threonine residues by members of the GALNT family. This initial addition of GalNAc residues forms the basis for further processing into several core structures, among which core 1, 2, 3, and 4 are the most common. Core 1 and core 2 are the most abundant and involve extension with galactose and N-acetylglucosamine, while core 3 and core 4 reflect alternative branching routes. From these cores, elongation and terminal modifications occur, with successive addition of galactose, N-acetylglucosamine, fucose, and sialic acid to generate a spectrum of extended glycans. Incomplete processing gives rise to truncated structures such as Tn and STn, which are frequently observed in cancer. The fully processed glycoproteins are packaged into vesicles and transported to the cell membrane, where they become part of the extracellular glycocalyx. Other glycosylation pathways, including N-glycans, O-mannose, O-fucose, O-glucose, O-GlcNAc, glycosphingolipids, glycosaminoglycans, hyaluronic acid, and GPI anchors, are represented alongside to contextualize O-GalNAc glycans within the full diversity of the cellular glycome. In cancer cells, this biosynthetic program is frequently remodeled, leading to accumulation of truncated structures such as Tn and STn, and to increased expression of terminally sialylated and fucosylated epitopes, including sialyl-Lewis-x and sialyl-Lewis-a. these cancer-associated O-glycan structures can alter the extracellular glycocalyx and influence tumor cell adhesion, immune recognition, and receptor signaling. Created with BioRender.comSchematic of O-GalNAc glycan biosynthesis and cancer-associated remodeling, showing formation of core structures, terminal modifications, and truncated tumor-associated glycans such as Tn and STn.What is the structural landscape of mucin-type O-GalNAc glycans in healthy and malignant epithelia?Historically, “mucin-type” O-glycosylation is synonymous with O-GalNAc glycosylation, which is now recognized as a widespread modification across the secretory pathway, with around 15,000 mapped sites distributed on the majority of proteins that traffic through the Golgi (Steentoft et al. 2013; Woo et al. 2015; Yang et al. 2018; Nielsen et al. 2022). Initiation occurs throughout the Golgi apparatus, where one of 20 polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferases (GALNTs) installs an α-linked N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) on serine, threonine or, less commonly, tyrosine residues to generate the Thomsen–nouveau (Gomes, et al.) determinant (GalNAcα1-O-Ser/Thr/Tyr) (Wandall et al. 2021). Collectively, the GALNTs create both densely decorated mucin and mucin-like domains as well as isolated sites on a wide spectrum of secreted and membrane proteins (de Haan et al. 2024). After the addition of the first glycan residue, O-glycans are elaborated into eight recognized “core” structures, of which cores 1–4 predominate (as reviewed in (de Haan et al. 2024)) (Fig. 1). These cores may then be extended with either type-1 (Galβ1–3GlcNAc) repeats, or the more prevalent type-2 (Galβ1–4GlcNAc; LacNAc) repeats. Both types of repeats can be further decorated to generate Lewis motifs and blood group antigens, with baseline Lewis expression shaped by FUT2 secretor status and FUT3/Lewis-negative phenotypes (Jajosky et al. 2023). In addition, sialyltransferases are able to cap terminal galactose with N-acetylneuraminic acid in either a α2–3, α2–6 linkage, and less commonly in a α2–8 linkage (Harduin-Lepers 2023). Furthermore, addition of sulphation can fine-tune recognition by selectins and siglecs (Sun et al. 2022; Goerdeler et al. 2026). Together, these elaborations produce a structurally rich glycocalyx at the epithelial surface.Cancer-associated remodeling of O-glycansMalignant transformation perturbs the normal glycosylation program, producing prominent tumor-associated carbohydrate antigens (TACAs) on cell surfaces. These TACAs appear both at single glycosylation sites and as high-density patches on individual glycoproteins, positioning them to influence adhesion, receptor signaling, and immune surveillance. Importantly, their surface expression, render them accessible therapeutic targets in contrast to many intracellular oncoproteins. As mentioned, the range of TACAs cover both the shorter truncated O-glycan structures (Tn, STn, and T (TF) antigens), and terminal structures, such as Lewis antigens (Lea,x,y, sLea,x,y), that can arise on several classes of glycoconjugates (Springer et al. 1975; Springer 1983; Thor et al. 1986; Yamada et al. 1995; Baldus et al. 1998; Yan et al. 2010). Evidence for the expression of short cancer-associated O-glycans across all carcinomas is very robust and correlated to poor outcome (Itzkowitz et al. 1989; Nakasaki et al. 1989; Kobayashi et al. 1992; Stowell et al. 2015; Romer et al. 2021). Although comparisons between studies can be challenging due to variable reagents, specimen handling, and scoring criteria, studies with both glycan-binding lectins and the more specific monoclonal antibodies have shown more consistent expression of Tn and STn across epithelial-derived malignancies (Springer et al. 1975; Springer 1983; Thor et al. 1986; Romer et al. 2021). In contrast, there does not seem to be a broad expression of truncated O-glycans in mesenchymal-derived cancers (Romer et al. 2021), although some expression has been reported in glioblastomas (Dusoswa et al. 2020). The expression of truncated O-glycans arises already in premalignant lesions and is consistent across different grades, with a minor non-significant dip in stage IV cancers (Itzkowitz et al. 1992; Conze et al. 2010; Romer et al. 2021; Dombek et al. 2022). The expression is frequently intratumorally heterogeneous, with truncation of O-glycans existing alongside areas expressing elongated glycans. Such spatial patterning likely reflects functional niches such as differences in biological functions at invasive fronts, in stem cell-like compartments, or within immune-excluded domains. Notably, while Tn expression is highly selective for neoplastic epithelia, STn can be induced in inflammation, particularly in the gut, where the healthy colon typically harbors 9−/7-O-acetylated STn, which is structurally distinct and prevents binding of classical STn targeting mAbs (Ta et al. 1997; Loureiro et al. 2018; Kudelka et al. 2020). Inflammatory signals, including microbial enzymes and host-driven changes in sialic-acid O-acetyl-esterase and the 9-O-acetyltransferase CASD1, can expose underlying STn, making it a less specific cancer marker when compared with Tn (Ta et al. 1997; Barresi et al. 2001; Kudelka et al. 2020). Also, the T antigen, often described as a cancer-associated carbohydrate antigen, is broadly expressed in select healthy tissues (for example, in epidermal keratinocytes and haematopoietic stem cells) and should therefore not be considered intrinsically tumor-exclusive (Radhakrishnan et al. 2014).Similar to truncated O-glycans, the expression of sialyl-Lewisa (sLea/CA19–9), sialyl-Lewisx (sLex/CD15s), and Lewisy/sialyl-Lewisy is correlated with poor prognosis and enhanced invasiveness (Nakamori et al. 1993; Takada et al. 1993; Renkonen et al. 1997; Amado et al. 1998; Brockhausen 2006). However, such structures are not cancer-specific. sLea, measured clinically as CA19–9, has particular biomarker value in pancreatic cancer, but its utility is limited by elevation in inflammatory and obstructive conditions and by FUT3-null/Lewis-negative patients. More broadly, sLea is found at low levels on normal GI and airway epithelia, in fetal/placental tissues, and in secretions, and its serum levels often rise in benign cholestasis, biliary obstruction, and pancreatitis. As we will discuss below, sLex is a physiological E-/P-selectin ligand on leukocytes and can be induced on endothelium and mucosa during inflammation, while Ley is present on normal secretory/ductal epithelia and in secretions (McEver and Cummings 1997). Therefore, although tumors, especially adenocarcinomas, commonly overexpress these elongated antigens to support adhesion and metastasis, their baseline and inflammation-related expression in non-malignant settings limits diagnostic specificity. Another circumstance limiting diagnostic utility is that it can be hard to determine if the Lewis structures are localized to O-linked glycans. Because Lewis antigens can terminate both N- and O-glycans (and glycolipids), deconvoluting the specific contribution of O-glycans remains a technical challenge when using classical carbohydrate probes. The recent advances in mass spectrometry imaging, as well as spatial strategies combining laser dissection and sensitive LC–MS/MS (which provides a richer identification both at sequence and composition-level, including isomer separation), will hopefully soon allow us to resolve the complexity and heterogeneity of expressed glycans and their carriers in human cancers (Madunić et al. 2021; de Haan et al. 2022; Pace et al. 2022; Samal et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024).How do cancer associated O-glycans emerge?Remodeling of O-glycans in carcinoma emerges from multiple events, including changes in enzyme expression, protein conformation, neighboring PTMs, Golgi residence time, donor-sugar supply, cation availability, and trafficking. The combined effects of these perturbations affect the biosynthetic pathways causing the spatial heterogeneity of O-glycans which is the characteristic of epithelial tumors. Loss of function in C1GALT1 or its obligate chaperone COSMC is the most direct way to generate expression of Tn/STn (Ju et al. 2008). However, deleterious mutations are uncommon, and more frequently, promoter methylation or lineage-specific transcriptional programs seem to be the main reason for O-glycan truncation (Radhakrishnan et al. 2014). Other mechanisms include the upregulation of the sialyltransferase ST6GALNAC1 capping Tn to STn and blocking further extension (Brockhausen et al. 2001; Marcos et al. 2011; Marcos et al. 2004;; Sewell et al. 2006). Looking beyond simple generation of the short O-glycans, Tn and STn, further examples of changes in expression of enzymes involved in O-glycan formation include loss of core-3 expression observed in colon cancer; or increased expression of core-2 branching, supporting selectin ligands (sLea/x) as mentioned above. Changes in galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases have also been observed, including B3GALT5 and ST3GALs that modulate the usage of type-1/type-2 chains to create tumor-associated termini such as CA19–9 (Hayashi et al. 2004; Cheung et al. 2016). The question remains how the expression of the enzymes is modulated. While the expression of some enzymes have been suggested to be influenced by inflammatory pathways and hypoxia (Sproviero et al. 2012), other studies suggest that they are affected downstream of oncogenic signaling, although the exact link between signals and changes in enzyme levels and glycans for the most part remains enigmatic.As an alternative explanation it has been suggested that cancer-associated changes in Rab/SNARE components and Golgi matrix proteins cause fragmentation of Golgi stacks resulting in mislocalization of enzymes (Zhang 2021; Bajaj et al. 2022). However, even with the massive fragmentation seen during other types of cellular insults, such as viral infections, O-glycan sialylation is intact (Bagdonaite et al. 2015), questioning the consistency of this idea. Other mechanisms that has been suggested includes retrograde trafficking of GALNTs to the endoplasmic reticulum (Gill et al. 2011). Mediated by Src-activation, this has been proposed to increase Tn antigen levels in the ER by allowing GALNTs to act on substrates in the ER without competition of elongating enzymes (Gill et al. 2011). This was done by forced overexpression of GalNAc-Ts in the ER, where it was shown that mislocalized GALNTs increase glycosylation of substrates ranging from proteases (e.g. MMP14) to chaperones (PDIA4, calnexin) influencing invasion and proteostasis (Gill et al. 2013; Nguyen et al. 2017; Ros et al. 2020). The question remains, however, whether this holds true in actual cancer lesions, where high expression of GALNTs in the ER remains to be detected. Another potential mechanism is represented by change in turnover of glycosyltransferases through shedding of luminal catalytic domains by proteases present in the secretory pathway such as SPPL3 (Voss et al. 2014; Hobohm et al. 2022). However, it is not known if this is relevant for O-glycans. In this context, it was recently shown that ablation of SPPL3 can be used to improve the generation of exhaustion resistant universal chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapies (Wu et al. 2025). Finally, the physicochemical environment of the secretory pathway, especially Golgi luminal pH, may also influence enzyme kinetics. In cancer, dysregulated V-ATPase activity often neutralizes Golgi pH (Galenkamp and Commisso 2021). Interestingly, it has been shown that neutralizing the pH gradient of the secretory pathway, either with the weak base ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) or the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A1 causes relocalizing glycosyltransferases which favors early capping with sialic acid over elongation (Axelsson et al. 2001). However, conflicting results exists on this with some studies showing inhibition of sialylation by hyper-acidification, while others show inhibition of sialylation by neutralizing pH (Campbell et al. 2001; Poschet et al. 2002). Such conflicting results could naturally stem from the different cells analyzed, or limitation of the method of analysis. Another suggestion is that changes in pH tune homo−/heteromeric assemblies and position of glycosyltransferases with the potential to destabilize and reduce their cooperative functions, which might influence the degree of sialylation (Rivinoja et al. 2009; Hassinen et al. 2011). Finally, large Crispr screens have shown a more defined role for cofactor availability (Mn2+ via SLC39/SLC30 and Zn2+ via Zip9) with a strong effect on O-glycosylation. Especially the loss of the Zn2+ transporter causing truncation of O-glycosylation (Yamaji et al. 2019; Romer et al. 2023). Together, these potentially interconnected mechanisms may explain the ubiquitous yet heterogeneous changes in O-glycans observed in epithelial cancers.How do cancer associated O-GalNAc-glycans drive cancer formation and progression?As described above, the structural reorganization of mucin-type O-GalNAc glycans goes into two principal directions: either global truncation (Tn, STn, TF) or selective elongation of glycans capped with functional motifs. However, how does such changes affect cancer formation? In murine models, tissue-restricted ablation of elongation enzymes has demonstrated that loss of elongated O-glycans in the gastrointestinal tract compromises the mucus barrier and precipitates microbiota-dependent, inflammasome-linked pathologies that increase the risk of carcinomas (An et al. 2007; Fu et al. 2011; Gao et al. 2016; Kudelka et al. 2016; Bergstrom et al. 2017; Liu et al. 2020). These observations further suggest that mucins have a central and protective function in this process, because elongated mucin-type O-glycans are major structural determinants of the mucus layer and a key interface with the microbiome. Thus, truncation of O-glycans is expected not only to weaken barrier function, but also to affect host–microbe interactions and the spatial organization of the microbiota, thereby amplifying inflammation-driven tumorigenesis (Fu et al. 2011; Kudelka et al. 2016; Bergstrom et al. 2017; de Ram et al. 2024). Mechanistically, truncated O-glycans may alter mucin conformation and reduce resistance to proteolysis inducing barrier problems (van der Post et al. 2013; Hanisch et al. 2014; Järvå et al. 2020; Wood et al. 2025). Besides such indirect but essential functions, the inherent role of elongated O-glycans in tissue homeostasis has been shown in models of human tissue, more specifically human skin epithelia, where truncation of O-glycans (COSMC or Core-1 KO) in precancerous cells produces hyperproliferation, invasive growth, loss of cell–cell adhesion, and delayed differentiation (Radhakrishnan et al. 2014). Tissues built with primary-like keratinocytes (N/TERT-1) confirmed that elongated O-glycans are important for basal cell architecture and cell–cell adhesion, but in these models failed to induce invasion; implying that truncation of O-glycans cooperates with oncogenic drivers to promote invasive behavior (Dabelsteen et al. 2020). Furthermore, proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses have indicated that loss of elongated glycans acts on multiple pathways simultaneously, destabilizing junctional proteins (adherens junction, tight junctions, desmosomes, hemidesmosomes) and altering kinase pathways (Radhakrishnan et al. 2014). In pancreatic models, combining truncation of O-glycans with mutant KRAS/TP53 accelerates aggressive disease, consistent with crosstalk between a loss of elongated glycans, receptor signaling and genetic lesions (Chugh et al. 2018). Notably, the prognostic impact of elongation enzymes can change dependent on the organ system and model investigated. For example, high C1GalT1 correlates with poor survival in breast cancer patients (Lloyd et al. 1996; Wan and Yu 2021), where deletion of C1GalT1 delays tumor onset in MMTV-ErbB2/PyMT mice (Song et al. 2015). This demonstrates lineage-specific effects and underscores the contextual functions of O-glycans.Site-specific O-glycosylation as a regulatory switch in cancer progressionBeyond shortening of O-glycans, the location of the individual O-glycans may shape signaling, adhesion and lineage control (Zhang and Ten Hagen 2019; Wandall et al. 2021). As mentioned above, the positions at which mucin-type O-glycans are installed are defined by the expression of one or several of the 20 GALNT enzymes influencing receptor functions, ectodomain shedding, adhesion, and differentiation (Bennett et al. 2012; Goth et al. 2018; Zhang and Ten Hagen 2019; Wandall et al. 2021). Altogether, it influences transformation, cell–cell and cell-matrix interactions, and hence the course of the disease. This interpretation has been further substantiated by isoform-specific O-glycoproteomics showing how discrete subsets of glycosites are governed by single GALNT isoforms, and how loss of individual GALNTs perturbs human tissue architecture more strongly than loss of O-glycan elongation (Lavrsen et al. 2018;Bagdonaite et al. 2020 ; Nielsen et al. 2022). These studies furthermore introduce the potential importance of occupancy of the individual glycosites, suggesting that changes in the most highly occupied, isoform-dependent sites are the most likely drivers of specific phenotypes and events. In the following we will provide a few examples of alteration of GalNAcTs and associated observations:Effects on signalingAltered GALNT expression has been reported to perturb cellular signaling, but the effects are highly context-dependent, and the mechanisms involved are generally still unclear and often highly speculative. Several studies suggest that individual GalNAcTs affect signaling directly through glycosylation of specific growth factor receptors. For example, studies find that GALNT1 is frequently upregulated in hepatocellular, breast, colorectal and bladder carcinomas, which is associated with poorer survival (Dyrskjot et al. 2009; Huang et al. 2015; Milde-Langosch et al. 2015). The poor survival has been suggested to be mechanistically linked to increased glycosylation of EGFR affecting motility and invasion (Li et al. 2016). However, this remains unclear, as further investigation of the associated mechanism is missing. Moreover, other studies suggest opposite functional consequences of glycosylation of the EGFR, with increased glycosylation causing inhibition of both the EGFR and other receptors like cMET and IGFR (Liu et al. 2016). Again, the data supporting these findings seem to be limited, which altogether questions the validity of the proposed mechanisms. Instead, the variable data likely reflects that function of site-specific O-glycans is contextual, and that the reported associations may be correlative rather than causal.Regulation of adhesion and tissue architectureSeveral lines of evidence suggest that changes in GALNTs affect epithelial adhesion. GALNT2 is overexpressed in colorectal, lung and oral carcinomas and gliomas and is associated with metastasis and poorer outcome (Kohsaki et al. 2000; Ho et al. 2014; Lin et al. 2014). Interestingly, GalNT2 loss-of-function in human tissue models causes compromised cell-matrix adhesion and defective O-glycosylation of adherence, including tight junctions, desmosomes and hemidesmosomes, coupled to altered phosphorylation (Bagdonaite et al. 2020; Nielsen et al. 2022). However, it should be stressed that these data are only correlative and a direct mechanistic link between site specific glycosylation and effect is still missing. Nevertheless, the observed changes are consistent with an effect on cell-matrix adhesion and a suggested role in glycosylation of ECM proteins, including collagens (Bagdonaite et al. 2020; Nielsen et al. 2022). In non-small cell lung cancer, GALNT2 is even suggested to directly O-glycosylate integrin α5 (ITGA5), modulate PI3K/AKT, and MAPK/ERK activity to promote migration and invasion (Sun et al. 2019). Developmental studies support such functional interactions, with the demonstration in Drosophila, that the fly orthologue, pgant3, is required for integrin-mediated adhesion, highlighting how site-specific O-glycans can control focal adhesion dynamics (Zhang et al. 2008). Moreover, such a role for GALNTs could explain the observation of increased GALNT2 expression at invasive fronts. Alternatively, this could be due to a potential role of GalNAc-T2 glycosylation of major ECM proteins deposited in such areas.Differentiation programs and EMTSite-specific initiation is suggested to affect epithelial differentiation and EMT. This is exemplified by GALNT3 and GALNT6, which have opposing influences on epithelial fate. GALNT3 helps maintain differentiation in human skin (Bagdonaite et al. 2020, Nielsen et al. 2022), where its loss promotes epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in mammary epithelium and trophoblast stem cells (Raghu et al. 2019). In contrast, overexpression of GALNT6 compromises epithelial differentiation (Park et al. 2011; Lavrsen et al. 2018) and GALNT6 upregulation is associated with dysplastic growth and EMT (Park et al. 2010; Freire-de-Lima et al. 2011; Tarhan et al. 2016; Kimura et al. 2020). Looking at patient specimens, the association between cancer and GALNT3 or GALNT6 seems to be dependent on both to stage and tumor type. For example, GALNT6 correlates with invasion and poor outcome in some colon and gastric cohorts (Gomes et al. 2009; Lavrsen et al. 2018), while it correlates with a favorable prognosis in other cohorts (Ogawa et al. 2022). The same is the case with GALNT3, which is linked to good prognosis in colorectal and lung cancers (Dosaka-Akita et al. 2002; Shibao et al. 2002; Yamamoto et al. 2004), yet associated with a poor prognosis in pancreatic and ovarian disease (Wang et al. 2014; Chugh et al. 2016; Sheta et al. 2017; Barkeer et al. 2018). These differential patterns could simply be related to the various subtypes investigated, or perhaps more likely to tumor stage. Collectively it emphasizes that the context, such as tissue type or cancer stage, defines whether a particular GALNT behaves as an oncogene or a suppressor.Metastatic disseminationChanges in GalNAcT expression has moreover been linked to metastatic dissemination, suggesting that defined O-glycosylation events can change the metastatic potential of individual cells. In prostate cancer, GALNT7 is upregulated in prostate cancer tissue and has been associated with altered O-glycoproteomes, increased Tn antigen exposure, tumor growth, migration and invasion (Scott et al. 2023). In hepatocellular carcinoma, GALNT7 has similarly been implicated in migration and invasion through O-glycosylation of MUC13 and activation of PI3K/AKT signaling (Liang et al. 2025). In xenografts of human neuroblastoma, GALNT11 and GALNT13 are selectively expressed in cells metastasizing to the bone marrow, while GALNT9 is expressed in primary tumors (Berois et al. 2013). Functional studies have implicated GALNT13 in the spread of lung cancer cell lines through the decoration of syndecan-1 with a trimeric-Tn cluster, which is suggested to enable syndecan-integrin-MMP9 complex formation through an unknown mechanism (Matsumoto et al. 2013). This complex formation increases cancer cell line motility and extracellular-matrix degradation, which would be consistent with clinical links between GALNT13 expression, metastasis and poor outcome in metastatic breast cancer, lung cancer, and neuroblastoma (Berois et al. 2006; Berois et al. 2013; Nogimori et al. 2016; Fernandez et al. 2021). Additional evidence suggests that other initiation enzymes, such as GALNT14, can also promote metastatic behavior in selected settings (Kwon et al. 2015; Song et al. 2016; Kwon et al. 2020). Importantly, GALNT dysregulation is often embedded in broader noncoding RNA networks. For example, the metastatic miR-30b/30d program suppresses GALNT7 and GALNT1 in melanoma, while GALNT7 is upregulated in colorectal cancer through lncRNA-SNHG7/miR-34a and in additional settings through regulators such as miR-214, miR-125a-5p, and lncRNA-CCDC144NL-AS1 (Gaziel-Sovran et al. 2011; Peng et al. 2012; Li et al. 2018; Cao et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2022). Finally, human genetics supports a role for initiation enzymes in cancer susceptibility. Inactivating germline and somatic variants in GALNT12 occur in subsets of colorectal cancers and have been associated with moderate-penetrance risk, although the gene-disease validity is limited and reflects heterogeneity across studies (Guda et al. 2009; Clarke et al. 2012; Evans et al. 2018; Fernandez et al. 2019). It would be expected that new O-glycoproteomic tools, including bump-hole reporters (Schumann et al. 2020) and BOCTAG (Cioce et al. 2022), now allow direct mapping of isoenzyme-specific glyco-barcodes and should help define which GALNT-dependent glycosylation events are causal for invasion and metastasis.Together, these data support a hierarchical view in which GALNT-encoded positional information creates a spatial code on receptors, adhesion molecules and immune ligands, while branching, extension, and capping enzymes (truncation versus elongation) define the global properties of the glycocalyx. It is the intersection of which sites are occupied, at what density, and how those sites are further elongated, as well as the carbohydrate receptor availability, that reprograms how glycans influence adhesion, signaling, immune evasion and metastatic behavior in epithelial cancers.Cancer progression through O-glycans and glycan-binding proteinsIn healthy organisms an important function of O-glycans is to orchestrate immune cell trafficking and to modulate immune tolerance through interaction with glycan-binding proteins (GBPs) (McEver and Cummings 1997; RodrIguez et al. 2018; Smith and Bertozzi 2021). In the developing tumor, such mechanisms are exploited to promote progression, metastasis, and immune evasion through changes in O-glycans. The functional impact of these glycans reflects the heterogeneous and context-dependent expression of O-glycans across tumor types, anatomical sites, timepoints, and differentiation states. In this way, the O-glycan landscape might reflect the adaptive plasticity of tumors within their evolving ecosystems. Several key carbohydrate receptors are involved, and the most prevalent and essential are reviewed below.Selectins and vascular adhesionSelectins (E, P, L) primarily recognize sialylated, fucosylated LacNAc motifs, with sialyl Lewis X (Neu5Acα2–3Galβ1–4[Fucα1–3]GlcNAc) as the canonical epitope and sialyl Lewis A as a weaker binding variant in some contexts (McEver and Cummings 1997; Smith and Bertozzi 2021). L-selectin prefers 6-sulfo-sLex (and related 6−/disulfated forms), while P-selectin binds sLex presented on core-2 O-glycans, classically on PSGL-1, where peptide Tyr-sulfation increases affinity. E-selectin engages sLex/a on densely displayed, often extended poly-LacNAc chains of glycoproteins or glycolipids, supporting multivalent interactions and thus boosting avidity. On tumor cells, elongated O-glycans terminating in Lewis structures create high-affinity selectin ligands, hijacking the physiological use of core-2 O-glycans on leukocytes to tether to vasculature, enabling intravascular invasion and metastasis (Takada et al. 1993; Shimodaira et al. 1997; Hagisawa et al. 2005; Hatakeyama et al. 2010). Interruption of sLex reduces metastatic dissemination (Opolski et al. 1998; Weston et al. 1999), while forced sLex expression amplifies EGFR signaling and, with KRAS activation, accelerates neoplastic outgrowth, providing a direct link between glycans and receptors (Engle et al. 2019). Similarly, constitutive E-selectin expression in the bone marrow sustains leukemic engraftment, mirroring stem-cell homing, while platelet P-selectin bridges tumor cells into protective platelet emboli that promote angiogenesis and shield from shear forces and immunity (Sackstein et al. 2008; Laubli and Borsig 2010; Paschos et al. 2010; Winkler et al. 2012). Though immunohistochemistry rarely distinguishes O- from N- or glycolipid carriers of selectin ligands, enzyme expression and glycomics implicate substantive O-glycan contributions, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract, typically in mosaic patches that coordinate vascular interactions with integrins, chemokine receptors, and other receptors (Hinneburg et al. 2017; Doi et al. 2020).Siglecs and immune checkpointsIn parallel, tumors upregulate clustered sialylated O-glycans, especially on mucins such as MUC1 and MUC16, to engage inhibitory Siglecs (Swanson et al. 2007; Beatson et al. 2016). Furthermore, site-specific glycosylation may encode molecular patterns dictating receptor engagement. For example, Siglec-7 preferentially binds ST/STn, especially when 6-O-sulfated, to suppress NK cytotoxicity and polarize macrophages (Hudak et al. 2014; Bull et al. 2021; Jung et al. 2025); Siglec-15 binds clustered STn to attenuate T-cell responses independently of PD-L1 (Wang et al. 2019); and Siglec-9, recognizing diverse α2–3-sialylated termini (Beatson et al. 2016; Rodriguez et al. 2021), contributes with Siglec-7 to an immunosuppressive milieu in pancreatic cancer (Beatson et al. 2016; Rodriguez et al. 2021). Siglec-10, via engagement with the heavily O-glycosylated CD24, transmits anti-phagocytic signals to macrophages, an axis reversed by interrupting the Siglec-10-CD24 interaction (Chen et al. 2009; Sammar et al. 2017; Forgione et al. 2020). Collectively, these interactions between O-glycans and siglecs impose tolerogenic signaling (ITIM/ITAM-coupled), suppress T cell receptor activity, and diminish cytotoxicity, thereby constituting parallel immune checkpoints to the classical checkpoints like PD1-PD-L1 (Angata et al. 2006; Engblom et al. 2017)(Fig. 2).Figure 2Cancer hallmarks influenced by changes in O-GalNAc-glycans and associated treatment opportunities. Alterations in O-glycosylation influence multiple hallmarks of cancer, creating a functional link between changes in O-glycans and malignant behavior. Truncated structures such as Tn and STn influence cell signaling and reduce cell–cell adhesion facilitating invasive behavior. Terminal modifications, including sialyl-Lewis antigens, enable vascular adhesion and extravasation through interactions with selectins, thereby promoting metastatic dissemination. Cancer associated glycans also engage lectin receptors such as galectins, Siglecs, and MGL to dampen immune recognition and enable immune evasion. Each of these glycan-driven traits is coupled to therapeutic opportunities: Antibodies and vaccines that target tumor-associated epitopes; inhibitors of glycan-lectin interactions prevent metastasis formation and disrupt immune check points; and enzymatic or metabolic strategies seek to remodel the tumor glycocalyx with similar effects. High density Tn recruits macrophage galactose-type lectin (MGL), which recognizes both glycan identity and carrier (Higashi et al. 2002; van Vliet et al. 2008; RodrIguez et al. 2018; Diniz et al. 2019; Gabba et al. 2021) (Fig. 2). It can therefore be speculated that clustered Tn-mucin shed from tumors promotes tolerogenic dendritic cell differentiation and IL-10 secretion. MGL+ antigen-presenting cells consequently inhibit CD4+ T-cell proliferation (Li et al. 2012; van Vliet et al. 2013; Gu et al. 2019) and dampen effector T-cell signaling via CD45 modulation (van Vliet et al. 2006). Clinically, the presence of MGL ligands is associated with poor outcome and oncogenic drivers (e.g. BRAF(V600E), PIK3CA) (Saeland et al. 2007; Lenos et al. 2015; Sahasrabudhe et al. 2019), demonstrating how the MGL-Tn interactions may form an independent immune checkpoint and, at least in explain the increased expression of Tn in human cancers.Galectin lattices and receptor controlGalectins add yet another dimension, oligomerizing on β-galactoside termini (LacNAc/poly-LacNAc; sometimes TF) to form lattices that stabilize receptors and regulate endocytosis (Liu and Rabinovich 2005; Elola et al. 2015; Thijssen et al. 2015) (Fig. 2). Galectin-1, often elevated in tumors (Thijssen et al. 2015), reduces neutrophil trafficking, induces T-cell apoptosis, promotes T-reg activity, and reprograms macrophages toward tumor associated macrophages expressing tolerogenic signals, including IDO1/PD-L1 expression (Yu et al. 2025). Galectin-3 binds clustered core-1 O-glycans (Modenutti et al. 2019) and has been suggested to interact with MUC1/MUC16 to stabilize EGFR dimers, reinforce endothelial adhesion, and enhance mitogenic signaling (Argueso et al. 2009; Cao et al. 2018). In melanoma, galectin-3 has also been suggested to cluster MUC18 to activate Akt-driven invasion (Pang et al. 2022). Similarly, Galectin-9 has been shown to interact with a mucin domain on TIM-3 to modulate Th1/T-reg balance and drive T-cell apoptosis (Seki et al. 2008; Wang et al. 2008; Nielsen et al. 2018), providing yet another suggestion of how O-glycan signals seem to be exploited as immune checkpoints.Tumors as multicellular and adaptive systemsTo make sense of the many different functions of O-glycans, one may view tumors as an adaptive multicellular system. This may explain the observed O-glycan heterogeneity, with variable expression of O-glycans across tumors, sites, and states reflecting functional differences. Based on this perspective, it could be speculated that a truncated program (Tn, STn) supports proliferation, motility, and immune evasion, while an elongated program (extended cores with Gal, GlcNAc, fucose, sialic acid) reinforces receptor stability and support metastasis formation. In this context, the dense display of O-glycans on mucins is particularly important, as weak monovalent glycan-lectin interactions can become strong through multivalent presentation, and mucins with cancer-associated glycans can thereby function as new contextual ligands or decoys. However, this interpretation is most likely too simple to capture the many different aspects of glycan functions during tumor formation and progression. Nevertheless, it is clear that some glycans are more dynamic than others, across tumors, and that therapies must make sure to target the most stable structures across multiple stages and present in the largest number of patients. So far, such structures seem to be short, truncated O-glycans like Tn and STn.Translating tumor-specific O-GalNAc motifs into safe, effective cancer therapiesThe selective expression of aberrant O-GalNAc glycans such as Tn and STn on carcinomas across all cancer stages (Romer et al. 2021) make them appealing tumor-associated targets (Fig. 2). Early vaccine efforts with monovalent conjugates have shown to induce a robust humoral immune response, but did not always achieve recognition of native tumor cells (e.g. Tn-, STn-, or T-KLH) (Ragupathi et al. 1999; Sørensen et al. 2006; Miles et al. 2011; Yin and Huang 2012). One of the most advanced examples is the use of the 5E5 antibody, primarily targeting Tn-MUC1 (Tarp et al. 2007), converted into a second-generation CAR format (Posey Jr et al. 2016). The 5E5 scFv retained specificity for MUC1-Tn with minimal cross-reactivity, and 5E5 CART cells demonstrated potent and selective cytolytic activity against Tn-expressing cancer cells while sparing normal human cells. Effect was seen in murine xenograft models (Posey Jr et al. 2016) leading to a clinical phase I trial in solid tumors (NCT04025216) (Gutierrez et al. 2021). Another Tn-targeting candidate, the 237Ab antibody, which recognizes a Tn-glycosylated epitope in murine podoplanin, was also adapted to a CAR format (Brooks et al. 2010). However, while the parental antibody displayed strong specificity, the 237CART cells became more promiscuous, highlighting potential loss of specificity during scFv conversion (He et al. 2019). More recently, the 4C8 antibody, developed against a Tn glycopeptide in CD44v6, was adapted into CARTs and demonstrated selective tumor targeting and cytotoxicity in vitro and in vivo using murine models (Aasted et al. 2023). Importantly, 4C8 CARTs overcame known cross-reactivity issues associated with CD44v6 of healthy tissues such as skin with selective targeting of cancer cells using mixed 3D models, underscoring the potential safety advantages of glycopeptide-specific targeting (Aasted et al. 2023). Beyond Tn, CART strategies have also been developed against the STn antigen, most notably using the B72.3 and CC49 antibodies, both of which recognize the tumor-associated glycoprotein TAG-72 (Kjeldsen et al. 1988; Muraro et al. 1988; Loy and Nashelsky 1993). Early B72.3-based CARTs induced IL-2 secretion and cytotoxicity against STn/TAG-72-positive colorectal adenocarcinoma cells (Hombach et al. 1997a; Murad et al. 2018), and CC49-based CARTs showed tumor-specific lysis both in vitro and in vivo (Hombach et al. 1998; McGuinness et al. 1999). A first-generation humanized CC49 CART entered clinical trials but failed, likely due to limited co-stimulation and immune responses against the scFv (Hege et al. 2017). To address this, a humanized CC49 CART incorporating a 4-1BB co-stimulatory domain was developed and demonstrated robust activity against ovarian cancer cell lines and xenografts (Murad et al. 2018). These collective findings supported the initiation of a clinical trial in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer patients (NCT05225363). More recently, a novel STn-specific monoclonal antibody (AM52.1) with high tumor specificity was engineered into a second-generation CAR construct. AM52.1 CART demonstrated potent activity against STn-expressing cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and multiple solid tumor models, including gastric, tubo-ovarian, and colorectal mucinous metastases (Abrantes et al. 2025). Nevertheless, challenges such as expression of STn in healthy or inflamed tissue remain obstacles for STn-directed therapies. Other elongated O-glycan structures have also been explored as CART targets, including Ley (Lewis Y antigen). The Hu3S193 antibody, which was humanized to generate second-generation Ley CARTs, showed selective cytotoxicity against cancer cells with medium to high Ley expression, while sparing normal cells with low expression, such as neutrophils (Westwood et al. 2005; Westwood et al. 2009). Importantly, Ley CART activity was not blocked by soluble antigen in patient sera. In a clinical phase I trial, four relapsed AML patients were treated with Ley CARTs without grade 3 or 4 toxicities (Ritchie et al. 2013). Additional phase I trials are underway to evaluate Ley CARTs in advanced lung cancer and solid tumors (NCT03198052, NCT03198052).Redirecting endogenous T-cells with CD3-engaging bispecifics (T-cell bispecifics; TCBs) offers an off-the-shelf complement to CART therapies. Although most clinical approvals to date are in hematologic malignancies, there is now clear precedent for efficacy in solid tumors. Importantly, recent engineering innovations, especially CD3 affinity attenuation and asymmetric valency, have improved the therapeutic index in settings with narrow safety margins (Lee et al. 2023). These insights are directly applicable to O-glycan targets, where reducing basal T-cell triggering is critical to mitigate bystander effects in tissues expressing low levels of target glycans. Indeed, TAG-72 × CD3 and STn × CD3 bispecifics concepts have shown preclinical proof-of-mechanism (Hombach et al. 1997b). Modern designs emphasize weaker CD3 arms and 2:1 tumor-antigen:CD3 stoichiometry, which can dissociate cytokine release from tumor killing (Bacac et al. 2016; Trinklein et al. 2019; Dang et al. 2021; Eigenmann et al. 2021). Moreover, protease-activatable pro-T-cell engagers (pro-TCEs) represent an important advance: these molecules remain inert until unmasked by tumor-localized proteases (Cattaruzza et al. 2023). Preclinical models have already demonstrated that such conditional activation can widen the safety margin for solid-tumor targeting (Geiger et al. 2020). Beyond CD3 engagers, bispecific antibodies combining a glycan-defined tumor arm with a second specificity can enhance selectivity and potency. Biparatopic designs on specific targets may illustrate how simultaneous engagement of two non-overlapping glyco-epitopes may increases avidity and tumor retention (Jasuja et al. 2024; Shrestha et al. 2026b).Antibody-drug conjugates targeting O-glycan epitopesTargeting cancer-associated O-glycans also offers a promising strategy to expand the therapeutic window of antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) for solid tumors, where off-tumor binding to healthy epithelia has historically limited both safety and efficacy. Early efforts focused on humanized anti-STn antibodies conjugated to monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) (Eavarone et al. 2018), which demonstrated nanomolar potency in vitro, tumor growth inhibition in both cell line and patient-derived xenograft models, and favorable toxicology in non-human primates (Eavarone et al. 2018). Despite these encouraging findings, concerns have persisted regarding STn expression in certain healthy, and particularly inflamed tissues (Julien et al. 2012).
