The importance of BRD4 as a 5’ elongation checkpoint factor mediating Pol II pause release is elegantly illustrated by defects in pause release, 3’-end mRNA processing, and transcription termination upon depletion of endogenous BRD4-L and BRD4-S, but not BRD2 and BRD3, using genome editing and a BRD4-specific degrader.23 It is clear that pause release requires BRD4 association with key elongation factors such as DSIF, Pol II-associated factor 1 complex (PAF1c), both Cyclin T1 and CDK9 subunits of P-TEFb, and histone chaperone/elongation factor SPT6,17,19,23 while the presence of 3’-end mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor (CPSF) and cleavage stimulatory factor (CstF) in the BRD4 complex is critical for 3’-processing and transcription termination.23Mechanistically, BRD4-recruited P-TEFb kinase phosphorylates the Pol II CTD at Ser2, DSIF subunit SPT5, and NELF subunits A and E, resulting in NELF dissociation, PAF1c binding, and release of paused Pol II.177,178 While BRD4 is essential for P-TEFb recruitment, its bromodomains seem dispensable since deletion of BD1 and BD2 does not affect BRD4 and P-TEFb association nor Pol II pause release.179 Such BD-independent interaction has also been observed in BD-deleted BRD4 association with Mediator, SPT5/DSIF, and SPT6,180 thus providing a molecular switch mechanism underlying BRD4 recruitment from bromodomain-dependent chromatin binding during initial breast cancer development to bromodomain-dispensable but Mediator-dependent association when tumors become insensitive to BET inhibitor treatment.83Depending on the molecular features of Pol II stalling, additional mechanisms have been described for release of promoter-proximal pausing. P-TEFb, besides existing as an active Cyclin T1-CDK9 dimer, is also sequestered as an inactive small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex containing 7SK small nuclear RNA (snRNA) and HEXIM1/2, MEPCE, and LARP7 proteins.181 Release of this inhibitory complex from the pause site can be potentially achieved by BRD4-dependent recruitment of JMJD6 (Jumonji domain-containing protein 6) to the anti-pause enhancer (A-PE).16 The A-PE-associated JMJD6 acts to remove the repressive dimethylated histone H4 arginine 3 (H4R3m2) chromatin mark and the 5’-methyl-cap in 7SK snRNA through long-range A-PE contact with the paused promoter bridged by BRD4, leading to resumed elongation of Pol II. Other pause-release mechanisms may also occur via BRD4-mediated recruitment of TFs or DNA/chromatin regulators to the pause sites. Documented examples include BRD4-recruited c-Myc17 to facilitate Pol II pause release rather than Pol II recruitment170 and BRD4-mediated Pol II CTD Ser2 phosphorylation that in turn stimulates DNA topoisomerase I activity to help overcome transcription-induced torsional stress in DNA topology after pause release.182 Moreover, how the positioning of the BRD4-enriched +1 nucleosome,160 promoter-proximal DNA/RNA sequence and structure,176,183 and m6A-modified nascent RNAs and 7SK snRNA184,185 functionally crosstalk with BRD4 and other pause release factors remains to be further investigated.5.Post pause releaseAfter pause release, Pol II resumes transcription typically in a highly processive manner until encountering roadblocks, such as positive supercoiling-generated DNA torsional stress, gene body-embedded nucleosomes, co-transcriptional mRNA processing events (e.g., splicing), and transcription-replication conflicts, that require additional factors to overcome these elongation barriers. DNA topoisomerase I, besides associating with promoter-engaged Pol II to facilitate PIC assembly and pause release, is also found in gene bodies extending to the transcription termination sites to help relieve DNA torsional stress in an enzymatic activity- and BRD4-dependent manner.182 Many of the BRD4-interacting proteins, e.g., 53BP1, BARD1, GLTSCR1, ATAD5, CHD4, JMJD6, and NSD3 (Figure 4B), possess chromatin-remodeling, histone-modifying, topologically-associating/scaffolding, or genome-surveillance activity to help Pol II pass through downstream roadblocks. CHD4 (chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4), as a subunit in the NuRD chromatin-remodeling complex, interacts with the ET domain of BRD4 to promote fusion oncoprotein access to super-enhancers in rhabdomyosarcoma186 where BRD4-L has recently been shown to act as an oncogenic factor93 in contrast to its tumor-suppressive role in breast cancer.54 Other examples include NSD3 (nuclear receptor-binding SET domain protein 3)-facilitated BRD4 association with CHD8 chromatin remodeler187 and c-Myc oncoprotein,188 as well as BRD4-ATAD5 (ATPase family AAA domain-containing 5)-regulated replication fork progression.29,30,148A specific class of BRD4-interacting proteins is involved in co-transcriptional RNA processing linked to Pol II elongation. This effector function of BRD4 mediated by direct protein-protein interaction (PPI) is distinct from the indirect transcriptional control of genes encoding RNA processing factors including select serine/arginine-rich splicing factors (SRSFs) and spliceosomal components.189 Besides interacting with the RPB1 CTD,116 the cohesin (SMC1/SMC3/RAD21) complex,190 and JMJD616 that forms a unique splicing hub controlling c-Myc-promoted cancer metabolic programs,191 BRD4 also modulates mRNA processing via direct contact with specific components of the mRNA splicing machinery such as heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein M (hnRNPM) and FUS (fused in sarcoma; also known as hnRNPP2).22 From BRD4 isoform IP-proteomic analysis33 performed in immortalized W12E keratinocytes, which are derived from a low-grade cervical lesion naturally harboring extrachromosomal HPV16 (ecHPV16) genomes, BRD4-L was indeed found to associate with JMJD6, RAD21, SRSF protein kinase 2 (SRPK2) and its substrate SRSF2,24 as well as many mRNA splicing components involved in spliceosome assembly and function (Figure 4C, green), splicing regulation (red), and RNA binding via RNA recognition motif (RRM)-containing proteins implicated in m6A recognition (blue).33In contrast, BRD4-S, while not showing direct association with these RNA processing factors in W12E nuclear extracts, was specifically enriched in gene bodies in genome-wide binding profiling performed in MDA-MB-231 TNBC cells,54 indicating that BRD4-S and BRD4-L may both be implicated in RNA processing via a mechanistically distinct and/or cell state-specific manner. This notion is supported by observations that (1) BRD4 inhibitor treatment consistently alters mRNA splicing patterns189,192 and RNA foci formation,193 and (2) BRD4-L-interacting RRM-containing YTHDC1 is involved in BRD4-regulated enhancer function,141 alternative spliceosome complex assembly, and splice site usage194 depending on its reading of m6A-modified enhancer RNA or precursor mRNA.Through interaction with distinct protein partners and ncRNA/pre-mRNA association, BRD4 controls multiple steps of chromatin dynamics, transcription, and co-transcriptional events. It is thus important to define the molecular mechanisms underlying BRD4-modulated proximity (i.e., short-range) and long/ultralong-range chromosomal organization and oncogenic ecDNA amplification, particularly the role of BRD4 protein isoforms and post-translational modifications in these processes.Distinct BRD4 Isoform Function in Cancer Development and Viral Latency/ReactivationMechanistic understanding of BRD4 isoform function is crucial for identifying key gene targets and regulatory pathways/factors for the development of therapeutic options. During disease progression, BRD4, with its growth-promoting/immunomodulatory function, often drives proto-oncogene and immune checkpoint gene expression, as seen with enhanced levels of c-Myc in leukemia and high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC),79,80,82 FosL1/AP-1 in lung adenocarcinoma,195 immunosuppressive programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) in T cells,196 and programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) in cancer cells.197 In most of these studies, the cancer-driving role of BRD4 is attributed to the more abundant BRD4-L, even though most of the experimental strategies involving pan-BRD4 RNAi or antibodies targeting the N-terminal region of BRD4 cannot readily distinguish the specific BRD4 isoform involved. This is particularly concerning, as a predominant BRD4-L degradation product comigrating with BRD4-S is often detected in SDS-PAGE and WB analysis. Without using isoform-specific antibodies (Figure 2) or conducting functional rescue with ectopically expressed isoforms, functional designation of BRD4-L and BRD4-S based purely on gel size detection could be misleading.Recently, opposing functions of BRD4-L and BRD4-S in cancer development and viral latency/reactivation have been defined mainly by parallel studies of individual BRD4 isoform knockdown and subsequent rescue in the same experimental setting. The demonstration of BRD4-L as a tumor suppressor versus the oncogenic function of BRD4-S in breast cancer, particularly the TNBC subtype, is thus convincingly established via cell-based 2D/3D proliferation, migration, and invasion assays, as well as in vivo xenograft and transgenic mouse models54 (Figure 5A). It appears that BRD4-S and BRD4-L both associate with acetylated nucleosomes and interact with the same TF, engrailed homeobox 1 (EN1), typically expressed in the brain but ectopically reactivated in TNBC cells. However, BRD4-S-upregulated matrisome (i.e., extracellular matrix-ECM network) gene expression through enhancer binding is distinct from the promoter association of BRD4-L, resulting in altered expression of matrisome genes encoding mucins (5AC, 5B), syndecans (SDC3, SDC4), type II cystatins (CST1, CST2, CST4), cathepsins (CTSB, CTSW, CTSZ), semaphorins (SEMA3B, SEMA3F, SEMA4D, SEMA6B), plexins (PLXNA2, PLXNA3, PLXND1), and many others (Figure 5A). This highlights the importance of location-dependent regulation of BRD4 isoform functions.A pro-leukemia function of BRD4-S versus a potential anti-leukemia role of BRD4-L198 in driving BCL2 and c-Myc oncogene expression has likewise been described in the mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL) fusion protein-positive (i.e., MLL-X, derived from chromosomal translocation/rearrangement) subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia (AML; Figure 5A). Similar BRD4-S-promoted colorectal cancer (CRC) cell proliferation/migration and tumor growth have also been described.94 In both CRC and MLL-X AML, SRSF protein kinase 1 (SRPK1)-mediated phosphorylation of SRSFs that regulate splice site recognition and spliceosome assembly seems to enhance BRD4-S 3’-terminal exon 12 usage (Figure 3), thus favoring pre-mRNA splicing towards BRD4-S over BRD4-L. This is consistent with the observation that inhibition of SRPK1 kinase activity by small-molecule inhibitor SPHINX31 leads to increased BRD4-L (i.e., reduced BRD4-S) transcript and protein levels without altering total BRD4 transcripts. However, the specific regulatory SRSF proteins involved, e.g., SRSF1/2 in MLL-X AML198 vs. DEAD-box RNA helicase DDX27-recruited SRSF6 in CRC,94 may vary by the cancer type and its tumor microenvironment. Although knockdown of BRD4-L shows only small, if any, effects in both studies, a precise role of BRD4-L remains to be clarified. Nonetheless, a tumor-suppressive role of BRD4-L in preventing aging-associated cancer development in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS), which is a premature aging disorder, has also been suggested based on oncogenic transformation resistance in HGPS patient-derived cell studies.199Context-dependent regulation is not constrained to the spatial locations where BRD4 isoforms bind to their regulated genes but also depends on subcellular compartmentalization, cell/tissue/organ-specific status, and the microenvironment. Unlike the opposing functions observed in breast cancer and MLL-X-positive AML, BRD4-L is the de facto oncogenic driver in rhabdomyosarcoma,93 where BRD4-S acts as a gatekeeper (i.e., suppressor) to restrict BRD4-L function in upregulating invasion/migration-associated integrin ITGA4/5 expression, particularly in fusion protein (FP)-negative embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (FP− ERMS; Figure 5B).While antagonizing activities seem to be a common feature in several of the examined cancer types, BRD4-L and BRD4-S can also act cooperatively or synergistically in subsequent disease progression or in other biological contexts. When cancer cells metastasize to distal organs, the opposing activities of BRD4-L and BRD4-S observed in primary breast tumors switch to functional dependency or cooperativity during lung metastasis, since knockdown of either isoform significantly diminishes TNBC metastasis to the lungs in an MDA-MB-231 lung metastasis (LM)-prone mouse xenograft model.54 This functional dependency/cooperativity of both BRD4 isoforms is also found in BRD4 locus-amplified, c-Myc-driven HGSOC in which Neuregulin 1 (NRG1) important for activating membrane tyrosine kinase receptor signaling is upregulated by BRD4-L and BRD4-S acting together with the tumor-promoting activity of the SWI/SNF complex, with each isoform additionally regulating unique gene signatures, e.g., BRD4-L-enhanced E2F1 versus BRD4-S-elevated VEGF pathways200 (Figure 5C). This indicates that BRD4-L and BRD4-S can both play an oncogenic role by targeting common and unique cellular pathways during disease progression.The recruitment of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler possessing tumor-promoting function by BRD4-S/L in HGSOC is distinct from a typically tumor-suppressive role of SWI/SNF, which in the case of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) is recruited mainly by BRD4-S, and not by BRD4-L, to the downstream BRD4-bound +1 nucleosome.69 BRD4-S-recruited SWI/SNF silences HIV-1 promoter activity during HIV-1 latency, particularly in CD4+ T cells, and likely suppresses endogenous retroelements in the host genome as well (Figure 5D). Reactivation of the latent HIV provirus can be achieved by treating cells with activating cytokines (e.g., TNF-α) or latency-reversing agents (LRAs) in the “shock-and-kill” regimen to displace the repressor complexes and/or remodel the chromatin environment. This triggers HIV transcription that can be further enhanced by BRD4-L-mediated recruitment of TFs (e.g., NFκB or AP-1) for transcription initiation and P-TEFb for Pol II pause release, or by the HIV-encoded transcriptional activator Tat in complex with P-TEFb during elongation (Figure 5D). Of note, P-TEFb recruitment by Tat or by BRD4-L is mutually exclusive.122 This intricate partner interaction switch from HIV latency to reactivation elegantly illustrates a highly coordinated molecular action mediated by distinct BRD4 isoforms in modulating viral gene expression.In HPV, viral latency is partly achieved by HPV-encoded full-length E2,13,201 double-spliced E2 C-terminal domain (dsE2C),13 E8^E2C (later simplified as E8^E2),202 and E1M^E2C203 transcriptional repressors that limit viral gene expression typically in the basal and parabasal epithelial layers. Full-length E2, in complex with BRD4-L and through binding to its cognate cis-elements in the E6 early promoter-proximal region, inhibits E6 and E7 oncogene expression primarily by blocking TFIID and Pol II entry in an acetylated nucleosome-dependent manner.13,134,204 This transcription-repressive function of E2 is separate from its transactivating role in gene regulation and its involvement, together with HPV-encoded E1 helicase, in initiating viral DNA replication,205 with functional distinction depending on specific DNA contexts and the partner proteins involved.206,207 When the repressor function of E2 is disrupted, often through viral genome integration into host chromosomes that partially truncates E1/E2-coding sequences, BRD4-L/S then works with cellular factors (e.g., AP-1)208 acting through the enhancer-containing HPV upstream regulatory region (URR) or integration-adjacent cellular enhancers to activate E6/E7 expression, leading to cellular hyperproliferation and sometimes oncogenic progression.13,206,207 Without integration, latent HPV genomes remain as episomal ecDNA and use NPS-phosphorylated BRD4-L/S to potentiate E1/E2-dependent early HPV replication.28,33 Upon epithelial cell differentiation, which is critical for viral capsid production and virion assembly, BRD4-L/S then recruits DDR factors, such as p53-binding protein 1 (53BP1), implicated in non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and BRCA1-associated RING domain 1 (BARD1), involved in homologous repair (HR), to help overcome replication stress associated with high-copy episomal ecHPV replication needed for the productive HPV infection cycle.33 This often occurs in a temporal and spatial-dependent manner, first through BRD4-L-enhanced E2 binding to the HPV origin of replication (ori), followed by BRD4-L-mediated recruitment of 53BP1 and BRD4-S, with the latter further bringing in BARD1 during the early stage of differentiation-dependent HPV genome amplification (Figure 5E). A switch of DNA repair pathways from error-prone NHEJ mediated by BRD4-L/53BP1 to error-free HR facilitated by BRD4-L/BARD1 occurs at a subsequent replication stage to ensure faithful genome replication,33 which is likely triggered by reduced levels of histone H4 lysine 20 dimethylation (H4K20me2) needed for stable 53BP1 binding,209 thus dislodging 53BP1 from replicating HPV chromatin.The recruitment of DDR factors through distinct BRD4 isoforms is crucial not only for alleviating the replication stress associated with productive viral genome replication but also for maintaining host genome integrity, whose disruption or instability/imbalance is often linked to carcinogenesis. DDR factors uniquely associated with BRD4-L, as identified by proteomic network analysis33, include 53BP1, RIF1 and NSD2 (also known as WHSC1) in NHEJ; BARD1 and BRCA1 in HR; INO80, MCRS1 and ACTR8 in global genome nucleotide excision repair (GG-NER); TFIIH, CDK9, XAB2 and Pol II in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER); and RFC1/2/3, PCNA, CUL4A and XPC in both GG-NER and TC-NER pathways (Figure 5F).6,25,33 In contrast, BRD4-S and BRD4-S(b) show selective association with HR factors BARD1/BRCA133 and DDR-shielding condensin II components SMC2/NCAPD334, respectively. Besides direct effector function, BRD4 isoforms also indirectly modulate the levels of DDR factors through transcriptional control, as evidenced by BRD4-L-regulated gene transcription of XRCC5/636 and CtIP37 involved individually in the NHEJ and HR repair pathways. Clearly, multi-tier regulation through protein effector function and transcriptional/posttranscriptional control is used by distinct BRD4 isoforms to modulate key steps in cancer progression and viral latency/reactivation.BRD4 Phosphorylation and Other Post-Translational Modification (PTM)The biological function of BRD4 isoforms lies not only in effector association and transcriptional regulation but is further dictated by post-translational modifications. PTMs can generate diversity in BRD4 protein isoforms by creating new PPI interfaces, altering protein stability, modulating enzymatic activities, and/or changing subcellular localization crucial for cancer/disease progression and viral latency/reactivation, making PTM sites potential biomarkers in targeted therapies. Reported PTMs in BRD4 include phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, sumoylation, and hydroxylation, which are typically identified by mobility shifts in SDS-PAGE, bioinformatic and computational analyses, in vitro modification assays, or highly sensitive and quantitative liquid chromatography electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS/MS) or liquid chromatography-matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (LC-MALDI) MS analysis. The identified PTMs are typically validated by site-directed mutagenesis and/or PTM-specific antibody-based detection (e.g., WB and cell imaging). Among these, the functional effects of BRD4 phosphorylation have been most extensively studied.Phosphorylation of BRD4 was first observed by a mobility difference in SDS-PAGE between bacteria- versus insect cell-expressed recombinant protein fragments containing either NPS or CPS. Analysis of amino acid sequences identified seven putative casein kinase II (CK2) consensus sites (pS/TxxE/D; x is any amino acid) in the NPS that were subsequently confirmed by dephosphorylating pNPS in insect cell-purified protein fragments with lambda or calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase and by phosphorylating NPS in bacteria-purified recombinant fragments with CK217 (Figure 6A). An additional phosphorylation site (T500) was independently identified by MS analysis. CK2 is a cell-intrinsic NPS kinase in both normal and cancer cells, as perturbation of CK2 expression and its kinase activity in keratinocyte-derived Ker-CT cells, primary neurons, and SUM159 TNBC cells by CK2 knockdown or inhibitor treatment shows reduced NPS phosphorylation of endogenous BRD4 proteins.17,83,125 Phosphorylation of NPS, particularly at S492 and S494, is critical for unmasking the chromatin-binding activity of BD1/2 and for BRD4-mediated transcriptional regulation typically via phosphorylation-dependent association with sequence-specific transcription factors and other pNPS interactors (see Figure 4B). This NPS region is conserved in all BET family proteins.17 Thus, NPS phosphorylation likely plays an important role in BRD2, BRD3, and BRDT function as well. Besides CK2, other kinases, such as protein kinase A (PKA),17 IκB kinase ɛ (IKKε),17 and CK1δ,210 can also phosphorylate the NPS, with CK1δ-phosphorylated BRD4 shown to be critical for cerebellar granule cell progenitor function and neurogenesis.210Phosphorylation in other regions of BRD4 has also been described (Figure 6A). Hyperphosphorylation of BRD4-L at T249/S1045/S1117/T1186 by cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1)/cyclin B occurs during mitosis.211 The CDK1-phosphorylated T1186 is recognized by polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1), which then phosphorylates BRD4-L at S24 and S1100 (Figure 6A), leading to recruitment of the APC/CCDH1 E3 ubiquitin ligase and proteasome-mediated degradation of BRD4-L.56 This mitosis-specific phosphorylation cascade (CDK1-PLK1-APC/CCDH1) could potentially reduce the elevated BRD4 protein levels observed in BBDi-resistant prostate cancer cells, thus resensitizing cancer cells to therapeutic drug treatment. Interestingly, T1186 and additionally T1212 are also phosphorylated by c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), which triggers BRD4-L release from chromatin212 and likely results in BRD4-L dissociation from metaphase chromosomes.50 This could partly explain why BRD4-L may not be a mitotic bookmarking factor.53 JNK-mediated phosphorylation seems to inactivate the reported HAT activity of BRD4 and in turn switch on its kinase activity, converting BRD4-L from a chromatin binder to a promoter regulator, which likely helps Pol II release from promoter-proximal pause sites through enhanced phosphorylation of Pol II CTD at Ser2, CDK9 at Thr186, and c-Myc at Thr58.212 It would be of great interest to examine whether BRD4-S, lacking S1100/T1186 found in BRD4-L, is in fact the authentic mitotic chromosome-bookmarking factor that provides a binding platform for viral genome tethering and conveys transcriptional memory upon cell reentry to the G1 phase.A key event in phosphorylation regulation is recognition of the modified phosphoresidues by reader proteins that trigger specific downstream signaling events. A BRD4-interacting protein, peptidyl-prolyl isomerase NIMA-interacting 1 (PIN1), is a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) shown to bind pS/T-Pro (P) motifs, such as pT204-P205 of BRD4,213 and functions as a post-phosphorylation regulatory factor to regulate substrate conformation. Although the pT204 kinase has not yet been identified, PIN1 binding to pT204, which is unique to BRD4 and not found in BRD2 and BRD3, converts pT204-P205 from the cis to trans configuration, thus enhancing BRD4 protein stability by reducing polyubiquitination and further stimulating BRD4 interaction and recruitment of CDK9, target gene transcription, and tumor-promoting function in gastric cancer cells.213Other phosphorylation sites that also confer BRD4 protein stability are tyrosine (Y) 97 and Y98 in BD1 of BRD4, as phosphorylation of both Y97 and Y98 by Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) in response to cytokine IL6/IL8 secreted by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in the tumor microenvironment of CRC enhances pBRD4 interaction with ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L3 (UCHL3), a BRD4 deubiquitinase highly active in CRC.214 UCHL3 is distinct from the earlier identified deubiquitinase DUB3132 that counteracts the poly-ubiquitinating activity of a BRD4 E3 ubiquitin ligase containing Cullin 3, RING, and BRD4-binding adaptor SPOP (speckle-type POZ protein).215–217 While Y97 crucial for BBDi binding is conserved among BET proteins, Y98 is only present in BRD4, but not BRD2 or BRD3, making BRD4 a unique substrate regulated by extrinsic IL6/IL8-JAK2 signaling in promoting cancer cell expansion. Importantly, phosphorylation at Y97/Y98 not only confers drug resistance in cancer cells but also enhances BRD4 binding to chromatin and interaction with JAK2-activated transcription factor STAT3 (signal transducer and activator of transcription 3) at growth-promoting enhancer/super-enhancer regions.214 This JAK2-dependent phosphorylation at Y97/Y98 is distinct from CK2-enhanced NPS phosphorylation in stimulating BRD4 chromatin association. It would be of great interest to examine whether these two phosphorylation events are interlinked or functionally independent.Clearly, distinct kinases (CK2, PKA, IKKε, CK1δ, CDK1, PLK1, JNK, and JAK2), acting in a context-dependent manner, create a combination of phosphorylation codes that trigger specific downstream signaling pathways to modulate cellular activities that are either uniquely (e.g., C-terminal modifications) or commonly (e.g., NPS phosphorylation) modulated by distinct BRD4 isoforms (Figure 6B). The degradation and chromatin release of BRD4-L, triggered by distinct phosphorylation events at its unique C-terminal extension, likely result in a dynamic BRD4-L turnover through cell cycle progression. In contrast, BRD4-S, albeit less abundant than BRD4-L in most cells, provides a more stable form in response to intra- and extracellular signaling events. The functions of the mostly cell type-specific and stress-induced BRD4-S(b) are yet to be defined.Besides phosphorylation, BRD4 is also modified by ubiquitination (Ub), sumoylation (SM), acetylation (Ac), methylation (Me), and hydroxylation (HO), based mostly on software prediction and/or mass spectrometry analysis, and some of the PTMs have been experimentally validated (Figure 6C). Ubiquitination of BRD4 by the SPOP E3 ubiquitin ligase, first described in prostate cancer,215–217 and deubiquitination by DUB3132 in prostate cancer and UCHL3214 in colorectal cancer mainly regulate BRD4 protein stability. Conjugation of a small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) protein to the ε-amino group of a lysine residue, analogous to ubiquitination, is another way to control protein stability and transcription activity, among other biological functions.218,219 Among multiple predicted sites, sumoylation at K1111 of BRD4 by E3 SUMO ligase chromobox homolog 4 (CBX4) is reported to stabilize BRD4 by antagonizing polyubiquitination, thus enhancing the expression of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 in synovial fibroblasts.220Acetylation of BRD4 at K332 by PCAF (p300/CBP-associated factor; i.e., KAT2B) has been shown to enhance BRD4 association with TF intestine-specific homeobox (ISX) that promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and lung cancer initiation/progression through the PCAF-ISX-BRD4 axis-enhanced expression of EMT-promoting TFs, such as TWIST1 and SNAIL1.104 Interestingly, ISX in complex with BRD4 also depends on PCAF-acetylated K69 in ISX for binding specifically to BRD4 BD2 (not BD1), similar to that described for TIP60-acetylated K73/K76 in TWIST1, which likewise contact uniquely BD2 to control BRD4-regulated EMT in basal-like breast cancer cells,103 and CBP-acetylated K146/K187 in SNAIL1 that are critical for BRD4-promoted gastric cancer cell invasion and metastasis.221In addition to acetylation, BRD4 can also be methylated at lysine residues by certain SET domain-containing lysine methyltransferases (KMTs) or at arginine residues by specific protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs). Mono-methylation of BRD4 by SET domain-containing protein 6 (SETD6) at K99 within BD1, which is also conserved in BRD2 and BRD3 but not BRDT, does not affect BD1 binding to acetylated chromatin but reduces BRD4 interaction with TF E2F1, leading to selectively reduced ribosomal gene transcription thus underlying SETD6-mediated BRD4 methylation in inhibiting protein translation.222 Unlike the inhibitory K99 methylation, PRMT1-mediated asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) formation at R179, R181, and R183 residues of BRD4, which are situated downstream of BD1 and not conserved in other BET proteins, is critical for BRD4-promoted ovarian cancer cell migration, invasion, and tumorigenesis.223 Methylation of these three arginine residues, counteracted by the JMJD6 demethylase and recognized by the Tudor domain-containing SPF30 reader protein, increases NPS phosphorylation needed for BRD4 binding to targeted chromatin and is functionally linked to TGF-β signaling.223 This PTM crosstalk between arginine methylation and NPS phosphorylation is also important for partial EMT and TGF-β1-induced kidney fibrosis, likely through PRMT1-enhanced BRD4 methylation and NPS phosphorylation that, besides regulating BRD4 target gene transcription, additionally modulates SNAIL1 acetylation and protein stability through direct protein-protein interaction.224 Surprisingly, DNA damage-induced arginine mono-methylation, and not the typical asymmetric di-methylation, at the same R179/R181/R183 residues by the PRMT2/PRMT4 complex likewise enhances BRD4 binding to acetylated chromatin and upregulates the expression of cell cycle, chromatin remodeling, and DNA repair genes in breast cancer cells, thus facilitating BRD4-mediated DNA repair and mouse xenograft mammary tumor growth.225Besides these canonical PTMs, BRD4 is found to be hydroxylated by the 2-oxoglutarate dioxygenase activity of JMJD6 at 19 lysine residues,226 of which 14 are situated in the positively charged BID (Figure 6C) that is important for transcription condensate formation,113 nucleosomal DNA binding,145 and intramolecular contact with the negatively charged pNPS to control factor recruitment and the acetyl-chromatin binding activity of BRD4.17 This oxygen level-dependent lysine hydroxylation, mostly detected in the BID, is also found in BRD2 and BRD3, although the extent of modification in BRD2 (four lysines) and BRD3 (six lysines) is significantly less than that found in BRD4. It would be of great interest to define whether any of these lysine-hydroxylated residues uniquely identified in BRD4 would alter the functional properties of BRD4 versus BRD2 and BRD3, e.g., the cellular distribution of BRD4 hydroxylated at K286/K289/K291 residues situated in the nuclear localization signal114 and whether K332-hydroxylated BRD4 blocks PCAF-mediated BRD4 K332 acetylation, acetyl-K332-dependent BRD4 interaction with ISX, and PCAF-ISX-BRD4 axis-regulated EMT and lung cancer progression.104Targeting IDR for BRD4 InhibitionThe extensive PTMs identified in BRD4 particularly at the negatively charged NPS (phosphorylation) and positively charged BID (hydroxylation), both situated within the internal IDR, suggest that NPS and BID, via intra/inter-molecular contact switches and combinatorial PTM fine-tuning, play a key role in regulating BRD4 dynamics and functional properties.136 This internal IDR with three charged clusters (NPS, BID, CPS) is distinct from the C-terminal proline-rich IDR (see Figure 2). A general feature of IDRs, often referred to as low complexity domains (LCDs) or low complexity regions (LCRs), is the conformational adaptability to form weak multivalent interactions with other IDRs or chemically compatible surfaces, whether unstructured or structured. The interface can be formed through hydrogen bonding, charge-charge, hydrophobic or π-π interactions, among others, to mediate assembly of diverse protein networks/hubs, foci/puncti, biomolecular condensates, liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), or liquid/hydrogel-like membrane-less compartments.227–233In drug development, folded domains (e.g., kinase, HDAC, bromodomain, etc.) are ideal targets for obtaining high-affinity compounds at nano/picomolar ranges through primarily structure-guided chemical modification. These pocket inhibitors, however, frequently exhibit off-target inhibition of other structurally and/or functionally related protein domains, incurring strong side effects and general toxicities (Figure 7A, left). On the other hand, targeting IDRs provides an innovative approach to modulate a contact interface created through cooperative multivalent, low-affinity interactions, often leading to a transition from a disordered-to-ordered structure that is distinct, highly selective, and not typically found in other functionally related proteins, thus significantly minimizing off-target inhibition and potential side effects (Figure 7A, right).With the unsatisfactory results of BBDi in clinical trials,4,9 identification of non-bromodomain inhibitors offers new hope for BRD4-directed therapies. Indeed, a new class of PPI inhibitors (PPIi) targeting pNPS in the internal BRD4 IDR that modulates chromatin accessibility of BD2/BD1, factor recruitment, and intra/inter-domain interaction has been developed.28,33 The identification of IDR-targeting PPIi, termed IDRi, is based on the phospho-switch mechanism in which acetylated chromatin-binding activity of BD1/BD2 is regulated by the phosphorylation state of NPS.17 When non-phosphorylated, the NPS masks BD2 and prevents BD1/BD2 from binding to acetylated chromatin via NPS-BD2 and BD2-BD1 interactions. Phosphorylation of NPS by CK2 switches intramolecular NPS contacts from BD2 to downstream BID, leading to activation of BD2/BD1 chromatin-binding activity and concurrently recruiting an active form of p53 to its target genes (Figure 7B). It is important to note that protein-protein contacts may not necessarily lead to active transcription, as only pNPS-recruited p53 is active in target gene regulation whereas BID-associated p53 is inactive in DNA binding.17 It should also be mentioned that besides the intramolecular contact switch, NPS phosphorylation could also modulate inter-molecular BRD4 dimerization, partly determined by the ionic strength of the solution (e.g., 250 mM NaCl).111 The phosphatase involved in this phospho-switch has been identified as protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), whose downregulation leads to increased BRD4 phosphorylation that correlates with TNBC and lung adenocarcinoma progression and drug resistance83,90,234 as well as neurodevelopment/neurodegeneration such as cerebellar neurogenesis,210 mouse learning/memory,125,235 cocaine addiction,236 and memory impairment in fragile X syndrome.18 As NPS phosphorylation represents the active form of BRD4 for chromatin regulation and factor recruitment, it is conceivable that pNPS is broadly involved in BRD4 biology and thus provides a targeted region for anticancer, anti-inflammatory responses, and antiviral therapeutics development.Through one-bead, one-compound microscopic screening of a 38,500 peptoid (i.e., amino acid-like N-substituted oligoglycines) library, two peptoids (DC-1: Nlys-Nlys-Nmea-Nlys-Ntyr-Nleu, and DC-2: Nlys-Nlys-Nffa-Nlys-Nleu-Napp) that bind specifically to pNPS, but not to non-phosphorylated NPS or another conserved CK2-phosphorylated region downstream of the ET domain (i.e., pCPS; see Figure 2), were identified (Figure 7C).237 DC-1, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 50 μM, has a 2-fold higher affinity than DC-2 (IC50 = 125 μM) for binding to the high-risk HPV16-encoded E2 (16E2) protein and effectively blocks pBRD4-dependent 16E2 binding to its cognate sequence situated ~1 kb upstream of the matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) TSS in proliferating keratinocytes. It also diminishes pNPS-driven and 16E2-enhanced NFκB binding to the MMP-9 promoter-proximal (−0.6 kb) NFκB binding site in differentiated keratinocytes, thus inhibiting BRD4-regulated MMP-9 gene transcription.28 Moreover, DC-1 and DC-2 both suppress pNPS-dependent transient HPV replication,33 highlighting the proof of concept in developing IDRi with protease/peptidase-resistant and cell-permeable protein-binding ligands.Although peptoids are highly selective ligands, their cell permeability and affinity toward target protein binding are generally low, which potentially thwarts further development of the initial hits. Through extension to large-scale high-throughput chemical library screening of 200,000 pharmacologically expandable small molecules, 83 compounds, of which 37 are commercially available, were identified to alleviate BRD4-E2 repressor complex-mediated inhibition of an HPV enhancer/promoter-driven luciferase reporter activity. One of the hits, compound 14, and its chemical derivative 90 show potent inhibition of HPV genome replication not only in differentiated keratinocytes but also in a three-dimensional (3D) HPV epithelial cell differentiation (i.e., raft) system mimicking the natural HPV infection life cycle without altering tissue integrity and epidermal differentiation.33 Both compounds exhibit significantly improved potency compared to peptoids, with low to sub-micromolar IC50 (14: 1.5–5.1 μM; 90: 0.4–1.6 μM) for inhibition of pNPS/pBRD4 interactions with viral 16E2, p53 and DDR factors 53BP1 and BARD1 (Figure 7D). Importantly, while effectively blocking HPV DNA replication, 14/90 have minimal perturbation of the genome-wide transcriptome and the chromatin landscape in HPV-infected keratinocytes, suggesting that the high selectivity of IDRi for a specific PPI interface does not disrupt global gene transcription and chromatin organization at least in a virus-infected cellular environment.Another IDRi, SDU-071, modified from compound 21 identified from the 200,000-compound library screen, has significantly improved IC50 (2.7–3.1 μM), compared with the parent compound (40.0–49.6 μM), for inhibition of pNPS-dependent interaction with full-length p53 or its C-terminal regulatory region (aa 309–393) and strongly suppresses MDA-MB-231 TNBC cell growth, invasion, migration, and orthotopic mouse xenograft mammary tumor growth.238 SDU-071 and compound 21 both preferentially inhibit BRD4 interaction with p53 over 16E2. These findings indicate that IDRi can block concurrent or sequential protein interactions with select phosphoresidues within a conformationally dynamic 20-amino acid region. Conceivably, pNPS can create a “combinatorial phosphorylation code” by using different positions/numbers of the eight phospho-S/T residues to contact different interactors such as TFs p53, NFκB, and AP-1, replication factors HPV E2 and E1, DDR factors 53BP1, BARD1, and other yet-to-be-identified chromatin regulators (Figure 7E). This is analogous to the CTD phosphorylation code239 that creates diverse signals and binding platforms within the heptapeptide repeats of RPB1 for distinct factor association with either non-phosphorylated or phosphorylated Pol II during PIC assembly and the initiation, elongation, and termination of transcription, along with co-transcriptionally regulated 5’ capping, mRNA splicing, and 3’ mRNA processing events (see Figure 4A).Besides the internal IDR, the C-terminal proline-rich IDR unique to BRD4-L may offer greater selectivity for BRD4-L-specific targeting. A natural product PCG (procyanidin C-13,3′,3″-tri-O-gallate), acting as an HIV latency-reversing agent through promoting Tat-dependent HIV transcription240 (see Figure 5D), has been shown to bind directly to either or both proline-rich segments (P1: aa 751–800, P2: 951–1031) of BRD4-L (see Figure 2) and convert BRD4-L nuclear condensates into static aggregates, thus inhibiting c-Myc and select target gene transcription.119 Interestingly, some histidine residues embedded within the P1 and P2 segments also play a key role in conferring the intracellular pH-sensing activity of BRD4-L in regulating macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses.241Other examples of IDR targeting include (1) compound EPI-7386 (masofaniten) that binds androgen receptor N-terminal AF-1 IDR, with IC50 = 0.421 μM in inhibiting the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) luciferase reporter activity in LNCaP prostate cancer cells, and exhibits greatly reduced toxicity in clinical trials against metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer;242,243 (2) compounds -G5 and -F4 that bind distinct IDR regions of the monomeric c-Myc bHLHZip domain (aa 363–381 and 402–412, respectively), preventing c-Myc/Max heterodimerization with IC50 = 0.8–7.0 μM, and induce myeloid differentiation in AML cells as well as neuronal differentiation and lipid accumulation in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cells;244,245 (3) compounds Nutlin-3 and RG7112 that bind MDM2 and disrupt its interaction with the p53 N-terminal transactivation domain IDR with IC50 = 0.018–0.3 μM, effectively inhibiting cell growth and viability of cancer cells expressing wild-type but not mutant p53;246,247 (4) compounds lipoamide and lipoic acid that disrupt FUS/TDP-43 condensates with IC50 = 13–17 μM and alleviate neuronal defects caused by Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)-associated FUS and TDP-43 mutants;248 and (5) compound A-485 that, through binding to the HAT domain of p300/CBP and at 10 μM, reduces p300 IDR-mediated LLPS and transcriptional capacity.249 Clearly, IDR targeting is feasible and represents a new direction for effective drug development that may minimize the strong side effects commonly encountered with pocket domain targeting during clinical trials and patient treatments.sTranscription is a highly coordinated event that requires RNA polymerases working in conjunction with an array of general and gene-specific transcription factors and cofactors to regulate distinct steps of the transcriptional process. This complexity of gene regulation is further complicated by the chromatin environment that adds another layer of regulation for TF access to enhancer/promoter regions. BRD4, as an epigenetic and transcriptional regulator, is a key factor bridging chromatin and DNA-driven processes by either acting as a scaffold/adaptor protein for locus-specific enhancer-promoter communications and long/ultralong-range chromatin interactions or as a checkpoint modulator controlling transcription progression and factor exchange. Three features underlying the action of a universal chromatin regulator for functioning as a gene/locus-specific factor are (1) post-translational modification, (2) isoform switch, and (3) partner association.The advances in multi-omics and computational tools allow network analysis and pathway identification through loss- and gain-of-function approaches, along with functional rescue, to identify specific factors and/or protein domains/regions crucial for their action and regulation. Besides genetic dissections, pharmacological agents with the use of target-selective chemical inhibitors and/or PROTAC (proteolysis targeting chimera) degraders further expand the repertoire of toolkits available for biological studies. In the case of BRD4, both genetic and chemical analyses have identified the unique and shared properties of universally expressed long (BRD4-L) and short (BRD4-S) isoforms, extending beyond the seemingly stress- and cell type-specific function of BRD4-S(b). While broad perturbation of BRD4 or BET protein functions using non-selective genetic or chemical inhibition makes it difficult to unambiguously pinpoint the specific factor involved, functional rescue by unique isoforms or other family members helps to identify the implicated entities and pathways.Among BET family proteins, the C-terminal proline-rich (sometimes referred to as HPQ-rich for histidine/proline/glutamine-rich) region is unique to BRD4-L. Thus, antibodies and genetic/chemical perturbations targeting epitopes or structural features residing in this IDR most likely reflect the functional properties of BRD4-L. Any reagents disrupting the functions of evolutionarily conserved N-terminal regions would require additional biological validation with the specific rescue factor(s) to designate the activity to unique BET family members (BRD4-L, BRD4-S, BRD3, BRD2). Moreover, target identification from in vitro analysis may not be fully validated by in vivo characterization, as the presence or absence of other cellular or viral proteins or macromolecules may mask or unmask the epitopes or surface features.While the internal IDR-targeting compounds (e.g., 14 and 90) appear to bind pNPS of full-length proteins or an IDR-only segment derived from purified recombinant BRD4-L, BRD4-S, BRD3, and BRD2 with comparable affinities in vitro, these compounds do show in vivo selectivity of specific BET proteins or isoforms in a context- and/or cell type-specific manner, presumably due to the presence of interacting partners that modulate the extent of surface exposure through direct complex formation and/or allosteric regulation. Comparison between in vitro and in vivo results is thus critical to provide a comprehensive and unbiased view of BET protein action and compound selectivity. It should also be mentioned that although off-target inhibition and general toxicity are often seen with BBD or other folded domain inhibitors and PROTAC degraders, the strong side effects can be potentially alleviated through development of domain (e.g., BD1 or BD2 only)-selective inhibitors, allosteric inhibitors, dual-target inhibitors, or combination therapy with much reduced concentrations. Gain- and loss-of-function mutations uniquely found in the folded domains can also be explored for developing mutant-selective inhibitors/modulators or antibodies that do not cross-react with other structurally or functionally related wild-type proteins.Beyond conventional wisdom in therapeutics design and optimization, targeting IDRs that are uniquely adapted to the partner-interacting interface is an innovative approach to circumvent the strong side effects encountered with domain-targeting inhibitors. In cases where BET members work jointly to control a biological process – e.g., in differentiation-dependent HPV genome amplification where BRD4-L, BRD4-S and BRD3 are all functionally involved,33 in BRD4-amplified HGSOC where both isoforms contribute to oncogenic c-Myc and NRG1 pathways (Figure 5C), and in breast cancer metastasis in which BRD4-L/S are both critical for lung metastasis54 – pNPS IDR-targeting and pan-BET inhibitors may be particularly effective in treating these diseases. However, in a context where BET members or BRD4 isoforms exhibit opposing activities such as in the TNBC and RMS tumor development, this non-selective pan inhibition may blunt the therapeutic efficacy by simultaneously blocking both oncogenic and protective functions.The success with phosphoresidue-based IDRi can be likewise applied to other PTM residues in therapeutics development. Moreover, enhancement of drug modeling algorithms with the aid of artificial intelligence (AI) to include IDR/PTM information based on biochemical/biophysical and protein structure studies will be beneficial. With more drug-like IDR modulators and in-depth molecular understanding of protein function and compound selectivity facilitated by integrated genomic technology and computational AI approaches, more effective treatment regimens tailored to individuals based on their unique genetic and molecular profiles (i.e., personalized medicine) can be achieved for patients with viral, cancer, or inflammation-associated diseases in BRD4-targeted therapy.

title: Context matters in PROTAC design: navigating the trade-off between degradation and developability
abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimaeras (PROTACs) couple target recognition to ubiquitin-dependent degradation, but their translation requires coordinated optimisation of degradation efficiency and developability. This review frames PROTAC design as a context-dependent medicinal chemistry problem rather than modular assembly of a warhead, linker and ubiquitin ligase (E3) recruiter. Linker length, rigidity, and exit vectors, together with warhead recognition topology, determine whether binary binding can form a cooperative, ubiquitination-competent ternary complex. Warhead binding mode further affects catalytic turnover and cellular degradation. Linker-free designs and disclosed clinical PROTAC structures show that beyond Rule of Five property control remains central to exposure. Conditional linkers and E3 ligase choice add biological constraints through stimulus-responsive activation, recruiter tractability, E3 expression, localisation, pathway biology, and safety liabilities. This review integrates these principles into a framework for PROTAC design. The framework aligns productive ternary complex assembly, effective exposure and biological-context compatibility within the intended therapeutic context.
full_text: As an emerging drug discovery technology, proteolysis-targeting chimaeras (PROTACs) have attracted broad attention from academia and the pharmaceutical industry for their potential to target previously “undruggable” proteins and overcome drug resistance1–3. Over the past two decades, PROTACs have evolved from an intriguing laboratory tool into a clinically validated therapeutic modality, with the first PROTAC now approved and many additional candidates advancing through clinical evaluation4–6. They were not discovered serendipitously along the route of traditional inhibitor optimisation, but were proposed in a chemical biology context aimed at “hijacking” the cell’s intrinsic protein degradation machinery7. PROTACs convert transient ternary recognition into ubiquitin-mediated elimination, enabling a pharmacological mechanism that is not solely dependent on sustained target occupancy8. Ubiquitination typically requires the concerted action of three enzymes, including a ubiquitin-activating enzyme (E1), a ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2), and a ubiquitin ligase (E3)9. The PROTAC acts as a bridging molecule, using one end to specifically recognise and bind the protein of interest (POI) and the other to engage the E3 ligase. The resulting POI-PROTAC-E3 ternary complex promotes POI ubiquitination, followed by proteasomal recognition and degradation (Figure 1).Figure 1.Mechanism of PROTAC-mediated protein of interest (POI) degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS). In the presence of a PROTAC, this complex is “hijacked” to engage the POI (cyan), yielding a ubiquitin-E2-E3-PROTAC-POI ternary complex. Polyubiquitinated POI is subsequently recognised and degraded by the 26S proteasome (rainbow-coloured complex), generating small peptide fragments. The background features a membrane structure to add context.This mechanism does not make effective degraders a simple matter of joining a warhead to an E3 recruiter. PROTAC optimisation therefore depends on how the warhead, linker, and E3 recruiter organise productive ubiquitination. The review follows the three structural elements of PROTAC design, including linker engineering, warhead optimisation, and E3 ligase selection. We define context at three interconnected levels, including productive ternary complex assembly, effective drug exposure and physicochemical property control and biological-context compatibility. By integrating these levels, this review aims to guide the development of PROTACs in which degradation performance and developability are aligned within the intended therapeutic context.Linker engineering in PROTAC optimisationStructural modulation of linkersGeometric explorationLinker optimisation often begins with linker length10. If the linker is too short, steric constraints may hinder simultaneous engagement of the POI and E3 ligase by the warhead and E3 recruiter. If it is too long, the molecule may adopt non-productive conformations that are unfavourable for productive ternary complex formation10–12. Because the relative arrangement of the POI and E3 ligase is often unknown during early-stage optimisation, flexible linkers such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) units or alkyl diols are commonly used to explore this geometric space10,13. However, this flexibility can also introduce absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) liabilities. PEG-rich linkers contribute additional hydrogen-bond acceptors (HBAs), generally increasing polar surface area and solvation capacity and thereby disfavouring passive cellular permeability14–16. Moreover, PEG-rich linkers increase polar atom content and HBA burden, which may contribute to permeability and efflux liabilities17. In contrast, alkyl-rich linkers tend to increase lipophilicity and hydrophobic surface exposure, which may improve permeability but can also increase non-specific plasma protein binding and reduce free drug exposure15,18,19. Thus, flexible linkers are valuable for early geometric exploration, but their utility must be balanced against the permeability, efflux, and metabolic liabilities they may introduce20.Conformational constraint and selectivity controlOnce a productive ternary complex geometry or a reliable binding pose has been identified, flexible linkers are often replaced with rigid linkers of similar atomic length. At this stage, the objective is no longer broad geometric exploration, but the reduction of conformational heterogeneity and the entropic penalty of ternary complex formation21. Macrocyclisation can preorganise the warhead and E3 recruiter within one constrained architecture. Ciulli and colleagues found that an early linear PROTAC adopted a horseshoe-shaped conformation within the interfacial cavity of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)-Elongin C-Elongin B complex (VCB)-bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) bromodomain 2 (BD2) complex, indicating cyclisation potential11. Based on this observation, macroPROTAC-1 (Figure 2(A)) was designed to favour cooperative ternary complex formation22. The cocrystal structure of macroPROTAC-1 with VCB and BRD4 BD2 showed that the cyclised linker occupied the interfacial cavity while preserving key interactions involving Arg107, Trp374, and His437. An important parameter in binding studies is the cooperativity factor α, defined as the ratio of the dissociation constant (Kd) of the PROTAC binary complex to that of the ternary complex. Values of α greater than 1 indicate positive cooperativity, whereas values below 1 indicate negative cooperativity23. Mechanistically, positive cooperativity is favoured by linker geometry that supports compatible POI-E3 positioning and stabilising interfacial contacts, whereas negative cooperativity reflects geometry that disfavours stable ternary complex formation. In the competitive fluorescence polarisation (FP) assay, macroPROTAC-1 displayed an α value of 10.5 with BRD4 BD2, exceeding those observed for bromodomain-containing protein 2 (BRD2) BD2 and bromodomain-containing protein 3 (BRD3) BD2. In line with these cooperativity measurements, macroPROTAC-1 most effectively degraded BRD4 in cells, with half-maximal degradation concentration (DC50) values of 25-125 nM, while BRD2 and BRD3 were degraded only at higher concentrations. This approach requires close spatial proximity between the warhead-bound POI and recruited E3 ligase11,24. This linker-free design reduced the physicochemical and conformational burden introduced by PEG linkers by lowering molecular weight (MW), the number of rotatable bonds (NRotB), and PEG-derived HBA density. These changes may reduce the entropic cost of productive ternary complex formation and the polar-solvation penalty that can limit cellular exposure. Consistent with this design logic, Pro-BA showed stronger degradation and antiproliferative activity than the PEG-linked analogues Pro-PEG1-BA and Pro-PEG3-BA in H3122 cells, with 13.0-fold and 5.6-fold improvements in DC50 and 17.0-fold and 4.6-fold improvements in half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), respectively. These activity gains were accompanied by improved exposure-related properties. Aqueous solubility of 1.8 M compared with 0.86 M for Pro-PEG3-BA and approximately 1.5-fold higher intracellular concentration. In mice, orally administered Pro-BA showed an elimination half-life of 3.4 h, maximum plasma concentration of 2.7 μg/mL, area under the curve of 4.9 h·μg/mL, and oral bioavailability of 35%. Pro-BA illustrates that linker deletion can improve degradation performance and exposure-related properties when spatial compatibility permits. This strategy should therefore be viewed as a context-dependent opportunity, not a general rule for PROTAC optimisation.Linker optimisation should be viewed as a progressive strategy for balancing ternary complex geometry, selectivity, and PROTAC developability. Flexible linkers are particularly useful for the early identification of productive ternary complex geometries, whereas rigid linkers can be employed to enhance conformational constraint and selectivity once such geometries have been defined. When spatial geometry permits, linker-free designs can reduce molecular complexity and improve exposure-related properties26–28.Conditional linker controlRedox-responsive linkersRedox-responsive linkers provide a representative strategy for conditional degrader activation in disease-relevant contexts. Jin and colleagues first established this concept using the folate-guided disulphide prodrug FA-S2-POMA29. In this system, folate serves as a targeting element because folate receptor 1 (FOLR1) is highly expressed in multiple myeloma and other cancer cells30,31, whereas other folate transport pathways display relatively lower affinity for folate, allowing folate conjugates to be preferentially delivered to FOLR1-positive tumours. FA-S2-POMA is not a bona fide PROTAC, but it validates reduction-responsive delivery (Figure 2(C)). It induced concentration- and time-dependent degradation of Ikaros family zinc finger protein 3 or Ikaros family zinc finger protein 1 in FOLR1-positive cells, inhibited MM.1S cell proliferation with an IC50 of 1.0 μM and was markedly more potent than the noncleavable control FA-C2-POMA. Moreover, increasing intracellular glutathione (GSH) with S-acetyl-l-GSH further enhanced its antiproliferative activity to an IC50 of 88 nM. Building on this redox-activated delivery strategy, the authors subsequently developed the bona fide folate-caged ALK PROTAC FA-S2-MS4048 together with the noncleavable control FA-C2-MS4048. In proliferation assays, FA-S2-MS4048 showed an approximately 20.4-fold improvement in IC50 relative to the noncleavable control FA-C2-MS4048 and S-acetyl-l-GSH pre-treatment further improved the IC50 by approximately 8.3-fold.This strategy exploits the pronounced difference in GSH concentrations between the intracellular cytosol and the extracellular milieu. Disulphide motifs are synthetically accessible and compatible with targeting elements. Intracellular thiol-disulphide exchange can then release the active degrader. However, this chemistry also creates stability liabilities. Highly reduction-labile linkers may undergo premature cleavage in the presence of extracellular reducing species such as cysteine or ascorbic acid, which can compromise site selectivity32,33. Redox-responsive linkers may offer better stimulus selectivity than hydrolytic systems. Their use still depends on balancing intracellular cleavage with systemic stability.Photoswitchable linkersPhotoswitchable linkers allow reversible optical control of degrader activity34. This strategy relies on embedding a photoisomerisable unit into the linker so that light-induced geometric changes alter the relative orientation of the warhead and the E3 recruiter. Trauner and colleagues demonstrated this concept using azobenzene-containing photochemically targeting chimaeras (PHOTACs; Figure 2(D)), in which trans-PHOTAC-I-3 remained less active until irradiation at 390 nm induced trans-to-cis isomerisation and improved the half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) in RS4;11 cells by approximately 7.1-fold, while irradiation at 500 nm enabled rapid conversion back to the trans isomer35. A related example was reported by Tate and colleagues with the arylazopyrazole-based degrader AP-PROTAC-136. This molecule reached photostationary states containing up to 78% E isomer under 457 nm irradiation and 85% Z isomer under 365 nm irradiation, while retaining reversible switching over 20 cycles. In HeLa cells treated with 100 nM AP-PROTAC-1 for 6 h, the E-enriched state induced approximately 2.5-fold higher BRD4 degradation than the Z-enriched state and also reduced BRD2 by 75%, whereas the Z-enriched state had little effect on BRD2.The different degradation profiles clarify how photoisomerisation regulates PROTAC activity. These linkers do more than add photosensitivity. These linkers alter the spatial relationship between the warhead and the E3 recruiter through photoisomerisation, thereby shifting the degrader between more and less productive ternary complex-forming states. This feature enables reversible and quantitatively tuneable optical control of PROTAC activity, with the extent of regulation influenced by wavelength, irradiation intensity, exposure duration, and the intracellular distribution of photoisomers. However, these advantages are accompanied by clear translational limitations. The limited tissue penetration of ultraviolet and visible light, potential phototoxicity associated with prolonged irradiation, and practical requirement for light-delivery devices all restrict the broader application of this strategy37.Warhead design and optimisationAllosteric ligands as warheadsAllosteric ligands are particularly useful as warheads when drug resistance is driven by mutations in the orthosteric binding pocket. The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) degrader DDC-01-163 reported by Gray and colleagues illustrates this design logic (Figure 3(A))38. The molecular docking model of EGFR and JBJ-07-149 shows that this design shifts target recognition away from the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding site (Figure 3(B)). JBJ-07-149 is linked to pomalidomide through its piperazine region, which extends from the EGFR allosteric pocket towards the solvent. Although conversion of JBJ-07-149 into a PROTAC reduced biochemical inhibition of EGFRL858R/T790M by approximately 41-fold, DDC-01-163 improved growth inhibition in Ba/F3 cells expressing the mutant EGFRL858R/T790M variant by approximately 51-fold and showed more than 100-fold selectivity over Ba/F3 cells expressing wild-type EGFR. It also retained stronger activity in Ba/F3 cells expressing the osimertinib-resistant EGFRL858R/T790M/C797S and EGFRL858R/T790M/L718Q variants, with approximately 2.3-fold and 3.4-fold improved potency relative to the EGFRL858R/T790M model, respectively. At 0.1 μM, DDC-01-163 reduced EGFR protein levels by 74% and 71% in these two resistant models, whereas osimertinib did not induce EGFR degradation or effectively inhibit normalised EGFR activity. These results indicate that allosteric warheads can shift degrader recognition topology and preserve activity against orthosteric-pocket resistance mutations. Wang and colleagues examined this issue using the same cereblon (CRBN) recruiter and the same linker and generated a reversible noncovalent PROTAC, an irreversible covalent PROTAC and a reversible covalent PROTAC (RNC-1, IRC-1, and RC-1; Figure 3(C)) by changing only Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK)-binding warhead39. Western blot analysis after 24 h of treatment in MOLM-14 cells showed that the reversible covalent PROTAC potently induced BTK degradation. RNC-1 displayed weaker degradation at low concentrations but showed activity comparable to that of RC-1 at 200 nM, whereas IRC-1 induced inefficient BTK degradation. In cell proliferation assays, RC-1 improved IC50 by approximately 13.2-fold and 8.7-fold relative to RNC-1 and IRC-1, respectively. In assays measuring cellular BTK target engagement, RC-1 improved IC50 by approximately 29.5-fold and 3.0-fold relative to RNC-1 and IRC-1, respectively. Using K′P,D (K′P,D = Kd,D/IC50,TE) to define relative intracellular accumulation, Wang and colleagues found that the intracellular accumulation of RC-1 was approximately sixfold higher than that of IRC-1 and 40-fold higher than that of RNC-1. Warhead binding mode may therefore affect degradation efficiency through target engagement and intracellular accumulation40. Reversible noncovalent PROTACs bind BTK exclusively through noncovalent interactions and may show weaker activity at lower concentrations when intracellular accumulation is limited. In contrast, irreversible covalent PROTACs may become trapped on the POI after covalent bond formation. This can reduce catalytic turnover and limit serial degradation. Reversible covalent PROTACs use an α-cyanoacrylamide-derived moiety to form a reversible bond with Cys481, a feature that may preserve PROTAC recycling while supporting higher intracellular accumulation.Target site and binding mode both affect degrader performance. Allosteric warheads can bypass resistance-prone orthosteric pockets. Reversible covalent warheads may improve POI engagement while preserving turnover. Therefore, an effective warhead needs more than affinity. Its topology and binding mode must support ternary complex formation and catalytic degradation.E3 ligase selection in PROTAC designCommonly used E3 ligasesCRBN and VHL are the two most extensively validated E3 ligases in targeted protein degradation41,42. Their use largely reflects the availability of well-characterised small-molecule recruiters43. CRBN recruitment is predominantly achieved using immunomodulatory imide drug (IMiD) ligands and their derivatives, such as thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide41,44. These ligands are compact, relatively drug-like and well suited to the CRBN binding pocket. They are now the most widely used recruiters in PROTAC design. Cocrystal structures of CRBN bound to pomalidomide, lenalidomide, and thalidomide reveal that the glutarimide moiety is anchored deep in the CRBN pocket through a conserved hydrogen-bonding network involving Trp382 and His380, whereas the phthalimide ring engages in a weaker π-alkyl interaction with Pro354 and is exposed to solvent (Figure 4). In pomalidomide and lenalidomide, the 4-amino group on the aromatic ring is commonly employed as the exit vector. In contrast, thalidomide does not contain a comparable amino handle for conjugation. Accordingly, incorporation of a linker into the thalidomide scaffold is generally accomplished by substitution on the phenyl ring of the phthalimide moiety. Even small changes in thalidomide linker position can alter degradation efficiency. In the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) degrader SK-575, isomeric PROTACs (26) with different thalidomide exit vectors showed significantly different activities in inhibiting cell proliferation (Figure 3(D))45. The ortho position was optimal in this PARP1 degrader series, yet clinically advanced CRBN-recruiting PROTACs such as ARV-110 and ARV-471 use the meta position for linker attachment (Figure 3(E)). Exit vector choice remains target dependent within the same recruiter class.
