CRBN recruiters can generate a broad neosubstrate landscape, complicating mechanistic interpretation and safety assessment48,49, whereas VHL recruiters impose a greater physicochemical burden because they are larger and contain more hydrogen-bonding functionality50. VHL also sits within the canonical hypoxia-inducible factor regulatory pathway, so perturbing this axis may introduce added biological complexity in some disease settings51. These limitations motivate the search for alternative E3 ligases.Early alternative E3 ligasesTo address the off-target liabilities associated with CRBN recruiters, as well as the physicochemical burden and biological constraints often imposed by VHL recruiters, researchers began to explore additional E3 ligases that could be engaged by tractable small-molecule recruiters. Among these, murine double minute 2 (MDM2) and inhibitor of apoptosis protein (IAP) were among the earliest and most representative alternative E3 ligases.MDM2 is a RING-type E3 ligase52. Early studies showed that MDM2 is often overexpressed in tumors53,54. Among the small-molecule antagonists developed to disrupt the p53-MDM2 interaction, idasanutlin effectively binds the p53-binding site on MDM2 and exhibits antitumor activity55,56. Repurposing this antagonist as an E3 recruiter provided a potential early alternative to CRBN and VHL. Docking of idasanutlin to human MDM2 (Figure 5(B)) suggested that chloro and fluoro substituents form a stable hydrophobic network with surrounding residues. The terminal hydroxyl group of idasanutlin serves as a suitable exit vector for efficient conjugation, and this design is expected to preserve occupancy of the p53-binding pocket after conjugation. A representative example is A1874 (Figure 5(D)), a degrader based on idasanutlin that degrades BRD4 while stabilising p53 in wild-type p53 cells, thereby producing synergistic antiproliferative effects56,57. This dual activity defines both the opportunity and the limitation of MDM2 recruitment. Coupling POI degradation with p53 pathway activation may be advantageous in tumours retaining functional p53, but MDM2 is not a biologically neutral E3 ligase option. Its degradation outcome and antiproliferative activity depend on p53 pathway status, MDM2 expression and normal-tissue tolerance to p53 activation58,59. In tumours lacking functional p53, the contribution of MDM2 antagonism may be diminished, whereas excessive p53 activation in p53-proficient normal tissues may narrow the therapeutic window60. MDM2-based degraders are best treated as context-restricted bifunctional agents, not general CRBN or VHL replacements.Several members of the IAP family function as RING-type E3 ligases involved in the regulation of cell survival, apoptosis and inflammatory signalling. Among these ligases, cellular inhibitor of apoptosis protein 1 (cIAP1) was recruited early for targeted protein degradation. Methyl bestatin (MeBS) binds the baculoviral IAP repeat 3 (BIR3) domain of cIAP1 with micromolar affinity61,62, providing a tractable small-molecule recruiter for IAP recruitment. Docking of MeBS into the cIAP1 BIR3 domain suggested that the recruiter forms hydrogen bonds with Arg308 and Glu319, while its terminal ester group was exposed to the solvent as an exit vector (Figure 5(C))63,64. In the construction of SNIPER (Figure 5(E)), MeBS is conjugated to a warhead through a linker, thereby inducing ubiquitination mediated by cIAP1 and degradation of the POI65. This strategy also has important limitations. IAP expression varies across cellular contexts, which can make degradation efficiency tissue- and cell-line-dependent66. In addition, many IAP recruiters trigger cIAP1 autoubiquitination and self-degradation, thereby depleting the recruited ligase and potentially competing with POI degradation67. IAP proteins regulate apoptosis and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB)-related signaling68,69. Their engagement can produce pathway effects that are difficult to separate from degradation. Thus, IAP recruitment may be useful when apoptosis pathway modulation is desirable, but it is less suitable as a broadly neutral E3 ligase option.MDM2 and IAP expanded the E3 ligase repertoire beyond CRBN and VHL. Their limited generalisability also clarifies a key selection principle. Alternative ligases should not be judged only by recruiter availability or degradation proof of concept. Their pathway biology, expression context, and intrinsic regulatory behaviour must also be compatible with the intended therapeutic setting. Early alternative ligases broadened PROTAC design. They also showed that chemical recruitability alone does not define a useful E3 option.Emerging recruitable E3 ligasesRecent efforts to expand the E3 ligase repertoire have moved beyond simply identifying bindable ligases and have shifted towards matching recruitment chemistry with the biological properties of each ligase70. Emerging recruitable E3 ligases can be grouped by covalent and noncovalent recruitment. This classification highlights how different recruitment modes use specific ligand fragments to engage E3 ligase pockets in distinct biological contexts.Covalently recruitable E3 ligasesAmong emerging E3 ligases, those amenable to covalent recruitment have provided an important route for expanding the PROTAC toolbox. Ring finger protein 114 (RNF114) is a RING-type E3 ligase71,72. It remained relatively underexplored until Nomura and colleagues discovered that the natural product nimbolide covalently binds RNF114 and stabilises specific cell-cycle regulatory proteins73. Nimbolide blocks substrate binding to RNF114 and hijacks the ligase, thereby indirectly stabilising tumour suppressors74. Based on this mechanism, nimbolide was conjugated to JQ1 to generate the degrader XH2, which reduced BRD4 abundance at nanomolar concentrations (Figure 6(A)). Although RNF114 was enriched by more than 10-fold using a nimbolide-alkyne probe, the same experiment also identified 114 additional proteins with more than 10-fold enrichment, indicating a substantial proteome-wide covalent background. Subsequent studies identified EN219 as a covalent recruiter that targets an N-terminal cysteine residue on RNF114 and is more tractable for derivatisation75. Compared with nimbolide, EN219 provided a more controllable synthetic starting point. It engaged RNF114 with an IC50 of 470 nM and modified Cys8 on purified RNF114. In cells, however, this improvement did not amount to complete proteome-wide selectivity. Competitive chemoproteomics showed that four proteins among 686 quantified cysteine sites displayed greater than twofold competition and EN219-alkyne profiling further detected 7–10 additional potential off-targets. Importantly, this moderate selectivity still supported functional degrader design. EN219-based ML2-14 and ML2-23 degraded BRD4 and breakpoint cluster region-Abelson.Figure 6.Representative PROTACs developed from emerging E3 ligases. (A) PROTACs that recruit ring finger protein 114; (B) PROTACs that recruit DDB1- and CUL4-associated factor 16; (C) a PROTAC that recruits DDB1- and CUL4-associated factor 1; and (D) a PROTAC that recruits aryl hydrocarbon receptor. This figure was created by the authors using ChemDraw software.Chemical structures of various PROTACs and their components, arranged in four panels, with annotations on biological activity.The figure features four panels (A-D) detailing chemical structures of PROTAC molecules and related compounds. Panel A showsRNF114-recruiting PROTACs, including XH2, ML2-14, and ML2-23, together with their corresponding recruiter and warhead components. Panel B illustrates DCAF16-recruiting PROTACs, including KB02-SLF, KB02-JQ1, C8, and A4, with associated activity data.Panel C presents the DCAF1 recruiter OICR-8268, a WDR5 ligand, and the corresponding PROTAC OICR- with activity data. Panel D depicts β-Naphthoflavone and all-trans retinoic acid, and the corresponding AhR-recruiting PROTAC β-NF-ATRA. Each structure's connectivity and biological relevance are meticulously documented.The Cravatt laboratory identified DDB1- and CUL4-associated factor 16 (DCAF16) as a component of the CUL4-DDB1 E3 ligase complex that contains multiple surface-exposed reactive cysteine residues and is thus suitable for covalent recruitment76. They employed a broad electrophile screening strategy to identify the chloroacetamide lead fragment KB02, which covalently engages specific cysteine residues on DCAF16, and used it to develop degraders targeting nuclear FK506-binding protein 12 (FKBP12) and BRD4 (Figure 6(B)). KB02-SLF markedly reduced nuclear FKBP12 at 2 μM, whereas KB02-JQ1 induced the most pronounced degradation of endogenous BRD4 at 20-40 μM. These results established KB02 as a functional first-generation DCAF16 recruiter, but its electrophilic scout-fragment origin also raised the question of proteome-wide selectivity. This limitation was quantified in a later comparative study using FKBP12 nuclear localisation sequence interactome profiling, in which KB02-SLF recruited DCAF16 and DDB1 but also enriched 13 additional proteins77. Later KB02-based degraders showed that DCAF16 recruitment remains useful for selected nuclear targets. Li and colleagues conjugated KB02 to olaparib and palbociclib to generate C8 and A4, which were designed to induce degradation of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 2 (PARP2) and cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6, respectively78,79. Compared with the corresponding parent inhibitors, C8 and A4 showed substantially enhanced degrader-related cellular activity.The key advantage of covalent E3 recruitment is that the degrader is anchored to the ligase rather than to the POI. As discussed in the section on warhead binding mode, irreversible covalent engagement by the warhead may trap the degrader on a single POI molecule, thereby limiting catalytic turnover. By contrast, a covalent E3 recruiter forms a long-lived E3-degrader complex while maintaining reversible POI binding80. This allows the E3-degrader complex to engage subsequent POI molecules for ubiquitination81,82. However, this does not mean that covalent recruitment is a universal solution for E3 selection. The electrophilic group that enables ligase engagement can also introduce off-target cysteine modification, making proteome-wide selectivity a decisive requirement for this strategy83. In addition, the biological function of the recruited ligase remains relevant after covalent engagement. RNF114 recruitment may perturb endogenous substrate recognition, particularly pathways linked to p21 regulation, cell-cycle control, NF-κB signalling, and T-cell activation. By contrast, DCAF16 recruitment is currently supported mainly in nuclear degradation settings, while its broader utility remains constrained by the still-incomplete understanding of its endogenous substrate biology within the CUL4-DDB1 complex. Therefore, covalent E3 recruitment is a context-dependent expansion strategy, not a general replacement for established ligases. Its successful application requires a more selective electrophilic recruiter, a productive ternary complex architecture and ligase biology compatible with the intended therapeutic context.Noncovalently recruitable E3 ligasesUnlike covalent recruitment, noncovalent recruitment does not rely on reactive amino acid residues to engage E3 ligases. It instead uses defined binding pockets and is more compatible with structure-guided design. DDB1- and CUL4-associated factor 1 (DCAF1) is a substrate receptor of the Cullin-RING ligase 4 (CRL4) E3 ligase complex84–86. Vedadi and colleagues identified OICR-8268, a noncovalent recruiter that engages the DCAF1 binding pocket, and incorporated it into a PROTAC (OICR- , Figure 6(C)) that induced measurable degradation of both endogenous and exogenous WD repeat-containing protein 5 (WDR5)87,88. This work provided a noncovalent chemical handle for DCAF1 and enabled structure-guided design of DCAF1-based PROTACs. In this design, the DCAF1 recruiter was functionalised through an amine exit vector for linker attachment. The resulting OICR- induced 49% degradation of WDR5 in cells at 40 nM.Among noncovalently recruitable ligases, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is distinctive because ligand-activated AhR can participate in a cullin 4B-based E3 ligase complex89,90. Building on this property, Naito and colleagues exploited an AhR ligand as a recruiter to induce degradation of targets including cellular retinoic acid-binding protein (CRABP) and BRD proteins91. In this PROTAC design (β-NF-ATRA, Figure 6(D)), β-naphthoflavone serves as an AhR recruiter that engages the E3 ligase complex associated with AhR and promotes CRABP degradation.DCAF1 and AhR illustrate both the appeal and the constraint of noncovalent recruitment among emerging E3 ligases. Compared with covalent recruitment, noncovalent recruiters avoid electrophile-driven cysteine off-target modification and are more amenable to structure-guided optimisation when a defined ligand-binding pocket is available. However, this chemical advantage does not make these ligases broadly interchangeable with CRBN or VHL. DCAF1-based degradation has so far been most clearly demonstrated in nuclear target contexts, suggesting that its utility depends on subcellular colocalisation between the ligase and the POI87. Its role as a CRL4 substrate receptor also means that DCAF1 engagement may intersect with endogenous regulatory pathways, including Merlin/neurofibromatosis type 2-linked tumour suppressive signaling92,93. AhR recruitment is especially context dependent. Although AhR is broadly expressed, broad expression does not provide intrinsic tissue selectivity, and its function as a ligand-activated transcription factor links AhR recruitment to xenobiotic metabolism, immune regulation, and wider transcriptional control94,95. Therefore, DCAF1 and AhR expand the E3 ligase repertoire, but their successful application still requires matching pathway biology with the intended therapeutic context.E3 ligase selection is a context-dependent medicinal chemistry decision. The E3 ligases discussed above converge on a common principle. Degradation outcomes depend on disease biology and cell context, not chemical recruitability alone. Recent reviews on DCAF-PROTACs and HDAC-targeting PROTACs further support this view. They extend this principle to disease setting, target-class biology, pharmacological selectivity, and translational developability96,97. Future E3 ligase discovery should define when each ligase is useful, not only add new recruiters. Useful E3 ligases must satisfy chemical and biological requirements. The recruiter should be selective and optimisable, and the ligase should be expressed in disease-relevant tissues. The ligase should also colocalise with the POI and should not introduce unacceptable toxicity or obscure the intended mechanism through its pathway biology. Accordingly, the next stage of E3 ligase selection will require the integration of chemoproteomics, structural biology, AI-assisted substrate mapping, and physiologically relevant degradation assays98–100. These tools can link E3 ligase biology with translationally meaningful degrader performance.Strategies for mitigating the hook effectThe hook effect reflects concentration-dependent imbalance in degrader binding. When the degrader is present at excessive concentrations relative to the POI and E3 ligase, productive POI-PROTAC-E3 ternary complex formation can be outcompeted by non-productive POI-PROTAC or E3-PROTAC binary complexes101. Accordingly, hook effect mitigation is not simply a potency optimisation problem. A more useful medicinal chemistry goal is to tune the concentration-dependent balance between non-productive binary complexes and productive ternary complex formation. The aim is to keep ubiquitination-competent ternary complexes favoured across the productive degradation window.Exit vector selection and ternary complex cooperativityThe bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) degrader series reported by Ciulli and colleagues provides an instructive example of how the exit vector influences hook effect behaviour102. The authors compared two BET inhibitor scaffolds, JQ1 and I-BET726, connected to the same VHL ligand through matched PEG-2, PEG-3, and PEG-4 linkers (Figure 7(A)). Although both warheads bind the canonical acetyl-lysine recognition pocket of BET bromodomains, their solvent-exposed exit vectors present the VHL ligand along different linker trajectories (Figure 7(B,C)). This distinction matters because the exit vector defines both linker attachment and POI-E3 positioning.Figure 7.Mitigation of the hook effect in PROTACs through warhead exit vector optimisation. (A) Chemical structures and key activity properties of degraders based on JQ1 and I-BET726 and (B, C) cocrystal structures of JQ1 and I-BET726 bound to bromodomain-containing protein 4 bromodomain 1 were used to visualise the solvent-exposed exit vectors. This figure was created by the authors using PyMOL and ChemDraw software.Chemical structures of JQ1 and I-BET726, binding data in a table, and molecular surface interactions with proteins.The figure has three panels (A, B, C). Panel A includes chemical structures for JQ1 (Kd = 100 nM) and I-BET726 (Kd = 4 nM), with a table detailing other compounds and their binding affinities. Panel B shows JQ1 bound to BRD4 BD1, with the solvent-exposed exit vector indicated by an arrow. Panel C presents I-BET726 bound to BRD4 BD1 in a similar protein surface context, also marked with an exit vector, illustrating the different binding orientation.The comparison showed that stronger binary POI binding did not necessarily produce a better degradation profile. The I-BET726-derived degraders retained higher BRD4 BD2 affinity, with Kd values of 3-8 nM, whereas the JQ1-derived degraders showed weaker BRD4 BD2 binding, with Kd values of 17-27 nM. However, the ternary complex behaviour followed the opposite trend. The JQ1-derived series formed positively cooperative VCB-PROTAC-BRD4 BD2 complexes, with α values of 4.7-7.4, whereas the I-BET726-derived series formed negatively cooperative complexes, with α values of 0.2-0.6. The I-BET726 series had stronger BRD4 binding but poorer ternary complex geometry. Its exit vector likely positioned VCB and BRD4 BD2 less productively.Linker length further modulated this geometric effect, but did not override the influence of the exit vector. In the JQ1-derived series, the PEG-3 degrader compound 6 showed the most favourable balance, with a ternary Kd of 9 nM, an α value of 7.4, and degradation of the BRD4 long isoform in HeLa cells with a DC50 of 2.5 nM and a maximum degradation (Dmax) of 100%. In the I-BET726-derived series, linker extension improved degradation from compound 8 to compounds 9 and 10, but all three compounds remained negatively cooperative. Consistent with this mechanistic pattern, compounds 9 and 10 showed high-concentration rebound of BET protein levels at 1-10 μM, and BRD2 levels even rose above the vehicle control.Combined with the E3 recruiter examples discussed in section “Commonly used E3 ligases”, control over linker trajectory should not be limited to the warhead side of the PROTAC. The exit vector on either the warhead or the E3 recruiter can redirect POI-E3 relative positioning and determine whether binary binding is converted into a cooperative ternary complex. Linker refinement can improve geometry within a given scaffold, but it cannot fully compensate for an attachment trajectory that intrinsically favours negative cooperativity. Thus, hook effect mitigation should prioritise attachment geometry that supports productive ternary complex formation, rather than simply increasing warhead or E3 recruiter affinity.Binary-affinity tuning to broaden the productive degradation windowEvans and colleagues addressed the hook effect in an Aurora A degrader series103. In this study, the authors did not define the hook effect using a separate scalar index. They defined the hook region from Aurora A HiBiT degradation curves. Data points above Dmax with at least 10% protein rebound were classified as hook behaviour. Using this criterion, the starting degrader JB170 showed nanomolar Aurora A degradation in MV4-11 cells, with a DC50 of 39 nM and a Dmax of 69%, but its concentration-response profile was limited by a severe hook effect and only moderate hydrolytic stability.The first stage focused on architectural refinement of the linker (Figure 8(A)). Compound 44 retained degradation activity comparable to JB170, with a DC50 of 37 nM and a Dmax of 63%, while improving hydrolytic stability from 25 to 46 h. Linker rigidification then generated compound 51, which improved the DC50 to 6.5 nM and enhanced Aurora A/CRBN ternary complex formation in the time-resolved fluorescence resonance energy transfer (TR-FRET) assay. The authors further analysed these TR-FRET profiles using a Han-derived equilibrium framework to estimate ternary complex cooperativity (Figure 8(B))104. This analysis indicated that compound 51 increased the estimated cooperativity factor from 24 for JB170 to 110. However, this improved ternary complex preorganisation did not translate into a higher maximal degradation response, because the Dmax of 51 remained 63%. These results show that linker optimisation improved potency, hydrolytic stability, and ternary complex formation. However, Dmax stayed below 70% and hook behaviour persisted.Figure 8.Binary-affinity tuning to mitigate the hook effect in Aurora A degraders. (A) Linker optimisation of the JB170 scaffold and representative degradation and stability data; (B) Han-derived ternary complex equilibrium framework used to describe POI-PROTAC-E3 assembly. P, L, and E denote the POI, PROTAC, and E3 ligase, respectively, and PLE denotes the ternary complex. KP1 and KE1 represent the binary equilibrium dissociation constants for PL and EL formation, whereas KP2 and KE2 represent the corresponding dissociation constants when the third binding partner is already engaged. The cooperativity factor α describes the relative preference for ternary complex formation; (C) CRBN ligand tuning on the compound 44 scaffold, showing CRBN binding affinity, Aurora A degradation parameters, hook effect behaviour and selected equilibrium parameters. This figure was created by the authors using ChemDraw software.Multi-panel figure showing chemical structures of PROTAC compounds, reaction equations, and data tables with biological activity metrics.The figure consists of three panels. Panel A displays the chemical structures of PROTAC compounds JB170, 44, and 51, highlighting a "Linker" in gray along with their Aurora A HiBiT DC50 values, Dmax, and hydrolytic stability. Panel B presents an equilibrium scheme showing complex formation among the POI, PROTAC, and E3 ligase, with equations for equilibrium constants and cooperativity. Panel C shows CRBN ligands with various substitutions alongside their properties, including IC50 values and PROTAC data, detailing interactions and biological metrics related to potency.CRBN ligand optimisation on compound 44 tested whether weaker CRBN binding could suppress the hook effect (Figure 8(C)). Stronger CRBN recruitment did not produce a better degradation profile. Compound 47, derived from the most potent CRBN ligand in the set with a CRBN FP IC50 of 200 nM, showed the most pronounced hook effect and the lowest Dmax value of 55%, despite retaining a DC50 of 18 nM. Compound 44, derived from CRBN ligand 52 with an IC50 of 710 nM, still showed an evident hook effect and a Dmax of 63%. Intermediate analogues showed partial improvement, with compounds 48 and 49 displaying reduced hook behaviour and increased Dmax values of 79% and 75%, respectively. CCT400028 gave the largest improvement. It was derived from compound 56, the weakest tested CRBN ligand, with a CRBN FP IC50 of 6300 nM. CCT400028 retained nanomolar Aurora A degradation with a DC50 of 29 nM, increased Dmax to 85% and showed no measurable hook effect within the tested concentration range.The ternary complex analysis supported this binding-balance interpretation. Relative to compound 44, CCT400028 showed a marked increase in the E3-PROTAC binary dissociation parameter from 550 to 5400 nM, indicating substantially weaker binary binding to CRBN, while the estimated α increased from 190 to 650. Compound 48 followed the same direction, with weaker CRBN binary engagement, increased cooperativity and reduced hook behaviour relative to 44. In this series, stronger binary affinity did not mitigate the hook effect. Weaker CRBN binding instead favoured productive Aurora A-PROTAC-CRBN complexes at high degrader concentrations.This binding-balance analysis defines a practical design rule for mitigating the hook effect. When the hook effect is driven by excessive binary binding, stronger E3 ligase, or POI binary binding may become counterproductive because it narrows the concentration range that favours productive ternary complex formation. In this situation, reducing excessive binary binding can increase the Dmax and suppress high-concentration rebound, provided that ternary complex cooperativity and chemical stability are maintained. Thus, CCT400028 shows that the more meaningful objective is to coordinate binary binding, ternary complex cooperativity and molecular stability to support a broader degradation window.Medicinal chemistry lessons from approved and clinically advanced PROTACsAs of 5 June 2026, we analysed 22 structurally disclosed approved and clinical-stage PROTACs from Cortellis Drug Discovery Intelligence (Figure 9(A))105. The analysis focused on warheads, linkers, recruited degradation systems, and key physicochemical properties. Most warheads in this dataset derive from established small-molecule scaffolds, not weak exploratory fragments. This tendency is evident across multiple target classes, including nuclear receptors, kinases, epigenetic or transcriptional regulators, apoptosis-related proteins, and ubiquitin pathway proteins (Figure 9(B)). Consistent with the design principles discussed in section “Exit vector selection and ternary complex cooperativity”, these mature scaffolds validate target binding and inform exit vector selection. They also help position the warhead for productive POI-PROTAC-E3 assembly. Therefore, in clinical PROTAC development, an ideal warhead is not defined by affinity alone. Its exit vector must also enable effective degradation.Figure 9.Medicinal chemistry features and physicochemical properties of approved and clinical-stage PROTACs. (A) Chemical structures, target classes, recruited degradation systems, and key physicochemical properties of the 22 structurally disclosed approved and clinical-stage PROTACs retrieved from Cortellis Drug Discovery Intelligence as of 5 June 2026; (B-D) distribution statistics of target classes, recruited degradation systems and linker lengths in the analysed PROTACs; (E) scatter-based distribution statistics of molecular weight (MW) and topological polar surface area (TPSA) in the analysed PROTACs; (F) scatter-based distribution statistics of hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA) count, hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) count, number of rotatable bonds (NRotB), and calculated LogP (cLogP) in the analysed PROTACs; (G) median physicochemical properties grouped by recruited degradation system and normalised to the corresponding median values of the 22-compound dataset. This figure was created by the authors using ChemDraw and GraphPad software.Figure illustrating chemical structures of various compounds, showing molecular weights, TPSA, and categorizations.This multi-panel figure presents a comprehensive analysis of chemical structures for protein degraders aimed at multiple biological targets. Panel A shows 22 compound structures with labels for unique IDs, molecular weights (MW in Da), topological polar surface area (TPSA in Å²), LogP, and their recruiting systems (CRBN, VHL, HSP90). Panel B offers a horizontal bar chart indicating quantities by target category, specifically highlighting Kinase and Epigenetic/Transcriptional with 7 degraders each. Panel C features a pie chart showing system distribution: CRBN (77.3%), VHL (18.2%), HSP90 (4.5%). Panel D illustrates degrader quantities by linker length, with 9-12 atoms being most common. Panels E and F comprise scatter-based distribution plots depicting MW, TPSA, HBA, HBD, NRotB, and cLogP. Panel G includes a heatmap and table presenting normalized physicochemical properties for CRBN, VHL, and HSP90, revealing key comparative insights.The recruited degradation systems reveal another clinical medicinal chemistry trend. CRBN-recruiting degraders account for the majority of the analysed PROTACs (Figure 9(C)). This distribution reflects the practical advantages of CRBN in clinical development. As discussed in section “Commonly used E3 ligases”, IMiD-derived CRBN recruiters are compact, structurally well characterised and supported by extensive linker exit vector precedent, thereby leaving more physicochemical space for the warhead and linker than hydroxyproline-based VHL recruiters. This may explain the frequent use of CRBN in orally oriented degrader programs. The advantage depends on acceptable CRBN neosubstrate liability. VHL-based degraders are less frequent in this dataset. They remain valuable when geometry, selectivity, or tissue safety justify the higher physicochemical burden. Heat shock protein 90 (HSP90)-associated degraders should be separated from classical E3-recruiting PROTACs. They rely on chaperone-associated degradation rather than direct E3 recruitment106,107.Consistent with the linker optimisation principles discussed in section “Linker engineering in PROTAC optimisation”, the linker statistics suggest that these compounds tend to balance geometric compatibility with whole-molecule developability (Figure 9(D)). The enrichment of 9-12-atom linkers suggests that these compounds commonly use a moderate linker length that is sufficient for simultaneous POI and E3 ligase engagement, but not so long as to add unnecessary conformational entropy, rotatable bonds, polar surface area, and metabolic liability. Linker composition further refines this balance. Most linkers in the analysed PROTACs display hybrid architectures. They combine limited adaptability with restricted motifs such as piperazine, piperidine, pyrrolidine, aryl, alkyne, or spirocyclic units. These fragments can reduce conformational heterogeneity and lower the entropic penalty of ternary complex formation108,109. They also tune polarity, basicity, exposed hydrogen bonding, and metabolic stability. Importantly, this role of the linker should be interpreted at the level of the whole degrader rather than as an isolated structural element. The warhead and E3 recruiter consume much of the MW, polarity, and lipophilicity budget. Linker optimisation can redistribute these liabilities through flexibility, polar exposure, charge, and metabolic stability110. Thus, the linker must preserve the required geometry while translating that geometry into a molecular architecture compatible with overall developability.The physicochemical profile further emphasises that PROTACs should be evaluated within a beyond Rule of Five (bRo5) framework, but this does not mean that property control can be relaxed. Scatter-based distribution plots of the analysed PROTACs show median values of 824.2 Da for MW, 168.9 Å2 for topological polar surface area (TPSA), 10.0 NRotB, 3.0 for hydrogen-bond donors (HBDs), 14.0 for HBAs, and 4.46 for calculated LogP (cLogP; Figure 9(E,F)). These values exceed conventional small-molecule space, yet they cluster around a developable property centre and provide an empirical reference for PROTAC optimisation. Median descriptor values were calculated separately by recruitment strategy and normalised to the corresponding overall median of the 22-compound dataset (Figure 9(G)). CRBN-based degraders remained closest to the dataset median. VHL-based degraders deviated more because of greater molecular size, hydrogen-bonding capacity, polarity, and flexibility. The HSP90 example displayed a distinct noncanonical profile. This indicates that such physicochemical deviation may be acceptable when it supports productive ternary complex formation, improves selectivity, or enhances drug exposure. When it does not support degradation, it becomes an avoidable developability liability.The case studies discussed above support viewing PROTAC optimisation as three context-dependent design problems, rather than as the isolated adjustment of the linker, warhead, or E3 recruiter (Table 1). A productive PROTAC must first assemble an effective ternary complex. Linker length and rigidity, warhead and E3 recruiter exit vectors, and warhead recognition topology collectively define the spatial trajectory by which the warhead, linker, and E3 recruiter position the two proteins. This positioning controls whether binary engagement becomes a cooperative, ubiquitination-competent ternary complex. Warhead binding mode further influences ternary complex productivity by preserving PROTAC catalytic turnover. These features ultimately determine ternary complex cooperativity, ternary Kd, degradation potency, Dmax, and hook effect behaviour. Effective exposure also depends on remaining near a developable property centre. In this context, physicochemical properties including MW, TPSA, HBD, HBA, NRotB, and cLogP should be evaluated together. Together they influence solubility, permeability, efflux, intracellular concentration, stability, and pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters. Linker-free design further illustrates this principle because, when spatial compatibility permits, removal of the linker can reduce molecular complexity and improve exposure-related properties. Biological context is equally important. For conditionally controlled linkers, this requires evaluating disease-relevant activation cues and tissue accessibility before assuming that stimulus-responsive activation will translate into selective degradation. For E3 ligase selection, recruiter tractability and selectivity, E3 ligase expression and localisation, recruitment mode, pathway biology and safety liabilities determine whether a chemically recruitable degradation system is biologically appropriate. Together, productive ternary complex assembly, effective drug exposure, physicochemical property control, and biological-context compatibility form an integrated framework. This framework helps judge whether a PROTAC modification improves both degradation performance and developability within the same therapeutic context.Table 1.Context-dependent framework for balancing degradation performance and developability in PROTAC design.Design contextKey variables emphasisedEvidence usedProductive ternary complex assemblyLinker length and rigidity, warhead and E3 recruiter exit vectors, warhead recognition topology and binding mode, binary binding balanceTernary complex structures, cooperativity factor α, ternary Kd, DC50, Dmax, and hook effect behaviourEffective drug exposure and physicochemical property controlLinker-free design and whole-molecule descriptors, including MW, TPSA, HBD, HBA, NRotB, and cLogPSolubility, permeability, efflux risk, intracellular concentration, metabolic or hydrolytic stability, PK parameters, and bioavailabilityBiological-context compatibilityConditional linker control, recruiter tractability and selectivity, E3 ligase expression and localisation, recruitment mode and pathway biologyProteomic selectivity, neosubstrate or off-target profiles, cell-type-dependent degradation, subcellular colocalisation, pathway effects, safety signals, and context-selective activitycLogP: calculated LogP; DC50: half-maximal degradation concentration; Dmax: maximum degradation; HBA: hydrogen-bond acceptor; HBD: hydrogen-bond donor; Kd: dissociation constant; MW: molecular weight; NRotB: number of rotatable bonds; PK: pharmacokinetic; POI: protein of interest; TPSA: topological polar surface area.s and outlookPROTAC optimisation requires joint control of degradation potency, ternary complex productivity, and developability. Productive degradation is not determined by the isolated quality of the warhead, linker, or E3 recruiter. It depends on POI-E3 orientation, binary-binding balance, intracellular exposure, and biological compatibility. Therefore, the practical goal is to sustain ubiquitination-competent ternary complexes within tractable physicochemical and disease contexts.Future PROTAC discovery should move from empirical degrader assembly towards predictive and context-guided design. Ternary complex modelling, live-cell degradation kinetics, bRo5 assessment, multi-omics, and AI-assisted design can support earlier optimisation111–113. These tools may help align ternary complex formation, effective exposure, and biological-context compatibility. The next stage of PROTAC research should not be defined simply by generating more degraders, but by establishing workflows that determine when a degrader is mechanistically productive, sufficiently exposed, and appropriate for the intended disease context.

title: Nuclear factor of activated T cells as a driver of tumor progression and a target for precision therapy
abstract: The Nuclear Factor of Activated T Cells (NFAT) family comprises closely related transcription factors. Numerous biological processes including angiogenesis, invasion, migration, proliferation, and cell survival are regulated by the NFAT family. NFATs are overexpressed and have increased transcriptional activity in a variety of human solid tumors and hematological cancers. Beyond tumor cell‐intrinsic roles, NFAT has also emerged as an important regulator of the tumor microenvironment (TME), where it can influence immune cell behavior and contribute to mechanisms of immune evasion. The discovery of the multifaceted functions of NFATs has driven the need to further unveil their role in cancer and provide new insights into other potential roles. This review provides a comprehensive narrative synthesis of current molecular and clinical studies, with particular emphasis on how NFAT shapes tumor immune interactions and modulates the TME. By integrating findings across different cancer types, we highlight how NFAT may contribute to both tumor progression and immune regulation. The review concludes by highlighting significant knowledge gaps and recommending future paths for translational and therapeutic research to leverage NFAT signaling as a potential target in precision cancer therapy.
full_text: 1INTRODUCTIONNuclear factor of activated T cells, commonly termed NFAT, was originally recognized as nuclear protein that binds upon activation of human and murine T cells to the interleukin 2 (IL2) promoter/enhancer. 1 , 2 Later experiments showed that this DNA‐binding activity is cyclosporin A (CsA) sensitive, which selectively reduces binding to the purine‐rich regions of the IL2 promoter. These findings provided key insights into the immunosuppressive action of CsA. 3 Although first described as the Pu‐box factor due to its presence in B cells, NFAT was later renamed by Crabtree to highlight its role in activated T cells. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 CsA, a compound derived from fungi, became widely used as an immunosuppressant, even before its exact mechanism was understood. 6 , 7 , 8 CsA dampens T‐cell activation by interfering with calcium signaling, blocking calcineurin and preventing NFAT from activating IL‐2 expression. 9 , 10 , 11 The first NFAT protein (NF‐ATp) was cloned in 1993 by Anjana Rao's laboratory and shown to regulate IL‐2 expression in T cells through interaction with AP‐1, while a related factor, NFATc, was later identified as a key integrator of calcium and protein kinase C signaling 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 The family of NFATs consists of 5 members with 4 calcium‐regulated genes (NFATc1–NFATc4) and a single osmotic stress‐responsive gene (NFAT5). 17 , 18 , 19 Activation happens by intracellular calcium influx via either the PLC‐γ or store operated calcium channels, with the exception of NFAT5. Hyperphosphorylated variants of the calcium‐responsive NFAT proteins are found in the cytoplasm and are activated by the rise of intracellular calcium levels, which causes calcineurin to dephosphorylate NFAT and thus leading to translocation to the nucleus. 20 , 21 Once in the nucleus, they bind directly to DNA and often cooperate with transcription partners like AP‐1 to mediate the transcription of downstream gene targets. 22 , 23 , 24 NFAT family members are increasingly recognized for their involvement in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell fate determination, proliferation, differentiation, and development. 25 In line with these roles, emerging evidence suggests that dysregulated NFAT signaling may contribute to tumor‐related processes such as angiogenesis, cell motility, and cell cycle progression. 23 Numerous cancer types, such as diffuse large B cell lymphoma, 26 , 27 aggressive T cell lymphoma, 28 pancreatic cancer, 29 breast cancer, 30 , 31 and Burkitt's lymphoma, have also been shown to overexpress or constitutively express NFAT family members. Along with the elevated protein concentration of the NFAT family members, the NFAT gene aberration has also been found. 22 With the growing evidence of NFAT involvement in both cancer cell intrinsic pathways and environmental pathways affecting tumor progression and therapeutic response, a systematic synthesis of NFAT biology in cancer is timely and necessary. Furthermore, advances in technologies such as single‐cell and spatial transcriptomics can provide deeper insights into the context‐specific functions of NFAT isoforms within tumors. While these findings highlight the potential relevance of NFAT signaling in cancer, its suitability as a therapeutic target remains to be fully established. This review therefore aims to summarize current knowledge and explore future directions in understanding NFAT signaling in cancer.2 NFAT FAMILY STRUCTURE AND MOLECULAR REGULATIONThe five members of the NFAT gene family in humans are NFATc1 (NFAT2/NFATc), NFATc2 (NFAT1/NFATp), NFATc3 (NFAT4/NFATx), NFATc4 (NFAT3), and NFAT5 (TonEBP/OREBP). 32 2.1Diversity and domain architecture of NFAT proteinsThe NFAT family proteins are regulated by calcium and have a conserved modular structure consisting of two large domains in tandem: (1) a regulatory domain, also called the NFAT homology region (NHR), and (2) a DNA‐binding domain (DBD), also called the Rel homology region (shown in Figure 1). Over a stretch of approximately 300 amino acid residues this factor showed more than 70% sequence similarity to NF‐ATp and the cloning of two further NFAT factors, designated as NF‐AT3 and NF‐AT4 (or NF‐ATx), 33 , 34 revealed the other two genuine members of NFAT factor family. Although this domain shares less than 20% sequence similarity with the Rel DNA binding domain of NF‐kB factors, its function as a DNA binding domain and organization in two loops and 10β strands at positions similar to the Rel domain 35 led to its designation as Rel Similarity (or Rel Homology) Domain, RSD (or RHD). The RSD mediates the binding of NFATs to their canonical ‘core’ binding DNA motif A/T GGAAA. In contrast to the RSD, the other parts of NFATs are less well conserved among the four factors. However, short conserved motifs for the interaction with Calcineurin, with the co‐factor CBP/p300, for nuclear import and export, phosphorylation and sumoylation have been identified in stretches near the 5′ and 3′ ends of both NFATc1, NFATc2 and the other NFAT proteins. Those sequences located outside of RSD domains exhibited a strong transactivation activity when tested in co‐transfection studies. 36 Conservation of the NHR is comparatively low, with only 22–36 sequence identities between various NFAT members. Two transcriptional activation domains (TAD) at the N‐ and C terminus are located on either side of the NHR and DBD domains. TADs differed greatly among NFAT's many isoforms and members. 32 , 37 , 38 FIGURE 1NFAT protein structure showing the NHR regulatory region containing calcineurin‐binding motifs, the DNA‐interacting DBD and the flanking TAD‐N and TAD‐C regions.TADs are anticipated to be regions where particular NFAT proteins interact with particular domains to regulate essential functions like cell death and proliferation. The N‐terminal motif, central motif, and C‐terminal motif are three highly conserved small motifs found in TADs, despite being the least conserved members of the NFAT family. It is hypothesized that these conserved sub‐regions provide the structural or functional anchoring sites required for specific interactions between proteins. 39 Through their conserved DBD and NHR domains, NFATs can interact with other proteins to either synergize 40 , 41 (like GATA‐3 42 ; ICSBP 43 ; C/EBP 44 ; AP‐1 40 ) or repress (PPAR‐γ 45 ; Mrj 46 ; Foxp3 47 ; ICER 48 ) NFAT‐mediated transcription. 49 2.2Canonical calcium–calcineurin‐dependent activationThe NFAT factors are normally inactive in the cytosol of unstimulated cells. Numerous cell surface receptor types, including G‐protein‐coupled receptors (GPCRs), T‐cell receptors (TCRs), and receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), stimulate these proteins in the cytoplasm. Actually, when these receptors are engaged by binding to their ligands, phospholipase Cγ (PLCγ) is activated, which causes phosphatidylinositol 4,5‐bisphosphate (PIP2) to be cleaved into inositol‐1,4,5‐triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). Then, IP3 joins forces with IP3 receptors that are attached to the ER to help release Ca2+ from ER Ca2+ storage. Store‐operated calcium channels (SOC) detect the ensuing Ca2+ depletion and cause these channels to open, allowing extracellular Ca2+ to enter the cytosol. 50 , 51 Ca2+ activates the Ca2+ sensor calmodulin (CaM) in the cytosol, which binds to and activates calcineurin (calcium‐binding protein CnA and CnB subunits). NFAT nuclear translocation is interrupted by the known phosphatase calcineurin which dephosphorylates multiple phosphoserines of NFATs. NFAT interacts with several transcription factors (e.g. ATF2, c‐Jun, c‐Fos, MEF2 and GATA4) in the nucleus in order to regulate numerous gene expression programmes. 22 , 37 In addition, within the nucleus, the NFAT proteins are rephosphorylated and inactivated by various kinases like casein kinase 1 [CK1], glycogen‐synthase kinase 3 [GSK3], Jun N‐terminal kinase [JNK2] and dual‐specificity tyrosine‐phosphorylation‐regulated kinase1/2 [DYRK1 and DYRK2] and move to the cytoplasm. 52 , 53 , 54 2.3Non‐canonical regulatory pathways governing NFAT activityThe more complex molecular activation of NFAT5 influences its definition. Under isotonic conditions regulated by tonicity stress, NFAT5 is constantly transferred between the cytoplasm and the nucleus. A hypertonic environment triggers NFAT5 transcription, translation, and nuclear importation, whereas the hypotonic environment triggers nuclear export of the proteins. 55 , 56 NFAT5 is turned on by diverse isotonic stimuli, including activation triggers of innate immunity receptors such as Toll‐like receptors (TLR), followed by the activation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitogen‐activated protein kinases (MAPK). Interestingly, NFAT5 has distinct characteristics in relation to osmotic activated response. 57 However, there is still uncertainty regarding the exact biochemical pathways and the connection between these two activation mechanisms. 58 Besides the classical calcium–calcineurin pathway, NFAT can be activated by a non‐conventional mechanism in early thymocytes. In thymocytes with pre‐TCR, NFATc1 is activated by IL‐7‐Jak3 signaling without calcineurin‐mediated dephosphorylation and interacts with STAT5 to control survival and differentiation programs, including the stimulation of transcription of anti‐apoptotic genes, such as Bcl‐2. These results highlight the fact that there are context‐dependent NFAT activation pathways involved in T‐cell differentiation and immune homeostasis. 59 2.4Post‐translational modificationsIn the cytosol of resting cells, NFAT is extensively phosphorylated at numerous Ser‐rich regions (SRR) and Ser‐Pro (SP) sequence motifs. An escalated amount of calcium results in the loss of these phosphate groups by the phosphatase calcineurin which exposes nuclear localization signals permitting the entry of NFAT into the nucleus to activate gene transcription. NFAT can be re‐phosphorylated by certain kinases to prevent this activity and it is re‐imported into the cytoplasm and silenced. A set of serine/threonine kinases specifically regulate the movement and activity of NFAT, such as GSK‐3 that phosphorylates NFAT upon priming by protein kinase A (PKA) 60 and which is in turn inhibited by PI3K‐Akt signaling, which is one of the most commonly deregulated cancer pathways. 61 NFAT is also regulated by other kinases, such as CK1 and MAPKs by phosphorylation of various motifs, which connects NFAT to cancer‐related signaling pathways. 62 , 63 Members of the DYRK family were found to be the key regulatory factors of NFAT. DYRK1 facilitates the export of NFAT out of the nucleus and DYRK2 plays a context‐dependent role both as tumor suppressor and an oncogene, making it a promising therapeutic target. 64 , 65 NFAT activation can also be controlled by other post‐translational modifications in addition to phosphorylation, such as sumoylation, which facilitates retention in the nucleus, and ubiquitination. A combination of these calcium‐dependent and kinase‐mediated actions indicates that the NFAT regulation is quite complex and is linked to significant cancer‐signaling pathways, which is why it is essential to regulate the cell growth and tumor progression. 23 3 NFAT SIGNALING IN CANCER PATHOGENESISNumerous cellular processes, including angiogenesis, invasion, migration, proliferation, and survival are regulated by the NFAT family of transcription factors. Many cancer types exhibit constitutively active and elevated NFAT isoforms, which drive the transcription of downstream targets important to the development and progression of cancer. and CsA blocks it 32 3.2 NFAT cross‐talk with signaling pathwaysIt has been known for some time that NFATs interact with numerous significant signaling pathways that are vital to the development of tumors (shown in Figure 2). The MAPK and PI3K‐AKT cascade is one of them. NFAT activation can occur via RTKs activating such pathways that cause NFAT‐mediated gene expression of cell proliferation, invasion and metastasis. NFAT is known to communicate with the Wnt/β‐catenin pathway and thus it can facilitate the advancement of several malignant traits including tumor growth and angiogenesis. 75 TGF‐β also has some cross‐talk with NFAT because TGF‐β may regulate NFAT in a Smad‐dependent fashion. 76 By encouraging invasion, the epithelial‐mesenchymal transition (EMT), and other pro‐tumorigenic processes, this NFAT‐TGF‐β cross‐linkage accelerates the growth of tumors. 77 Besides the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway, NFAT also interacts with the non‐canonical Wnt signaling pathways, such as the Rac1‐JNK pathway that enhances tumor cell migration, invasion, and other malignant characteristics. 78 To conclude, NFAT has been discovered to interact with important carcinogenic signaling pathways such as MAPK, PI3K‐AKT, Wnt and TGF‐β. This enables NFAT to promote numerous cancer characteristics such as proliferation, invasion, metastasis and angiogenesis, which facilitates general tumor development. 32 , 79 FIGURE 2NFAT‐ calcineurin activation and cross‐talk with other signaling pathways. IP3 causes the release of calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum, which is detected as calcium channels by STIM proteins and keeps the calcium influx. Activated AKT suppresses the activity of the kinase GSK3β, which normally inactivates NFAT and other substrates through phosphorylation. The inhibition of GSK3β by AKT increases the duration of the action of NFAT within the nucleus, thereby increasing expression of cancer related genes. Moreover, NFAT is able to promote the expression of pro‐angiogenic molecules such as VEGF, which stimulates the development of new blood vessels to sustain tumor development and metastasis. These angiogenic and invasion‐related genes are regulated by NFAT, which adds to the general growth, invasion and metastatic potential of the tumor. Overall, the cross‐talk between NFAT and signaling cascades, including TGF‐β and angiogenic pathways, enables NFAT to be a critical mediator of EMT, invasion and metastasis, which are characteristic of tumor aggression. 23 , 32 , 79 4 NFAT IN CANCER STEM CELL BIOLOGY4.1 NFAT regulation and mechanistic roles in cancer stem cell self‐renewalCancer stem cells (CSCs), a subpopulation of tumor cells, have the ability to self‐renew, grow, and start tumors. These CSCs have been linked to the development, spread, metastasis, and treatment resistance of tumors. NFAT is essential in controlling the malignant behavior of CSCs by a comprehensive form of cross‐talk among other vital signaling pathways. For instance, the NFATc2‐NDEL1‐ERK axis has been demonstrated to stimulate cell multiplication, invasion, and a cancerous phenotype in glioma stem cells. 80 Similarly, the Ca2+/NFATc2 pathway has been found to play a role in lung cancer regulating stem cell traits, such as tumor growth, cell motility, and resistance to drugs. NFAT interacts with the PI3K‐AKT cascade as well as promoting the resilience to drugs and self‐renewal of CSCs. 71 The TRPC3‐Ca2+‐AKT/GSK‐3β/CNB2‐NFATc2 axis has been demonstrated to induce the stemness of gastric cancer stem cells in gastric cancer. 81 Additionally, the resistance of pancreatic cancer stem cells to apoptosis is mediated via the CUX1‐WNT5A‐NFATc2 axis, which is downstream of the PI3K‐AKT pathway. 82 NFAT signaling also interacts with Wnt and TGF‐β signaling to maintain stemness and malignant phenotype in CSCs. Similarly, the TGF‐β‐NFAT pathway has been linked to the control of the malignant nature of breast cancer stem cells. 32 4.2 NFAT interaction with stemness pathwaysThe NFAT transcription factor family maintains CSC properties by interacting with important stemness pathways such as Hippo, NOTCH, and SOX2. For instance, NFATc2 has been shown to interact with the Hippo‐YAP1 pathway promoting self‐renewal and stemness in colorectal CSCs. 70 Furthermore, current research suggests that the NFAT‐Notch axis controls tumor development and progression by modulating CSC features. 83 Additionally, NFAT has been connected to the control of the stemness transcription factor SOX2. It has been demonstrated that NFATc2 increases SOX2 expression, which leads to the maintenance of gastric CSCs via a similar NFAT‐SOX2 axis and the induction of drug resistance and CSC characteristics in lung adenocarcinoma. 71 These findings emphasize NFAT's critical function in cross‐talk between NFAT and stemness related pathways, which can contribute to CSC malignancy and tumor growth.5 NFAT'S ROLE IN THE TUMOR IMMUNE MICROENVIRONMENT5.1Regulation dynamics of T cellsIn the tumor microenvironment (TME), NFATs have a pivotal role in controlling T cell activation. In reaction to TCR stimulation, NFAT proteins go to the nucleus, where they activate expression of genes necessary for effector functions. Only tumor‐induced CD8+ T cell exhaustion requires NFAT5, an NFAT protein without an AP‐1 docking site, which has been shown to be highly expressed in exhausted CD8+ T cells during persistent infections and tumors. Due to increased expression of the exhaustion‐associated proteins TOX and PD‐1, which eventually reduce anti‐tumor activity, excessive expression of NFAT5 in CD8+ T cells has been shown to reduce tumor control. 84 NFATc2 (NFAT1) can have a role in both cell‐intrinsic tumor suppression and extrinsic tumor promotion, depending on the host parenchyma and tumor microenvironment. NFATc2 expression is a prospective focus for targeted treatment of some advanced cancers since it can stimulate the proliferation of transformed cells and is probably TGF‐β dependent but independent of IL‐4. 85 5.2 NFAT control of immune checkpointNFAT directly regulates the transcription of the checkpoint molecules PD‐1 and CTLA‐4, which are significant inhibitors of T cell activation in cancer. NFATc1 and NFATc2 bind directly to the PD‐1 (Pdcd1) gene promoter and activate transcription in response to the stimulation of TCR, coupling PD‐1 expression strength to TCR signaling intensity. 86 When stimulation stops, Blimp‐1 inhibits NFATc2 and silences PD‐1. 87 In chronically activated or “exhausted” T cells, NFATc2 continues to drive PD‐1 production independently of AP‐1, resulting in immunological suppression. 88 Meanwhile, FoxO1 and BATF promote PD‐1 expression and T cell malfunction, creating a feedback loop that maintains exhaustion over prolonged antigen exposure. 89 6DYSREGULATED NFAT SIGNALING IN SPECIFIC CANCER TYPESNFAT signaling exhibits a variety of roles in human cancers, affecting tumor growth through context‐dependent molecular processes.6.1GliomasGliomas are malignant tumors of the CNS, marked by rapid invasiveness, neovascularization, and resilience to combination therapy. 90 NFAT has an important function in the growth and survival of gliomas. NFATc2 increases the promoter activity of IL6 and IL6R, which contributes to the hostile nature of gliomas. The NFATc2‐regulated IL6 signaling pathway facilitates the growth, invasion and tumor initiation of glioma stem cells (GSCs). 91 Furthermore, by upregulating invasion‐related genes such MMP‐7, MMP‐9, and COX‐2 (shown in Figure 3), NFATc2 promotes invasion rather than cell proliferation in glioblastoma multiforme, which is the most aggressive kind of glioma. 92 This suggests that NFATc2 may be crucial in controlling the malignancy of GSCs. Since APLNR, a receptor associated with advanced gliomas and a poor prognosis, adversely regulates NFAT5, it is also involved in the progression of gliomas. The persistence of GSC traits and tumor aggressiveness may be attributed to the deregulation of the NFAT5‐APLNR axis. 93 FIGURE 3Glioma progression and maintenance of stemness by calcium activated NFATc1/c2. The influx of calcium via calcium release‐activated calcium (CRAC) channels causes activation of the phosphatase calcineurin in glioma cells, which dephosphorylates and translocates NFATc1 and NFATc2 to the nucleus. In the nucleus, NFATc1 works together with histone deacetylase1 (HDAC1) to modulate the NF‐kB pathway linked to a mesenchymal subtype of glioma, controlling the expression of genes that cause the aggressive tumor phenotype. NFATc2 promotes the transcription of targets NDEL1, cyclooxygenase‐2 (COX‐2), and interleukin‐6 (IL‐6), as well as downstream effectors, to stimulate glioma stem cell (GSC) growth, invasion and inflammation. Such pathways incorporate calcium‐calcineurin signaling to suppress glioma progression by mediating the growth and invasion of tumor cells and maintenance of tumor cell phenotype.6.2Breast cancerBreast cancer is caused by unregulated epithelial cell proliferation and breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) have a poorer prognosis. 94 NFAT regulates a variety of actions in breast cancer cells. The Cn/NFAT pathway was discovered to be active in cases of breast cancer and contributes to the tumorigenicity and progression of breast tumor cell lines. 95 NFAT may increase the migration of breast cancer cells by activating pro‐metastatic proteins such as COX‐2 and prostaglandin production. 96 Importantly, NFAT modulates breast cancer angiogenesis. NFATc3 was discovered as a key facilitator of VEGF‐induced angiogenesis in breast tumors and inhibiting NFATc3 using the traditional Chinese herb Qingdu granule inhibited tumor angiogenesis. 97 , 98 The TGF‐β signaling pathway promotes the oncogenic nature of BCSCs. 99 In breast cancer, TGF‐β regulates NFAT, which modulates the expression of cell cycle regulators and EMT‐related genes driving tumor growth. 76 , 77 Furthermore, the Ca2+‐NFAT axis may be critical in retaining BCSC stem cell properties, as calcium signaling has been found to enhance self‐renewal and chemoresistance. 100 6.3Liver cancerLiver cancer is a very common cancer with a relatively high mortality rate. Treatment resistance, metastasis, and tumor recurrence are all associated with liver cancer stem cells (LCSCs). 101 NFAT promotes the development of liver cancer in a number of ways. NFATc2 inhibits p53 activation while promoting the growth of liver cancer cells via binding to the MDM2 promoter and activating it through transcription in a p53‐independent way. 102 However, it has also been shown that NFATc1 increases the expression of FasL and Egr2, which reduces the invasiveness of liver cancer cells and accelerates their apoptosis. 103 Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) tissues and cell lines exhibit downregulated NFAT5, whereas its overexpression results in apoptosis and inhibits cellular invasion. Nonetheless, it has been demonstrated that the MOR‐NFAT axis improves the proliferation, migration, and self‐renewal of hepatocellular carcinoma stem cells, 104 and that the FGF19/FGFR4‐SOCE/NFATc2 signaling pathway is necessary for LCSC self‐renewal. 105 Furthermore, NFAT5 starts ATM‐regulated NF‐kB activation, which boosts LCSC stemness and self‐renewal through the ATM‐NF‐kB‐SOX2 55 axis (shown in Figure 4).FIGURE 4NFAT signaling of hepatic cancer promotes stemness, growth, and metastasis. NFATc1 causes apoptosis and inhibits invasion by Egr2 and FasL. The MOR‐NFAT pathway also controls HCC proliferation, migration and self‐renewal via MAPK, c‐Myc, WNT and COX2 pathways. NFAT5 also triggers the ATM‐NF‐kB‐SOX2 pathway to stimulate LCSC self‐renewal, which disrupts tumor remission and leads to an unfavorable prognosis.6.4Colorectal cancerColorectal cancer stem cells (CCSCs) play a part in tumor resistance and recurrence. Colorectal cancer is the third most common cause of cancer‐related death worldwide. 106 Both the growth of colorectal cancer and the creation of CCSCs are encouraged by NFAT proteins. Colorectal cancer cells that were exposed to acid expressed more of the acid‐sensitive ion channel ASIC2, which activated the calcineurin/NFATc2 pathway and promoted the growth, invasion and metastasis of CRC cells to the liver. 69 According to a recent study, the NFAT and Hippo‐YAP1 pathways cooperate and the Hippo‐YAP1 signaling pathway is essential for maintaining CCSC stemness. NFATc2 specifically inhibits YAP phosphorylation, hence increasing its transcriptional activity and enhancing CCSC stemness. 70 The calcium route is also critical for CCSC promotion as epithelial calcineurin increases CCSC survival and proliferation through NFAT. 107 Additionally, the NFAT5‐JMJD2B‐NANOG axis was discovered to regulate dedifferentiation and stemness in colorectal cancer. 72 6.5Squamous cell carcinoma NFAT5 is a crucial factor for accelerating oral cancer cell growth. NFAT5 exerts this function by upregulating DPAGT1 expression which facilitates the translocation of EGFR to the plasma membrane from the endoplasmic reticulum. DPAGT1 activation and EGFR subcellular translocation, which are linked with OSCC tumor progress, depend on hypertonic‐induced NFAT5 translocation. 108 In oral squamous cell carcinoma, prolonged ethanol exposure stimulates the NFAT signaling system, which increases CSC populations and stem cell characteristics like ALDH activity, self‐renewal ability, stem cell marker expression and migratory potential. 109 Orai stimulates NFATc3, which enhances OCT4 expression by increasing OCT4 promoter activity. The NFATc3‐OCT4 axis enhances stem cell survival and self‐renewal in oral squamous cell cancer. 110 6.6Lung cancerLung cancer development is significantly influenced by the NFAT family. As2O3 has been shown to prevent SCLC metastasis and endothelial cell activation through the calcineurin NFAT signaling pathway. NFATc2 was shown to be highly expressed in lung tumor tissues, and NFATc2 knockdown dramatically decreased lung cancer cell invasion, migration, and proliferation. 111 Furthermore, it was shown that NFAT5 modulates the expression of AQP5, which in turn influences the proliferation and migration of human lung adenocarcinoma cells. 73 Anomalies in calcium signaling may contribute to the malignant nature of lung cancer stem cells (CSCs). Voltage‐gated calcium channel α2δ1‐expressing SCLC cells exhibited CSC traits and were treatment‐resistant. 112 The Ca2+/NFATc2 pathway is one novel regulator of lung CSC properties, including tumor sphere formation, cell mobility, carcinogenesis, and therapeutic response. Furthermore, CSC traits and treatment resistance in lung cancer are caused by the NFATc2/SOX2/ALDHA1 axis, and NFATc2 enhances SOX2 expression via its 3′ enhancer. In conclusion, via regulating lung CSCs, the NFAT family plays a major role in the development of the malignant characteristics of lung cancer cells, including their invasiveness, ability to spread, and resistance to treatment. 71 6.7Gastric cancerA malignant transformation of the gastric epithelium is termed gastric cancer (GC). Aberrant activation of calcium signaling increases the survival of gastric cancer stem cells (GCSCs). TRPC3 enhances Ca2+ influx and induces the carcinogenic nuclear translocation of NFATc2 in gastric cancer cells. 81 Blocking the STAT3/MSK1/NFATc2 signaling axis has been found to prevent the multiplication of gastric cancer cells as well as the formation of xenogeneic tumors. This shows that aberrant epigenetic and transcriptional pathways involving NFAT could be used to produce new targets for the treatment of gastric cancer. 113 NFATc1 participates in cell control and epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) programming by creating a complex with SOX2 that is attracted to the Snai1 promoter by the collagen‐bound receptor tyrosine kinase DDR2. This mechanism contributes to the maintenance of gastric CSC stemness. 114 In summary, the NFAT signaling system, notably the activation of NFATc2 and NFATc1, contributes to the malignant phenotype of gastric cancer cells while also maintaining the stemness of GCSCs. Targeting NFAT‐mediated transcriptional networks may have therapeutic benefits in gastric cancer.6.8Pancreatic cancerAn extremely aggressive form of malignancy with a dismal prognosis is pancreatic cancer. The inhibition of NFAT promotor causes NFATc2 to silence p15INK4b and stimulates the growth of pancreatic cancer tumors both in vitro and in vivo. Targeting the calcineurin‐NFATc2 pathway may be therapeutic for pancreatic cancer since NFATc2 inactivation has been shown to hamper the disease's progression. 115 Intracellular calcium signals that trigger the CaM/NFAT pathway cause pancreatic cancer cells to divide and multiply. 116 One important mechanism for C‐MYC activation in pancreatic cancer is the stimulation of the NFATc1 and Ca2+/CaM signaling pathways. NFATc1 has been demonstrated to bind to C‐MYC and increase its transcription in pancreatic cancer cells. This NFATc1‐mediated C‐MYC overexpression increases the malignant phenotype of pancreatic cancer stem cells (PCSCs) including proliferation, stemness and EMT. 29 Furthermore, NFATc1 has been shown to coordinate the expression of EMT‐related genes and stem factors in a SOX2‐dependent way, hence a stem‐like state in pancreatic cancer cells is maintained. This emphasizes the importance of the NFAT‐SOX2 axis in controlling the malignant transformation and stemness of PCSCs. 117 In conclusion, the NFAT family, notably NFATc2 and NFATc1, plays a pivotal part in accelerating the proliferation, tumor growth, and maintenance of the stem‐like phenotype in pancreatic cancer, making it a prospective therapeutic target in this aggressive malignancy.7THERAPEUTIC TARGETING OF NFAT 7.1Pharmacological strategies to inhibit NFAT signalingThere are three approaches to targeting the NFAT signaling pathway as a potential cancer therapy. (1) Targeting Upstream Regulators of NFAT. Drugs such as cyclosporin A (CsA), tacrolimus (FK‐506) and ISA247 inhibit the calcineurin phosphatase that dephosphorylates and activates NFAT. There are also other inhibitors such as BTP2 and McKeon compounds that inhibit calcium signaling upstream of NFAT. (2) Directly targeting NFAT. Compounds such as ST‐1959, Roc‐1/2/3, helenalin, genistein and zoledronic acid have a direct effect on inhibiting the expression of NFAT and its nuclear translocation or promoting its degradation. (3) Blocking binding of NFAT to DNA. UR‐1505, triflusal, caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE), punicalagin, and vitamin D3 are some of the compounds that prevent the binding of NFAT to its target DNA sequences, thereby interfering with its transcriptional activity. These approaches will inhibit the NFAT signaling axis that plays a role in many cancer hallmarks such as cell number expansion, invasion, metastasis and angiogenesis. 22 7.2Preclinical and clinical evidence across cancer typesNFAT plays a multifaceted role in cancer progression and responses to therapy by controlling tumor growth, immune evasion, drug resistance and metastatic behavior via the Ca2+‐calcineurin‐NFAT signaling pathway. InuA‐mediated suppression of NFATc2 prevents MDM2 transcription and prostate cancer proliferation, migration and invasion regardless of p53 or androgen receptor status. 118 NFATc2 enhances immune evasion by stimulating PD‐L1 in renal cell carcinoma and is maintained in sunitinib resistant tumors through overactivation of PI3K/AKT/GSK3β. In addition, FOXA1 and SETD2 suppress its degradation through inhibition of FBW7. 119 Triterpenoids block ASIC2 and NFATc2 in colorectal cancer, blocking downstream MMP‐2/MMP‐9 expression and invasion. NFATc2 nuclear translocation and Fas/FasL are increased with combined TMZ and lithium treatment to repress the growth of glioma. 120 In contrast, NFATc1 promotes proliferation and prevents DNA damage, thereby mediating the resistance to carboplatin in lung cancer, and indeed, its silencing can restore drug susceptibility of high glucose‐induced lung cancer, which underscores its clinical application in diabetic non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). 121 miR‐194 regulates the progression of lung cancer by targeting NFAT5 and predicts its treatment of diabetic NSCLC. 122 NFAT5 is also highly expressed in inflammatory breast cancer, where it is a biomarker of aggressive subtypes, and a combination of NFAT expression and CA72‐4 levels predicts the prognosis in ovarian clear cell carcinoma through the regulation of CHAD. Also, AM404, an acetaminophen metabolite, suppresses NFAT and COX‐2 expression in neuroblastoma, which may indicate the possibility of its use as an anti‐inflammatory and anti‐cancer agent. 123 , 124 Table 2 summarizes a brief overview of the types of cancer, NFAT‐targeting approaches and the mechanistic consequences of these approaches.TABLE 2Cancer specific targeting strategies and mechanistic outcomes of NFAT pathway inhibition.Cancer typeTherapeutic targeting strategyKey findings and mechanismsGliomaCalcineurin inhibitors (CsA, FK506); NFATc2‐NDEL1 axis targetingInhibition of NFATc2 reduces glioma invasiveness and tumor growth by suppressing IL‐6 signaling and invasion‐related genes. to be a revolutionary technology to analyze the architecture of tumor microenvironments, cell–cell interactions, immune checkpoint landscapes, and transcriptional heterogeneity in multiple types of cancer, such as lung, colorectal, gastric, breast, and brain tumors. 127 , 128 , 129 ST has revealed significant information about the TME, macrophage reprogramming, immune checkpoints and immunosuppressive alteration in brain metastases in lung cancer, which may serve as prognostic biomarkers and treatment options for immune and fibrotic pathways. 130 , 131 In colorectal cancer, ST has assisted in a study of genetic and epigenetic co‐evolution that has shown the effects of chromatin and transcription factor changes on tumor progression and metastasis. 132 , 133 The TME cellular components and interactions between them play a significant role in tumor progression, metastasis and prognosis, and are possible new targets of precision therapy. 134 In gastric cancer, ST can be utilized to investigate the biological characteristics of the tumors of the gastrointestinal tract using the various levels of tissues, identify the differences of gene expression between tumor and the surrounding normal tissues, and obtain valuable information about the early diagnosis of the tumor and predict the recurrence in the tumor. 135 However, in spite of these recent developments in spatially mapping transcriptional factors and cell ecosystems, there are still no studies that have used ST to comprehensively map NFAT isoform distribution across different cell types and their spatial locations in tumors, which is an urgent gap since NFAT family members have specific, often opposite roles in different cell types, with some isoforms inducting tumors and others repressing tumor progression. The exploitation of ST platforms that have been able to map immune and metabolic programs to decode the complexity of NFAT is an important next step in creating isoform‐selective, spatially‐informed therapeutic approaches that can bypass the limitations of pan‐NFAT inhibitors, which have historically failed due to severe immunosuppression because of their inability to differentiate between beneficial and adverse NFAT functions in various cellular compartments.8CONCLUSIONThe NFAT transcription factor family was initially discovered in T cells and shown to be important in the regulation of the immune response. Later research has demonstrated that NFAT proteins are ubiquitously expressed and have a wide range of regulatory functions in most types of cells, including those implicated in the development of cancer. The NFAT transcription factors have been implicated in regulating extensive variety of cellular functions that are essential in cancer such as in survival of cells, cell growth, cell migration, cell invasion, and angiogenesis. Notably, NFAT isoforms are often constitutively engaged and/or overexpressed in diverse human malignancies, leading to malignant phenotypes and tumor development. Considering the central role of NFAT in cancer, the pharmacological or genetic targeting of NFAT signaling pathway has been proposed as a promising approach to cancer prevention and treatment. Moreover, NFAT inhibitors of various classes have shown promising anti‐cancer effects in preclinical research.Even with substantial progress, there are still important gaps in our knowledge of NFAT signaling in cancer that should be addressed in the future. To determine context‐dependent functions of individual NFAT members in the tumor microenvironment, isoform and cell type‐specific NFAT mouse models especially focused on tumor‐associated fibroblasts, macrophages, endothelial cells and regulatory T cells will need to be developed. Moreover, although spatial transcriptomics has been successfully applied to map immune checkpoint landscapes, metabolic programs, and transcription factor activities in a variety of cancer types, no research has so far be done to profile systematically NFAT isoform distribution using spatial technologies. Spatial resolution may provide important insights into NFAT biology since within a cellular and spatial context NFAT isoforms often have opposed functions, which cannot be determined by bulk RNA sequencing or traditional immunohistochemistry. Combining spatial transcriptomics with NFAT biology could help clarify which isoforms contribute to oncogenic and tumor suppressive programs in particular tumor areas and cellular subsets to inform the design of spatially targeted therapeutic interventions. The existing pharmacological inhibitors of calcineurin‐NFAT, for example, cyclosporin A and FK506, are not isoform‐selective but instead cause systemic immunosuppression, which highlights the need for more selective approaches, for example, isoform‐specific small molecules, peptide disruptors, or PROTAC‐based degraders. Moreover, despite the evidence of NFAT being involved in immune evasion and regulation of PD‐L1, its contribution to immunotherapy resistance to immune checkpoint blockade and CAR‐T therapy has not yet been fully studied and no clinical trials are currently available that have attempted to combine NFAT targeting with immunotherapy. Although NFAT plays a role in cancer stem cell maintenance in a variety of malignancies, downstream transcriptional programs that regulate self‐renewal and chemoresistance have yet to be clearly determined. Moreover, a diagnostic or prognostic biomarker of NFAT5 and combined NFAT‐CA72‐4 has yet to be clinically validated at large scales and detection of NFAT signatures using liquid biopsy is not available. Together, filling these gaps will be important for improving the translational understanding of NFAT biology to achieve effective and accurate cancer therapeutics.AUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS Hira Khan: Formal analysis; investigation; methodology; writing – original draft; writing – review and editing.
