title: Actinomycin Derivatives: Structural Diversification and Biological Activities
abstract: Actinomycins constitute a class of bioactive compounds known for their potent cytotoxic properties. Among them, actinomycin D, isolated in the 1940s from Streptomyces antibioticus, is the most extensively studied derivative. Structurally, actinomycins are characterized by a planar phenoxazinone chromophore flanked by two cyclic pentapeptides. They exert their biological effects primarily through DNA intercalation and transcription inhibition. Despite its remarkable bioactivity, the clinical application of actinomycin D is limited by significant adverse effects, including hepatotoxicity and restricted selectivity. These limitations underscore the need for structurally optimized analogs with improved therapeutic profiles and reduced toxicity. Over the decades, natural product discovery, precursor‐directed biosynthesis, and synthetic modification have yielded more than 70 structurally distinct derivatives, incorporating variations in both the peptide rings and the chromophore core. These structural modifications have resulted in diverse antibacterial, antiviral, and cytotoxic activities. Thus, this review critically examines the historical development, chemical diversity, and in vitro and preclinical bioactivity of actinomycin derivatives, highlighting key structural modifications over time and discussing their implications for future drug development.
full_text: 1IntroductionActinomycins are a family of chromopeptide antibiotics produced predominantly by Streptomyces species, although they have also been reported from other actinomycetes, including Micromonospora. Structurally, actinomycins consist of a phenoxazinone chromophore linked to two cyclic pentapeptide lactones with variable amino acid compositions [1, 2, 3]. Further diversity is introduced into the peptide structure through rearrangements, such as β‐ring threonine modifications or the incorporation of heteroatoms. However, recent studies have also identified derivatives with modifications on the phenoxazinone chromophore, indicating that structural diversity extends beyond the peptide rings. Depending on whether the amino acid composition of the two cyclic pentapeptides is identical, actinomycins can be classified as iso‐ or aniso‐actinomycins. Collectively, these structural variations define the A‐Z‐type subclasses, which exhibit distinct biological activity profiles [4, 5]. Up to date, more than 70 structurally distinct actinomycin derivatives have been reported, along with several analogs obtained via precursor‐directed biosynthesis, synthesis, and semisynthesis [5, 6]. Among these, the best‐known member, actinomycin D (AMD), was discovered in the 1940s. AMD exerts its biological activity primarily through DNA intercalation and subsequent inhibition of RNA synthesis, which underlies both its potent antitumor efficacy and dose‐limiting toxicity [6, 7, 8]. The findings ultimately led to its clinical development as one of the earliest chemotherapeutic agents [9, 10, 11]. Given its clinical relevance, further studies have demonstrated that structural modifications profoundly influence biological activity. For example, replacing N‐methylvaline (MeVal) with N‐methylalanine (MeAla) markedly reduced antitumor activity, whereas substituting MeVal with N‐methylleucine (MeLeu) enhanced in vitro potency [12, 13].Despite the identification of distinct actinomycin derivatives over seven decades, AMD remains the sole clinically approved member of this family. This lack of clinical translation, despite promising preclinical activities, reflects fundamental challenges in achieving sufficient therapeutic selectivity and acceptable toxicity profiles. Consequently, actinomycins are no longer considered a major focus of anticancer drug development, although they remain valuable tools for chemical biology and mechanistic studies.This review summarizes actinomycin derivatives, focusing on their chemical structures and, where available, their biological activities, to provide an overview of their chemical diversity, biological activities, and translational potential. In addition, it outlines the historical progression of actinomycin discovery and clarifies inconsistencies in nomenclature and synonym usage across the literature, thereby consolidating fragmented reports into a coherent framework.2Naturally Occurring Actinomycins2.1Actinomycin Type DActinomycin D (AMD, 5) comprises a 2‐amino‐4,6‐dimethylphenoxazin‐3‐one‐1,9‐dicarboxylic acid chromophore linked to two cyclic pentapeptide lactones (Figure 1). The three‐dimensional structure of AMD has been elucidated by X‐ray crystallography and NMR studies, revealing a nonplanar phenoxazinone chromophore stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding and conformational constraints imposed by the cyclic pentapeptides [14, 15]. AMD binds DNA through a dual recognition mechanism in which the phenoxazinone chromophore intercalates between adjacent base pairs while the cyclic pentapeptides occupy the minor groove. The planar chromophore intercalates preferentially at GpC steps within double‐stranded DNA [2, 16].FIGURE 1Schematic overview of AMD‐mediated transcriptional inhibition and its mechanistic downstream effects in mammalian (green sector) and microbial cells (purple sector). The AMD–DNA complex was generated from the crystal structure of the d(GAAGCTTC)2‐AMD complex (PDB ID: 173D) (created in BioRender. https://BioRender.com/het7ha0). As the first step in biosynthesis, tryptophan is converted to the precursor 4‐methyl‐3‐hydroxyanthranilic acid (4‐MHA) via a multi‐step pathway shown in Figure 2a [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Actinomycin biosynthesis is orchestrated by a nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) system. During peptide assembly, integrated methyltransferase domains catalyze N‐methylation of amino acids, while epimerization domains convert L‐amino acids to D‐configuration. These modifications occur co‐translationally as the peptide chain is assembled on the NRPS, not as post‐assembly tailoring steps. The depsipeptide macrocycle is formed through intramolecular esterification between the threonine hydroxyl group and the thioester‐linked MeVal, followed by oxidative coupling of the two pentapeptide halves via phenoxazinone synthetase (PHS) [22, 23, 24, 25, 26] (Figure 2b,c).FIGURE 2Biosynthesis of AMD. (a) Biosynthetic pathway for the formation of 4‐methyl‐3‐hydroxyanthranilic acid (4‐MHA). (b) Assembly‐line organization of the nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) system. (c) Proposed final step in actinomycin biosynthesis. Abbreviations: ACMS I, actinomycin synthetase I; ACMS III, actinomycin synthetase III; AcmACP, actinomycin acyl carrier protein; A, adenylation domain; T, thiolation domain; PCP, peptidyl carrier protein; C, condensation domain; E, epimerization domain; M, methyltransferase domain; TE, thioesterase domain; Thr, threonine; Val, valine; Pro, proline; Gly, glycine (created in BioRender. https://BioRender.com/xzy6iq4). 1.1Molecular Mechanisms of AMDThe antitumor activity of AMD is primarily mediated through transcriptional inhibition following DNA binding. AMD binds strongly but reversibly to DNA by intercalating its phenoxazinone chromophore between adjacent base pairs, while the cyclic pentapeptides interact with the minor groove. This interaction preferentially occurs at GpC‐rich sites and impedes RNA polymerase progression, with transcription elongation being more sensitive than initiation. Among the three nuclear RNA polymerases, RNA polymerase I (RNAP I) is the most sensitive target, followed by RNAP II and RNAP III, resulting in pronounced inhibition of ribosomal RNA synthesis at nanomolar concentrations [27, 28, 29, 30]. Although transcriptional inhibition represents the principal mechanism of action, AMD has also been reported to inhibit DNA topoisomerases I and II in human cells. Further investigation revealed that AMD forms stable coordination complexes with Cu(II), which enhance oxidative DNA strand cleavage, particularly in the presence of H2O2, suggesting a redox‐mediated mechanism [31]. This interference is particularly damaging to rapidly proliferating cells, such as cancer cells, which rely heavily on efficient DNA and RNA synthesis for their uncontrolled growth. AMD ultimately leads to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis (programmed cell death) in malignant cells, thereby reducing tumor burden. However, this mechanism also affects healthy rapidly dividing cells such as bone marrow and gastrointestinal epithelium, leading to the side effects.Inhibition of ribosomal RNA synthesis triggers nucleolar stress, a hallmark of AMD activity. Previous studies demonstrated reversible translocation of nucleophosmin (B23), accompanied by suppression of RNA synthesis and cell proliferation, in HeLa cells [32, 33].Nucleolar disruption further promotes the sequestration of MDM2 by ribosomal proteins, thereby stabilizing and activating p53 in sensitive cells [34]. These signaling events contribute substantially to AMD's antiproliferative effects.Downstream of transcriptional inhibition and nucleolar stress, AMD induces apoptosis through both p53‐dependent and p53‐independent mechanisms. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells, AMD activated stress‐activated protein kinase/c‐Jun N‐terminal kinase (SAPK/JNK) signaling and increased Bax expression independently of p53 or Bad, leading to apoptosis in different pancreatic cancer lines (PANC‐1, CAPAN‐1, and T3M4) [35, 36]. In addition, AMD induced mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by mitochondrial membrane depolarization, cytochrome c release, activation of caspase‐9 and caspase‐3, and loss of anti‐apoptotic proteins, including MCL‐1, in several tumor models [37, 38, 39]. These findings highlight the dual p53‐dependent and p53‐independent apoptotic mechanisms of AMD.2.1.2Cytotoxic Activity and Combination StudiesNumerous studies have investigated the cytotoxic activity of AMD across diverse cancer cell types, either as monotherapy (Table 1a) or in combination with other agents (Table 1b). CellMiner (release 2025.3) data from the NCI‐60 drug screen (sulforhodamine B assay) were analyzed to evaluate AMD's cell line‐dependent cytotoxicity. CellMiner (release 2025.3) data from the NCI‐60 drug screen (sulforhodamine B assay) showed that AMD is among the most potent compounds in the panel, with GI50 values predominantly in the picomolar to nanomolar range. AMD displayed broad cytotoxicity across most cell lines, with a mean GI50 of approximately 0.0014 μM. Hematopoietic malignancies were particularly sensitive, with all leukemia cell lines exhibiting subnanomolar GI50 values, whereas several solid tumor lines, including breast, colon, and melanoma, showed comparatively reduced sensitivity. For example, HL‐60 (TB) leukemia cells exhibited a GI50 of approximately 0.0002 μM, whereas MCF‐7 breast cancer and SK‐MEL‐28 melanoma cells required concentrations of approximately 0.2–0.3 μM to achieve comparable growth inhibition. These findings indicate marked cell line–dependent differences in AMD sensitivity and suggest that rapidly proliferating hematopoietic tumors are particularly susceptible to transcriptional inhibition.TABLE 1In vitro cytotoxic activities of AMD.a. Similarly, a combination of AMD with the recombinant immunotoxin RG7787 produced synergistic activity against mesothelin‐positive cancer cells and was associated with enhanced NF‐κB signaling [57]. Synergistic interactions have also been reported between AMD and echinomycin in DNA mismatch repair‐deficient HCT116 colon cancer cells (combination index ≈0.5) [58]. In addition, co‐treatment with resveratrol potentiated antiproliferative activity by activating p53 signaling and upregulating p21, PUMA, and GDF15, accompanied by reduced Ki‐67 expression in vivo [59].2.1.3Clinical Applications and LimitationsAMD remains the only clinically approved member of the actinomycin family. It is used primarily in pediatric oncology for the treatment of Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma, as well as in gynecologic oncology for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia and in selected patients with metastatic nonseminomatous germ cell tumors. In clinical practice, AMD is rarely administered as monotherapy and is generally incorporated into multi‐agent chemotherapy regimens, including VAC (vincristine‐AMD‐cyclophosphamide) for rhabdomyosarcoma and vincristine/AMD‐based protocols for Wilms tumor and other pediatric sarcomas [60, 61, 62]. In addition, AMD has been employed as a component of regional perfusion protocols for the palliative or adjunctive treatment of locally recurrent or locoregional solid malignancies. Because of poor gastrointestinal absorption, AMD is administered exclusively by the intravenous route. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate that the drug undergoes limited metabolism, preferentially accumulates in nucleated cells, exhibits poor penetration across the blood–brain barrier, and has a terminal plasma half‐life of approximately 36 h. About 30% of an administered dose is recovered in urine and feces within 1 week. Despite its clinical efficacy, the therapeutic application of AMD is constrained by dose‐limiting toxicities, particularly myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and gastrointestinal adverse effects. Moreover, resistance mechanisms, including drug efflux and enhanced DNA repair, may reduce therapeutic efficacy in certain tumor types [63, 64, 65]. Additionally, AMD can cause a “radiation recall” phenomenon, where skin reactions (erythema, blistering) potentially occur in previously irradiated areas, even months or years after radiation therapy. Long‐term treatment regimens incorporating AMD have also been associated with an increased risk of secondary malignancies, further limiting its therapeutic window.2.1.4Other Bioactivities2.1.4.1Antibacterial and Anti‐Virulence ActivityAMD exhibits antibacterial activity against both Gram‐positive and Gram‐negative pathogens and has additionally been reported to interfere with biofilm formation, quorum sensing, and bacterial virulence mechanisms. In various research, AMD exhibited bioactivity against both methicillin‐sensitive and methicillin‐resistant S. aureus strains, inhibiting bacterial growth, suppressing biofilm formation, and modulating the expression of virulence‐associated genes [66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 74]. Resistance in MRSA could be partially overcome by treatment with D‐serine (Ser) or D‐threonine (Thr), which alter the composition of the peptidoglycan precursor, or by subinhibitory concentrations of tunicamycin, an inhibitor of teichoic acid biosynthesis, thereby enhancing bacterial susceptibility to AMD [72]. In addition, AMD inhibited biofilm formation in Staphylococcus epidermidis ATCC in a dose‐dependent manner, reducing biofilm biomass by more than 90% at 1.5 µg/mL by disrupting the ica operon [75].AMD has also demonstrated activity against several other bacterial pathogens. Although only weak inhibition of Mycobacterium tuberculosis pantothenate synthetase was initially reported [76], subsequent studies showed antibacterial activity against M. tuberculosis H37Ra and H37Rv strains, with protein kinase B (PknB) identified as a potential molecular target [77, 78]. Additional antibacterial effects have been described against Klebsiella pneumoniae [79], whereas proteomic analyses identified the flagellar motor switch protein FliN as a potential target in Vibrio parahaemolyticus [80]. Beyond growth inhibition, AMD exhibited pronounced anti‐virulence effects. Treatment reduced hemolysin production, motility, and biofilm formation in Aeromonas hydrophila [81]; inhibited the alternative peptidoglycan biosynthesis enzyme MurD2 in Xanthomonas oryzae [82]; and interfered with quorum sensing pathways in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, resulting in reduced motility phenotypes and altered expression of quorum sensing–associated genes [83, 84].Despite these promising in vitro activities, the antibacterial application of AMD is severely limited by its pronounced cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells. Thus, it has not been developed as a clinically useful antibacterial agent.2.1.4.2Antifungal and Antiparasitic ActivityAntifungal activity has also been reported for AMD‐producing Streptomyces isolates. For example, AMD was obtained from the endophytic Streptomyces sp. Tc022, isolated from Alpinia galanga roots, and exhibited weak activity against Colletotrichum musae and Candida albicans [85]. Streptomyces sp. IA1 was isolated from Saharan soil and produced antifungal activity against a broad range of fungi, exhibiting inhibition zones of 19–45 mm against Fusarium culmorum, Fusarium equiseti, Fusarium moniliforme, Fusarium proliferatum, Aspergillus carbonarius, Aspergillus niger, and Umbelopsis ramanniana. Notably, AMD significantly reduced disease symptoms of chocolate spot (Botrytis fabae) in field bean by up to 91.7% and Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum) in flax by nearly 60% [86]. Lately, AMD was identified as an inhibitor of polysaccharide deacetylase (Agd3) in Aspergillus fumigatus, weakly reducing biofilm biomass at a concentration of 100 µM [87].AMD has also demonstrated antiparasitic activity, although available studies remain limited. In Leishmania major, AMD showed activity against promastigotes, with an EC50 of 1.90 µg/mL. However, the corresponding cytotoxic concentration (CC50 = 0.10 µg/mL) resulted in a very low selectivity index (SI = 0.053), indicating poor selectivity toward the parasite relative to mammalian cells and thereby limiting its therapeutic potential [88].2.1.4.3Antiviral ActivityAMD has demonstrated antiviral activity against several RNA and retroviruses. Early studies showed that AMD inhibited replication of Pichinde virus in BHK‐21 fibroblast cells in a dose‐dependent manner at concentrations ranging from 0.4 to 4 µg/mL. Notably, administration up to 12 h post‐infection still resulted in a 50% reduction in viral yield. The data indicated that AMD did not inhibit viral RNA synthesis but rather interfered with a late stage of viral maturation, likely involving host membrane glycoproteins required for virion assembly [89]. Similarly, AMD inhibited human coronavirus 229E replication, with a 50% inhibitory dose (ID50) of 0.1 µg/mL [90]. In simian rotavirus (SA11)–infected cells, treatment with 2.5 µg/mL AMD reduced virus‐specific fluorescence by more than 50% and decreased cytoplasmic metachromasia by approximately 25%, without affecting viral RNA replication [91].The antiviral activity of AMD has also been investigated against HIV‐1. AMD inhibited several stages of reverse transcription, including DNA‐dependent DNA synthesis and strand transfer reactions, primarily through binding to viral nucleic acids [92, 93, 94]. However, paradoxical enhancement of HIV‐1 replication has also been reported at low concentrations, accompanied by altered cytokine signaling and reduced susceptibility to certain nucleoside analogs [95, 96]. These findings highlight the complex and context‐dependent effects of AMD on HIV replication.Collectively, the antiviral effects of AMD are highly context‐dependent. Because AMD primarily targets host transcriptional machinery rather than virus‐specific proteins, both antiviral and proviral effects have been reported depending on the virus, host cell, and experimental conditions.2.1.5Other D‐Type AnalogsMethylated actinomycin D (mAMD) displayed potent cytotoxicity against multiple cancer cell lines while exhibiting lower toxicity toward normal HL‐7702 liver cells, suggesting a modest improvement in selectivity relative to AMD. Mechanistic studies indicated that mAMD induces caspase‐dependent apoptosis through both mitochondrial and Fas‐mediated pathways [97]. In 2018, four analogs, actinomycins D1–D4, were isolated together with AMD (Figure 3). The compounds were generally less cytotoxic than AMD toward WI‐38 fibroblasts, although all retained antibacterial activity against MRSA, with actinomycin D1 exhibiting an MIC of 0.125 μg/mL. In contrast, N‐acetylation (D3) or a Val‐to‐Ala substitution (D4) did not confer a clear biological advantage over AMD [98]. Overall, all four analogs were less cytotoxic, suggesting that the structural modifications introduced in D1–D4 did not improve the antiproliferative effect.FIGURE 3Chemical structures of actinomycins D1 (1), D2 (2), D3 (3), D4 (4), and D (5); 7‐aminoactinomycin D (6); neo‐actinomycin D (7); and hemiactinomycin (8). 7 macrophages (IC50 = 15.41 ± 0.66 μM) [99]. These findings demonstrate that even minor structural modifications within the actinomycin scaffold can substantially influence biological activity in vitro.2.2Actinomycin Type XAmong actinomycin subtypes, X‐type derivatives represent the second most studied group after D‐type analogs. Actinomycin X2 (synonymous with actinomycin V; 9) is a widely studied analog that differs from AMD by the presence of a 4‐oxoproline (OPro) moiety. In contrast, actinomycin X0β (synonymous with actinomycin A1, 10) contains trans‐4‐hydroxyproline (Hyp) instead of proline (Pro) in the β‐ring (Figure 4). Early studies established that actinomycin X preparations consisted of several closely related analogs differing mainly in the oxidation state and stereochemistry of the proline residue. Subsequent structural studies identified additional members, including X0α (11), X0δ (12), and X1a (13), thereby expanding the X‐type subclass (Figure 4) [100, 101]. Although Sharma and Manhas (2019) labeled one of their purified compounds as actinomycin V, the depicted structure and chromatographic characteristics are consistent with those of actinomycin X0β. In the broader literature, actinomycin V is synonymous with actinomycin X2, not with actinomycin X0β, indicating that the compound assignment in the original publication was likely incorrect [102].FIGURE 4Chemical structures of actinomycins X2 (9), X0β (10), X0α (11), X0δ (12), X1a (13), and Bis(hyp)‐X1 (14). Differences to AMD (5) are shown in bold letters. All amino acids are L‐configured except when indicated otherwise. Abbreviations: Thr = threonine, D‐Val = D‐valine, Pro = proline, Sar = sarcosine, MeVal = N‐methylvaline, Hyp = trans‐4‐hydroxyproline, OPro = 4‐oxoproline, αHyp = cis‐4‐hydroxyproline. Actinomycin X2, isolated from Streptomyces sp. MITKK‐103, demonstrated pronounced activity against HL‐60 leukemia cells (LC50 = 8 nM), markedly exceeding that of AMD (45 nM) and X0β (>100 nM) [103]. In lung cancer models, apoptosis induction by actinomycin X2 was cell‐type dependent. A549 cells exhibited a substantial increase in apoptotic fraction (6.19% to 45.23%), whereas NCI‐H1299 cells showed minimal sensitivity (4.23% to 6.39%) [104]. Similarly, across various breast cancer cell lines, actinomycin X2 displayed sub‐nanomolar potency (IC50 = 0.83–4.16 nM), corresponding to 4.29–18.25‐fold greater cytotoxicity than AMD [105, 106]. Comparable trends were observed in colorectal cancer models (IC50 = 6.38–8.65 nM), while substantially reduced toxicity was noted in nonmalignant QSG‐7701 and HEK‐293T cells (IC50 = 68.3 and 82.6 nM, respectively), suggesting partial tumor selectivity. Mechanistically, actinomycin X2 induced apoptosis via mitochondrial dysfunction, involving the activation of caspase‐9, caspase‐3, and PARP, and the inhibition of the phosphatidylinositol 3‐kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathway [107]. Notably, actinomycin X2 from Streptomyces sp. ZZ338 exhibited nanomolar cytotoxicity, with IC50 values ranging from 0.42 to 1.80 nM against glioblastoma and astrocytoma cell lines, and surpassed doxorubicin in selected models [108]. Collectively, available studies indicate that oxidation of the β‐ring proline residue, particularly to 4‐oxoproline, consistently enhances cytotoxic potency relative to AMD, potentially through altered steric and hydrogen‐bonding interactions within the peptide periphery. Despite consistently superior in vitro potency, actinomycin X2 has not yet advanced to clinical evaluation.Furthermore, X‐type actinomycins demonstrated broad antimicrobial activity, although potency varies considerably across species. Actinomycins X2, X0β, and AMD, from Streptomyces sp. MS449, inhibited Mycobacterium bovis BCG and M. tuberculosis H37Rv, with MICs ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 µg/mL and 1.0 to 8.0 µg/mL, respectively [109]. AMD and actinomycin X2 demonstrated MICs ranging from 1.95 to 31.25 μg/mL against vancomycin‐resistant Enterococcus (VRE), Bacillus subtilis, E. coli (S1‐LF), MRSA, and K. pneumoniae subsp. pneumoniae [102]. Further, actinomycin X0β and AMD inhibited the spore germination, hyphal growth, and biomass accumulation of Verticillium dahliae in a dose‐dependent manner [110]. Actinomycins X2 and D exhibited IC50 values of 17.6 and 29.6 μM, respectively, for inhibiting pyoverdine production in Pseudomonas cichorii SPC9018, while actinomycin X2 further displayed antibacterial activity, with an MIC of 0.25 µg/mL against MRSA ATCC and 1.56–12.5 µg/mL against various other Gram‐positive pathogens [111, 112, 113]. In a study, actinomycin X2 was reported with MIC values of 0.08, 0.12, and 0.83 µM against S. aureus, E. coli, and C. albicans, respectively [108]. In silico analyses proposed isoleucyl‐tRNA synthetase as a potential antimicrobial target, while penicillin‐binding protein‐1a was the least favorable target [113]. However, assigning specific antibacterial targets solely on the basis of docking studies should be further evaluated, as the physiological relevance of this interaction remains uncertain.To enhance potency against Gram‐negative pathogens, combinatorial antimicrobial strategies have also been explored. In a study using E. coli ATCC , synergistic effects were observed when actinomycin X2 and AMD were combined with polymyxin B and kanamycin (most synergistic area scores >10, as indicated by SynergyFinder results). In contrast, actinomycin X0β showed no synergistic effect with the tested antibiotics [114]. Further, actinomycin X2 inhibited Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri at 31.25 µg/mL (versus 62.50 µg/mL for AMD and X0β) and demonstrated greater antifungal potency against Penicillium italicum, while X0β was inactive [115]. Additional studies showed inhibition of spore germination and ROS induction in postharvest citrus pathogens [116]. In addition, actinomycins X2 and X0β displayed antimalarial activity against Plasmodium falciparum (IC50 = 0.241 and 7.69 nM, respectively). Notably, both compounds exhibited higher selectivity indices over AMD [117].Alternative applications beyond systemic therapy have explored actinomycin X2 as an antimicrobial dye for silk materials and as a functional component of fiber‐blend membranes and multifunctional hydrogels, demonstrating retained or enhanced antibacterial activity, along with improved mechanical properties [118, 119, 120, 121, 122]. Actinomycin X2‐containing wound‐healing films further promoted wound closure in rat models [123]. While these findings highlight physicochemical robustness, their translational relevance to systemic therapy remains unclear. Targeted delivery strategies have also been investigated. Folate‐modified liposomal formulations of actinomycin X2 achieved a tumor inhibition rate of 77.2% in hepatocellular carcinoma models, representing a 4.17–fold enhancement relative to free compound [124]. Overall, antimicrobial activities are broad but highly strain‐dependent and, like AMD, may primarily reflect global transcriptional inhibition rather than selective target engagement. A major unresolved challenge remains the separation of desirable biological activity from the intrinsic toxicity associated with the actinomycin scaffold.2.3Actinomycins Type A, B, and CThe A‐, B‐, and C‐type actinomycins constitute relatively small subclasses whose distinguishing features arise primarily from modifications of the chromophore rather than extensive alterations of the peptide rings. Historically, actinomycin A1 (synonymous with actinomycin X0β) and A2 (synonymous with actinomycin II and F8) were identified [125]. More recently, structural diversification within the A‐ and B‐type subclasses was expanded by the discovery of neo‐actinomycin A (15) and neo‐actinomycin B (16) from the marine‐derived Streptomyces sp. IMB094. These analogs feature a tetracyclic 5H‐oxazolo[4,5‐b]phenoxazine chromophore formed via condensation of the classical actinomycin scaffold with tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates. Neo‐actinomycin A contains a carboxyethyl‐substituted oxazole ring, while neo‐actinomycin B features a methyl‐substituted oxazole ring (Figure 5). Neo‐actinomycin A exhibited moderate cytotoxicity (IC50 38.7 nM in HCT116; 65.8 nM in A549) and antibacterial activity against MRSA and VRE (MIC 16–64 μg/mL), whereas neo‐actinomycin B showed ∼10‐fold lower cytotoxicity and negligible antibacterial activity (MIC > 128 μg/mL) [126]. These findings suggest that chromophore extension alone does not uniformly enhance potency and that substituent identity on the oxazole ring significantly influences activity.FIGURE 5Chemical structures of neo‐actinomycins A (15), B (16), and C (17) and actinomycins C2 (18) and C3 (19). Structural variations relative to the classical actinomycin scaffold are highlighted. aureus and M. tuberculosis, with activities comparable to or exceeding those of AMD [127]. Consistently, an earlier study reported that actinomycin C2, actinomycin VII (synonymous with actinomycin C3), and AMD inhibited the Shc signaling adaptor protein/Grb2 (growth factor receptor‐bound protein 2) interaction while blocking MAP kinase (Erk1/Erk2) phosphorylation in B104‐1‐1 cells at 1 µM [128]. These observations suggest that certain actinomycins may influence signaling pathways beyond their canonical role as transcription inhibitors. Nevertheless, whether these effects represent direct target engagement or secondary consequences of transcriptional suppression remains unclear. In a recent investigation, neo‐actinomycins C (17) and D (7) were isolated from Streptomyces sp. S22. Structurally, both of the compounds retain the characteristic chromophore, as seen in neo‐actinomycins A and B; however, neo‐actinomycin D is distinguished by the presence of an N‐methyl‐N‐(p‐tolyl)formamide moiety attached to the chromophore. Neo‐actinomycin D demonstrated enhanced antibacterial activity compared to neo‐actinomycin C, with 4‐ to 32‐fold lower MICs against ESKAPE pathogens (E. faecium, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, P. aeruginosa, and Enterobacter sp.) and cytotoxicity against the HepG2 liver carcinoma cell line [129], underscoring the likely impact of appended aromatic substituents on antimicrobial activity.2.4Actinomycins Type G, S, Y, and ZG‐ and Z‐type actinomycins are characterized by the substitution of N‐MeAla in place of N‐MeVal at position 5 of the α‐peptidolactone unit, along with selective methylation and oxidation of the proline residues (Figure 6). Actinomycin G1 (20), isolated in the early 2000s from Streptomyces sp. HKI‐0155, had a moderate activity against B. subtilis ATCC 6633 [130]. Furthermore, actinomycins G2–G6 were produced by Streptomyces iakyrus DSM isolated from the rhizosphere of an orange tree. These derivatives displayed distinct structural variations compared to AMD. In particular, the R‐ring incorporated trans‐3‐hydroxy‐cis‐5‐methylproline (HMPro), while the β‐ring contained MeAla and either chlorinated or hydroxylated threonine residues. Additional G3–G6 (21 –25) analogs differ through positional isomerism, hydroxylation patterns, chromophore‐ring cyclization, or conversion of one peptidolactone into a cyclopeptide, further expanding the structural diversity of the G‐type subclass [131].FIGURE 6Chemical structures of actinomycins G1 (20), G2 (21), G3 (22), G4 (23), G5 (24), G6 (25), and S (26). coli, S. aureus, and B. subtilis in a disc diffusion assay (50 µg/disc), while actinomycin G3 showed no activity against E. coli but inhibited S. aureus and B. subtilis (21 and 33 mm). Actinomycin G5 was only active against S. aureus (10 mm) and B. subtilis (20 mm), whereas actinomycin G6 showed no detectable activity. Later, cytotoxicity assays indicated that actinomycin G2 had an GI50 of 0.0013 µM and a TGI (total growth inhibition concentration) of 0.0043 µM, which were better than those of AMD (GI50, 0.0016 µM; TGI, 0.0064 µM) against HM02 gastric adenocarcinoma cells [131]. Thus, the hydroxylated and methylated proline derivatives can be accommodated within the actinomycin scaffold without loss of activity and may even enhance cytotoxic potency relative to AMD.Later, biosynthetic investigations identified a dedicated acmG gene cluster containing accessory hydroxylase and halogenase enzymes responsible for the characteristic hydroxylated and chlorinated amino acid residues found in G‐type actinomycins [132].Actinomycin S (26) was isolated from Streptomyces sp. S22. Structurally, it features an aspartic acid residue in place of Pro in the β‐peptidolactone ring. This substitution resulted in moderate antibacterial activity (MIC 1.25–80 μg/mL) against ESKAPE pathogens and induced G0/G1 arrest in HepG2 cells [129]. In an earlier study, actinomycins S2 (synonymous with AMD) and S3 were isolated from Streptomyces sp. 1048A. Structural characterization identified actinomycin S3 as containing OPro residue instead of Pro. The presence of OPro in actinomycin S3 suggests partial structural convergence with X‐type derivatives [133], indicating that β‐ring oxidation patterns may influence bioactivity.Later, Bitzer et al. [134] reported that Y‐type actinomycins (Y1–Y5; 27 –31) (Figure 7) were isolated from Streptomyces sp. strain Gö‐GS12. Y‐type actinomycins feature unique amino acid compositions, such as Hyp or OPro, that distinguish them from Z‐ and G‐type analogs. Among the Y‐series, actinomycin Y1 was the most potent analog, whereas replacement of OPro with Hyp (Y2) substantially reduced activity. Structural simplification in Y4 and Y5 resulted in a marked loss of both cytotoxic and antimicrobial potency [134]. Further studies done using Streptomyces sp. strain Gö‐GS12 identified novel aniso‐actinomycins Y6 (32), Y7 (33), Y8 (34), Y9 (35), and iso‐actinomycin ZP. Structural analyses revealed β‐ring rearrangements in actinomycin Y6 and a rare 5‐methylproline (MPro) in actinomycins Y9 and Zp. Antibacterial activity tests showed Y9 as the most bioactive one (MICs between 0.012 and 0.003 µg/mL), followed by Y8 (0.031–0.003 µg/mL) and Zp (0.047–0.006 µg/mL) against S. aureus, Micrococcus luteus, and B. subtilis. Strikingly, aniso‐actinomycins Y9 and Zp exhibited sub‐nanomolar cytotoxicity (EC50 0.16–0.74 nM) comparable to or exceeding AMD [4]. These data suggest that specific β‐ring rearrangements and incorporation of 5‐methylproline enhance potency, particularly when combined with halogenation.FIGURE 7Chemical structures of actinomycins Y1 (27), Y2 (28), Y3 (29), Y4 (30), Y5 (31), Y6 (32), Y7 (33), Y8 (34), and Y9 (35). These compounds lack unmodified Pro but contain MeAla and rare Pro derivatives, such as MPro (Z5), 4‐keto‐5‐methylproline in Z1 and Z5, and HMPro in Z1 [136, 137, 138, 139, 140]. Some variants, including Z1, also contain 4‐hydroxythreonine (HThr), an uncommon amino acid among actinomycins [141]. In a study, Z‐type actinomycins isolated from S. fradiae were structurally elucidated and denoted as actinomycins Z1 (36), Z2 (37), Z3 (38), Z4 (39), and Z5 (40). These analogs contain rare amino acids, such as 4‐chloro‐L‐threonine (ClThr). Z3 and Z5 demonstrated particularly strong cytotoxicity (IC50 ∼ 0.1 μM), surpassing AMD in HM02, HepG2, and MCF‐7 cell lines [142].FIGURE 8Chemical structures of actinomycins Z1 (36), Z2 (37), Z3 (38), Z4 (39), Z5 (40), and Z6 (41). KIB‐H714. Actinomycin Z6 was distinguished by the presence of an additional oxygen‐bridged ring linking the chromophore to the β‐peptidolactone. Although Z6 displayed cytotoxicity across HL‐60 leukemia, SMMC‐7721 liver carcinoma, A549 lung carcinoma, MCF‐7 breast carcinoma, and SW480 colon carcinoma cell lines, the strongest activities were observed for actinomycins Z3 and Z5, both exhibiting IC50 fivefold lower activity, while reductions against S. aureus reached 17‐ to 20‐fold. These data suggest that subtle steric alterations at the imino acid position critically affect DNA intercalation efficiency and antibacterial activity [150, 151]. Streptomyces antibioticus produces novel actinomycin derivatives when cultured with DL‐pipecolic acid, yielding three compounds: actinomycins Pip1α (57), Pip1β (58), and Pip2 (62). These analogs differ from typical actinomycins by incorporating pipecolic acid and its derivative 4‐oxopipecolic acid (OPip) at the imino acid positions, alongside standard residues such as threonine, valine, sarcosine, and N‐MeVal. Specifically, actinomycin Pip2 contains two pipecolic acid residues, while actinomycin Pip1β has one pipecolic acid and one proline. Nevertheless, actinomycin Pip1α contains pipecolic acid linked to OPip, an uncommon amino acid found in several peptide antibiotics. Biological activities of actinomycins Pip1α and Pip2 had reduced antibacterial activity compared to AMD, particularly against penicillin‐resistant S. aureus, where MIC values increased from 0.1 µg/mL (AMD) to 5.0 µg/mL (actinomycin Pip1α) and 1.5 µg/mL (actinomycin Pip2) [152, 153]. Therefore, the expansion of the five‐membered proline ring to a six‐membered pipecolic acid ring was found to be unfavorable for antibacterial activity.Another study in the 1960s published that feeding Streptomyces antibioticus with non‐proteinogenic amino acids, such as azetidine‐2‐carboxylic acid (AzC) and pipecolic acid, yielded novel actinomycins in which AzC or pipecolic acid replaced one or both proline residues [154]. Consistently, another study reported that S. antibioticus, when cultured with AzC, produced novel actinomycins, named azetomycins I (synonymous with azetomicin I, 63) and II (64), in which one or both proline residues are replaced by AzC, respectively. Unlike most proline replacements, azetidine substitution largely preserved antibacterial potency while increasing total antibiotic production. This observation reflects that ring size reduction is better tolerated than ring expansion and highlights the flexibility of the actinomycin biosynthetic machinery [155].Another example of biosynthetic manipulation was observed when Streptomyces chrysomallus and S. parvulus were cultured in media supplemented with 3‐hydroxyanthranilic acid (3‐HA), a structural analog of the chromophore precursor 4‐MHA. This led to the formation of C‐demethylactinomycins, namely mono‐C‐demethylactinomycin D and di‐C‐demethylactinomycin D. Although C‐demethylactinomycins constituted only 7%–8% of total actinomycin production, their natural occurrence (up to 0.8%) in non‐supplemented cultures suggests 3‐HA formation via a minor diversion from the 4‐MHA biosynthetic pathway [156]. In a mutasynthesis approach, 10 new halogenated derivatives of actinomycin D were generated by feeding halogenated (F−, Cl−, Br−, I−) or methoxy‐substituted 4‐MHA to a Streptomyces mutant strain. Among the resulting analogs, compounds 5 (4,6‐dichloro), 7 (4,6‐dibromo), 10 (4,6‐diiodo), and 12 (6‐iodo) showed the antibacterial activity against eight different S. aureus strains, M. luteus ML01, E. faecium ATCC , E. faecalis ATCC , and Bacillus thuringiensis BT01 with MIC values ranging 128 µg/mL) [158]. Thereafter, precursor‐directed biosynthesis reveals limited but exploitable tolerance of the actinomycin scaffold to structural modification, delineating the boundaries of its structural flexibility. The spirolinked architecture of actinomycins L1 and L2 demonstrates that noncanonical chromophore modifications can be achieved through precursor‐directed approaches; however, the resulting compounds showed only moderate antibacterial activity and no clear advantage over established actinomycins.FIGURE 10Chemical structure of actinomycin L1 (65). Using a modular total synthesis approach, novel Bis(hyp)‐X1 (14) and naturally occurring actinomycins X0β and X0δ were obtained. Actinomycin Bis(hyp)‐X1 contains trans‐4‐hydroxyproline residues in both peptide rings in place of proline [101], demonstrating that the imino acid position tolerates certain hydroxylated substitutions. However, available data suggest that hydroxylation alone does not confer a substantial pharmacological advantage over naturally occurring X‐type analogs. Furthermore, a study evaluated the SAR of 13 synthetic AMD analogs. It indicated that modifications at the cyclic peptide backbone's Val and/or MeVal positions significantly influenced both Grb2‐SH2 domain binding and cellular antiproliferative activity. Among synthetic analogs, compounds containing tyrosine displayed the strongest IC50 values of 0.5 and 0.8 µM against B104‐1‐1 cell line, respectively. However, they showed weaker cell growth inhibition, likely due to poor cellular permeability. In contrast, analogs containing phenylalanine, O‐methyltyrosine (Ome), or Val showed potent antiproliferative effects, with IC50 values ranging between 0.9 and 2 µM against HeLa cells. By comparison, analogs with threonine substitutions were significantly less active [159]. This infers aromatic or hydrophobic side chains are generally preferred at these positions, whereas polar substitutions compromise activity, likely through unfavorable effects on DNA binding and/or cellular permeability.Subsequently, in 2008, a novel analog, L‐MeLeu5AMD ([D‐Val2, L‐MeLeu5]2‐AMD), was synthesized, in which MeVal was replaced with MeLeu. Further bioactivity assays demonstrated antiproliferative activity against SGC‐7901 human gastric carcinoma cells, with an IC50 of 10 nM. Mechanistic studies confirmed that L‐MeLeu5AMD induced apoptosis via the mitochondrial pathway, mitochondrial membrane potential disruption, and downregulation of Bcl‐2 expression. In vivo testing in S‐180 sarcoma‐bearing mice showed dose‐dependent tumor suppression, with tumor weight inhibition (TWI%) reaching 63.42% at 102 μg/kg, exceeding AMD (53.8% TWI at 140 μg/kg) [160]. Notably, L‐MeLeu5AMD is among the few synthetic analogs reported to outperform AMD in both in vitro and in vivo models, highlighting the importance of N‐methyl amino acid substitutions within the peptide ring. Another study investigated AMD analogs generated by replacing the D‐Val and MeVal residues within the cyclic depsipeptide rings with alternative amino acids, including D‐Phe, L‐ and D‐N‐MeVal, N‐methylisoleucine (MeIle), MeLeu, N‐methylphenylalanine (MePhe), MeAla, and Sar. Most analogs carrying substitutions at the D‐Val position exhibited substantially reduced antimicrobial and cytotoxic activities relative to AMD, indicating that the native D‐Val residue is critical for biological activity. The acute toxicity of L‐MeLeu5‐AMD was comparable to that of AMD, whereas L‐MeIle5‐AMD was approximately 1.25‐fold more toxic. The three analogs exhibited cytotoxicity against prostate carcinoma (PC‐3), bladder carcinoma (Biu‐87 and EJ), and cervical carcinoma (HeLa) cells, with IC50 values ranging from 0.017 to 0.121 μM, demonstrating that replacement of the MeVal residue is generally well tolerated and may modestly improve potency in selected cases, although no clear advantage in therapeutic profile was established. In antimicrobial assays, L‐MeIle5‐AMD and D‐MeLeu5‐AMD retained potent antibacterial activity, exhibiting submicromolar MIC values against E. coli, S. aureus, and B. subtilis [161]. Together, these studies revealed that substitutions at the MeVal position are among the most productive modifications explored within the actinomycin family. Replacement with larger hydrophobic residues such as MeLeu or MeIle can preserve or enhance biological activity, whereas smaller or more polar residues generally reduce potency. Unlike peptide modifications aimed at improving pharmacological properties, certain chromophore modifications have primarily been used as research tools rather than as therapeutic leads.7‐Aminoactinomycin D is a semisynthetic derivative of AMD and is widely used as a fluorescent marker in viability assays to discriminate between apoptotic and necrotic cell death [162, 163, 164]. Overall, synthetic studies have provided valuable SAR insights and consistently indicate that modifications within the peptide periphery are better tolerated than extensive chromophore alterations. However, despite occasional improvements in potency, none of the reported derivatives has demonstrated a sufficiently improved therapeutic index to warrant clinical development.4Summary and OutlookActinomycins constitute one of the most extensively investigated families of chromopeptide natural products. To date, more than 70 naturally occurring, precursor‐directed, semisynthetic, and synthetic derivatives have been reported, revealing considerable structural diversity within both the phenoxazinone chromophore and cyclic peptide rings.Several consistent structure–activity relationship trends emerge from these studies. Modifications within the peptide periphery generally exert a greater influence on biological activity than alterations of the chromophore. In particular, oxidation, methylation, and halogenation of certain amino acid residues frequently enhance cytotoxic or antimicrobial potency, whereas extensive replacement of proline or the introduction of highly polar residues typically reduces activity. Likewise, substitution of N‐methyl amino acid residues, especially with larger hydrophobic residues such as MeLeu or MeIle, can preserve or improve biological activity. In contrast, extensive chromophore modifications rarely confer clear pharmacological advantages and are often associated with reduced activity.The biological activity of actinomycins remains fundamentally linked to DNA intercalation and the subsequent inhibition of transcription. Although numerous additional molecular targets and biological effects have been proposed, many reported activities are likely secondary consequences of this primary mechanism. Several derivatives, including actinomycin X2, Leu5AMD, and selected Y‐ and Z‐type analogs, exhibit enhanced preclinical potency relative to AMD. Nevertheless, these improvements have not translated into clinical application, and AMD remains the sole clinically approved member of the family. Importantly, no structural modification reported to date has successfully uncoupled antitumor efficacy from the intrinsic toxicity associated with DNA intercalation and transcriptional inhibition.The absence of new clinically useful actinomycins after more than seven decades of investigation highlights fundamental limitations of the scaffold. DNA intercalation and transcriptional inhibition are inherently nonselective processes that affect both malignant and normal proliferating cells, resulting in a narrow therapeutic window. Consequently, structural modifications that enhance potency rarely improve tumor selectivity, whereas those that reduce toxicity frequently compromise efficacy.Future progress is therefore unlikely to arise solely from the discovery of additional analogs. Instead, greater translational potential may lie in strategies designed to overcome the intrinsic limitations of the actinomycin scaffold. Preliminary studies have demonstrated that targeted delivery approaches for AMD, including cell‐penetrating peptides, antibody‐mediated delivery platforms, and nanoparticle‐based formulations, can enhance intracellular delivery, modify biodistribution, or improve antitumor efficacy in preclinical models [165, 166, 167]. However, these approaches remain at an early stage of development, and whether they can provide sufficient improvements in therapeutic selectivity and safety to enable broader clinical application remains uncertain. In parallel, actinomycins are expected to remain valuable chemical biology tools for investigating transcriptional regulation and other DNA‐dependent processes.Conflicts of InterestThe authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: Synergistic p53 Pathway Activation Through Sono‐Gene Therapy Induced by Ultrasound‐Triggered Theranostic Mesoporous Nanoparticles
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) poses a significant global health burden due to its high mortality. The modest efficacy of single‐agent treatments is spurring the quest for combinatorial approaches. Sonodynamic therapy and gene therapy offer promising therapeutic approaches, yet they are limited by restricted tumor specificity and inefficient delivery. In this work, we developed a multifunctional mesoporous silica‐based nanoplatform co‐delivering indocyanine green (ICG) and CD24 small interfering RNA (siRNA) (siCD24), and the surface was engineered with lactobionic acid (LA) to enable active targeting and 2,3‐dimethylmaleic anhydride (DMMA) to confer tumor microenvironment‐responsive charge reversal, thereby enhancing specific accumulation and release. Under ultrasound irradiation, the nanoplatform concurrently activates dual mechanisms: ICG‐mediated sonodynamic action generates reactive oxygen species, while synchronized CD24 silencing modulates downstream effectors, such as p14 alternative reading frame and MDM2. This leads to coordinated regulation of the p53, resulting in the upregulation of the Cleaved caspase‐3 and p21, alongside the downregulation of Cyclin D1. Evaluations in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that combinatorial therapy exerts superior antitumor efficacy compared to monotherapy. Notably, the nanoparticles significantly enhanced ultrasound imaging. Our work validates the concept of a unified theranostic platform for sono‐gene therapy and ultrasound imaging, representing a promising advance in HCC treatment.
full_text: 1IntroductionThe clinical profile of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is marked by insidious onset, aggressive progression, and a typically grave prognosis [1, 2]. Despite recent advances in diagnostic and therapeutic technologies, HCC continues to pose a significant challenge due to its poor overall prognosis and alarmingly low 5‐year survival rate, particularly in late‐stage disease [3, 4], underscoring the urgent need for innovative treatment strategies. Moreover, the disconnect between diagnosis and treatment can exacerbate tissue damage and side effects, which also limits the overall efficiency and precision of anticancer therapy. Therefore, the development of an integrated theranostic platform that combines diagnostic and therapeutic functions holds significant potential for improving cure rates and survival outcomes in HCC patients.CD24 is well‐established as both an overexpressed oncoprotein and a poor prognostic marker in various malignancies, such as oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma [5], HCC [6], breast cancer, and ovarian cancer [7]. Studies employing antibody blockade, gene silencing, and ectopic or inducible expression have confirmed its contribution to tumor growth [8, 9]. Beyond proliferation, CD24 also participates in metastasis [10, 11]. The underlying mechanism involves fucosylated CD24 binding to P‐ and E‐selectins, which mediates endothelial rolling and promotes distant invasion [12]. Interestingly, a groundbreaking study in prostate cancer reveals that p14 alternative reading frame (ARF) is stabilized within the nucleolus through its interaction with nucleophosmin (NPM), while CD24 competitively inhibits the binding between ARF and NPM. This leads to the destabilization of ARF, resulting in increased MDM2 abundance and ultimately a reduction in p53 [13]. This finding positions CD24 as a novel upstream oncogenic regulator. We hypothesize that a similar CD24‐ARF‐p53 regulatory axis may exist in HCC, and silencing CD24 expression could represent a promising therapeutic strategy.However, achieving efficient gene therapy faces multiple challenges, including the inherent instability of nucleic acid drugs in vivo and their insufficient targeting capability [14, 15]. In recent years, nanomedicine has emerged as a promising strategy for gene/drug delivery and enhanced cancer therapy. Among various nanocarriers, mesoporous silica nanoparticle (MSN) has attracted significant interest due to their unique advantageous properties [16, 17], such as robust mesoporous frameworks, high surface area, tunable pore dimensions, and volumes, as well as modifiable surface characteristics [18]. Moreover, recent review articles have well documented that MSN serves as excellent nanocarriers for small interfering RNA (siRNA) delivery [19, 20, 21], thereby enabling efficient CD24 gene silencing. Despite the promising potential of MSN for gene therapy, conventional MSN‐based platforms still suffer from several typical drawbacks [22, 23], including insufficient active targeting ability, lack of tumor microenvironment‐responsive release behavior, and single therapeutic modality. To address the limitation of single therapeutic modality and further enhance antitumor efficacy via synergistic therapy, we loaded a sonosensitizer into MSN to realize combined gene therapy and sonodynamic therapy (SDT) under ultrasound (US). Furthermore, the MSN‐based system demonstrates favorable US imaging performance, laying a foundation for the development of image‐guided synergistic theranostic platforms [24].Apart from the above improvement of therapeutic modality, the insufficient active targeting capability and lack of tumor microenvironment‐responsive release still remain to be optimized. Extensive studies have demonstrated that rational framework reconstruction, surface functionalization, and morphology design can effectively address these limitations and endow MSN with improved responsiveness and delivery performance [25, 26, 27]. Unlike conventional single‐component modification, we employed biocompatible natural chitosan (CS) as the coating layer [28], whose abundant hydroxyl and amino groups provide sufficient reactive sites for subsequent dual‐functional decoration with lactobionic acid (LA) and 2,3‐dimethylmaleic anhydride (DMMA). Specifically, LA conjugation enables the nanoplatform to actively target hepatocellular carcinoma cells (e.g., Huh7) by specifically recognizing the asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR) [29]. Meanwhile, DMMA forms acid‐labile β‐carboxylic amide bonds with chitosan, endowing the platform with pH‐triggered charge reversal responsiveness within the tumor microenvironment [30]. This dual‐functional design achieves precise tumor targeting and site‐specific drug/gene release, effectively improving therapeutic efficacy, and reducing non‐specific off‐target damage.Encouraged by the above background and structural design advantages, we herein fabricated a novel dual‐functional modified MSN nanoplatform loaded with indocyanine green (ICG) and CD24 siRNA (siCD24), and coated with an LA‐CS‐DMMA (LCD) outer protective shell, which integrates targeted responsiveness, synergistic sono‐gene therapy, and US imaging capabilities (Scheme 1). When compared with reported similar nanotherapeutic systems, polythiophene‐based platforms have achieved SDT‐gene synergistic therapy [31], yet they are constructed with soft organic frameworks rather than rigid porous MSN structure, and fail to integrate imaging guidance as well as tumor microenvironment‐responsive charge reversal. Moreover, most current MSN‐based sonodynamic platforms merely combine SDT with chemotherapy, hyperthermia, or immunotherapy [32, 33, 34], while few designs introduce specific gene silencing to intervene key oncogenic signaling pathways. Distinct from these reported designs, our nanoplatform simultaneously integrates tumor targeting, microenvironment‐triggered charge reversal, co‐delivery of sonosensitizer and therapeutic gene, and US imaging‐guided therapy, which is rarely reported in conventional MSN designs. Notably, almost no MSN‐based nanoplatform has been engineered to regulate the CD24‐ARF‐MDM2‐p53 signaling axis for HCC therapy, which further highlights the novelty and originality of our design. Herein, we systematically characterize the physicochemical properties, in vitro performance and in vivo therapeutic efficacy of the as‐prepared nanoplatform. This multifunctional nanoplatform is expected to efficiently target HCC and suppress tumor growth via synergistic sono‐gene therapy, offering a promising experimental foundation for targeted clinical HCC therapy.SCHEME 1Schematic representation of ultrasound‐mediated ICG/siCD24@MSN‐LCD from nanostructure to synergistic sono‐gene therapy in HCC. ICG/siCD24@MSN‐LCD actively targets asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR) via its LA‐CS‐DMMA (LCD) shell, and the LCD coating dissociates and sheds off specifically after binding, followed by the release of loaded ICG and siCD24, which exert synergistic effects. The core mechanism involves ultrasound‐guided sonodynamic therapy (SDT) by ICG and CD24 knockdown by siCD24, both activating the p53 axis to inhibit tumor progression. Specifically, on the one hand, siCD24 mediates CD24 knockdown to release the competitive inhibition of ARF‐nucleophosmin (NPM) interaction, the restored ARF stability suppresses MDM2 activity, thereby attenuating MDM2‐induced p53 ubiquitination and degradation. On the other hand, ICG serves as a sonosensitizer to generate ROS under ultrasound, and the produced ROS also participates in activating the p53 signaling pathway. The accumulated p53 further activates downstream target genes including p21/CDKN1A to realize synergistic sono‐gene therapy. Integrated with ultrasound imaging capabilities, it constitutes a novel all‐in‐one theranostic strategy for HCC.2Experimental Section2.1MaterialsHexadecyltrimethylammonium p‐toluenesulfonate (CTAT), tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), and triethylamine (TEA) are obtained by Sigma‐Aldrich (MO, USA). Chitosan, RNase A solution, and crystal violet are sourced from Solarbio (Beijing, China). LA is procured from Bide (Shanghai, China). DMMA and ICG are acquired from Macklin (Shanghai, China). Human/Mouse CD24 siRNA and EdU‐567 Kit are supplied by RiboBio (Guangzhou, China). The sequence of human CD24 siRNA was CAACTGGAACTTCAAGTAA, and the sequence of mouse CD24 siRNA was CCCGGTAACCAGAATATTT. 2′,7′‐Dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (DCFH‐DA), Dihydroethidium (DHE), and the Live/Dead Staining Kit are supplied by Beyotime (Shanghai, China). Rabbit anti‐CD24 is purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Rabbit anti‐ARF, rabbit anti‐p53, rabbit anti‐p21, and Cleaved caspase‐3 antibodies are purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (Boston, USA). Rabbit anti‐Ki67 antibody and TUNEL kit are procured by Servicebio (Wuhan, China). DMMA bears pH‐responsive functional groups that remain negatively charged under neutral pH conditions, ensuring nanoparticle stability in physiological environments. However, in acidic conditions, DMMA dissociates, leading to a reversal of the nanoparticle charge from negative to positive. Charge conversion capability was assessed by monitoring changes in zeta potential (Figure 2A). At pH 6.5, the zeta potential shifted from ‐16.9 ± 4.8 to +18.6 ± 4.7 mV, confirming the charge reversal behavior of ICG/siCD24@MSN‐LCD in an acidic condition. Due to the pH‐responsive nature of ICG/siCD24@MSN‐LCD, its surface charge becomes positive at an acidic microenvironment, causing repulsion between the positively charged outer LCD coating and the internally positively charged ICG/siCD24@MSN, which promotes the detachment of the LCD layer. After the removal of the LCD coating, the siCD24/CS complex is directly exposed on the surface. Once internalized into the cytoplasm, siCD24 gradually dissociates from CS, and this process can be reasonably explained by three factors: the intracellular electrostatic shielding effect [43], the decreased protonation degree of CS under neutral pH [44], and the competitive binding with negatively charged endogenous biomacromolecules [45]. Along with the gradual disassembly of the surface siCD24/CS complex, sustained diffusion and release of both siCD24 and encapsulated ICG can be achieved. Therefore, we investigated the in vitro release profiles of ICG (Figure 2D) and siCD24 (Figure 2F) from ICG/siCD24@MSN‐LCD under different pH conditions. Within 10 h, the cumulative release of ICG was only 17.8% ± 2.4% at pH 7.4, while it increased prominently to 60.0% ± 5.6% at pH 6.5. Similarly, after 8 h of incubation, the siCD24 release rate reached 80.4% ± 3.7% at pH 6.5, whereas only 28.3% ± 6.4% was released at pH 7.4.
