addition, researchers can utilize phylogenetic inference to rebuild tumor cell lineages and order the chronology of mutations that occurred over time.22 Moreover, a novel liquid biopsy technology can noninvasively collect blood samples at multiple time points in the process of disease progression to isolate and profile circulating tumor cells (CTCs)23–25 and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).26,27 Liquid biopsy makes it possible to obtain multiple longitudinal tumor samples to study clonal dynamics over time and in response to treatment.Based on advancements in sequencing and biopsy technologies, researchers have developed various competing tumor evolution models, including Darwinian evolution, neutral evolution, and punctuated evolution.7,20,22 Furthermore, decades of exploration have shown that tumor cells face various selective pressures throughout development.28 Tumor evolution is shaped not only by genetic mutations but also by factors such as the tumor microenvironment, immune system interactions, metabolic reprogramming, and other extrinsic influences. Recent breakthroughs in genomic sequencing, bioinformatics, and imaging technologies have provided valuable insights into the mutational landscapes of tumors and the molecular pathways regulating tumor evolution. Despite significant advances in the field, there remains a critical gap in understanding the full spectrum of regulatory mechanisms driving tumor evolution. The complexity of these interactions remains incompletely understood, and much work is still required to translate these findings into clinically effective therapies.In this review, we offer a comprehensive and multidimensional analysis of the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, from genetic and epigenetic changes to the role of the tumor microenvironment and antitumor therapies. By exploring the current state of knowledge on tumor evolutionary dynamics, we aim to highlight the critical mechanisms driving cancer progression and therapeutic resistance. While tumor evolution is a universal process across cancer types, this review primarily focuses on carcinomas, melanomas, brain tumors, and hematological malignancies, as these represent the most extensively studied models of evolutionary trajectories and therapeutic response. Additionally, we will discuss how these insights can be leveraged to identify actionable therapeutic targets, ultimately improving cancer management. We believe that a deeper understanding of tumor evolution will not only enhance our knowledge of cancer biology but also pave the way for more effective, personalized treatment strategies to overcome the challenges posed by tumor heterogeneity and treatment resistance. Ultimately, the goal of this review is to provide a detailed, up-to-date perspective on tumor evolution, offering insights that can guide future research and clinical interventions aimed at improving the lives of cancer patients worldwide.Developmental history of tumor evolutionOur understanding of tumor evolution has significantly advanced, progressing from early theoretical models to technology-driven insights that form the foundation of contemporary research (Fig. 1). Foundational theories, such as clonal evolution, cancer stem cell (CSC) theory, and genomic instability, introduced critical concepts, including tumor heterogeneity and the adaptive nature of cancer. These early models provided a framework for understanding tumor evolution through genetic and phenotypic diversification, offering a basis for studying tumor progression, resistance, and metastasis from an evolutionary perspective.Fig. 1Historical timeline of milestones in tumor evolution research. The first hypothesis about the origin of tumors can be traced back to the 1950s, and the introduction of clonal evolution theory in 1976 marked the beginning of tumor evolution studies. Due to technological limitations, it was not until the 21st century that the concept of tumor evolution began to receive widespread attention and develop rapidly. Abbreviations: CSC, cancer stem cell; ITH, intratumor heterogeneityHowever, as research advanced, the limitations of these early theories became apparent. It was only with the technological breakthroughs of the 21st century that the field of tumor evolution gained significant momentum. Emerging technologies such as high-throughput sequencing, single-cell genomics, and spatial transcriptomics have provided researchers with essential tools to explore the dynamic and branching nature of tumor evolution. These technologies have demonstrated that cancer progression is not linear; instead, it is characterized by continuous diversification, clonal selection, and adaptation.The integration of foundational evolutionary theories with modern technological advancements has transformed our understanding of cancer as a complex, evolving system. While early theoretical frameworks provided valuable insights, the advent of cutting-edge technologies has allowed for a more refined exploration of the molecular mechanisms driving tumor evolution. This evolving understanding underscores the necessity of therapeutic strategies that account for the dynamic and adaptive nature of tumors, shifting from the traditional one-size-fits-all approach to more personalized, evolution-informed treatments.Early foundational theories of tumor evolutionThe origins of tumor evolutionary theory can be traced back to 20th-century observations of intratumoral heterogeneity and the application of Darwinian evolutionary theory in oncology. Foundational paradigms such as the clonal evolution theory, cancer stem cell (CSC) theory and genomic instability theory have each provided distinct yet complementary perspectives on how genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity arise and are maintained in malignant tissues. These early paradigms not only laid the groundwork for modern cancer biology but also continue to inform contemporary approaches to diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic resistance.Clonal origin of cancerAs Darwin succinctly articulated, “multiply, vary, let the strongest live and the weakest die”. Darwin’s framework provided a powerful lens through which somatic selection, diversification, and extinction could be understood, grounded in the principles of variation, heredity, and selection.29 In line with this evolutionary logic, many clonal lineages that once dominated may ultimately reach evolutionary dead ends and vanish, while only a select few persist and propagate.As early as the 1950s, the term “evolution” was occasionally invoked to describe cancer progression, although not always with a strict Darwinian connotation.30,31 During this era, seminal studies of cancer cell karyotypes lent empirical support to Theodor Boveri’s hypothesis that chromosomal abnormalities—often arising from defective mitoses—could drive tumorigenesis by conferring selective growth advantages to certain clones.32 Karyotyping, functioning as one of the earliest genome-wide assays at the single-cell level, not only revealed gross chromosomal alterations but also revealed striking variability in chromosome number across tumor cells. These observations raised foundational questions: were tumors composed of multiple stable subclones, each defined by a fixed karyotype, or were the karyotypes themselves mutable and subject to selection?Later, cytogeneticists began to consider whether such variations were stochastic or heritable and whether they conferred differential fitness under selective pressures. T.S. Hauschka directly invoked a “mutation–selection sequence analogous to phylogeny”, arguing that certain tumor karyotypes may confer competitive survival advantages.33 This notion of selection acting on somatic variation was further articulated by C.E. Ford, who posited that unbalanced karyotypic changes could alter a cell’s likelihood of survival and proliferation, thereby shaping the cytogenetic architecture of tumor cell populations.34Collectively, these investigations converged on the model of a clonal origin of cancer, wherein intratumoural heterogeneity arises not from simultaneous transformation of many cells but from ongoing genetic diversification within a single ancestral clone. Although evolutionary principles were often implicit rather than explicitly stated in these early works, the conceptual groundwork was laid for the modern view of cancer as an evolutionary system—subject to the same rules of variation, selection, and adaptation that govern biological species. These insights now form the backbone of contemporary models of tumor progression, resistance evolution, and clonal dynamics.Clonal evolution theoryThe systematic proposal of the tumor clonal evolution hypothesis can be traced back to 1976. After observing tumor heterogeneity in advanced malignant tumors, Peter Nowell and his colleagues proposed that the Darwinian principle also drives cancer initiation, progression, and adaptation.7 Despite the conceptual significance of this proposal, Nowell’s evolutionary view was initially underappreciated as the dominant paradigm at the time envisioned tumor development as a linear, stepwise progression. Under this linear model, sequential driver mutations arise in a single progenitor lineage, each conferring a selective advantage that enables successive clonal sweeps. Consequently, tumors were thought to be composed of a relatively homogeneous population of cells descended from the latest, most fit clone.22This view was later challenged in 1984 by Gloria Heppner and her colleagues,35,36 who provided compelling evidence that tumors consist of genetically and phenotypically diverse subclones exhibiting fundamentally distinct behaviors. Applying principles from population genetics, Heppner argued that tumors should be conceptualized as “societies highly adapted for survival” that generate new variants to circumvent both natural and therapeutic selection.35 This paradigm shift gave rise to the branched evolution model, in which multiple subclones derived from a common ancestor diverge and expand in parallel, each following its own evolutionary trajectory depending on selective pressures and local ecological conditions.37CSC theoryEvolutionary theory posits that natural selection operates in any system composed of entities with differential reproductive potential. In cancer evolution—during both tumorigenesis and posttherapy relapse—the primary unit of selection is the cell. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) with self-renewal properties and genomic instability are considered to be the engine of tumor evolution. Initially proposed in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) during the 1990s38 and subsequently validated in solid tumors such as breast cancer,39 the CSC theory posits that only a subset of cancer cells, termed cancer stem cells, possesses long-term self-renewal and substantial replicative potential. These CSCs not only fuel tumor growth and metastasis but also exhibit resistance to conventional therapies, making them critical sources of tumor recurrence and metastasis.40Accumulating evidence has further substantiated the CSC model across diverse tumor types. Cancer cells often display activation or deregulation of signaling pathways fundamental to normal stem cell biology, including Wnt,41 BMI1,42,43 and Notch.44,45 Moreover, molecules associated with stem cell migration and homing—such as the chemokine receptor CXCR4—are expressed in both normal hematopoietic stem cells and malignant cells and have been implicated in metastatic dissemination.46,47 The fact that metastases often retain the hierarchical organization of the primary tumor suggests that stem-like cancer cells are involved in the colonization of distant sites.48Functional validation of CSCs has relied on their ability to initiate tumors in immunodeficient mice. This approach was pioneered in 1994, when a subpopulation of AML cells—identified by surface markers shared with normal hematopoietic stem cells—was shown to be tumorigenic in severe combined immune-deficient (SCID) mice.49 Since then, similar assays have identified CSC-like populations in multiple solid malignancies, including those of the lung, brain, skin, prostate, and colon.50–54 In breast cancer specifically, the existence of normal mammary stem cells has long been hypothesized based on the organ’s developmental plasticity, particularly during pregnancy.55 Experimental evidence has shown that single mammary cells can regenerate an entire functional ductal tree,56,57 supporting the view that mammary stem cells may serve as a cell of origin for tumorigenesis. A landmark study in 2003 provided the first definitive identification of breast cancer stem cells. Al-Hajj isolated a subpopulation of human breast cancer cells with a CD44⁺CD24⁻/low phenotype, which efficiently initiated heterogeneous tumors in immunocompromised mice—recapitulating the cellular complexity of the original tumor—while other subpopulations lacked this capability.39Research progress driven by technological revolutionsThe study of tumor evolution was previously constrained by the technological limitations of the late 20th century. However, the advent of the 21st century ushered in a significant paradigm shift, driven by breakthroughs in molecular and genomic technologies. These advancements have facilitated the detailed analysis of cancer evolutionary dynamics with unprecedented resolution, transforming the field and providing novel insights into tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and therapeutic resistance. This progress has not only deepened our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer but also highlighted the need for therapeutic strategies that account for the dynamic nature of tumor evolution, steering the field toward more personalized, evolution-informed approaches.High-throughput sequencing: revolutionizing cancer genomicsThe previous generation of genomics technologies, such as automated Sanger sequencing, was constrained by their reliance on hybridization and probe-based methods. While these techniques were valuable for analyzing copy number variations (CNVs), single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and known transcript expression, they could only detect genomic variations identifiable by probes with predefined sequences.58 Recent advancements in cancer genomics, driven by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) technologies and bioinformatics tools, have overcome these limitations.59 The launch of the Roche 454 FLX Pyrosequencer in 2004 marked the beginning of a new era for commercially available sequencing technologies, collectively known as next-generation sequencing (NGS) or HTS.60,61 The term “next” in NGS signifies the transformative technological advancements that enable the massive parallel sequencing of DNA fragments, similar to performing millions of individual Sanger sequencing reactions concurrently.62 This high-throughput “shotgun” approach facilitates the comprehensive and rapid analysis of tumor genomes, providing a more detailed understanding of somatic sequence variations, genomic configurations, and the expression of previously unannotated transcripts.63 HTS has revealed the genetic diversity within tumors, uncovering mutations that drive tumor progression and metastasis, including somatic mutations, copy number alterations, and structural variations contributing to intratumoral heterogeneity.64 Furthermore, HTS has facilitated the discovery of novel cancer-related genes, and large-scale medical resequencing of human DNA is revolutionizing medicine and providing new opportunities for therapeutic targeting. For example, whole-exome sequencing (WES), an application of next-generation technology, has distinguished the variations of all coding regions, or exons, of hundreds of genes.65 HTS has also been pivotal in revealing the genetic basis of subclonal populations within tumors. For instance, Gerlinger et al. employed whole-exome multiregion spatial sequencing to identify distinct clonal populations in renal cell carcinomas, illustrating the branching evolution of tumors and the emergence of subclones with unique genetic signatures.9 This insight into tumor evolution underscores the necessity for therapies that target these subclonal populations to prevent relapse and treatment resistance.Single-cell sequencing: decoding tumor heterogeneity at the cellular levelBuilding on the transformative insights provided by high-throughput sequencing (HTS), which has revolutionized our understanding of genomic alterations in tumors, single-cell sequencing further refines this understanding by offering a higher resolution at the cellular level. Beginning with the introduction of the first single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) method for profiling copy number variations in human tissues in 2011, the field of single-cell genomics has advanced significantly, fostering deeper investigations into tumor evolution.66,67 Single-cell sequencing allows for the analysis of individual tumor cells, providing a level of resolution previously unattainable with bulk sequencing methods.68 By examining single cells, researchers can capture the full spectrum of genetic and epigenetic variations within a tumor. ScRNA-seq enables the profiling of gene expression at the individual cell level, revealing the dynamic behavior of tumor cells in response to intrinsic and extrinsic factors.17,18 Recent studies utilizing scRNA-seq have uncovered the existence of cellular plasticity within tumors, particularly in CSCs, which drive tumor progression and resistance to therapy. For instance, Gimple et al. highlighted how brain tumor stem cells exhibit resilience through adaptive plasticity and hierarchical heterogeneity, which enables their survival in hostile environments and contributes to therapeutic resistance.69 Similarly, it has been demonstrated that single-cell sequencing of bladder cancer stem cells identified genetic alterations that enhance self-renewal capabilities, shedding light on the molecular mechanisms that drive tumor initiation and maintenance.70 While scRNA-seq enables the analysis of gene expression at the single-cell level, it is also important to acknowledge its technical limitations, including high noise, dropout rates, and challenges in CNV calling and cell state classification. These factors can impact the accuracy of gene expression profiles and hinder the detection of subtle genomic changes or rare cell populations, which must be considered in data interpretation.The capability to profile thousands of individual cells within a single tumor has yielded critical insights into the evolutionary dynamics driving cancer progression. These discoveries highlight the importance of precision medicine strategies that consider intratumoral clonal diversity, as targeting a single clone may be insufficient to eradicate the entire tumor population.Spatial transcriptomics: mapping tumor evolution in 3DAlthough significant progress has been made in scRNA-seq, it still requires cell isolation from tissues, leading to the loss of spatial context—an essential aspect for studying intercellular interactions and functional relevance.71,72 Recently, emerging spatial omics technologies have offered powerful tools for analyzing cellular spatial information and promising insights into spatiotemporal tumor evolution, with spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) being named the “Method of the Year” in 2020.68,73 While high-quality spatial DNA sequencing remains under development and is not yet widely implemented,74 SRT technologies, which measure RNA from thousands of spatial locations within tissue, have been extensively used to analyze the spatial organization of transcriptionally defined cell types in tumors.75–77 Although SRT does not directly detect somatic mutations in DNA, identifying copy number alterations (CNAs) through transcriptomic data—where deletions typically lead to underexpression and amplifications to overexpression—offers promise for studying somatic evolution in tumors.75Moreover, integrating gene expression profiling with spatial information, SRT enables the investigation of tumor evolution across distinct regions. SRT is particularly valuable for characterizing spatial heterogeneity and understanding how subclonal populations evolve within diverse tumor microenvironments.75,78 It has facilitated the reconstruction of tumor phylogeography by mapping the spatial distribution of mutations and tracking the emergence and expansion of subclones. For instance, the CalicoST algorithm integrates SRT data with genomic profiling to infer allele-specific CNAs and reconstruct the tumor’s evolutionary trajectory.75 This approach has revealed that spatially distinct subclones exhibit unique genetic profiles, shedding light on how tumors adapt to their microenvironment. The ability to study tumor evolution in 3D opens new opportunities to explore how clonal populations interact and evolve under selective pressures, such as immune evasion or therapeutic treatment.Lineage tracing and molecular recorders: tracking clonal and phenotypic evolutionWhile genomic and transcriptomic technologies have provided detailed snapshots of tumor heterogeneity, emerging lineage-tracing and molecular-recording systems now allow investigators to dynamically map how individual cancer cells diversify, adapt, and acquire metastatic competence. Classically, tumor phylogenies were reconstructed using naturally occurring somatic variations—such as point mutations or copy-number changes—as de facto lineage markers, but this approach provides only limited resolution and captures evolution indirectly.79To overcome these limitations, evolving lineage-tracing systems have been coupled with single-cell RNA-seq to directly track clonal diversification and cell-state transitions in vivo. In a Kras;Trp53 (KP)-driven lung adenocarcinoma model, such an integrated system enabled tumor evolution to be followed from single transformed cells to metastatic lesions with unprecedented resolution.80 Tumors progressed from an initial alveolar type II–like state through a transient burst of plasticity before committing to distinct transcriptional programs that drove rapid expansion, metastasis, and ultimately clonal sweeps of the most fit subclones. These findings demonstrated that tumor evolution follows stereotyped trajectories, while additional tumor-suppressor perturbations generate alternative evolutionary routes and accelerate progression.Building on these advances, recent CRISPR-based barcoding and molecular-recording systems have further transformed the field by enabling the continuous accumulation of heritable edits that encode the evolutionary history of individual cells. A representative example is the macsGESTALT system, an inducible CRISPR–Cas9 recorder that simultaneously captures lineage edits and single-cell transcriptomes.81 Applied to metastatic pancreatic cancer, macsGESTALT reconstructed high-resolution phylogenies and revealed a continuous EMT spectrum, with metastatic competence enriched in rare late-hybrid EMT states arising from epithelial ancestors. These states were associated with poor survival in human cancers, and S100 family programs were found to converge across distinct clones, suggesting microenvironment-driven phenotypic similarity independent of lineage history.Together, these next-generation lineage-tracing and molecular-recording systems provide a dynamic and temporally resolved view of cancer evolution.Other emerging technologies in tumor evolutionLiquid biopsy, which involves the analysis of tumor cells and tumor-derived products detectable in blood and other biofluids, was first introduced by Pantel and Alix Panabières.82 In addition to circulating tumor cells (CTCs), circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as the second major analyte in liquid biopsy, garnering significant interest in the last decade.83 Unlike traditional tissue biopsies that provide a single-time snapshot of the tumor’s genetic landscape, liquid biopsies allow real-time tracking of genetic alterations throughout treatment, providing a dynamic perspective on tumor evolution and revealing intratumoral temporal heterogeneity.84,85 ctDNA reflects the genetic changes present in the tumor, such as CNAs and driver mutations, offering a noninvasive method for assessing tumor progression, therapeutic response, and resistance mechanisms. One of the key advantages of ctDNA is its ability to detect minimal residual disease (MRD) and monitor tumor progression during treatment, as demonstrated in studies of high-risk neuroblastoma84,85 and urothelial carcinoma.86,87 Liquid biopsies also facilitate the early detection of resistance mutations, often identifying genetic alterations before they are detectable using traditional imaging techniques. For example, ctDNA profiling has provided valuable insights into the genomic evolution of neuroblastoma under ALK inhibitor therapy, revealing actionable mutations and offering crucial information about therapeutic resistance.84 Ultimately, technologies such as ctDNA sequencing provide actionable data that can inform clinical decision-making, improving precision oncology by enabling timely adjustments to therapeutic strategies.In addition, by integrating genomic, transcriptomic, and clinical data, computational models simulate the processes driving cancer progression and predict tumor responses to various therapies.88,89 These models allow researchers to identify key drivers of tumor evolution, uncovering complex patterns of clonal diversification and selection that unfold within tumors over time. An example of computational modeling mentioned before is CalicoST, a tool that combines SRT data with genomic profiling to infer allele-specific CNAs and reconstruct tumor phylogeography.75 Computational platforms such as OncoGEMINI also contribute significantly by analyzing somatic mutations across multiple tumor samples, providing insights into tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution during treatment.90 Such models are crucial for understanding complex tumor behaviors, including resistance mechanisms, and for predicting patient-specific treatment outcomes.Furthermore, recent deep learning (DL) methods for predicting tumor genetics from H&E images have demonstrated significant potential.91 For instance, DL models applied in both organ-specific cancer research92,93 and pancancer94,95 have successfully predicted the presence of genetic mutations across various cancer types, including lung, breast, kidney, and colorectal cancers. DL algorithms offer innovative approaches to resolve the complexities of intratumoral heterogeneity with unprecedented detail. Recently, it has been demonstrated that DL can infer genetic heterogeneity and mutation status at subclonal spatial resolution, providing a more nuanced understanding of the tumor’s genetic landscape. For instance, DL models have been applied to analyze clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), enabling the identification of mutations in the BAP1, PBRM1, and SETD2 genes, which are frequently altered in ccRCC.91 These models demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity in predicting mutation status, with BAP1 mutations correlating strongly with clinical outcomes such as disease-specific survival. The ability of deep learning to resolve intratumoral mutation heterogeneity makes it an invaluable tool for both diagnostic and prognostic purposes, especially in cases where traditional methods might overlook subtle but clinically significant alterations.Intratumoral heterogeneity: a trait allows tumor evolutionBefore delving into tumor evolution, it is essential to understand intratumor heterogeneity (ITH), which refers to the diversity observed within tumor cell populations across genomic, phenotypic, and metabolic characteristics. ITH forms the basis for tumor evolution by providing tumor cells with various survival strategies and adaptive pathways, thereby driving adaptive evolution during treatment. With the advent of high-throughput sequencing, tumor heterogeneity has begun to be understood at the genomic level. Furthermore, the rapid development of technologies such as single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, and liquid biopsies has expanded this understanding to the individual cellular and spatiotemporal levels. Regarding the contribution of heterogeneity, although heterogeneity has been broadly considered a trait that allows tumors to overcome evolutionary pressures, it can also reflect vulnerabilities that could be exploited therapeutically.96 The evolution of tumor cells in different treatment stages and microenvironments illustrates how this heterogeneity selectively promotes the survival and expansion of certain clones under selective pressures. As mentioned above, ITH originates from intrinsic genetic instability and is further amplified by mutations at the epigenetic, transcriptional, or protein levels, ultimately manifesting in both temporal and spatial dimensions.97Temporal heterogeneity arises during the dynamic processes of tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis.97,98 In recent years, the development of time-resolved tools such as live-cell imaging, sequential liquid biopsy, and lineage tracing has enabled longitudinal monitoring of mutation accumulation and clonal evolution, thereby drawing increasing attention to temporal heterogeneity.99–102 Live-cell imaging, for example, is an emerging tool for studying tumor temporal heterogeneity due to its high temporal resolution.100 By continuously monitoring cellular processes, it provides valuable insights into the dynamic nature of tumor behavior, including treatment responses and the evolution of cellular states. These technologies enable researchers to track tumor cells across various stages of development and treatment, revealing how cellular features, such as morphology and signaling dynamics, evolve over time. Due to intrinsic mechanisms such as genomic instability or selective pressure from tumor-targeted therapies, clonal heterogeneity within a single tumor can evolve over time.10 For example, although trastuzumab has shown success in HER2-positive breast cancer, researchers in the T-ACT study observed a HER2 loss rate of up to 69% in HER2-positive gastric or gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) tumor after first-line anti-HER2 therapy, as detected by conventional IHC and FISH methods.103 This HER2 status change, often driven by clonal evolution, represents a form of temporal heterogeneity and may contribute to the development of acquired resistance to anti-HER2 therapies.104,105 Furthermore, compared to pretreatment samples, secondary mutations associated with resistance to anti-HER2 therapy were detected in posttreatment primary tumor samples at higher frequencies, including deletions in exon 16 of the HER2 gene and mutations in the KRAS and PI3K signaling pathways.105 Temporal heterogeneity resulting from clonal evolution suggests that analysis of pretreated tumors may not fully represent the evolutionary changes occurring in longitudinal samples, which may undergo different mutation processes and selective pressures.106Unlike temporal heterogeneity, spatial heterogeneity refers to the variation in genetic, phenotypic, and metabolic characteristics of tumor cells within the same tumor or across different tumors at a specific point in time.97 It can be studied using spatially resolved tools such as multiregion sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, which enable the mapping of gene expression profiles in distinct tumor regions.107,108 The evolutionary differences between primary and metastatic tumors can significantly influence treatment decisions, especially in the management of metastatic cancers. The number of shared mutations between primary and metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) ranges from 20% to 90%, indicating considerable heterogeneity in the mutational landscape across different tumor sites.109,110 Moreover, studies have shown that the proportion of private mutations in the primary site (compared to the metastatic site) ranges from 6% to 57%, while the proportion of private mutations in the metastatic site (compared to the primary tumor) ranges from 11% to 80%.110 Similarly, studies on copy number alterations and genomic instability in primary and metastatic neuroendocrine tumors have revealed that chromosomal abnormalities are significantly more frequent in metastatic tumors than in primary tumors.111 In addition, differences arising from the evolution of distinct subclones within the same tumor are also observed. In clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), multiple biopsies are required to more accurately assess the true extent of genomic heterogeneity and clinically relevant mutations.112 For instance, mutations in the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway can lead to resistance to everolimus, and such mutations are found in some, but not all, tumor regions.9,112 In summary, spatial heterogeneity in solid tumors can lead to substantial sampling bias.10Since tumors develop and progress under the influence of various internal and external factors, the interactions between these factors lead to ITH across both temporal and spatial dimensions. Temporal heterogeneity reflects the dynamic changes in tumor cells over time, while spatial heterogeneity captures the differences in tumor cells across distinct regions of the tumor. Both forms of heterogeneity are critical and complementary for understanding tumor evolution, as they provide insights into how tumors adapt to therapy not only over time but also across different tumor regions. Therefore, ITH is a crucial prerequisite for tumor evolution and offers a tangible manifestation of tumor evolution at the cellular and tissue levels.In summary, the understanding of tumor evolution has significantly progressed over the years, transitioning from early theories to the incorporation of modern technological advancements. Foundational models such as clonal evolution and cancer stem cell (CSC) theory have provided key insights into the complexity of tumor progression. However, the limitations of these models, such as their inability to fully capture the dynamic nature of tumor evolution, became evident. The technological breakthroughs of the 21st century, such as high-throughput sequencing, single-cell genomics, and spatial transcriptomics, have refined our understanding, showing that cancer progression is nonlinear and driven by continuous diversification and adaptation. This evolving understanding stresses the importance of personalized therapeutic strategies tailored to the specific evolutionary trajectories of individual tumors.Models explaining tumor evolutionAt the onset of the 21st century, an explanatory mechanism of tumor evolution that gained significant attention is clonal evolution: through the accumulation of gene mutations and epigenetic changes, the adaptability of tumor cells is changed, eventually leading to clonal expansion or contraction by natural selection. With the observation of heterogeneity in advanced malignant tumors, Peter Nowell pioneered the hypothesis that tumorigenesis is an evolutionary process in 1976, suggesting that Darwinian principles can be applied to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the formation and progression of cancer.7 After Nowell’s elegant summary of the clonal evolutionary model of cancer, it was not until the 21st century, when high-throughput sequencing began to rapidly develop, that research on clonal evolution accelerated.20 While a Darwinian framework has been historically adopted to develop models of clonal evolution and therapy resistance, studies have demonstrated that models of accumulating genetic changes subject to selective pressure are not fully sufficient to explain the full spectrum of cancer evolutionary histories. Researchers have observed that a large number of genomic aberrations may occur in cancer cells in a short time, which is not in line with the assumption that mutations in the Darwinian evolution model are gradually acquired over time.29 Non-Darwinian evolution concepts such as neutral evolution and punctuated tumor evolution have been proposed and have received extensive attention in recent years.22 With increasing evidence, we have a more complex picture of how tumors change over time. Different clonal evolution models, including Darwinian and non-Darwinian types, help us understand how cancer grows and evolves over time (Fig. 2).Fig. 2Models of tumor evolution. Various evolution models, including Darwinian and non-Darwinian types, have been developed to help us understand how cancer evolves over time. The Darwinian Evolutionary Model section includes four distinct models, and their common feature is based on natural selection: in linear evolution, the characteristic is a selective sweep of dominant clones and accumulates mutations linearly; in branched evolution models, without selective sweeps, multiple subclones can expand under continuous clonal evolution; convergent evolution and parallel evolution refer to similar changes that occur between independent tumors of the same patient or between different subclones within the same tumor, respectively. Non-Darwinian Evolution Models featured by the absence of selective pressure or fitness change: in Neutral Evolution, random mutations accumulate over time, leading to genetic drift and extensive intratumor heterogeneity; Punctuated Evolution suggests that large-scale genomic alterations occur in rapid bursts rather than gradually over time, typically during the early stages of tumor progression; Neutral Evolution can coexist with Parallel EvolutionDarwinian evolution modelsThe application of evolutionary concepts to understand cancer formation and development can be attributed to the clonal evolution theory proposed by Peter Nowell. Quoting Darwin “the strongest live and the weakest die”, Nowell’s model stated that most cancers originate from a single neoplastic cell and evolve through a process of selection for somatic alterations, leading to the proliferation and survival of the most aggressive clones.Linear evolution modelOne of the most renowned models of Darwinian evolution is linear evolution (LE), suggesting that mutations accumulate linearly in a stepwise fashion and result in more malignant stages of cancer.113 In this linear model, driver mutations induce a significant survival advantage in some tumor cells and lead to a characteristic selective sweep, which refers to a process in which a dominant clone with high fitness occurs and encompasses other clones.114 Driver mutations refer to mutations that provide a selective advantage, whereas passenger mutations do not impact fitness. This increased fitness can drive clonal expansions, where a specific genotype becomes more prevalent within the tumor mass. After selective sweep, the phylogenetic tree of linear evolution mostly consists of the dominant clone produced by each selective sweep, with only a limited number of intermediates representing previously residual dominant clones. Initial evidence for LE was derived from profiling X inactivation in tumors.22 Unlike most somatic tissues, which typically exhibit random inactivation of either the maternal or paternal X allele, human tumors often display inactivation of one single clonal X allele across the entire tumor mass. These results suggest that human tumors originate from clonal expansion of dominant clones. Fearon et al. further proposed that colon cancers progress through a linear series of stepwise mutations leading to sequentially more malignant stages of tumor growth in colorectal cancer.114 However, most early data supporting LE primarily derive from studies focused on single genes without genome-wide markers, potentially overlooking heterogeneous mutations that distinguish distinct clones.18 With advances in genome-wide sequencing technologies, in certain cancer types, instances of linear evolution have also been documented through phylogenetic and subclonal analysis,115 including in breast cancer,116,117 acute myeloid leukemia,118 chronic lymphocytic leukemia,119 and VHL-associated clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).120Branched evolution modelThe recognition that tumors consist of genetically distinct subclones exhibiting significant behavioral variability—known as ITH—has questioned the traditional linear evolution model. This insight supported a branched evolution (BE) model in which tumors evolve in a nonlinear, branched manner, with multiple subclones originating from a common ancestor, diverging and expanding simultaneously with distinct fitness advantages.6,37 BE is characterized by ongoing clonal evolution, wherein novel driving mutations constantly emerge to facilitate clonal expansion. The BE model has been reinforced by numerous next-generation sequencing (NGS) studies, which have profiled point mutations through techniques such as single-cell DNA sequencing,67,113,121–123 multiregion sequencing9,112 and deep sequencing.124–126 These studies have consistently reported evidence of branched evolution in a wide range of human cancers, including leukemia,127 breast cancer,121,124,125 liver cancer,128 colorectal cancer,129,130 ovarian cancer,131 prostate cancer,132 kidney cancer,9,112 melanoma,133 and brain cancer.134–136Although many tumors exhibit a branched evolutionary pattern, some may encounter shared selective pressures from the tumor microenvironment or constraints inherited from the parental founder cell, driving different subclones to independently converge on similar cellular processes.137 This crucial observation lays the foundation for understanding the mechanisms behind genetic changes in tumorigenesis.Other Darwinian evolution modelsWhile many tumors exhibit a branching evolutionary pattern, it is likely that common selective pressures from the tumor microenvironment or constraints inherited from the founding parental cell drive the different subclones to independently evolve similar cellular processes. Therefore, in addition to branching evolution, growing interest in convergent and parallel evolution has emerged alongside advancements in multiregion and single-cell sequencing technologies.Convergent evolution refers to the process of independent tumors within the same patient acquiring (epi)genetic alterations in similar genes, protein complexes, or signaling pathways.138 This phenomenon can be seen as a direct consequence of shared selective pressures. When different tumors or subclones within a tumor are subjected to similar environmental pressures or inherit similar constraints, they are more likely to evolve in a way that leads to the adoption of similar survival strategies. These strategies manifest as genetic alterations that enhance their fitness within the given selective context. Conversely, parallel evolution refers to subclones derived from the same parental clone inside a tumor acquiring (epi)genetic alterations in similar genes, protein complexes, or signaling pathways.112,138 This process is also influenced by shared selective pressures and inherited constraints, but it started with a common ancestral clone. This resulted in an evolutionary pattern where distinct subclones, despite evolving independently, ultimately converge on similar genetic changes due to selective pressures from the tumor microenvironment and constraints imposed by their cellular lineage.However, models based on the accumulation of genetic changes under selective pressure are insufficient to account for the entire range of cancer evolutionary histories. Growing evidence suggests that the evolutionary dynamics of cancer frequently deviate from Darwinian principles, and non-Darwinian mechanisms play a crucial role in tumor evolution.Non-Darwinian evolution modelsNeutral evolution modelUnlike the Darwinian evolutionary models that select the most suitable subclones, some tumors show little evidence of natural selection. In that case, Sottoriva et al. proposed a neutral evolution (NE) model.129 This model posits that selective pressure or significant fitness changes are absent during most of the tumor’s lifespan. Instead, random mutations accumulate over time, leading to genetic drift and contributing to extensive ITH. Evidence for NE was constituted by a linear relationship between the number of mutations and inverse mutant allele frequency. A mathematical neutral evolution model is consistent with genetic data in approximately one-third of solid tumors,139 multiple myeloma140 and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia.141 Ling et al. used multiregion sequencing to profile 309 spatial regions of a single patient with hepatocellular carcinoma and reported 35 polymorphic SNVs that defined 20 subclones.128 The frequencies of mutations among sections and their spatial arrangements were consistent with a model of NE in an expanding population, showing no evidence of positive Darwinian selection. The extremely high genetic diversity observed in a single tumor reflects the prevalence of non-Darwinian cell evolution. Together, these results provide evidence that neutral evolution may occur in a significant fraction of tumors. It has also been indicated that neutral evolution may play a crucial role in the development of several cancers, including cervical squamous cell carcinoma, endocervical adenocarcinoma, colorectal, gastric, lung, prostate, bladder, and urothelial cancers.139Punctuated evolution modelThe traditional linear, branched, and neutral evolution models often propose that mutations accumulate in a stepwise and progressive manner over time. However, recent findings indicate that in certain tumors, catastrophic events that occur at the early stage of tumorigenesis, such as massive genomic aberrations, result in multiple different subclones that burst in a short time.22,29 Subsequently, one or more of the dominant clones stably expand to promote the occurrence of tumor evolution. Drawing from the concept of “punctuated equilibrium” in evolutionary biology, this model has been termed “punctuated evolution (PE)”. PE is characterized by three key principles: evolution occurring in short bursts, stable clonal expansions, and the absence of gradual intermediates that persist throughout the evolutionary process.22 Furthermore, evidence of PE has been observed in prostate cancer, where significant genomic alterations occur in a limited number of catastrophic events, a phenomenon known as chromoplexy.142,143 Such evolutionary dynamics were observed in various cancers, including breast cancer113,144 and colorectal cancer,145 as well as in pancancer studies.146Extensive observations and tests have corroborated the theoretical significance of the clonal evolution model. Darwinian evolution emphasizes how selective pressures favor the survival of dominant clones, leading to increased malignancy of tumors and the emergence of treatment failure or drug resistance.6,7,147 The neutral evolution model advocates that rather than natural selection, tumors evolve through gene drift caused by the gradual accumulation of random mutations.129,140 Conversely, punctuated evolution suggests that tumor evolution is not gradual but rather triggered by the burst of catastrophic genomic events, followed by the stable expansion of dominant clones.143,144,148 However, clonal evolution models cannot fully explain the phenotype of cancer. Putting the same cancer cells in different microenvironments alters their behavior, suggesting that phenotypic intratumoral heterogeneity may exist independently of genetics.149–152 Recently, phenotypic plasticity has been increasingly acknowledged as a significant factor in intratumoral heterogeneity and therapy evasion.153–156 Although epigenomic heterogeneity is not directly inherited through DNA sequence changes such as gene mutations, it can be effectively passaged in tumors through mechanisms such as epigenomic reprogramming, stochastic changes and lasting memory, providing an important basis for tumor evolution.157In summary, tumor evolution is a complex, dynamic process shaped by a range of genetic and selective factors. The clonal evolution model laid the groundwork for understanding tumor progression through genetic mutations and selective pressures. However, other models, such as branched and non-Darwin evolution, have been proven to better capture the complexities of tumor heterogeneity. Although studies on advanced carcinomas do not support the LE model, mathematical modeling indicates that it may occur during the early stages of tumor progression in small, fixed population sizes.158 As the tumor population grows, the evolution may transition from LE to BE. More research is needed to compare early-stage cancers (e.g., colon adenomas) with advanced carcinomas to assess whether LE is more prevalent in early neoplasms. Similarly, it has been suggested that tumor evolution may transition from PE to NE in colon cancer.139 This hybrid model proposes that all driver mutations occur early in tumor development, after which clonal expansion takes place without further selection. Notably, much experimental data suggest that point mutations adhere to a BE model, while CNAs and chromosomal structural variants follow a PE model. Moreover, NE can coexist with PE, where a single catastrophic genomic event leads to the emergence of multiple species without exerting selective pressure on the dominance of any particular clone.159–161Together, these models reveal that tumor progression is driven by more than just a linear accumulation of mutations; it is shaped by the interplay of genetic, environmental, and therapeutic pressures. As our understanding of these evolutionary models deepens, it becomes increasingly clear that the regulatory mechanisms behind tumor evolution play a pivotal role in guiding these processes. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of how tumors evolve and respond to treatments, it is essential to explore the multifaceted regulatory mechanisms that drive these dynamics, which will be discussed in the next section.Multidimensional regulatory mechanisms of tumor evolutionThe progression of tumors from localized growth to metastatic malignancy is governed by a complex array of interacting signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms. As discussed in the previous section on evolutionary models, tumor evolution is a dynamic, multifactorial process shaped by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. The evolutionary trajectory of cancer cells is influenced not only by genetic alterations inherent to the tumor but also by the cellular and environmental contexts in which these alterations occur. These regulatory mechanisms operate across three critical dimensions—intracellular, extracellular, and exogenous levels—each playing a crucial role in orchestrating tumor evolution (Fig. 3).Fig. 3Overview of multidimensional regulatory factors in tumor evolution. Tumor evolution is regulated by multiple driving factors from three dimensions: cell-intrinsic level (including genomic instability, epigenetic plasticity and metabolic reprogramming), cell-extrinsic level (including tumor microenvironment, immune escape and intercellular communication), and exogenous level (including therapeutic interventions, environmental factors, characteristics of patients). These factors interact closely and ultimately manifest in the form of tumor heterogeneity in both temporal and spatial dimensions. Abbreviations: MSI, microsatellite instability; CIN, chromosomal instability; EMT, epithelial–mesenchymal transitionAt the cellular level, intrinsic factors such as genomic instability, epigenetic modifications, and metabolic reprogramming drive the clonal diversity that characterizes cancer progression. These factors, often acting synergistically, facilitate the selection of tumor cells with growth advantages, enabling them to survive and proliferate under both physiological and therapeutic stresses. Meanwhile, the tumor microenvironment (TME), consisting of stromal cells, immune cells, and extracellular matrix components, exerts a significant influence on tumor evolution, promoting processes such as invasion, immune evasion, and resistance to treatment. Additionally, extrinsic factors, including environmental influences and therapeutic interventions, introduce selective pressures that further shape the tumor’s evolutionary landscape.As discussed below, we will examine the signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms that regulate tumor evolution across these three dimensions. By integrating insights from these diverse mechanisms, we aim to develop a comprehensive understanding of tumor evolution, ultimately facilitating the creation of more effective and targeted therapeutic strategies.Cell-intrinsic regulatory mechanisms in tumor evolutionCell-intrinsic regulatory mechanisms are central to understanding how cancer cells acquire and sustain their malignant phenotypes. These intrinsic factors, such as genomic instability, epigenetic plasticity, and metabolic reprogramming, are pivotal in enabling tumor cells to adapt to selective pressures, accumulate mutations, and proliferate uncontrollably. A deeper understanding of the molecular pathways and cellular processes governing these mechanisms is crucial for elucidating the evolution of tumors and their resistance to therapeutic interventions.Genomic instabilityGenomic instability is one of the most defining features of tumor evolution. It manifests in various forms, such as genetic mutations, chromosomal aberrations, and aneuploidy. These changes can drive the acquisition of oncogenic traits, clonal diversity and resistance to therapies. A thorough understanding of the molecular mechanisms driving genomic instability is crucial for understanding how tumors evolve and adapt to both endogenous and exogenous stresses.One of the most significant contributors to gene mutations in various cancer types is the activity of the APOBEC3 family of cytidine deaminases. APOBEC3 enzymes, particularly APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, induce mutations through the deamination of cytosine residues, leading to “C to T” and “C to G” substitutions. The mutational signatures associated with APOBEC3 activity have been identified as a hallmark of multiple cancers, contributing to tumor mutational burden (TMB) and overall genomic instability.162,163 APOBEC3-mediated mutations are particularly prevalent in late-stage tumor subclones and contribute to the evolution of tumor heterogeneity. Studies have shown that APOBEC3-induced mutations play a key role in the branching evolution of tumors, contributing to clonal diversification and resistance to therapeutic interventions.164,165 For instance, in bladder cancer, APOBEC3G expression was found to induce a distinct mutational signature that correlated with poor patient survival.163 This mutational process is not uniform but rather episodic, with bursts of mutagenesis triggered by factors such as viral infection, DNA replication stress, and inflammation.166 Moreover, APOBEC3 activity is not limited to driving somatic mutations. It also plays a role in modulating the immune environment of tumors. While some cancers, such as melanoma and breast cancer, exhibit immune-activating properties due to APOBEC3-induced mutations, others, such as renal cell carcinoma, exploit APOBEC3-induced mutations to escape immune surveillance.167–170 These dual roles highlight the complex nature of APOBEC3 in tumor progression, offering potential therapeutic targets to control its mutagenic activity.Another manifestation of genomic instability in tumors is the formation of extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), which plays a critical role in tumor evolution. EcDNA is a circular, acentric DNA molecule distinct from chromosomal DNA. These DNA fragments, typically ranging from 50 kb to 5 Mb in size, carry oncogenes, immunoregulatory genes, and enhancers, playing a crucial role in tumor progression by facilitating high-level transcription and promoting cancer heterogeneity.171–173 The unique nature of ecDNA, particularly its lack of centromeres, enables it to be distributed unequally to daughter cells during cell division, resulting in heterogeneous tumor populations and promoting clonal diversity.174,175 This irregular inheritance creates a dynamic environment within the tumor, where subclonal populations emerge rapidly and adapt to selective pressures, accelerating tumor progression.176,177 EcDNA can also undergo structural rearrangements, contributing to further genomic instability.167 These rearrangements enable ecDNA to amplify oncogenes and facilitate rapid evolutionary changes. Multiple ecDNA species may coexist within a single tumor, and their structural complexity tends to increase over time, particularly as the tumor progresses.167,178,179 The presence of different ecDNA species contributes to the formation of a multifocal and highly heterogeneous tumor population, fostering adaptability and enhancing the likelihood of therapy resistance.171,177 Moreover, these extrachromosomal elements can reintegrate into chromosomal DNA, leading to genetic rearrangements that influence gene activation and contribute to the malignant transformation of tumor cells.180The role of ecDNA in tumor evolution is further underscored by its interaction with mutagenic processes. More than 30% of ecDNAs are associated with APOBEC3-induced kataegis, a mutagenic process that contributes to the sequence diversity of ecDNA and drives the evolution of therapy-resistant clones.181,182 As mentioned before, these APOBEC3-mediated mutations are particularly significant in promoting genomic instability, enhancing the diversity of ecDNA sequences, and contributing to the adaptability of cancer cells under therapeutic stress.181,183 The ability of ecDNA to accumulate mutations, coupled with its rapid inheritance and amplification, makes it a central player in the evolution of malignancies and their resistance to treatment.184Furthermore, ecDNA can form transcriptional hubs, where clusters of ecDNA molecules aggregate in specific regions of the nucleus.185 These hubs are associated with increased transcriptional activity and play a crucial role in regulating gene expression within the tumor.186 Transcriptional regulation within ecDNA hubs is closely tied to proteins such as BRD4, which mediate the formation of these hubs and facilitate the transcription of oncogenes that drive tumor progression.185 Therefore, the dynamic properties of ecDNA, including its ability to undergo structural rearrangements, amplify oncogenes, and interact with mutagenic pathways such as APOBEC3, highlight its critical role in promoting cancer heterogeneity and accelerating tumor evolution. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent in cancers exhibiting high genomic instability, such as those induced by CRISPR/Cas9-based mutagenesis. The amplification of ecDNA can increase oncogene dosage and enhancer-driven transcription, thereby supporting intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) and providing a reservoir for further mutational evolution.187 Notably, the formation of ecDNA has been associated with resistance to targeted therapies and contributes to the adaptability of tumors in response to environmental stressors and therapeutic pressures.The role of genomic instability in tumor evolution is not restricted to mutagenic enzymes and ecDNA formation. Chromosomal instability (CIN) is also a critical driver of tumor evolution. CIN is primarily caused by errors during the mitotic process, leading to chromosomal structural and numerical abnormalities, including copy number alterations (CNAs), aneuploidy, chromoplexy and chromothripsis. Recent studies have demonstrated that CIN enhances tumor evolution by providing rapid adaptive opportunities through genome doubling and copy number alterations, promoting tumor aggressiveness and metastasis. In a comprehensive study of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) from the TRACERx cohort, the role of CIN in shaping ITH was emphasized.188 Tumors with high levels of CIN exhibited increased chromosomal complexity and a higher frequency of subclonal copy number variations, which were linked to phenotypic changes such as increased proliferation and reduced clonality. These findings underscore the pivotal role of CIN in the development of tumor heterogeneity, which is essential for the clonal evolution of aggressive tumor subpopulations.Aneuploidy, the presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes, is another fundamental aspect of genomic instability in cancer. It often results from CIN and plays a crucial role in facilitating tumor evolution by allowing cells to adapt to selective pressures, including therapeutic interventions. High levels of aneuploidy have been associated with poor patient outcomes due to their role in promoting tumor progression and treatment resistance. The mechanisms by which aneuploidy drives tumor evolution include the alteration of gene dosage, leading to the upregulation of oncogenes or the loss of tumor suppressor genes.189 This can result in the activation of key signaling pathways that promote cell survival, proliferation, and metastasis. Aneuploidy has been described as a “bet-hedging” mechanism in tumor evolution, where genetic instability provides an opportunity for cells to rapidly adapt to changing environmental conditions, including therapeutic pressures.190 By accumulating diverse chromosomal aberrations, tumor cells enhance their adaptability, allowing them to thrive under selective pressures that would typically lead to cell death. This ability to tolerate high levels of CIN and aneuploidy is particularly relevant in the context of cancer treatment, where treatment resistance is a major barrier to therapeutic success. A recent study examining colorectal cancer organoids demonstrated the role of CIN in promoting tumor progression, with cells exhibiting varying levels of tolerance to mitotic errors.191 This variability in CIN tolerance led to the formation of distinct karyotypic landscapes, contributing to tumor heterogeneity and resistance to treatment. Such findings highlight the dynamic nature of CIN and its critical role in shaping the tumor genome and its response to therapy.Chromoplexy and chromothripsis are representative examples of single catastrophic events that can drive tumor evolution, suggesting their involvement in the punctuated model of cancer evolution. Rather than a gradual accumulation of mutations, chromoplexy and chromothripsis can cause sudden and dramatic changes in the genome, leading to rapid evolutionary shifts in tumor populations. This model contrasts with traditional linear or branching models of tumor evolution and highlights the importance of catastrophic genomic events in shaping tumor heterogeneity and therapeutic resistance.Chromoplexy refers to a catastrophic genomic event involving complex, simultaneous chromosomal rearrangements.192 Chromoplexy is triggered by the occurrence of multiple double-strand breaks in the genome, typically in regions of the genome prone to such damage. These breaks lead to highly complex repair mechanisms, often involving nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) or alternative end-joining pathways, which result in the rearrangement of chromosomal segments.193–195 Disrupted chromosomal regions can lead to the formation of fusion genes, creating new oncogenic drivers that promote tumor progression. In prostate cancer, for example, chromoplexy often involves the rearrangement of genes such as the fusion between TMPRSS2 and ERG, contributing to cancer cell proliferation and survival.196 These fusions serve as a significant driver of tumorigenesis, highlighting the role of chromoplexy in creating oncogenic gene combinations. Moreover, several key signaling pathways are associated with chromoplexy-driven tumor evolution. For example, the androgen receptor (AR) signaling pathway in prostate cancer is influenced by chromoplexy-induced gene fusions, such as TMPRSS2:ERG.192 These fusions activate downstream targets involved in cell survival and proliferation. Additionally, chromoplexy can affect pathways such as PI3K/AKT and MAPK signaling, which are crucial for cancer cell growth and survival. Chromoplexy-induced mutations contribute to the evolution of aggressive cancer phenotypes, as the genomic chaos generated by chromoplexy can alter the function of key regulatory genes, facilitating tumor survival and metastasis. This phenomenon underscores the role of chromoplexy in the early stages of cancer development, where a single catastrophic event can lead to a cascade of mutations and clonal evolution.Chromothripsis refers to a catastrophic genomic event characterized by massive, localized chromosomal fragmentation followed by incomplete repair, leading to highly complex genomic rearrangements.197 Unlike chromoplexy, which involves multiple chromosomes, chromothripsis typically affects a single or few chromosomes, generating a fragmented, shattering pattern.159 These fragmented chromosomes are then improperly repaired, resulting in structural variations such as deletions, duplications, translocations, and inversions, all of which contribute to genomic instability in tumors. Chromothripsis often occurs during cellular stress, such as replication or telomere dysfunction, and has been linked to abnormal mitosis. This leads to chromosomal shattering, which, when repaired by NHEJ or alternative end joining (alt-EJ), results in an array of structural variants. These variants disrupt the normal function of key tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes, thus fostering the clonal evolution of the tumor. In prostate cancer, for example, chromothripsis contributes to the formation of fusion genes such as TMPRSS2:ERG, which further drives tumor progression. Additionally, in breast cancer, chromothripsis has been observed in a significant proportion of cases, particularly in metastatic tumors.197 This event has been linked to the generation of recurrent fusions that drive tumor progression, with several well-known oncogenes, such as CCND1, ERBB2, and CDK12, being affected. Chromothripsis also influences the activation of pathways such as the PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways, which promote cell survival, growth, and metastasis. Interestingly, chromothripsis is frequently associated with kataegis, a mutational signature characterized by clustered point mutations, suggesting that chromothripsis plays a dual role in both structural and mutational changes that facilitate tumor evolution. Strategies to target CIN, such as inhibitors of mitotic checkpoint kinases or drugs that induce chromosomal instability, may offer new avenues for cancer therapy. In addition, recent advancements in genomic sequencing technologies, such as single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, have allowed for a more detailed characterization of CIN and aneuploidy at the single-cell level. These technologies provide a deeper understanding of how chromosomal aberrations contribute to tumor evolution and offer the potential for more personalized treatment strategies.Furthermore, research involving single-cell copy number profiling and exome sequencing from the same breast cancer patients has revealed that CNAs emerge early in evolution as punctuated bursts, followed by stable expansion. In contrast, point mutations accumulate gradually throughout the tumor’s progression, driving clonal expansions over time.121 Similarly, studies employing whole-genome sequencing of matched longitudinal breast tumor samples from hyperplasias, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), and invasive carcinomas have demonstrated that copy number evolution occurs early, while point mutations evolve more gradually and branch throughout disease progression.198 This indicates the correlation between tumor evolution models and the molecular mechanisms driving tumor evolution. In the early stages of tumor development, genomic instability events, such as CNAs, chromoplexy, and chromothripsis, emerge rapidly in an explosive manner. These events drive tumor evolution in accordance with the punctuated equilibrium model. In contrast, point mutations, which accumulate gradually due to defects in DNA repair pathways and errors in DNA polymerases, often drive branching tumor evolution.199,200In conclusion, genomic instability is a central driver of tumor evolution, contributing to the accumulation of mutations, the formation of clonal diversity, and the development of resistance to therapies. The mechanisms underlying genomic instability—ranging from the activity of mutagenic enzymes such as APOBEC3G to the formation of ecDNA and the accumulation of chromosomal aberrations—provide critical insights into how tumors evolve and adapt. Understanding these processes is essential for identifying potential therapeutic targets aimed at disrupting the evolutionary dynamics of tumors and preventing the emergence of therapy-resistant clones.Epigenetic plasticityEpigenetic modifications play a crucial and dynamic role in tumor evolution, contributing to the establishment of cellular diversity and the adaptability of cancer cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Unlike genetic mutations, which are typically irreversible, epigenetic changes are reversible, allowing for plasticity that enables tumor cells to respond to environmental pressures such as hypoxia, immune attack, and therapeutic intervention. These alterations, which include DNA methylation, histone modification, and chromatin remodeling, provide a mechanism for tumor cells to acquire malignant phenotypes without changing the underlying genetic sequence. This ability to undergo epigenetic reprogramming is a key feature that drives tumor progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. In this section, we will discuss how epigenetic plasticity drives tumor evolution, focusing on various molecular mechanisms and pathways.DNA methylation is a critical epigenetic modification that contributes to the regulation of gene expression in tumors. Aberrant DNA methylation patterns, such as hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes and hypomethylation of oncogenes, are frequently observed in various cancers and contribute to tumorigenesis and progression. Early in tumorigenesis, abnormal DNA methylation can establish a foundation for subsequent genetic alterations, thereby contributing to tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution. These methylation changes are not random but often follow specific patterns that can provide insight into tumor evolution.201In the context of tumor progression, DNA methylation plays a pivotal role in regulating the expression of genes involved in immune evasion. For example, the expression of immune checkpoint molecules such as PD-L1 can be modulated by methylation at gene promoter regions, allowing tumors to escape immune surveillance. This process is further compounded by the silencing of immune-related genes, which can be reversed by demethylating agents, offering potential therapeutic strategies to counteract immune evasion.202 As tumors evolve, the accumulation of DNA methylation changes can also lead to the stabilization of specific gene expression profiles, which support the adaptive capabilities of the tumor under therapeutic pressures.In addition to DNA methylation, histone modifications play a critical role in regulating gene expression during tumor evolution. Modifications such as acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, and ubiquitination of histones can alter the chromatin structure, either promoting or repressing transcriptional activity. Histone acetylation, for example, is associated with an open chromatin structure and active transcription, while histone methylation can result in either gene activation or silencing depending on the specific context and the histone residues involved. One of the most well-studied histone modifications in cancer is H3K27ac, which marks active enhancer regions in the genome. It has been demonstrated that the activation of enhancers, as indicated by increased H3K27ac levels, is associated with phenotypic heterogeneity within tumors.203 These changes in enhancer activity reflect the dynamic adaptation of tumors to their environment and are closely linked to therapeutic resistance. In the case of endocrine-resistant breast cancer, for example, changes in enhancer activity drive the expansion of specific subclones that exhibit resistance to treatment, highlighting the role of epigenetic regulation in modulating tumor heterogeneity.203Furthermore, chromatin remodeling complexes such as SWI/SNF and the chromatin-modifying enzymes EZH2 and KDM1A are frequently altered in cancer.204,205,206 These proteins regulate chromatin accessibility and the expression of key oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Mutations or altered expression of these chromatin regulators can contribute to tumorigenesis by altering the transcriptional landscape, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation and survival. These modifications often result in an epigenetic “memory” that persists even in the absence of the initial genetic alteration, providing a lasting advantage to the tumor.204Epigenetic plasticity is not only critical for tumor initiation and progression but also plays a central role in metastasis and therapeutic resistance. Tumor cells that undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) represent a well-characterized example of phenotypic plasticity, while phenotypic plasticity can also manifest through other processes, including the acquisition of stem-like states and therapy-induced transcriptional reprogramming.207,208 EMT-associated epigenetic reprogramming allows tumor cells to acquire invasive and migratory capabilities. The dynamic and reversible nature of EMT, as mediated by epigenetic modifications, enables cancer cells to adapt to different microenvironmental niches and resist therapeutic intervention.209 This process is often driven by transcription factors such as ZEB1, which regulate both the expression of EMT markers and the epigenetic landscape of the cell.Epigenetic reprogramming also contributes to the acquisition of therapy resistance. Cancer cells can undergo reversible epigenetic changes that allow them to survive in the face of chemotherapy or immunotherapy. For instance, certain subpopulations of tumor cells may enter a dormant or “persister” state through chromatin modifications, enabling them to evade the cytotoxic effects of treatment. Upon cessation of therapy or changes in the microenvironment, these cells can “wake up”, initiating tumor relapse and contributing to poor therapeutic outcomes. Such epigenetic mechanisms, which are independent of genetic mutations, underscore the complexity of cancer evolution and highlight the need for novel therapeutic strategies that target both genetic and epigenetic drivers of resistance.210A significant aspect of epigenetic plasticity in tumor evolution is its role in immune evasion. Tumor cells frequently exploit epigenetic mechanisms to modulate the expression of immune-related genes, thereby escaping immune surveillance. The epigenetic regulation of genes involved in immune recognition, such as MHC molecules, plays a key role in determining whether tumor cells are visible to the immune system. The CSDE1 protein regulates immune recognition by modulating STAT1 phosphorylation.211 The differential expression of CSDE1 in nascent tumorigenic cells, regulated by SMYD3-mediated H3K4 trimethylation, dictates whether these cells exhibit high or low immunogenicity. This epigenetic pathway represents a crucial determinant of tumor immune visibility and contributes to immune evasion during early tumor evolution. In particular, the modulation of CSDE1 expression through mechanical signaling in the TME underscores the importance of the microenvironment in shaping the epigenetic landscape of tumor cells and their ability to evade immune detection.211Metabolic reprogrammingAs tumors progress, they encounter environmental stresses such as hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, and immune surveillance, which trigger changes in metabolic pathways to sustain cellular functions and promote malignancy. These metabolic alterations offer a significant advantage in tumor evolution. The following discussion explores the molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways involved in metabolic reprogramming and their contribution to the dynamic evolution of tumors.The Warburg effect, first described by Otto Warburg in the 1920s, is a fundamental aspect of metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells.212 This phenomenon is characterized by increased glucose consumption and lactate production, even in the presence of oxygen, a process known as aerobic glycolysis. Tumor cells often exhibit this metabolic shift, which supports rapid ATP generation and the biosynthesis of key macromolecules needed for growth and proliferation. This shift away from oxidative phosphorylation is thought to be driven by oncogenic signaling pathways, including the activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MYC pathways, which promote glycolysis by upregulating glycolytic enzymes such as hexokinase 2 (HK2) and lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA).213 The Warburg effect is not just a metabolic quirk but an adaptive response to the microenvironment of rapidly growing tumors, which often face limited oxygen and nutrient availability. The metabolic flexibility conferred by the Warburg effect allows tumor cells to thrive in hypoxic conditions and provides a mechanism for survival in hostile environments, a key feature in tumor progression and metastasis.214In addition to the Warburg effect, cancer cells undergo extensive reprogramming of multiple metabolic pathways to meet the energy demands of their rapid growth and survival in a hostile microenvironment. These changes include alterations in glucose metabolism, lipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial function. Glucose is a critical nutrient for cancer cells, and its metabolism is heavily altered in tumors. In glycolysis, glucose is converted to pyruvate, which, under normal conditions, enters the mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation. However, in many cancers, pyruvate is converted to lactate by LDHA, even under aerobic conditions, ensuring continued ATP production via glycolysis.215,216 This shift is particularly evident in aggressive cancers and is a key feature of the metabolic adaptation that supports tumor progression. Furthermore, the activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway enhances glucose uptake through increased expression of glucose transporters (GLUTs) and key glycolytic enzymes.217 This metabolic shift is essential for the rapid cell division and growth seen in tumors.218Lipid metabolism is another critical aspect of metabolic reprogramming in tumor cells. Tumor cells increase fatty acid synthesis to provide lipids for the construction of cell membranes and to produce signaling molecules. Fatty acid synthase (FASN) is a key enzyme in this process, and its overexpression is common in many cancer types, including breast cancer.219 Elevated levels of FASN drive the synthesis of fatty acids, which are integral for the formation of phospholipids in cellular membranes, a requirement for tumor cell proliferation. Additionally, altered lipid metabolism contributes to the regulation of cell signaling pathways involved in tumor progression. For example, the accumulation of specific lipid species can activate oncogenic pathways such as the PI3K-AKT pathway, further fueling the aggressive growth of tumors.220Furthermore, amino acids are essential for protein synthesis and cellular growth, and their metabolism is often reprogrammed in cancer cells.
