One prominent example is the reprogramming of glutamine metabolism. Glutamine is used as a carbon and nitrogen source for biosynthesis and mitochondrial energy production in cancer cells. In some tumors, the glutamine transporter SLC1A5 is upregulated to increase glutamine uptake, and glutamine is converted into α-ketoglutarate, which enters the TCA cycle to fuel anabolic pathways.221 Moreover, altered amino acid metabolism can influence the tumor microenvironment (TME) by modulating immune cell function. For instance, elevated levels of tryptophan metabolites, such as kynurenine, can suppress T-cell activation and promote immune evasion.222As tumors evolve, they experience metabolic selection pressures that drive the acquisition of specific genetic alterations, particularly those that promote survival under metabolic stress. Copy number alterations (CNAs) in metabolic genes are common in tumors, particularly those involved in glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis, and amino acid metabolism.213,223 These alterations provide a survival advantage to tumor cells by enhancing their ability to adapt to changing metabolic conditions, thus driving tumor progression. For example, the amplification of glycolytic genes such as hexokinase and enolase is frequently observed in tumors with high metabolic activity, highlighting the selective advantage conferred by metabolic reprogramming.223Metabolic reprogramming is a critical factor in tumor evolution, enabling cancer cells to adapt to the harsh conditions of the tumor microenvironment while promoting uncontrolled growth and survival. Key metabolic alterations, including the Warburg effect, changes in lipid and amino acid metabolism, and adaptations to hypoxic stress, are all crucial to understanding how tumors evolve over time. These metabolic shifts are not only essential for tumor growth and progression but also represent potential therapeutic targets for future cancer treatments. By targeting these metabolic pathways, it may be possible to disrupt tumor evolution and improve clinical outcomes for patients.In summary, cell-intrinsic mechanisms are essential drivers of tumor evolution, shaping the genetic and epigenetic landscape of tumors while facilitating their adaptation to therapeutic pressures. Genomic instability, through mechanisms such as APOBEC3-mediated mutations and the formation of ecDNA, contributes to the diversification of tumor clones and the development of resistance to therapies. Epigenetic plasticity, marked by reversible changes in DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin remodeling, further enhances tumor adaptability and progression, enabling cells to evade immune surveillance and therapeutic interventions. Additionally, metabolic reprogramming allows tumor cells to thrive under stress conditions, fostering uncontrolled growth and contributing to metastasis. These intrinsic mechanisms work synergistically to promote the heterogeneity and aggressiveness of tumors, underscoring the complexity of cancer evolution. As we transition to the next section, we will explore how external factors, such as the tumor microenvironment and immune system, also play a pivotal role in driving tumor progression and shaping evolutionary dynamics.Cell-extrinsic regulatory mechanism of tumor evolutionThe complexity of the tumor ecosystem is shaped in space and time by diverse cell-extrinsic factors stemming from the tumor microenvironment, immune system, intercellular interactions and other extracellular driving factors. These external cues do not act passively. Instead, they actively sculpt clonal dynamics, influencing which cancer cell populations survive, expand, or are eliminated.Tumor microenvironmentWhile these extrinsic factors convey evolutionary pressure to the distinct clones within the tumor, cancer cells themselves are also capable of reconstructing a tumor-supportive microenvironment by recruiting and reprogramming noncancerous host cells and by remodeling angiogenesis and the extracellular matrix (ECM).224,225 Hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment induces vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression and polarizes tumor-associated stromal cells (e.g., tumor-associated macrophages, tumor-associated fibroblasts), driving tumor microenvironmental remodeling, which exacerbates intratumoral heterogeneity and evolutionary potential.226 In addition to its effects on stromal dynamics, hypoxia also promotes genomic instability through multiple mechanisms, including the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated DNA damage, impaired replication restart fidelity, and suppression of DNA damage response (DDR) pathways, including mismatch repair and methylation silencing of BRCA1.227Cancer cells actively remodel their surroundings through the recruitment and reprogramming of nonmalignant host cells, including fibroblasts, immune cells, and endothelial cells. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), for instance, secrete a wide array of mitogenic growth factors, including hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), fibroblast growth factors (FGFs), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and stromal-derived factor 1 (SDF-1/CXCL12).228–230 These paracrine signals complement oncogenic mutations and enable clonal expansion even under therapeutic selective pressure. Moreover, immunosuppressive factors in the TME, such as CXCL12, CXCL14, and IL-6, secreted by inflammatory-like cancer-associated fibroblasts pan-iCAF and pan-iCAF-2, contribute to tumor evolution by promoting immune evasion, cancer stem cell renewal, and the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages.231Immune systemThe immune system exerts one of the most potent forms of selection on developing tumors. The immunoediting framework—comprising elimination, equilibrium, and escape—describes how nascent tumors are initially constrained by immune surveillance but may eventually adapt to survive in an immunosuppressive niche.232 Immune escape is also an important driver of tumor evolution. For example, the progression of breast ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) to invasive ductal carcinomas was accompanied by a transition to a suppressed immune milieu characterized by fewer activated CD8 + T cells, increased PD-L1 and CTLA4 expression, more regulatory T cells (Tregs), and less diverse T-cell receptor (TCR) clonotypes.233 Weeden et al. revealed that tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells, while normally providing local immune defense, can shape tumor evolution through chronic immune pressure.234 In ever-smokers, heightened TRM-like activity prior to tumor onset enhances immune surveillance but also promotes immune escape by selecting tumor clones that downregulate MHC class I and resist immune checkpoint blockade (ICB).Importantly, immune escape should not be viewed as a static or terminal event but rather as a dynamic and evolving process shaped by selective pressures throughout tumor progression. Tumor clones may acquire partial escape mechanisms early on and refine or diversify these strategies as immunologic conditions change, particularly under the influence of therapy. As a result, the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions—such as immune checkpoint blockade—depends not only on the presence of immune-competent cells but also on the specific timing, mechanism and evolutionary stage of immune escape.To address this challenge, real-time evolutionary monitoring of tumor-immune dynamics is essential. Approaches such as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling, neoantigen landscape tracking, and spatial immunogenomic analysis can help identify emerging escape subclones and adapt treatment strategies accordingly. By integrating such evolutionary surveillance into clinical decision-making, it may be possible to anticipate immune evasion, guide rational combinations, and prolong the window of therapeutic vulnerability.Intercellular interactionsRecent advances in computational analysis and modeling have revealed a diversity of intercellular signaling networks, revealing how complex intercellular interactions are integrated to promote the evolution of tumor.225,235 There are multiple mechanisms by which this intercellular dialog is regulated, including cell‒cell contact and paracrine signaling.236 Contact-dependent communication is mediated by adhesion molecules, including integrins, cadherins, selectins, and immunoglobulin superfamily members, and via gap junctions and tunneling nanotubes.225 For instance, aberrant glycan sialylation on cancer cells regulates numerous interactions, including interactions with Siglec-expressing immune cells, promoting immune evasion and tumor evolution.237 In addition to direct cell‒cell contact, paracrine signaling through the release of cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and proteases is also critical for intercellular communication.225 These molecules are secreted in response to cancer-intrinsic features and cellular stress, exerting direct and indirect actions on target cells by ECM remodeling or binding to receptors. Moreover, extracellular vesicles (EVs), particularly exosomes, have emerged as pivotal carriers of intercellular messages. These vesicles transport bioactive molecules—proteins, lipids, RNAs, and DNA fragments—to recipient cells, influencing their behavior in a context-dependent manner. For example, melanoma-derived exosomes enriched in PD-L1 can suppress T-cell activation systemically, contributing to immune evasion.238 In breast cancer, exosomal miR-105 derived from metastatic cells has been shown to disrupt tight junctions in endothelial cells by targeting ZO-1, promoting vascular permeability and premetastatic niche formation.239 Similarly, glioma-derived exosomes carrying EGFRvIII can transform neighboring astrocytes, facilitating an invasive tumor microenvironment.240Spatial transcriptomics and tools such as CellPhoneDB241 and NicheNet242 have further uncovered complex cell–cell communication networks within tumors, revealing that stromal and immune cell subsets preferentially interact with specific cancer subclones. These interaction patterns are not static but evolve over time in response to selective pressures such as nutrient gradients or immune responses.243 Aberrant glycosylation patterns—such as hypersialylation—also mediate intercellular crosstalk by engaging inhibitory Siglec receptors on immune cells, promoting immune tolerance and escape.244Other extracellular driving factorsIn addition to well-characterized components such as the tumor microenvironment, immune system and intercellular interactions, biophysical and physiological factors within the tumor ecosystem also exert profound evolutionary influence.Temporal fluctuations in blood flow are a hallmark of malignant tumors, yet their evolutionary significance has often been overlooked. These variations stem from the eco-evolutionary dynamics of tumor angiogenesis, where cancer cells—acting as local units of selection—respond solely to proximal microenvironmental cues.245 As a result, neovessels commonly emerge from the nearest available vasculature without coordination or regard for functional capacity, giving rise to a chaotic vascular architecture and pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in perfusion and tissue conditions.246This unstable hemodynamic landscape imposes shifting selective pressures that fuel cancer cell adaptation, promoting phenotypic plasticity, enhanced motility, invasiveness, and metabolic versatility.247 Clinically, fluctuating blood flow intensifies intratumoral hypoxia, hampers effective drug delivery, and accelerates the selection of resistant clones—collectively shaping treatment outcomes and long-term disease evolution.248Beyond fluctuations in blood flow and perfusion, a diverse array of biophysical forces—including mechanical stress, interstitial pressure, osmotic gradients, and extracellular acidosis—further contribute to tumor evolution by shaping the selection landscape. As tumors grow within confined anatomical spaces, cancer cells are subjected to increasing solid stress and tensile strain from the surrounding stroma and ECM. These forces influence cell fate decisions by modulating mechanotransduction pathways, such as integrin–FAK–YAP/TAZ signaling, which in turn promote survival, proliferation, and stem-like phenotypes in subclones capable of withstanding mechanical challenge.247 Chemical and ionic gradients also impose powerful selective constraints. Acidic extracellular pH, resulting from aerobic glycolysis and impaired clearance of metabolic waste, not only favors clones with altered pH-regulating transporters (e.g., CAIX, MCT4) but also induces mutagenic stress and immune suppression.249 Subclones that thrive in acidic environments often exhibit enhanced treatment resistance and invasive potential.250 Hyperosmotic stress, on the other hand, as seen in densely packed or poorly perfused regions, can activate stress-adaptive signaling such as the p38 MAPK and HSP pathways, selecting for more resilient cellular phenotypes.251Collectively, these physical and chemical factors define microenvironmental niches that filter cancer cell populations based on mechanical resilience, metabolic adaptability, and signaling plasticity. The result is a highly heterogeneous tumor composed of subclones fine-tuned to distinct ecological constraints—an evolutionary mosaic continually reshaped by nongenetic, extrinsic forces.Exogenous regulatory mechanism of tumor evolutionBuilding upon the cellular-extrinsic factors discussed in the previous section, tumor evolution is also profoundly influenced by a range of exogenous regulatory mechanisms. These factors, which include therapeutic interventions, environmental influences, and the diverse clinical characteristics of the patient population, serve as additional evolutionary pressures that shape the dynamics of tumor progression. Unlike intrinsic cellular alterations, exogenous factors exert a force on tumors from outside the cellular realm, providing selective pressures that influence clonal selection, adaptation, and therapeutic resistance. While these external forces may act synergistically with intrinsic mutations and cellular plasticity, their contribution to the tumor evolutionary process often determines the trajectory of the disease, influencing both its aggressiveness and response to treatment.Therapeutic interventionsTumor evolution can naturally occur due to intrinsic genomic instability and stochastic processes. However, therapeutic interventions accelerate and redirect these evolutionary pathways by imposing strong selective pressures. Each treatment modality targets specific vulnerabilities, which inevitably alters the competitive fitness landscape of tumor cells, promoting the emergence of resistant clones and adaptive phenotypes. Understanding these treatment-driven evolutionary dynamics is essential for developing more durable and adaptive therapeutic strategies. Moreover, persister cells, which are transiently drug-tolerant subpopulations within tumors, play a crucial role in cancer progression and therapy resistance. These cells are not genetically resistant but instead exhibit adaptive mutability, allowing them to survive under therapeutic stress and acquire mutations that can lead to permanent resistance. The mechanisms driving this phenomenon include changes in DNA repair pathways, the upregulation of error-prone DNA polymerases and microsatellite instability (MSI).252ChemotherapyChemotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment and the only systemic treatment for certain cancer subtypes associated with poor clinicopathologic features. By exerting strong cytotoxic effects on cancer cells, chemotherapeutic agents not only eliminate sensitive subclones but also impose intense selective pressures that reshape the clonal landscape of tumors, inadvertently promoting the survival and expansion of resistant populations. In breast cancer patients, following paclitaxel treatment, the E545K mutation of the PIK3CA gene became significantly enriched, with the mutation allele frequency increasing from 14% prior to treatment to 34% posttreatment.253 This mutation promotes cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis by activating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, ultimately leading to resistance to paclitaxel.254 Moreover, whole exome sequencing of tumor biopsies collected before treatment, at the point of therapy switch, and after sequential treatment with epirubicin and docetaxel monotherapy revealed that docetaxel induced a profound redistribution of subclones in breast cancer.255 This redistribution was characterized by the regression of sensitive clones and the expansion of clones carrying mutations associated with treatment resistance, including TP53 and PIK3CA, driving tumor recurrence and evolution.256 Two germline mutations in the TEKT4 gene (c. A541G and c. A547G), associated with reduced disease-free survival and overall survival, were significantly enriched in basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) patients postpaclitaxel-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NCT).257 Encoding the microtubule stabilizing protein Tektin4, the ectopic expression of TEKT4 mutations antagonizes paclitaxel-induced microtubule stabilization, contributing to increased paclitaxel resistance.257–259In addition, gene fusion also plays an important role in paclitaxel-driven tumor evolution. ABCB1 encodes multidrug resistance protein (MDR1), an ATP-binding cassette member involved in the cellular efflux of chemotherapeutic drugs.260,261 In high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) and breast cancer, a study found that the ABCB1 gene enhances promoter-driven self-expression through transcriptional fusion events with other genes, such as SLC25A40, resulting in overexpression of MDR1.262 MDR1 overexpression reduces the cytotoxicity of drugs by increasing the ability of cells to efflux paclitaxel. After chemotherapy with paclitaxel or other MDR1 substrate drugs, resistant clones harboring the ABCB1 fusion are selectively expanded.262Notably, paclitaxel-resistant cells are more likely to enter this drug-tolerant persistence state under EGFR-TKI treatment pressure than cells without paclitaxel resistance, eventually evolving into stable resistance.263 With the upregulation of stemness markers such as Nanog and CD133, this process represents a key step in the evolution of tumor cells from paclitaxel resistance to stable resistance to EGFR-TKIs.264–266 However, this drug-tolerant persistence state can be reversed after drug removal.267 While paclitaxel-resistant tumor cells were proven to maintain their resistant phenotype by regulating FOXO3a,264 this stable resistance to EGFR-TKIs following paclitaxel resistance does not require known resistance-promoting mechanisms such as MET amplification and KRAS G12 missense mutation. It is primarily driven by a range of cellular phenotypic changes and nongenetic mechanisms, including stemness enrichment, metabolic rewiring, and alterations in apoptosis regulation.Platinum-based chemotherapeutics, another key component of cancer chemotherapy, introduce a different set of evolutionary dynamics by targeting DNA integrity via the formation of intra- and interstrand crosslinks. A study demonstrated that the newly defined cisplatin-specific single nucleotide variation (SNV) and short insertion/deletion mutations of either base to thymine at AG putative intrastrand crosslinks are causes of the reversion of BRCA2 mutations in emerging cisplatin-resistant clones.268 Cisplatin-specific mutation signatures with significantly increased C>A and T>A mutations were observed in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), urothelial carcinoma (UC), muscle-invasive bladder cancer and high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), and the mutation frequency was positively correlated with drug dose in ESCC.86,269,270 These studies suggest that cisplatin-based therapy can directly induce resistance-causing mutations.Moreover, patients with HGSOC carrying BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations are particularly sensitive to platinum-based drugs due to the lack of homologous recombination repair ability, resulting in a longer recurrence-free survival period.271 However, some patients exhibit However, despite their specificity, targeted agents are not exempt from tumor evolution by introducing selective pressures that favor the emergence of resistant clones harboring secondary mutations, bypass signaling, or phenotypic plasticity.Among various targeted therapies, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors represent a key advancement in the treatment of cancers driven by aberrant EGFR signaling, such as non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The evolutionary dynamics induced by EGFR inhibitors have been extensively studied in lung cancer. Gefitinib, an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is widely used to treat EGFR mutation-positive NSCLC patients. The T790M mutation is the primary mechanism of acquired resistance in NSCLC during EGFR inhibitor therapy, occurring in 50–60% of patients.264,280 Research has shown that T790M mutations arise through two pathways: selection of preexisting T790M clones and genetic evolution of drug-tolerant cells. Therefore, the significant restoration of HRD-related gene mutation expression induced by olaparib treatment, representing epigenetic reversal, may be related to resistance. Different classes of endocrine therapies, including anti-estrogen agents, anti-androgen agents, and aromatase inhibitors, exert selective pressures on tumor cells by disrupting hormonal signaling pathways essential for tumor growth.Research on anti-estrogen therapies primarily focuses on hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative (HR+/HER2-) advanced breast cancer. Tumor genome evolution and treatment resistance are common during combination therapy with antiestrogenic drugs (such as bazedoxifene or fulvestrant) and the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib. Mutations in the ESR1 gene, particularly the Y537S mutation, and PIK3CA mutations are well-established drivers of fulvestrant resistance and play a dominant role in posttreatment resistance mechanisms.294,295,300 These mutations significantly impact progression-free survival (PFS). Furthermore, LBD truncating rearrangements in the AR gene have been observed in resistant patients, allowing ligand-independent activation of AR and further promoting therapeutic resistance. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), such as anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 therapies, have ushered in a new era of cancer treatment by enhancing antitumor immunity. When treated with the immune checkpoint inhibitors nivolumab and pembrolizumab, melanoma, NSCLC and glioblastoma (GBM) patients who respond to treatment exhibit selective killing of tumor cells with high neoantigen loads, leading to the enrichment of low-immunogenic subclones.309–313 This process is referred to as clonal contraction or immunoediting. In contrast, tumors from resistant patients show mutational expansion, indicating that therapeutic pressure has triggered an increase in tumor clonal diversity. Similarly, in immune checkpoint inhibitor nonresponders, accelerated mutation accumulation posttreatment is observed, manifested as linear evolution.314 This suggests that treatment pressure may contribute to resistance by facilitating the expansion of subclonal populations.Moreover, in nivolumab-resistant melanoma patients, the loss of CDKN2A and an increase in B2M mutations are significantly observed.309 Frameshift mutations in B2M, along with heterozygous loss, are a typical mechanism of acquired resistance to PD-1 therapy.309–311 In NSCLC, reductions in the copy number of B2M and antigen-presentation genes (such as TAP1, TAP2, and HLA-A) have been shown to be associated with nivolumab resistance.311 Additionally, in some nivolumab-resistant clear cell renal carcinoma (ccRCC) patients, HLA loss of heterozygosity (HLA LOH) and deletions of CDKN2A/B copy numbers have been observed, significantly reducing antigen presentation ability and promoting tumor immune evasion.312 In regions with a significant immune response posttreatment, HLA LOH or CDKN2A/B loss is typically absent. The mechanisms behind HPD remain complex and multifactorial. One of the key mechanisms contributing to HPD is the alteration of the tumor microenvironment (TME). ICIs can shift the immune landscape, leading to the expansion of immunosuppressive cells, such as myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and macrophages, which may promote tumor progression rather than inhibit it.316,317 These cells can suppress T-cell activity, facilitating tumor growth. Moreover, T-cell exhaustion or dysfunctional T-cell phenotypes have been linked to HPD. Consequently, NK cells and macrophages can eliminate T cells via antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) or antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP), potentially leading to T-cell depletion and facilitating rapid tumor progression.319 Genomic alterations, such as mutations in driver genes and alterations in oncogenic pathways, contribute to HPD. Specific mutations, such as copy number alterations in MDM2/MDM4 and EGFR, have been shown to drive aggressive tumor behavior in response to ICI therapy. This occurs through the induction of PD-L1 expression on tumor cells, leading to resistance to immune surveillance.321RadiotherapyRadiotherapy is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, influencing tumor evolution by imposing selective pressures that shape tumor growth and response dynamics. The effectiveness of radiotherapy often leads to the expansion of resistant subclonal populations, contributing to relapse and therapeutic resistance. Recent studies have revealed several key signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms that mediate tumor evolution in response to radiotherapy.A critical aspect of tumor evolution following radiotherapy involves alterations to the tumor microenvironment, particularly immune cell dynamics. For instance, radiation can enhance the accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which play a pivotal role in immune suppression and tumor progression.322 By interacting with T cells and natural killer (NK) cells, these cells exert immunosuppressive effects that contribute to tumor survival and metastasis. Moreover, radiotherapy induces genetic mutations and genomic instability, fueling the clonal evolution of tumors. In undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS), radiotherapy has been shown to drive a shift toward subclonal selection, where specific mutations, such as those in calcium signaling pathways, are linked to radiosensitivity.323 Radiation causes significant changes in subclone abundance, with subclone contraction correlating with alterations in calcium signaling pathways. Targeting calcium transporters has been shown to enhance UPS cell radiosensitivity, highlighting the crucial role of calcium signaling in radiotherapy resistance.323 Therefore, radiotherapy not only induces DNA damage and mutations in tumor cells but also plays a significant role in tumor evolution through immune modulation and selective subclone expansion. A deeper understanding of the signaling pathways involved in radiotherapy-induced tumor evolution, including immune regulation and genomic instability, is essential for developing targeted strategies to enhance treatment efficacy and minimize relapse. Moreover, in lung tumors during radiotherapy, a patient-specific model based on a partial differential equation was built to predict the evolutionary trajectory, showing a satisfying agreement between the predicted tumor contours and those drawn by an expert.324In conclusion, treatment-induced tumor evolution plays a central role in the development of therapeutic resistance, complicating the efficacy of various cancer treatments. Chemotherapy, immunotherapy, endocrine therapy and targeted therapies all exert selective pressures that drive tumor cells to adapt through genetic alterations, clonal expansion, and the activation of alternative signaling pathways. In chemotherapy, resistance often arises through mutations in drug target genes or by upregulating drug efflux pumps. Immunotherapy resistance is primarily driven by immune escape mechanisms, such as tumor-induced immune suppression. In targeted therapies, mutations in key oncogenes such as EGFR or PI3K lead to the emergence of resistant clones, while endocrine therapies for HR+ breast cancer are hampered by mutations such as ESR1. These evolving tumor dynamics underscore the need for personalized and combination treatment strategies that account for tumor heterogeneity and adaptive resistance, ultimately optimizing therapeutic efficacy and improving patient outcomes.Environmental factorsEnvironmental factors are significant external regulators of tumor evolution, influencing cancer progression, metastasis, and therapy resistance. These factors include a variety of physical, chemical, and biological elements, such as diet, air pollution, UV radiation, and infection, each of which can induce specific genetic and epigenetic changes in tumor cells. Environmental exposure creates selective pressures that shape tumor evolution, driving the selection of clones that are better suited to survive and thrive in the given microenvironment. This section will focus on the impact of environmental factors on tumor evolution, highlighting key molecular pathways and mechanisms through which these factors influence cancer progression.UV radiation is one of the most well-known environmental carcinogens and is primarily associated with skin cancers, such as melanoma.325 UV radiation induces DNA damage in skin cells, leading to the formation of pyrimidine dimers and the activation of DNA repair mechanisms. However, the accumulation of unrepaired DNA damage can promote genetic mutations and drive tumor evolution. UV radiation-induced DNA damage is primarily repaired through nucleotide excision repair (NER) and other repair pathways. However, defects in these repair mechanisms, particularly in genes such as XPC and ERCC2, increase the likelihood of mutations, which may contribute to the development of skin cancers.326 UV radiation also activates cellular stress responses, including the activation of p53, a key tumor suppressor protein involved in the DNA damage response and cell cycle regulation. However, chronic exposure to UV radiation can lead to mutations in the p53 gene itself, which may allow for the accumulation of additional mutations and the progression of cancer. Furthermore, UV-induced DNA damage is often associated with the activation of oncogenic pathways such as the MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways, which promote cell survival and proliferation. These pathways can be upregulated in response to DNA damage, creating a feedback loop that supports tumorigenesis and drives the evolution of resistant subclones. UV radiation also influences the immune system by suppressing local immune responses, thereby facilitating tumor survival and growth. This immune suppression is partly mediated by the induction of regulatory T cells (Tregs), which inhibit antitumor immune responses and support the evolution of immune-resistant tumor cells. Thus, UV radiation is a powerful environmental factor that induces DNA damage and promotes tumor evolution by selecting for mutations that enhance tumor survival and resistance to immune surveillance. It has also been found to shape dendritic cell leukemia transformation in the skin by promoting plasma-cytoid dendritic cell (pDC) expansion and mutagenesis.327 The impact of UV radiation on tumor progression underscores the importance of protecting against environmental factors that promote genetic instability and drive cancer development.Chemical carcinogens, such as those found in tobacco smoke, industrial chemicals, and pollutants, are another major environmental factor influencing tumor evolution. These substances induce DNA damage by forming adducts with DNA bases, leading to mutations that can contribute to tumorigenesis. One of the most well-studied examples of chemical carcinogenesis is the role of tobacco smoke in the development of lung cancer. Tobacco smoke contains numerous mutagenic compounds, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), which cause DNA damage and mutations that promote tumor evolution.328 Adler et al. investigated how exposure to tobacco carcinogens induces mutations in key cancer-related genes, such as TP53, EGFR, and KRAS, leading to the development of drug-resistant subclones. These mutations are often selected for in response to the selective pressures imposed by the carcinogen, driving the evolution of a genetically diverse tumor population. Additionally, the accumulation of mutations in DNA repair genes, such as those in the base excision repair pathway, further accelerates the rate of mutation and contributes to the generation of subclonal diversity.Chemical carcinogens also modulate signaling pathways that drive tumor progression. For example, PAHs and other carcinogens can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), which regulates the expression of detoxification enzymes and can influence tumor growth and metastasis.329 The activation of AhR and other signaling pathways by chemical carcinogens promotes tumor evolution by creating a proinflammatory and prosurvival microenvironment, further facilitating the development of therapy-resistant tumor clones.Additionally, infections, particularly viral infections, also contribute significantly to tumor initiation and progression.330 For instance, human papillomavirus (HPV) is linked to cervical cancer, while chronic hepatitis B and C infections lead to hepatocellular carcinoma. These infections often cause genomic instability, inflammation, and changes in epithelial cell differentiation, which contribute to the tumorigenic process. Vaccination against HPV has been shown to reduce the incidence of early neoplasias and cervical cancers by inducing regression of precancerous lesions, demonstrating how infection-related carcinogenesis can be prevented at early stages.Lifestyle habits of patientsLifestyle habits of individual patients also influence the development of cancer not only through direct genetic alterations but also by promoting a favorable environment for mutated cells to thrive and evolve into invasive tumors.Smoking and alcohol consumption are two of the most significant lifestyle-related risk factors for cancer.330,331 Smoking introduces mutagenic compounds into the body that directly damage DNA, leading to oncogenic driver mutations. In addition to these mutagenic effects, smoking also acts as a promoter by creating a proinflammatory environment, enhancing cell proliferation, and suppressing immune responses, which collectively promote tumor progression. For example, smoking is linked to several cancers, including lung, oral, and esophageal cancers, where inflammatory markers such as cytokine production in lung myeloid cells play a pivotal role. Alcohol, another major lifestyle factor, affects cancer risk through hormonal alterations (such as increased estrogen levels) and through changes in metabolic processes.332 Alcohol consumption has been associated with a decrease in immune function, particularly through the reduction of CD8 + T-cell responses, thus facilitating tumor growth.Dietary factors are emerging as important contributors to tumor evolution. Certain diets, particularly those high in fat, sugar, and processed foods, can create a metabolic environment that supports tumor growth and progression. These dietary factors can influence signaling pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation, and DNA repair, driving tumor evolution. For example, a high-fat diet has been shown to activate the mTOR signaling pathway, which regulates cell growth, metabolism, and survival. This activation promotes tumor growth by enhancing nutrient uptake and increasing cell proliferation.333 A high-fat diet also promotes cancer evolution by inducing gut microbiota-mediated leucine production and myeloid cell differentiation.334 Similarly, diets rich in antioxidants have been shown to suppress oxidative stress, thereby reducing DNA damage and slowing the rate of mutagenesis. Conversely, diets that promote inflammation, such as those high in processed foods and red meat, can exacerbate tumor progression by activating proinflammatory cytokines and signaling pathways such as NF-κB, further driving the evolution of therapy-resistant tumor cells.333 Thus, dietary factors can influence tumor evolution by modulating key signaling pathways, such as those involved in metabolism, inflammation, and DNA repair, contributing to the development of more aggressive and resistant tumor clones.Clinical consequences of tumor evolutionary dynamicsEvolutionary principles govern the trajectory of cancer from its earliest stages to treatment resistance.28 Tumors evolve as dynamic ecosystems of competing clones shaped by mutation, selection, drift, and environmental constraints. These evolutionary dynamics have profound implications for all stages of cancer—tumor initiation, malignant progression, metastasis, and therapeutic response (Fig. 4). These evolutionary dynamics profoundly influence every stage of malignancy, from the earliest neoplastic transformation and silent clonal expansion within normal tissues to the development of invasion and metastasis and ultimately to therapeutic response and resistance. Each of these clinical phenomena reflects a distinct evolutionary phase characterized by selective bottlenecks, adaptive strategies, and ecological trade-offs.Fig. 4Clinical outcomes in tumor evolutionary trajectories. There is a dynamic and complex interplay between tumor evolutionary trajectories and clinical consequences. Key evolutionary phases, such as tumor initiation with clonal expansion, malignant progression involving invasion, metastasis, and recurrence, and the emergence of drug resistance, highlight therapeutic bottlenecks and promising targetsTumorigenesis and early clonal expansionTumorigenesis is fundamentally an outcome of an evolutionary process that is characterized by the accumulation of somatic mutations, clonal selection, and adaptive expansion.335 Initial somatic mutations, often in genes regulating the cell cycle, DNA repair, or apoptosis, provide the raw material for clonal expansion. However, the emergence of neoplastic clones depends not only on acquiring “driver” mutations but also on navigating the ecological landscape of the tissue niche. Mutations that confer even a modest proliferative advantage may enable certain clones to expand at the expense of others, especially in the face of resource limitation or immune surveillance. This early clonal selection represents the first clinically relevant consequence of tumor evolution: the silent expansion of genetically distinct clones in histologically normal or premalignant tissues. Normal tissues impose strict physiological constraints—such as architectural organization, metabolic homeostasis, and stromal regulation—that act as ecological barriers to malignant transformation. These barriers must be overcome incrementally.37 Accordingly, early mutations confer a selective advantage only within specific microenvironmental contexts—such as hypoxia, inflammation or nutrient stress—rather than functioning as universally transforming events. For instance, the pro-proliferative effects of oncogenic RAS or loss of TP53 may only become advantageous when the tissue environment becomes disrupted, highlighting the context-dependent nature of clonal fitness.336Over time, continued mutational input—amplified in some cases by mutator phenotypes or epigenetic drift—leads to a branching pattern of clonal diversification. These coexisting subclones may compete (clonal interference), coexist, or sweep to dominance depending on their relative fitness in the given microenvironment. For instance, recurrent disruption of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex or activation of the PI3K pathway through distinct mutations in mTOR, TSC1, PTEN, and PIK3CA has been frequently observed in different subclones within the same renal cancer, highlighting how multiple subclonal trajectories can converge on similar functional pathways through divergent genetic alterations.337 Critically, this phase is often clinically covert, as evidenced by the high prevalence of premalignant clonal expansions in tissues such as the prostate, breast ducts, and esophageal epithelium that rarely progress to cancer.338In this view, tumor initiation reflects the stepwise selection of phenotypes that gradually overcome niche-level constraints. The evolutionary process is constrained not only by mutation supply but also by the tissue’s ability to buffer or eliminate aberrant clones. Cellular phenotypes that allow partial circumvention of spatial confinement, altered metabolic demands (e.g., aerobic glycolysis), or resistance to apoptotic signaling gain incremental footholds in the tissue ecosystem.339 These cells are not inherently malignant but are better equipped to survive and adapt within localized pockets of ecological disturbance. This idea reframes early tumorigenesis as a trajectory across successive adaptive peaks, where the malignant phenotype emerges only after passing through multiple intermediate states of partial fitness under local selection. Early tumor evolution sets the stage for future malignancy, not by deterministic progression but by generating a reservoir of genetic diversity from which aggressive phenotypes may later emerge. In this context, the tissue ecosystem acts as both a barrier and a selective filter, shaping which clones survive, expand, or are eliminated. Only those clones able to adapt to niche constraints—such as hypoxia, growth factor scarcity, or immune pressure—advance along the path toward transformation.Progression to advanced disease: invasion, recurrence and metastasisIn the tumor’s primary habitat, cancer clones are initially restrained by physical architecture and resource limitations. For instance, intestinal stem cells are sequestered in crypts, an anatomical niche that naturally suppresses uncontrolled proliferation.340 However, through the acquisition of traits such as enhanced migratory capacity, resistance to apoptosis, and angiogenic potential, cancer cells can circumvent these constraints, gaining invasive and metastatic competence.Local invasion itself can be understood as an evolutionary response to ecological stress within the tumor microenvironment. As expanding clones compete for limited space, oxygen, and nutrients, they encounter increasing selective pressure that favors phenotypes capable of escaping their original niche.28 This includes the emergence of EMT-like features, cytoskeletal remodeling, and the secretion of proteolytic enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), enabling cells to degrade basement membranes and invade adjacent stroma.341 From an ecological standpoint, invasion represents a form of habitat escape—an adaptive response to spatial confinement and environmental degradation, whereby mobile clones migrate toward new, less competitive niches at the invasive front.Metastasis, in turn, represents a more complex evolutionary progression wherein successful dissemination and colonization at distant sites require not only cellular adaptability but also active modification of target tissues. Increasing evidence supports the existence of a “premetastatic niche”, an environment primed by tumor-secreted factors—such as exosomes, inflammatory cytokines (e.g., S100A8/9), and VEGF—that condition distant organs even before the arrival of disseminated tumor cells (DTCs).342 These signals recruit bone marrow–derived myeloid progenitors, remodel the extracellular matrix, suppress immune surveillance, and enhance vascular permeability, effectively constructing a supportive niche that improves the fitness landscape for incoming tumor cells. The evolution of this long-range intercellular communication can thus be seen as a strategic adaptation that anticipates and mitigates the severe bottlenecks associated with colonizing foreign microenvironments.Spatial heterogeneity in resource availability continues to act as a potent selective pressure that fosters cell migration. Upon dissemination to distant tissues, cancer cells encounter novel environmental challenges, which further shape subclonal diversification. This ecological perspective helps explain the evolutionary rationale for metastasis. Indeed, in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, Yachida et al. demonstrated that distant metastases tend to emerge late during the clonal evolution of the primary tumor, suggesting that only clones with an optimal suite of adaptive traits—what might be termed a “complete fitness package”—are capable of successful colonization of distant sites.343Recurrence represents a reiteration of this evolutionary process. On the one hand, it may reflect the expansion of therapy-resistant clones or cancer stem cells that evaded initial eradication. On the other hand, recurrent tumors often exhibit greater aggressiveness, potentially linked to enhanced self-renewal capacity. In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), for example, progression to blast crisis is accompanied by loss of p53-mediated checkpoint control and upregulation of stemness-associated programs, leading to an increased frequency of leukemia-initiating cells and more rapid disease progression.344Evolutionary dynamics of treatment sensitivity and resistanceTherapeutic intervention introduces a potent and often abrupt form of artificial selection into the tumor ecosystem. Cytotoxic chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents dramatically reshape clonal dynamics by eliminating a large fraction of tumor cells while simultaneously selecting for preexisting or therapy-induced resistant variants.345 This process mirrors natural selection in accelerated form—massive cell death generates intense evolutionary pressure, and survivors, often harboring resistant phenotypes, are poised to repopulate a remodeled landscape.While initial responses may be profound, long-term disease control remains elusive in most advanced or metastatic cancers. The failure of therapy is frequently attributable to the evolutionary resilience of residual cancer cell populations. CSCs, in particular, represent a persistent reservoir of clonal regeneration. Their relative quiescence, niche protection, and intrinsic plasticity confer resistance to therapies that predominantly target proliferating cells.346 Moreover, if CSCs possess intrinsic genetic instability, these further fuel the diversity of resistant phenotypes and enhance their adaptive potential. Heritable epigenetic variation, reversible cellular states such as dormancy, and nongenetic plasticity—including oncogene bypass and pathway rewiring—also contribute to escape mechanisms.347Following therapy, the tissue ecosystem itself becomes an evolutionary force. Antitumor therapy may drastically alter the tumor microenvironment, depleting not only cancer cells but also altering stromal composition, immune surveillance, and nutrient availability.348 This “ecological reset” provides both new selective pressures and ecological niches that favor the expansion of surviving clones.Despite optimism surrounding the precision oncology paradigm—exemplified by the early success of targeted agents such as imatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)—most solid tumors lack such monoclonal vulnerability. Even in CML, resistance inevitably arises either through secondary kinase mutations or persistence of quiescent CSCs.349 Thus, to overcome resistance, treatment strategies must shift from static targeting to dynamic management—anticipating clonal evolution, applying combination therapies to preclude escape routes and modulating the fitness landscape to suppress resistant lineages. Integrating real-time evolutionary monitoring into clinical care may represent a critical step toward sustained disease control.350Combination therapies, especially those modeled on antiviral treatment paradigms such as for HIV, have been proposed as a means to prolong disease control.351 However, unlike viruses with a small number of genetic targets, cancer cells possess thousands of genes and regulatory elements capable of mediating resistance. Even so, the range of resistance mechanisms appears finite in specific contexts. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), for example, at least 12 distinct mechanisms of resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as erlotinib, have been identified, with the most common being the EGFR T790M mutation.352 This observation has spurred rational combination strategies—such as pairing EGFR TKIs with EGFR-directed antibodies—to delay or prevent resistance emergence. A similar principle has shown clinical efficacy in ERBB2-positive breast cancer, where combined blockade with trastuzumab (a monoclonal antibody) and lapatinib (a small-molecule inhibitor) has achieved durable responses.353These adaptive treatment strategies exploit evolutionary trade-offs. In hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, resistance to anti-estrogen therapy is often mediated by upregulation of growth factor signaling pathways (e.g., EGFR, IGF1R, TGF-β, FGF), which suppress estrogen receptor (ER) expression.354 Conversely, inhibition of these pathways may resensitize cells to hormone therapy. Such reciprocal plasticity between signaling axes offers an opportunity to design “evolutionarily futile cycles”, in which sequential therapies exploit the tumor’s adaptive responses to corner clonal trajectories into vulnerable states.Promising therapeutic targets and clinical research progress on tumor evolutionTo bridge the gap between preclinical findings and clinical applications, we focus on strategies to disrupt adaptive resistance and tumor evolutionary dynamics. Tumor evolution is driven by genetic instability, epigenetic reprogramming, and interactions with the tumor microenvironment, making it crucial to target these mechanisms for effective cancer treatment. We will discuss promising therapeutic targets identified in preclinical models (Table 1), as well as targets actively being tested in clinical trials (Table 2). By understanding the drivers of tumor evolution, such as genomic instability, immune evasion, and metabolic adaptation, we can develop precision therapies to directly combat resistance and adaptability. Additionally, adaptive treatment strategies that adjust to tumor pressures will be explored. These approaches are vital for translating preclinical insights into clinical strategies, ultimately improving long-term cancer outcomes and overcoming resistance mechanisms inherent in tumor evolution (Fig. 5).Fig. 5Promising therapeutic targets for tumor evolution. Pembrolizumabactive, not recruitingADT adaptive androgen deprivation therapy, mCRC metastatic colorectal cancer, MSS microsatellite-stable, MMR mismatch repair-proficientBlocking the origin of tumor evolutionA promising approach to halting tumor evolution is to target its origins, focusing on the mechanisms that drive genetic instability and tumor adaptability. By disrupting the initial steps of tumor evolution, such as metabolic reprogramming, immune evasion, and genomic instability, it is possible to limit the ability of tumors to evolve and adapt to therapy. This strategy holds potential in preventing the emergence of resistant clones and halting tumor progression at its source. By understanding and targeting these foundational mechanisms, we can develop therapies that not only treat the existing tumor burden but also prevent further evolution and therapeutic resistance.One promising strategy to block the origin of tumor evolution focuses on polyamine metabolism, particularly in immune cells within the tumor microenvironment. Polyamines, such as spermine and spermidine, are essential for maintaining cell growth, survival, and function, particularly in the context of immune cells such as tumor-associated myeloid cells (TAMCs).355 Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits a prominent infiltration of TAMCs and a marked deficiency in T cells.356 TAMCs play a crucial role in promoting immunosuppression, acting as a significant obstacle to effective immunotherapy in gliomas.357,358 In glioblastoma, TAMCs use highly basic polyamines to buffer acidic environments, thereby supporting their survival and immunosuppressive functions in the harsh tumor microenvironment.356 Inhibition of polyamine synthesis with agents such as difluoromethylornithine (DFMO) has shown therapeutic potential by reducing the intracellular pH in TAMCs and disrupting their survival, thus enhancing immune responses and improving animal survival in glioblastoma models.359 This strategy is particularly effective when combined with immunotherapy or radiotherapy, as it targets the metabolic adaptations that tumor-associated immune cells use to promote tumor survival and immune evasion.359,360 These findings indicate that disrupting the polyamine axis not only targets the immune cells that contribute to tumor progression but also reduces the tumor’s ability to adapt to its microenvironment, preventing further evolutionary adaptations.Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3), a crucial mitochondrial deacetylase, plays a multifaceted role in cancer, affecting tumor progression through its regulation of cellular metabolism, oxidative stress, and DNA damage repair.361–363 SIRT3 has a context-dependent role in cancer, either promoting or inhibiting tumor progression depending on the specific tumor type and stage.364 For instance, in cancers with high oxidative stress, such as clear-cell renal carcinoma (ccRCC), SIRT3 mitigates excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) to facilitate tumor growth.365 Conversely, in cancers such as breast and prostate cancer, SIRT3 acts as a tumor suppressor by controlling mitochondrial functions and inhibiting epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT).366,367 Additionally, the involvement of SIRT3 in regulated cell death (RCD) pathways, such as apoptosis and autophagy, contributes to both tumor suppression and resistance, making it a promising target for therapeutic modulation.368–370 Several small-molecule inhibitors and activators targeting SIRT3 have shown potential in preclinical models, emphasizing the need for further exploration of SIRT3 modulation in cancer therapy. SIRT3 inhibitors, such as 3-triazolylpyridine and 4′-bromo-resveratrol, disrupt the deacetylation process of key mitochondrial proteins, leading to impaired tumor cell proliferation and migration.371–373 These inhibitors, developed using structure-based designs, have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models, including leukemia, ovarian, and colon cancers. On the other hand, SIRT3 activators such as honokiol and compound 33c enhance mitochondrial function and autophagy, showing significant promise in reducing tumor cell growth and promoting apoptosis.374,375 Despite these promising results, further research is needed to optimize these modulators for clinical use, considering the complex, context-dependent roles of SIRT3 in various cancers. Additionally, new strategies, such as allosteric inhibitors and proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), are being explored to improve SIRT3-targeted therapies.364,376 The therapeutic potential of modulating SIRT3 holds considerable promise but requires careful consideration of tumor-specific factors for maximum efficacy.As mentioned before, APOBEC3 enzymes, particularly APOBEC3B, have been implicated as significant sources of somatic mutagenesis in cancer. In cancers such as breast cancer, APOBEC enzymes drive tumor evolution by inducing mutations that fuel tumor progression and metastasis, as well as contributing to therapy resistance.377 Inhibiting these enzymes could prevent the emergence of such pro-cancerous mutations. Notably, A3B, a key driver of APOBEC3-induced mutations, is nonessential in humans, as demonstrated by the presence of a gene deletion allele in the general population.378 Although the concept of APOBEC mutagenesis in cancer is relatively recent, efforts to develop specific inhibitors are still in the early stages. However, the recent release of the A3A-ssDNA and A3Bctd-ssDNA cocrystal structures has provided valuable insights into the binding interactions between A3 enzymes and their ssDNA substrates.379,380 This structural knowledge will facilitate the rational design of small-molecule inhibitors targeting A3 enzymes. Consistent with this rationale, APOBEC3 inhibition can be framed as blocking the mutational fuel of tumor evolution. Restricting APOBEC3B splicing plasticity suppresses A3B expression and mutagenic activity, while bladder cancer genomic data link APOBEC signatures with progression from non-muscle-invasive to muscle-invasive disease.381,382 Because APOBEC-driven mutagenesis promotes subclonal diversification, chemotherapy resistance and STING-dependent dissemination in A3A-driven tumors, targeting APOBEC3 activity or its downstream inflammatory axis may restrain evolutionary progression.383–386 Additionally, a potential “therapy-by-hypermutation” strategy could be explored, where small molecule agonists increase mutagenesis to toxic levels, thereby promoting cancer cell death, although this approach is more complex than the inhibition of A3B.387 Conversely, APOBEC3 activation may be exploitable when mutational stress creates therapeutic vulnerability. APOBEC3A/B-induced mutagenesis can increase neoepitope generation and T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity, improving responses to immune checkpoint blockade in melanoma and breast cancer.388,389 It may also sensitize tumor cells to cisplatin and DNA-damage response inhibitors, including ATR, Chk1/2, WEE1 and PARP inhibitors, across breast cancer, leukemia, osteosarcoma, p53-deficient and pancreatic cancer models.384,390–393Moreover, the ARETHUSA trial in the context of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) employed a two-phase treatment strategy, focusing on temozolomide (TMZ) to induce hypermutation, followed by immunotherapy with pembrolizumab in patients with RAS-mutant, microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors.394 The first phase involved TMZ as a priming agent to create a mutational burden increase, potentially making the tumors more immunogenic. This was based on the concept that pharmacologic inactivation of mismatch repair (MMR) could transform immunologically “cold” tumors into “hot” ones by increasing tumor mutational burden (TMB) and neoantigen presentation, thus enhancing their susceptibility to immune checkpoint blockade. Similarly, the MAYA trial explored a related strategy, combining TMZ priming with immune checkpoint inhibitors, specifically low-dose ipilimumab and nivolumab, in patients with MGMT-silenced, MSS mCRC.395 TMZ treatment induced hypermutation, which increased TMB, thereby sensitizing tumors to subsequent immunotherapy. This approach, initially showing promising results, highlights the potential of combining conventional chemotherapy with immunotherapy to overcome resistance mechanisms and enhance treatment efficacy in otherwise resistant mCRC. Both trials underscore the potential of manipulating the tumor mutational landscape as a therapeutic strategy, converting immunologically unresponsive tumors into those amenable to immune system targeting, thus offering a novel approach to tackle tumor evolution and resistance.Preventive combination therapy for tumorsThe evolution of tumors, driven by genomic instability, clonal selection, and adaptive resistance mechanisms, is a major challenge in cancer treatment. While targeted therapies have made significant strides, the emergence of resistance remains a critical issue. One promising strategy to overcome this challenge is preventive combination therapy, which aims to preemptively target both traditional therapeutic targets and the mechanisms underlying potential secondary treatment resistance. By using combination therapies from the outset, clinicians can block multiple signaling pathways involved in tumor evolution, reducing the likelihood of resistance development and improving patient outcomes.Preclinical studies have shown that early intervention with combination therapies targeting key oncogenic drivers can significantly delay the onset of resistance. For instance, dual-targeted therapy for tumors harboring mutations in genes such as EGFR and BRAF has been shown to provide more durable responses than monotherapy.396–398 In particular, targeting both EGFR and MEK has been shown to inhibit the reactivation of alternative signaling pathways, such as the MAPK pathway, thereby preventing the emergence of resistance due to bypass signaling.397 Moreover, targeting multiple components within the same pathway can reduce the possibility of the tumor adapting through mutational changes that activate alternate pathways.The PALOMA-3 study on metastatic breast cancer demonstrated that combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with endocrine therapy significantly improved progression-free survival in patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, even in cases of acquired endocrine resistance.399 This combination therapy also illustrated the importance of preventing the emergence of resistance by targeting both tumor growth drivers and mechanisms of treatment resistance. Such strategies are crucial not only for managing existing treatment resistance but also for potentially preventing resistance from developing.Additionally, combination therapies are being explored in the context of immunotherapy. Tumors often evolve immune evasion mechanisms, complicating treatment. By combining immune checkpoint inhibitors with targeted therapies, such as EGFR inhibitors or HER family-targeting agents, researchers aim to prevent immune resistance and enhance the immune system’s ability to recognize and destroy tumor cells.400 The Pan-HER antibody mixture, for example, targets multiple HER family receptors, overcoming the tumor’s ability to adapt to one receptor’s inhibition and providing a broader approach to tackling tumor heterogeneity.400In the case of RAS-driven tumors, mTOR and HDAC inhibitors are being studied as potential combination treatments to induce catastrophic oxidative stress, thereby targeting tumors that lack a single actionable driver.401 By inducing oxidative stress in a cooperative manner, these inhibitors disrupt the tumor’s protective mechanisms, ultimately preventing tumor adaptation and survival. Such combination approaches are especially critical in cancers lacking clear, targetable mutations but characterized by complex, evolving resistance profiles.In summary, the key to preventing tumor evolution lies in the strategic use of combination therapies. By targeting multiple drivers of tumor growth and resistance from the outset, it is possible to delay or prevent the emergence of resistant clones. These strategies, incorporating both molecularly targeted agents and immunotherapy, hold significant promise in improving treatment outcomes and managing the dynamic challenges posed by tumor evolution. The integration of preventive combination therapies into clinical practice represents a critical next step in the fight against cancer.Dynamic adjustment of adaptive treatment strategiesThe concept of adaptive therapy (AT) has gained significant attention in recent years as a strategy to address the challenges posed by tumor evolution and the development of treatment resistance. Traditional cancer treatment paradigms often focus on maximizing tumor cell death, typically through the use of maximum tolerated doses of chemotherapy or targeted therapies. However, this approach may accelerate the emergence of resistant clones, leading to treatment failure. In contrast, adaptive therapy aims to exploit the evolutionary dynamics of tumors, particularly the fitness costs associated with resistance mechanisms, by dynamically adjusting treatment schedules to maintain a balance between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant tumor populations. This strategy seeks to inhibit the growth of drug-resistant clones while promoting the survival of sensitive clones, ultimately achieving long-term tumor control.One of the key benefits of adaptive therapy is the potential for long-term disease control without the need for continuous high-dose treatment. This concept has been explored in various cancers, including ovarian cancer and prostate cancer, with promising results. Studies have demonstrated that adaptive therapy can extend progression-free survival and reduce the overall drug dose required for effective tumor control.402,403 By modulating the timing and dosing of therapies based on the dynamic tumor response, adaptive therapy aims to prevent the rapid emergence of resistance and prolong the effectiveness of treatment.In ovarian cancer, a disease often characterized by high rates of chemoresistance, adaptive therapy with carboplatin has shown significant promise. It has been demonstrated that carboplatin-based adaptive therapy could maintain long-term control of chemotherapy-resistant ovarian cancer.403 The therapy exploits the selective fitness costs associated with the resistant populations under low-resource conditions, causing a decline and apoptosis of these resistant cells while allowing the regrowth of drug-sensitive cells during treatment breaks. In both preclinical models and clinical trials, adaptive therapy caused fluctuations in the sensitive/resistant tumor population size and significantly extended the survival of tumor-bearing mice.403 The study also revealed that these fluctuations in resistant cell populations correlated strongly with disease burden, providing further evidence that adaptive therapy could effectively control tumor progression without inducing the rapid emergence of resistance.The integration of evolutionary dynamics into adaptive therapy is facilitated by mathematical and computational models that predict tumor growth patterns and guide treatment schedules. These models, such as the Lotka-Volterra equations used to simulate competition between different tumor clones, provide valuable insights into how tumors evolve under treatment pressures. Zhang et al. applied these models to the treatment of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, showing that adaptive therapy, guided by tumor-specific dynamics, significantly increased the time to progression (TTP) compared to conventional dosing schedules.402 In this study, a pilot clinical trial demonstrated that adaptive therapy resulted in stable tumor oscillations and reduced cumulative drug use by nearly 50%, with the median TTP extending to at least 27 months. This computational approach not only validated the clinical potential of adaptive therapy but also underscored the importance of using dynamic treatment schedules based on real-time tumor monitoring.Adaptive therapy has also shown potential in breast cancer, particularly in models of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). A study applied an evolution-guided treatment strategy in preclinical models of breast cancer, including both TNBC and estrogen receptor-positive (ER + ) breast cancer.404 The study used algorithms linked to tumor response, monitored by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), to adjust treatment doses dynamically. The findings showed that adaptive therapy could maintain tumor control with progressively smaller doses of chemotherapy over time. In 60-80% of animals, continued tumor size decline allowed treatment-free intervals of up to several weeks, indicating that adaptive therapy could significantly reduce the need for continuous treatment while still maintaining disease control.404 Moreover, it has been proven that adaptive therapy leads to vascular normalization and reduced tumor necrosis, suggesting that the treatment not only controls tumor growth but also improves the tumor microenvironment. These results highlight the potential of adaptive therapy to provide long-term tumor control while minimizing the side effects typically associated with continuous high-dose chemotherapy.Despite the promising results from preclinical models and early clinical trials, there are several challenges in translating adaptive therapy into widespread clinical practice. One key issue is the need for continuous and accurate monitoring of tumor dynamics. Adaptive therapy requires real-time data on tumor growth and treatment resistance profiles to adjust treatment schedules accordingly. This necessitates the development of advanced imaging techniques and biomarker identification strategies to track tumor evolution in a noninvasive manner.405 Another challenge is the integration of adaptive therapy with existing treatment regimens. For adaptive therapy to be successful, it must be carefully tailored to individual patients, taking into account factors such as tumor heterogeneity, patient-specific responses, and the presence of specific mutations or resistance mechanisms. The development of robust computational models that can predict optimal treatment schedules for individual patients will be crucial in overcoming these challenges and ensuring the success of adaptive therapy in clinical settings.Several clinical trials are currently exploring the efficacy of adaptive therapy in various cancers, including metastatic prostate cancer, ovarian cancer, and melanoma.405 These trials aim to validate the preclinical findings and provide evidence for the clinical feasibility of adaptive therapy. The results of these trials will be critical in determining the future role of adaptive therapy in cancer treatment. Future directions in adaptive therapy include the integration of immunotherapy with adaptive strategies. By combining immune checkpoint inhibitors with adaptive dosing, it may be possible to enhance the immune system’s ability to target resistant tumor clones, thereby providing a more comprehensive approach to cancer treatment.405 Additionally, advancements in personalized medicine and liquid biopsy techniques could enable more precise monitoring of tumor dynamics and improve the customization of adaptive therapy protocols for individual patients.Other therapeutic targets and clinical research progress on tumor evolutionOne of the most exciting and innovative strategies to target tumor evolution involves nanomedicine. As tumors constantly evolve in response to environmental pressures, therapeutic agents must adapt to remain effective. Recent advancements in nanomedicine have provided new insights into leveraging nanoparticles as tools not only for drug delivery but also as agents capable of targeting evolving tumors. Researchers have critically reviewed the use of nanomaterials as therapeutic agents, emphasizing their ability to target the dynamic nature of tumor evolution.406 Nanoparticles offer several advantages over conventional molecular agents, including tunability, tumor-targeting properties, and multiple possible mechanisms of action. These properties make them particularly well suited to counteract tumor evolution, which often renders traditional therapies ineffective. The use of nano-based delivery systems for drugs targeting multiple pathways simultaneously could offer a solution to the evolving nature of cancer cells, providing a new frontier in tumor treatment.406Furthermore, nanoparticle-mediated copper chaperone inhibition has shown potential in restoring the immunogenicity of tumor cells, enhancing chemotherapy and immunotherapy efficacy. By manipulating copper-dependent signaling pathways, these nanoparticles promote reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, triggering immunogenic cell death (ICD) and stimulating a robust antitumor immune response.407 Such strategies underline the role of nanotechnology not only in drug delivery but also in shaping the tumor microenvironment and promoting the immune system’s ability to fight evolving cancer cells.Another significant challenge in tumor evolution is the role of dormant cancer cells in therapy resistance and metastasis. Cancer cell dormancy, or quiescence, is a central mechanism by which tumors evade treatment, particularly in response to chemotherapy or targeted therapies. Francescangeli et al. reviewed the complex interplay between stemness, dormancy, and therapy resistance, focusing on how these factors contribute to tumor progression.333 Dormant cells, which may not be actively proliferating, remain capable of reactivating and contributing to disease relapse. This phenomenon is particularly problematic in cancers such as breast cancer and lung cancer, where dormant cells are often found in metastatic sites. The understanding of dormant cancer cells (QCCs) has profound therapeutic implications. Recent studies have shown that QCCs not only are resilient to chemotherapy but also exhibit metabolic plasticity and immune evasion capabilities, making them difficult to target.333 Developing therapeutic strategies that target the core transcriptional programs and metabolic features of QCCs could provide a novel approach to prevent recurrence. Additionally, therapies that exploit the plasticity of cancer stem cells (CSCs) and their ability to switch phenotypes could be pivotal in overcoming therapy resistance.408–413 By targeting these cells during their dormant phase or preventing their reactivation, we may be able to achieve a more effective and durable response in cancer treatment.A promising strategy to understand and predict tumor evolution involves computational modeling. Pénisson et al. introduced a mathematical framework for modeling tumor evolution, focusing on the endogenous mutational processes that drive cancer risk and progression.414 By combining DNA sequencing data from healthy human tissues with predictions of somatic mutations, this model aims to quantify the mutational load within various tissues over time. The findings suggest that endogenous mutations account for a significant portion of cancer risk, and understanding these processes could lead to better prevention and early detection strategies. This model also highlights the potential of using mathematical frameworks to predict how tumors evolve in response to treatments, offering insights into the timing of mutational events and the emergence of resistance. The integration of such models with clinical data could enable the prediction of individual patient outcomes and help tailor therapies to prevent tumor progression before resistance mechanisms emerge.414Immunotherapy continues to be one of the most promising areas in cancer treatment. However, as tumors evolve, they often develop resistance to immune-based therapies, complicating treatment efforts. The effectiveness of immunotherapy is heavily influenced by the tumor’s ability to respond to immune modulation. Immune “hot”, “altered”, and “cold” tumors—terms used to describe the presence or absence of a baseline immune response—require different therapeutic approaches.415 Tumors that are “hot” typically respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors, while “cold” tumors, lacking immune infiltrates, show minimal response. Combination therapies, including checkpoint inhibitors and other immune-modulating agents, have shown promise in transforming cold tumors into hot tumors. Recent advancements in combination immunotherapy aim to harness the tumor’s ability to adapt to the immune system, promoting the reactivation of suppressed immune responses. For instance, combining STING agonists with immune checkpoint blockade can significantly enhance the immune response against tumors by activating the STING pathway, which is involved in the innate immune response to cancer.416 Such approaches are particularly effective in cancers with a low mutational burden, where the immune system’s recognition of tumor cells may be compromised.As tumors evolve, they often accumulate mutations that can serve as useful biomarkers for predicting treatment response. Recent advances in liquid biopsy technologies have enabled the detection of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) as potential biomarkers for tracking tumor evolution and therapeutic efficacy.417 These technologies allow for real-time monitoring of treatment response and the emergence of resistant subclones, providing valuable insights into tumor dynamics without the need for invasive tissue biopsies. In metastatic breast cancer, for example, a digital RNA signature derived from CTCs has been shown to predict early therapeutic responses, allowing clinicians to adjust treatment regimens more effectively.417 By identifying specific mutations within CTCs, it is possible to detect the onset of resistance mechanisms before clinical progression is evident, enabling earlier intervention.Protein kinase inhibitors (PKIs), particularly tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), are among the most rapidly growing classes of cancer drugs. These inhibitors target signaling pathways that are often dysregulated in cancer, including the BRAF, EGFR, and ALK pathways. However, the development of resistance to TKIs remains a significant challenge.418 One approach to overcoming this challenge is the development of combination therapies that target both tumor cells and the mechanisms underlying resistance. The concept of a drug resistance index for cancer (DRIC) has been proposed to help predict the likelihood of resistance development and tailor treatment strategies accordingly.418 By combining TKIs with other agents, such as immune modulators or inhibitors of compensatory signaling pathways, it may be possible to reduce the risk of resistance and prolong treatment efficacy.The concept of precision medicine has made significant strides in recent years, allowing for treatments tailored to the specific genetic makeup of individual tumors. By identifying specific mutations or gene expression profiles, clinicians can more accurately target therapies to the underlying causes of cancer. However, as tumors evolve, they often develop new mutations that render initial treatments ineffective. The dynamic nature of tumor evolution, combined with the heterogeneity observed in many cancers, means that adaptive strategies must continuously evolve alongside treatment regimens. The use of personalized approaches that incorporate tumor evolution models into clinical decision-making will likely become the norm in the future. These models can predict how tumors will evolve in response to treatment, allowing for proactive adjustments in therapy to counter resistance before it emerges.419,420Emerging therapeutic strategies targeting the dynamic process of tumor evolution offer promising avenues for overcoming resistance mechanisms. From nanomedicine and immune modulation to precision medicine and computational modeling, these strategies are poised to enhance current treatment regimens and provide new options for patients with resistant or metastatic cancers. Continued research into the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, coupled with the development of targeted therapies, holds the potential to revolutionize cancer treatment and improve patient outcomes.s and perspectivesIn conclusion, we offer a comprehensive multidimensional analysis of the signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms governing tumor evolution. Based on early foundational theories, innovative technologies such as high-throughput sequencing and liquid biopsy greatly enhanced our understanding of tumor evolution at the cellular and spatiotemporal levels. The dynamic interplay of multidimensional factors shapes the evolutionary trajectories of tumors, promoting their survival and adaptability.
