CircRNAs are widely expressed in almost all cell types, with a significant portion regulating gene expression by binding to miRNAs and proteins. circRNAs can also produce peptides in a cap-independent mechanism. These intrinsic features have positioned synthetic circRNA as a promising candidate for RNA-based therapeutics. circRNA has demonstrated superior efficacy over linear RNA in various therapeutic areas such as vaccines, protein replacement, and gene editing. The multiple binding sites on circRNA can sustainably interact with miRNA and RBPs, effectively repressing oncogenic pathways. circRNA vaccines yield higher abundance proteins than linear mRNA, inducing stronger immune responses with prolonged immune efficacy. circRNA can also serve as a vector for gene editing to achieve precise knockout of pathogenic genes.Table 3Exogenous circRNA in tumor therapy.Table 3circRNADelivery vectorMechanismRef.TI-0093LNPEncodes HPV16 E7/E6 to induce immunity (clinical trial)172Apt-circRNAsSubcutaneous injectionEncodes tumor neoantigens (first-in-human trial)125acircRNAExosomeThe aptamer inhibits CTNNB1 and NFKB pathways in BCa cells115circRNACARLNPPrimarily activates the vitality of immune cells by encoding CAR122circOVAGSer-CARTInduces a strong T cell response by encoding OVA170GSDMDENG circRNALNPThe translated GSDMD leads to mtROS leakage, triggering antitumor immunity; mitochondrial autophagy mediates adaptive immune responses173circREREAAVIt stabilizes MAVS expression by adsorbing miR-6837-3p, thereby activating the type I IFN signaling pathway113circRNAanti−CD19 CARElectroporation transfectionEncodes anti-CD19 CAR protein in T cells101circRNA 3 × PTPN2LNPEncodes the liver cancer-specific tumor neoantigen Ptpn2_I383T124cmRNAIntratumoral injectionEncodes multiple cytokine126circ-SHPRHAAVCirc-SHPRH induces the expression of P21 by encoding SHPRH-146aa, inhibiting the CDK4-cyclin D complex and blocking the cell cycle progression117hsa_circ_0000520LentivirusesActs as a scaffold to promote the ubiquitination and degradation of LIN28A174circFAM53BLiposomeEncodes peptides with high affinity for HLA-I and HLA-II to enhance infiltration of T cells69Circ-arRNALNPActs for the in vivo RNA editing-mediated repair of the TP53-W53X nonsense mutation134circFOXO3 plasmidsGold nanoparticlesInduces cell apoptosis54circUGP2 plasmidsLNPUpregulates ADGRB1 expression by sponging miR-3191-5p and acts as a transcriptional co-activator of PURB114circRNA-IL23LNPCombines IL-23 and MSA-2-Pt to inhibit tumor127AAV, adeno-associated virus; LNP, lipid nanoparticle.High-throughput screening and AI-assisted design have accelerated the identification of functional circRNA structure. These structures can be synthesized and cyclized in vitro using enzymatic ligation, chemical ligation, or ribozyme self-splicing methods. Currently, the PIE is the most widely applied method, producing circular transcripts through rearranging the intron structure, followed by spontaneous splicing within GTP and Mg2+ and other reactions. Residual linear precursors, free introns, template DNA, and other byproducts are removed through exonuclease degradation and electrophoresis or chromatography to minimize the non-specific immunogenicity. Nano drug delivery systems have brought promising strategies for the in vivo expression of circRNA. Delivery platforms such as LNP, VLP, and exosomes have been employed to encapsulate circRNA due to their good safety, targeting specificity, and stability. The tissue- and cell-targeting potential of circRNA is achieved through structural modifications and surface engineering of these carriers. The LVP-based Tornado system facilitates intracellular self-circularization of circRNA while maintaining high biological activity, expanding the application in circRNA delivery.Despite these advantages, several barriers still impede the mechanism exploration and clinical transformation, including identifying high-quality targets, scaling industrial circRNA production and purification, improving encapsulation, as well as mitigating immunogenicity of the material itself. Future research will focus more on overcoming these obstacles to make breakthroughs. Firstly, in terms of mechanism exploration, the sheer abundance of circRNAs far exceeds that of upstream genes; thus, it remains challenging to ascertain how tumor circRNAs are dysregulated through genetic inheritance. Genetic alterations, epigenetic modifications, and protein-level perturbations may all contribute to dysregulated circRNA expression185. A single circRNA may have multiple competitive binding sites, and the expression profiles vary significantly across different cell types and subcellular localizations, resulting in distinct functionalities. It remains unclear whether modulating circRNAs within a specific pathway may perturb competitive interactions and inadvertently influence unrelated signaling networks. Advances in RNA-Seq, CRISPR-Cas9 editing, and BSJ-specific probes have the potential to minimize false positives in screening differential circRNAs. Emerging nano-omics tools such as nanopore sequencing offer new opportunities to dissect relationships of circRNA and tumors186. However, there is still a lack of a gold standard algorithm for quantifying circRNA abundance. Additionally, the lack of a comprehensive circRNA library further complicates the screening process, hindering the efficient identification41.The advancement of circRNA therapeutics is further constrained by the limited efficiency of current preparation strategies. It is essential to first cyclize the long or structurally complex sequence. The incorporation of specific RBP motifs can enhance the efficiency of circularization by promoting the proximity of splice sites. For instance, the introduction of QKI allows for binding to two distant regions of RNA, forming a dimer that brings the two ends closer together187. For effective circRNA translation, modifications are often required to obtain sufficient translation levels. Incorporation of translational enhancers, such as Poly(A)-binding protein binding sequence EIF4G, into the 5′ UTR of circRNA can improve the translation efficiency. However, such modifications may result in an excessively long transcript that subsequently reduces cyclization efficiency and increases susceptibility to degradation188. Regarding the IRES-dependent translation mechanism, various truncated IRES optimization strategies have consistently led to reduced translation efficiency, as maintaining the stability in the secondary structure of IRES is critical. One feasible solution involves incorporating a series of minimal spacer sequences, which can nearly double cyclization efficiency with only a slight increase in transcript length188. Additionally, alternative RNA modifications have emerged as compelling alternatives, such as non-IRES-dependent m6A modifications that utilize YTHDF3 m6A readers to recognize m6A within a short DRACH and initiate translation. Additionally, the m6A motif can be specifically recognized by YTHDF2 within phase-separated condensates, thereby preventing RIGI exposure and reducing immunogenicity110. However, m6A modification may also induce changes in secondary structure folding, potentially impacting normal function. Furthermore, YTHDF2 is capable of binding to RNase P/MRP via HRSP12, which initiates rapid degradation of circRNA. Consequently, further investigation into m6A and other modifications is warranted189. Other motifs, such as a diverse array of 5′ modifications, may reveal additional functionalities. A comprehensive understanding of methylation modifications or capping necessitates further exploration from immunological, stability-related, and efficiency perspectives. In addition, for large molecular proteins like traditional Cas9 (>3000 nt), Compact alternatives, such as Cas12a with its smaller size, low off-target effect, and A/T-rich regions preference, represent an alternative solution130. Simultaneously, it is crucial to seek an alternative circularization method to achieve the desired length and structure. Researchers have also promoted circularization by design, circRNA-promoting RNA (cpRNA) to increase the stable pairing of the flanking introns by bringing the terminal sequences of precursor RNA closer together40. At the manufacturing level, purification remains a major unmet need. Various purification techniques, such as HPLC and electrophoresis, can improve the resolution of products; they are currently limited to small-scale laboratory applications, leaving industrial-scale purification technology still under development. Another major challenge in preparation is immunogenicity. Although the immunostimulatory effect of circRNA is considerably lower compared to the corresponding linear RNA, Chen et al.190 have shown that circRNA spliced with the intron from the T4 phage td gene can induce the expression of RIGI, while endogenous introns appear to mitigate this effect. Some researchers have also proposed that RNA modification may regulate immune gene expression, but there is currently no standardized experimental protocol for verifying immunogenicity88. In addition, studies have explored leveraging the immunogenic properties of circRNA by delivering it as an immune adjuvant in conjunction with soluble proteins to elicit specific immune responses191.The delivery of circRNA remains a critical issue. Although the stability of circRNA is better than that of linear RNA, it still requires an appropriate carrier to prevent nonspecific degradation and ensure bioavailability. Active targeting modifications are particularly important, especially in the high osmotic pressure environment of solid tumors. LNP, VLP, and exosomes demonstrate excellent biocompatibility and structural stability. Further improvements are needed in material modification and loading capabilities. Enhancing loading efficiency must be balanced against risks such as particle aggregation, elevated immunogenicity, and other side effects that may arise from alterations in parameters such as Zeta and particle size. Overcoming circRNA inactivation presents another significant obstacle. While delivery-associated immunogenicity has received increasing attention, a comprehensive and systematic safety assessment remains insufficient. In addition to adverse reactions stemming from residual impurities, potential off-target effects and immune inflammation induced by repeated dosing necessitate further investigation. Intravenous carriers tend to accumulate in the liver, with this accumulation exacerbated by high doses or chronic administration192. Chronic toxicity to non-target organs such as the kidneys and lungs, alongside the liver, also warrants additional scrutiny. Immune responses or neutralizing antibodies elicited by components of the carrier itself can result in unexpected immune reactions and may alter existing immune recognition, thereby diminishing efficacy193,194. Furthermore, different administration routes may lead to distinct profiles of innate immune activation. A more detailed quantitative analysis of pharmacokinetics, biodistribution analyses to define delivery, clearance, and tissue-specific accumulation is essential within biological systems. The functional degradation effects associated with industrial storage and transportation of carriers also require ongoing clarification. For viral vectors specifically, potential genome insertion represents the most critical concern. Employing non-integrating viral particles has substantially mitigated this risk; additionally, mechanisms such as integration site monitoring are utilized to further reduce this concern. Concurrently, the development of novel carrier systems remains an important direction. For example, the Selective Endogenous eNcapsidation for cellular Delivery system utilizes a mechanism involving certain retrotransposon-derived proteins in mammalian genomes, which can form capsid particles that encapsulate their own mRNA for transfer via vesicles. The PEG10 protein derived from human retrotransposon factors was selected and modified to encapsulate the target specifically UTR sequence modified with PEG10 at both ends by reprogramming PEG10-VLP. The specificity of cellular targeting was further enhanced through fusing targeting peptides, facilitating the successful delivery and expression of the CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo. Theoretically, the same mechanism could be applied to circRNA or its precursor sequences through UTR reprogramming195. In addition, achieving efficient overexpression of circRNA in vivo remains an urgent challenge that must be solved. The transposon transfection method previously discussed offers a feasible strategy that utilizes specific drivers to enable controlled expression in targeted cells. However, this approach also requires the delivery capabilities of an effective vector.CircRNA-based therapy presents an unprecedented method for precision treatment. Several diagnostic clinical trials are underway to investigate circRNA dysregulation. Concurrently, clinical trials focusing on exogenous circRNA delivery have begun to advance. For example, TI-0093 is currently undergoing Phase I clinical trials for advanced recurrent or metastatic solid tumors associated with HPV16+, which involves five intramuscular injections aimed at evaluating safety and early efficacy. Additionally, the multivalent neoantigen circRNA vaccine apt-circRNA-KR2 has already shown preliminary safety and immune responsiveness in first-in-human trials125,172. Beyond oncology, exogenous circRNA therapeutics are being explored for ischemic heart failure and radiation-induced xerostomia. It is evident that with deeper insights into the structural biology, intracellular dynamics, and regulatory mechanisms of circRNA-coupled with advancements in circRNA production, purification, and delivery technologies. This innovative RNA therapeutic approach holds considerable promise for application in oncology and potentially facilitates precise tumor treatment.Author contributionsXu Shi and Yue Zhao and Yunkai Tang contributed to the data collection and organization, writing-original draft preparation, figure and table drawing. Gang Fu and Chen Qian and Feng Li collected and provided part of the literature data. Zheyu Yang and Wenguo Cui contributed to the manuscript proofreading and correction. Wei Cai contributed to determining the general direction and objectives of the research, and revision of the manuscript.Conflicts of interestThe authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: Comprehensive Experimental and Computational Characterization of a Phenylacetamide‐Based Molecule
abstract: The aim of this study was to synthesize Tetrahydroisoquinoline Derivative 1 (M1) and to evaluate its biological activities in the SH‐SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line. Theoretical calculations for the investigated molecule were performed using the Gaussian software package at the B3LYP, HF, and M062X levels with the 6‐31g, 6‐31++g, and 6‐31++g(d,p) basis sets. Subsequently, the activity of the compound against SH‐SY5Y cancer–related proteins (PDB IDs: 2F37, 3PBL, and 5WIV) was assessed. In addition, the molecule‐likeness properties of the molecule were evaluated through ADME/T analyses. The cytotoxic activity of M1 in the SH‐SY5Y cell lines was determined using the MTT assay. Following treatment with M1, the expression levels of apoptosis‐related genes (MYC, CASP2, BAX, and NF‐κB1) and genes associated with DNA repair mechanisms (TP53, RAD51, BRCA2, and MDM2) were analyzed by RT‐PCR. Enzyme activities were also measured in M1‐treated SH‐SY5Y cells. The results demonstrated that M1 exerted its highest cytotoxic effect in the SH‐SY5Y cell line after 72 h of incubation. Compared with the control group, M1 showed a stronger effect on G6PDH activity in SH‐SY5Y cells, while catalase activity increased by 78% following M1 treatment. Moreover, M1 markedly reduced cell viability in SH‐SY5Y cells relative to the control group. In conclusion, these findings indicate that Tetrahydroisoquinoline Derivative M1 exhibits pronounced cytotoxic activity in SH‐SY5Y neuroblastoma cells and significantly modulates oxidative stress–related enzyme activities as well as the expression of genes involved in apoptosis and DNA repair pathways, suggesting that M1 may represent a novel and promising candidate for neuroblastoma therapy.
full_text: 1. Cancer and neurodegenerative diseases represent a growing public health challenge due to their rising global incidence. Due to their structural adaptability and ability to modulate several cancer‐related pathways, isoquinoline derivatives represent a key class of multitarget therapeutic agents. Several natural and synthetic isoquinoline alkaloids (ellipticine, palmatine, berberine, etc., analogs) exhibit significant anticancer effects on neuroblastoma (NB) cells, as extensively reviewed in the literature [1–4]. Inspired by these reports, our work employs acetoacetanilide in multicomponent reactions to access a variety of heterocyclic systems, notably isoquinoline derivatives [2–5]. Here, we present the biological evaluation of the compound, complementing its synthesis (Scheme 1) and crystallographic characterization reported previously [6].Scheme 1The synthesis of M1.NB is a type of neuroblastic tumor that arises from primitive neural crest cells located in the sympathetic nervous system, with 65% of cases originating from the adrenal medulla [7, 8]. While NB constitutes 8%–10% of childhood cancers, it represents approximately 15% of cancer‐related fatalities among children [9]. NB symptoms begin to appear in children aged 18 months, and 90% of them are diagnosed after the age of 10 [10]. Approximately 40% of patients diagnosed with NB are classified in the high‐risk group [11]. Various treatment methods, such as surgery and induction chemotherapy, autologous peripheral blood stem cell support, radiation, biological agents, and immunotherapy, are applied to high‐risk NB patients [12, 13]. Despite intensive treatment, children diagnosed with high‐risk NB are resistant to treatment, and their overall survival rate is approximately 50% [8]. Enhanced induction chemotherapy correlates with better overall survival rates [14, 15]. Doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, cisplatin, and etoposide are used as chemotherapeutic agents [16–20]. Despite current therapeutic advances and research, there is an unpredictable clinical situation for advanced NB. Rapid development of new strategies and targeted therapies is needed to cure the disease [21]. Apoptosis refers to a form of programmed cell death that involves genetic pathways crucial for development and the maintenance of homeostasis in healthy tissues. Apoptosis is important for maintaining tissue homeostasis in a multicellular organism [22]. Even in cases where very few cells undergo apoptosis, tumor formation may occur even if there is no proliferation rate [23]. Delayed activation of apoptotic pathways is an important phenomenon for NB regression and therapy resistance. Avoidance of apoptosis is not only involved in the gradual process of tumorigenesis but is also one of the hallmarks of human cancers, including NB. Current treatment regimens of cancer cells, namely, the response to chemo‐, radio‐, or immunotherapy, are largely due to the induction of apoptosis in neoplastic cells, combining resistance to apoptosis and resistance to therapy for response to cytotoxic treatments [24–26]. Dysregulation of cell cycle progression is seen in many human cancers. Accordingly, cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis may be affected, resulting in tumorigenesis [27]. Antitumor growth drugs that “accelerate” or “brake” excessive cell turnover may be a powerful treatment option for unfavorable NBs [28].Upon a thorough examination of the most recent studies, it becomes evident that theoretical calculations and experimental methodologies produce consistent results that mutually reinforce one another [29]. This scenario started to be utilized for the synthesis and design of more active and effective molecules in theoretical research conducted prior to experimental investigations [30]. Docking study is one of the most frequently employed techniques for comparing the biological activities of various molecules [31]. The molecular docking technique is employed to evaluate the efficacy of various molecules in relation to enzymes, aiming to identify those with the greatest biological activity. Experimental studies are guided by these calculations. For the theoretical calculations of the studied molecule, calculations were made at B3LYP, HF, and M062X [32–34] levels on the 6‐31g, 6‐31++g, and 6‐31++g(d,p) basis sets using the Gaussian package program. Afterwards, the activity of the studied molecule against the SH‐SY5Y cancer protein (PDB ID: 2F37, 3PBL, and 5WIV) [35–37] was examined. Ultimately, the characteristics of the M1 molecule associated with the molecule under investigation were assessed through the execution of ADME/T analysis.This study is among the limited number of investigations that address the biological effects of an isoquinoline‐derived compound on NB cells within an integrated framework combining experimental biochemical analyses and molecular docking approaches. Although numerous studies have reported the anticancer potential of isoquinoline alkaloids, the majority of these investigations are either restricted to experimental cytotoxicity data or fail to establish a direct link between theoretical calculations and biological validation. One of the most significant aspects of the present study is that the isoquinoline derivative, whose synthesis and crystallographic characterization were previously reported, was evaluated for the first time in a NB (SH‐SY5Y) cell line by analyzing expression changes in key apoptosis‐related genes (MYC, CASP2, BAX, and NF-κB1), as well as cell cycle–associated genes of major relevance in cancer biology (TP53, RAD51, BRCA2, and MDM2). In addition, the effects of the isoquinoline derivative on antioxidant defense mechanisms in SH‐SY5Y cells were investigated by measuring the activities of glutathione (GSH), glutathione S‐transferase (GST), glucose‐6‐phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH), catalase (CAT), and superoxide dismutase (SOD).2. Materials and 2.1. Chemistry SectionMelting points were measured using a Stuart SMP30 melting point apparatus, and no corrections were applied. The 1H and 13C NMR spectra of established chemicals were obtained using a Bruker Avance II+300 (UltraShieldTM Magnet) instrument, with measurements conducted in DMSO at frequencies of 300 and 75 MHz, respectively. With solvent resonance in DMSO‐d6 solutions serving as the internal standard, chemical shifts from tetramethylsilane were reported in parts per million. All chemicals available for commercial purchase were obtained from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany) and Fluka (Buchs, Switzerland) and utilized without additional purification. The reactions were observed using TLC on silica gel 60 f254 plates.The target compound (1) was synthesized via a multicomponent reaction involving acetoacetanilide, malononitrile, and piperazine hydrate in an ethanol–water medium. The reaction proceeds through condensation and subsequent cyclization steps at room temperature, affording the isoquinoline‐based phenylacetamide derivative. Detailed experimental conditions are provided in the supporting information file and Figures S1, S2, S3 and S4.2.2. Cell CultureSH‐SY5Y NB cells were maintained at 37°C in an incubator with 5% CO2 in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 100 U/mL penicillin. Cells were routinely passaged, and the culture medium was refreshed upon reaching the appropriate confluence.2.3. In Vitro Cytotoxicity Determination (MTT [(3‐(4,5‐Dimethylthiazol‐2‐yl)‐2,5‐Diphenyl Tetrazolium Bromide)])Cells were seeded into 96‐well plates at 1 × 104 cells/well, a density selected based on preliminary optimization to ensure appropriate confluence and a linear MTT response over 24–72 h, consistent with commonly used SH‐SY5Y MTT protocols. After 24 h, cells were treated with M1 at concentrations ranging from 1 to 100 μM and incubated for the indicated exposure times. Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay [38, 39]. Following incubation with MTT, the supernatant was aspirated, and 100 μL DMSO was added to each well to dissolve the formazan crystals. Plates were incubated for 15 min, and absorbance was measured at 570 nm. IC50 values were calculated using GraphPad Prism 7. All experiments were performed in triplicate (n = 3), and results are presented as the mean of three independent measurements.2.4. Extraction of RNA From Cell Culture SamplesThe SH‐SY5Y cell line was retreated with the IC50 dose of the M1 molecule, determined by the MTT assay at 48 h. Following an additional 48‐h incubation period, RNA isolation was performed in accordance with the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany, Cat No.: ) protocol. RNA isolation was performed from cells given the M1 molecule, from cells given the M1 molecule solution, and from control cells that received nothing.2.5. Complementary DNA (cDNA) SynthesisTo determine the expression levels of apoptosis‐related genes (MYC, CASP2, BAX, and NF-κB1) and genes associated with cell regulation/DNA repair mechanisms (TP53, RAD51, BRCA2, and MDM2), cDNA was synthesized from RNA in accordance with the manufacturer′s kit (RT First Strand Kit [Qiagen, Germany, Cat. No.: ]) protocol for subsequent RT‐PCR analysis.2.6. Real‐Time PCR AnalysisUtilizing the enhanced RT2 SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix Kit, the expression of apoptosis (MYC, CASP2, BAX, and NF-κB1) and cell cycle (TP53, RAD51, BRCA2, and MDM2) genes (RT2 qPCR Primer Assay [Qiagen, Germany]) was evaluated using the Δ CT technique on an RT‐PCR equipment. GAPDH was used for housekeeping. RT‐qPCR experiments were performed in triplicate (n = 3) for each experimental group, and the reported values represent the mean of three independent measurements. In this investigation, SYBR Green was utilized as a fluorescent dye. A 25 μL qPCR mix was made from samples containing cDNA in accordance with the kit instructions, and statistical calculation of the results acquired in the device was accomplished by use of the Δ CT method utilizing https://dataanalysis2.qiagen.com/pcr software.2.7. Determination of Antioxidant Levels2.7.1. Glutathione (GSH) DeterminationSH‐SY5Y cells were plated in six‐well plates and subsequently treated with the M1 molecule. The cells were trypsinized, and the supernatant was removed after 48 h. A volume of 250 μL was obtained from each cell sample, and the procedure was followed. The methodology that was suggested by Giustarini et al. [40] was used to determine the GSH level. The protocol proposed by Giustarini et al. is designed for the determination of GSH and glutathione disulfide (GSSG) concentrations in blood, cell lysates, and various tissues. The concentration of GSSG is subsequently quantified spectrophotometrically using the GSH recycling assay, which is based on the reduction of GSSG to GSH by GSH reductase in the presence of NADPH, followed by its reaction with 5,5 ′‐dithiobis‐(2‐nitrobenzoic acid).2.7.2. Glutathione‐S‐Transferase (GST) DeterminationOne hundred and fifty microliters was taken from each of the M1 samples treated with SH‐SY5Y cell lines, and the methodology suggested by Ghelfi et al. [41] was used to determine the GST level. According to this method, the assay is based on the conjugation of reduced GSH with the substrate 1‐chloro‐2,4‐dinitrobenzene (CDNB). The reaction mixture consisted of potassium phosphate buffer (0.1 M, pH 6.5), GSH, CDNB, and an appropriate amount of sample. Formation of the GS–DNB conjugate was monitored by measuring the increase in absorbance at 340 nm at 25°C. Enzyme activity was calculated using the molar extinction coefficient of the conjugate and expressed as nanomoles per minute per milligram of protein. Protein concentrations were determined prior to the assay, and all measurements were performed under conditions in which the reaction rate was linear with respect to time and protein concentration [41].2.7.3. Determination of Glucose‐6‐Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PDH) Enzyme ActivityG6PDH is located in the pentose phosphate pathway in cells and serves to protect the cell from damage caused by oxidants. One hundred and fifty microliters of M1 was added to the cell culture medium, and the following methodology was used. The methodology that Olive et al. [42] recommended was used to determine the G6PDH level. According to this method, G6PDH activity in cell lysates was determined spectrophotometrically based on the rate of NADP+ reduction. Briefly, the reaction mixture contained Tris–HCl buffer (pH 7.8), glucose‐6‐phosphate as the substrate, NADP+ as the coenzyme, and an appropriate amount of sample. The reaction was initiated by the addition of glucose‐6‐phosphate, and the formation of NADPH was monitored by recording the increase in absorbance at 340 nm at 25°C. Enzyme activity was calculated using the molar extinction coefficient of NADPH and expressed as nanomoles of NADPH formed per minute per milligram of protein. Protein concentrations were determined prior to the assay, and all measurements were performed under conditions in which the reaction rate was linear with respect to time and protein concentration [42].2.7.4. Catalase (CAT) DeterminationCAT is one of the enzymes that catalyze the splitting of hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen. One hundred microliters of M1 was taken up in cell culture, and the protocol was applied. CAT amount was determined according to the protocol recommended by Aebi [43]. According to the method described by Aebi, CAT activity in cell lysates was determined spectrophotometrically based on the rate of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) decomposition catalyzed by CAT. The principle of the assay relies on the strong absorbance of H2O2 at 240 nm and the progressive decrease in absorbance as H2O2 is degraded by CAT. Briefly, the reaction mixture was prepared to contain phosphate buffer at an appropriate concentration (pH 7.0–7.4), a defined initial concentration of H2O2, and an appropriate amount of cell lysate. The reaction was initiated by the addition of the cell lysate, and the decrease in absorbance at 240 nm due to H2O2 degradation was monitored at 25°C over a defined period. CAT activity was calculated from the rate of change in absorbance (ΔA/min) using the molar extinction coefficient of H2O2 and was expressed as the amount of H2O2 decomposed per minute per milligram of protein. Protein concentrations were determined prior to the assay, and all measurements were performed under conditions in which the reaction rate was linear with respect to time and protein concentration [43].2.7.5. Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) DeterminationIt is the standard procedure for determining cytotoxicity in membrane integrity studies. The course of cytotoxicity caused by the molecule in cell cultures is quantitatively evaluated by measuring the activity of LDH in the supernatant. For 48 h, the cells were exposed to IC50 doses of M1 medication, and 100 μL of M1 was taken in cell culture media. The methodology suggested by Decker and Lohmann‐Matthes [44] was used to assess LDH activity. LDH activity was experimentally determined as an indicator of cellular cytotoxicity based on the quantification of LDH released into the culture medium following cell damage. Briefly, after incubation of the cells under appropriate conditions, culture supernatants were collected and added to the reaction mixture for LDH analysis. The assay principle is based on the LDH‐catalyzed oxidation of lactate to pyruvate, accompanied by the reduction of NAD+ to NADH, which subsequently drives the reduction of a tetrazolium salt to form a colored formazan product. The intensity of the developed color was measured spectrophotometrically at a specific wavelength, and absorbance values were considered proportional to the amount of LDH released into the extracellular medium. LDH release was interpreted as a marker of compromised cell membrane integrity, and the results were expressed as percentage cytotoxicity or relative LDH activity compared with the control group. This experimental approach enables rapid and reliable quantitative assessment of cell death associated with cellular cytotoxicity [44].2.7.6. Superoxide dismutase (V) DeterminationSun et al. used a spectrophotometric apparatus to detect SOD activity, following the approach that was provided by [45]. SOD activity was determined using a spectrophotometric method based on the ability of SOD to inhibit reactions mediated by superoxide anions. The principle of the assay relies on the generation of superoxide radicals through the xanthine–xanthine oxidase system, which, under normal conditions, reduces an indicator compound, such as nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT). SOD present in the cell lysate catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide anions, thereby suppressing this reduction reaction. Briefly, cell lysates were added to the reaction mixture, and the color change resulting from NBT reduction was monitored spectrophotometrically at a specific wavelength. SOD activity was calculated based on the percentage inhibition of NBT reduction, and one unit of SOD activity was defined as the amount of enzyme required to produce 50% inhibition under the assay conditions [45].2.8. Statistical AnalysisAll data are expressed as mean ± SD. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism (Version 8, GraphPad Software, United States). For MTT time‐course experiments (24, 48, and 72 h), differences were evaluated using one‐way repeated‐measures ANOVA with Greenhouse–Geisser correction. Biochemical assay results and RT‐PCR data were compared between two groups using Student′s t‐test. For RT‐PCR, relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2−Δ ΔCT method, with CT values and fold‐change calculations performed using QIAGEN′s GeneGlobe RT2 Profiler PCR Data Analysis software. Values are presented as means with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical comparisons were performed using Student′s t‐test. ∗ p 500 is great. c 80% is high.Various characteristics, including molecular mass, dipole moment, total solvent accessible surface area (SASA), and the number of hydrogen bonds given or received, are critical characteristics of molecules. Nevertheless, considering the biological characteristics of the molecules, the anticipated IC50 for HERG K+ channel inhibition, which serves as a model for the gut‐blood barrier, the prediction of the brain/blood partition coefficient, the estimated skin permeability, the unanticipated apparent MDCK cell diffusion, the forecast of binding to human serum albumin, and the predicted qualitative characteristics of human oral absorption are among the various parameters that have been computed [88].Their amounts should be in the criteria in order for these traits to be assigned to different organs. Additionally, two characteristics, RuleOfFive [89, 90] (number of violations of Lipinski′s rule of five) and RuleOfThree [91] (number of violations of Jorgensen′s rule of three), are evaluated quantitatively to ascertain whether a compound satisfies the criteria for being categorized as a drug. It is predicted that the number of these two characters will be zero.4. Collectively, the present data demonstrate that M1 exerts anticancer effects in SH‐SY5Y NB cells and is associated with significant modulation of apoptosis and cell cycle/DNA repair–related gene expression, together with alterations in enzyme activity and redox/oxidative stress markers. Complementary in silico analyses supported these observations: Quantum chemical calculations (B3LYP, HF, and M062X) coupled with ESP mapping delineated plausible reactive regions, and molecular docking predicted the strongest interaction with 5WIV, followed by 3PBL and 2F37. Moreover, ADME/T profiling indicated acceptable drug‐like characteristics within the applied criteria. These findings provide a rationale for subsequent studies to verify M1′s mechanism of action and molecular targets and to evaluate its efficacy and safety in advanced in vitro platforms and in vivo models.Author Contributions Tugba Agbektas: investigation, formal analysis, conceptualization, writing – review and editing. title: Cuproptosis: A Potential Target for the Treatment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disease characterized by multi-organ involvement and broad immunological abnormalities, including persistent positive anti-nuclear antibodies. Different from many other autoimmune disorders, SLE is associated with significant disruption of copper homeostasis. Accumulating clinical evidence demonstrates elevated serum copper concentrations in SLE patients, which are closely associated with disease activity and inflammatory status. Despite advances in disease management, effective therapeutic options for SLE remain limited. Most SLE patients still require nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, immunosuppressants, and glucocorticoids, yet these treatments are frequently associated with adverse events and variable efficacy, particularly with long-term glucocorticoid use. For refractory SLE cases and patients experiencing chronic glucocorticoid-related toxicity, novel therapeutic strategies targeting cuproptosis are urgently required. Although biologic therapies have broadened available treatment options, their high cost and increased infection risk limit widespread clinical application. Its complex pathogenesis and pronounced clinical variability make personalized management strategies highly challenging. Identifying new molecular mechanisms and therapeutic targets, therefore, remains a major focus in SLE research. Recent studies have revealed a newly recognised form of programmed cell death, termed cuproptosis, within SLE-related pathological processes. Copper-mediated cuproptosis is driven by enhanced mitochondrial metabolism and excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation, processes that may promote immune-cell activation and inflammatory injury in SLE. Several key regulators are involved in this pathway, including ferredoxin 1 (FDX1); the lipoic-acid synthesis and protein lipoylation enzymes lipoic acid synthase (LIAS), lipoyltransferase 1 (LIPT1), and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD); pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC) subunits PDHA1 and PDHB, and dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase (DLAT); as well as additional regulatory factors, including glutaminase (GLS), metal-regulatory transcription factor 1 (MTF1), and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A). This review explores the relationship between cuproptosis and ten associated genes, their roles in dysregulated immune responses, and the emerging opportunities and challenges in developing therapeutic targets and clinical interventions.
full_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the prototype autoimmune disease characterized by involvement of multiple organ systems and the presence of diverse autoantibodies in the serum. It follows a course of fluctuating activity with episodes of relapse and remission that are difficult to control, severely affecting work, sleep, and overall physical and mental health.1,2 Due to the complexity and heterogeneity of SLE and the variability in treatment responses, a standard management approach remains under exploration.3,4 This underscores the need to identify new molecular mechanisms and therapeutic targets of SLE that may offer more precise diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.Disturbances in cell death pathways are associated with the pathogenesis of SLE. Impaired clearance of apoptotic cells leads to self-antigen exposure, triggering pathological autoimmune responses.5 Abnormal apoptosis in immune cells, such as lymphocytes, disrupts immune tolerance and promotes autoantibody production.6 Neutrophil NETosis (neutrophil extracellular trap) releases nuclear material and granule proteins that act as potent self-antigens and strongly drive pathological type I interferon signaling.7 Macrophage pyroptosis, driven by cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway activation, releases interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and other pro-inflammatory mediators that increase tissue inflammation.8 Beyond these well-established pathways, a novel form of regulated cell death, cuproptosis, has been identified. Recent advances have characterized cuproptosis as a cytotoxic mechanism in which copper binds directly to acylated components of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, causing aggregation of these components, loss of iron–sulfur (Fe–S) cluster proteins, and protein-toxicity stress that leads to cell death.9Copper is an essential trace element that serves as a cofactor for several enzymes involved in immune responses and oxidative stress. Multiple studies have reported elevated serum copper levels in SLE patients, suggesting a possible role in disease development.10 Tóth et al11 reported increased serum copper concentrations in SLE patients and a shift in copper-binding patterns: copper was predominantly albumin-bound in SLE, whereas ceruloplasmin was the major carrier in healthy individuals, suggesting disruption of metal-metabolism homeostasis during chronic inflammation. Other studies have confirmed that elevated serum copper is associated with increased SLE risk and correlates positively with C-reactive protein levels.12,13 Copper may exacerbate inflammatory reactions and sustain chronic inflammation by interacting with pro-inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress pathways.14 Current evidence suggests that copper’s effects on SLE primarily involve its role in oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling, both of which are central to disease progression.15To better understand these relationships, a systematic literature search was conducted on cuproptosis, cuproptosis-related genes, and SLE using databases including PubMed and Web of Science. The objective was to clarify how copper metabolism and copper-dependent cytotoxic pathways may contribute to SLE and to provide a theoretical basis for developing new therapeutic strategies.The Relationship Between Cuproptosis and SLEVarious forms of programmed cell death have been linked to the pathogenesis of SLE, and growing evidence indicates potential interactions between cuproptosis and the immunopathology of this disease. Immune infiltration studies have shown increased numbers of neutrophils, memory B cells, plasma cells, macrophages, and activated dendritic cells in SLE patients.3 Neutrophils contribute to pathology through several mechanisms, including the induction of plasma-cell–like dendritic cells that drive interferon production and promote disease progression. Although NETosis is an important antimicrobial defence mechanism of neutrophils, excessive or inadequately cleared neutrophil extracellular traps can damage tissues and stimulate inflammatory cells, thus promoting disease progression.16,17 Research has shown that reactive oxygen species (ROS) strongly promote NETosis, and the interactions between ROS and NET formation are bidirectional.18,19 Cuproptosis involves ROS generation via disruption of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, leading to oxidative stress in blood vessels and connective tissues and contributing to chronic inflammation.20 Therefore, ROS may represent a mechanistic link between cuproptosis and NETosis in SLE pathogenesis.The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway is a key regulator of cellular growth, metabolism, and autophagy, and dysregulated mTOR signaling has been implicated in several autoimmune disorders, including SLE.21 Copper can interfere with autophagy through multiple mechanisms, including increased expression of autophagy-related (ATG) proteins, regulation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-mTOR signaling, and induction of oxidative stress. Moreover, deficiency of the copper-export protein ATPase copper transporting beta (ATP7B) or intracellular copper accumulation activates transcription factor EB (TFEB), a major regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, enhancing autophagic activity.22 Effector T cells also rely on mTOR-dependent metabolic pathways and exhibit increased glycolytic uptake of glucose and enhanced glutaminolysis of glutamine, which may indirectly influence cuproptosis by altering substrate availability.23Glycolysis is a metabolic pathway that converts glucose into pyruvate through sequential enzymatic reactions mediated by enzymes such as hexokinase and pyruvate kinase, supplying ATP required for cellular activity.24 In SLE, M1 macrophages depend predominantly on glycolytic metabolism and release multiple pro-inflammatory mediators that contribute to disease progression. Co-stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interferon-γ stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and promotes metabolic reprogramming toward glycolysis in M1 macrophages.25 Recent findings by Ou et al26 identified hexokinase domain-containing protein 1 (HKDC1), a mitochondrial-associated hexokinase that interacts with heat shock cognate B (HSCB) and the cuproptosis regulator FDX1, increasing intracellular copper accumulation and initiating cuproptosis. In LPS-stimulated THP-1 macrophages, HKDC1 knockdown altered FDX1 activity and modified the expression of copper-transport proteins ATP7B and solute carrier family 31 member 1 (SLC31A1).26 These results suggest that glycolytic reprogramming and cuproptosis may be functionally interconnected in M1 macrophages during SLE progression, providing new insight into disease-associated metabolic regulation. The potential roles of cuproptosis-related genes in specific immune-cell populations are summarized in Table 1. no direct diagnostic data.Targeting LIPT1-related lipoylation may improve mitochondrial function in SLE fibroblasts.[60–62]DLDDihydrolipoamide DehydrogenaseT cells, natural killer cells, macrophages, neutrophilsDLD affects mitochondrial autophagy and cellular energy production.Associated with mitochondrial autophagy and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation in SLE.Modulating DLD activity may reduce ox-mtDNA release and type I IFN production.[32, 51, 63]PDHA1PDHA1 may contribute to SLE development through its regulatory role in glycolysis. As the catalytic core of the PDHC, PDHA1 controls the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA within the tricarboxylic acid cycle by oxidizing decarboxylated pyruvate. Its involvement in metabolic control has been widely reported in various tumors. For example, PDHA1 plays an inhibitory role in the proliferation and aerobic glycolysis of cervical cancer cells,64 and its downregulation in gastric cancer promotes cancer cell growth, invasion, and glycolytic activity.65 In prostate cancer, knockdown of PDHA1 increases glutamine-dependent survival and drives metabolic reprogramming,66 while PDHA1 knockout in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma promotes cell proliferation, migration, and chemotherapy tolerance.67Immune cells undergoing activation or inflammatory stimulation require rapid metabolic shifts to meet increased bioenergetic and biosynthetic demands. During activation and differentiation, these cells shift from catabolic metabolism to anabolic metabolism and rely on glycolysis to rapidly produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and metabolic intermediates.68 Pro-inflammatory effector cells in SLE—such as M1 macrophages, activated B cells, and effector T cells—prefer glycolysis for energy and intermediate products production, accompanied by increased activity of the pentose phosphate pathway and glutamine utilization, whereas the level of fatty-acid synthesis remains relatively reduced.69,70 This metabolic pattern suggests that PDHA1 may be inhibited in effector cells (such as M1 macrophages, activated B cells, and effector T cells) in SLE, favouring a glycolytic state and supporting cellular activation and expansion.In addition to its role in metabolic regulation, PDHA1 may also affect SLE by regulating inflammatory responses. Activation of the NOD-like receptor heat protein domain-associated protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome and the release of downstream inflammatory mediators are key pathogenic features of SLE.71 Inhibition of pyruvate oxidation through reduced activity of mitochondrial pyruvate carrier 2 (MPC2) or PDHA1 increases NLRP3 inflammasome activation, indicating that impaired mitochondrial pyruvate transport and increased lactate fermentation support the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome.27 NLRP3 inflammasome activation leads to the release of pro-inflammatory mediators, including mitochondrial pyruvate carrier 2 (MPC2) and others.27 Macrophages, which drive the inflammatory cascade in SLE, are sensitive to this regulation. Loss of the silencing regulatory protein 3 (SIRT3) reduces PDHA1 activity by increasing lysine acetylation, leading to intracellular lactate accumulation and reduced macrophage pH, controlling NLRP3 and IL-1β secretion by macrophages.28 In vitro models using LPS-stimulated macrophages have further elucidated this pathway.72 Melatonin receptor 1 (MT1) reduces LPS-induced aerobic glycolysis and suppresses inflammatory responses by increasing PDHA1 expression and affecting oxidative phosphorylation.29 MT1 has already been associated with SLE pathogenesis through its effects on the Th1/Th17 balance and the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT), extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling pathways, which regulate pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and IL-1β, exerting anti-inflammatory effects.73PDHA1 appears to serve as a key regulatory element linking glycolytic reprogramming and inflammation and is regulated by multiple transcriptional mechanisms. Its exact role in SLE, however, requires further in-depth research through continued mechanistic studies.PDHBThe PDHC is a tetramer composed of two alpha subunits (PDHA1) and two beta subunits (PDHB). PDHB, as an essential catalytic component, participates in the decarboxylation of pyruvate and plays a key role in glycolysis-related energy metabolism, similar to the function of PDHA1.30 DJ-1 (encoded by PARK7), a key familial Parkinson’s disease gene, is known to act as a regulatory factor for PDH activity in CD4⁺ regulatory T cells. DJ-1 binds to PDHB and inhibits PDH phosphorylation, supporting PDH activity and oxidative phosphorylation. Given the significant dysregulation of Treg homeostasis in SLE, the DJ-1–PDHB axis represents a potential regulatory target for maintaining or restoring Treg stability.31Xia et al32 used machine-learning approaches combined with single-cell sequencing and animal experiments to identify molecular pathways associated with cuproptosis in SLE. Their findings showed that, based on ROC curve analyses, the cuproptosis–related genes PDHB and GLS hold strong diagnostic relevance. Among all immune cells with high PDHB expression, macrophages accounted for the most significant proportion, while plasma cells showed the highest PDHB expression intensity. GLS expression was also highest in plasma cells. These observations highlight the diagnostic importance of PDHB and GLS in SLE pathophysiology.Disruption of ERK signalling in CD4⁺ T-cell populations has been implicated in SLE pathology.74 Studies by Tang et al demonstrated that PDHB inhibits RasV12-driven ERK signalling and limits cell growth.33 This suggests that PDHB may suppress excessive lymphocyte activation in SLE by inhibiting ERK pathway activity. Reduced PDHB expression may reprogram glucose metabolism toward a glycolytic state, inhibit the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and exacerbate immune-cell dysfunction. These changes may reflect a cellular adaptation to copper-related metabolic stress.GLSGLS exists as two isoenzymes, GLS1 and GLS2, both of which catalyze the first step of glutamine catabolism. The functional differences between these isoforms arise from the presence of PDZ-domain-binding motifs in GLS2; their absence impairs GLS2’s ability to control ROS levels and support IL-2 production. GLS1 is required for Th17-cell differentiation, and its inhibition can suppress autoimmune pathology in animal models. Hisada et al34 reported reduced GLS2 expression in CD4⁺ T cells from lupus-prone mice and patients with SLE. Overexpression of GLS2 restored ROS balance in lupus mice and SLE patients and recovered IL-2 production by CD4⁺ T cells.Although GLS1 and GLS2 both convert glutamine to glutamate, their downstream biological effects differ significantly. In various cancer cell lines, GLS1 upregulation supports tumor growth, whereas GLS2 expression is associated with quiescent or differentiated states.35 GLS1 is known to drive Th17-cell differentiation, and either pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of GLS1 has been shown to slow disease progression in MRL/lpr mice.36 GLS2 lowers ROS levels through a glutathione (GSH)-dependent antioxidant system. Excessive intracellular ROS is associated with various pathological states, including malignancies and SLE.75 Within the immune system, moderate ROS levels are required for T-cell signalling, but excessive ROS compromises T-cell survival and inhibits IL-2 production.76 Impaired IL-2 production is a key immunological defect in SLE, and restoring this pathway is considered clinically relevant.75Studies have shown that GLS2 expression is downregulated in CD4⁺ T cells from MRL/lpr mice and SLE patients, whereas GLS2 overexpression reduces ROS and restores IL-2 production.34 These observations suggest that GLS2-centred signalling may represent a promising therapeutic direction for SLE. GLS appears to affect plasma cells, Th17 cells, and CD4⁺ T-cell subsets in SLE by regulating the differentiation of inflammatory cells and supporting the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines.LIASLIAS is a key mitochondrial enzyme responsible for the biosynthesis of iron–sulfur clusters and for generating the endogenous antioxidant α-lipoic acid (LA). LA also acts as an essential cofactor in the PDHC and the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, both of which contribute to mitochondrial energy metabolism.37 As mitochondria serve as the primary source of intracellular ROS, disturbances in mitochondrial redox homeostasis are closely associated with the immunopathogenesis of SLE. Excessive oxidative stress has been shown to aggravate inflammation, trigger apoptosis, and disrupt immune tolerance, thus contributing to disease progression.77LIAS has been identified as a copper-toxicity–related gene and may affect SLE through its role in immune-cell composition in affected tissues. Immune-infiltration analyses revealed strong associations between LIAS expression and multiple immune-cell subsets, including Treg cells, Th1 cells, Th2 cells, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, natural killer cells, CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells, neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and platelets.38 These populations have well-established relevance to SLE pathophysiology, particularly in aberrant cytokine secretion, autoantibody formation, and tissue injury.78–80Functional enrichment analyses showed that LIAS-related gene sets were significantly enriched in the JAK–STAT signalling pathway, especially within type I interferon responses.38 Genes associated with LIAS expression are widely involved in multiple central regulatory mechanisms in this pathway, including suppressor of cytokine signaling-1 (SOCS1)- and SOCS3-mediated inhibition of JAK kinase activity, Src homology region 2 domain-containing phosphatase-1 (SHP-1)-dependent JAK1 dephosphorylation, and STAT2 phosphorylation. These events shape interferon-α and interferon-β signalling, underscoring the importance of LIAS in immune regulation.39Further analysis of two GEO datasets (GSE122459 and GSE61635) demonstrated that LIAS achieved the highest diagnostic performance among a panel of 10 cuproptosis-related genes, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 86.5%.38 This suggests that LIAS may serve as a potential biomarker for SLE. These results indicate that copper-related oxidative stress and downstream inflammatory responses associated with LIAS may contribute to disease development and carry diagnostic value.DLATAutophagy is closely associated with the immunopathology of SLE. Increased numbers of autophagosomes have been reported in T cells from SLE patients, and increased autophagy may support the survival of autoreactive lymphocytes.81 Autoantibodies isolated from the serum of SLE patients can also trigger autophagy in neuroblastoma cells, underscoring the regulatory importance of this process in disease activity. DLAT, a core component of the PDHC, has been associated with autophagy induction when expressed at high levels on the cell surface; however, this evidence is primarily derived from cancer and neurological disease models, and direct experimental validation in SLE models remains lacking.32The association between DLAT and SLE may be indirectly reflected through complications related to steroid exposure. Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) is a common cause of disability, and corticosteroid use is a major risk factor for its occurrence and progression. Because steroids are routinely administered in SLE management, steroid-induced ONFH (SIONFH) has become a significant clinical concern.82 Currently, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are recognised pathological features of SIONFH. Copper dysregulation may contribute to this process, as copper ions can bind to multiple lipid-acylated mitochondrial enzymes, including PDHB and DLAT within the PDHC complex. Such interactions interfere with enzyme function and impair the tricarboxylic acid cycle, the central metabolic pathway responsible for mitochondrial energy production. Dysfunction of the tricarboxylic acid cycle decreases electron transport chain activity, lowers ATP synthesis, and increases ROS generation through electron leakage to oxygen molecules.40,41 These mechanisms suggest that DLAT, through its sensitivity to copper-induced dysfunction, may participate in oxidative stress–related pathways relevant to SLE pathogenesis and its complications. However, direct evidence supporting the involvement of DLAT in SLE pathogenesis remains limited, and further investigations using SLE animal models and patient samples are required to validate these proposed mechanisms.FDX1FDX1 encodes a small acidic iron–sulfur protein that functions as an electron-transfer carrier for the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 system and participates in metabolic pathways involving steroid hormones, vitamin D, and bile acids.42 Evidence from Sun et al43 indicates that FDX1 supports mitochondrial stability, and its downregulation may trigger mitochondrial depolarization and oxidative stress. Excessive ROS can damage mitochondria, induce mitochondrial depolarization, and trigger mitochondrial autophagy.83 ROS can also activate the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway through several mechanisms.84 In SLE patients, this pathway remains persistently activated, with increased secretion of inflammatory factors. Phosphorylation of PI3K activates AKT, which, in turn, regulates downstream apoptotic factors such as Bax and Caspase-3, aggravating inflammatory injury and platelet apoptosis.85Studies in inflammatory models further highlight FDX1’s relevance to immune-mediated pathology. Che J44 reported that in IL-1β-stimulated chondrocytes and monocytes, expression of cuproptosis-related genes was significantly altered, and copper-dependent cytotoxic stress increased FDX1 expression levels while promoting chondrocyte apoptosis. These observations suggest that FDX1 upregulation during copper-dependent stress may also occur in chondrocyte injury associated with SLE, supporting the possibility that copper-induced cytotoxicity contributes to joint damage in this disease.Zhou et al45 reported a strong correlation between FDX1 and the copper transporter SLC31A1. FDX1 is a mitochondrial reductase that converts Cu(II) to the more cytotoxic Cu(I), which drives aggregation of lipid-acylated proteins and initiates cuproptosis. Its overexpression has been associated with poor outcomes in several malignant tumours, suggesting that FDX1 may serve as a therapeutic target in disorders with mitochondrial metabolic dependence.46 FDX1 also shows differential associations with immune-cell infiltration, including CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, and macrophages,47 and displays close relationships with signalling pathways such as HIF-1α/mTOR, p53, and Notch.48 These pathways are widely implicated in SLE pathogenesis, suggesting that FDX1-related copper-dependent mechanisms may play an important role in disease development.MTF1Hypoxic microenvironments, characterized by reduced tissue oxygen concentration, are essential to the pathogenesis and progression of several autoimmune diseases. The transcription factor HIF-1α coordinates cellular responses to low oxygen and remains highly active in an inflammatory microenvironment.86 Cytokines released within inflamed regions, including granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), TNF-α, IL-1β, and interferons, support HIF-1α activity and inhibit neutrophil apoptosis.87 Neutrophils from patients with SLE show abnormal ROS formation, with elevated O2−, H2O2, and HO• levels,88 indicating that HIF-1α contributes to neutrophil accumulation and the secretion of inflammatory mediators.A significant overlap between MTF1 and HIF-1α signalling has been reported. Dubé et al49 demonstrated that MTF1 increases HIF-1α activity, while HIF-1α improves MTF1 function, forming a reciprocal regulatory axis. Activation of MTF1 requires phosphorylation by several kinase pathways, including PKC, PI3K, c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), and protein tyrosine kinase (PTK).49 In SLE, these pathways do not work in isolation, but form a sophisticated signaling network. PTK acts as an upstream switch following immune-receptor engagement. PTK triggers PI3K signalling, which supports cell survival and metabolic shifts, and activates PKC, which facilitates lymphocyte activation and differentiation. PKC then activates MAPK pathways, such as JNK and the NF-κB cascade, leading to increased production of inflammatory factors, proliferation and persistence of autoreactive lymphocytes, and class-switching events that promote high-affinity autoantibody production.89,90Metal ions play essential roles in various cellular processes, including cellular proliferation, migration, metabolic regulation, and cell death. It is worth noting that metal ions regulate the functions of many immune cells and molecules in the body and have been widely reported in recent years.50 Metallothionein, encoded by MTF1, is a cysteine-rich protein that binds zinc, cadmium, copper, and related ions with high affinity, enabling detoxification and free-radical scavenging.51,52 Serum zinc concentrations are reduced in patients with SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren syndrome, and zinc-finger proteins are closely associated with the pathology of these diseases.91 These results indicate that MTF1 participates in SLE pathogenesis by maintaining metal-ion balance, limiting oxidative stress, and regulating transcriptional programmes associated with immune activation and metal-related toxicity.CDKN2ADysregulated B-cell function is a defining feature of SLE. Loss of regulatory control increases the survival of autoreactive B cells, allowing these cells to bypass tolerance checkpoints and undergo clonal expansion. They can further differentiate into long-lived plasma cells that release large quantities of pathogenic autoantibodies. These antibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissues, cause inflammation, and contribute to multi-organ involvement.92–94 Azizan et al53 reported dysregulation of the CDKN2A–MDM2–p53 axis in SLE B cells. Expression of TP53 and CDKN2A was reduced in both resting and activated B cells, with higher reductions in patients with active or inactive disease, whereas MDM2 expression was increased, particularly in activated B cells from patients with active SLE. Reduced TP53 and CDKN2A, together with elevated MDM2, may shift the balance toward increased B-cell survival rate. CDKN2A functions as a negative regulator of MDM2, stabilizing and activating p53 by inhibiting MDM2 and p14ARF, supporting p53-mediated cell death.54,55 Altered CDKN2A expression in SLE may therefore disturb this regulatory balance and favour the persistence of autoreactive B cells.CDKN2A encodes two tumour-suppressor proteins, p16INK4A and p14ARF, which participate in cell ageing by regulating the cell cycle and are considered hallmark molecules of this process.56 Compared with healthy individuals, SLE patients show increased CDKN2A expression,38 consistent with the close association between cellular ageing and chronic inflammation.57 Monocytes from SLE patients display a senescence-like phenotype, characterized by increased CDKN2A expression and elevated senescence-associated β -galactosidase (SA-β-Gal) activity.58 Upregulated genes in SLE monocytes include several ageing-related markers (CDKN2A, CDKN2B, CDKN2D) and DNA-damage-response genes (CHEK1, CHEK2), whereas downregulated genes include CDK4, CDK6, and others that drive cell-cycle progression and are directly inhibited by CDKN2A.58 Peripheral activation of SLE monocytes promotes IFN-α production through TLR7-driven plasmacytoid dendritic-cell responses and cGAS-STING-mediated pathways in monocytes, both of which exacerbate systemic inflammation.DNA methylation changes in immune-related genes, including interferon-regulated genes, MMPs, TGF-β, STAT3, CXCL12, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-10, have been studied as diagnostic markers for SLE and other autoimmune diseases.95–98 Gravand et al59 reported a significant association between CDKN2A promoter hypomethylation and disease-activity indices in SLE patients. Patients showed pronounced hypomethylation of the CDKN2A promoter compared with healthy controls, indicating that low CDKN2A methylation can serve as an alternative biomarker for evaluating disease activity. At an optimal threshold, CDKN2A methylation yielded a specificity of 77.30% and a sensitivity of 81.33% for distinguishing SLE from healthy subjects. CDKN2A methylation levels correlated positively with C3 and C4 and negatively with anti-dsDNA concentrations. DNA methylation differences were also observed between patients with onset before age 18 and those with onset after age 18. These results indicate that reduced CDKN2A methylation is associated with higher disease activity. However, confirmation in larger cohorts remains necessary due to sample-size limitations.LIPT1Cuproptosis occurs when intracellular Cu2⁺ binds to unstable thiol-containing proteins, causing their abnormal aggregation, mitochondrial metabolic disruption, and, eventually, cell death.99 Protein lipoylation is a two-step enzymatic process in which LA is first activated to lipoyl-AMP and then transferred to target apoproteins through a covalent reaction catalysed by the LIPT1-encoded enzyme.60 Studies in mutant cell models reported reduced LIPT1 expression, accompanied by decreased levels of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins, findings associated with defective mitochondrial function, iron accumulation, reduced membrane potential, and increased oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation.61 LIPT1 dysfunction has been identified as a limiting factor contributing to the pathogenic phenotype of SLE fibroblasts. Disturbance of cellular metabolic homeostasis in these cells exacerbates their pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic behaviour, driving disease progression and aggravating tissue injury in SLE.62 Although these findings suggest a possible association between LIPT1 and SLE pathogenesis, careful interpretation is warranted, as most mechanistic evidence regarding LIPT1 function, particularly its involvement in cuproptosis, derives from studies conducted in cancer and neurological disease models.100–104 Whether these mechanisms are directly applicable to SLE pathophysiology remains unclear. Therefore, the biological role of LIPT1 in autoimmune diseases requires further experimental investigation.DLDDLD encodes dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, a core mitochondrial enzyme in energy metabolism whose dysfunction can trigger mitochondrial autophagy.32,51 DLD is shared by three major mitochondrial enzyme complexes: the PDHC, the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and the branched α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. DLD is an essential catalytic core in these complexes. Loss of DLD activity disrupts these complexes and may cause mitochondrial membrane potential loss, accompanied by a sharp increase in ROS, changes known to activate the PINK1/Parkin pathway and initiate mitochondrial autophagy.63 Evidence indicates that mitochondrial autophagy contributes to the development and functional regulation of T cells, natural killer cells, and macrophages.75 In SLE, defective mitochondrial autophagy allows neutrophils to retain oxidised mitochondrial DNA (ox-mtDNA), which can be released and recognised as a potent autoantigen. This recognition supports dendritic cell activation, type I interferon production, and autoantibody formation, promoting disease progression.105 It is worth noting that the mechanisms governing mitochondrial autophagy are highly complex and involve the coordinated action of ATG proteins, mitochondrial receptors, endocytic machinery, and mitochondrial dynamics regulators. Because of this complexity, the functional status and impact of mitochondrial autophagy regulation cannot be fully inferred from isolated mechanistic studies on mitochondrial autophagy regulation and autoimmunity.106 However, DLD is likely to be an important cuproptosis-related gene with a considerable role in mitochondrial autophagy dysregulation in SLE, warranting further detailed investigation. This process involves the core cuproptosis execution module, including FDX1, LIAS, LIPT1, PDHA1, PDHB, DLAT and DLD, which are shown in a box with arrows indicating their interactions. Mitochondrial dysfunction results in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). GLS is shown interacting with the mitochondria. ROS production activates several pathways: the mTOR pathway, leading to abnormally activated T cells; NETosis; and the NLRP3 inflammasome. Another box shows upstream regulatory genes GLS, MTF1 and CDKN2A modulating cellular processes, leading to cellular inflammasome activation. Arrows indicate the flow and interaction between these components and processes.sMultiple cuproptosis-related genes may contribute to the pathogenesis of SLE. PDHA1 has been implicated in immune-cell metabolism and inflammatory regulation, whereas PDHB appears important for maintaining T-cell stability. GLS and LIAS are associated with antioxidant defense and oxidative-stress regulation, respectively. DLAT and FDX1 have been linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic reprogramming. MTF1 and CDKN2A may contribute to autoimmune activation and cellular senescence, whereas LIPT1 and DLD participate in tricarboxylic-acid cycle regulation and mitochondrial autophagy. As a recently identified form of programmed cell death, cuproptosis has attracted increasing attention, and research in this field is progressing rapidly. A previous bioinformatics study conducted by Li et al107 identified cuproptosis-related genes and established machine-learning models for SLE prediction, highlighting IFIT3, PLSCR1, CCR1, IL1RN, and ETV7 as potential biomarkers. However, this review focuses specifically on ten core regulatory genes directly involved in the cuproptosis pathway and summarizes their biological functions and potential mechanisms in SLE pathogenesis, thereby providing a theoretical framework for future experimental validation (Figure 2). As SLE serves as a prototype of systemic autoimmune disorders, elucidating its new molecular pathways and therapeutic targets may offer fresh perspectives for the diagnosis and treatment of other autoimmune diseases. However, due to an incomplete understanding of cuproptosis mechanisms, direct clinical evidence associating cuproptosis with SLE remains lacking. Therefore, future studies should extend beyond literature-based and mechanistic analyses and prioritize experimental validation using established SLE animal models, including MRL/lpr and NZB/W F1 mice. Particular attention should be paid to FDX1 and DLAT, given their key roles in the cuproptosis pathway and their potential as therapeutic targets. Moreover, future studies should stratify SLE patients by disease activity to investigate the expression profiles of cuproptosis-related genes across different pathological conditions. Such approaches may facilitate the identification of clinically relevant biomarkers and support the development of targeted therapeutic strategies and early-phase clinical studies. Furthermore, therapeutic approaches targeting cuproptosis, including copper chelators, ionophores, and dietary copper restriction, warrant further investigation as potential interventions for SLE.Figure 2Ten core cuproptosis-related genes — PDHA1, PDHB, GLS, LIAS, DLAT, FDX1, MTF1, CDKN2A, LIPT1, and DLD — are mapped to their respective immune cell targets in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), including macrophages, T cells, B cells, neutrophils, and others. Each gene is depicted as regulating key cellular processes such as metabolic reprogramming, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, and inflammatory signaling. These interactions collectively indicate that cuproptosis-related pathways contribute to immune dysfunction and tissue damage in SLE.Cuproptosis genes′ roles in immune regulation in lupus.The diagram illustrates the roles of ten core cuproptosis-related genes in immune cell regulation within systemic lupus erythematosus. The genes PDHA1, PDHB, GLS, LIAS, DLAT, FDX1, MTF1, CDKN2A, LIPT1 and DLD are mapped to various immune cells, including macrophages, T cells, B cells and neutrophils. PDHA1 and CDKN2A are shown regulating glycolysis and P53 in B cells. PDHB and GLS influence CD4 positive T cells through ERK and ROS pathways. FDX1 and LIAS affect CD8 positive T cells via PI3K/AKT and JAK/STAT pathways. LIPT1 and PDHA1 are involved in macrophage regulation, affecting M1 and M2 polarization. DLAT and PDHA1 contribute to T cell proliferation and effector function. DLD and MTF1 are linked to autophagy and NET formation in neutrophils. The diagram highlights interactions such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory signaling, indicating their contribution to immune dysfunction and tissue damage in systemic lupus erythematosus.
