title: Regulated cell death programs shaping cancer therapy
abstract: Regulated cell death has long been central to cancer therapy, with apoptosis historically regarded as the principal mechanism underlying treatment efficacy.Main bodyIncreasing evidence now demonstrates that tumors engage a diverse array of regulated cell death programs, including apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, cuproptosis, autophagy-associated death processes, and emerging stress-induced modalities such as parthanatos and disulfidptosis. These pathways can be broadly conceptualized as protein-governed, metabolism-driven, or stress-induced programs, reflecting distinct mechanistic principles and differing degrees of mechanistic definition and translational maturity. Their activation or suppression can influence tumor progression, immune modulation, and therapy resistance. While therapeutic induction of specific death modalities offers opportunities for tumor control, death-associated signaling may also paradoxically promote tumor adaptation and immune evasion under certain conditions.sThis review integrates current understanding of regulated cell death programs to highlight their plasticity in cancer and underscores the importance of mechanism-guided targeting of death pathways to improve cancer therapy outcomes.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.
full_text: The fundamental principle underlying many cancer therapies is the selective induction of cell death in malignant cells. For decades, the paradigm of regulated cell death in oncology has been dominated by apoptosis, a highly orchestrated process essential for tissue homeostasis and development. The therapeutic effects of conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy have largely been attributed to their ability to indirectly trigger apoptotic pathways. However, the pervasive development of therapy resistance underscores the limitations of interpreting cancer therapy through a single death modality. Cancer cells can evade apoptosis through genetic, epigenetic, and metabolic adaptations, and such resistance has motivated increasing interest in whether alternative regulated cell death programs can be therapeutically engaged [1].Recent advances have moved beyond the traditional apoptosis-necrosis dichotomy, revealing a diverse repertoire of regulated cell death programs, each with distinct molecular triggers, execution mechanisms, and immunological consequences. These include inflammatory lytic deaths such as necroptosis and pyroptosis, metabolism-driven processes such as ferroptosis and cuproptosis, and stress-responsive pathways such as parthanatos and disulfidptosis [2–5]. Concurrently, autophagy, primarily a stress-adaptive survival mechanism, can restrain tumor initiation by preserving cellular homeostasis but support established tumors under metabolic or therapeutic stress [6]. Although these modalities are often investigated as separate pathways, selected examples of pathway crosstalk indicate that they do not always operate in isolation. For instance, caspase-8 activity can influence the balance between apoptosis and necroptosis [7, 8], whereas caspase-3-mediated cleavage of GSDME can shift apoptotic signaling toward pyroptosis in GSDME-expressing cells [9]. These observations suggest that therapeutic response may depend not only on activation of an individual death pathway, but also on the cellular context that permits, suppresses, or shifts the engagement of specific death programs.This review synthesizes the evolving landscape of regulated cell death into a unified framework, grouping pathways into protein-governed, metabolism-driven, and stress-induced programs. These categories are intended to reflect distinct mechanistic principles, not a strict hierarchy of evidence, although the included modalities differ substantially in mechanistic definition and translational development. Protein-governed pathways rely on dedicated molecular executioners, metabolism-driven processes link metabolic state to cell fate, whereas stress-induced modalities arise from catastrophic cellular perturbations and remain less mechanistically defined. After examining these modalities individually, this review further compares selected upstream regulatory themes that recur across death programs and shape pathway engagement. By integrating pathway-specific mechanisms with therapeutic targeting strategies, resistance mechanisms, immunological consequences, and shared regulatory constraints, this review highlights how a more precise understanding of regulated cell death may inform mechanism-guided cancer treatment strategies.Main textPart I: Canonical regulated cell death pathways with defined molecular executionersThis section focuses on three canonical forms of regulated cell death—apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis—defined by their reliance on well-characterized molecular executioners. Although these pathways differ in immunological outcome, they share an executor-centric architecture that renders them both frequent targets of oncogenic suppression and central nodes for therapeutic reactivation in cancer.ApoptosisThe term apoptosis was introduced by Kerr, Wyllie, and Currie in 1972 to describe a morphologically distinct form of cell death [10]. Apoptosis is a highly regulated form of cell death characterized by membrane blebbing, cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, DNA fragmentation, and subsequent phagocytic clearance [11]. It is mainly initiated through intrinsic mitochondrial and extrinsic death receptor pathways. The intrinsic pathway is regulated by the BCL-2 family of proteins, comprising anti-apoptotic proteins (BCL-2, BCL-XL, BCL-W, MCL-1, BFL-1/A1), pro-apoptotic pore-formers (BAX, BAK, BOK), and pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins (BAD, BID, BIK, BIM, BMF, HRK, NOXA, PUMA, etc.) [12, 13]. Intracellular stress signals, such as DNA damage, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, or growth factor deprivation, activate this pathway (Fig. 1a). These signals activate BH3-only proteins which either directly activate effector proteins BAX/BAK or neutralize anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members [14–16]. Once activated, BAX/BAK oligomerize on the mitochondrial outer membrane, causing mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), which results in the release of cytochrome c and SMAC (second mitochondria-derived activator of caspase). In the cytosol, cytochrome c binds APAF-1, forming the apoptosome complex, which activates initiator caspase-9. Caspase-9 then cleaves and activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3/7, culminating in irreversible proteolytic degradation of cellular components and cell demise [17, 18]. In parallel, inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs), particularly XIAP, restrain caspase activation, whereas mitochondria-released SMAC antagonizes IAP-mediated caspase inhibition by binding to their baculoviral IAP repeat (BIR) domains [19–21]. The extrinsic pathway is initiated by extracellular death ligands, including FAS ligand, TNF-α, or TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL), which bind to their respective cell surface receptors (FAS, TNFR1, or DR4/5). This binding triggers caspase-8-dependent activation of caspases and downstream effector caspases [22]. FAS ligand or TRAIL binding causes the receptors to trimerize, and the death domain (DD) within the intracellular domain of the receptors recruits intracellular adaptor proteins, such as FAS-Associated Death Domain protein (FADD) [23, 24]. FADD contains a death effector domain (DED) that further recruits and activates caspase-8/10, forming a multiprotein complex known as the death-inducing signaling complex (DISC) [25]. The anti-apoptotic protein cFLIP (cellular FLICE-inhibitory protein), a structural homologue of caspase-8, can disrupt DISC formation by competing with caspase-8 for recruitment to FADD [26]. In type I cells, such as lymphocytes, caspase-8 activation is sufficient to cleave and activate caspase-3/6/7, whereas type II cells, such as hepatocytes and pancreatic β-cells, require mitochondrial amplification to overcome XIAP-mediated inhibition of executioner caspases. This amplification is achieved through caspase-8-mediated cleavage of the BH3-only protein BID into its truncated form (tBID), which activates the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. The subsequent release of mitochondrial proteins, including the IAP antagonist SMAC, counteracts XIAP’s inhibition and permits apoptosis to proceed [27, 28].Impairment of apoptotic mechanisms plays a critical role in tumorigenesis. Many oncogenes that drive cell division, including MYC, E1A, E2F1, and cyclin D, can also induce apoptosis [29]. During tumor development, hypoxia, oxidative stress, the absence of external survival factors and nutrients can activate apoptosis. Consequently, apoptosis evasion is imperative for cancer cell survival. Several mechanisms lead to the deregulation of apoptosis: (1) Imbalance in BCL-2 family proteins: Overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 has been reported in various tumors, including prostate cancer, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and melanoma [30–32]. Additionally, MCL-1 upregulation is observed in a broad spectrum of tumors including chronic myeloid leukemia, myeloma, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [33–35]. (2) Overexpression of IAPs and/or downregulation of SMAC: Many solid tumors exhibit amplifications at the 11q21-q23 locus, leading to increased copy numbers of c-IAP1 and c-IAP2. XIAP is frequently upregulated and serves as an independent poor prognostic marker in various cancers [36]. Conversely, reduced SMAC expression has been associated with poorer prognosis in renal cell carcinoma, oral squamous cell carcinoma, and colorectal cancer [37–39]. (3) Impaired wild-type p53 function: p53 can transcriptionally activate targets like CDKN1A, BAX, PUMA, and NOXA to regulate cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [40]. (4) Loss or functional inactivation of caspases: Key examples include epigenetic/genetic inactivation of the CASP8 gene in neuroblastoma, and the frequent loss of caspase-10 protein expression in breast and lung carcinomas [41–43]. Fig. 1Regulatory network and crosstalk between apoptosis and necroptosis. a, Regulatory network of the intrinsic and extrinsic apoptosis pathways. The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, activated by cellular stress, is regulated by BCL-2 family proteins, leading to cytochrome c release and caspase activation. The extrinsic (death receptor) pathway is initiated by ligand-receptor binding and DISC formation, activating caspase-8. Both pathways converge on effector caspases to execute apoptosis, with cross-talk mediated by BID cleavage. b, Necroptosis pathway and its switch with apoptosis. TNF-α binding initiates Complex I assembly, where ubiquitinated RIPK1 promotes NF-κB activation. Upon deubiquitination, RIPK1 can recruit active caspase-8 to induce apoptosis. Conversely, FAS/TRAIL-induced apoptosis via the DISC can switch to necroptosis upon caspase-8 inhibition. LPS-activated Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) signaling and ZBP1 sensing endogenous Z-nucleic acids can also trigger necroptosis through the RIPK1-RIPK3-MLKL axis Most conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy induce apoptosis indirectly, primarily by blocking DNA synthesis, damaging DNA, or inhibiting DNA replication [44]. In contrast, BH3-mimetic drugs directly engage mitochondrial apoptosis by structurally mimicking the BH3 domain of pro-apoptotic proteins and liberating pro-apoptotic counterparts from pro-survival BCL-2 family proteins [45]. Venetoclax was the first Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved, BCL-2-specific small-molecule inhibitor, indicated for the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) with 17p deletion in patients who have received at least one prior therapy [46]. CLL is characterized by a dependency on the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2, which contributes to apoptosis resistance in malignant B cells. A classic mechanism of BCL-2 dysregulation in B-cell malignancies is the t(14;18) translocation, which places BCL2 under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer [47, 48], leading to its constitutive expression and conferring apoptosis resistance in malignant B cells [49]. As a BH3-mimetic, venetoclax binds to the hydrophobic groove of BCL-2 (with high affinity, Ki 1.0×ULN) [80].AutophagyAutophagy is a fundamental cellular process responsible for the degradation and recycling of cytoplasmic components via lysosomes, playing a significant role in maintaining cellular homeostasis, adapting to stress, and promoting survival. This evolutionarily conserved pathway, most commonly referring to macroautophagy, is orchestrated by a suite of core autophagy-related (ATG) proteins that coordinate the formation of double-membraned autophagosomes, the sequestration of cargo, and subsequent fusion with lysosomes for content degradation [6]. This machinery can function as a non-selective bulk clearance mechanism or be deployed with precision to remove specific organelles, such as mitochondria (mitophagy) or the endoplasmic reticulum (reticulophagy) [244]. Beyond this well-established cytoprotective role, the autophagic apparatus itself can, under specific conditions, directly execute a distinct form of regulated cell death, known as autophagy-dependent cell death (ADCD) [245]. As outlined by the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death, ADCD strictly applies to scenarios where genetic or pharmacological inhibition of autophagy prevents cell demise, indicating the autophagic apparatus acts as the direct effector of death [4]. A specific, molecularly defined subtype within this category is autosis, characterized by its unique reliance on the plasma membrane Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. This reliance makes autosis susceptible to inhibition both in vitro and in vivo by pharmacological antagonists like cardiac glycosides or by genetic knockdown of the pump’s α1 subunit [246]. Furthermore, it is crucial to differentiate these mechanistically defined forms from the broader term autophagy-mediated cell death, which refers to contexts where autophagy facilitates cellular demise by enabling or amplifying canonical cell death pathways, for instance, by degrading ferritin to promote ferroptosis or by removing IAP proteins to facilitate necroptosis [247]. Fig. 4Dual roles of autophagy in tumor progression and therapy. Autophagy exhibits a stage-dependent function during tumorigenesis: it initially acts as a tumor suppressor but switches to a cytoprotective, pro-survival mechanism that facilitates metastasis in established tumors. This functional duality also dictates therapeutic responses. In glioma, temozolomide-induced autophagy promotes cell death, and its combination with the mitophagy inducer cannabidiol shows synergistic efficacy. Conversely, in breast cancer treated with the mTOR inhibitor everolimus, therapy-induced autophagy sustains cell survival; co-treatment with the autophagy inhibitor hydroxychloroquine blocks autophagic flux to overcome resistance Typically, autophagy plays a stage-dependent dual role in cancer, initially suppressing malignant transformation and later supporting tumor progression and metastasis (Fig. 4). First, autophagy prevents malignant transformation by maintaining cellular homeostasis through the removal of damaged organelles, misfolded proteins, and reactive oxygen species, preserving genomic integrity and limiting oncogenic signaling [6]. In breast and ovarian cancers, the E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin 3 (CUL3), utilizing KLHL38 as an adaptor, promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of the core autophagy protein Beclin1. This suppression of autophagy promotes tumor cell proliferation and is associated with poor patient prognosis, revealing a ubiquitin-dependent mechanism of autophagy inhibition in cancer progression [248]. Similarly, the preservation of organelle homeostasis through selective autophagy is also vital for tumor suppression. Loss of the mitophagy regulators PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and Parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase (PARK2) promotes pancreatic tumorigenesis by disrupting mitochondrial iron homeostasis. The subsequent iron overload drives several important tumor-promoting pathways, including metabolic reprogramming and immunosuppression caused by inflammation [249]. Furthermore, evidence from a colorectal cancer model conversely demonstrates that enhancing mitophagy can be therapeutic: STAT3 loss in intestinal epithelial cells amplifies mitophagy, triggering a cascade of lysosomal iron(II) accumulation, membrane permeabilization, and protease release, which boosts major histocompatibility complex class I(MHC-I) antigen presentation and potentiates antitumor immunity [250]. Similarly, autophagy also facilitates the release of ATP from chemotherapy-treated tumor cells to promote the recruitment of dendritic cells and T lymphocytes [251]. In established tumors, however, autophagy is co-opted to promote cancer cell survival and growth by supplying metabolic substrates under nutrient stress, sustaining mitochondrial function, and facilitating adaptation to oncogenic drivers such as RAS and BRAF mutations [252]. In KRAS-driven lung cancer, Atg7-mediated autophagy enables tumor survival not only by providing essential biosynthetic and bioenergetic precursors during nutrient stress, but also by sustaining mitochondrial fitness to prevent p53 activation and proliferative arrest [253, 254]. Under hypoxic conditions, autophagy promotes tumor cell survival by degrading NK cell-derived granzyme B within autophagosomes, directly impairing the effector function of NK cells and conferring resistance to immune-mediated lysis [255]. Autophagy also facilitates tumor immune evasion by mediating the lysosomal degradation of MHC-I molecules, thereby impairing antigen presentation and allowing cancer cells to escape CD8+ T cell surveillance [256]. During metastasis, autophagy exhibits context-specific functions: it supports dissemination by enhancing resistance to anoikis, survival in circulation, and adaptation to foreign microenvironments, yet also restricts metastatic outgrowth and colonization by maintaining tumor dormancy and degrading pro-metastatic factors [257]. This multifaceted and context-dependent role of autophagy in cancer underscores its complexity and highlights the need for stage-specific therapeutic strategies.Harnessing the dual role of autophagy in cancer presents a promising therapeutic avenue, primarily focused on inhibiting pro-tumorigenic autophagy or conversely, hyperactivating it to induce selective cancer cell demise. Strategies include the direct pharmacological inhibition of autophagy using agents like chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), which block autophagosome-lysosome fusion. A recent phase Ib/2 trial (NCT05953350; first submitted June 12, 2023) revealed that combining HCQ with a high-dose CDK4/6 inhibitor overcame resistance conferred by p62-selective autophagic degradation of PTEN, achieving a 41.4% objective response rate in resistant HR+/HER2- breast cancer [83]. Based on these results, a phase III confirmatory trial (NCT07061717; first submitted May 05, 2025) has been registered. Another randomized phase II trial (NCT01978184; first submitted October 30, 2013) showed that adding high-dose HCQ to gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel improved pathological response and CA19-9 reduction in resectable pancreatic cancer, with evidence of autophagy inhibition and enhanced immune infiltration, though no significant improvement in overall survival was observed [82]. In parallel with targeting established tumors, autophagy inhibition represents a promising strategy to eradicate dormant disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) that drive cancer recurrence. Preclinical evidence indicates that both autophagy and mTOR signaling are critical for DTC survival and reactivation [258, 259]. The subsequent phase II trial (NCT03032406; first submitted January 24, 2017) demonstrated that combining HCQ with the mTOR inhibitor everolimus was highly effective, with an estimated 87% reduction in DTC burden, surpassing the effects of either agent alone. The combination also achieved a 100% 3-year recurrence-free survival rate, supporting further evaluation of this strategy for targeting minimal residual disease and preventing relapse [84]. In addition to suppressing pro-tumorigenic autophagy, a promising alternative strategy aims to induce excessive, lethal autophagy in cancer cells. Combined treatment with repurposed, clinically approved tricyclic antidepressants and P2Y₁₂ inhibitors synergistically elevates intracellular cAMP in gliomas via the EPAC pathway, a cAMP-responsive signaling axis, thereby inducing excessive autophagic flux and triggering non-apoptotic, autophagy-associated tumor cell death in preclinical glioma models [260]. Another preclinical study demonstrates that cannabidiol (CBD) exerts antitumor effects in glioma by activating the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) channel to induce lethal mitophagy and shows synergistic activity with temozolomide [261]. A phase I/II trial (NCT01812603; first submitted March 14, 2013) evaluating the cannabinoid spray Nabiximols (an oral mucosal spray containing CBD) combined with dose-intense temozolomide reported an acceptable safety profile and a survival difference favoring the Nabiximols group at one year [81]. Of note, the phase I/II study had a limited sample size; a phase II trial (NCT05629702; first submitted November 07, 2022) is ongoing to validate these findings. Another study utilized myxoma virus-infected CAR-T or T cell receptor-engineered T cells to induce tumor cell autosis, a process driven by synergistic IFN-γ and viral signaling that enhanced tumor cell killing and overcame primary and acquired resistance in vitro [262].Part III: Emerging stress-induced cell death pathwaysThis section focuses on emerging cell death programs activated by catastrophic cellular stress, including parthanatos, disulfidptosis, sodium overload‑induced necrosis, and mitoxyperilysis. These processes are primarily described under conditions of severe pathological or experimental stress and generally lack the well‑defined execution machineries characteristic of canonical cell death pathways. Their clinical translation remains at a very early stage, with evidence derived mostly from foundational mechanistic studies and preclinical models. Nonetheless, these pathways reveal how catastrophic perturbations in DNA repair, redox balance, ion homeostasis, cytoskeletal integrity, and mitochondrial function may create cancer-cell vulnerabilities that warrant further investigation.ParthanatosParthanatos is a regulated, caspase-independent form of cell death triggered by PARP-1 overactivation in response to severe DNA damage. This overactivation leads to an excessive accumulation of PAR polymers, which signals the release of apoptosis-inducing factor from the mitochondria. AIF then translocates to the nucleus, where it induces large-scale DNA fragmentation, ultimately resulting in irreversible cell death. The term parthanatos is derived from a combination of PARP and Thanatos, the Greek word for death [263]. In acute myeloid leukemia, the frontline regimen of cytarabine and idarubicin has been shown to induce parthanatos, with this cell death response correlating positively with improved clinical outcomes [264]. Beyond its role in necroptosis, MLKL also regulates parthanatos in RIPK3-deficient hepatocellular carcinoma by maintaining ER-mitochondrial Mg²⁺ dynamics, and targeting this axis induces parthanatos, illustrating functional crosstalk between these two cell death pathways [265].DisulfidptosisDisulfidptosis is a recently characterized form of regulated cell death triggered by disulfide stress, specifically occurring in cells with high SLC7A11 expression under glucose deprivation [5]. The underlying mechanism involves a critical metabolic vulnerability: high cystine import via SLC7A11 consumes massive amounts of NADPH, which is primarily generated from glucose through the pentose phosphate pathway. Glucose starvation depletes NADPH, disrupting the cytosolic reducing environment and leading to the aberrant accumulation of disulfide molecules. This disulfide stress promotes excessive disulfide bond formation within actin cytoskeleton proteins, causing the actin network to contract, detach from the plasma membrane, and ultimately collapse, resulting in cell death. The Rac-WAVE regulatory complex-Arp2/3 signaling axis, which promotes branched actin polymerization, contributes to this process by providing a dynamic actin network that is vulnerable to disulfide crosslinking [266]. Furthermore, cellular stress responses like endoplasmic reticulum stress can act as protective signals during disulfidptosis. Inhibiting these responses enhances disulfidptosis independently of NADPH levels [267]. Recent studies have shown that ferroptosis resistance can be converted to lethal disulfidptosis by co-loading ferroptosis-inducing nano-agents with glucose metabolism inhibitors, such as glucose oxidase or glucose transporter inhibitors, a strategy supported by preclinical models [268, 269].Necrosis by sodium overloadNecrosis by sodium overload is a non-canonical pathway of regulated necrotic cell death, primarily driven by the persistent activation of the TRPM4 ion channel by the specific agonist Necrocide-1 (NCI). This activation causes catastrophic sodium influx, leading to membrane depolarization, osmotic swelling, and ATP depletion. This pathway can be blocked by drugs like the antifungal agent clotrimazole, which directly competes for the TRPM4 binding site, and by dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as benidipine [270]. In a separate mechanistic study, certain anticancer agents, such as BHPI and ErSO, were found to induce necrosis by activating TRPM4 through elevated intracellular calcium, its physiological activator. This calcium-mediated activation similarly triggers sodium influx and cell swelling, amplifying upstream death signals and driving immunogenic necrosis [271].MitoxyperilysisMitoxyperilysis is a newly proposed, lytic form of regulated cell death triggered by the synergistic co-activation of innate immune and metabolic stress signals. Under this combined stress, two independent but indispensable pathways are initiated: glutathione depletion coupled with BAX/BAK1/BID-dependent mitochondrial damage, which generates the necessary oxidative stress; and a separate process activated by innate immune signals strictly dependent on mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) function. The essential role of mTORC2 is highlighted by the complete prevention of cell death upon its genetic or pharmacological inhibition. mTORC2 promotes death by suppressing cytoskeletal dynamics through RhoA inhibition, a mechanism that traps the damaged, ROS-producing mitochondria in prolonged contact with the plasma membrane, leading to local oxidative damage, membrane rupture, and cell lysis. Notably, mitoxyperilysis operates independently of traditional cell death executioners, which may be activated but are non-essential, suggesting potential redundancy or crosstalk with other oxidative stress-related death modalities [272]. Mitoxyperilysis resembles a synthetic lethal-like strategy based on the co-activation of two non-lethal signals, although the precise molecular crosstalk and regulation between the two arms remain to be elucidated.Cross-pathway regulation and functional stratification of regulated cell death programsAlthough the preceding sections have examined individual death modalities separately, several upstream regulatory themes recur across regulated cell death programs. Figure 5 summarizes representative regulatory checkpoints within each major death program in parallel, rather than depicting a unified map of direct pathway cross-talk. These shared nodes do not erase the mechanistic distinction between death modalities, but help explain why tumor genotype, metabolic state, redox pressure, and stress signaling can bias cancer cells toward different death outcomes under therapy. For example, p53 can promote mitochondrial apoptosis through PUMA, NOXA, and BAX, while also influencing ferroptosis through repression of SLC7A11 [40, 273]. Conversely, NRF2 reinforces antioxidant defense by sustaining the SLC7A11–GPX4 axis, thereby restraining ferroptosis and contributing to therapy resistance [191, 274]. Redox and mitochondrial states similarly recur across multiple modalities, contributing to apoptotic stress signaling, Tom20/BAX/caspase-3/GSDME-mediated pyroptosis [275], electron transport chain-associated lipid peroxidation in ferroptosis, and mitochondrial metabolic dependence in cuproptosis, as discussed in the corresponding sections above. Metabolic sensing provides another shared regulatory layer, as AMPK/mTORC1 signaling controls autophagy through ULK1 and the Beclin1 complex, while AMPK-linked lipid remodeling can also restrain ferroptosis under defined metabolic conditions [276]. Other pathway-specific checkpoints, including NF-κB-induced A20 and cFLIP in necroptosis, HIF-1α-mediated cuproptosis resistance, and promoter methylation of GSDME in pyroptosis [277–279], further illustrate how upstream regulatory states can determine whether a death program is engaged or suppressed. Together, these recurring regulatory themes suggest that therapeutic responses may depend not only on which death pathway is targeted, but also on the upstream cellular state that permits, restrains, or shifts the engagement of regulated cell death programs. Fig. 5Representative regulatory nodes across major regulated cell death pathways in cancer. a, Apoptosis. DNA damage, oncogenic stress, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) activate p53, which induces pro-apoptotic mediators such as PUMA, NOXA, and BAX, thereby promoting mitochondrial apoptosis. Anti-apoptotic proteins counteract this process. b, Necroptosis. TNF-α/TNFR1 signaling promotes RIPK1/RIPK3-dependent necroptosis. NF-κB restrains this pathway by inducing A20 and cFLIP, which inhibit RIPK1/RIPK3 signaling directly or through the caspase-8 checkpoint. c, Pyroptosis. Oxidative stress promotes pyroptosis through a Tom20/BAX/caspase-3/GSDME pathway, whereas promoter methylation suppresses GSDME expression and limits pyroptotic execution. d, Ferroptosis. p53 suppresses SLC7A11 to weaken the SLC7A11–GPX4 antioxidant axis, whereas NRF2 reinforces this defense program. In parallel, ETC-derived ROS promotes lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. e, Cuproptosis. Under hypoxic conditions, HIF-1α promotes cuproptosis resistance through induction of PDK1/3, which suppresses DLAT, and metallothionein, which limits mitochondrial Cu(I) availability. f, Autophagy. Energy stress activates AMPK, whereas growth factors and nutrient availability promote mTORC1 signaling. AMPK stimulates autophagy by directly activating unc-51-like kinase 1 (ULK1) and by suppressing mTORC1, while mTORC1 inhibits ULK1. ULK1 subsequently activates the Beclin1 complex to promote autophagosome formation The therapeutic relevance of this cross-pathway view is evident in resistance settings where tumor cells either acquire a new death dependency or suppress multiple death outputs simultaneously. The clearest evidence comes from ferroptosis. A landmark study showed that a broad therapy-resistant high-mesenchymal state is characterized by a selective dependence on GPX4-mediated protection from ferroptosis [172]. A complementary study extended this concept to drug-tolerant persister cells, demonstrating across multiple cancer types and treatment contexts that residual persister populations acquire GPX4 dependency, undergo selective ferroptotic death upon GPX4 loss, and can be prevented from driving relapse in vivo [280, 281]. Together, these studies indicate that resistance does not simply extinguish cell death, but can redirect tumor cells toward alternative dependencies that remain therapeutically targetable. This principle is not confined to ferroptosis. In apoptosis-resistant colorectal cancer, caspase-8 deficiency creates a therapeutic vulnerability to SMAC mimetic-induced necroptosis, leading to tumor regression in vivo [282]. Conversely, apoptosis resistance does not always unmask a new death vulnerability. When a therapy engages multiple death outputs, resistant tumors may instead suppress several of these outputs simultaneously, as illustrated by loss of chemotherapy-induced canonical pyroptosis in chemoresistant lung and pancreatic cancer models and by RIP3 silencing that attenuates the necroptotic component of chemotherapeutic killing [283, 284]. A related, but mechanistically distinct, layer of cross-talk is provided by autophagy, which can, in specific contexts, facilitate other death programs by degrading ferritin or selected inhibitory proteins [285, 286]. These patterns suggest that therapeutic failure may reflect either redirection toward a newly targetable death dependency or collapse of a composite death response, underscoring the need for mechanism-informed therapeutic design.A parallel cross-pathway principle is evident in the immunological consequences of regulated cell death. Rather than being determined by pathway identity alone, immune outcomes are shaped by the kinetics and completeness of execution, the extent of membrane rupture, and the balance between released DAMPs and suppressive signals such as suppressing/inhibiting DAMPs (SAMPs). Among these pathways, acutely executed necroptosis and GSDME-mediated pyroptosis are generally among the more immunogenic forms, whereas efficiently cleared apoptosis is predominantly tolerogenic. Ferroptosis generally shows an immunogenic bias when induced in tumor cells, whereas autophagy produces more indirect and variable immune outputs; chronic or incomplete necroptotic signaling can become immunosuppressive. Apoptosis, particularly when efficiently cleared by efferocytosis, is classically tolerogenic, as it promotes the release of pro-resolving SAMPs that actively drive Treg differentiation and suppress Th1/Th17 responses [287]. In contrast, necroptosis and pyroptosis, when triggered acutely and fully executed, typically release immunogenic DAMPs. For instance, pyroptosis releases pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that promote T cell recruitment and activation [127, 128, 130], while necroptosis triggers mitochondrial DNA release and type I interferon production via the cGAS-STING pathway, thereby fostering T cell-dependent antitumor immunity [94–96]. However, chronic or sublethal necroptosis-associated signaling can promote immunosuppression through chemokines such as CXCL1 and IL-8, leading to MDSC recruitment or PD-L1 upregulation [98–101]. Ferroptosis is generally immunogenic when induced in tumor cells during antitumor therapy, particularly through CD8⁺ T cell-derived IFN-γ or radiotherapy combined with immune checkpoint blockade [178–180]. However, ferroptosis of KRASG12D-mutant pancreatic cancer cells or spontaneous ferroptosis of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells can generate immunosuppressive effects [182, 183]. Autophagy influences antitumor immunity more indirectly: it can enhance immunogenicity by promoting ATP release in response to chemotherapy or supporting MHC-I antigen presentation upon STAT3 loss [250, 251]; nevertheless, it can facilitate immune escape by degrading NK cell-derived granzyme B under hypoxic conditions and by promoting lysosomal degradation of MHC-I in pancreatic cancer [255, 256]. Understanding these determinants will be critical for designing therapies that exploit immunogenic cell death while avoiding unintended immune suppression.Because death-pathway susceptibility depends on tumor state, future translation will require functional diagnostics that identify actionable death dependencies in real time. BH3 profiling is a leading example with two major translational applications [288]. First, dynamic BH3 profiling (DBP) measures drug-induced increases in mitochondrial priming by quantifying cytochrome c release after short ex vivo drug exposure. Because this response can be assessed within 48 h, DBP provides a faster functional readout of therapeutic sensitivity than conventional viability assays and has been applied or further developed in hematologic malignancy settings, including acute myeloid leukemia and chronic lymphocytic leukemia [289–292]. Second, BH3 profiling can define anti-apoptotic dependencies by using selective BH3 peptides to identify pro-survival BCL-2 family members, thereby guiding rational BH3 mimetic combination strategies. For example, DBP revealed that ibrutinib (a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor) does not induce cell death in CLL cells as a single agent but increases their dependence on BCL-2, providing the mechanistic rationale for combining ibrutinib with venetoclax, a strategy later supported by subsequent clinical evidence [293–295]. Complementing this approach, metabolic vulnerability mapping provides a conceptual framework linking tumor metabolic states to specific cell death susceptibilities. For example, a lipid peroxidation–prone state creates dependence on GPX4-mediated detoxification, thereby sensitizing cells to ferroptosis, whereas tumors with elevated mitochondrial TCA cycle activity exhibit increased susceptibility to copper-induced cell death [3, 172]. In this context, metabolic states can define therapeutically exploitable liabilities by predisposing cancer cells to specific modes of regulated cell death. Large-scale resources such as the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) further support this framework by identifying candidate dependencies across diverse cancer cell lines [281, 296], whereas patient-derived organoid models provide a scalable platform for functionally validating these tumor-specific liabilities in clinically relevant settings. For example, DepMap-guided analyses identified heme biosynthesis as a selective dependency in acute myeloid leukemia, linking a lineage-specific metabolic vulnerability to cuproptosis induction and suggesting opportunities for rational combination strategies [234]. These emerging functional and systems-level approaches should help define tumor-specific death dependencies more precisely and inform rational therapeutic combinations.s and future perspectivesRegulated cell death is not merely an endpoint of cancer therapy, but a dynamic determinant of therapeutic sensitivity, resistance, and immune remodeling. Across established and emerging death programs, differences in molecular execution, metabolic dependency, inflammatory potential, and translational maturity shape how tumors respond to treatment. Apoptosis evasion can create dependence on alternative survival pathways, metabolism-linked programs such as ferroptosis and cuproptosis expose state-specific vulnerabilities, and lytic death modalities such as necroptosis and pyroptosis can either stimulate antitumor immunity or promote inflammatory immune evasion depending on the cellular and microenvironmental context. These observations indicate that therapeutic failure may reflect not only resistance to a single death pathway, but also broader remodeling of death dependencies under treatment pressure. A central challenge for future cancer therapy is therefore to define which death programs are available, suppressed, or therapeutically exploitable in each tumor context. Rather than treating regulated cell death as a fixed downstream consequence of therapy, future strategies should combine mechanism-guided pathway targeting with functional assessment of tumor-specific vulnerabilities to improve patient stratification and rational therapeutic combinations. This framework may help transform regulated cell death from a descriptive mechanism of treatment response into a more precise basis for therapeutic design.

title: O-GlcNAcylation at the tumor–immune interface: a metabolic post-translational code driving immune evasion and therapy resistance in cancer
abstract: Protein O-GlcNAcylation has evolved from a metabolic curiosity into a master post-translational modification that enables cancer cells to translate nutrient availability into coordinated programs of proliferation, therapy resistance, and immune evasion. In this review, we argue that hyper-O-GlcNAcylation is not merely a passive consequence of the Warburg effect but an actively maintained stress-adaptive state that drives malignancy through parallel substrate-selective circuits rather than a single unified axis. We synthesize recent advances in four interconnected dimensions. Metabolically, OGT integrates glucose, lipid, and nucleotide metabolism by modifying key rate-limiting enzymes and is regulated by lineage-specific mechanisms. O-GlcNAcylation modulates responses to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, reinforces DNA damage repair, and controls senescence. Immunologically, it promotes tumor immune evasion by stabilizing PD-L1, reprogramming macrophages, suppressing NK and T cell function, and modulating cGAS–STING signaling, thereby influencing checkpoint blockade efficacy. In the tumor microenvironment, O-GlcNAc signaling remodels the extracellular matrix, drives angiogenesis, and maintains cancer stemness and mechanoadaptation. Collectively, we propose that substrate-selective O-GlcNAc circuits, rather than global OGT activity, are the key drivers of context-dependent malignancy. This framework highlights opportunities for developing next-generation low-toxicity therapeutics, including substrate-selective inhibitors and PROTAC degraders, in rational combinations with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy.
full_text: 1IntroductionProtein post-translational modifications (PTMs) are covalent alterations that occur during or after protein synthesis and profoundly impact protein functions (1, 2). Among the more than 300 identified PTMs (3), glycosylation is one of the most diverse and abundant, encompassing N-linked, O-linked, C-linked, and glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored subtypes (4, 5). Aberrant glycosylation is now recognized as a hallmark of malignancy that shapes tumor proliferation, metastasis, and immune evasion across virtually every cancer type (6, 7). Within the O-linked class, O-GlcNAcylation, which involves the addition of a single N-acetylglucosamine residue to serine and threonine residues of cytoplasmic, nuclear, or mitochondrial proteins (8), has emerged as a particularly consequential regulator of oncogenic signaling (9, 10). Unlike conventional protein glycosylation, O-GlcNAcylation is dynamic and reversible. O-GlcNAcylation is highly responsive to a wide range of extrinsic stimuli, including osmotic, oxidative, hyperthermic, and genotoxic stress (11, 12). The dynamic cycling of this modification is reversibly regulated by a single pair of antagonistic enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT), which adds the sugar moiety, and O-GlcNAcase (OGA), which removes it, in a manner that is highly responsive to nutrient availability and cellular stress (11). This nutrient-sensitive PTM thus serves as a rapid molecular rheostat linking cellular metabolism to signaling, transcription, and stress responses (13).The Warburg effect drives elevated hexosamine biosynthesis pathway (HBP) flux and global hyper-O-GlcNAcylation, a feature documented largely by pan-O-GlcNAc immunostaining across breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, liver, and hematologic malignancies (10, 14–16). O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is concurrently upregulated in virtually every tumor examined, and its silencing suppresses transformed phenotypes (17, 18). Mechanistically, O-GlcNAcylation regulates the core hallmarks of cancer, including proliferation, survival, invasion, metastasis, energy metabolism, and epigenetic reprogramming (9, 19–23). Specific substrates couple HBP activity to oncogenic output: O-GlcNAcylation of phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1) at Ser529 diverts glycolytic intermediates into the pentose phosphate pathway (24), malate dehydrogenase 1 (MDH1) at Ser189 sustains glutamine catabolism in pancreatic cancer (25), and STAT5 drives oncogenic transcription in myeloid malignancies (26). The HBP–OGT axis further promotes tumor immune evasion by stabilizing programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1). O-GlcNAcylation of the endosomal sorting component HGS impairs its interaction with PD-L1 and blocks lysosomal degradation of PD-L1 (27), whereas HBP hyperactivation upregulates PD-L1 translation by bypassing signal peptide-mediated elongation arrest (28), collectively licensing checkpoint-mediated immune evasion. Hyperglycemia-driven O-GlcNAcylation induces alternative (M2) macrophage polarization in the tumor microenvironment, reinforcing immunosuppression (29).Despite significant advances, the mechanisms by which substrate-selective O-GlcNAc circuits, rather than a unified OGT–cancer axis, orchestrate metabolic reprogramming, therapy resistance, and immune evasion across different tumor lineages remain poorly understood. A methodological caveat must be stated at the outset, because it conditions how the entire literature below should be interpreted. The evidence for “global” hyper-O-GlcNAcylation across tumor types, together with most of the prognostic correlations discussed in later sections, rests predominantly on pan-O-GlcNAc detection using the monoclonal antibodies RL2 and CTD110.6. By design, these reagents integrate signals across thousands of substrates and therefore cannot distinguish oncogenic from tumor-suppressive site-specific modifications. More fundamentally, CTD110.6 is now known to cross-react with terminal β-N-acetylglucosamine on complex N-linked glycans, such that a portion of the “O-GlcNAc” signal recorded in bulk immunoblotting or immunohistochemistry may not reflect the intracellular modification (30, 31). Therefore, we interpreted bulk-level associations as hypothesis-generating tissue signatures rather than mechanistic evidence. Throughout this review, we deliberately focused on studies that resolve O-GlcNAcylation of defined substrates and modification sites. This distinction is not merely technical; it is foundational to the central thesis developed below, that substrate-selective O-GlcNAc circuits, rather than bulk OGT activity, drive context-dependent cancers. We revisit its translational consequences in detail in the Limitations and Unresolved Questions section. Critical questions remain regarding lineage-specific OGT regulation, O-GlcNAc–phosphorylation crosstalk, and the predictive value of substrate-resolved versus global O-GlcNAc profiles for therapeutic vulnerability. Addressing these gaps is essential for advancing O-GlcNAc biology toward substrate-directed and context-aware therapies. Here, we present a unifying framework in which hyper-O-GlcNAcylation acts as an actively maintained stress-adaptive state that drives malignancy through four interconnected axes: metabolic integration, therapeutic resistance, immune evasion, and tumor microenvironment remodeling. We also outline how this perspective can inform the design of next-generation O-GlcNAc-targeted interventions. Although O-GlcNAcylation in cancer has been reviewed previously, covering its cancer-associated inflammation (32) and immunotherapy links (33) and its role in therapy resistance (34), these accounts largely catalogue functions cancer-by-cancer and treat global OGT activity as broadly oncogenic. Here we instead advance a unifying, falsifiable convergence framework centered on substrate-selective, site-specific circuits, integrate the most recent (2024–2026) site-resolved and immune cell-intrinsic studies, and add an explicit translational lens (prognostic vs predictive biomarkers, evidence grading, and CNS-safety constraints).2O-GlcNAcylation machinery and hexosamine biosynthesis in cancer: a metabolic primerThe HBP end-product UDP-GlcNAc acts as a nutrient rheostat, and its elevation in tumor cells drives the coordinated O-GlcNAcylation of the metabolic machinery and OGT itself. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), glucose upregulates CARM1, which methylates OGT at arginine 348 to recruit the deubiquitinase USP9X, stabilizing OGT, and amplifying global O-GlcNAcylation to drive glycolysis, c-Myc induction, and tumor growth (35). Glycolytic enzymes are direct O-GlcNAc targets. In colon cancer, phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) is O-GlcNAcylated at T255 to enhance lactate production and translocate into mitochondria, where it functions as a kinase that inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex and suppresses oxidative phosphorylation (36). In NSCLC, hexokinase 2 (HK2) O-GlcNAcylation preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential, suppresses ROS, and promotes proliferation and invasion (37). Together, these circuits establish a glucose → CARM1 → OGT → glycolytic enzyme axis that constructs the metabolic ground state for downstream oncogenic programs.Beyond glycolysis, O-GlcNAcylation acts as a multi-input integrator, converging on rate-limiting enzymes across orthogonal metabolic streams (modification sites in Table 1). In the lipogenic stream, it modifies ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY) to enable CoA binding and de novo lipogenesis, independent of EGF-driven phosphorylation (38). In nucleotide metabolism, it drives hexamer formation of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase 1 (PRPS1), relieving feedback inhibition and AMPK restraint to boost purine, pyrimidine, and NAD synthesis and to confer chemoradiotherapy resistance in lung cancer (39). In glutamine catabolism, the modification of malate dehydrogenase 1 (MDH1) sustains the redox-supporting pathway of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer (25). The same logic extends to systemic and tumor-suppressive inputs: dietary fructose raises microbiota-derived acetate to elevate hepatic UDP-GlcNAc and hyper-O-GlcNAcylate eEF1A1 in hepatocellular carcinoma (40), while glucose-dependent O-GlcNAcylation of CK2 promotes CRL4^COP1-mediated p53 degradation, bypassing the p53 checkpoint without mutation (41). Two mechanistically complementary studies have addressed post-translational PD-L1 stabilization. O-GlcNAcylation of HGS, a key endosomal sorting component, impairs its interaction with intracellular PD-L1, blocking lysosomal degradation and elevating surface PD-L1 levels to suppress T cell immunity (27). OGT inhibition or a competitive HGS glycosylation peptide inhibitor restored degradation and synergized with anti-PD-L1 antibody in immune-competent mouse models (27). Independently, GFPT1 upregulation in breast cancer elevates global O-GlcNAcylation and stabilizes PD-L1 through O-glycosylation, whereas GFPT1 silencing reduces PD-L1 levels and attenuates tumor immune escape in vivo (45). These studies converge on O-GlcNAc-dependent PD-L1 stabilization operating through spatially distinct nodes, endosomal sorting, and direct protein glycosylation, which could be targeted combinatorially. O-GlcNAcylation, which is elevated by cytokine stimulation, is a permissive modification required for full NK effector function, and genetic stabilization offers a tractable strategy for NK-based immunotherapy. Two independent studies established that IL-2 and IL-15 stimulation increases O-GlcNAcylation in NK cells and that OSMI-1-mediated OGT inhibition comprehensively impairs cytotoxic capacity by reducing NKG2D, NKG2A, and NKp44 expression, diminishing granzyme B, perforin, granulysin, TNF-α, and IFN-γ, and abrogating tumor killing in a lymphoma xenograft model (53). Proteomics has identified LRPPRC as a key O-GlcNAc-modified NK cell regulator (52), although its mechanistic link to effector function requires further investigation. Critically, the studies diverge on enhancement: one study found that OGA inhibition or shRNA-mediated OGA knockdown did not augment cytotoxicity (53), whereas another demonstrated that Thiamet G and, more robustly, genetic deletion of the OGT intronic splicing silencer (ISS) stabilized O-GlcNAcylation, preserved potent cytotoxicity under TME-mimicking conditions, and enhanced in vivo tumor killing (52). Transcriptomic profiling of OGT-ISS-deleted NK92 cells revealed downregulated TGF-β and upregulated Type I interferon signalling, providing a molecular framework for TME suppression resistance (52). This discrepancy likely reflects the distinction between acute pharmacological and stable genetic O-GlcNAcylation elevation, which is a critical methodological caveat. This licensing logic broadly parallels observations in activated T cells, where TCR engagement drives a c-Myc–dependent HBP feed-forward loop in which O-GlcNAcylation stabilizes c-Myc and sustains glucose/glutamine flux to support clonal expansion (63). Whether analogous c-Myc or NFAT-centered circuits operate in cytokine-stimulated NK cells is untested, and the apparent NK-specific requirement for an LRPPRC-linked mitochondrial node (52) argues that effector-lineage-specific substrate maps, not T cell-derived frameworks, should guide rational O-GlcNAc engineering in NK cells. A recent study provides preliminary evidence that O-GlcNAcylation participates in both activating and inhibitory NK signalling downstream of the ILT-2 receptor (54), although the substrate identity and mechanistic details remain unresolved. Future studies should map the NK O-GlcNAc proteome under cytokine stimulation and TME suppression and identify the substrates that differentially govern cytotoxicity and exhaustion. At the adaptive immune interface, GFPT1-driven OGT activity O-GlcNAcylates CD39 at Ser239, stabilizing this ectonucleotidase to generate an immunosuppressive adenosine-rich microenvironment. GFPT1 silencing enhances CD8+ T cell infiltration and cytotoxicity in breast cancer (60). Site-specific O-GlcNAcylation of ENO1 at Ser249 blocks the ENO1–STUB1 interaction, preventing STUB1-mediated PD-L1 degradation, orthogonally to ENO1-Thr19 glycosylation, which promotes glycolytic dimer formation (Table 2) (61).Future studies should determine whether OGT inhibitor-induced cGAS–STING activation converts immunologically cold tumors into inflamed phenotypes and whether sequencing OGT inhibition before checkpoint blockade can maximize immune-priming. The ENO1 site-selective glycosylation model provides a template for bivalent inhibitors that simultaneously restrict both metabolic and immunosuppressive O-GlcNAc functions.3.6Cell-intrinsic O-GlcNAcylation across immune subsets: a divergent, lineage-specific logicThe preceding sections reveal that cell-intrinsic O-GlcNAcylation does not impose a single immunological direction; rather, its functional valence is lineage-specific and frequently opposite between effector and suppressor compartments. In cytotoxic effectors, O-GlcNAcylation is permissive for antitumor function: cytokine-induced O-GlcNAc is required for NK cell cytotoxicity, and its pharmacological removal collapses NKG2D expression and granzyme/perforin output (52, 53), while in CD8+ T cells, an O-GlcNAc-dependent β-catenin–Tcf7 axis preserves stemness and restrains exhaustion (56), and an HBP–c-Myc feed-forward loop sustains clonal expansion (63). In immunosuppressive and protumoral compartments, the same modification performs the opposite work: Glut3-driven O-GlcNAcylation of c-Rel sustains the tumor-specific suppressive program of intratumoral Tregs (55), and in tumor-associated macrophages, O-GlcNAcylation of EGR2 and lysosomal Cathepsin B, together with the GFPT2–YBX1–IL-18 axis, enforces M2-like, metastasis- and chemoresistance-promoting polarization (49, 50, 66), an effect amplified under hyperglycemia (29) and reversible by OGT suppression (51). Antigen-presenting cells occupy an intermediate, less-resolved position: in human monocyte-derived dendritic cells, OGT inhibition reshapes differentiation and maturation, altering AKT and MEK/ERK signaling, co-stimulatory and HLA-DR expression, and the IL-10/IL-6 balance, with downstream consequences for T-cell priming, the net tumor-relevant direction of which remains undefined (67).This divergence has direct and underappreciated translational consequences. Because systemically delivered, non-selective OGT inhibition engages every immune compartment simultaneously, it is expected to disarm the effectors that mediate tumor rejection (NK and CD8+ T cells) while disabling the suppressors that enforce immune privilege (Tregs and TAMs). Therefore, the net effect on antitumor immunity cannot be deduced from tumor-intrinsic data and will depend on the dose, schedule, and dominant immune contexture of a given tumor. This logic tempers the optimistic reading of OGT inhibition as a uniform immune sensitizer and instead predicts a narrow, context-gated therapeutic window, reinforcing, from the immune side, the case for the cell-type-selective, substrate-directed, and tumor-restricted strategies developed in the Targeting O-GlcNAcylation section. It also exposes how much of the relevant landscape remains uncharted: cell-intrinsic O-GlcNAc biology in intratumoral dendritic cells and essentially all of its biology in myeloid-derived suppressor cells, B cells, neutrophils, and innate lymphoid cells, have not been mechanistically defined (68). Two studies identified distinct substrates, UGDH and Hsp47, that converge on ECM composition and immune exclusion. O-GlcNAcylation of UGDH at Ser350 reinforces hydrogen bonding within the UDP-binding domain and enhances enzymatic activity, elevating hyaluronic acid (HA) synthesis (69). Molecular dynamics simulations provided atomic-level support, and CyTOF analysis confirmed an inverse correlation between UGDH O-GlcNAcylation and CD8+ T cell infiltration (69). O-GlcNAcylated UGDH also exerts a non-metabolic function by binding to KPNA2, displacing STAT1, blocking nuclear translocation, suppressing CXCL10 transcription, and impairing T cell recruitment (69). Tumors expressing O-GlcNAcylation-deficient UGDH exhibited reduced xenograft growth and improved survival rates.In colorectal cancer, O-GlcNAcylation of the collagen chaperone Hsp47 promotes maturation and secretion of type I collagen. (70). Kaempferol disrupts this by reducing UDP-GlcNAc levels, downregulating OGT, impairing Hsp47 localization, and blocking collagen secretion both in vitro and in vivo (70). O-GlcNAc-modified Hsp47 has been proposed as a predictive biomarker for the OGT–collagen axis in the kidney. Together, these studies establish O-GlcNAcylation as a dual ECM remodeler that operates through enzymatic enhancement and chaperone regulation. However, both findings should be interpreted against the established principle that the bulk of the tumor ECM, including fibrillar collagens and HA, is deposited and crosslinked by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and other stromal cells rather than by epithelial tumor cells (71). Because neither study resolves the contribution of stromal OGT activity to overall matrix deposition, it remains unclear whether tumor-intrinsic UGDH and Hsp47 modifications constitute the quantitatively dominant source of immunosuppressive ECM or a fine-tuning overlay on a predominantly CAF-driven program, a distinction with direct implications for the clinical positioning of OGT inhibitors. Future studies should investigate whether UGDH-driven HA and Hsp47-driven collagen cooperate to create a unified immune-exclusion barrier and whether OGT inhibition combined with checkpoint blockade can dismantle this barrier in ECM-dense, immunologically cold tumors.4.2O-GlcNAc-dependent promotion of tumor angiogenesisRecent studies have established O-GlcNAcylation as a pro-angiogenic signal converging on VEGF regulation via cell-autonomous and intercellular mechanisms. In hepatocellular carcinoma, FOXM1 upregulates HBP flux, elevating O-GlcNAcylation and promoting VEGF secretion to drive angiogenesis; OGT inhibition significantly impairs this response (72). FOXM1 and SPP1 have been identified as hub HBP genes that correlate with poor prognosis, positioning HBP expression as a clinically informative prognostic signature (72).A mechanistically precise intercellular axis was uncovered in bladder cancer, where tumor cells transfer GFAT1 to endothelial cells (ECs) via small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), reprogramming EC glucose metabolism by increasing hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) flux and O-GlcNAcylation (73). O-GlcNAcylation of SerRS at Ser101 promotes ubiquitination and degradation, while impairing importin α5-mediated nuclear translocation (73). Intranuclear SerRS suppresses VEGF transcription by binding to the GC-rich proximal promoter; its loss de-represses VEGF and drives neovascularization in the retina. GFAT1 knockout in tumor cells abrogated SerRS O-GlcNAcylation in ECs and attenuated angiogenesis in vivo, whereas sEV-mediated GFAT1 delivery restored angiogenic activity in GFAT1-knockout mice (73). Together, these studies reveal that O-GlcNAcylation promotes angiogenesis via VEGF secretion and transcriptional de-repression, which are complementary outputs of the same metabolic pathway. Nonetheless, these findings should be interpreted in the context of the broader recognition that tumor angiogenesis is predominantly governed by hypoxia-driven HIF-1α–VEGF signalling and stromal cues from CAFs and tumor-associated macrophages (74), rather than by a single metabolic input. Whether HBP-driven O-GlcNAcylation acts as an independent pro-angiogenic axis or converges on canonical hypoxia signalling, for example, by stabilizing HIF-1α, remains untested in either model, and the apparent quantitative dominance of the FOXM1 and sEV-GFAT1 mechanisms may reflect model-specific vascular dependencies rather than a pan-tumor principle. Future studies should establish whether the sEV-GFAT1 axis operates in other vascularized solid tumors and whether SerRS O-GlcNAcylation at Ser101 is detectable in circulating ECs as a minimally invasive angiogenesis biomarker for these tumors.4.3Intercellular metabolic communication via O-GlcNAc signalingO-GlcNAc signalling functions as a metabolic sensor that translates extracellular nutrient cues into oncogenic programs. Two studies have demonstrated distinct modes of microenvironment-driven O-GlcNAcylation during intercellular tumor–stromal communication. In nasopharyngeal carcinoma, hypoxic tumor cell-derived exosomes (H-exo) carrying low LKB1 remodel adjacent adipocytes by inhibiting the STK11/LKB1–AMPK axis and activating the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) flux (75). O-GlcNAcylation of VPS4B promotes its interaction with ANXA5, triggering lipid droplet (LD) maturation and release; tumor cells then internalize these LDs via macropinocytosis to fuel progression (75). This bidirectional circuit, in which tumor-derived exosomes program stromal adipocytes to supply lipid cargo, represents O-GlcNAc-dependent metabolic symbiosis in the TME.In a systemic context, diabetic hyperglycemia elevates HBP flux and O-GlcNAcylation in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), promoting proliferation, invasion, and lymph node metastasis via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway (76). DM status correlated with advanced T stage, depth of invasion, and Ki-67 in patients with OSCC; OGT knockdown or OSMI-1 reversed these phenotypes (76), reinforcing systemic glucose excess as a druggable determinant of tumor behavior.Together, these studies illustrate that O-GlcNAcylation links local hypoxia-exosomes and systemic hyperglycemia inputs to tumor progression. The hyperglycemia–O-GlcNAc axis defined here for OSCC parallels earlier observations in colorectal cancer, where patients with diabetes exhibit skewing of tumor-associated macrophages toward immunosuppressive M2-like phenotypes via elevated HBP flux (29), suggesting that systemic glucose excess may act concurrently on tumor-intrinsic and myeloid compartments rather than on a single cell type. Whether the adipocyte-centered VPS4B circuit is similarly amplified under hyperglycemic conditions or remains a hypoxia-restricted mechanism has not been tested, which is a gap that tempers the direct extrapolation of either study to broader metabolic disease contexts. Future studies should map O-GlcNAc proteomic changes in adipocyte–tumor cocultures under nutrient stress and determine whether glycemic control in patients with diabetes and cancer reduces tumor O-GlcNAcylation and improves treatment response, a clinically tractable hypothesis warranting prospective investigation.4.4O-GlcNAcylation in tumor stemness, mechanoadaptation, and cytokine regulationO-GlcNAcylation regulates tumor progression through three functionally distinct programs: mechanical stemness, cytokine suppression, and transcription factor-driven cytokine induction, all of which are unified by HBP flux as a shared metabolic sensor. The most mechanistically resolved axis involves Notch1 O-GlcNAcylation during chordoma recurrence. Stiff ECM drives ligand-independent EPHA2 phosphorylation, sequentially activating LYN kinase and OGT via phosphorylation at Y989 and Y418; enhanced OGT activity then induces NICD1 O-GlcNAcylation at T2063, T2090, and S2162, activating transcription of mechanical and stemness-related genes (77). MIR31 deletion amplifies this cascade by upregulating LYN expression and enhancing the perception of stiffness. MIR31 loss has been proposed as a patient stratification biomarker for Notch- or OGT-targeted therapy (77). This circuit represents a rare example of mechanotransduction directly and site-specifically coupled to glycosylation, with substantial therapeutic implications for recurrent chordomas. At the cytokine level, elevated TME O-GlcNAcylation, modelled using OGT-transgenic mice bearing B16 melanoma, suppresses p38 MAPK activity, upregulates ERK1/2 signalling, and downregulates macrophage NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory cytokine production, thereby promoting tumor growth (78). This inverse relationship between TME O-GlcNAcylation and antitumor inflammation provides a mechanistic explanation for the elevated cancer morbidity observed in patients with diabetes and systemic hyperglycemia (78). A contrasting cytokine axis has been identified in pancreatic cancer, where GFPT2-mediated O-GlcNAcylation promotes the nuclear translocation of YBX1, which transcriptionally activates IL-18 and drives macrophage M2 polarization, creating an immunosuppressive TME (66). Recent studies converge on macrophage reprogramming through mechanistically orthogonal routes, NF-κB suppression versus YBX1-mediated IL-18 induction, a distinction with direct implications for therapeutic targeting in macrophage-rich tumors (66, 78). Translationally, consensus clustering of 34 O-GlcNAcylation-related genes in gastric cancer identified subgroups with divergent TME profiles. A principal component analysis (PCA)-derived prognostic score validated across five real-world cohorts demonstrated that patients with low scores had better prognosis and greater immunotherapy benefit (79), positioning O-GlcNAcylation gene signatures as a clinically actionable predictive framework (Figure 4). The clearest example of this is Erbin, a tumor suppressor that represses homologous recombination (HR). In 5-FU-resistant colorectal cancer, hyper-O-GlcNAcylation of Erbin promotes its degradation, lifting HR suppression, and enabling repair of 5-FU lesions. A mechanistically distinct case is that of topoisomerase IIα (TOP2A). Rather than altering stability, O-GlcNAcylation directly enhances chromatin binding and catalytic activity, promoting adriamycin resistance in breast cancer cells and xenografts (91).
