title: The role, regulatory mechanisms, and therapeutic implications of FTO in gastrointestinal cancer
abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most common post-transcriptional modification in mRNA, playing a crucial role in cancer development by modulating RNA stability, translation, and nuclear export. As the first discovered m6A demethylase, FTO catalyzes m6A demethylation in a Fe2+/α-KG-dependent manner, functioning as either an oncogene or a tumor suppressor to mediate cancer progression via reducing m6A levels and thereby modulating RNA metabolism. Numerous studies have elucidated the mechanisms by which upstream regulators affect FTO expression, as well as the post-translational modifications that impact its protein stability, translocation, and degradation. Moreover, inhibitors targeting FTO demonstrate significant therapeutic potential. In this review, we summarize recent research on the role and regulatory manner of FTO in gastrointestinal cancer and discuss its potential clinical application in cancer therapy.
full_text: In eukaryotes, RNA metabolism relies not only on transcriptional control of genes but also on RNA modifications at the post-transcriptional level. Among the more than 170 known RNA modifications, RNA methylation is the most prevalent, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the total, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A), N1-methyladenosine (m1A), 5-methylcytidine (m5C), and 7-methylguanosine (m7G). To date, m6A is the most extensively studied modification occurring in mRNA, tRNA, lncRNA, microRNA, and circRNA.1, 2, 3, 4, 5 In 2012, the development of the whole transcriptome m6A detecting method (m6A-seq) provided key tools for the identifying m6A modifications, which accelerated the exploration of the role of m6A in cancers.6, 7, 8 Previous studies have revealed that m6A mainly occurs at the RRm6ACH (R = G or A; H = C, A, or U) motif, and can be recognized by m6A reader proteins to affect RNA fate.9, 10, 11, 12, 13 Extensive evidence demonstrates that m6A mediates nearly all aspects of RNA metabolism, including mRNA stability, export, translation, splicing, and degradation, which mediates the progression of various cancers.14, 15, 16Mechanistically, m6A is dynamically regulated by “writers” and “erasers” and recognized by “readers” to mediate RNA fate. The reported m6A methyltransferase complex consists of methyltransferase-like 3/14 (METTL3/14) and WT1-associated protein (WTAP). Among them, METTL3 acts as the catalytic subunit, which deposits m6A modification to the substrate in an S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM)-dependent manner.17 Structural analysis revealed that METTL3 and METTL14 form a heterodimer modulating the m6A deposition on nuclear RNA.18 Previous studies have demonstrated that WTAP plays a role in mediating mRNA splicing and regulating alternative splicing.19,20 Pinget al. revealed that WTAP is essential for the localization of METTL3 and METTL14 into nuclear speckles.21 Additionally, METTL16, vir-like m6A methyltransferase-associated (VIRMA), Cbl proto-oncogene-like 1 (HAKAI, zinc finger CCCH-type containing 13 (ZC3H13), and RNA-binding motif protein 15/15B (RBM15/15B) also interact with methyltransferase complex to mediate m6A methylation on specific targets.22, 23, 24, 25, 26 At present, two AlkB family proteins have been identified as m6A demethylases, including FTO and AlkB homolog 5 (ALKBH5). ALKBH5 primarily recognizes m6A-modified mRNA, while FTO can recognize various types of RNA, including mRNA, snRNA, and tRNA. Moreover, FTO shuttles between the cytoplasm and the nucleus, whereas ALKBH5 is predominantly localized in the nucleus. Additionally, they remove m6A methylation in different ways. FTO first catalyzes m6A to generate N6-hydroxymethyladenosine (hm6A) and N6-formyladenosine (f6A). Subsequently, these two intermediate products are converted to adenosine (A) under conditions at 37 °C.27 In contrast, ALKBH5 accomplishes the progression of m6A demethylation in a single step.28 Ueda et al found that ALKBH3 specifically recognizes m6A in tRNA within cancer cells.29 In addition, the m6A “reader” proteins are crucial regulators that direct m6A-modified RNA into various metabolic pathways. The YTH domain family contains the largest group of m6A readers (YTHDF1/2/3, and YTHDC1/2), which modulate m6A RNA stability, translation, and nuclear export.11, 12, 13,30IGF2 mRNA binding protein (IGF2BP1/2/3) recognizes m6A-modified RNA to enhance mRNA stability and translation.31 The heterokaryotic nuclear RNA protein family (HNRNPC, HNRNPG), acting as readers of m6A RNA, mediates pre-RNA alternative splicing and microRNA processing.32, 33, 34In the course of m6A-related studies, the identification of the first m6A demethylation enzyme, alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase (FTO), represents a significant landmark discovery. This finding confirms the dynamic nature of m6A and positions it as one of the most prominent targets in epigenetics.35 Meanwhile, FTO is one of the most extensively studied m6A regulators in cancers. Considering its widespread distribution, substrate diversity, and functional variability, this review summarizes recent advances in understanding the role and molecular mechanisms of FTO in gastrointestinal cancer (GICs), including the known upstream regulators and posttranslational modifications of FTO, and discusses the progress in the development of small-molecule inhibitors targeting FTO for cancer treatment.Structure and function of FTOFTO, a member of the AlkB family, catalyzes the demethylation of substrates in a Fe2+/α-ketoglutarate (α-KG)-dependent manner. The reported catalytic substrates of FTO include m6A, m1A, and the N6, 2′-O-dimethyladenosine cap (m6Am) modification. In the nucleus, FTO demethylates m6A and m6Am in small nucleus RNA (snRNA), N1-methyladenine (m1A) from tRNA, and m6A in mRNA. When localized in the cytoplasm, FTO can demethylate m6A and m6Am in mRNA and m1A from tRNA 36, 37, 38 (Fig. 1). Crystal structure analysis has revealed that FTO consists of an Alkb-like domain (NTD, residues 32–326) and a carboxy-terminal domain (CTD, resides 327–498). The NTD serves as the catalytic core of FTO, containing the binding sites for Fe2+ and N-oxalylglycine. The CTD stabilizes the conformation of the NTD, thereby maintaining FTO demethylase activity.39 The R316Q mutation has been identified a key site for enzymatic activity through genetic analysis of a family with growth retardation and polymalformative syndrome.40Figure 1The substrate and function of FTO in RNA metabolism. FTO recognizes mRNA, tRNA, and snRNA, and catalyzes the demethylation of m1A, m6A, and m6Am in a Fe2+/α-KG-dependent manner, which mediate RNA metabolism, including mRNA export, splicing, degradation, and translocation.Figure 1The role of FTO in gastrointestinal cancerAs one of the most widely reported m6A medication regulators, FTO has been verified to be tightly involved in the development of various cancers by mediating RNA stability, nuclear export, and translation. GICs represent one of the foremost contributors to cancer-related deaths across the globe.41 Here, we summarize recent studies elucidating the role of FTO as both a pro-tumor and tumor suppressor factor in GICs (Table 1).Table 1Role of FTO in gastrointestinal cancer.Table 1CancerRoleUpstreamTargetReaderFunctionGCOncogenePI3K/AktGC malignancy42GCOncogeneMOXD1GC malignancy43GCOncogeneCaveolin-1GC tumor growth44GCOncogeneMAP4K4Tumorigenesis and metastasis45GCOncogenecircFAM192AGC cells proliferation46GCOncogeneSP1Invasion and LNM47GCOncogeneHDAC3/FOXA2MYCTumorigenesis48GCOncogeneDDIT3Chemosensitivity49GCSuppressorMYCFOSIGF2BP1/2Migration and invasion50LCOncogeneGPNMBYTHDF2Proliferation, migration and invasion51LCOncogeneFTO-IT1PKM2/GLUT1YTHDF2Glycolysis and proliferation52LCOncogeneULK1YTHDC2Autophagy53LCOncogeneAMD1SOX2Stem-cell property54LCSuppressorERBB3/TUBB4AProliferation, migration, and tumorigenesis55LCSuppressorCircGPR137BCell growth, tumorgenetics56LCSuppressorCUL4AGlucose metabolism57CRCOncogeneAKTGPX4YTHDF2Protect from ferroptotic cell death58CRCOncogenePD-L1Impact PD-L1 expression59CRCOncogeneZNF687Tumor growth, metastasis, and angiogenesis60CRCOncogeneG6PD/PARP1Chemo-Resistance61CRCOncogeneSIVA1Chemo-Resistance62CRCSuppressorHK2IGF2BP2Glycolysis63CRCSuppressormicroRNA-96MYCProliferation and apoptotic64PCOncogenePDGFCYTHDF2Proliferation65PCOncogeneLINC01134Chemoresistance66PCOncogenemiR-383–5pIGF2BP1Cell viability, metastasis, stemness67PCOncogeneUSP7NEDD4Chemoresistance68PCOncogeneTFPI-2YTHDF1Growth, migration, and invasion69PCOncogeneGATA6-AS1SNAI1Epithelial-mesenchymal70PCSuppressorPJA2YTHDF2Proliferation, invasion and metastasis71GC, gastric cancer; CRC, colorectal cancer; LC, liver cancer; PC, pancreatic cancer.Gastric cancerGastric cancer (GC) ranks as the fifth most prevalent and fatal cancer globally. In 2022, over 968,000 new cases of GC were diagnosed, resulting in nearly 660,000 deaths.72 Nonetheless, the exact mechanisms contributing to the high prevalence of GC remain poorly understood. Therefore, identifying key molecules that influence the progression of GC is critical for the development of potential therapeutic approaches. Bioinformatics and experimental studies confirmed a significantly correlation between the FTO gene and gastric cancer at both the genetic and transcriptional levels.73,74 GC patients with up-regulated FTO present markedly lower overall survival rates, which are mediated through multiple mechanisms. For instance, Zhu et al and Lai et al found that FTO promotes GC malignancy by upregulating the PI3K/Akt signaling and DBH-like monooxygenase 1 (MOXD1) expression, respectively.42,43 Yin et al found that FTO promotes GC progression by suppressing MAP4KA degradation and activating MAPK/JNK signaling pathways.45 As a prognostic marker in GC, FTO reduces caveolin-1 mRNA by enhancing its degradation in an m6A-dependent manner, which promotes GC cell malignancy and tumor growth by inducing mitochondrial fusion and metabolism.44 Besides the most common mRNA, FTO could modulate circRNA fate to affect GC progression. Zhou, et al proved that FTO could recognize circFAM192A and remove its m6A methylation, thereby protecting it from degradation and enhancing the stability of interacting protein leucine transporter solute carrier family 7 member 5 (SLC7A5). As a result, the amount of SLC7A5 significantly increased on the membrane, activating the mTOR signaling pathway to promote GC cell proliferation.46 Functionally, FTO has been demonstrated to mediate proliferation and migration of various types of GC cells75,76 and to enhance cellular malignancy by promoting the stemness of GC cells.77 Recently, Zeng et al reported that FTO correlates with tumor size, advanced nerve invasion, and lymph node metastasis (LNM) in GC patients. They revealed that FTO increases the levels of specificity protein 1 (SP1) and Aurora Kniase B by removing its methylation, leading to the dephosphorylation of P53 and promoting GC tumorigenesis and progression.47Viral infection is a significant factor in the onset of gastric cancer,78 and FTO regulates the efficiency of viral infection, thereby modulating the development of gastric cancer. Gui et al found that Helicobacter pylori infection significantly increases both the mRNA and protein levels of FTO in both human gastric mucosal epithelial cells and Mongolinan gerbil gastric tissues. The knockdown of FTO significantly reduces the abilities of migration and invasion in Helicobacter pylori -infected GC cells, suggesting that FTO may serve as a potential therapeutic target to reduce virus-infected GC malignancy.79 Interestingly, FTO is also highly expressed in Epstein–Barr virus-associated gastric cancer (EBVaGC), but it restrains EBVaGC cell migration, invasion, and tumor metastasis. FOS was identified as a critical downstream target of FTO by MeRIP-seq, while IGF2BP1/2 binds to the m6A modification of FOS nascent transcripts to maintain its mRNA stability. Its upstream regulator EBV activates myelocytomatosis viral oncogenehomolog (MYC) binding to the promoter of FTO to elevate FTO expression in EBVaGC cells.50In addition, several upstream regulators, including transcription factors and clinical drugs, can regulate the development and treatment efficacy of gastric cancer by targeting FTO. Yang et al found that the transcription factor A2 (FOXA2) binds to the FTO promoter, leading to a decrease in FTO expression in GC. Mechanistically, FOXA2 inhibits FTO to remove the m6A methylation of MYC), thereby stabilizing MYC mRNA and promoting gastric cancer progression. Combination therapy may represent the most expedient approach to investigate this purpose.s and prospectsIncreasing evidence demonstrates that abnormal expression of FTO is significantly associated with cancer occurrence and development. FTO functions not only as an oncogenic factor but also acts to inhibit tumor progression in GICs. Five major cancer-promoting pathways have been reported: (i) FTO demethylates the m6A modification of oncogenes such as MYC and DDIT3,48, 49, 50 which enhances their mRNA stability and translation efficiency, thereby promoting the proliferation of cancer cells; (ii) FTO modulates metabolic reprogramming by regulating the m6A levels of metabolism-related genes (GLUT1, PKM2,52 and HK263), thereby promoting cancer progression; (iii) FTO inhibits the activity of T cell by mediating the m6A modification of the immune checkpoint factor PD-L1, contributing to cancer immune escape.59 (vi) FTO mediates drug resistance through reducing the m6A levels of chemoresistance-related gene NEDD4.68 (v) FTO counteracts ferroptosis in CRC cells, promoting tumorigenesis via enhancing the expression levels of solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4).58,159 Conversely, FTO can improve cancer cell stemness,89 facilitates metabolic reprogramming,63,160 reduce m6A modification of antioncogenes,64 and enhances ferroptosis159 to suppress the development of GICs. The current understanding of regulatory networks is insufficient to distinguish the bidirectional role of FTO in GICs. The application of artificial intelligence may offer new insights41 to establish a clear classification method.In addition to its role as an m6A demethylase that influences various biological processes, such as viral infection,161 DNA damage,162,163 and stress response, via modifying m6A levels,164, 165, 166 FTO also mediates cellular metabolism in an m6A(m)-independent manner. Kim et al found that FTO mediates canonical WNT/β-Catenin signaling via downregulating DKK1 in an RNA methylation-independent manner, thereby promoting cell migration.167 These findings highlight the necessity of exploring multiple perspectives in the function and regulatory mechanisms of FTO in future research.Despite significant advances in the development of FTO regulators, various aspects warrant further exploration. (i) As a primary m6A demethylase, FTO not only function as an oncogene in GICs, but also has been shown to inhibit cancer progression across various malignancies. To date, nearly all reported FTO regulators are designed to suppress its pro-tumor function based on its substrate and structural characteristics. For instance, Wang et al found that NADP directly binds to FTO, enhancing its activity.168 Additionally, Huang et al demonstrated that regulating NADPH levels with branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) could mediate FTO expression.169 However, no related FTO activators have been identified so far. Therefore, further studies are needed to elucidate the structural basis and regulatory mechanisms of FTO's function to develop dual-action regulators. (ii) As an m6A and m6Am demethylase, the sensitivity and specificity of FTO regulators warrant closer attention. (iii) Previous studies have demonstrated that FTO inhibitors, such as MO-I-500, CS1/CS2, and , can effectively inhibit FTO activity in breast cancer. Dac51 has been shown to synergize with anti-PD-L1, promoting T cell infiltration.151 However, further clinical trials are still needed to validate their clinical practicability. (vi) With ongoing research, the regulatory mechanisms of FTO are being progressively elucidated, encompassing upstream regulators and PTMs, which provide new insight for the developing of FTO regulators to accelerate the advancement of relative drug development.In summary, FTO plays a crucial role in GICs, which may serve as a potential diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target. We anticipate that future studies will further reveal its regulatory mechanisms, facilitating the development of both inhibitors and activators, and ultimately advancing their application in clinical treatment.CRediT authorship contribution statementXinxin Zhang: Writing – original draft, Resources, Project administration. title: Wise as a Serpent and Gentle as a Dove: Pharmacological Targeting of NRF2/KEAP1 Pathway from Treasure Trove of Mother Nature
abstract: Discovery of NRF2 in 1994 was once assumed simplistic and classical but the following years witnessed phenomenal breakthroughs that led to a rapid increase in the components of complex molecular web. Emerging evidence has enabled us to develop a better understanding of the spatio-temporally placed molecular machinery both upstream and downstream to the NRF2 in different contexts and diseases. The exciting voyage to unravel the multifaceted roles of NRF2 in human diseases has catalyzed innovations in therapeutic approaches, inspiring the design of compounds for pharmacological modulation of NRF2 in disease prevention and intervention. In this review, we have set the spotlight on sketching a detailed landscape both upstream and downstream to the central signaling node of NRF2. Identification of the natural products having unique ability to pharmacologically target NRF2-associated networks. Later, we expand our discussion about ongoing and completed clinical trials related to multifaceted roles of NRF2 as an oncogene and a tumor suppressor. We argue that a holistic view of NRF2-driven upstream and downstream signaling is necessary for the identification of preventive or therapeutic opportunities.
full_text: The multifaceted nature of cancer is becoming increasingly complex and intriguing because of the rapidly growing list of breakthroughs in molecular oncology. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) in biological systems are transient but essential molecules. These molecules are generated by specific enzymatic pathways and eliminated by a delicately balanced antioxidant defense system.1–3 From transformation and tumor initiation to metastatic dissemination, increasing ROS in cancer cells can paradoxically promote or suppress the tumorigenic process. This “double-edged sword” behavior depends on the extent of redox stress, its spatiotemporal characteristics and the tumor microenvironment. The NRF transcriptional factors NRF1, NRF2, and NRF3, are a subset of Cap “n” collar transcriptional regulators involved in regulating the expression of genes harboring antioxidant-response element (ARE) sequences within their promoter regions. KEAP1 interacts with the N-terminal located Neh2 domain of NRF2 and blocks its nuclear translocation. KEAP1 enhances the rate of the proteasomal degradation of NRF2 (Figure 1).4,5 Figure 1The transcriptional factor NRF2 and its principal negative regulator, the E3 ligase adaptor KEAP1, are critical in the maintenance of redox. In the cytoplasm, NRF2 is ubiquitinated by the KEAP1-CUL3 ubiquitin E3 ligase complex to mark it for proteasomal degradation.The image illustrates the interaction between KEAP1 and NRF2, leading to NRF2 degradation. KEAP1 is depicted with domains labeled NTR, BTB, IVR and CTR and cysteine residues Cys-151, Cys-273, Cys-288 and Cys-489. NRF2 is shown with domains Neh2, Neh4, Neh5, Neh7, Neh6, Neh1 and Neh3. KEAP1 binds to NRF2, facilitating its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the proteasome. The process ends with NRF2 being broken down into smaller fragments, labeled as degraded NRF2.Diagram showing KEAP1-NRF2 interaction leading to NRF2 degradation via the proteasome.KEAP1/NRF2 is an important regulatory pathway and existing evidence highlights different mutations in this cascade.6–9 NRF2 mutations, particularly, R34G (Arg34Gly) had been shown to induce drug resistance in cancer cells.10 Therefore, status of NRF2 activity in aggressive and drug resistant cancers holds vital importance. Positron emission tomography imaging has provided analysis of NRF2 activation in patient-derived, orthotopic and genetically engineered rodent models. Combination of imaging and targeted treatment with activating NRF2/KEAP1 mutations may open new horizons for therapy-resistant cancer patients.11Site-directed mutagenesis was used for detailed analysis of the functional role of different amino acids in KEAP1. It was shown that Cys151 in the BTB domain of KEAP1 had a central role in the regulation of NRF2. Adduction or oxidation at Cys151 induced conformational change in KEAP1 that resulted in dissociation of KEAP1 from CUL3, thereby inhibiting NRF2 ubiquitination.With the aid of high-throughput technologies and the landmark discoveries of significant functionalities of NRF2, our connaissance of the regulatory roles of NRF2 in different stages of cancer development has evolved substantially. It is worth mentioning that NRF2 mechanistically modulates the expression of its target genes and centrally steers multiple stages of cancer.There are some good reviews related to the role of KEAP1/NRF2 in different diseases and how this signaling axis can be exploited pharmacologically for an efficient and durable treatment option.12–15 In this review, we have addressed the dualistic roles of KEAP1/NRF2 signaling in different cancers. We have summarized how KEAP1/NRF2 signaling served as an oncogenic pathway and a tumor suppressor pathway in different cancers. How inputs through multiple effectors and crosstalks with other transduction cascades play a role in regulation of carcinogenesis and metastasis. Another important aim of this review is to rationalize these conflicting perspectives by critiquing the context dependence of NRF2 functions and pharmacological modulation for the inhibition of carcinogenesis and metastasis.Exclusion and Inclusion CriteriaIn this review, we have exclusively selected high-quality research articles using Scopus, PUBMED, and clinicaltrials.gov. We used different keywords “NRF2”, “KEAP1”, metastasis, “mice”, “natural products”. The selected references were primarily taken from 2020–2026. However, seminal studies published before 2020 were also included for a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms (Figure 2). Figure 2Exclusion and inclusion criteria for the selection of seminal studies and structuring of the review.A flowchart of selection, exclusion and inclusion criteria with article counts for a review.Role of NRF2/KEAP1 in CarcinogenesisNRF2 signaling has been shown to centrally drive multiple stages of carcinogenesis and metastasis. In this section, we have summarized how different proteins enhanced the stability and activity of NRF2 by inhibition of KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2.Peptidylprolyl isomerase A (PPIA) is required for the stability of NRF2. PPIA physically binds to NRF2 and prevents the accessibility of KEAP1 to NRF2, thus inhibiting the degradation of NRF2. Cyclosporin A, an FDA-approved drug, impairs the interaction of NRF2 with PPIA, thus inducing the ubiquitination and degradation of NRF2. NRF2-KLF5 signaling transcriptionally stimulates glutamine transporter SLC1A5 in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells (Figure 3). Transportation of glutamine into cells through plasma membrane transporters (SLC1A5) is converted to glutamate by glutaminase to fuel the growth of cancer cells. Targeting of glutaminase for cancer inhibition is also an exciting area of research. Glutaminase inhibitor (CB-839) and cyclosporin A efficiently impeded the growth of the tumors in mice injected with A549 cells.16 Thus, the stability of NRF2 is regulated by different proteins that interfere with KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2. Figure 3(A and B) PPIA (Peptidylprolyl isomerase (A)) physically binds to NRF2 and pre-vents the accessibility of KEAP1 to NRF2, thus inhibiting the degradation of NRF2. NRF2-KLF5 signaling transcriptionally stimulates glutamine transporter SLC1A5. Transportation of glutamine into cells through plasma membrane transporters (SLC1A5) is converted to glutamate by glutaminase to fuel the growth of cancer cells. (C–E) KAT5 (Lysine acetyltransferase 5) and FosB synergistically stimulate the expression of oncogenic DPP4. DPP4 potentiates the activation of NRF2 signaling and triggers NRF2-mediated transcriptional upregulation of p62. Consequently, p62 interferes with KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2. (F) DPP4-silenced cancer cells did not form pulmonary and hepatic metastasis in mice. (RED CROSS Symbolizes inhibition).The image consists of two parts. The left part shows a cellular diagram illustrating NRF2 signaling and glutamine transport. Peptidylprolyl isomerase A binds to NRF2, preventing KEAP1 from accessing NRF2, thus inhibiting its degradation. NRF2-KLF5 signaling stimulates the glutamine transporter SLC1A5. Glutamine enters the cell and is converted to glutamate by glutaminase. Lysine acetyltransferase 5 and FosB stimulate DPP4 expression, which activates NRF2 signaling and upregulates p62. p62 interferes with KEAP1-mediated NRF2 targeting. The right part shows a mouse model with DPP4-silenced TPC-1 cells, indicating inhibition of pulmonary and liver metastasis. Red crosses symbolize inhibition of metastasis in the lung and liver.Diagram showing NRF2 signaling, glutamine transport and DPP4′s role in cancer metastasis inhibition in mice.Dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DPP4) has an oncogenic role. Lysine acetyltransferase 5 (KAT5) and FosB synergistically stimulate the expression of DPP4 in papillary thyroid cancer (Figure 3). DPP4 potentiates the activation of NRF2 signaling and stimulation of p62. Resultantly, p62 competitively inhibits KEAP1-NRF2 interaction and triggers the activation of NRF2-mediated signaling. There was a considerable reduction in the number of hepatic and pulmonary metastatic nodules in mice injected with DPP4-silenced TPC-1 cells, while further overexpression of KAT5 or FosB led to an increase in the number of metastatic nodules.17DPP9 is also an oncogenic protein. It contains ETGE and ESGE motifs. Mechanistically, DPP9 physically interacts with KEAP1 through ESGE and protects NRF2 from degradation by KEAP1 (Figure 4). Consequently, NRF2 levels are high in DPP9-overexpressing cancer cells. DPP9 overexpression suppresses ferroptotic death and induces sorafenib resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) cells primarily through NRF2-mediated transcriptional upregulation of SLC7A11. SLC7A11 is a transporter of cystine for GSH biosynthesis, thereby protecting cells from oxidative stress and ferroptotic death (Figure 4). DPP9 knockout led to marked regression of tumors formed by 786-O cells and potentiated sorafenib-induced tumor inhibitory effects.18 Overall, targeted inhibition of DPP9 is necessary for the activation of KEAP1. Figure 4(A) DPP9 interacts with KEAP1 and interferes with the binding of NRF2 and KEAP1. NRF2 mediates transcriptional upregulation of SLC7A11. SLC7A11 is a transporter of cystine for GSH biosynthesis, thereby protecting cells from oxidative stress. (B and C) KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2 is inhibited by UCHL3 and long non-coding RNAs. (D) NRF2 stimulates pro-metastatic PRPS1. (E and F) Heme promotes FBXO22-mediated degradation of BACH1. However, NRF2-mediated upregulation of Heme oxygenase promotes the catabolism of heme. UCHL3, PRPS1 and BACH1 promote the metastatic colonization of cancer cells to secondary organs.The diagram illustrates the interaction of DPP9 with KEAP1, affecting NRF2 regulation. In section A, DPP9 binds KEAP1, allowing NRF2 to translocate and upregulate SLC7A11, which transports cystine for glutathione synthesis. Section B shows UCHL3 inhibiting KEAP1, stabilizing NRF2. Section C depicts lncRNA-EBLN3P interfering with KEAP1, enhancing NRF2 activity. Section D shows NRF2 upregulating PRPS1, while section E shows NRF2 upregulating Heme Oxygenase-1. Section F illustrates heme promoting FBXO22-mediated degradation of BACH1, while NRF2-induced Heme Oxygenase catabolizes heme. The right side shows a mouse model with pulmonary metastasis, highlighting pro-metastatic roles of UCHL3, PRPS1 and BACH1.Diagram: DPP9 interacts with KEAP1, NRF2 and pathways UCHL3, PRPS1, BACH1.Ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2C (UBE2C) overexpression promotes the interaction between p62 and KEAP1, thus interfering with the interaction between NRF2 and KEAP1. UBE2C-mediated inhibition of the interaction between NRF2 and KEAP1 leads to nuclear accumulation of NRF2. Notably, p62 depletion causes significant suppression in UBE2C-mediated increase in NRF2 levels. Furthermore, the silencing of UBE2C also inhibits the nuclear accumulation of NRF2.19Carnitine palmitoyltransferase (CPT1B) interacts with KEAP1 and promotes the activation of NRF2. There is a considerable regression of the tumors and reduction in NRF2 expression in mice inoculated with CPT1B-knockdown MiaPaCa-2 cells. Gemcitabine-mediated chemotherapeutic effects were found to be enhanced in mice inoculated with CPT1B knockdown cancer cells.20EIF4A is a component of eukaryotic initiation factor 4F (EIF4F) complex. CR-1-31B (CR-31), a synthetic rocaglate has been shown to potently inhibit eIF4A-mediated translation of NRF2. Tert-butylhydroquinone (tBHQ), a chemical oxidative stress inducer caused activation of NRF2. Loss of oncogenic NRF2 sufficiently blocked osteosarcoma growth, metastasizing ability and phenocopied the inhibitory effects of CR-1-31B on metastatic dissemination. Likewise, clinical-grade eFT226 (zotatifin), an EIF4A1 inhibitor enhanced oxidative stress and blocked the metastatic phenotype of tBHQ-treated osteosarcoma cells. CR-1-31B efficiently inhibited spontaneous lung metastasis in mice orthotopically implanted with MNNG cells.21Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) promoted nuclear accumulation of NRF2 with concomitant increase in the NRF2-regulated gene networks. High doxorubicin-resistance-induced pro-angiogenic, pro-proliferative and invasive effects were found to be impaired upon depletion of SIRT1. Findings indicated a considerable increase in tumor formation and invasion in mice xenografted with MDA-MB-231 high Dox-Res cancer cells.22NADP+ is generated by phosphorylation of NAD+ by NAD+ kinase (NADK). Isoform 3 of NAD+ kinase is transcriptionally stimulated by NRF2. It has previously been revealed that metastasizing melanoma cells are fueled by NADPH regenerating pathways. Low NADPH/NADP+ ratio indicates higher level of oxidative stress. Importantly, ratio of NADPH/NADP+ was noted to be reduced in metastatic nodules as compared to the subcutaneous tumors. Cancer cells, both in circulation and during metastatic colonization undergo high levels of oxidative stress. While most cancer cells do not survive the metastatic cascade, but successful metastatically competent cancer cells gradually overcome oxidative stress. NADK Isoform 3 is specifically upregulated in metastatic nodules compared to the primary tumors. NADK Isoform 3 provides antioxidant protection to melanoma cells increasing extravasation and organ colonization by metastasizing melanoma cells.23Nearly 50 years ago, researchers observed that cells in culture “exfoliated” small sacs of mysterious functions. Pioneering works have shown that these structures, now known as exosomes or extracellular vesicles, can contain RNA, proteins and other molecules. Exosomes are packaged by parent cells and delivered to recipient cells. Cells seem to use them to communicate with each other. Circ- is secreted in exosomes by breast cancer cells. Circ- -loaded exosomes are taken up by tumor-associated macrophages and promote the polarization of macrophages to M2-phenotype (Figure 5). circ- acted as a scaffold and enhanced the interaction between the deubiquitinating enzyme ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7) and NRF2 in macrophages. Circ- induced USP7-mediated deubiquitination of NRF2 (Figure 5). Whereas HIF-1α stimulated the expression of circ- in breast cancer cells (Figure 5). Injections of circ- -silenced exosomes not only caused a reduction of the volume and weight of tumors but also prolonged the survival time of tumor-bearing mice. There was a considerable reduction in the population of F4/80+CD206+ M2-macrophages within tumor tissues of mice treated with circ- -silenced exosomes. Furthermore, metastatic dissemination of 4T1 cancer cells was severely impaired in mice injected with circ- -silenced exosomes.24 Overall, these findings indicated that oncogenic non-coding RNAs enhanced the stability of NRF2. There is a gradual increase in the multi-layered regulation of NRF2 by non-coding RNAs through intricate interplay between long non-coding RNAs/microRNAs and circular RNAs/microRNAs. (B) Circ- -loaded exosomes are taken up tumor-associated macrophages and promoted the polarization of macrophages to M2-phenotype. circ- enhances the interaction between the deubiquitinating enzyme ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7) and NRF2 in macrophages. In section A, breast cancer cells release exosomes containing Circ- , stimulated by HIF-1 alpha. These exosomes are shown moving towards macrophages. In section B, Circ- -loaded exosomes are taken up by CD206 and CD163 positive M2 macrophages. Circ- enhances the interaction between ubiquitin-specific protease 7 and NRF2, promoting NRF2 activity. In section C, a mouse model is depicted with circ- -silenced exosomes, showing inhibition of pulmonary metastasis. The red cross symbolizes inhibition of metastasis to the lung.Diagram showing breast cancer cell exosome release, macrophage uptake and metastasis inhibition in a mouse model.ΔNp63α is frequently overexpressed in ESCC and drives transcriptional upregulation of Plectin (PLEC). PLEC impairs KEAP-mediated targeting of NRF2. ΔNp63α knockdown led to a significant reduction in the levels of NRF2. Moreover, low-dose irradiation induces NRF2 activation, consequently upregulating the expression of ΔNp63α.25Free heme is a potent oxidative molecule that directly binds to BACH1 and promotes its proteasomal degradation. However, in response to stress, NRF2 is activated and it sequentially triggers the expression of genes involved in the catabolism of heme. Mechanistically, heme promotes FBXO22-mediated degradation of BACH1 (Figure 4). BACH1 depletion reduced metastases of tumors but FBXO22 depletion potently enhanced metastases in mice. Importantly, concomitant loss of BACH1 significantly impaired the formation of metastasis induced by the depletion of FBXO22, suggesting that BACH1 induced metastatic dissemination in the absence of FBXO22. An increase in the levels of BACH1 through the loss of KEAP1 or FBXO22 induced metastasis.26Hepatitis B X-interacting protein (HBXIP) interacts with KEAP1 via its GLNLG motif and impairs KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2. LM-436 cells are a lung specifically metastatic sub-line obtained through four consecutive rounds of lung metastasis selections, after resection of the primary orthotopically implanted tumors. HBXIP knockdown led to significant reduction in the pulmonary metastatic nodules in mice injected with cancer cells.27RagD belongs to small G protein family and a potent activator of mTOR pathway. There is a significant reduction in NRF2-mediated upregulation of RagD in NRF2-mutated cancer cells. NVP-BEZ235, a dual PI3K-mTOR inhibitor, efficiently inhibited tumor growth in xenografted rodent models. Mutant NRF2-expressing tumors demonstrated poorly differentiated carcinoma with increased mitotic activity and highly aggressive characteristics, such as invasion into the surrounding muscle and adipose tissues. Furthermore, there was occasional hepatic metastasis, which suggested that mutant NRF2 promoted invasive and metastasizing capacities of cancer cells.28Cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR) is a metabolite of NAD catalyzed by CD38. There is a considerable reduction in tumor growth and metastatic dissemination in immuno-competent mice inoculated with CD38 mutant and CD38 knockout tumor cells. 8-Br-cADPR (CD38 inhibitor) significantly inhibited tumor growth and tumor mass in mice inoculated with CD38-WT-expressing LLC-cells. Similarly, 8-Br-cADPR also increased the infiltration of CD3+ T cells within the tumor tissues. cADPR physically interacts with TRPM2 (ion channel) and induces the mobilization of intracellular Ca2+ via TRPM2 channels. There is a marked increase in the levels of KEAP1 in CD38 mutant and CD38 knockout tumor cells.29 Overall, these findings indicated that KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 in CD38-mutant or knockout tumor cells inhibited carcinogenesis and metastasis.lncRNA-EBLN3P, an oncogenic long non-coding RNA, interferes with KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2 and enhances radio-resistance in NSCLC cells (Figure 4). However, targeted inhibition of lncRNA-EBLN3P enhanced radio-sensitivity of NSCLC cells.30Ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L3 (UCHL3) potently promotes metastasis of cervical cancer cells. Overexpression of UCHL3 suppressed ubiquitination-mediated degradation of NRF2 in C3AA cells (Figure 4). Knockdown of UCHL3 significantly inhibited metastatic dissemination of cervical cancer cells and reduced the pulmonary metastatic nodules.31Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase 1 (PRPS1) has been shown to fuel the melanoma cells. NRF2 transcriptionally upregulates the expression of PRPS1 in melanoma cells (Figure 4). PRPS1 overexpression reduced the apoptotic death in melanoma cells but knockdown of PRPS1 increased the apoptosis in melanoma cells. Overexpression of PRPS1 in A875 cells significantly promoted tumor growth. BALB/c nude mice carrying PRPS1-overexpressing A875 cells significantly enhanced the formation of lung-specific metastasis and the expression levels of PRPS1 were correlated positively with the number of tumor foci.32UBE2E2 overexpression induced an increase in the levels of NRF2 in A2780 and SKOV3 cells. UBE2E2 enhances the stability of SNAIL by inhibiting its ubiquitination. UBE2E2-depleted OvCa cells formed fewer tumor nodules in orthotopically established ovarian cancer xenografted models and intraperitoneal xenograft models.33Broad complex, Tramtrack and Bric-a-Brac (BTB) domain of KEAP1 has mutations at two sites in CDDP-resistant cells. The BTB domain is involved in the physical interaction of KEAP1 with CUL3 and NRF2. Mutations in BTB domain are loss-of-function (LOF) mutations which abolish KEAP1 functions thus causing the activation of NRF2 signaling. Cisplatin-resistant HNSCC cells (HN30-R8) demonstrated potent ability to metastasize to the lungs and elevated rates of regional lymph node metastasis. Cisplatin effectively induced shrinkage of NRF2-silenced HN30-R8 tumors. Whereas reconstitution of cancer cells with wild-type KEAP1 markedly improved the response to cisplatin and significantly impaired tumor growth. Importantly, cisplatin considerably inhibited the metastatic dissemination of NRF2-silenced or wild-type KEAP1-overexpressing HN30-R8 cells in the rodent models.34 Collectively, these findings indicated that NRF2 hyperactivation strongly promoted cisplatin resistance and tumor-forming abilities of HNSCC cells.Importantly, NRF2 signaling has a linchpin role in promoting the carcinogenesis and metastasis by transcriptional upregulation of the oncogenic regulatory networks. In the next section, we have discussed important natural products having unique ability to regulate KEAP1/NRF2 signaling in different cancers.Natural Products Mediated Targeting of NRF2-Driven PathwayDevelopment of resistance against different therapeutics is a challenging clinical issue. Interdisciplinary research work has propelled the field of natural product research, and we have witnessed ground-breaking discoveries in translational oncology.Understanding the surprising complexity of the bioactive molecules from natural sources provides a roadmap for the development of novel compounds.35–38 Research over decades has generated empirical evidence about cancer chemopreventive role of natural products. Biologically active molecules obtained from natural sources have demonstrated exceptional ability to pharmacologically target deregulated oncogenic pathways and inhibit the progression and metastatic spread of cancer cells.In this section, we have provided a summary of proof-of-concept studies which underscore significant cancer chemopreventive role of natural products mainly through regulation of NRF2 pathway in cell culture studies and tumor-bearing mice.Oroxylin AOroxylin A, a naturally bioactive O-methylated flavone isolated from Scutellaria baicalensis has been shown to regulate NRF2 signaling. Oroxylin A increased the levels of NRF2 and promoted the nuclear accumulation in HCT-116 cancer cells. Oroxylin A efficiently caused shrinkage of the tumors in mice xenografted with HCT-116 cancer cells. Orally administered Oroxylin A did not show gross toxicity in experimental mice.39 KEAP1-interacting region (KIR) present within p62 forms hydrogen bonds with KEAP1 and promotes NRF2 activation. However, caspase-mediated cleavage caused a loss of KIR domain that impaired the interaction between KEAP1 and p62 (Figure 6A). Oroxylin A inhibited NRF2 activation by enhancing caspase-mediated cleavage of p62. Oroxylin A induced shrinkage of the tumors derived from SMMC-7721 cancer cells in tumor-bearing mice.40 Figure 6(A) KIR domain of p62 interacts with KEAP1 and inhibits KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2. Casapse-8 proteolytically processes p62 and cleaved p62 fails to interact with KEAP1. Oroxylin A promotes caspase-8-mediated processing of p62. (B and C) STAT3 transcriptionally upregulates TRIM40. TRIM40 degrades KEAP1 and promotes nuclear accumulation and activity of NRF2. Oroxylin A-mediated anticancer effects can be enhanced by inhibition of TRIM40 to promote KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2. Lines with flat head mean inhibition. Importantly, STAT3 transcriptionally upregulates oncogenic TRIM40 in esophageal cancer (Figure 6B). Degradation of KEAP1 promotes nuclear accumulation of NRF2 and transcriptional activation of target gene network (Figure 6C). Depletion of TRIM40 led to significant reduction in the tumor growth rates and tumor weights.41 Collectively, these findings indicated that TRIM40 exerted carcinogenic effects and promoted esophageal cancer. Therefore, targeting of TRIM40 promotes KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2 and enhances the anticancer effects of Oroxylin A.CurcuminCurcumin is an important bioactive component isolated from Curcuma longa. Because of initial success, curcumin has been extensively studied against different cancers. Multiple analogs of curcumin have also been designed to improve the efficacy with minimum off-target effects.42–44 Mass spectrometric analysis suggests that curcumin binds to Cys151 in KEAP1. Cells transfected with a mutant KEAP1 (cysteine 151 replaced by serine) were used to establish the cause-and-effect relationship of KEAP1 and NRF2. Findings indicated that curcumin-mediated NRF2 transactivation was severely reduced in cells transfected with a mutant KEAP1.45 Curcumin-inspired mono-carbonyl piperidinone analogs covalently modify Cys-151 and Cys-288 residues at KEAP1 and inhibit KEAP1-mediated targeting of NRF2.46 Curcumin has been shown to dualistically regulate NRF2 in cancer inhibition. In the next paragraphs, we will discuss how curcumin exerts cancer inhibitory effects either through activation or inhibition of NRF2.Curcumin-Mediated Activation of NRF2 for Cancer InhibitionCurcumin increased the nuclear fraction of NRF2 and stimulated NRF2-mediated upregulation of tumor suppressor miR-34a/b/c. Targeted inhibition of miR-34a by antagomirs led to partial restoration of metastases after treatment with curcumin. Five weeks after injection, resected lungs were devoid of macroscopically visible metastases in animal models injected with curcumin-treated SW620 cells. There was a significant reduction in the metastatic nodules in mice injected with curcumin-treated cells. Whereas SW620 cells concomitantly treated with curcumin and miR-34a-antagomirs formed pulmonary metastatic nodules in rodent models.47In some other studies, it has been shown that curcumin derivatives epigenetically activated NRF2 and inhibited proliferation and colony formation of murine TRAMP C1 prostate cancer cells.48,49Curcumin-Mediated Inhibition of NRF2 for Cancer InhibitionNOTCH signaling is initiated by the interaction of Delta like ligands or Jagged ligands with NOTCH receptors. Following ligand binding, multiple cleavages occur in the transmembrane region of NOTCH. NOTCH intracellular domain (NICD) moves to the nucleus and binds to Recombination signal binding protein for immunoglobulin κ J region (RBPJ) transcription factors. Within the promoter region, multi-component molecular machinery comprising NICD and RBPJ displaces co-repressors and recruits co-activators for the transcriptional upregulation of different genes.50 Overexpression of NOTCH1 or RBPJ resulted in the enrichment of RBPJ within the promoter region of NRF2, thereby stimulating the expression of NRF2. Modification of cysteine residues in KEAP1 has a regulatory role. Different natural products have been shown to chemically modify cysteine residues in KEAP1. It has previously been reported that NRF2 activation and upregulation of HO-1 by ascorbic acid are likely mediated through modifications at Cys151, 273, and 288 residues in KEAP1 (Figure 8).55 Figure 8Different natural products (Vitamin C, xanthohumol and deoxynyboquinone) have been shown to modify the cysteine residues in KEAP1. Therefore, molecular analysis of patient-derived drug-resistant xenografts is an essential strategy to evaluate multi-targeting facets of natural products.Clinical Trials Related to Pharmacological Targeting of Oncogenic NRF2NRF2-driven signaling has garnered tremendous spotlight because of its ability to pleiotropically modulate a myriad of gene networks. Ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related (ATR) is involved in the repair of damaged DNA. NRF2 interacted with ATR and induced its activation at double-stranded breaks. Therefore, targeted inhibition of NRF2 and ATR provided an effective avenue to overcome radio-resistance in NSCLC patients.95,96 Phase II HUDSON study (NCT03334617) has evaluated ceralasertib and olaparib in combination with durvalumab in locally advanced or metastatic LKB1/KEAP1-deficient NSCLC patients.97Drug repurposing is also a dynamic dimension of clinical research. Sapanisertib is a potent, selective inhibitor of mTORC1/2 in NRF2-mutated NSCLC patients (NCT05275673). 6-Diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON) is a glutamine antagonist. VVD- is being tested for safety, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and preliminary efficacy in participants with advanced solid tumors (NCT05954312). The pharmacokinetic activity of bardoxolone methyl is characterized by slow oral absorption and a relatively long biological half-life.104Concluding RemarksIncreasingly, it is being realized that dysregulations of spatio-temporally controlled intracellular signaling cascades are contributory in cancer development and progression. Signaling cascades modulate different molecular activities through multiple effectors and also by crosstalks with other transduction cascades. Multi-layered regulation of KEAP1/NRF2 pathway is highly complicated and different upstream activators have been shown to activate NRF2 pathway (Figure 10). Different compounds have been investigated to chemically interact with KEAP1 and enhance NRF2 activity. title: Immunotherapy: the Mega Weapon to Cure Cancer
abstract: Objective:Cancer is one of the most complex genomic diseases that can gain abilities to resist different therapies. These capabilities, known as the hallmark of cancer, allow specific and personalised therapies such as immunotherapy.Materials and methods:This review paper discusses how different immunotherapies, such as immune checkpoint blockade, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell, and Oncolytic viral therapy, which are currently being used and researched to overcome cancer cell capabilities by using the patient’s immune system.Results:Immune checkpoint blockade therapy is used to block immune inhibitory pathways using anti-PD-1 receptor and anti-CTLA-4 receptor antibodies, which make lymphocytes more responsive towards cancer cells. Then, it is discussed how CAR T-cells are designed to make cancer antigens more easily identified by T-cells for a more specific immune response. Furthermore, it is shown that oncolytic viruses directly destroy cancer cells and, indirectly, make them more vulnerable to the immune system.Conclusion:It is proposed that oncolytic viral therapy is a bridge between Immune checkpoint and CAR T-cell therapies for a more effective and more specific immune response towards cancer.
full_text: Cancer is the disease of the genome. Cancer cells are self-centred cells that reproduce uncontrollably and stop functioning as they should in a specific organ. Most cancer types progress through five different stages (1). Organ cells start from a premalignant status and progress to stage IV (metastasis), in which cancer cells have invaded other organs (2). When a cell becomes premalignant, it means it has acquired gene mutations or gene activation of a few genes, which can potentially lead to over replication. These mutations can be called abilities in a way that cancerous cells gain over time at every stage, and with each capability that they gain, they become more invasive and more unstable (3). A total of 606,520 deaths are expected in 2020, only in the US, as a result of cancer (4). The earliest description of cancer dates back to 3000 BC, which was written in ancient Egypt, in which was noted to be untreatable (5). Since then, many therapies have been developed to treat this disease. In modern times, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and cancer removal surgery have saved millions of lives. However, many people still die due to having more aggressive cancer types and metastasis as a result of late diagnosis or fast progression of the disease. Cancer cells continuously evolve to survive on their own. This means that cancer cells become multi-drug resistant by gaining the ability to pump drugs out by activating a family of ATP-dependent transporters (6). This is why general chemotherapy was mixed with targeted chemotherapy. However, cancer cells also evolve to evade targeted treatments by changing the drug target structure. For instance, imatinib is used for chronic myelogenous leukaemia, but overtime BCR-ABL protein structure changed so that imatinib cannot inhibit its ATP binding site (6). Cancer cells gain twelve capabilities that allow them to grow, resist different treatments, and become metastatic. Some of these phenotypic abilities are as follows: evading growth suppressors, inducing angiogenesis, resisting cell death, sustaining proliferative signalling, and avoiding immune destruction (7).Many different therapeutic strategies have been developed to tackle these cancer capabilities. Consequently, a new type of oncology treatment has emerged, known as personalised cancer therapy. In this strategy, cancer capabilities are found by cancer genome sequencing, and accordingly, the patient is administered medication that is not bypassed by the cancer cells (8). This implies that cancer can relapse with a more vicious type (more phenotypic abilities) or progress to metastasis within the patient. Therefore, in the past decade, scientists have undertaken extensive research on immunotherapy. In personalised immunotherapy, the patient’s immune system is used or assisted in detecting cancer cells better (9). Our immune system detects and destroys cancer cells every day from birth. When a cell becomes cancerous, one of the main capabilities it has gained to survive is to camouflage and not be detected by the immune system. Hence, much advancement such as immune checkpoint blockade, CAR T-cell therapy, and oncolytic viruses (OVs) have been developed to aid in increasing detection, targeted cancer cell destruction, and loss of capabilities in cancer cells. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of these therapies and to discuss how these therapies can complement each other to cure this formerly known untreatable disease.Immune checkpoint blockade:Immune cells such as T-cells, B-cells, APC, and NK cells are continually scanning somatic cells to identify cancer cells and destroy them by inducing apoptosis and secreting cytotoxins. This process of scanning is carried out by a series of immune checkpoint receptors present on T-cells, such as PD-1, CTLA-4, and CD-28 receptors (10). T-cells scan somatic cells by binding their T-cell receptors (TCR) to the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) of the self-cell, which is followed by PD-1 receptor present on T-cell binding to the PD-L1 ligand present on the same cell (11). These bindings will signal the inhibition of T-cell activation, which means the bound cell to the T-cell is non-cancerous or a cancer cell over expressing PD-1 and being recognised as self (Figure 1A) (12). Similarly, CTLA-4 receptors of the T-cell are attached to a dendritic cell or an APC (Antigen-presenting cells) to T-cells for antigen recognition and processing (9). When an APC is attached to the T-cell to present an antigen sample, it expresses different subtypes of B7 ligands (CD-80 and CD-86) (13). These subtypes of B7 compete to bind to CD-28 and CTLA-4 receptors on T-cells, depending on their expressed concentration on the APC (13). If B7 binds to CTLA-4, T-cell proliferation is inhibited, and if it binds to CD-28, the T-cell is activated (13, 14). This T-cell activation then leads to cytokine release for clonal expansion, T regulatory cell inhibition, and lymphocyte migration to the site of tumour or infection (14, 15). Thus, due to this immune checkpoint system, most cancer cells are identified and destroyed by the immune cells. However, based on the hallmarks of cancer, one of the expected abilities that cancer cells gain is increasing expression of PD-L1 and B7 ligands, which results in immune suppression (7, 13). Then, this immune inactivity towards the cancer cells leads to cancer progression. Currently, there are a few humanised antibodies developed that bind to the PD-1 receptor, blocking it, such as Nivolumab, Pembrolizumab, and Cemiplimab (16–18). Whilst for CTLA-4 blockade, monoclonal antibodies like Ipilimumab have been developed (19). These are known as Immune checkpoint blockade therapies, which help T-cell activation towards the cancer cells (Figures 1B and 1C). These drugs have been approved by the FDA and are currently being used clinically to treat many cancer types such as leukaemia, prostate cancer and sarcoma (20–22). However, PD-1 blockade alone is inefficient for solid tumours and progressed cancers (surpassing stage 3); consequently, a combination of PD-1 and CTLA-4 blockade therapy is currently being used as a more aggressive treatment (20).Figure 1:PD-1 and CTLA-4 immune checkpoint regulationA) Attachment of PD-1 receptor to PD-L1 ligand increases T regulatory cell proliferation and reduced CD8 T-cell proliferation and survival with reduced cytokine production. B) PD-1 blockade results in cancer cell detection, increased CD8 T-cell proliferation, cytokine release and T regulatory cell deactivation. C) Higher number of CTLA-4 binding to B7 than CD-28 results in CD8 T-cell inactivation, T reg cell activation reduced IL-2 production and cancer progression. Blockade of CTLA-4 causes T reg inactivation, cancer detection, CD8 T-cell proliferation and increased IL-2 secretion (10). “Created in BioRender. Rt, Z. (2026) https://BioRender.com/og0jcpo “.For instance, for the treatment of Metastatic Esophagogastric Cancer, a group of patients who received combination therapy had a 9% higher progression-free survival rate than the group of patients who only received PD-1 blocker over 12 months (19). It also should be noted that these immune checkpoint blockade therapies are not free of risks and may lead to autoimmune diseases due to blockade of PD-1 and CTLA-4 receptors, which act as T-cell off switches (23).CAR T-cell:T-cells are one of the primary lymphocytes that scan the body for cancer cells and destroy them if identified. However, in some people, their immune system does not recognise or does not fully respond to cancer cells, which is due to their genetic make-up, genome composition, and epigenetic regulation (24). Previously, it was shown that this lack of response could be due to immune checkpoint inhibitory pathway activation, but there are other reasons for this lack of response. There are many genes that regulate transcription of many surface receptors and cytokine production of lymphocytes other than PD-1 and CTLA-4, such as IL-2R (α, β, and γ) and TCR (CDR3 α, β, γ, and δ control VJ and VDJ recombination) (15, 25).These mutations affect tumour antigen recognition and lymphocyte activation and survival (25). Therefore, when these genes are downregulated, cancer cells are not recognised and continue to progress. In order to overcome this problem, scientists have been working on a new technology called CAR T-cell therapy. In this TCRs of the T-cells are designed for a specific tumour antigen as receptors called CARs (Figure 2A) (26). Then, the genetic code for this CAR is transferred ex vivo to the patient’s T-cells using Lentiviruses and other nanoparticles (27). The advancement in this technology has created new generations of CARs, which have signalling capability for T-cell activation (28).Figure 2:Chimeric antigen receptor design and CAR T-cell administration.A) CAR is designed based on cancer specific antigen antibody’s variable region, and its gene is delivered to the T-cells via AAV vectors before CAR T-cells’ administration to the patient. B) First-generation CARs were designed by fusing CD3ζ signalling protein (intracellular domain) to the variable fragment (extracellular domain) for T-cell activation. Second and third-generation CARs have additional CD1 and CD2 intracellular signalling proteins that were fused to first-generation CAR. In fourth and fifth-generation CARs extra inducible IL-12 and IL-2Rβ chains were infused with second-generation CARs (26). “Created in BioRender. Rt, Z. (2026) https://BioRender.com/ozv6hj7 “.These signalling capabilities can be added to CARs intracellular domain to make up for signalling pathways that patients’ T-cells lack, such as IL-12 (29). Currently, three generations are being utilized in clinical trials, and further generations four and five are being developed in mouse models capable of inducing the production of one or more cytokines (Figure 2B) (28). CARs target tumour-specific antigens that are typically overexpressed in different cancer types. For instance, Anti-CD19 is CAR T-cell therapy that has been made to treat acute lymphatic leukaemia since CD19 is overexpressed on B cells in this disease (30). Multiple CARs are developed for different cancer antigens in order to treat different types of cancer, as shown in Table 1 (31). However, since these targeted antigens are expressed and presented at different levels, unfortunately, CAR T-cell therapy may occasionally lead to autoimmune diseases, cytokine release syndrome, and neurotoxicity (28).Table 1:Some examples of CARs developed for solid tumors (31) Targeted antigen Disease Vector CAR Generation FRaOvarian cancerRetrovirusFirstMesothelinPancreatic cancermRNASecondc-METBreast cancermRNASecondEGFRvlllGlioblastomaLentivirusSecondCEACAM5Colorectal cancerRetrovirusFirstCEAColorectal cancerLentivirusSecondGD2NeuroblastomaRetrovirusFirstCD133Colorectal cancer, Pancreatic cancer, Hepatocellular carcinomaLentivirusSecondNevertheless, even with such adverse effects, this study has shown a promising success rate of 68% to 93% with a low relapse rate of 40% to 50% of patients (32).Oncolytic Viruses:Viruses are small particles that carry a small genome and are responsible for many diseases. These are capable of causing disease by entering a host cell and disturbing the cell’s normal function by using the cell’s machinery to transcribe and translate its genome. This characteristic of viruses allows scientists to apply them as vessels to transfer specifically designed viral genomes into the cancer cells, also known as OVs. Such viruses can be configured to have a cancer-specific surface protein, which will allow them to infect cancer cells solely (33, 34). In order to make this viral infection and expression, more specific cancer distinct promoters are used in their designed genome; therefore, in case of entry to healthy cells, they will not be expressed (33). These viral vectors lack disease-causing genes, so they are unable to cause illness in patients. Many different genes can be inserted into the viral vector which will destroy cancer cells; these occur through two primary mechanisms, tumour tropism and tumour cell lysis (35). Viral replicative genes lead to tumour cell lysis due to viral particle production and assembly (Figure 3A) (36). On the other hand, tumour tropism can be a bridge between many cancer therapies, such as CAR T-cell therapy and immune checkpoint blockade therapy. It can also take away the abilities that tumour cells have gained, as mentioned is a crucial quality of cancer. For instance, Oncolytic adenovirus can carry a p53 gene aimed for cancers with p53 tumour suppressor gene mutation to induce apoptosis in them (Figure 3E) (37). Another example of tumour tropism would be the introduction of an anti-PD-1 receptor antibody gene (Figure 3C) (38). In a mouse animal model, oncolytic viral therapy was used to treat five mice in which anti-PD-1was detected, and four of them had reductions in tumour size and volume with 80% success rate (39). OVs are capable of altering the microenvironment of the tumour by suppressing angiogenesis and establishing production of prodrug activating enzymes such as Vasculostatin and yeast cytosine deaminase uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (yCD–UPRT) (Figures 3D, 3G) (40, 41). Last but not least, OVs can be designed to carry genes that produce IL-12, which promotes clonal expansion and T-cell activation, expressing specific membrane-bound antigens on cancer cells (Figures 3F, 3B) (42). For instance, CLDN6 is only expressed in early stages of embryonic development and not in adult cells (43). Expressing CLDN6 in cancer cells via OVs, flags cancer cells and makes them easy targets for the immune cells to identify (43-45). Thus, oncolytic viral therapy directly kills cancer cells and, through the tumour tropism mechanism, makes cancer cells a better target for the immune system in addition to creating an overall harsh environment for them to survive.Figure 3:Oncolytic virus different applications for cancer therapy.A) Viral replication leads to cancer cell stress and death. B) Membrane bound tumour cell specific antigen production. C) Anti-PD-1 antibody production. D) Prodrug activating enzyme production. E) Tumour suppressor gene activation. F) IL-12 expression and release. G) Angiogenesis inhibitor drug production. All these expressions happen by the cancer cell due to the viral vector transfection (33). “Created in BioRender. Rt, Z. (2026) https://BioRender.com/zvht8my ”.Scanning somatic cells to identify cancer cells and destroy them is carried out by a series of immune checkpoint receptors present on T-cells. Immune checkpoint blockade therapies are not free of risks and may lead to autoimmune diseases due to blockade of PD-1 and CTLA-4 receptors, which act as T-cell off switches (23). Multiple CARs are developed for different cancer antigens in order to treat different types of cancer, as shown in Table 1 (31). However, since these targeted antigens are expressed and presented at different levels, unfortunately, CAR T-cell therapy may occasionally lead to autoimmune diseases, cytokine release syndrome, and neurotoxicity (28). Nevertheless, even with such adverse effects, this study has shown a promising success rate of 68% to 93% with a low relapse rate of 40% to 50% of patients (32).Oncolytic viral therapy directly kills cancer cells and, through the tumour tropism mechanism, makes cancer cells a better target for the immune system in addition to creating an overall harsh environment for them to survive.In summary, the hallmark of cancer has shown the capabilities that cancer gains to progress and to resist usual therapies such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Hence, immunotherapy has become more popular since it uses the best weapon against diseases, which is our immune system. Immune checkpoint blockade therapy development and implications make immune cells more responsive towards cancer cells by blocking inhibitory receptors such as PD-1 and CTLA-4. Next, it was demonstrated how CAR T-cell therapy trains T-cells to identify tumour-specific antigens readily and as a result, make the treatment more effective. CAR T-cells are designed using the variable region of cancer specific antibodies, which are fused with various signalling proteins to enhance tumour detection and destruction. Attention must be kept on how to overcome the possible autoimmune disease side effects as a result of immune checkpoint blockade therapy. Finally, the way OVs, directly and indirectly, weaken and destroy malignant cells was able to be determined. OVs have tumour lysis and tropism capability, which reduces cancer cell survival and progression. OVs can be combined with immune checkpoint therapy and CAR T-cell therapy and act as a bridge between these two treatments.For future applications, this review paper proposes to utilize all three therapies together to treat cancer. OVs can be designed to give rise to specific membrane tumour antigens that our own cells do not express, in addition to the production of immune checkpoint blockade antibodies. Furthermore, fourth-generation CAR T-cells can be designed for the tumour antigen coded by the OVs and an inducible IL-12 domain. This could theoretically increase the T-cell response to cancer cells expressing the antigen and limit their activation to the tumour microenvironment, and where only cancer cells are present. Thus, this combined therapy can increase immune response and infiltration towards cancer cells while reducing future off-target effects to become the mega weapon to cure cancer.

title: The Potential of AI-Driven High-Content Imaging in Drug Discovery
abstract: We have authored a compelling and timely review that highlights the transformative potential of high-content imaging for discovering small molecules (SMs). SMs are crucial for advancing drug potency, selectivity, and precision, and their assessment through specialized cellular assays accelerates drug development. High-content imaging (HCI), which seamlessly integrates automated microscopy with sophisticated image analysis powered by artificial intelligence (AI), is revolutionizing cell-based assays by enabling a comprehensive evaluation of cellular parameters following drug treatment. The rich multivariate data generated by HCI from multiplexed assays unlock unprecedented insights into the cellular and subcellular effects of lead compounds, making it an indispensable tool in modern drug discovery.
full_text: Low-molecular weight organic compounds or SMs offer unparalleled versatility, capable of modulating a vast array of biological targets. Their favorable pharmacokinetic properties, including oral bioavailability and membrane permeability, enable convenient dosing and high patient compliance, offering a distinct advantage over other therapeutic modalities. Nearly 90% of pharmaceutical drugs are SMs due to established, scalable manufacturing processes and well-defined regulatory pathways, underscoring their vital role in medicine. A wide array of advanced assays exists for their characterization, including gradient-based microfluidics, , protein-based assays on protein-SM interaction, bulk read-out assays, − and cell-based assays. , These assays harnessing SMs can significantly accelerate scientific discovery and innovation in the biomedical fields.Design Strategies for SMsEffective SM drug discovery and development hinge on innovative design strategies paired with a deep understanding of disease biology and the target. The most impactful SM design strategies are structure-based drug design (SBDD), ligand-based drug design (LBDD), fragment-based drug design (FBDD), molecular hybridization, prodrug strategies, physicochemical optimization, and polypharmacology and network pharmacology, as shown in Figure .1Strategies in SM drug design.Experimental Strategies for SMs ScreeningScreening SMs stands as a cornerstone in advancing not only drug development but also numerous scientific disciplines. By employing a variety of innovative methodologies and approaches, researchers can identify compounds with specific, desirable activities, ultimately accelerating the discovery process. The importance of diverse screening techniques cannot be overstated, as each offers unique advantages. The most common SM screening methods are high-throughput screening (HTS), virtual screening, fragment-based screening, cell-based screening, biochemical assays, phenotypic screening, biophysical screening, and structure-based screening, as shown in Figure .2Strategies in SMs drug design.A significant constraint in SM phenotypic screening is the scarcity of compounds that exhibit the necessary selectivity and are documented as being efficacious against specific protein targets. To illustrate, while there are an estimated 1.3 billion compounds accessible for virtual screening, with about 16 million of these being obtainable from suppliers, the number of compounds confirmed active in target-specific tests, as recorded in public repositories like ChEMBL or those cataloged by ZINC, is less than a million.High-Content Imaging, Screening, or AnalysisIn contrast to other biochemical assays, the rapid advancement in microscopy has enabled the screening of hundreds of compounds for mechanistic toxicity and the identification of lead compounds. HCI provides a fundamentally different approach to drug discovery compared with traditional biochemical (BAs) or cellular assays (CAs). While conventional methods offer a simplified, population-averaged snapshot, HCI presents a detailed, multiparametric view of complex biological processes.
