InvitrogenThermo ScientificClick-iT TUNEL Alexa Fluor imaging assays for microscopy and HCSC10245screening of apoptotic cells , C10246C10247InvitrogenThermo ScientificHCI, HCS, and HCA are indispensable tools in modern biology and drug discovery. While often used interchangeably, the terms highlight distinct aspects of a powerful integrated technology.HCI provides cutting-edge imaging technology, utilizing automated microscopy to acquire detailed, high-resolution images of cells that were previously impossible to capture efficiently. HCS is the expansion of this capability into a high-throughput platform, enabling researchers to rapidly screen vast libraries of compounds or genetic modifications, accelerating discoveries and enabling more precise phenotypic observations. HCA completes this cycle by offering advanced data analysis, quantitatively extracting vital biological insights from complex image data sets (Figure ). Together, these technologies revolutionize research, offering unprecedented speed, accuracy, and depth of understanding. Investing in or using these integrated tools is essential for anyone aiming to stay at the forefront of biological innovation and therapeutic development.3High-content data acquisition and analysis resulting in lead compounds.HCI can perform the automated acquisition and analysis of cellular imaging data. It is now a well-established method for profiling and optimizing compounds. A remarkable advantage of HCI is its ability to be conducted in multiwell plates (96 or 384), allowing researchers to simultaneously analyze a vast array of cell types, treatments, and readouts in real-time (Table lists standard plates used in HCI). Cellular imaging techniques predominantly utilize fluorescence labeling to precisely target and visualize specific cellular components such as organelles or proteins, enhancing the depth and accuracy of analysis. Moreover, advanced multiplexed cell painting methods enable the capture of distinct cellular events within each well, significantly boosting the data richness. Importantly, with the rise of machine learning (ML) and AI, it is now possible to extract valuable information from unlabeled cells, further expanding the scope and sophistication of cellular analysis. These technological innovations collectively position HCI as an indispensable tool for cutting-edge biomedical research.3Specialized Plates Required for HCIproductssourcedescriptionrefsμ-plates 96, 384 well square, or round89606black 96/384-well culture plate with square or round wells and a flat, clear bottom for high-throughput microscopy – 8962788407Ibidicorning high-content imaging microplateCLS4581black cyclic olefin copolymer (COC), 96/384-well culture plate with flat bottom, sterile, film bottom – CLS4517CLS4518CorningBIOFLOAT 96-well platesF202301fully inert, and cell-repelling surface, spheroid cultivation , F224384faCellitateStemoniX microBrain 3D platformAxoSim3D neural spheroid system in 96 and 384-well format Image-based HCI assays identify different cell populations in a single well. Cellular features are extracted via image segmentation and independently analyzed for meaningful results. Many HCI assays are used globally, such as subcellular localization, cell death (apoptosis, autophagy, and necrosis), cell cycle, protein aggregation, anchorage independence, biomarker discovery, epigenetic modifications, and cell motility. Other customized assays include receptor internalization, degradation, translocation, transcription factors, protein modifications, and more. , While HCS shows great promise for research and industry, it has not yet become the main screening method. This offers opportunities for growth by tackling challenges such as lengthy assay development, limited microscopy throughput, and the need for specialized expertise. Recent advancements position HCI as a transformative tool. Our review explores HCI’s informational potential and the growing body of research, though a gap remains in the depth of data sharing. Improving data analysis could unlock more benefits, making HCI essential for future scientific and industrial progress. HCI provides an excellent opportunity to generate highly reliable qualitative and quantitative data for screening SMs. It can be effectively utilized across various stages of the drug discovery workflow, enhancing the efficiency and accuracy. It begins with hit identification, particularly in HTS, where researchers can systematically evaluate a wide range of targets and compounds. This initial phase is crucial, as it allows scientists to identify potential therapeutic candidates early in the drug discovery pipeline.Once a promising hit compound is identified, the next step involves optimization, which can be significantly enhanced through HCA. This approach generates predictive, translatable data essential for subsequent in vivo studies, helping researchers understand how the compound may behave in living organisms. Furthermore, HCA is not limited to in vivo applications; it is also applicable to ex vivo studies. These studies offer valuable insights into the compound’s effects on biological systems outside the living organism, providing additional data to support further development before proceeding to safety assessments.An important aspect of HCI is managing a substantial number of samples and images, which pose a variety of challenges. This process can be exceptionally time-consuming due to the sheer volume of data that must be handled. Each sample generates a wealth of images that require extensive digital storage to protect them and organize effectively. Without adequate storage, the risk of data loss or corruption increases, underscoring the need for reliable systems.In addition to storage requirements, analyzing these data necessitates sophisticated, specialized software. This software is crucial for conducting automatic analyses that account for numerous parameters, enabling researchers to derive meaningful insights from complex data sets. The challenge arises when the efficiency of image acquisition, facilitated by rapid-response cameras and high-resolution imaging systems, outpaces the capacity for subsequent data processing.Although rapid image capture is impressive, it often causes major bottlenecks during analysis. The shift from capturing to analyzing images can become slow, especially when data is transferred to storage systems and managing it efficiently. These delays can slow research progress and demand extra resources, highlighting the need to improve workflow efficiency in HCI applications that deal with large data sets. By solving these issues, researchers can boost their productivity and obtain more value from their data.HCI: Applications in Drug DiscoveryHCI has numerous applications within well-organized Integrated Drug Discovery programs, targeting therapeutic areas such as cancer and neuroscience. By leveraging this technology, researchers can streamline the drug development process, improve candidate selection, and increase the likelihood of successful clinical outcomes. Figure illustrates a typical HCI setup layout.4Schematic representation of a typical drug treatment assay.Several HCI setups and protocols have successfully identified small molecules for various diseases, all of which are listed in Table along with their targets. In summary, SMs that promote neurogenesis have been identified using HCl assays that monitor neural markers, such as Tuj1 (a neuron-specific β-tubulin), in neural progenitor cells (NPCs). These phenotypic screens on a SMs library enable the discovery of molecules that stimulate differentiation or protect neuronal cells. 4A List of SMs Identified from Libraries Using HCIA high-throughput assay screened 28,864 SMs for AP-4 deficiency and identified BCH-HSP-C01, which reversed ATG9A mislocalization in patient fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons. HCS of 1280 molecules uncovered off-target proteasome activity of EGFR inhibitor tyrphostin AG555 and synergy between MEK inhibitors and disulfiram, highlighting the value of this approach. A HCI platform with integrated image analysis screened a bioactive lipid library, validating known raft modulators such as epigallocatechin gallate, miltefosine, and C6- and C8-ceramide while also finding novel modulators. HCS technology enabled automated quantitative assessment of multiple cellular features, effectively identifying small molecules that manipulate human ES and iPS cells for treating degenerative diseases while uncovering novel differentiation mechanisms. An automated centrosome-duplication assay screened 16,320 SMs, identified five potent inhibitors that spare microtubule dynamics and protein synthesis, demonstrating an approach broadly applicable to studying centrosome regulation and other biological processes. An HCI assay screening 3317 compounds identified SMs that inhibit colon cancer cell growth via apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, or adhesion disruption, providing chemical probes for new mechanisms and potential therapies with reduced nonspecific toxicity. A phenotypic cell-imaging assay enabled concurrent screening of multiple targets under physiological conditions, reducing an initial ∼250,000 compounds to ∼400 validated small-molecule autophagy inhibitors through rigorous triage. A fluorometric imaging plate reader (FLIPR)-based assay screening 45,000 compounds identified diverse Akt1 translocation inhibitors, demonstrating HCS effectiveness in elucidating small-molecule mechanisms across the Akt pathway. A sophisticated HCA technique has been developed to harness a robust phenotypic profiling strategy for studying vascular modulation, including processes like angiogenesis. A dependable HCI assay screening 344 traditional Chinese medicine compounds identified eight anti-renal fibrosis agents, six previously unreported: Hydroxysafflor Yellow A, glycyrrhizic acid, astragaloside IV, gypenosides, crocin, and licorice marking the first successful application of this approach to Chinese herbal remedies. An image-based HCS system that evaluates the full viral replication cycle identified nelfinavir mesylate from 1280 compounds as an inhibitor of human adenovirus multicycle plaque formation but not single-cycle infection, demonstrating the utility of this approach. An image-based HCS strategy screening 849 protease inhibitors identified four broad-spectrum antiviral compounds (F694-1532, G202-0362, C795-0925, and D011-2120) against RVFV and other RNA viruses, confirming HCI’s value in antiviral discovery, mechanistic understanding, and safety assessment. A comprehensive HCS campaign using an AR-TIF2 PPI biosensor screened 143,535 compounds, yielding three hit series hydrobenzo-oxazepins (S1), thiadiazol-5-piperidine-carboxamides (S2), and phenyl-methyl-indoles (S3) with distinct binding modes (S3 at the BF-3 allosteric site; S1 and S2 near the DHT orthosteric site), advancing mechanistic understanding and providing leads for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Using AstraZeneca’s chemo genomic library and multiplexed HCS screen of 13,000 compounds in hiPSC-derived hepatocytes identified small molecules that protect against ER stress-induced steatosis by inhibiting the cyclin D3-CDK2/4, C/EBPβ, and DGAT2 pathway, validating this phenotypic platform for fatty liver drug discovery. Using HCS with validated algorithms on morphology and proliferation markers, over 300 natural product-like compounds were tested, identifying 13.6% with harmful cellular responses, offering a rapid and cost-effective approach for early toxicity assessment. A cell-based HCS process with integrated high-resolution imaging screened a modest library of 400 diverse compounds, leading to the discovery of Micropolyin, a novel inhibitor of microtubule dynamics, and enabling rapid hit identification and target progression. A high-content screen of 160 kinase inhibitors using live-cell imaging identified JNJ- (J101) as a compound that specifically triggers prometaphase mitotic arrest in glioblastoma-derived neural stem cells without affecting normal neural stem cells. A HCS assay using NeuriteIQ screened 1040 compounds for Aβ-induced neurite loss, identifying 36 protective SMs and suggesting NSAIDs and PPARγ agonists as potential therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer’s disease. A screen of 13,000 small molecules using DAPI staining and a nonparametric statistical method identified a compound that induces mitotic arrest, confirmed by phosphohistone H3 detection and impairs proliferation across multiple cancer cell lines. A suite of HCI screens targeting autophagy regulators identified eight SMs (Penitrem A, Wiskostatin, Fluspirilene, Niguldipine, Trifluoperazine, Nicardipine, Rapamycin, and Nigericin) from 480 compounds, including seven FDA-approved drugs with unexpectedly low toxicity that stimulate autophagic degradation and reduce misfolded protein accumulation. A large-scale HCS screen of 23,406 molecules identified 84 compounds that induce FoxA2 expression and endodermal differentiation in mESCs, notably revealing that ROCK inhibition by Fasudil promotes endoderm and PDX1-positive pancreatic progenitors in both mouse and human ESCs. An HCI-based screen of 50,000 heterocycles in primary human CD34+ cells identified naphthyridinone derivatives that promote megakaryocyte differentiation from common myeloid progenitors by inhibiting PDGFR, offering potential for treating thrombocytopenia. A refined HCA method screened 56 pharmaceutical compounds, identifying eight agents, including crizotinib, bosutinib, and rapamycin, that modulate NET (neutrophil extracellular trap) as inducers, inhibitors, or biphasic regulators. A refined phenotypic HCS assay screened 488 bioactive compounds and identified vanilloids, including capsaicin, as a novel class of inhibitors of PMA-induced NET formation. An image-based multiparametric HCS assay screened 1600 compounds, identified celastrol as a hit that induces prolonged HSP70 expression under stress without affecting nonstressed cells, offering a promising strategy for protein misfolding disorders. Using HCS and proteomics to screen 273 kinase inhibitors, the multikinase inhibitor BX795 was identified as a promising neuroprotective candidate that reverses neurodegenerative phenotypes in a Parkinson’s disease patient-derived model. Utilizing Cell Painting to Identify SMsA system pharmacology network was built combining drug-target-pathway-disease links with cell painting morphological profiles. A chemogenomic library of 5000 SMs targeting various biological processes and diseases was created. This platform and library aim to identify targets and understand mechanisms in phenotypic assays. From ChEMBL, 2473 chemical–target interactions were identified and linked to the Cell Painting profiles. At the scaffold level, associations between scaffolds, proteins, and morphological profiles can be proposed. In U-2 OS cells, 218 compounds were used to generate cell painting profiles that reveal how different substances cause distinctive cellular morphologies. These compounds, including cytoskeletal toxins, electrophiles, genotoxins, and redox substances, serve as reference standards for cellular damage in high-content assays. An analysis of 30,616 compounds from the NIH Molecular Libraries Initiative at 10 μM showed that those with reduced cell counts often display strong phenotypes in the CP assay. The cell painting assay has produced a publicly accessible data set that includes morphological characteristics and pictures of 30,000 SM treatments. This data set demonstrates the value of high-content data in identifying symptoms linked to genes and clarifying small-molecule drugs’ mechanisms of action (MOA), including their target identification. Such comprehensive profiling offers a valuable resource for advancing our understanding of cellular responses and accelerating drug discovery efforts. 19,555 SMs were profiled using eight esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) cell lines and tissue-matched controls, including 16,608 chemical and lead-like substances and 2947 medications. The study showed that pharmacological modes of action (MOA) across different cell lines can be classified by combining machine learning with the Cell Painting assay. This method identified phenotypic clusters enriched with related pharmacological classes, such as methotrexate and other antimetabolites, demonstrating how this EAC screening platform can find new compounds with selective activity against EAC cell morphologies and known drug classes. To build the largest Cell Painting data set, a new academic-industry partnership called the Joint Undertaking in Morphological Profiling with Cell Painting (JUMP-CP) was established. This enormous project profiled cells under over 140,000 situations, including genetic alterations and SMs. The resulting morphological atlas serves as a comprehensive resource for connecting diseases, drugs, and genes. By providing an extensive reference data set, JUMP-CP sought to enhance cell-based phenotypic screening, improve the prediction of MOA and cellular toxicities, and uncover new opportunities for drug repurposing opportunities. Fluorescently Tagged Small Molecules for Tracking and LocalizationSMs tagged with fluorescent dyes are invaluable in biological and chemical research. They facilitate the visualization, tracking, and localization of molecules inside cells, tissues, or organisms. These molecules are often linked to fluorescent dyes or tags, causing them to emit light when exposed to a specific wavelength. This method is commonly employed in live-cell imaging, drug discovery, and molecular biology research (Figure ). There are three key components of FTSMs: the molecule of interest (e.g., a drug, metabolite, or probe) that is being studied, a fluorophore (e.g., FITC, Rhodamine, Cyanine dyes, Alexa Fluor, or GFP derivatives) that emits light upon excitation, and a chemical spacer that connects the small molecule to the fluorescent tag, ensuring the tag does not interfere with the molecule’s function. Background noise, cytotoxicity, steric hindrance, and accurate quantification of fluorescence signals can be a few of the challenges associated with FTSMs. 5Schematic representation of a typical drug treatment assay.Recent advances in FTSMs include click chemistry for site-specific fluorescent labeling, environment-sensitive probes with environment-dependent emission, nanoparticle-based delivery systems for in vivo tracking, and multiplexing for the simultaneous tracking of multiple molecules.The Power and Complexity of Activatable ProbesActivatable fluorophores, including environment-sensitive probes that report on parameters such as pH, viscosity, or polarity, and fluorogenic substrates that respond to specific enzyme activities (e.g., proteases, kinases, and cytochrome P450s), provide a powerful window into dynamic biochemical processes. Unlike always-on fluorescent tags, these probes remain optically silent until they are engaged with their target stimulus, enabling high-contrast, wash-free imaging with minimal background interference. This “off/on” switching capability is particularly valuable for reporting specific enzymatic activities in living systems, offering direct mechanistic insight into drug action and disease pathology. However, the very properties that make these probes informative also pose significant analytical challenges that must be addressed to ensure reliable HCS.Analytical Challenges in Activatable Probe-Based HCISignal-to-noise ratio and dynamic range are limited by fluorogenic substrates, which convert nonfluorescent molecules into highly fluorescent products. Incomplete quenching creates background fluorescence, reducing dynamic range and detection sensitivity, especially for low-abundance enzymes or subtle activity changes. The 1:1 substrate-to-product stoichiometry makes the signal directly proportional to enzyme concentration, demanding a very low background to detect small variations.Probe Retention and Spatial ResolutionConventional fluorogenic substrates release small, hydrophilic fluorophores that diffuse away, reducing spatial resolution and hindering accurate mapping of enzymatic activity. Self-immobilizing strategies trap fluorophores at reaction sites but can disrupt enzyme function and signaling, creating a trade-off between resolution and biological fidelity.Multiplexing ConstraintsBiological processes frequently involve the coordinated action of multiple enzyme species. However, conventional fluorogenic substrates exhibit broad emission spectra that limit the number of distinguishable channels, restricting the ability to simultaneously monitor multiple enzymatic activities in the same sample. This spectral crowding complicates efforts to elucidate the cooperation among different enzymes in complex biological pathways.Quantitative Accuracy and Stoichiometric UncertaintySingle-enzyme kinetics studies have revealed that many fluorogenic substrates suffer from poorly defined stoichiometry, where the relationship between the fluorescence intensity and enzyme turnover number is not strictly linear. This uncertainty complicates efforts to derive quantitative kinetic parameters from imaging data and can lead to misinterpretation of enzyme inhibition or activation in drug screening campaigns.Phototoxicity and Cellular PerturbationExtended imaging of activatable probes, particularly those requiring ultraviolet or short-wavelength excitation, can induce phototoxic effects that alter cellular physiology and potentially confound phenotypic readouts. This is especially problematic for time-lapse studies of dynamic enzyme activities, where repeated imaging over extended periods may perturb the biological processes under investigation.AI-Driven Solutions for Activatable Probe AnalysisRecent advances in AI and ML are providing powerful tools to address these analytical challenges, enabling the more robust and informative use of activatable probes in HCS.AI-Driven Probe DesignInstead of relying solely on empirical screening, researchers now use AI strategies to design fluorogenic substrates with optimized properties based on first principles. For example, NFa is a highly specific oral fluorogenic substrate for imaging CYP3A4 activity. By combining an AI-selected drug-like fragment with a CYP3A4-preferred fluorophore, the probe shows isoform-specificity, ultrahigh sensitivity, excellent spatial resolution, and good safety. This approach demonstrates how ML accelerates the development of probes that address specificity, sensitivity, and biocompatibility in one molecular framework.DL for Signal Enhancement and DenoisingDeep neural networks have demonstrated a remarkable capability in extracting signals from noisy imaging data. For voltage imaging data sets, which face similar signal-to-noise challenges as activatable probe imaging pipelines, such as VolPy, incorporate automated denoising and spike extraction algorithms that dramatically improve signal detection. These approaches can be adapted for activatable probe analysis, enabling reliable quantification of weak enzymatic signals that might otherwise be indistinguishable from the background. Similarly, DL-based localization algorithms can achieve state-of-the-art detection accuracy, even at high fluorophore densities, providing uncertainty estimates that improve quantitative reliability.AI-Enabled Multiplexing through Spectral UnmixingML approaches are increasingly capable of unmixing overlapping emission spectra, effectively increasing the multiplexing capacity of fluorescence imaging. By training neural networks to recognize the characteristic spectral signatures of different fluorogenic products, it becomes possible to resolve multiple enzymatic activities within the same sample despite spectral overlap, addressing a key limitation of conventional activatable probe multiplexing.Morphological Profiling as an Alternative MeasurementAn intriguing alternative to direct fluorogenic signal quantification is the use of bright-field imaging combined with deep learning to infer the mechanism of action without any fluorescence at all. The BF-MoA framework demonstrates that CNNs trained on bright-field images alone can predict compound mechanisms of action with accuracy comparable to or exceeding that of fluorescence-based CellProfiler features. This approach entirely circumvents issues of phototoxicity, photobleaching, and fluorophore diffusion, suggesting that for some applications, AI may enable mechanism-of-action prediction without the need for activatable probes altogether.Correction of Diffusion ArtifactsML models can be trained to estimate and correct for fluorophore diffusion artifacts by learning the relationship between the observed fluorescence distributions and underlying enzymatic activity patterns. By incorporating spatial context and temporal dynamics, these models can infer the original sites of enzyme activity even when fluorophores have undergone significant postreaction diffusion.Implications for HCIThe convergence of activatable probe chemistry with AI analysis is transforming phenotypic drug discovery. AI-designed probes like NFa demonstrate that computational methods can create fluorogenic substrates with drug-like properties such as oral bioavailability, isoform specificity, and safety profiles that are difficult to achieve. When paired with DL image analysis, these probes allow functional imaging of enzyme activities with high spatial and temporal resolution, supporting mechanistic studies and HCS. For HCI campaigns using activatable probes, key considerations include: (i) choosing or designing probes with optimized signal-to-noise and minimal diffusion artifacts; (ii) applying AI-powered denoising and quantification; and (iii) exploring label-free options using morphological profiling to infer mechanisms without fluorescent perturbation.Utilization of FTSMsThese FTSMs can be utilized in live cell imaging to track the localization and dynamics of small molecules within living cells in real time and study cellular processes like endocytosis, membrane trafficking, and organelle targeting. In drug discovery, the uptake, distribution, and binding of drug candidates in cells or tissues are visualized, and drug–target interactions and pharmacokinetics are assessed. They can also be used as probes to detect specific enzymes, receptors, or biomarkers in biological systems, and in diagnostics, the FTSMs can be used to detect disease biomarkers or pathogens in clinical samples. − They have also been used to study molecular interactions and signaling pathways. Recently, FTSMs have been used in super-resolution microscopy (e.g., STORM, PALM, or STED) to achieve nanoscale resolution of small-molecule localization. Design Considerations for FTSMsCritical design considerations for FTSMs include photostability; the choice of fluorophores that are resistant to photobleaching for long-term imaging, brightness; high-quantum-yield fluorophores for better signal detection, wavelength; select fluorophores with excitation/emission wavelengths compatible with available microscopy equipment (Table lists all the commercially available HCI instruments), minimal perturbation; ensuring the fluorescent tag does not alter the small molecule’s biological activity or binding affinity, solubility, and permeability; optimize the molecule for cellular uptake and solubility in aqueous or lipid environments. 5Instruments for HCIinstrumentsourcefeaturesrefsInCell analyzerGE Healthcaresuperfast, sensitive, and flexible wide-field cell imaging system ScanROlympus Life Sciencesmodular microscope-based imaging platform, fully automated image acquisition and data analysis through deep-learning technology , IncuCyteSartoriusautomated live cell imaging and analysis systems , Pathway 435BD Biosciencescompact, benchtop, endpoint (fixed cell) biological assays TTP LabTech Acumen ExplorerTTP Labtechflow cytometry-based cellular screening instrument Yokogawa CV8000Yokogawahigh-speed confocal scanner, water immersion lens, up to four high-field-of-view cameras, cell cultivation environment, and an integrated robotic pipetter , Yokogawa CQ3000Yokogawahigh-speed and high-resolution 3D live cell imaging. sCMOS camera. Many are larger than the small molecules they label (over 400–800 Da vs 300–500 Da), causing steric hindrance and disrupting binding, especially in tight pockets, as with fluorescent fipronil derivatives that require click chemistry. Binding affinity or kinetics may decrease. Fluorophores’ polyaromatic, hydrophobic nature can alter small molecules’ properties and cell permeability. Hydrophilic groups, such as sulfonates, limit membrane crossing, complicating intracellular tracking. Large fluorophores can also alter subcellular localization, leading to artifacts.Phototoxicity and Cellular PerturbationBeyond structural alterations, fluorescent labels can themselves perturb cellular biology through phototoxic effects during imaging. The generation of reactive oxygen species upon excitation can induce cellular stress responses, alter cell viability, and potentially confound phenotypic readouts in high-content imaging experiments.Strategies for Minimal, Non-Perturbative Fluorescent LabelingRecognition of these limitations has driven the development of several innovative approaches to minimize fluorophore-induced perturbations while maintaining the imaging capability.Ultra-Compact FluorophoresA promising direction involves the discovery and engineering of exceptionally small fluorophores that approach the size of the parent molecule. 3-Hydroxyisonicotinealdehyde (HINA) represents a remarkable example: consisting of only 14 atoms (123 g/mol), it functions as a green-emitting push–pull fluorophore in water with a quantum yield of 15%. Despite its minimal size, HINA exhibits a ratiometric emission response to biologically relevant pH differences (pK a2 ∼ 7.1) and is readily taken up by cells, demonstrating that compact size need not compromise functionality. Such ultrasmall fluorophores dramatically reduce the risk of steric hindrance and off-target physicochemical alterations.Environment-Sensitive Fluorogenic ProbesThey remain nonfluorescent until binding, enabling wash-free, high-contrast imaging. The MaP platform uses probes that switch from nonfluorescent to fluorescent upon target binding, allowing intracellular protein imaging in live cells without extensive washing. The GLF-MINFLUX approach leverages this for sequential labeling and tracking of proteins with 7.8 nm accuracy at high speed.Minimal Quencher ApproachesBackbone thioamide substitutions are a minimally invasive method for distance-dependent measurements. Thioamides, which replace the carbonyl oxygen with sulfur, act as fluorescence quenchers via FRET or PET. They can be incorporated at almost any protein position, allowing pairing with larger fluorophores that are tolerated only at select sites. This method effectively monitors peptide–protein interactions, unfolding, and aggregation with minimal structural disruption.Click Chemistry for Controlled ConjugationThe method of fluorophore attachment significantly influences the degree of perturbation. As demonstrated in the fipronil example, the choice of conjugation chemistry can determine both the stability of the probe and its functional integrity. Click chemistry approaches (e.g., azide–alkyne cycloaddition) offer bioorthogonal, stable ligation with minimal perturbation, providing a versatile platform for attaching fluorophores to SMs at optimized positions that minimize interference with target binding.Implications for FTSM Design in HCIChoosing an appropriate fluorescent labeling strategy involves balancing factors such as fluorophore size, physicochemical properties, photostability, brightness, and compatibility with imaging equipment. For high-content screening with thousands of compounds, an ideal FTSM should: (i) preserve target binding affinity and selectivity, (ii) maintain cell permeability and proper subcellular distribution, (iii) have sufficient photostability, and (iv) limit phototoxicity and cellular perturbations. Developing ultracompact and fluorogenic probes can expand FTSM applications and reduce labeling artifacts.There are many examples of FTSMs, such as the fluorescently labeled anticancer drug doxorubicin-FITC to study its intracellular distribution and the microtubule-binding drug Paclitaxel-Cy5 for live cell tracking. There are a couple of metabolic probes: 2-NBDG, a fluorescent glucose analogue used to monitor glucose uptake in cells, and BODIPY-labeled fatty acids to track lipid metabolism and trafficking. Fluorogenic substrates for proteases, kinases, or phosphatases are used to study enzyme activity. DNA/RNA Binders, such as Hoechst , are fluorescent dyes that bind to DNA and are used for nuclear staining. Meanwhile, SYTO RNA Select is used to label RNA in live cells.Nevertheless, FTSMs continue to revolutionize our understanding of biological systems, offering insights into molecular mechanisms and enabling the development of novel therapeutics.ML and DL Approaches for HCIThe integration of AI and ML with HCI fundamentally transforms drug discovery by shifting the paradigm from descriptive analysis to predictive and mechanistic insight. ML approaches are already used in de novo drug design. , Big pharmaceutical companies are rapidly collaborating to harness the immense transformative potential of AI for SM drug design, signaling a new era of innovation. Equally, automation and AI are revolutionizing imaging and image analysis, unlocking unprecedented insights. The critical challenge lies in efficiently integrating the vast amounts of imaging data generated during screening assays, a task that demands cutting-edge, high-performance computing and sophisticated analytical tools.ML approaches are essential for interpreting the complex cellular features extracted post-treatment, dramatically enhancing our understanding. HCI analysis relies heavily on DL techniques, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which facilitate critical tasks such as image classification, segmentation, and feature extraction, essential steps in accelerating drug discovery and disease diagnosis. For example, a deep learning framework for predicting ferroptosis and apoptosis based on cell painting was recently developed. Another example is the classification of antibiotic mechanisms of action from bacterial images, even for unseen compounds, while vision transformers like NOVA provide an unbiased, holistic view of organellar changes to distinguish patient-derived disease models from healthy controls. Beyond classification, multimodal foundation models such as PhenoModel directly link a molecule’s chemical structure to its phenotypic fingerprint, enabling in silico virtual screening campaigns. , Additionally, advanced models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), stacked autoencoders (SAEs), and generative adversarial networks (GANs) play crucial roles in analyzing temporal dynamics, facilitating unsupervised feature learning, and generating synthetic data, respectively (Figure ). This predictive power is further demonstrated by generative models such as MorphDiff, which can simulate cellular morphological responses to unseen perturbations, effectively prescreening compounds before a physical experiment is conducted. Furthermore, active learning frameworks such as DrugReflector have demonstrated the ability to dramatically improve screening efficiency, achieving up to a 17-fold increase in hit rate by iteratively refining predictions based on experimental data. 6Schematic representation of ML and DL approaches in HCI.These powerful methods process raw image data to extract meaningful insights, offering markedly more accurate and efficient analysis in comparison to traditional techniques. Furthermore, cell-based readouts can be seamlessly processed with commercially available modules or freely accessible software such as CellProfiler, while custom-designed pipelines enable tailored analysis of specific cellular events, ultimately driving faster, more reliable breakthroughs in biomedical research. and analysis by Revvity https://www.revvity.com/product/harmony-5-2-office-revvity-hh17000019 Collectively, these AI-driven approaches are transforming HCI into a high-precision engine capable of not only identifying novel therapeutics but also elucidating their mechanisms with unprecedented depth and efficiency. The potential of AI to revolutionize drug discovery is substantial, and HCI represents a cost-effective and accessible experimental modality. As these technologies continue to evolve and integrate, they hold significant potential to facilitate the rapid discovery of novel therapeutics The field has recently undergone a revolution, driven by significant breakthroughs in AI and ML. These advancements, combined with a surge in computational power, are profoundly reshaping the drug discovery process, impacting each phase of the drug development pipeline from identifying potential therapeutic targets to conducting clinical trials.This transformative shift is attributed mainly to remarkable improvements in computational capabilities, particularly the accessibility of consumer-grade graphics cards that now deliver teraflops of performance. Furthermore, the collaborative and open nature of the scientific community has resulted in the widespread release of powerful open-source toolkits, democratizing access to cutting-edge technologies. Consequently, AI and machine learning techniques are increasingly applied to HCI data, facilitating the classification of cell phenotypes and enhancing our ability to predict mechanisms of action for various therapeutics.Within this context, artificial neural networks (ANNs) and DL have emerged as pivotal components in biological image analysis, being employed across a multitude of prediction tasks. Notably, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have had a tremendous impact on image analysis, allowing researchers to apply deep architectures and sophisticated techniques in both unsupervised and supervised environments, particularly for predicting the mechanisms by which small molecules exert their effects.The term “phenomics” was introduced to encapsulate the comprehensive study of phenotypes, which provides crucial functional insights into genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data. Achieving a holistic systems-biology-level understanding of cell phenotypes and therapeutic mechanisms of action requires integrating HCI data with other multiomics data types, leveraging AI and ML.Collaboration across various disciplines in academia and industry is ushering in a groundbreaking era of “phenomics drug discovery”, where HCI stands at the forefront of developing treatments that are more relevant to the complexities of diseases and provide deeper mechanistic insights. , In the following discussion, we delve into the evolution and influence of HCI, considering both academic and industrial perspectives. We will illuminate significant strides in HCI analysis and the development and application of multiparametric phenotypic profiling, which has the potential to redefine the field. Additionally, we will address the essential roles of image data repositories and image data-sharing standards in further progressing the capabilities of HCI. Finally, we will present our vision for the future evolution of HCI hardware and software, outlining the possibilities that lie ahead in this dynamic field.One recent and interesting innovation is bright field imaging, an AI-based approach that dramatically enhances various live-cell analysis workflows by offering notable advantages. One of the most significant benefits is the remarkable precision it achieves. Traditionally, workflows often require genetic modification and nuclei labeling, which could be time-consuming and complex. However, these steps are rendered unnecessary with the advent of bright-field imaging. This streamlines sample preparation and allows researchers to dedicate the fluorescence channel to additional markers, providing more flexibility in the experimental design. Moreover, the use of bright field imaging significantly reduces the time cells are exposed to light. Shorter exposure times, especially under low-light fluorescence conditions, minimize the risk of phototoxicity. This reduction in light exposure helps protect delicate live cells, fostering healthier conditions for observation and analysis, while also saving valuable time throughout the research process. Overall, this AI-driven technique represents a transformative advancement in live-cell imaging and analysis.The debate over whether AI/ML tools for HCI require custom development for each new assay or are moving toward generalizable architectures highlights a key shift in computational bioimaging. In the past, each HCI assay required unique segmentation algorithms, feature engineering, and model training, leading to duplicated efforts, steep learning curves, and limited reproducibility between laboratories. However, the rise of self-supervised learning and vision foundation models is changing this landscape quickly. Models like Cat-Vision, based on frameworks such as DINOv2 with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), allow researchers to extract detailed features from unlabeled images and adapt pretrained models to new assays with little additional data and computing power. Likewise, HistoLite shows that lightweight, contrastive learning architectures can achieve strong domain generalization with only minor performance reductions across various imaging platforms.A critical enabler of transferability is the BioImage Model Zoo, a community-driven repository that provides standardized model formats and cross-compatibility across multiple end-user tools (ilastik, deepImageJ, QuPath, StarDist, and others), embodying the FAIR principles of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability. Platforms such as DL4MicEverywhere further democratize access by enabling researchers to train and deploy models across diverse computational environments from laptops to high-performance clusters.Despite these advances, significant challenges remain. Foundation models remain susceptible to domain shift and scanner bias, with recent studies showing performance drops when identical samples are imaged on different platforms, underscoring the need for careful validation before deployment. Furthermore, a trade-off exists between lightweight models that generalize broadly and massive foundation models that achieve peak performance on specific tasks, suggesting that the optimal architecture depends on the application context.In summary, while fully generalizable “one-size-fits-all” solutions remain elusive, the field is rapidly converging toward adaptable foundation models, interoperable platforms, and community-driven repositories that dramatically reduce, though do not eliminate, the need for bespoke development. The trajectory is clear: future HCI analysis will increasingly involve fine-tuning pretrained, generalizable architectures rather than building from scratch, lowering barriers to entry, and enhancing reproducibility across the drug discovery community.The HCI field is evolving from custom AI for each assay to more general models. Traditional methods needed unique algorithms per cell type or stain, but now, self-supervised foundation models and transfer learning allow adaptation of pretrained networks with minimal data. Platforms such as CellProfiler and Harmony incorporate these tools, enabling DL in familiar interfaces instead of building from scratch. Resources like the BioImage Model Zoo offer pretrained models that are usable across software. Challenges include domain shift and scanner bias, which require validation on new platforms. Although universal solutions are not here yet, the trend is toward fine-tuning general architectures, reducing barriers, and improving reproducibility in drug discovery.ChallengesDespite its transformative potential, the widespread adoption of HCI in drug discovery is constrained by several significant limitations. First, the sheer volume of data generated, often terabytes per screen, creates substantial bottlenecks in storage, processing, and computational analysis, requiring specialized infrastructure and bioinformatics expertise that may not be readily available in all laboratories. Second, while AI and ML have advanced image analysis, challenges remain in standardizing experimental protocols and image-analysis pipelines across platforms and laboratories, leading to issues with reproducibility and data comparability. Third, HCI assays typically require more complex experimental design and optimization compared to traditional biochemical assays, including the need for multiplexed fluorescent labeling that can itself perturb cellular biology or introduce phototoxicity during imaging. Fourth, the dimensionality of the data, while a strength, also presents a challenge: distinguishing biologically meaningful signals from technical noise or nonspecific phenotypic changes requires rigorous statistical frameworks and can lead to overinterpretation if not carefully controlled. , Finally, despite improvements in automation, HCI still generally offers lower throughput than biochemical assays and involves higher per-well costs for reagents and consumables, which can be prohibitive for ultralarge-scale screening campaigns exceeding several million compounds. HCI in 3DWhile 2D cell models often serve in HCS, they oversimplify the complex 3D microenvironment in vivo. The shift to 3D imaging marks a move toward greater biological realism. Models like spheroids, organoids, and cocultures mimic native tissue features such as cell interactions, oxygen and nutrient gradients, and spatial microenvironments, which influence drug responses. These features enable 3D systems to model complex diseases such as tumor heterogeneity, metastasis, and neurodegeneration with higher fidelity than monolayer cultures. As a result, 3D HCI can identify compounds that affect disease phenotypes more predictively, thereby reducing drug failure rates. Although 3D imaging requires advanced technology for deeper tissue imaging, faster data collection, and complex analysis, their ability to reveal otherwise invisible biological phenomena justifies this investment.Analyzing 3D bioimages presents unique challenges compared to those of 2D images. Key difficulties include increased complexity, sample heterogeneity, data segmentation, object detection, noise, artifacts, interpretation, and quantitative analysis. 3D images from confocal and light-sheet microscopy generate larger data sets, requiring more storage, computational power, and efficient algorithms. Balancing spatial resolution in all three dimensions (x, y, and z) is challenging, especially with common anisotropic resolution, complicating analysis. Identifying object boundaries is more complex due to overlapping structures, noise, and varying intensities across slices. 3D objects have intricate shapes and connectivity, making segmentation harder, especially for touching or overlapping cells or organelles. Noise from imaging limitations such as photobleaching, scattering, or low signal-to-noise ratio affects image quality. Imaging artifacts such as striping, shadowing, and distortion are more pronounced and difficult to correct.Analyzing 3D images is computationally intensive and requires efficient algorithms and high-performance resources. Handling large data sets can strain memory, especially with operations like deconvolution or ML. Rendering and visualizing 3D structures is challenging; tools like volume rendering, max-intensity projection, and surface rendering have limitations. Understanding 3D structures and spatial relationships requires expertise and interactive exploration. Quantitative analysis, including metrics like volume and shape, demands robust algorithms, which are more complex than those in 2D. Biological sample variability complicates generalized analysis. Time-lapse 3D data add complexity, requiring object tracking over time. Solutions include advanced algorithms such as watershed, level sets, and graph-based segmentation and techniques such as deconvolution and deep learning architectures such as 3D CNNs and U-Nets.In summary, while 3D bioimage analysis is challenging, advances in imaging technology, computational methods, and machine learning continually improve our ability to extract meaningful insights from complex 3D data sets.Recommendations and Future PerspectivesThe field of HCI has significantly evolved and expanded across various industries and academic research institutions since its inception in the early 1990s. According to a recent report, its market was valued at approximately USD 3.4 billion in 2024. This market is projected to grow significantly, reaching around USD 5.1 billion by 2029. This increase reflects a robust compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.40%, indicating strong expanding interest in advanced screening and imaging technologies across various research and pharmaceutical sectors. HCI involves the automated acquisition and analysis of microscopic images from multiple biological sample types. By integrating HCI microscopes with multiwell-plate handling robotics, researchers can perform HCI at scale, enabling medium- to high-throughput screening of pharmacological, genetic, and environmental perturbations in complex biological systems. These systems can range from 2D cell cultures to 3D tissue organoids and small model organisms. Advancements in automated HCI play a crucial role in the contemporary landscape of hypothesis-free “discovery science”, complementing traditional hypothesis-driven research methodologies. The pharmaceutical industry is rapidly adopting HCI technology, largely motivated by significant gains in efficiency and the expedited identification of potential therapeutic targets, chemical starting points, and early toxicity predictions.In today’s scientific landscape, there is an urgent need for a sophisticated, fully automated system that harnesses AI to swiftly capture images of organoids and intricate 3D cultures. It is widely recognized that the behavior and interactions of cells in 3D environments differ markedly from those in traditional 2D monolayer cultures. Therefore, a critical component of any HCI system lies in its capacity to analyze the substantial volumes of data that it generates. To facilitate meaningful data interpretation, whether for targeted studies or comprehensive assessments, it is essential to employ specialized ML tools that streamline the analytical process. These tools can significantly enhance our understanding of complex biological systems, paving the way for groundbreaking advances in cellular biology research.Concluding RemarksHCI is a sophisticated technique designed to maximize the data collection in imaging experiments. This goal can be achieved through several methods, including optimizing imaging efficiency to make the process as fast and accurate as possible, minimizing dead time between sessions to increase data gathering, and performing standardized imaging experiments thousands or even millions of times. Such extensive repetition is crucial for obtaining a large, representative sample, which improves the reliability of the data. The ability to perform high-throughput experiments is one of the key benefits of HCI, making it particularly valuable in various research fields. Neuroscience, for instance, allows researchers to study complex cellular behaviors and interactions among numerous variables. In drug discovery, HCI can be instrumental in quickly and efficiently screening potential drug candidates by assessing their effects on cells or tissues at a scale. Additionally, in lab-on-a-chip applications, this imaging technique enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple samples or conditions, further increasing the potential for discovery and innovation.Academic institutions have significantly contributed to this field by providing robust, accessible image analysis software, and ML applications. These facilitate deep phenotyping of cellular biology, including therapeutic mechanisms of action, and accommodate increased biological sample complexity. The pharmaceutical industry is rapidly adopting HCI technology, primarily motivated by significant gains in efficiency and the expedited identification of potential therapeutic targets and chemical starting points as well as early toxicity predictions. Through collaborative efforts, academia and industry have achieved substantial progress in collecting and analyzing the HCI data.

title: Chemicals in cow milk and soy beverages: Neurotoxicity and neuroprotection
abstract: Cow milk constitutes a fundamental component of the human diet. Along with high nutritional value, contains neuroprotective components, caseins, lactoferrin, phospholipids and tryptophan. However, due to the use of pesticides in agriculture, veterinary drugs in livestock, and the presence of other contaminants, cow milk is frequently contaminated by these chemicals posing a risk to human health, namely through neurotoxicity. Strategies to decrease these contaminants include detoxification via microorganisms. Concomitantly, increased consumption of plant-based protein to substitute animal sources has been seen globally, being soy beverages (SB) utilized as an alternative to cow milk. Soy products are almost equivalent to animal sources in protein quality, and moreover, soy isoflavones like genistein, daidzein and glycitein and saponins, as well as soy peptides, may play neuroprotective roles. Conversely, neurotoxic risks associated with the consumption of soy beverages also exist, mainly due to the presence of excess of manganese, mycotoxins and consequences of human interventions during cultivation, resulting in pesticide residues, and pollution of soils, namely with metals. Due to the neurotoxicity and bioaccumulation of these contaminants, the fact that both cow milk and soy beverages are routinely ingested by all ages, and represent key ingredients in many processed foods, including baby foods, strict surveying of their levels is suggested.
full_text: 1.Milk and its derivatives constitute one of the fundamental components of the human diet, particularly due to their protein and mineral content (Woźniak et al., 2022). Milk is widely consumed by children and adults and, consequently, is a very important food item. However, in the last few decades, the increased consumption of plant-based protein as a substitution for animal sources has been seen globally. In turn, soy beverages (SB) can be utilized as an alternative to cow milk by individuals who are vegan, lactose intolerant or allergic to cow milk, which is one of the most common food allergies in infancy. It can also be a substitute for cow milk where cow milk is not accessible in adequate amounts (Andrade et al., 2023). In this chapter, we will explore aspects related to general health, neuroprotection, and neurotoxicity associated with cow milk and soy beverages consumption, particularly focusing on contaminants found in these foods. We will also mention methods to reduce contamination in both cow milk and plant-based alternatives, such as and soy beverages.2.Introduction to cow milkCow milk (CM) is considered a major part of human diet worldwide because of its overall nutritional value (Jadhav et al., 2019; Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022; Cimmino et al., 2023). Cow milk and its products are essential components of a balanced human diet as they have tremendous nutritional values regarding a good proportion of proteins, fats, and important minerals (Ćosić et al., 2021).Milk is a fluid secreted by the mammary glands of female mammals and fulfils the nutritional requirements of the neonate, including the energetic part (provided by lipids, lactose, and in excess by proteins), essential amino acids, and amino groups necessary for the biosynthesis of non-essential amino acids (provided by proteins), essential fatty acids, vitamins, inorganic elements, and water (Raheem and Niamah, 2021; Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022).Bovine milk is the most consumed food product representing about 48 percent of the total milk consumed globally. The European Union, Australia, and New Zealand are the most important producers, followed by the United States and India (Wiley, 2007; Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022). Global CM production has increased by about 20 percent in the last decade, from 694 million tons in 2008 to 843 million tons in 2018. One mechanism by which CM is introduced and promoted in countries throughout the world is school milk programs (Wiley, 2007).Given the clear disparity in dairy consumption trends, and an overall increase in CM production, growth potential in the dairy market is the greatest in developing countries. Stable or declining CM consumption in western countries is related to demographic trends, notably the aging of the population, as well as increased competition with other beverages introduced in the market (Wiley, 2007). The consumption of CM and its derivatives belongs to the most ancient eating practices, since these products have been considered as the most balanced food found in nature, containing major sources of nutrients, especially for children, adults, and the elderly people (Nag, 2010; Boudebbouz et al., 2022). However, despite its nutritional value and high consumption, the use of pesticides in agricultural practices and antibiotics in livestock production, CM is frequently contaminated by these chemicals (Zhao and Wang, 2012; Akhtar and Karam, 2017; Welsh et al., 2019).3.Chemical contamination in cow milkPesticide residues may appear in both CM and its products from direct or indirect sources, such as herbage, contaminated drinking water, and the application of various chemicals from preventing diverse diseases (Nag, 2010; Welsh et al., 2019; Cimmino et al., 2023). Thus, antibiotics and hormones are administered to cows orally, by injection, or as intramammary infusions to treat diseases, promote animal growth and increase milk production (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022). Due to its nutritional and supplementary value, CM is being consumed by people of different age groups; therefore, those residues in CM represent an immediate attention of researchers and regulators (Akhtar and Karam, 2017).Additionally, other common environmental contaminants are mycotoxins, and metals consumed by cattle through feed, forages, and water (Raheem and Niamah, 2021; Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022). In addition, direct contamination may occur during CM processing from milking, handling, storage and even pasteurization. During the industrialization process, CM may contain metals, residues of cleaning products, mycotoxins, among others (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022). Thus, due to various direct and indirect contamination sources, different chemical and microbiological contaminants have been found in CM. Nevertheless, as population and industrial growth increased, new contaminants appeared, and with this, contamination of CM also increased not only by compounds of biological origin, but also by compounds of chemical origin (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022).Among the various chemical contaminants in CM, we will give special attention to chemicals with neurotoxic effects that may cause neurotoxicity on a direct or indirect way. Neurotoxic chemicals may target neuronal axons, myelin or neurotransmission causing neurotoxic effects. These effects depend on the chemical’s potency and the repeatability of the exposure. The loss of neurons can happen affecting or losing some functions (Costa et al., 2008). As an example of chemical contaminants with neurotoxic effects we may include the group of pesticides and some veterinary drugs. Indeed, all the above referred cow milk contaminants, pesticides but also veterinary medicines residues, may derive in health risks to humans due to the consumption of contaminated CM and dairy products (Raheem and Niamah, 2021).4.Pesticides residues in cow milkPesticides are defined by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations as a substance or mixture of substances attended for controlling, preventing, destroying any pest, animal, or human disease-causing vectors, undesirable plants, or animal species affecting food production, managing, selling, storage, and transportation (WHO, 2020). Pesticides play a key role in agriculture and food production by controlling the insects, weeds, plant pathogens and microbial contaminations (Ćosić et al., 2021). These pesticides are used before harvest and during the storage period, and these pesticides transfer through the food chain from simple plants and animals to high-end animals which leads to the bioaccumulation of pesticides in animal products such as meat, milk, fats and eggs (Akhtar and Karam, 2017; Raheem and Niamah, 2021). A pesticide found in water is another source of residues in milk through drinking water (Akhtar and Karam, 2017; Ćosić et al., 2021).The global consumption of pesticides in 2019 was approximately 4.19 million metric tons, where China was by far the largest pesticide-consuming country (1.76 million metric tons), followed by the United States (408 thousand tons), Brazil (377 thousand tons), and Argentina (204 thousand tons) (Fernández-González et al., 2015; Rajak et al., 2023; Kiruthika et al., 2024). Although pesticides are valuable in several aspects such as agriculture and public health, their inappropriate application may cause health problems, including carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, neurodegenerative diseases and disruption of endocrine system (Mohammadi et al., 2021; Schopf et al., 2022).Milk and dairy products, although present considerable socioeconomic importance, their contamination with pesticide residues is a matter of a worldwide serious public health concern, since they are widely and repeatedly consumed by infants, children and elderly population (Battu et al., 2004; Khaniki, 2007; Ćosić et al., 2021; Schopf et al., 2022). Infant exposure to these residues poses serious health risks, especially owing to the lack fully active enzymatic and metabolic systems having a detoxification role (Shaker and Elsharkawy, 2015). In addition to the great importance for human diet, milk has been studied as a bio-concentration process indicator of the environmentally persistent organic pollutants, such as some pesticides (Ćosić et al., 2021). Occurrence of pesticide residues in milk is not so rare, especially for CM (EFSA, 2019).4.1Different classes of pesticidesThere are several different classes of pesticides, with different uses, mechanisms of action in target species, and toxic effects in nontarget organisms. Pesticides are usually classified according to their target species. The three major classes (and their target pests) are those of insecticides (insects), herbicides (weeds), fungicides (fungi, molds) (Costa et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 2019). Within each class, several subclasses exist, with substantially different chemical and toxicological characteristics (Costa et al., 2008).Depending on climate and the type of crops, countries may preferentially apply greater amounts of insecticides, herbicides or fungicides (Costa et al., 2008). Pesticides are one of the most found contaminants, not only in raw CM but also after the pasteurization and Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) process. Their presence in CM, even below the maximum permitted levels, represents a health risk to the consumer (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022). Some studies report that animal origin food is responsible for 90 percent pesticides entry in the human body (Akhtar and Karam, 2017). Pesticides source in dietary rout (products like milk, meat, fat and eggs) is main way of chronic exposure to these substances (Abd-Rabo et al., 2016; Akhtar and Karam, 2017). Organochlorine, organophosphates, synthetic pyrethroid and/or triazine were all pesticides’ chemical classes found in fluid CM, powder products, yogurts, cheese, butter, and sour cream. (Schopf et al., 2022).Many pesticides and their residues that enter the human body through the food chains are recognized as causative agents or primarily contributory factors in several serious human diseases, such as disruption of the endocrine system, neurological and immune system disorders, sterility, different cancer types (breast, lung, cervix, and prostate), heart diseases, Alzheimer’s and Parkinsonism (Nath et al., 2013; Bedi et al., 2015). Insecticides play a relevant role in the control of insect pests. All the chemical insecticides in use today are neurotoxicants, and act by poisoning the nervous systems of the target organisms. The target sites for insecticides in insects are also found in mammals, hence insecticides are, for the most not species-selective regarding targets of toxicity, and mammals, including humans, are highly sensitive to their toxicity (Costa et al., 2008).As noted, insecticides have higher acute toxicity toward nontarget species compared to other pesticides. There are several classes of insecticides; the most widely used are the cholinesterase inhibitors (organophosphates and carbamates), followed by the pyrethroids, and by other more recently developed compounds, such the neonicotinoids. The organochlorine compounds (e.g., DDT) (also insecticides) were widely used until most of them were banned in the mid-1970s; however, some are still used in certain countries, and exposure of the general population still occurs, given their high environmental persistence (Costa et al., 2008).4.2OrganophosphorusOrganophosphorus are a commonly used group of pesticides and constitute roughly 38 percent of the total pesticide utilized universally (Boudebbouz et al., 2022). Organophosphorus compounds were developed in the early 1940s, while carbamates were introduced as insecticides in the 1950s. Compounds of both classes although having a common target of toxicity, the enzyme acetylcholinesterase (AChE), display different toxicological features.Exposure to organophosphorus can cause known effects—acute (short) and chronic (longer-term)—to humans as well as to animals (Richardson et al., 2019; Perry et al., 2020; Ajiboye et al., 2022). The primary target for organophosphorus is AChE, whose physiological role is to hydrolyse acetylcholine, a major neurotransmitter in the central and peripheral (autonomic and motor-somatic) nervous systems. Inhibition of AChE by organophosphates causes accumulation of acetylcholine at cholinergic synapses, with overstimulation of cholinergic receptors of the muscarinic and nicotinic type, with symptoms such as weakness or paralysis of the muscles (Costa et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 2019; Perry et al., 2020). Two additional areas of concern regarding the neurotoxicity of organophosphates are possible long-term CNS effects in adults, and developmental neurotoxicity (Costa et al., 2008).Abundant evidence exists in support of pre- and/or post-natal exposure to organophosphates-induced developmental neurotoxicity (Costa et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 2019). Organophosphates can disrupt various cellular processes (e.g., DNA replication, neuronal survival, neurite outgrowth), alter non-cholinergic pathways, induce oxidative str, ess, and cause various behavioral abnormalities (Costa, 2006; Costa et al., 2008). The intensive use of organophosphates is mainly due to their broad spectrum of action and to their lesser persistence and accumulation in the environment in comparison with organochloride pesticides (Soares et al., 2019; Mulla et al., 2020). However, despite this relatively low stability, organophosphates can accumulate in the food chain including CM (Bolles et al., 1999). This is due to the ability of organophosphates to covalently link to proteins in milk; in fact, it has been proved that casein, mainly with its seryl and phosphoseryl residues, can bind with organophosphates (Deiana and Fatichenti, 1992; Pagliuca et al., 2006).Since CM can be one of the human dietary sources of organophosphates, the detection of these residues in this food is important to correctly evaluate the overall consumer risk with particular attention to the safety of infants and children (Pagliuca et al., 2006). Nonetheless, despite their wide use, there is a relatively low number of studies (12 publications) reporting organophosphate pesticides analysis in raw CM compared to other related pesticides such as organochlorine (Boudebbouz et al., 2022).4.3CarbamateCarbamate insecticides (carbaryl, carbofuran, and aminocarb) are organic compounds derived from carbamic acid, having different degrees of acute oral toxicity, ranging from moderate to low toxicity (carbaryl), to extremely high toxicity (e.g., aldicarb) (Costa et al., 2008). Carbamate insecticides are used abundantly by households and for agriculture purposes (Blodgett and Means, 2013). Milk contamination with carbamate pesticides could cause a serious risk to humans and animals since these compounds have been linked with cancer, reproduction toxicity and neurotoxic effects (Vidair, 2004; Herbert et al., 2021; Boudebbouz et al., 2022).The mechanism of toxicity of carbamates is similar to organophosphates, as they also inhibit AChE, although in case of carbamates the inhibition of the enzyme is transient and rapidly reversible. Nevertheless, the sign and symptoms of carbamate poisoning are similar to those of organophosphates (Costa et al., 2008).4.4Organochlorine pesticidesOrganochlorine pesticides, polychlorinated biphenyls, dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans are widely distributed halogenated aromatic compounds which persistently contaminate the environment (Mrema et al., 2013). These compounds are chemically stable with long biological half-life which leads to high biomagnification in the food chain across a wide range of trophic levels (Serrano et al., 2008; Boudebbouz et al., 2022).Milk-producing animals accumulate pesticides from contaminated feed and by inhaling contaminated air. Organochlorine pesticides due to their lipophilic properties are initially stored in fat-rich tissues and subsequently translocated and excreted in milk (Deti et al., 2014). The organochlorine insecticides are categorized into three groups namely dichlorodiphenylethane (include DDT, DDD and dicofol), chlorinated cyclodienes (Includes aldrin, dieldrin and heptachlor) and hexachlorocyclohexanes (include lindane only). These compounds exist in the form of residues in all food chains from soil to animals, but these may vary in toxic doses, skin absorption levels, metabolism and even elimination from the body (Hayes and Laws, 1982; Muhammad et al., 2021).Organochlorine pesticides, although known endocrine disrupting chemicals (Martins et al., 2019), can also cause impaired immune function, a wide variety of cancers and neurobehavioral disorders (Singh, 2016). In addition, exposure to these chemicals can induce a wide range of adverse health effects including possible long-term effects on intellectual function in infants and negative effects on central nervous system functioning (Zhao et al., 2007).Most of the organochlorine insecticides employ their hazardous effects by injuring the insect nervous system. DDT exerts its insecticidal activity by causing voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) to remain open, leading to persistent depolarization and hyperactivity in the nervous system (Richardson et al., 2019). These chemicals follow the same mechanism for humans by attacking the nervous system, although the lethal doses may differ for insects and humans. Due to the dependence of the organism on the dose for strong toxic effects, care should always be taken when these pesticides encounter humans (Muhammad et al., 2021). It was suggested that the chronic exposure to organochlorine insecticides may be related to the increase of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD). Recently, Richardson and co-workers (2019) reported that serum levels of DDE (a DDT metabolite) were approximately four-fold higher in AD patients, and this was associated with increased risk of AD diagnosis.It is noteworthy that organochlorine pesticides such as hexachlorocyclohexane, dichlorodiphenyl trichloroethane, and endosulfan are still present despite having been banned since the 1970s (between 1970 and 1980). They are commonly detected in CM because of their high persistence in the environment. This indicates that they are still used in agriculture and animal husbandry. In addition, and internationally, DDT has been recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for malaria eradication, which has increased its usage in recent years (van den Berg et al., 2017). Additionally, with a few exceptions (cyhalothrin, cypermethrin, fenvalerate, deltamethrin, permethrin, and diazinonella), most pesticides found in CM are not regulated by Codex and the EU (Raheem and Niamah, 2021). This demonstrates the low efficiency of the regulatory controls of these contaminants in the unprocessed and post-processed product, leading to an inefficient safety of CM (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022).The presence of organochlorine insecticides (such as HCB, Lindane, Aldrin and DDT) in CM has been verified with values exceeding the Minimal Risk Level (MRL), according to the WHO, which may eventually cause a large risk on human health due to its biological accumulation, and the consequent negative effects already mentioned (Rêgo, 2019). Notably some pesticide residues disappeared with skim milk and buttermilk during the production process. Yogurt has low level of pesticides due to heat treatment (it will be mentioned ahead) (Raheem and Niamah, 2021). Among the organochlorine pesticides reported in 32 studies in raw CM, DDTs have the highest monitoring frequency (27 publications), followed by endosulfan (20 publications), hexachlorocyclohexane (HCH) (19 publications), drins (16 publications), heptachlor (11 publications), and endrin (8 publications) (Boudebbouz et al., 2022).Endosulfan and HCH with its isomers, were also considered persistent organic pollutants in 2011 by the Stockholm Convention. Although their use has been restricted by several countries, it is still used in developing countries due to the absence of other organic choices and/or regulation lacking (Sathishkumar et al., 2021). Heptachlor, another chlorinated hydrocarbon insecticide besides being considered carcinogenic to humans, can attack the central nervous system and causes neurological disorders such as Lewy pathology (Ross et al., 2019).4.5PyrethroidsPyrethroids are synthetic organic insecticides derived from the naturally occurring flowers of pyrethrums (Chrysanthemum coccineum and Chrysanthemum cinerariae folium) (Zacharia, 2010). They are used worldwide since 1980 and are considered as the safest compounds for use in food due to their photo degradation, effectiveness against various insects, and the low toxicity compared to other classes of pesticides (Yoo et al., 2016). The mechanism of action of pyrethroids is the same in insects and in mammals, as they bind to the sodium channels and slow its activation, as well as the rate of inactivation, leading to a stable hyperexcitable state (Costa et al., 2008).However, despite low toxicity, recent evidence suggests that exposure to pyrethroids during pregnancy or childhood may be associated with childhood behavioral problems and could affect the nervous system (Furlong et al., 2017). Exposure to these compounds in utero or during childhood can contribute to a variety of neurodevelopmental and neurological disorders. Developmental neurotoxicants may also cause silent damage, which would manifest itself only as the individual ages, and may contribute to neurodegenerative diseases such as PD or AD (Giordano and Costa, 2012).5.Strategies to decay pesticide residues in milkAs it was mentioned before, milk products might contain undesired organophosphate or organochlorine pesticides when dairy cows are fed with pesticides-polluted forages or drinking water (Battu et al., 2004; Schopf et al., 2022).Several processing technologies can be utilized to destroy pesticide residues or reduce its concentration in food and dairy products through its degradation (Gafour, 2018). These technologies reducing the pesticide residues in CM, may indirectly contribute to the decrease of eventual neurotoxic effects caused by the pesticides. Recently, detoxification via microorganisms such as lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and probiotics has been extensively studied and degradation of pesticides through hydrolytic enzymes has been introduced as the possible mechanism, and it has been highlighted that some probiotics harbor pesticide-degrading genes (Mohammadi et al., 2021). In fact, microorganisms play a significant role in the breakdown of pesticides and have been recognized for their influence and many uses in human welfare (Kafilzadeh et al., 2015).Lactic acid bacteria are gaining global attention, especially due to their role as a probiotic. Besides their role in food processing, LAB also have a significant role in degrading insecticide residues in the environment (Kiruthika et al., 2024). Lactic acid bacteria are a group of Gram-positive, non-spore forming, immobile and catalase negative bacteria, which excretes lactic acid as major end product and generally recognized as safe (Kiruthika et al., 2024). The key enzymes produced by LAB, such as phosphatase and esterase, play a vital role in breaking down insecticide molecules (Kim et al., 2005; Kiruthika et al., 2024).Biosorption methods employing the use of microorganisms prove to be efficient in the removal of pesticides, metals, and mycotoxins. Biosorption with LAB managed to eliminate organophosphate pesticides from CM, being more effective for chlorpyrifos, fenitrothion, and malathion (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022). According to Schopf et al. (2022) although the application of LAB was shown to be an effective method for removing diazinon, dimethoate, and methyl parathion in CM it was not very selective since it cannot eliminate all the organophosphates studied. However, Zhou and Zhao (2014) observed that such LAB species present in CM (Lactobacillus casei, L. bulgaricus, L. rhamnosus, L. acidophilus and Streptococcus thermophilus) could degrade organophosphorus insecticides, namely, chlorpyriphos, chlorpyriphos-methyl, diazinon, dichlorvos, fenthion, malathion, phorate, pirimiphos-methyl and trichlorphon.Ayoub et al. (2012) showed that the sterilization process of raw CM is the most effective method for reduction the pesticide residues to minimum value. Concerning the study of organochlorine pesticides residues in CM, Ayoub as well as Abou-Zied before (1994) concluded that sterilization of CM is the most effective method for reduction of p,p’-DDE residues in milk followed by boiling and finally pasteurization. Raheem and Niamah (2021) also noted that the concentration of residues of pesticides in CM decay after heat process. The heat treatment had affected highly the residue in CM sample and the sterilization and boiling provided effective degradation of HCH isomers (organochlorine insecticide). Analysis of organophosphorus pesticides results also indicated that the pesticides degraded faster at higher temperature in CM during heat treatment; and among the pesticides methyl parathion was the most unstable one. Heat treatment and lactic acid fermentation could reduce the level of organophosphorus pesticide in dairy products (Bo, 2010).
