Gafour (2018) found that in the dairy industry field, the heat treatments such as pasteurization, boiling, and sterilization had a significant positive impact on malathion reduction.Moreover, ultrasound technology has the potential to increase microbial metabolic activity; so, Yuan et al. (2020) explored the stimulatory effect of ultrasound pre-treatment on the degradation of four common organophosphate pesticides (fenitrothion, chlorpyrifos, profenofos, and dimethoate) during milk fermentation by Lactobacillus plantarum. The authors observed that the ultrasonic pretreatment significantly accelerated the degradation of the four pesticides studied during yogurt fermentation (Yuan et al., 2020). The enhancement of pesticide degradation by ultrasound may be promoted by the activity of phosphatase in CM, which was the main mechanism for L. plantarum to degrade organophosphorus pesticides (Yuan et al., 2020).6.Veterinary drug residues in cow milkThe common use of veterinary medicines by livestock breeders are utilized mainly to enhance the production of CM and its products besides treating diseases such as mastitis and parasites. The failure to know the adequate period for disposal of these medicines by the animal, is one of the causes that leads to their presence or residues in animal-derived foods, including CM, with potential dietary exposure to humans (Piñeiro et al., 2021; Raheem and Niamah, 2021).The presence of drug residues in food products has become a growing concern because of the adverse health risks and regulatory implications. Drug residues in food refer to the presence of pharmaceutical compounds or their metabolites in products such as meat, fish, eggs, milk, poultry and ready-to-eat foods, which are intended for human consumption. These residues can come from the use of drugs in the field of veterinary medicine, such as antibiotics, antiparasitic agents, growth promoters and other veterinary drugs given to livestock with the aim of providing them as prophylaxis, therapy and for promoting growth (Beyene, 2016; Pratiwi et al., 2023). Compliance with the maximum residue limit (MRL) is very important for food manufacturers according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or European Union (EU) regulations (Pratiwi et al., 2023). The residues of these drugs in food animals can have various potential adverse effects on humans, including carcinogenic, allergic, toxic, neurologic disorders and microbiological effects (Babapour et al., 2012; Rana et al., 2019; Pratiwi et al., 2023).6.1AntibioticsThe presence of antibiotics in human food has been linked to several negative public health outcomes, including gastrointestinal disturbance, kidney damage, and neurological diseases (Apata, 2009). Due to their availability and low cost, antibiotics have been widely used in the dairy, livestock, poultry, aquaculture and honey production industries in various countries around the world. Currently, approximately 80 percent of food animals receive antibiotics for part or most of their lifetime, which may lead to residue accumulation in animal products (Rana et al., 2019).Antibiotics are natural products of a micro-organism, identical synthetic products or similar semi synthetic product that inhibit the growth of or destroy microorganisms. In veterinary medicine antibiotics are used for therapeutic, prophylactic, metaphylactic and nutritive purposes (Babapour et al., 2012; Beyene, 2016; Pratiwi et al., 2023). Cows eliminate antibiotics and their metabolites through milk, depending on the dose and route of application, level of milk production, type and degree of mammary disease, and time between treatment and milking (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022).The presence of antibiotics residues in human food is associated with several adverse public health effects including hypersensitivity, tissue damage, gastrointestinal disturbance like perturbation of the intestinal microbiome and modification of the antimicrobial resistance profile of the human intestinal microbiota and neurological disorders (Babapour et al., 2012; Piñeiro et al., 2021). These antimicrobial drug classes are currently used and licensed in many jurisdictions for therapeutic indications in food animal veterinary medicine. However, some regulatory agencies no longer approve their use as growth promoters in food-producing animals (Beyene, 2016). Antimicrobials used according to label directions should not result in residues at slaughter. However, reasons for residue presence in edible tissues include non-adherence to recommended label directions or dosage (extra-label usage); non observance of recommended withdrawal periods; administration of too large a volume at a single injection site; use of antibiotic-contaminated equipment, or failure to properly clean equipment used to mix or administer drugs, and also mixing errors (Okocha et al., 2018).While the process varies among national authorities, all antimicrobial new animal drugs are assessed for toxicological and pharmacological hazards as appropriate to the drug class and to the specific drug under consideration. These can include, but are not limited to carcinogenicity, haemotoxicity, genotoxicity, immunotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, developmental toxicity, and reproductive effects (Cerniglia et al., 2016).The natural intestinal bacteria serve as a protective barrier, preventing incoming pathogens from taking hold and causing illnesses; hence, intestinal microorganisms play a key role in maintaining the body’s homeostasis. Recent experimental findings suggest that dysbiosis (reduced diversity) of the gut microbiome is linked to systemic inflammatory diseases including AD (Khalifa et al., 2024). Consequently, maintaining the homeostasis of the intestinal microbiota is essential. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are frequently implicated in disrupting intestinal flora, leading to gastrointestinal disorders (Yang et al., 2021; Khalifa et al., 2024). Tetracycline, oxytetracycline, penicillin, and amoxicillin are prevalent antibiotics found in milk (Calahorrano-Moreno et al., 2022).Antibiotic treatment can disrupt both short- and long-term conditions of microbial balance in the gut (Yang et al., 2021). In turn, antibiotics residues in CM can induce neurotoxicity owing to the disruption of the microbiota in the gut (Helaly et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021). To reiterate the previous point, Ke et al. (2024) report that the intestinal microbiota helps maintain the integrity of the intestinal barrier, which may provide protection against the neurotoxic effects induced by methylmercury (MeHg).. The balance of the microbial population has been considered as an independent biological factor that affects the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Antibiotic abuse caused the animals to show anxiety-related disorders (Golubeva et al., 2015).The neurotoxic effect result from abuse of antibiotics works by both local and more prominent systemic mechanisms (Helaly et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021). It can be said that antibiotic abuse is a cofactor behind the rise of neuropsychiatric diseases (Helaly et al., 2019). Corroborating these observations, it was observed that long-term antibiotic therapy for tuberculosis has been reported to induce clear neurotoxicity including cognitive disorders and delusional thinking (Helaly et al., 2019).Excess use of antibiotics like Amoxicillin Clavulanic combination induced neurotoxic effects demonstrated by neurobehavioral tests and histopathology in vivo studies. Neomycin induced hippocampal excitability that reflected calcium binding protein activity. The neurobehavioral tests in mice showed potential impaired memory, cognition and motor function in a remote way (Helaly et al., 2019). A study performed by Vuong et al. (2020) using mice demonstrated that antibiotic maternal exposure could influence fetal neurodevelopment (Vuong et al. 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Patangia et al. 2022). This study is relevant concerning the exposure of fetus to antibiotic residues in milk consumed by the mothers. However, concerning Rahman et al. opinion (2021) that although most of the milk samples of the study area possess veterinary antibiotics residue above the MRL value, it would not be detrimental to humans’ health following consumption. This statement may be very debatable because the consumption of CM varies very much between each one, depends also on the age and health status of the consumer as well as on the type of diet and medicines that are taken.6.2Antiparasitics6.2.1CoccidiostatsCoccidiostats, also referred to as antiprotozoal agents, are compounds extensively used as additives or drugs for the prevention and treatment of livestock coccidiosis (Peek and Landman, 2011; Kant, 2013). Specifically, these drugs are used to treat or control the disease caused by parasites, organisms of the genus Eimeria, known to damage the intestinal mucosa of the host animal (Zhao et al., 2018). They primarily impact poultry and ruminant animals (Tuck et al., 2016). However, coccidiostats may cause residue accumulation in edible animal products and, consequently, posing serious health risks to the consumer (Kadykalo et al., 2018; Rana et al., 2019). Excessive anticoccidial residues in animal-derived food have been associated with toxicological effects such as teratogenicity, hepatotoxicity, or neurotoxicity (Tuck et al., 2016; Pratiwi et al., 2023).6.2.2AvermectinsAvermectins (AVM)s have widespread global application in veterinary and human medicine to control parasitic infections. The AVMs are the most widely used anti-parasitic drugs in veterinary field with sales exceeding one billion US dollars annually (Salman et al., 2022). Among the AVMs, ivermectin was one of the first, broad-spectrum antiparasitic agents extensively used for the prevention and treatment of parasites in food-producing animals. It has been widely used for over 25 years and is listed in the WHO essential medicines for several parasitic diseases (Campillo et al., 2021; Suvarna, 2023). It is indicated for use in the treatment of strongyloidiasis (Strongyloides stercoralis) and onchocerciasis (Onchocerca volvulus), diseases caused by the referred parasites.All AVMs including ivermectin are highly lipophilic, implying a long withdrawal period and presence (accumulation) in the edible parts of the treated animals, specifically those with high fat content (Rana et al., 2019; Campillo et al., 2021). According to Campillo et al. (2021) Ivermectin application at the label dose for beef cattle will cause detectable CM residues that may persist for an extended period.From a human safety perspective, the administration of ivermectin to food producing animal species entails potential risks related to the presence of drug residues in edible tissues, CM, and other derived products (Escribano et al., 2012). The AVMs may pose a serious toxicity threat to animals (Salman et al., 2022). Ivermectin has been regarded as potential neurotoxin; it acts mainly by binding to the glutamate-dependent chloride channels of invertebrate nerve and muscle cells, causing an increase in membrane permeability leading ultimately to neuromuscular paralysis and death of certain parasites (Salman et al., 2022). Generally, the use of AVMs in animals has a wide safety margin as far as the nervous system is concerned (Lankas et al., 1997; Salman et al., 2022). However, in some species like rats and dogs the AVMs exhibit nervous effects by damaging the cerebral cortex and inducing diffused cerebellar dysfunction (Salman et al., 2022).In neurotoxicity studies various signs are observed like depression, tremors, salivation, ataxia, convulsions, mydriasis, coma, and ultimately death in animals like dogs, cattle, and lions (Lankas et al., 1997; Campillo et al., 2021; Salman et al., 2022). Serious neurological adverse events were also reported in public health programs in Africa to eliminate onchocerciasis through community-based ivermectin treatment. Therefore, it has been considered free of the potential to cause neurological adverse drug reactions, except in situations of overdose (Campillo et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2018). Various regulatory authorities including the Joint Expert Committee of Food Additives and Contaminants (JECFA) and European Union have fixed the MRL of ivermectin in CM at 0.01 mg/kg. Therefore, monitoring of ivermectin residue levels in the various food products of animal origin is of great importance to ensure the safety of consumers (Suvarna, 2023).7.Cow milk—General protectionMilk proteins have also been reported for their biological activities, with peptides derived from their gastrointestinal digestion playing an influential role. These activities include nutrient uptake, immunoregulation, and postprandial hormone secretion. In addition milk has antioxidant protective effects (Erukainure et al., 2020).Several studies have analyzed the anti-inflammatory effects of various CM-derived molecules including protein isolates, fractions of bio-active lipids and calcium. The milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) which chaperones encases CM lipids, contains an estimated 120 proteins, some of which have been demonstrated to potently modulate immune function. In one study, lactadherin, a protein naturally enriched in CM, markedly suppressed inflammation in mice induced with a fluid percussion injury. Similarly, mucins have been shown to play a role in the innate immune system and may attenuate bacterial infections (D’Alonzo et al., 2020).8.Cow milk neuroprotection8.1CaseinsCaseins are amongst the milk proteins and abundant in most mammalian species, making 80 percent of CMs proteins (Kunz et al., 1999). They are regarded as micelles owing to their assembly in supra-macromolecular structures (Erukainure et al., 2020). The results from Erukainure et al. (2020) study indicate a neuroprotective effect of casein micelles from CM. There have been increasing interests on cognitive impairment as it has been recognized as a major age-related neuropathology (Berr, 2000). Oxidative stress has been implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of the two major types of cognitive impairment: AD and vascular dementia (VaD). Treatment of oxidative brain injury in vivo using isolated casein micelles resulted in a significant enhancement of the brain’s antioxidant defense systems. Specifically, levels of key enzymatic antioxidants including glutathione (GSH), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and catalase (CAT), were markedly increased, indicating a reinforced capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate oxidative stress. Moreover, the treatment also led to elevated expression of ecto-nucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase (E-NTPDase), an enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of extracellular nucleotides, which plays a crucial role in modulating neuroinflammation and facilitating tissue repair. Additionally, levels of 5’-nucleoside-triphosphatase, another enzyme implicated in nucleotide metabolism, were also increased, further supporting the therapeutic potential of casein micelles in restoring homeostasis in oxidatively stressed neural tissues. These findings suggest a multifaceted neuroprotective mechanism by which casein micelles not only counteract oxidative damage but also support inflammatory resolution and regenerative pathways in the brain (Feldbrügge et al., 2018). Treatment with the isolated casein micelles led to complete depletion of oxidative stress generated lipid metabolites, while deactivating oxidative-activated lipid metabolic pathways. These results indicate the microstructural properties, particle size, elemental composition, and antioxidant neuroprotective effect of casein micelles from CM (Erukainure et al., 2020).8.2Lactoferrin (Lf)Lactoferrin is a multifunctional glycoprotein with approximately 80 kDa molecular mass and 700 amino acids, that is usually known for its presence in CM. lactoferrin’s is found in different regions of the body, especially in the brain, exerting antioxidant, antibacterial, antiviral and anti-inflammatory effects (Le Parc et al., 2017; Eker et al., 2023). To no surprise, lactoferrin can decrease the number of proinflammatory cytokines that are secreted from glial cells under certain circumstances (Xu et al., 2019).8.3Phospholipids and tryptophanBovine dairy milk phospholipids reduce endoplasmic reticulum stress in neuronal cells, implicated in development of neurodegenerative disorders. Moreover, relevant to brain function, CM phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin, were found to promote cell structural integrity (D’Alonzo et al., 2020). In addition, tryptophan, which is abundant in CM, is a precursor of the neuroactive compounds, serotonin and melatonin (Joung et al., 2021).9.Soy and soy beverages consumptionSoybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] is originated from China since over 5000 years ago; in 1830, travelled a great distance to Europe, and from there spread throughout the world to North America, South America, India, and other regions (Cao et al., 2022; Yip et al., 2023). Nowadays, is the most important oil plant worldwide and the major oil crop, which also provides plant protein to the food industry, with a global oil plant cultivation area of 46 percent in 2017 (Heydebreck, 2021; Cao et al., 2022; Yip et al., 2023). In this same year, 14.4 million tons and 20.8 million tons of soybeans and soybean meal, respectively, were imported to the European Union (EU), being the majority of soybeans imported from the USA and Brazil (>70 percent), whereas about 87 percent of soybean meal was originated from Brazil and Argentina (Heydebreck, 2021). In 2018, the average per capita per year of soybean food consumption was 7.94 Kg in Japan, 3.61 kg in China, 0.21 kg in the USA and 0.28 kg in Europe (Cao et al., 2022; Yip et al., 2023).Noteworthy is the fact that the average global warming potential of soybean production (0.58 kg CO2-eq/Kg) is much lower than beef (28.73 Kg CO2-eq/Kg), lamb (27.91 Kg CO2-eq/Kg), pork (5.85 Kg CO2-eq/Kg) or chicken (4.12 Kg CO2-eq/Kg) meat. Therefore, soy products have been increasingly recognized as an alternative to livestock production to reduce climate changes (Cao et al., 2022; Yip et al., 2023). The use of soy in foodstuffs is quite diverse with unfermented foods including tofu, edamame, soy nuts and sprouts, while fermented soy products comprise miso, tempeh, natto and soy sauce.Currently, soy-based beverages are one of the most consumed plant-based beverages, which is a global trend in the food market, representing an alternative for cow milk (Pérez-Rodríguez et al., 2023). Although the consumption of milk and dairy products are recommended in numerous national dietary guidelines, their inclusion in the daily diet is declining in both Europe and USA. Such is due to lactose intolerance and milk protein allergies, as well as to a growing tendency for vegan or flexitarian diets in the belief of improved health and lowered environmental impact (Sterup Moore et al., 2024). For vegans and vegetarians, soy and soy products such as SB successfully took its place due to its high protein content, which is estimated to be 36.49 mg/100g according to United States Department of Agriculture Food Composition Databases; in the case of SB, the product contains 7 g of protein per 236.6 mL which is similar to the protein content of dairy milk. Moreover, SB is inexpensive, refreshing, nutritional and contains different functionally active components responsible for beneficial roles in the body (Paul et al., 2020).The SB is made by triturating soybeans with water, filtering the aqueous extract, and heat processing the aqueous extract to inactivate enzymes, particularly trypsin inhibitors, and pasteurizing the product (Haisman, 2011). Therefore, the main soy sources in SB are the beans, the hydro soluble extract, and the isolate protein. The isolate protein is an end-product of the soy processing and contains more than 90 percent of protein, in dry base (McArdle and Hamill, 2011). With regards to the terminology of SB, although soy-based drinks are known as soy milk all over the world, the European regulation prohibits the use of the word milk for drinks that are not made from mammary secretions. In a different way, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers the legality of using the term “milk” in plant-based dairy alternatives. Nowadays, soy-based drinks are referred to as “soy milk,” “soy drinks,” or “soy beverages” (Olías et al., 2023).10.Nutritional value of soy beverages and general effects on healthThe nutritional content of plant-based beverages varies markedly depending on their plant origin, fortification, and industrial processing, and consequently, the commercial brand. In truth the largely variable composition of the plant-based beverages available on the market impairs a fair nutrient calculation (Sterup Moore et al., 2024). In the case of SB, since the food industry continually innovates to enhance nutritional and sensory qualities to make it more attractive to consumers, the market is full of different products (Olías et al., 2023). A study in Spain based on the labeling information, leaded to consider that the average soybean content was approximately 11 percent (w/v) in these beverages (Olías et al., 2023). In turn, soybeans contain around twice the amount of protein compared to other commonly consumed beans and legumes, which is 35–40 percent of protein on a dry-weight basis and is the only plant source containing all the nine essential amino acids; moreover, the leucine content of soybeans is comparable to levels found in fish and eggs. Soy products are almost equivalent to animal sources in protein quality, with the additional benefit of containing less saturated fat and no cholesterol (Jones et al., 2008; Chatterjee et al., 2018; Belobrajdic et al., 2023). They also contain higher amounts of poly unsaturated fatty acids, including both omega-6 and omega-3 essential fatty acids, than other common legumes. Soybeans have a similar dietary fiber content to other beans and pulses, mainly in the form of oligosaccharides, and contain non-starch polysaccharides which include pectic polysaccharides, xyloglucan and cellulose. They are also a good source of several micronutrients, often limited in plant-based diets, such as iron, zinc and calcium; the high calcium content of soybeans, coupled with the fact that this calcium is efficiently absorbed, makes them particularly amenable to be used as a dairy alternative (Belobrajdic et al., 2023).Despite the already mentioned nutritional variations among SB brands, SB is considered an excellent source of high-quality protein, vitamin B and unsaturated fatty acids, and the fortification these beverages by the industry turn the nutritional gap with cow milk successfully bridged (Olías et al., 2023). Of brief reference are the infant soy formulas as well as milk-based formulas, that fed millions of infants worldwide and promoted growth and development (Badger et al., 2009). Soybeans and derived foods (which includes SB) have been considered healthy for humans, with their phytochemicals such as isoflavones, saponins, proteins or peptides, phospholipids, phenolic acids, trypsin inhibitors, and phytic acid, believed to be responsible for several health benefits (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Chen and Chen, 2021; Kim et al., 2021). Actually, more than 100 phytochemicals were identified in soybeans and soy food (Chatterjee et al., 2018) and in this chapter, general health effects due to the presence of isoflavones, saponins, proteins or peptides will be described.Epidemiological studies have associated soy consumption with reduction of the risk for chronic diseases such as obesity, cardiovascular disease, insulin-resistance/type II diabetes, immune disorders, certain type of cancers, such as breast and prostate cancers, as well as better bone health, and relief of menopausal symptoms (Jones et al., 2008; Chatterjee et al., 2018). Other authors mention antioxidative properties, antiaging, antithrombotic effects, anti-renal failure, diuretic action, prevention of gallstone formation, anti-obesity, relief from constipation, prevention of osteoporosis, promotion of liver function, lower blood pressure and boosting of immunity; soy phytochemicals can also inhibit HIV (Kim et al., 2021).The major bioactive compounds in soybeans are the isoflavones and both soy foods and soy-based infant formulas are rich sources of isoflavones, containing 1–4.2 mg isoflavones/g, which are associated with soy proteins (Jones et al., 2008; Chatterjee et al., 2018; Messina et al., 2022). Jackson et al. (2002) describes mean recoveries of isoflavones in SB, in relation to their initial concentration in raw soybeans, of 54 percent. Biologically inactive glucoside isoflavones are broken down by intestinal bacteria into the biologically active aglycones genistein, diadzein and glycitein, which account for approximately 50, 40 and 10 percent, respectively, of the total isoflavone content of soybeans (Soni et al., 2014; Chatterjee et al., 2018). Limited research exists regarding the bioavailability and pharmacodynamics of isoflavones, but it is achieved that gender and form of the soy product has the potential to influence those processes. Peak concentrations of daidzein after soy consumption have higher levels in women, while in SB, isoflavones are absorbed faster and peak levels are attained earlier than with other soy products (Soni et al., 2014).Isoflavones are often referred to as phytoestrogens because they structurally resemble 17β-estradiol and can affect estrogen-mediated processes through binding to both estrogen receptors (ER) α and β (ERα/β), although their affinity for Erβ is higher (Lee et al., 2005; Chatterjee et al., 2018). ERα is expressed in various tissues and organs, and, ERβ have been found to be expressed in bone, cardiovascular system, and in the brain (Lee et al., 2005). Genistein is the most potent isoflavone, whereas daidzein and glycitein have affinities to ERs approximately 100–500 times lower than genistein (Soni et al., 2014). The levels of genistein, diadzein and glycitein vary considerably across soy food products (Lee et al., 2005). A study in which SB was subjected to various heat treatments at 95, 121 and 140°C for various lengths of time, showed that heating may cause an increase or decrease in the genistein content of SB which depends on the temperature and time used. Even so, genistein showed greater stability to heat treatment than daidzein and glycitein, with both daidzein and glycitein contents decreasing rapidly during the early stage of heating, despite on continued heating the rates of decrease were much slower (Huang et al., 2006). An interesting study with postmenopausal women, aimed to compare the pharmacokinetics of genistein and daidzein after ingestion of SB with the ingestion soy extract capsules; the results showed that the bioavailability of daidzein following a single oral administration of SB was significantly less than that of soy extract capsules, whereas the bioavailability of genistein from both soy preparations were comparable (Anupongsanugool et al., 2005).The estrogenic activity of isoflavones raise some concern regarding their potential to act as endocrine disruptors, and such is truth in the case of infants and small children because their hormone-sensitive organs, including the brain and reproductive system, are still undergoing sexual differentiation and maturation; their susceptibility to the endocrine-disrupting activities of soy phytoestrogens may be especially high (Patisaul, 2017). However, whether soy phytoestrogens are beneficial or harmful to human health is neither straightforward nor universally applicable to all groups (Patisaul, 2017). In male rats, continuous exposure to low and high doses of isoflavones is described as promoting hormonal imbalance, resulting in a decrease in circulating and testicular androgen and an increase in estrogen levels, associated reduced sperm quality parameters and testicular weight (Caceres et al., 2023). Contradictorily a review from Messina et al. (2022) concludes that in adult humans, soy isoflavone intake do not negatively affect testosterone or estrogen levels, sperm or semen parameters in men, as well as thyroid function, breast, endometrial tissue or estrogen levels in women, in which although the menstrual cycle length may be slightly increased, ovulation is not prevented (Messina et al., 2022). It is described that when endogenous levels of circulating estrogen are high (e.g., during the ovulatory menstrual cycle phase in pre-menopausal women) phytoestrogens can act as ER antagonists by competing with the activity of natural estrogens, but with a lower potency; when circulating estrogen is low (e.g., in men or post-menopausal women), phytoestrogens can operate as ER agonists (Soni et al., 2014). The most effective way of relieving menopausal syndrome is hormone replacement therapy. However, such treatment has also been associated with increased risks for coronary heart disease, stroke and breast cancer. As an alternative, the estrogenic activity of isoflavones affords efficacy in post-menopausal women, with epidemiological data showing a connection between the consumption of soy and reduced vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause, including hot flush, sweating and palpitations (Chen and Chen, 2021).Isoflavones has also beneficial impacts on the risk factors for cardiovascular disease by lowering liver or blood triglycerides, total and LDL cholesterol levels, and by increasing the HDL cholesterol and the HDL/LDL cholesterol ratio (Jones et al., 2008). Other studies suggested that isoflavones may be protective against age-related diseases such as osteoporosis. Furthermore, estrogen receptor-independent actions of isoflavones include antioxidant action, inhibition of DNA topoisomerases, inhibition of cell cycle progression and inhibition of angiogenesis and tumor invasiveness (Wong et al., 2008). Other benefic compounds found in soy are saponins, due to their potential anti-colitic, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, hepato- and cardio-protective, estrogen-like and anti-carcinogenic effects. Soyasapogenol B, a metabolite of soyasaponin I, has been reported to inhibit the proliferation of human breast cancer cells (Hong et al., 2013; Chatterjee et al., 2018).With respect to soy proteins, they can be partially hydrolyzed enzymatically to physiologically active soy peptides (Kim et al., 2021). Several soybean peptides that have been discovered over the last decade, some of them with antihypertensive, antithrombotic, hypocholesterolemic, anti-diabetic, immunostimulating, anti-inflammatory, chemopreventive, antimicrobial, opiate-like, mineral-binding and antioxidative properties, due to their structure, composition, and amino acid sequence (Cabanos et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021).11.Neuroprotection11.1IsoflavonesLately, there is a growing interest in the physiological functions of soy isoflavones, especially in whether they affect positively cognitive functions and have beneficial effects on neurodegenerative diseases (Lee et al., 2005). In several studies it was observed that soy isoflavones can improve cognitive function in humans (Cui et al., 2020). However, while soy isoflavones appear to improve cognitive function in postmenopausal women, very few works have involved men; one study demonstrated that soy isoflavones appear to be harmful to the cognitive function in middle-aged men. In another study (Lee et al., 2005), participants received a daily intake of 100 mg of soy isoflavones, a dosage considerably higher than that typically consumed in Western diets. Over the course of the intervention, both short-term and long-term memory performance demonstrated statistically significant improvements. In addition to memory, executive functions, particularly mental flexibility, the ability to adapt cognitive strategies in response to changing stimuli or demands were also enhanced. Importantly, these cognitive benefits were observed in both male and female participants, suggesting a broad, non-sex-specific neurocognitive effect of isoflavone intake. The findings support the hypothesis that soy isoflavones, which exhibit phytoestrogenic and antioxidant properties, may modulate cognitive function through mechanisms such as estrogen receptor-mediated neuroprotection, enhanced cerebral blood flow, or improved cholinergic signaling in brain regions responsible for memory and executive processing. These results add to a growing body of evidence that dietary flavonoids can positively influence brain function even in healthy, non-elderly populations.In recent years, the interest in soybean as a neuroprotective nutrient in the management of Alzheimer disease (AD) has increased, with clinical studies demonstrating that soy isoflavones can have beneficial effects on the cognition of older adults, especially older adults with AD (Lu et al., 2018). While the underlying mechanisms of improved brain function have yet to be fully characterized, the administration of soy isoflavones in mice with chronic ethanol-induced dementia significantly improved their cognitive performance, regulated the acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity and acetylcholine (Ach) levels, elevated synaptic plasticity-related protein expressions and inhibited neuron apoptosis-related protein expressions in the cortex and in the hippocampus (Lu et al., 2020). Being achieved the estrogenic effect of isoflavones, it is also reported that they may improve the cognitive functions by mimicking the effects of estrogen in the brain; in fact, the mammalian 17β-estradiol has been shown to protect neurons and positively affect the cognitive function. Some studies suggest that estrogen affects neuron survival and growth, synaptic plasticity and brain function via an ER-mediated pathway and/or antioxidant properties. The effects of estrogen on ERs can also modulate brain functions by regulating gene transcription and second messenger systems (Lee et al., 2005).11.2GenisteinGenistein can pass through the blood–brain barrier (BBB) and induce neuroprotective effects through antioxidant, anti-inflammation, and estrogenic properties (Li et al., 2022). It is broadly known that the amyloid β protein (Aβ) is the main component of neuritic plaques in AD, produced from the amyloid precursor protein (APP) by sequential proteolytic cleavages by β-secretase and γ-secretase; since its accumulation is the molecular driver of ADs pathogenesis and progression, Aβ is currently the prime target for the development of AD therapy (Hur, 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Genistein might be a promising isoflavone in the management of AD, since has been shown to reduce neuronal loss, ameliorate Aβ-induced cell death in vivo, and even downregulate Aβ generation possibly by serving as an inhibitor of γ-secretase (Soni et al., 2014; Li et al., 2022). Furthermore, while the initial neurologic change in AD patients is the activation of microglia around the Aβ deposition site, thereby increasing proinflammatory cytokine levels, genistein possess (as mentioned) the capability of mediating anti-inflammatory effects. One of the mechanisms is the inhibition of inflammatory factor levels, with proven decrease of proinflammatory chemokines, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, which is a mediator that recruit monocytes in various inflammation models and diseases. It also induces an interleukin-6 mRNA decrease, being interleukin 6 produced in response to tissue injuries, having its dysregulated continual synthesis a pathological effect on chronic inflammation (Tanaka et al., 2014; Hosaka et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2021).Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common degenerative disorder of the central nervous system, and it has been suggested that genistein may have therapeutic or preventive value on PD due to their anti-inflammatory properties. Antioxidant capabilities through ROS-scavenging via redox-sensitive signaling pathways is another cited mechanism (Uddin and Kabir, 2019; Li et al., 2022). In agreement, it was already observed a significant dose-dependent decrease in oxidative stress and an increase in dopamine content in genistein-exposed PD flies, more concretely transgenic Drosophila flies with key PD features such as age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons (Li et al., 2022).Since most neurodegenerative diseases share some common etiologies such as oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, beneficial effects of genistein are also described by Li et al. (2022) on Huntington’s disease, spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, multiple sclerosis, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.11.3DaidzeinIn the same way as genistein, daidzein can pass through the BBB exerting antioxidant, anti-inflammation, and estrogenic effects (Soni et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2022). In vitro study (Liu et al., 2009) have demonstrated that daidzein, a major soy isoflavone, exerts notable anti-inflammatory effects, which may contribute to reducing the risk or slowing the progression of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Specifically, daidzein has been shown to downregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) in microglial and astrocytic cultures activated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides. These cytokines are key mediators of neuroinflammation, a central feature of AD pathogenesis. Daidzein also appears to inhibit activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway, which plays a critical role in the transcription of inflammatory genes. Furthermore, it has been shown to reduce inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression, thereby limiting the production of neurotoxic reactive nitrogen and oxygen species. Through these mechanisms, daidzein not only curbs inflammation but may also help preserve synaptic integrity and neuronal viability in models of neurodegeneration. Although these effects have yet to be fully validated in vivo or in clinical settings, the mechanistic data suggest that daidzein’s anti-inflammatory actions could offer neuroprotective benefits and potentially mitigate the inflammatory cascades that drive AD progression. Moreover, in the same way as genistein, diadzein was already associated with a reduction in tau protein phosphorylation associated with neurofibrillary tangle formation (Soni et al., 2014).In vivo studies demonstrated that daidzein partly improves the symptoms of PD by restoring dopamine levels and regulating antioxidant systems, with reduced loss of dopaminergic neurons and improvement of movement disorders (Wang et al., 2022). Daidzein was shown to confer neuroprotective effects in Parkinson’s disease (PD) models by modulating both dopaminergic signaling and oxidative stress responses. Specifically, daidzein treatment was associated with a partial restoration of striatal dopamine levels, which are typically depleted due to the progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. This preservation of dopamine was accompanied by a reduction in the loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons, indicating a protective effect on the nigrostriatal pathway. In parallel, daidzein significantly improved motor deficits, as assessed by behavioral assays such as the rotarod and open-field tests, reflecting a functional recovery of motor coordination and balance. Mechanistically, these benefits were linked to daidzein’s ability to enhance endogenous antioxidant defenses, including upregulation of superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), and catalase (CAT), thereby reducing lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the brain. Collectively, these findings suggest that daidzein may ameliorate PD-related pathology by targeting both dopaminergic neurodegeneration and oxidative damage, offering promise as a complementary or preventive therapeutic strategy (Wang et al., 2022). Additionally, genetic studies have advocated the role of improper protein phosphorylation caused by a dysfunction in kinases from the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase family, as an important player in the progression and pathogenesis of PD. The MAP kinases, which is responsible for intracellular signaling, comprises four main groups: the extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1 and 2 (ERK1/2), the ERK5, the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNKs) and the p38 mitogen activated protein kinase (p38) (Bohush et al., 2018). The dysregulation of ERK1/2, JNK, and p38 is associated with various stages of inflammatory processes, contributing to age-related neurodegenerative diseases (Ahmed et al., 2020). Hence, controlling inflammation through the regulation of MAP kinase could be a worthwhile approach against neurodegenerative diseases and 6,7,4′-trihydroxyisoflavone, a major metabolite of daidzein, can reduce in vitro the phosphorylation of JNKs, p38 and ERK1/2; these results are suggestive that this isoflavone might be an attractive choice for the prevention of PD (Ahmed et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022).11.4GlyciteinGlycitein can only be obtained via soy in the diet and is the least studied of the three mentioned estrogenic aglycones (Soni et al., 2014). Still, glycitein (as well as genistein and daidzein) is known to possess significant neuroprotective activity in humans, via suppression of the activities of monoamine oxidases, β-secretase, AChE and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), which dysregulation is involved in the neurodegenerative process of AD and PD. Glycitein might be regarded a beneficial phytochemical for alleviating depression and dementia associated with neurodegenerative diseases (Prajapati et al., 2021). It is also described that glycitein have the ability to trigger increased activity of ROS scavenging enzymes, like superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT), being these properties pointed by some authors as potentially useful in the management of neurodegenerative diseases, such as PD (Dong and Yang, 2022).11.5Saponins and soy peptidesTwo major saponins from soybeans were already isolated to investigate their learning- and memory-enhancing effects. Memory impairment was induced in rats using intracerebroventricular injection of amyloid-beta (Aβ1−42) to mimic Alzheimer’s disease-like pathology, and behavioral performance was assessed using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests. Rats were then administered soyasaponin I orally over a set period to evaluate its therapeutic efficacy. Such events were proposed to occur via the promotion of proliferation and differentiation of neural precursor cells in the hippocampus facilitating neuronal regeneration, and by minimizing neuroinflammation (Hong et al., 2013).As regards to soy peptides, a study involving subjects with mild cognitive impairment which received soy peptide supplementation demonstrated that they significantly improved the delayed memory score and tended to improve immediate memory, compared with placebo; in addition, the soy peptide intake significantly increased serum dopamine, known to be associated with memory function (Maebuchi et al., 2013). In vivo experiments support these findings through the proposal that some soy peptides improve long-term memory and neurogenesis by activating cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB)-mediated downstream proteins as a molecular memory pathway. These peptides have also been reported as having positive effects on brain wave and neurotransmitter control, in patients with mild cognitive impairment; their role in preventing aging-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases, such as AD are also referred (Kim et al., 2021).12.NeurotoxicityThe risks associated with the consumption of soy and their products, including SB, are mainly due to the presence of Manganese (Mn), mycotoxins and human interventions during cultivation; soybean crops are often treated with large amounts of pesticides, and pollution of soils, namely with metals can result in high concentrations of potentially toxic elements in food (Gil-Serna et al., 2020; Rubio et al., 2021). However, it should be mentioned in brief that despite the previously described neuroprotective properties genistein and daidzein, when these compounds are present in high dose, they can have toxic effects on neurons in vitro, possibly through interference with GABA (Jin et al., 2007).12.1ManganeseDespite Mn is a metal, it will be considered here in the context of its natural occurrence in soy, and not as a contaminant; effectively, this essential mineral nutrient is found at high levels in plants, such as soy (Cockell et al., 2004). As regards to SB, high levels of Mn are reported in soy baby formulas, leading to elevated serum levels in the consumers (Mitchell et al., 2020). In another work the calculated mean Mn intakes from SB for children with 1–3 years old, when assuming complete substitution of cow milk by these products (0.78 L/day), approached the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) for this age range; no UL for Mn is available for infants under 1 year of age (Cockell et al., 2004).Excessive Mn exposure increases the risk of adverse neurological effects, being demonstrated that mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, inflammation and excitotoxicity are involved in Mn-induced neurotoxicity (Cockell et al., 2004; Dobson et al., 2004; Pajarillo et al., 2021). In particular, the accumulation of Mn in the brain may cause a neurodegenerative disorder known as manganism, which has Parkinson-like symptoms. The similarities between the two disorders can be partially explained by the fact that the basal ganglia accumulate most of the excess Mn compared with other brain regions, and dysfunction in the basal ganglia is also the aetiology of PD (Dobson et al., 2004). Mn accumulates in several other brain regions, apart from the basal ganglia, such as the frontal cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum. Exposure to Mn may also be a risk factor for AD, with relatively recent studies beginning to show links between brain Mn concentration and the development of AD or AD-like symptoms; increases in plasma Aβ peptides were showed to be associated with increased concentrations of Mn. Additionally, overexposure to Mn increase the risk of the abnormal neurodevelopment, abnormal behavior, cognitive decline and learning deficits in infants and children (Martins et al., 2019; Pajarillo et al., 2021).12.2MycotoxinsMycotoxins are fungal secondary metabolites that are a considerable threat to food safety, since are toxic to humans. More than 300 mycotoxins are identified, although ochratoxin A (OTA), aflatoxins (AFT), trichothecenes (T2), zearalenone (ZEN) and fumonisins (FUM) are considered among the most important due to their high toxicity and frequent occurrence in food products (Gil-Serna et al., 2020). The complete eradication of mycotoxins is difficult as they are formed both pre- and post-harvest under natural environmental conditions (Niyibituronsa et al., 2018). Soy is susceptible to the growth of moulds that produce mycotoxins and in accordance, the Dsm-Firmenich World Mycotoxin Survey performed from January to March, in 2024, have indicated the presence of all the mentioned mycotoxins in soybean meal; in SB, T-2 have been detected (Niyibituronsa et al., 2018; Azam et al., 2021; Dsm, 2024). The occurrence of emerging mycotoxins, such as enniatins and beauvericin in plant-based milks, was also evaluated by leading to found that 12.5 percent of SB, were contaminated by at least one of these mycotoxins (Gil-Serna et al., 2020). Quite concerning is the fact that the European Commission has not yet set guidelines for the maximum mycotoxin concentrations in plant-based beverages, nor has the European Food Safety Authority conducted a risk assessment (Pavlenko et al., 2024). According to the authors of the mentioned Survey, monitoring mycotoxins in all soybean meals every year is always advisable (Dsm, 2024).Pertaining to the neurotoxicity of mycotoxins, several of them can cross the BBB and accumulate in the brain disrupting its normal function (Pei et al., 2021). Although research on OTA mediated neurotoxicity has increased greatly in recent years, detail knowledge about their induced neurotoxic effects in humans is currently inadequate. Nevertheless, it is already known that OTA, namely OTAA, has a high affinity with the brain where induces ROS generation, lipid peroxidation and apoptosis. Neuroinflammatory response associated with repeated exposure to OTA A is also demonstrated in three-dimensional whole-brain aggregate in vitro cultures (Obafemi et al., 2023). In vivo, OTA can cause male-specific autism by combining microRNA and X-chromosomes (Pei et al., 2021; Obafemi et al., 2023). The toxicity of OTA toxicity can lead to AD progression, with in vivo studies showing that upon OTA administration, moderately high levels of OTA can accumulate in the hippocampus, which is an essential site of neurodegeneration in AD. Among several proposed mechanisms for this neurodegeneration, an interesting one is the induction of diminished expression of the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in a dose-dependent way. Indeed, BDNF abnormal expression in the brain leads to leads to oxidative stress and apoptotic assault, being associated with AD and even with other disorders, which include schizophrenia, Huntington’s disease and PD (Niaz et al., 2020). Indeed, the association of OTA A sub chronic exposure with PD is demonstrated by both in vitro and in vivo studies; OTA can trigger some of the key pathological features of this disease, such as the loss of striatal dopaminergic innervation and dopaminergic cell dysfunction, accompanied with motor impairments, and increased phosphorylated alpha-synuclein levels (Arce-López et al., 2021).Among AFT, aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is the most toxic congener of 21 identified AFTs, with in vivo studies indicating that AFB1 exposure can provoke anxiety, lethargy disorders, depression-like behavior, cognitive, learning and memory defects, and decreased feeding behavior. Mechanistically, AFB1 exposure has been associated with lipid peroxidation, ablation of non-enzymatic and enzymatic antioxidant defence systems and decreased neurotransmitter levels, as well as neuroinflammation; DNA damage, apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction in the brain tissue, is also demonstrated (Dai et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023). This mycotoxin can additionally indirectly affect in vivo neurons, by disturbing the function of glial cells, and potentially by activating immune cells in the bloodstream, causing neurodevelopmental and function abnormalities (Pei et al., 2021). After observing a growing trend of neuronal deterioration in vivo with continuous increasing time of AFT administration, few authors considered that chronic exposure to aflatoxin or dose accumulation could lead to neurodegeneration events like Huntington disease or AD (Alsayyah et al., 2019). Additionally, the observation that oral exposure to AFB1 trigger α-synuclein pathology and cause dopaminergic neurotoxicity, leaded also to propose a contributing role of AFB1 exposure to PD aetiology (Wang et al., 2023).During the last decade, the neurotoxicity of T2 toxin has been a major concern. This toxin crosses the BBB by altering permeability and induces oxidative stress responses, including ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, and protein carbonyl formation. Exposure to T2 can interfere with certain signal transduction pathways, such as the inhibition of Nrf2/hemeoxygenase-1 (HO-1) and the activation of the p53 pathway, which leads to oxidative stress and apoptosis; changes in brain dopamine levels and decreases in ganglion area are also reported (Zhang et al., 2020). It has been reported that the concentration of T2 in the serum of subjects with a history of mycotoxin exposure was significantly increased, concomitantly with hindered neurodevelopment, and weakened exercise balance, visual function, reaction speed, cognitive ability, and emotional management ability; a decrease in frontal cortex activity was also detected by quantitative electroencephalogram (Pei et al., 2021). The T2 toxins exert also mitochondrial dysfunction, being of notice that mitochondrial dysfunction dependent diseases include neurobehavioral and psychiatric diseases, such as autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, and bipolar and mood disorders; important changes occur also in mitochondrial dynamics in neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington’s, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, and in AD and PD (Islam et al., 2018; Alqahtani et al., 2023). In the case of AD, Aß and tau problems both have effects on mitochondria, which leads to mitochondrial malfunction and, ultimately, the onset of the disease, while in PD disease, α-synuclein aggregation, and inflammation, results from reduced brain mitochondria activity (Alqahtani et al., 2023).The available information on the neurotoxic effects of ZEN is very much limited (Venkataramana et al., 2014). However, being achieved that even at low doses, ZEN causes estrogenic effects, negative effects of this mycotoxin on the nervous system are reported, and these effects are related to the presence of estrogen receptors in the brain (Makowska et al., 2017). The underlying mechanisms behind sex hormonal modulation of neural circuits are not well understood, but sex differences are apparent in AD and PD, with so far, ERs ascribed has having important roles in the risk and progression of these neurodegenerative diseases (Maioli et al., 2021). To investigate the neurotoxic effects of zearalenone (ZEN), differentiated SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells were treated with varying concentrations of ZEN. Following exposure, several biomarkers of cellular stress and damage were assessed. Changes in gene expression related to oxidative stress pathways were quantified, alongside measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, a marker of lipid peroxidation. Mitochondrial integrity was evaluated through assessment of mitochondrial membrane potential, and DNA damage was quantified using appropriate assays. All observed effects—including ROS generation, MDA elevation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and DNA damage—were found to be dose-dependent, consistent with findings reported by Pei et al. (2021) and Venkataramana et al. (2014).Several studies on experimental animals or on cell cultures of neural origin have established that FUM has a neurodegenerative potential, although the mechanism of its neurotoxicity is still vague (Domijan, 2012). However, it should be mentioned that FUM B1 can inhibit sphingolipid biosynthesis in cultured cerebellar neurons, affecting the formation of sphingomyelin; actually, sphingolipids are especially abundant in central nervous system compared with other parts of the organism, where play different signaling roles (Merrill et al., 1993; Mei et al., 2023).12.3PesticidesIt is estimated that >899 million litters of pesticides has been sprayed in soybean, corn and sugar cane crops since 2015. Within the pesticides used in soybean crops, the most frequently applied are glyphosate, fipronil, and imidacloprid. Of particular concern, is the demonstration in vitro that this mixture of pesticides elicits significant synergistic effects regarding cytotoxicity, which were greater than the expected by both addictive predictions, as ahead will be described (Conte et al., 2022).12.4GlyphosateGlyphosate is a controversial herbicide due to concerns regarding public health risks. Hence, there is an intense debate, namely in Europe, around glyphosate, with a vote in 2023 on renewing its marketing authorization (Bloem and Boonstra, 2023). Studies on glyphosate residues in food are scarce, existing a study performed in USA showing that glyphosate residues above the limit of quantification were not found in SB (Guo, 2014). Most of the studies on nervous systems effects used concentrations of glyphosate-based herbicides or glyphosate that are much higher than the ones to which most humans are likely to be exposed (Madani and Carpenter, 2022). Even so, chronic exposure to glyphosate scenarios should not be relaxed since several scientific works demonstrated that glyphosate can cross and affect the BBB and cause various types of short-term or long-term disturbances in the human nervous system. Exposure to glyphosate appears to affect neuronal development, altering the expression of molecules involved in the growth and maturation of neurons, induce oxidative stress, potentiates inflammatory responses by upregulating the expression of the proinflammatory cytokine IL-6 genes, interferes with neurotransmission, namely cholinergic and dopaminergic transmission, and with the glutamatergic system. In fact, the glutamatergic system is the one of most affected, exhibiting neuronal death due to autophagy, necrosis, or apoptosis, with the appearance of behavioral and motor disorders (Faria et al., 2021; Costas-Ferreira et al., 2022; de Castro Vieira Carneiro et al., 2023; Costas-Ferreira et al., 2024). A study in a rural area leaded to suggest a possible relationship between exposure to glyphosate during prenatal and childhood stages and an increased risk of developing autism (Costas-Ferreira et al., 2022). In a publication by Winstone et al. (2022). It is mentioned that the recent rise in glyphosate application to soy crops correlates positively with increased death rates due to AD and other neurodegenerative disorders (Winstone et al., 2022). There is also evidence that exposure to glyphosate is a risk factor for PD, since individuals who attempted suicide by glyphosate-based herbicides ingestion, but survived to this acute exposure, developed PD several months later (Madani and Carpenter, 2022).12.5FipronilFipronil is an insecticide of the phenylpyrazoles class, for which very little information exist regarding it neurotoxicity. However, it is demonstrated that fipronil elicits neurotoxicity in mammals by inhibition of GABAA-gated chloride channels, producing hyperexcitability of the central nervous system (Gupta and Anadón, 2018). In turn, while the status of fipronil as a potential developmental neurotoxicant is still under debate, as several in vivo and in vitro studies suggests it, other in vitro studies do not confirm this concern (Schmitz et al., 2021).12.6ImidaclopridAmong the neonicotinoid’s insecticides, imidacloprid is the most used in soy crops. In general, neonicotinoids are antagonists of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR), and therefore they cause constant nerve stimulation, generating lethal effects in insects (Conte et al., 2022). Although neonicotinoids are thought to have minimal mammalian toxicity, several studies suggested that prolonged imidacloprid exposure can induce various health problems in humans (Hassanen et al., 2023). A potent neurotoxic effect of imidacloprid is reported in vivo by neurobehavioral and neuropathological alterations and a reduction of both acetylcholine esterase activity, and dopamine, serotonin, and γ-aminobutyric acid levels in the brain. In this organ it was also observed elevated levels of MDA and reduced antioxidant capacity, as well as upregulation of the transcription levels of nuclear factor-κB, interleukin-1 β, and tumor necrosis factor genes, as well as strong caspase-3 and inducible nitric oxide synthase expression (Hassanen et al., 2023). Imidacloprid can affect mammals brain function during development, affecting proliferation and neural formation, and memory and cognitive functions (Kara et al., 2015; Conte et al., 2022).12.7Pesticide mixturesAs mentioned, in soybean crops it is common to use glyphosate, fipronil, and imidacloprid in combination. A study performed to evaluate the individual and the mixture effects of fipronil, glyphosate and imidacloprid in human HepG2 cells, showed that this pesticides mixture elicited significant synergistic effects. Decreased mitochondrial membrane potential were observed, justifying the need for a more realistic approach in safety evaluations to better predict the effects to human health (Conte et al., 2022). Given such information, studies on the neurotoxicity of this mixture are deemed necessary.12.8MetalsNumerous human activities including mining, smelting, agriculture, waste disposal, and traffic and transportation have resulted in the release of significant quantities of metals to the environment. Soy belongs to a group of crops that strongly accumulate metals, and these include, neurotoxic metals, such as lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd) and copper (Cu) (Zhuang et al., 2013). In addition, soy consumption can also lead indirectly to metal toxicity because soy foods contribute to low levels of cysteine, zinc, pantothenic acid and other factors needed for detoxification. This can result in a buildup of mercury, cadmium, arsenic, aluminum and other toxic metals in the body, ultimately affecting every metabolic process (Daniel, 2009).12.9LeadLead primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the developing brain, making children to be at a greater risk than adults. The ability of Pb to pass through the BBB is due in large to its ability to substitute for calcium ions; once in the brain, Pb induce damage in the prefrontal cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum, may leading to a variety of neurological disorders, such as mental retardation, behavioral problems, nerve damage, and possibly AD, PD, and schizophrenia (Polido et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2009; Bakulski et al., 2012; Rubio et al., 2021).12.10CadmiumOnce ingested, Cd exerts toxic effects that pose a significant threat to human health, being the nervous system particularly vulnerable to prolonged, low-dose Cd exposure. Within the nervous system, Cd disrupts mitochondrial respiration by decreasing ATP synthesis and increasing the production of ROS. The metal can also impair the BBB, neurotransmission, and change the regulation of glycogen metabolism, and such cumulative nervous system damage can increase the risk for neurological and neurodegenerative disorders (Cheng et al., 2021; Arruebarrena et al., 2023; Ojo et al., 2023). A Cd-dependent neurotoxicity has been related to neurodegenerative diseases such as AD and PD, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and multiple sclerosis (Branca et al., 2018).12.11CopperPractically any data is available regarding Cu levels in SB, but it is known that although women are a hundred times more likely to become copper toxic than men, anyone who uses soy as meat or dairy replacements or who adheres to a vegetarian diet is at risk for copper toxicity (Daniel, 2009). Excessive Cu intake cause Cu accumulation in the brain, leading to apoptosis or cuproptosis in neuronal cells, while neuronal loss leads to memory deficits and cognitive impairment. On the other hand, ROS production, which attack biological macromolecules, leading to oxidative damage to the proteome, lipids, and DNA, inducing apoptosis, exacerbates neuronal toxicity and dysfunction; elevated glutamate, malondialdehyde, and caspase-3 in the frontal cortex and hippocampus of Cu-exposed mice is also described (Duan et al., 2023).13.Strategies to decay contaminants in soyMost of the available work has been performed in the reduction of microbiological risk and indeed decrease of metal levels but under a perspective o heavy metal stress induced in the plants rather than public health concerns. Therefore, described approaches are focused on heavy metal tolerance mediated by the plants (Shaffique et al., 2023). Even so, a work developed in China mention the production of low Cd crop varieties through genotypic selection as a means to reduce the risk of Cd migration into human diet, since physical, chemical and biological methods for remediation of heavy metal contaminated soil, have been shown to be insufficient in effectiveness, sustainability and economy (Zhi et al., 2020), Another work mention the need of reducing the chlorpyrifos content essential for food safety, with methods such as gamma irradiation, pulsed electric field, high-pressure processing and ultrasound pointed as some of the effective non-thermal treatments used in pesticide degradation. However, operational safety (irradiation), limited application to solids foods (PEF) and freshness modification (HPP & US) are some of the constraints associated with these technologies (Anbarasan et al., 2022). Regarding mycotoxins prevention methods, including pre-harvest field management and post-harvest storage management, are still the most effective strategies, since mycotoxins are hardly to be eliminated once they are present in the ingredients. Methodologies involving physical, thermal, chemical methods, and mycotoxin controlling feed additives so far, show evident mycotoxin reducing effects, but of different consistencies and limited by various practical conditions such as costs of high grain mass loss (Peng et al., 2018).14.sNowadays, cow milk and soy beverages are the two main nutritive beverages ingested by humans at birth, during childhood, and for a lifetime, and they are also important ingredients in many processed foods including baby foods (Vitoria, 2017; Andrade et al., 2023; Bakshi, 2023). Therefore, the consumption of dairy products together with other contaminated food may expose consumers to unexpected levels of chemicals with emphasis on some pesticides and metals (Waliszewski et al., 2003; Armendáriz et al., 2004).The effects on human health, particularly children to the exposure of these contaminants in cow milk or soy beverages, even below the permissible levels, are unpredictable because human beings are not only exposed to these food contaminants; they are also exposed to contaminants from other foods, exposed to chemicals in the environment, medicines, as well as chemicals at homes. Many of these chemicals are neurotoxic and their final consequences of the exposure to these mixtures may be very harmful mainly after chronic exposure.Nevertheless, due to the toxicity and neurotoxicity and bioaccumulation of some of these chemical contaminants, the fact that these foods are routinely ingested by all ages, mainly children, and represent key ingredients in many processed foods, including baby foods, we suggest strict surveying of these chemical residue levels in cow milk and soy beverages.
