title: Hydrazone–heterocyclic hybrids as promising anticancer agents: a comprehensive review
abstract: Hydrazones have gained significant attention in the field of medicinal chemistry because of their ease of preparation, crystalline nature, structural flexibility and broad-spectrum biological activity. Additionally, N-containing heterocycles have always contributed to anticancer drug discovery, with 73% of FDA-approved anticancer drugs based on them. Recently, the idea of hybrid drug design that synergistically combines two or more pharmacologically active molecules has become an effective strategy in discovering new anticancer drugs. Hence, combining two bioactive fragment hydrazones and N-containing heterocycles can be considered an effective strategy for discovering potent anticancer drugs. Among these, heterocycle–hydrazone hybrids derived from quinoline, indole, triazole, benzimidazole and isatin have displayed promising anticancer activities, with some of the studies even approaching in vivo evaluation. Overall, this review focuses on the anticancer activities of these hydrazone hybrids, their in vitro cytotoxic results, the proposed mechanism of action of the most active compound, cell death pathway results, docking studies, and cell cycle-arrest results. In addition, various synthetic strategies of hydrazones, including conventional methods, microwave and ultrasonication irradiation techniques, diazonium salt-derived methods and solvent-free reaction conditions, have been reported. Furthermore, the kinetics of hydrazone synthesis is described in brief.
full_text: 1.Cancer is a major global health problem, and India has the third-highest cancer cases worldwide after China and the USA, according to the Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN), which estimates a 57% rise in the number of cancer cases by 2040.1 Cancer is caused when the abnormal cells divide uncontrollably in the human body, which is not only due to genetics but also caused by poor lifestyle or habits.2 DNA damage is caused by various exogenous and endogenous processes, such as exposure to chemicals, exposure to radiation, generation of free radicals, and topological changes, and is another important condition for the generation of cancerous cells.3 What makes cancer the deadliest disease is its diverse symptoms in diagnosis, with its signs being similar to those caused during mild illness.4 In particular, the current state of knowledge in tumour biology over the last decade has positively impacted the discovery of anticancer drugs.5 However, the drug resistance and lack of selectivity of the drug molecules, as reported in several studies6 and clinical trials, have urged the discovery of new bioactive molecules that are capable of exhibiting cancer-specific cytotoxic activities, and the discovery of anticancer drugs is still a topic of interest among researchers.Hybrid drug design linking two pharmacologically active molecules has become an effective strategy in the field of medicinal chemistry.7 The incorporation of two biologically active fragments into a single molecule can exert synergistic effects by enhancing pharmaceutical applications via targeting multiple receptor sites.8 Among the various fragments that can be used to scaffold heterocycles, hydrazones (–C Created by potrace 1.16, written by Peter Selinger 2001-2019 N–NH–) provide proven benefits, such as easier synthetic methods, flexibility, and the ability to interact with various target proteins and display broad-spectrum biological applications.9 The free rotation around the N–N single bond and the presence of a carbonyl group maintaining molecular planarity are the characteristic features of their azomethine linkage. In addition, hydrazones are not just the final products of the reaction, but they can also be used as intermediates to prepare heterocycles.10Heterocycles are cyclic compounds containing at least one heteroatom, such as oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur.11 Owing to their importance in drug discovery, more than 85% of FDA-approved drugs are made of heterocycles.12 More specifically, approximately 75% of FDA-approved drugs contain N-heterocycles, highlighting their importance in drug discovery.13 Combining these heterocycles with hydrazone hybrids enhances the biological activities of the resultant hybrids.14 Previously, Popiolek has studied the antimicrobial activity of various hydrazone derivatives.15,16 In addition, the authors studied the antimicrobial, antifungal, antitumor, antidepressant, insecticidal and enzyme inhibition activities of benzene–sulfonyl hydrazone derivatives.17 Mali et al. studied various biological activities such as antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, and antitubercular functions including synthesis aspects.18 Socea et al. reported the synthesis, spectral characterization, and antitumour, antimicrobial, antiviral, antiparasitic, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, antioedematous, antidiabetic and antioxidant action of various acyl hydrazones.19 Tafere et al. reported anticancer and antimicrobial activities of copper, silver and gold complexes of hydrazones.20 In addition to their antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and anticancer applications, Wahbeh et al. reported the role of hydrazones in the prevention of platelet aggregation.21 Omidi and Kakanejadifard studied the biological activities of hydrazones of curcumin.22 Angelova et al. studied the anticonvulsant activity of acetyl-, benzoyl-, GABA-, nicotinic acid-, indole-, thiophene-, 2-chloroquinolinyl, coumarin-, chroman- and chromene–hydrazone derivatives in animal models.23 Furthermore, reviews addressing the anticancer activities of quinoline,24 indole,25 triazole,26 benzimidazole27 and isatin28 have been extensively reported, but a review collectively explaining the anticancer activities of these heterocyclic hydrazones has not yet been conducted.While there is growing research interest in heterocyclic–hydrazone hybrids in anticancer drug discovery, understanding the current developments in the synthetic methodologies of hydrazone derivatives and the biological applications of heterocycle–hydrazone hybrids is vital. In this context, this review summarizes various synthetic strategies and kinetic effects of catalyst, solvent, pressure and irradiation techniques on hydrazone synthesis. In addition, the recent advances in the anticancer activities of various N-containing heterocycle–hydrazone hybrids, particularly quinoline, indole, benzimidazole, triazole and isatin hydrazones, are summarized along with docking studies to understand their binding interactions with target proteins (such as EGFR, topoisomerase, ERα, and various kinase domains), briefly describing the enzyme inhibition results wherever reported in the anticancer study, the mechanism of action of the most active compounds, and cell-cycle arrest results to collectively present the results of various studies and provide readers with a collective overview of this area of research. With these insights, structure–activity relationship studies have been conducted to help the researchers to understand different substitution patterns and structural arrangement to design potent bioactive molecules with effective anticancer activity.2.Synthetic methodologies of hydrazones2.1.Classical condensation of hydrazides and aldehydesBaşaran et al. synthesized acyl hydrazones by the initial conversion of ester 1 to hydrazide 2 using hydrazine hydrate in ethanol at RT. Subsequent treatment of these hydrazides with various aldehydes yielded hydrazones 3a–g in good yields of 76–89% (ref. 29) [Scheme 1].29Scheme 1Classical condensation of hydrazide 1 with aldehydes to yield hydrazones 3a–3g.2.2.Using acid catalystsUdhayanithi et al. prepared hydrazones 6a–e in 80–90% yield by condensing hydrazide 4 with aromatic aldehydes 5a–e in ethanol at reflux using acetic acid (catalyst)30 [Scheme 2].30Scheme 2Synthesis of hydrazones 6a–e using acid catalysts.2.3.Using a base catalystKarimatu et al. synthesized hydrazone 9 by refluxing 2,4,5-trimethoxyacetophenone 7 and 4-nitrophenylhydrazine 8 in ethanol in the presence of sodium hydroxide31 [Scheme 3].31Scheme 3Synthesis of hydrazone 9 using the base catalyst.2.4.From diazonium saltsSalah et al. synthesized hydrazone 15 from an aryl diazonium intermediate 12, which was synthesized from chloroanthranilic acid 10 using an aqueous solution of sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid. To this, a solution of acetylacetone 13, sodium hydroxide, water and ethanol was added. Subsequently, the solid precipitate was filtered to yield the target hydrazone32 [Scheme 4].32Scheme 4Synthesis of hydrazone 15via an aryl diazonium intermediate.2.5.Microwave-assisted synthesisMagda et al. conducted microwave-assisted synthesis of hydrazones 18a–o by dissolving 2-phenylacetohydrazide 16 and various benzaldehydes 17a–o in ethanol and subjecting the reagents to microwave radiation (300 W of power, for 7 min at 155 °C). The reduced reaction time and sustainable approach in the synthesis serve as an important advantage of such reactions33 [Scheme 5].33Scheme 5Microwave-assisted synthesis of hydrazones 18a–o.2.6.Solvent-free reactionsAbu-Melha et al. reported solvent-free synthesis of hydrazone 21 employing a grinding technique in the condensation of ketone 19 and hydrazide 20 using acetic acid (catalyst)34 [Scheme 6].34Scheme 6Grinding technique to synthesize hydrazone 21.2.7.Ultrasonic irradiation techniqueRezki et al. utilized an ultrasound irradiation technique to synthesize the desired hydrazone 24 from isoniazid 22 and 4-fluorobenzaldehyde 23 using acetic acid (catalytic) in ethanol35 [Scheme 7].35Scheme 7Ultrasonic irradiation technique employed to synthesize hydrazone 24.3.Kinetics of hydrazone synthesis3.1.Effect of solventsBharanidharan et al. tested the effect of various solvents on the synthesis of hydrazone 27 using ZnO–Tis nanoparticles as catalysts in the reaction36 [Scheme 8].36 Generally, reactions performed in polar solvents such as methanol and ethanol were completed in shorter reaction times, providing higher yields than reactions employing nonpolar solvents (such as chloroform and dichloromethane), as described in Table 1.36Scheme 8Synthesis of hydrazone 27 using zinc nanoparticles.Table 1Effect of solvents on the reaction time and percentage of yield of hydrazoneS. No.SolventTime (h)Yield (%)1Methanol3752Ethanol3893Water10Trace4CDCl36605DCM5653.2.Effect of catalystAl-Saleem et al. studied the effect of citric acid and acetic acid on the percentage yield in the synthesis of hydrazones 30a–o (ref. 37) [Scheme 9].37 The result indicated that the reaction with citric acid provided a higher yield than that with acetic acid employed as a catalyst, as depicted in Table 2.37Scheme 9Synthesis of hydrazones 30a–o using citric acid and acetic acid as catalysts.Table 2Effect of catalysts on the synthesis of hydrazones 30a–oCompoundYield (%)Citric acidAcetic acid30a948530b928330c928230d908330e908130f908230g908030h928130i908030j887830k887930l888030m888130n888230o88803.3.Effect of pressureCosta and coworkers synthesized hydrazones 33a–i [Scheme 10]38 by condensing hydrazides 32 and aldehyde 31 at room temperature without employing solvent with increasing pressure from 0.001 to 3.8 kbar using atmospheric pressure as the control and found that the reaction occurring at the lowest pressure of 0.001 kbar provided a yield of up to 80%. Increasing the pressure up to 0.7 kbar increased the yield by 11%, providing over 90% yield. A successive increase in pressure had a minimal effect on increasing the yield without a notable increase, terming that it could only favour the reaction conditions. Since there was no further increase in yield after 1.4 kbar, further investigation with this pressure being used in 10 cycles yielded 96% yield, which could be treated as the optimal condition for the synthesis. In addition, as depicted in Scheme 10, reactions proceeded under high hydrostatic pressure and provided a higher yield than that obtained in the control conditions.38Scheme 10Effect of pressure on the percentage yield of hydrazones 33a–i.3.4.Effect of irradiationAl-Rasheed et al. used ultrasonic radiation to enhance the rate of hydrazone formation and compared the yield and reaction time to the conventional technique [Scheme 11].39 The ultrasonic irradiated reactions were carried out at 40 °C, whereas conventional reactions were performed at reflux temperature in ethanol. The reactions carried out using ultrasonic radiation significantly improved the yield (>90%) at time intervals of 30 to 60 minutes, while conventional reactions gave approximately 70% yield at 4–5 h.39Scheme 11Effect of ultrasonication on the synthesis of hydrazones 36a–o.Olayinka et al. used microwave irradiation technique to synthesize target hydrazones and compared the percentage yield and time with those of conventional techniques.40 The target hydrazones 39a–d were synthesized with a higher yield of 73–91% at 1-minute intervals than the yield of 59–70% at 180 minutes as depicted in Scheme 12.40Scheme 12Microwave-assisted synthesis of compounds 39a–d.4.Quinoline hydrazide–hydrazones and their anticancer activitiesQuinoline is a fused heterocyclic molecule with the molecular formula of C9H7N, comprising a pyridine ring fused with a phenyl ring.41 These pharmaceutically active molecules are less toxic and their diverse biological applications have gained significant attention from researchers, making them important heterocycles in the field of medicinal chemistry.42 The presence of a nitrogen atom (−I effect) contributes to its anticancer properties, since it can bind to various amino acid residues in target proteins.43 There are various quinoline-based anticancer drugs such as bosutinib,44 cabozantinib,45 and topotecan,46 as depicted in Fig. 1. Furthermore, introducing a hydrazone functionality into the quinoline group can enhance the structural adaptability and biomolecular interactions.47 Hence, due to this synergistic combination, quinoline–hydrazones have gained prominence in tumor studies.Fig. 1Quinoline-based anticancer drugs.Bingul et al. synthesized various quinoline hydrazones 44a–f and nonquinoline hydrazones 45a–c and investigated their antitumor activities against various cancer cells using cell viability assays.48 Compound 44d, bearing two methoxy substituents at the 5th and 7th positions of the quinoline ring, exhibited the highest cytotoxicity against both breast (33% and 38% cell reductions with respect to MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 cell lines, respectively) and neuroblastoma cell lines (82% and 96% cell reductions in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cell lines, respectively). Compound 44c demonstrated the second-best cytotoxicity, with 68% and 88% of SH-SY5Y and Kelly cancer cell reductions, respectively. The three nonquinoline hydrazones displayed lesser activity than the quinoline hydrazones, with cell reductions of less than 10% against MCF-7 cancer cell lines, and being even less active towards neuroblastoma cells, thus highlighting the importance of the quinoline ring in cytotoxic activity. In the dose-response experiments, compound 44d displayed IC50 values of 1.3 and 2.9 µM against the Kelly and SH-SY5Y cells, respectively. In addition, compound 44d reduced only 30% of normal lung fibroblast, displaying their selectivity towards cancerous cells. Further, it reduced the cell count in the S phase and G2/M phase, which indicates that compound 44d prevents cell proliferation and induces cell cycle arrest by upregulating p27kip1 (ref. 48) (Fig. 2).48,49 Jia-Xing Lu et al. synthesized quinoline-based dihydrazones, and the in vitro cytotoxic study revealed that compound 45b displayed pronounced anticancer activities against BGC-823 (IC50 = 9.12 ± 0.19 µM), BEL-7402 (IC50 = 10.22 ± 0.12 µM), MCF-7 (IC50 = 7.05 ± 0.05 µM) and A549 (IC50 = 7.32 ± 0.05 µM) cancer cells, even superior to that of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) (IC50 values = 15.18 ± 0.05, 15.81 ± 0.01, 11.32 ± 0.78, and 11.77 ± 0.89 µM, respectively); however, it was less cytotoxic than the standard sorafenib. It displayed less cytotoxicity towards normal cell lines (IC50 > 100 µM) than 5-FU (IC50 = 20.83 ± 0.05 µM), indicating better selectivity. Compound 45c displayed potent cytotoxicity against BEL-7402 (IC50 = 11.14 ± 1.02 µM) and MCF-7 (IC50 = 10.39 ± 0.52 µM) cancer cell lines, superior to that of 5-FU, with better selectivity (IC50 > 100 µM against normal cells). These two compounds had a phenyl group on the pyrimidine backbone, which enhanced the conjugation, which can be attributed to their increased anticancer effects. In addition, compound 45a (IC50 = 7.01 ± 0.26 µM) displayed superior cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cancer cells relative to the standard. The docking results revealed that compounds 45a and 45b had BEs of −7.9 kcal mol−1 and −7.2 kcal mol−1, respectively, indicating stronger binding with DNA. Compound 45b formed H-bonding interactions with DG-8 and DG-34 DNA base pairs, while compound 45c formed H-bonding interactions with DG-8 DNA base pairs. Molecular docking studies carried out on the CDK2 active binding site, which is an enzyme that plays an important role in cell division, revealed that compounds 45a and 45b displayed better binding interactions with the enzyme than the rest of the derivatives, which was in accordance with the in vitro results. Notably, the N-atom in the hydrazone linkage in 45a displayed strong H-bonding interaction with the Lys-88 amino acid residue, while 45b formed H-bonding interaction with the Arg-199 residue. The quinoline ring formed π–π stacking interactions with Ala-201 and Asp-92 residues49 (Fig. 3).49,50 Puskullu et al. studied the cytotoxic activities of the synthesized quinoline hydrazones against A549 and MCF-7 cancer cell lines by an MTT assay. At 100 µM, compound 46 displayed better cytotoxicity by reducing the percentage viability to 59.28% in A549 cancer cells50 (Fig. 3).51 Özcan et al. synthesized quinoline-based sulfonyl hydrazones and studied their cytotoxicity against breast cancer cell line using the MTT assay. Compounds were found to be more active against the ER-negative MDA-MB-231 cells. More specifically, compounds 47a (IC50 = 6.8 µM) bearing chloro at the 2nd and 4th positions, 47b (IC50 = 6.96 µM) bearing a trifluoromethyl group and 47c bearing a chloro substituent (IC50 = 8.6 µM) emerged as potent anticancer agents, displaying potent activity against MDA-MB-231 cancer cells, similar to cisplatin (IC50 = 6.93 µM). Hence, their selectivity was also evaluated by treating them against the normal fibroblast cell line L929, and it was found that compounds 47a (IC50 = 42.64 µM), 47b (IC50 = 297.6 µM) and 47c (IC50 = 96.2 µM) displayed much lower cytotoxicity than the standard (IC50 = 18.36 µM). Hence, compounds with electron-accepting halogens displayed better cytotoxicity than those bearing EDGs, primarily, disubstituted halogens. In addition, compound 47b (p pyridyl > phenyl > furan ring systems and as substituents moved from para- to ortho-positions. In addition, docking studies conducted on the EGFR protein (PDB ID: 3W2S) suggested that compound 90 formed the highest binding interactions with the enzyme with a docking score of −11.533 kcal mol−1, forming hydrophobic interactions (LEU718A, VAL726A, and ALA743A), and H-bonding interactions (LYS745A at 2.11 and 2.67 Å distances), which validates its superior in vitro cytotoxicity72 (Fig. 15).73 Sreenivasulu et al. synthesized indole hydrazides and hydrazones and tested their in vitro anticancer activity against various cancer cells using the MTT assay. Compound 91 (IC50 = 0.793 ± 0.29 µM) displayed superior cytotoxicity against A549 cells to that of doxorubicin (IC50 = 0.89 ± 0.26 µM). Compound 91 was found to be less cytotoxic towards normal HEK-293 cells (IC50 > 200 µM) similar to doxorubicin (IC50 > 200 µM), which indicates its higher selectivity. Time-dependent apoptosis induction was observed, where 76% of the cells appeared in late apoptosis, while 26% appeared in early apoptosis, when the cells were treated with compound 91 at a concentration of 1 µM after 16 h treatment, indicating apoptotic cell death in MCF-7 and HeLa cancer cells. Overall, compound 91 induced apoptosis via p53-dependent and MAPK-mediated pathways, thus being an important biomolecule in anticancer drug discovery73 (Fig. 15).74 The authors also synthesized indole–indazolyl hydrazones and the MTT assay results showed that compound 92 (IC50 = 1.93 ± 0.25 µM) displayed potent cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cancer cells, but was twofold less potent than doxorubicin (IC50 = 0.98 ± 0.14 µM). The docking studies conducted in tubulin receptor protein revealed that the –NH group of the indole and indazole rings formed H-bonding interactions with Val315 and Val238 residues. Additionally, the –NH group of the hydrazone formed additional H-bonding with the Asn258 residue, and the nitro group present in the indazole ring displayed side-chain H-bonding with the Lys352 residue, which can account for its higher cytotoxicity than the rest of the derivatives74 (Fig. 15).75 Kilic-Kurt et al. synthesized indole-based hydrazones and evaluated their anticancer activity against three panels of cancer cells, namely MCF-7, HepG2 and PC3. Compound 93 (IC50 = 3.01 µM), bearing a 4-chloro substituent at the benzylidene part and a methoxy substituent attached to the 5th position in the indole ring, displayed potent cytotoxicity against breast cancer cells at a concentration of 20 µM after 48 h, with a cell viability of 23.03% ± 3.51%. Compounds 94 (IC50 = 5.48 µM) and 95 (IC50 = 7.32 µM) bearing 3,4-dichloro substituents followed closely with cell viabilities of 22.15% ± 4.59% and 15.09% ± 1.37%, respectively. Compound 93 increased the MCF-7 cell population to 45.6% ± 1.13% in the G0/G1 phase compared with 1.7% ± 0.14% in the control, indicating cell cycle arrest at the G0/G1 phase (p 50 µM) normal cells with cell viability up to 77.09%, owing to its improved selectivity. The cytotoxicity of compounds with various substituents was observed in the following order: 99 > 100 (furan, 19.2 ± 0.4 µM, 23.53%) > 101 (pyridine, 21.4 ± 0.2 µM, 23.44%), 102 (naphthyl, 26.6 ± 0.1 µM, 30.59%) > 103 (benzyl, 43.4 ± 0.2 µM, 44.16%). With this structure–activity relationship, the effect of phenyl and benzyl substituents can be easily identified, where compound 99 containing a phenyl group was the most cytotoxic derivative, while compound 102 containing a benzyl group was the least active cytotoxic agent. With respect to substitution patterns, EWGs present at the para-position were found to be more active than those in the ortho position. This can be evidenced by 104 (p-Br, 21.8 ± 0.2) and 105 (o-Br, 26.4 ± 0.2). Further, docking studies conducted on the target protein EFGR (PDB ID: 3W2S) revealed that compound 99 formed stable binding with the protein with a BE of −10.523 kcal mol−1, thus accounting for its highest cytotoxicity79 (Fig. 16).80 Dipanwita et al. tested the cytotoxicity of bis-indolyl hydrazones against A549 cells using MTT assay. Compound 106 bearing a methoxy substituent at the 5th position of the indole ring displayed superior cytotoxicity with an IC50 value of 2 µM among other derivatives, but was less cytotoxic than colchicine (IC50 = 0.02 µM). Its positional isomer 107 bearing a methoxy group at the 6th position displayed lesser cytotoxicity (IC50 = 6 µM), thus highlighting the effect of substituent modification on cytotoxicity. The most active cytotoxic compound 106 (IC50 = 48.5 µM) displayed less cytotoxicity against WI38 healthy cells, indicating its high selectivity. Further, cervical cancer cells treated with both compounds resulted in nuclear condensation, nuclear shrinkage and loss of shape compared with the control, indicating the apoptotic cell death pathway when tested by DAPI staining110 (Fig. 28).Table 6Most potent benzimidazole hydrazone-based anticancer agentsCompoundActivityReference146Superior cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cells compared with cisplatin, with 3-fold less cytotoxicity against healthy NIH3T3 cells 100 147 and 148Superior cytotoxicity against A549 and MCF-7 cancer cells compared with cisplatin 101 149Superior activity against MCF-7 cancer cells compared with cisplatin 101 150Potent cytotoxicity against HT29, MCF-7, C6 cancer cells with less cytotoxicity towards healthy L929 102 151Superior cytotoxicity against A549 cancer cells compared with paclitaxel 103 152 and 153Potent cytotoxicity against HCT-116 and MCF-7, superior to that of sunitinib 104 154, 155, 157 and 158Potent cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cancer cells, superior to that of sunitinib 104 160Superior cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cancer cells compared with doxorubicin 105 161 and 162Potent cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cells, superior to that of 5-FU and carboplatin 107 169Potent cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cells, exceeding that of doxorubicin 108 172Potent cytotoxicity against A549 cells, exceeding that of 5-FU and gefitinib 109 Fig. 28Cytotoxic benzimidazole hydrazones 172–174.109,110With respect to substitution patterns, most of the compounds comprised electron-donating methoxy or electron-withdrawing halogens in their structure, which were responsible for the superior cytotoxicity of the molecule. In addition, compounds induced cell cycle arrest in the G0/G1 and G2/M phases, preventing DNA synthesis and replication and inducing apoptosis.8.Isatin hydrazide–hydrazone anticancer activitiesIsatin (1H-indole-2, 3-dione) is a natural, plant-derived organic molecule that is capable of exhibiting anticancer activity.111 Among the diverse biological applications exhibited by isatins, their anticancer activities have been studied extensively, with several isatin-based anticancer drugs, namely, toceranib, semaxanib and orantinib (Fig. 29) known to exhibit superior anticancer effects with semaxanib and orantinib still under clinical trials,112 which makes it important to develop anticancer drugs containing isatin groups, with isatin–hydrazones being a suitable choice moving forward.Fig. 29Isatin-based anticancer drugs.Ibrahim et al. synthesized bis-isatin hydrazones and evaluated their cytotoxicity against HCT-116, MCF-7 and HepG2 cancer cells.113 Compound 178, bearing a methoxy substituent, displayed potent anticancer activity against MCF-7 (IC50 = 1.84 ± 0.29 µM) and HCT-116 (IC50 = 3.31 ± 0.83 µM) cancer cells, superior to that of doxorubicin (IC50 = 2.57 ± 0.43, 3.70 ± 0.18 µM, respectively). Further, it displayed effective EGFR inhibitory activities (IC50 = 1.26 ± 0.07 µM); however, it was less effective than the reference inhibitor erlotinib (IC50 = 0.11 ± 0.03 µM). In addition, compound 184 (IC50 = 7.3 ± 0.52, and 6.7 ± 0.17 µM, respectively) displayed superior cytotoxicity to gefitinib. Seliem synthesized various isatin–thiazole hybrids and evaluated their cytotoxicity against breast cancer cells. The docking studies conducted on Bcl-2 antiapoptotic protein (PDB ID: 4LVT, 2XAO) suggested that compound 191 displayed the most effective binding with BE values of −7.8 kcal mol−1 and −10.7 kcal mol−1 in the two proteins, respectively, higher than navitoclax (−5.4 kcal mol−1 in 4LVT) and tamoxifen (−8.3 kcal mol−1 in 2XAO), forming H-bonding interactions through hydrazone nitrogen and coumarin oxygen atoms with LYS C:57 and SER C:60 residues, respectively, with the isatin group involved in various hydrophobic interactions, thus improving the binding affinity119 (Fig. 31).Fig. 31Cytotoxic isatin hydrazones 183–191.117–119Arif et al. evaluated the cytotoxicity of synthesized isatin–hydrazone derivatives against breast cancer cells and compound 192 (IC50 = 9.29 ± 0.97 µM), without any substitution at the benzene ring, displayed effective cytotoxicity.120 Apart from this, compound 193 (IC50 = 13.34 ± 2.53 µM) bearing an o-hydroxyl substituent displayed potent cytotoxicity, and the cytotoxicity increased in compound 194 (IC50 = 12.09 ± 4.08 µM) bearing a trihydroxy substituent, displaying the effect of an electron-donating hydroxyl substituent on cytotoxic activity. Quinoline hydrazones bearing electron-withdrawing halogens or nitro groups displayed superior anticancer activity compared with the standard employed.50–52,54,59,60,62A similar effect was observed for indole-based hydrazones where compounds bearing electron-withdrawing halogens displayed superior cytotoxicity.71,74,75,77,78,81,82,84 Although some of the compounds in triazole–hydrazone hybrids88,94,96,97 and benzimidazole–hydrazone hybrids101,106,107 containing electron-withdrawing substituents displayed superior anticancer activity, the majority of these derivatives consisted of electron-donating groups.Finally, isatin–hydrazone derivatives containing electron-withdrawing substituents displayed prominent cytotoxic activities.115,117,118 Overall, across various heterocyclic–hydrazone hybrids, electron-withdrawing halogens, primarily chloro and fluoro, displayed superior cytotoxicity, which could be a positive take when designing anticancer drugs.9.2.Effect of electron-donating substituentsMost of the quinoline hydrazones displaying significant cytotoxicity consisted of electron-withdrawing groups as discussed above. While a significant number of indole–hydrazone hybrids bearing electron-withdrawing halogens displayed superior cytotoxicity, the effects of electron-donating hydroxy, methoxy, methyl and amine groups were equally prominent, with superior anti-proliferative activity.68,70,72,76,80,82 Most of these derivatives consisted of methoxy substituents as the electron-donating group, and attached to the 4th position of the aromatic ring. With respect to substitution in the indole ring, the methoxy group occupied the 5th or 6th position. In addition, triazole–hydrazones consisted of hydroxy or methoxy groups as electron-donating substituents, primarily occupying the 3rd or 4th position of the benzene ring.89–92,95The electron-donating substituents primarily contributed to the anticancer activity with respect to benzimidazole-based hydrazones. These derivatives consisted of methoxy and hydroxy substituents linked to the aromatic rings and benzene ring of the benzimidazole moiety. The methoxy and hydroxy substituents were primarily found at the 3rd and 4th positions of the aromatic ring, and these substituents were present at the benzylidene which could be considered a positive approach when designing benzimidazole–hydrazone-based anticancer drugs.101,103–105,107,108,110In addition, substituting isatin-based hydrazones with electron-donating groups seems to increase the anticancer activities of the resulting compounds. Isatin hydrazones consisting of electron-donating methoxy and hydroxy substituents enhanced the anticancer activities of the resulting compounds.113,116,117,120–122 Similar to the observations of benzimidazole hydrazones, these electron-donating substituents occupied the 3rd and 4th positions of the benzene rings.9.3.Effect of heterocyclesQuinoline hydrazones have displayed superior cytotoxicity compared with nonquinoline hydrazones, owing to the importance of the quinoline ring.48 In addition, bis quinoline hydrazones displayed significantly higher cytotoxicity as reported in one of the studies.49 Furthermore, quinoline combined with various heterocycles such as oxazole,55 thiazole,56 indole,58 isatin60 and triazole62 has displayed superior cytotoxicity to the standard employed in the in vitro assays.Bis-indole moieties linked through hydrazone linkages were studied for indole-based hydrazones, where the derivatives displayed superior cytotoxicity.69,80,82,84 In addition, indole was linked to heterocycles, such as triazole and benzothiazole groups,83,85 and was used as a positive approach in designing anticancer drugs. Furthermore, triazole-based hydrazones linked to heterocycles such as furan, isatin, benzothiazole and indole88,89,93,95,97 displayed superior cytotoxicity. Benzimidazole groups linked to thiophene, thiazole and furan groups displayed significant anticancer activity in the in vitro assays.100,102,106,107 Furthermore, bis-isatin113 (104), and isatin groups linked to pyridine,114,116,120 thiazole,119 quinoline and quinazolines121 displayed enhanced cytotoxicities. Hence, combining two similar heterocycles or with heterocycles such as thiazole, furan and triazole groups has been used frequently among the different N-containing heterocycles that have been listed in this review, which could be considered a positive molecular design in the development of anticancer drugs.9.4.SelectivityAmong various N-heterocycles, most of the cytotoxic triazole-based hydrazones displayed cancer-specific activity.91,92 Furthermore, the triazole group combined with heterocycles, such as isatin,84,95 furan88 and imidazo[2,1-b]thiazole94 displayed significant cancer-specific cytotoxicity results. Furthermore, owing to the cancer-specific cytotoxicity of isatin derivatives, which are not limited to the above-mentioned isatin–triazole hybrids, isatin–indole84 and isatin hydrazone individually115 displayed significant selectivity. In addition, bis-quinoline hydrazone49 and benzimidazole hydrazone linked to thiophene102 and thiazole106 groups displayed cancer-specific cytotoxic results.Overall, quinoline-, indole- and isatin-based hydrazones with electron-withdrawing groups such as chloro and fluoro groups displayed superior anticancer activities, while benzimidazole hydrazones with electron-donating substituents such as hydroxy and alkoxy groups enhanced the antiproliferative activity. With respect to heterocycles, bis-indole hydrazones and isatin–pyridine hydrazone hybrids displayed excellent cytotoxicity. In addition, thiazole, a heterocycle, was combined with all the N-containing heterocyclic hydrazones reviewed, which resulted in a positive approach in enhancing the cytotoxicity. Furthermore, triazole- and isatin-based hydrazones have displayed significant cancer-specific activities, which can be useful in the designing of anticancer drugs. In addition to the heterocyclic scaffolds, the hydrazone linkage is involved in various binding interactions with essential amino acid residues in the target protein in different molecules, marking the importance of this molecular fragment in targeting receptor sites and enhancing the anticancer activities.10.In conclusion, in recent years, significant work evaluating the anticancer potential of N-heterocycle–hydrazone has been conducted, and these hybrid molecules have displayed promising anticancer activity. Hydrazones are combined as a bioactive scaffold with N-heterocycles because of their ease of synthesis, easy isolation due to crystallinity and structural flexibility. Overall, this review presents various synthetic strategies involved in the synthesis of hydrazones including conventional condensation, acid- and base-catalysed reactions, from azo compounds, microwave and ultrasonic irradiation techniques. The kinetic effects of solvents, catalysts, pressure and irradiation techniques have been briefly presented to understand their effects on the reaction rate and yield. Most importantly, a comprehensive explanation of the anticancer activities of various N-heterocyclic hydrazones including quinoline-, indole-, triazole-, benzimidazole-, and isatin–hydrazones has been presented in detail, along with the mechanism of action, cell-cycle arrest results, docking interactions and cell death pathway results to provide the readers with combined information on these aspects, which can help in understanding the current state of development and future drug designs.Among all the derivatives displaying potent in vitro antiproliferative activity, compound 82, a bis-indole hydrazone derivative, and compound 126, a triazole hydrazone linked to furan and naphthalene groups, comprising fluorine, methoxy and nitro groups, were the stand-out molecules because of their significant pre-clinical in vivo results. Compound 82 reduced 46% solid tumour mass in Ehrlich carcinoma (breast cancer)-bearing mice, comparable to 5-fluorouracil (58% growth inhibition). Compound 126, following its superior in vitro anticancer activity against prostate cancer cells (PC3 cells), displayed significant cancer-specificity by accumulating in the prostate of mice after 6 h when the fluorescence intensity of urogenital organs was studied.The structure–activity relationship analysis revealed the positive influence of electron-withdrawing halogens, primarily fluorine and chloro substituents and nitro groups, and electron-donating substituents, primarily methoxy and hydroxy groups, with this observation being consistent across all the hybrids. Further, enzyme inhibition studies marked a plausible mechanism of action. The docking studies conducted on various target proteins (EGFR, ERα, CDK, tubulin, VEGFR, etc.) displayed various binding interactions between heterocyclic and halogen fragments with various amino acid residues at the active site of the protein contributing to the stable binding interactions. Further, the most active compounds listed induced apoptosis with cell cycle arrest in the G0/G1 and G2/M phases, preventing DNA replication.Despite these advances, several challenges remain. First, detailed work covering drug design, bioavailability, toxicity profiles, in vitro efficacy studies, and enzyme inhibition studies to provide mechanistic insights, docking studies, simulations, QSAR models, cell-death pathways, cell cycle arrest and in vivo study results is still lacking in the literature. Further optimization should target success in clinical trials and commercialize the drug molecule to contribute to cancer treatment.Based on structure–activity relationship studies, linking two heterocyclic moieties into a single molecule using hydrazone linkage has resulted in positive results with respect to anticancer activity due to synergistic effects. Further, researchers can concentrate on trying different combinations of these heterocycles to obtain positive results. In addition, incorporating electron-withdrawing groups into quinoline-, indole- and isatin-based hydrazones and electron-donating groups into benzimidazole hydrazones resulted in significant enhancement in the anticancer activity of the resulting compounds. Most of the molecules contained chloro and fluoro substituents as EWGs, and hydroxy and methoxy substituents as EDGs. Hence, researchers can consider these structural arrangements in designing potent anticancer drugs with respect to N-heterocyclic hydrazones.Author contributionK Nagaraj Pai: conceptualization, writing-original draft, investigation. title: WDR72 Promotes Neuroblastoma Stemness and Progression by Sequestering TRIM31‐Mediated Degradation of CBX8
abstract: Cancer stem cells are pivotal in cancer progression, yet the mechanisms underlying the stemness properties of neuroblastoma cells remain largely unclear. By analyzing data from the TARGET‐NBL and GEO databases, WDR72 is identified as a cancer stem cell marker that significantly correlates with high‐risk of neuroblastoma and poor prognosis in neuroblastoma patients. It is found that knocking down WDR72 in neuroblastoma cells suppresses cell proliferation and migration, while inducing apoptosis. An increased expression of WDR72 is detected in neuroblastoma cells with enhanced stemness properties, while silencing WDR72 reduces the stemness of these cells. Mechanistically, we find that the upregulation of WDR72 is mediated by m6A modifications in its 3’ UTR induced by the METTL14‐IGF2BP1 axis. Further investigation into the downstream regulatory mechanisms of WDR72 demonstrates that WDR72 interacts with TRIM31, blocking the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of the CBX8 protein. This interaction stabilizes CBX8, contributing to the maintenance of neuroblastoma cell stemness. This study reveals that the upregulation of WDR72 via the METTL14‐IGF2BP1 axis enhances the stemness properties of neuroblastoma cells by stabilizing CBX8 through interaction with TRIM31. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms driving neuroblastoma malignancy and offer potential therapeutic targets for patients with neuroblastoma.
full_text: 1IntroductionNeuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children and a leading cause of cancer‐related mortality in pediatric patients [1]. This malignancy arises from neural crest cells, and develops into a heterogenous pediatric tumor of the sympathetic nervous system [2]. Neuroblastoma primarily affects infants and young children, displaying a wide spectrum of clinical behaviors, ranging from spontaneous regression to aggressive metastatic disease. Prognosis is highly variable in neuroblastoma, with high‐risk patients associated with poorer outcomes compared to the low/intermediate‐risk ones [3].The heterogeneous nature of neuroblastoma has made it a major focus of research, particularly regarding cancer stem cells (CSCs) or tumor‐initiating cells. CSCs share properties with normal stem cells, including the ability to self‐renew and differentiate into multiple tumor cell types. These cells are considered key drivers of tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and resistance to conventional therapies [4]. In neuroblastoma, the presence of CSCs complicates treatment, as they can survive chemotherapy and contribute to tumor relapse and metastasis. Understanding the characteristics and behavior of CSCs in neuroblastoma is crucial for developing targeted therapies that effectively eradicate these cells and improve patient outcomes.Research efforts increasingly focus on identifying specific markers and signaling pathways associated with CSCs in neuroblastoma. These markers provide insights into the mechanisms underlying CSC maintenance and offer potential therapeutic targets [5, 6]. Emerging strategies include the use of small molecules, monoclonal antibodies, and gene therapies to selectively eliminate or inhibit CSCs. Targeting these cells aims to develop more effective and less toxic treatments for neuroblastoma patients.One promising research area involves WD repeat domain 72 (WDR72), a member of the WD40‐repeat domain superfamily [7]. Proteins in this family are implicated in various cellular processes, including cell cycle regulation, signal transduction, and transcription. While WDR72 has primarily been associated with amelogenesis imperfecta, a genetic disorder affecting tooth enamel development [8, 9], recent findings suggest an oncogenic role in lung cancer, where it promotes stemness and tumor progression [10, 11]. Besides, a report also revealed WDR72 as a CSC‐related gene in gastric cancer [12]. However, the role of WDR72 in neuroblastoma remains largely unexplored.In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of WDR72 in neuroblastoma by analyzing data from the TARGET‐N BL and GEO databases. Our preliminary analysis identified WDR72 as a potential marker for CSCs in neuroblastoma, with its expression correlating with high‐risk neuroblastoma and poor prognosis. This suggests that WDR72 may play a significant role in the malignant progression of neuroblastoma, potentially through its influence on CSC properties. To our knowledge, the specific role of WDR72 in neuroblastoma has not been previously reported.The primary objective of this study is to elucidate the function of WDR72 in regulating CSC‐induced malignant progression in neuroblastoma cells. We hypothesize that WDR72 contributes to the maintenance and proliferation of CSCs, thereby promoting tumor aggressiveness and treatment resistance. Additionally, we aim to explore the upstream and downstream regulatory mechanisms associated with WDR72, including its potential interactions with other proteins and signaling pathways involved in neuroblastoma pathogenesis. By gaining a deeper understanding of WDR72's involvement in neuroblastoma, we hope to contribute to the understanding of neuroblastoma pathogenesis and identify novel therapeutic targets for this aggressive pediatric malignancy. Our findings could pave the way for the development of targeted therapies that specifically address the CSC population in neuroblastoma, ultimately improving treatment outcomes and survival rates for affected children.2Methods2.1Clinical SamplesTissue samples from 17 cases of metastatic neuroblastoma and 9 cases of non‐metastatic neuroblastoma were collected by Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center. These samples were used to analyze the expression of focused genes via qPCR and western blot. The clinical, prognostic, and pathological information of the patients was included. The sponsors fully understood and agreed to the research. The procedures of this study were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center (No.[2023]064B00) and conducted in accordance with the Code of Ethics of the World Medical Association. The experimental methods comply with the Helsinki Declaration.2.2Tissue MicroarrayThe tissue microarray analyses were accomplished by bioaitech company, with the microarray numbered N264001. The microarray included 22 cases of neuroblastoma tissue and 4 cases of normal adrenal tissue from healthy donors, and 8 of 22 neuroblastoma cases were with lymph node metastasis or distant metastasis.2.3Bioinformatics AnalysesTARGET‐NBL database was applied to obtained genes with high risk or poor prognosis of neuroblastoma patients. GSE90789 was used to analyze differential genes in spheres of tumors from relapsed and newly‐diagnosed neuroblastoma patients. Since CSCs are able to isolated as tumor sphere, we set those genes upregulated in relapsed spheres as CSCs markers. Genes related to high risk of neuroblastoma patients was selected via Log2FC>1.5 and adjP 0.3, P 0.1. CSCs markers were screened via log2FC>1.5. The genes associated with high risk or poor prognosis of neuroblastoma patients obtained from TARGET‐NBL, and CSCs markers acquired from GSE90789, were all listed in Supplementary table 1.2.4AnimalsAll experiments were performed in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and authorized by Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center (No. G20230376). Six to eight‐week‐old NOD/SCID/IL‐2Ry‐null (NSG) mice were purchased from Guangdong Medical Laboratory Animal Center and maintained under specific pathogen‐free conditions. Specifically, the air humidity was maintained between 40% and 70%. The temperature was controlled at approximately 22°C, with a permissible fluctuation of ±2°C. Additionally, we employed a light/dark cycle of 12 h each. Regarding their diet, the mice were provided with standard sterile food and water ad libitum. Subcutaneous xenograft models were established by injecting 2×106/100 µl SK‐N‐SH cells in PBS into the left axilla of each mouse (n = 5 each group). The tumors were recorded every three days from Day 7 to Day 28, and the tissues were acquired and weighted after mice sacrifice. The in vivo metastasis model was set by injecting 2×107 IMR‐32 cells transfected with shNC or shWDR72 into the NSG mice (n = 4 each group) via the tail vein. Four weeks later, mice were sacrificed and the lungs were obtained to analyze the metastatic nodules. The orthotopic neuroblastoma animal model was established based on previous experimental methods [13]. Five‐week‐old female SCID mice were used for this model. Different treated IMR‐32 cells were resuspended in HEPES buffer to a concentration of 1.25 × 107 cells mL−1. A total of 20 µl of the cell suspension was injected into the adrenal gland of the left kidney of each mouse (n = 4 each group). The mice were monitored twice weekly for their health status after the injection. Tissue samples were collected in the third week of modeling for subsequent experiments. This study was conducted with ethical approval and review.2.5Cell Culture and TreatmentTwo neuroblastoma cell lines (SK‐N‐SH and IMR‐32) and 293T cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA). Routine short tandem repeat (STR) testing was performed to confirm the authenticity of the cell lines and exclude contamination. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) and maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. Cells were treated with 20 µM MG132 for 4 h, 50 µg mL−1 cycloheximide (CHX) for 0, 6, and 12 h, and 100 nM bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) for 1 h.2.6TransfectionsShort hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting WDR72 (sh‐WDR72#1 and sh‐WDR72#2) and METTL14 (sh‐METTL14#1 and sh‐METTL14#2) were synthesized by GenePharma (Jiangsu, China). The full sequences of WDR72, METTL14, and TRIM31 were synthesized and cloned into pcDNA 3.1 vectors to generate corresponding overexpression constructs. For transient transfections, siRNAs or plasmids were mixed with Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) in OptiMEM (Gibco) to form complexes, and then transfected into cells for 48 h. Cells were subsequently harvested for further experiments.2.7Quantitative Reverse Transcription Real‐Time PCR (RT‐qPCR)Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol (TransGen Biotech, China) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis was performed using M‐MLV reverse transcriptase (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). RT‐qPCR was conducted with SYBR Green master mix (Vazyme) on an ABI Prism 7500 Sequence Detector (Applied Biosystems, USA). mRNA levels were normalized to the internal control gene GAPDH, and relative mRNA expression levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method [14].2.8Cell Counting Kit‐8 (CCK‐8) AssayFor the CCK‐8 assay, cells were seeded in a 96‐well plate at a density of 2 × 103 cells per well and incubated for 24 h. CCK‐8 solution (10 µL; Beyotime, China) was added to each well at 24, 48, and 96 h, followed by incubation for 2 h at 37°C. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader.2.9Colony Formation AssayCells were seeded in 6‐well plates at a density of 500 cells per well to assess proliferation. After 14 days, colonies were washed with phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS), fixed with 70% ethanol, and stained with 0.5% crystal violet. Colonies were counted and recorded.2.10Transwell AssayCells transfected with the indicated plasmids were starved in serum‐free medium. A cell suspension of 0.2 mL DMEM was added to the upper chamber of a Transwell insert (8‐µm pore size, Corning, New York, USA) pre‐coated with 50 µl Matrigel (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) for the invasion assay, or uncoated for the migration assay. DMEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) was added to the lower chamber. After 48 h of incubation, non‐migrated cells were removed from the upper chamber using a cotton swab. Cells that had migrated or invaded to the lower side of the upper chamber were fixed with methanol, stained with 2% crystal violet for 10 min, and counted in five random fields under a microscope.2.11Flow Cytometry AssayCells were treated as indicated, incubated for 48 h, and harvested for flow cytometry. Apoptosis was assessed using an Annexin V‐FITC/PI apoptosis detection kit (Multi Sciences, Hangzhou, China) following the manufacturer's protocol, and analyzed with a flow cytometer (BD Biosciences).2.12Sphere Formation AssayHarvested cells were resuspended as single cells in serum‐free medium and seeded into 96‐well plates at a density of 200 cells per well, with each well containing 200 µl of serum‐free medium. Medium was changed every 2 days. Sphere formation was observed and recorded using an optical microscope (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany).2.13Western BlotCells were lysed using RIPA buffer (CWBio, Beijing, China) containing protease inhibitors. Lysates were mixed with loading buffer and denatured at 100°C for 10 min. Proteins were separated by 10% SDS‐PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA). Membranes were blocked and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies: anti‐WDR72, anti‐ALDH1, anti‐Nanog, anti‐CBX8, anti‐TRIM31 (all 1:1000, Abcam, USA), and anti‐GAPDH (1:1000, Abcam). Secondary antibody incubation followed (1:2000, Abcam), and bands were visualized using ECL substrate (Millipore).2.14RIP AssayRIP assay was performed using Protein A/G Agarose Resin (YEASEN, China). Cell lysates were extracted with NP‐40 lysis buffer (Beyotime, China), and 100 µL lysate was incubated with NP‐40 buffer containing Protein A/G beads conjugated to anti‐m6A, anti‐METTL3, anti‐METTL14, or anti‐METTL16 antibodies at 4°C overnight. Protein‐RNA complexes were isolated, digested with protease K (YEASEN), and RNA was extracted for RT‐qPCR to identify the enrichment of WDR72 3'UTR.2.15Coimmunoprecipitation (Co‐IP) Assay and Mass SpectrometryCell lysates were incubated with primary antibodies (anti‐WDR72, anti‐TRIM31, and anti‐CBX8) or rabbit IgG (negative control) at 4°C overnight. Protein A/G agarose (20 µl; Bioworld Technology, St. Louis Park, MN, USA) was added and incubated at 4°C for 2 h. After washing, Protein‐antibody complexes were collected by centrifugation and subjected to Western blot or mass spectrometry analysis as previously described [15]. The data reported in this paper have been deposited in the OMIX, China National Center for Bioinformation / Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/omix: accession numbers OMIX010833, OMIX010974) [16, 17].2.16Immunofluorescence AssayCells were processed, fixed, and incubated with specific primary antibodies including anti‐CBX8 (PA5‐ , 1 µg mL−1, Invitrogen), anti‐TRIM31 ( ‐1‐AP, 1:200 dilution, Proteintech), anti‐Ub‐K48 (ab140601, 1:500 dilution, Abcam), anti‐Ub‐K63 (14‐6077‐82, 1:300 dilution, Invitrogen), anti‐WDR72 (ab222307, 4 µg mL−1, Abcam), followed by washing and incubation with fluorescent‐labeled secondary antibodies. Samples were washed, stained, and observed under a fluorescence microscope.2.17Immunohistochemistry (IHC)The metastatic and non‐metastatic neuroblastoma tissues subjected to fixation via 4% paraformaldehyde were cut into slices of 4 µm‐thickness. Following being dewaxed by xylene and hydrated by gradient ethanol, the tissue slides were boiled for 20 min and cooled down. After that, the slides were treated with primary antibodies including anti‐TRIM31 ( ‐1‐AP, 1:200 dilution, Proteintech) and anti‐CBX8 (PA5‐ , 1:50 dilution, Invitrogen) for 1 h at room temperature, followed by incubation with HRP‐coupled secondary antibody at room temperature for another 1 h. The staining of TRIM31 or CBX8 was visualized via 3,3‐N‐diaminobenzidine (DAB), and hematoxylin was used to counterstain the nuclei. Following dehydrated, cleared, and sealed, the samples were observed under an inverted microscope. The percentage of stained area in total area were calculated as staining positivity.2.18M6A Dot Blot AssayThe m6A dot blot assay was conducted as previously described [18]. In brief, after being dissolved in 3 times volume of RNA incubation buffer and denatured, RNA samples were divided into subgroups of 400, 200, and 100 ng, and then mixed with ice‐cold 20*SSC buffer (Sigma–Aldrich, Germany). After that, the samples in different subgroups were all loaded to an Amersham Hybond‐N+ membrane (GE Healthcare, USA) installed in a Bio‐Dot Apparatus (Bio‐Rad, USA). Then, the membrane was UV crosslinked, washed, stained with 0.02% Methylene blue (Sangon Biotech, China), scanned, and blocked with BSA, followed by incubation with specific m6A antibody ( ‐1‐Ig, 1:2000 dilution, Proteintech) overnight at 4°C. After further incubation with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibody for 1 h at room temperature, the dot blots were visualized via an imaging system (Bio‐Rad, USA). The integrated density of each dot was counted by ImageJ, and relative m6A level was calculated as the ratio of integrated density of experimental dots to that of control dots.2.19Ubiquitination AssayTo detect polyubiquitinated CBX8, whole cell lysates were prepared with RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitors. Lysates were subjected to immunoprecipitation of endogenous CBX8, and ubiquitination levels were analyzed by Western blot using an anti‐Ub antibody.2.20GST Pull DownTo validate protein binding in vitro, TRIM31 was tagged with a His tag and CBX8 was tagged with a GST tag, and both were expressed in engineered 293T cells. After lysing the cells, the supernatant was collected by centrifugation, and the purified GST fusion protein (bait protein) was obtained using glutathione agarose beads. The bait protein‐GSH magnetic bead complex was then incubated with the lysate of His‐TRIM31‐overexpressing cells for 3–4 h. Subsequently, the bait‐captured protein complex was eluted, and the eluted products were analyzed by Western blot. The experiment was conducted using the GST pull‐down kit (Agarose) (Elabscience, Wuhan, China, EA‐IP‐K008), following the protocol provided in the kit instructions.2.21Dual‐luciferase Reporter AssayAfter constructing the 3’ UTR region of WDR72 into the psicheck2 vector, the psicheck2‐WDR72 vector was co‐transfected with METTL14 or IGF2BP1 vectors into adherent cells using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen). After 48 h of transfection, relative luciferase activity was measured using a dual‐luciferase reporter assay system (Meilunbio, Dalian, China).2.22Statistical AnalysisExperiments were conducted in triplicate, and results are presented as means ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 22.0 software (IBM, USA). Student's t‐test was used to compare two groups, while one‐way ANOVA or Two‐way repeated measures ANOVA was used for multiple groups. A p‐value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. We declared that no other scripts and software were used other than those mentioned in the methods section.3Results3.1WDR72 Expression Correlates with Neuroblastoma MalignancyTo search factors significant in neuroblastoma, we began our study by analyzing data from the TARGET‐NBL and GSE90789 databases. Such analyses highlighted four potential CSC markers (including KIRREL2, NCAN, EPPK1 and WDR72) which were simultaneously associated with high‐risk and poor prognosis in neuroblastoma patients (Figure 1A). The survival curve of neuroblastoma patients with high or low expressions of above four factors were shown in Additional file 1: Figure S1. Next, we collected tissue samples from 9 non‐metastatic and 17 metastatic neuroblastoma cases. Our analysis revealed that only WDR72 among above four genes showed a significant upregulation in metastatic tissues compared to non‐metastatic samples (Figure 1B). This observation was further supported by Western blot analysis, which demonstrated elevated WDR72 expression in randomly selected metastatic tissues (6 non‐metastatic and 6 metastatic cases) (Figure 1C). Additionally, tissue microarray analysis confirmed the marked upregulation of WDR72 in metastatic neuroblastoma tissues (Figure 1D). To further elucidate the role of WDR72 in metastatic neuroblastoma, we evaluated the expression levels of stem cell markers ALDH1 and Nanog in these samples (Figure 1E). Likewise, the enhancement of WDR72 overexpression on neuroblastoma cell proliferation and sphere formation was abrogated after CBX8 knockdown (Additional file 1: Figure S6E,F). These data demonstrated that CBX8 acts as a critical downstream effector of WDR72 in maintaining CSC properties. This functional rescue provides strong evidence supporting the mechanistic link between WDR72 and CBX8, confirming their combined role in promoting neuroblastoma cell stemness.Together, these findings elucidate a novel regulatory mechanism in which WDR72 stabilizes CBX8 protein through de‐ubiquitination, thereby enhancing neuroblastoma cell stemness.3.6WDR72 Inhibits TRIM31‐Mediated Ubiquitination of CBX8 to Enhance Its StabilityOur previous findings suggested that WDR72 mediates the de‐ubiquitination of CBX8, enhancing its stability. To explore the underlying mechanism, we first performed an IP assay to determine whether WDR72 directly regulates CBX8. However, no direct interaction was observed between the two proteins (Additional file 1: Figure S7A).Next, we identified potential CBX8 interactors through IP and mass spectrometry analysis (Figure 6A). Among the candidates, TRIM31, a newly identified E3 ubiquitin ligase of the TRIM family involved in autophagy, inflammation, antiviral immunity, and cancer, caught our attention. We confirmed the interaction between TRIM31 and CBX8 using Co‐IP and Western blot analyses (Figure 6B), suggesting TRIM31's potential regulatory role. Functional assays revealed that TRIM31 interference enhanced proliferation, sphere‐forming ability, and CBX8 activity in neuroblastoma cells (Additional file 1: Figure S7B–D), indicating its negative regulatory role on CBX8.FIGURE 6WDR72 Inhibits TRIM31‐Mediated Ubiquitination of CBX8 to Enhance Its Stability. (A) TRIM31 protein was screened using IP‐MS analysis. (B) Co‐IP was performed to detect the interaction between CBX8 and TRIM31. (C) Western blot analysis was conducted to investigate the regulatory effect of TRIM31 overexpression on CBX8 expression. (D) Analysis of CBX8 degradation after TRIM31 overexpression in the presence of CHX to inhibit protein synthesis. (E) GST pull down assay to determine if CBX8 is a substrate of TRIM31. (F) Co‐IP experiment to analyze the ubiquitination level of CBX8 and the effect of TRIM31 overexpression on CBX8 ubiquitination. (G) Co‐IP experiment to examine the impact of WDR72 overexpression on the interaction between TRIM31 and CBX8. (H) IF co‐localization experiment to analyze the effect of WDR72 overexpression on the binding of TRIM31 and CBX8. (I) In vitro ubiquitination assay to determine the impact of TRIM31 and WDR72 on CBX8 ubiquitination. Two‐way repeated measures ANOVA was used to analyze data of D. ** p<0.01.To further elucidate the mechanism, we overexpressed TRIM31 in neuroblastoma cells and observed a reduction in CBX8 protein levels (Figure 6C). Western blot analysis showed that TRIM31 overexpression shortened the half‐life of CBX8 (Figure 6D). GST pull down assays confirmed that CBX8 is a substrate of TRIM31 (Figure 6E), and TRIM31 overexpression significantly increased CBX8 ubiquitination both exogenously and endogenously (Figure 6F and Additional file 1: Figure S8A), demonstrating TRIM31's role in promoting CBX8 ubiquitination.Given the opposing roles of WDR72 and TRIM31 in CBX8 ubiquitination, we investigated their potential interaction. While WDR72 overexpression did not alter TRIM31 levels (Additional file 1: Figure S8B), Co‐IP assays confirmed interactions between WDR72 or CBX8 and TRIM31 (Additional file 1: Figure S8C). WDR72 overexpression disrupted the TRIM31‐CBX8 interaction in adherent cells (Figure 6G and Additional file 1: Figure S8D), whereas WDR72 interference enhanced this interaction in spheroids (Additional file 1: Figure S8E). Immunofluorescence assays further validated the WDR72‐TRIM31 interaction and its impact on TRIM31‐CBX8 binding (Figure 6H and Additional file 1: Figure S8F). Ubiquitination assays demonstrated that WDR72 effectively reduces TRIM31‐induced CBX8 ubiquitination (Figure 6I).Notably, we observed lower TRIM31 expression in metastatic neuroblastoma tissues (Additional file 1: Figure S9A–C). Meanwhile, we also detected the staining of CBX8 in the same tissues used in Figure S9C, and the data showed that CBX8 staining was elevated in metastatic neuroblastoma tissues compared to non‐metastatic controls (Additional file 1: Figure S9D). More importantly, the staining of CBX8 in these samples was negatively correlated with that of TRIM31 (Additional file 1: Figure S9E), further supporting that CBX8 was inhibited by TRIM31‐mediated ubiquitination. In summary, our findings indicate that WDR72 impedes the TRIM31‐CBX8 interaction, thereby stabilizing CBX8 protein.3.7WDR72 Stabilizes and Activates CBX8 by Inducing K63‐linked Ubiquitination and Repressing K48‐linked Ubiquitination Through Interaction With TRIM31The type of polyubiquitination chain plays a crucial role in determining the fate of proteins [22]. After confirming that TRIM31 mediates CBX8 ubiquitination, we sought to identify the specific type of ubiquitination involved. Using Co‐IP and Western blot analyses, we found TRIM31 overexpression significantly reduced K63‐linked ubiquitination while increasing K48‐linked ubiquitination of CBX8 (Figure 7A). Conversely, TRIM31 interference decreased K48‐linked ubiquitination of CBX8 (Figure 7B). Importantly, these effects were abolished when both K48 and K63 ubiquitin chains were mutated (Figure 7C). Furthermore, the TRIM31 C36A mutant, which lacks E3 ligase activity, failed to inhibit K63‐linked ubiquitination and also enhanced K48‐linked ubiquitination of CBX8 (Figure 7D,E), indicating that TRIM31's E3 ligase activity is essential for modulating these ubiquitination patterns.FIGURE 7WDR72 Stabilizes and Activates CBX8 by Inducing K63‐linked Ubiquitination and Repressing K48‐Linked Ubiquitination through Interaction with TRIM31. (A) Construction of ubiquitin chain‐tagged vectors for Co‐IP experiment to elucidate the specific ubiquitin chain mediated by TRIM31 on CBX8. (B) Co‐IP experiment to analyze the impact of TRIM31 knockdown on the ubiquitination level of the CBX8 K48 chain. (C) Co‐IP experiment after mutating K63 and K48 to analyze the role of TRIM31. (D,E) Analysis of the changes in the roles of TRIM31‐mediated K63 and K48 ubiquitination after mutating the E3 ubiquitin ligase active site of TRIM31 (C36A). (F) Schematic representation of TRIM31's domain constructs. (G) Co‐IP experiment to analyze the binding region between TRIM31 and CBX8. (H) Schematic representation of CBX8's domain constructs. (I) Co‐IP experiment to analyze the binding region between CBX8 and TRIM31. ** p<0.01.Immunofluorescence co‐localization assays revealed that WDR72 overexpression in adherent cells or knockdown in spheroid cells altered the levels of K48‐ and K63‐linked ubiquitination of CBX8. Specifically, WDR72 overexpression increased K63‐linked ubiquitination while decreasing K48‐linked ubiquitination (Additional file 1: Figure S10A), whereas, WDR72 knockdown had the opposite effect (Additional file 1: Figure S10B). These findings strongly suggest that TRIM31 promotes K48‐linked ubiquitination of CBX8 via its E3 ligase activity, a process regulated by WDR72.TRIM31 comprises three functional domains: a RING‐finger domain (amino acids 16–57), a B‐box domain (amino acids 90–129), and a C‐C domain (amino acids 126–307) [23]. To identify the domain responsible of TRIM31's interaction with CBX8, we generated truncation mutants of TRIM31 (Figure 7F). Co‐IP experiments showed that TRIM31‐WT, TRIM31‐∆R, TRIM31‐∆N, and TRIM31‐∆C mutants retained their ability to interact with CBX8, while the Flag‐TRIM31‐∆C‐C mutant and the control (beads alone) did not (Figure 7G). Western blot, clone formation and sphere formation assays, demonstrated that the deletion of the CC domain (∆C‐C) or the disruption of the RING domain (either ∆R deletion or C36A mutation) in TRIM31 abolished its ability to suppress CBX8 activity (Additional file 1: Figure S11A–C).To further delineate the interaction domains within CBX8, we divided CBX8 into five segments based on its structural domains and constructed tagged vectors (Figure 7H): Myc‐CBX8‐1 (amino acids 1–60), Myc‐CBX8‐2 (amino acids 61–300), Myc‐CBX8‐3 (amino acids 131–240), Myc‐CBX8‐4 (amino acids 241–300), and Myc‐CBX8‐5 (amino acids 301–389). Co‐IP assays revealed that TRIM31 specifically interacts with the Myc‐CBX8‐4 segment (amino acids 241–300) (Figure 7I).In summary, our results demonstrate that WDR72 stabilizes and activates CBX8 by promoting K63‐linked ubiquitination and suppressing K48‐linked ubiquitination through its interaction with TRIM31. This regulatory mechanism is mediated by specific domains within TRIM31 and CBX8, highlighting the intricate interplay between these proteins in modulating CBX8 stability and activity.3.8K48 And K63 Ubiquitin Chains Target K227 and K295 Sites of CBX8 Respectively, and Cooperatively Regulate Its UbiquitinationTo precisely map the ubiquitination sites associated with K48‐ and K63‐linked polyubiquitin chains on CBX8, we conducted bioinformatics analysis, which identified four potential ubiquitination sites (Figure 8A). Using site‐directed mutagenesis, we generated mutant CBX8 constructs and performed immunoprecipitation assays. Our results revealed that the K227R mutation specifically impaired K48‐linked ubiquitination, while the K295R mutation disrupted K63‐linked ubiquitination of CBX8 (Figure 8B).FIGURE 8K48 and K63 ubiquitin chains target K227 and K295 sites of CBX8 respectively, and cooperatively regulate its ubiquitination. (A) Bioinformatics website screening for ubiquitination sites of CBX8. (B) Co‐IP experiment to screen for ubiquitination sites. (C) Immunofluorescence analysis of ubiquitin chains on CBX8 in adherent cells and cell spheroids after treatment with MG132.To further characterize the ubiquitination patterns of CBX8 under different cellular conditions, we treated cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 and analyzed ubiquitin chain modifications in both adherent and sphere‐forming cells. Notably, K48‐linked ubiquitination was predominantly observed in adherent cells, whereas K63‐linked ubiquitination was significantly enriched in sphere‐forming cells (Figure 8C).In functional assays, including colony formation and sphere formation, we found that overexpression of TRIM31 inhibited the promoting effects of CBX8 on the colony formation and sphere formation capabilities of neuroblastoma cells. Additionally, transfection with either the CBX8‐K295R mutant or the CBX8‐K227R mutant weakened the degradation effect of TRIM31 on CBX8, with the CBX8‐K227R mutant exhibiting a stronger inhibitory effect. Importantly, simultaneous mutations at both sites (K227R + K295R) made it resistant to TRIM31‐mediated degradation, restoring CBX8 function (Additional file 1: Figure S11D,E).4DiscussionCancer stem cells (CSCs) are key drivers of tumor progression, recurrence, and therapeutic resistance, playing a central role in tumor malignancy [24, 25]. In this study, we identified WDR72 as a CSC marker associated with high‐risk neuroblastoma and poor prognosis through integrated analysis of the TARGET‐NBL and GEO databases. Importantly, our work is the first to systematically elucidate the functional roles and regulatory mechanisms of WDR72 in neuroblastoma stemness and progression, providing novel insights into its contribution to neuroblastoma pathology.Previous studies have implicated WDR72 in various cancer types. For instance, WDR72 has been proposed as a biomarker for predicting recurrence in bladder cancer [26], aiding in the diagnosis of esophageal cancer [27], and functioning as a tumor suppressor linked to prognosis in renal cell carcinoma [28]. Our findings expand on these observations by demonstrating that WDR72 silencing significantly suppresses neuroblastoma cell viability and proliferation while markedly increasing apoptosis. Furthermore, WDR72 knockdown impaired the migratory and invasive capabilities of neuroblastoma cells, establishing a strong positive correlation between WDR72 expression and neuroblastoma cell malignancy.A pivotal aspect of our study is the exploration of WDR72's role in regulation neuroblastoma cell stemness. We observed that WDR72 expression is significantly upregulated in neuroblastoma cell spheroids compared to adherent cells, a finding consistent with the enhanced stemness potential of spheroids. Functional assays revealed that WDR72 overexpression increases the expression of stemness markers such as ALDH1 and Nanog, while also promoting the sphere‐forming capacity of both adherent cells and spheroids. These results collectively demonstrate that WDR72 is a critical enhancer of neuroblastoma cell stemness, which has been previously suggested in lung cancer as well [10]. Also, the finding is consistent with previous report that proposed WDR72 as CSC‐related genes in gastric cancer [12].To unravel the mechanism underlying WDR72 upregulation in neuroblastoma cell spheroids, we employed bioinformatics analysis and identified multiple m6A modification sites in the WDR72 3’UTR. m6A modification is a well‐characterized post‐transcriptional regulatory mechanism that influences mRNA stability and translation, thereby impacting tumor progression. For example, METTL3‐mediated m6A modification of HDGF mRNA facilitates gastric cancer progression [29], while IGF2BP2‐dependent m6A modification of HMGA1 drives colorectal cancer proliferation and metastasis [30]. Our m6A‐RIP assays confirmed m6A modification of WDR72, with higher m6A enrichment observed in the WDR72 3’UTR of neuroblastoma cell spheroids. Among the m6A writers (METTL3, METTL14, and METTL16) and the readers (IGF2BP1, IGF2BP2, and IGF2BP3) [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36], we found that METTL14 and IGF2BP1 were significantly upregulated in neuroblastoma cell spheroids and could directly bind to the WDR72 3’UTR. These findings reveal for the first time that the METTL14‐IGF2BP1 axis mediates m6A modifications that drive the upregulation of WDR72 in neuroblastoma cell spheroids.Beyond m6A regulation, we investigated the downstream target of WDR72 and their roles in neuroblastoma cell stemness. Proteins often exert their oncogenic effects by modulating downstream target [37, 38, 39]. Through proteomic analysis, we identified CBX8 as a key effector of WDR72 in neuroblastoma. Mechanistic studies revealed that WDR72 stabilizes CBX8 protein by reducing its ubiquitination levels. CBX8 has been implicated as potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for several common cancers including hepatocellular carcinoma, kidney renal clear cell carcinoma, and ovarian cancer [40]. Also, it has been proved as a tumor promoter in colon cancer [41, 42], and laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma [43], and lung cancer [44]. More importantly, CBX8 is suggested to be highly associated with cancer stemness as well [19]. However, our study is the first to link CBX8 to neuroblastoma stemness. Since WDR72 does not directly interact with CBX8, we further identified TRIM31, an E3 ubiquitin ligase [23], as a CBX8‐interacting partner. Our results demonstrate that TRIM31 promotes CBX8 ubiquitination, while WDR72 inhibits the TRIM31‐CBX8 interaction, thereby stabilizing CBX8 protein. This discovery underscores the role of WDR72 in modulating CBX8 stability through a TRIM31‐dependent mechanism.Our study demonstrates that WDR72 promotes neuroblastoma stemness and progression through a multi‐layered regulatory mechanism. First, WDR72 is upregulated through m6A modifications mediated by the METTL14‐IGF2BP1 axis, thereby enhancing the specific stability of its mRNA in neuroblastoma cell spheroids. Second, WDR72 stabilizes CBX8 by disrupting its interaction with the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM31, thereby inhibiting TRIM31‐mediated ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. These findings elucidate a previously unrecognized molecular axis driving neuroblastoma malignancy and highlight WDR72 as a potential therapeutic target for future interventions in neuroblastoma treatment.Author Contributions Yan Zou, Huijuan Zeng and Tianyou Yang designed the experiments. Jiliang Yang, Jiahao Li, and Zhang Zhao performed IHC and some animal experiment. Tianzhu Long and Liyu Zhang supervised the analysis. Chao Hu drafted the initial manuscript. Gautam Sethi, Tianyou Yang and Yan Zou revised the manuscript. All authors have read and approved the final manuscript.Ethics StatementThe procedures of this study were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center (No.[2023]064B00) and conducted in accordance with the Code of Ethics of the World Medical Association. The experimental methods comply with the Helsinki Declaration.
