title: Targeting DOT1L Reactivates HERV-K to Drive Cell-Autonomous and Paracrine Senescence in Adenocarcinoma of the Esophagogastric Junction
abstract: Pharmacological DOT1L inhibition not only reactivates HERV-K to trigger autonomous senescence through a STING-mediated immune response but also promotes formation of HERV-K–derived retrovirus-like particles that propagate senescence, suppressing gastrointestinal cancer progression.
full_text: Adenocarcinoma of the esophagogastric junction (AEG), defined as tumors occurring within a 5-cm range proximal and distal to the esophagogastric junction (1–3), represents a significant global health burden. Despite declining rates of certain gastric cancers over recent decades, AEG exhibits persistently high incidence and mortality, ranking among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide (4–7). A substantial number of new AEG cases are diagnosed annually (4, 8, 9). This therapeutic challenge highlights the need to identify novel mechanistic targets for AEG.Human endogenous retroviruses (HERV) make up about 8% of the human genome, dispersed across around 700,000 components (10, 11). Due to the threat posed by retroviral gene expression to genome integrity and somatic homeostasis, the activity of endogenous retroviruses is strictly regulated by a series of epigenetic modifications (12). Epigenetic therapies reactivating HERVs offer promising immunomodulatory strategies. Inhibitors targeting DNA methylation can induce HERV-derived nucleic acids, triggering viral mimicry immune responses (13, 14). Recent studies suggest that HERV activation may promote cellular senescence through specific signaling pathways. Certain HERV, HERV-K, inhibits cellular stemness (15) and propagates senescence phenotypes (16). However, the epigenetic regulators controlling HERVs in AEG remain unidentified.Disruptor of telomeric silencing 1–like (DOT1L), also denoted as KMT4, is the sole methyltransferase in mammals capable of catalyzing the mono-, di-, and trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 79 (H3K79; ref. 17). Aberrant overexpression of DOT1L has been identified in numerous human malignancies, and dysregulation of H3K79 methylation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of acute myeloid leukemia and several solid tumors (18–23). DOT1L governs core stem cell genes that are essential for cancer stem cell self-renewal, tumorigenesis, and multidrug resistance (24). Recent investigations have positioned DOT1L as an attractive therapeutic target in cancer research (25–29). DOT1L regulates gene expression in an environment-dependent manner via H3K79 methylation (H3K79me2/3), and it can both activate (30) and repress transcription (31). However, the efficacy and underlying mechanisms of targeting DOT1L in AEG remain unelucidated.Here, our findings establish DOT1L as a novel epigenetic regulator of HERV-K in AEG. Specifically, we demonstrate for the first time that DOT1L silences HERV-K transcription via locus-specific H3K79me2 deposition, whereas its overexpression correlates with poor prognosis. Furthermore, we reveal a dual mechanism. Pharmacologic DOT1L inhibition not only reactivates HERV-K to trigger autonomous senescence through STING-mediated innate immune responses but also promotes the formation of HERV-K–derived retrovirus-like particles (RVLP). Critically, these RVLPs propagate senescence via paracrine signaling, thereby establishing a self-amplifying antitumor response.Materials and Clinical data collectionAll studies are performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki principles under a protocol approved by the Ethics Committee of Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, and written informed consent was obtained from all subjects. Paraffin-embedded tissue specimens and clinical data of AEG in Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital were collected. Complete clinical data, paraffin-embedded tissues, and follow-up information of patients with AEG from 2011 to 2019 were included.MiceAnimal experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital. Female BALB/c nude mice (5–6 weeks old) were obtained from Guangdong Medical Laboratory Animal Center. All mice had free access to food and water. The mice were randomly assigned to each group to minimize the effects of little difference between them.Animal experimentsOE19 cells were suspended in PBS and subcutaneously injected into the dorsal flank of BALB/c nude mice. Tumor growth was monitored every 2 or 3 days using Vernier calipers, with volume calculated as V = length × width × width/2.DOT1L inhibitor treatment in animal experimentsOE19 cells (2 × 106 cells per mouse) were suspended in 100 μL of PBS and injected subcutaneously into the dorsalis of each BALB/c nude mouse. After reaching the desired tumor size (50–80 mm3), mice were treated with SGC0946 (MCE, HY- ; 5 mg/kg/mouse/day) or EPZ004777 (MCE, HY- ; 5 mg/kg/mouse/day) or PBS via intraperitoneal injection.Abacavir antagonism of DOT1L inhibitor treatment in animal experimentsOE19 cells (4 × 106 cells per mouse) were suspended in 200 μL of PBS and injected subcutaneously into the dorsalis of each mouse. After reaching the desired tumor size (100 mm3), mice were treated with both SGC0946 (5 mg/kg/mouse/day) and abacavir (MCE, HY-17423A; 50 μg/mouse/day) via intraperitoneal injection. All procedures followed institutional animal care guidelines.Cell lines and cell cultureHuman AEG cell lines, including OE19 and SKGT4, were obtained from the Shanghai Cell Bank Type Culture Collection Committee. HEK293T cell line was obtained from Servicebio. These cell lines were verified by short tandem repeat assays for their identification and tested negative for Mycoplasma contamination.OE19 and SKGT4 were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Pricella, PM150210) with 10% FBS (ExCell Bio, FSP500) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Cells were incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2. The culture medium was refreshed every 2 to 3 days to maintain cells in the logarithmic growth phase. Plasmids (MiaoLing Plasmid), pMD2.G (VSV-G envelope), and the packaging vector psPAX2 were cotransfected into HEK293T cells using PEI MAX transfection reagent (Polysciences). OE19 cells were transduced with lentiviral supernatant supplemented with 8 μg/mL polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich). Lentivirus infection was performed to establish OE19-DOT1L-sh, OE19-STING-sg, and OE19-HERVK-CRISPRi cell lines. Positive clones were selected with 2 μg/mL puromycin 48 hours after transduction.The sequences of the short hairpin RNAs (shRNA) and single-guide RNAs (sgRNA) used for CRISPR-Cas9 and the sgRNAs used for CRISPRi-dCas9 and the matching Negative Control (NC) are listed in Supplementary Tables S1, S2, and S3.Cell Counting Kit-8 assayCell viability was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Yeasen, 40203ES60) assay, a colorimetric technique utilizing WST-8. Cells in logarithmic growth were trypsinized, resuspended, and seeded into 96-well plates at ≥1,000 cells/well. Peripheral wells were filled with buffer to minimize evaporation. After preincubation at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 12 to 24 hours, CCK-8 reagent (10 μL/well) was added, and plates were incubated until a color change occurred. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader in triplicate. Cell viability (%) was calculated using a specified formula based on the absorbances of experimental, control, and blank wells.Clonal expansion assayTwo thousand cells were seeded in one well of a 6-well plate precoated and treated with DOT1L inhibitors or control vehicle for approximately 10 days. The cells were then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 minutes and stained with 10% crystal violet for 30 minutes. The relative cell integral density was calculated using ImageJ software.Lactate dehydrogenase cytotoxicity assayCytotoxicity was assessed using a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) assay kit (Beyotime, C0016). AEG cell lines were cultured in serum-free or low-serum (1% FBS) 1,640 medium. High-background control (cells + lysis buffer, 37°C for 30 minutes) and low-background control (medium only) were set. After treatment, supernatants were collected by centrifugation (250 × g, 3 minutes), mixed with the working solution, and incubated in the dark for 15 to 30 minutes, and the absorbance at 490 nm was measured. The stop solution was added, and the absorbance was remeasured. Cell damage rate (%) = (A − C)/(B − C) × 100 (A, sample absorbance; B, high-control absorbance; C, low-control absorbance). All experiments were performed in triplicate.5-Ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine proliferation testCells were seeded on coverslips placed in 6-well plates and treated with DOT1L inhibitors or a control vehicle for the indicated time points. 5-Ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) was added to the culture medium for 2 hours prior to fixation. EdU incorporation was then detected using a Click-iT EdU kit (Rio Bio, C10310-3), following the manufacturer's instructions.Senescence-associated β-galactosidase stainingThe cells were fixed, and a staining solution was prepared according to the instructions of the senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-Gal) kit (Beyotime, C0602). They were then incubated with the staining solution at 37°C for an optimal duration. The presence of SA-β-Gal activity was observed as blue staining under a microscope, and optionally, the staining intensity was quantified for analysis.ImmunofluorescenceFor immunofluorescence staining, cells seeded on coverslips were washed three times with PBS, fixed in 4% PFA, and permeabilized in 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS. Coverslips were incubated with anti–HERVK-Env (AUSTRAL Biologicals, HERM-1811-5) in blocking buffer at 4°C overnight and then with one or two types of secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature. The cells or tissues were then incubated for 5 minutes with 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) for nucleus staining. Finally, images were obtained with fluorescence and laser confocal microscopes. The fluorescence intensity was detected using ImageJ software.ImmunohistochemicalTissue samples were first fixed to maintain cellular morphology and structure, followed by dehydration through a graded series of ethanols and embedding in paraffin. Subsequently, thin sections were cut and subjected to antigen retrieval to unmask the epitopes of interest. Specific primary antibodies, anti-Ki67 (9449s, Cell Signaling Technology), anti–HERVK-Env (AUSTRAL Biologicals, HERM-1811-5), and anti-P21 (HA500156, HUABIO), were applied to the sections and allowed to bind to their respective antigens. After washing to remove unbound antibodies, a chromogenic substrate was introduced to visualize the antibody–antigen complexes, resulting in stained areas indicating the presence and distribution of the target antigens. The stained slides were then examined and analyzed under a light microscope for statistical analysis.Transmission electron microscopy and immunoelectron microscopyCells were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 mol/L cacodylate buffer, postfixed with 1% osmium tetroxide, dehydrated, and embedded in Epon. Thin sections were stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate for transmission electron microscopy (TEM). For immunoelectron microscopy, sections were incubated with primary antibodies against HERVK-Env, followed by incubation with secondary antibodies conjugated to gold particles. The samples were observed under a transmission electron microscope (HT7800, Hitachi), and images were obtained.Immuno-TEMFor TEM, the cells were collected by electron microscope fixative (car: G1102, Servicebio). After a serial procession of agarose pre-embedding, fixation, dehydration, resin penetration and embedding, polymerization, ultrathin sectioning, and staining, the samples were observed under a transmission electron microscope (HT7800, Hitachi) and images were obtained.Western blottingCellular or tumor tissue lysates were lysed in RIPA buffer with protease and phosphatase inhibitors, and protein concentrations were determined using the bicinchoninic acid assay. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies: anti–HERVK-Env (AUSTRAL Biologicals, HERM-1811-5), anti-P21 (HA500156, HUABIO), anti-P16 (SU0702, HUABIO), anti-P53 (SY010-6, HUABIO), anti–Bcl-XL (R22508, ZenBio), anti–cleaved PARP (5625, Cell Signaling Technology), anti-STING ( , Cell Signaling Technology), anti-TBK1 (3504, Cell Signaling Technology), anti–phosphorylated TBK1 (anti–p-TBK1; 5483, Cell Signaling Technology), anti-IRF3 ( , Cell Signaling Technology), anti–phosphorylated IRF3 (anti–p-IRF3; , Cell Signaling Technology), anti-DOT1L (ABclonal, A12329), anti-tubulin (2146, Cell Signaling Technology), anti–β-actin (HA722023, HUABIO), anti-GAPDH ( , Cell Signaling Technology), anti–histone H3 (PTM-6621, PTMab), anti–di-methyl-histone H3 (Lys79; PTM-5159, PTMab), anti–di-methyl-histone H3 (Lys79; PTM-5157, PTMab), anti–mouse IgG [horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–linked; 7076, Cell Signaling Technology], and anti–rabbit IgG (HRP-linked; 7074, Cell Signaling Technology). After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and visualized using an ECL detection kit (BL520A, Biosharp). All steps included thorough TBST washing to ensure specificity. In addition, relevant information about the drugs is provided as follows: EPZ5676 (TargetMol, T3099), ABT-737 (KKL, KM14441), and cycloheximide (CHX; KKL, KM10397).RNA extraction, reverse transcription, and quantitative reverse transcriptase PCRRNA was extracted from cellular or tumor tissue samples using the EZB kit and quantified spectrophotometrically. Reverse transcription was performed with 1 μg of RNA. Quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-qPCR) was performed using SYBR Green and specific primers, with cycling conditions consisting of initial denaturation at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method, normalized to GAPDH or actin, and analyzed statistically. All primers used for RT-qPCR are listed in Supplementary Table S4.Purification of microvesicle particles from conditioned mediumCells were cultured in medium supplemented with 10% exosome-depleted fetal bovine serum (Systembio, EXO-FBS-50A-1) for 48 hours before medium collection (16). The conditioned medium was collected, and the corresponding cell number was counted. Medium from the same number of cells was used for microvesicle purification by centrifugation at 300 × g for 10 minutes to eliminate cell contamination and 3,000 × g for 20 minutes, followed by filtration through a 0.22-μm filter (Pall Corporation) and then ultracentrifugation at 110,000 × g for 2 hours (16). Pellets were collected and resolved in an equal volume of PBS and subjected to RNA isolation or Western blotting (WB).RNA sequencing of OE19 cellsCell samples were divided into untreated control and SGC0946-treated groups (1 and 5 µmol/L) and sent to Chibio Biotech Co., Ltd., for RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). Briefly, total RNA was extracted, and its purity and integrity were verified to ensure subsequent experimental reliability for sequencing library construction. The raw sequencing reads were quality-controlled using fastp (version 0.24.0; ref. 32). Clean reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38) with additional annotation on liftovered ERV coordinates (Supplementary Table S5, originated from Paces and colleagues; ref. 33) using Salmon quant (version 0.12.0; ref. 34) with parameters “libType A–validateMappings–useVBOpt–numBootstraps 25.” The generated abundance files were used to generate counts for differential analysis using the R package DESeq2 (version 1.30.1; ref. 35). Expression on Transcripts Per Million (TPM) and Fragments Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads (FPKM) was also generated for comparison between groups and downstream analysis. The Reactome_cellular_senescence and Fridman_senescence_up gmt file was downloaded from Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) to generate heatmaps, visualizing gene enrichment in the cellular senescence pathway.Cleavage Under Targets and TagmentationWe performed two Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) experiments under the kit (Vazyme TD904 and TD202) guidelines in this study. In the first experiment, the wild-type (WT) OE19 cells were treated with SGC0946 or DMSO, harvested, and then incubated with DOT1L and H3K79me2 antibody. In the second experiment, the DOT1L-knockdown and WT OE19 cells were harvested and incubated with H3K79me2 antibody. After library construction and sequencing (Berry Genomics Corporation, China, and JMDNA, China), analysis was performed following the Sparse Enrichment Analysis for CUT&RUN (SEACR) guidelines (version 1.3; ref. 36). Briefly, raw fastq reads were filtered using cutadapt (version 5.0; ref. 37) and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38) and spike-in DNA (Supplementary Table S6) using Bowtie 2 (version 2.5.4; ref. 38). Then, peaks were called by SEACR with default parameters. Finally, the target ERVs were visualized based on the spike-in depth-normalized bigWig files via profile plot and track plot by deepTools (version 3.5.5; ref. 39) and pyGenomeTracks (version 3.9; ref. 40).DOT1L-mediated inhibition of HERV-K is a potential therapeutic target for AEG HERVs are typically epigenetically silenced, with methyltransferases playing a pivotal role in this process (12, 41, 42). To pinpoint the primary methyltransferases responsible for regulating HERV expression in AEG, we applied a HERV analysis workflow (43). This workflow systematically examined the HERV transcriptome and compared its expression to 169 methyltransferase protein-coding genes. Initially, we quantified the expression levels of all annotated mRNAs and HERVs. Subsequently, using a subset of robustly expressed HERVs and mRNAs, we computed the correlation between all pairwise genes and summarized the results to identify genes exhibiting correlated or inversely correlated expression patterns with HERVs (Fig. 1A). For our study, we utilized two independent public datasets: one comprising bulk RNA-seq data from tumor tissues and adjacent normal tissues of 83 patients with AEG (3) and the other containing bulk RNA-seq data from tumor tissues of 37 patients with AEG (44). Across all datasets, we consistently identified 43 candidates among the top 50% of methyltransferases negatively correlated with HERVs (Fig. 1B and C; Supplementary Table S7).Figure 1. DOT1L expression negatively correlated with HERVs in AEG. A, Schematic workflow outlining the computational pipeline applied to each dataset for alignment, quantitation, normalization, and correlation calculation between HERV and mRNA expression. B, Venn diagram illustrating the overlap of top HERV anticorrelated methyltransferases (MTs) (top 50% with >25th percentile expression) across AEG tumor tissue datasets (GSE183924 in blue; PRJNA788008 in yellow) and AEG matched normal adjacent tissue (NAT) dataset (PRJNA788008 in red). Overlap counts are shown, and MT gene names are listed in the boxes that are matched to the color of the respective overlap region. C, Bar plots presenting the median Spearman rank correlation values for 43 MTs consistently anticorrelated across AEG tumor tissue datasets (GSE183924 in blue; PRJNA788008 in yellow) and AEG NAT dataset (PRJNA788008 in red). D, Venn diagram depicting the overlap of MTs that were robustly associated with AEG prognosis and negatively correlated with HERV expression under different count modes and grouping bases. The diagram showed the overlap counts, and the names of the MTs are listed in boxes matching the colors of the corresponding overlap regions. E, Survival analysis curve based on DOT1L expression levels (divided by median FPKM counts) in the AEG tumor tissue cohort (PRJNA788008). F, Proteomic evalution of DOT1L level in tumor and adjacent tissues from the AEG cohort (PRJNA788008). EdgeR exact t test, adjusted P value= 2.511157e-06. G, Scatter plot showing Spearman bicorrelation between DOT1L and intact HERVs in two AEG cohorts: GSE183924 (x-axis) and PRJNA788008 (y-axis). Significant bicorrelations are highlighted in red, and an intact HERV-K is highlighted in a red box. H, Survival analysis curve based on HML2-1284 expression levels (divided by median FPKM counts) in the AEG tumor tissue cohort (PRJNA788008). I, Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of AEG tissue section from two patients showing the typical tumor morphology (left). Multiplex immunofluorescence staining of a consecutive section for DAPI, DOT1L, and HERVK-Env (middle). The white dashed line demarcates the border between the target region (right).To further identify a potential methyltransferase target in AEG, we conducted a survival analysis for 43 candidate methyltransferases. We found that 22 of them were related to the prognosis of patients with AEG. Specifically, DOT1L, PRMT1, NSUN4, COQ3, METTL7B, METTL2A, TRMT44, COMT, and ANTKMT were adverse prognostic factors for AEG. METTL1, TRMT2B, EEF1AKMT4, CAMKMT, CARM1, METTL13, METTL25B, SETD1A, METTL2B, SHMT1, PCMT1, PRMT7, and TRMT1 were favorable prognostic factors for AEG (Fig. 1D; Supplementary Fig. S1, S2, and S3A). Among them, only DOT1L and PRMT1 were significantly associated with poor prognosis of AEG under the preliminary grouping (median gene expression) condition (Fig. 1E). Previous studies have shown that pharmacologic inhibition of PRMT1 significantly suppressed the growth of refractory melanoma in vivo experiments and increased CD8+ T cells within tumors in vivo (45). However, the regulatory mechanisms by which DOT1L modulates HERVs, especially the effects of pharmacologic inhibition of DOT1L on HERV expression, remain poorly understood (46). Consequently, our study focused on investigating DOT1L.We analyzed a public AEG cohort with clinical data to observe the DOT1L protein expression in tumor tissues compared with the paired adjacent normal tissues (3). We found that DOT1L protein was highly expressed in AEG (Fig. 1F). By consulting the TCGA database, we also found that DOT1L was highly expressed in many other tumors (Supplementary Fig. S3B). We quantified the expression of intact HERVs in PRJNA788008 and GSE183924 datasets and then examined the correlation between DOT1L expression and the expression of these HERVs based on Spearman rank correlation test. The results of the screening were presented as scatter plots representing the correlation values of DOT1L–HERV pairs in the two datasets. A significant co-negative correlation was observed between DOT1L and HML2-1284, an intact HERV-K (Fig. 1G). In addition, elevated HML2-1284 expression correlated with improved overall survival (Fig. 1H; Supplementary Fig. S3C and S3D). To further verify the negative correlation between DOT1L and HERV-K in clinical samples, we performed immunofluorescence double staining of AEG clinical samples targeting DOT1L and HERV-K envelope protein (HERVK-Env). The results show that the red signal representing DOT1L is not in the same region as the green signal representing HERVK-Env (Fig. 1I). Taken together, our data suggest that the expressions of DOT1L and HERV-K are negatively correlated in AEG.DOT1L inhibitor induces HERV-K expression by decreasing H3K79 methylation and induces cellular senescence through the innate immune responseTo investigate the regulatory role of DOT1L on HERVs, we performed RNA-seq on the OE19 cell line treated with SGC0946 and DMSO, respectively. The RNA-seq results reveal that higher concentrations of DOT1L inhibitor significantly activated more HERVs (Fig. 2A–C). We subsequently conducted experiments to examine the changes in HERV mRNA expression in the OE19 cell line treated with varying concentrations of the DOT1L inhibitor. We evaluated different HERV transcript families, including HERV-E, HERV-F, HERV-K, human mouse mammary tumor virus–like 2 (HML2), and ERVL using RT-qPCR assays. Unpaired two-tailed Student's t test was used for comparisons between two groups in L, N. **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001.To further determine whether altered HERV expression profiles in SGC0946-treated OE19 cells were linked to reduced H3K79 methylation, we performed CUT&Tag assays on the OE19 cell line treated with either SGC0946 or DMSO. Under baseline (DMSO-treated) conditions, DOT1L protein and its catalytic product H3K79me2 were markedly enriched at the transcription start sites (TSS), gene bodies, and transcription termination sites (TTS) of HERV genomic loci (Fig. 2F). Collectively, these experimental data support our hypothesis that DOT1L mediates H3K79 methylation across full-length HERV sequences, and this modification functions to repress HERV transcriptional activation. HERV- K induces cellular senescence through innate immune response (16). We speculated that DOT1L inhibitors exert a comparable effect in AEG. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the DOT1L inhibitor activates the HERV-K and induces cellular senescence.DOT1L inhibitor induces cellular senescence in AEG cells through HERV-K triggering innate immune responseTo confirm that the DOT1L inhibitor induces cellular senescence in AEG cells, we conducted a series of comprehensive experiments. Unpaired two-tailed Student's t test was used for comparisons between two groups in C, H, I, and M. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001, ns, not significant.Next, we performed KEGG pathway enrichment analysis based on RNA-seq data from DOT1L inhibitor–treated cells. ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test was used for comparisons among multiple groups in E, G, H, and I. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001, ns, not significant.DOT1L inhibitor induces bystander cell senescence by paracrine HERV-K RVLPsPrevious studies have shown that senescent cells release HERV-K RVLPs into culture media (16, 50). Unpaired two-tailed Student's t test was used for comparisons between two groups in G and H. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001; ns, not significant.We further hypothesized that DOT1L inhibitors may produce significant antitumor effects by inducing HERV-K RVLP–mediated bystander cell senescence. RT-qPCR and WB showed that HERV-K RNA and HERVK-Env protein levels were significantly higher in SGC-CM compared with DMSO-CM (Fig. 7B and C). ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test was used for comparisons among multiple groups in E, F, G, J, and K. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001, ns, not significant.Our study establishes DOT1L as a critical epigenetic regulator in AEG pathogenesis through its suppression of HERV-K elements. There are three key findings. Firstly, DOT1L maintains transcriptional repression of HERV-K via H3K79me2-mediated chromatin modification. The HERV-K activated by DOT1L inhibitors may depend on the cGAS–STING axis (16), triggering a robust innate immune response characterized by TBK1/IRF3 phosphorylation and interferon-stimulated gene upregulation. Secondly, pharmacologic DOT1L inhibition triggers innate immune response through HERV-K, inducing autonomous senescence and RVLP production. Lastly, the RVLPs propagate senescence via STING-dependent paracrine signaling, establishing an amplified antitumor response.In other tumor-related studies, researchers have predominantly targeted epigenetically modified proteins or genes to activate ERV in tumor cells, triggering an innate immune response and inducing immunogenic death in vivo (45) or providing new epitopes for tumor cells to induce specific immunity (51). Combining these approaches with immune checkpoint inhibitors can achieve remarkable antitumor effects (45, 52). The discovery of DOT1L-mediated HERV-K silencing extends current understanding of retroelement regulation in AEG malignancies. Although DNA methylation and H3K9me3 modifications have been implicated in ERV control (13, 42), our work identifies H3K79me2 as a novel chromatin mark maintaining HERV-K repression. This finding aligns with emerging evidence that DOT1L-mediated methylation regulates heterochromatic regions (53), though its specific targeting of HERV-K elements reveals a previously unrecognized layer of retroelement regulation. The conventional paradigm holds that H3K79me2/3 acts as a signature of transcriptional activity (30). However, a study has clarified that the transcriptional effect (activation or repression) of DOT1L-catalyzed H3K79me2/3 modification is strictly contingent upon the histone modification landscape of the local chromatin context (31). This effect relies on the unique chromatin profile of HERV gene bodies, which are extensively marked by H3K79me2. In contrast to single-copy genes, DOT1L-mediated H3K79 methylation acts as a repressive epigenetic mark that restricts HERV transcription and DOT1L inhibitor treatment abolishes this modification, removing the epigenetic constraint and thus enabling global HERV transcription and subsequent RVLP production. The resultant RVLP-mediated senescence propagation represents a self-sustaining therapeutic mechanism distinct from direct cytotoxic approaches. Notably, the RVLP-induced bystander senescence effect addresses a key limitation of senescence-focused therapies, the potential for senescent cell accumulation (54). The coupling of autonomous senescence with paracrine propagation enables our strategy to generate significant spatial amplification of therapeutic effects, thereby minimizing the risk of systemic toxicity.In addition, our recent single-cell analysis of AEG revealed that T cells in the AEG immune microenvironment are depleted (55), and it has been recently reported that patients with AEG with immune desert type have a poor prognosis. These suggest that DOT1L inhibitors hold great potential for clinical treatment of AEG through nonspecific immune-dependent antitumor effects. Future studies are needed to validate its efficacy and safety in a larger cohort of clinical samples and to explore its synergies with existing treatment options, ultimately optimizing treatment strategies.Collectively, our data uncover a crucial phenomenon. Pharmacologic DOT1L inhibition not only reactivates HERV-K to trigger autonomous senescence through STING-mediated innate immune response but also promotes the formation of HERV-K–derived RVLPs. Critically, these RVLPs propagate senescence via paracrine signaling, thereby establishing a self-amplifying antitumor response.Limitations of the studyAlthough this work elucidates the DOT1L–HERV-K regulatory axis, certain limitations warrant consideration and several key questions remain unresolved. The precise molecular interactions between HERV-K-derived nucleic acids and STING pathway components require structural validation, though prior studies have established this mechanism in other systems (16). Furthermore, the specificity of DOT1L-mediated regulation of HERV-K, which we found to be inhibited via H3K79 methylation (H3K79me2) in AEG cells in vitro, requires additional validation. A significant constraint of this study is the reliance on models lacking an intact immune microenvironment. Our in vivo observations of HERV-K expression and tumor senescence were conducted in nude mice lacking functional T cells. Current xenograft models similarly lack intact immune microenvironments, which limits the assessment of HERV-K RVLP–mediated immunomodulation. The development of orthotopic AEG models with competent immune systems is therefore urgently needed.Complexity of Immune Modulation and Therapeutic Translation: The translatability of our findings to immunocompetent settings is complicated by the potential for HERV-K, SASP, and DOT1L inhibitors to modulate the immune system, possibly leading to different outcomes compared with nude mice. Notably, the role of DOT1L in T cells is highly complex and stage dependent: earlier studies showed reduced DOT1L activity impairs CD8+ T-cell survival and antitumor immunity (56), whereas recent research demonstrated that DOT1L deletion or inhibition enhances mature CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity without affecting survival (57). Such dual effects may introduce confounding factors when evaluating the direct antitumor activity of RVLPs. Consequently, the clinical application of DOT1L-targeted therapy for AEG in patients with intact immune systems remains challenging, and combining DOT1L inhibitors with immunomodulatory therapies may be necessary to optimize clinical efficacy. In the future, addressing these limitations through advanced organoid coculture systems (58–60) and spatial transcriptomic analysis (61, 62) will be crucial for enhancing the clinical translation of this therapeutic paradigm.Supplementary upplementary Figure S1Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of HERV negative correlated methyltransferases in the AEG cohort (PRJNA788008, FPKM-based grouping); linked to Figure 1C.Supplementary Figure S2Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of HERV-negative correlated methyltransferases in the AEG cohort (PRJNA788008, TPM-based grouping); linked to Figure 1C.Supplementary Figure S3DOT1L-HERV negative correlation analyses in AEG, including methyltransferase Kaplan-Meier survival curves (FPKM-median grouping, PRJNA788008; linked to Figure 1C), pan-cancer DOT1L expression comparison (TCGA, normal vs tumor), and HML2-1284 Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (FPKM/TPM-cutpoint grouping, PRJNA788008); linked to Figure 1I.Supplementary Figure S4DOT1L inhibitor induces HERVK-associated cellular senescence rather than apoptosis in AEG cells, including LDH, Western blot and RT-qPCR assays for cell injury, apoptosis and HERV expression, KEGG enrichment analysis of DEGs, cellular senescence gene clustering heatmap, and impact of abacavir on the expression of aging-related genes CDKN1A and CDKN2A.Supplementary Table S1shRNA sequences targeting DOT1L.Supplementary Table S2sgRNA sequences targeting STING.Supplementary Table S3sgRNA sequences targeting HERVK.Supplementary Table S4Primer sequences used for RT-qPCR.Supplementary Table S5Up intact ERVs linked to Figure 2C.Supplementary Table S6Sequences of Spike-in DNA.Supplementary Table S7Methyltransferases expression negatively correlated with HERVs in AEG (linked to Figure 1C).

title: Rucaparib – drug evaluation: a PARP inhibitor for the treatment of BRCA-mutated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
abstract: Rucaparib (RUBRACAⓇ) is the first FDA-approved poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor for men with BRCA mutation-associated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Rucaparib’s efficacy in patients with mCRPC associated with DNA damage repair (DDR) deficiency was demonstrated in the TRITON2 and TRITON3 trials. In TRITON2, rucaparib demonstrated meaningful antitumor activity in men with measurable BRCA-mutated disease, with objective responses observed across both germline and somatic mutations. In TRITON3, rucaparib improved radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) over physician’s choice of therapy (docetaxel or a second-generation androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor [ARPI]). Rucaparib is the only drug to have shown improved rPFS versus docetaxel in mCRPC. Rucaparib demonstrated a consistent and manageable safety profile similar to other PARP inhibitors, with the most common adverse events being fatigue/asthenia, musculoskeletal pain, nausea, and anemia/decreased hemoglobin. Men with mCRPC face prolonged and complex treatments, during which maintaining quality of life, minimizing toxicity, and preserving functional status are major priorities. For patients with BRCA mutations, rucaparib offers a targeted oral alternative to chemotherapy that can delay mCRPC progression while reducing many of the logistical, physical, and clinical burdens commonly associated with chemotherapy. Its oral administration and flexible dosing enable an individualized approach that reduces treatment interruptions and maximizes clinical benefits.
full_text: 1.Introduction/overview of the fieldDeleterious BRCA mutations are found in approximately 12% of men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) (BRCA1, 2%; BRCA2, 10%) [1–3]. Compared with non-BRCA prostate cancer (PCa), BRCA-mutated PCa is known to be more aggressive (e.g., higher risk of nodal involvement and distant metastasis), with poorer prognosis, worse survival, and faster progression on androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) [4–7]. In a targeted screening for PCa in men with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, the cancers diagnosed were predominantly intermediate and high-risk disease [8]. Therefore, BRCA screenings are crucial to identifying appropriate patients that could benefit from targeted therapies such as poly (adenosine diphosphate [ADP]-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors [9,10].Along with PARP inhibitors, treatment options for advanced PCa include monotherapy with ADT and treatment combinations with taxane-based chemotherapy, androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs), or radiopharmaceuticals [9,11]. However, a persistent challenge in PCa treatment is the limited duration of clinical and survival benefit due to the emergence of primary and acquired treatment resistance.Recent research has provided insight into the molecular landscape of advanced PCa and the mechanisms behind treatment resistance [12–14]. Of note, mutations in genes involved in the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) damage repair (DDR) pathway have been reported in patients with advanced PCa [1–3]. This finding provides a unique opportunity to develop therapeutic strategies that leverage a decreased ability of the cancer cells to repair DNA damage [12,15].PARP inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in cancer cells harboring BRCA1/2 mutations in mCRPC and more recently, in DDR-deficient cancer cells in hormone-sensitive PCa (mHSPC), while sparing non-mutated healthy cells [16,17]. Rucaparib (RUBRACAⓇ) is the first FDA-approved PARP inhibitor for men with mCRPC through the accelerated approval pathway, after being granted Breakthrough Therapy designation [18,19]. In December 2025, rucaparib received full FDA-approval for the treatment of adult patients with deleterious BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations (germline and/or somatic)-associated mCRPC, who have been previously treated with an ARPI [19]. It is also approved in the United States for the maintenance treatment of patients with deleterious BRCA mutation-associated recurrent ovarian cancer [19]. In Europe, it is approved for the first-line maintenance treatment of advanced ovarian cancer and maintenance treatment of platinum-sensitive relapsed ovarian cancer [20]. In this review, we will discuss the relevant background, pharmacology, clinical efficacy, and safety of rucaparib for the treatment of mCRPC.2.Introduction to the compoundRucaparib (Figure 1) is a potent, small-molecule inhibitor of PARP enzymes that has been shown to be active against tumor cells that have an impaired ability to repair DNA damage [21–24]. Through a mechanism known as synthetic lethality, rucaparib induces cytotoxicity in cancer cells via enzymatic inhibition of PARP proteins in the presence of defects in the DDR pathway (e.g., mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2) (Figure 2) [23–25]. In vitro studies indicate that rucaparib-induced cytotoxicity may involve increased formation of PARP-DNA complexes (specifically via stabilization of PARP1, PARP2, and PARP3, and to a lesser extent other PARP isoforms) resulting in DNA damage, apoptosis, and cancer cell death [19,21]. In tumor cell lines with BRCA1/2 and other DNA repair gene deficiencies, rucaparib demonstrated increased cytotoxicity and anti-tumor activity compared with tumor cell lines without such DNA repair deficiencies [19,25]. Additionally, preclinical studies have reported chemosensitization and radiosensitization effects, supporting the potential of treatment combinations [22,26]. Figure 1.Chemical structure of rucaparib.Rucaparib is a small-molecule PARP inhibitor designed to target the catalytic domain of PARP enzymes. Its chemical structure consists of a tricyclic indole-derived core system that facilitates binding to the NAD⁺ site of PARP, connected via a linker to a substituted phenyl ring and a terminal secondary amine. In its clinically used form, rucaparib is present as the camsylate salt, which includes a secondary bicyclic sulfonate moiety.Chemical structure of rucaparib with two distinct molecular parts.Rucaparib is a small molecule PARP inhibitor. The figure shows the tricyclic indole-derived core and appended phenyl ring.Abbreviations: PARP = poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase. Figure 2.Mechanism of action of PARP inhibitors.The diagram illustrates the mechanism of action of PARP inhibitors on DNA repair. It begins with a single strand break in DNA. Without a PARP inhibitor, PARP proteins facilitate DNA repair, resulting in repaired DNA. With a PARP inhibitor, PARP activity is inhibited, leading to different outcomes based on cell type. In non-DDR-mutated cells, DNA is repaired despite PARP inhibition. In DDR-mutated cells, the inhibition leads to double strand breaks and tumor cell death. The diagram highlights the role of PARP inhibition in exploiting DNA repair deficiencies in DDR-mutated cells to induce cytotoxicity.Diagram: PARP inhibitors affect DNA repair in cells, causing repair or death in DDR-mutated cells.This schematic illustrates how poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, such as rucaparib, exploit deficiencies in the DNA damage repair (DDR) pathway. In normal cells (left), DNA damage is repaired as usual, allowing cancer cells to continue proliferating. When PARP is inhibited in cells without DDR mutations (middle), DNA repair can still occur through intact repair mechanisms, and cancer cells continue to proliferate. In contrast, in cells with BRCA or other DDR gene mutations (right), DNA repair is impaired; accumulated damage cannot be resolved, leading to cell death through synthetic lethality.Abbreviations: PARP = poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase; DDR = DNA damage repair.3.Pharmacology3.1.DosageThe recommended dose of rucaparib is 600 mg (two 300 mg tablets) taken orally twice daily with or without food (a total daily dose of 1,200 mg) [19]. If needed, to manage adverse events, treatment interruptions or dose reduction(s) may be considered; recommended rucaparib dose modifications include stepwise reductions to 500 mg twice daily (two 250 mg tablets), 400 mg twice daily (two 200 mg tablets), and 300 mg twice daily (one 300 mg tablet) [19]. Patients receiving rucaparib for mCRPC should also receive a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analog concurrently or should have had bilateral orchiectomy [19].3.2.Pharmacokinetic profileThe pharmacokinetic (PK) profile of rucaparib monotherapy has been characterized in patients with advanced solid tumors [27].Pharmacokinetic values of oral rucaparib were obtained from a 3- open-label, phase I and II study (NCT01482715) [27]. In 55 patients with locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors who had progressed on standard treatment received doses from 40 mg to 500 mg once daily (QD) and 240 mg to 840 mg twice daily (BID) [27]. Single-dose and steady-state PK were evaluated on day 1 and day 15, respectively [27]. Overall, the plasma concentration of rucaparib demonstrated a dose-dependent increase following a QD or BID dosing schedule [27]. Median time to maximum plasma concentration, Tmax, was 1.5–4 hours and 1.5–6 hours for the QD and BID dosing schedules, respectively, which suggests relatively fast absorption [27]. Steady-state was achieved after 8 days for both the QD and BID dosing schedules [27]. The steady-state accumulation ratio for area under concentration-time curve (AUC) ranged from 1.60–2.33 and 1.47–5.44 following QD and BID dosing schedules, respectively [27].Steady-state exposure at the recommended dose level of 600 mg rucaparib BID using the commercial tablet formulation was evaluated in 18 patients in of the study [27]. Arithmetic mean (coefficient of variation %) for steady-state Cmax (Cmax,ss) and AUC0-tau were 1940 ng/mL (54%) and 15,800 ng·h/mL (58%), respectively [27].3.2.1.Absorption and distributionAbsorption and distribution data for rucaparib were obtained from a separate phase I study (NCT01009190), which enrolled 85 patients with advanced solid tumors [28]. Rucaparib demonstrated a dose-independent mean oral bioavailability of 36% (range 30–45%) based on the ratio of dose-normalized AUC [19,28]. Following administration with a high-fat meal, rucaparib exposure was moderately increased, with a ~ 20% increase in Cmax, a ~ 38% increase in AUC0-24 h, and a delay in Tmax of approximately 2.5 hours compared with fasted conditions [19,27]. However, these changes are not considered clinically significant, and rucaparib may be administered with or without food [27]. Following a single intravenous dose of rucaparib 12–40 mg, rucaparib had a steady-state volume of distribution of 113–262 L [19,28].3.2.2.Metabolism and excretionMetabolism and excretion data were obtained from an analysis of PK data from several studies including NCT01009190, NCT01482715, and NCT01891344. At the approved rucaparib 600 mg BID dosage, apparent rucaparib clearance at steady state is 44.2 L/h, and the half-life is 26 hours [19,27,29]. In a population PK study of rucaparib 600 mg BID, no apparent difference in rucaparib PK was observed among patients with different phenotypes of CYP1A2 (normal n = 28; hyperinducer n = 136) and CYP2D6 (poor metabolizer n = 9; normal metabolizer n = 76; intermediate metabolizer n = 71; ultra-rapid metabolizer n = 4) [30]. For patients with mild to moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance 30–89 mL/min, as estimated by the Cockcroft-Gault method), no dosage modification is recommended [19]. Rucaparib has not been studied in patients with creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min or patients on dialysis [19].3.2.3.Drug-drug interactionIn vitro studies indicated that the risk of drug-drug interactions impacting rucaparib exposure was low [31]. However, there is potential for drug-drug interactions impacting substrate exposure with rucaparib. If rucaparib is administered concomitantly with certain CYP1A2, CYP3A, CYP2C9, or CYP2C19 substrates, the exposure of the substrate increases [32], which may lead to increased risk of adverse events [19]. To reduce this potential risk, decrease the substrate dose as indicated in its approved prescribing information [19].4.Clinical efficacyRucaparib’s efficacy in men with mCRPC associated with DDR deficiency was evaluated in the TRITON2 (phase II) and TRITON3 (phase III) clinical trials (Table 1).Table 1.Summary of Phase II and III clinical trial results of rucaparib.TrialNamePhaseObjectiveMethodologySubgroupMedian rPFS (mo)ORR(%) [n/N]PSA50(%) [n/N]Median OS (mo)sReferencesTRITON2IISafety and efficacy of rucaparib in DNA damage repair- deficient mCRPCOpen-label, single-arm studyRucaparib 600 mg BID (n = 277)Patients who progressed after 1–2 ARPI and ≥1 taxane-based chemotherapyBRCAPALB2ATMCDK12CHEK2Other[BARD1, FANCA, NBN, RAD51, RAD51B, BRIP1]10.713.65.3NANA5.846 [37/81]100 [4/4]0 [0/23]0 [0/9]0 [0/4]25 [3/12]53 [92/172]55 [6/11]3.4 [2/59]6.7 [1/15]14 [1/7]23 [3/13]17.217.714.613.911.110.5Rucaparib showed meaningful antitumor activity in patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC[33]TRITON3IIIEfficacy of rucaparib compared to physician’s choice of abiraterone acetate, enzalutamide, or docetaxel in BRCA or ATM mutated mCRPCOpen-label, double-arm studyRandomized (2:1) into rucaparib 600 mg BID (n = 270) or physician’s choice (docetaxel or second-generation ARPI) (n = 135)Chemotherapy-naïve patients who progressed after 2nd generation ARPIBRCA RucaparibPhysician’s ChoiceITT RucaparibPhysician’s Choice11.26.4(HR 0.50, p < 0.001)10.26.4(HR 0.61, p < 0.001)45 [37/82]17 [7/41]35 [37/106]16 [9/55]55 [NR/201]27 [NR/101](HR 0.52)42 [NR/270]27 [NR/135](HR 0.63)23.221.2(HR 0.91,p = 0.50)NRNR(HR 0.99)Rucaparib provided a longer duration of rPFS vs physician’s choice (docetaxel or a second-generation ARPI) in patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC[38,39]Abbreviations: rPFS = radiographic progression-free survival; ARPI = androgen receptor pathway inhibitor; HR = hazard ratio; ITT = intent-to-treat; NR = not reported.4.1.TRITON2 (NCT02952534)Rucaparib received accelerated FDA approval in 2020 based on its meaningful objective response rate (ORR) in patients with measurable disease, the primary endpoint of the TRITON2 clinical trial [18,19]. TRITON2 was an international, open-label, single-arm, phase II study evaluating rucaparib in patients with mCRPC associated with DDR deficiency [33]. Eligible patients had a deleterious germline or somatic mutation in one or more genes: BRCA1, BRCA2, or another prespecified DDR gene that may confer sensitivity to PARP inhibition [33]. Enrolled patients had progressed after one to two lines of second-generation ARPI therapy and one taxane-based chemotherapy for castrate-resistant disease [33]. Patients received a starting dose of 600 mg oral rucaparib twice daily [33].The TRITON2 study enrolled a total of 277 patients. ORR (primary endpoint), duration of response (DOR; secondary endpoint), and radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS; secondary endpoint) were assessed by independent radiology review (IRR) in 133 evaluable patients. The other secondary endpoints of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response, clinical benefit rate (CBR), overall survival (OS), and safety were analyzed in all 277 enrolled patients [33]. In the final TRITON2 analysis, within the BRCA subgroup, 37/81 (46%) patients with IRR-evaluable disease had a confirmed objective response (Figure 3), with a median DOR by IRR of 15.5 months (95% CI 6.4-not reached [NR]) [33]. The confirmed ORR was 48% and 30% for patients with a BRCA2 and BRCA1 mutation, respectively (Figure 3) [33]. The ORR was 45% for patients with a germline BRCA mutation and 46% for those with a somatic mutation, respectively [33]. The ORR was similar in patients with or without co-occurring TP53, PTEN, or RB1 mutations [33], although ORR was numerically lower for patients with co-occurring BRCA and RB1 mutations (23%; 95% CI 5.0–54, Figure 3) [33]. In an interim analysis of the TRITON2 BRCA-mutated population, which included 115 patients at the time of data cutoff, the ORR among patients with and without homozygous BRCA loss was 70% (95% CI 34.8–93.3%) and 40% (95% CI 12.2–73.8%), respectively [34]. Eur Urol. 2023;84(3):321–330.Reprinted with permission.In the final TRITON2 analysis, a PSA50 response occurred in 92 of 172 patients (53%; 95% CI 46–61%) in the BRCA subgroup (Figure 3), with a median time to PSA progression of 6.5 months (95% CI 5.7–7.5) [33]. PSA50 response rates were 59% and 18% for those with a BRCA2 and BRCA1 mutation, respectively (Figure 3) [33]. Of patients with germline and somatic BRCA mutations, 59% (95% CI 46–70%) and 49% (95% CI 39–60%), respectively, had a PSA50 response [33]. There was no difference in PSA50 response rates among patients with co-occurring mutations in TP53, RB1, or PTEN [33]. Additional outcomes in the BRCA subgroup included a median rPFS of 10.7 months (95% CI 8.7–13), median OS of 17.2 months (95% CI 15–20), and a CBR of 58% at 6 months [33].There were 4 patients with measurable disease by IRR and a PALB2 mutation, all of whom had a confirmed objective response (100%; 95% CI 40–100), with a median duration of objective response (DOR) of 10.1 months (95% CI NR-NR) [33]. Six of 11 patients (55%; 95% CI 23–83) with a PALB2 mutation had a PSA50 response, with a median time to PSA progression of 7.5 months (95% CI 4.7–12) [33]. Additional outcomes in the PALB2 subgroup included a median rPFS of 13.6 months (95% CI 7.1–25), median OS of 17.7 months (95% CI 7.1-NR), and a CBR of 82% at 6 months [33].No objective responses by IRR were observed in the ATM, CDK12, or CHEK2 subgroups [33]. Among patients with IRR-evaluable disease in the Other DDR gene subgroup, defined as patients with gene mutations in BARD1, FANCA, NBN, RAD51, RAD51B, or BRIP1, 3 of 12 patients (25%; 95% CI 5.5–57%) had a confirmed objective response [33]. These responders had mutations in FANCA, RAD51B, and BRIP1; however, the patient with a BRIP1 mutation was later found to have a co-occurring homozygous BRCA2 deletion at enrollment [33].PSA responses were limited across the non-BRCA groups. A PSA50 response occurred in 2 of 59 patients (3.4%; 95% CI 0.4–12%) in the ATM subgroup, with a median time to PSA progression of 3.1 months (95% CI 2.8–3.7) [33]. A PSA50 response also occurred in 1 of 15 patients (6.7%; 95% CI 0.2–32%) in the CDK12 subgroup, 1 of 7 patients (14%; 95% CI 0.4–58%) in the CHEK2 subgroup, and 3 of 13 patients (23%; 95% CI 5.0–54%) in the Other DDR gene subgroup [33].Across the ATM, CDK12, CHEK2, and Other DDR gene subgroups, median rPFS by IRR ranged from 5.3 to 5.8 months, median OS ranged from 10.5 to 14.6 months, and CBR ranged from 13% to 31% at 6 months and from 0% to 23% at 12 months [33].The study population of TRITON2 consisted largely of patients with measurable disease burden; measurable visceral disease was observed in patients harboring BRCA (37%), non-BRCA (ATM = 43%, CDK12 = 22%, PALB2 = 50%), and Other DDR gene (17%) mutations [33]. In an interim analysis of the TRITON2 BRCA-mutated population, which included 115 patients at the time of data cutoff, those with visceral disease demonstrated an ORR of 47.6% (10/21; 95% CI 25.7–70.2%) and a PSA50 response rate of 63.6% (14/22; 95% CI 40.7–82.8%) [35].Overall, results from the TRITON2 trial led to FDA accelerated approval of rucaparib for mCRPC in 2020 based on the ORR and DOR in patients with measurable disease [18,19]. This positioned rucaparib as the first PARP inhibitor to receive FDA approval for the treatment of mCRPC [18,19,36]. Rucaparib was shown to be effective across BRCA mutation types (e.g., germline, somatic, homozygous, and heterozygous), as loss of function enabling synthetic lethality occurs in all cases [33,34]. The presence of co-occurring mutations did not diminish rucaparib’s efficacy [33]. Additionally, TRITON2 enrolled a high proportion of patients with visceral disease [33], indicating that rucaparib is effective for the treatment of patients with measurable disease burden.4.2.TRITON3 (NCT02975934)In December 2025, rucaparib received FDA approval confirming its 2020 accelerated approval and expanding its indication to a broader population of patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC, based on the significant improvement in rPFS (the primary endpoint of TRITON3) compared with physician’s choice of therapy in patients with BRCA-mutated disease (11.2 vs 6.4 months; hazard ratio [HR] 0.50; 95% CI 0.36–0.69; p < 0.001) [37]. TRITON3 was an international randomized, controlled, open-label, phase III trial evaluating rucaparib in patients with mCRPC and a BRCA1, BRCA2, or ATM mutation [38]. All patients had a history of disease progression after treatment with one previous second-generation ARPI (abiraterone acetate, enzalutamide, apalutamide, or an investigational agent) [38]. Unlike patients in TRITON2, patients in TRITON3 had not been treated with chemotherapy for castration-resistant disease [38]. Previous taxane-based chemotherapy for castration-sensitive disease was permitted [33,38]. Patients were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive oral rucaparib (600 mg twice daily) or a physician’s choice of therapy (docetaxel or a second-generation ARPI [abiraterone acetate or enzalutamide]) [38]. Prior to randomization, investigators chose the next choice of therapy (docetaxel, abiraterone acetate, or enzalutamide) for each patient [38]. Patients randomized to the physician’s choice arm were given the opportunity to cross over to the rucaparib arm after confirmation of disease progression [38]. The primary efficacy outcome was rPFS, and key secondary outcomes included OS and objective response according to independent radiology review [38].In TRITON3, 270 patients were assigned to the rucaparib arm and 135 were assigned to the physician’s choice arm (intention-to-treat [ITT] population) [38]. Among the patients in the rucaparib arm, 201 had a BRCA mutation (BRCA2 n = 172; BRCA1 n = 29) [38]. In the physician’s choice arm, 101 patients had a BRCA mutation (BRCA2 n = 86; BRCA1 n = 15) [38]. The demographics of patients enrolled in TRITON3 (e.g., gender, age, genomic features) were generally an accurate representation of the real-world population at risk for PCa, except that there were fewer men of African descent compared to the general population with advanced PCa [38].At 62 months, the median duration of rPFS was significantly longer in the rucaparib arm than in the physician’s choice arm, both in the BRCA subgroup (11.2 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.36–0.69; p < 0.001) (Figure 4(a)) and the ITT population (10.2 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.47–0.80; p < 0.001) (Figure 4(b)) [38]. Exploratory efficacy analyses compared rucaparib to each physician’s choice of therapy in the BRCA subgroup. Rucaparib significantly prolonged rPFS compared with docetaxel (11.2 vs 8.3 months; HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.37–0.77) (Figure 4(c)) and with abiraterone acetate or enzalutamide (11.2 vs 4.5 months; HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.25–0.58) (Figure 4(d)) [38]. Reprinted with permission.After an overall median follow-up of 44 months, median OS in the BRCA subgroup was 23.2 months (95% CI 19.1–25.2) in the rucaparib arm and 21.2 months (95% CI 18.0–23.1) in the physician’s choice arm (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.68–1.20; p = 0.50) [39]. Median OS in the ITT population was similar between rucaparib and physician’s choice (HR 0.99; 95% CI 0.78–1.26) [39]. The confirmed ORR in the BRCA subgroup was 45% (37/82) in the rucaparib arm and 17% (7/41) in the physician’s choice arm [38]. In the ITT population, the confirmed ORR was 35% (37/106) and 16% (9/55) for the rucaparib and physician’s choice arm, respectively [38]. In the ATM subgroup, no meaningful differences in OS and ORR were observed between treatment arms [38,39].Additional subgroup analyses of TRITON3 demonstrated consistent benefit with rucaparib across BRCA mutation types, liver metastases status, and in patients who crossed over to rucaparib following progression on physician’s choice of therapy. In the BRCA population, rucaparib improved rPFS compared with physician’s choice in both the germline and somatic mutation groups (germline: HR 0.52; 95% CI 0.32–0.84; somatic: HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.25–0.59), with a median rPFS of 11.2 months with rucaparib in both subgroups compared with 8.4 months for those in the physician’s choice arm with germline mutations and 5.6 months for those with somatic mutations [40]. Median OS was 24.8 vs 22.7 months (rucaparib vs physician’s choice) in the germline subgroup [40]. In patients with somatic BRCA mutations, the survival difference was more pronounced, with median OS of 24.2 months for rucaparib compared with 16.3 months for physician’s choice [40].In subgroup analyses of patients with BRCA mutations by liver metastases status, rucaparib improved median rPFS compared with physician’s choice in patients with liver metastases (4.8 vs 2.6 months; HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.23–1.25) and those without liver metastases (11.3 vs 7.1 months; HR 0.45; 95% CI 0.32–0.63) [41]. However, the subgroup with liver metastases was small, with 20 patients in the rucaparib arm and 10 patients in the physician’s choice arm [41]. Median OS was similar between treatment arms (~11 months) in patients with liver metastases; patients without liver metastases had a median OS of 24 months with rucaparib and 22 months with physician’s choice of therapy [41]. The ORR was higher with rucaparib than with physician’s choice in patients with and without liver metastases [41]. Among patients with liver metastases, partial responses occurred in 41% (7/17) of those treated with rucaparib versus 22% (2/9) receiving physician’s choice, with no complete responses observed in either arm [41]. Among patients without liver metastases, 46% (30/65) in the rucaparib arm achieved a complete or partial response compared with 16% (5/32) in the physician’s choice arm [41].Exploratory analyses were conducted in patients with BRCA mutations who crossed over to rucaparib from physician’s choice arm after disease progression [42]. Seventy of the 101 patients with BRCA mutation in the physician’s choice arm were eligible for crossover [42]. Of the 70, 53 crossed over to rucaparib [42]. Response was assessed in 31 patients with measurable disease [42]. Among patients initially treated with docetaxel during randomization phase, ORR was similar with docetaxel and after crossover to rucaparib (35% vs 33%) [42]. Among patients initially treated with an ARPI, ORR was higher following crossover to rucaparib (9% vs 46%) [42]. The median DOR following crossover to rucaparib was 5.4 months among patients who crossed over after initial docetaxel and was not reached among those initially treated with an ARPI [42]. Together, these analyses suggest that rucaparib may remain effective in patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC who have received at least one ARPI and progressed on another ARPI or docetaxel.Overall, rucaparib is the only PARP inhibitor evaluated in a randomized phase III study comparing a PARP inhibitor with docetaxel [38]. Clinical benefit was primarily driven by patients with BRCA mutations, which comprised the largest proportion of enrolled patients and demonstrated clear treatment effect with rucaparib, including longer rPFS and higher objective response rates compared with the physician’s choice of therapy [38]. The trial also had a high rate of crossover from physician’s choice to rucaparib after progression, with a majority of eligible patients crossing over; OS was similar between arms, likely reflecting this crossover [39].5.Safety and tolerabilityRucaparib demonstrated a consistent and manageable safety profile in patients with mCRPC across TRITON2 and TRITON3 (Tables 2 and 3) [33,38]. The most common adverse events in the pooled safety population of 373 patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC from TRITON2 and TRITON3 included fatigue/asthenia, musculoskeletal pain, nausea, and anemia/decreased hemoglobin [19,33,38]. Fatal adverse events were rare in both trials. In TRITON2, fatal adverse events occurred in 1.7% of patients who received rucaparib, including acute respiratory distress syndrome and pneumonia (1 patient each) [19,33]. In TRITON3, fatal adverse events occurred in 1.5% of patients treated with rucaparib, including cardiac failure, myocardial ischemia, and sepsis (1 patient each) [19,38].Table 2.Proportions of patients with adverse events reported in ≥20% of patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC on Rucaparib in TRITON2 and TRITON3 [19] Percent (%). These elevations were generally low grade, early in onset, reversible with continued treatment, and not associated with liver or kidney toxicity [33].The safety profiles of rucaparib and physician’s choice (docetaxel or ARPIs) were summarized in Figure 5. TRITON3 investigators noted that thromboembolic events (a side effect associated with olaparib and talazoparib) in the rucaparib arm were lower than or similar to those associated with physician’s choice [38,43,44]. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) or acute myeloid leukemia (AML) was reported in 1% (2/201) of patients with a BRCA mutation receiving rucaparib [19]. In patients who developed secondary MDS/AML, the duration of rucaparib treatment ranged from 1.4–2.3 years [19]. Additionally, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) in TRITON3 were analyzed by age groups: <65 years, 65–74 years, and ≥75 years [45]. Anemia/decreased hemoglobin was more common in older patients in both the rucaparib and physician’s choice arms, while the incidence of decreased appetite was higher in older patients only in the rucaparib arm [45]. No clear, age-related patterns were observed for the other most common TEAEs [45]. For Grade 3 or higher TEAEs, the incidence of fatigue/asthenia and anemia/decreased hemoglobin was highest in the oldest age group (≥75 years) for patients treated with rucaparib [45]. Figure 5.Proportion of Patients with Adverse Events in ≥10% of Patients with BRCA-Mutated mCRPC–Rucaparib vs Physicians’ Choice [19].The phase III TRITON3 trial evaluated rucaparib versus physician’s choice in patients with BRCA mutated metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). The most frequent AEs included fatigue/asthenia, musculoskeletal pain, nausea, decreased appetite, and constipation, with grade 3–4 events occurring infrequently in both arms.The data in this tornado plot represent the percentage of patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC who experienced adverse events (AEs) in ≥10% of patients.
