Advances in RNA biology have uncovered its structural diversity, dynamic interactions, and broad regulatory roles2, particularly in cancer, where RNA-mediated processes contribute to tumor initiation, progression, and therapy response3.One of the most versatile layers of RNA regulation is chemical modification, collectively known as RNA epitranscriptome4. These modifications introduce reversible marks that influence RNA metabolism, analogous to DNA and histone modifications in the epigenome. Over 170 RNA modifications have been identified across coding and non-coding RNA species, including messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), and chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs). Among these, N6-methyladenosine (m6A), 5-methylcytosine (m5C), pseudouridine (Ψ), N1-methyladenosine (m1A), and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing are the most extensively studied in physiological and disease contexts. Additional modifications, such as 2′-O-methylation (Nm), which is highly abundant due to widespread snoRNA-guided installation, as well as N7-methylguanosine (m7G) and N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C), add further layers of regulatory complexity5,6. These chemical marks are deposited, removed, and recognized/interpreted by specialized proteins, namely writers, erasers, and readers, respectively, which collectively shape RNA splicing, localization, stability, and translation in a context-specific manner.RNA modifications function within integrated regulatory networks7. At the molecular level, they influence nearly every stage of RNA fate. At the systems level, they interact with core signaling pathways that govern cancer cell proliferation, metabolism, immune escape, stemness, and resistance to therapy. This multi-layered coordination positions RNA modifications as system-wide regulators of tumor plasticity.Rapid advances in epitranscriptomics have created new translational opportunities. RNA-based platforms, including mRNA vaccines, antisense oligonucleotides, and RNA interference therapies, have already entered the clinic. Meanwhile, RNA-modifying enzymes are emerging as druggable nodes within oncogenic, immune-evasive, and therapy-resistant pathways. Small-molecule inhibitors targeting m6A or m5C machinery have entered preclinical development7–9, while modified mRNA technologies now integrate epitranscriptomic features to enhance mRNA stability and translation10. These advances underscore RNA modification as both a key mechanism in cancer biology and a promising therapeutic frontier, highlighting the need for deeper, context-specific understanding of the functional landscape of RNA epitranscriptome in malignancies.In this review, we provide a mechanistic overview of how RNA modifications shape cancer biology. We highlight advances in detection technologies, single-cell and spatial profiling, and targeted perturbation tools. A central focus is our framework linking RNA modification regulators to cancer hallmarks and oncogenic signaling networks. We also discuss their emerging roles as therapeutic targets and biomarkers offering an integrated perspective on the epitranscriptome’s impact on cancer and translational potential.2.RNA Modification Enzymes and Mapping Technologies2.1Major epitranscriptomic marks and their regulatory complexes m6AAmong RNA modifications, m6A is the most abundant internal mark in eukaryotic mRNA, and its writers, erasers, and readers have been well characterized (Figure 1). The m6A in mRNA is mainly installed by the METTL3-METTL14-WTAP methyltransferase complex (MTC), and the deposition can occur co- or post-transcriptionally depending on context11–14. METTL3 provides catalytic activity, while METTL14 enhances substrate recognition. WTAP, together with other accessory subunits such as VIRMA, RBM15, RBM15B, and ZC3H13, regulates the subcellular localization of the complex, promotes recruitment to RNA-binding sites, and contributes to substrate specificity15–17. Additional m6A writers such as METTL16, METTL5, and ZCCHC4 have been identified18–20, each targeting distinct RNA species including mRNA, structured ncRNAs and rRNAs. Two m6A erasers have been characterized: FTO and ALKBH5. Both belong to the ALKBH superfamily and α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase family. FTO, the first RNA demethylase discovered, acts on a broad set of methylated adenosines, including m6A, N6, 2′-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am), and m1A in both mRNA and tRNA21,22. ALKBH5, by contrast, selectively demethylates m6A but not m6Am23.m6A reader proteins fall into three mechanistic classes. The YTH domain family (YTHDF1-3, YTHDC1/2) recognizes m6A-marked RNAs through YTH domains and affects multiple stages of RNA fate, including splicing, nuclear export, translation, and stability24–27. The IGF2BP family (IGF2BP1-3) binds m6A-modified transcripts via KH3-KH4 tandem domains28. IGF2BPs stabilize mRNAs by recruiting partners such as ELAVL1, MATR3, and PABPC128,29, and by antagonizing miRNA-mediated decay30. They also modulate translation in a context-dependent manner: IGF2BP2 can enhance initiation by recruiting eIF4A131, whereas IGF2BP3 can either promote cap-independent translation via eIF4G232 or repress translation by routing target mRNAs to P bodies while preserving stability33. A third class includes hnRNPA2B1, hnRNPC, and hnRNPG, which bind to regions whose structure is altered by m6A through the m6A switch mechanism34,35. In addition to readers, certain factors counteract m6A output. G3BP1 and G3BP2 act as m6A anti-readers, preferentially binding unmethylated motifs and being disfavored by m6A, indicating that absence of the mark can itself be regulatory36,37. Additional suppressive influences also occur at the installation level, such as site shielding by RNA structure or competition from other RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) that limit methyltransferase access and reduce methylation at selected motifs.m5C5-methylcytosine (5mC) is a conserved chemical modification first identified in DNA38, and its RNA counterpart m5C39 has since been found in tRNA, rRNA, mRNA, and lncRNA. Similar to 5mC in DNA, RNA m5C is formed by the enzymatic transfer of a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to the fifth carbon of cytosine (Figure 1). Although less abundant than m6A, m5C accounts for approximately 0.02%−0.09% of all cytosine residues in mRNA40. The deposition of m5C is catalyzed by two main families of enzymes: the NOL1/NOP2/Sun (NSUN) domain-containing family (NSUN1-7) and the DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) family, primarily DNMT2 and, in certain contexts, DNMT3A. These enzymes mediate site-specific methylation and each with distinct substrate preferences across RNA classes41. The TET family of dioxygenases (e.g., TET2) has been shown to oxidize RNA m5C to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (hm5C) and possibly further oxidized derivatives, while ALKBH1 has been implicated in direct demethylation of m5C, particularly in tRNA42 43. Beyond writers and erasers, several m5C “readers” have been identified that recognize and functionally interpret this mark. ALYREF and YBX1 mediate nuclear export and cytoplasmic stability of methylated mRNAs, respectively44 45. Additional m5C readers include MeCP246, MBD547, MBD648, SRSF249 and YTHDF250.ΨPseudouridine (Ψ), the C5-isomer of uridine, is generated by repositioning the glycosidic bond from N1-C1′ to C5-C1′, creating a stable C-C linkage51 that renders the modification essentially irreversible (Figure 1). In eukaryotes, Ψ occurs in rRNA, snRNA, snoRNA, tRNA, and mRNA52, with an estimated Ψ/U ratio of 0.2–0.6% in mammalian mRNA53 and 1.4% in rRNA54. Ψ is catalyzed by two major classes of enzymes: (1) stand-alone pseudouridine synthases (such as PUS1-PUS10, TRUB family and RPUSD family), and (2) the H/ACA box snRNP complex, where dyskerin (DKC1) serves as the catalytic component55 56. PUS enzymes act independently and site-specifically, whereas DKC1 relies on H/ACA guide snoRNAs to direct modification57. Notably, PUS1, PUS4, and PUS7 catalyze mRNA pseudouridylation55 58 59; TRUB1 modifies Ψ55 in both mitochondrial and nuclear-encoded RNAs60,61; and RPUSD3, RPUSD4, and TRUB2 mediate Ψ formation in mitochondrial rRNA and mRNA, supporting mitochondrial translation and oxidative phosphorylation62,63.A-to-IAdenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is a type of RNA modification in which adenosine (A) is deaminated to inosine (I), which is interpreted as guanosine (G) during translation (Figure 1). It is the most prevalent RNA nucleotide modification in humans and occurs primarily in non-coding regions enriched in double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), especially within inverted repeat elements such as Alu sequences in introns and untranslated regions64. In mammals, A-to-I editing is catalyzed by the adenosine-deaminase-acting-on-RNA (ADAR) family (ADAR1 and ADAR2), which contain 2–3 dsRNA-binding domains (dsRBDs), a C-terminal catalytic deaminase domain, and a nuclear localization signal (NLS). ADAR1 uniquely harbors an N-terminal Z-DNA/Z-RNA-binding domain (ZBD), conferring distinct structural and functional properties and contributing to substrate specificity, for example, preferential editing of short dsRNA substrates, with its third dsRBD essential for efficient recognition and catalysis65.ac4C, Nm, m1A, m7G, and beyondN4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) is a conserved RNA modification catalyzed by N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10), which primarily acetylates cytidines within mRNA coding sequences5. In mammalian mRNA, ac4C abundance has been reported at ~0.01– ~0.2%66,67. NAT10 transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the N4 position of cytidine (Figure 1). Functionally, ac4C enhances mRNA stability and translation efficiency, potentially by modulating local RNA structure or interacting with RNA-binding proteins such as the YTHDF family68.2′-O-methylation (Nm) refers to the addition of a methyl group to the 2′-hydroxyl of ribose, catalyzed by 2′-O-methyltransferases (Figure 1). Nm occurs in tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and mRNA69, with reported levels in mRNA ranging from ~0.012% (Am/A) to ~0.15% (Um/U)69 54. Beyond internal residues, Nm also present at the RNA cap, where it contributes to RNA stability, structural flexibility, and protein interactions70. Known Nm writers include FTSJ171, FTSJ372, and CMTR1/CMTR273. Meanwhile, the fibrillarin (FBL) complex with NOP56, NOP58, and SNU13, particularly for rRNA modification74. However, to date, no definitive readers or erasers of Nm have been identified.N1-methyladenosine (m1A), first discovered in the 1960s, is formed by methylation at the N1 position of adenosine75 (Figure 1). m1A is present in tRNA, rRNA, mRNA, lncRNA and mitochondrial RNA, with an estimated m1A/A ratio of ~0.02% in human mRNA76. The functional impact of m1A is context-dependent77 78: m1A within coding sequences of nuclear or mitochondrial mRNAs generally suppresses translation, whereas m1A in the 5′UTR correlates with enhanced translation efficiency78. m1A is dynamically regulated by dedicated writers, readers, and erasers. Its installation involves TRMT6, TRMT61A, TRMT61B, TRMT10C, and nucleomethylin (NML), with TRMT6-TRMT61A forming a heterotetramer in which TRMT61A provides catalytic activity and TRMT6 mediates tRNA substrate recognition. This complex installs m1A58 in cytoplasmic tRNA, critical for tRNA stability and efficient translation79. In mitochondria, TRMT61B and TRMT10C catalyze m1A modifications on mitochondrial tRNAs and mRNAs. YTH family proteins have been reported as m1A readers, while ALKBH1, ALKBH3, and FTO function as erasers21,80–82.N7-methylguanosine (m7G) occurs in multiple RNA species, including mRNA, tRNA, and circular RNA. In mammalians, m7G abundance ranges from 0.002%−0.05% in mRNA6, whereas in tRNA levels can reach 60%−85%54,83. The METTL1-WDR4 complex installs m7G at GGACU motifs. Functionally, m7G influences RNA stability and translation through recognition by RBPs: QKI isoforms (QKI5/6/7) were the first identified internal readers, enhancing mRNA stability while suppressing translation84, whereas IGF2BP3 was recently reported to promote m7G-mediated mRNA decay85.Overall, RNA modifications act as dynamic or static, multilayered regulators of the RNA lifecycle, influencing transcription, splicing, export, translation, and decay in both coding and non-coding RNAs. By shaping transcript fate through context-dependent mechanisms, they link molecular decisions to cellular phenotypes, thereby underpinning their involvement in cancer hallmarks and tumor evolution.2.2Global and site-specific mapping technologiesRecent advances in transcriptome-wide mapping of m6A and other RNA-modifications, particularly at single-nucleotide resolution, have significantly deepened our understanding of its distribution and function in normal and malignant settings (see Supplementary Table 1). These methods enhance detection precision and enable functional dissection of RNA modification dynamics across developmental, tumor progression, and therapy response.Global mapping technologies for RNA modificationsEarly m6A profiling relied on antibody-based enrichment with high-throughput sequencing. The foundational, m6A-seq and MeRIP-seq86,87, enabled transcriptome-wide mapping but were limited to peak-level resolution (~100–200 nucleotides) and required substantial RNA input. Subsequent refinements, including PA-m6A-seq, miCLIP, m6A-CLIP, m6A-LAIC-seq, m6ACE-seq, m6A-seq2, and SLIM-seq88–94, improved resolution, quantification, or input requirements, but still relied on antibody specificity, potential cross-reactivity, and/or inability to deliver stoichiometric measurements at single-nucleotide resolution.To overcome these limitations, enzyme- and chemistry-based strategies were developed, offering antibody-free alternatives and, in some cases, absolute quantification. MAZTER-seq and m6A-REF-seq use methylation-sensitive cleavage at ACA motifs95,96; m6A-SEAL and m6A-label-seq apply chemical derivatization for selective pull-down97,98; and methods such as m6A-SAC-seq, GLORI, and eTAM-seq99–101 brought direct mapping with improved accuracy, reduced background, and stoichiometric estimation. New technologies have further improved resolution, sensitivity, and compatibility with low-input or structured RNAs. For example, CAM-seq, a mild chemical deamination method, preserves m6A to enable single-base resolution without enzymes or antibodies, and works with nanogram-level RNA, making it suitable for low-input or structured RNA samples102. GLORI has been further upgraded to GLORI-2.0 and −3.0, which integrate one-pot deamination and carrier-RNA strategies to enable absolute m6A quantification from as few as ~500 cells, while retaining its core advantage of single-nucleotide stoichiometric accuracy and improving applicability to rare clinical samples103.For m5C, transcriptome-wide detection has been achieved using both antibody-based methods (e.g., m5C-RIP104 and miCLIP-m5C105) and adapted bisulfite sequencing protocols (RNA-BisSeq106, TAWO-seq107 and UBS-seq108). While bisulfite-seq remains the gold standard, its application to RNA is challenged by incomplete conversion and sensitivity to RNA structure. Ψ mapping has been enabled by chemical derivatization approaches such as Ψ-seq and Pseudo-seq55,58, which use CMC to block Ψ during reverse transcription, as well as metabolic labeling (e.g., CeU-seq) and crosslinking-based methods. Quantitative stoichiometry for Ψ can now be achieved with emerging methods, including BID-seq, PRAISE and BACS for transcriptome-wide mapping and absolute quantification109,110,111,112. For Nm, methods like RiboMeth-seq113 and Nm-seq114 enable high-resolution mapping by leveraging Nm’s resistance to chemical or enzymatic cleavage. Other modifications, such as ac4C and m7G, are being explored using targeted chemical pulldown and selective reactivity, although transcriptome-wide approaches for these marks remain at an early stage115 116.Together, these advances have shifted the field from peak-level detection to true precision epitranscriptomics, enabling base-resolved, stoichiometric, and sequence-specific mapping even from scarce or structured RNA. Although this section focuses on bulk global profiling, emerging direct RNA, single-cell, spatial, and editing-based approaches further expand resolution and will be discussed later. Despite ongoing challenges in standardization, sensitivity, and multi-modification integration, current global tools have established a strong foundation for dissecting the regulatory roles of RNA modifications in health and disease.Direct RNA sequencingUnlike cDNA-based methods that erase many native marks during reverse transcription and amplification, nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) profiles RNA in its native state and preserves chemical modifications. Modifications are inferred from characteristic changes in ionic current and, in some cases, dwell time as bases pass through the nanopore. Several computational tools leverage these raw signals for m6A detection: xPore usees a Bayesian framework to identify differential m6A sites by comparing wild-type and methyltransferase-deficient samples117, while m6Anet applies a multiple instance learning model trained on matched miCLIP and DRS datasets to predict m6A at DRACH motifs118. More recent algorithms expand beyond m6A. NanoPsu and nanoRMS enable detection of Ψ by analyzing alterations in current intensity and dwell time119.DeepEdit detects A-to-I RNA editing by identifying consistent basecalling mismatches at known editing sites120. modCnet simultaneously identifies m5C and ac4C from native DRS signals using a deep learning framework trained on chemically modified datasets121. Similarly, TandemMod uses transfer learning to detect m6A, m5C, and Ψ across species122; mAFiA estimates site-specific m6A stoichiometry at single-molecule resolution123; Uncalled4 improves RNA and DNA modification calling through signal-based deep learning124; and NanoSPA enables transcriptome-wide detection of m6A and Ψ via multi-class classifiers125. Additional tools such as RedNano126 and the benchmarking initiative from the RMaP Challenge127 further enhance prediction fidelity and reproducibility. Notably, CHEUI supports single-molecule co-detection of m6A and m5C and has revealed widespread co-occurrence of these marks across transcriptomes128. This ecosystem continues to grow rapidly as nanopore-based epitranscriptomics advances.Despite these developments, limitations remain. The subtle signal shifts induced by modifications require well-trained models, adequate read depth, and high-quality controls129. Current approaches provide only approximate stoichiometry, and detection of low-abundance or structurally complex transcripts, especially in bulk or heterogeneous clinical samples, remains challenging130. Sequencing cost also remains relatively high. Nevertheless, DRS provides full-length, native RNA profiling and integrates with long-read transcriptomics. As basecalling and validation continue to improve, it is poised to become a key tool for high-resolution epitranscriptomics, particularly in disease studies.Epitranscriptomic editing and perturbation toolsEpitranscriptomic editing and perturbation platforms enable functional interrogation of RNA modifications. These include CRISPR/dCas13 fusions, synthetic oligonucleotide mimics, and enzyme knockdown, knockout, or degradation. dCas13-based systems now allow site-specific m6A editing: Wilson and Chen showed that targeting METTL3 variants to nuclear or cytoplasmic compartments enables programmable methylation131, and Xia et al. demonstrated efficient locus-specific m6A installation or removal using dCasRx-METTL3 or dCasRx-ALKBH5 with minimal off-target activity132. While m6A remains the primary target, emerging efforts aim to expand editing to m5C and A-to-I.Beyond editing, synthetic RNA mimics containing chemically installed modifications and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) that block modification sites or alter local RNA structure represent versatile tools to study modification-mediated control of splicing, translation, and stability133.Single-Cell and Spatial Mapping of m6AEmerging single-cell and spatial profiling now reveal RNA modification heterogeneity with high granularity. Building on scDART-seq, which detects m6A via programmable base-editing readout, newer approaches now extend sensitivity and biological scope134. picoMeRIP-seq enables antibody-based m6A mapping from picogram-scale inputs, suitable for rare cell populations135,136. Scm6A infers single-cell m6A levels using machine-learning models trained on scRNA-seq features137. sn-m6A-CT adapts single-nucleus CUT&Tag for simultaneous profiling of m6A methylation and transcriptomic identity across thousands of nuclei138. Computational models such as SigRM reconstruct cell-type-specific modification trajectories from sparse data139, while spatially approaches like Select-seq integrate transcriptomic and positional data, enabling in situ epitranscriptomic landscapes140. TARS141 enables fluorescence-based, site-specific m6A quantification in single cells using padlock probe ligation and gap-filling amplification141. Together, these technologies establish a foundation for capturing RNA modification dynamics in single cells and structured tissues.Orthogonal validation: mass spectrometry (MS) and chromatographyWhile next-generation sequencing yields transcript-level maps of RNA modifications, MS and chromatography offer a complementary, chemistry-driven view142. Nucleoside LC-MS workflows, based on enzymatic hydrolysis, chromatographic separation, and stable-isotope labeled standards, established robust stoichiometry. Advances such as UHPLC, targeted MRM/SRM, and high-resolution MS have since expanded sensitivity and dynamic range for biomarker and pharmacodynamic studies143. At a more targeted level, partial-digest LC-MS/MS can localize modifications on specific oligonucleotides without antibody dependence, albeit with narrower coverage than transcriptome-wide assays144,145. In addition, MS-based proteomics is critical for identifying and characterizing RNA-binding proteins that interpret or regulate these marks.3Mechanistic Map: RNA Modifications and Cancer HallmarksRNA modifications are frequently dysregulated across cancers. With most regulators aberrantly overexpressed and some downregulated in specific contexts (see Figure 2). These alterations influence key cancer processes, including proliferation, stemness, metastasis, metabolic reprogramming, immune evasion, and therapy resistance. To support evidence-based interpretation, Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 summarize key regulators, alongside evidence tiers (human genetics, patient/PDX, mouse, cell lines), prognostic associations, and therapeutic relevance, enabling transparent appraisal while keeping the mechanistic narrative focused.We frame this review with reference to the updated Hallmarks of Cancer146, retaining six themes most strongly supported by current evidence and translational relevance: Sustaining Proliferative Signaling and Cell Survival; Enabling Cancer Cell Stemness; Activating Invasion & Metastasis; Reprogramming Metabolism; Immune Evasion & TME Interaction; and Therapeutic Resistance.Among these, the strongest evidence to date highlights stemness, metabolic reprogramming, and immune evasion as particularly critical hallmarks shaped by RNA modifications in cancer. Supplementary Table 4 maps the 2022 hallmarks to the six themes and indicates where each is covered in the review. Throughout, we qualify key claims by model and evidence tier, noting that “oncogenic” or “tumor-suppressive” roles are often context-dependent and may reflect essential RNA homeostasis rather than cancer-specific functions. This section examines how specific RNA modifications and regulators contribute to these cancer hallmarks (Figures 3 and 4, and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3).3.1Sustaining Proliferative Signaling and Cell SurvivalUncontrolled proliferation and resistance to growth-inhibitory cues are defined features of malignancy. A major growth-promoting mechanism is enhancement of oncogenic mRNA expression. METTL3/METTL14 install m6A on transcripts such as MYC, SOX2, EGFR, and TAZ in leukemia, glioblastoma (GBM), and lung cancers21,147–150. These marks are decoded by reader proteins (see Section 2.1) to enhance gene expression, YTHDF1 promotes translation and IGF2BP1-3 stabilize oncogenic transcripts such as KRAS and CDK6, sustaining proliferative signaling151. IGF2BPs also stabilize m6A-modified noncoding RNAs, including circNSUN2, circMDK, and lncRNA ZFAS1, reinforcing growth programs by modulating signaling and RNA-protein interactions152–154. m6A can also restrain cell proliferation. YTHDF2 promotes degradation of oncogenic mRNAs such as EGFR, acting as a negative regulator155. While YTHDF2 restrains gene expression post-transcriptionally, other m6A-interacting factors act earlier; RBFOX2, a noncanonical reader, recruits the methyltransferase complex to promoter-associated RNAs to drive chromatin-linked methylation, suppress differentiation programs, and sustain AML proliferation156.Whether m6A promotes or inhibits growth is highly context-dependent. FTO acts as an oncogenic driver in AML and glioma by demethylating and stabilizing MYC and CEBPA transcripts147,157,158. yet in HCC, ovarian, and thyroid cancers, its activity varies and may be growth-suppressive159–161. ALKBH5 similarly promotes proliferation in glioma and breast cancer162,163, but inhibits non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) growth by reducing m6A on YAP mRNA164. These contrasting outcomes underscore lineage-specific regulatory effects shaped by cell type, mutational status, and microenvironmental cues.Similarly, non-m6A RNA modifications also drive tumor growth through analogous mechanisms, sustaining proliferative signaling and cell survival by enhancing oncogene expression and/or repressing tumor-suppressive pathways. For instance, TET2 deficiency enhances m5C modifications on caRNA, promoting MBD6-mediated chromatin remodeling and activation of leukemogenic genes via global DNA hypomethylation48,165. Ψ also plays a crucial role in tumor proliferation. PUS1 enhances translation of oncogenic mRNAs such as IRS1 and MYC, supporting liver cancer progression166. TRUB1-mediated Ψ modification stabilizes oncogenic transcripts including ERH, SCP2, AMFR and CDC6109. DKC1 stabilizes ribosomal protein mRNAs (RPL10A, RPL22L1, etc.) through pseudouridylation in colorectal cancer, enhancing ribosome biogenesis and supporting rapid tumor cell proliferation167. A-to-I editing by ADARs modulates proliferative signaling in a context-dependent manner. For example, editing of COPA promotes tumor growth in breast cancer and its absence drives AML and liver cancer168–170. 2′-O-Me promotes translational efficiency of PARP1 and enhance endometrial cancer cell proliferation171. NAT10-catalyzed ac4C modification stabilizes CD2BP2-DT and promotes CDK1 expression, enhancing breast cancer proliferation172. TRMT6/61A-driven m1A modification in bladder cancer modulates the unfolded protein response to maintain tumor growth173. In uveal melanoma, ALKBH3 removes m1A from SP100A, impairing YTHDF1 recognition and destabilizing the tumor-suppressive PML complex174. METTL1-mediated m7G methylation enhances tRNA stability and translation of proliferation-associated genes (e.g., those in the EGFR pathway), driving intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma175. In ESCC, METTL1 and WDR4 support tumor survival by mTORC1 signalingl176. Similarly, enrichment of m7G-modified tRNAs such as Arg-TCT-4-1 selectively boosts AGA codon-driven oncogene translation177.Collectively, these RNA modifications orchestrate oncogenic programs by enhancing pro-proliferative and survival pathways and/or suppressing growth-inhibitory signals. They play central roles in sustaining proliferation and evading cell death across diverse cancers through both gene-specific and network-level mechanisms, underscoring RNA modification regulators as attractive therapeutic targets.3.2Maintaining Cancer Cell StemnessCancer stem cells (CSCs) retain long-term self-renewal and tumor-regenerating capacity, enabling differentiation evasion and post-therapy relapse. RNA modifications act as key post-transcriptional regulators that maintain stem-like states and tumor-initiating potential.The m6A machinery places a central role in CSC maintenance. METTL14 enhances leukemia stem/initiating cell (LSCs/LIC) self-renewal by increasing m6A on MYB and MYC, thereby promoting their stability and translation21. METTL16 is overexpressed in AML, particularly in LSCs/LICs, and supports their self-renewal178. In liver CSCs, METTL16 promotes rRNA maturation and mRNA translation, while METTL3 increases FZD10 expression via m6A to activate WNT/β-catenin and YAP1 signaling179,180. As an m6A eraser, ALKBH5 promotes LSC/LIC self-renewal in AML via enhancing expression of key targets such as TACC3 and AXL, and enhances NANOG and FOXM1 expression to maintain undifferentiated states in GBM and breast cancer162,163,181,182. IGF2BP2 supports CSC maintenance by stabilizing pluripotency-linked transcripts in glioma, liver cancer, and AML7,183–185. Notably, YTHDF2, typically decay-promoting, stabilizes MYC and VEGFR transcripts in GBM CSCs186. YTHDC1 forms phase-separated nuclear condensates that sequester m6A-modified RNAs in AML, preventing their decay and sustaining LSC self-renewal while sparing normal progenitors187.Beyond m6A, multiple non-m6A RNA modification machineries have also emerged as critical regulators of CSC self-renewal. Li et al. demonstrated that TET2 deficiency leads to increased m5C in Tspan13 mRNA to enhance its stability, leading to the activation of the Tspan13-Cxcr4 signaling axis and thereby enhanced LSC homing/self-renewal and leukemogenesis188. PUS7 is overexpressed and correlates with poor patient survival in GBM, in which PUS7-dependent tRNA pseudouridylation programs codon-specific translation to promote glioma stem cell (GSC) stemness189. The tRNA m1A methyltransferase TRMT6/TRMT61A promotes liver CSC self-renewal by boosting PPARδ translation, thereby enhancing cholesterol biosynthesis and activating Hedgehog signaling190. 2′-O-methylation cooperates with other RNA marks to control CSC-linked translation. In HCC, m6A-driven MIR4435-2HG stabilizes NOP58, lowers rRNA 2′-O-Me, and promotes IRES-dependent oncogene translation, reinforcing CSC traits191.In summary, RNA modifications preserve CSC identity by dynamically regulating gene expression post-transcriptionally, stabilizing self-renewal programs and suppressing differentiation, thereby sustaining tumor-initiating potential and revealing new therapeutic opportunities.3.3Activating Tumor Invasion and MetastasisEmerging evidence shows that RNA modifications also regulates tumor invasion and metastasis. In prostate cancer, altered m6A patterns, particularly at loci such as VCAN, associate with tumor invasion and poor prognosis192. METTL3 promotes metastasis across colorectal, gastric, lung, breast, and liver cancers by regulating pro-metastatic targets such as HDGF and ZMYM1, and pathways like MAPK and YTHDF2-SOCS2; collectively enhancing epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), invasion, and metastatic colonization148,193–197. In contrast, METTL14 restricts metastasis in hepatocellular, colorectal, renal, and bladder cancers by repressing pro-metastatic mRNAs (SOX4, ARRDC4, Notch1) and promoting of tumor-suppressive miRNA processing198–204. Their divergent roles likely reflect METTL3’s METTL14-independent functions and/or context-dependent regulatory specificity. Noncoding RNAs are key metastatic drivers, with their functions often shaped by m6A and reader-dependent mechanisms. In colorectal cancer, circNSUN2 promotes liver metastasis by enabling IGF2BP2-dependent stabilization of HMGA2, whereas circ-YAP increases a YAP-derived peptide via YTHDF3 to drive dissemination153,205. lncRNAs such as NEAT1 and XIST undergo YTHDF2-mediated degradation following methylation by METTL14; loss of METTL14 leads to their accumulate, which in turn promotes metastasis in renal and colorectal cancers206,207. In TNBC, demethylated LINC00115 escapes YTHDF2-dependent decay, activates HIF1α signaling, and drives chemoresistant dissemination208.Non-m6A RNA modifications also shape metastatic trajectories. NSUN5 binds the SMAD3 promoter to enhance its chromatin accessibility and transcription, elevating SMAD3 expression and activating EMT to drive HCC progression209. A-to-I editing of miR-589-3p at position +6 redirects its targeting from PCDH9 to the pro-invasive ADAM12 in GBM; while the unedited form promotes proliferation and migration, the edited form suppresses these traits, illustrating the context-dependent role of RNA editing in metastasis.210. Furthermore, ALKBH1, promotes colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis by demethylating the m1A-modified METTL3 mRNA, thereby driving EMT and metastatic progression211.Together, these findings illustrate how both m6A and non-m6A epitranscriptomic mechanisms coordinate complex regulatory networks that govern cancer cell plasticity, invasion, and dissemination.3.4Reprogramming Cancer MetabolismCancer cells adapt to nutrient and oxygen scarcity by rewiring glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism to balance biomass production and stress resistance. RNA modifications support this metabolic plasticity by controlling mRNA stability, translation, and localization.Glucose Metabolism and Stress AdaptationCancer cells preferentially adopt aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect) to support anabolic growth and survive in hypoxic, nutrient-poor environments212,213. m6A-dependent RNA regulation contributes to this shift by controlling glycolytic gene expression in both proliferative and stress-adaptive contexts. METTL3 promotes glycolysis across multiple cancers by altering rate-limiting enzymes and transporters (e.g., HK2, SLC2A1, ENO2, PDK4, SLC2A1, SLC2A4) through reader-mediated controls194,214–216. METTL14 is context-dependent, it augments glycolysis in gastric cancer (via LHPP downregulation) but reduces glycolysis in HCC and renal carcinoma (by destabilizing BPTF and stabilizing USP48, respectively)199,217,218. The m6A erasers also show cancer-type specificity. FTO promotes glycolysis in leukemia and several solid tumors (e.g., via PFKP/LDHB or chromatin programs) but reduces glycolysis in lung adenocarcinoma by dampening m6A-dependent MYC translation219,220,221. ALKBH5 facilitates glycolysis in breast cancer yet shifts metabolism toward oxidative phosphorylation in cervical and liver cancers216,222. Under stress, m6A also sustains glucose metabolism: in pancreatic cancer, ALKBH5 stabilizes HDAC4 to promote glycolysis and hypoxic adaptation through a HIF1α-feedback loop223.Lipid MetabolismCancer cells also reprogram lipid biosynthesis for membrane production and energy storage. In HCC, METTL3 stabilizes the lncRNA LINC00958 to increase lipogenic enzymes (FASN, ACC1)224. Similarly, in CRC, METTL3-mediated methylation upregulates POU6F2-AS1, which recruits YBX1 to activate FASN and drive lipid accumulation225. As an m6A eraser, FTO also links cellular metabolic status to RNA methylation. The metabolite NADP has been shown to activate FTO enzymatic activity, thereby enhancing m6A demethylation and promoting adipogenesis226. In contrast, ALKBH5 suppresses fatty acid synthesis in esophageal cancer by downregulating ACLY and ACC1, while hnRNPA2B1 counteracts this effect by promoting their expression227.Amino Acid MetabolismAmino acids supply nitrogen, carbon, and redox intermediates essential for tumor proliferation. m6A-dependent regulation provides flexible control of these pathways228. In AML, METTL3 and METTL14 enhance the stability and translation of transcripts encoding key glutaminolysis regulators (MYC and GPT2) and the transporter (SLC1A5) via IGF2BP2, thereby sustaining leukemic proliferation and LSC self-renewal29. Conversely, FTO loss in VHL-deficient renal carcinoma leads to hypermethylation and decay of SLC1A5, limiting glutamine uptake and impairing tumor viability229. These opposing roles illustrate how m6A dynamics fine-tune glutamine flux in a cancer-type-specific manner. m6A also governs BCAA metabolism. In AML, METTL16 methylates the transcripts of BCAT1/2 transcripts to promote BCAA catabolism, promoting leukemia progression178. The m6A reader IGF2BP3 stabilizes serine biosynthesis transcripts PHGDH and PSAT1, reinforcing serine-driven nucleotide synthesis and redox balance in AML230.Non-m6A modifications also play a role in regulating tumor metabolism. In MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma, PUS7 is transcriptionally activated by MYC/MYCN and drives metabolic reprogramming; its knockdown suppresses amino acid biosynthesis and related metabolic pathways, highlighting its role in sustaining tumor metabolism231. Transcriptome-wide profiling shows widespread PUS7-dependent pseudouridylation in neuroblastoma, reinforcing its role in metabolic gene regulation232. In osteosarcoma, NSUN2 stabilizes FABP5 mRNA to enhance lipid lipolysis and fatty acid metabolism, promoting tumor progression233. ALYREF also influences tumor metabolism by stabilizing PKM2 mRNA234. In TNBC, NAT10 increases ac4C on JunB mRNA to upregulate JunB and LDHA, enhance glycolysis, and drive malignant progression with immune suppression235. NAT10-mediated ac4C enhances translation of SLC1A4, HOXA9, and MENIN to boost serine uptake and synthesis, thereby promoting leukemia progression236.Together, RNA modifications enable cancer cells to post-transcriptionally rewire metabolism in a nutrient- and context-dependent manner. By regulating anabolic enzymes and stress-adaptive pathways, they link environmental cues to the metabolic programs that support malignant growth.3.5Immune evasion & microenvironmental interactionTo evade immune surveillance, tumors create an immune-cold microenvironment characterized by impaired antigen presentation, dampened innate activation, and increased immunosuppressive infiltration. RNA modifications regulate these processes in diverse, context-specific ways. This section summarizes how they help establish and sustain an immune-cold tumor microenvironment (TME).Blocking Immune Recognition by Adaptive Immunitym6A modification regulates immune checkpoint expression through context-specific mechanisms. In AML, FTO promotes the m6A-dependent upregulation of PD-L1, PD-L2, and LILRB4, supporting immune evasion and disease progression158. In melanoma, inhibiting ALKBH5 enhances the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy237. In HCC, IGF2BP1 stabilizes m6A-modified PD-L1 transcripts, correlating with reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration238. Conversely, YTHDF2 promotes PD-L1 decay in other settings, highlighting context dependence239.m6A also influences antigen presentation and interferon signaling. In AML, METTL3 and IGF2BP3 stabilize CD47 and LGALS9, impairing T- and NK-cell recognition50. In dendritic cells (DCs), YTHDF1 enhances translation of lysosomal cathepsins, accelerating antigen degradation and impaired cross-presentation via MHC-I240. METTL3 promotes DC-mediated T-cell priming by increasing co-stimulatory molecules (CD40, CD80, TIRAP)241. m6A also shapes interferon signaling: METTL3/METTL14 methylate IFNB1 mRNA for YTHDF2-mediated decay, and loss of this pathway stabilizes IFNB1 and elevates IFN-β production242,243. Together, these mechanisms weaken adaptive antitumor immunity.Suppressing Innate Immune TriggersTumors also silence innate immune activation through m6A-dependent regulation of RNA sensing and inflammatory signaling. Endogenous circRNAs carry m6A marks that recruit YTHDF2, preventing their detection as non-self and limiting innate activation, whereas unmodified exogenous circRNAs trigger strong immune responses, indicating that m6A serves as a molecular “self” signature244. Consistently, METTL3 inhibition restores innate sensing by promoting dsRNA accumulation and activating type I IFN signaling245. Ψ in-vitro transcribed (IVT) mRNA has also been shown to suppress innate immune triggers246,247, highlighting its role in regulating innate immune response.Establishing and Reinforcing an Immunosuppressive MicroenvironmentRNA modifications contribute to immunosuppressive TME remodeling in cancer. In myeloid cells, METTL3 enhances JAK-STAT3 signaling, which promotes the immunosuppressive activity of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs)248. In CRC, ALKBH5 sustains an immunosuppressive TME by stabilizing AXIN2, activating Wnt signaling and inducing DKK1-mediated expansion of suppressive myeloid populations249. In CD4+ T cells and Tregs, METTL3 promotes IL-7 and IL-2-STAT5 signaling by destabilizing SOCS transcripts250. In NK cells, METTL3 and YTHDF2 facilitate terminal maturation and cytotoxic activity251. In macrophages, METTL14-mediated methylation regulates EBI3 expression, indirectly contributing to CD8+ T cell exhaustion252. These effects are reinforced by microenvironment stress. Hypoxia and NF-κB activation, common features of solid tumors, upregulate FTO and ALKBH5, thereby enhancing m6A-dependent stabilization of immune-suppressive transcripts and immune checkpoint regulators7,253,254. This establishes a feedback loop in which environmental stress sustain immune evasion through epitranscriptomic modulation. System-wide coordination across tumor and immune cells further amplifies these effects. In AML, METTL3 and IGF2BP3 not only regulate immune evasion within leukemic cells but also reprogram Tregs, TAMs, and DCs, creating an immunosuppressive network resistant to therapy255.Recent studies have also highlighted the immunomodulatory potential of non-m6A RNA modifications, including A-to-I editing, m1A, m5C, and m7G. ADAR1-mediated A-to-I editing maintains innate immune tolerance. Its loss reduces editing of interferon-stimulated dsRNA, triggering MDA5 activation, elevating type I interferons, and enhancing antitumor immunity in melanoma, thereby sensitizing tumors to PD-1 blockade and overcoming resistance256. ADAR1 can also drive immune escape: by editing DDX58, it induces PTIR1, which engages the deubiquitinase UCHL5 to suppress immunoproteasome activity, impair neoantigen processing, and block T-cell recognition, promoting immunotherapy resistance257. TRMT61A functions in both immunosuppressive and immune-activating contexts. In HNSCC, it enhances MYC translation to upregulate PD-L1 and promote immune evasion258, whereas in CD8+ T cells, TRMT61A-mediated m1A boosts ACLY translation, strengthening cytotoxic function and antitumor immunity259. NAT10 is upregulated upon TCR engagement, and its T cell-specific deletion reduces naïve T cells and weakens antiviral responses, indicating a role in T cell homeostasis and activation260. In HCC and HNSCC, it promotes tumor progression and immune suppression by enhancing the translation of TGF-β2 and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, respectively261 262. Conversely, in prostate cancer, METTL1 loss generates tRNA fragments that enhance translation of immune effector genes, thereby strengthening antitumor immunity263.In summary, RNA modifications shape the immune-cold phenotype by limiting antigen recognition, suppressing innate sensing, and remodeling the immune milieu. These layered effects position the epitranscriptome as a central driver of immune escape and a promising therapeutic axis to restore antitumor immunity and overcome resistance to immunotherapy.3.6Influencing Drug Sensitivity and Therapeutic ResistanceTherapy resistance remains a major challenge in cancer, driving relapse, metastasis, and poor outcomes. RNA modifications play key roles in regulating responses to chemo-, radio-, targeted, and immunotherapies by post-transcriptionally controlling DNA repair, apoptosis, metabolism, and immune evasion pathways.As a major m6A writer, METTL3 contributes to therapy resistance. In GSCs, it methylates and stabilizes SOX2 mRNA to enhance DNA repair and promote radioresistance150. METTL3 enhances LDHA translation in CRC, supporting glycolysis-dependent resistance to 5-FU264, and methylates FZD10 mRNA in HCC, promoting lenvatinib resistance180. In melanoma, METTL3 increases EGFR translation, contributing to acquired resistance to BRAF inhibitors265. Its depletion sensitizes pancreatic cancer to gemcitabine, cisplatin, and 5-FU253,266. Reader proteins also control resistance. IGF2BP1 forms condensates that shield m6A-marked ITGB1 mRNA from degradation, promoting survival under cisplatin treatment267. In CRC, YTHDF1 drives 5-FU and oxaliplatin resistance, and its loss restores drug sensitivity268, while YTHDF2 supports immunosuppressive myeloid programs, and its depletion enhances antitumor immunity and radiosensitivity249.m6A erasers introduce additional resistance control. In AML, inhibition of FTO by R-2-hydroxyglutarate (R-2HG) increases m6A levels and destabilizes oncogenic transcripts, thereby sensitizing leukemic cells to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), 5-azacytidine, decitabine, and daunorubicin157. In BRCA-mutant ovarian cancer, FTO downregulation increases m6A on FZD10, reducing resistance to PARP inhibitors269. In GBM, ALKBH5 supports radioresistance by maintaining the expression of DNA repair genes270. In cervical squamous cell carcinoma, FTO demethylates and stabilizes β-catenin mRNA, increasing ERCC1 activity and promoting chemoradiotherapy resistance271.m6A-modified noncoding RNAs also drive resistance. In hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, METTL16 increases m6A on circCUX1 to enhance tumor cell survival under irradiation272. In HCC, circMAP3K4 is methylated and recognized by IGF2BP1, promoting translation of a peptide that suppresses apoptosis and enhances cisplatin resistance273. In ovarian cancer, circPLPP4 is stabilized by m6A and functions as a sponge for miR-136, leading to increased PIK3R1 expression and reduced cisplatin sensitivity274. Transcriptomic profiling in breast cancer stem-like cells exposed to paclitaxel revealed m6A-regulated long noncoding RNAs associated with chemoresistance208.Non-m6A RNA modifications also shape therapy resistance. NSUN2-driven m5C methylation, including stabilization of TREX2 mRNA, limits cytoplasmic dsDNA accumulation, dampens cGAS-STING signaling, and promotes immune evasion under PD-L1 blockade275. ALKBH1 is overexpressed in AML and essential for LSC self-renewal while dispensable for normal hematopoiesis276. By installing f5C at tRNA wobble sites, it reprograms codon-biased translation to enhance OXPHOS, leukemogenesis, and venetoclax resistance; ALKBH1 inhibition markedly sensitizes AML to venetoclax, and triple therapy with venetoclax and azacitidine shows strong synergistic activity, highlighting ALKBH1 as a promising target to overcome drug resistance276. In NSCLC, YBX1 recognizes m5C-modified QSOX1 mRNA to enhance its translation, driving gefitinib resistance and tumor recurrence277. A-to-I editing also modulates therapeutic responses in a transcript-specific manner. Pan-cancer analyses show that editing of COG3 and GRIA2 correlates with increased sensitivity to selected targeted drugs, whereas AZIN1 editing is linked to reduced responsiveness278. In T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), ADAR1-mediated editing of immunogenic dsRNA supports LSC/LIC self-renewal, drives relapse, and contributes to chemotherapy resistance279. In HCC, METTL1-mediated m7G tRNA modification enhances translation of DNA-PKcs and LIG4 after irradiation, promoting non-homologous end joining and increasing radioresistance280. As readers of m7G, QKIs, especially QKI7, also influence therapy response by modulating translational programs relevant to drug sensitivity84.Overall, evidence most strongly links RNA modifications to cancer stemness, metabolic reprogramming, and immune modulation, highlighting these processes as especially promising for translational exploration.4Functional Interdependencies and Emerging Concepts4.1Cross-talk among different RNA modificationsRNA modifications function within an interconnected system rather than as isolated marks. Crosstalk among m6A, A-to-I editing, m5C, and Ψ is increasingly evident in cancer (see Figure 5 upper panel). A prominent example is the interaction between m6A and A-to-I editing, which can be antagonistic or cooperative depending on context. In human stem cells, m6A limits A-to-I editing by disrupting dsRNA structures required for ADAR1 recognition281. Depletion of METTL3 or METTL14 increases A-to-I editing levels across hundreds of sites, suggesting that m6A suppresses ADAR1 substrate accessibility by altering RNA conformation281. In tumor, this relationship can reverse. In GBM, METTL3 adds m6A to ADAR1 mRNA, which is recognized by YTHDF1 to promote translation282. Under cytokine stimulation, m6A-YTHDF1 signaling increases expression of the IFN-inducible ADAR1p150 isoform, elevating A-to-I editing and modulating innate immune responses283.m6A also interacts with m5C in cancer-related pathways. On the p21 transcript, METTL3-mediated m6A promotes nearby NSUN2-catalyzed m5C, and the co-modified mRNA exhibits enhanced stability and translation under stress284. At systems level, m6A and m5C pathways appear co-regulated. For instance, m6A effectors such as METTL14, WTAP, and YTHDF2 are co-expressed with m5C writers and readers including NSUN4, ALYREF, and YBX1285. These modules are enriched in pathways related to mitochondrial metabolism, translation, and chromatin regulation, key hallmarks of tumor adaptation285.YTHDF2 represents a central node in this crosstalk. In B cell malignancies, it binds both m6A- and m5C-modified RNAs but executes distinct functions50. As an m6A reader, YTHDF2 destabilizes immune-related transcripts, whereas as an m5C reader, it stabilizes mRNAs encoding mitochondrial ATPase components to support tumor metabolism50. This dual-reader capability allows cancer cells to integrate modification signals across different layers of post-transcriptional control. Supporting this interdependency, single-molecule mapping confirms that m6A and m5C frequently co-occur on the same transcripts across cell types, including cancers128.The relationship between m6A and Ψ is indirect but functionally relevant: m6A promotes local unwinding, whereas Ψ stabilizes base stacking. These opposing structural effects can converge on shared outcomes—for example, both weaken RBP binding (e.g., PUM2), and when co-present, further reduce binding affinity286. Nanopore-based single-molecule sequencing further reveals opposing transcriptome-wide co-occurrence patterns for m6A and Ψ, yet synergistic and hierarchical effects on mRNA translation125.Together, these findings show that RNA modifications in cancer rarely act alone but form cooperative or competitive relationships through spatial proximity, structural effects, and shared readers. Current evidence highlights co-occurrence and context-dependent coordination among m6A, A-to-I, m5C, and Ψ; however, whether distinct marks form stable hierarchical relationships (e.g., a reader of one mark recruiting a writer or eraser of another) remains unclear. Mapping these interdependencies will help explain how cancer cells use RNA modifications to fine-tune gene expression, respond to stress, and maintain fitness, and underscores inter-mark crosstalk as an important area for future investigation.4.2Crosstalk Between RNA Modifications and Chromatin/DNA Regulation in CancerRNA modifications are embedded in the DNA/histone epigenetic landscape, forming a bidirectional relationship in which chromatin features shape RNA-modification patterns, and RNA modifications, in turn, influence chromatin state, histone marks, DNA methylation, and transcription. This layered regulatory architecture is particularly relevant in cancer (Figure 5 lower panel).Chromatin marks can locally guide RNA modification deposition. A key example is H3K36me3, which is added co-transcriptionally and directly recognized by METTL14 to promote m6A installation on nascent pre-mRNAs at exons and 3′UTRs, linking active chromatin to mRNA stability and translation13. Chromatin can also regulates RNA-modifying enzymes. In AML, the histone demethylase KDM4C remodels chromatin at the ALKBH5 locus, elevating expression of this m6A eraser, which stabilizes oncogenic transcripts such as AXL by removing m6A marks, thereby promoting LSC maintenance287.Just as chromatin guides RNA modification, modified RNAs can reciprocally influence chromatin structure, histone marks, and DNA methylation, with m6A readers linking these RNAs to chromatin modifiers. FXR1 recruits TET1 to m6A-marked RNAs, guiding site-specific DNA demethylation and chromatin opening, thereby regulating gene transcription in an m6A-dependent manner288. In human embryonic stem cells, YTHDC2 binds m6A-modified HERVH RNAs to recruit TET1, maintaining DNA hypomethylation at these elements and linking RNA modification to chromatin regulation289. RNA modifications also affect heterochromatin. TET2 oxidizes m5C on retrotransposon RNAs, which are bound by MBD6 to recruit a deubiquitinase that removes H2AK119ub and promotes chromatin de-repression290. Conversely, m6A-marked repetitive RNAs such as LINE1 and IAP recruit YTHDC1, which scaffolds SETDB1 and TRIM28 to deposit H3K9me3, reinforcing silencing and maintaining epigenetic stability291–294. RNA modifications also regulate chromatin modifiers post-transcriptionally. In stratified epithelia, METTL3-mediated m6A promotes degradation of histone methyltransferase mRNAs; METTL3 loss stabilizes these transcripts, increases H3K4 methylation, and disrupts gene expression, a pattern also observed in head and neck cancer295. CFL1 acts as a METTL3 cofactor to enhance m6A on super-enhancer RNAs, which recruit YTHDC2 and MLL1 to promote co-transcriptional H3K4me3, increase chromatin accessibility, and drive oncogene transcription in PDAC296.Together, these studies show that RNA modifications act as both integrators and modulators of chromatin state. By recruiting histone modifiers, altering DNA methylation, and regulating chromatin-regulating transcripts, RNA modifications establish feedback that enables cancer cells to tune epigenetic states, maintain stemness, repress transposable elements, and activate lineage-defining enhancers to support tumor progression and plasticity.4.3Epitranscriptomic Heterogeneity at Single-Cell and Spatial ResolutionHigh-resolution single-cell and spatial profiling now reveals extensive heterogeneity in RNA modifications. Marks such as m6A and A-to-I vary across cell types and even among individual cells within the same tissue, adding regulatory nuance that may underlie tumor phenotypic diversity.Single-cell m6A mapping shows that bulk averages mask substantial variation in methylation stoichiometry. scDART-seq uncovered cell-specific m6A patterns independent of transcript abundance or cell cycle, with low-bulk sites highly modified in select subpopulations134. In cancer, such heterogeneity may fuel lineage plasticity, environmental adaptability, and therapy-resistant reservoirs.Achieving true single-cell epitranscriptomic resolution remains challenging. Methods like scDART-seq rely on engineered reader-editor fusions (e.g., APOBEC1-YTH) to mark m6A via base editing, limiting use in primary samples and in vivo contexts. Additional barriers include background editing noise, context-dependent RNA accessibility, and limited detection of m5C and Ψ, though emerging computational frameworks help extend current method. SigRM, a recent model-based framework, improves single-cell m6A site detection and enables inference of cell type-specific methylation trajectories and regulatory networks260. These advances are key steps toward quantitative maps of RNA modifications in complex tissues, though further refinement is needed to extend across modification types and biological contexts.Spatial epitranscriptomics is beginning to resolve tissue architecture of RNA modification programs. Select-seq mapped A-to-I editing in TNBC, revealing CSC-enriched regions with elevated GPX4 editing linked to ferroptosis resistance and outcomes, underscoring the clinical relevance of spatial RNA modification140. However, limitations such as RNA degradation in sections, low throughput of laser-capture-based methods, and read accuracy still constrain detection of rare or transient events.As single-cell and spatial profiling advance, linking RNA modifications to cellular states, lineage trajectories, and tumor niches will become increasingly feasible. High-resolution mapping of epitranscriptomic diversity will help dissect intratumoral heterogeneity and reveal context-specific vulnerabilities. Integrating these data with proteomic, epigenomic, and spatial chromatin maps will be essential for a multidimensional understanding of cancer cell identity.5Therapeutic Insights and ProspectsRecognizing RNA modifications as adaptive regulators of cancer phenotypes is accelerating their translation into therapies (Figure 6). Owing to their dynamic and reversible nature, these marks offer a programmable layer for intervention, and their regulatory machinery, including writers, erasers, readers, and cofactors across m6A and non-m6A pathways, represents an attractive entry point for precision oncology.5.1Targeting m6A RegulatorsSmall-molecule inhibitors against dysregulated m6A regulators (writers, erasers and readers) have introduced a new dimension to cancer therapy (see Supplementary Table 5 for the relevant inhibitors reported so far). FTO is the most intensively studied, particularly in AML, GBM, and lung cancer. Early inhibitors such as Rhein and meclofenamic acid (MA and MA2) restored m6A methylation and suppressed oncogenic programs297–299. Later-generation agents such as FB23-2 and CS1/CS2 improved selectivity and metabolic stability, enabling in vivo efficacy in leukemic models158,300. Dac51 further expanded this class by targeting FTO to impair immune evasion and metabolic resilience through PD-L1 degradation and glycolytic suppression220. Other strategies exploit metabolic vulnerabilities: the oncometabolite R-2HG inhibits FTO enzymatic activity and sensitizes AML cells to ATRA and hypomethylating agents157. A more recent compound, FTO-04, targets stemness programs in glioma cells via FTO’s catalytic pocket301. Beyond enzymatic inhibition, PROTAC degraders such as FP54, derived from the FTO inhibitor FB23, selectively degrade FTO in AML, increase m6A on ribosome biogenesis transcripts, enhance YTHDF2-mediated decay, disrupt ribosome assembly and translation, and suppress AML progression302. Parallel advances have been made for the demethylase ALKBH5. Inhibitors such as MV1035 and 20m increase m6A levels and impair GBM and leukemia progression303,304, while ALK-04 has emerged as a promising candidate for immunomodulatory combinations305. Recent covalent ALKBH5 chemotypes (e.g., 18I) show selective, cell-active inhibition, underscoring tractability and providing clearer PD linkage in preclinical models306.Therapeutic inhibition of writers has gained traction with the development of METTL3-selective compounds. The tool compound STM2457 demonstrated promising anti-leukemic activity with minimal toxicity in preclinical systems307. Other methyltransferase inhibitors, such as UZH1a and UZH2, are now available to support chemical probe validation294. A first-in-human METTL3 inhibitor, STC-15, is now in Phase I, with interim PK/PD and activity readouts reported, establishing clinical feasibility for writer targeting308.Targeting m6A reader proteins has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy in cancer and immune regulation. Among the YTH domain-containing proteins, YTHDF2 has been the most actively explored. Small-molecule inhibitors such as CCI-38 disrupt YTHDF2-m6A/m5C interactions, suppress tumor growth, restore CD19/MHC-II expression, and enhance CAR-T efficacy in B-cell malignancies50. DC-Y13-27 impairs YTHDF2 function in MDSCs, enhancing radiosensitivity by reducing MDSC-mediated immunosuppression and promoting antitumor immunity309. Droperidol, repurposed from clinical use, selectively binds the YTH domain to inhibit YTHDF2-driven translation and reverse paclitaxel resistance310. Y2-IN-1, discovered via virtual screening, also targets the YTHDF2-m6A interaction and is under early-stage evaluation311. DF-A7, preferentially induces YTHDF2 degradation, which shows a potent antitumor effect alone but a better effect when combined with anti-PD-L1 or anti-PD-1 antibodies312. For YTHDC1, a nuclear reader regulating splicing and mRNA export, inhibitor such as compound 40 selectively target the m6A-binding pocket and induce apoptosis in leukemia313. The IGF2BP family (IGF2BP1/2/3), which stabilizes oncogenic mRNAs like MYC and KRAS, has also gained traction. IGF2BP1 inhibitors such as BTYNB block RNA-binding domains, destabilize target transcripts, and suppress tumor growth; IGF2BP2 inhibitors such as CWI1-2 and JX5 interfere with KH domain-mediated RNA binding and show efficacy in leukemia and glioma models, respectively; Direct inhibitors for IGF2BP3 remain elusive, though its expression can be downregulated indirectly via BET inhibition29,314,315.Together, these compounds (Supplementary Table 5) represent the first generation of m6A regulator-targeted therapeutics. While most remain preclinical, clinical evaluation has begun for a METTL3 inhibitor, and these agents collectively establish proof-of-concept for drugging m6A recognition and catalysis.5.2Targeting non-m6A RegulatorsGiven the key role of m5C regulators in cancer, targeting m5C “writers” like NSUN2 and NSUN3 has become a growing focus. Cysteine-directed activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) technology identified a stereoselective covalent NSUN2 inhibitor, azetidine acrylamide, which blocks tRNA binding, reduces m5C levels, and suppresses tumor progression316. Nsun2-i4 is a small-molecule inhibitor targeting NSUN2, which inhibits CRC progression, showing its safety and synergy with PD- . A novel bipyridine derivative, B19, designed based on the structure of carubicin A, can specifically bind to the NSUN3 protein and inhibit CRC proliferation and migration318.Currently, some inhibitors targeting pseudouridylation enzymes have been gradually characterized. Mogroside IV-E was identified as a specific PUS1 inhibitor, which exhibits a strong anti-metastatic effect on prostate cancer by reducing the expression of PUS1319. C17 is a chemical inhibitor of PUS7, which can prevent the pseudouridylation mediated by PUS7 and inhibit tumorigenesis189. Combination of a DKC1 inhibitor (pyrazofurin) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor) has been shown to synergistically inhibit the growth of CRC cells167.ADAR1 inhibitor, ZYS-1, significantly inhibits prostate cancer growth and metastasis, while enhancing anti-tumor immune response255. Rebecsinib, another ADAR1 inhibitor, impairs LSC self-renewal, showing favorable toxicokinetics and pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) profiles320. AVA-ADR-001 targets the Zα domain of ADAR1p150 and exerts multi-faceted anti-tumor effects by enhancing immune responses, promoting interferon accumulation, and activating PKR, leading to inhibited protein translation and cell cycle arrest321. 8-azanebularine, a free nucleoside, inhibits the ADAR2 response322.5.3Combination Strategies: Enhancing Therapeutic EfficacyRather than functioning as stand-alone interventions, RNA modifications-targeted agents appear to act as sensitizers, disrupting resistance circuits and amplifying the effects of immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy. In the immunotherapy context, compounds like FTO inhibitors CS1, CS2 and Dac51 and ALKBH5 inhibitor ALK-04 have demonstrated synergy with T-cell therapy or PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in AML, lung cancer and melanoma158,220,237. Similarly, YTHDF2 inhibitor CCI-38 can overcome tumor immune evasion by restoring CD19 and MHC-II expression and enhancing CAR-T cell efficacy in B-cell malignancies50. m6A regulation also intersects with chemoresistance. Suppression of FTO, either genetically or via R-2HG, restores sensitivity to agents such as ATRA, azacitidine, and daunorubicin in AML and glioma, while METTL3 knockdown sensitizes pancreatic cancer to cisplatin and 5-FU157,266. The YTHDF2 inhibitor droperidol blocks YTHDF2-driven translation and reverses paclitaxel resistance310. For radiotherapy, m6A regulators modulate DNA damage responses. METTL3-driven stabilization of transcripts such as H2AX, SOX2, and circCUX1 mediates resistance in NSCLC and glioma150,272,323, while ALKBH5 and FTO contribute to post-radiation survival via chromatin and signaling reprogramming270,271. The YTHDF2 inhibitor DC-Y13-27 enhances radiosensitivity by targeting YTHDF2 in MDSCs, reducing immunosuppressive activity and promoting antitumor immunity309. Lastly, m6A modulation has been linked to targeted therapy outcomes. METTL3 enhances resistance to BRAF inhibitors by promoting EGFR translation in melanoma265, and FTO activity drives adaptive resistance to BCR-ABL1 TKIs in CML297. In BRCA-mutant ovarian cancer, FTO and ALKBH5 depletion reactivates homologous recombination via FZD10 hypermethylation, reducing PARP inhibitor efficacy269. Together, these findings suggest that RNA modification-targeted therapies may serve as “response amplifiers” that augment existing therapies by disrupting resistance and immunosuppressive programs. This reinforces the rationale for pairing RNA-modification-regulator inhibitors (i.e., RNA-modulating agents) with existing regimens in future clinical designs.Beyond pairing RNA-modulating agents with cytotoxic, targeted, or immune therapies, dual targeting across epitranscriptomic axes represents a plausible next step. Published in vivo combination data across distinct RNA-modification pathways remain limited; testable hypotheses include m6A-pathway modulation with A-to-I (ADAR1) inhibition to amplify endogenous dsRNA/type I IFN signaling, writer-reader co-inhibition to curtail compensatory stabilization/translation, and joint m6A and m7G (METTL1) targeting to converge on translational control in MYC-high contexts. Prospective evaluation should incorporate mechanism-linked pharmacodynamic biomarkers and safety monitoring.5.4Emerging Technologies and Biomarker PotentialBuilding on pharmacologic and combinatorial advances, recent efforts have turned to leveraging the regulatory logic of RNA modifications for diagnostic innovation and precision intervention. Rather than simply inhibiting RNA modification regulators, these approaches leverage the sequence specificity and dynamic nature of RNA marks to improve diagnosis, classification, therapeutic design, and disease monitoring. Complementary advances are occurring in epitranscriptomic editing. Although still in early conceptual stages, editing tools such as CRISPR-Cas13 and programmable RNA modification writers or erasers have been proposed for selectively editing specific marks on target transcripts, offering a route to post-transcriptional therapeutic control without altering the genome7.m6A and its regulators are emerging as diagnostic and predictive biomarkers. The landscape of m6A as well as the expression levels of METTL3, FTO, and IGF2BPs have been associated with prognosis, recurrence risk, and therapeutic response across several cancers7,192,253. The differential m6A modifications can distinguish PDAC patients into two subtypes with different prognosis outcome324. More recently, He and colleagues showed that tumor-specific m6A patterns correlate with disease aggression and prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma and prostate cancer, further underscoring the potential of m6A dysregulation as a clinically informative biomarker192,325. Refined tools such as the “m6A score” derived from multi-gene expression models, have been shown to stratify patients by likely benefit from chemotherapy or immunotherapy326. In addition, m6A-modified circulating RNAs detected in plasma or serum have shown promise as non-invasive biomarkers for early detection and treatment monitoring in cancer, though further development and clinical validation of standardized detection platforms are needed327. Circulating cell-free RNA (cfRNA) offers a promising biomarker for cancer detection. He and colleagues developed low-input multiple methylation sequencing to profile RNA modifications in cfRNA, revealing diverse human and microbiome-derived tRNAs and small noncoding RNAs; notably, microbiome cfRNA modification patterns reflect microbial activity and enable early colorectal cancer detection328.During tumorigenesis, cancer cells accumulate numerous mutations, including synonymous mutations that do not alter the amino acids. Thousands of synonymous mutations in cancer genomes that can disrupt m6A modification, with functional evidence showing that some serve as oncogenic drivers329,330. This mechanism may help explain cancer pathogenesis in patients without missense or nonsense mutations but carrying synonymous alterations. These mutations may also serve as promising clinical biomarkers and targets for editing-based therapeutics.Together, these advances highlight the potential of the m6A machinery as a programmable layer linking RNA biology to clinical application. As these technologies mature, RNA modification-guided strategies may become essential tools in personalized RNA-centric cancer care.6.s, Challenges and Future DirectionsRNA modifications have emerged as critical regulators of cancer biology, shaping RNA fate and function through context-specific and dynamically regulated mechanisms. These marks intersect with key oncogenic signaling pathways such as MYC, PI3K/AKT, and TP53, and influence nearly every cancer hallmark, from proliferation and metabolic rewiring to immune evasion, stemness, and therapy resistance. Rather than acting in isolation, RNA modifications function within integrated regulatory networks, where their impact depends on cell state, environmental cues, and cross-regulation with other epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms.Despite major advances, several challenges remain. One key gap is understanding the functional specificity of each RNA modification in a given tumor context. It remains unclear how the same chemical mark can exert distinct effects across different cell types, disease stages, or oncogenic settings. Another emerging question involves the interplay between modifications: how multiple RNA marks on the same or different transcripts might cooperate or compete to fine-tune gene expression. Additionally, the temporal dynamics of RNA modifications in response to extrinsic stressors such as therapy, inflammation, or metabolic perturbation are only beginning to be explored. Emerging links between RNA modifications and replicative immortality and cellular senescence warrant systematic investigation.From a translational standpoint, RNA modifications offer a promising but still underdeveloped therapeutic frontier. Writers and erasers are enzymatically active and often druggable, and several small-molecule inhibitors targeting regulators of m6A and other modifications are in preclinical development. However, targeting their readers is more challenging. Tumor heterogeneity further complicates translation, as the impact of RNA modification perturbation can vary substantially across subclones and microenvironmental niches. The dual and sometimes opposing roles of regulators such as METTL3, which is oncogenic in some contexts but tumor-suppressive in others, underscore the need for context-aware models and predictive biomarkers that capture disease stage, lineage, and molecular dependencies. Several enzymes, such as METTL3 and METTL16, exert both catalytic and non-catalytic functions in cancer, which may limit the efficacy of inhibitors that target only their enzymatic activity. Furthermore, challenges remain in achieving isoform-specific inhibition, minimizing off-target effects, and identifying predictive biomarkers of response. Moreover, the clinical integration of RNA modification-based diagnostics and therapeutics will require robust functional validation, spatiotemporal profiling, and context-aware modeling of RNA regulation across diverse cancers.Moving forward, addressing these challenges will require interdisciplinary efforts combining structural biology, single-cell and spatial epitranscriptomics, proteogenomics, and high-throughput perturbation screens. Elucidating how RNA modifications contribute to tumor plasticity, immune escape, and therapeutic resistance will unlock new opportunities for precision oncology. Ultimately, the integration of RNA modification biology into clinical paradigms holds immense potential to reshape cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.Supplementary Material1Supplementary Table 1: Global mapping technologies.Supplementary Table 2: Overview of RNA m6A modifications, associated regulators, hallmark functions, and related tumor typesSupplementary Table 3: Overview of RNA non-m6A modifications, associated regulators, hallmark functions, and related tumor typesSupplementary Table 4: Alignment of RNA modification-associated processes with updated cancer hallmarks (Hanahan, 2022).Supplementary Table 5: Overview of inhibitors targeting RNA -modification regulators
