title: Mitotic catastrophe–related six-gene signature predicts prognosis, tumor immune landscape, and therapeutic response in lung adenocarcinoma
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) exhibits significant molecular and immune heterogeneity, limiting the prognostic and therapeutic value of single biomarkers. Mitotic catastrophe (MC) is a key biological axis, but externally validated MC-related gene (MCRG) signatures integrating immune and pharmacologic annotations remain lacking.We obtained datasets from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) databases. Differentially expressed genes overlapping with mitotic catastrophe–related genes (MCRGs) were screened. GSVA-derived MCRG scores guided WGCNA to identify associated modules; after KEGG/GO-BP enrichment and mutation analysis, a six-gene RiskScore model was constructed via LASSO-Cox and multivariate Cox regression. Immune microenvironment was analyzed by ESTIMATE and MCPcounter; ICI responsiveness by TIDE; drug sensitivity by pRRophetic. Wet-lab validation included qPCR, CCK-8, and siRNA-mediated GNPNAT1 knockdown assays.A total of 2,290 upregulated and 1,959 downregulated genes were identified, with 266 overlapping MCRGs. The turquoise module showed the highest correlation with MCRG scores, and 940 overlapping genes were enriched in pathways like p53 signaling. The six-gene model (GNPNAT1, etc.) effectively stratified OS, PFI, and DSS in TCGA and was validated in GSE31210. High-risk tumors had lower immune scores, depleted key immune lineages, poor ICI response, and correlated with various drug IC50 values. Wet-lab assays confirmed abnormal expression of target genes in LUAD cells, and GNPNAT1 silencing inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion.The MC-related molecular axis integrates tumor proliferation-metabolism-immunity networks, providing actionable guidance for perioperative and translational therapeutic stratification.We proposed an MC-anchored six-gene signature integrating prognostic, immune, and therapeutic dimensions in LUAD. This exploratory study has biological plausibility, but prospective multi-center studies are required before clinical application.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at
full_text: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common histological subtype of non–small-cell lung cancer and exhibits pronounced heterogeneity at molecular, pathological, and tumor-microenvironmental levels [1–3]. This cross-genomic, histologic, and immunologic heterogeneity directly affects staging assessment, prognostication, and treatment-response prediction, thereby increasing the complexity of precision oncology [4–6]. Although advances in targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in both perioperative and advanced-disease settings have improved outcomes for selected patients, overall population-level survival gains remain limited, and optimal patient selection and treatment sequencing are not yet fully defined [7, 8]. Real-world studies further show that, among patients lacking actionable driver alterations or those receiving later-line therapy after prior chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy, median survival remains suboptimal, underscoring the clinical need for improved stratification tools [9]. The performance of single biomarkers (e.g., PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, TMB) varies across assay platforms, clinical contexts, and temporal/spatial heterogeneity, which constrains their generalizability and decision utility [10–12].Mitotic catastrophe (MC) refers to cell death or irreversible growth arrest associated with aberrant mitosis that is triggered by perturbations such as DNA damage, defects in the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), or mitotic slippage, and it is regarded as an important tumor-suppressive barrier [13, 14]. MC is tightly linked to chromosomal instability (CIN) and aneuploidy dynamics—genomic events that can drive tumor progression and co-evolve with therapy resistance [15, 16]. Therapeutically, microtubule inhibitors, DNA-damage/DNA-damage-response (DDR) pathway inhibitors, and cell-cycle checkpoint agents can induce MC, thereby potentiating radio-/chemotherapy effects and exhibiting synergy with immunotherapy [17]. Targeting G2/M gatekeepers such as WEE1 can precipitate premature mitotic entry and induce MC, demonstrating sensitization to platinum agents, radiotherapy, and ICIs across multiple tumor models [18]. In addition, modulation of the autophagy–cGAS–STING axis can enhance MC-associated antitumor immunity, suggesting a therapeutic window at the MC–immunity interface [19]. Cross-tumor evidence further indicates that molecular features built from MC-related genes (MCRGs) can jointly characterize prognosis, the tumor immune microenvironment, and potential treatment responsiveness—validated in cohorts of breast, colorectal, and liver cancers—supporting their promise as a biologically interpretable risk axis [20, 21].Against this background, the present study aims to develop a LUAD-oriented MCRG transcriptomic signature using TCGA-LUAD for model construction and to externally validate it in GSE31210, thereby unifying prognostication, tumor-immune microenvironment profiling, and prediction of potential therapeutic benefit within a single framework. Methodologically, we integrate differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) [22], and penalized Cox modeling for robust variable selection to enhance interpretability and generalizability. For functional and immune annotation, we apply widely used transcriptome-based inference of immune/stromal infiltration together with the TIDE framework to evaluate immune evasion and predict ICI responsiveness [23, 24]. At the pharmacologic level, we employ oncoPredict and its standardized workflow to translate large-scale cell-line drug-sensitivity data into individualized drug-response predictions [25, 26].Materials and Data acquisition and preprocessingTCGA-LUAD Clinical and RNA-seq data were retrieved via the GDC API [27]; samples with missing overall survival (OS) time/status or OS ≤ 0 days were excluded; expression values were converted to FPKM and log2-transformed as log2(FPKM + 1); a total of 500 tumor and 59 normal samples were retained.GEO (GSE31210) [28]Microarray data were downloaded, and probe IDs were mapped to official gene symbols using the platform annotation; samples lacking follow-up or OS information were removed; 226 tumor samples were retained. In addition, for GSE30219, we retained only tumor samples with pathological diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, excluded normal lung tissues, and constructed overall survival (OS) variables. Samples with OS.time ≤ 0 or missing information were removed, resulting in 83 LUAD patients for analysis. For GSE3141, we selected samples with CellType = “A” (adenocarcinoma) based on clinical annotations, yielding 58 LUAD patients for external validation. The TCGA-LUAD cohort was used for training, while GSE31210, GSE30219, and GSE3141 served as independent external validation cohorts.Gene set source MCRGs were curated from published research [29].Differential gene identificationIn the training cohort (TCGA-LUAD), differential expression was assessed using the limma R package by fitting linear models with empirical Bayes variance moderation to compare tumors versus normal [30]; multiple testing was controlled by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to obtain adjusted P values (FDR); genes were designated as differentially expressed if |log2FC| > log2(1.5) and P.adj 0.01, and further removed the 25% of genes with the lowest MAD values. The remaining high‑variability genes were used as input for WGCNA. Next, the pickSoftThreshold function was applied to determine the optimal soft‑thresholding power β, balancing scale‑free topology fit and mean connectivity. Using the selected β, we constructed a gene‑gene adjacency matrix and transformed it into a topological overlap matrix (TOM). Average‑linkage hierarchical clustering based on TOM dissimilarity generated a gene dendrogram, from which co‑expression modules were identified using the dynamic tree‑cut algorithm with a minimum module size of 60 genes. For each module, we calculated the module eigengene (ME) and evaluated its correlation with the MCRGs score using Pearson correlation. The module showing the strongest correlation with the MCRGs score was selected for downstream analyses, and the genes belonging to this module were extracted for further model development and functional enrichment.Risk model construction and evaluationUsing the differentially expressed module genes as candidates, we first performed LASSO-Cox penalized regression (glmnet) in the training cohort (TCGA-LUAD), selecting the optimal penalty parameter via 10-fold cross-validation to reduce dimensionality and mitigate multicollinearity; the retained features were then entered into a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model followed by bidirectional stepwise selection based on the Akaike information criterion (AIC) to finalize the gene set and coefficients. For each patient, a risk score was computed as RiskScore = Σ(βi × Expi), where Expi denotes the expression of gene and βi is its multivariable Cox coefficient; the resulting linear predictor was applied to the external validation dataset (GSE31210). An optimal single cutoff for dichotomizing patients into high- and low-risk subgroups was determined in the training set using survminer::surv_cutpoint (maximally selected rank statistics) and carried forward unchanged to the validation cohort to avoid information leakage. Survival differences were assessed with Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test, while model discrimination was quantified using time-dependent ROC analysis; the proportional hazards assumption was examined (Schoenfeld residuals) when appropriate to ensure model validity.Immune microenvironment analysis and immunotherapy predictionUsing the TCGA-LUAD expression matrix, we applied ESTIMATE (estimate R package) to derive the ImmuneScore, StromalScore, and ESTIMATEScore [31]; used MCPcounter to infer the abundance of predefined immune and stromal cell populations [32]; and computed per-sample enrichment scores for 28 tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) signatures via ssGSEA implemented in GSVA [33]. Associations between the model risk score and immune metrics were quantified with Spearman correlation, and differences between high- and low-risk groups were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test; multiple testing was controlled by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to estimate the FDR. Predicted responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors was evaluated with the TIDE framework by supplying normalized expression matrices according to the developer’s guidelines to obtain patient-level ICI response propensity.Drug sensitivity analysisUsing the TCGA-LUAD expression matrix, we applied the pRRophetic R package to predict half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) [34], yielding patient-level sensitivity estimates to commonly used chemotherapeutic/targeted agents. The model RiskScore was then treated as a continuous trait to compute Spearman rank correlations (ρ) with predicted IC50 values for each drug, with two-sided P values reported; a Wilcoxon rank-sum test comparing high- vs. low-risk groups was additionally performed as a consistency check, and multiple testing was controlled using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.Cell culture and transfectionHuman normal bronchial epithelial cells BEAS-2B (CRL-3588, ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) and human lung cancer cell lines A549 (CRM-CCL-185, ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) and NCI-H838 (CRL-5844, ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were used. Cells were cultured in DMEM (PM150210, Procell, Wuhan, China) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) ( , Procell) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Procell) under standard conditions (37 ℃, 5% CO2, saturated humidity) in a tri-gas incubator (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Cells were passaged at 70–80% confluence using Trypsin-EDTA and were routinely tested to be mycoplasma-free. Short tandem repeat (STR) identification has been carried out on the cells, and the outcome of mycoplasma detection shows negativity. For gene silencing, small interfering RNAs targeting GNPNAT1 (si-GNPNAT1) and a non-targeting negative control siRNA were obtained from GenePharma (Shanghai, China); the sequences were si-NC (5’-UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT-3’), si-GNPNAT1#1 (5’-GAGUCAGAAUACAGCUACATT-3’), and si-GNPNAT1#2 (5’-GCAAGAAACUGAACUGUUACATT-3’). Transfections were performed in A549 and NCI-H838 cells using Lipofectamine™ 3000 ( , Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions.Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT–PCR)Total RNA was isolated from cultured cells with TRIzol reagent (15596026CN, Invitrogen, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions, and RNA yield/purity were verified using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). First-strand cDNA was generated with the Beyotime Reverse Transcription Kit (D7178S, Shanghai, China). Quantitative PCR was then carried out with SYBR Green qPCR Mix (D7260, Beyotime) on an Applied Biosystems real-time PCR platform (Applied Biosystems, USA). The thermocycling conditions were: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min; 30 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s, 60 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 1 min; and a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. Relative transcript abundance was determined by the 2−ΔΔCt approach using GAPDH as the reference gene. Primer sequences are provided in Table 1. Each sample was analyzed in technical triplicate, and no-template controls were included in every run. Cell viability was quantified using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; C0037, Beyotime): 10 µL reagent was added to each well and incubated for 4 h, after which absorbance at 450 nm was measured on a microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Percent viability was determined as (OD450(sample) – OD450(blank)) / (OD450(siNC) – OD450(blank)) × 100%. Background-corrected signals normalized to the si-NC control. Each condition included ≥ 3 technical replicates, and experiments were performed independently at least three times.Wound-healing assayFor migration assays, cells were plated in 6-well dishes (2 mL complete medium per well) and cultured at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO₂ incubator until a uniform confluent monolayer formed. A linear scratch was created with a sterile 200-µL pipette tip, detached cells were removed by two PBS rinses, and serum-free DMEM was added. Phase-contrast images were acquired at 0 and 48 h using an inverted microscope. The wound-healing rate was calculated as the percentage decrease in mean wound width at 48 h relative to the initial width. Each condition was analyzed in triplicate and repeated in at least three independent experiments.Transwell assayFor invasion assays, transwell inserts (Corning, USA) were pre-coated with 30 µL Matrigel and put on the upper-chamber membrane. Cells were seeded into the upper chambers, while the lower chambers were filled with medium containing FBS as a chemoattractant. After incubation for 48 h at 37 °C, non-invading cells on the upper surface were gently removed. Cells that had traversed the membrane were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with crystal violet for 10 min, then imaged and enumerated under an inverted microscope.Statistical analysisR was used for TCGA/GEO: limma with BH-FDR (FDR log21.5); KM/log-rank and Cox (HR, 95% CI); LASSO–Cox (glmnet) + stepwise AIC; time-dependent ROC, C-index; PH checked by Schoenfeld; Spearman/Wilcoxon with FDR where applicable. Experimental data were analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 and presented as mean ± SD (≥ 3); two groups: unpaired two-tailed t-test; multi-group: one-/two-way ANOVA with Tukey. Two-sided P log2(1.5) and P.adj < 0.05) identified 2,290 upregulated and 1,959 downregulated genes (Fig. 1A). Intersecting these differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with the curated MCRGs yielded 266 differentially expressed MCRGs (Fig. 1B). Somatic mutation profiling of the 266 differential MCRGs—summarized by a waterfall plot of the top 20 mutated genes—revealed the highest mutation frequencies in TP53, KRAS, and DMD (Fig. 1C). C Waterfall plot of somatic mutations for the top 20 differentially expressed MCRGs WGCNAStarting from the differential MCRGs, we computed per-sample MCRGs score using GSVA and retained the top 75% of the most variable protein-coding genes (by SD) for network construction. WGCNA was then applied to identify co-expression modules associated with the MCRGs score: to approximate a scale-free topology, we selected a soft-thresholding power of β = 7, performed hierarchical clustering on the topological overlap matrix with dynamic tree cutting, and obtained 25 co-expression modules after module merging (Fig. 2A–B); the grey module contained genes not assigned to any other module. Correlating module eigengenes with the MCRGs score revealed the turquoise module as the most strongly associated Fig. 2C–D), which was prioritized for downstream analyses. C Heatmap of correlations between MEs and the MCRGs score. D Scatter plot of module membership vs. gene significance for the MCRGs score in the turquoise module Enrichment analysisIntersecting the turquoise module genes with the DEGs yielded 940 differentially expressed module genes (Fig. 3A). Using clusterProfiler with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (P.adjust < 0.05), KEGG enrichment indicated significant overrepresentation of cancer-relevant pathways, notably the p53 signaling pathway, Cell cycle, and Central carbon metabolism in cancer (Fig. 3B). GO–Biological Process terms were predominantly associated with positive regulation of cell cycle process, cell cycle checkpoint, and regulation of DNA metabolic process (Fig. 3C). Fig. 3Functional enrichment of turquoise module–derived genes. A Venn diagram intersecting TCGA DEGs with turquoise module genes. B KEGG pathway enrichment analysis results. C GO–biological process enrichment analysis results Construction and validation of the prognostic modelAmong the 940 intersecting genes, univariable Cox proportional hazards regression (P < 0.01) identified candidate prognosis-related features, which were further reduced by LASSO–Cox penalization (Fig. 4A–B) and finalized by multivariable Cox modeling to derive the coefficients (Fig. 4C). The resulting six-gene model computed the risk score as RiskScore = 0.254×GNPNAT1 + 0.102×GPR37 + 0.362×LDHA + 0.219 ×MELTF + 0.150×PTPRH − 0.188×STK32A. Patients were dichotomized into high- and low-risk groups using the optimal cutoff; in the training cohort, time-dependent ROC analyses demonstrated consistently favorable AUCs across 1–5 years (Fig. 4D), indicating strong discriminative ability. Kaplan–Meier curves further showed significantly poorer outcomes for the high-risk group across OS, progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-specific survival (DSS) (all P < 0.05; Fig. 4E–G). Applying the same formula and carrying forward the training cutoff to the external GSE31210 cohort, the model retained high AUCs at 1–5 years (Fig. 4H), and KM analysis again revealed significantly worse survival in the high-risk subgroup (P < 0.05; Fig. 4I). Finally, we conducted additional validation in two independent LUAD cohorts. As shown in Figure S1A–B, in the GSE30219 dataset, the AUC values for overall survival at 1 to 5 years were all greater than 0.7, and high-risk patients had a poorer prognosis. In the GSE3141 dataset, the ROC curves demonstrated that the risk model also exhibited good discriminatory ability, and patients in the high-risk group had significantly shorter overall survival compared to those in the low-risk group (Figure S1C–D). These results further confirm the stability and clinical applicability of our MC‑related six‑gene signature across different external datasets. C Forest plot of the multivariable Cox model (HRs with 95% CIs) for the six-gene signature. D, E TCGA-LUAD: time-dependent ROC curve for OS and Kaplan–Meier survival curve by risk group. F TCGA-LUAD: Kaplan–Meier curve for PFI. G TCGA-LUAD: Kaplan–Meier curve for DSS. MCPcounter–based comparisons (Fig. 5B) revealed significantly lower abundances of B lineage, myeloid dendritic cells, and neutrophils in the high-risk group. Consistently, leveraging ssGSEA-derived TIL scores (Fig. 5C), eosinophils, immature dendritic cells, and mast cells were significantly negatively correlated with the RiskScore. TIDE analysis (Fig. 5D–F) further indicated higher Exclusion and lower Dysfunction scores in the high-risk group, along with a markedly smaller proportion of predicted ICI responders, supporting an immune-excluded phenotype in high-risk patients. Notably, a higher overall TIDE score may reflect stronger tumor immune evasion and is associated with a poorer response to immune checkpoint inhibitors. B MCPcounter-inferred immune/stromal cell abundances by risk group. C Correlation bubble plot of 28 TIL signatures in TCGA. D, E TIDE-derived Exclusion and Dysfunction scores compared between risk groups. F Stacked bar plot of predicted ICI responder proportions by risk group. *Statistical significance is indicated as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 Drug sensitivityUsing pRRophetic predictions, we compared chemotherapeutic susceptibilities between risk strata and assessed RiskScore–IC50 associations via Spearman correlation (Fig. 6). RiskScore correlated positively with the IC50 of rapamycin and PHA-665,752, suggesting greater resistance in high-risk patients; conversely, RiskScore correlated negatively with cisplatin, paclitaxel, BI-2536, pyrimethamine, GW843682X, and vinorelbine IC50 values, indicating higher predicted sensitivity in the high-risk group. Scatter plots showing Spearman correlations between RiskScore and predicted IC50 (pRRophetic) for the indicated agents Expression profiling of the signature genes and functional validation of GNPNAT1First, we quantified mRNA levels of the six-gene signature (GNPNAT1, GPR37, LDHA, MELTF, PTPRH, and STK32A) in normal airway epithelial cells (BEAS-2B) and two lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) cell lines (A549 and NCI-H838). GNPNAT1, GPR37, LDHA, MELTF, and PTPRH were overall upregulated in cancer cells, whereas STK32A was downregulated, with consistent differences between A549/NCI-H838 and BEAS-2B (Fig. 7A). Focusing on the key gene GNPNAT1, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown in A549 and NCI-H838 and verified silencing efficiency by qPCR (Figs. 7B–C). Both si-GNPNAT1#1 and si-GNPNAT1#2 markedly reduced GNPNAT1 transcript levels; the knockdown effect of si-GNPNAT1 is better, si-GNPNAT1#1 was therefore used for subsequent experiments. Functionally, CCK-8 assays demonstrated that GNPNAT1 knockdown decreased proliferation in both cell lines, with OD450 values significantly lower than controls across 24–72 h (Figs. 7D–E). In motility and invasion assays, wound-healing experiments showed a significant reduction in wound closure at 48 h in GNPNAT1-silenced A549 cells (Fig. 7F), and Transwell assays further revealed markedly fewer transmembrane cells in both cell lines (Fig. 7G). Consistently, GNPNAT1 knockdown in NCI-H838 also led to a significant reduction in wound closure at 48 h (Fig. 7H), and invasion assays likewise showed decreased numbers of transmembrane cells in both cell lines (Fig. 7I). Data are presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments (n = 3 per group). Statistical analysis was performed using two‑way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons test. B, C qRT‑PCR validation of GNPNAT1 knockdown efficiency in A549 (B) and NCI-H838 (C) cells transfected with si‑NC or si‑GNPNAT1#1. Data are presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments (n = 3 per group). Statistical analysis was performed using one‑way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. D, E CCK-8 proliferation curves for LUAD cells A549 (D) and NCI-H838 (E) following GNPNAT1 knockdown or control treatment across indicated time points. Data are presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments (n = 3). Two‑way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test was used. F, H Migration assay (wound-healing) in LUAD cells A549 (F) and NCI-H838 (H) with representative images and quantification of wound closure at 48 h. Scale bars, 200 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments (n = 3 per group). Statistical analysis was performed using unpaired t-test. G, I Invasion assay (Matrigel Transwell) in LUAD cells A549 (G) and NCI-H838 (I) with representative images and quantification of cells per field (migration or invasion as specified). Scale bars, 200 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments (n = 3 per group). Statistical analysis was performed using unpaired t-test. *Statistical significance is indicated as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001 LUAD is highly heterogeneous, and traditional single biomarkers often show limited generalizability across assay platforms and disease stages, underscoring the need for integrative stratification tools with stronger biological interpretability [35–38]. In recent years, numerous studies have revealed, from various perspectives, the heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment (TME) in LUAD and its profound impact on prognosis and treatment [39, 40]. For example, a study using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to thoroughly analyze the dual roles of macrophages in LUAD found that signaling pathways such as SPP1 and MIF are more active in tumor tissues, suggesting that macrophages may promote tumor progression through specific signaling axes [41]. Another study focused on immunogenic cell death (ICD) and, by integrating scRNA-seq with machine learning algorithms, constructed an ICD-related gene signature comprising 11 core genes [42]. Furthermore, addressing the unique pathological feature of LUAD known as “spread through air spaces” (STAS), a study innovatively combined scRNA-seq with digital spatial mapping to reveal that M2a-type macrophages activate the β-catenin signaling pathway via the CCL17/CCR4 axis, thereby promoting the development and progression of STAS [43]. These studies demonstrate that polygenic signature models based on specific biological axes can effectively integrate information regarding prognosis, the TME, and treatment response in LUAD, providing important contextual support and theoretical justification for the MC-centric signature developed in this study. Anchored on MC—a core process intertwined with chromosomal instability/aneuploid dynamics and mechanistically interfacing with chemo-radiotherapy and immunotherapy—we developed and externally validated a six-gene transcriptional prognostic signature (GNPNAT1, GPR37, LDHA, MELTF, PTPRH, STK32A). The model yielded stable AUCs and clear Kaplan–Meier separation in the TCGA training set and retained discriminative performance in the independent GSE31210 cohort, with functional annotation implicating p53 signaling, cell-cycle control, and central carbon metabolism. Importantly, beyond in silico evidence, wet-lab assays corroborated the biology: in BEAS-2B versus LUAD cell lines (A549, NCI-H838), GNPNAT1/GPR37/LDHA/MELTF/PTPRH were upregulated while STK32A was downregulated; targeted silencing of GNPNAT1 reduced proliferation (CCK-8) and impaired motility/invasion (wound-healing and Transwell), thereby providing functional support for the signature’s mechanistic plausibility. Consistent with these axes, the high-risk subgroup exhibited an immune-excluded phenotype, and drug-sensitivity inference suggested higher susceptibility to microtubule/cell-cycle agents (cisplatin, paclitaxel, BI-2536, vinorelbine) but relative resistance to rapamycin and PHA-665,752. Collectively, these findings indicate that an MC-related molecular axis can coherently capture tumor proliferation–metabolism–immunity ecology while offering actionable guidance for perioperative and translational therapeutic stratification.From a mechanistic standpoint, the six genes delineate a coherent circuit linking metabolism, receptor/kinase signaling, and cell-cycle/stress control. (i) LDHA, a glycolytic gatekeeper, promotes lactate accumulation and microenvironmental acidification, supporting high proliferative demand while suppressing effector T-cell functions consistent with the immune-cold/excluded features seen in the high-risk group [44, 45]. (ii) GNPNAT1, a rate-limiting enzyme in the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, augments O-GlcNAcylation to facilitate cell-cycle progression and motility [46]; its oncogenic and adverse-prognostic roles in LUAD align with an MC axis characterized by “high proliferation under high stress [47, 48].” (iii) MELTF intersects with EGF/FAK signaling and cell adhesion/migration, and is associated with malignant progression across cancers, serving as a potential interface between stress adaptation and invasive programs—states that frequently co-occur under MC induction or CIN [49]. (iv) PTPRH, a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase, when inactivated can lead to aberrant EGFR phosphorylation and actionable EGFR-TKI sensitivity, highlighting crosstalk between growth signaling and mitotic checkpoint control [50]. (v) GPR37, an orphan GPCR linked to cellular stress responses, has been implicated in proliferation, migration, and cell-cycle regulation—including LUAD contexts via CDK6 engagement [51], while GPCR-coupled ER stress/UPR pathways are widely recognized in tumor adaptation to hypoxia and metabolic pressure, resonating with shifts in the MC stress threshold [52]. (vi) STK32A, a serine/threonine kinase, has been reported to modulate the cell cycle and transcription-factor phosphorylation; its protective coefficient in our model suggests a braking function in LUAD or indicates a specific differentiation state [53].The immune-excluded or “cold” microenvironment observed in the high-risk group—characterized by reductions in several myeloid subsets and B-lineage cells, elevated TIDE Exclusion scores, decreased Dysfunction scores, and a lower proportion of predicted responders—provides an immunologic explanation for poorer survival and putative insensitivity to ICIs. Methodologically, TIDE models immune escape through T-cell dysfunction and exclusion, concepts that have been validated across multiple cancer immunotherapy settings [54]. Beyond correlative patterns, there are mechanistic links between CIN/MC and immune evasion: persistent chromosome mis-segregation generates aberrant cytosolic DNA and remodels the cGAS–STING axis, potentially driving chronic, tolerance-prone inflammation and enhanced metastatic competence. These insights converge with our high-risk group’s immune-cold signature, reinforcing the biological plausibility that MC/CIN dynamics shape—and are shaped by—the tumor–immune ecosystem [55–57]. Emerging evidence from other tumor types further illustrates how tumor‑intrinsic and microenvironmental factors can convert “cold” tumors into “hot” ones, thereby modulating ICI responsiveness. For instance, antibody‑drug conjugates (ADCs) that induce ICD can function as in situ vaccines, promoting dendritic cell activation and T‑cell infiltration [58]. Conversely, molecules such as PAK2 have been shown to negatively regulate anti‑tumor immune status and suppress immune cell infiltration in head and neck cancer [59]. Aberrant glycosylation patterns, which affect immune recognition and cytokine activity, have also been linked to immunotherapy response in breast cancer [60]. Moreover, disulfidptosis‑related signatures reflect tumor immune characteristics and predict ICI responsiveness across cancers [61]. These findings, although derived from different malignancies, support the concept that reshaping the TME—whether through ICD induction, targeting immunosuppressive drivers, or exploiting novel cell death pathways—can overcome immune exclusion. Our MC‑anchored signature, which captures a similar immune‑cold phenotype in LUAD, may therefore guide rational combinations with ICD‑inducing agents or inhibitors of immunosuppressive axes to enhance ICI efficacy.Pharmacologically, the predicted vulnerability of the high-risk subgroup to microtubule and cell-cycle agents (cisplatin, paclitaxel, BI-2536, vinorelbine) accords with the notion that highly proliferative tumors operating near a mitotic-stress ceiling are more readily forced into MC by spindle or checkpoint perturbation. The PLK1 inhibitor BI-2536 induces mitotic arrest and MC, with early-phase clinical studies supporting the mechanistic direction and tolerability [62]. Leveraging MC as a therapeutic fulcrum, inhibition of G2/M gatekeepers such as WEE1 can precipitate premature mitotic entry, amplify DNA damage, and synergize with platinum chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and potentially immunotherapy. These data collectively support perioperative strategies—e.g., “cell-cycle inhibitors and/or radiochemotherapy ± ICI”—for biomarker-defined high-risk LUAD [63, 64]. In contrast, the observed trend toward resistance to rapamycin (mTOR inhibition) and PHA-665,752 (MET inhibition) is biologically plausible: mTORC1 blockade has shown limited single-agent activity in NSCLC with frequent feedback and adaptive compensation, and clinically meaningful responses to MET inhibition are largely confined to biomarker-enriched subsets (e.g., MET exon 14 skipping and amplification) rather than non–oncogene-addicted contexts [65, 66]. It should be noted that our study found that although the high-risk group was predicted to have higher sensitivity to cisplatin and paclitaxel, these patients had significantly poorer overall survival in the TCGA-LUAD cohort. Several factors may explain this discrepancy. First, the efficacy of chemotherapy is critically modulated by the TME; an immune‑excluded or “cold” TME, as observed in our high‑risk group, can compromise chemotherapy‑induced ICD, which is essential for eliciting durable antitumor immunity [67]. Without an effective T‑cell response, the intrinsic chemosensitivity of tumor cells may not translate into prolonged survival. Second, the TCGA‑LUAD cohort is retrospective and heterogeneous in treatment allocation; not all patients received the specific platinum‑based regimens for which their tumors were predicted to be sensitive. Third, transcriptome‑based drug sensitivity prediction (e.g., pRRophetic) captures baseline intrinsic responsiveness but does not fully account for in vivo pharmacokinetics, drug tolerance, or adaptive resistance mechanisms. Finally, the high‑risk signature includes metabolically aggressive genes that may drive rapid progression and early metastasis, potentially overriding any short‑term chemosensitivity [55]. Collectively, these observations suggest that for high‑risk LUAD patients, the immune‑excluded TME may override predicted chemosensitivity, indicating that chemotherapy alone is insufficient. Rational combinations—such as ICD‑inducing chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint blockade or TME‑remodeling agents—are warranted to convert chemosensitivity into meaningful survival benefits [68].Several limitations warrant emphasis. First, this is a retrospective study integrating multi-platform data (TCGA RNA-seq FPKM for training; GEO microarrays for validation). Despite standardization and batch-effect mitigation, residual cross-platform bias cannot be fully excluded, and external validation relied on a single public cohort—highlighting the need for multi-center, real-world, prospective evaluation. Second, predicted immunotherapy response was inferred solely with TIDE without prospective testing in ICI-treated patients; drug sensitivity was estimated via pRRophetic/cell-line pharmacogenomic mapping, which is vulnerable to expression-to-drug-response domain shift and may not capture adaptive resistance. Third, although our wet-lab assays (qPCR, CCK-8, wound-healing, Transwell) lend functional plausibility—showing GNPNAT1 knockdown suppresses proliferation and motility/invasion in A549 and NCI-H838—these experiments were limited to two LUAD lines, focused on a single target gene, and lacked rescue and in vivo validation; off-target effects and the absence of protein-level/phenotypic complementation cannot be excluded. Causal links between all six genes and the MC/immune axis therefore remain to be established. Future work will prioritize prospective, multi-center validation (including decision-curve and net-benefit analyses), spatial/single-cell profiling of the immune microenvironment, and mechanistic studies using CRISPR perturbation with rescue, proteomic/phosphoproteomic readouts, xenograft/organoid models, and biomarker-driven trials testing “WEE1/PLK1 inhibitors + platinum/radiotherapy ± ICI” to determine the clinical utility of this signature in perioperative and translational settings.We present an MC-anchored six-gene signature that integrates prognostic, immune, and therapeutic dimensions in LUAD. External validation together with targeted wet-lab assays supports its biological plausibility and potential clinical relevance. This framework may enable more reliable risk stratification and treatment selection, and it provides a rationale for prospective multi-center evaluation and biomarker-driven trials.Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1.
