title: Dual PI3K/AKT and CDK4/6 inhibition reveals selective sensitivity in an SHH medulloblastoma stem cell model
abstract: Medulloblastoma (MB) is a brain tumor for which current treatments cause serious side effects and are not curative for all patients, highlighting the need for more effective and brain‐protecting therapies. Recently, we combined phosphoinositide 3‐kinase (PI3K) inhibitor (BYL719), fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitor (JNJ‐ ) and cyclin‐dependent kinase (CDK)4/6 inhibitor (PD‐ ) in MB cell lines, and discovered synergistic effects. In the current study, we investigate the most efficient therapies in a normal/tumorigenic neural stem cell model. A sonic hedgehog (SHH)‐MB model, including a Gorlin syndrome patient neuroepithelial stem cell line (NES) and its tumor derivative (tNES), was used to evaluate single and combined treatments of PI3K, AKT, FGFR, and CDK4/6 inhibitors (BYL719, AZD5363, JNJ‐ , and PD‐ , respectively). Effects on viability, cell confluence and apoptosis were tested on NES and tNES cells cultured as 2D monolayers and 3D spheroids. We found that 2D tNES cells were generally more sensitive to the inhibitory effects of both single and combination treatments compared to 2D NES cells. In the 3D setting, all single drugs were more effective against tNES than NES, except for JNJ‐ , which showed the opposite trend. Drug combinations in 3D cultures generally resulted in synergistic or additive effects on cell viability in NES and tNES. This study illustrates that single and combined administrations of PI3K, FGFR, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors in a NES/tNES model have dose‐dependent and additive/synergistic anti‐MB activity impacting tumor growth. Their effects on tNES cells were generally more pronounced than on NES; however, the difference in proliferative capacity between the cells should be considered.
full_text: Abbreviations2DTwo dimensional3DThree dimensionalAKTProtein kinase BATPAdenosine triphosphateBSABovine serum albuminCC3Cleaved caspase 3CDK4/6Cyclin‐dependent kinases 4 and 6CTChemotherapyDAB3,3′‐DiaminobenzidineDMEM/F12Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium/Nutrient Mixture F‐12DMSODimethyl sulfoxideEGFEpidermal growth factorFDAFood and Drug AdministrationFGF2Fibroblast growth factor 2FGFRFibroblast growth factor receptorGLI2GLI family zinc finger 2HASHighest single agentHRPHorse‐radish peroxidaseIHCImmunohistochemistryiPSInduced pluripotent stem cellsMBMedulloblastomaNBNeuroblastomaNESNeuroepithelial stem cellso/nOvernightPBSPhosphate‐buffered salinePI3KPhosphoinositide 3‐kinasePTCH1Patched 1RbRetinoblastoma proteinRTRoom temperatureSDStandard deviationSHHSonic hedgehogSMOSmoothenedSUFUSuppressor of fusedtNESTumor‐derived neuroepithelial stem cellsTP53Tumor protein p53WNTWingless‐related integration siteWST‐1Water‐soluble tetrazolium salt‐1; cell viability assay1IntroductionMedulloblastoma (MB) is a highly aggressive childhood brain malignancy originating in the cerebellum, with significant molecular and clinical heterogeneity [1, 2]. Based on molecular profiles, MB is classified into four major subgroups: WNT‐activated, SHH‐activated (subdivided into TP53 wild‐type and TP53 mutant), and a non‐WNT/non‐SHH group, which includes Group 3 and Group 4 [2, 3]. The SHH‐driven subgroup accounts for approximately 30% of all MB cases and is marked by aberrant activation of the SHH signaling pathway, which is crucial for tumor cell proliferation and growth [2, 4, 5]. Dysregulated SHH signaling is often linked to mutations in key components such as PTCH1, SMO, SUFU, or GLI2 [6, 7, 8]. Notably, SHH‐MB is also frequently associated with cancer predisposition syndromes, particularly Gorlin syndrome, caused by germline mutations in PTCH1 or SUFU [9, 10].Despite advances in treatment, including surgery, chemotherapy (CT), and radiotherapy (RT), current therapies cause long‐term side effects and often fail to specifically target the molecular mechanisms driving tumor growth, leading to treatment resistance [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. In this context, applying various targeted therapies could offer a novel approach to improve treatment efficacy.Multiple signaling pathways and tumor drivers are involved in MB tumor development and progression [20, 21]. The phosphoinositide 3‐kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT) pathway plays a critical role in MB cell survival, differentiation, proliferation, and metabolism, and mutations in the PI3K/AKT pathway are also found in MB [22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. Moreover, mutations in the catalytic subunit alpha of PI3K have been shown to enhance tumor growth and promote metastasis in SHH‐MB mouse models [27]. Alongside the PI3K/AKT pathway, cyclin‐dependent kinases (CDK) 4 and 6 are key regulators of the cell cycle and are often amplified in MB, leading to uncontrolled cell division [26, 28, 29]. Hence, the CDK4/6/cyclin D/Rb pathway has been proposed as a potential therapeutic target for all non‐WNT MB [30]. In addition, fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) activation promotes invasiveness and cell growth in MB cells, making it an important therapeutic target [31, 32].Previously, we targeted some of the above pathways and demonstrated that combinations of Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved BYL719 (PI3K), with AZD5363 (AKT), PD‐ (CDK4/6) or JNJ‐ (FGFR) produced synergistic effects in MB cell lines [33, 34, 35, 36, 37].Here, to compare the effects of targeted therapies under normalized vs. tumor‐like conditions, a pilot study was performed. More specifically, neuroepithelial stem (NES) cells derived from induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells of a Gorlin syndrome patient with a germline PTCH1 mutation and its tumor‐derived counterpart tNES from the same patient were used [38]. The tNES cells, which resemble SHH‐driven MB, were originally generated from tumors derived from NES cells transplanted into mouse cerebellum [38].More specifically, the therapeutic effects of the PI3K, CDK4/6, and FGFR inhibitors mentioned above, along with the newly FDA‐approved AKT inhibitor AZD5363 (33), were tested both alone and in combination, in parallel on NES and tNES cells grown in two‐dimensional (2D) monolayer cultures and three‐dimensional (3D) spheroid cultures.2Materials and 2.1Cells and culture conditionsGeneration of NES and tNES cells has been described previously [38]. Both NES and tNES have been provided from Associate Prof. Margareta Wilhelm, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell biology, Karolinska Institutet. They were both cultured as monolayers in flasks coated with 20 μg·mL−1 Poly‐L‐ornithine (Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) and 1 μg·mL−1 laminin (L2020, Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck) in DMEM/F12 medium (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) containing 1% Penicillin–Streptomycin (Pen/Strep) (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% N2 (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific), 0.1% B27 (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific), 10 ng·mL−1 FGF2 (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 10 ng·mL−1 EGF (PeproTech, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Rocky Hill, NJ, USA). All cells used in this study were routinely tested and confirmed to be mycoplasma free.For monolayer (2D) growth, NES and tNES cells were seeded in 96‐well tissue culture plates coated with 20 μg·mL−1 Poly‐L‐ornithine (Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck) and 1 μg·mL−1 laminin (Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck) and for the viability assay they were seeded at cells in 90 μL medium/well.To establish 3D cultures (spheroids) of 300–400 μm in diameter, 5000 and 3000 single‐cell suspensions of NES and tNES, respectively, were seeded in 100 μL medium in 96‐well, Nunclon Sphera‐Treated, U‐Shaped‐Bottom Microplates ULA (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and cultured for 72 h before drug treatment. The cultures were then followed for viability assay, measurement of spheroid growth, and immunohistochemistry (IHC).2.2InhibitorsThe FDA‐approved PI3K inhibitor BYL719 (alpelisib), AKT inhibitor AZD5363 (Capivasertib), CDK4/6 inhibitor PD‐ (palbociclib), and FGFR inhibitor JNJ‐ (erdafitinib) were all purchased from TargetMol (San Diego, California, USA). All initial stocks were prepared in DMSO and later diluted in PBS to each drug's working stock concentration (0.05–1 μm) after proceeding with initial drug titrations.2.3 WST‐1 cell viability assay for 2D studiesTo assess cell viability in 2D cultures, the WST‐1 assay (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) was used. This colorimetric method indicates viable cells and was performed according to the previously described protocol [39].2.4 CellTiterGlo 3D cell viability assayFor 3D cultures, viability was measured with the CellTiterGlo reagent (Promega, Madison, WI, USA), according to the manufacturer's instructions. This method utilizes ATP quantification to mark metabolically active cells. Viability was measured 24, 48, and 72 h after treatment, where 100 μL CellTiterGlo reagent was added to each well at room temperature (RT), followed by 5 min of shaking. After 25 min incubation at RT, luminescence was measured using the Varioskan™ LUX multimode microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The viability was calculated by averaging the luminescence, subtracting the blank, and normalizing to the PBS‐treated control.2.5Spheroid growth assayed by the Incucyte® S3 live‐cell analysis instrumentAfter the spheroid formation, as described in the section ‘Cells and culture conditions’ the spheroids were treated with our tested drugs (mentioned in the Section ‘Inhibitors’), and the Incucyte® S3 Live‐Cell Analysis Instrument (Sartorius, Göttingen, Germany) was used for live imaging. Images of each spheroid were captured every 2 h, and their size was calculated as the largest object area in each image using the Incucyte software 2024A.2.6ImmunohistochemistrySpheroids treated for 48 h and corresponding controls were collected from a 96‐well spheroid plate and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA) overnight (o/n) at 4 °C. After changing to 70% ethanol, the samples were stored at 4 °C. The fixed spheroids were dehydrated in an automated tissue processing machine (LOGOS, Milestone Srl, Sorisole, Bergamo, Italy), embedded in paraffin, cut into 4 μm thick sections, and mounted on glass slides (Superfrost, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). All slides were heated at 56 °C for 3 h.Before staining, the slides were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated in decreasing concentrations of ethanol. Heat‐induced epitope retrieval was performed in Citrate buffer pH 6 (Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck, C‐9999, Schnelldorf, Germany) using a Decloaking Chamber (Biocare Medical, Pacheco, California, USA) set for 5 min at 110 °C. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked by incubation with 0.15% hydrogen peroxide for 30 min at RT. Further blocking with Biocare Medical Background Sniper (Biocare Medical, Pacheco, California, USA) for 15 min was done to reduce non‐specific background staining. The tissue sections were incubated o/n at 4 °C in a humidity chamber with the primary antibodies, anti‐Ki67 (1 : 800, DAKO, #A0047, Lot nr, RRID, UK Ltd., Cambridgeshire, UK) to assess proliferation or anti‐cleaved caspase 3 (anti‐CC‐3) (1 : 2000, Cell Signaling, #9661, Lot nr, RRID: AB_2341188 Danvers, MA, USA) to assess apoptosis. Both antibodies were diluted in PBS with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA). Detection was done using the Bio Biocare Medical Mach‐1 Universal Horse‐Radish‐Peroxidase (HRP)‐Polymer Kit (MIU539L10, Biocare Medical, Pacheco, California, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol and developed for 5 min with 3,3′‐diaminobenzidine (DAB) (Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck, Schnelldorf, Germany). After counterstaining with Mayer's hematoxylin (Sigma‐Aldrich, Merck) for 1 min, the sections were dehydrated in an increasing gradient of ethanol and xylene and then mounted using Pertex (Histolab, Gothenburg, Sweden). The images were obtained using the Olympus BH‐2 microscope (Tokyo, Japan) and DMK 33UX264 series monochrome industrial camera (The Imaging Source, Bremen, Germany).2.7Synergy calculation and statistical analysisThe effectiveness of the drug combinations was assessed using the Synergy FinderPlus computational tool (https://synergyfinderplus.org/), with the highest single agent (HSA) approach. HSA values greater than 10 indicate synergistic effects of the drugs, values between −10 and 10 suggest additive effects, and values less than −10 indicate antagonism [40, 41]. All experiments were repeated at least three times and are depicted as mean values with standard deviations (SD). The difference between the combinational treatments and the corresponding single treatments was estimated using two‐way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test, P < 0.05 was considered significant. All reported P values are referred to 72 h unless they are specified.3Results3.1Impact of single and combined FGFR, PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors on cell viability in 2D cultures of NES and tNES cells (i.e., 2D NES and 2D tNES)3.1.1Single treatments on 2D NES cellsAlthough all 0.05–1 μm doses of the FGFR inhibitor JNJ‐ inhibited NES cell viability up to 50% only the highest dose showed significant effect (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1A). PI3K and CDK4/6 inhibitors, BYL719 and PD‐ respectively, significantly decreased cell viability in the highest doses (P < 0.05). (Fig. 1B,C). In contrast, similar doses of the AKT inhibitor (AZD5363) had almost no effect on cell viability (Fig. 1D).Fig. 1Impact of single and combined treatments with FGFR, PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors JNJ‐ , BYL719, PD‐ , and AZD5363, respectively, on the viability of NES and tNES monolayers. Cell viability of 2D NES (A–G) and tNES (H–N) cultures was assessed by absorbance measurements at 24, 48, and 72 h following treatment. Data represent independent biological replicates as follows: panel A, E, N, n = 3; panel B, D, F, (J), K, L, n = 5; panels C, n = 7; panels G, (I), n = 4; panels H, (M), n = 6. Error bars indicate standard deviation (SD). Most of the combinations of BYL719 and JNJ‐ significantly decreased NES cell viability (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1E). A 50% decrease in NES viability was only obtained with the two highest drug doses, that is, 0.5 μm and 1 μm of the BYL719 and PD‐ combination (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1F), while for the AZD5363 and PD‐ combination this was only obtained with the highest drug dose 1 μm (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1G).3.1.4Combined treatments on 2D tNES cellsAll 0.05–1 μm BYL719 and JNJ‐ , BYL719 and PD‐ , as well as AZD5363 and PD‐ combinations significantly decreased the tNES viability by at least 50% compared to the PBS control, except for the two lower concentrations (0.05 μm and 0.1 μm) of the AZD5363 and PD‐ combination (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1L–N).To summarize, tNES cells were generally more sensitive than NES cells to both single and combination treatments in 2D cultures.3.2Impact of single and combined FGFR, PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors on cell viability in 3D cultures of NES and tNES cells (i.e., 3D NES and 3D tNES)3.2.1Single treatments on 3D NESIn 3D NES, JNJ‐ had the most pronounced impact among the single treatments, like 2D NES, with all tested doses 0.05–1 μm significantly reducing cell viability by more than 50% at all time points (P < 0.005) (Fig. 2A). BYL719 also inhibited cell viability by more than 50% at the highest concentration 1 μm compared to the PBS control (P < 0.05) (Fig. 2B). 3D NES, showed however similar to 2D only moderate to mild reductions in cell viability upon AZD5363 and PD‐ single treatments (Fig. 2C,D).Fig. 2Impact of single and combined treatments with FGFR, PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors JNJ‐ , BYL719, PD‐ , and AZD5363, respectively, on the viability of NES and tNES spheroids. Cell viability of NES (A–G) and tNES (H–N) spheroids was assessed by luminescence measurements at 24, 48, and 72 h following treatment. Data represent independent biological replicates as follows: panels A, B, C, E, L, N, n = 4; panels D, H, J, M, n = 5; panels F, G, n = 3; panels I, K, n = 6. Error bars indicate standard deviation (SD). Moreover, while the treatments generally had stronger effects on 3D tNES than on 3D NES, JNJ‐ showed weaker cell viability reduction in 3D tNES, whereas BYL719 exhibited comparable efficacy across both models (Fig. 2A–D,H–K).3.2.3Combined treatments on 3D NES and tNESThe combinations of 0.05–1 μm BYL719 with JNJ‐ considerably decreased cell viability in 3D NES and 3D tNES, with 3D NES showing greater sensitivity (Fig. 2E,L).Most of the tested combination doses of BYL719 with PD‐ produced a similar trend in both 3D NES and 3D tNES, considerably reducing cell viability compared to the PBS control at both 48 and 72 h, with a more pronounced effect observed in 3D tNES (P < 0.005) (Fig. 2F,M).Likewise, 0.05–1 μm combination doses of AZD5363 and PD‐ were generally more effective in 3D tNES, with a marked reduction in viability in the latter observed at 48 and 72 h (P < 0.05) (Fig. 2G,N).To summarize, all single‐drug treatments, except for JNJ‐ , tended to be more effective on 3D tNES compared to 3D NES. Moreover, combination treatments generally enhanced the effects on viability in both 3D NES and 3D tNES; however, also here JNJ‐ exhibited stronger viability reduction in 3D NES than in 3D tNES.3.3Synergistic effects of inhibitor combinations in 3D NES and 3D tNES The synergistic potential of BYL719, AZD5363, and PD‐ combinations was further evaluated in 3D NES and 3D tNES using 3D cell viability data (Fig. 3). Here, we aimed to determine whether significant differences existed between 3D NES and 3D tNES regarding the synergistic effects of the treatments. However, since JNJ‐ alone and combined with BYL719 were highly effective, causing rapid cell death in 3D NES, the latter combination was not further investigated in detail, or compared with regard to its effects on 3D tNES.Fig. 3Evaluation of drug interactions between BYL719, PD‐ , and AZD5363 in NES and tNES spheroids 72 h after treatment. Drug interaction analyses were performed in NES and tNES spheroids using the SynergyFinder Plus platform. Heatmap plots (A–D) and 3D surface maps (E–H) display the interaction profiles and optimal combination doses of BYL719, PD‐ , and AZD5363 based on the Highest Single Agent (HSA) model. The synergy score reflects the interaction: values greater than 10 indicate a synergistic effect, values between −10 and 10 suggest an additive effect, and values below −10 indicate an antagonistic effect. In this model, HSA values greater than 10 indicate synergy, values between −10 and 10 indicate additive effects, and values below −10 represent antagonism.In 3D NES, predominantly synergistic interactions were observed between BYL719 and PD‐ as well as between AZD5363 and PD‐ , except for the lowest dose combinations (0.05 μm) which exhibited additive effects (Fig. 3A,B,E,F).The same trend was observed in 3D tNES, with mostly synergistic effects between BYL719 and PD‐ , except at the lowest doses, which were additive (Fig. 3C,G). In comparison, the AZD5363 and PD‐ combination mainly induced additive effects in tNES spheroids, with only one instance of synergy (Fig. 3D,H).To summarize, BYL719 and PD‐ combinations exhibited primarily synergistic effects in both 3D NES and 3D tNES, while AZD5363 and PD‐ combinations had mainly synergistic effects in 3D NES and predominantly additive effects in 3D tNES.3.4Growth response of NES and tNES spheroids to PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitionTo further explore the effects of JNJ‐ , BYL719, AZD5363, and PD‐ administered alone or in combination on 3D NES and 3D tNES in real time, the Incucyte® S3 Live‐Cell Analysis system was used. Representative images of 3D NES (A1–30) and 3D tNES (B1–30) are shown 72 h after treatment from three independent biological experiments (n = 3). Scalebar = 400 μm. NES, neuroepithelial stem cells; tNES, tumor‐derived neuroepithelial stem cells; FGFR, fibroblast growth factor receptor; PI3K, phosphoinositide 3‐kinase; CDK4/6, cyclin‐dependent kinases 4 and 6; AKT, protein kinase B; JNJ, JNJ‐ ; BYL, BYL719; PD, PD‐ ; AZD, AZD5363.3.4.1Single treatmentsThe size of NES spheroids remained mostly unaltered compared to the controls throughout the observation period with all drugs, suggesting little to no visible effect on growth (Figs 4A–D and 5A, 1–18).In 3D tNES, PD‐ had the strongest effect on growth, leading to the greatest reduction in spheroid size in a dose‐dependent manner (Figs 4J and 5B, 11–14). In addition, the two highest doses (0.5–1 μm) of AZD5363 also decreased spheroid growth, while the same doses of BYL719 had a slight impact compared to the control (Figs 4I,K and 5B, 7–10,15–18).In contrast, JNJ‐ did not affect spheroid size compared to the control (Figs 4H and 5B, 1–6).3.4.2Combined treatmentsIn 3D NES, combinations of BYL719 with PD‐ and AZD5363 with PD‐ had no or minimal impact on growth, with spheroid size remaining largely unchanged (Figs 4E–G and 5A, 19–30). However, the combination of AZD5363 with PD‐ led to the appearance of a halo‐like structure indicative of cellular shedding, suggesting cell dissociation from the main spheroid body (Fig. 5).In 3D tNES, among combination treatments, BYL719 with PD‐ and AZD5363 with PD‐ , profoundly inhibited spheroid growth, with spheroid size decreasing in a concentration‐dependent manner (Figs 4L–N and 5). Similar to 3D NES, the two highest doses of AZD5363 and PD‐ induced spheroid dispersal in tNES spheroids, indicating cellular dissociation (Fig. 5).3.5Immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis of PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors on apoptosis and proliferation in 3D NES and 3D tNES IHC was performed to further investigate the impact of the treatments on proliferation and apoptosis in 3D NES and 3D tNES. Staining was done on 3D NES and 3D tNES 48 h after treatment with efficient single (0.1 μm AZD5363, 0.5 μm BYL719, 0.1 and 0.5 μm PD‐ ) and combined treatments (0.1 μm AZD5363 with 0.1 μm PD‐ and 0.5 μm BYL719 with 0.5 μm PD‐ ).The analysis included markers for proliferation (anti‐Ki67) and apoptosis (anti‐cleaved caspase 3, CC‐3) as shown in Fig. 6A,B respectively.Fig. 6Histological analysis of NES and tNES spheroids 48 h after treatment with single doses of BYL719, PD‐ , AZD5363 and their combinations. Representative images of NES and tNES spheroid sections stained for the proliferation marker Ki67 (A) and the apoptosis marker cleaved caspase‐3 (CC‐3) (B) are shown. Ki67 staining is shown for NES (A1–4 and A9–11) and tNES (A5–8 and A12–14), and CC‐3 staining is shown for NES (B1–4 and B9–11) and tNES (B5–8 and B12–14). Images were captured at 20x magnification. Experiments were repeated independently three times (n = 3), with similar results. Scalebar = 100 μm. NES, neuroepithelial stem cells; tNES, tumor‐derived neuroepithelial stem cells; BYL, BYL719; PD, PD‐ ; AZD, AZD5363.In the control groups, 3D NES showed moderate Ki67 staining, reflecting normal proliferative activity, while 3D tNES exhibited strong Ki67 staining, indicating high tumor cell proliferation (Fig. 6A, 1,5). However, a notable reduction of Ki67 staining was observed at the center of control 3D tNES, suggesting lower proliferative activity, likely due to nutrient deprivation, hypoxia, or high cell density (Fig. 6A, 5).3D NES proliferation (Ki67) was affected mainly with single 0.5 μm PD‐ and combined treatments of 0.1 μm AZD5363 and 0.1 μm PD‐ or 0.5 μm BYL719 and 0.5 μm PD‐ as compared to the control, but none of these treatments had a noticeable impact on spheroid size (Fig. 6A, 1–4,9–11).In 3D tNES, strong inhibitory effects on proliferation (Ki67) were observed with all single treatments (0.1 and 0.5 μm) of PD‐ as well as with combinations of 0.1 μm AZD5363 with 0.1 μm PD‐ or 0.5 μm BYL719 and 0.5 μm PD‐ compared to the control (Fig. 6A, 5–8,12–14). All treatments also led to a noticeable reduction in spheroid size compared to the control, suggesting a considerable impact on both cell division and overall spheroid growth (Fig. 6A, 5–8,12–14).Control 3D NES and 3D tNES showed minimal CC3 staining, indicating low apoptotic activity (Fig. 6B, 1,5). However, the centers of control tNES spheroids exhibited an increased CC3 staining, suggesting a higher apoptosis due to nutrient deprivation, hypoxia, or cellular stress, consistent with the reduced Ki67 staining (Fig. 6B, 5).CC3 staining was increased with all treatments in 3D NES (Fig. 6B, 1–4,9–11). Similarly, an enhanced apoptotic response in 3D tNES was observed with all single treatments, though 0.1 μm AZD5363 and combination treatments 0.1 μm AZD5363 with 0.1 μm PD‐ and 0.5 μm BYL719 with 0.5 μm PD‐ all had weaker effects (Fig. 6B, 5–8,12–14). Nevertheless, in general, the effects of the inhibitors were more pronounced in 3D tNES than in 3D NES.4DiscussionIn this study, the effects of single and combination treatments with the FGFR, PI3K, CDK4/6, and AKT inhibitors JNJ‐ , BYL719, PD‐ , and AZD5363, respectively, on viability and growth were evaluated on 2D and 3D NES and tNES cultures, both derived from a Gorlin syndrome patient SHH‐MB model. Although it is derived from a Gorlin syndrome patient (which is a very limited patient group)— PTCH1 mutations are the most common mutations in SHH‐MB and therefore a valid model system [38, 42, 43].In general, 2D tNES cells were more sensitive to the inhibitory effects of both single and combined treatments compared to 2D NES cells. Likewise, in the 3D setting, all single‐drug treatments, except for JNJ‐ , tended to be more effective in reducing viability in 3D tNES than in 3D NES; this was also the case when combining the drugs, except for combinations including JNJ‐ . Notably, JNJ‐ alone or in combination with BYL719 exhibited a very pronounced impact on viability in 3D NES compared to 3D tNES.The initially observed stronger inhibition of cell viability by most drugs, used alone or in combination, on 2D tNES compared to 2D NES was very promising. It suggested that these drugs could be more effective against the tumorigenic tNES cells than the normal NES cells, which is important for minimizing treatment‐related side effects while effectively targeting tumors. However, upon testing NES and tNES as spheroids revealed a more complex pattern. Although single‐drug treatments again tended to affect 3D tNES more than 3D NES, this was not the case for the FGFR inhibitor JNJ‐ . Moreover, the tested inhibitors generally exhibited greater potency in 3D spheroid cultures compared to 2D monolayers. We hypothesize that the differences between 2D and 3D cell viability data could to some extent be due to altered cell–cell interactions, drug penetration, or the presence of a hypoxic core within spheroids.Notably, combining the drugs, especially BYL719 and PD‐ , generally showed synergistic effects on viability for both 3D NES and 3D tNES, while AZD5363 combined with PD‐ showed mainly synergistic effects in 3D NES and predominantly additive effects in 3D tNES. The latter may suggest that AKT signaling might not be as critical in 3D tNES, or the cells can bypass AKT inhibition via other survival routes.The combination of BYL719 and JNJ‐ was effective in both 3D NES and 3D tNES; however, due to the high sensitivity of NES cells to JNJ‐ alone, this combination was not investigated further. The high sensitivity to JNJ‐ could be a result of the crucial role of FGFR in stem cells, making the signaling pathway essential for survival [44]. This highlights the importance of carefully evaluating FGFR inhibitors in the context of normal brain tissue to avoid potential adverse effects on healthy neural stem cells.Finally, we also investigated growth, proliferation, and apoptosis in the 3D setting. Overall, the effects were more pronounced on the 3D tNES, which, consistent with their tumorigenic nature, displayed higher proliferative capacity compared to the 3D NES cells. This observation was supported by stronger Ki67 staining in control 3D tNES compared to 3D NES. Further support came from the increased CC3 levels in the core of control 3D tNES after 72 h of growth, suggesting elevated apoptosis likely due to nutrient deprivation, hypoxia, or cellular stress.Additionally, the tested single and combined inhibitors had minimal effects on 3D NES size, suggesting that 3D NES growth remained mostly unaffected. On the other hand, growth was less prominent in general for 3D NES as compared to 3D tNES during the 72‐h observation period. In contrast, 3D tNES were more responsive, with single treatments of PD‐ and AZD5363, as well as combinations of PD‐ with BYL719 and PD‐ with AZD5363, showing the strongest growth‐inhibitory effects. Notably, single PD‐ and the same combination treatments greatly reduced proliferation and increased apoptosis in 3D tNES, whereas in 3D NES, proliferation was also inhibited by these treatments, but apoptosis induction remained minimal.The CDK4/6 inhibitor (PD‐ ) alone or in combination with PI3K (BYL719) or AKT (AZD5363) inhibitors selectively suppressed tumor spheroid growth by both reducing proliferation and increasing apoptosis, whereas in 3D NES they mainly reduce proliferation without triggering cell death or affecting overall growth. This indicates a selective response where tumor cells were more sensitive to both growth arrest and apoptosis, while normal cells mainly show slowed proliferation without much cell death and shrinkage.This selective response of tNES versus NES cells suggests a potential therapeutic window, in which tumor cells are effectively targeted while sparing normal neural stem cells, potentially reducing treatment‐related side effects in patients. Furthermore, the observed synergistic effects of some combinations indicate that targeting multiple signaling pathways simultaneously may overcome intrinsic or acquired resistance mechanisms in SHH‐driven MB. Clinically, these findings highlight the potential for rational combination therapies that maximize tumor suppression while minimizing harm to healthy brain tissue.Clearly, the NES/tNES model offers notable advantages, as it allows for the direct comparison of drug responses between a normalized neuroepithelial stem cell line and its tumorigenic counterpart. However, the data should be interpreted with caution, as tNES cells inherently possess a higher growth capacity, which may make them more susceptible to drug‐induced effects overall and this must be considered when interpreting the data.This study has some limitations. First, it was based on a single NES/tNES cell model derived from one Gorlin patient, which may not fully capture the biological variability seen across different patients. Second, the drug screen included a relatively limited number of drugs and concentrations, primarily focusing on drugs and doses previously tested in MB cell lines [36, 37]. Moreover, this study was restricted to the MB SHH subtype, which comprises approximately 30% of all cases. Future studies should include in vivo evaluation using established SHH‐MB mouse models to assess both efficacy and systemic tolerability of these inhibitors. Consequently, the drug responses observed in tNES cells with PTCH1 mutations may not fully reflect responses in MB with other distinct genetic s.Nevertheless, the study illustrates how a normalized/tumorigenic NES/tNES model can be used to test various drugs, although the specific features and proliferative capacities of the two counterparts in the model need to be taken into account when interpreting the obtained data.5ConclusionsTo sum up, 2D tNES cells were generally more sensitive to the inhibitory effects of both single and combined treatments compared to 2D NES cells. In the 3D setting, all single‐drug treatments, except for the FGFR inhibitor JNJ‐ , exerted stronger effects on cell viability in 3D tNES than in 3D NES, while for JNJ‐ the opposite occurred, and for combined treatments, synergistic/additive effects were relatively similar for both NES and tNES. This NES/tNES model therefore holds promise for evaluating drug responses, but further studies on additional NES/tNES models should be pursued, and the specific cell features and proliferation capacity of the cells should be taken into account when evaluating the data.Conflict of interestThe authors declare no conflict of interest.Author contributionsML: Writing – review and editing, writing – original draft, visualization, validation, methodology, investigation, funding acquisition, formal analysis, data curation. title: Nanoceria–curcumin nanoplatform enhances radiotherapy efficacy in triple-negative breast cancer via microenvironmental redox modulation and TNF-α–NF-κB/inflammatory program suppression
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) derives only limited clinical benefit from radiotherapy (RT), partly due to abnormalities in the tumor microenvironment and dysregulated signaling pathways. By integrating TNBC cases from the METABRIC and TCGA cohorts, we implemented an analysis framework centered on RT-by-gene interaction terms, implicating TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and inflammatory response as potential effect modifiers of RT benefit. Based on a pathway-guided polyphenol–gene interaction screen, curcumin (Cur) was prioritized as a modulator of TNF-α–NF-κB/inflammation-related programs. We then engineered a multifunctional nanoplatform (TCC) that couples catalytic modulation of the tumor microenvironment with suppression of adaptive pro-survival programs. TCC was built on pH-responsive nanoceria (CeO2 nanozymes) to modulate redox homeostasis and alleviate hypoxia, loaded with Cur, and coated with D-α-tocopherol polyethylene glycol succinate (TPGS) to improve stability and cellular uptake; cRGD was further introduced to generate cRGD-TCC for enhanced tumor targeting. In vitro and in vivo, TCC promoted G2/M-phase arrest, amplified RT-induced reactive oxygen species generation and DNA damage, and attenuated TNF-α–NF-κB/inflammatory programs and markers of inflammation, survival, and invasion. Collectively, TCC provides an integrated radiosensitization strategy that addresses microenvironmental barriers and adaptive tumor signaling, thereby potentially enhancing RT response in TNBC.
full_text: 1IntroductionBreast cancer is one of the most common malignancies among women, and its molecular subtypes exhibit substantial heterogeneity that leads to marked differences in treatment response and prognosis [1]. Within multimodal therapy, radiotherapy (RT) remains indispensable for local control and recurrence prevention. However, multiple clinical studies have reported that the benefit of RT varies significantly across subtypes, with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) generally showing the least improvement in clinical outcomes [[2], [3], [4]]. This suggests that the RT response in TNBC is regulated by complex subtype-specific mechanisms rather than by radiation dose or treatment regimen alone. Defining the core drivers of RT resistance in TNBC is therefore essential for improving radiosensitivity.Ionizing radiation exerts its cytotoxic effect primarily through direct DNA damage and oxidative damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS) [5,6]. Tumor cells rapidly activate the DNA damage response (DDR) and antioxidant defenses to counter radiation-induced stress, enabling their survival and fostering radioresistance [7]. The canonical DDR pathway, mediated by kinases such as ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK, coordinates DNA repair and activates cell-cycle checkpoints to maintain cell survival [8]. Radiation-induced DNA damage and ROS also act as secondary messengers that stimulate pro-survival signaling pathways, including PI3K/AKT, MAPK, and NF-κB, thereby enhancing cellular antioxidant defenses and repair capacity [9,10]. Beyond intrinsic signaling, the hypoxic and poorly perfused tumor microenvironment (TME) in TNBC weakens the oxygen-fixation effect of RT and favors hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) stabilization, glycolytic reprogramming, lactate buildup, and immune suppression, which together compromise the therapeutic efficacy of RT [[11], [12], [13]]. Radiation-induced stress can also promote epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and enhance stemness, endowing tumor cells with greater repair capacity and increased invasiveness [14]. These findings suggest that RT resistance in TNBC is not driven by a single pathway but emerges from the convergence of multiple adaptive responses.Targeting DNA repair represents one of the most direct strategies for radiosensitization. Inhibiting ATM, ATR, CHK1/2, or PARP can block DDR activation and impair DNA repair, thereby increasing the cytotoxicity of radiation [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. Nonetheless, when DDR is suppressed, tumor cells frequently activate compensatory pro-survival pathways, such as PI3K/AKT and NF-κB, which can diminish the overall sensitization effect [19]. Enhancing oxygen availability or boosting ROS generation may also strengthen the response to RT [20], but HIF-1α–driven glycolytic reprogramming and vascular remodeling often re-establish metabolic and microenvironmental homeostasis, limiting the durability of these approaches [21]. Excessive ROS can intensify oxidative injury but may also introduce nonspecific toxicity, while tumor cells retain the capacity to rapidly detoxify ROS through robust antioxidant defenses [22]. These compensatory adaptations clarify why single-target strategies seldom yield durable radiosensitization and underscore the necessity of coordinated, multi-level interventions.Nanomedicine provides new opportunities for multidimensional radiosensitization. High-atomic-number inorganic nanomaterials can enhance local radiation energy deposition through the photoelectric effect [23]. Metal oxide nanozymes such as nanoceria (CeO2) and MnO2 display catalase (CAT)-like and peroxidase (POD)-like activities that modulate redox balance, alleviate hypoxia, and amplify free-radical production [[24], [25], [26]]. Among these nanozymes, nanoceria possesses reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ cycling and pH-responsive catalytic activity that enable it to shift between oxygen generation and oxidative-stress amplification in response to the local tumor microenvironment, offering clear advantages for RT enhancement [27,28]. Constructing nanoceria into multifunctional nanocomposites enables the incorporation of drug loading, surface modification, and targeted delivery, thereby allowing coordinated modulation of both the tumor microenvironment and oncogenic signaling within a single platform [29].In recent years, dietary polyphenols have gained increasing attention for their broad regulatory activity across inflammatory, metabolic, and stress-response pathways [30,31]. Unlike single-target small-molecule inhibitors, which frequently trigger compensatory signaling [32,33], natural polyphenols can modulate multiple nodes within oncogenic and stress-adaptation networks while maintaining an excellent safety profile [34]. These multi-target and low-toxicity features make polyphenols attractive candidates for radiosensitization, particularly in TNBC, where therapy resistance often arises from the concurrent activation of several adaptive pathways [35]. Among dietary polyphenols, Cur is one of the most extensively studied and has been shown to inhibit NF-κB and multiple downstream pro-survival signaling cascades [36,37]. D-α-tocopherol polyethylene glycol succinate (TPGS) improves nanoparticle stability, cellular uptake, and delivery efficiency [38], while cyclic RGD peptide (cRGD) further enhances tumor targeting [39]. Together, these components provide key functional elements for constructing a cooperative radiosensitizing system.This study analyzed the METABRIC and TCGA datasets to identify key pathways associated with RT resistance in TNBC. Accordingly, a multifunctional nanocomposite (TCC) was developed for targeted intervention. Built around nanoceria, the platform modulates oxygen metabolism and ROS generation, delivers Cur to suppress radiation-induced pro-survival and inflammation-associated signaling, and incorporates TPGS and cRGD to enhance delivery efficiency, cellular uptake, and tumor targeting. By integrating clinical data mining with material engineering and mechanistic validation, this study establishes a multidimensional radiosensitization strategy that addresses both microenvironmental remodeling and oncogenic signaling interference (Scheme 1).Scheme 1Schematic illustration of TCC construction and its proposed radiosensitization mechanism. (a) Stepwise synthesis of the multifunctional TCC nanoplatform. (b) TCC enhances RT by alleviating hypoxia, amplifying ROS generation, and suppressing TNF-α–NF-κB signaling to promote apoptosis. Abbreviations: TCC, TPGS-nanoceria-curcumin; RT, radiotherapy; ROS, reactive oxygen species.2Materials and 2.1Data sources and patient inclusion criteriaData for this study were obtained from two publicly available breast cancer (BRCA) genomic cohorts: the Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium (METABRIC) and The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA-BRCA) cohort. METABRIC expression and clinical data were accessed via the cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics, and TCGA-BRCA data were downloaded from the UCSC Xena Browser. Both datasets include clinical annotations such as age, clinical stage, radiotherapy status, immunohistochemistry (IHC)-based subtype, and survival outcomes. METABRIC expression profiles were generated using the Illumina HumanHT-12 v3 microarray platform and are provided as log2-normalized values. TCGA expression data were generated using the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform, quantified by the RSEM algorithm, and provided as log2(x + 1)-transformed matrices.Only primary tumor samples with complete IHC-based subtype information, radiotherapy records, and overall survival (OS) follow-up were included. Molecular subtyping was based on IHC for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). Patients were classified as triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC; ER−/PR−/HER2−) or non-TNBC (positive for ≥1 marker). RT status was defined as a binary exposure variable (RT = “yes” if the patient received RT at any time per cohort records; otherwise “no”). As METABRIC and TCGA are fully de-identified public datasets, no additional ethical approval or patient consent was required.2.2Survival analysis and interaction-guided gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA)Within each cohort, patients were grouped as RT or non-RT according to treatment records. OS was estimated and visualized using Kaplan–Meier (KM) curves. Analyses were performed in R (v4.3.0) using the survival and survminer packages. Hazard ratios (HRs) for RT (RT vs non-RT) shown alongside KM curves were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models with RT as the only covariate (univariable Cox). HRs are reported with 95% confidence intervals derived from the Cox model, and p values for KM curves were obtained from two-sided log-rank tests.To identify molecular programs associated with heterogeneous RT benefit in TNBC, gene-wise Cox proportional hazards models were fitted in the TNBC subset of METABRIC and TCGA, adjusted for age and clinical stage, and including an RT×gene interaction term. Gene expression was z-standardized prior to modeling. The RT×gene interaction Wald z-statistic indicates effect modification: z > 0 suggests reduced RT benefit at higher expression, whereas z 0 indicates enrichment toward genes with z > 0, whereas NES 1 with adjusted p 0.05), so downstream interpretation focused on three pathways with consistent interaction patterns: TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, inflammatory response, and mitotic spindle.Overall, TNBC showed limited population-average association between RT and OS in METABRIC, alongside concordant enrichment of TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and inflammatory response consistent with reduced RT benefit, whereas mitotic spindle was enriched in the RT-favorable direction. Importantly, these pathway enrichments and corresponding interaction patterns were directionally consistent in TCGA (Fig. 1d and e). Given their cross-cohort consistency in the radioresistance direction and greater pharmacological tractability, we prioritized TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and inflammatory response to guide compound selection and subsequent nanoplatform design.3.2TNF-α–NF-κB and inflammatory pathway profiling prioritizes Cur as a lead natural polyphenolWe performed a pathway-guided screen of dietary polyphenols to identify candidates that could modulate the resistance-associated programs. After excluding phenolic acids and non-phenolic metabolites from the Phenol-Explorer database, 579 polyphenols were curated. CTD mapping showed highly uneven evidence depth across compounds, spanning from no curated targets to thousands of reported interactions (Fig. 2a).Fig. 2Polyphenol screening and pathway-based characterization of Cur. (a) CTD-annotated target-gene counts for representative polyphenols. (b) Coverage of the TNF-α–NF-κB/inflammatory union signature across the top 50 polyphenols. (c) Specificity versus union-signature coverage; bubble size denotes interaction score. (d) Hallmark enrichment of Cur-associated genes. (e) Venn diagram showing gene overlap among TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, inflammatory response, hypoxia, EMT, and apoptosis. (f) STRING PPI network of Cur-associated genes within the selected pathways. Abbreviations: Cur, curcumin; CTD, Comparative Toxicogenomics Database; EMT, epithelial–mesenchymal transition; PPI, protein–protein interaction.Among the 579 polyphenols, 155 had at least one curated interaction record in CTD and were taken forward for downstream analysis. We defined a TNF-α–NF-κB/inflammatory union signature as the union of the Hallmark TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and inflammatory response gene sets (Fig. 2b), and quantified union-signature coverage for each compound. Coverage was generally low, with only a small subset showing broad overlap. We therefore focused on the top 5% by union-signature coverage, yielding eight candidates. Because coverage can be inflated by broadly acting compounds, we additionally considered pathway specificity and an interaction score. Under this combined evaluation, Cur showed the most consistently favorable profile and was prioritized for subsequent validation (Fig. 2c).Functional enrichment of Cur-associated genes indicated strong involvement of TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and the inflammatory response, with additional enrichment in hypoxia, EMT, and apoptosis-related programs (Fig. 2d). Accordingly, hypoxia, EMT, and apoptosis were included as supplementary modules, together with TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and inflammatory response, to visualize pathway overlap (Fig. 2e). These five programs showed appreciable gene intersection and overlap. Consistently, the STRING PPI network constructed from the overlapping genes showed a connected core with hub-like nodes including FN1, TNF, and TP53, supporting the over-representation of EMT/extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and TNF-α–NF-κB–linked inflammatory modules, together with a TP53-centered stress and tumor-suppressive response axis, within the Cur-associated network (Fig. 2f). On this basis, Cur was selected as the lead polyphenol for downstream validation and nanomaterial studies.3.3TCC exhibits structural stability and tunable redox catalytic activityGuided by the bioinformatic features associated with RT resistance in TNBC, a multifunctional nanoplatform (TCC) was constructed to integrate microenvironmental regulation with signaling interference (Fig. 3a). The physicochemical properties and redox behavior of TCC were subsequently characterized in detail. TEM imaging showed that the as-synthesized nanoceria possessed a uniform spherical morphology with an average diameter of approximately 5 nm (Fig. 3b). After TPGS modification, an organic TPGS-associated coating was introduced around the nanoceria, increasing the overall particle diameter to approximately 40 nm and enabling stable dispersion in aqueous media (Fig. 3c). Further Cur loading enlarged the particle size to 70–80 nm, accompanied by a characteristic deep-red appearance (Fig. 3d and e).Fig. 3Design and physicochemical characterization of the TCC nanoplatform. (a) Schematic illustration of the synthetic procedure from nanoceria to TPGS-nanoceria and TCC. (b–d) TEM images of nanoceria, TPGS-nanoceria, and TCC, accompanied by corresponding digital photographs. (e) Digital photographs of TCC aqueous dispersions at different concentrations. (f) Hydrodynamic size distribution of TCC measured by DLS. (g) Colloidal stability of TCC over 7 days, n = 3. (h) STEM image and EDS elemental maps of Ce and O in TCC. (i) FT-IR spectra of nanoceria, TPGS, Cur, and TCC. (j) UV–Vis absorption spectra of nanoceria, TPGS, Cur, and TCC. (k) Fluorescence emission spectra of nanoceria, TPGS, Cur, and TCC, with excitation at 320 nm. (l) Ce 3d XPS spectrum of TCC with fitted Ce3+/Ce4+ components. (m, n) CAT-like (m) and POD-like (n) activities of TCC under different pH conditions. Scale bars: 20 nm. Abbreviations: TCC, TPGS-nanoceria-curcumin; Cur, curcumin; CAT, catalase; POD, peroxidase.DLS measurements showed that TCC had a hydrodynamic diameter of 78.7 ± 2.5 nm, a ζ-potential of −38.6 ± 0.2 mV, and a PDI of 0.18 (Fig. 3f). Comparative DLS analysis showed that the hydrodynamic diameter increased from 52.4 ± 1.7 nm for TC to 78.7 ± 2.5 nm for TCC and 92.1 ± 5.8 nm for cRGD-TCC, whereas their ζ-potentials remained similarly negative (−37.2 ± 0.7, −38.6 ± 0.2, and −37.6 ± 0.5 mV, respectively; Fig. S4a–b). TCC maintained stable particle size and PDI for 7 days in PBS and RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% FBS (Fig. 3g, Fig. S5). Quantitative drug-loading and release analyses showed a Cur DLC of 12.6%, an EE of 86.1%, and mildly pH-dependent Cur release, with cumulative release reaching approximately 42.1%, 38.2%, and 25.5% at pH 5.0, pH 6.5, and pH 7.4, respectively, at the final time point (Fig. S7).Spectroscopic and structural analyses further confirmed the successful assembly of all components. STEM–EDS mapping (Fig. 3h) demonstrated homogeneous distributions of Ce and O, supporting the successful incorporation and preservation of nanoceria within the TPGS/Cur-associated composite. FT-IR spectra (Fig. 3i) showed characteristic bands corresponding to Ce–O (450-550 cm−1), the ester C=O stretching of TPGS (1720-1730 cm−1), and the aromatic C=C stretching vibrations of Cur (1500-1600 cm−1). UV–Vis spectra revealed the intrinsic broad absorption of nanoceria together with the characteristic Cur band at 420 nm, which showed a slight red shift to approximately 430 nm in TCC (Fig. 3j) [40].The 1H NMR spectrum (Fig. S6) displayed resonances attributed to the alkyl chains of TPGS and aromatic protons of Cur. Fluorescence spectra (Fig. 3k) exhibited both the blue emission of nanoceria (400–450 nm) and the slightly red-shifted Cur emission (540–555 nm). TGA (Fig. S8) showed a dominant mass loss of TCC over ∼250–450 °C, corresponding to the decomposition of organic constituents, and a final residue of ∼26.4% at 1000 °C. Notably, the thermal profile of TCC was distinct from those of the individual components, supporting the successful incorporation of the TPGS coating and Cur payload into TCC.XRD patterns (Fig. S9) confirmed the fluorite structure of nanoceria, with diffraction peaks at 2θ = 28.6°, 33.1°, 47.5°, and 56.4°, consistent with JCPDS -0394. In TCC, the thick organic coating attenuated the diffraction intensity and produced a broadened peak near 28°. Raman spectroscopy was further performed as a supplementary structural characterization of TCC; however, the Raman signal was broad and weak under the current acquisition conditions, without clearly resolved bands in the locally enlarged region (Fig. S10). XPS spectra (Fig. 3l) showed the coexistence of Ce3+ and Ce4+, with a Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio of approximately 1:4, supporting the presence of redox-active cerium sites and oxygen-vacancy-related surface characteristics. Catalytic activity assays revealed that TCC exhibited pH- and concentration-dependent enzyme-mimicking behavior (Fig. 3m–n, Fig. S11). Under neutral pH (7.4), TCC mainly showed CAT-like activity, whereas acidic pH (6.5–5.0) significantly enhanced its POD-like activity, reflected by increased TMB oxidation. These findings indicate that TCC can dynamically adjust its catalytic mode in response to the local tumor microenvironment.3.4TCC enhances radiosensitivity in vitro by modulating oxygen metabolism and cell-cycle progressionWe first examined uptake kinetics and intracellular distribution of TCC in 4T1 cells. Flow cytometry showed that TCC-Cy7 was rapidly internalized, with the proportion of cells exhibiting detectable Cy7 fluorescence increasing markedly at 0.5 h and reaching a steady level by 1 h. Thereafter, the fluorescence peak continued to shift rightward, indicating progressive intracellular accumulation despite a relatively stable fraction of Cy7-positive cells (Fig. 4a). CLSM imaging further confirmed stronger and more homogeneous cytoplasmic fluorescence for TCC-Cy7 compared with free Cy7 (Fig. 4b), suggesting that TPGS modification markedly enhances cellular uptake and intracellular retention. Lysosomal colocalization studies revealed that TCC predominantly accumulated within lysosomal compartments and remained detectable for up to 24 h (Fig. S12), a feature that may facilitate activation of the POD-like catalytic function of nanoceria in the acidic lysosomal environment.Fig. 4TCC enhances cellular radiosensitivity by promoting intracellular uptake, improving oxygenation, elevating ROS levels, and inducing G2/M arrest. (a) Flow cytometry analysis of TCC-Cy7 uptake in 4T1 cells after 0.5–4 h of incubation. (b) CLSM images showing cellular uptake of free Cy7 and TCC-Cy7. (c) Viability of 4T1 cells treated with TCC for 12 h with or without 4 Gy irradiation. (d) Cell-cycle distribution of 4T1 cells after PBS, TCC, or TCC + RT treatment. (e) Annexin V–FITC/PI staining analysis of apoptosis. (f) Intracellular hypoxia assessed using the [Ru(dpp)3]Cl2 probe. (g) Intracellular ROS detected by DCFH-DA staining. (h) Scratch-wound images at 0, 12, and 24 h. (i, j) Quantification of wound-healing area at 12 h (i) and 24 h (j), n = 3. (k) Representative colony formation images of 4T1 cells after 0, 2, 4, and 6 Gy irradiation with or without TCC pretreatment. Scale bars: 50 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SD. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001; ns, not significant. Abbreviations: TCC, TPGS-nanoceria-curcumin; ROS, reactive oxygen species; TCC-Cy7, Cy7-labeled TCC; CLSM, confocal laser scanning microscopy; RT, radiotherapy; PI, propidium iodide; DCFH-DA, 2′,7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate.CCK-8 assays demonstrated that TCC or RT alone induced modest cytotoxicity, whereas their combination substantially reduced cell viability. The viability of 4T1 cells after treatment with TCC (10 μg/mL), RT, and TCC + RT was 91.58%, 78.26%, and 53.80%, respectively (Fig. 4c), indicating that TCC significantly augments RT-induced cell killing. Cell-cycle analysis revealed that TCC (30 μg/mL, 12 h) increased the G2/M population from 20.7% in the PBS group to 32.9% in the TCC group, and TCC + RT further increased this fraction to 48.1% (Fig. 4d). As cells in G2/M are known to exhibit heightened sensitivity to ionizing radiation, TCC-induced G2/M enrichment is expected to potentiate radiation-induced DNA damage. Consistently, flow cytometry showed that late-stage apoptosis increased from 10.2% in the RT group to 30.6% in the TCC + RT group (Fig. 4e).To further evaluate the redox-modulating capability of TCC, intracellular hypoxia and ROS levels were examined. Imaging with the hypoxia probe [Ru(dpp)3]Cl2 revealed strong red fluorescence in the PBS and RT groups, whereas the signal was markedly reduced in the TCC-treated groups (Fig. 4f), indicating effective alleviation of hypoxia. ROS detection showed that TCC or RT alone induced moderate ROS accumulation, while the combination produced the highest DCF fluorescence intensity (Fig. 4g), demonstrating that TCC can amplify RT-induced oxidative stress.Functionally, scratch-wound assays showed that TCC + RT significantly inhibited cell migration, with only 8.42% wound closure at 24 h compared with 66.68% in PBS and 41.95% in RT (Fig. 4h–j). Colony formation assays were further performed across increasing radiation doses of 0, 2, 4, and 6 Gy in the presence or absence of TCC pretreatment (Fig. 4k). TCC markedly reduced clonogenic survival at each radiation dose compared with RT alone. The dose-response survival curves were fitted using the linear-quadratic model, yielding a sensitizer enhancement ratio of approximately 1.84 at 10% surviving fraction (Fig. S13). These results provide quantitative evidence that TCC enhances the long-term radiosensitivity of 4T1 cells. Transwell assays further showed that migration and invasion areas in the TCC + RT group were reduced to 12.7% and 13.5% of the PBS group, respectively (Fig. S14), both significantly lower than either treatment alone.These data show that TCC is efficiently taken up and retained, reduces hypoxia, increases ROS accumulation, promotes G2/M accumulation, and suppresses clonogenic survival, consistent with enhanced RT response in vitro.3.5TCC exhibits favorable tumor accumulation and targeted delivery in vivoIn vivo fluorescence imaging was performed to evaluate biodistribution and tumor targeting in a 4T1 subcutaneous tumor model. After injection, free Cy7 showed rapid systemic dispersion and minimal tumor-associated signal under the same imaging settings (Fig. 5a). In contrast, TCC–Cy7 enabled an earlier appearance of a distinguishable tumor-to-background contrast, and the tumor ROI signal gradually decreased over time, consistent with progressive clearance after systemic distribution. Notably, cRGD functionalization further improved the detectability of tumor signals at early time points and prolonged intratumoral retention, resulting in a more favorable tumor-to-background profile across the imaging window.Fig. 5In vivo biodistribution and tumor-targeting performance of TCC and cRGD-TCC in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice. (a) In vivo fluorescence images of tumor-bearing mice after intravenous injection of free Cy7, TCC-Cy7, or cRGD-TCC-Cy7 at different time points. (b) Ex vivo fluorescence images of tumors and major organs collected at 24 h post-injection. (c) Quantification of fluorescence intensity in tumors and major organs based on ROI analysis, n = 3. (d) CLSM images of tumor cryosections collected at 12 h post-injection showing the intratumoral distribution of Cy7-associated formulations in the marginal and central regions of tumors. Scale bars: 50 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SD. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001; ns, not significant. Abbreviations: TCC, TPGS-nanoceria-curcumin; cRGD-TCC, cyclo(Arg-Gly-Asp-D-Phe-Cys)-modified TCC; Cy7, cyanine 7; ROI, region of interest; CLSM, confocal laser scanning microscopy.Ex vivo organ imaging (Fig. 5b and c) further supported these findings. Free Cy7 was primarily distributed in the liver and kidneys, with weak tumor signals. Both TCC-Cy7 and cRGD-TCC-Cy7 showed evident tumor accumulation, whereas cRGD-TCC-Cy7 displayed substantially enhanced tumor-associated fluorescence.Quantitative analysis revealed that cRGD-TCC-Cy7 achieved significantly higher tumor fluorescence intensity than unmodified TCC-Cy7 (p < 0.05), together with notably increased tumor-to-liver and tumor-to-kidney fluorescence ratios (p < 0.05), indicating improved targeting efficiency conferred by cRGD modification (Fig. S15) [41].To assess intratumoral penetration, tumors were harvested 12 h post-injection for cryosectioning (Fig. 5d). Free Cy7 remained sparsely distributed and confined to the tumor periphery. TCC-Cy7 penetrated more uniformly throughout the tumor mass, while cRGD-TCC-Cy7 exhibited the deepest and strongest intratumoral fluorescence. These results demonstrate that TCC possesses intrinsic tumor-accumulating and retaining properties, and cRGD functionalization further enhances its penetration and residence within tumor tissues.3.6TCC markedly enhances in vivo radiotherapy efficacy without overt toxicityThe radiosensitizing efficacy of TCC was further evaluated in a 4T1 subcutaneous tumor model (Fig. 6a). As shown in Fig. 6b, RT alone exerted only modest tumor-growth inhibition, with tumor volume reaching 866.3 ± 170.3 mm3 on day 14. Treatment with TCC (691.4 ± 135.6 mm3) or cRGD-TCC (513.8 ± 117.3 mm3) alone moderately delayed tumor progression. In contrast, combining these formulations with RT further reduced tumor volume compared with RT alone. Tumor volume in the TCC + RT group decreased to 249.5 ± 76.5 mm3, and further to 144.3 ± 44.1 mm3 in the cRGD-TCC + RT group, which also showed the lowest tumor weight (0.15 ± 0.03 g; Fig. 6d and e). These findings indicate that cRGD modification enhances intratumoral accumulation and thereby strengthens the therapeutic response. Histological analyses further elucidated the mechanisms underlying the enhanced therapeutic outcome.Fig. 6In vivo radiosensitizing efficacy of TCC in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice. (a) Treatment regimen for the saline, RT, TCC, cRGD-TCC, TCC + RT, and cRGD-TCC + RT groups. (b, c) Tumor growth curves (b) and body weight changes (c) over the 14-day study period, n = 6. (d) Photographs of excised tumors collected on day 14. (e) Tumor weights on day 14, n = 6. (f) Representative images of tumor sections stained with H&E, HIF-1α, p-p65, γ-H2AX, and TUNEL. (g–j) Quantification of HIF-1α-positive nuclei (g), p-p65-positive nuclei (h), γ-H2AX-positive nuclei (i), and TUNEL-positive apoptotic index (j). Scale bars: 50 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SD. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001; ns, not significant. Abbreviations: TCC, TPGS-nanoceria-curcumin; RT, radiotherapy; cRGD-TCC, cyclo(Arg-Gly-Asp-D-Phe-Cys)-modified TCC.H&E staining revealed extensive necrosis in the TCC + RT group, with even more pronounced tissue destruction in the cRGD-TCC + RT group. Immunohistochemistry (Fig. 6f–h) demonstrated that TCC + RT reduced the expression of the hypoxia marker HIF-1α and the NF-κB activation-related marker p-p65, whereas cRGD-TCC + RT produced stronger suppression, consistent with its higher tumor accumulation. γ-H2AX (Fig. 6i) and TUNEL staining (Fig. 6j) further confirmed that combined treatment markedly increased DNA double-strand breaks and apoptosis. Representative high-magnification insets of p-p65 and γ-H2AX staining are shown in Fig. S16.Additional immunohistochemical analysis showed that CD8+ T-cell infiltration was increased after TCC-based combined treatment, with the highest level observed in the cRGD-TCC + RT group (Fig. S17a–b). In contrast, Hsp90 expression was elevated after RT and was reduced in TCC- or cRGD-TCC-treated tumors, particularly compared with RT alone (Fig. S17a and c). These findings provide preliminary evidence that TCC-mediated radiosensitization may be associated with increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and attenuation of stress-response-related Hsp90 expression.Body weights remained stable in all groups (Fig. 6c). H&E staining of major organs revealed no detectable pathological abnormalities (Fig. S18), and serum biochemical parameters (ALT, AST, CRE, BUN) remained within the normal range (Fig. S19). Thirty-day biodistribution and biosafety assessment showed that Ce was mainly detected in the liver and spleen, whereas relatively low levels were observed in the heart, lung, and kidney. Despite partial liver/spleen retention, day-30 H&E staining and serum biochemical analysis did not reveal obvious tissue injury under the current experimental conditions (Fig. S20). Hemolysis testing showed that TCC at 10–50 μg/mL induced less than 5% hemolysis (Fig. S21), confirming the good hemocompatibility of the nanoplatform.3.7TCC reverses radiotherapy-resistance signatures through multidimensional gene regulationRNA-seq was performed on 4T1 cells treated with PBS, RT, or TCC + RT to examine transcriptomic correlates of radiosensitization. PCA revealed clear separation of the three groups at the transcriptomic level: PC1 (98% variance) separated TCC + RT from PBS and RT, whereas PC2 (2% variance) further distinguished RT from PBS (Fig. 7a). Differential expression analysis identified 1007 DEGs in RT versus PBS, including 812 upregulated and 195 downregulated genes (Fig. 7b). In TCC + RT versus RT, 7733 DEGs were detected (3863 upregulated and 3870 downregulated; Fig. 7c), consistent with a broader transcriptional response upon adding TCC to RT.Fig. 7Transcriptomic and Western blot analyses of RT-associated resistance programs. (a) PCA of 4T1 cell transcriptomes from PBS, RT, and TCC + RT groups, n = 3 per group. (b) Volcano plot of DEGs for RT vs PBS. (c) Volcano plot of DEGs for TCC + RT vs RT. (d) ssGSEA scores for TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, inflammatory response, hypoxia, and EMT across groups, n = 3. (e–h) GSEA plots for TCC + RT vs RT: TNF-α–NF-κB signaling (e), inflammatory response (f), hypoxia (g), and EMT (h). (i–k) Heatmaps of representative gene modules: TNF-α–NF-κB signaling (i), hypoxia/glycolysis (j), and EMT/ECM-remodeling (k). (l) Western blot analysis of p65, p-p65, IκBα, p-IκBα, and COX-2 in 4T1 cells after indicated treatments. Data are presented as mean ± SD where applicable. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001; ns, not significant. Abbreviations: TCC, TPGS-nanoceria-curcumin; RT, radiotherapy; PCA, principal component analysis; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; ssGSEA, single-sample gene-set enrichment analysis; GSEA, gene-set enrichment analysis; EMT, epithelial–mesenchymal transition; ECM, extracellular matrix.ssGSEA showed higher scores for TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, inflammatory response, and EMT in RT compared with PBS (adjusted p < 0.05). Notably, adding TCC led to a more pronounced reduction in the hypoxia score in TCC + RT relative to RT, accompanied by concurrent decreases in TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, inflammatory response, and EMT (adjusted p < 0.05; Fig. 7d). GSEA of TCC + RT versus RT showed significant negative enrichment of hypoxia and the other pathways (adjusted p < 0.05; Fig. 7e–h), indicating that TCC attenuates hypoxia-related transcriptional programs while suppressing RT-associated TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, inflammatory response, and EMT programs. Heatmaps of representative gene modules were consistent with the pathway-level analyses. Relative to RT, TCC + RT showed reduced expression of genes in the TNF-α–NF-κB module and the hypoxia/glycolysis module (Fig. 7i and j), together with a coordinated shift in the EMT/ECM-remodeling module (Fig. 7k). In addition, antioxidant/apoptosis-related gene changes further supported enhanced stress and cell-death signaling after TCC + RT treatment (Fig. S22). Western blot analysis further confirmed suppression of NF-κB-related proteins after TCC-based combined treatment (Fig. 7l). Together, these transcriptomic and protein-level findings indicate that TCC attenuates RT-associated resistance programs while reinforcing pro-death responses under combined treatment.4DiscussionThe cohort analyses suggested that TNBC derives limited survival benefit from RT and highlighted resistance-linked TNF-α–NF-κB signaling and inflammatory programs. Motivated by these observations, we developed a nanoceria–curcumin nanoplatform (TCC) and tested it as an RT adjuvant in 4T1 models, where the combination significantly improved tumor control relative to RT alone.At near-neutral pH, nanoceria predominantly exhibits CAT-like activity [42], decomposing hydrogen peroxide and potentially improving local oxygen availability, which may facilitate oxygen-dependent fixation of radiation-induced DNA lesions. Consistent with this possibility, tumors treated with TCC showed reduced HIF-1α staining. Under acidic tumor-related or intracellular conditions, CeO2-based nanoparticles may exhibit enhanced pro-oxidant/POD-like activity, thereby facilitating ROS generation and amplifying irradiation-associated oxidative stress [43]. In the present study, the coexistence of Ce3+ and Ce4+ in TCC, together with its pH-dependent CAT-/POD-like activities, supports the potential of TCC to participate in local redox modulation. This redox adaptability is generally attributed to oxygen-vacancy-related surface defects and reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ cycling, which are key determinants of nanoceria enzyme-like activity [44]. During irradiation, water radiolysis and radiation-induced oxidative stress may further interact with these redox-active surface sites, supporting continuous ROS modulation. Therefore, the observed increase in ROS, enhancement of γ-H2AX staining, promotion of apoptosis, and reduction in hypoxia-related signals may result from the combined effects of pH-dependent enzyme-like activity and these redox-active surface characteristics [45]. However, the current XPS data mainly reflect the initial surface oxidation state of TCC before irradiation, and direct quantitative monitoring of Ce3+/Ce4+ changes within tumor tissues remains technically challenging because of the low cerium abundance in biological samples.In line with prior reports on metal-polyphenol coordination systems, Cur can chelate Ce3+/Ce4+ through its β-diketone and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which can improve loading stability and reinforce the organic-inorganic interface within the nanocomposite [46]. Cur release from TCC followed a mildly pH-dependent profile rather than an acid-triggered burst-release or disassembly pattern, suggesting that acidic conditions may moderately facilitate Cur diffusion from the coordination-assisted TPGS/CeO2 matrix. Similar mildly pH-facilitated release behavior has been observed in other Cur-loaded nanocarriers, including hyaluronic acid-crosslinked zein nanogels and HA/TPGS-based nanoparticles [47,48]. In addition to its role in nanocomposite assembly, Cur can modulate multiple resistance-associated pathways, particularly NF-κB-related signaling. Mechanistically, Cur has been reported to reduce IKK activity, stabilize IκBα, and limit p65 nuclear translocation [49,50]. This interpretation was further supported by western blot analysis, which showed that TCC + RT attenuated RT-associated increases in p-p65, p-IκBα, and COX-2 compared with RT alone. These protein-level results link the transcriptomic suppression of TNF-α–NF-κB/inflammatory programs to canonical NF-κB pathway inhibition. Cur has also been linked to EMT suppression through NF-κB–Snail signaling, consistent with the reduced migration and invasion observed after TCC + RT [51].The therapeutic effect of TCC should therefore be interpreted as a cooperative outcome of microenvironmental modulation and signaling intervention. Nanoceria improves the physical and chemical basis for RT by modulating oxygen availability and ROS generation, whereas Cur attenuates irradiation-induced inflammatory and pro-survival signaling. G2/M-phase enrichment and dose-response clonogenic assays further support this functional radiosensitizing effect.To improve tumor delivery and selectivity, TCC incorporates TPGS and cRGD. TPGS enhances colloidal stability and nanoparticle-membrane interactions, which can promote cellular uptake and intracellular accumulation [52,53]. The nearly unchanged ζ-potential after Cur loading and cRGD modification likely reflects the dominant contribution of the TPGS-based outer layer to the interfacial properties of TCC, a phenomenon also reported in RGD/cRGD-functionalized PEGylated nanoparticles [54]. In parallel, cRGD enables integrin-directed targeting via αvβ3 binding, thereby facilitating tumor cell association and internalization [55]. In tumor cryosections, cRGD-TCC-Cy7 showed stronger fluorescence signals in deeper regions. When considered alongside the biodistribution results, this pattern is suggestive of enhanced integrin-mediated uptake and retention rather than passive penetration alone [56]. These features may increase intratumoral exposure and thereby support local redox modulation and signaling inhibition.In addition to tumor-intrinsic redox and signaling regulation, immune microenvironment remodeling may also contribute to the therapeutic response. Radiotherapy can promote CD8+ T-cell infiltration and antitumor immune responses, while Cur has also been reported to restore CD4+/CD8+ T-cell populations and favor Th1-type immunity [57,58]. Consistently, CD8+ T-cell immunohistochemistry showed increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration after TCC-based combined treatment. From a translational perspective, the 30-day organ distribution data provide further information on the safety profile of TCC. Cerium was mainly detected in the liver and spleen, consistent with reticuloendothelial system-associated distribution of inorganic nanoparticles after systemic administration [59]. Although hepatic cerium showed an overall decreasing trend, day-30 H&E staining and serum biochemical analysis did not reveal obvious pathological abnormalities or liver dysfunction under the current experimental conditions. Nevertheless, the relatively persistent splenic retention indicates that longer-term pharmacokinetic, excretion, repeated-dose, and chronic toxicity studies are still needed.Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, some aspects of TCC characterization require further validation. Although the initial Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio and pH-dependent enzyme-like activities support the redox-modulating potential of TCC, the current XPS and catalytic activity data do not directly quantify oxygen-vacancy density, and in vivo monitoring of Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio shifts during or after RT was limited by the low cerium abundance in recovered biological samples. In addition, although TEM/STEM–EDS mapping supported the morphology and elemental distribution of TCC, HAADF-STEM or cryo-STEM would be required to more clearly define its internal spatial organization. Second, although the data support a cooperative mechanism involving nanoceria-mediated microenvironmental modulation and Cur-mediated NF-κB/inflammatory signaling inhibition, their relative contributions were not quantitatively separated. Third, immune analysis was limited to CD8+ T-cell immunohistochemistry, and broader immune remodeling, including macrophage polarization and T-cell activation status, remains to be investigated. Finally, although the 30-day biosafety evaluation did not reveal obvious organ toxicity, partial splenic retention indicates that longer-term pharmacokinetic and chronic safety assessments are still needed.5ConclusionA nanoceria–Cur nanoplatform (TCC) was developed here that combines microenvironment-responsive redox modulation with suppression of resistance-associated signaling and incorporates TPGS and cRGD to support tumor delivery. In 4T1 models, TCC potentiated RT-induced oxidative stress, DNA damage, and apoptosis and improved tumor control without overt short-term toxicity. This integrated design couples redox remodeling with suppression of NF-κB–linked pro-survival and inflammatory programs to improve RT response in TNBC.This work was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of China ( [grant number ]; and the Natural Science Foundation [grant numbers 2024AFD436, 2024AFD452].CRediT authorship contribution statementLongqing Hu: Visualization, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing.
