title: Bibliometric analysis of retinoblastoma research over the past decade
abstract: Background:Retinoblastoma (RB), the most prevalent primary intraocular malignancy in children, has emerged as a model disease for exploring the molecular underpinnings of pediatric cancer. Over the past decade, research in this field has accelerated, propelled by advances in genomics, diagnostic imaging, targeted therapies, and global scientific collaboration.Methods:This study systematically retrieved RB-related publications from 2015 to 2024 using the Web of Science Core Collection. A total of 4990 articles were included. CiteSpace and VOSviewer were employed to perform bibliometric and visual analyses across multiple dimensions, including countries, institutions, authors, journals, and thematic evolution.Results:The United States and China were identified as the leading contributors, jointly accounting for over 40.55% of all publications. US-based journals led in both publication volume and citation impact, underscoring their global influence. Cluster analysis revealed 4 major research domains: clinical diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis; molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways; gene and protein function studies; and research methodologies and experimental models.Conclusion:RB research is transitioning into an era of precision oncology, characterized by molecular subtyping, novel therapeutic targets, and individualized treatment approaches. While diagnostic and therapeutic outcomes have markedly improved in high-income countries, significant disparities persist in low- and middle-income regions due to limited access to early detection and comprehensive care. Future priorities should include the refinement of preclinical models, investigation of drug resistance mechanisms, and promotion of international collaboration to standardize diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. These efforts are critical to improving global outcomes for children with RB.
full_text: 1. Retinoblastoma (RB) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, and a well-established model disease in oncology due to its clearly defined genetic basis.[1] Characterized by its rapid progression and aggressive clinical course, untreated RB can lead to irreversible visual impairment, enucleation, and ultimately, death.[2] Over recent decades, the management of RB has evolved substantially, shifting from radical surgery towards multimodal, sight-preserving strategies, which have dramatically improved patient survival.[3–5] This therapeutic progress has been paralleled by a rapid expansion of the related scientific literature, a trend quantitatively evidenced in recent analyses of the field’s research output.Given the accelerating volume and complexity of publications, there is a pressing need to move beyond traditional narrative reviews and adopt systematic, data-driven approaches to map the intellectual landscape of RB research. Bibliometric and scientometric methods provide powerful tools for this purpose, enabling the objective analysis of large publication corpora to visualize knowledge structures, identify key contributors and collaborative networks, and trace the evolution of research themes.[6,7]To address this need and provide a comprehensive overview of the current research frontier, this study conducts a bibliometric analysis of RB-related publications from 2015 to 2024. Utilizing data from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and analytical tools including CiteSpace and VOSviewer, we aim to: identify the most productive and influential countries, institutions, authors, and journals; visualize global and institutional scientific collaboration networks; delineate the thematic structure and its temporal evolution over the past decade; and provide a strategic overview to guide future research directions and foster interdisciplinary collaboration in RB precision oncology.2. Material and 2.1. Database and search strategyThe bibliometric data for this study were systematically extracted from the Science Citation Index Expanded within the WoSCC. A comprehensive search was conducted on April 10, 2025, using the query TS= (“Retinoblastoma” OR “RB” OR “Retinoblastoma of the eye” OR “Congenital retinoblastoma” OR “Hereditary retinoblastoma” OR “Sporadic retinoblastoma” OR “Bilateral retinoblastoma” OR “Unilateral retinoblastoma” OR “Childhood retinoblastoma” OR “Malignant retinoblastoma” OR “Retinoblastoma tumor” OR “Retinoblastoma lesion”) with no initial restrictions, which yielded 26,160 records. To focus on the most recent decade of research, the publication year was restricted to 2015 to 2024, resulting in 6398 records. Subsequently, a systematic screening was performed. First, we excluded non-research document types, including: Biographical-Item (4), Book Chapters (16), Correction (43), Early Access (11), Editorial Material (181), Expression of Concern (4), Letter (115), Meeting Abstract (860), News Item (4), Proceeding Paper (24), Publication with Expression of Concern (1), Reprint (2), Retracted Publication (54), and Retraction (42). This step yielded 5037 records, comprising 4222 Articles and 768 Review Articles. Then, we limited the results to publications in English, excluding records in all other languages (47). This refined the dataset to the final 4990 publications for analysis. No duplicate records were identified. The complete screening process is detailed as Figure 1 shown.Figure 1.Flowchart illustrating the systematic screening process and search strategy utilized in this study.2.2. Data analysisIn this study, we systematically retrieved and processed bibliographic information, including article titles, keywords, authors, s, publication years, citation counts, references, countries/regions, and institutional affiliations, from the WoSCC database. All data were stored in plain text format to facilitate subsequent analysis. To accurately evaluate the impact of journals and ensure the reliability of the analysis, we utilized the 2021 edition of the Journal Citation Reports for determining journal impact factors. To conduct the bibliometric analysis based on the retrieved and processed data, we employed 2 specialized software tools: VOSviewer and CiteSpace. VOSviewer (version 1.6.18) was utilized for constructing and visualizing co-occurrence networks of author keywords and co-citation networks of references.[6,8] The analyses in VOSviewer were conducted with the following specific parameters: we used the full counting method; the similarity matrix was normalized using the association strength measure; and clusters were identified using the VOS clustering algorithm. For the keyword co-occurrence analysis, from an initial set of 16,597 author keywords, a minimum occurrence threshold of 61 was applied chosen to balance inclusiveness and interpretability, resulting in 100 high-frequency keywords. These were further refined by manually merging synonyms (e.g., “retinoblastoma protein” and “rb1”), yielding a final set of 83 keywords for network mapping and thematic analysis. Comprehensive instructions and guidelines for using VOSviewer can be accessed at https://www.vosviewer.com/getting-started. CiteSpace (version 6.4.R2 Advanced) was employed to identify emerging trends, pivotal publications, and the dynamic evolution of the research field through timeline visualization and burst detection.[9] The software was configured with the following parameters to ensure reproducibility: the time span was sliced into 1-year intervals from 2015 to 2024; for each time slice, the top 50 most cited references were selected for network construction; to simplify the network structure, the Pathfinder and Pruning the Sliced Networks algorithms were applied; clusters within the network were labeled using the log-likelihood ratio algorithm to extract the most representative terms; and Kleinberg burst detection algorithm was used to identify publications that experienced a sharp increase in citation frequency over a specific period. The official website and documentation for CiteSpace can be accessed at https://citespace.podia.com/. Statistical summaries and the visualization of annual publication trends were performed using Microsoft Excel 2021. This multi-method approach, utilizing complementary tools with explicitly defined parameters, allowed for a comprehensive, rigorous, and reproducible analysis of the RB research landscape.3. 3.1. Quantitative analysis of publications and citationsThe number of publications and citations serve as critical indicators for identifying research hotspots, development trends, and frontier directions in a specific field. As illustrated in Figure 2, a systematic literature screening identified 4990 RB-related articles published between 2015 and 2024, providing robust data for analyzing trends in publication and citation counts within this domain. The analysis of publication numbers reveals that, although annual publication counts in the RB field exhibited fluctuations from 2015 to 2022, they remained consistently high (ranging from 458 to 589 articles), with a peak observed in 2020 (589 articles). However, a notable decline in publication numbers occurred after 2022, with publication numbers decreasing to 386 articles in 2023 and showing a modest rebound to 415 articles in 2024. This trend may reflect a phased shift in research intensity, where the initial period was characterized by substantial resource allocation and steady output, while the later period may have been influenced by strategic adjustments in research priorities and resource reallocation, leading to a reduction in publication volume.Figure 2.Temporal trends in annual publication and citation counts for retinoblastoma research from 2015 to 2024, reflecting the growth trajectory and scholarly impact of the field over the past decade.Notably, the citation count demonstrated a distinct trajectory compared to the publication count. In 2015, the citation count stood at a relatively low level of 459. However, from 2015 to 2022, citations experienced rapid and sustained growth. Although minor fluctuations occurred after 2022 (with a slight decline in 2023), the overall trend remained upward, culminating in a peak of 18,657 citations in 2024. This pattern suggests that, despite the decline in publication numbers in the later period, the impact of research outputs in this field continued to expand. The accumulation of foundational research has facilitated the advancement of subsequent studies, resulting in increased citation frequency of related works and heightened recognition of their contributions to the academic community. Moreover, the enduring influence of high-quality research outputs underscores their long-term academic value, which persists and disseminates through continuous citation and engagement, even as the production of new research diminishes. This analysis highlights that the RB research field transitioned from a phase of high output to one of refined research between 2015 and 2024, with a potential shift in focus from broad exploration to in-depth investigation. This evolution underscores the importance of prioritizing research quality and fostering innovative breakthroughs to sustain and enhance the academic influence of this field.3.2. Analysis of prolific authors and academic impactAs summarized in Table 1, publication cumulative citation count, and the H-index are widely recognized indicators of academic productivity and influence. Abramson, David H. leads the field with 80 publications, accumulating 2055 citations (including 214 self-citations) and attaining an H-index of 25, underscoring his prominent role in RB research. Shields, Carol (70 publications; H-index: 23) and Chantada, Guillermo Luis (60 publications; H-index: 22) follow closely, each surpassing 2000 citations and reflecting sustained scholarly impact. Particularly noteworthy is Munier, Francis, who demonstrates the highest average citation rate (37.95 citations per article), highlighting the exceptional academic quality and visibility of his work. Among prolific authors, Abramson and Shields exhibit both high research output and significant citation influence, reaffirming their leadership in the RB research community. Collectively, these metrics illustrate the pivotal contributions of these scholars in shaping the trajectory and academic impact of RB research.Table 1The 14 most prolific authors in retinoblastoma research.RankResearcher profilesPublicationsCiting articlesWithout self-citationsTimes citedTimes cited without self-citationsAverage per itemH-Index1Abramson, David H. .69252Shields, Carol70137613372155203130.79233Francis, Jasmine H. .1224Kaliki, Swathi6364560188277614155Chantada, Guillermo Luis60117611282036182233.93226Berry, Jesse L54630594107194519.38187Moll, Annette458067761147107325.49198Munier, Francis43110110701632155037.95169Schaiquevich, Paula3848044879067720.791610Khetan, Vikas3567365994791427.061711Dunkel, Ira J. .111712Sagoo, Mandeep S. .111413Kim, Jonathan W. .791814Zhao, Junyang348308091094104432. .3. Analysis of the contributions of journals and countriesFigure 3A presents a dual-map overlay that comprehensively illustrates the disciplinary distribution and contribution patterns of academic journals across distinct research domains. Each journal cluster is clearly labeled according to its respective academic domain, and color-coded citation trajectories visually represent the flow of knowledge, mapping research pathways and core contribution directions within specific disciplines. The citing journals encompass a broad spectrum of disciplines, including Physics, Materials Science, Chemistry, Ecology, Earth Sciences, Geophysics, Veterinary Science, Animal Science, Mathematics, Systems Science, Molecular Biology, Immunology, Clinical Medicine, Economics, Political Science, Psychology, Education, Health Sciences, Neuroscience, and Ophthalmology. Similarly, the cited journals exhibit substantial disciplinary diversity, Spanning Systems Science, Computer Science, Environmental Science, Toxicology, Nutrition, Ecology, Earth Sciences, Geophysics, Chemistry, Materials Science, Physics, Health Sciences, Nursing, Medicine, Psychology, Education, Social Sciences, Molecular Biology, Genetics, Anatomy, Sports Medicine, Botany, Ecology, Geophysics, Veterinary Science, Parasitology, Economics, Political Science, Dermatology, Dentistry, Surgery, Ophthalmology, History, and Philosophy. This extensive interdisciplinary footprint, bridging fundamental sciences with clinical and even social sciences, underscores that RB has transcended its traditional domain to become a nexus for integrative research, attracting attention far beyond ophthalmology and pediatric oncology. The analysis identifies 2 primary citation pathways: an orange pathway representing the flow of knowledge from Molecular Biology and Genetics to Molecular Biology and Immunology, and a green pathway illustrating the migration of knowledge from Molecular Biology and Genetics to Clinical Medicine. These pathways not only underscore the typical patterns of interdisciplinary knowledge dissemination but also provide robust empirical evidence for the pivotal contributions in key research areas. Specifically, they delineate the core translational axis of the field: foundational discoveries in genetics and molecular biology directly fuel advances in immunomodulatory strategies and clinical therapeutics, highlighting RB’s role as a paradigm for bench-to-bedside research. Figure 3B presents the publication trajectories of the top 5 journals in the field of RB from 2015 to 2024. The analyzed journals include Cancers, International Journal of Molecular Sciences, Pediatric Blood & Cancer, PLOS One, and Scientific Reports. Among these, Cancers exhibits a remarkable growth trajectory, particularly from 2020 to 2024, with its publication count surging from 18 to 93 articles. Similarly, International Journal of Molecular Sciences demonstrates a comparable growth trend, with publications increasing from 12 to 89 articles between 2018 and 2024. In contrast, Pediatric Blood & Cancer, PLOS One, and Scientific Reports show relatively moderate growth, with publication counts rising from 6 to 86, 19 to 81, and 8 to 80 articles, respectively. Although the growth rate of all journals slows after 2024, they continue to maintain an upward trend. This analysis highlights that, from 2015 to 2024, the leading journals in RB research consistently experienced a steady increase in publication with Cancers and International Journal of Molecular Sciences demonstrating the most significant growth. The pronounced growth in broad-scope, high-impact oncology and molecular science journals (Cancers, IJMS), compared to more specialized or multidisciplinary journals, suggests a strategic shift in publication venues. It indicates that cutting-edge RB research is increasingly perceived as relevant to wider audiences in general oncology and molecular mechanisms, potentially enhancing its visibility and cross-disciplinary impact. This trend underscores the sustained academic vitality and escalating research momentum in this field, driven by the increasing scientific and clinical interest in RB. Figure 3C depicts the geographical distribution of 147 countries and regions engaged in RB research, highlighting their global contributions based on academic publication output. The visualization reveals a highly concentrated research landscape, with the bulk of productivity originating from North America, East Asia, and Western Europe, which aligns with global patterns of biomedical research investment and infrastructure. Furthermore, Figure 3D presents the publication trends of the top 10 most research-active countries globally, offering essential data insights into the evolving dynamics of this research domain. The longitudinal data not only confirms the sustained dominance of the United States but also captures the rapid ascendancy of China in recent years, signaling a potential rebalancing of global research leadership and the emergence of new collaborative hubs in the field.Figure 3.Using a dual-map overlay, line graph, geographical distribution map and bar graph to respectively illustrate interdisciplinary journals, publication trends of top journals, global spatial distribution and the top 10 productive countries/regions in retinoblastoma research. (A) Overlay dual-map highlighting journals associated with retinoblastoma research, illustrating the interdisciplinary connections and knowledge flow within the field. (B) Line graph depicting the publication trends of the top 5 journals in retinoblastoma research, providing insights into their evolving contributions over time. (C) Geographical distribution of global research output in retinoblastoma, visualizing the spatial patterns of research activity across countries and regions. (D) Bar graph showcasing the top 10 most productive countries/regions in retinoblastoma research, highlighting their relative contributions to the domain.3.4. Analysis of keywordsFigure 4A presents a comprehensive network visualization of keyword co-occurrence, based on terms appearing more than 61 times. Using VOSviewer, a total of 16,597 initial author keywords were processed. By applying a minimum occurrence threshold of 61, 100 high-frequency keywords were identified. After merging synonyms, 83 keywords were retained for co-occurrence network analysis. The VOS clustering algorithm was employed, grouping these keywords into 4 distinct thematic clusters representing major research areas in RB. The network map illustrates the strength of co-occurrence via the thickness of connecting lines, where thicker lines represent stronger associations. Cluster 1 (Red Cluster): Focuses on clinical diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of the disease. Key terms include RB, breast-cancer, childhood-cancer, lung-cancer, neuroblastoma, hepatocellular-carcinoma, children, eyes, prognosis, diagnosis, management, survival, outcomes, risk, epidemiology, international-classification, classification, enucleation, intra-arterial chemotherapy (IAC), chemotherapy, chemoreduction, therapy, radiotherapy, melphalan, carboplatin, and combination. Cluster 2 (Green Cluster): Centers on molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways. Key terms include pathway, cell cycle, apoptosis, proliferation, differentiation, migration, invasion, metastasis, tumorigenesis, angiogenesis, autophagy, oxidative stress, DNA-damage, senescence, resistance, inactivation, activation, inhibition, phosphorylation, degradation, down-regulation, promotes, transcription, transcription factor, binding, complex, methylation, kinase, and nf-kappa-b. Cluster 3 (Blue Cluster): Emphasizes gene and protein research. Key terms include RB1, p53, E2F, RB protein (pRb), RB tumor-suppressor,tumor-suppressor, gene, gene-expression, protein, cyclin d1, Palbociclib, microRNAs (miRNAs), transcription factor, stem-cells, and family. Cluster 4 (Yellow Cluster): Highlights research methods and models. Key terms include in vitro, in vivo, target, identification, features, and association. Figure 4B displays the top 25 keywords with the highest citation burst rates, revealing dynamic shifts in research focus over time. The timeline visualization provides a dynamic view of research hotspots associated with different keywords, clearly illustrating temporal patterns and trends. By aligning documents from the same cluster on the same horizontal axis, the timeline progresses from left to right, reflecting the evolution from earlier to more recent research. The number of documents within each cluster underscores the depth and significance of research outputs in that area, offering critical insights into the developmental trajectory of RB research. The visualization reveals distinct temporal waves of research interest. Early citation bursts (approximately 2015–2017) for keywords such as “in vivo” and “senescence” correspond to a period dominated by foundational mechanistic studies. Subsequently, later and sustained bursts for keywords including “signaling pathway,” “radiotherapy,” and “prognosis” mark a discernible shift in research focus towards clinical applications and therapeutic optimization. Notably, the pronounced citation burst for “uveal melanoma” around 2021 suggests a growing research interest in the association between RB and other ocular malignancies. Collectively, these evolving temporal patterns underscore the field’s progression from foundational basic science towards increasingly translational and clinical research domains, a trajectory consistent with broader trends in oncology. Figure 4C delineates the research landscape of RB through 2 key dimensions: development degree (density) and relevance degree (centrality). Research themes are categorized into 4 quadrants: Niche Themes (upper-left quadrant), Motor Themes (upper-right quadrant), Emerging or Declining Themes (lower-left quadrant), and Basic Themes (lower-right quadrant). Niche Themes, such as endothelial growth factor, macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy, exhibit low centrality but high density. These themes represent emerging or specialized directions within RB research, characterized by limited connectivity in the overall research network but high research activity, indicating potential for future development. Motor Themes, including RB, management, chemotherapy, children, and survival, demonstrate high centrality and density. These themes constitute the core research directions in RB studies, with significant academic impact and active progress, driving knowledge accumulation and clinical advancements in the field. Emerging or Declining Themes, such as breast cancer, cell cycle, combination, palbociclib, and squamous cell carcinoma, show low density and centrality. These themes are characterized by limited research activity and weak connections to other research areas, necessitating further exploration to determine their scientific relevance and future potential. Basic Themes, including expression, cancer, pRb, proliferation, and apoptosis, exhibit high centrality but low density. These themes form the theoretical foundation and core concepts of RB research, playing a critical role in shaping the research framework and supporting subsequent studies despite their lower research density. This analysis underscores the importance of Basic Themes as the cornerstone of the research field while highlighting the transformative potential of Motor Themes in driving innovation and progress. Additionally, it identifies opportunities for exploration in Niche and Emerging Themes, providing a strategic roadmap for prioritizing impactful research directions in the vital domain of RB studies. Significantly, the positioning of “chemotherapy” and “management” firmly within the Motor Themes quadrant validates that treatment optimization and clinical care delivery are not only active but also central to the current RB research agenda, effectively bridging basic molecular insights with patient-centered outcomes.Figure 4.Three visualizations for retinoblastoma research. (A) Comprehensive network visualization map illustrating keyword co-occurrence patterns in retinoblastoma research, highlighting key thematic clusters and their interconnections. (B) Temporal analysis of the top 25 references with the strongest citation bursts. The bursts were detected using Kleinberg algorithm, highlighting periods of sharp increase in citation frequency for key publications. (C) Thematic map categorizing research themes in retinoblastoma based on 2 dimensions: relevance (centrality) and development (density), providing a strategic overview of core, emerging, niche, and foundational research areas in the field.Figure 5A presents a visual analysis of the thematic evolution and research trends in the field of RB, revealing the research hotspots and development directions in this domain. Each term represents a key research topic, with the size of the circles corresponding to the frequency of occurrence or research popularity in the literature. Topics such as “RB,” “expression,” “proliferation,” and “retinoblastoma protein” maintained high research popularity throughout the study period, particularly peaking between 2018 and 2019. These topics focus on the molecular mechanisms, gene expression regulation, and tumor proliferation in RB, underscoring their significance as core research directions in the field. The topics “access” and “history” reached their peak research popularity in 2024, reflecting a growing focus on the accessibility of medical resources and historical research related to RB. These topics may emerge as important future research directions, particularly in the areas of healthcare policy and historical data analysis. Topics such as “American Joint Committee,” “etoposide,” and “choroidal melanoma” showed high research popularity in 2023, likely related to updates in clinical practice guidelines, the application of specific chemotherapeutic agents, and studies on the association between RB and other ocular tumors, such as choroidal melanoma. The topics “care,” “multicenter,” “lineage plasticity,” and “childhood cancer” exhibited high popularity between 2022 and 2023, indicating increased attention to improving patient care quality, conducting multicenter clinical studies, exploring tumor cell lineage plasticity mechanisms, and comprehensive management of childhood cancers. Topics such as “impact,” “cell,” “cancer,” “chemotherapy,” and “children” have also maintained high research popularity in recent years, addressing the impact of RB on patients’ quality of life, the molecular mechanisms of tumor cells, optimization of chemotherapy regimens, and personalized treatment strategies for pediatric patients. Topics such as “breast cancer,” “differentiation,” “in vivo,” and “tumorigenesis” were prominent between 2017 and 2018, potentially reflecting research on the molecular associations between RB and breast cancer, mechanisms of tumor cell differentiation, development of in vivo experimental models, and tumorigenesis. Topics like “hereditary RB,” “progenitor cells,” “cell cycle control,” and “dependent kinase inhibitors” highlight researchers’ focus on the molecular basis of hereditary RB, the role of progenitor cells, mechanisms of cell cycle regulation, and the development of kinase inhibitors. Topics such as “RB family,” “transgenic mice,” and “dependent degradation” primarily involve functional studies of the RB gene family, the application of transgenic mouse models, and mechanisms of protein-dependent degradation. This progression mirrors the field’s expansion from understanding disease mechanisms to addressing clinical implementation and broader health service challenges. Figure 5B visually illustrates the key stages, research hotspots, and development directions in RB research, identifying 11 major research clusters, including “childhood cancer,” “intra-arterial chemotherapy (IAC),” “oxidative stress,” “identification,” “intraarterial chemotherap,” “PD ,” “differentiation,” “uveal melanoma,” “activation,” “cell cycle arrest,” and “therapy.” Keywords are color-coded according to their time periods, and their directional changes, frequency of occurrence, and connections with other keywords demonstrate significant advancements in academic research. Keywords such as “IAC,” “identification,” “differentiation,” and “therapy” have maintained high popularity over time, indicating their enduring importance in RB research. Future RB research will increasingly emphasize interdisciplinary collaboration and technological innovation, particularly in the development of early diagnostic markers, novel targeted drugs, optimization of immunotherapy strategies, and the formulation of individualized treatment plans. Additionally, research on oxidative stress, cell cycle regulation, and the tumor microenvironment (TME) will provide new perspectives on the molecular mechanisms of RB.Figure 5.The temporal evolution of research themes and trends in RB. (A) Temporal analysis of key research themes in RB, highlighting the evolution of research hotspots and their relative popularity over time. (B) Timeline visualization and keyword clustering map depicting the progression of research trends in RB, with color-coded keywords representing their temporal emergence and interconnections. RB = retinoblastoma.4. 4.1. Global research status and trendsBased on global publication data analysis, the United States and China are the most productive contributors to RB research, with 1586 and 1469 publications, respectively. Together, they account for 40.55% of total publications in the field, indicating their significant involvement in advancing RB research. In terms of publication quality and citation impact, the United States leads globally, as reflected in higher average citation rates and journal influence metrics of its outputs. Analysis of authors’ publication and citation data shows that the top 3 most prolific authors are affiliated with US institutions, reflecting a productive and impactful research community in the country. Among the top 11 research institutions in RB research, 6 are based in the United States, 2 in China, 1 in France, 1 in the United Kingdom, and 1 in Canada. These institutions have played a key role in driving RB research progress, illustrating the interplay between global academic collaboration and knowledge exchange. These findings clarify the international distribution of RB research efforts and provide a reference for promoting future cross-border academic partnerships.4.2. Research keyword analysisIn this study, we performed a cluster analysis of 83 keywords with a frequency exceeding 61 in the field of RB to identify research hotspots and emerging trends. The cluster analysis categorized these keywords into 4 distinct clusters: Cluster 1 (Red Cluster), which focuses on the clinical diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of RB; Cluster 2 (Green Cluster), which centers on molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways in RB; Cluster 3 (Blue Cluster), which emphasizes gene and protein research in RB; and Cluster 4 (Yellow Cluster), which highlights research methods and models in RB. Through co-occurrence analysis, this study elucidated the key research directions and emerging trends in the field. Based on timeline analysis and an examination of the top 25 high-frequency keywords, it was found that during the early stage (2015–2018), high-frequency keywords (e.g., in vivo, tumorigenesis, PD , mice, DNA methylation, transcription factors, induction, lung cancer, NF-κB, senescence, and kinase) primarily focused on the molecular mechanisms underlying RB, therapeutic strategies, and experimental models. In the mid-stage (2018–2021), high-frequency keywords (e.g., combination, prognosis, signaling pathway, radiotherapy, long noncoding RNA, and inhibitor) shifted toward translational research, bridging molecular mechanisms with clinical applications to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize treatment regimens, and enhance patient outcomes. In the recent stage (2021–2024), high-frequency keywords (e.g., migration, uveal melanoma, cell, liquid biopsy, multicenter, and aqueous humor) predominantly addressed RB metastasis mechanisms, liquid biopsy techniques (e.g., aqueous humor analysis), multicenter collaborative research, and molecular characterization of tumor cells, thereby advancing precision medicine and individualized treatment strategies. This evolution from basic mechanisms to translational and clinical applications, as revealed by keyword analysis, sets the stage for a detailed discussion of each thematic cluster. From 2015 to 2024, significant advancements have been achieved in RB research, encompassing research directions, methodological innovations, clinical practices, interdisciplinary collaborations, and multicenter studies. These developments not only reflect the dynamic evolution of the field but also provide critical insights for future research. By comprehensively analyzing the 4 clusters, this study identifies key research domains and future directions in RB, offering valuable insights for both academic research and clinical practice.4.3. Red Cluster: clinical diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of RBRB represents the most prevalent primary intraocular malignancy in pediatric populations, exerting profound effects on vision, survival outcomes, and overall quality of life. Globally, the incidence is estimated at approximately 1 case per 15,000 to 20,000 live births.[1] RB predominantly affects children under the age of 5 and shows no significant sex predilection. It can be classified into hereditary (germline RB1 mutation) and sporadic forms, with hereditary cases accounting for approximately 40% of diagnoses. Germline mutations are commonly associated with bilateral disease and increase the risk of secondary malignancies such as osteosarcoma, breast cancer, and lung cancer.[1,10] Although advancements in diagnosis and therapy have markedly improved survival – particularly in high-income countries – disparities in prognosis persist due to unequal access to medical care and treatment modalities.[11]RB diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical examination, imaging, and genetic testing. Funduscopy may reveal leukocoria, strabismus, or other ocular abnormalities. Modern imaging techniques – including ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and optical coherence tomography – are essential for evaluating tumor extent and guiding treatment planning.[12] The International Classification of RB stratifies disease into Groups A to E, which informs therapeutic decision-making.[13] Early diagnosis is critical, as Group D or E disease is associated with poorer prognosis and higher rates of enucleation.[14,15]Substantial advancements have been achieved in the management of RB, with treatment paradigms evolving from primary enucleation toward eye-preserving strategies. Nevertheless, enucleation continues to serve as the definitive therapeutic modality for advanced unilateral RB. Conventional systemic chemotherapy, commonly consisting of carboplatin, etoposide, and vincristine, has been increasingly replaced by more targeted and regionally administered modalities, including IAC and intravitreal injection. In response to the need for more effective and less toxic localized therapies, IAC has emerged as a pivotal advancement. Among these approaches, IAC – particularly employing melphalan alone or in conjunction with topotecan – has emerged as a cornerstone modality for ocular salvage in Group C–E RB. This approach is particularly effective for unilateral involvement, yielding high ocular salvage rates while minimizing systemic toxicity.[16,17] In bilateral RB, chemoreduction – typically involving carboplatin, etoposide, and vincristine – followed by focal interventions such as laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, remains the standard therapeutic approach.[18] Although radiotherapy remains effective, it is now reserved for refractory cases due to the increased risk of secondary malignancies and long-term sequelae.[19,20] Recent investigations have further emphasized the therapeutic efficacy of melphalan in IAC, highlighting its critical role in tumor burden reduction and prognostic enhancement.[21,22]RB generally carries a favorable prognosis, with survival rates surpassing 95% in high-income nations when diagnosed early and treated.[23,24] In contrast, outcomes remain markedly inferior in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), primarily due to delayed diagnosis and restricted access to advanced therapeutic modalities.[25,26] Key adverse prognostic indicators encompass advanced-stage presentation, extraocular extension, and germline RB1 mutations, which predispose patients to bilateral disease and increased risk of secondary malignancies including osteosarcoma, lung cancer, and breast cancer.[27] Comprehensive long-term surveillance is critical for detecting tumor recurrence, secondary neoplasms, and treatment-associated complications. Improving RB outcomes requires prioritization of early detection, especially in LMICs, facilitated through public health strategies and telemedicine-based interventions.[28] Emerging advances in molecular diagnostics and targeted therapeutics – such as PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway inhibitors – offer promising avenues for addressing refractory disease.[18,29] Furthermore, international cooperation and protocol standardization are essential for minimizing global disparities and enhancing RB outcomes on a worldwide scale.[26,30]In conclusion, accurate diagnosis integrated with multimodal therapeutic strategies is fundamental to improving both prognosis and quality of life in patients with RB. Future directions should prioritize innovative modalities including gene editing, molecularly targeted agents, and immunotherapies to maximize ocular preservation and mitigate long-term.4.4. Green Cluster: molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways in RBBuilding upon the clinical landscape, a deep understanding of RB’s molecular pathogenesis is crucial for developing targeted therapies. RB is a paradigmatic model for dissecting the molecular basis of tumorigenesis, particularly in pediatric oncology, owing to its well-defined genetic etiology and rapid onset during early development. The disease is initiated primarily by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene, a key regulator of the cell cycle, apoptosis, and differentiation.[1] While RB1 loss is the rate-limiting event in Rb initiation, recent genomic and transcriptomic analyses have revealed that tumor progression is driven by extensive interplay among diverse oncogenic signaling networks involved in proliferation, invasion, and angiogenesis.[31]The defining genetic hallmark of Rb is complete RB1 inactivation, which disrupts the G1/S checkpoint and leads to deregulated activity of E2F transcription factors. Under physiological conditions, the pRB restrains E2F-mediated transcription to prevent unscheduled DNA synthesis. In the absence of pRB, constitutive E2F activity accelerates cell cycle progression and promotes genomic instability, thereby facilitating tumor evolution.[32,33]RB1 deficiency also triggers activation of oncogenic cascades that cooperate to sustain tumor cell survival. Among these, the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway is frequently upregulated, promoting growth through enhanced translation, metabolic reprogramming, and resistance to apoptosis.[32,34] In parallel, MYCN amplification – a common feature of high-risk Rb – is associated with proliferative advantage and poor prognosis, due to its role in modulating genes involved in cell cycle regulation and DNA repair.[32]Resistance to apoptosis is a critical trait of Rb cells. Loss of RB1 attenuates the expression of pro-apoptotic mediators such as BAX and PUMA, while simultaneously increasing antiapoptotic proteins like BCL-2 and survivin.[35] Tumor cells also engage additional cytoprotective mechanisms, including enhanced DNA damage repair, autophagy, and oxidative stress adaptation. Notably, persistent activation of the NF-κB pathway further supports chemoresistance by sustaining the expression of survival genes under therapeutic stress.[36]The TME significantly contributes to Rb progression. Hypoxic conditions stabilize HIF-1α, leading to upregulation of VEGF and other angiogenic factors, thereby promoting neovascularization and tumor expansion.[37] Additionally, transcription factors such as SNAIL and TWIST drive epithelial–mesenchymal transition, endowing tumor cells with migratory and invasive capacities that underpin local invasion and metastatic potential.[38,39]Epigenetic dysregulation has emerged as another key contributor to Rb pathobiology. Aberrant DNA methylation and histone modifications frequently silence tumor suppressor genes, including RASSF1A and CDKN2A, facilitating oncogenic transformation.[40] Concurrently, overactivation of kinases such as CDK4/6 and Aurora kinases has been implicated in uncontrolled proliferation and represents a promising avenue for targeted therapy.[41] Selective inhibitors targeting these kinases have demonstrated potent antitumor activity in preclinical models.Beyond canonical pathways, emerging evidence implicates the Sonic Hedgehog pathway in Rb pathogenesis. High expression of GLI1 and GLI2 has been observed in patient-derived tumors and correlates with more aggressive disease.[42] Similarly, dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway – particularly in the context of pRB loss – has been shown to synergize with LEF1 and MYCN, further driving tumor invasiveness.[43]miRNAs are increasingly recognized as critical posttranscriptional regulators in Rb. For example, miR-224-3p has been shown to inhibit apoptosis and promote proliferation by suppressing LATS2 and inactivating the Hippo-YAP pathway.[44]With the rise of high-throughput sequencing technologies, an expanding array of actionable molecular targets has been identified in Rb. Therapeutic strategies directed against PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MYCN, CDK4/6, and angiogenic mediators are currently under preclinical or early-phase clinical evaluation.[32,34,41,45] Nevertheless, due to pathway redundancy and intertumoral heterogeneity, combination therapies targeting multiple oncogenic axes – such as cell cycle, apoptosis, and angiogenesis – may yield superior clinical efficacy. Integration of molecular profiling into therapeutic decision-making could enable personalized treatment approaches and improve outcomes for Rb patients.[46]In conclusion, the oncogenesis and progression of RB are orchestrated by a multifactorial network of genetic lesions, epigenetic alterations, dysregulated signaling pathways, and microenvironmental inputs. Continued efforts to map these interconnected mechanisms will be essential for the development of effective, mechanism-based therapeutic interventions.[47]4.5. Blue Cluster: gene and protein research in RBThe dysregulation of signaling pathways, as discussed, is fundamentally rooted in genetic and proteomic alterations, which constitute the focus of this section. RB is a rare pediatric intraocular malignancy that arises primarily from biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene, which encodes the pRb. pRb plays a central role in cell cycle regulation, particularly at the G1/S checkpoint, through its inhibitory interaction with E2F transcription factors that drive the expression of genes essential for DNA replication and cell proliferation. Loss of RB1 function results in dysregulated cell division and is recognized as a fundamental initiating event in RB tumorigenesis. Moreover, accumulating evidence highlights the functional crosstalk between RB1 and other tumor suppressors such as TP53, revealing a more intricate landscape of genetic interactions underlying disease progression.[35,48]Beyond its role in E2F inhibition, pRb is tightly regulated by cyclin D1-CDK4/6 complexes, which phosphorylate and functionally inactivate pRb, thereby releasing E2F and enabling S-phase entry. This mechanistic axis has been explored therapeutically, with CDK4/6 inhibitors – such as palbociclib – showing antitumor activity in preclinical RB models.[49] Nonetheless, resistance mechanisms and off-target toxicities present ongoing clinical challenges, underscoring the need for combination strategies and precision-guided regimens.Recent studies have also elucidated the role of miRNAs as posttranscriptional regulators of tumor suppressors, including RB1 and TP53. Dysregulated miRNA expression profiles have been documented in RB, with some miRNAs (e.g., members of the miR-17-92 cluster) functioning oncogenically by targeting RB1, while others (e.g., miR-34a, a TP53-regulated miRNA) exhibit tumor-suppressive properties. Comprehensive profiling of miRNA networks in RB offers promising opportunities for the identification of molecular biomarkers and therapeutic targets.[50]The involvement of cancer stem-like cells (CSCs) in RB pathogenesis is gaining recognition. These subpopulations exhibit self-renewal, differentiation potential, and therapeutic resistance – features that contribute to tumor heterogeneity and relapse. RB specimens have been shown to harbor CSC-like cells expressing classical stem cell markers, displaying resilience to conventional chemotherapeutic agents.[51] Therapeutically, targeting CSCs via Wnt/β-catenin and Notch signaling pathways represents a rational approach for overcoming treatment resistance and improving long-term disease control.Genetic predisposition is another critical determinant of RB development. Approximately 40% of RB cases are heritable, arising from germline RB1 mutations that follow autosomal dominant inheritance. Early diagnosis through genetic counseling and surveillance of at-risk individuals enables timely intervention, often at a curable stage. Advances in next-generation sequencing have enhanced the detection of RB1 mutations and other pathogenic alterations, thereby facilitating personalized treatment strategies.[1,32]Together, these findings depict RB as a genetically and molecularly heterogeneous tumor, shaped by disrupted tumor suppressor pathways, regulatory noncoding RNAs, stem cell-like subpopulations, and inherited susceptibility. Despite significant progress in delineating its molecular underpinnings, the translation of these insights into effective clinical therapies remains an ongoing challenge. Future efforts should focus on unraveling RB’s molecular heterogeneity, refining targeted therapeutics, and integrating immunological approaches for more durable disease control.4.6. Yellow Cluster: research methods and models in RBThe insights into genes, proteins, and pathways discussed above are largely derived from sophisticated experimental models, which are the focus of this final thematic cluster. RB research has made significant progress through the application of in vitro and in vivo models, which have provided key insights into its molecular mechanisms, target identification, and therapeutic strategies. In vitro models, such as the Y79 and WERI-Rb1 RB cell lines, have been crucial in investigating the fundamental characteristics of tumor cells, including proliferation, apoptosis, and responses to therapy. These models serve as essential platforms for high-throughput screening of potential therapeutic agents and for elucidating critical molecular pathways, such as the RB1–E2F axis and the involvement of cyclin-dependent kinases in regulating cell cycle progression.[52] However, in vitro models have limitations, such as the absence of the TME and heterogeneity, which necessitates the use of complementary in vivo models.In vivo models (including genetically engineered mouse models and patient-derived xenograft models) are essential for linking genetic alterations with tumorigenesis. Genetically engineered mouse models with conditional knockout of the RB1 gene in retinal progenitor cells recapitulate the genetic and histological features of human RB, providing a platform to study tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis.[53] Patient-derived xenograft models, created by transplanting patient tumor tissue into immunodeficient mice, retain the original tumor’s genetic and phenotypic characteristics, making them invaluable for preclinical drug testing and personalized medicine research.[54,55]The integration of omics technologies (such as genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics) has further advanced the identification of molecular targets and biomarkers for RB. For instance, next-generation sequencing has revealed recurrent mutations and copy number variations in RB1 and other genes (such as MYCN and BCOR), which are associated with tumor invasiveness and prognosis.[56] Transcriptomic analyses have identified dysregulated signaling pathways, such as PI3K/AKT and Wnt/β-catenin, which could serve as potential therapeutic targets. Proteomic studies have identified key proteins involved in tumor metabolism and drug resistance, providing new insights for developing novel therapeutic strategies.[57]Despite these advancements, translating the findings from preclinical models into clinical applications remains a challenge. The heterogeneity within and between tumors complicates the identification of universal therapeutic targets. Furthermore, the emergence of resistance to targeted therapies, such as palbociclib, highlights the need for combination therapies and the exploration of alternative targets, such as miRNAs and epigenetic regulators.[58] Additionally, ethical and practical limitations in pediatric research necessitate the development of more complex in vitro systems (such as 3D organoid cultures and microfluidic devices) that can better replicate the TME and intercellular interactions.In conclusion, the combination of in vitro and in vivo models with advanced omics technologies has significantly enhanced our understanding of the biological characteristics and therapeutic potential of RB. Future research should focus on refining these models, identifying new targets, and developing personalized therapeutic strategies to improve the prognosis of patients with this malignant disease.5. LimitationsThis study is subject to several limitations. First, the exclusive inclusion of English-language literature may have introduced language bias by omitting potentially significant contributions published in other languages, such as Chinese, German, or Japanese. Second, recently published high-quality studies may not yet have accrued sufficient citations to influence bibliometric analyses, thereby limiting the sensitivity of hotspot and trend detection. Despite these constraints, the present analysis provides meaningful insights into the thematic evolution, emerging research frontiers, and future directions in the field of RB.6. RB, the most prevalent intraocular malignancy in children, serves as a foundational model in cancer biology due to its well-defined genetic etiology and rapid clinical course. Over the past decade, RB research has undergone substantial evolution, driven by global scientific contributions, technological innovation, and interdisciplinary collaboration. This bibliometric and thematic analysis reveals that the United States and China have emerged as dominant contributors, jointly accounting for over 40% of global RB publications. Leading institutions and influential researchers in these regions have played pivotal roles in shaping the trajectory of the field. Clustering and temporal analyses delineate 4 major domains of RB research: clinical diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis; molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways; gene and protein function; and experimental models and methodological advances.Clinically, the shift from enucleation to eye-salvaging treatments – including intra-arterial and intravitreal chemotherapy – has markedly improved patient outcomes, particularly in high-resource settings. However, outcome disparities persist in LMICs due to diagnostic delays and limited treatment accessibility. At the molecular level, RB1 inactivation, aberrant oncogenic signaling (e.g., PI3K/AKT/mTOR and Wnt/β-catenin), epigenetic reprogramming, and the involvement of miRNAs and CSCs are central to RB pathogenesis. These insights provide promising targets for therapeutic intervention and biomarker development. The integration of in vitro and in vivo models with multi-omics platforms has enabled high-throughput drug screening and mechanistic studies. Nonetheless, challenges remain in translating preclinical findings to clinical benefit, due largely to intratumoral heterogeneity and therapeutic resistance. Future directions should emphasize the development of advanced model systems (e.g., 3D organoids and microfluidic tumor chips), integration of personalized genomic data, and combinatorial therapeutic strategies that target both intrinsic genetic drivers and extrinsic microenvironmental factors. RB research is entering a transformative era characterized by precision oncology, collaborative synergy, and translational innovation. To realize equitable therapeutic outcomes globally, future efforts must prioritize early detection strategies, international harmonization of treatment protocols, and the seamless integration of molecular insights into personalized clinical care.Author contributionsConceptualization: Jinxiang Zhao.Data curation: Liping Wang, Tong Fu, Xu Zhang.Formal analysis: Jun Feng.Funding acquisition: Jinxiang Zhao.Investigation: Jun Feng.Methodology: Tong Fu.Project administration: Jinxiang Zhao.Resources: Xu Zhang, Jinxiang Zhao.Software: Tong Fu, Jian Zhang.Validation: Jun Feng, Xu Zhang.Visualization: Jun Feng.Writing – original draft: Liping Wang.Writing – review & editing: Jian Zhang, Fan Xie, Jinxiang Zhao.

title: Multi‑omics identification of MSI2 as a super-enhancer‑driven vulnerability in MYCN‑amplified neuroblastoma
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children and is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity and poor prognosis. MYCN amplification drives NB tumorigenesis through epigenetic reprogramming and is frequently accompanied by a copy-number gain of the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q). Epigenetic dysregulation of enhancer landscapes—particularly large regulatory elements termed super‑enhancers (SEs), which are enriched for H3K27ac and bound by lineage-specific master transcription factors (TFs)—establishes distinct NB cellular identities and states. These SE domains demarcate oncogenes that function as critical regulators of cell proliferation and apoptosis. Therefore, SE-driven genes represent tumor vulnerabilities, offering selective therapeutic opportunities.By integrating ATAC-seq data from 22 NB cell lines, the intratumoral heterogeneity of MYCN-amplified NB was characterized at the level of chromatin accessibility. Subsequently, based on H3K27ac ChIP-seq data from 38 NB cell lines, the ROSE algorithm was employed to identify SE-driven oncogenes. The synergistic mechanism between MYCN amplification and the 17q SE-driven gene MSI2 was investigated through genome‑wide CRISPR/Cas9 loss‑of‑function screens. At single‑cell resolution, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the characteristics of heterogeneous tumor subpopulations and their immune microenvironment features. This analysis was performed using multiple bioinformatics workflows, including AUCell scoring, SCENIC analysis, copy‑number inference, cell differentiation‑state evaluation, neighborhood abundance tests, and separability tests. Finally, functional validation was performed using NB cell lines (MYCN‑amplified and non‑amplified) to assess gene perturbations.Pronounced epigenetic heterogeneity was observed within MYCN-amplified NB. MSI2 is an SE‑driven oncogene and is highly expressed in MYCN‑amplified NB. MSI2 and MYCN are co-expressed, may be mutually dependent, and are both correlated with cell cycle-related pathways. At the single-cell level, we identified and redefined an NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype characterized by malignant transcriptional features, an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and poor patient prognosis. Building on this, combined targeting of MSI2 and MYCN markedly reduced proliferation and migration in MYCN‑amplified NB cells.sThe NB‑MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype defines a clinically aggressive, therapy‑refractory state characterized by high proliferation, metabolic reprogramming, and immunosuppression. For patients with MYCN-amplified NB, MSI2 is both a prognostic biomarker and a candidate therapeutic target.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at
full_text: NB is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children, predominantly affecting those under 10 years of age. Patients with low- and intermediate-risk NB may experience spontaneous regression without intervention, whereas high-risk patients exhibit extensive tumor metastasis and poor prognosis. This pronounced clinical heterogeneity makes NB a key focus in pediatric oncology research [1–4].Alterations in chromatin structure within the epigenetic landscape critically influence cellular identity and state transitions [5, 6]. SEs are clusters of enhancers spanning several kilobases in close genomic proximity that are characterized by dense occupancy of H3K27ac and H3K4me1 and strong transcriptional activation potential [7]. Across a wide range of cancers, including NB [8], small-cell lung cancer, medulloblastoma, and breast and gastric cancers, SEs are newly established during tumorigenesis. These cancer-specific SEs drive the expression of key oncogenes and are fundamental to maintaining the oncogenic state [9, 10].Oncogenic signaling pathways converge at transcriptional SEs [11]. Core transcriptional regulatory circuitries (CRCs), composed of specific genes driven by SEs, establish NB’s adrenergic (ADRN) and mesenchymal (MES) phenotypes through self-regulatory mechanisms and feedforward loops. These phenotypic differences are closely associated with dysregulated epigenetic networks, which not only partially explain the origin of NB heterogeneity but also provide crucial therapeutic targets [12–15]. Notably, MYCN amplification on chromosome 2 remodels transcriptional programs through enhancer invasion [16], and synergizes with 17q gain to significantly reduce long-term patient survival rates [17]. Therefore, in MYCN-amplified NB, targeting the oncogenic storm mediated by SE-driven genes in the 17q region holds significant therapeutic potential.MSI2, located on 17q, encodes an RNA-binding protein (RBP) involved in neural development and cell cycle regulation. Studies indicate that MSI2 is aberrantly expressed across multiple tumor types. It promotes malignant transformation in hematopoietic lineages and intestinal epithelial tissues, while maintaining tumor cell stemness and drug resistance [18–21]. In addition, increased MSI2 expression in cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma, revealing complex multicellular co-regulatory interactions [22]. Recently, MSI2 was found to interact with the SE-driven long non-coding RNA PRKCQ-AS1 in non-MYCN-amplified NB, thereby promoting tumor cell proliferation [23]. However, the functional role of MSI2 in MYCN-amplified NB remains undefined.Here, we identified MSI2 (chr17:57,255,851–57,701,581) on 17q as an SE-driven oncogene that is significantly upregulated in MYCN-amplified NB. The regulation of MSI2 and MYCN expression is potentially interdependent. Subsequently, we defined a distinct NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype characterized by enhanced proliferative and migratory capacities and poor clinical outcomes. In vitro experiments showed that combined knockdown of both genes synergistically inhibited MYCN-amplified NB cell proliferation and migration and induced apoptosis. Collectively, these findings suggest that MSI2 could be a promising therapeutic target for MYCN-amplified NB.Materials and Raw data collection and processingRaw data were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and processed under standardized environmental conditions to minimize batch effects during data analysis. Single-cell raw FASTQ data were processed using Cell Ranger 7.1.0, with the refdata-gex-GRCh38-2020-A genome as the reference, to generate downstream expression matrices. The immune cell atlas of human NB, including cell subtype annotations and cell embeddings, was obtained from the GEO dataset GSE147766 [24]. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq reads were aligned to the hg38 genome sequence after MACS2 peak calling (Bowtie2 2.5.3, Picard 2.27.5, Samtools 1.9, MACS2 2.2.9.1). ATAC-seq downstream matrices were merged from replicate BAM files, shifted by + 4/-5 bp, and normalized for GC content and gene length. BigWig files were generated from bedGraph files using deepTools. Finally, visualization was performed by selecting “scale-regions” mode, running ComputeMatrix, and plotting heatmaps.Identification of SE-driven genes by ROSE analysisFor each sample, H3K27ac ChIP-seq BAM files were analyzed together with matched input controls. Peak summits overlapping ENCODE blacklist regions were excluded. SE-driven genes were identified using the ROSE algorithm (https://bitbucket.org/young_computation/rose) with the following parameters: genome = hg38, stitching distance = 12.5 kb, and default ranking settings. Duplicate SE-driven genes identified across the same cell lines or biological replicates were removed from the dataset. BigWig files were smoothed and visualized using R.DepMap data processingGene expression, gene effect, gene dependency, and gene copy number data for cancer cell lines were extracted from the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap). Log2-transformed gene copy numbers were dichotomized using a cutoff of 1.58 (diploid baseline = 2; copy number ≥ 3 indicating amplification). After retaining 18,119 genes with complete information across 802 common cell lines, median differences in gene dependency scores between MYCN_AMP and WT groups were calculated for cancer cell lines. Cell lines were grouped according to tissue of origin. Tissue types retaining at least 3 mutant cell lines (Mut ≥ 3) and at least 5 wild-type cell lines (WT ≥ 5) were included. These groups were then directly compared, and the difference in mean gene dependency between mutant and wild-type cohorts was calculated. Differential analysis of gene dependency scores for SE-driven genes between NB and pan-cancer was performed using limma (v3.58.1), with results visualized in volcano plots.Univariate Cox regression analysis and survival analysisHazard ratios (HRs) were calculated using univariate Cox regression and visualized in forest plots for the top-ranked SE genes with significant differences in dependency. Using the median expression level of the MSI2 gene and MYCN status, we constructed a joint grouping variable. Death and disease recurrence were defined as endpoint events. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were generated using the survfit function, while the survdiff function was employed for log-rank tests and pairwise group comparisons. Survival curves were plotted using ggsurvplot, with the shaded area representing the 95% confidence interval (CI) and the risk table at the bottom displaying patient attrition during follow-up.Relative correlation analysisBy calculating average gene-expression profiles across NB tumor cell subpopulations, we identified the top 2000 genes with the highest variance. Rank correlation coefficients were used to assess the similarity of expression patterns between subpopulations, and results were visualized using pheatmap. Applying the same analytical strategy, we generated scatter plots of correlations between gene expression and CRISPR screen phenotypic scores. The strength of correlation was quantified using the correlation coefficient (r) and its statistical significance (t-test), with the gray-shaded area around the regression curve representing the 95% CI.Gene set enrichment analysisThe gene sets utilized in this study were obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB), encompassing Gene Ontology (GO) biological processes (BP), cellular components (CC), and molecular functions (MF), Hallmark gene sets, the Reactome Pathway Database, and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). Enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was performed using clusterProfiler (v4.10.0) based on the hypergeometric test. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) based on gene ranking was employed. Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) was applied to quantify pathway activity scores at the sample level. P-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.Pseudobulk construction for single-cell samplesCells from different individuals were distinguished by sample identifiers (orig.idents). The dgCMatrix was extracted, and gene expression values were summed across all cells. This process was iteratively applied to generate a whole-sample matrix, converting single-cell-level counts into pseudobulk expression values for each sample. To correct for sequencing depth variations and facilitate cross-sample comparisons, expression values for each gene were divided by their column sums and multiplied by 10^6 to achieve CPM normalization. Natural logarithms were then applied to every value in the normalized matrix, making the data more closely approximate a normal distribution. Finally, hierarchical clustering of samples was performed using Euclidean distance to achieve grouping.Single-cell data processingSingle-cell RNA count matrices underwent standardization and normalization for preprocessing, with doublet identification performed by DoubletFinder (v2.0.3) and DecontX to calculate doublet rates and ambient RNA contamination rates [25, 26]. During the initial quality control step, cells with mitochondrial gene content exceeding 10% or erythrocyte gene expression exceeding 1% were removed, and cells with fewer than 500 or more than 9000 genes (nFeatures 9000) were filtered. Subsequently, we performed regression analysis on cell cycle genes and conducted principal component analysis (PCA) dimensionality reduction using 2,000 highly variable genes (HVGs). The top 30 principal components were selected for batch effect correction across samples using the Harmony algorithm. Cell type annotation was based on canonical marker genes for known biological cell types, as reported in the literature and in the CellMarker database (http://xteam.xbio.top/CellMarker). DEGs for each cluster were identified using the FindAllMarkers function (thresholds: |log2FC| ≥ 0.25, expression ratio ≥ 0.25, adj.p 0.1, P < 0.05), 132 genes with significant dependency differences were identified (Supplementary Material 2). GO enrichment analysis showed significant overrepresentation of terms related to nervous system development, stem cell maintenance, metabolic and hormone responses, cell proliferation, and transcriptional activators. The top-ranked dependency-upregulated genes were CRC TFs MYCN, HAND2, GATA3, PHOX2A, and PHOX2B, as well as other genes, including IRS2, ALK, and MSI2 [13]. We also identified genes functionally linked to the CRC, such as ASCL1, CCND1, and TBX2 (Fig. 1F) [14, 44, 45]. The univariate Cox regression analysis revealed that among dependency-attenuated SE genes, SP1 and SCD exhibited the highest HRs, while among dependency-upregulated SE genes, PPP1R15B, ALK, MSI2, and MYCN showed the most pronounced changes in HR (Fig. 1G; Supplementary Material 3). Given that chromosome 17q harbors numerous “essential genes” for MYCN [46], MSI2 emerged as a key component and exhibited an HR comparable to that of MYCN. Their co-upregulation patterns, including both HR elevation and dependency upregulation, suggest an intrinsic functional linkage. Pan-cancer analysis across 33 cancer types revealed that, compared with adjacent normal tissues, MSI2 expression was elevated in most primary tumors, including BRCA, CESC, CHOL, COAD, and LUAD (Fig. S1A), suggesting a potential oncogenic role [47].MYCN amplification promotes activation of the MSI2 epigenetic landscapeBy integrating SE-driven gene predictions across 38 NB cell lines, we identified high-confidence SE-driven genes defined by H3K27ac signal values exceeding 10,000 in at least 10 cell lines (Supplementary Material 4). The MSI2 locus met these criteria and was selected. Given that enhancer invasion can remodel MYCN transcriptional regulation [16], we observed markedly elevated H3K27ac enrichment across a 620-kb genomic region surrounding the MSI2 locus in MYCN-amplified NB cell lines (Fig. 2A and B). When enhancer regions were delineated by H3K4me1 signals, abundant enhancer marks were observed across the MSI2 locus regardless of MYCN status (Fig. 2C). Its enhancer region resides in a poised state, providing the foundation for potential activation into a functional enhancer. Histone modification of H3K27ac distinguishes active enhancers from poised enhancers [48]. In the context of MYCN amplification, the high H3K27ac signal at the MSI2 enhancer region is associated with increased transcriptional activity. Active promoters are marked by RNA Pol II, H3K4me3, and H3K27ac, while transcription elongation regions are characterized by RNA Pol II Ser2P [49, 50]. In the MSI2 locus of IMR-32, ATAC signals indicate a high level of chromatin openness; RNA Pol II and abundant H3K4me3 at the promoter provide the fundamental conditions for transcription, and RNA Pol II Ser2P across the gene body indicates active elongation (Fig. 2D). A limited set of essential TFs—MYCN, HAND2, GATA3, PHOX2B, ISL1, and TBX2—serve as CRC members maintaining the cellular state of MYCN-amplified NB [13]. Among these, HAND2, GATA3, and PHOX2B drive NB lineage addiction, thereby defining their ADRN phenotypic identity [12]. We observed co-localization of MSI2 enhancer peaks with binding peaks for HAND2, GATA3, PHOX2B, and MYCN, accompanied by enhanced activation marker H3K27ac and diminished repressive marker H3K27me3. This suggests that the recruitment of CRC master TFs to the MSI2 enhancer contributes to MSI2 transcriptional activation and may reinforce ADRN lineage programs. Compared to the MES phenotype, the induced ADRN-phenotype cell lines showed higher H3K27ac signals at the MSI2 locus [51], further supporting this regulatory propensity. Cellular differentiation potential was estimated based on gene-expression abundance and diversity [29]. Compared to other subtypes, the NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype exhibited higher developmental potential (Fig. 4G). Pseudotime trajectory inference revealed that most of these cells clustered at the initiation end of low-differentiation branches (Cell State 1). With pseudotime progression, they diverged at Branch Point 1 toward NB-SOX6 and NB-HOXC8 differentiation trajectories (Fig. 4H). Using T/B cells and monocytes/macrophages as normal references, the NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype exhibited an increased copy-number burden on chromosome 17q (Fig. 4I), consistent with aggressive NB genomics [52]. Concurrently, this subtype is highly enriched in malignant proliferation programs (Program1/6) characterized by the expression of MKI67, PCNA, TOP2A, and eukaryotic translation initiation factor family genes (Fig. 4L) [53]. After extracting and annotating immune cell subsets (Fig. 7A and B), the constructed single-cell pseudobulk transcriptomes were used to stratify patients through hierarchical clustering and PCA dimensionality reduction (Fig. 7C). Quantitative analyses of cellular abundance revealed significant differences between the two groups of immune cells in both overall proportions and the number of local neighborhoods. To explore specific functional changes underlying these subpopulations, we reconstructed the NB immune cell reference atlas for reference mapping [24]. This reduction directly correlated with diminished long-term survival rates in patients.
