I: Correlation scatter plots showing the relationships between stromal score, immune score, tumor purity, and MSI2 and MYCN expression in NB tumor samples (n = 498) NB arises from dysregulated cell differentiation due to developmental abnormalities [1, 2] and is thus metaphorically described as “differentiation goes awry” [61]. Although the origin of NB remains debated [62], lineage tracing and single-cell sequencing studies have provided critical clues for decoding gene perturbations in disease states [53, 63]. Regardless of their origin, the determination of NB cell identity is governed by transcriptional networks disrupted through epigenetic dysregulation [13, 37].During this regulatory process, cell type-specific master TFs occupy enhancer regions of target genes, thereby controlling key identity-determining genes and directing dominant transcriptional programs of cell differentiation [42]. Notably, SEs—large regulatory elements formed by clustered enhancers—serve as pivotal regulatory hubs due to their potent transcriptional activation capacity [64]. Based on SE characteristics, NB can be classified into four epigenetic clinical subtypes: MYCN-amplified, high-risk MYCN-non-amplified, low-risk MYCN-non-amplified, and a fourth subtype exhibiting mesenchymal features [14]. According to dependency on the CRC TFs, these can be classified into the ADRN phenotype—dominated by master TFs such as HAND2, GATA3, and PHOX2B through feedforward loops—and the MES phenotype driven by PRRX1 and characterized by the AP-1 TF (FOS/JUN) [12, 15]. Because distinct lineages exhibit interconvertible properties, such plasticity potentially underlies treatment resistance and tumor recurrence [15]. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that intratumoral heterogeneity in NB is not stochastic but governed by specific epigenetic contexts, with MYCN amplification status playing a predominant regulatory role.As a key TF in NB, MYCN amplification drives pluripotency programs and serves as a marker of high-risk clinical subtypes and poor prognosis [52, 65]. ATAC-seq data reveal highly accessible chromatin near TSSs in MYCN-amplified NB, with epigenetic heterogeneity primarily governed by distal regulatory elements. Additionally, MYCN promotes a highly dependent oncogenic transcriptional network and maintains its activity by hijacking SEs of relevant genes [16, 41]. By integrating H3K27ac ChIP-seq data from multiple NB cell lines, we identified a group of SE-driven genes and performed a differential comparison with pan-cancer dependency scores. These NB-specific SE-driven genes were enriched for the GO terms “nervous system development” and “cell proliferation.” Among these, some SE-driven genes were uniquely present in MYCN-amplified NB cell lines. Through univariate Cox regression modeling, MSI2 and MYCN were identified as high-risk oncogenes.ChIP-seq signals revealed that MSI2 SE regions are occupied by master TFs of the ADRN phenotype. Although H3K4me1 is broadly enriched at MSI2 enhancer regions and maintains a primed state, only MYCN-amplified NB cell lines exhibit relatively high H3K27ac levels indicative of active enhancers. Multi-omics integration confirmed a positive correlation between MSI2 and MYCN expression, which is associated with a 17q gain [17, 46]. Immunofluorescence localized MSI2 predominantly to the cytoplasm, whereas MYCN was mainly present in the nucleus. Subsequently, the CRISPR/Cas9 library was screened to compare essential gene differences between oncogene-dependent cell lines and their non-dependent counterparts [66, 67], revealing MSI2 as a synthetic lethality partner of MYCN. The CRC members HAND2, GATA3, and PHOX2B identified concurrently reflect MYCN’s preference for the ADRN phenotype [13]. Interaction analysis demonstrated a mutual dependence between MSI2 and MYCN, with dependency scores positively correlated with expression levels of both genes. Mechanistic perturbations indicate that MYCN knockdown reduces MSI2 mRNA and protein levels by approximately 40%, yet basal expression persists, suggesting both MYCN-dependent and -independent regulatory inputs. Beyond direct MYCN regulation, TFs associated with the ADRN phenotype may sustain residual transcriptional activity by binding to the SE regions of MSI2. Notably, although MSI2 functions as an RBP, MSI2 knockdown did not alter MYCN mRNA levels but resulted in an approximately 60% reduction in MYCN protein. However, Co-IP failed to detect a stable direct MSI2–MYCN PPI. This indicates that MSI2 does not directly regulate MYCN at either the transcriptional or protein-stability level. Instead, MSI2 likely modulates MYCN protein abundance indirectly by influencing its translational efficiency. Functional validations demonstrated that individual overexpression of either MSI2 or MYCN promoted NB cell proliferation. Notably, MSI2 overexpression potentiated the inhibitory effect of MYCN knockdown, suggesting that increased MSI2 levels may increase cellular dependence on MYCN signaling. We propose a model in which MYCN, together with ADRN-type TFs (HAND2, GATA3, and PHOX2B), binds to the MSI2 SE region to transcriptionally activate MSI2 expression, while MSI2 in turn enhances MYCN protein levels post‑transcriptionally. This reciprocal interaction forms a positive feedback regulatory loop that reinforces survival pathways and promotes tumor progression (Fig. S3). Furthermore, the expression of ALK—a malignant proliferation marker in NB [68]—correlates positively with both MSI2 and MYCN, while ALK-mutant peripheral nervous system cell lines demonstrate heightened dependency on MSI2. This implies that ALK may participate in the MSI2/MYCN oncogenic circuit, and together they may drive malignant progression in NB.Intratumoral transcriptomic comparisons frequently serve as the cellular and molecular foundation for establishing tumor heterogeneity [69]. At single-cell resolution, we defined the NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype characterized by lower differentiation, aberrantly activated metabolic pathways, and concurrent 17q gain. Comparative analysis revealed that the transcriptional profile of the NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype resembles the malignant proliferation program of NB and exhibits migratory potential associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Although this subtype showed an attenuated ADRN signature, it did not shift toward the MES phenotype, reflecting MYCN addiction to the ADRN lineage [56]. On the other hand, given that MSI2 can confer stemness to tumor cells and enhance drug resistance [18–20], the MSI2/MYCN co-expression state is conducive to tumor cells acquiring chemotherapy tolerance while maintaining rapid proliferation.Prognostic analysis demonstrates extremely poor outcomes in the MSI2 + MYCN+ patient cohort. Both transcriptomic data and immunohistochemical results from patients with NB across different INSS stages collectively indicate that MSI2 outperforms MYCN in clinical staging, suggesting that MSI2 may serve as a novel molecular biomarker for prognostic evaluation in patients with NB. Pathway enrichment analysis in the MSI2 + MYCN+ patient group reveals significant activation of cell proliferation-related programs, including DNA replication, E2F targets, G2/M checkpoint, and cell cycle. Co-knockdown of MSI2 and MYCN resulted in comprehensive downregulation of the transcriptional levels of key cell-cycle regulators, including CDK2, PCNA, and E2F1, consistent with their role in sustaining high proliferative activity.The dependency of tumors on SE-driven genes provides critical therapeutic targets [10]. Because MSI2 is SE-driven and exhibits synthetic lethality with MYCN, we propose that the MSI2/MYCN interaction may represent a potential therapeutic target. Our experimental results demonstrate that MYCN-amplified NB cell lines exhibit heightened sensitivity to MSI2 knockdown. Compared with single-target knockdown, dual targeting of MSI2 and MYCN more effectively suppressed NB cell proliferation and invasion while inducing apoptosis.Although MSI2 has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in MYCN‑amplified NB, RBPs remain difficult to drug because most lack conventional catalytic pockets for small‑molecule inhibition [70]. While no potent and selective MSI2 inhibitors are currently available, several small-molecule MSI2 inhibitors with partial activity have been reported, indicating that MSI2 is not entirely undruggable [21]. Given that MSI2 expression is driven by SEs and influences cell‑cycle progression, selectively eliminating cancer cells may be achievable by blocking SE‑driven oncogenic transcription using BRD4 or CDK7 inhibitors [8, 10]. In addition, combinatorial strategies, including co-treatment with MYCN inhibitors or retinoic acid, which induces neuronal differentiation and proliferation arrest, may offer additional therapeutic benefit and warrant further investigation.It must be emphasized that alterations in the immune microenvironment surrounding cancer cells similarly impact long-term patient survival [4], manifested specifically through changes in tumor-suppressive and tumor-supportive immune cell phenotypes. In the MSI2 + MYCN+ patient cohort, T-cell abundance decreased significantly while myeloid-cell abundance markedly increased. Reference mapping of the NB immune cell atlas revealed diminished pro-inflammatory capacity in myeloid cells, which concurrently demonstrated tumor growth-promoting effects [24]. CTLs and highly cytotoxic activated NK cells primarily exhibited a marked reduction in population size [60]. Taken together, these shifts in immune composition and state suggest MSI2/MYCN likely facilitates immune evasion by remodeling the immunosuppressive microenvironment.This study has limitations. Although we have validated the MSI2-MYCN association through multidimensional approaches, the precise molecular mechanism governing their reciprocal regulation remains incompletely understood. Regarding the tumor microenvironment, although patients in the MSI2 + MYCN+ group exhibit overall immunosuppressive features, the spatial heterogeneity of such tumor cells within tissues and their interactions with immune-infiltrating components warrant further investigation. Future research should integrate proteomics and spatial transcriptomics with more sophisticated in vivo models and molecular mechanism experiments to systematically elucidate the complex molecular networks that drive the development of the NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype.sIn summary, this study identified the SE-driven oncogene MSI2 on chromosome 17q in MYCN-amplified NB and untangled its underlying oncogenic circuitry from an epigenetic regulatory perspective. Through multi-omics analyses and functional validation, we demonstrated that MSI2 is co-expressed with MYCN and represents a vulnerable target in MYCN-amplified NB. On this basis, we defined an NB-MSI2 + MYCN+ subtype with distinct molecular characteristics. Tumors of this subtype display a malignant transcriptional program, an ADRN phenotype characterized by attenuated differentiation, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Finally, we proposed a combined therapeutic strategy targeting both MSI2 and MYCN, which holds clinical translational value for the treatment of MYCN-amplified NB.Supplementary InformationBelow is the link to the electronic supplementary material. title: Immunotherapy in Acute Myeloid Leukemia: The Antibodies, TriKEs, and CARs on the Arduous Road to Cure
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a complex, heterogeneous and aggressive hematopoietic clonal disorder with limited curative options beyond allogeneic stem cell transplantation. The disease presents significant challenges due to high relapse rates resistance to chemotherapy, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. The immune system plays an important role in leukemia survival and resistance. Various immunotherapeutic approaches, ranging from the use of monoclonal antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTE’s), chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells, vaccines and therapeutic infusions of NK cells, are currently being tested with promising, yet conflicting results. We review the various types of immunotherapies in pre-clinical and clinical development and discuss how best to use them in clinical practice from the point of view of a clinical hematologist.
full_text: Despite therapeutic advances, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains a largely fatal disease, with a 5-year survival rate of 32.9% and an estimated 11,090 deaths in 2025 according to the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program [1]. AML is biologically and clinically heterogeneous disease with outcomes shaped by diverse clinical, cytogenetic, and molecular factors. For decades, intensive induction chemotherapy with the “7+3” regimen (cytarabine + daunorubicin) followed by consolidation chemotherapy and/or allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) in patients at high of relapse, has constituted the standard of care [2, 3]. Although the introduction of newer targeted molecules including Fms-like tyrosine kinase (FLT)-3, isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 (IDH-1), IDH2 and B-cell lymphoma (BCL)-2 inhibitors has expanded treatment options, overall outcomes remain suboptimal, particularly for relapsed/refractory (r/r) disease and for older or medically unfit patients [4]. The effectiveness of conventional chemotherapy is strongly influenced by the malignant hematopoietic lineage at diagnosis and by leukemia-intrinsic genomic alterations with important biological and clinical implications [5, 6]. Allo-HSCT provides a potent antileukemic effect through donor-mediated immune cytotoxicity known as the graft vs. leukemia (GvL) effect and represents the earliest successful application of cellular immunotherapy [7]. However, its utility is limited by transplant-related mortality (TRM), graft vs. host disease (GvHD), secondary malignancies, and restricted eligibility due to age, frailty, or comorbidities. Moreover, many transplanted patients ultimately relapse, often driven by immune escape mechanisms [8]. Given the close interactions between myeloid cells and the immune system, AML is an appealing target for immunotherapy. Progress, however, has been hindered by the lack of leukemia-specific antigens (LAAs) that clearly distinguish leukemic blasts from normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) resulting in off-target toxicity. There is therefore a critical need for more effective, less toxic, and individualized therapies. Multiple immunotherapies including monoclonal antibodies (MoAbs), chemo-immunoconjugates, bispecific antibodies (bsAbs), antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), immune-checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), T cell recruiting antibody constructs, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells, and dendritic cell vaccination are now under active investigation particularly in r/r AML. This review provides a comprehensive overview of these emerging therapies with a focus on their safety, efficacy and clinical development.1.Monoclonal Antibodies (MoAbs)Monoclonal Antibodies (MoAbs) target leukemia cells through multiple mechanisms and represent a promising therapeutic strategy due to their specificity and potentially lower toxicity compared to conventional chemotherapy. Their primary mechanism involves antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), where immune effector cells recognize antibody-coated leukemic blasts and induce cell lysis. Tumor fragments are subsequently processed by the antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and presented via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II molecules, activating cytotoxic T lymphocytes and enhancing antitumor activity [9]. MoAbs can also induce complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) and stimulate innate immune responses in treating AML. AML blasts express several surface antigens that serve as therapeutic targets including CD33, CD123 [10], CD32, CD371, CD38, CD47 [11, 12], CD44, CD56, CD30, CD7, CD25, CD70, CD96, C-type lectin, and CD64 [13, 14]. Various antibody-based platforms are under investigation, including monospecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates that deliver linked drugs, toxins, or radioactive payloads to malignant cells. Key AML antigen targets and their antibodies are shown in Figure 2.1.1Anti CD33 Targeting Monoclonal AntibodiesMost of the research on antibody-based therapy in AML has primarily focused on the myeloid differentiation antigen CD33 (sialic acid binding immunoglobulin-like lectins [SIGLEC-3]), a glycoprotein expressed on more than 90% of leukemic blasts but absent on normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and mature granulocytes. This allows selective malignant cell elimination while sparing healthy progenitors [15, 16]. CD33 expression is highest in AML patients with NPM1 mutations and lower in complex karyotypes and t(8;21) translocations [17].1.1.1Unconjugated antibodies: Lintuzumab (SGN-333, HuM195)Unconjugated humanized murine monoclonal antibody Lintuzumab (SGN-333,HuM195) was evaluated in phase II and III trials in combination with mitoxantrone, etoposide, and cytarabine (MEC) in the salvage setting; however, no survival benefit was observed leading to discontinuation of its development [18–20]. In contrast, BI836858, a fully humanized Fc-engineered anti-CD33 antibody, demonstrated manageable tolerability and preliminary signals of efficacy when combined with decitabine in elderly patients with r/r AML [21]. A phase 1 study of lintuzumab-Ac225 combined with CLAG-M (cladribine/cytarabine/filgrastim/mitoxantrone) (NCT03441048) reported a CRc (composite complete response rates (CR/CRi) of 56.6%, including 50% in TP53-mutated AML and 38.5% in patients previously treated with venetoclax (ven). MRD-negativity was achieved in 8 of the 12 responders. The estimated 2-year overall survival (OS) was 23.1% and 1-year progression-free-survival (PFS) was 30.8%. The regimen was well tolerated. Lintuzumab is currently being evaluated either as a single agent (NCT00283114, completed) and in combination with ven (NCT03867682, unknown status) or low dose cytarabine in clinical trials (NCT00528333, study completed).1.1.2Conjugated Anti-CD33 antibodies1.1.2.1Gemtuzumab Ozogamicin (GO; Myelotarg)Gemtuzumab Ozogamicin (GO) is the most extensively studied antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) in AML. GO comprises a humanized anti-CD33 IgG4 monoclonal antibody covalently linked calicheamicin, a potent DNA damaging cytotoxic agent. Binding of GO to CD33 on leukemic blasts leads to internalization of antibody-antigen complex, intracellular release of calicheamicin, induction of double-stranded DNA breaks and apoptotic cell death. GO became the first ADC approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2000 for older patients with CD33-positive AML in first relapse based on phase II trials demonstrating an overall response rate (ORR) of 30% (CR+ CRi [complete response with incomplete count recovery]) in patients with de-novo or relapsed AML [22, 23]. The initial regimen consisted of GO monotherapy at 9mg/m2 on days 1 and 14, repeated every 14 days for 2 doses, producing modest response durations. A subsequent phase III trial (SWOG S0106) designed to meet the FDA post-approval requirements, evaluated a lower dose of GO at 6mg/m2 combined with the standard induction chemotherapy in younger patients [24]. The study failed to show improvements in OS or remission rates and reported higher induction mortality in the GO arm (5.5% vs. 1.4%). Significant safety concerns emerged, particularly life-threatening VOD, observed in 9–14% of patients receiving higher GO doses. Risk was greatest in patients with pre-existing liver disease, exposure to hepatotoxic agents, and those undergoing allo-HSCT within 3 months of GO therapy. These toxicities, attributed to calicheamicin-mediated hepatocyte injury and uptake by CD33+ cells residing within the hepatic sinusoids, ultimately led to voluntary withdrawal of GO from US markets [25, 26]. The SWOG trial design was later criticized for suboptimal dose selection and lack of cytogenetic-risk stratification.Following its withdrawal, several large, randomized trials in the U.S. and Europe reevaluated adding GO to standard induction chemotherapy in newly diagnosed adults with AML using lower and/or fractionated dosing strategies. These studies demonstrated that adding GO to standard induction chemotherapy significantly improved OS, particularly in younger patients with favorable and/or intermediate risk cytogenetics. In older patients, GO improved relapse risk (RR), event-free survival (EFS), and OS without increasing early mortality rate, although response rates were largely unchanged [27–30]. The pivotal phase III ALFA-0701 trial (NCT00927498) evaluated fractionated low-dose GO in patients aged 50 to 70 years, and demonstrated substantial improvements in EFS, reduced relapse rates, and a more favorable safety profile. These findings led to the reapproval of GO by the FDA in 2017 for newly diagnosed and r/r CD33-positive AML [30]. A meta-analysis of 3,325 patients from randomized trials confirmed GO’s benefit. Adding a single 3mg/m2 dose to induction reduced the risk of relapse (HR 0.8; 95% CI 0.72–0.89, p<0.001), improved relapse-free survival (RFS) (HR 0.8, 95% CI 0.76–0.94; p=0.001), and improved OS (HR 0.89; 95%CI 0.82–0.97;p=0.01), with the greatest benefit in patients with favorable and intermediate risk cytogenetics [31]. More recent data suggest that a second dose of GO on day 4 may enhance measurable residual disease (MRD) clearance and improve OS in older patients without adverse cytogenetics [32]. A broader meta-analysis including 15 randomized and 15 retrospective studies further confirmed GO’s survival advantage in patients with favorable or intermediate-risk cytogenetics, as well as those with NPM1 mutations and FLT-3 wild type (FLT3-wt) disease [33]. Genetic profiling studies also indicate greater benefit in patients classified as favorable or intermediate risk by European Leukemia Net (ELN) criteria with higher CD33 expression [34].GO has been studied in combination with hypomethylating agents (HMAs). In a phase I/II trial evaluating azacytidine (aza) and GO in r/r AML, the combination achieved a CRc rate of 24% without dose-limiting toxicities or cases of VOD [35]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 clinical trials comparing GO monotherapy with GO combined with HMA found the combination more effective in unfit AML patients, with a higher ORR (48% vs 25%), and CRc rates (42% vs 25%). In r/r AML, however, pooled analyses showed no major difference in response outcomes between monotherapy and combination therapy. Overall, the regimen was well tolerated with relatively low toxicity supporting its use in older or frail patients [36]. Emerging data also suggest GO can be safely combined with liposomal daunorubicin and cytarabine (CPX-351). A pilot study in adults with newly diagnosed favorable or intermediate risk, FLT3-ITD negative AML treated with GO plus CPX-351 demonstrated a 95% CR rate, with 42% achieving MRD-negativity. The estimated 18-month leukemia-free-survival (LFS) and OS were 80% and 95% respectively. The regimen did not result in prolonged cytopenias, although subclinical cardiotoxicity was observed in 25% of patients [37]. These findings support ongoing evaluation of this combination.Finally, GO has been explored in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). In combination with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), the CR rate was 84% (16/19), with all evaluable patients (twelve patients were evaluable) becoming PCR-negative within 2 to 4 months of remission [38]. In high-risk APL, combining GO with arsenic trioxide (ATO) yielded a 5-year EFS of 84% suggesting a potential anthracycline-sparing curative strategy [39].Overall, GO’s clinical trajectory from initial approval to withdrawal and subsequent reintroduction highlights the importance of dose optimization, patient selection and molecular risk stratification. GO remains the most validated ADC in AML and continues to play an important role in frontline and salvage treatment strategies for CD33-positive AML with favorable or intermediate-risk cytogenetics.1.1.2.2 AVE9633, another anti-CD33 antibody showed limited activity in a phase I study [40]. IMGN779, a human anti-CD33 MoAb demonstrated response rates exceeding 50% with weekly dosing and 35% with biweekly dosing in a phase 1 trial (NCT02674763), but further development was stopped for strategic reasons by the drug company [41].1.1.2.3Vadastuximab talirine (SGN33A)Vadastuximab is a next generation anti-CD33 ADC linked to a pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimer that induces DNA damage, cell cycle arrest, and leukemia cell apoptosis. In a phase I trial (NCT01902329), SGN33A monotherapy showed a CRc rates of 28% with dose limiting toxicities including pulmonary embolism and myelosuppression [42]. In another phase I trial, combination with HMA yielded ORR of 28% in r/r AML and 73% in newly diagnosed AML, with nearly 47% of responding patients achieving MRD-negativity, although severe myelosuppression was common [43]. The phase III CASCADE trial comparing HMA with or without vadastuximab in untreated AML was terminated early because of increased infection-related mortality in the experimental arm [44]. A phase Ib study (NCT02326584), combining vadastuximab with 7+3 showed a 78% CRc, but all patients experienced grade 4 myelosuppression. However, there were no cases of VOD and the 60-day mortality rate was 7% [45]. Due to the increased number of deaths on several phase 1 trials, FDA placed a hold on this drug in December 2016, and the manufacturer discontinued all patient enrollment and treatment in 2017.1.2Anti-CD123 Monoclonal AntibodiesCD123, or the interleukin-3 receptor alpha chain (IL-3Rα) is a 75 kDa transmembrane protein highly overexpressed on leukemic stem cells (LSC) and myeloid blasts. The overexpression of CD123 correlates with increased blast proliferation, disease relapse, and drug resistance [46, 47].1.2.1Unconjugated Anti CD123 Antibodies1.2.1.1Talacotuzumab (CSL362/JNJ- )Talacotuzumab is a second generation, fully humanized anti-CD123 monoclonal antibody, Fc engineered to enhance NK-cell binding via CD16 and promote ADCC. In a phase 1 trial (NCT0162852) involving 25 patients in first or second CR with high-risk features for relapse, CSL362 demonstrated potent activity with acceptable safety profile. Among the 20 evaluable patients, 10 maintained CR for a median duration exceeding six months, and three of the six patients assessed for MRD achieved MRD-negativity. Adverse events occurring in ≥ 10% of subjects included infusion reactions, hypotension, hypertension, and increased C-reactive protein. In a randomized phase II trial (NCT02472145), comparing talacotuzumab with decitabine vs. decitabine alone in 316 older, newly diagnosed AML patients ineligible for intensive chemotherapy, no improvement in outcomes was observed leading to discontinuation of drug development [48]. Similarly, the investigator-initiated phase II SAMBA trial (NCT02992860) evaluated talacotuzumab monotherapy in HMA-refractory AML and high-risk MDS. Among 24 patients, the ORR was 8.3% (2 patients, one CRi and one hematologic improvement [HI]), with three additional cases of stable disease (SD). Median OS was 3.6 months, and median response duration was 57 days (range: 1–374 days). Higher toxicity including infections, cytopenias, gastrointestinal and cardiac events, infusion reactions, and rare neurological complications led to early study termination [49].1.2.1.2CSL360, another antiCD123 antibody was evaluated in a phase 1 trial (NCT00401739) with minimal efficacy[50].1.2.2Conjugated Anti CD123 Antibodies1.2.2.1Tagraxofusp (SL-401; DT388IL3, TAG)Tagraxofusp (TAG) is a first- in-class CD123-targeted recombinant fusion protein composed of the truncated diphtheria toxin linked to human IL-3 ligand. Upon binding to CD123 and subsequent internalization, the toxin inhibits protein synthesis, ultimately inducing apoptosis [51]. Based on a multicenter trial demonstrating a 53.8% CR response in treatment-naïve patients, the FDA proved TAG in December 2018 for the treatment of blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) [52]. The therapeutic utility of TAG is now being actively explored in AML. In a phase 2 study (NCT04342962) of r/r CD123+ AML, TAG monotherapy yielded an ORR of 34.8%, which included two MRD-negative CRs and six PRs [53]. Emerging data suggests synergistic potential when TAG is combined with ven and HMA. A phase Ib trial (NCT03113643) evaluated TAG in combination with ven and aza in intensive chemotherapy-ineligible patients. The triplet regimen achieved a 39% CR and 19% CRi rate. Notably, 12% of patients achieved morphologic leukemia-free state (MLFS). The triplet combination showed significant efficacy in high- risk populations; among 13 patients with TP53 mutations, 54% achieved a response (CR:4; CRi: 2, MLFS:1). Furthermore, 12 of the 17 responders achieved MRD-negativity. The median OS was 14 months (95% CI, 9.5-NA) with a median PFS of 8.5 months (95%CI, 5.1-NA) [54]. Currently, there are several trials incorporating TAG with other agents. The TRILLIUM trial (NCT06456463), a phase II study is recruiting older, untreated CD123+ AML patients to receive TAG with ven and aza. A phase II study (TAGALONG Trial) is evaluating TAG and aza with or without ven in newly diagnosed secondary AML patients after previous exposure to HMA (NCT05442216) [55]. Finally, TAG is being studied in combination with cladribine and low-dose cytarabine (LDAC) for patients with r/r AML after treatment with a ven combination (NCT06561152).1.2.2.2Pivekimab sunirine (IMGN632)Pivekimab sunirine, a CD123 targeted ADC, showed a 21% ORR (95% CI 8–40; six of 29) and 17% CRc rate in a phase 1/II study (NCT03386513) [56]. Pivekimab sunirine combined with aza and ven demonstrated high activity in newly diagnosed unfit AML. With 10-month median follow-up, CR occurred in 63.3% and CR/CRi in 79.6%, with MRD negativity in 92% of CR and 90% of CR/CRi cases [57]. It also showed high, durable activity in Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm (BPDCN) in the CADENZA trial [58]. It is now being evaluated in a phase Ib/II study in combination with aza and ven in newly diagnosed patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy (NCT04086264).1.3AntiCD38 Monoclonal antibodiesCD38, a 45 kDa transmembrane glycoprotein, is expressed on more than 70% of AML blasts, making it a potential therapeutic target [59, 60]. Daratumumab is an FDA-approved anti-CD38 IgG1ĸ MoAb for the treatment of multiple myeloma. A phase I/II trial of daratumumab in r/r AML and high risk MDS (NCT03067571) was terminated, with no results yet reported. Isatuxumab, another anti-CD38 MoAb, was evaluated in a phase I/II pediatric leukemia trial (NCT03860844), and showed a CRc rate of 60.9%, with a median OS of 9.4 months. However, serious adverse events occurred in 62.9% of patients and prespecified efficacy thresholds were not met, leading to trial termination [61].1.4Anti-CD371 Monoclonal antibodies (CLL-1, CLEC12A)Anti -CD371 (anti-CLL-1/CLEC12A) MoAb DCLL9718S was evaluated in a phase I dose escalation trial (NCT03298516) in r/r AML and no CR or PR were observed, the was terminated early due to severe hepatotoxicity and lack of efficacy [62].1.5Anti CD56 Monoclonal antibodiesCD56, also known as NCAM1 (neural cell adhesion molecule 1), is aberrantly expressed in a variety of hematological malignancies including AML and is associated with poor survival and shorter OS [63–66].1.5.1 Lorvotuzumab mertansine is a CD56 MoAb conjugated to maytansinoid DM1. It was evaluated in a phase II trial in patients with CD56+ hematologic malignancies including AML, myelofibrosis, and BPDCN (NCT02420873), results of which are not reported. This drug has been withdrawn from further development.1.6Anti-FLT3 Monoclonal AntibodiesFMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), a class III receptor tyrosine kinase, is highly expressed on AML blasts and LSCs, and high FLT3 levels correlate with unfavorable prognosis, high relapse rates, and chemotherapy resistance [67, 68]. Activating mutations in the internal tandem duplication (ITD) are among the most frequent genetic abnormalities occurring in approximately 30% of newly diagnosed AML patients. Multiple MoAbs targeting FLT3 have been evaluated in clinical trials in patients with r/r AML, including AGS62P1, an ADC conjugated with the microtubule toxin amberstatin 269 (NCT02864290) [69] and IMC-EB10 (LY3012218), (NCT00887926) with poor efficacy leading to closure of drug development [70]. A phase I study of FLYSYN, an Fc-optimized anti-FLT3 antibody, demonstrated encouraging MRD reduction; 65% of MRD+ AML patients showed dose-dependent decreases in bone marrow MRD, and two achieved MRDnegativity [71].1.7Anti-CD25 Monoclonal AntibodiesCD25, also known as IL-2RA, expression on AML blasts is associated with failure of induction therapy, increased risk of relapse, and shorter OS [72, 73]. Camidanlumab tesirine, a CD25-targeting ADC was evaluated in a phase 1 trial (NCT02588092). Two patients achieved CRi, and the drug showed a manageable safety profile with no serious adverse events. The study was terminated during of dose escalation due to programmatic reasons [74].1.8Anti CD30 AntibodiesCD30 (TNFRSF8/Ki-1) is a 120 kDa transmembrane glycoprotein expressed in a subset of AML[75, 76]. Brentuximab vedotin (BV; SGN-35) is a chimeric ADC composed of an anti-CD30 monoclonal antibody linked to the microtubule disrupting agent monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) via a protease-cleavable linker. After binding to CD30-expressing cells and internalization, MMAE is released, causing G2/M phase cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. BV is FDA approved for treatment of Hodgkin lymphoma and anaplastic large cell lymphoma, and its activity in other CD30-positive malignancies is being explored [77, 78]. In a phase I dose escalation study (NCT01830777), BV was combined with MEC chemotherapy in r/r AML. The CRc rate was 36% overall and increased to 42% at the highest BV dose (1.8 mg/kg). Among responders the median DFS was 6.8 months, and median OS was 9.5 months. Notably, 55% of patients successfully bridged to consolidation therapies, including allo-HSCT or donor lymphocyte infusion (DLI). The regimen demonstrated acceptable safety with toxicity comparable to MEC alone, supporting further evaluation in randomized studies and across various cytogenetic and molecular subgroups[79].1.9Anti CD44 Monoclonal AntibodiesCD44 is an adhesion molecule expressed on hematopoietic precursors, macrophages, lymphocytes, and leukemic blasts [80]. A phase 1 trial with anti-CD44 antibody RGN356 (RO5429083) in r/r AML showed one patient achieving CRp, another achieved PR, and one SD with hematologic improvement among the 44 enrolled patients. Toxicities were mostly mild although grade 3 hemolysis and drug induced aseptic meningitis were noted in 2 patients [81].1.10AntiCD70 Monoclonal AntibodiesCD70, a ligand belonging to tumor necrosis factors, exhibits aberrant overexpression among multiple hematologic and solid malignancies. CD70 is a very promising target due to its consistent expression on LSCs and AML blasts [82, 83].1.10.1 Cusatuzumab (ARGX-110) is a high affinity, anti-CD70 MoAb that blocks CD70/CD27 signaling, inhibiting LSC proliferation, reducing leukemic blasts, impairing regulatory T-cell survival thereby preventing tumor immune escape, and restoring normal myeloid differentiation [82–85]. As normal HSCs lack CD70 or CD27, this pathway represents an attractive therapeutic target. In a phase I/II trial (NCT03030612), cusatuzumab was evaluated with aza in treatment-naïve AML patients. After an initial 14-day cusatuzumab monotherapy lead-in, aza was introduced to the regimen. Among 12 participants, all achieved a clinical response, eight achieved a CR, two achieved CRi and two patients achieved PR. MRD-negativity was confirmed in four patients, and treatment significantly depleted the LSC pool, suggesting potential for durable disease control [82, 86, 87]. The multicenter phase I/II CULMINATE trial (NCT04023526), further assessed cusatuzumab in combination with aza for treatment naïve AML patients ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy. Patients received a 14-day cusatuzumab monotherapy lead in at escalating doses (range:1–20mg/kg), followed by 28-day combination cycles with aza (75mg/m2 for 7 days). During dose-escalation, the regimen produced a CRc of 50%. A dose of 10mg/kg was selected as the recommended phase II dose. The regimen was well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicities. Median duration of response (mDOR) was 4.5 months, and a median OS was 11.5 months [88]. Further evaluation of cusatuzumab is ongoing in the ELEVATE trial (NCT04150887), a phase 1b study assessing cusatuzumab with ven, with or without aza, to determine whether these combinations have synergistic clinical benefits to improve clinical outcomes [89]. Select clinical trials and their key outcomes are summarized in table 1 below:Limitations of MoAbs and future directions:AML heterogeneity and lack of AML specific target antigens have historically hindered antibody-based therapies, often resulting in poor efficacy or off-target toxicity. However, the field is rapidly evolving through identification of novel agents and a deeper understanding of immune checkpoint signaling crosstalk. Concurrently, advancements in molecular bioengineering have facilitated the development of next generation MoAb constructs with optimized pharmacokinetics, enhanced stability, and superior effector recruitment. Emerging modalities including TCR-mimic, anti-FcγR, and anti-IL-1 receptor accessory protein (IL1RAP) antibodies, alongside targets like CD96, CD105, CD157 and CD200 are currently under preclinical and early clinical investigation. Research into synergistic combinations of MoAbs with chemotherapy, HMAs, and other novel inhibitors is expanding. Thes innovations signal a transformative era in AML treatment, offering the potential to overcome historical limitations and significantly expand the therapeutic armamentarium for patients and clinicians.2.0Radioimmunotherapy via targeted radio-conjugated antibodiesRadioimmunotherapy (RIT) utilizes MoAbs conjugated to radionuclides to deliver targeted continuous ionizing radiation to antigen expressing leukemic cells. Radiolabeled antibodies induce apoptosis and necrosis primarily through unrepaired DNA strand breaks [102]. The therapeutic profile of RIT depends on the radionuclide used. In AML, the most commonly employed radionuclides are 131I (iodine 131) and 90Y (Yttrium 90), both β-emitters with relatively low linear energy transfer (LET), relative biological effectiveness (BE) and manageable safety characteristics [103, 104]. Clinically, RIT has been incorporated mainly into the conditioning regimens before allo-HSCT, to enhance immunoablation, reduce leukemic burden, and prevent graft rejection [105–109]. The most extensively studied RIT targets in AML is CD45, a key regulator of hematopoietic and immune cell signaling that is broadly expressed on hematopoietic and immune cells [110]. Anti-CD45 radioimmunoconjugates including 131I-BC-8 (Iomab-b) and 131I-Apamistamab have been combined with fludarabine and TBI to enhance cytoreduction prior to allo-HSCT.The phase III SIERRA trial (NCT02665065), an open label 1:1 randomized, controlled, optional one-way crossover study, evaluated 131I-apamistamab followed by fludarabine-TBI (Flu-TBI) and allo-HSCT versus the investigator’s choice of therapy in patients ≥ 55 years with active r/r AML. The conventional arm comprised salvage therapy followed by standard of care allo-HSCT if patients achieved CR or CRp within 28–42 days of treatment initiation. Patients with a CR/CRp per bone marrow assessment could proceed to conventional allo-HSCT or continue treatment. Patients without CR/CRp, or who had AML progression from day 14, could cross over to receive 131I-apamistamab and Flu-TBI followed by allo-HSCT. The primary endpoint was durable CR (dCR), defined as CR/CRp lasting ≥ 180 days from first assessment in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population. The dCR required CR/CRp before transplant in the conventional care arm and after transplant in the 131I-apamistamab arm. Secondary endpoints, such as OS was defined as time to death from random assignment and EFS was defined as time from random assignment to (1) failure to receive allo-HSCT in the 131I-apamistamab group, (2) salvage treatment failure in the conventional group, (3) morphologic relapse, or (4) death, whichever came first. The ITT population included 153 patients (131I-apamistamab [n=76]; conventional care [n=77]). In total 44 of the 77 conventional care arm patients crossed over and 40 of the 77 (52%) received 131I-apamistamab and allo-HSCT, with six patients (13.6%) experiencing dCR. In the ITT population, the dCR was significantly higher with 131I-apamistamab (17.1% [95% CI, 9.4–27.5]) than the conventional care (0% [95% CI,0–4.7]; p<.0001). The OS hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.70–1.41; p=0.96) and the EFS HR was 0.23 (95% CI, 0.15–0.34), favoring 131I-apamistamab. Grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 59.7% and 59.2% of the 131I-apamistamab and conventional care groups respectively [111]. Although the trial met its primary endpoint, the FDA did not support the biologics license application (BLA) filing and requested an additional head-to-head randomized trial (Iomab-B plus RIC vs. RIC) to demonstrate an OS benefit. Despite these encouraging results, γ-emissions from 131I require patient isolation, prompting evaluation of alternative isotopes such as 90Y which emits β particles and thus does not require lead-lined isolation units [108].Other RIT agents have been tried in small studies. In a phase I trial combining 90Y-DOTA-BC8 with fludarabine and 2-Gy TBI prior to allo-HSCT, 13 of the 15 (87%) high-risk AML/MDS patients achieved CR. Relapse occurred in six patients with one- and two-year OS of 66% and 46%, and PFS of 46% (NCT01300572) [112]. Innovative approaches have explored combining multiple radionuclides to enhance the crossfire effect. In a small study of three patients with refractory AML, 90Y-labeled anti-CXCR4 peptide and 188Re-labeled CD66 antibody were administered, with one patient also receiving a third conjugate (153Sm EDTMP). All three patients achieved a CR following a second allo-HSCT with RIC [113].RIT has also been combined with chemotherapy to intensify myeloablative conditioning. Two antibodies, an anti-CD45 antibody, apamistamab and an anti-CD66 antibody, besilesomab have been studied in this context. In a phase I/II trial, 131I-apamistamab combined with targeted dose busulfan and cyclophosphamide in intermediate- or high-risk AML patients in first remission yielded a 3-year non-relapse mortality (NRM) of 21% and DFS of 61% without excess organ toxicity or GvHD. Compared with 509 similar registry controls from the Center for International Bone Marrow Transplant Registry (CIBMTR), outcomes suggested feasibility of antibody augmented conditioning, the adjusted mortality risk was 0.65 (95% CI: 0.39–1.08; p=.09) [107]. Another study evaluated 188Re-labeled anti-CD66 antibody besilesomab with either TBI/cyclophosphamide or busulfan/cyclophosphamide in high-risk AML and MDS patients in first CR or PR. RIT delivered an additional mean marrow dose of 15.3Gy, with relapse rates of 20% in patients transplanted in remission and 30% for those with active disease. NRM and GvHD rates were not increased, although renal toxicity occurred due to instability of the conjugate [114]. This issue was addressed by switching to 90Y with MX-DTPA chelation allowing higher bone marrow doses without added organ toxicity [115].Outside of transplant setting, α-emitter- labelled RITs have shown promising activity. Lintuzumab labeled isotopes such as 231Bi and 225Ac have demonstrated meaningful CR rates in patients with r/r AML patients who are unfit for intensive chemotherapy. However, hematologic toxicity remains dose limiting, and ongoing studies are evaluating optimal dosing and combination strategies for 225Ac-labeled lintuzumab [116–118].Limitations and future directions:Current AML research increasingly focuses on eliminating LSCs. Targeted therapies face challenges due to LSC heterogeneity and the close biological relationship between LSCs and HSCs which contributes to hematologic toxicity. RIT may offer an advantage by delivering radiation capable of eradicating both antigen-positive and antigen-negative LSCs through the crossfire effect. However, several practical limitations remain. These include concerns about the long-term effects of low dose radiation, logistical challenges associated with radioactive isolation and radiation safety, limited availability of therapeutic nuclides (particularly α-emitters), complex dosimetry protocols, and the cost and regulatory requirements of producing antibody-radionuclide conjugates under good manufacturing practice (GMP) standards. Despite these challenges, continued improvements in radionuclide chemistry, targeting strategies, and combination approaches may expand the role of RIT in AML treatment [119].3.Bispecific Antibodies including BiTEs®, DARTs, BiKEs and TriKEsBispecific antibodies (bsAbs) are an emerging immunotherapeutic strategy that enables simultaneous targeting of tumor surface antigens and activation of immune effector cells. Conventional antibodies cannot directly recruit T-cells because T-cells lack Fcγ receptors [120]. BsAbs overcome this limitation by binding both a tumor associated antigen and an effector cell antigen such as CD3 on T-cells or CD16 on NK-cells. This dual binding brings immune effector cells into close proximity with tumor cells and triggers effector cell activation [121, 122]. As a result, bsAbs can induce potent, MHC-independent cytotoxicity without the need for co-stimulatory signaling, thereby overcoming a key mechanism of tumor immune evasion [123]. As of May 2025, 17 bsAbs have received regulatory approval across various diseases [124].Several bsAb platforms have been developed. Bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs®) consist of two single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) connected in tandem, one targeting the TAA and the other engaging CD3 on T cells [125]. Dual-affinity retargeting molecules (DARTs®) use a stabilized diabody backbone often incorporating an Fc-region to extend half-life [126, 127]. Other approaches include bispecific killer engagers (BiKEs) which target CD16 to activate NK cells, and trispecific killer engagers (TriKEs) which include an IL-15 linker to enhance NK-cell function [128, 129]. A key toxicity associated with immune-effector cell activation by bsAbs is cytokine release syndrome (CRS). This “on-target” effect results from a rapid cytokine release and can range from mild symptoms such as fever, headache, myalgia, and rash to severe manifestations including shock, hypoxia, and multiorgan failure. Bystander immune cells and endothelial cells may also contribute to the development and severity of CRS [130, 131]. CRS is also seen with other cellular therapies.3.1CD33 directed bispecific antibodiesMultiple CD33 × CD3 BiTE® constructs targeting CD33 including emerfetamab (AMG673; NCT03224819), eluvixtamab (AMG330; NCT02520427), vixtimotamab (AMV564; NCT03144245), JNJ- (NCT03915379), and GEM33 (NCT03516760) have been evaluated in early phase clinical trials for r/r AML. Across studies, a consistent finding was significant toxicity, particularly CRS, occurring in up to 78% with eluvixtamab and 50% with emerfetamab. Emerfetamab was also associated with elevated liver enzymes (17%), leukopenia (13%), thrombocytopenia (7%), and febrile neutropenia (7%). In view of these safety concerns and limited clinical efficacy, development of several of these agents, including emerfetamab, GEM33, and eluvixtamab, was discontinued by sponsors. JNJ- was halted due to lack of efficacy. Additionally, 90% (27/30) of patients receiving emerfetamab discontinued treatment due to disease progression [132–135]. Currently, no active trials are evaluating CD33-targeting bsAbs in AML. Table 2 lists the published clinical trials with bsAbs.3.2CD123 directed bispecific antibodiesVibecotamab is a humanized CD3 × CD123 bsAb with an Fc-domain that prolongs its half-life to 6.2 days [136]. In a phase I trial involving 120 patients with r/r AML, CRS was the most common adverse event (AE) (59.2%), and 16 patients experienced at least one dose limiting toxicity (DLT). Among 111 evaluable patients, the ORR was 10%, with responses (MLFS or better) observed only at doses ≥0.75μg/kg (n=87) and more frequently in patients with lower marrow blast burden ( <25% blasts) [137]. A subsequent phase II study (NCT05285813; closed to accrual) in MDS/CMML after HMA failure (cohort 1) and MRD+ AML (cohort 2) has shown encouraging early activity, with meaningful remission rates. In early reporting of 37 treated patients, out of 19 patients in the MDS/CMML cohort, 12 achieved bone marrow CR and one hematologic improvement (HI), while 5 of the 18 MRD+ AML patients achieved MRD-negative CR. There was minimal myelosuppression, and manageable infusion-related reactions, and no observed DLTs [138].Mipletamig is a recombinant CD123 × CD3 ADAPTIRÒ™ bsAb designed to redirect T-cells independent of MHC. In a phase Ib dose-escalation study of the 46 patients with r/r AML and MDS, infusion related reactions occurred in 28.3% patients and CRS in 21.7% (grade 3–4 in 8.7%). Anemia was the most common hematological toxicity, and one patient experienced acute renal failure following grade 2 CRS. Among 34 evaluable r/r AML patients, 22 achieved SD and two patients with primary AML achieved CR [139]. In a separate phase Ib study (NCT05303076) combining mipletamig with aza and ven in newly diagnosed AML patients (n=13), infusion reactions were the most common non-hematologic adverse event, and elevated AST was the most frequent grade ≥3 toxicity Notably, no CRS was observed. Among nine evaluable patients, seven achieved CR (five MRD-negative) and one achieved a PR, supporting promising safety and efficacy [139, 140]. This study is currently actively enrolling at higher dose levels and further analyses are awaited.Flotetuzumab is a novel CD123 × CD3 DART® bsAb with preferential binding to CD123 than CD3 to enhance leukemia targeting while sparing HSCs [141, 142]. In a phase I/II trial (NCT02152956), in 30 primary induction failure or early relapse patients, the ORR was 30%, including CR in 5 patients (16.7%), with a median OS of 10.2 months. The 6- and 12-month survival rates were 75% (95% CI, 0.450–1.05) and 50% (95% CI, 0.154–0.846) respectively. CRS was common but mostly low grade (1–2), one patient experienced grade 3 CRS [143]. Transcriptomic profiling of the bone marrow identified a 10-gene signature predictive of response more accurately than the ELN risk classification, while high baseline leukemic PD-L1 expression correlated with rapid progression within 2 weeks. Despite promising activity, the combination trial of flotetuzumab and the anti-PD-1 antibody, MGA102, has been discontinued by the manufacturer. A Children’s Oncology Group (COG) phase I trial of flotetuzumab in pediatric r/r AML is currently active but not recruiting (NCT04158739). A second-generation CD123 × CD3 DART, MGD204, with longer half-life permitting intermittent dosing is currently under investigation (NCT05362773).Further developments of two other CD123 × CD3 targeting bsAbs, JNJ- (NCT02715011) and SAR440234 (NCT03594955), were terminated owing to poor tolerability and safety challenges; see table 2 for details [144].3.3CLEC12A/CLL-1 directed bispecific antibodiesMCLA-117 is a full length IgG1 CLL-1 × CD3 bsAb that activates and redirects T-cells to lyse CLEC12A+ AML blasts, with its Fc containing structure supporting weekly or biweekly dosing [145]. A phase I trial (NCT03038230) enrolled 50 adults with newly diagnosed or secondary AML but was terminated for strategic reasons. No DLTs were observed; TRAEs included nausea, chills, pyrexia and CRS (32%). Four of the 26 evaluable patients had ≥50% blast reduction in bone marrow, including one MLFS [146].3.4Tri-specific Killer Engagers (TriKEs in AML)Tri-specific killer engagers (TriKEs) are a novel class of engineered immunotherapeutic agents designed to engage and activate NK-cells, thereby enhancing immune-mediated elimination of cancer cells [129, 147]. A TriKE consists of three functional domains constructed from antigen-specific antibodies or antibody fragments. TriKEs can be broadly categorized into IgG-like formats containing Fc-region and non-IgG-like formats composed of smaller antibody-derived components such as antigen-binding fragments (Fab), single-chain variable fragments (scFv), or single-chain domain antibodies (sdAb). These smaller domains improve tissue penetration and flexibility[148, 149]. Most TriKE constructs incorporate an anti-CD16 domain to activate NK cells and an IL-15 moiety to enhance NK-cell survival, expansion, and cytotoxic function.Early, first-generation TriKEs used anti-human CD16 scFv along with an N72D modified human IL-15 super-agonist [150, 151]. However, the relatively large size of the dual scFvs produced steric hindrance that reduced IL-15 bioavailability, resulting in markedly diminished IL-15 activity compared to recombinant human IL-15 [129, 152]. To overcome this limitation, researchers replaced the anti-CD16 scFv with a smaller humanized heavy-chain camelid as antibody. This modification enhanced IL-15 accessibility and improved NK-cell activation, eliminating the need for the N72D IL-15 mutant [148, 149, 152]. These advances led to the second-generation TriKEs that incorporate anti-CD16 sdAbs paired with wild-type IL-15, enabling stronger NK-cell activation and improved tumor targeting.GTB-3550 (CD16/IL-15/CD33 TriKE) is a fusion protein containing two anti-CD33 scFVs and an anti-CD16 domain flanking a human IL-15 linker [129]. A phase I trial (NCT03214666) enrolled 12 patients before early termination due to sponsor prioritization of a second-generation product (GTB-3650). Four patients demonstrated blast count reductions starting at dose level (DL) of 25 μg/kg/day dose level with GTB-3550. Development has shifted to GTB-3650, a camelid nanobody-based second generation TriKE with improved NK-cell engagement; a phase I study is ongoing (NCT06594445), though no peer-reviewed clinical results have been presented or published.SAR443579, a CD123 × NKp46 × CD16 TriKE was evaluated in a phase I/II study (NCT05086315) and enrolled 42 r/r AML patients and one HR-MDS patient (including 13 post allo-HSCT). Grade ≥3 AEs were observed in 28 patients (65.1%), including one grade 4 neutropenia. Only two grade 1 CRS events were observed and the CRc rate was 12% (5 patients). The study was terminated by the sponsor for strategic reasons despite good safety [153].A novel HLA -A2*0201 restricted, TCR mimetic, bispecific T-cell engager targeting cathepsin G1 (CG1) is currently recruiting patients. So far there is no clinical data available on this trial (NCT06994676).A second generation TriKE containing humanized anti-CD16 heavy chain camelid sdAb, wild-type IL-15 moiety, and a scFv targeting CLEC12A, in pre-clinical studies, induced robust NK-cell proliferation, enhanced NK-cell activation, and potent killing of AML cell lines and primary AML blasts, while sparing healthy HSCs [152].Challenges and future directions with bsAb therapiesDespite having a novel mechanism of action, bsAb-based therapies have not been resoundingly successful in improving treatment outcomes, especially CD33-targeting therapies, none of which are now in active clinical trials. Apart from concerns due to safety (such as hepatoxicity with JNJ- ), other factors that hinder bsAb efficacy include the profoundly immunosuppressive bone marrow niche in AML which can be further worsened with exhausted and dysfunctional effector T-cells that have been rendered ineffective by prior chemotherapies leading to poor T-cell recruitment by bsAbs [154]. Thus, giving bsAb-based therapies earlier in the disease course could be beneficial and needs to be explored. Preclinical studies with AMG330 showed that T-cell activation correlates with upregulation of immune-checkpoints like programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) leading to poor effector cell function which could be overcome with the use of a bifunctional checkpoint inhibitory T cell-engaging (CiTE) antibody [155]. While the combination of flotetuzumab with MGA102 has been discontinued, future studies should evaluate this combination. Patients responding to AMG330 also had lower disease burden at baseline, which could also prompt exploration to the use of these therapies in the setting of MRD-eradication following induction.4.0Immune Checkpoint InhibitorsImmune checkpoints (IC) are inhibitory receptors on immune cells that dampen immune activation when engaged by their ligands [157]. Tumor cells frequently exploit these pathways by expressing IC ligands, enabling escape from immune surveillance. Because ICs are cell-surface molecules, they can be effectively blocked with monoclonal antibodies. Immune check point inhibitors (ICIs), have transformed therapy for multiple solid tumors with previously limited therapeutic options [158]. In AML, multiple clinical trials evaluating the use of ICIs, especially in combination with HMAs are currently under active study.4.1PD-1/PD-L1 Axis InhibitorsThe programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1 or CD279) is an inhibitory receptor expressed on the activated immune cells. By binding its ligands, PD-L1 or PD-L2, it suppresses innate and adaptive immune responses [159]. In AML, PD-1 is upregulated in Tregs and CD8+ effector T-cells [160]. There is evidence that HMAs can upregulate PD-L1 or PD-L2, creating rationale for combination therapy [161]. Multiple trials have examined PD-1/PD-L1 blockers either alone or in combination, particularly in r/r AML.Pembrolizumab, a humanized IgG4 MoAb, blocks PD-1 interaction with its ligands reversing T-cell exhaustion and restores cytotoxic T-cell effector function [162]. In a pilot study (NCT02996474) combining pembrolizumab with decitabine in r/r AML, 6 out of 10 patients achieved SD or better. Surprisingly, patients achieving CRs did not experience irAEs [163]. In another phase II study (NCT02845297) of pembrolizumab with aza that enrolled 37 r/r AML and 22 newly diagnosed patients, 14% of r/r AML patients and 47% of newly diagnosed older adults achieved CR/CRi. There were higher grade irAEs in r/r disease (24%) than in newly diagnosed patients (14%)[164]. A phase II study (NCT02768792) using pembrolizumab after high dose cytarabine (HiDAC) showed patients with refractory or early relapse had longer OS than those with late relapse (13.2 vs 7.0 months) [165].These studies suggest pembrolizumab should be used earlier in the disease course for effective response. Finally, the use of pembrolizumab prior to allo-HSCT did not increase acute or chronic GvHD, and one-year survival was comparable between pembrolizumab exposed and unexposed patients [166].Nivolumab, another PD-1 inhibitor, was evaluated in a phase Ib/II trial in combination with aza for r/r AML. Fifty three patients were enrolled, with a median age of 68 years, the CRc was 21% and 14% patients had HI. Responses were durable, with most CRc patients (9 out of 11) alive at one year. Grade ≥3 irAEs occurred in 14% of patients and all responded to steroids [167]. In newly diagnosed AML and high risk MDS, a phase II study combining nivolumab with idarubicin and cytarabine showed an impressive response with CRc in 77 with 53% achieving MRD-negativity. Median OS was 18.5 months, and 41% patients proceeded to an allo-HSCT. Six patients experienced grade ≥ 3 irAEs [168]. Nivolumab has also been used as maintenance therapy in high-risk AML patients ineligible for an allo-HSCT. Among the 14 patients treated up to 12 months, median CR duration was not reached at 11-month follow up; CR duration rates were 79% and 71% at 6 months and 12 months, respectively [169].Clinical trials using PD-L1 antagonists avelumab and durvalumab have largely failed to show benefit in combination with other agents and increased toxicity [170–172].4.2CTLA-4/B7 Axis InhibitorsThe cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) is an inhibitory immunoglobulin superfamily receptor with higher affinity for CD80 and CD86 expressed on AML blasts, than the co-stimulatory ligand CD28 thereby suppressing T-cell activation. While CTLA-4 plays essential physiological roles in immune tolerance and Treg induction, its overexpression in AML contributes to impaired immune-surveillance [173, 174]. Steroid-responsive chronic GvHD occurred in 4 post allo-HSCT patients [176]. Ipilimumab monotherapy was also tested in 28 patients with progressive or persistent AML after allo-HSCT. Toxicities included IrAEs (21%, including one death) and GvHD requiring discontinuation of ipilimumab in four patients. Responses were seen only at the 10mg/kg dose and included 23% CR and 9% PR rates. Notably, 4 CRs occurred in patients with extramedullary disease [177]. In another phase I study combining ipilimumab and nivolumab in 29 patients with post allo-HSCT relapse, multitudes of IrAEs like pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis and endocrinopathies were observed; GvHD occurred in four patients (14%), with one grade IV lower gastrointestinal GvHD and seven patients (24%) experienced fatal grade 5 toxicities. Median PFS was 109 days (95% CI: 48 days–NA). The further development of sabatolimab was discontinued in early 2024 in both AML and MDS following failure of the phase III STIMULUS-MDS2 to meet its primary endpoint.4.4CD47/SIRPs Axis InhibitorsCD47 is a widely expressed transmembrane protein that interacts with the signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) on macrophages and dendritic cells to inhibit phagocytosis.
