Clinical trials with ICIs are listed in table 3 below.Challenges and future perspectives with ICI therapiesAlthough ICIs are supported by a strong scientific rationale, their clinical efficacy in AML has been limited compared with solid tumors. One explanation is the relatively low mutational burden of AML and the generally intact DNA mismatch repair system, both of which limit neoantigen generation and reduce immune recognition [159, 205]. Although AML with TP53 mutations or complex cytogenetics may exhibit a higher mutational burden providing a potential rationale for checkpoint blockade, this hypothesis was not confirmed in the phase III ENHANCE-2 trial [206]. Moreover, T-cells within the AML bone marrow microenvironment frequently express multiple inhibitory receptors beyond PD-1/PD-L1, including LAG-3 and TIM-3, which promote immune evasion and may contribute to resistance to checkpoint inhibition [160]. The AARON (NCT03017820) study is evaluating nivolumab with relatlimab in combination with aza in patients with AML. However, dual checkpoint inhibition may increase toxicity as observed with tremelimumab plus durvalumab combined with aza [179]. ICIs may ultimately prove more beneficial in settings of lower disease burden. Potential roles may include maintenance therapy for high-risk disease or treatment of MRD. Immunotherapies such as bsAbs appear to be most effective earlier in the disease course. This concept is supported by studies evaluating nivolumab in the maintenance setting, where its use was associated with prolongation of complete remission (CR) duration [169].5.0NK Cells and Vaccine therapy for AML5.1Natural Killer (NK) Cellular TherapyNatural Killer (NK) cells are group 1 innate lymphoid cells defined by CD56 expression and absence of CD3. They comprise 2–18% of circulating lymphocytes and eliminate tumor cells in an MHC-unrestricted manner, allowing recognition of tumor cells that have lost MHC class I after malignant transformation [207, 208]. In AML, blasts induce an immunosuppressive microenvironment by downregulating activating NK-receptors, such as NKG2D, impairing cytotoxicity [209, 210]. A key advantage of NK-cell based therapies is that they do not require HLA matching and rarely cause GVHD.NK cell therapy in AML is a newer treatment, and all studies are phase I or II featuring limited number of patients. These are summarized in table 4 below. The studies are heterogeneous and some of them lack a focus on a specific hematologic disease and result in varying OS, EFS and relapse risk based on the underlying disease.Challenges and research directions with NK-cell therapy:Despite their potential, several limitations have hindered the widespread clinical success of NK cell-based therapies in AML [244]. While autologous NK-cells are generally safe, they have demonstrated limited efficacy in AML. This poor clinical response is primarily due to the expression of inhibitory receptors on autologous NK cells that recognize self-MHC class I molecules on cancer cells, thereby suppressing NK cell activation [245, 246]. Furthermore, NK cells derived from cancer patients often reside in an immunosuppressive state characterized by diminished functionality, which severely impairs their antitumor capacity. Allogeneic NK-cell therapies offer a promising alternative but face distinct challenges, including the need for rapid ex vivo expansion, poor in vivo persistence, and suboptimal clinical activation [247, 248]. A major bottleneck for allogeneic approaches is the difficulty in generating a sufficient quantity of highly functional cells. Consequently, recent research has focused on optimizing expansion and activation strategies to enhance therapeutic potency. While systemic cytokine administration may improve antitumor responses, the use of IL-15 to stimulate ex vivo expanded autologous NK cells has been associated with CRS in some AML patients [249]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a formidable barrier to both engineered and non-engineered NK cell efficacy. Immunosuppressive cytokines, particularly transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), impair NK cell function by downregulating activating receptors and inhibiting interferon-γ (IFN-γ) production, thereby neutralizing antitumor responses [250]. To circumvent this, researchers have utilized CRISPR-Cas 9 gene editing to knock out the TGF-β receptor2 gene (TGFBR2) in primary human NK cells. This genetic modification confers resistance to TGF-β mediated immunosuppression, preserving cellular potency within the TME [251].Beyond biological barriers, significant logistical challenges persist in the clinical translation of NK cell therapies. The isolation and ex-vivo expansion of NK cells from peripheral or umbilical cord blood are labor-intensive processes characterized by low initial yields. Generating a clinically sufficient dose typically requires a 4-to 10-week expansion period. Furthermore, NK cells exhibit marked sensitivity to cryopreservation, with freeze-thaw cycles often compromising their survival and cytotoxic potential. While post-thaw incubation with IL-2 can partially restore functional activity, optimizing these manufacturing and storage protocols remains essential [251]. Ultimately, addressing these multifaceted technical and biological constraints is critical to realizing the full therapeutic potential of NK cell-based immunotherapy for AML.5.2Vaccine therapy in AMLTherapeutic cancer vaccines aim to enhance tumor antigen presentation, strengthen T-cell immunity, and promote selective elimination of AML blasts while sparing normal cells [252]. Tumor vaccines are designed to induce tumor-specific T-cell responses, particularly cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells, and have been explored in AML for several decades. Their effectiveness depends on identifying immunogenic leukemic antigens and developing platforms capable of generating durable immune responses [253, 254]. AML vaccines are broadly categorized as peptide vaccines or dendritic cell (DC)-based vaccine constructs [255]. The most extensively studied LAAs/TAAs (tumor associated antigens) include Wilms’ Tumor 1 (WT1), preferentially expressed antigen of melanoma (PRAME), receptor for hyaluronic acid-mediated motility (RHAMM), Proteinase 3 (Pr3), New York esophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1 (NY-ESO-1) and mucin 1 (MUC1), with WT-1 being the most actively investigated [256–259]. Each can elicit antigen-specific cytotoxic T-cell responses [254]. Recently, a multiepitope vaccine targeting KIT mutations and incorporating CD8+ and CD4+ epitopes has shown strong immunogenicity in AML [260].5.2.1Peptide vaccinesPeptide vaccines present short antigenic epitopes to antigen-presenting cells (APCs), prompting the expansion of antigenic CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells [255]. The currently developed peptide vaccines primarily target WT1, RHAMM, Pr3, and MUC1 [256, 257]. Each of these antigenic targets has demonstrated the capacity to elicit robust, antigen-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocyte responses. Peptide vaccines in various clinical trials and their efficacy and toxicity is summarized in the table 5A below.Among the current peptide vaccine candidates, Galinpepimut-S, a multivalent WT1 vaccine, has emerged as a particularly promising agent. The efficacy of this vaccine was evaluated in a phase II clinical trial involving 22 adult patients with a median age of 64 years in CR1 (NCT01266083). The treatment regimen consisted of an initial six doses of the vaccine administered over 10 weeks, with an optional extension of six-monthly doses for patients maintaining CR. The vaccine was well tolerated and safe, the most common adverse events were low grade injection site reactions (46%), fatigue (32%) and skin induration (32%). Of the 14 evaluable patients, 64% exhibited detectable immune responses measured via CD4+ T cell proliferation or CD8+ interferon-γ secretion confirming the vaccine’s ability to stimulate an adaptive anti-tumor response. At the close of the study, the median DFS from the time of CR was 16.9 months, and notably the median OS from diagnosis has not yet been reached, projecting survival exceeding 67.6 months [256].5.2.2Dendritic cell (DC) vaccinesDendritic cell (DC)-based vaccination strategies aim to activate DCs in vivo or infuse ex vivo-generated DCs capable of presenting LAAs and stimulating robust antileukemic immunity [255, 265–268]. DC-vaccines can be whole cell, peptide, or protein (free or bound to antibodies), viral vector-based, mRNA or DNA vaccines [266, 269]. Two major platforms are in use: monocyte derived DCs (moDCs) which require ex vivo loading with LAAs (peptides, tumor lysate, RNA, viral vectors) and the leukemia derived DCs (AML-DCs) which are generated directly from AML blasts, inherently presenting multiple endogenous LAAs [267, 270]. Vaccination strategies with DC vaccines are mainly divided into two groups: autologous DC vaccines loaded with ex vivo AML antigenic peptides or RNA and peptide or genetic material vaccines targeting DCs in vivo [271]. DC-AML fusion vaccines represent a personalized approach to treat AML, in which fusion hybrids of autologous moDCs and patient derived AML cells are used to stimulate antileukemic responses [272]. Like AML-DCs, ex vivo antigenic loading is not required for DC-AML fusion vaccines [270]. Several studies have explored the use of DC- based vaccines as a treatment option for AML and these are summarized in the table 5B below.In summary, vaccines for AML seem to have the greatest clinical utility in maintenance therapy following conventional chemotherapy in high-risk patients who achieve CR but are not eligible for an allo-HSCT. However, isolated vaccinations do not show a sustained immune response and this calls for broader immunotherapeutic approaches such as combination therapies with ICIs targeting PD-1 or CAR T-cell therapy [283, 284]. In vitro studies support the therapeutic potential of ICIs in conjunction with anti-AML immunizations. Additionally, combining these vaccines together with CAR T-cells is an exciting strategy. AML specific monoclonal antibodies also synergize with vaccination therapy since antibody induced cellular cytotoxicity triggers the release of antigens. However, no clinical studies have been developed employing this therapeutic strategy. Combination therapies have the advantage of simultaneously targeting different aspects of immunomodulation for a multidimensional approach overcoming resistance to therapies, relieving immune evasion mechanisms and improving responses [285].6.CAR T-Cell TherapyChimeric antigen receptor T-cells (CAR T-cells) are T-lymphocytes genetically modified to express synthetic receptors that recognize specific cell surface antigens. Most CAR constructs include an antigen-binding domain, a hinge (spacer) region, a transmembrane domain, a costimulatory domain, and a T-cell signaling domain. The antigen binding domain is typically an scFv composed of the variable heavy and light chains of a monoclonal antibody. The hinge region connects the scFv to the transmembrane domain and can influence CAR flexibility, signaling, and epitope recognition [286–288]. The intracellular signaling region contains CD3ζ signaling domain whose immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMS) are phosphorylated upon antigen binding, initiating ZAP70-mediated signaling and downstream cytotoxic activity through the release of perforins, granzymes, and cytokine secretion [289].Over time, CAR T-cells have undergone significant innovation with each new generation of CAR T-cells pursuing a novel mechanism to improve efficacy and persistence. While the first-generation CAR T-cells only had an scFv and intracellular signaling region, second generation CAR T-cells incorporated co-stimulatory proteins to enhance cytotoxicity and persistence; third generation CAR T-cells incorporated multiple costimulatory domains. The fourth generation CAR T-cells, also known as TRUCKs (T-cells Redirected for Universal Cytokine-mediated Killing), are able to release cytokines and finally the fifth generation (latest generation) CAR T-cells have an additional integrated membrane receptors (most commonly IL2RB) which can promote activation of the broader immune system and also enhance memory T-cell formation [290–295]. Beyond innovations in improvement through each new generation of CAR T-cells, multiple other advanced platforms like use of adapter targeting modules which can be easily turned off to balance cell killing and toxicity, gene editing technology to reduce GvHD risk with allogeneic products, and the use of nanobody-based heavy chains are discussed in pertinent sections and illustrated in figure 3.A major advantage of CAR T-cells is their ability to target tumor cells without MHC restriction. This adoptive cellular therapy has transformed treatment for B-cell malignances and multiple myeloma with five CD19 and two BCMA (B-cell maturation antigen) directed products currently approved by the FDA [296]. However, efficacy in AML has lagged behind due to disease heterogeneity, antigen overlap with normal hematopoiesis, and challenges with persistence and trafficking. A meta-analysis of 57 AML patients treated across ten trials and three case reports showed an ORR of 65.2% and CR rate of 49.5% but the responses were often not durable [297].6.1Lewis Y (LeY)The first phase I AML CAR T-cell study targeted the Lewis Y antigen, a difucosylated carbohydrate expressed on AML but minimally expressed in normal tissues. Four patients received autologous, second generation, LeY-CAR T-cells, with good tolerability and without grade ≥3 CRS. Three patients experienced disease responses, including one cytogenetic remission. The investigators also described CAR T-cell infiltration into leukemia cutis lesions in one patient. However, all responding patients eventually relapsed, and the trial was discontinued [298].6.2CD33CD33 has been targeted using CAR T-cells in several early phase studies. The first-in-human case involved escalating doses of a second-generation autologous CART-33 in a 41-year old man, producing transient blast reduction but had disease progression by week nine. Infusions caused grade 4 chills and fever, persistent neutropenia, and transient hyperbilirubinemia [299]. In a phase I trial using 4–1BB /CD3ζ CAR co-expressing truncated human EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor; (HER1t)), successful CAR manufacture occurred in only four of the ten enrolled patients, and three were infused. No anti-leukemic responses were observed, and toxicities included CRS (in two patients), immune-effector cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) in one patient, tumor lysis syndrome-associated acute kidney injury, and liver dysfunction [300]. A phase I/II multicenter study in children and young adults treated 19 of the 24 enrolled patients with an autologous CD33 CAR T-cells across four dose levels. Grade ≥ 3 CRS occurred in 21% and ICANS in 1 patient. Two patients achieved MRD-negative CR at dose level 4 (DL4, highest dose), both accompanied by myeloid aplasia. One patient proceeded to an allo-HSCT and remained in CR at day +100; the other relapsed after declining transplant. Transient CAR expansion occurred in nearly half (47.4%) of the patients [301].While CD33 remains and actively pursued antigen target, development of effective therapies have been met with significant challenges including prolonged myeloid aplasia, antigen escape, heterogenous expression, poor persistence, and manufacturing difficulties due to prior receipt of lymphodepleting therapies. Multiple novel strategies are now being employed to overcome these challenges including simultaneously targeting multiple antigens including CD33, base-editing to knock out TCR and CD52 as bridge to allo-HSCT (NCT05942599), dose modulation, and logic gating [302, 303]. Ongoing CD33-directed CAR T-cell trials continue to refine safety, potency and persistence and are listed in the table 5.6.3NKG2D LigandsThe Natural Killer Group 2, Member D (NKG2D) receptor complex is a type II C-type lectin-like transmembrane protein with activating and co-stimulatory functions. Expressed as a homodimer on γδ T-cells, subsets of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, and NK-cells, NKG2D plays a key role in immunosurveillance [304]. Its ligands (NKG2DL), include MHC class I-chain related proteins A and B (MICA and -B), UL16 binding protein 1 (ULBP1), murine ULBP-like transcript 1 (MULT1), and retinoid acid early family of proteins 1 (RAE-1). They are typically absent or expressed at low levels under normal conditions but are upregulated during stress and tumorigenesis, including in AML and solid tumors, making them attractive immunotherapy targets [305].The first phase I clinical trial of a first generation NKG2DL targeted CAR T-cells (CYAD-01), enrolled 12 patients with AML and r/r multiple myeloma (MM) and administered CYAD-01 across four DLs (dose levels) without lymphodepleting chemotherapy. No DLTs, CRS, or neurotoxicity occurred. No objective responses were observed although one AML patient treated at DL4 had a transient hematologic improvement [306]. The subsequent THINK study, an open-label, phase I, dose escalation trial, delivered three CYAD-01 infusions two weeks apart, with optional consolidation dosing in sixteen patients without lymphodepletion. Grade ≥ 3 CRS occurred in five (31%) patients, including one dose limiting CRS at DL3. Among 12 r/r AML patients, three achieved objective responses, and two proceeded to allo-HSCT and remained in remission [307]. The maximum tolerated dose was not reached in this study.The same company (Ceylad Oncology) later launched two additional phase 1 studies; DEPLETHINK (NCT03466320), evaluating CYAD-01 with lymphodepletion, and CYCLE-1 trial (NCT04167696) testing CYAD-02, engineered with shRNA to reduce fratricide by suppressing MICA and MICB expression on CAR T-cells. Among 17 DEPLETHINK and 12 CYCLE-1 participants, grade ≥ 3 CRS occurred in one and four patients, respectively. Three fatal events included disease progression, sepsis, and VOD. No objective responses occurred with CYAD-01, whereas CYAD-02 showed a 17% ORR and demonstrated improved CAR T-cell persistence [308].6.4CD123The first reported human use of CD123 CAR T-cells, involved a fourth-generation construct (4SCAR123) incorporating a CD123scFv, three costimulatory domains (CD28, CD137, and CD27), a CD3ζ intracellular domain, and an inducible caspase 9 (iCasp9) killer switch. This product was infused in a 47-year-old patient with post allo-HSCT relapsed AML who developed severe CRS requiring tocilizumab and had only a modest improvement in bone marrow blasts (59% to 45% at day 20) [309].Early phase I studies of autologous or donor derived CD123 CAR T-cells have demonstrated acceptable tolerability but limited antileukemic efficacy. In a small study of five patients who received autologous CD123 CAR-T cells, two developed grade ≥ 3 CRS, and no responses were observed following which the trial was terminated [310]. A pediatric study using CD20 switch CD123 CAR T-cell product treated 5 AML patients at two DLs; no DLTs occurred, but only one patient at the higher dose achieved a transient CR, and another patient who received the product off study achieved morphologic CR [311]. In another clinical trial, seven patients (six AML, one BPDCN) were treated across two DLs with an autologous or donor-derived CD123 CAR T-cells. Grade 1–2 CRS occurred in five patients, and one patient developed grade 3 rash secondary to drug hypersensitivity. Responses included one MLFS at DL1, two CRs at DL2, and one CR in BPDCN [312].While CD123 is an attractive therapeutic target in AML, higher rates of CRS and limited antileukemic efficacy remain significant challenges. CRS has been a recurrent toxicity across multiple trials evaluating CD123-directed CAR T-cell therapies, highlighting the narrow therapeutic window and the persistent trade-off between antileukemic activity and treatment-related toxicity. To address these limitations, several novel strategies have been developed to improve the safety and expansion of CD123 CAR-T cells. One such approach is UCART123v1.2, an allogeneic product generated using TALEN® gene editing. This construct lacks CD52 and TRAC (T-cell receptor alpha constant), enabling the use of alemtuzumab-based lymphodepletion while reducing the risk of GvHD. In the phase 1 AMELI-01 trial, involving 16 patients, CRS occurred in 15, including one death from CRS at DL2. Responses included one SD, one MLFS in the FC (fludarabine/ cyclophosphamide) lymphodepletion arm, and one SD and one MRD-negative CR in the FCA (fludarabine/cyclophosphamide/alemtuzumab) arm, with the CR sustained beyond eight months [313].Another novel strategy involves the development of an adapter CAR-T system, UniCAR02-T-CD123, in which a universal CAR-T cell (UniCAR-T) is activated only in the presence of a separately administered CD123-targeting module (TM). This target module is delivered as a continuous infusion, allowing dynamic control of CAR-T activity. In a study of 19 treated patients, grade 3 CRS occurred in three cases but was rapidly reversed following discontinuation of the TM infusion, highlighting the controllable safety profile of this platform. The ORR was 53% (8/15) among patients with r/r AML and 75% (3/4) in patients with MRD+ disease. One patient in the MRD+ arm became transplant eligible while another patient who had relapsed post allo-HSCT achieved a CR which was sustained until last follow up (five months) [314].6.5CLL-1Multiple phase I clinical trials have evaluated CLL-1 directed CAR T-cell therapy in r/r AML. In a large phase 1 study (ChiCTR2000041054), 30 patients received autologous or donor-derived CAR T-cells. All patients experienced CRS, including 11 with grade 3 and one with grade 4 CRS; one patient developed grade 4 ICANS. Despite toxicity, the ORR was 73.33% with 40% (12 patients) achieving MRD-negative CRc and 33% (10 patients) achieving MRD + CRc [315]. A related study treating 12 post-transplant relapse disease using donor derived CLL-1 CAR T-cells showed similar toxicity patterns and yielded seven MRD-negative and two MRD+ CR/CRi responses [316].Novel CAR designs are emerging to overcome immune-escape and microenvironment suppression. In one small study, two patients with post-transplant r/r AML received CLL-1 directed CAR T-cells incorporating PD-1 silencing. Both developed CRS (grade ≤ 2),and achieved durable MRD-negative CRi, remaining in CR at three months after treatment [317]. Another strategy has explored dual targeting of CLL-1 and CD33 using a compound CAR (cCAR) approach in nine patients with r/r disease. CRS occurred in eight patients, predominantly grade 1–2, while three patients developed grade 3 ICANS. Seven patients achieved MRD-negative CR, and six subsequently proceeded to allo-HSCT. These findings highlight the potential of dual-antigen targeting strategies to mitigate antigen escape and enhance the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapies [318]. A phase I study evaluating fourth-generation, IL-18–secreting “armored” CAR T-cells targeting CLL-1 treated five patients with r/r AML. The CAR T-cell product was successfully manufactured for all patients. CRS occurred in all patients, including one case each of grade 3 and grade 4 CRS, while one patient developed grade 3 CANS. Three patients achieved MRD-negative CR, while in MLFS [319]. Collectively, these studies highlight the potential of innovative CAR T-cell strategies in AML, including fourth-generation CAR T-cells, PD-1–silencing approaches, and dual-targeting CAR constructs, to enhance antileukemic activity while addressing mechanisms of resistance.6.6CD7CD7 is a transmembrane immunoglobulin superfamily glycoprotein expressed on early pluripotent HSCs and retained on mature T- and NK-cells while myeloid and B-cells lose CD7 expression upon maturation [320, 321]. Although primarily associated with T-cell malignancies, 12–32% of AML patients express CD7 on LSCs [322]. A recent phase I study evaluated CD7-targeted nanobody-derived dual variable heavy chain antibody (dVHH) based CAR T-cells (NS7CAR-T) in 10 AML patients, showing mild CRS in most patients (80%) and no neurotoxicity. Seven patients (70%) achieved CR, with relapses linked to loss of CD7 expression [323].A novel strategy employing sequential allogeneic CD7-targeting CAR T-cells followed by haploidentical allo-HSCT was evaluated in seven patients with AML. No cases of grade ≥3 CRS were reported, and one patient developed CAR T-cell associated grade 2 acute GvHD. Six patients achieved MRD-negative CR, while one achieved MRD+ CR. At the last follow-up, five patients remained alive, with two deaths reported. Among the two patients who relapsed, both exhibited CD7-negative disease at relapse, suggesting antigen escape. Notably, the investigators did not administer GvHD prophylaxis, yet no severe GvHD occurred. This observation raises the possibility that CD7-directed CAR T cells may eliminate donor-derived alloreactive CD7⁺ T cells, thereby reducing the risk of severe GvHD [324].6.7CD38A phase I study evaluating daratumumab-based CD38 scFv CAR T-cells in six post-transplant relapsed AML patients reported grade 1–2 CRS and one case of grade 4 hepatoxicity. One CR and three CRi responses were observed, with median OS and LFS of 7.9 and 6.4 months, respectively [325]. Another phase I study using CD38 CAR-T cell was terminated (NCT05442580).CAR NK-cellsChimeric antigen receptor-engineered natural killer cells (CAR-NKs) represent a promising immunotherapeutic modality for AML. Because NK cells do not cause GVHD, they enable the use of allogeneic NK cells as “off-the-shelf” cellular products and may offer a more favorable toxicity profile compared to allogeneic CAR-T cells [326–328]. The first-in-human study of CD33-directed CAR NK-cells (CD33-CAR NK-92) was conducted in 3 patients with r/r AML. Patients received CD33-CAR NK-92 cells incorporating 4–1 BB and CD28 co-stimulatory domains (a third generation CAR-product). One patient achieved an MRD+ CR at one month but relapsed within three weeks, while the remaining patients relapsed within one month. Treatment-related toxicity was minimal with only one reported case of high-grade fever [329]. In a separate study involving 10 patients with r/r AML treated with CD33 CAR NK-cells, grade 4 hematologic toxicity was frequently observed. Six patients achieved MRD-negative CR by day 28, however, all but a one (who underwent an allo-HSCT) relapsed by day 100 [330].A donor derived CAR-NK product targeting NKG2DL (NKX101) was evaluated in a phase I study involving six patients with r/r AML who received fludarabine and cytarabine for lymphodepletion. High grade toxicities included infections and myelosuppression; however, no cases of CRS, ICANS, or GVHD were reported. Four patients achieved CRc, including three with MRD-negative CR. One patient subsequently proceeded to an allo-HSCT. Responses were described as sustained, though exact duration of response was not reported (NCT04623944) [331]. Multiple clinical trials with CAR NK-cells are ongoing, including an off-the-shelf logic gated product SENTI-202 targeting CD33 and/or FLT3 (NCT06325748), and a CD123-directed CAR-NK therapy for AML and BPDCN (NCT06690827). Clinical trials using CART cells in r/r AML are summarized below in table 6A (completed) and 6B (ongoing).7.TCR-TherapyT-cell receptor (TCR) therapies represent an important form of adoptive cell therapy using genetically-modified T-cells engineered to express αβ TCRs that recognize TAAs via peptide presentation on MHC class I molecules on the malignant cells [334, 335]. Unlike CAR T-cells which target surface antigens independent of MHC, TCR-based therapies are HLA-restricted and rely on intracellular peptide presentation [336]. They require fewer antigens to trigger activation, form longer-lasting immune synapses, and exhibit greater persistence, though they generally show lower binding affinity and slower cytolytic kinetics [337]. In AML, TCR-based therapies offer a compelling alternative to CAR T-cell therapies because they can target numerous intracellular antigens unreachable by CAR T-cells [338]. Preclinical efforts have identified several AML-relevant TAAs, including lineage restricted antigens (e.g., WT1), overexpressed antigens (telomerase and survivin), cancer-testis antigens (CTA), minor histocompatibility antigens (HA-1), and neoantigens [334].WT1 is among the most extensively studied TCR targets in AML [339]. In the first-in-human WT1 TCR-T trial, WT1 specific TCRs were transduced using a retroviral vector and were restricted to HLA-A*24:02. Patients also received WT1-peptide vaccine after the second dose of TCR T-cells. Five of the eight treated patients demonstrated long-term TCR persistence, no off-target toxicity was observed, and two patients showed a reduction in bone marrow blasts [340]. In another phase I/II study, autologous gene-modified WT1-TCR cells restricted to HLA-A*02:01 were administered to 10 patients with AML, MDS, or CML who were ineligible for allo-HSCT. CRS occurred in one patient. All six AML patients achieved CR and remained alive at last follow up (7–12.8 months), and TCR persistence was detected in seven patients. In contrast, 2 of the 3 patients with MDS died from disease progression [340]. A separate WT1-directed strategy employed an allogeneic HLA-A*02:01-restricted TCR targeting WT1 (TCRC4), in which TCRs were introduced into EBV-specific donor CD8+ cells in patients who had previously undergone allo-HSCT for AML. This cohort achieved a 100% RFS at a median follow-up of 44-months, which was significantly superior to historical controls; however, the study closed early due to slow accrual [341].Minor histocompatibility antigens such as HA-1 have also been explored as targets for TCR-based therapies. In a phase I trial, allogeneic HA-1-specific TCR T-cells were infused into HLA-A*02:01 positive patients with post-transplant recurrent leukemia. Among the nine treated patients (six with AML/MDS), self-limited fever was the most common adverse event. Two patients exhibited reductions in bone marrow blast counts, and two achieved remission with bridging therapy that persisted following TCR T-cell infusion [342]. In a second HA-1H-directed study, CMV/EBV-specific T-cells were retargeted with HA-1HTCRs (a hematopoiesis-restricted TAA). However, products could be manufactured for only five patients, and in vivo expansion of T-cells was limited [343]. Currently a clinical trial targeting HA-1 and HA-2 in HLA-A*02:01 AML is ongoing (NCT05473910). Clinical trials targeting the PRAME LAA were terminated by the sponsor (NCT03503968, NCT02743611). Finally, an ongoing trial is evaluating autologous neoantigen-specific TCR-T cells for AML with TP53 or RAS mutations using seven mutation-specific, HLA-restricted TCRs in patients with r/r AML (NCT06904066).Collectively, the expanding repertoire of LAAs has enabled the development of multiple antibody-based and immune-targeted therapeutic strategies in AML. The principal antigenic targets highlighted throughout this review are summarized schematically in figure 4.Although immunotherapies are reshaping the AML treatment landscape, their clinical impact remains limited, with allo-HSCT still representing the most effective immunotherapeutic treatment for high-risk disease. To date, GO is the only FDA-approved MoAb for AML, while several additional agents such as MoAbs, ICIs, CAR-T/NK cells, TCR-based therapies, and vaccine are in early or advanced clinical trials, generally showing modest activity in r/r patients. AML’s marked biological heterogeneity means that patients respond differently to immunotherapies depending on disease stage, clonal characteristics, and antigen expression. Current research is focused on optimizing each immunotherapeutic platform and exploring rational combinations that pair immune-activating approaches with strategies that block immune-suppressive pathways. Preclinical and early clinical studies suggest that immunotherapy, alone or in combination with other treatments, may ultimately enable durable, mechanism guided, and personalized management of AML patients, potentially reducing reliance on intensive chemotherapy and eventually, even allo-HSCT.

title: Effects of n-Myc and c-Myc on the expression of p53 family members and their transcriptional targets in human neuroblastoma cells
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is an embryonic malignancy causing 15 % of pediatric cancer fatalities. Amplification of the MYCN gene is one of the major NB drivers and biomarkers of high-risk NB. MYCN amplification is associated with high p53-coding gene expression and decreased survival rates in patients. Importantly, only 1–2 % of NB cases harbor TP53 mutations. Moreover, both high TP53 and low MYC expression levels are unfavorable prognostic markers for NB patients, which is not typical for most types of tumors. In this study we analyzed the effect of MYCN amplification on the expression of genes coding p53 family members – TP63 and TP73. We show that, unlike TP53, TP63 and TP73 levels are higher in MYCN-amplified samples. Furthermore, high TP63 and TP73 expression is a favorable prognostic marker for NB patients’ survival. That MDM2 inhibition contributes to p53 stabilization and augments the cytotoxic activity of doxorubicin in NB cells prompted us to test the cytotoxic effects of three small-molecule inhibitors of MDM2 that differ in their mechanisms: Nutlin-3a, Mel23, and SP-141. Our results showed that despite the same target, MDM2, these compounds displayed different cytotoxic effects and synergy with doxorubicin on two widely used NB cell lines, IMR-32 and SH-SY5Y that vary in the amount of MDM2 expression. Collectively, our results suggest that except Nutlin-3a, the other two inhibitors, Mel23 and SP-141, employ additional Mdm2-independent mechanisms of cytotoxicity in NB cells that warrants further investigation.

Neuroblastoma (NB) is an embryonic malignancy causing 15 % of pediatric cancer fatalities. Amplification of the MYCN gene is one of the major NB drivers and biomarkers of high-risk NB. MYCN amplification is associated with high p53-coding gene expression and decreased survival rates in patients. Importantly, only 1–2 % of NB cases harbor TP53 mutations. Moreover, both high TP53 and low MYC expression levels are unfavorable prognostic markers for NB patients, which is not typical for most types of tumors. In this study we analyzed the effect of MYCN amplification on the expression of genes coding p53 family members – TP63 and TP73. We show that, unlike TP53, TP63 and TP73 levels are higher in MYCN-amplified samples. Furthermore, high TP63 and TP73 expression is a favorable prognostic marker for NB patients’ survival. That MDM2 inhibition contributes to p53 stabilization and augments the cytotoxic activity of doxorubicin in NB cells prompted us to test the cytotoxic effects of three small-molecule inhibitors of MDM2 that differ in their mechanisms: Nutlin-3a, Mel23, and SP-141. Our results showed that despite the same target, MDM2, these compounds displayed different cytotoxic effects and synergy with doxorubicin on two widely used NB cell lines, IMR-32 and SH-SY5Y that vary in the amount of MDM2 expression. Collectively, our results suggest that except Nutlin-3a, the other two inhibitors, Mel23 and SP-141, employ additional Mdm2-independent mechanisms of cytotoxicity in NB cells that warrants further investigation. Keywords Neuroblastoma MYC MYCN p53 p63 MDM2 Abbreviations NB neuroblastoma TAD transactivation domain DBD DNA binding domain Mb Myc box 1 Introduction Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric malignancy of the sympathetic nervous system arising from embryonic cells forming the neural crest. The median age at NB diagnosis is 2 years, and more than 40 % of infant patients receive the diagnosis within the first 3 months of life. About half of NB patients are diagnosed with low-risk NB and demonstrate favorable therapy response and even spontaneous regression or transformation into benign tumors, while the other half of NB cases belong to high-risk NB that is characterized by older age at diagnosis or MYCN gene amplification, high probability of metastasis, and poor outcome. Despite the significant progress in NB research and treatment, it is the cause of nearly 15 % of pediatric cancer fatalities [1 ,2 ]. Indeed, MYCN amplification along with TERT rearrangement and ATRX mutations are considered the main drivers and biomarkers of high-risk NB. MYCN is a human gene coding for n-Myc protein which is a member of the Myc protein family. NB is characterized by expression of two of three members of the Myc family – c-Myc (MYC) and n-Myc (MYCN). The third Myc family member, l-Myc (MYCL), is expressed at low levels in NB cells and does not appear to contribute significantly to this disease. C-Myc and n-Myc are transcription factors sharing the identical domain structure composed of the transactivation domain (TAD), the central region, and the DNA-binding domain (DBD) which is also responsible for dimerization with Max protein (Fig. 1 A). TAD and the central region encompass six conservative Myc boxes (Mb) that are responsible for transactivation and trans -repression activities of Myc proteins. Furthermore, covalent modifications of these regions are responsible for the protein stability [3 ]. Two nuclear localization sites (NLSI and NLSII) are localized in the central region and DBD of c-Myc and n-Myc proteins. Importantly, both c-Myc and n-Myc form a stable heterodimer Myc/Max, which binds to the E-box elements (CACGTG) to regulate the transcription. Expectedly, when comparing the amino acid sequences of human c-Myc and n-Myc, DBDs of these two proteins are the regions displaying the highest homology (Fig. 1 B). It is well known that the Myc family proteins act as oncogenes through controlling the expression of numerous regulatory genes, e.g. p21, p27, Cyclins D and E, Bcl −2, HK2, LDHA and others whose products are involved in proliferation, cellular metabolism, cell death, and survival [4 ]. In particular, both c-Myc and n-Myc directly activate the expression of the major tumor suppressor p53 and sensitize cancer cells to p53-dependent apoptosis [5 ]. It is important to emphasize that neuroblastoma belongs to rare type of malignancies in which p53 is mutated at extremely low rate (1–2 % of cases) [6 ]. This makes the stabilization of p53 a particularly promising strategy for neuroblastoma treatment. In addition, two other pro-apoptotic members of the p53 protein family – p63 and p73 – may potentially contribute to cell death activation of neuroblastoma cells. The major p53 negative regulator, ubiquitin ligase MDM2, has been considered a target for anticancer therapy for more than 20 years. Importantly, the expression of the MDM2-coding gene, HDM2, is regulated by all p53 family members. This study was focused on the c-Myc and n-Myc mutual regulation in neuroblastoma as well as on the effects of Myc family proteins on p53, p63, and p73 expression. We also analyzed the efficiency of three different MDM2 inhibitors on susceptibility of neuroblastoma cells to the genotoxic drug, doxorubicin. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Cell cultures Neuroblastoma cancer cells SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 were obtained from the Russian Cell Culture Collection of Vertebrate Cells (St. Petersburg, Russia) and cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum, 0.05 mg/ml gentamicin, and 2 mM L-glutamine. 2.2 RNA extraction and quantitative PCR Total RNA was extracted from cells using ExtractRNA (Evrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. For each sample, 2 μg total RNA was used as a template for cDNA synthesis using the MMLV RT kit (Evrogen). qPCR was carried out with SYBR green master mix (Evrogen). mRNA expression levels were calculated relative to GAPDH using the ΔΔCt method. The primer sequences are given in Refs. [7–9 ] and Supplementary Fig. S1 . 2.3 Western blotting The whole-cell extracts were prepared for Western blot analysis. The primary antibodies against the analyzed proteins were used: c-Myc, PUMA, p21, MDM2 (Cell Signaling); p53, n-Myc (Merck Millipore); GAPDH, p73 (Santa Cruz), p63 (Abcam). 2.4 MTT assay Cell culture 96-well plates were used for the MTT experiment. The next day, at 50 % confluence, cells were treated with Nutlin-3a, doxorubicin, DMSO (Sigma-Aldrich), Mel23, SP-141 (Macklin), and their combinations. After 24h incubation, 10 μl of 5 mg/ml of Triazolyl Blue (MTT) solution was added to each well for 4h. Then the medium was removed, and MTT-formazan salt was diluted with 100 μl DMSO per well. iMark reader (BioRad) was used for measuring the optical density (OD) at 570 nm and 630 nm. 2.5 Bioinformatics and statistics The NB patients' data from the GDC portal was used (TARGET-NBL project) [10 ]. The GDC Application Programming Interface (API) v.7.7.0 was used to obtain the mRNA expression data in log2 (FPKM-UQ+1) units. All samples were divided into two groups based on the MYCN amplification status. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to assess the significance of differences between the 2 groups. The correlation score was determined by Spearman's correlation analysis. Overall survival analysis of NB patients was calculated using the gene expression data from the GSE62564 dataset. To plot Kaplan–Meier curves, the entire sample was divided into two groups based on the median expression level of the corresponding gene. The statistical significance of differences in survival was tested using the Log-rank test. The IC50 concentrations were calculated using the “Quest Graph™ IC50 Calculator” tool (https://www.aatbio.com/tools/ic50-calculator ). The synergistic effects of drug combinations were assessed by determination of combination indexes (CI) by the Chou-Talalay algorithm using the CompuSyn software. 3 Results 3.1 Amplification of the MYCN gene results in increased corresponding mRNA expression, downregulation of MYC, and decreased survival for patients with neuroblastoma As the first step, we analyzed the NBL dataset of GDS portal containing the data on 152 NB patients from whom samples were collected for RNAseq [10 ]. For 103 samples from this set, the status of p53 family genes was determined: no TP53 and TP73 mutations and one patient with a TP63 mutation was identified. We divided the samples into two groups depending on the presence of MYCN amplification: 123 samples did not harbor changes in MYCN copy number, and in 29 samples, MYCN was amplified. Importantly, MYCN amplification was shown to augment MYCN expression level (Fig. 1 C). Furthermore, MYC expression was significantly reduced in MYCN-amplified samples, which is consistent with other NB studies [11 ,12 ] (Fig. 1 D). Additionally, we analyzed the effect of MYC and NMYC expression levels on survival of NB patients using GEO dataset GSE62564. Expectedly, MYCN high expression strongly correlated with increased mortality rate, while high MYC expression was an explicit favorable prognostic marker for NB patients (Fig. 1 E and F). 3.2 MYCN amplification distinctly affects TP53, TP63, and TP73 expression in NB patients’ samples Next, we analyzed whether MYCN amplification affects the genes of all three p53 family members — TP53, TP63, and TP73. Surprisingly, in contrast to upregulation of p53, we observed a reduction in the levels of p63 and p73 mRNA in MYCN-amplified samples (Fig. 2 A). We also estimated the correlation between MYC/MYCN and p53 family genes in NB samples and showed that the expression of MYC negatively correlated with TP53, especially in the MYCN-amplified group (Fig. 2 B). Conversely, TP63 and TP73 positively correlated with MYC, in particular in the MYCN-amplified sample cohort (Fig. 2 B). The analysis of correlation between the expression of p53 family members and MYCN revealed a strong positive correlation of MYCN with TP53 and TP73, and inverse correlation with TP63 in the MYCN-amplified group (Fig. 2 B). The investigation of dependence of NB patients' overall survival on the expression of p53 family members revealed the negative prognostic value of TP53 expression, while TP63 and TP73 demonstrated a significant positive impact on the patients’ life expectancy (Fig. 1 C–E). 3.3 Investigation of the mRNA and protein levels of the p53 family members and their transcriptional targets in human NB cell lines, SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 Having discovered that p53, p63, and p73 exhibit distinct effects on NB patients’ survival, we decided to investigate the expression of these onco-suppressors on both mRNA and protein levels along with their transcriptional targets in SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 human NB cell lines. The SH-SY5Y cells harbor the non-altered MYCN copy number whereas in IMR-32 cells MYCN is amplified. We also treated these cells with doxorubicin for the induction of the p53/p63/p73-dependent signaling cascades. As a result, we found that mRNA levels of all three p53 family members were generally higher in IMR-32 cells compared to SH-SY5Y (Fig. 3 A). Notably, in IMR-32 cells all three p53 family members as well as their shared transcription targets – CDKN1A (p21-coding gene), HDM2 (MDM2-coding gene), and BBC3B (PUMA-coding gene) were increased in response to doxorubicin (Fig. 3 A). Next, we examined the protein products of these genes and discovered that MYC-expressing SH-SY5Y cells displayed low levels of p53/p73 and their transcriptional targets p21 and MDM2 (Fig. 3 B). At the same time, SH-SY5Y cells expressed relatively high levels of p63 and PUMA, arguing that these cells have developed a strong anti-apoptotic response. On the contrary, the MYCN-amplified IMR-32 cells expressed both p53 and p73, but not p63 (Fig. 3 B). Doxorubicin treatment of IMR-32 stabilized p53 and p73 and promoted the expression of their targets, p21, MDM2, and PUMA (although to a lesser extent) (Fig. 3 B), suggesting that p53/p73 are functional in these cells. 3.4 SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 respond differently to Nutlin-3a, Mel23, and SP-141 MDM2 inhibitors According to our results, both NB cell lines express the wild-type TP53 gene. Yet, only IMR-32 cells showed a proper p53/p73-dependent response. Thus, we decided to compare the cytotoxic effects of several MDM2 inhibitors, Nutlin-3a, Mel23, and SP-141, on IMR-32 cells with high expression of MDM2 and SH-SY5Y cells with low levels of MDM2 (Fig. 3 C). We observed that Nutlin-3a, which competes MDM2 away from p53, elicited cytotoxicity in IMR-32 cells at IC50 that was five times lower than that for SH-SY5Y (8.33 μM and 41.91 μM, respectively) (Fig. 3 C). Notably, that despite the high level of toxicity of Nutlin-3a, its derivatives RG7112 and Idasanutlin are in clinical trials as anticancer drugs [13 ]. Another MDM2 inhibitor, Mel23, which apparently prevents the MDM2/MDMX-mediated ubiquitination of p53 [14 ], failed to demonstrate a significant cytotoxicity in either NB cell line (Fig. 3 C). Even at high concentrations (up to 240 μM), the viability of SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 cells did not decrease below 60 % and 40 %, respectively (Fig. 3 C). The last compound tested was SP-141, which was shown to target MDM2 for degradation in cancer cells [15 ,16 ]. Both cell lines demonstrated susceptibility to SP-141 irrespective of MDM2 levels. The calculated IC50 for SH-SY5Y was 35.14 μM and for IMR-32 -12.46 μM, respectively. Collectively, this result suggests that Mdm2 may not be the bona fide target for SP-141 in these cells. 3.5 The combined effect of doxorubicin and MDM2 inhibitors on NB cells Doxorubicin is one of the first-line drugs for NB treatment. To investigate the ability of MDM2 inhibitors tested above to sensitize NB cells to doxorubicin we analyzed the combined effects of these molecules with different concentrations of doxorubicin (Fig. 4 A). The doxorubicin concentrations for SH-SY5Y cells were within the range 0–10 μM, while IMR-32 cells showed far greater susceptibility to this drug (0–100 nM), according to our observations and the previously published data [17 ]. Expectedly, we observed a high synergy level for the doxorubicin + Nutlin-3a combination in IMR-32 cells. The combination index (CI) was close to 0 at high doxorubicin concentrations indicating a strong synergy of the doxorubicin + Nutlin-3a combination in IMR-32. On the contrary, this combination did not demonstrate any synergy in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 4 A and B). Whereas Nutlin-3a stabilized p53 and activated its transcriptional targets, MDM2 and p21, in IMR-32, no accumulation of the p73 protein was observed (Fig. 4 C). Testing the combination of doxorubicin + Mel23 on IMR-32 cells revealed additive effects of these compounds (mean CI = 1.19), while SH-SY5Y cells treated with doxorubicin and Mel23 demonstrated a strong antagonistic effect (mean CI = 2.26) Fig. 4 A and B). Notably, we observed a strong stabilization of c-Myc in SH-SY5Y cells treated with Mel23, which may contribute to the antagonistic effect observed (Fig. 4 C). As shown in Fig. 4 C, Mel23 significantly increased the protein levels of MDM2, p53, p21, and even p73 in IMR-32, which, however, did not augment its cytotoxic effect. In contrast, SP-141 in combination with doxorubicin showed a certain level of synergy in both NB cell lines with more pronounced effect in IMR-32 compared to SH-SY5Y (mean CI = 0.19 vs CI = 0.71, respectively) (Fig. 4 A and B). On the protein level, SP-141 moderately attenuated the levels of MDM2 and p21 in IMR-32, while in SH-SY5Y, only p21 downregulation was observed compared to the untreated cells (Fig. 4 C). 4 Discussion NB is a malignancy which has extremely rare molecular characteristics and predictive biomarkers. The fact that only 1–2 % of NB cases harbor TP53 mutations is still enigmatic [6 ]. One can hypothesize that the wild-type form of p53 may be required for the expression of non-coding and coding genes [18 ] that perturb the immune homeostasis and hence promote this neurological malignancy [19 ]. Furthermore, p53 interacts with a number of chromatin modifiers and hence may alter the transcriptional program of neuronal cells [20–22 ]. Moreover, both high TP53 and low MYC expression levels are unfavorable prognostic markers for NB patients, which is not typical for the most types of tumors. Importantly, the high-risk NB type is driven by MYCN gene amplification, which is found in ∼25 % of NB cases and associates with the reduced survival rate, TP53 upregulation and a decrease in MYC expression [23 ]. In this study, we aimed to determine the effect of MYCN amplification on the expression of two other genes of the p53 family – TP63 and TP73, which share pro-apoptotic transcription targets and antitumor functions with p53 and thus may contribute to the targeted NB cells elimination. Using publicly available RNAseq data, we found that, unlike TP53, TP63 and TP73 expression levels were higher in MYCN-amplified NB samples and positively correlated with MYC expression (Fig. 2 A and B). Additionally, both TP63 and TP73 were found favorable prognostic markers for NB patients’ overall survival (Fig. 2 C–E). It has previously been demonstrated that the p63 transcription factor can suppress MYCN [24 ], therefore the mutual regulation of these two proteins can be carried out through the negative feedback loop. Importantly, through the analysis of two human NB cell lines, SH-SY5Y and IMR-32, with non-amplified and amplified MYCN, respectively, we did not find this inverse correlation of TP63 and TP73 expression with MYCN status that was observed for p53 (Fig. 3 A). These findings indicate the importance of thorough examination of cellular models of NB for the extrapolation of obtained data on patients’ cases. The presence of wild-type TP53 in most cases of NB makes stabilization and activation of the p53 protein an attractive and promising strategy for NB therapy. We tested three inhibitors of MDM2 both as single-agent treatment and in combination with doxorubicin on SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 cell lines. Since the MDM2 level was significantly higher in IMR-32 cells, we expected a more pronounced effect in this cell line. Additionally, we aimed to analyze the effect of tested inhibitors on p63 and p73 stability. Out of three tested compounds, only Nutlin-3a demonstrated the convincing differential effect on SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 cell lines irrespective of whether used as monotherapy or in combination with doxorubicin (Figs. 3C and 4 A,B). Despite the stabilization effect on p53, p63, and p73 in NB cells treated with Mel23, we observed low sensitivity to doxorubicin in both cell lines and a lack of synergy between these compounds. In contrast, SP-141 combined with doxorubicin showed a synergistic effect in SH-SY5Y and IMR-32 cells, suggesting that it works through an Mdm2-independent molecular mechanism(s). This phenomenon requires further investigation. Interestingly, p63 and p73 do not appear to contribute to anticancer activity of the examined MDM2 inhibitors. The stabilization of p63 was observed in SH-SY5Y cells in response to all treatments irrespective of their cytotoxic effects, while the most prominent accumulation of p73 in IMR-32 was achieved by the Mel23 compound, which, on the other hand, displayed the least cytotoxic effect (Fig. 4 C). Thus, our findings demonstrate that MYCN amplification in NB affects not only p53 but also p63 and p73 expression levels. We also show that using the p53-MDM2 interaction inhibitors, particularly the Nutlin derivatives, has high therapeutic potential for treating high-risk NB, while overcoming NB with non-amplified MYCN requires targeting alternative pathways. title: TRIM59-mediated ferroptosis enhances neuroblastoma development and chemosensitivity through p53 ubiquitination and degradation
abstract: Neuroblastoma, predominantly afflicting young individuals, is characterized as an embryonal tumor, with poor prognosis primarily attributed to chemoresistance. This study delved into the impact of tripartite motif (TRIM) 59, an E3 ligase, on neuroblastoma development and chemosensitivity through mediating ferroptosis and the involvement of the tumor suppressor p53. Clinical samples were assessed for TRIM59 and p53 levels to explore their correlation with neuroblastoma differentiation. In neuroblastoma cells, modulation of TRIM59 expression, either through overexpression or knockdown, was coupled with doxorubicin hydrochloride (DOX) or ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) therapy. In vivo assessments examined the influence of TRIM59 knockdown on neuroblastoma chemosensitivity to DOX. Co-immunoprecipitation and ubiquitination assays investigated the association between TRIM59 and p53. Proliferation was gauged with Cell Counting Kit-8, lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS) were assessed via flow cytometry, and protein levels were determined by Western blotting. TRIM59 expression was inversely correlated with neuroblastoma differentiation and positively linked to cell proliferation in response to DOX. Moreover, TRIM59 impeded lipid ROS generation and ferroptosis by directly interacting with p53, promoting its ubiquitination and degradation in DOX-exposed neuroblastoma cells. Fer-1 countered the impact of TRIM59 knockdown on neuroblastoma, while TRIM59 knockdown enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of DOX in xenograph mice. This study underscores TRIM59 as an oncogene in neuroblastoma, fostering growth and chemoresistance by suppressing ferroptosis through p53 ubiquitination and degradation. TRIM59 emerges as a potential strategy for neuroblastoma therapy.

Neuroblastoma, predominantly afflicting young individuals, is characterized as an embryonal tumor, with poor prognosis primarily attributed to chemoresistance. This study delved into the impact of tripartite motif (TRIM) 59, an E3 ligase, on neuroblastoma development and chemosensitivity through mediating ferroptosis and the involvement of the tumor suppressor p53. Clinical samples were assessed for TRIM59 and p53 levels to explore their correlation with neuroblastoma differentiation. In neuroblastoma cells, modulation of TRIM59 expression, either through overexpression or knockdown, was coupled with doxorubicin hydrochloride (DOX) or ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) therapy. In vivo assessments examined the influence of TRIM59 knockdown on neuroblastoma chemosensitivity to DOX. Co-immunoprecipitation and ubiquitination assays investigated the association between TRIM59 and p53. Proliferation was gauged with Cell Counting Kit-8, lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS) were assessed via flow cytometry, and protein levels were determined by Western blotting. TRIM59 expression was inversely correlated with neuroblastoma differentiation and positively linked to cell proliferation in response to DOX. Moreover, TRIM59 impeded lipid ROS generation and ferroptosis by directly interacting with p53, promoting its ubiquitination and degradation in DOX-exposed neuroblastoma cells. Fer-1 countered the impact of TRIM59 knockdown on neuroblastoma, while TRIM59 knockdown enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of DOX in xenograph mice. This study underscores TRIM59 as an oncogene in neuroblastoma, fostering growth and chemoresistance by suppressing ferroptosis through p53 ubiquitination and degradation. TRIM59 emerges as a potential strategy for neuroblastoma therapy. Keywords Neuroblastoma TRIM59 Ferroptosis Lipid ROS p53 1 Introduction Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumor of the sympathetic nervous system, predominantly impacting young children [1 ]. It constitutes around 8% of all malignant tumors in childhood and 15% of pediatric cancers [2 ,3 ]. Patients with low- and intermediate-risk neuroblastoma exhibit a high 5-year survival, while those with high-risk neuroblastoma face a 40% survival rate [4 ,5 ]. Chemoradiotherapy stands as the primary mainstay strategy for neuroblastoma patients with a poor prognosis [4 ]. The primary challenges in this field revolve around devising innovative strategies to mitigate or overcome chemoresistance and enhance the sensitivity of neuroblastoma to chemotherapy. Neuroblastoma originates from sympathetic nervous system cells, specifically sympathoadrenal progenitor cells, and progresses to sympathetic ganglion and adrenal chromaffin cells [6 ]. The differentiation of sympathoadrenal precursor cells is linked to alterations in various genetic factors, including TP53 (the gene encoding p53) deletions, NGF and MYCN amplification, ALK amplifications or mutations, and ATRX deletions or mutations [6–9 ]. p53, a well-established tumor suppressor protein, plays a significant role in the cellular response to diverse stressors such as malnutrition, oncogene activation, hypoxia, and DNA damage [10 ]. p53 modulates survival and death in response to stress through acetylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and other modifications [11 ]. Furthermore, p53 inactivation is pivotal in relapsed neuroblastoma and may contribute to chemoresistance [12 ]. Recent studies have unveiled p53 as a novel regulator of ferroptosis in malignancies both in vitro and in vivo [13–15 ]. However, this aspect not been explored in neuroblastoma, and the precise underlying mechanism remains unknown. Ferroptosis is a form of regulated cell death characterized by iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation [16 ]. Mechanistically, the inhibition of GPX4, essential for clearing ROS, triggers ferroptosis. p53's interference with cysteine uptake sensitizes cells to ferroptosis by downregulating SLC7A11 and GPX4 expression, thereby reducing antioxidant capacity and ROS accumulation [17 ]. Diverse oxidative and antioxidant systems converge on cellular degradation machinery to influence the ferroptotic response [18 ]. The induction of ferroptosis emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy to induce cell death in brain tumors [19 ,20 ]. Recent findings indicate a connection between ferroptosis and neuroblastoma prognosis. In stage 1 neuroblastoma, as opposed to stage 4, a majority of ferroptosis-related genes (26 out of 27) exhibited increased expression and correlated with overall survival (OS) [21 ]. Moreover, the suppression of ferroptosis is linked to chemoresistance and the progression of various tumor types [22 ,23 ]. Stimulating ferroptosis, such as through PTC596 or PKCα inhibition, has been reported to enhance multidrug resistance in neuroblastoma [24 ,25 ]. The ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) serves as the primary mechanism for degrading proteins labeled with ubiquitin. However, the key pathway through which UPS facilitates ferroptotic cell death is not well understood [26 ]. Recently, there has been growing interest in TRIM and TRIM-like proteins, which function as E3 ligases. TRIM proteins play roles in various physiological functions, including antimicrobial immunity, oncogenesis, cell death regulation, signal transduction, and gene regulation [27 ]. A study has demonstrated that TRIM members act as oncogenes in neuroblastoma by stimulating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway [28 ]. Furthermore, multiple studies have highlighted the regulatory effects of TRIM59 and p53 on various tumor processes, including clone formation, cell proliferation, migration and invasion, and chemosensitivity [29–31 ]. Furthermore, TRIM59-mediated ferroptosis has been implicated in nonalcoholic non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and pancreatic cancer development [32 ,33 ]. However, in neuroblastoma, no evidence of an association between TRIM59 and p53 has been found. Our research reveals that TRIM59 regulates ferroptosis in neuroblastoma by ubiquitinating and degrading p53. Notably, TRIM59 knockdown enhances neuroblastoma susceptibility to DOX. These findings contribute to the understanding of TRIM59 as a potential therapeutic target for neuroblastoma. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Clinical samples Six adjacent mediastinal, six moderately differentiated, and 12 poorly differentiated mediastinal neuroblastoma tumor tissues were acquired from the patients at Fudan University's Children's Hospital. Written informed consent was obtained from the patients. Protein content evaluation of the samples was conducted through Western blotting. 2.2 Cells The human neuroblastoma cell lines SH-SY5Y, SK-N-BE2, and SK-N-SH were obtained from the Chinese Academy of Sciences Cell Bank (Shanghai, China). Cell cultivation followed the procedures outlined in a prior study [28 ]. 2.3 Lentivirus TRIM59 overexpression and knockdown lentiviruses, as well as p53 overexpression lentiviruses were generated by GeneChem Company (Shanghai, China). The sequences and primers used are detailed in Table 1 . Lentivirus injection into wells was based on colony-forming units. Subsequently, cells were seeded onto 6-well plates for 12 h and then cultivated for 48 h with or without medications. Infection efficiency in cells was assessed using Western blotting. 2.4 Cell viability assays A total of 3 × 104 cells were seeded into 96-well plates and exposed to DOX/ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) for 48 h. Cell proliferation was assessed at different time points (0, 12, 24, and 48 h) using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The optical density at 450 nm was then measured using a microplate reader (BioTek, VT, USA). 2.5 Lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS) measurement Cultured cell lipid ROS levels were determined using a Reactive Oxygen Species Assay Kit (S0033S, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Flow cytometry (BD Biosciences, NJ, USA) was employed to analyze the cell sample with an excitation wavelength of 480 nm and an emission wavelength of 525 nm. 2.6 Co-immunoprecipitation (CO-IP) and ubiquitination assays The interaction between TRIM59 and p53 was examined using a co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assay following previously described procedures [34 ]. IP was carried out using anti-IgG (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-2027, CA, USA), anti-TRIM59 (Novus Biologicals, NBP1- , Beijing, China), and anti-p53 (CST #2527, MA, USA) antibodies. Western blotting was performed using anti-TRIM59 (Proteintech, -1-AP, IL, USA), anti-p53 (Proteintech, -2-Ig, IL, USA), and anti-ubiquitin (Abcam, ab7780, Shanghai, China) antibodies. 2.7 Real-time quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) For the measurement of p53 mRNA expression, qRT-PCR was employed, utilizing the primers specified in our previous research (Table 2 ) [28 ]. The expression of the target gene was normalized to ACTB and calculated using the 2−ΔΔ Ct method. 2.8 Western blotting Total protein was extracted from cell lysate, and the protein concentration was determined using a BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). Following established procedures [28 ], 35 μg of protein from each sample was separated through sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Protein levels were assessed using primary antibodies: anti-TRIM59 (1:800, Proteintech, -1-AP, IL, USA), anti-p53 (1:1000, CST #2527), anti-SLC7A11 (1:2000, Abcam, ab37185), anti-GPX4 (1:1000, Abcam, ab125066), and anti-β-actin (1:2000, Abcam, ab8227). Lastly, the protein bands were analyzed and digitized using ImageJ software (NIH, USA). 2.9 Xenograph mouse model Male BALB/c nude mice, 7 weeks old (n = 96 mice), were provided by the Shanghai Experimental Animal Center (Shanghai, China). Approval for this study was obtained from the Animal Ethics Committee of our hospital. Subcutaneous injection of neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells (1 × 106 ) into the left posterior flanks of the mice was carried out. DOX (8 mg/kg, twice weekly) was administered to the mice for 4 weeks, and mouse specimens were sacrificed (six mice per group). Throughout this period, the growth curve of the subcutaneous tumor was documented. TUNEL labeling, following established procedures, was used to assess tumor cell death [35 ], with the examination of tumor cells conducted using a fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Japan). Furthermore, the survival rate of 90-day-old nude mice was analyzed (16 mice per group). 2.10 Statistical analysis The data are expressed as means ± standard deviations. Group differences were assessed using one-way analysis of variance, Tukey's post hoc test, and Student's t . Statistical significance was defined by p values < 0.05. 3 Results 3.1 TRIM59 is positively related to the viability of neuroblastoma cells exposed to DOX We observed higher TRIM59 abundance in SH-SY5Y and SK-N-SH cells but lower levels in SK-N-BE2 cells [28 ]. Initial exploration involved evaluating the impact of TRIM59 shRNA (two shRNA sites, sh#1, and sh#2) on SH-SY5Y and SK-N-SH cell proliferation, followed by examining the effects of TRIM59 overexpression (OE) on SK-N-BE2 cell proliferation. CCK-8 assay results demonstrated that DOX treatment (2, 5, and 10 μg/mL) suppressed cell proliferation (Fig. 1 ). Notably, TRIM59 knockdown intensified the inhibitory effect of DOX on cell proliferation (Fig. 1 A and B), while TRIM59 overexpression attenuated it (Fig. 1 C). This indicates a positive association between TRIM59 and the viability of neuroblastoma cells exposed to DOX. 3.2 TRIM59 knockdown promotes ferroptosis in neuroblastoma cells We also explored the effects of TRIM59 shRNA (sh#1 and sh#2) on ferroptosis in SH-SY5Y and SK-N-SH cells. Transfecting TRIM59 shRNA lentivirus into these cells led to reduced growth (Fig. 2 A and B). Flow cytometry revealed that TRIM59 shRNA induced lipid ROS production in both SH-SY5Y and SK-N-SH cells (Fig. 2 C–F). Notably, TRIM59 shRNA downregulated the protein levels of TRIM59, GPX4, and SLC7A11, key ferroptosis repressors [18 ]. Moreover, TRIM59 shRNA treatment induced p53 expression in SH-SY5Y and SK-N-SH cells (Fig. 2 G–P). 3.3 TRIM59 overexpression inhibits ferroptosis in neuroblastoma cells SK-N-BE2 cells were transfected with TRIM59 overexpression lentivirus, and cultured for 48 h. Subsequent examinations included assessing cell proliferation, lipid ROS levels, and protein levels of p53, TRIM59, SLC7A11, and GPX4. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , TRIM59 overexpression significantly enhanced the proliferation of SK-N-BE2 cells compared to the empty plasmid vector (EPC) at 24 and 48 h post treatment (Fig. 3 A). Moreover, TRIM59 overexpression led to a reduction in lipid ROS levels (Fig. 3 B and C). Furthermore, TRIM59 overexpression increased the protein levels of TRIM59, GPX4, and SLC7A11 while decreasing the protein levels of p53 (Fig. 3 D–H). This collectively indicates that TRIM59 overexpression mitigates ferroptosis in SK-N-BE2 cells. 3.4 TRIM59 induces degradation of p53 by ubiquitination We proceeded to examine the association between TRIM59 and p53 expression and its correlation with neuroblastoma cell differentiation. The interaction between TRIM59 and p53 was also investigated. As shown in Fig. 4 , TRIM59 protein levels were lower in adjacent mediastinal (AM) tissues and higher in moderately differentiated (MD) neuroblastoma tumor tissues (Fig. 4 A). Conversely, p53 showed an inverse relationship with TRIM59 (Fig. 4 A). Furthermore, TRIM59 knockdown in SH-SY5Y and SK-N-SH cells and TRIM59 overexpression in SK-N-BE2 cells did not affect mRNA expression of p53 (Fig. 4 B–D). Therefore, we investigated the protein interaction between p53 and TRIM59. The Co-IP assay conducted on SH-SY5Y cells confirmed the interaction between TRIM59 and p53 proteins (Fig. 4 E and F). Furthermore, we investigated p53 ubiquitination degradation in SH-SY5Y cells with TRIM59 interference, revealing that TRIM59 shRNA inhibited p53 ubiquitination degradation (Fig. 4 G). 3.5 TRIM59 and p53 are involved in the sensitivity of neuroblastoma cells to DOX In this section, we explored the effects of TRIM59 and p53 overexpression (OE) on SK-N-BE2 cells treated with DOX (5 μg/mL). Following transfection into SK-N-BE2 cells, which were then cultured for 24 h, the efficacy of the p53 overexpression vector was tested using qRT-PCR and Western blotting (Fig. 5 A–C). Our findings indicate that under DOX exposure, TRIM59 overexpression increased the proliferation of SK-N-BE2 cells, while p53 overexpression had the opposite effect at 24 and 48 h (Fig. 5 D). Furthermore, DOX increased lipid ROS levels, further induced by p53 overexpression. In contrast, TRIM59 overexpression reduced lipid ROS levels, irrespective of the absence or presence of p53 (Fig. 5 E and F). Furthermore, SLC7A11 and GPX4 protein levels were upregulated by TRIM59 overexpression but downregulated by p53 overexpression. Concurrently, p53 protein levels exhibited an opposing trend (Fig. 5 G–J). Moreover, p53 overexpression significantly reversed the changes induced by TRIM59 overexpression in SK-N-BE2 cells exposed to DOX (Fig. 5 D–J). 3.6 TRIM59 knockdown promotes ferroptosis and increases neuroblastoma cell sensitivity to DOX We investigated the impact of TRIM59 knockdown on the sensitivity of SH-SY5Y cells to DOX. SH-SY5Y cells were transfected with either TRIM59 shRNA or shNC and then subjected to DOX (5 μg/mL) and Fer-1 (10 μM) treatment for 48 h. Subsequent assessments involved examining the proliferation and lipid ROS levels of SH-SY5Y cells. The results presented in Fig. 6 indicate that the proliferation of SH-SY5Y cells was reduced by DOX. Additionally, Fer-1 enhanced the proliferation of SH-SY5Y cells exposed to DOX, while TRIM59 shRNA exerted an inhibitory effect. Notably, Fer-1 treatment counteracted the impact of TRIM59 shRNA on SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 6 A). Furthermore, the lipid ROS content displayed an inverse relationship with cell proliferation (Fig. 6 B and C). 3.7 TRIM59 knockdown increases neuroblastoma cell sensitivity to DOX In this section, we initiated TRIM59 knockdown in SH-SY5Y cells and established a xenograft mouse model. As illustrated in Fig. 7 , both TRIM59 knockdown and DOX treatment contributed to a reduction in tumor growth (Fig. 7 A and B). Furthermore, the combined effect of TRIM59 knockdown and DOX treatment improved the survival rates of 90-day nude mice (Fig. 7 C). Moreover, tumor cell death was observed following TRIM59 knockdown and DOX treatment (Fig. 7 D and E). In addition, TRIM59 knockdown resulted in an increase in p53 protein levels and a decrease in SLC7A11 and GPX4 protein levels (Fig. 7 F–I). These results suggest that TRIM59 knockdown increases the sensitivity of neuroblastoma cells to DOX. 4 Discussion Neuroblastoma stands out as one of the prevalent solid tumors in children, and ferroptosis, a distinct iron-dependent cell death pathway, deviates from apoptosis. Generally, antitumor medications induce ferroptosis as part of their therapeutic action [36 ]. This investigation reveals the pivotal role of TRIM59 in modulating the susceptibility of neuroblastoma cells to DOX through the mediation of ferroptosis. TRIM59 expression exerts a beneficial influence on neuroblastoma cell proliferation. Furthermore, TRIM59 overexpression demonstrated a capacity to reduce lipid ROS levels, whereas TRIM59 knockdown led to their elevation. Notably, TRIM59 protein levels exhibited an inverse correlation with neuroblastoma differentiation. Furthermore, our observations indicated that cell ferroptosis suppressing proteins SLC7A11 and GPX4 were negatively regulated by TRIM59. The downregulation of TRIM59 increased neuroblastoma sensitivity to DOX, both in vitro and in vivo . This mechanism is intricately linked to the inhibition of p53 ubiquitination and degradation. TRIM proteins, functioning as E3 ligases, are implicated in diverse biological activities [27 ]. Their crucial roles in the regulating of cellular biological processes in tumor cells have been established through various studies [37 ]. Several studies reveal a reciprocal relationship between p53 and TRIM proteins: p53 regulates the expression of certain TRIM proteins, while TRIM proteins modulate regulate p53 activity and levels. This regulatory interplay plays a pivotal role in influencing the biological behaviors of tumors and other diseases [38–40 ]. The inactivation of p53 signaling is a pivotal event in the formation and development of human cancers, making it an attractive target for cancer treatment [41 ]. TRIM59, identified as an oncogene in numerous tumor types, including breast cancer [42 ], non-small cell lung cancer [43 ], ovarian cancer [44 ], and retinoblastoma [45 ], and is implicated in various signaling pathways. The findings from this study elucidate that TRIM59 ubiquitinates and degrades the tumor suppressor p53. TRIM59 knockdown induces ferroptosis in neuroblastoma cells by enhancing p53 expression and lipid ROS generation, while decreasing the expression of SLC7A11 and GPX4. Interestingly, TRIM59 exhibits a dual role in neuroblastoma, being associated with neuroblastoma differentiation and promoting its development by reducing ferroptosis. However, TRIM59 knockdown induces ferroptosis and enhances neuroblastoma susceptibility to DOX. Furthermore, the combined treatment of TRIM59 knockdown and DOX exhibits improved therapeutic effects in xenograft mice. Ferroptosis, a relatively recent form of cell death, is characterized by its dependence on iron and the accumulation of lipid peroxide [15 ]. Various pathways, including Nrf2, P53, heme oxygenase-1, BECN1, and FANCD2 regulate ferroptosis in tumors [46 ]. p53, a crucial regulator of ferroptosis, is known to be involved in various tumor processes, encompassing cell cycle arrest, senescence, apoptosis, genome stability maintenance, metabolism modulation, autophagy, and the recently identified ferroptosis [47 ]. p53 plays dual roles in ferroptosis induction under different conditions [13 ]. In this study, TRIM59 was found to directly interact with p53, promoting its ubiquitination and degradation. This interaction subsequently induced SLC7A11 and GPX4 expression, inhibiting ferroptosis. SLC7A11, recognized as a ferroptosis inhibitor, is overexpressed in numerous cancers. It functions as a cystine importer, enhancing antioxidant defense and glutathione production [48 ]. SLC7A11 upregulation was associated with tumor formation through both ferroptosis-independent and ferroptosis-dependent mechanisms, and inhibiting SLC7A11 inhibition has been suggested as an effective tumor suppression strategy [49 ]. The present study demonstrated a reduction in the ferroptosis suppressors SLC7A11 and GPX4 by shTRIM59 in neuroblastoma, both in vitro and in vivo . Moreover, shTRIM59 improved neuroblastoma chemosensitivity to DOX, with the mechanism associated with the decreased ubiquitination and degradation of p53 and the induction of cell ferroptosis. 5 Conclusion In summary, this study highlights the significance of TRIM59 in the advancement of neuroblastoma. Higher TRIM59 expression correlates with both tumor progression and chemoresistance in neuroblastoma. Diminishing TRIM59 levels may enhance neuroblastoma ferroptosis, thereby augmenting the sensitivity of neuroblastoma cells to DOX. Consequently, targeting TRIM59 emerges as a potentially valuable strategy in treating neuroblastoma. title: Improving neuroblastoma therapy with a new p53 family-activating agent
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is among the most common malignancies in children and represents a therapeutic challenge in pediatric oncology. p53 family proteins play a critical role in protecting cells from genomic instability and malignant transformation. However, in NB, their activities are often inhibited by interacting proteins such as MDM2. The interplay between p53 family pathway and N-Myc, a key biomarker of poor prognosis, is also a critical factor in NB pathogenesis. Herein, we disclose 1-(dibromomethyl)-3,4,6-trimethoxy-9H-xanthen-9-one (LEM3) as a new p53 family-activating agent with potent NB anticancer activity. At 0.13–2.1 μM, LEM3 inhibited the growth of several NB cell lines. Its activity was further evidenced in spheroids, patient-derived NB cells, and in a vasculature stiffness-based model of MYCN-amplified NB cells. This growth-inhibitory effect was associated with cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, in SH-SY5Y and SK-N-BE(2) NB cells, without apparent acquisition of resistance. LEM3 inhibited cell migration and invasion and reduced the expression of NB-related prognostic markers, particularly MYCN mRNA and protein levels. LEM3 released p53, TAp63, and TAp73 from their interaction with MDM2 both in a yeast-based assay and NB cells; for p53, this led to increased protein stabilization, DNA-binding ability, and transcriptional activity. Fluorescence quenching and docking analyses suggested that LEM3 binds to p53, TAp63, and TAp73 at the MDM2-binding site within their transactivation domain. LEM3 also synergies with doxorubicin and cisplatin in NB cells. Given the central role of the p53 family-MDM2-MYCN axis in NB pathogenesis, our findings support LEM3 as a promising compound for advancing NB targeted therapy.
