Department of Life Science National Institute of Technology Rourkela Odisha India Neuroblast cells play a pivotal role in adult neurogenesis. However, the detailed mechanisms underlying the acquisition of pluripotency or the process of differentiation remain unknown. Herein, the role of the AT-hook protein AKNA in regulating pluripotency and stemness in neuroblastoma cells is demonstrated through gene knockdown, immunofluorescence, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), localization of AKNA, signaling interactions, and transcriptional activity. AKNA was detected primarily in the nucleus during the induction of pluripotency and was retained in the cytosol by FAK signaling during differentiation. Loss of AKNA disrupts both the stemness and differentiation potential of neuroblastoma cells. In the nucleus, colocalization and physical association between AKNA and KDM6B promote H3K27me3 demethylation and subsequently H3K27ac deposition on the promoters of stemness genes, triggering their transcription. These findings establish AKNA as a critical regulator of neuroblast cell fate determinants in association with epigenetic modifiers and signaling pathways, offering potential targets for neuroblastoma therapies and regenerative medicine for neurodegenerative diseases. Graphical abstract Unlabelled Image Keywords AT-hook AKNA Neuroblastoma Stemness Differentiation Chromatin dynamics FAK signaling Data availability Data will be made available on request. 1 Introduction AT-hook containing proteins are a class of proteins characterized by a small AT-motif, which is sufficient to bind to the DNA minor groove and plays important roles in regulating chromatin remodeling and gene expression from plants to animals [1,2] . One such protein is AKNA, which garnered attention due to its roles in immune system regulation and development. Earlier, it was characterized as a nuclear localized transcription factor (TF) in CD40 and CD40L promoters during the secondary immune response [3–5] . Later, AKNA was described as a centrosomal protein that regulates neurogenesis by modulating microtubule organization. It also regulates the epithelial to mesenchymal transition in neural stem cells delamination in the subventricular zone of the brain [6] . Shifting of transcription regulatory proteins from the nucleus to the cytosol or vice versa is an established phenomenon for multifaceted functions. For example, Inhibitor of differentiation 1 (ID1), a helix-loop-helix protein, is a stemness like gene that promotes survival and proliferation. ID1 is re-localized in the cytoplasm after treatment with retinoic acid in SH-SY5Y cells [7] . Coordination between chromatin modifiers, TFs, and DNA architecture modifying proteins regulates gene expression. Among the chromatin modifiers, histone methyl transferases (HMTs) and demethylases (KDMs) are some of the important enzymes has taken the lead with their crosstalk with different TFs [8] . The remarkable capacity of TFs to cell fate determination depends on chromatin remodeling at target loci by recruiting specific epigenetic modifiers. Many AT-hook containing proteins themselves act as chromatin remodelers like ALL1, SWI/SNF, TAFII250, Ash1, etc. [2,9–12] . During pluripotent stem cells' (PSCs) self-renewal and differentiation, epigenetic regulation preserves cell identity by shaping unique epigenetic landscapes. Bivalent domains, marked by both the repressive histone H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and the activating H3K4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), are uniquely positioned at lineage-specific genes in embryonic stem cells (ESCs), poising them for precise activation or repression during fate transitions. Research indicates that deposition of H3K4me3 often precedes the removal of H3K27me3, thereby priming genes for activation while they remain transcriptionally repressed until H3K27me3 is demethylated by KDM6 family demethylases (e.g., KDM6A/UTX and KDM6B/JMJD3) [13,14] . Temporal control seems important; H3K4me3 can be deposited at promoters even when there is H3K27me3, setting up a poised chromatin configuration. Resolution of this bivalency by demethylation of H3K27me3 allows transcription elongation [15,16] . Current research suggests that KDM6B plays a more pivotal role in the brain cells than KDM6A and is essential for neuronal development, synaptic plasticity, and cognitive function, with disruptions in its activity linked to cognitive impairments. In contrast, the role of KDM6A in brain function appears to be less prominent [17–20] . H3K27me3 is associated with repression of CD133, NESTIN, CD44, and SOX2 gene expression [21,22] , which are known for important stemness and pluripotency factors. KDM6B is known to be a transcription activator epigenetically on CD44 and SOX2 gene promoters in different cancer cells [23] and maintains pluripotency in hematopoietic stem cells in a context dependent manner [24] . KDM6B is reported as an important epigenetic modifier in the maintenance and establishment of neuronal stem cells in the dentate gyrus in mice [25] . KDM6B is reported to be recruited at the transcription start site by interacting with different DNA binding proteins like T-Box TFs, Smad proteins, estrogen receptors, and KLF4 [26–29] . Another well-known transcription factor, p53, is reported to be a lineage determinant in RA induced differentiation by recruiting H3K27me demethylase KDM6B on target gene promoters [30,31] . P53 is reported to be physically associated with AT-hook protein like HMG1, p300, and TAFII250 for different cellular functions and nuclear localization [32–35] , and might have an accessory role in AKNA's functions. Nodal signaling dependent developmental reprogramming is H3K27me3 demethylation dependent, which is catalyzed by smad2/3 dependent KDM6B recruitment on the targeted gene promoter [36] . There are other examples also where KDM6B either accumulated in the nucleus or recruited to the promoter by different nuclear proteins [37,38] . As per available literature, the prevailing view is that different TFs and nuclear proteins assist the localization and functions of epigenetic modifiers like KDM6B and reprogram the gene expression pattern, depicting cell fate. Centrosomal functions and specifically transcription regulation by AKNA are poorly understood. Further investigation of how AKNA brings these two roles might provide further insights into cellular differentiation, immune response, and tumorigenesis. Herein, we have investigated how AKNA functions as a context-dependent regulator for chromatin function, in which context AKNA is retained in the cytosol, and how AKNA becomes indispensable for both stemness and differentiation. This study elaborates on the molecular mechanisms of AKNA in histone modifications, essential for the activation of genes associated with neuroblastoma lineage determinations. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Culture of neuroblastoma cell lines IMR32 and SH-SY5Y cell lines were procured from NCCS, Pune, India. These cell lines were grown in DMEM and F12 media, respectively. 10% serum (Gibco −10,270,106) supplement and 1× antibiotic-antimycotic were added to the cultured media and incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator. For induction of stemness, DMEM/F12 (1:1) was used instead of the cultured media for the cell lines. To treat the cells with different chemical agents, cells were counted and seeded according to their rate of cell division. For microscopy based analyses, cells were plated at 10–15% initial confluency according to the diameter to avoid overgrowth during the experiment. 2.2 Drug treatments and MTT assay To check the cytotoxicity of different treatments, cell viability was assessed using MTT (Himedia-TC191) in live cells. Cells were seeded at 103 to 1.5*103 per well in a 96-well cell culture plate. After 24 h of incubation in a CO2 incubator, cells were treated with different concentrations of drugs for 48 h because the downstream experiments need a long exposure time. After that, the drug media was replaced with MTT media and incubated for 4–6 h. followed by DMSO (HiMedia - AS121) mediated solubilization of formazan crystals. The absorbance was captured at 570 nm, which was used to calculate cell viability as follows, % Viability =100 * mean OD (drug)/mean OD (control). Drugs used in this study: Retinoic acid (Sigma- R2625), OAC1 (Santa Cruz- sc-397,046), PF- (PZ0117 - Sigma), Na3VO4 (sc-3540 -Santa Cruz). 2.3 Neurosphere formation assay Spheroid and organoid culture systems offer physiologically relevant three dimensional models that more accurately reflect in vivo organization and cellular heterogeneity, making them valuable tools in biological and translational research [39–41] . To determine the presence and prevalence of stem cells in cultured cells in different treatments, a neurosphere formation assay was performed. Trypsinized SH-SY5Y and IMR32 cells were seeded at a density of 1 × 104 cells/well on a low attachment culture plate containing DMEM/F12 growth media. Cultures were kept in a CO2 incubator for 5–7 days at 37 °C. Every 2 days, the culture media were replaced with fresh media. These cells readily form neurospheres, and the images were taken using a phase contrast microscope (Olympus), as established earlier [42] . Spheres were collected at the indicated time points for immunocytochemistry and protein extraction. 2.4 In Vitro neuronal differentiation IMR32 and SH-SY5Y cell lines were seeded at a density of 1 × 105 cells per 6-well culture plate coated with poly-l -lysine in normal growth media, followed by overnight incubation for attachment. After 24 h culture media was replaced by 2.5% FBS containing DMEM media with 10 μM retinoic acid (RA) (Sigma-R2625-100MG) for SH-SY5Y and 5 μM for IMR32. From the next day, half of the culture media from each well was replaced by fresh RA containing media for up to 5 days. Neurite outgrowth was assessed under a phase contrast microscope. Three different time points (1,3 &5th day) differentiated cells were used for downstream experiments to study the gradual molecular changes during differentiation. Although different groups of researchers differentiate for variable time points according to their research interests. In this study, we intended to induce differentiation for up to 5 days to induce higher expression of differentiated neuronal markers, and that was confirmed with the expression of differentiation markers in downstream experiments in previous study [43,44] . 2.5 Colony formation assay Single cells were seeded in a 35 mm Petri dish (500/well) and incubated for 24 h, followed by replacement of the growth media with respective treated media and incubated for another 10–15 days, depending on the cell line. Then the colonies were fixed with formaldehyde and stained with crystal violet. Excess stain was washed with tap water, and the image was captured as described earlier [45] . 2.6 siRNA and plasmid transfections Transfection was performed using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen L3000–15) in Opti-MEM media following the manufacturer's instructions and incubated for 48 h. Different concentration of siRNA (AKNA; KDM6B) was used and validated in western blotting for knockdown efficiency confirmation. For overexpression, 3–5 μg of plasmid [CoMiP (# Addgene); KDM6B (# Addgene); FAK(# Addgene)] was used, depending on the culture plate size and cell density. siRNA sequences are given below AKNA: CAGAUGAGAAGCUCGCUGU[dT][dT]; ACAGCGAGCUUCUCAUCUG[dT][dT] KDM6B: CUCGAAAUCCCAUCACAGU[dT][dT]; ACUGUGAUGGGAUUUCGAG[dT][dT] 2.7 Apoptosis assay Cells were seeded at per well on a coverslip inside a 6-well plate. Then, after attachment, cells were treated with the respective treatment and incubated for another 48 h. After that, cells were washed with PBS and stained with acridine orange (100 μg/mL) and EtBr (100 μg/mL) for 5 min, followed by imaging under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus). 2.8 Caspase-3/7 activity assay Protein extracted from SH-SY5Y cells after different treatments was quantified, and 20 μg protein from each sample was incubated with Caspase-Glo® 3/7 (Promega, USA) for 2 h in the dark at room temperature to check the cleavage of luminescent substrate. Luminescence was measured by a luminometer and normalized with total protein content. 2.9 RNA isolation and qRT-PCR For gene expression quantification using qRT-PCR, RNA samples were isolated using TRIzol (Thermo - 15,596,018) method and phenol chloroform (Himedia-MB063) precipitation. RNA samples were washed with 70% ethanol (Himedia-MB228) and, after drying, dissolved in nuclease-free water. After qualitative and quantitative analysis of RNA samples in agarose gel electrophoresis and nanodrop (Eppendorf), cDNA synthesis was performed using reverse transcriptase (Genesure - PGK163A) according to the manufacturer's instructions. For qRT-PCR, 1 μg of cDNA and 300 nM respective gene primer were taken with SYBR-green PCR mix (Thermo - A25742) and performed qRT-PCR in the previously described method [46] . Data analysis was performed according to Livak's method (∆∆CT calculation) using ACTB as the housekeeping gene. 2.10 Nuclear and cytosolic protein fractionation To obtain nuclear and cytosolic fractions, cells were incubated in low salt buffer (10 mM HEPES/KOH, pH 7.9, 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 1× Protease inhibitor cocktail) for 10 min at 4 °C in a rotor. For neurospheres, the incubation time increased to 15 min. After centrifugation (2000 g -5mins), the supernatant was taken as the cytoplasmic fraction. The remaining pellets were rewashed with a low salt buffer to remove any residual cytoplasmic contamination. After that, the remaining pellets were dissolved in high salt buffer (20 mM HEPES/KOH, pH = 7.9; 420 mM NaCl; 1.5 mM MgCl2; 200 uM EDTA; 23% glycerol; 1xPIC) followed by incubation at 4 °C for 20 min and centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 10 min. 2.11 Immunoblotting Whole cell lysates were extracted using RIPA buffer (sigma –R0278-50ML), followed by centrifugation (12,000 rpm-15mins), and immunoblotting was performed by following the protocol adapted from [47] . In brief, the protein samples were separated on 8–12% SDS-PAGE gels based on target protein molecular weight, resolved and transferred to nitrocellulose membrane (Axiva -160300RI) using a semidry transfer system (BioRad), blocked with 5% skim milk for 1 h at RT. All primary antibodies were diluted in 1% BSA (Himedia-MB083) dissolved in PBST, and the blots were incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. After removing the primary antibodies, blots were washed with PBST three times (10 min* 3), then they were probed with either anti-rabbit (Invitrogen-65-6120) or anti-mouse (Santa Cruz - SC516102) secondary antibody for 1 h at RT. Then, the blots were washed with PBST three times (3*10mins), followed by visualization using ECL substrate (Thermo- 34,580) in a ChemiDoc instrument (BioRad). Antibody details are described in the supplementary data file. 2.12 Immunostaining Immunoblotting was performed as per the previous standard protocol [48] . Cells were seeded on a coverslip in a 6-well plate or on a chambered slide with 15 to 20% confluency. After being treated with different agents for different time points according to the requirements, followed by fixation using 4% formaldehyde for 5 min. For the neurosphere, the same conditions were applied, but done in eppendorf tubes. Then the cells were permeabilized with PBST on ice for 10 min and incubated for 1 h with 1% BSA for blocking. Then, the cells were incubated with the desired primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. Next, the cells were washed with PBS (10 min × 3) and incubated with Alexa647/Alexa488 (anti-mouse - ab150119 or anti-rabbit - ab150077). Unbound secondary antibodies were washed with PBS three times. For nuclear staining, DAPI (1 mg/mL) was used in PBS, and dry coverslips were mounted with ProLong™ Gold Antifade Mountant (Thermo P36930). 2.13 Confocal microscopy Images of immunostained samples were captured in an inverted confocal microscope (DMi8/STELLARIS 5; Leica) with lasers 405, 488, and 638 nm with constant acquisition parameters (laser power, gain, pinhole, and scan settings) controlled by LAS X Stellaris Control software. ImageJ software was used to quantify the signals of different channels. Line scan intensity profiling was executed by the ImageJ software. A straight line ROI (3–5 pixel width) was drawn across the longest axis of a region of interest (A-B), and fluorescence intensity of each channel was measured by analyzing the plot profile. Intensity values were normalized (0–100%) for each channel in GraphPad software and represented as a line scan. Quantitative analysis of nuclear and cytoplasmic localization was performed using ImageJ software. Based on DNA staining, the nuclear region was defined and measured, and excluded from cytoplasmic quantification. The nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio was measured by dividing the mean nuclear intensity by the mean cytoplasmic intensity and plotted as violin plots using GraphPad Prism. Statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett's multiple comparisons test) was performed to check the significance. 2.14 Coimmunoprecipitation Whole cell lysates were used for the co-immunoprecipitation assay. Protein samples (300 μg) were incubated with respective primary antibodies (anti-AKNA, anti-KDM6B, and anti-HA) overnight at 4 °C. The next day, each sample was poured with pre-cleared A/G beads and incubated for 2 h at 4 °C. For the negative control, a mouse IgG antibody was used. Then, immunoprecipitated complexes were washed with wash buffer three times, followed by elution with 20 μL Laemmli buffer and heating. Protein-protein interactions were analysed by western blotting. 2.15 Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay Chromatin immunoprecipitation assay was performed using a kit method (Sigma-Imprint chromatin immunoprecipitation kit – CHP1) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Treated and control cells were fixed with 1% formaldehyde in PBS for 10 min under shaking conditions. Formaldehyde neutralized by using 1.25 M glycine for 5 min at RT. Centrifuged and washed with PBS and lysed (on ice) for 10 min in 300 μL of ChIP lysis buffer, followed by sonication (0.3 mm probe sonicator) on ice for 10 min on 30s ON-30s OFF cycles at 30% efficiency, and a small fraction was checked after every 2–3 cycles for the fragment length (approx. 200–1000 bp) standardization. Then the samples were diluted with an equal amount of ChIP dilution buffer. 1 μg of specific antibody for respective samples was incubated overnight at 4 °C in shaking conditions to avoid nonspecific binding. 1 μL of mouse IgG was used as a negative control. The rest of the protocol was followed as mentioned in the kit. The DNA samples were purified using a PCR purification kit (Qiagen). % input was calculated according to the standard method, as described earlier [49] . The sequence of ChIP primers was presented in the supplementary data. 2.16 Statistical analysis Either student's ‘t’ test or two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni correction were performed in Prism5 software to test the significance with sample number ≥ 3, and the test employed along with the p -values (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.001. ns, no significance) and their inference is mentioned in figure legends. 3 Results 3.1 OAC1 induces pluripotency and stemness in neuroblastoma cells In neuroblastoma cell lines (IMR32 and SH-SY5Y), dose dependent treatment of reprogramming agent OAC1 [50] showed that a 5 μM concentration significantly induced all the tested stemness and pluripotency markers expression (Suppl. Fig. S1). Whereas higher concentration above 30 μM shows significant cell death (data not given). OAC1(5 μM) treatment led to a significant increase in colony formation capacity and neurosphere generation, with a greater number and larger size of spheres (Fig. 1 A-C ). These findings suggest that OAC1 enhances stem-like properties in these cells. To further investigate this, we assessed the expression of stemness and pluripotency markers. Western blot analysis revealed a time dependent upregulation of CD133, CD44, OCT4, SOX2, and PAX6, with 24 to 48 h of treatment being sufficient to induce robust expression of these markers (Fig. 1 D-E). To evaluate whether OAC1 treatment represses neuronal differentiation, we performed immunostaining for the neuronal differentiation marker TUBB3, which showed a marked reduction in expression after 48 h of treatment. In contrast, the expression of the neuroepithelial marker, Nestin, was significantly increased. The upregulation of PAX6 and SOX2 was further confirmed by immunostaining, reinforcing the observation that OAC1 drives a transition toward a pluripotent, stem-like state in these neuroblastoma cell lines (Fig. 1 F). These findings demonstrate that OAC1 treatment effectively reprograms neuroblastoma cells toward a stem-like state by inducing pluripotency genes and suppressing neuronal differentiation. 3.2 AKNA expression gradually increases during both OAC1 and retinoic acid induced cell fate transitions Treatment of both IMR32 and SH-SY5Y cells with OAC1 is associated with multiple cell clustering and sphere like forms, indicating the direction toward an enhanced stem-like state compared to control cells, which have more differentiated, attached morphology. Treatment with RA drives neuronal like differentiation, with elongated, neurite-like extensions (Fig. 2 A ). There is a strong, time dependent increase in AKNA mRNA with OAC1 treatment (24 h, 48 h, 72 h) in both cell lines, with a maximum at 72 h. Conversely, RA (10 μM) (dose derived from viability assay; data not given) treatment also increases AKNA, albeit less so than OAC1. AKNA protein expression reflects the mRNA findings, with a robust time dependent increase in OAC1 treated cells. RA treated cells also exhibit AKNA upregulation, although the increase is less than with OAC1. The quantified data validate that AKNA protein levels increase substantially with time with OAC1 treatment and, to a lesser extent, with RA. Maximum expression is seen at 72 h of OAC1 treatment, whereas RA treatment is moderately induced (Fig. 2 B-E). These findings suggest that OAC1 treatment induces robust expression of AKNA at the mRNA and protein levels, and this is concurrent with morphological changes characteristic of stemness. RA treatment induces upregulation of AKNA, but this is concurrent with morphological markers of neuronal differentiation. These indicate that AKNA can exert a context-dependent function in mediating stemness and differentiation in neuroblastoma cells. 3.3 AKNA is indispensable to induce pluripotency and stemness in neuroblastoma cells As the earlier figure (Fig. 1 ) showed that OAC1 induces stemness and pluripotency, whereas retinoic acid, known as a differentiation inducer, upregulates the expression of AKNA, the effects of loss of function of AKNA in stemness and differentiation were assessed. AKNA knockdown was performed using siRNA, and knockdown efficiency was confirmed by western blotting (Suppl. Fig. S2). In AKNA knockdown, it was observed that stemness and pluripotency markers OCT4, SOX2, CD133, CD44, NES, and PAX6 expression were significantly downregulated. These results were also reflected in neurosphere as well as in colony formation efficiency of the treated cells, as a smaller number of colonies and smaller neurospheres were observed in AKNA KD cells (Fig. 2 F-G; Suppl. Figs. S3–4). To uncover the role of AKNA in OAC1 induced stemness, AKNA KD cells were treated with OAC1. Interestingly, it was observed that in the absence of AKNA, OAC1 does not induce pluripotency and stemness in neuroblast cells, confirmed by immunoblotting (Fig. 3 A ). This was further reflected in the colony formation and neurosphere formation capacity of neuroblast cells. In the absence of AKNA, both neurosphere and colony formation capacity decrease even though the OAC1 is present in the medium (Fig. 3 B-C, Suppl. Fig. S5). To nullify any off-target effects of chemically synthesized small molecule, OAC1, on stemness and pluripotency induction, a pluripotency inducing vector (CoMiP) [51] was transfected independently and in the absence of AKNA. In CoMiP transfected cells, pluripotency and stemness markers were significantly upregulated as expected, but in the absence of AKNA, it failed to induce the expression of pluripotency and stemness markers at both transcriptional and translational levels in neuroblast cells (Fig. 3 D-E). To nullify the effects of OAC1 or CoMiP on AKNA expression, neurosphere formation was performed without any stemness inducing agents, followed by immunostaining and immunoblotting. It was noted that AKNA expression persists, along with increased expression of CD133, CD44, Nestin, and OCT4 in the presence or absence of OAC1. It was also observed that TBR1 expression decreased during neurosphere formation. Immunoblotting of neurosphere protein extracts confirmed that AKNA expression was significantly upregulated during neurosphere formation. Immunoblotting also confirmed that AKNA expression increases along with higher expression of stemness markers like CD133 (Fig. 3 F-G; Suppl. Fig. S6). This result further strengthens the importance of AKNA in maintaining stemness in neuroblast cells. 3.4 AKNA is also crucial for the differentiation of neuroblastoma cells into mature neuron like cells To check the outcomes of AKNA knockdown on differentiation, lineage-specific markers expression was analysed. Terminal differentiation markers like TUBB3, NEFM, and NEFL were also downregulated in AKNA knockdown cells, but intermediate progenitor and immature neuronal markers like TBR2 and TBR1 do not show any significant changes (Fig. 4 A ; Suppl. Fig. S7). To identify the role of AKNA in RA induced differentiation, AKNA KD cells were treated with RA. In the absence of AKNA, RA failed to differentiate neuroblastoma cells into fully matured neuronal cells, and a greater number of bipolar morphological neuronal cells were observed (Fig. 4 B). During differentiation, intermediate progenitor markers like TBR2 protein expression are not hampered in the absence of AKNA, indeed slightly upregulated when RA is present. But postmitotic neuronal marker, TBR1, and mature neuronal markers like NEFL and NEFM expression were significantly decreased when AKNA is absent during RA mediated differentiation induction (Fig. 4 C). Functional maturation assays, such as electrophysiological measurements and other studies, should be tested in the AKNA background. As the cells neither differentiate nor show pluripotency in the absence of AKNA, it prompts us to check the state of the cells. For that, a cell cycle assay was performed, and an increased G2/M phase arrest was observed in AKNA knockdown cells (Fig. 4 D; Suppl. Fig. S8). To precisely known about AKNA effects on the cell cycle, in AKNA knockdown cells, chromosomal spreading was visualized using a nuclear DNA specific dye (Suppl. Fig. S8). In AKNA knockdown, it was visible from flow cytometry data that the cells that were arrested in G2/M phase were mostly arrested in mitotic stages, confirmed by immunostaining and immunoblotting with M-phase specific marker (H3S10P) (Fig. 4 E-F). This mitotic arrest possibly leads to apoptotic cell death, as observed by pharmacological inhibition of docetaxel (Metaphase blocker) (sublethal dose 10 nM) treatment in a time dependent manner upregulates H3S10P, and subsequent cleaved Caspase3 expression (Suppl. Fig. S9). Apoptosis in AKNA knockdown was also determined by caspase glow assay and AO-EtBr staining. Increased expression of Bax, Caspase 3, and cleaved Caspase 3 in AKNA knockdown further strengthens the effects. It is also evident that the apoptotic cell death is p53 dependent because p53 inhibition by Pifithrin-alpha (PFT-α) (5 μM) reduces the apoptosis (Fig. 4 G-H; Suppl. Fig. S10). Physical association between AKNA and p53 (Suppl. Fig. S11) was observed, strengthening the p53 axis. 3.5 AKNA exhibits dynamic localization during stemness and differentiation induction and is regulated by FAK signaling Studying the dual fate directional role of AKNA, it prompts us to study the cellular localization of the AKNA protein in different treatment conditions. Surprisingly, it was observed that OAC1 induces more nuclear localization of AKNA compared to the untreated cells, as seen in the confocal microscopy and immunoblotting assay of nuclear and cytosolic fractions. On the other hand, it has been found that RA treatment retains more AKNA protein outside the nucleus. Whether OAC1 drives AKNA's nuclear localization or not, nontreated neurosphere fractions were immunoblotted. Interestingly, even though neurospheres were generated in the absence of OAC1, nuclear localization of AKNA greatly increased (Fig. 5 A-D , Suppl. Fig. S12). Sodium orthovanadate (Tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor) treatment significantly increases AKNA's cytosolic retention even in the presence of OAC1 (Fig. 5 E-H, Suppl. Fig. S12). IMR32 cells treated with Na3VO4 (A tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor [52] ) at different time points showed that pFAK expression was significantly upregulated, while FAK expression was almost similar to the earliest condition. To check the effects of FAK signaling on AKNA transcription, FAK signaling was inhibited by PF- (Tyr397 -FAK inhibitor) [53] and activated by FAK overexpression. In both these conditions, AKNA expression remains unchanged (Fig. 6 A-B ). However, from immunocytochemistry data, it was visible that FAK retains more AKNA in the cytosol, whereas inhibition of FAK phosphorylation significantly enriches AKNA inside the nucleus even in the FAK overexpressed cells (Fig. 6 C-D, Suppl. Figs. S13–14). FAK signaling inhibition also disrupts the RA mediated neuronal differentiation in the neuroblastoma model (Suppl. Fig. S15), and our recent report also supports the regulatory functions of FAK in neuronal differentiation [54] . This result suggests that AKNA's dynamic localization is important for fate transition and is regulated by FAK phosphorylation. 3.6 Accumulation of AKNA and reduction of H3K27me3 mark by KDM6B on gene promoters are associated with OAC1 induced pluripotency and stemness To elucidate the mechanisms of AKNA mediated transcriptional activation of stemness and pluripotency, a ChIP assay was performed. It was observed that in OAC1 treatment, occupancy of AKNA significantly increased on the tested gene (NES, CD133, SOX2, and OCT4) promoter. In the same condition, transcriptional repressor mark H3K27me3 occupancy significantly decreased on the tested gene promoters. In time dependent OAC1 treatment, it was noted that H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B upregulated gradually in both cell lines. Promoter occupancy of KDM6B also increased on tested gene promoters in OAC1 treatment (Fig. 7 A-D , Suppl. Fig. S16). To verify the independent effects of KDM6B on pluripotency and stemness, knockdown and overexpression were performed, followed by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting. In KDM6B KD, a significant reduction of stemness and pluripotency markers expression was observed in mRNA and protein levels as well. Reverse results were observed in the overexpression condition in both cell lines (Fig. 7 E-F; Suppl. Fig. S16). It was also observed that KDM6B overexpression increases the neurosphere formation efficiency in both cell lines (Fig. 7 G). ChIP data confirms that KDM6B upregulates the tested genes by removing repressive H3K27me3 from the gene promoters (Fig. 7 H). This data suggests that AKNA is possibly associated with KDM6B to drive gene transcription in this tested model. However, another H3K27me3 demethylase, KDM6A observed to be the least expressed in neuroblastoma cells when compared to a positive cell line (HaCaT) at the mRNA level and observed to be unaltered in KDM6B KD cells (Suppl. Fig. S17). As the neuroblastoma cells fail to recover the expression of stemness associated markers in the presence of KDM6A, the importance of KDM6B as an H3K27me3 demethylase in neuroblastoma cells can be drawn from here. 3.7 AKNA is essential for KDM6B mediated H3K27me3 demethylation and subsequent acetylation of H3K27 to H3K27ac for gene expression To assess the functional interdependency, KDM6B was overexpressed in AKNA knockdown cells. Interestingly, the KDM6B stability was not changed in AKNA knockdown cells, and global H3K2me3 status was also unchanged (Suppl. Fig. S18). Still, in the absence of AKNA, KDM6B overexpression failed to rescue the transcription of stemness and pluripotency associated genes (CD133, CD44, NES, OCT4, SOX2, and PAX6), which were otherwise induced by KDM6B overexpression. It was further validated by immunoblotting data (Fig. 8 A-B ; Suppl. Fig. S19). Neurosphere formation capacity was also compromised in KDM6B overexpressed cells when AKNA was absent (Fig. 8 C). To find out the possible mechanisms of KDM6B dependency on AKNA, promoter occupancy was checked. It was clearly detected that when AKNA is less occupied on the tested gene promoters, KDM6B occupancy also compromised (Fig. 8 D-E; Suppl. Fig. S21B). This data confirmed that H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B heavily relies upon AKNA for transcription activation of pluripotency and stemness related genes in neuroblastoma cells. 3.8 AKNA and KDM6B interaction is indispensable for stemness factors and pluripotency associated gene expression To further confirm the effects of interdependency between AKNA and KDM6B, a ChIP experiment was performed. It was observed that H3K27me3 is high in AKNA KD, and when AKNA is absent, KDM6B overexpression is not sufficient to demethylate H3K27me3 from the tested gene promoters. The mechanism behind such a finding was that when AKNA was absent, KDM6B failed to occupy the gene promoters as compared to the KDM6B overexpression only (Fig. 9 A-B ). Further, it was also traced that H3K27 acetyl transferase p300/CBP complex, along with H3K27ac depositions, was higher in KDM6B overexpressed cells but decreased the occupancy when AKNA was knocked down in cells, irrespective of normal or ectopic overexpression of KDM6B (Fig. 9 C, Suppl. Fig. S20). KDM6B physically interacts with different TFs to activate gene transcription by removing methylation from H3K27me3, and from the above observation in this study, its dependency on AKNA was evoked to study their physical association. From immunocytochemistry data, it was apparent that AKNA and KDM6B colocalize in the neuroblast cells, and further immunoblotting data confirmed that AKNA protein physically interacts with KDM6B in different treatment conditions. Although it started with an equal amount of whole cell protein samples, the magnitude of interaction between KDM6B and AKNA is high in stemness induction. Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed that AKNA pull down recovered HA-KDM6B specifically in the transfected cells, whereas HA immunoprecipitation enriched AKNA relative to the input fraction (Fig. 9 D-E). So, AKNA possibly promotes the occupancy of KDM6B on gene promoters during the induction of stemness in neuroblastoma cells. 4 Discussion This study demonstrated that AKNA functions as a key regulator for neuronal lineage fate determinant in the neuroblast cell model in a context dependent manner. OAC1, which induces pluripotency [50] , reprogrammed IMR32 and SH-SY5Y cells into enhanced pluripotent stem-like cells with enhanced self renewal and proliferation capacity. Simultaneously, OAC1 suppressed the differentiation, as seen in the reduction in expression of TUBB3, a well-known differentiation marker [55] . The molecular mechanism of TUBB3 downregulation during the induction of stemness needs further experimentation [56] . Although total PAX6 protein levels appeared modestly altered under OAC1 treatment, the increase in cytoplasmic PAX6 signal is consistent with previously reported context dependent changes in PAX6 localization during neural differentiation [57] . These results aligned with the established theory of small molecules or factors' capacity to reprogram fate determined cells into pluripotent cells [50,58,59] . In opposite directions, retinoic acid (RA) induces neuronal differentiation characterized by neurite extension and apparent morphological changes [43,60] (Figs. 1–2 ). Since the expression of AKNA was upregulated in both stemness and differentiation, demonstrating its dual impact in the cellular and molecular context. The shortfall of pluripotency inducing CoMiP plasmid (OCT4-SOX2-KLF4-cMYC tetrad) [51] to induce stemness in the absence of AKNA makes it a unique TF from other TFs, like LIN28 and NANOG, specifically in neuronal lineage [59,61] (Figs. 3–4 ). Future studies employing targeted perturbation of OCT4 independent of global stemness induction will be required to definitively establish directionality between OCT4 or other TFs and AKNA. AKNA expression alone is not sufficient but is instead regulated by subcellular localization and molecular interactions. In stemness, AKNA was localized to the nucleus, whereas during differentiation, AKNA was retained predominantly in the cytosol, correlated with the expression of neuronal differentiation markers and neurite formation [62,63] . Earlier reports suggest Ser/Thr phosphatase inhibition disrupts the centrosomal localization of AKNA [6] , and here in this study, it was observed that Tyrosine phosphatase inhibition retained AKNA in the cytosol. The role of tyrosine phosphorylation in the localization of AKNA need further investigation. RA is known to activate FAK signaling [54,64] and is described for its importance in neurodevelopmental processes [65] . Although FAK activity strongly correlates with cytoplasmic retention of AKNA and regulates the fate of neuroblastoma (Fig. 6 ) [54] , we did not detect a physical interaction between pFAK and AKNA in the neuroblastoma model. AKNA has been reported to be associated with centrosomal microtubule organization [6] , and FAK signaling is known to regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and microtubule associated trafficking [66,67] . It is plausible that FAK indirectly influences AKNA nucleocytoplasmic distribution through modulation of cytoskeletal to centrosomal signaling networks rather than through direct phosphorylation of AKNA [68] . These dynamic shifts of AKNA in the subcellular compartment for fate determination are very much similar to those of other TFs like SOX2, depending on the cellular context and interactions [69,70] . In the absence of AKNA, disruption of neuronal differentiation (e.g., TUBB3, NEFL, NEFM downregulated) without affecting intermediate progenitor cell identity (e.g., TBR2 unchanged) [71] and generation of bipolar neuron like cells in the presence of RA. Cytosolic AKNA possibly governs the later stages of neuronal differentiation, possibly post mitotic neuronal cells, as mitotic phase arrest is observed in the knockdown condition. Such stage specific role are well known in cortical neurogenesis, where different TFs sequentially orchestrate the process [72,73] . This mitotic arrest aligned with the previous findings of AKNA's role in CD40 and CD40L regulation in lymphocyte maturation and its important role in M-phase transition [5,74,75] . Prolonged mitotic arrest in the absence of AKNA with or without fate determining signals induce p53 dependent apoptotic cell death (Figs. 4–6 ). Although AKNA depletion induces both mitotic arrest and apoptosis, whether apoptosis is a direct consequence of mitotic arrest or is independently regulated by AKNA remains to be determined. The dynamic localization of AKNA and physical interaction with p53 directs a new molecular mechanism of neuronal cell survival that needs to be determined, when high p53 expression is reported in RA mediated neuronal differentiation [76,77] . The dual functions of AKNA on fate and self-proliferation warrant further studies, plausibly through differentiation stage-specific single-cell RNA sequencing to decipher the dynamics of AKNA in fate determination [78] . The OAC1 induced stem like states reflect the transcriptional landscape of embryonic stem cells, in which OCT4, SOX2, and PAX6 form a pluripotency network hub [79–81] . These genes were upregulated with simultaneous nuclear accumulation of AKNA protein in a time-dependent manner, irrespective of any external cues, which sites AKNA as a possible transcriptional regulator in neuroblast stemness. This is reinforced by the physical interaction between AKNA and KDM6B, important for activating pluripotency and stemness by removing the methylation mark [82,83] . The interdependency between KDM6B and AKNA is illustrated by the insufficiency of KDM6B to maintain stemness in the absence of AKNA, which reflects the molecular basis of neural stem cells, where epigenetic modifiers associated with TFs that establishes different lineages [84–86] . Strikingly, without altering the expression of KDM6B and global H3K27me3 dynamics, AKNA knockdown abolishes the efficiency of KDM6B to occupy the promoters of pluripotency and stemness genes (OCT4, SOX2, CD133, NES), evidenced by ChIP data (Fig. 7 ; Suppl. Fig. S18). This is allied with the role of KDM6B in neurodevelopment [87–89] . Although KDM6A can demethylate H3K27me3 [89] , KDM6B depletion was sufficient to repress stemness related genes, suggesting that endogenous unaltered KDM6A is not sufficient to compensate for the loss of KDM6B in the tested lines. Interaction between AKNA and KDM6B delivered a mechanistic axis link between epigenetic modification and transcriptional control on neuroblast plasticity. Induction of stemness and pluripotency upregulates KDM6B during OAC1 treatment, which reduces the repressive H3K27me3 mark on promoters that are aligned with its prevalent functions in neuronal stem cell maintenance [23,25,90] . In the absence of AKNA, occupancy of KDM6B is decreased in KDM6B overexpression conditions, suggesting that AKNA promotes and may stabilize the binding of KDM6B, as found in other TFs and demethylase complexes [14] . Whether AKNA has any role in the catalytic activity of KMD6B other than promoter occupancy should be determined by biochemical studies. These results will reinforce the understanding of neuronal development and the differentiation process. Retinoic acid drives neuronal differentiation and is a recognized model for studying neuronal lineage commitment for embryogenesis [91] , whereas OAC1 drives stemness by AKNA, advocating dual regulating mechanisms. However, the context dependent role of AKNA entangles the mechanism and prerequisites of the upstream regulation study, like FAK signaling, possibly through post translational modifications [92] of AKNA, and its functions in neuronal lineage commitment [93] . AKNA expression alone is not sufficient to dictate cell fate. Instead, our data support a model in which AKNA functions as a context dependent permissive regulator, whose activity is governed by subcellular localization and interaction with chromatin modifying partners or signaling molecules. In conclusion, AKNA emerges as a molecular keystone for neuronal lineage commitment by integration of transcription factors with epigenetic cues through an association with KDM6B. This work demonstrated a novel regulatory horizon that guides the balance between stemness and differentiation, presenting a foundation for the orchestration of neurodevelopmental plasticity with broadscale implication in developmental biology and regenerative medicine. title: Gain of chromosome 17 is an early genetic abnormality in neuroblastoma with PPM1D emerging as a strong candidate oncogene driving tumor progression
abstract: Segmental gain of chromosome 17q is the most common genetic aberration in high-risk neuroblastoma, but its role in disease progression is poorly understood. This study aims to address the contribution of 17q gain to neuroblastoma malignancy. We analyzed the genetic and transcriptional landscape of 417 neuroblastoma patients across various risk groups and clinical stages using multi-omic approaches. Single-cell RNA/DNA sequencing and SNP arrays were combined to characterize genomic aberrations, while evolutionary trajectories were mapped to explore the accumulation of genetic changes in patients with neuroblastoma. Additionally, DNA and RNA sequencing were used to assess mutational burden and gene expression patterns. Our findings suggest that chromosome 17 gain is an early genetic event acquired during neuroblastoma development, correlating with the accumulation of additional chromosomal aberrations and poor prognosis. Increased segmental gains of chromosome 17q were observed during clonal evolution, relapse disease and metastasis. We identified PPM1D, a p53-inducible Ser/Thr phosphatase located on chr17q22.3, as a key player activated by segmental 17q-gain, gene-fusion, or gain-of-function somatic and germline mutations, further promoting neuroblastoma development/progression. Gain of chromosome 17 is an early driver of genetic instability in neuroblastoma, with PPM1D emerging as a potential candidate gene implicated in high-risk disease progression.

mmc1.pptx APPLICATION CAN S0304-3835(25) -0 Fig. 1 Segmental chromosome 17q gain in neuroblastoma. A. Chromosome 17 gain with indicated break-points. Summary of segmental gains of chromosome 17 in the extended Swedish neuroblastoma cohort (n = 417). 192 samples displayed segmental gain of chromosome 17 as indicated by red horizontal bars with regions displaying additional level of gain (more copies) indicated by dark red color. An additional 127 cases showed whole chromosome gain of chromosome 17 (not shown in the figure). B. Gain of 17q correlates with poor survival in neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma survival probability according to Kaplan-Meier analysis in a Swedish population-based patient material in relation to chromosome 17 status in the tumor tissue shows worse overall survival (OS) for children with 17q segmental gain (n = 124; green line, 48.0 % 5 year OS) vs children with no segmental 17q gain (n = 141; blue line, 82.8 % 5 year OS). Fig. 1 Fig. 2 Chromosome 17 gain is an early event in neuroblastoma development. A . Evolutionary trajectories of chromosomal aberrations in neuroblastoma. Multiregional tumor sampling discloses chromosome 17 copy number (CN) accumulation in high-risk neuroblastoma. (I) Genome array analysis of pre-treatment biopsies (B1-B3), post-chemotherapy resection specimens (P1-P2) and concurrent bone marrow metastasis (M) from a female (F) 6-month-old (mo.) patient with a low-risk neuroblastoma (NB), having a whole genome profile with only numerical (NUM) changes (I, left). Evolutionary reconstruction (I, center) shows 15 aberrations in the phylogenetic stem, i.e. present in >90 % of tumor cells in all samples, followed by several additional whole chromosome changes at subclonal levels (arrows with numbers in blue type), distributed over a subset of samples. Segmental gain of chromosome 17q is the most common genetic aberration in high-risk neuroblastoma, but its role in disease progression is poorly understood. This study aims to address the contribution of 17q gain to neuroblastoma malignancy. We analyzed the genetic and transcriptional landscape of 417 neuroblastoma patients across various risk groups and clinical stages using multi-omic approaches. Single-cell RNA/DNA sequencing and SNP arrays were combined to characterize genomic aberrations, while evolutionary trajectories were mapped to explore the accumulation of genetic changes in patients with neuroblastoma. Additionally, DNA and RNA sequencing were used to assess mutational burden and gene expression patterns. Our findings suggest that chromosome 17 gain is an early genetic event acquired during neuroblastoma development, correlating with the accumulation of additional chromosomal aberrations and poor prognosis. Increased segmental gains of chromosome 17q were observed during clonal evolution, relapse disease and metastasis. We identified PPM1D , a p53-inducible Ser/Thr phosphatase located on chr17q22.3, as a key player activated by segmental 17q-gain, gene-fusion, or gain-of-function somatic and germline mutations, further promoting neuroblastoma development/progression. Gain of chromosome 17 is an early driver of genetic instability in neuroblastoma, with PPM1D emerging as a potential candidate gene implicated in high-risk disease progression. Keywords Neuroblastoma Chromosome 17q p53 WIP1 PPM1D 1 Introduction Chromosomal instability (CIN), caused by errors in DNA replication and chromosomal segregation during mitosis, is a hallmark of most human cancers [1 ]. CIN frequently results in structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities, leading to intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity, which disrupts key cancer pathways that give rise to phenotypic variations, posing challenges for therapeutic interventions [2 ]. Neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor of the sympathetic neural system, typically exhibits, like most childhood tumors, a low burden of somatic mutations [3 ]. Instead, CN alterations play a dominant role, where focal amplification of the MYCN oncogene, re-arrangements within the TERT locus on chromosome 5, segmental gains of chromosome 17q, and loss of chromosomes 1p36 and 11q all associated with high-risk disease and poor survival [4 ]. The most common cytogenetic abnormality in neuroblastoma is segmental or whole chromosomal gain of chromosome 17, detected in over 80 % of tumors [5 ]. Segmental gain of 17q21 extending to 17qter is observed in more than 60 % of tumors and is the most frequent genetic aberration linked to high-risk disease and poor prognosis of neuroblastoma patients [6 ]. Recent studies have added to the genomic complexity by revealing significant spatial genetic heterogeneity within neuroblastomas [7 ,8 ]. Furthermore, these tumors display distinct cell-type states, which may coexist within the same tumor [9 ]. While no genetic differences between these cell-type states have been reported, they are distinguished by variations in their transcriptional and epigenetic profiles [10 ]. Characterization of the genetic events during neuroblastoma evolution has shown that chromosomal gains crucial to disease pathogenesis typically occur early, within the first trimester of pregnancy [11 ]. This suggests that the intra-tumor heterogeneity may arise from the stepwise accumulation of genetic aberrations during embryonic development, with cells at different developmental maturation stages contributing to the heterogeneity observed in patient samples. Inactivating mutations of the tumor suppressor gene TP53 is a hallmark of adult cancers and lead to impaired DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoint arrest and apoptosis, ultimately resulting in accumulation of DNA mutations and CIN's [12 ]. Pediatric cancers, on the other hand, including neuroblastoma, rarely exhibit TP53 mutations [3 ]. Nevertheless, p53 activity is frequently compromised in neuroblastoma, particularly in relapsed tumors, where the incidence of TP53 mutations increases [13 ]. This suggests that inactivation of p53 remains critical for tumorigenesis, with alternative mechanisms likely contributing to its attenuation during early neuroblastoma development. One such mechanism may involve PPM1D , a gene located on chr17q22.3, which is frequently gained in high-risk neuroblastomas [5 ]. PPM1D encodes the nuclear serine/threonine phosphatase WIP1 (wild-type p53 induced phosphatase 1), a key regulator of DNA damage response and cell cycle progression, controlling the activity of p53, ATM, CHK1/2 and other key molecules involved in DNA repair, cell cycle progression and apoptosis [14–18 ]. In concordance, PPM1D mutations, amplifications and WIP1 overexpression have been identified in various cancers [19–27 ], and we recently demonstrated that overexpression of WIP1 in mice can drive tumor development, including neuroblastoma, by repressing p53 activity, promoting apoptotic escape, inducing genomic instability, and impairing growth arrest [28 ,29 ]. This suggests that PPM1D might acts as an oncogene, facilitating malignant tumor development. In this study, we use multi-omics approaches to investigate the genetic development of neuroblastoma, focusing on the most common aberration, gain of chromosome 17q, and the oncogenic role of PPM1D and the p53 regulating phosphatase WIP1. We demonstrate that gain of chromosome 17 is an early event in CIN during neuroblastoma development, with additional copies acquired through clonal evolution in aggressive and metastatic disease. Moreover, PPM1D gene fusions resulting in high expression levels of PPM1D as well as activating germline and somatic mutations were detected, suggesting a pivotal role of PPM1D in neuroblastoma disease progression. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Patient-derived tumor material and clinical data The collection of neuroblastoma tissue samples from Swedish patients was performed after either written or verbal consent obtained from parents/guardians according to ethical permits approved by the local Ethics Committee (Karolinska Institutet and Karolinska University Hospital, registration number 03–736, 2009/1369-31/1 and 2022- -1. Fresh tumor tissue was collected at surgery and snap-frozen and stored at −80o C until analysis. All patients were diagnosed, managed and treated according to national and international guidelines and protocols. 2.2 Neuroblastoma tissue genomics and transcriptomics 2.2.1 Patient material for genetic analysis DNA was extracted from frozen tumors or blood using DNeasy blood and tissue kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to manufacturer's protocol and evaluated through absorbance measurements, fluorometric quantitation and DNA integrity assessment on Agilent Tapestation (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA). Demographic and genomic data of patients are outlined in Table S1 . 2.2.2 SNP-microarray analysis Microarray analysis was performed on a consecutive series of samples from an unselected cohort of 417 neuroblastoma patients using Affymetrix CytoScan HD SNP microarrays (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). These analyses include the majority of cases from Sweden whereof 362 had sufficient tumor content and quality for assessment of copy number aberrations. Some tumors were staged according to the International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) and INRG criteria. Handling of the microarrays has been described previously [6 ,30 ]. Primary data analysis was performed using GeneChip Command Console Software version 5.0.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) prior CN analysis using Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS v.3.3.0; Thermo Fisher Scientific). All cases of chromosomal gain, loss, or amplification or allelic imbalances were scored, both segmental and numerical aberrations, including detailed information about the breakpoint positions when applicable. For practical reasons, all notations of gain and loss were considered in relation to a nominal tumor karyotype and a chromosomal break in a tumor was defined as a clear change in gene dose level in the genomic profile. All genomic position annotations are stated based on the hg19 build (http://genome.ucsc.edu/ ) of the human genome. 2.2.3 Analysis of 17q clonal evolution Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays including the Oncoscan (formalin fixed paraffins embedded samples) and Cytoscan HD (fresh frozen samples) platforms (Affymetrix Inc.) were retrieved from and subjected to comparisons of 17q CN. Evolutionary trajectories were formalized as phylogenetic ideograms along the lines described in the original publication [7 ]. In all, 100 multiregional samples collected from 23 patients with neuroblastoma were analyzed. Each patient was assigned to one of three simplified clinical-genetic risk groups, including children T; p.Q510∗), resulting in a premature truncation of the protein (Fig. 3 A). This mutation was found in a 26-month-old boy diagnosed with metastatic stage 4 (INSS/stage M, INRGSS) neuroblastoma originating in the left adrenal gland with bone metastases. The patient exhibited clinical features resembling previously described cases of children with intellectual disabilities and dysmorphic features associated with PPM1D germline mutations (Fig. S3B ). The tumor lacked MYCN amplification, and the patient had a poor clinical outcome after relapse and disease progression, despite multimodal clinical therapy. A detailed clinical description of this patient can be found in the Supplementary Methods section. Hence, the neuroblastoma-associated PPM1D mutations both resulted in C-terminal truncated variants of WIP1, similar to those gain-of-function variants identified in other cancers (Fig. 3 A) (http//:www.cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic/mutation/ ). In addition, by FusionCatcher analysis of RNA-sequencing data from neuroblastoma tumors we identified a gene fusion between PPM1D and the breast carcinoma amplified sequence 3 (BCAS3) gene located on chromosome 17q23.2 in a tumor from a patient enrolled in the Therapeutically Applicable Research to Generate Effective Treatments (TARGET) neuroblastoma dataset. This fusion was associated with high expression of PPM1D and a predicted WIP1 isoform with a truncated C-terminal (Fig. 3 B). These findings, together with the evidence that chromosome 17q gain is an early event in neuroblastoma tumorigenesis, suggest that genes within this chromosomal region, particularly PPM1D , play a key role in neuroblastoma progression. Given PPM1D 's known functions in DNA repair, cell cycle regulation, and apoptosis, it is a strong candidate for driving further genomic instability and tumor evolution. 3.4 Overexpression of PPM1D in neuroblastoma correlates with unfavorable clinical and biological features Our data demonstrating that the PPM1D gene is altered in CN and/or structure in the majority of 17q gained high-risk neuroblastomas, incited us to investigate the clinical prognostic and biological features of PPM1D gene expression in neuroblastoma. Our results demonstrate that higher expression levels of PPM1D was associated with several neuroblastoma risk factors, including metastatic stage 4 disease, older age at diagnosis (>18 months), MYCN -gene amplification and classification into the INRG high-risk (HR) group as defined by combined clinical and biological features associated with unfavorable clinical outcome [36 ] (Fig. 4 A). Notably, the highest PPM1D expression was observed in non-MYCN amplified HR-neuroblastoma tumors (nMN HR; Fig. 4 A), which predominantly correspond to cases with 11q-deletions, a group frequently harboring segmental 17q gains. Next, we correlated PPM1D expression with CN alterations, using data from CGH arrays, WES and WGS. CN gains were separated into numerical gains that included whole chromosome 17 and segmental gains that included the sub-region containing PPM1D . Correlation analysis revealed a significant gene dosage effect, with PPM1D expression increasing proportionally with the number of 17q copies (Fig. 4 A and B). Moreover, high PPM1D expression was strongly linked to poor clinical outcome, with significantly lower overall survival (OS; 59 % vs. 83 % at five years, p T (p.Gln510∗) somatic mutation has been reported previously in a malignant melanoma [66 ]. We also detected a gene fusion of PPM1D and BCAS3 expressed at high levels in a neuroblastoma patient. The fusion is predicted to generate a C-terminal truncation and cause augmented WIP1 protein levels. Similarly, a fusion between PPM1D and C1QTNF1 in an Ewing sarcoma patient has been reported to drive high WIP1 expression (https://pecan.stjude.cloud ). Additional PPM1D fusions, such as an intragenic region of RPSK6B1 and a PPM1D-ZNS655 fusion, have been described in patients with diffuse cerebellar glioma and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), although without further investigation on the effect on WIP1 protein stability and abundance [67 ] (https://pecan.stjude.cloud ). Given that PPM1D gene amplifications and C-terminal mutations are frequently detected in a wide spectrum of cancers [65 ] suggests that PPM1D is a pivotal gene on 17q contributing to neuroblastoma pathogenesis by promoting CIN and allowing tumor cells to evade p53-mediated apoptosis. In primary neuroblastoma, mutations of genes in the p53 pathway are rare, occurring in only 1–2 % of primary cases [39 ], but they become more common in relapsed disease (15 %) [39 ], where p53 inactivation appears to be linked to therapy resistance [68 ,69 ]. Mechanisms that inactivate p53 in neuroblastoma include MDM2 gene amplification or overexpression mediated by MYCN amplification, hypermethylation or deletion of CDKN2A , miR-380-5p-mediated repression of p53, or its inactivation by the methyltransferase SETD8 [13 ,70–73 ]. Under normal conditions, WIP1 attenuates p53 activation by inhibiting p53-mediated transactivation of promoters by dephosphorylating p53 at Ser15 [74 ]. Additionally, WIP1 indirectly inhibits p53 activity by dephosphorylating Mdm2 and upstream p53 activating kinases [14–18 ]. Amplification and gain-of-function mutations of PPM1D are proposed to only partially inhibit p53 activity, given that p53 undergoes multiple post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation, acetylation and ubiquitination that mediate p53-dependent beyond WIP1's regulatory influence [75 ]. Our recent mouse studies support this, showing that transgenic mice overexpressing PPM1D generate tumors phenotypically similar to Trp53 loss-of-function derived tumors29 rather than the spectra of tumors observed in Trp53 knock-out mice. The effects of this partial inhibition of p53 activity together with the WIP1-mediated delay in DNA repair processes [65 ] suggest that PPM1D activating mutations and/or overexpression disrupt the fidelity of DNA repair and DNA replication, allowing for accumulation of mutations and chromosomal aberrations that eventually result in malignant transformation. Our study demonstrates that gain of chromosome 17 is an early event in neuroblastoma and that additional copies of 17q, harboring PPM1D locus, are associated with high-risk, metastatic and relapsed disease. High WIP1 expression in neuroblastoma appears to allow for the accumulation of cells with SNV and CIN in neural crest cells during development, ultimately resulting in the emergence of neuroblastoma with increased tumor aggressiveness and resistance to treatment. Therefore, inhibiting WIP1 could be a valuable addition to neuroblastoma treatment, with potential benefits extending to other pediatric and adult cancers exhibiting WIP1 dysregulation. As segmental gain of chromosome 17q is the most common genetic aberration associated with high-risk neuroblastoma, other genes, in addition to PPM1D , located within the 17q21-17qter chromosomal region have been suggested to be involved in neuroblastoma initiation and/or development of high-risk disease [48–50 ]. Insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA binding protein-1 is encoded by the IGF2BP1 gene located on chromosome 17q21.32. IGF2BP1 is highly expressed in high-risk neuroblastoma and has been shown to induce neuroblastoma in transgenic mice where IGF2BP expression is driven by the dopamine hydroxylase promoter (dbh ) expressed in sympathoadrenal cells during development. IGF2BP1 has been shown to interact with Mycn in a feed-forward manner in which MYCN acting as a transcription factor induce the expression of IGF2BP1 whereas IGF2BP1 acting as an RNA binding protein stabilizes MYCN mRNA leading to increased half-life of Mycn proteins promoting the expression of other oncogenes contributing to the aggressive nature of high-risk neuroblastoma [50 ]. The T-box 2 transcription factor (TBX2 ) located on chromosome 17q21.22 is also overexpressed in high-risk neuroblastoma. TBX2 has been described as a super-enhancer included in the core regulatory circuitry (CRC) of transcription factors that regulate the expression of genes important for keeping neuroblastoma cells in an undifferentiated cellular state [48 ]. BIRC5 located on chromosome 17q25.3 encoding the anti-apoptotic protein survivin has for more than 25 years been shown to be associated with neuroblastoma and poor patient survival [49 ]. Although pharmacological or genetic repression of survivin inhibit the growth of neuroblastoma cells, this growth suppression was shown to be independent on 17q gain [5 ]. Moreover, a recent study combining DNA CN profiles and systems biology applying protein-protein networks analysis in high-risk NB harboring Chr 11q deletions identified five regulatory nodes corresponding to BIRC5, BRCA1, PRKCA, SUMO2 , and GPS1 all located on Chr 17q and that this may affect chromatin remodeling and DNA repair [76 ]. Although Chr 11q deletions has been considered to be a late chromosomal event in NB [59 ], this may contribute to the chromosomal heterogeneity observed in high-risk NB. In summary, our data position 17q gain as an early and possibly the initial event in neuroblastoma development, with PPM1D emerging as a strong candidate oncogene driving tumor progression through p53 pathway modulation and CIN promotion. Targeting WIP1 in neuroblastoma in combinations with current treatment modalities may address the challenge of genetic instability and therapy resistance, representing an avenue for improving outcomes in high-risk and relapsed pediatric neuroblastoma as well as other PPM1D -driven cancers. title: T-2 toxin induces senescence in human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells by regulating the HIF-1α/p53/p21 pathway
abstract: The mechanisms by which T-2 toxin induces senescence in neurons, along with the involvement of hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), remain poorly understood. Using human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells as a model, T-2 toxin (6 nM, 1–48 h) induced senescence in SH-SY5Y cells, leading to cell cycle arrest. This was mediated by the upregulation of proteins involved in cell cycle regulation and stimulation of IL-6 and NF-κB expression. T-2 toxin rapidly triggered the expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase, disrupted mitochondrial function, and altered the levels of Alzheimer’s disease-associated proteins (Tau, p-Tau, and APP). T-2 toxin also transiently elevated HIF-1α levels. Notably, HIF-1α regulated the expression of cell cycle inhibitory proteins (p16, p21, p53) and senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors (IL-8, IL-6, CCL2), along with the expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase, thereby exacerbating T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence. These findings underscore the vital role of HIF-1α in T-2 toxin-induced senescence in SH-SY5Y cells.
