T-2 toxin has diverse toxicological effects, raising concerns due to its potential to cross the blood-brain barrier, accumulate in the central nervous system, and invoke neurotoxic effects (Zhang et al., 2020 ). Its neurotoxic mechanisms are multifaceted, involving a series of interconnected pathways including inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and glial cell activation (Pei et al., 2021 ). The interplay of these pathways culminates in neuronal injury, which manifests in a spectrum of neurological dysfunctions and pathological alterations (Shahba et al., 2021 ). Cellular senescence represents a complex biological phenomenon that integrates various facets of cellular distress and numerous molecular pathways, encompassing persistent DNA damage responses, impairment of telomere integrity, and activation of oncogenes (Di Micco et al., 2021 ). Senescence research has yet to identify a universal or model-specific biomarker within culture medium or tissue specimen that is capable of reliably distinguishing senescent cells (Gorgoulis et al., 2019 ). At present, the identification of senescent cells is predicated on an array of markers, which include the enhanced expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), the buildup of lipofuscin, notably altered and flattened cellular morphology, and an increased cytoplasm-to-nucleus size ratio (Di Micco et al., 2021; Lopez-Otin et al., 2023 ). Moreover, a defining feature of cellular senescence is the notable upregulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (CDKNs), with p16 and p53 being the most important proteins that inhibit the cell cycle (Kandhaya-Pillai et al., 2023 ). The activation of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) unfolds as a dynamic sequence in tandem with cellular senescence. Expression of cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and CCL2, which constitute the SASP core, is observed in almost all senescent cell types cultured in vitro (Hawthorne et al., 2023 ). Certain mycotoxins, such as aflatoxin G1, can disrupt cellular metabolic activities and impinge upon NF-κB and c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling cascades, precipitating anomalous cellular functions and expediting the onset of senescence (Li et al., 2023a ). In the field of cellular biology, the ramifications of hypoxic environments on intracellular dynamics have garnered considerable interest. The hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) emerged as a critical regulatory element, orchestrating the activation of a multitude of genes during periods of low oxygen within cells, a phenomenon that appears to be widespread across cellular systems (Hayashi et al., 2019 ). Emerging evidence indicates that HIF-1α plays a consequential role in various physiological and pathological contexts, such as cancer biology, inflammatory responses, and angiogenic processes (Brockmueller et al., 2023 ). Pertinent research has revealed a strong correlation between crop-associated mycotoxins, particularly T-2 toxin, and hypoxia (Wu et al., 2020 ). This connection extends to immunological implications where HIF-1α is implicated in facilitating “immune evasion” mechanisms through the activation of the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway in the context of T-2 toxin exposure (You et al., 2022 ). Moreover, exposure to deoxynivalenol, a type B trichothecene mycotoxin, upregulates HIF-1α via the STAT3 signaling pathway, designating HIF-1α as an essential mediator of deoxynivalenol-elicited immunosuppressive responses (Zhang et al., 2023 ). In addition, emerging evidence suggests a significant link between mycotoxins (including T-2 toxin) exposure and the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Pei et al., 2021 ). The neurotoxic effects of T-2 toxin, particularly its ability to induce oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, mirror the pathological hallmarks observed in AD, including amyloid-beta plaque formation and tau hyperphosphorylation (Zhao et al., 2024 ). This connection underscores the importance of understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying T-2 toxin-induced neurotoxicity to develop potential therapeutic strategies and mitigate the risk of neurodegenerative diseases associated with environmental toxins. Within this framework, the potential involvement of mycotoxins, especially T-2 toxin, in triggering cellular senescence and the specific role of HIF-1α in this process have not been thoroughly investigated. Notably, a growing body of both in vivo and in vitro evidence underscores the brain as highly susceptible to mycotoxin-induced neurotoxic effects. This susceptibility may be associated with neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) (Pei et al., 2021; Mateo et al., 2022 ). The SH-SY5Y cells exhibit stable characteristics and demonstrate similar properties to neuronal cells in terms of signal transduction, and have been widely used in neuroscience research, particularly in studies of NDs (Wang et al., 2022 ). In this study, we employed the human neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y as an in vitro model to conduct both experimental and analytical assessments of the potential involvement of T-2 toxin in the critical process of cellular senescence within SH-SY5Y and the underlying function of HIF-1α in this context. The findings are anticipated to enhance the comprehension of the neurotoxic effects exerted by T-2 toxin and to offer prospective targets for intervention and therapeutic strategies against T-2 toxin-induced cellular damage. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Chemicals T-2 toxin was acquired from Qifa Experimental Reagent, Shanghai, China. Minimum Essential Medium (MEM), Ham’s F-12 medium, non-essential amino acids, sodium pyruvate, and GlutaMAX-1 were all purchased from iCell Bioscience, Shanghai, China. Dimethyl sulfoxide and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) transfer membranes for western blotting were obtained from Merck. Trypsin was obtained from Hyclone, Logan, USA. YC-1, an inhibitor of HIF-1α, was obtained from Bidepharm, Shanghai, China. Propidium iodide (PI) staining solution was purchased from Servicebio, Wuhan, China. The Senescence β-Galactosidase Staining Kit and Cell Counting Kit-8 were obtained from Beyotime, Shanghai, China. All the chemicals utilized in our study possess exceptional purity levels (≥99%). The primary and secondary antibodies used for western blotting are summarized in Supplementary Table 1 . 2.2 Cell culture and treatments Human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells were obtained from iCell Biotechnology, Shanghai. Cells were grown in MEM/F12 medium added with 10% fetal bovine serum (Tianhang Bio-technology, Hangzhou, China), 1% non-essential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate, 1% GlutaMAX-1, and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Solarbio, Beijing, China), kept in a humidified incubator (Changjin, Changsha, China) at 37°C and 5% CO2 . Cultured SH-SY5Y cells were inoculated from T-25 culture flasks into six-well plates at a density of 1×106 cells/mL (Cell counting using the TC20; Bio-Rad Automatic Cell Counter, USA). Based on CCK-8 assay results, the experimental concentration of T-2 toxin was defined as 6 nM. SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to T-2 toxin (6 nM) for 1, 2, 6, 12, 24 and 48 h. Simultaneously, a negative control (NC) group was treated only with MEM/F12 complete medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum, whereas a positive control group was treated with 100 μM CoCl2 for comparison of HIF-1α expression levels. In certain experiments, cells were first treated with the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1 (10 μM) for 24 h (Hu et al., 2020 ) and then incubated with T-2 toxin (6 nM) for the indicated times. 2.3 Western blotting Cellular protein extraction was conducted on ice, with pre-cooled sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), EP tubes, and a centrifuge, all maintained at 4°C, to ensure optimal conditions. Treated cells were lysed at 4°C for 20 min in RIPA buffer (Servicebio) containing protease inhibitors. After centrifuging the lysate, the supernatant was collected. The protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay kit (Beyotime). The protein concentration was diluted to 20 μg/μL, and 40 μg protein sample was transferred to each western blot lane. Extracted cellular proteins were isolated using sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis gels and moved to PVDF membranes, then left to incubate overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies (1:2000) mixed in TBST containing 5% skimmed milk powder (Servicebio). After rinsing three times with TBST, the membrane was incubated with the secondary antibody (1: ) for 1 h at room temperature (18–25°C). The PVDF membranes were developed with ECL luminescence reagent (Meilun Biotechnology, Dalian, China). 2.4 Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) For qPCR analysis, we referred to experimental methods previously described by our research group (You et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In brief, total RNA was isolated using an RNA Extraction Kit (Tiangen Biotech, Beijing, China). RNA was reverse-transcribed using cDNA synthesis premix reagent (Tiangen Biotech). The qPCR was performed using a CFX96 Thermal Cycler system (Bio-Rad, USA) as follows. The initial phase involved pre-denaturation at 95°C lasting 30 s, succeeded by a 15 s denaturation phase at the same temperature, and the subsequent phase encompassed a 30 s annealing and extension step at 60°C. After 40 cycles, the fluorescence signal was recorded. The sequences of the specific primers are presented in Supplementary Table 2 . Results were computed using the 2-ΔΔCT method. 2.5 Flow cytometry The cultured cells were digested by trypsin, washed with pre-cooled PBS 1× at 4°C, and centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 min. The cells were fixed with pre-cooled 75% ethanol at −20°C and kept away from light overnight at 4°C. Subsequently, cells were rinsed with pre-cooled PBS. To remove RNA, RNaseA (1 mg/mL, 2 μL; Solarbio) was added to the solution kept in a 37°C water bath for 40 min. Fluorescence labeling was performed by staining with 100 µL of 100 µg/mL PI staining solution for 20 min protected from light. Flow cytometry was performed using an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength of 585±21 nm. The cell cycle distribution was analyzed with Modfit software (Modfit LT 5.0 software, USA). 2.6 SA-β-gal staining SA-β-gal activity was assessed using a Senescence-associated β-Galactosidase Staining Kit. SH-SY5Y cells, cultured in six-well plates at a density of approximately 1×106 cells/mL, were rinsed with PBS, followed by a 15 min fixation step and three wash steps. PBS was aspirated, each well was supplemented with 1 mL of SA-β-gal staining solution, the six-well plates were wrapped with parafilm to avoid evaporation, and the cells were plated overnight at 37°C with staining solution, protected from light. The cells were observed and photographed using an inverted microscope. ImageJ software (version 1.53q, National Institutes of Health, USA) was used for image analysis to assess the proportion of positive cells to the total cell count in each group. The experiment was performed three times. 2.7 Transmission electron microscopy The medium was discarded from the grouped cultured cells, trypsin was added, and the cells were gently blown and centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was discarded, electron microscope fixative (Servicebio) was added, and cell pellet was resuspended. After fixation for 30 min at room temperature away from light, the cells were kept at 4°C. Subsequently, the cells were embedded in agar, fixed in osmium acid, dehydrated in ethanol at room temperature gradient for 15 min, impregnated with acetone:812 embedding agent, and subsequently embedded in pure 812 embedding agent. The cells were sectioned with an ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems, Weztlar, Germany), stained, and observed under a transmission electron microscope (HT7800; Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan). The images captured for analysis. 2.8 Statistical analyses Each experiment was repeated three times. GraphPad Prism (version 9.0.0, San Diego, USA) software was used for analyzing the data and creating graphs. Values were summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and intergroup variations were evaluated using one-way analysis of variance (one-way ANOVA) to assess statistical significance. p -values <0.05 were regarded as significant. 3 Results 3.1 T-2 toxin induces HIF-1α expression in SH-SY5Y cells Human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells were maintained in cultures, the morphology of the adherent cells was epithelioid with short extensions, and the cells tended to grow in clusters (Supplementary Figure 1). Initially, to evaluate the cytotoxic effects of T-2 toxin on SH-SY5Y cells, the CCK-8 assay was employed, revealing that T-2 toxin decreases cell viability in a time- and concentration-dependent manner ( Fig. 1 A). To balance inducing measurable toxic effects with retaining survivable cell populations, a T-2 toxin concentration of 6 nM was selected for subsequent experiments. Subsequent assays were aimed at exploring whether exposure to T-2 toxin can increase HIF-1α levels in SH-SY5Y cells. qPCR and western blotting experiments were conducted to analyze the changes in HIF-1α expression levels across a time frame spanning 1–48 h (Fig. 1 B, C). CoCl2 , a chemical agent acknowledged as a hypoxia mimic capable of upregulating HIF-1α levels, was deployed at a 100 μM concentration to act as a positive control in these experiments (Nowak-Stepniowska et al., 2022 ). The HIF-1α expression levels in cells subjected to CoCl2 were markedly and significantly elevated (p <0.01). Intriguingly, the pattern of HIF1A expression induced by T-2 toxin exposure fluctuated over time (Fig. 1 B). The overall protein expression results were consistent with the trends observed at the gene level—initially rising, subsequently diminishing, before ultimately rising again—with the apex of HIF-1α expression at 6 h (Fig. 1 C). Collectively, these observations substantiate the premise that T-2 toxin can upregulate HIF-1α expression in the human neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y. 3.2 T-2 toxin activates the expression of senescence-associated regulators in SH-SY5Y cells To confirm the induction of senescence in SH-SY5Y cells by T-2 toxin, we quantified the expression levels of senescence-associated biomarkers, including proteins such as p16, p21, p53, IL-6, and NF-κB and lncRNAs such as TERC , PINT , and DINO . These biomarkers were measured at various time points using western blotting and qPCR ( Fig. 2 ). Compared to the NC group, the p16 expression was notably decreased upon the administration of T-2 toxin for 1 h. This was followed by a continuous increase from 2 to 12 h, culminating in the highest expression level at 12 h. In contrast, p21 levels rose steadily during T-2 toxin exposure, reaching significant increases of 3.58-fold and 6.94-fold after 24 and 48 h, respectively (both p <0.01). The p53 protein exhibited a marked elevation (p <0.01) between 2 and 12 h of T-2 treatment, with the zenith at 6 h. IL-6 levels were significantly upregulated starting 1 h post-treatment and remained elevated from 12 to 48 h. The apex of IL-6 expression occurred at 24 h with a 1.68 times higher level than that observed in the NC group (p <0.01). For NF-κB expression, an initial significant decrease after 1 h of T-2 toxin treatment was observed, followed by a pronounced upregulation from 2 to 48 h, peaking at 12 h to a level 1.19 times that of the NC group (p <0.01; Fig. 2 A, B). These findings suggest that T-2 toxin catalyzes the activation of pivotal cellular senescence-associated proteins in SH-SY5Y cells, prompting senescence. To further dissect the senescence induction in SH-SY5Y cells attributed to T-2 toxin, we assessed using qPCRs the expression of the lncRNAs TERC , PINT , and DINO —key telomerase components, integrally linked with cellular senescence—at 2, 6, 12, and 24 h after-T-2 toxin exposure. Administration of T-2 toxin resulted in a general downregulation of TERC and PINT levels. TERC expression was decreased at 2 and 6 h relative to that of the NC group, hitting a low of 0.23-fold, and showed an increase at 12–24 h while remaining below the NC group benchmarks. PINT showed reduced expression levels from 2 to 12 h, with its nadir at 0.47-fold that of the NC group, and an increase at 24 h not surpassing the NC group levels. Strikingly, DINO levels were consistently upregulated from 2 to 24 h, reaching up to 3.77-fold those of the NC group at baseline (Fig. 2 C). These data signal that T-2 toxin exerts its effect by hindering the synthesis of the telomerase complex and instigating DNA damage within cells. 3.3 T-2 toxin induces senescence of SH-SY5Y cells by inducing cell cycle arrest and stimulating the expression of SA-β-gal Cellular senescence is characterized by a permanent cessation of the cell cycle, heightened activity of SA-β-gal, alterations in cell morphology, and mitochondrial dysfunction—all of which serve as indicators of the senescent state (Gorgoulis et al., 2019 ). This study identified senescent cells using flow cytometry and SA-β-gal staining assays. In addition, we noted the occurrence of ultrastructural damage in SH-SY5Y cells after exposure to T-2 toxin. While senescent cells retain metabolic functions for a limited time, they are insensitive to mitogenic signals, resulting in sustained cell cycle arrest (Di Micco et al., 2021 ). Flow cytometric analysis was employed to examine the cell cycle distribution. Supplementary Figure 2 demonstrates that the proportion of cells in the G1 phase relative to the whole population rose from 64.61% at 6 h after T-2 toxin treatment to 66.01% at 24 h. These findings suggest that the interruption of both pre- and post-DNA synthesis processes increased progressively with the duration of T-2 toxin exposure. SA-β-gal is a glycoside hydrolase, and X-gal can be hydrolyzed by β-gal at pH 6.0 to form a blue-green precipitate that accumulates in cells, serving as a hallmark of senescent cells ( Fig. 3 ). Analyses of SA-β-gal staining showed that the area ratio of SA-β-gal-positive cells in the NC group was 4.30±2.65%, which increased rapidly 2 h after T-2 toxin treatment to 43.69±33.77%, and the area ratios were 18.34±10.81% and 17.39±12.01% after 6 and 24 h, respectively. The administration of the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1 followed by T-2 toxin resulted in area ratios of 17.72±8.37% and 6.10±1.32% after 6 h and 24 h, respectively, whereas the area ratios were 1.07±1.14% for YC-1 administration alone (Fig. 3 ). These results showed a substantial increase in senescent markers in T-2 toxin-treated cells, suggesting that T-2 toxin rapidly upregulated the expression of cellular SA-β-gal in a short period of time, which manifested early senescence. HIF-1α appeared to modulate the expression of this enzyme during extended T-2 toxin exposure. Transmission electron microscopy analyses demonstrated that the morphology of NC SH-SY5Y cells was normal, with clear edges of the cell membrane. Moreover, the mitochondria were structurally intact, uniformly distributed, and numerous. After 24 h of T-2 treatment, the cells were abnormally enlarged and flattened, and the cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio was disproportionately increased. In the YC-1+T-2 toxin-treated group, the nucleus morphology showed irregular contractions. The NC group showed mitochondria with clear double membrane structures and a uniform distribution of mitochondrial cristae. The numbers of mitochondria in the T-2 and YC-1+T-2 groups were significantly decreased compared to that of the control group. Cellular morphology of the T-2 and YC-1+T-2 groups observed under a transmission electron microscope showed that the mitochondria had blurred cell membranes and sparse cristae; some mitochondrial inner membranes were broken with vacuole-like degeneration ( Fig. 4 ). The transmission electron microscopy results suggest that T-2 toxin can evoke the morphological features of substantial cellular senescence and induce senescence of SH-SY5Y cells by damaging mitochondria. 3.4 HIF-1α plays a crucial regulatory role in T-2-induced cellular senescence Having established that T-2 toxin upregulates HIF-1α expression and induces cellular senescence in SH-SY5Y cells, we hypothesized the crosstalk between HIF-1α and T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence. The HIF-1α-specific inhibitor YC-1 was used to confirm the regulatory role of HIF-1α in cellular senescence. Evaluating the levels of the CDKNs p16 and p21 is a way to detect cells in cell cycle arrest, and p53 can arrest cell cycle progression in several ways. After specifically blocking HIF-1α with 10 μM YC-1 before T-2 toxin treatment, the levels of the cell cycle arrest-relevant proteins p16, p21, and p53 were significantly inhibited (p <0.01) at 6 h compared to those of the toxin group ( Fig. 5 ). This suggests that HIF-1α increases the T-2 toxin-induced expression of p16, p21, and p53 to some extent, exacerbating their inhibitory effect on the cell cycle. Activation of SASP is a hallmark of senescence. After inhibiting HIF-1α during T-2 toxin treatment, IL-6 expression was increased relative to that of the toxin group. After the administration of YC-1 alone, IL-6 levels were remarkably elevated compared to those of the NC and toxin groups, suggesting that HIF-1α suppressed the expression of IL-6 to a certain extent. The overall expression trends of IL-8 and CCL2 were similar. Unlike IL-6, IL-8 and CCL2 were significantly downregulated after the addition of YC-1, suggesting that HIF-1α positively regulates IL-8 and CCL2 expression. NF-κB levels after T-2 toxin treatment were significantly increased (1.53-fold, p <0.01) compared to those of the NC group. After co-incubation with T-2 toxin and YC-1, the NF-κB levels did not exhibit as significant changes as observed in p16, p21, and p53 compared to the toxin group, suggesting that the inhibitory effect of HIF-1α on NF-κB was not as obvious as the inhibition of the cell cycle (Fig. 5 ). These results indicate that T-2 toxin-induced senescence occurs in SH-SY5Y cells, with HIF-1α being a pivotal mediator in the regulation of toxin-induced cellular senescence. 3.5 T-2 toxin changes the activation of Tau, p-Tau, and APP—Key proteins of Alzheimer’s disease T-2 toxin is recognized as a potent neurotoxin. Growing evidence suggests a link between mycotoxin metabolites and NDs (Nguyen et al., 2022a ), and an increasing interest exists in uncovering additional associations between T-2 toxin and AD. In this context, we investigated the effects of T-2 toxin on pivotal AD-related proteins—including Tau, phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), and amyloid precursor protein (APP)—and the expression of the lncRNA BACE1-AS , which is highly specific and transcribed in the brains of patients with AD (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Furthermore, our study delved into how HIF-1α modulates the expression of these proteins following T-2 toxin exposure ( Fig. 6 ). After 1 and 2 h of T-2 toxin treatment, p-Tau expression was suppressed, followed by a notable rise at 6–24 h (p <0.01) in comparison to that of the NC group. Tau levels were markedly increased (p <0.01) at 1 h of T-2 toxin treatment, then aligned gradually with those of the NC group at 2 and 6 h, and were significantly decreased (p <0.01) at 12–48 h. After the addition of YC-1 to T-2 toxin, p-Tau expression was markedly reduced relative to that of the toxin group (p <0.01), and Tau expression levels were considerably decreased compared with those of the NC and toxin groups (p <0.01; Fig. 6 A). Given that amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques in the brains of patients with AD predominantly result from APP cleavage by β- and γ-secretases, we also measured APP expression. APP levels were not significantly different from those of the NC group at 1 h; however, they were notably downregulated at 2, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h following T-2 toxin treatment. According to these results, 12 h was chosen as the time point to investigate the influence of HIF-1α on T-2 toxin-triggered APP expression. In line with the results of the time-dependent experiments, APP expression was markedly reduced after 12 h of T-2 toxin treatment. The addition of YC-1 to T-2 toxin treatment markedly reduced the APP levels compared to those of the NC group but markedly upregulated them compared to those of the toxin group (p <0.01). BACE1-AS was significantly downregulated by T-2 toxin at 12 h (Fig. 6 B). These findings indicate that T-2 toxin may provoke alterations in the expression of crucial AD proteins, hinting at the possible involvement of HIF-1α in the pathogenesis of mycotoxin-induced NDs in humans. 4 Discussion T-2 toxin is associated with various adverse negative health effects, including neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates a potential link between mycotoxin exposure and cellular aging or senescence (Li et al., 2023b ). The effects of mycotoxin exposure, including T-2 toxin, on cell senescence is an area of active research, requiring further investigation to thoroughly comprehend the scope and mechanisms of mycotoxin-induced cellular senescence (Wu et al., 2022 ). In the current study, we investigated the possibility of T-2 toxins inducing cellular senescence, with a focus on the involvement of HIF-1α activation. Mycotoxins can induce hypoxia (Wu et al., 2020; You et al., 2022 ). Mycotoxins inhibits mitochondrial function, resulting in the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which further damages cellular components and impairs oxygen utilization (You et al., 2021 ). The stabilization and activation of HIF-1α under mycotoxin exposure suggest a cellular attempt to adapt to a hypoxic environment. We treated SH-SY5Y cells with CoCl2 to establish an in vitro hypoxia model as a positive control. Our results showed that SH-SY5Y cells undergo intermittent hypoxia in response to T-2 toxin (Fig. 1 B, C). Similarly, in RAW264.7 cells, deoxynivalenol persistently activated Hif1a , displaying a similar intermittent upregulation (Zhang et al., 2023 ). We further showed that T-2 toxin induces senescence in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 2 ). CDKNs are negative regulators of cell cycle progression; p21 and p16 are known inducers of senescence, and p53 and pRb are critical for establishing cell-cycle arrest; prolonged overexpression of any of these elements is sufficient to induce senescence (Zarneshan et al., 2023 ). In our study, p16, p21, and p53 were activated, peaking at 12, 48, and 6 h after T-2 toxin treatment, respectively. When cells are subjected to DNA damage or other stress stimuli, p53 is usually activated, and its expression is increased compared to that of other proteins (Zhou and Liu, 2022 ). These findings suggest that T-2 toxin-induced cell cycle arrest may proceed through the p53/p21 pathway, and the p16/pRb pathway may also be involved. Nonetheless, the intricate interplay between the upstream and downstream components of the HIF-1α/p53/p21 pathway, as influenced by T-2 toxin, requires further validation through subsequent research. In our study, we observed a significant increase in NF-κB levels following T-2 toxin treatment. The increase in NF-κB levels suggests that T-2 toxin induces a cellular stress response, likely mediated by oxidative stress, DNA damage, and inflammatory signaling pathways, leading to the activation of NF-κB. lncRNAs play vital roles in diverse physiological and pathological conditions. T-2 toxin treatment inhibited the expression of the lncRNAs TERC and PINT but increased lncRNA DINO expression (Fig. 2 C). The classical function of TERC , a core component of telomerase, is to provide a template for telomerase extension (Mao et al., 2016 ). Insufficient telomerase activity leads to diseases associated with senescence. In the presence of DNA damage, PINT , as a negative regulator of cell cycle arrest, negatively regulates the p53 pathway. DINO is a p53-dependent gene for DNA damage in response to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Therefore, our findings suggest that T-2 toxin causes a DNA damage response that activates p53 and impairs the telomere balance by inhibiting the synthesis of the lncRNA TERC telomerase complex, potentially contributing to cellular senescence through telomere shortening. Flow cytometry analysis (Supplementary Figure 2) showed a gradual increase in G1 and G2 phase arrests with T-2 toxin treatment duration. Cells undergoing senescence typically stall in the G0 or G1 phases, reducing proliferation capacity, similar to previous observations in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from amnestic mild cognitive impairment (Salech et al., 2022 ). SA-β-gal expression, a biomarker to detect and quantify cellular senescence, was enhanced after 2 h of T-2 toxin exposure (Fig. 3 ). In our study, we did not conduct a statistical analysis comparing the T-2 toxin and YC-1 co-treatment group with the T-2 toxin alone group to determine any significant effects on cellular SA-β-gal. However, this does not entirely eliminate the potential for differences between the two groups, particularly at the 2-h and 24-h marks. After 24 h of T-2 treatment, cells appeared to be wrinkled compared to cells at 6 h, which corresponded to the transmission electron microscopy results. Apart from cellular flattening and morphological abnormalities, we noted that T-2 toxin treatment resulted in increased cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratios, as well as changes in mitochondrial number and structure, in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 4 ). All these findings suggest that T-2 toxin induces the SH-SY5Y cell senescence. We further focused on the role of HIF-1α in mycotoxin-induced cellular senescence. Current research suggests that hypoxia might have a dual role in cellular senescence, acting both as a physiological regulator of stress-induced senescence and preventing cellular senescence processes (Otero-Albiol and Carnero, 2021; van Vliet et al., 2021 ). Our results showed that HIF-1α positively regulated p16, p21, p53, IL-8, and CCL2, suggesting HIF-1α is involved in the promotion of T-2 toxin-induced SH-SY5Y cell senescence (Fig. 5 ). In addition, inhibition of HIF-1α exacerbated in our study the damage to mitochondrial structures (Fig. 4 ), suggesting a protective effect of HIF-1α on mitochondria. Similarly, prior studies have shown that HIF-1α can attenuate mitochondrial damage by promoting energy metabolism (Zhuonan et al., 2015 ). Moreover, HIF-1α regulates mitochondrial function and reduces the production of reactive oxygen species, providing a protective effect (Li et al., 2019 ). Under hypoxic conditions, HIF-1α stabilizes and translocates to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of genes involved in glycolysis and reduces mitochondrial oxygen consumption by downregulating mitochondrial biogenesis and function (You et al., 2021 ). This shift in metabolic pathways reduces the production of ROS by limiting the electron transport chain's activity, thereby minimizing oxidative stress and potential cellular damage. In addition, we observed that T-2 toxin treatment led to HIF-1α activation and induced cellular senescence. This suggests that the role of HIF-1α in cellular stress response can lead to senescence through specific signaling. Even with normal mitochondrial function, mitochondrial DNA mutations and altered energy metabolism can exacerbate senescence (Atamna et al., 2018 ). Thus, HIF-1α may exhibit different biological effects and depend on the type of stress, cellular environment, and interactions with other pathways. Our findings highlight the dual protective and senescent roles of HIF-1α under specific conditions and stressors. In addition to the relationship between T-2 toxin and cellular senescence, we were also interested in the connection between T-2 toxin and key factors of AD. We showed that T-2 toxin consistently reduced APP expression, whereas HIF-1α negatively regulated APP. BACE1-AS was downregulated 12 h after T-2 toxin exposure, could be indicative of a cellular response aimed at counteracting the toxic effects of T-2 Toxin. Considering that T-2 toxin induces cellular senescence through the HIF-1α/p53/p21 pathway, it is conceivable that the down-regulation of BACE1-AS forms part of a comprehensive adaptive response to oxidative stress and DNA damage, designed to alleviate additional neuronal harm. Related studies demonstrated that BACE1-AS expression is significantly upregulated in the brains of patients with AD and promotes Aβ production (Zhang et al., 2018 ). A study reported that chronic hypoxia favors NDs in a mouse model of Leigh’s syndrome, that normobaric respiration at 11% O2 protects against neurodegeneration in patients with Leigh’s syndrome, and that hypoxia prevents and even reverses brain damage in mice with late neuropathology (Ferrari et al., 2017 ). Moreover, intermittent hypoxic acclimation of transgenic AD mice protected against anxiety-like behaviors as well as memory and learning impairments, markedly decreased cortical Aβ levels, markedly elevated glucose levels in the cerebral cortex, and significantly improved cognition and recovery of mitochondrial bioenergetic profiles (Correia et al., 2021 ). Our findings suggest a potential additional link between mycotoxin T-2 toxin and NDs (Nguyen et al., 2022b ). Nevertheless, our study using one cell line is not sufficient to generalize pathway activation. Furthermore, although signaling pathways can be triggered in vitro cell models, it remains unclear whether they are activated in vivo . Our study has some limitations. Future research should test multiple cell lines or animal models, and additional molecules in autophagy-regulated signaling pathways should be analyzed to further validate and expand the breadth of our findings. In addition to HIF-1α, HIF-1β could also be explored to elucidate the mechanisms of T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence in cellular hypoxic microenvironments. Given that RNA interference exhibits potential immunostimulatory properties, we did not employ the HIF-1α knockdown methodology in our study. Nonetheless, in future studies, we can refine the knockdown experiments to more definitively ascertain the function of HIF-1α within the cellular senescence process. 5 Conclusion Our research elucidated that T-2 toxin induces cell senescence in SH-SY5Y cells by upregulating the expression of cellular senescence-associated factors, such as p16 (peaked 12 h), p21, and IL-6, and by increasing the activity of SA-β-gal (at 2 h), which leads to cell cycle arrest (G1 phase). Notably, HIF-1α is a critical target of T-2 toxin and participates in T-2 toxin-induced cellular senescence by affecting the expression of CDKNs (p16, p21, p53) and SASP factors (IL-8, IL-6, CCL2), along with the expression of SA-β-gal. Furthermore, a link between T-2 toxin and NDs may exist, with HIF-1α being a target of T-2 toxin regulating key AD proteins, including Tau, p-Tau, and APP (Supplementary Figure 3). This study offers insights into the field of mycotoxin-induced cellular senescence and further elucidates the information on the interaction between HIF-1α and cellular senescence mechanisms. title: Differential chromatin accessibility response to retinoic acid in neuroblastoma with ATRX in-frame-deletions versus ATRX loss-of-function
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer, arising in the developing sympathetic nervous system. Differentiation therapy with 13-cis-retinoic acid (RA) is given to children with neuroblastoma to prevent relapse, however there is little understanding of which patients benefit. ATRX alterations are identified in 10 % of high-risk neuroblastomas and associated with poor outcomes. The commonest type of ATRX alterations in neuroblastoma are in-frame multi-exon deletions, followed by nonsense mutations predicted to result in loss-of-function (ATRX LoF). We treated paired ATRX wild-type and LoF neuroblastoma cell-lines with RA: cells with ATRX LoF fail to upregulate direct RA target genes and show reduced chromatin accessibility differentiation and development related genes following RA treatment. Conversely, neuroblastoma models with in-frame deletions mount an appropriate epigenetic response to RA. Taken together this shows that the mechanism of differentiation in ATRX-altered neuroblastoma depends on the type of ATRX alteration, with implications relating to both oncogenesis and therapeutic response.

Results ATRX LoF neuroblastoma cells have an impaired chromatin response to RA compared to their wild-type counterparts To investigate the role of ATRX in differentiation, we used paired ATRX wild-type (ATRX WT) and LoF induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) [10 ] to generate human axial progenitor (HAP) cells, as the first step in differentiation towards neural crest lineage (Fig 1 A, Fig S1A-D) [11 ]. We saw no significant difference in the expression of the pluripotency markers OCT4 and NANOG in ATRX LoF iPSCs compared with ATRX WT iPSCs, although did see a significant downregulation of SOX2 expression (Fig 1 A). This is consistent with findings in glioma models identifying suppression of SOX2 expression with ATRX depletion [33 ]. Upon HAP differentiation, we saw a robust induction of expression of the axial progenitor marker CDX2 in both ATRX WT and LoF iPSCs (Fig 1 B), however this was only associated with induction of HOXC gene expression in ATRX WT cells (Fig 1 C). In normal embryonic development, CDX2 co-ordinates the spatial and temporal expression of HOX genes together with RA [34 ,35 ]. Given that RA is also used clinically as a differentiation therapy for patients with neuroblastoma, we next asked if a similar phenotype was seen when ATRX LoF neuroblastoma cells were treated with RA. Paired ATRX WT (p53(2)) and ATRX LoF (E6) neuroblastoma cells [36 ] were treated with RA and evaluated for expression of known RA target genes: CYP26A, HOXA1 and HOXA4 [37 ]. Concordant with our findings in ATRX LoF iPSCs, we also identified a failure of upregulation of direct RA target genes in neuroblastoma cells with ATRX LoF (Fig 2 A-B). We next analyzed sensitivity to RA in the paired cell lines by clonogenic assay. We saw no difference in sensitivity to RA between ATRX WT and LoF cells (Fig 2 C) however, the parental cell line was already highly retinoic acid resistant. Of note, the parental cell line is derived from a SH-EP cell [36 ] which is known to be a mesenchymal cell line with a super-enhancer landscape that associated with RA resistance [38 ]. Therefore, we next decided to evaluate the direct effects of ATRX LoF on chromatin accessibility by ATAC sequencing (Fig 2 D-J). We identified widespread differences in chromatin accessibility in ATRX LoF compared with ATRX WT neuroblastoma in both vehicle control conditions (Fig 2 D, Table S1) and upon treatment with RA (Fig 2 E, Table S1). Transcription factor binding motif analysis of differentially accessible peaks in response to RA also identified that a greater number of both over and under-represented peaks were seen in response to RA in ATRX WT cells compared with ATRX LoF cells (Fig 2 F, Table S1). However, both ATRX wild-type and ATRX LoF cells appropriately opened chromatin at the transcription factor binding motifs for the RA response elements RARA in response to RA (Fig S2A-B). We performed gene ontology (GO) analysis of differential accessibility in gene promoter regions between ATRX LoF and WT cells. Given the large number of terms identified, we used REVIGO [23 ] to summarize and remove redundant GO terms (Fig 2 G-H). The key GO terms with an increase in accessibility in ATRX LoF cells were in acute inflammatory response pathways (Fig 2 G-H), consistent with our work identifying an immunogenic phenotype in ATRX- altered neuroblastoma [9 ]. We also evaluated for differences in individual GO terms related to differentiation between ATRX LoF and WT cells which identified decreased accessibility in multiple critical pathways in embryonic development in ATRX LoF cells compared with WT cells in both vehicle control and RA treated conditions (Fig 2 I-J, Table S1). The top 3 differentiation related GO terms with reduced accessibility in ATRX LoF cells compared with wild-type cells, showed similar patterns in both vehicle control and RA treated conditions, however in all cases a greater number of genes were identified with differentially closed chromatin in ATRX mutant cells following RA treatment compared with vehicle control. These were: Pattern Specification Process (97 genes with less accessible chromatin in vehicle control conditions, 141 genes with RA treatment); Regionalization (90 genes with less accessible chromatin in vehicle control conditions, 132 genes with RA treatment); and Embryonic Organ Development (85 genes with less accessible chromatin in vehicle control conditions, 141 genes with RA treated treatment) (Table S1 ). Genes from the top enriched differentiation associated GO terms that became accessible following RA treatment of ATRX wild-type but not LoF cells included multiple HOX genes (HOXA7, HOXA10, HOXA9 , Table S1). Chromatin at the RARA and RARB genes was differentially closed in ATRX LoF cells compared with wild-type cells in both vehicle control and RA treated conditions (Table S1 ). Together with the transcription factor binding motif analysis this suggests that the defect in chromatin accessibility in ATRX LoF cells may directly be related to RA response element gene accessibility rather than downstream failure to regulate chromatin accessibility at RA response element binding sites. Maintenance of epigenetic response to RA is seen in neuroblastoma cell lines with ATRX IFF’s We next assessed whether RA treatment induced expression of direct RA HOX -gene targets in two neuroblastoma cell lines with in-frame ATRX deletions: SK-N-MM and CHLA-90 [6 ]. In contrast to ATRX LoF cells, cell lines with the ATRX IFF were able to upregulate direct RA HOX -gene targets following treatment with RA (Fig 3 A). We then performed ATAC sequencing in the ATRX IFF cell lines to evaluate changes in chromatin accessibility following RA treatment (Fig 3 B). Large changes in chromatin accessibility in response to RA were seen in SK-N-MM (Fig 3 C, Table S2) and more limited changes in chromatin accessibility were seen in CHLA-90 (Fig 3 D, Table S2). Although comparisons could not be made with matched wild-type cells in these models, we noted that both cell lines showed highly significant increases in chromatin accessibility at the direct RA genes DHRS3, CYP26A and CYP26B in response to RA, alongside EXOC6B which sits adjacent to CYP26B on 2p13.2. Both cell lines also appropriately opened chromatin at both the RARA and RARB genes (Table S2 ) and the transcription factor binding sites for these RA response elements (Fig S2C-D ). Taken together, this identifies that ATRX IFF neuroblastoma can differentially open chromatin in response to RA at relevant gene sites. ATRX -IFF neuroblastoma shows in-vitro sensitivity to RA We next analyzed RA sensitivity in available ATRX aberrant models. To our knowledge there are no currently available patient derived neuroblastoma cell lines with ATRX LoF. We identified a patient derived xenograft (PDX) neuroblastoma model with an ATRX p.Gly1748 mutation and treated this model with a clinically relevant dose of RA [28 ], 10 days after xenograft injection, and found no difference in tumour latency or growth in RA treated PDXs versus vehicle control (Fig S3A ). We next evaluated sensitivity to RA in ATRX IFF models. Others have shown that a non-canonical function of the ATRX IFF in blocking neuronal differentiation results in sensitivity to EZH2 inhibition [6 ]. Therefore, we hypothesized that the combination of RA with EZH2 inhibition may have an additive effective for ATRX IFF neuroblastoma. Both ATRX IFF neuroblastoma cell lines showed sensitivity to RA as a single agent (Fig 4 A-D) and their clonogenicity was further reduced with the addition of either tazemetostat or the EZH2 degrader MS1943, at doses sufficient to reduce H3K27me3 levels (Fig 4 A-E). Given the promising in-vitro results in ATRX IFF models, we evaluated in-vivo sensitivity to RA alone, and in combination with tazemetostat in the AMC772 ATRX IFF xenograft model. However here we saw no significant response to either agent alone, or in combination (Fig 4 F). Given the limitations in identifying in-vivo response to differentiation agents used in a minimal residual disease setting in a rapidly growing xenograft model, we next assessed response to these agents in an organoid model developed from the AMC722 xenografts. Here, we identified in-vitro sensitivity to RA but did not see any sensitivity to tazemetostat at doses sufficient to reduce H3K27me3 levels (Fig 4 G-I). Finally, we were able to generate one cell line with an ATRX -IFF from the RA sensitive cell line SH-SY5Y (Fig S4 ). This cell line retained full sensitivity to RA, however both the parental and ATRX IFF cell line were resistant to tazemetostat at doses sufficient to reduce H3K27me3 levels (Fig 4 J-L). Interestingly, RA treatment increased H3K27me3 levels both when given as a single agent and in combination with tazemetostat in both the SH-SY5Y parental cell line and the ATRX IFF cell line, suggesting RA treatment may counteract the effects of tazemetostat (Fig 4 L). Taken together, our results identify that in-vitro sensitivity to RA is consistent across multiple ATRX IFF models. However, our data does not support clinical development of tazemetostat either alone or in combination with RA for ATRX IFF neuroblastoma. Discussion Despite increasing evidence that neuroblastoma consists of distinct molecular subgroups with different clinical phenotypes [2 ], all children with high-risk neuroblastoma are currently treated uniformly. RA has been used as maintenance therapy in the minimal residual disease setting for neuroblastoma for decades, with evidence of clinical benefit for some children [39 ]. However, it is extremely challenging to identify which patients are likely to benefit from RA given that it is used at the end of treatment in the minimal residual disease setting. In pre-clinical studies, neuroblastoma with MYCN amplification has been shown to be generally sensitive to RA [40 ]. Here, we identify that ATRX IFF neuroblastoma is also generally sensitive to RA, and that ATRX IFF cell lines mount an appropriate epigenetic response to RA. In direct contrast, the epigenetic response to RA is impaired in ATRX LoF neuroblastoma. Our data suggests a high likelihood of RA resistance in ATRX LoF neuroblastoma, although the limitation of our study is that we were unable to directly evaluate sensitivity due to a lack of relevant models. Thus far, we have been unable to induce ATRX LoF via CRISPR-Cas9 in a RA sensitive cell line. We are limited on cell lines that can be used for these experiments, given that many RA sensitive cell lines are MYCN amplified, and that MYCN amplification is mutually exclusive with ATRX alterations [2 ]. We have attempted to induce ATRX LoF mutations in the SH-SY5Y cell line, which is a known MYCN non-amplified, RA sensitive cell line. However, in our experience induction of ATRX LoF is lethal in SH-SY5Y cells. We have also generated ATRX LoF clones from the NBL-S cell line [9 ]. However, NBL-S is highly RA resistant and does not upregulate direct target genes upon RA treatment (data not shown). This is likely to be because NBL-S carries an NF1 mutation [41 ], which is has also been shown to result in RA resistance [42 ]. Other commonly used non-MYCN -amplified cell lines such as SK-N-AS and GI-ME-N have also been shown to express low levels of NF1 and are RA resistant [42 ]. This highlights one of the significant challenges in the field, with a lack of appropriate models that reflect the heterogeneity of neuroblastoma seen in the clinic. Because of the challenges in CRISPR Cas9 gene editing the SH-SY5Y cell line and our previous experience showing that TP53 inactivation is required to generate ATRX altered cell lines [9 ], we also attempted to induce both LoF and IFF alterations in SH-SY5Y in after transfection with a TP53 dominant negative mutant plasmid to transiently inhibit p53 function. Although we were unable to generate an ATRX LoF model, we did generate one ATRX IFF clone using this methodology, albeit with mutant TP53 plasmid integration. Our finding of general sensitivity to RA was consistent across all ATRX IFF models used in this study. We also confirmed previous reports that the CHLA-90 and SK-N-MM models of ATRX IFF neuroblastoma were sensitive to the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat [6 ]. However, the additional ATRX IFF models used in this study did not show sensitivity to tazemetostat. As in patients with ATRX IFF neuroblastoma, each model used in this study has a different genetic background and differences in precise co-ordinates of the in-frame deletion, which will likely also affect therapeutic sensitivities. This highlights an additional layer of complexity when trying to identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for this group of patients. Here, our novel insight into the effects of ATRX LoF on neuroblastoma cell differentiation was triggered by an initial observation made in ATRX LoF iPSCs. Stem-cell models are increasingly being used to understand the underlying mechanisms of oncogenesis in neuroblastoma [43 ] and here, we show their potential to also give clinically relevant insight. Ongoing work in our laboratory and others to model the biological effects of specific ATRX alterations at later stages of neural crest differentiation will provide further insight, in addition to much needed pre-clinical models of neuroblastoma for future studies. In conclusion, we demonstrate differences in chromatin response to RA in neuroblastoma according to type of ATRX alteration and propose that within the ATRX subgroup, there is likely to be significant heterogeneity in response to differentiation therapies depending on the precise type of alteration. This emphasises the need for improved patient stratification based on molecular features in the upfront treatment setting, alongside the need to develop novel approaches for certain subgroups of patients. Our work also highlights one of the major challenges in the field as we identify increasingly smaller molecular subgroups, each with differing underlying biology, within this already rare disease. title: Targeting the p53-MDM2 pathway for neuroblastoma therapy: Rays of hope
abstract: Despite being the subject of extensive research and clinical trials, neuroblastoma remains a major therapeutic challenge in pediatric oncology. The p53 protein is a central safeguard that protects cells against genome instability and malignant transformation. Mutated TP53 (the gene encoding p53) is implicated in many human cancers, but the majority of neuroblastomas have wild type p53 with intact transcriptional function. In fact, the TP53 mutation rate does not exceed 1–2% in neuroblastomas. However, overexpression of the murine double minute 2 (MDM2) gene in neuroblastoma is relatively common, and leads to inhibition of p53. It is also associated with other non-canonical p53-independent functions, including drug resistance and increased translation of MYCN and VEGF mRNA. The p53-MDM2 pathway in neuroblastoma is also modulated at several different molecular levels, including via interactions with other proteins (MYCN, p14ARF). In addition, the overexpression of MDM2 in tumors is linked to a poorer prognosis for cancer patients. Thus, restoring p53 function by inhibiting its interaction with MDM2 is a potential therapeutic strategy for neuroblastoma. A number of p53-MDM2 antagonists have been designed and studied for this purpose. This review summarizes the current understanding of p53 biology and the p53-dependent and -independent oncogenic functions of MDM2 in neuroblastoma, and also the regulation of the p53-MDM2 axis in neuroblastoma. This review also highlights the use of MDM2 as a molecular target for the disease, and describes the MDM2 inhibitors currently being investigated in preclinical and clinical studies. We also briefly explain the various strategies that have been used and future directions to take in the development of effective MDM2 inhibitors for neuroblastoma.
