It majorly occurs in the adrenal glands but also been found in paraspinal, superior cervical, and celiac ganglia [1] . It is the most frequently occurring paediatric cancer with approximately 15 % mortality in all paediatric cancer cases [2] . The disease pathophysiology communicates the involvement of polycomb protein, Bmi1, which is highly expressed in neuroblastoma pathology and corelates with its tumorigenicity [3,4] . Bmi1 regulates downstream signalling at CDKN2A locus with the support from transcription factor, Myc-N, and controls the p53 pathway in neuroblastoma [5] . Bmi1 functions as E3 ligase along with Ring1A/B and induces an epigenetic hallmark, H2A monoubiquitination at lysine 119 position (uH2A) for chromatin remodeling in different cellular processes like DNA damage response, proliferation, senescence and stemness of the malignant cells [6] . In addition, the transcription factor, Oct3/4, is involved in the stemness maintenance of cancer stem cells and tumorigenesis [7,8] . Interestingly, it has been reported that Oct3/4 is regulated by ubiquitination and its stability is subjected to function of the ubiquitin proteosome system and known as oncogene in several cancers [9] . However, the relationship between E3 ligase, Bmi1, and Oct3/4 is still unexplored wherein both are vastly involved in neuroblastoma progression pathways and stemness of cancer stem cells. The cancer stem-like cells characteristics correlates with the cancer metastasis and epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) [10] pathways through EMT transcription factors such as TWIST, Slug, SNAIL, and Vimentin [11] . The expression of Vimentin increases with cancer progression and is a known marker for mesenchymal transition in metastasis. In an earlier proteomic report, the expression of Vimentin and Oct3/4 are correlated during osteogenesis [12] , however, their direct relation in neuroblastoma is yet to be explored. Moreover, Bmi1 is strongly overexpressed in 90 % cells of neuroblastoma which established Bmi1 as a potential target for therapeutic treatment of neuroblastoma [5] . Bmi1 expression is repressed by specific inhibitors like PRT4165, for neuroblastoma therapy. PRT4165 inhibits Bmi1 expression and its E3 ubiquitin ligase function disrupting the epigenetic hallmark, Histone H2A monoubiquitination at lysine 119 position (uH2A) [13] . However, treating neuroblastoma with PRT4165, its off targeting remains a limitation apart from its poor solubility and stability in physiological conditions. These therapeutic limitations can be evaded by encapsulation of PRT4165 in biocompatible and biodegradable nanoparticles of human serum albumin (HSANPs) [14] modified with the neuroblastoma biomarker, GD2. GD2, a disialoganglioside and complex acidic glycolipid, is highly expressed on neuroblastoma cells and is being utilized in antibody-driven neuroblastoma immunotherapy [15] . Targeting neuroblastoma cells with Anti-GD2 antibody modified nanoparticles can provide the efficient and specific delivery of therapeutic agent [16] like PRT4165 which can further target Bmi1 and its function. So, the PRT4165-encapsulated and anti-GD2-conjugated HSA nanoparticles (PRT@HSANPs@GD2) are hypothesized for an alternative targeted nanotherapy for neuroblastoma under in vitro and in vivo xenograft conditions. The anti-GD2 antibody was conjugated to HSANPs using the maleimide-thiol click chemistry and characterized. The anti-GD2 antibody conjugation increased the intracellular localization of HSA nanoparticles and enhanced the cytotoxicity through apoptosis pathway in neuroblastoma cell line, SHSY-5Y. PRT@HSANPs@GD2 efficiently and superiorly reduced the tumor volumes in xenograft mice. PRT@HSANPs@GD2 downregulated the expression of Bmi1, and associated epigenetic hallmark, uH2A in tumor tissues. Here, for the first-time, Bmi1 and Oct3/4 are shown to exhibit an interaction wherein our nanoformulation also repress this interaction along with suppression of Oct3/4-Vimentin axis. The superior therapeutic efficacy exerted by PRT@HSANPs@GD2 hold novel translational potential towards improving the off targeting limitations of current therapies. 2 Methodology 2.1 Synthesis and characterization of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles The Human Serum Albumin nanoparticles (HSANPs) were synthesized by desolvation method using 90 % ethanol as desolvating agent. The desolvated nanoparticles were cross-linked with 8 % glutaraldehyde (1.175µl/mg of HSA protein) at room temperature for 24 hrs. The ethanol was removed from the nanoparticles` reaction using rotary evaporator at 37 °C and purified with distilled water 5 times by centrifugation for 30 min at rpm. The stabilized and purified nanoparticles were then lyophilized. Further, 10 mg lyophilized HSANPs were dissolved in 4 ml 10 mM phosphate buffer saline (PBS) (pH7.4) and mildly sonicated for proper resuspension in the liquid. To this, 1 mg N-hydroxysuccinimidyl 4-Maleimidobutyric acid (NS 4-MB) was added and pH was monitored to 7.5 and incubated for 100 min at 25 °C under constant stirring. NS 4-MB was removed by centrifugation for 30 min at rpm. The activated nanoparticles were resuspended in 10 mM PBS (pH 7.4) and marked this solution as ‘A’. In addition, 10 µg/ml GD2 antibody (GD2 Mab) was diluted in 10 mM PBS supplemented with 5 mM EDTA and 10-folds 2-iminothiolane was added. This reaction mixture was incubated at room temperature for 60 min and extra unreacted 2-iminothiolane was removed through Amicon filters (cutoff, 3KDa). The GD2 Mab-SH recovered and marked as ‘B’. The Maleimide-Thiol click chemistry was followed by mixing ‘A’ and ‘B’ for 2 hrs at room temperature [17,18] . Afterwards, anti-GD2-conjugated HSA nanoparticles (HSANPs@GD2) were purified by centrifugation at rpm for 30 min and the anti-GD2-conjugated HSANPs were recovered and marked as ‘C’ (HSANPs@GD2). Further, 3 mg PRT4165 was dissolved in 3 ml ethanol (1mg/ml) and mixed with product ‘C’ (HSANPs@GD2), and HSANPs, separately, for 60 min followed by rotary evaporator to remove ethanol. The PRT4165 loaded anti-GD2-conjugated HSA nanoparticles (PRT@HSANPs@GD2) and PRT4165 loaded HSANPs (PRT@HSANPs) were then purified by centrifugation at rpm for 30 min and lyophilized. The blank and modified nanoparticles were characterized using dynamic light scattering (DLS), Zeta potential, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis. The antibody conjugation was assessed by the surface modification of HSANPs with Gold-functionalized antibody using above Maleimide-Thiol click chemistry method and characterized by energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) analysis using the field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM). The Alexa Flour (AF) 750-conjugated IgG antibody was conjugated HSANPs as above Maleimide-Thiol click chemistry method antibody and AF750 fluorescence of antibody was estimated in the supernatants of nanoparticles using Tecan Multiplate Reader. The exact antibody conjugation efficiency was enumerated using AF750 fluorescence standard curve (Figure S1 ) and following formula.% Antibody Conjugation Efficiency = Initial Antibody amount − Antibody Amount in Supernatant Initial Antibody amount x 100 % Furthermore, 1 mg PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and PRT@HSANPs were dissolved in ethanol, and PRT4165 was extracted for overnight at room temperature under constant shaking as described earlier [14] . The nanoparticles were centrifuged at rpm for 30 min and amount of PRT4165 was quantified using UV-Visible spectroscopy to calculate the drug loading efficiency. 2.2 In vitro studies of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles Furthermore, in vitro studies were performed on neuroblastoma cell line, SH SY-5Y [18] . These cells were procured from NCCS, Pune and maintained on Dulbecco's modified eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), Non-essential amino acid, L-Glutamine, and Penstrap antibiotics. When confluency is reached to 80 %, the cells were split by trypsinization, and 105 cells were seeded onto the sterilized coverslips in a 35 mm culture dish for cellular uptake study of nanoparticles. The 1mg/ml blank and modified HSA nanoparticles were tagged with fluorescent dye, 50 µM rhodamine B or Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) for overnight by incubating at rotary shaker. The tagged nanoparticles were centrifuged at rpm for 30 min and resuspended in 10 mM PBS and the cells on coverslips were treated with 100 µg of rhodamine B-tagged blank and modified HSA nanoparticles for 3 hrs. Afterwards, the cells were washed with 10 mM PBS, fixed with 4 % formaldehyde for 30 min at 4°C and stained with 100ng/ml DAPI for 10 min. The coverslips were mounted on glass slides and analyzed in Confocal Laser Scanning Microscopy (CLSM). Additionally, the SH SY-5Y cells were blocked with anti-GD2 antibody (1 µg per 106 cells) for 30 min and further treated with 100 µg rhodamine B-tagged HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 for 3 hrs following CLSM analysis as previously. SH SY-5Y cells were blocked with anti-GD2 antibody (1 µg per 106 cells) for 30 min and further treated with 100 µg FITC-tagged HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 for 3 hrs. These cells were harvested, washed for performing flow cytometric analysis in GD2+ subset of SH SY-5Y cells. Further, 104 cells were seeded in 100 µl of media in treated 96-wells microtiter plate. After overnight incubation, the cells were monitored for adherence and treated with different amounts of PRT4165, PRT@HSANPs, PRT@HSANPs@GD2, HSANPs@GD2, and HSANPs. After 24 and 48 hrs of separate treatment, 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide (MTT) dye was added to each well and incubated for 3 hrs before dissolving the insoluble formazans with Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). The absorbance was read at 530 nm using multi-plate reader (M-plex infinity, Tecan) and percentage cell viability was calculated using non-treated cells as control. The IC50 dose for treatments were enumerated using non-linear regression analysis. The IC50 dose of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and equivalent doses of PRT4165, PRT@HSANPs, HSANPs@GD2 and HSANPs were used for the further in vitro studies in SHSY-5Y cells. Additionally, SH SY-5Y cells were blocked with anti-GD2 antibody (1 µg per 106 cells) for 30 min and further treated with IC50 dose of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and equivalent dose of PRT@HSANPs for 48 hrs followed by cell viability assessment using MTT assay as previously. The normal cell line, HEK 293, were treated with 25 µM, 50 µM and 75 µM dose of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and equivalent doses of PRT4165, PRT@HSANPs, HSANPs@GD2 and HSANPs for 48 hrs followed by cell viability assessment by MTT assay as previously. Furthermore, 105 SH SY-5Y cells were seeded in 6-wells plate and treated with IC50 dose of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and equivalent doses of PRT4165, PRT@HSANPs, HSANPs@GD2 and HSANPs. After 48 hrs of treatment, the cells were washed with 10 mM ice cold PBS and scraped in 1X Annexin V binding buffer followed by staining with FITC-conjugated Annexin V and Propidium Iodide (PI) solution. The dual stained and treated cells along with unstained and mono-stained controls were analyzed in a flow cytometer (FACS Aria Fusion, BD). 2.3 In vivo biodistribution of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles All experimental animals used in the present study were complied with the guidelines of the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) and approved by the Institutional Animal Ethical Committee (IAEC) of the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Mohali (IISER, Mohali; Approval No IISERM/SAFE/PRT/2022/005) and National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute (NABI, Mohali; Approval No NABI/2039/CPCSEA/IAEC/2021/13). Furthermore, HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 were tagged with Indocyanine Green (ICG) using physical adsorption method. 100 µM ICG was incubated overnight with 1mg/ml HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 followed by centrifugation at rpm for 30 min. 200 µl of ICG-tagged HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 were administered intravenously through tail vein of female Balb/c mice. The time-dependent photoluminescence of ICG was recorded with In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS) (Perkin Elmer, USA) till 24 hrs. Afterwards, the animals were sacrificed with CO2 inhalation and distribution of ICG photoluminescence as a function of localization of nanoparticles was recorded in the major organs. 2.4 In vivo studies of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles in neuroblastoma xenograft All experimental animals used in the present study were complied with the guidelines of the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) and approved by the Institutional Animal Ethical Committee (IAEC) of the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Mohali (IISER, Mohali) and National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute (NABI, Mohali). In addition, 2 million SH SY-5Y cells were injected subcutaneously and orthotopically into dorsal right flanks of athymic nude mice to generate the neuroblastoma xenograft mouse model. The animals were monitored tumor development and the change in tumor volume were enumerated using this formula [19] . Tumor volume = ½ (L x W2 ) where L is length and W is Width of the tumor. When tumor volume reached approximately 100 mm3 , the mice were randomized. The ten cycles of 5 mg/kg PRT4165 and equivalent doses of PRT@HSANPs and PRT@HSANPs@GD2 were administered intraperitoneally to developed xenograft mice for 15 days [20] . Post-necropsy, tumor regression was observed. The animals were monitored for percentage change in the body weight along with tumor development and the change in tumor volume were enumerated [19] . The tumor tissues were fixed in the formalin and sectioned for the immunofluorescence analysis of cleaved Caspase 3. The sectioned tissues were blocked with bovine serum albumin and stained with primary antibody and counterstained with secondary antibody and DAPI for CLSM analysis. Furthermore, the tumor tissues were homogenized in RIPA buffer and protein was isolated. The proteins were transferred to the PVDF membrane for immunostaining with primary antibody and counter staining with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody to evaluate the change in protein expression (β-Actin, Bmi1, uH2A, Oct3/4, and Vimentin) after treatment regimen. Separately, 100 µg protein lysate were pulldown with anti-Bmi1 and anti-Oct3/4 antibodies followed by immunoblotting with Oct3/4 and Vimentin, respectively. In addition, the chromatin from the tumor tissues were isolated and anti-Oct3/4 chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay was performed, respectively, using Vimentin promoter-specific primers (supplementary Table S1 ). 3 Results and discussion 3.1 Synthesis and characterization of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles The nanoparticles of human serum albumin (HSANPs) are widely utilized as efficient and effective nanocarriers owing to their biodegradability, biocompatibility, drug interaction and surface characteristics. These characteristics help HSANPs to exhibit the high drug loading capacity and surface modification with antibodies for the development of a superior targeted cancer nanotherapy [21,22] . The HSANPs are synthesized with desolvation method wherein the HSA is titrated with desolvating agent, ethanol, to fabricate the monodispersed nanoparticles [23] . Here, the synthesized HSANPs were purified, and characterized for the hydrodynamic size distribution and zeta potential with Zetasizer and found the maximum hydrodynamic size population of 190 nm and surface charge of −18.06 ± 1.6 mV ( Fig. 1 A & 1D). The hydrodynamic size and surface charge of HSANPs relates with earlier reports of HSANPs encapsulating Doxorubicin for neuroblastoma drug delivery [24] . In neuroblastoma, a disialoganglioside, GD2, is highly expressed which can be a potential surface target for anti-GD2 antibody conjugated HSANPs to deliver the therapeutic agents [15,16] . The antibody conjugation to HSANPs is performed through Maleimide-Thiol click chemistry [25] . Here, the antibody thiolation with 2-iminothiolane provide the (-SH) groups to antibodies which has higher affinity to maleimide groups present in activated HSANPs by N-hydroxysuccinimidyl 4-Maleimidobutyric acid (NS 4-MB) [26] . When HSANPs were conjugated with anti-GD2 antibody changed the maximum hydrodynamic size population to 318 nm and surface charge to + 2.47 ± 1.6 mV (Fig. 1 A & 1D). These changes in the hydrodynamic size and surface potential of HSANPs are the primary indication for the conjugation anti-GD2 antibody onto the HSANPs surface which is supported by anti-HER2 antibody conjugation for cancer application [27] . The scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) and elemental analysis revealed the presence of Gold in the Gold-functionalized antibody conjugated HSANPs as a function of antibody conjugation (Fig. 1 G-I). The Gold-functionalized antibodies provide a wide range of application and can be used for the calculation of percentage of antibody conjugation to the nanoparticles surface as the elemental Gold can easily be estimated through elemental analysis with EDX [28] . The antibody conjugation to nanoparticles was enumerated to be 40 % using AF750 fluorescence standard curve of AF750-conjugated IgG antibody (Figure S1 ). The Neuroblastoma cells express the polycomb protein, Bmi1, in high quotients to regulate downstream signalling which make it a suitable molecular target for Neuroblastoma therapy [5] . The specific inhibitor of Bmi1, PRT4165, suppresses the H2A monoubiquitination function of Bmi1 and represses the downstream signalling in cancer [13] . The physiological instability and insolubility along with off target toxicity obstruct the therapeutic application of PRT4165 [14] which can be circumvented by encapsulation in HSANPs and GD2-functionalized HSANPs (HSANPs@GD2). The PRT4165 loading to HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 exhibited the zeta potential of −23.6 ± 2.05 mV and −17.16 ± 0.8 mV, respectively, wherein size was changed to 255 nm and 230 nm, respectively (Fig. 1 A & 1D). The PRT4165 loading efficiency for PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and PRT@HSANPs were found to be 18.2 % and 19.5 %, respectively. These analyses for PRT4165 loading to nanoparticles are supported by Obidoxime adsorption to HSANPs [29] and folate-functionalized docetaxel encapsulated HSANPs for drug delivery applications [30] . The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis demonstrated the spherical shaped and monodispersed HSA nanoparticles (Fig. 1 C-F). The spherical morphology of HSANPs correlate with the peptide-decorated [31] and Docetaxel-encapsulated and anti-PD1-conjugated HSANPs for cancer drug delivery application [32] . 3.2 Anti-GD2 antibody conjugation increases in vitro neuroblastoma therapeutics GD2 is biosynthesized by GD2 synthase with high enzymatic activity in Neuroblastoma causing high surface presence of GD2 molecules. The surface expression of GD2 in Neuroblastoma prompt the targeting of neuroblastoma cells for cancer cell toxicity [33] . The high expression of GD2 in neuroblastoma provide a suitable surface target for anti-GD2 antibody conjugated nanoparticles [15,16] and provide a superior PRT4165-mediated inhibition of polycomb signalling in neuroblastoma through the suppression of H2A monoubiquitination function of the polycomb protein, Bmi1 [13] . When antibody was conjugated, the targeting effect of anti-GD2 conjugation was evaluated by confocal microscopy as cellular uptake of anti-GD2-conjugated nanoparticles exhibited higher cellular localization compared to non-targeted nanoparticles. Nanoparticles were found to be located at nuclear periphery and cytoplasm ( Fig. 2 A). As reported in the earlier study, the anti-GD2 conjugation to iron oxide nanoparticles increases the cellular internalization of nanoparticles in GD2+ neuroblastoma cell line as monitored through the magnetic resonance imaging and fluorescence microscopy [34] which support our findings. The enhanced cellular internalization of therapeutics through GD2-decorated nanoparticles further increases the efficiency of therapeutic agents [35] . The therapeutic molecule, PRT4165, downregulates the Bmi1 expression which is vastly involved in cellular processes such as self-regeneration, proliferation, differentiation and aging [36] . The pharmacological inhibition of Bmi1, suppress the cancer cell proliferation [37] . The cytotoxicity assay for 24 and 48 hrs by MTT exhibited the more effective killing of the neuroblastoma cell line, SH SY-5Y for PRT@HSANPs@GD2 compared to non-targeted nanoparticles. The MTT assay explained the dose-dependent killing of PRT@HSANPs and PRT@HSANPs@GD2 for 24 and 48 hrs wherein 48 hrs treatment was found to be more effective. The PRT@HSANPs@GD2 exhibited the superior cytotoxicity against neuroblastoma cells and the IC50 of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 was found to be ∼50µM after 48 hrs of treatment (Fig. 2 B & 2 C). When anti-GD2 antibody was functionalized to HSANPs, the cellular internalization of the HSANPs@GD2 increased by 15 % in the GD2+ subset of SH SY-5Y cells. Further, when GD2 antigen was pre-blocked on cell surface by anti-GD2 antibody, the cellular internalization of the HSANPs@GD2 reduced by 81.2 % in the GD2+ subset of SH SY-5Y cells ( Fig. 3 A & 3B). CLSM analysis revealed that GD2 functionalization increased the cellular internalization of the HSANPs@GD2 by ∼2.6-folds and pre-blocking GD2 antigen with anti-GD2 antibody on the cell surface reduced the cellular internalization of the HSANPs@GD2 by ∼2.4-folds in SH SY-5Y cells (Fig. 3 C & 3D). MTT assay revealed that biocompatibility of HSANPs and HSANPs@GD2 as non-significant cytotoxicity in normal cells, HEK 293, was observed at different doses whereas lower level of cytotoxicity with ∼27 % and ∼20 % killing, respectively, were recorded at IC50 dose of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 and equivalent dose of PRT@HSANPs (Figure S1 ). In addition, pre-blocking GD2 antigen on the cell surface with anti-GD2 antibody, obstructed the PRT@HSANPs@GD2-mediated cytotoxicity of SH SY-5Y cells by ∼1.3-folds compared to GD2-unblocked SH SY-5Y cells (Fig. 3 E). The annexin-V and propidium iodide staining exhibited comparatively high number of apoptotic cells after the treatment of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 compared to other groups suggesting apoptotic mechanism of cytotoxicity (Fig. 2 D & S2). The Bmi1 expression help in the survival of neuroblastoma cells under the condition of the DNA-induced apoptosis [3] and suppression of Bmi1 overturn this pathway forcing neuroblastoma cells to follow apoptosis [6] . In summary, the GD2 functionalization increases cellular internalization of nanoparticles carrying the therapeutic agent, PRT4165, and increases the cytotoxicity in neuroblastoma cells through apoptosis pathway. 3.3 In vivo biodistribution of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles Furthermore, the in vivo biodistribution analysis by IVIS system revealed a longer circulation time for HSANPs@GD2 compared to HSANPs when the time-dependent ICG photoluminescence was recorded for ICG-tagged nanoparticles ( Fig. 4 A). The nanoparticles exhibited the renal clearance by reticuloendothelial system (RES) as presence of ICG photoluminescence was recorded in the liver and kidneys (Fig. 4 E) of HSANPs@GD2-treated mice (Fig. 4 D) compared to the control (Fig. 4 B) and HSANPs-treated mice (Fig. 4 C). The HSA nanoparticles are biodegradable and known for renal clearance as per the explanation from the previous biodistribution study for bovine serum albumin nanoparticles [38] . The in vivo biocompatibility study of HSA nanoparticles prompts for further in vivo therapeutic applications. 3.4 In vivo studies of GD2 antibody conjugated HSA nanoparticles in neuroblastoma xenograft In order to study the therapeutic application of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 for the neuroblastoma therapy, the in vivo studies are required to study the Bmi1 involvement and its suppression in the neuroblastoma condition. Neuroblastoma cell line-based mouse xenografts are routinely utilized for drug discovery and testing neuroblastoma therapy. We have utilized the subcutaneous xenograft model for neuroblastoma tumor development by injecting 2 million SH SY-5Y cells into the dorsal right flank of athymic nude mice and our previous studies have used this model for nanotherapeutics [39,40] . Fig. 5 A schematically represents the xenograft model development in athymic nude mice. After 15 days, the tumors were formed with appropriate tumor volume (approximately 100 mm3 ) when compared with time of injection (Fig. 5 B). Following the treatment regimen, the tumor volume reduction was observed in tumor-bearing mice-treated with PRT4165, PRT@HSANPs and PRT@HSANPs@GD2 (Fig. 5 B). The percentage reduction in xenograft mice body weight was ∼27 % for PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated xenograft mice groups compared to control wherein both PRT@HSANPs and PRT4165-treated xenograft mice groups exhibited ∼20 % reduction in body weight compared to control xenograft mice (Fig. 5 C). The tumor volume reduction was highest for PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated groups, and the reduction was found to be ∼10.2-folds, ∼8.5-folds and ∼2.3-folds, respectively, compared to control, PRT4165 and PRT@HSANPs-treated xenograft mice groups (Fig. 5 D-F). Previous studies demonstrated the larger size of tumor volumes (up to 4000–5000 mm3 ) in the control mice of Neuroblastoma xenograft model [41] . The tumor regression in our Neuroblastoma xenograft model is supported by earlier studies where Bmi1 inhibition promotes the anti-tumor effects in Neuroblastoma xenograft mice [42] . The Neuroblastoma xenograft study demonstrated a superior, efficient and targeted nanotherapy by PRT@HSANPs@GD2. GD2 targets the neuroblastoma cells and efficiently delivers PRT4165 which specifically inhibits the Bmi1 and its downstream signalling [43] . Furthermore, immunofluorescence assay showed the higher relative expression of the cleaved Caspase 3 in tumor tissues by ∼2.3-folds, ∼1.8-folds, and ∼1.3-folds, respectively, from PRT4165, PRT@HSANPs and PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated xenograft mice compared to that of the control xenograft mice (Fig. 5 G & 5 H). The cleaved Caspase 3 expression in tumor tissues from PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated xenograft mice increased by ∼1.3-folds and ∼1.7-folds compared to that of PRT@HSANPs and PRT4165, respectively (Fig. 5 H). The suppression of Bmi1 in the neuroblastoma condition leads to repression of tumorigenesis as explained by the Bmi1 knockdown studies [3] . The superior therapeutic efficiency of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 in neuroblastoma xenograft model is a testimony of the future translational development wherein GD2-targeted polycomb signalling is obstructed for the first time in neuroblastoma. 3.5 PRT@HSANPs@GD2 obstruct Bmi1-mediated downstream signalling in neuroblastoma The Polycomb protein, Bmi1, is direct target of Myc-N which transcriptionally regulates the function of Bmi1 and suggests the involvement of Bmi1-dependent signalling pathway excluding the p14ARF/p16INK4a locus regulation by Bmi1 [36] . Bmi1 has E3 ligase function and epigenetically regulate its target genes through depositing the monoubiquitination mark on H2A at lysine 119 position (uH2A) [20] . The western blot analysis demonstrated the Bmi1 downregulation by ∼1.5-folds, ∼1.9-folds, and ∼4.3-folds, in the tumor tissues of PRT4165-treated, PRT@HSANPs-treated, and PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated xenograft mice, respectively. The Bmi1-associaated epigenetic hallmark, uH2A, was downregulated by ∼3.9-folds, and ∼6.8-folds in the tumor tissues of PRT@HSANPs-treated, and PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated xenograft mice, respectively ( Fig. 6 A & 6B). The enhanced suppression of Bmi1 and its associated epigenetic hallmark, uH2A, are proof for the GD2-targeted delivery of PRT4165 in Neuroblastoma condition. The Oct3/4, Vimentin, and Snail were, respectively, downregulated by ∼26.5-folds, ∼2.9-folds and ∼4.4-folds, in the tumor tissues of PRT@HSANPs@GD2-treated xenograft mice (Fig. 6 A & 6B). PRT4165 is a specific inhibitor of Bmi1 and the enhanced suppression of Bmi1 by PRT@HSANPs@GD2 is the confirmation of effects of GD2 targeting in neuroblastoma. This superior molecular downregulation of Bmi1 helps downregulate downstream signalling. In neuroblastoma, the Bmi1 and Oct3/4 are greatly involved as oncogenes and control several downstream pathways in cancer progression and stemness of cancer stem cells which is involved in the epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway [6,9] . The superior effects on Bmi1 downregulation by treatment of PRT@HSANPs@GD2 blocks the expression of EMT makers, Vimentin and Sox which suggested the reversal of EMT pathway in neuroblastoma. The western blot analysis reveals that when Bmi1 is downregulated and Oct3/4 is also downregulated suggesting an interaction. However, the interrelationship between Bmi1 and Oct3/4 is yet to be explored. The co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) studies revealed the interaction between Bmi1 and Oct3/4 as presence of Oct3/4 expression after pull down with anti-Bmi1 antibody wherein PRT@HSANPs@GD2 obstructed this relationship and reduced the Oct3/4 expression. For the first-time, our findings suggest the presence of an interaction between Bmi1 and Oct3/4 in neuroblastoma condition and our nanoformulation, PRT@HSANPs@GD2 obstruct this interaction. The expression of Oct3/4 and Vimentin are correlated during osteogenesis [12] and also, our western blot analysis reveals that when Oct3/4 is downregulated and Vimentin is also downregulated suggesting an interaction. However, their direct relationship is still not explored in neuroblastoma. The additional co-IP studies revealed and interaction between Oct3/4 and Vimentin as the presence of Vimentin expression after the pull down with anti-Oct3/4 antibody wherein the PRT@HSANPs@GD2 obstructed this relationship and reduced the Vimentin expression (Fig. 6 C). This is for the first-time we report an interaction between Oct3/4 and Vimentin in neuroblastoma and our nanoformulation, PRT@HSANPs@GD2 obstruct this interaction. The co-IP studies confirm the downstream signalling cascade where Bmi1 interacts with Oct3/4 to further regulate the EMT marker, Vimentin, wherein our nanoformulation, PRT@HSANPs@GD2 block this signaling cascade. Further anti-Oct3/4 chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay revealed the Oct3/4 binding to the Vimentin promoter region of (-1902–1824bp) which reduced by the PRT@HSANPs@GD2 treatment wherein the other tested Vimentin promoter regions did not exhibit binding to Oct3/4 (Fig. 6 D & 6E). The binding of Oct3/4 to the Vimentin promoter region (-1902–1824bp) is illustrated in Fig. 6 F. The current nanotherapy exhibits the GD2-targeted neuroblastoma therapeutics which prove to be effective in athymic nude xenograft model. 4 Conclusion The high expression of polycomb protein, Bmi1, in neuroblastoma make it a suitable and potential molecular therapeutic target and can provide superior therapy when specifically suppressed by Bmi1 inhibitor, PRT4165. The nanoformulation prepared by encapsulating PRT4165 to HSANPs-functionalized with anti-GD2 antibody (PRT@HSANPs@GD2) exhibit an enhanced cellular internalization and cytotoxicity through apoptosis pathway in the GD2+ neuroblastoma cells. In neuroblastoma xenograft model, PRT@HSANPs@GD2 superiorly suppress the tumor growth and execute the suppression of Bmi1 and its signalling. The interaction between Bmi1 and Oct3/4 is reported for the first time and PRT@HSANPs@GD2 obstruct this relationship in neuroblastoma. Also, PRT@HSANPs@GD2 suppress the Oct3/4-Vimentin axis in neuroblastoma. Bmi1 suppression through GD2-targeted delivery of PRT4165 in the neuroblastoma is a promising strategy to provide a new avenue for future translational development. title: Combining selinexor with alisertib to target the p53 pathway in neuroblastoma
abstract: Neuroblastoma accounts for 15% of cancer-related deaths in children, highlighting an unmet need for novel therapies. Selinexor is a small molecule inhibitor of XPO1. XPO1 shuffles cargo proteins with a nuclear export sequence from the nucleus to the cytosol, many of which are essential for cancer growth and cell maintenance. We systematically tested the effect of selinexor against neuroblastoma cells in vitro and in vivo and used an advanced proteomic and phosphoproteomic screening approach to interrogate unknown mechanisms of action. We found that selinexor induced its cytotoxic effects in neuroblastoma through the predominantly nuclear accumulation of p53 and global activation of apoptosis pathways. Selinexor also induced p53 phosphorylation at site S315, which is one initiating step for p53 degradation. Since this phosphorylation step is undertaken mostly by aurora kinase A (AURKA), we used the clinically available AURKA inhibitor, alisertib, and found p53-mediated lethality could be further augmented in three orthotopic xenograft mouse models. These findings suggest a potential therapeutic benefit using selinexor and alisertib to synergistically increase p53-mediated cytotoxicity of high-risk neuroblastoma.

Expression of XPO1 in NB. (A) Comparison of XPO1 levels in normal adrenal gland (AG), neural crest (NC), and NB show significantly higher levels in NB (P = 3.0e-35; one-way ANOVA). (B) Analysis of XPO1 expression demonstrate higher expression levels in NB compared to acute lymphoblastic (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), rhabdoid tumor (RT), or Wilms’ tumor (WT; P 60% enrichment for transduced cells. PDX cells were transduced with freshly prepared concentrated lentivirus particles and rested for 24 hours in full RPMI medium and on Matrigel-coated plates (Corning Inc.) before injection into mice. After one passage in mice, tumors were processed into a single-cell suspension and cryopreserved when comprising a population of >60% of transduced cells Transient transfections Transient transfections were performed as previously described.10 A set of four ON-TARGETplus siRNAs targeting XPO1 and negative control siRNAs were obtained from Horizon (Cat. # LQ- -00-000) and transiently transfected into IMR-5 cells using the Nucleofector with solution L and program C-005 (Amaxa Biosystems). The knockdown efficiency was tested by reverse transcription (RT) quantitative PCR (qPCR) and immunoblotting. The impact of XPO1 knockdown on cell viability was quantified by conducting longitudinal confluence assays with the Incucyte system (Sartorius). Drug compounds The drug compounds used in this study were commercially obtained (i.e., selinexor from Selleckchem; temozolomide [TMZ] and alisertib from MedChemExpress) and resuspended as per the manufacturer's instructions for in vitro and in vivo use. Animals and orthotopic tumor cell injections Animals were housed under pathogen-free conditions. All animal studies were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Cancer Institute (protocol number: PB-023-2). Under anesthesia with isoflurane, CD1-Foxn1nu immunodeficient mice were positioned in a lateral right recumbent position. A 1.0 cm transverse cutaneous incision was made at the height of the spleen and carefully dissected down. Upon penetration of the peritoneum, the spleen was lifted cranially to visualize the left adrenal gland. PDX cells were resuspended as a single-cell solution in Matrigel to allow the injection of 1.0e6 cells in 20 μL into the periadrenal fat pad.11 The PDX lines grew orthotopically within 3-4 weeks from the implantation date. In vitro drug assays NB cells were dissociated into a single-cell suspension and grown in culture in 96-well flat-bottom plates (Corning Inc.) at 37°C in 5% CO2 incubators for 24 hours prior to the experiment. Plating densities were optimized for each cell line. The respective compound was added to culture wells for the duration of 72 hours. The CellTiter-Glo luminescent cell viability assay (Promega) was used according to manufacturer instructions to quantify cytotoxicity. A plate reader (SpectraMax M3) measured the luminescence in relative light units (RLU). Cytotoxicity was calculated with the following formula: c e l d e a t h ( % ) = 1 − R L U t r e a t e d R L U u n t r e a t e d . The Compusyn software was used to calculate synergism for drug combinations.12 Synergism was defined as a combination index (CI) 1. Protein isolation and immunoblotting For assessment of protein levels, cells were lysed using RIPA buffer supplemented with HaltTM protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The protein concentration was determined by using the Bradford dye reagent protein assay (Bio-Rad Laboratories). For nuclear and cytosolic separation, we used the NE-PERTM Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction Reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cell lysates in SDS-containing buffer were denatured for 10 minutes, and 10 µg of total protein was resolved by 4–20% SDS-PAGE and electroblotted onto a polyvinylidene difluoride membrane. Primary antibodies as listed in Supplementary Table 2 were incubated overnight at 4°C in 5% BSA in Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) and 0.02% sodium azide. Secondary antibodies were incubated for 1 hour at room temperature in 5% non-fat dry milk in TBST. Protein bands were detected using a goat anti-rabbit or -mouse IgG-HRP conjugated secondary antibody (200 µg/ml; Santa Cruz Biotechnology) and the SuperSignalTM West Femto Maximum Sensitivity Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific), visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence (Bio-Rad Laboratories). Quantification was performed with the ImageJ software. Real-time PCR Total mRNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) as per the manufacturer's protocol. cDNA was generated with the High-Capacity RNA-to-cDNATM kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The quantitative measurements of expression levels were conducted in technical triplicates with the Bio-Rad CFX Touch Real-time (RT) PCR detection system. Primer sequences are shown in Supplementary Table 3. Pharmacodynamic analysis Tumor-bearing mice were treated with oral selinexor (15 mg/kg) for three consecutive days to reach steady state drug levels. Six hours after the last dose, tumors were isolated, and protein or RNA were extracted from the tumors as described above. Transcriptomic changes in BIRC5 and XPO1 and changes in the protein level of survivin and XPO1 were determined for pharmacodynamic assessment. In vivo drug testing We confirmed that tumor-bearing mice with bioluminescence signals ≥10e7 p/s/cm2 /sr form small tumors. Thus, we screened, enrolled, and randomized animals based on their bioluminescence signal to receive vehicle (group 1); selinexor 15 mg/kg orally once on day 1 and 3 of each week for 3 weeks (group 2); alisertib 10 mg/kg orally twice daily for 7 days (group 3); TMZ 16.5 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days (group 4); or the combinations of selinexor with alisertib (group 5); or selinexor with TMZ (group 6). Each group comprised 5 animals. Three orthotopic tumor models (i.e., SH-SY5Y, IMR5, and SJNBL012407_X1) were tested. The mice received one therapy cycle lasting 3 weeks, mimicking clinical administration schedules. Weekly bioluminescence imaging was conducted to monitor tumor growth. Based on the kinetic curve for each tumor model, animals were injected with 3mg of luciferin (Perkins Elmer) intra-peritoneally and imaged 6 minutes after luciferin injection with an acquisition time of 1 minute. Imaging data was processed using the Living Image Software (Perkins Elmer). We waited one additional week after the completion of the therapy cycle before terminating the experiment to reveal residual tumor which might have been undetectable immediately after completion of therapy but would have grown to a detectable size during that time. Proteomic analysis Proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling were carried out via an advanced TMT-LC/LC-MS/MS platform as in previous studies.13-18 Briefly, around 8 million cells per sample were lysed in 0.5 mL of lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES, pH 8.5, 8 M urea, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 1 × PhosStop Phosphatase Inhibitor cocktail) at 4°C.19 Protein concentration was measured by BCA assay (Thermo Fisher). Cell lysates were first digested by Lys-C (100:1, w/w) for 2 hours, followed by an overnight trypsin digestion (50:1, w/w) at room temperature.20 Peptides were desalted, labeled with TMT16-plex reagents, and pooled together in equal amounts.13 Pooled peptides were then fractionated by basic pH reverse-phase liquid chromatography and concatenated to a total of 40 fractions. Ninety-five percent of each fraction was used for TiO2 -based phosphopeptide enrichment, and the remaining 5% was used for whole proteome analysis.21 , 22 Each fraction was then sequentially loaded on an acidic pH reverse phase LC-MS/MS instrument for proteomic or phosphoproteomic analysis (Q Exactive HF, Thermo Scientific).23 Acquired data were analyzed by JUMP software suites for protein and phosphopeptide identification and quantification.24-26 A target-decoy base FDR 1. We detected synergy in 12 drug ratios and antagonism in 19 conditions, which predominantly comprised TP53 -mutant NB lines. Although, we also noted CI < 1 (synergy) for SK-N-BE2C (MYCN- amplified and TP53 mutant) in all ratios except 4:1, the levels of measured cell death were much lower compared to the other sensitive cell lines (see heatmap). TP53- WT SH-SY5Y (MYCN single copy) showed limited to no synergy but high levels of cell death, predominantly due to high sensitivity of this line to alisertib (EC50 = 13nM). We next examined the protein changes in KCNR and SH-SY5Y cells when treated with single-agent selinexor or alisertib or a combination of both for 24 hours (Figure 4 C). Compared with controls, selinexor treatment and dual inhibition of XPO1 and AURKA caused an increase in nuclear p53 (Figure 4 D). The combination induced lower p-p53 S315 levels compared to single-agent therapy in the MYCN -WT line SH-SY5Y but not in the MYCN- amplified line KCNR. Cleaved caspase 3 (cCASP3) as a fraction of total caspase 3 (tCASP3) was also markedly elevated with the combination (KCNR) and with single-agent alisertib or dual inhibition (SH-SY5Y). Both drugs down-regulated MYCN protein levels in the cytosol of the MYCN- amplified cell line KCNR. Altogether, these experiments demonstrate that the combination of selinexor with alisertib causes synergistic cytotoxicity in vitro in a variety of NB cell lines with TP53- WT status and is agnostic of the MYCN status. At 24 hours after combination treatment, nuclear p53 and cCASP3 levels increase, while the addition of alisertib inhibits the phosphorylation of site S315 in one of the two cell lines. Dual inhibition of XPO1 and AURKA induces regression of NB in an orthotopic mouse model We evaluated the preclinical activity of selinexor combined with alisertib in one MYCN -WT (SH-SY5Y) and two MYCN -amplified preclinical xenograft models with established orthotopic NB (IMR-5 and SJNBL012407_X1). We chose these cell lines because we have thoroughly characterized their orthotopic growth behavior in vivo . We confirmed target inhibition for selinexor (Supplementary Fig. 7). We performed a head-to-head comparison of this combination with selinexor and TMZ, which is a clinically accepted regimen and a possible consideration for NB given that some backbones of second-line therapies include TMZ.28 , 29 In the experiment with SH-SY5Y, we only compared selinexor and alisertib as single-agent therapy or combination. Animals were randomized according to their bioluminescence signal and received therapy with one treatment cycle of: 1. Vehicle (VEH); 2. Selinexor twice weekly for 3 weeks (SEL); 3. TMZ for 5 days (TMZ); 4. Alisertib twice daily for 7 days (ALI); or the combinations 5. Selinexor and TMZ (SEL+TMZ); or 6. Selinexor and alisertib (SEL+ALI; Figure 5 A). All drug schedules are according to clinical NB regimens.28 , 30 We waited one additional week after the completion of the therapy cycle before terminating the experiment to reveal residual tumor which might have been undetectable immediately after completion of therapy but would have grown to a detectable size during that time. The combination therapy with alisertib and selinexor induced the most tumor regression in SH-SY5Y-bearing mice (Figure 5 B). In IMR-5 tumor–bearing mice, longitudinal imaging revealed the largest decline in bioluminescence signal in response to therapy with SEL+ALI compared with the remaining groups (Figure 5 C, Friedman test, P = 0.001). Tumor sizes (Figure 5 D) and tumor weights (Figure 5 E) were consistent with this observation. Animals that were implanted with the PDX, SJNBL012407_X1, had a less impressive response detected with bioluminescence imaging (Figure 5 F), though more significant changes in tumor sizes (Figure 5 G) and weights (Figure 5 H). Animals across all groups had maintained or increased weights and did not exhibit any signs of overt toxicity, thus indicative of a well-tolerated regimen (Supplementary Fig. 8). Taken together, we demonstrated in vivo that the novel combination of selinexor with alisertib induced tumor regression in three orthotopic NB xenograft models. Discussion NB is a deadly solid tumor of childhood for which there is an unmet need for novel therapies. Selinexor is a pharmacologic XPO1 inhibitor that has shown therapeutic benefits in the treatment of adult cancers.31-33 Though regarded as a targeted agent, there are more than 300 proteins that are dependent on XPO1 for their nuclear export and therefore potentially implicated in selinexor's mechanism of action.6 We used unbiased proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses to identify critical target proteins and pathways that illuminated mechanisms mediating selinexor's effects in NB. We found that selinexor increases predominantly the nuclear retention of p53 in NB cells and induces apoptotic pathways, evident by increased cleaved caspase 3 levels. Analysis of the phosphoproteome associated with selinexor treatment revealed the concomitant phosphorylation of p53 at site S315, which is an initiating step for p53 degradation.9 Our synergy screen with p53-targeting agents revealed that AURKA showed synergy with selinexor and prevents the phosphorylation of p53, thereby, increasing the total p53 levels in some of the tested cell lines. This combination showed significant efficacy in three orthotopic NB xenograft models, suggesting potential therapeutic benefit in children with high-risk NB. Several mechanisms of action of selinexor have been previously reported in NB. For example, reports have suggested that selinexor acts in NB by decreasing the level of survivin, thereby activating the apoptosis pathway.34 In another more recent study, selinexor was used in combination with bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor. The authors of this study showed that selinexor increases the intracellular nuclear retention of IkB and bortezomib prevents its degradation. The cytotoxic activity of this combination was further mediated through inhibition of the NF-kB pathway by IkB and led to cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis.35 Mitra et al. have studied the subcellular distribution of p53 and the role that NBAT1 and XPO1 play in this context. They demonstrated that low levels of NBAT1 are associated with high levels of XPO1, which in turn skews the distribution of p53 towards the cytoplasm, highjacking p53 tumor suppressor gene pathways.36 Using the IMR-32 cell line, they demonstrated that p53 is predominantly expressed in the cytosol, but nuclear expression can be restored by treating cells or mice with selinexor. Our study supports these findings, demonstrating predominantly nuclear accumulation of p53 and a global activation of the apoptosis pathways. These molecular alterations are conceivably responsible for the observed cytotoxic effects of NB cells herein and provide a mechanistic underpinning that harmonizes previously reported findings. Our in vitro data demonstrate that TP53 -mutant cells are more resistant to selinexor than WT-TP53 cells. TP53 mutations are in fact quite rare in newly diagnosed NB with approximately 2% detection compared to adult cancers37 but do increase anywhere from 15-50% in relapsed/refractory NB. Despite this, the majority of relapsed/refractory NB remain WT-TP53, indicating a substantial portion of relapsed/refractory patients that may benefit from such a therapeutic approach.38 Our studies would warrant molecular analysis of this gene as criteria for study enrollment. Analysis of the selinexor-stimulated phosphoproteome revealed increases in p53-S315 phosphorylation. In vivo data have been conflicting as phosphorylation at this site was shown to be both significant and dispensable for the function of p53.39 , 40 Phosphorylation at this site can occur following genotoxic and endoplasmic reticulum stress but also during cell-cycle progression.41 , 42 In addition, p53-S315 phosphorylation has been postulated to occur as one initiating step of p53 degradation.9 The phosphorylation at site S315 is undertaken by several kinases, including cyclin-dependent kinases and glycogen synthase kinase-3β.41 , 43 However, the main kinase implicated in this process is AURKA.9 Given the importance of p53 levels in selinexor treatment, we reasoned that combining selinexor with alisertib, an AURKA inhibitor, would lead to higher p53 levels and toxicity. Our studies clearly confirmed this hypothesis and show that alisertib synergizes with selinexor to increase NB cell death in vitro and improve tumor growth control in three orthotopic PDX models with established NB in vivo . Nevertheless, our mechanistic studies show that these cytotoxic effects correspond with a decrease in p-p53 S315 and reflexive increase in total nuclear p53 only in some of the treated cell lines, suggesting that other pathways may be involved in cell lines that do respond but fail to show respective molecular changes. Alisertib was first recognized as a possible drug candidate in NB owing to its ability to stabilize MYC proteins.44 , 45 It has since been promoted in clinical development for NB46 and has demonstrated both tolerability30 and efficacy.46 Patients with tumors harboring both MYCN amplification and AURKA expression particularly benefitted from the therapy, though the finding was only detailed in three patients. Paradoxically, results from the phase II study of alisertib combined with irinotecan and temozolomide demonstrated inferior progression-free survival in patients with MYCN amplification.46 The authors of this study hypothesized that a contributory factor was that this cohort was more heavily pre-treated than the phase I cohort. We propose that the potential therapeutic benefit of selinexor combined with alisertib may apply to a broader cohort of children with high-risk NB. Future studies in relapsed disease models could reveal whether and for how long these tumors remain sensitive to the combination. In the MYCN -amplified cell line KCNR, we showed that single or combination therapy decreased cytosolic MYCN levels. We observed selinexor-induced cytotoxicity against both MYCN- WT and -amplified NB cells, which suggests that the sensitivity to selinexor is agnostic of the MYCN status. Furthermore, when examining the interdependency of the MYCN status and XPO1 expression for patient outcome, we found that survival was predicted by XPO1 levels but not affected when we compared MYCN -amplified with WT tumors. Thus, we hypothesize that the effect on the MYCN targets is an additive effect to induce cytotoxicity in NB cells. This suggests that patients with either MYCN -amplified or -WT tumors may benefit from XPO1 inhibition. We have modeled our animal study according to a regimen that we foresee administering to patients with relapsed/refractory NB and WT-TP53 status. Both agents tested herein, selinexor and alisertib, are commercially available and their therapeutic indices and toxicities have been well documented, which would facilitate the expeditious movement into patient trials. The most frequent grade 3 and 4 toxicities observed in children who received single-agent alisertib were thrombocytopenia (21%), leukopenia (33%), and neutropenia (52%).47 Selinexor was primarily associated with grade 3 and 4 hyponatremia in a pediatric trial,48 though several adult studies have found thrombocytopenia in treated patients.49 Thus, we anticipate thrombocytopenia as one of the shared toxicities caused by our combination. This assumption is corroborated by preclinical work that has shown severe thrombocytopenia in AURKAnull mice.50 In addition, selinexor inhibits the nuclear export of STAT3, which is part of the thrombopoietin pathway that leads to a maturational arrest of megakaryocytes from progenitor cells causing thrombocytopenia.51 Though alisertib is a selective inhibitor of AURKA, it has low affinity to AURKB.52 The described toxicities with alisertib were primarily attributed to AURKB and could be avoided by using more selective inhibitor of AURKA. In a clinical trial, we would propose a regimen where alisertib is administered at 45 mg/m2 using oral solution as daily doses for 7 days46 and selinexor at a starting dose of 45 mg/m2 per dose orally on days 1, 3, 8, 10, 22, and 24 escalated to 55 and 70 mg/m2 according to a rolling-six design.48 Altogether, this study uncovered a milieu of relevant targetable pathways, most notably those of the p53 pathway by which selinexor can induce cytotoxicity in NB. Furthermore, synergism can be mediated through the inhibition of AURKA to further suppress tumor growth in relevant preclinical models. As such, translational studies are warranted to ascertain clinical efficacy for pediatric patients with high-risk disease. title: POLQ mediated end-joining promotes DNA damage tolerance in neuroblastoma
abstract: Segmental chromosomal alterations, including 11q deletion and 17q gain, are the strongest predictors of pediatric neuroblastoma relapse. These alterations result from unbalanced translocations linked to erroneous DNA repair. Breakpoint sequence analysis suggests that these abnormalities arise through a nonhomologous end-joining mechanism, indicating a potential therapeutic opportunity. While the exact components driving this DNA end-joining process in neuroblastoma remain unknown, polymerase theta-mediated end-joining (TMEJ) has been implicated in other homologous recombination-deficient cancers. Our previous work demonstrated that high-risk neuroblastoma expresses elevated levels of TMEJ components, including DNA Ligase III and Ligase I, while downregulating classical NHEJ factors (DNA Ligase IV and Artemis). Here we show that POLQ, a critical enzyme in TMEJ, is significantly upregulated in neuroblastoma. POLQ knockout impairs proliferation, enhances sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and reduces tumor growth in vivo. These findings suggest that POLQ facilitates DNA damage tolerance in neuroblastoma and represents a viable therapeutic target.

S1936-5233(25) -0 Fig. 1 POLQ overexpression found in high-risk neuroblastoma cell lines and patient tumors, predicts poor survival outcomes in neuroblastoma. (A & B) neuroblastoma cells with high-risk genotypes (SK-N-BE(2), IMR-32, and LA1–55n cells) expressed significantly higher mRNA, detected by qRT-PCR (A ) and protein levels of POLQ in Western blot normalized to GAPDH (B ) compared to non-tumorigenic SH-EP1 cells and intermediate risk SH-SY5Y cells. (****p < 0.0001, **p < 0.01, *p < 0.05). The R2 microarray analysis platform was used for analysis and is the data source. For POLQ expression in patient tumors and Kaplan-Meier survival curves we used the study with accession noGSE45547. (C ) POLQ expression in neuroblastoma patients across INSS stage was investigated. Stage 4 and Stage 3 groups of patient’s tumors have high expression of POLQ when compared stages 1, 2 and 4. (D ) POLQ expression between MYCN amplified and non-amplified tumors demonstrates high POLQ expression in MYCN amplified neuroblastoma tumors when compared to non-MYCN amplified. (E ) Scan modus was used for cutoff determination with a minimum group size of 8 to determine the best P value, and P values were corrected for multiple testing (Bonferroni). Gene expression was correlated with survival. Kaplan-Meier curve revealed that high POLQ expression had worse overall survival probability (29 %) compared with patients with low Lig3 expression (81 %), cutoff 2294.7, P = 4.3e-13. (F) Kaplan-Meier curve of event free survival revealed that high POLQ expression had worse event free survival probability (39 %) when compared to low POLQ expression patients (75 %), cutoff 1559.4, p = 2.48e-12. Fig 1 Fig. 2 POLQ knockout by CRISPR-Cas9 induces cell cycle arrest in high-risk neuroblastoma LA1–55n cells. (A ) Genomic PCR results shows POLQ targeting in clone KO-Q6 and KO-Q63. The upper panel diagram of genomic PCR Primer design, two set of primer were utilized to detect the left and right integration junctions (LF, LR: Forward and reverse PCR primer to amplify the left integration junction; RF, RR: Forward and reverse PCR primer to amplify the right integration junction). Lower left panel show left integration junction PCR products and lower right panel show right integration junction PCR products amplified from blasticidin selected colonies in 1.5 % agarose gel. (B ) Immunoblot validation of POLQ expression knockout in KO-Q6 and KO-Q63 colonies. (C ) mRNA POLQ expression was measured in LA1–55n control, KO-Q6 and KO-Q63 colonies (*** p < 0.001) (D ) Cell growth time was observed using MTS/PMS assay in Control and KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) cells. Cell growth was reduced in POLQ KO groups when compared to Control (**** p < 0.0001) (E ) The ability to form colonies of LA1–55n Control and POLQ KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) was investigated. The number of colonies in POLQ KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) groups were significantly less than the control group. Fig 2 Fig. 3 POLQ silencing sensitizes high-risk NB cells to anti-cancer therapies. (A ) Effect of etoposide on LA1–55n control and POLQ-KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) cell lines was assessed using MTS/PMS assay. LA1–55n control and POLQ-KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) cells were treated with varying concentrations of etoposide for 72 h. The IC50 of POLQ-KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) groups decreased significantly when compared to the control group. (B ) Sites of DNA damage were measured with yH2AX foci expression post 4 Gy irradiation at 2 time points (0.5 h and 24 h). At 0.5 h no difference was observed between control and POLQ-KO (KO-Q6 and KO-Q63) groups. At 24 h the number of yH2AX foci/cell was significantly elevated in POLQ-KO groups relative to the control group suggesting the failure to repair DSBs in the absence of POLQ in these high-risk NB cells. Scale Bar: 10 um. Fig 3: Fig. 4 POLQ knockout halts high-risk neuroblastoma progression in vivo. LA1–55n Control or KO-Q6 2 × 105 cells were injected into left adrenal gland of NSG mice (n = 7). Tumor growth was monitored weekly using ultrasound. (A ) Tumor growth curves measured by ultrasound demonstrates that POLQ absence slows tumor progression (****p < 0.0001). (B ) Representative picture of harvested tumors. (C ) Immunoblot demonstrates POLQ and PCNA expression was down in a KO-Q6 harvested tumor when compared to a control tumor. (D ) Histologic images of control tumors with local infiltration into adjacent musculature. (E ) Micro-metastasis to the lungs (arrows). Scale Bar: 200 um. Fig 4: Fig. 5 Knockout of POLQ augments expression of BMP and activates Smad1/5/9 signaling pathway in high-risk neuroblastoma LA1–55n cell. (A ) Expression profile of knockout POLQ vs control in LA1–55n cells. The top 50 upregulated and downregulated genes in response to POLQ knockout are listed. (B ) Western blot of POLQ knockout cell lines shows increased phospho-Smad1/5/9 relative to total Smad5 and GAPDH as loading controls. (C ) Important enriched gene sets reflecting the consequences of POLQ knockout. Fig 5 Fig. 6 Gain of POLQ by stable transfection in SH-EP1 cells. (A ) immunoblot demonstrates overexpression of POLQ in clone POLQ-8 and clone POLQ-12. (B ) upper panel: SH-EP1 control cells grow as flattened epithelioid cells and do not aggregate or float. Overexpression of POLQ (POLQ-8 and POLQ-12) tended to cause cells to aggregate or float (lower panel shows colony formation of floating cells in condition medium from control or overexpressed POLQ cells). The experiments were repeated three times. (C ) SH-EP1 Control, POLQ-8 and POLQ-12 cells were seeded in 96 well plate and either not treated or treated with 5 uM etoposide. Hospital Dr. SPC 4211 Ann Arbor USA Segmental chromosomal alterations, including 11q deletion and 17q gain, are the strongest predictors of pediatric neuroblastoma relapse. These alterations result from unbalanced translocations linked to erroneous DNA repair. Breakpoint sequence analysis suggests that these abnormalities arise through a nonhomologous end-joining mechanism, indicating a potential therapeutic opportunity. While the exact components driving this DNA end-joining process in neuroblastoma remain unknown, polymerase theta-mediated end-joining (TMEJ) has been implicated in other homologous recombination-deficient cancers. Our previous work demonstrated that high-risk neuroblastoma expresses elevated levels of TMEJ components, including DNA Ligase III and Ligase I, while downregulating classical NHEJ factors (DNA Ligase IV and Artemis). Here we show that POLQ, a critical enzyme in TMEJ, is significantly upregulated in neuroblastoma. POLQ knockout impairs proliferation, enhances sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and reduces tumor growth in vivo. These findings suggest that POLQ facilitates DNA damage tolerance in neuroblastoma and represents a viable therapeutic target. Keywords DNA repair POLQ Neuroblastoma Therapy resistance Introduction Neuroblastoma (NB) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy arising from developing neural crest stem cells, representing the most common extracranial tumor in children [1 ]. Despite intensive multimodal therapy, high-risk NB remains a major clinical challenge, with relapse rates exceeding 50 %. The genetic landscape of NB is characterized by both numerical and segmental chromosomal alterations, with 11q deletion and 17q gain serving as critical predictors of poor prognosis. These segmental aberrations, which frequently occur in treatment-resistant tumors, are thought to result from defective DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair mechanisms that contribute to genomic instability and tumor evolution [2 ,3 ]. The integrity of the genome is safeguarded by two major DSB repair pathways: non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR) [4 ]. However, in cancers with HR deficiencies, such as high-risk NB, alternative repair mechanisms become indispensable for cell survival. One such mechanism is polymerase theta-mediated end-joining (TMEJ), an error-prone process that utilizes POLQ to facilitate DNA repair under conditions of genomic stress [5 ]. Our prior work demonstrated a distinct pattern of DNA repair protein expression in high-risk NB, including the suppression of canonical NHEJ factors (LIG4 and Artemis) and upregulation of alternative TMEJ components (LIG3, LIG1, and PARP1) [6 ]. This suggests a functional reliance on POLQ-mediated repair for maintaining NB genomic stability. POLQ, a highly conserved helicase-polymerase, has emerged as a key player in tumor adaptation to genotoxic stress. Elevated POLQ expression has been observed in multiple cancers and is associated with poor clinical outcomes due to its ability to drive error-prone repair, foster chromosomal rearrangements, and promote therapeutic resistance[7–9 ]. Elevated POLQ expression correlates with poor outcomes in multiple cancers [7 ,10–12 ], yet its role in neuroblastoma remains unexplored. We hypothesize that POLQ facilitates DNA damage tolerance and tumor maintenance in neuroblastoma . Given the distinct DNA repair landscape in high-risk NB, we hypothesized that POLQ serves as a critical mediator of DNA damage tolerance and tumor maintenance. To test this, we investigated the functional role of POLQ in NB DSB repair, evaluating its impact on proliferation, response to DNA-damaging agents, and tumor progression. Our findings provide new insights into NB repair pathway dependencies and highlight POLQ as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in this aggressive childhood cancer.
