Neuroblastoma (NB) is a type of paediatric cancer that originates from embryonic sympathoadrenal cells. Despite its paediatric origin, NB is mostly treated with strategy of non-small cell lung cancer like adults due to lack of specific therapeutic approach. To improve treatment outcome for NB patients, developing drugs that specifically target the genetic mutations or molecular pathways involved in neuroblastoma is necessary. Overexpression of the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R) has been linked to various malignancies, including paediatric cancers. We hypothesized that inhibiting IGF1R with ALK (NB specific mutation) by phytochemical compound could effectively treat NB while avoiding undesirable cytotoxic effects. We evaluated the efficacy of Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP) as IGF1R inhibitor, for treatment of NB. The IC50 value of PPP on SH-SY5Y, NB cells after 24 h of treatment was found to be 0.501 μM. Molecular docking studies revealed that PPP had a binding score of −7.5 kcal/mol with IGF1R and − 8.8 kcal/mol with ALK. This suggests that PPP not only binds to and inhibits IGF1R but also has a strong affinity for ALK. Gene expression studies, densitometric analysis, scratch assays, and AO/EtBr differential staining were used to evaluate the efficacy of PPP in NB cells. Transcript expression and densitometric analysis revealed that PPP could downregulate IGF1R and ALK in NB cells. Downregulation of SNAIL , a mesenchymal marker, and upregulation of E-cadherin , an epithelial marker, indicated a mesenchymal to epithelial transition in NB cells, suggesting that PPP treatment inhibited NB cell migration and proliferation. This was further supported by scratch assay results in our study. Furthermore, gene expression analysis of p53 , BAX and BCL2 indicated that PPP induces apoptosis in NB cells. AO/EtBr differential staining revealed apoptotic phenomena in NB cells after 24 h of PPP treatment. Although further research is needed to explore the receptor targeting approach using PPP for IGF1R and ALK inhibition. Graphical abstract Unlabelled Image Keywords Neuroblastoma Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP) ALK IGF1R Epithelial to mesenchymal transition Apoptosis 1 Introduction Neuroblastoma (NB), originating from sympathetic nerve cells, is the most common extracranial paediatric solid tumor. It accounts for 8–10 % of occurrence of malignant tumors in children [1 ]. The overall survival of children with high-risk NB is around 40–50 % despite the aggressive treatment protocols consisting of intensive chemotherapy, surgery, radiation therapy, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation [2 ]. One of the most common phenomena associated with different cancers is sustained signaling by growth factors. During development, growth factors regulate cellular differentiation and division in a controlled manner to maintain cellular physiology, however, its uncontrolled signaling leads to cancer metastasis. The ligand-receptor interaction of Insulin-like growth factor (IFG) with Insulin-like growth factor 1 Receptor (IGF1R) plays a pivotal role in regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis [3 ,4 ]. Multiple studies have characterized the pro-oncogenic role of IGF1R in NB cells and tumor models [5–9 ]. Furthermore, overexpression of ALK gene and protein, another tyrosine kinase receptor has been firmly established over the last two decades in certain subsets of neuroblastoma [10–15 ]. Considering the complex nature of the cancer disease, its treatment has been a continuous hassle with relatively little success. In NB patients, the response to current standard treatments is highly heterogeneous, varying from total regression to the development of multi-drug resistance and severe toxicities [16 ]. A promising approach for the development of treatment strategies for neuroblastoma could involve the inhibition of IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases and the signaling networks that they are connected to. Currently available specific IGF1R tyrosine kinase inhibitor and ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors are associated with adverse events which impairs patient's quality of life [17–19 ]. Better treatment options may be developed without the related negative effects of chemotherapy if both of these tyrosine kinases were inhibited by a single phytochemical medication. Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP), derived from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum , is a phytochemical tyrosine kinase inhibitor reported to inhibit IGF1R in different cancers such as hepatoma, non-small cell lung cancer rhabdomyosarcoma [20 ,21 ]. As IGF1R and ALK both are receptor tyrosine kinase, we predicted that PPP could be able to inhibit both of this receptor tyrosine kinases. We aimed to evaluate, if PPP possessed dual inhibitory nature on IGF1R and ALK in SH-SY5Y NB cells. 2 Material and methods 2.1 Compound Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP) (5R,5aR,8aS,9R)-5-hydroxy-9-(3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl)-5a,6,8a,9-tetrahydro-5H-[2]benzofuro[5,6 f][1,3]benzodioxol-8-one, a known IGF1R inhibitor, with a molecular weight of 414.41 was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (T9576). 2.2 Cell line SH-SY5Y, neuroblastoma cell line was obtained from NCCS, Pune. Cells were cultured in MEM media with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1× antibiotics (penicillin-streptomycin; Gibco, 15,140,122) in 5 % CO2 at 37 °C. (The known characteristic feature of SH-SY5Y cells is that the plasma membrane is strongly enriched for ALKWT whereas both ALKWT and ALKF1174L are present in intracellular compartments) [22 ]. 2.3 Molecular docking The binding affinity of PPP was checked with tyrosine kinase receptors: ALK and IGF1R. The 3D structure of Picropodophyllotoxin was obtained from PubChem (PubChem Id: ) in SDF format to analyses the binding affinity of PPP with ALK (PDB Id: 5FTO ) and IGF1R (PDB Id: 5FXQ ). Ligand in SDF format was retrieved into the workspace of AutoDock tools 1.5.7. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina 1.5.7. For 2D visualization of the docked file, BIOVIA Discovery Study Visualizer 2021 was used. For 3D visualization of the docked file, PyMOL 2.5 software was used. 2.4 Evaluation of cytotoxicity SH-SY5Y cells were seeded into 96-well plates at the density of 5 × 104 cells. Cells were treated with various concentrations of PPP (0.89, 0.68, 0.48, 0.20, and 0.068 μM) and incubated for 24 h to measure the cytotoxicity. After exposure to PPP, MTT treatment was given for 4 h. Formazan crystals were dissolved using 200μL of DMSO and the intensity of color was measured at 570 nm (nm) using a microplate reader (InfiniteM200pro, Nanoquant Multimode reader, Tecan). 2.5 Gene expression analysis Cells were exposed to PPP for 24 h and used for RNA isolation. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 15,596,018). After assuring the quality and quantity of RNA, it was used for cDNA synthesis (Bio-Rad iScript cDNA, 1,708,891). qPCR was performed with triplicate assays using the SYBR Green mix (Bio-Rad iTaq Universal SYBR Green Supermix, 1,725,121). Primers for IGF1R, PI3KCB, AKT, BAX, BCL2, CDH1, SNAIL, NANOG, TWIST, TUBULIN, CDK8, p53, ALK, MYCN, NFKB and GAPDH were designed using the Primer-BLAST tool NCBI. GAPDH was used as an internal control. Data analysis was done by CT value and fold change expression was calculated by the 2-ΔΔC T method. 2.6 Western blot analysis After 24 h of PPP treatment to SH-SY5Y, cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89,900). The protein concentration was estimated by Pierce BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23,227). After SDS-PAGE, protein was transferred onto PVDF membrane (Bio-Rad, 1,620,177). Blocking was performed with 5 % BSA (HiMedia, MB083) in TBS for 1 h followed by overnight incubation with primary antibody at 4 °C. The blot was washed thrice with TBS-T buffer and incubated with HRP conjugated Goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody (Invitrogen, 656,120) in bocking buffer (1:1000 dilution) for 2 h. The intensity of the bands was observed in iBright CL100 Chemidoc (Thermo Fischer) and densitometric analysis was carried out using ImageJ software. 2.7 Immunocytochemistry Cells were incubated on Poly-d -lysine (Gibco, 1108) coated coverslip in 6 well plate. After PPP treatment for 24 h, the cells were washed with cold PBS and permeabilized with 1 % Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 min. Blocking was performed for 2 h in buffer containing 2 % BSA (HiMedia, MB083) in PBS with 0.1 % Tween-20 (HiMedia, MB067). Cells were washed in chilled PBS and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. After primary antibody incubation, cells were washed with PBS and incubated with secondary antibody (Alexa Fluor 488 antibody, Invitrogen, A32731) for 1 h at room temperature in dark. Cells were observed under confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM 710 Confocal Microscope). Captured images were analyzed by ImageJ software. 2.8 Scratch healing assay The monolayer of SH-SY5Y cells was wounded with 100 μL pipette tip. Cells were incubated for 24 h with PPP. The migrated distance of cells was measured and three randomly chosen fields were analyzed for each well to observe the anti-migratory and anti-proliferative potency of PPP. 2.9 Cell death analysis (morphological analysis) SH-SY5Y cells were treated with PPP at 50 % confluency for 24 h. Cells were fixed in methanol and stained with Acridine orange (AO) (HiMedia, TC262) and Ethidium bromide (EtBr) (HiMedia, MB071) stain (a mixture containing 100 μg/mL AO and 50 μg/mL EtBr) for 10 min at room temperature in dark. Cell morphology was examined under a fluorescent microscope (Zeiss Axio Observer A1 Fluorescence Inverted Microscope). 2.10 Statistical analysis All data is expressed as Mean ± SEM. Data was analyzed on GraphPad prism software using student's t -test. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. * denotes p ≤ 0.05, ** denotes p ≤ 0.01, *** denotes p ≤ 0.001 and **** denotes p ≤ 0.0001. 3 Results 3.1 Molecular docking of PPP to IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases PPP is a phytochemical that is known to inhibit IGF IR, a receptor tyrosine kinase by binding to the ATP binding domain and reducing its phosphorylation. We had hypothesized that PPP could be able to inhibit ALK too, as it is a receptor tyrosine kinase and PPP is an ATP binding competitor. In order to evaluate our speculation, molecular docking was performed. Docking score/binding affinity of PPP with IGF1R is −7.5 kcal/mol, while the docking score/binding affinity of PPP with ALK is 8.8 kcal/mol (Fig. 1 ). Docking score of ALK when compared with IGF1R suggest that PPP could be a potent inhibitor of ALK as well. 3.2 Cytotoxic potential of PPP We assessed the cytotoxicity of PPP in neuroblastoma cell line upon exposure for 24 h by MTT assay. Our documented IC50 of PPP in SH-SY5Y cells is 0.501 μM (Fig. 2 ). Investigators have previously found the IC50 value of PPP in other IGF1R-positive tumor cells in the range of 0.05 μM – 0.5 μM (Menu et al., 2006; Tarnowski et al., 2017). Our results are in accordance with the findings of previously mentioned investigators. However, MTT assay serves as an indirect measurement of the cell viability, and not a specific test for apoptosis. For further experiments, a dose of 16 nM PPP was used, which upon morphological examination under microscope revealed that it induces only apoptosis while avoiding necrosis in the cells. 3.3 PPP as a dual inhibitor of IGF1R and ALK To evaluate our docking results, gene expression analysis and, post-translational analysis by western blotting was performed. Expression of IGF1R gene was downregulated upon PPP treatment (p ≤ 0.0001), which is also supported by the decreased expression of IGF1R protein in the densitometric analysis of blots (p ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 3 ). Immunocytochemistry was performed to further validate the IGF1R expression (Fig. 4 ). Image analysis revealed a significant downregulation in IGF1R expression (p ≤ 0.001) in NB cells upon PPP treatment. Interaction of IGF1 and IGF1R results in autophosphorylation of IGF1R at specific tyrosine residues, which stimulates further downstream signaling [23 ]. We assessed, if PPP inhibited autophosphorylation of IGF1R. The protein expression level of phosphorylated IGF1R was significantly lower than that of the non-treated NB cells (p ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 3 ). Furthermore, downregulation of ALK was observed at translational (p ≤ 0.01) and post-translational levels (p ≤ 0.001) (Fig. 3 ). Downregulation of ALK was further evaluated through immunocytochemistry (Fig. 4 ). Image analysis revealed significant downregulation of ALK (p ≤ 0.0001), which further supports the gene expression and densitometric analysis. Gene expression and post-translational results strongly suggest that PPP effectively inhibits IGF1R and ALK in NB cells, acting as a dual inhibitor. 3.4 PPP alters downstream signal cascade activated by IGF1R and ALK IGF1R and ALK autophosphorylation can result in activation of multiple downstream signaling cascades, one of the prominent being PI3K/AKT [24 ,25 ]. To evaluate if inhibition of IGF1R and ALK by PPP results in diminished expression of these downstream kinases, gene expression analysis of PI3K and AKT was carried out, which revealed their significant downregulation (p ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 5 A ). CDK is another kinase involved in cell cycle regulation [26 ]. Uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation occurs as a result of abnormal CDK activation. Hyperactive PI3K/AKT pathway could increase CDK expression via activation of Cyclin D1 [27 ,28 ]. CDK8 is a member of the CDK family, serving crucial role in cell cycle regulation and it has been identified as a key oncogenic driver in many cancers [29 ,30 ]. It could thus be speculated that perturbed PI3K/AKT pathway leads to diminished expression of CDK8. Downregulated expression of CDK8 gene (p ≤ 0.0001) validates our speculation (Fig. 5 A). Furthermore, PI3K/AKT signaling enhances cell survival via NF-κB and MYCN [25 ,31 ]. Gene expression analysis implies suppression of MYCN and NF-κB gene was observed upon PPP treatment (p ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 5 B). Additionally, immunocytochemical localisation of NF-κB was performed which indicated its significant downregulation (p ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 5 C). Diminished MYCN and NF-κB expression further supports the speculation of PI3K/AKT inhibition. 3.5 PPP inhibits migration of SH-SY5Y NB cells One of the fundamental abnormalities of neoplastic cell is its unregulated migration. Cancer cells lose their migratory ability upon perturbation of migratory and proliferative signals via mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET). The role of insulin-like growth factors as potent chemotactic agents stimulating cancer migration is evident from the literature [32 ,33 ]. Increasing number of studies report the involvement of IGF1R signaling in EMT mediated tumor metastasis and drug resistance [34 ]. We thus assessed, whether PPP induced IGF1R inhibition could impair cancer cell migration. Gene expression analysis in PPP treated SH-SY5Y cells, when compared to control cells showed downregulation of TUBULIN , SNAIL , TWIST and NANOG mesenchymal markers (p ≤ 0.0001). While upregulation of E-cadherin (CDH1) epithelial marker was observed (p ≤ 0.0001) (Fig. 6 ). These data implies that PPP induced IGF1R inhibition via Mesenchymal to Epithelial transition could impede metastatic ability of the NB cell. Furthermore, the in vivo ability of cancer cells to migrate in an uncontrolled manner is mimicked by their in vitro behavior. Scratch assay was performed on SH-SY5Y cells to validate the anti-migratory ability of PPP. We observed that after 24 h of exposure, PPP was indeed able to attenuate cell migration in NB cells (Fig. 7 ). The observed wound enclosure of NB cells in control condition was measured to be 1.45 mm, whereas upon PPP exposure it was measured to be 1.88 mm. PPP treatment was thus able to hamper the characteristic uncontrolled growth and migratory feature of SH-SY5Y cells to a certain degree. 3.6 PPP alters morphology and induces apoptosis in SH-SY5Y NB cells IGF1R is known to impart anti-apoptotic properties in different types of cells [35 ]. Furthermore, studies have reported that cancer cells undergo regression upon IGF1R inhibition [36 ,37 ]. Therefore, we investigated if PPP mediated inhibition of IGF1R is able to induce apoptosis in NB cells as well. Low level expression of p53 is a phenomenon common to cancer cells, enabling them to proliferate in an uncontrolled manner. We thus postulated that upon inhibition of mitogenic IGF1R signaling through PPP, p53 expression in NB cancer cells may increase, ultimately driving the neoplastic cells towards programmed cell death. Gene expression analysis of p53 found increase expression of its transcript by 5.625 ± 0.16 fold (p ≤ 0.0001). In addition to the p53 gene, BAX and BCL2 genes play a significant role in regulating apoptosis. Gene expression analysis of transcripts of BAX, pro-apoptotic marker and BCL2, anti-apoptotic marker revealed a significant upregulation of BAX (p ≤ 0.0001) and a significant downregulation of BCL2 (p ≤ 0.0001) in the PPP treated SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 8 A ). Cell viability and apoptosis were further evaluated in SH-SY5Y cells via AO/EtBr differential staining (Fig. 8 B, C). Acridine orange stains viable cells which gives green fluorescence, but with early apoptotic cells it gives yellow fluorescence whereas with late apoptotic cells along with ethidium bromide its gives orange fluorescence. EtBr is only taken up by necrotic cells and it gives red fluorescence. Nuclear condensation and cell shrinkage are the characteristic features of apoptotic cells that was observed due to PPP treatment. We observed a greater number of cells in the apoptotic phase on treatment of IGF1R inhibitor. These results along with p53 , BAX upregulation and BCL2 downregulation implies that PPP could inhibit growth and induce apoptosis in NB tumor cells. 4 Discussion Neuroblastoma, a highly aggressive childhood cancer, poses significant challenges due to its resistance to conventional chemotherapeutic approaches and limited success with surgical interventions. The current treatment options for neuroblastoma have yielded low cure rates, underscoring the urgent need for the development of more targeted and effective therapeutic strategies [38 ]. Altered expression of IGF1R and ALK resulting in oncogenic signaling which drives the Neuroblastoma has been very well established over last couple of decades [8–10 ,12 ]. Picropodophyllotoxin (PPP), an epimer of podophyllotoxin, derived from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum is known to act as an inhibitor of IGF1R tyrosine kinase [39 ,40 ]. Furthermore, PPP has exhibited notable anti-tumor activity in ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL) cancer [41 ]. This study aims to demonstrate the potential of the phytochemical PPP as a dual inhibitor of IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma (NB) cells. Molecular docking analysis indicated favourable binding affinities of PPP to both IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases, suggesting its ability to competitively inhibit their ATP binding domains. Indeed, the findings of molecular docking analysis indicate the potential of the phytochemical PPP, as a dual inhibitor of IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases. To evaluate the cytotoxic potential of PPP, the MTT assay was performed in the SH-SY5Y NB cells. The obtained IC50 value of 0.501 μM is consistent with previous reports of PPP's efficacy against IGF1R-positive tumor cells [42 ,43 ]. As our docking results implied that PPP could be an inhibitor of ALK along with IGF1R, we validated this speculation by gene expression analysis, western blotting, and immunocytochemistry. The expression of IGF1R gene and protein was significantly downregulated upon PPP treatment, indicating effective inhibition at both transcriptional and translational levels. The inhibition of IGF1R autophosphorylation further confirmed the disruptive effect of PPP on IGF1R signaling in NB cells. Inhibition of IGF1R autophosphorylation by PPP has previously been also reported in 5 T33 multiple myeloma cells [42 ]. Similar downregulation was observed for ALK, supporting the speculation that PPP acts as a dual inhibitor of both tyrosine kinases. To gain insights into the molecular mechanism of PPP treatment, we investigated the downstream signaling cascades activated by IGF1R and ALK, including the PI3K/AKT pathway [24 ,25 ]. Through gene expression analysis, a significant downregulation of PI3K and AKT was observed, indicating the inhibition of this pro-survival pathway. The findings were further supported by the downregulation of CDK8, a critical regulator of cell cycle progression [44 ], confirming the disruption of cancer cell proliferation by PPP. Moreover, we observed the suppression of MYCN and NF-κB genes, both known to play pivotal roles in promoting cell survival [45 ,46 ]. These results highlight the potential of PPP to target multiple signaling pathways simultaneously, further emphasizing its promising therapeutic implications. Uncontrolled migration is a hallmark of cancer, and IGF1R and ALK signaling has been implicated in tumor metastasis [24 ,47 ]. We investigated the effect of PPP on the migratory ability of NB cells using gene expression analysis and scratch assay. Our findings revealed that treatment with PPP resulted in a significant downregulation of key mesenchymal markers including TUBULIN , SNAIL , TWIST , and NANOG . Concomitantly, there was a remarkable upregulation of the epithelial marker E-cadherin. These alterations in gene expression profiles strongly suggested a shift in the phenotype of NB cells towards a less migratory and more epithelial-like state. To further substantiate this effect, we performed scratch assay to evaluate cell migration. Scratch assay demonstrated attenuation of NB cell migration upon PPP treatment. These collective findings indicate the potential of PPP as a promising anti-metastatic agent in NB cancer. The induction of apoptosis represents a critical goal in the development of effective anticancer therapies [48 ]. Our investigations revealed a substantial upregulation of the transcript of tumor suppressor protein p53, a key regulator of apoptosis [49 ], upon PPP treatment. Additionally, the transcript expression of BAX, a pro-apoptotic protein [50 ], was significantly elevated, while the transcript expression of BCL2, an anti-apoptotic protein [51 ], was notably reduced. These alterations in gene expression patterns collectively indicate the activation of apoptotic pathways in NB cells following PPP treatment. To complement the gene expression analysis, we employed AO/EtBr staining, a well-established method for visualizing apoptotic cells [52 ]. PPP-treated cells exhibited characteristic features of apoptosis, including nuclear condensation and cell shrinkage, as observed through microscopic examination. These morphological changes further confirm the ability of PPP to induce apoptosis in NB cells. 5 Conclusion Neuroblastoma is an aggressive childhood cancer, often resistant to the most aggressive chemotherapeutic and surgical interventions. Since the current cure rate of NB is very low, there is a need to develop target specific treatment options. The findings of current study demonstrates that PPP exhibits dual inhibitory effects on IGF1R and ALK tyrosine kinases in NB cells. PPP effectively disrupts the downstream signaling pathways of these kinases which contribute to the suppression of cancer cell migration and induction of apoptosis. Although, further in vivo evaluations are necessary to support our study, through in vitro experiments on SH-SY5Y NB cells, we have demonstrated that PPP could effectively attenuate embryonic cancers such as NB, highlighting PPPs therapeutic potential. PPP is currently being used in clinical trials in other solid cancer under the name AXL1717 [53 ]. PPP, thus could be used to develop treatment strategies to remediate NB as well, which reflects the clinical significance of our study. title: The paracrine TAC1-TACR1 signaling promotes endothelial senescence and metastatic progression in neuroblastoma
abstract: Distal metastasis remains a major clinical challenge in neuroblastoma (NB), the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. However, the molecular mechanisms mediating tumor-endothelial crosstalk and NB metastasis remain incompletely understood. By integrating single-cell omics analyses of clinical NB samples with experimental validations, we established the molecular subtypes of NB and identified a C2 subtype marked by MYCN amplification and dual positivity for TWIST1 and TAC1 expressions. This aggressive tumor subpopulation exhibited enhanced secretion of the neuropeptide substance P (encoded by TAC1), which was regulated by the transcription factor TWIST1. TAC1 signaled to tumor-associated endothelial cells with elevated TACR1 expression, consequently leading to endothelial senescence and disrupted vascular integrity. Remarkably, TAC1 overexpression was sufficient to accelerate NB tumorigenesis, circulating tumor cell (CTC) generation and metastatic progression in vivo. Clinically, TWIST1+TAC+ CTCs were significantly enriched in the blood samples of metastatic NB patients compared to the non-metastatic group. As a proof-of-principle study, we further demonstrated that the TACR1 antagonist aprepitant could effectively suppress endothelial senescence, tumorigenesis, and CTC-mediated metastatic progression in vivo, presenting a potential therapeutic strategy for NB patients with TAC1-TACR1 activation.

Box plot showing the mRNA expression level of gene related SASP in both CD31 high expression and TACR1 high expression patients. ∗∗∗∗P 99.95% leukocyte depletion, substantially enhancing the purity of isolated CTC populations. 5.20 Sample preparation and scRNA sequencing Four fresh specimens subjected to single-cell sequencing were stored in Tissue Preservation Solution (Singleron Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China) and placed on ice. After samples were washed 3 times with HBSS, GEXSCOPE™ Tissue Dissociation Solution (Singleton Biotechnologies) was added to each sample. Subsequently, the tissue was finely cut into small pieces with scissors and then digested at 37 °C for 8 min to dissociate the tissue into single cells. The single-cell suspension (1 × 105 cells/mL) was then loaded onto microfluidic devices and scRNA-seq libraries were constructed according to Singleron GEXSCOPE™ protocol by GEXSCOPE™ Single-Cell RNA Library Kit (Singleron Biotechnologies). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument with 150 bp paired end reads. Five fresh specimens for 10x Genomics Cell Preparation Guide describes best practices and general protocols for washing, counting and concentrating cells from both abundant and limited cell suspensions (greater than or less than total cells, respectively) in preparation for use in10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols. Cell viability was measured with Acridine Orange/Propidium Iodide (AO/PI) kit. scRNA-seq libraries were prepared using ChromiumTM Single Cell G Chip and Chromium Single Cell 5’ Library & Gel Bead Kit v2 and sequencing was accomplished on an Illumina NovaSeq6000 System using a paired-end 150 bp. 5.21 Single‐cell transcriptome sequencing collection and data analysis For Singleron single-cell transcriptome sequencing and data preprocessing, the Telescope software (version 1.5.1) was used for the preprocessing of the sequencing reads. Briefly, the reads in FASTQ format were aligned to human genome reference (GRCh38) using STAR [49 ], and then “RNA multi-samples” were used to derive a gene expression matrix for each sample. For 10X Genomics single-cell transcriptome sequencing and data preprocessing, the Cell Ranger Single-Cell toolkit (v7.2.0) was applied to align reads for this case based on the human reference genome GRCh38. Downstream analysis of single-cell data was performed using the Seurat R package [50 ]. First, we removed cells with mitochondrial RNA content exceeding 20%, as well as those with UMI counts below 200 or above 6000. Potential doublets were predicted and filtered using ‘DoubletFinder’ R package [51 ], with a doublet removal rate set at 4% per patient. The analysis was performed using five principal components and a default pN value of 20%. The filtered gene expression matrix for each sample was normalized and scaled using the “NormalizeData” and “ScaleData” functions in Seurat R package. Batch effects across different patients were adjusted using the Harmony R package [52 ], and gene expression matrices from all samples were integrated. Principal component analysis (PCA) was then performed on the adjusted expression matrix, utilizing highly variable genes (HVGs) identified by the “FindVariableFeatures” function. Next, the “RunPCA” function was used to perform the PCA and the “FindNeighbors” function was used to construct a K‐nearest‐neighbor graph. The most representative principal components (PCs) selected based on PCA were used for cluster analysis with the ‘FindCluster’ function to identify different cell types. Those with high PECAM1 and VWF expressions were identified as endothelial cells; those with high CHGA and CHGB expressions as neuroblast cells. Following unsupervised clustering, we performed cell subpopulations based on their specifically expressed marker genes and named each subpopulation according to its most significantly enriched gene. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in each subpopulation were identified using the ‘wilcoxauc’ function from the presto R package, assessing significance based on log2-transformed fold changes (log2FC) and P -values. We consider differentially expressed genes with log2FC > 0.3 and P -value 1 for a subpopulation in each tissue indicates that the cluster is enriched in that tissue. 5.23 Copy number variation calling The inferCNV R package (inferCNV of the Trinity CTAT Project, provided at https://github.com/broadinstitute/inferCNV ) was used to infer large-scale chromosomal copy number variations in each cell. All other parameters were set to their default values. 5.24 Chip-seq and data analysis All chip-seq data for TWIST1 were downloaded in public database ChIP-Atlas [55 ]. We used IGV to visualize the genomic regions, and the enhancer regions were divided into nonoverlapping windows of different sizes (the windows with reads ≤1/20 of window size were filtered out). 5.25 Unsupervised clustering analysis in TARGET-NBL cohort We used the “wilcoxauc” function in presto R package (version 1.0.0) to identify specifically highly expressed genes of each malignant neuroblast cells that formed the cluster-specific gene signatures, with a |log2(FC)| value of >0.58 and a P value of 0.3 and P 0.3 and P 0.3 and P < 0.05 was considered significant. Log-rank test was used for univariate survival analyses and showed as the Kaplan-Meier plot. All statistical analyses and visualization were performed using R or GraphPad Prism. The lines in the middle of the box plot are median and the upper and lower lines indicate 25th and 75th percentiles. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The number of replicates and statistical tests used in figures were shown in corresponding figure legends. title: Focal adhesion kinase and p53 synergistically decrease neuroblastoma cell survival
abstract: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and is responsible for over 15% of pediatric cancer deaths. Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase that is important in many facets of neuroblastoma tumor development and progression. The p53 oncogene, although wild type in most neuroblastomas, lacks significant function as a tumor suppressor in these tumors. Recent reports have found that FAK and p53 interact in some tumor types. We have hypothesized FAK and p53 coordinately control each other's expression and also interact in neuroblastoma. In the present study, we showed that not only do FAK and p53 interact but each one controls the expression of the other. In addition, we also examined the effects of FAK inhibition combined with p53 activation in neuroblastoma and showed that these two, in combination, had a synergistic effect on neuroblastoma cell survival. The findings from this present study help to further our understanding of the regulation of neuroblastoma tumorigenesis and may provide novel therapeutic strategies and targets for neuroblastoma and other pediatric solid tumors.

S0022-4804(15) -9 Fig. 1 Association of FAK and p53 in neuroblastoma cell lines. (A) Immunoblotting of cell lysates from SH-EP, WAC (2), and SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells for FAK, MDM2, and p53 were performed, confirming that all three proteins were present in the cell lines under study. Immunoblotting for β-actin was used to demonstrate equal protein loading. (B) Immunoblotting for p21 in the SH-EP, WAC (2), and SH-SY5Y lysates showed that p21 was present in all three cell lines. Immunoblotting for β-actin demonstrated equal protein loading. (C) Immunoprecipitation followed by Western blotting was used to detect FAK and p53 interaction in neuroblastoma cell lines. Immunoprecipitation with p53 antibody followed by Western blotting for FAK showed a band for FAK at the expected 125 kDa in all cell lines examined (left top panel). Immunoblotting the same membrane for p53 detected a band at the expected 53 kDa (left bottom panel). Immunoprecipitation with FAK antibody followed by Western blotting for p53 detected a band at the expected 53 kDa (right bottom panel) and a FAK band at 125 kDa (right top panel) in all cell lines. (D) Because the MOPC control band for the immunoprecipitation blots (C) was located near the band for p53, immunoprecipitation experiments were also completed with rabbit IgG as the control. Again, immunoprecipitation with p53 antibody followed by immunoblotting for FAK revealed a band at the expected 125 kDa (upper left panel). The reverse immunoprecipitation with FAK and Western blotting for p53 showed a band at the expected 53 kDa level (lower right panel). Immunoblotting for the immunoprecipitated protein with their respective antibodies showed bands at the expected levels for p53 and FAK (lower left and upper right panels, respectively). Fig. 2 Association of FAK and p53 in neuroblastoma cell lines. Dual immunofluorescence staining followed by confocal microscopy was used to evaluate FAK and p53 colocalization in the SH-SY5Y cell line. (A) Representative photograph of immunofluorescence staining for p53 in SH-SY5Y cells (red). (B) These same cells were stained for FAK (green). (C) When the stains were merged, there was overlap between the two stains resulting in a yellow color. (D) Image of overlap staining at higher magnification (white box in (C). FAK and p53 were noted to co-localize in both the cytoplasm (white closed arrow) primarily in the perinuclear area, and in the nucleus (white open arrow). (E) Dual immunofluorescence staining was performed in SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cell lines, and confocal microscopy was used to quantitate the amount of overlap between the two stains by calculating Manders' coefficients. Manders' M1 and M2 coefficients have a value between 0 and 1 with zero indicating no overlap and one representing perfect overlap. There was a large amount of overlap detected between FAK and p53 staining in all three cell lines. (Color version of the figure is available online.) Fig. 3 Expression of p53 in the SH-SY5Y cell line was inversely correlated to FAK. (A) SH-SY5Y cells were transfected with transfection agent alone (control), FAK plasmid, or with empty vector (EV) and cell lysates collected. Immunoblotting was used to detect FAK and p53. Transfection with FAK plasmid resulted in overexpression of FAK protein. Expression of p53 was diminished after FAK overexpression. Densitometry confirmed increased FAK and decreased p53 in the FAK-transfected cells. Transfection agent alone or transfection with empty vector had no effect on FAK or p53 expression. (B) SH-SY5Y cells were transfected with either Lipofectamine alone, negative control siRNA (siNeg) or siRNA to FAK (siFAK) for 48 h. Cell lysates were examined with immunoblotting. FAK expression was decreased with siRNA treatment, and p53 expression increased with decreased FAK. Fig. 4 Expression of FAK in neuroblastoma cell lines was inversely correlated to p53. (A) SH-SY5Y cells were treated with 2 Gy of irradiation to upregulate p53. Cells were harvested, and lysates made at increasing times after irradiation. Immunoblotting was performed, which showed an increase in p53 and p21 (indicating p53 activity) beginning at 1 h after irradiation. As p53 increased after irradiation, FAK protein decreased. (B) Pharmacologic manipulation of p53 with 5-FU was examined. SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cells were treated for 24 h with increasing concentrations of 5-FU. Cell lysates were examined with immunoblotting. 5-FU treatment led to increased p53 and a decrease in FAK in all three cell lines. (C) SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cell lines were treated with increasing concentrations of nutlin-3 for 48 h and immunoblotting was performed on cell lysates. Increasing concentrations of nutlin-3 resulted in increased p53 and a concomitant decrease in FAK expression. (D) Pifithrin-α was used to inhibit p53 in the SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cells. Cell lines were treated with pifithrin-α (25 μM) for 48 h and cell lysates examined for FAK and p53. In all three cell lines, there was a decrease in p53 expression after pifithrin-α treatment and an increase in FAK. Densitometry was performed on all the blots and verified that p53 and FAK expressions were inversely correlated. Fig. 5 FAK inhibition and p53 activation individually decrease neuroblastoma cell survival. (A) SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cells were treated for 24 h with increasing concentrations of PF-573,228, and cell lysates were examined for immunoblotting. PF-573,228 treatment resulted in decreased FAK expression in all three cell lines, and as observed previously, p53 expression was inversely related to FAK. (B) SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cells were treated for 24 h with increasing concentrations of PF-573,228, and cell survival was measured by alamarBlue assay. There was a significant decrease in cell survival in all three cell lines beginning at 5 μM concentration. (C) SH-SY5Y cells were treated with increasing concentrations of nutlin-3 for 24 h. Cell survival was measured with alamarBlue assay. There was a significant decrease in SH-SY5Y cell survival with nutlin-3. (D) SH-EP and WAC(2) cell lines were treated with increasing concentrations of nutlin-3 for 24 h. Cell survival was measured with alamarBlue assay. There was a significant decrease in cell survival with nutlin-3 in these two cell lines also. Fig. 6 FAK inhibition combined with p53 activation acted synergistically to decrease neuroblastoma cell survival. (A) SH-SY5Y cells were treated with PF-573,228 (PF) and nutlin-3 combined for 24 h and cell survival measured with alamarBlue assay. CIs were calculated and isobolograms constructed. The straight line connects the LD50 of PF with that of nutlin-3 when each drug was administered alone. CI values above this line suggest an antagonistic effect, those below the line a synergistic effect, and those on the line represent an additive effect. In SH-SY5Y cells, the CIs fall below the line (less than one) suggesting the two treatments together resulted in a synergistic effect. (B) As described in (A), SH-EP cells were treated with PF and nutlin-3 combined for 24 h, cell survival detected, and an isobologram constructed. As with the SH-SY5Y cell lines, the CI values were less than one suggesting that the two treatments combined resulted in a synergistic fashion to decrease survival. (C) WAC (2) cells were treated as described in (A) and (B) Again, the CI for both drugs combined was less than one and suggested a synergistic effect of the two treatments to decrease survival. Keywords FAK p53 SH-EP WAC(2) Neuroblastoma 1 Introduction Neuroblastoma, a tumor of neural crest cells, is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood. Children affected by this tumor most often present with advanced stage disease, and despite significant advances in both medical and surgical pediatric oncologic care, continue to have a dismal prognosis, with a survival of less than 30% [1] . Clearly, novel therapies will need to be developed to improve the outcomes for children with neuroblastoma. Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is a 125 kDa nonreceptor protein tyrosine kinase that has been shown to be important in the tumorigenesis of a number of human tumors. FAK is involved in tumor cell proliferation, motility, survival, and apoptosis [2,3] , and the inhibition of FAK through a number of different means affects tumorigenesis. Inhibition of FAK with ribonucleic acid interference resulted in decreased motility in glioblastoma cells [4] . In other studies, FAK abrogation with antisense oligonucleotides or a dominant-negative FAK protein resulted in decreased melanoma, colon cancer, and breast cancer cell growth [5–7] . Small molecule inhibition of FAK has led to decreased growth and increased apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells [8] and breast cancer cells [9] . Previous studies have shown that FAK messenger RNA and protein were associated with aggressive neuroblastomas [10] and that FAK inhibition in neuroblastoma through a number of different mechanisms resulted in decreased tumor survival [11,12] and metastasis [13] . The tumor suppressor protein, p53 (encoded by the human gene, TP53 ), is a transcription factor that regulates cell signaling pathways involved in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Mutations in the TP53 gene are reported to occur in almost every type of cancer at varying rates resulting in mutant expression or inactivation of p53, leading to increased cellular proliferation, avoidance of apoptosis, and resistance to chemotherapy. In neuroblastoma, most tumors are actually wild-type p53 but conflicting data exist about p53 pathway signaling in this tumor, as activity of p53 is often diminished despite its wild-type status. It is unknown whether p53 activity is decreased due to upregulation of p53 inhibitors, sequestration of p53 in the cytoplasm, or ubiquitination of p53. Slack [14] reported that mouse double minute 2 (Mdm2), the primary inhibitor of p53, is upregulated by MYCN , a proto-oncogene that is amplified in many aggressive, treatment resistant neuroblastomas [15] . On a more general level, some investigators have suggested that proteins, such as FAK, may bind p53, thus sequestering it in the cytoplasm of the cell and preventing it from entering the nucleus and functioning as a transcription factor [16] . Others reported that FAK may facilitate p53 turnover via an MDM2-dependent ubiquitination [17] . There have been recent reports describing the protein–protein interaction between FAK and p53 in breast cancer cell lines and showing that disruption of this interaction with homologous peptides or small molecules resulted in decreased tumor cell survival [18,19] . The present studies were designed to test the hypothesis that in neuroblastoma FAK and p53 each coordinately regulate the other's expression in a biologically significant fashion. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Cells, cell culture, and transfections The human neuroblastoma cells line, SH-SY5Y (CRL-2266; American Type Culture Collection, Manassas, VA) was maintained in 1:1 mixture of minimum Eagle's medium and Ham's F-12 medium with 10% fetal bovine serum, 2 mM L-glutamine, 1 μM non-essential amino acids, and 1 μg/mL penicillin and/or streptomycin. SH-SY5Y cell line was chosen because this cell line was p53 wild type [20] , MDM2 non-amplified [21] , and MYCN non-amplified [22] . SH-EP (MYCN −) and the isogenic WAC (2) (MYCN +) human neuroblastoma cell lines were generously provided by Dr M. Schwab (Deutsches Krebsforschungszentrum, Heidelberg, Germany) and have been described in detail previously [23] . SH-EP and WAC (2) cell lines were maintained in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1 μg/mL penicillin and/or streptomycin. These two cell lines were chosen as they were also p53 wild type [20] , MDM2 non-amplified [21] , and are isogenic for MYCN , with the SH-EP cells being MYCN negative [23] and the WAC (2) cell line stably transfected with a MYCN vector [23] . For these experiments, transfection of plasmids was completed with SuperFect Transfection Reagent (Qiagen Inc, Valencia, CA) as previously described [11] . FAK plasmids, including wild-type FAK (pKH3-FAK) and empty vector (pKH3-EV), were generously provided by Dr JL Guan (University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH) and have been previously described [24] . All plasmids were sequenced at the DNA Sequencing and Analysis Core, Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of Alabama, Birmingham. 2.2 Antibodies and reagents Monoclonal mouse anti-FAK (4.47) and rabbit polyclonal anti-phospho-FAK (Y397) antibodies were obtained from Millipore (1:1000, 05-537; EMD Millipore, Billerica, MA) and Invitrogen (1:1000, 71-7900; Invitrogen Corp, Carlsbad, CA), respectively. Mouse monoclonal antibodies for MDM2 (1:1000, AB-1) and p53 (1:1000, PB53-12) were from Millipore (EMD Millipore) and for p21 from BD Biosciences (1:1000, 2G12; BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA). Anti-MYCN polyclonal rabbit antibody was from Cell Signaling (9405; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA). Monoclonal mouse anti-GAPDH was from Millipore (1:3000, MAB374; EMD Millipore), and anti-β-actin was from Sigma (1:2000, A1978; Sigma–Aldrich Corp, St. Louis, MO). The small molecules were as follows: PF-573,228 (C22 H20 F3 N5 O3 S) from Pfizer (New York, NY); pifithrin-α from Sigma; 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) from EMD Biosciences Millipore; and nutlin-3 from Enzo Life Sciences (Farmingdale, NY). Antibodies used for immunofluorescence were as listed: primary antibody to FAK (4.47) was a rabbit polyclonal (1:1000, C-20; Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA) and to p53 a mouse monoclonal (1:1000, BP53-12; EMD Millipore). Secondary antibodies for immunofluorescence were from Invitrogen and included goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488 (green, 1:200, A- , Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA) and goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 594 (red; 1:200, A- , Thermo Fisher). 2.3 Small interfering RNAs transfection Small interfering RNAs (siRNA) were obtained from Qiagen (Qiagen Inc) for the following FAK target sequence: 5′-CCGGTCGAATGATAAGGTGTA-3’. Transfection was carried out as previously described [25,26] . Briefly, cells were plated (3 × 105 cells per well) on 6-well culture plates and allowed to attach overnight. Cells were treated with HiPerFect (Qiagen) alone, HiPerFect plus 20 nM Negative Control siRNA ( ; Qiagen), or HiPerFect plus FAK siRNA (Hs_PTK2_10 FlexiTube siRNA [NM_005607; Qiagen]) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Cells were incubated for 24–48 h after transfection and then used for experiments. FAK inhibition by siRNA was confirmed using immunoblotting. 2.4 Immunoblotting Western blots were performed as previously described [12] . Briefly, cells were treated with the agent under study, then lysed on ice for 30 min in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCL, (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton-X (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA), 0.5% NaDOC, 0.1% SDS, 5 mM EDTA, 50 mM NaF, 1 mM NaVO3 , 10% glycerol, and protease inhibitors: 10 leupeptin, 10 PMSF, and 1 μg/mL aprotinin. The lysates were cleared by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 30 min at 4°C. Protein concentrations were determined using a Bio-Rad kit (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA), and proteins were separated by electrophoresis on sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gels. Antibodies were used according to manufacturer's recommended conditions. Molecular weight markers (Precision Plus Protein Kaleidoscope Standards; Bio-Rad) confirmed the expected size of the target proteins. Immunoblots were developed with Luminata Classico or Crescendo ECL (EMD Millipore). Blots were stripped with stripping solution (Bio-Rad) at 37°C for 15 min and then reprobed with selected antibodies. Immunoblotting with antibody to β-actin or GAPDH provided an internal control for equal protein loading. 2.5 Immunofluorescence Cells were plated on glass chamber slides and allowed to attach for 24 h after which they were fixed with 3% paraformaldehyde. Cells were permeablized with 0.15% Triton X-100, and the first primary antibody (anti-FAK, C-20, 1:1000; Santa Cruz) was added and incubated at room temperature (RT) for 1 h followed by the addition of the second primary antibody (anti-p53, BP53-12, 1:1000; Invitrogen) that was also incubated for 1 h at RT. The Alexa Fluor 488 secondary antibody (1:200) was added for 45 min at RT. After washing, the second secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 594, was added and incubated as mentioned previously. Prolong Gold antifade reagent with DAPI (P36931; Invitrogen) was used for mounting. Imaging was performed with a Zeiss LSM 710 Confocal Scanning Microscope with Zen 2008 software (Carl Zeiss MicroImaging, LLC, Thornwood, NY) using a 63 × objective with a zoom of 0.9. Analysis of the images and detection of confocal overlap were accomplished using the MetaMorph Microscopy Image Analysis Software (version 7.6; Analytical Technologies, Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA). Manders overlap coefficients were calculated for each of the cell lines [27] . Manders M1 and M2 coefficients have a value between 0 and 1 (0 = no overlap and 1 = perfect overlap) and provide the proportion of the overlap of each channel with the other. The M1 and M2 coefficients were calculated as follows: M1 (green) = the sum of the intensities of green pixels that had a red component divided by the total sum green intensities and M2 (red) = the sum of the intensities of red pixels that had a green component divided by the total sum of red intensities. 2.6 Cell viability and apoptosis Equal numbers of cells were plated and allowed to attach for 24 h. Cells were treated with PF-573,228 or nutlin-3 in varying concentrations. Cellular viability was measured using alamarBlue (Invitrogen) assay. In brief, cells were plated 1.5 × 103 cells per well on 96-well culture plates and allowed to attach. After treatment, 10 μL of alamarBlue dye was added to 200 μL of cell medium. After 4–6 h, the absorbance at 595 nm was measured using a kinetic microplate reader (BioTek Gen5; BioTek Instruments, Winooski, VT). 2.7 Peptides and cell proliferation Peptides were used to interrupt the binding of FAK and p53. The functional peptide (RP-TAT) and the control peptide (TAT) were synthesized with the assistance of P. Mayakonda at the UAB Protein Synthesis Core. The peptide (RP-TAT) and control (TAT) have been described previously [18] . RP-TAT corresponds to the 7 amino-acid peptide binding site on the N-terminal domain of p53 that interacts with the N-terminal domain of FAK. This peptide with the sequence (RMPEAAP) was coupled to a TAT sequence (YGRKKRRQRRR) to allow for improved cellular penetration. The TAT sequence alone was used as a control. Cells were treated with peptides for 48 h at 10-μM concentrations and then stained with trypan blue to assess proliferation. Results were reported as fold change in the ratio of dead to live cells. 2.8 Data analysis Experiments were repeated at least in triplicate, and data were reported as mean ± standard error of the mean. Densitometry of immunoblots was performed using Scion Image Program (http://www.nist.gov/lispix/imlab/prelim/dnld.html ). An analysis of variance or Student t -test was used as appropriate to compare data between groups. Statistical significance was determined at P ≤ 0.05. 3 Results 3.1 Association of FAK and p53 in neuroblastoma cell lines First, we documented that the targets of study were present in the cell lines that we chose for the experiments. Immunoblotting was performed on whole cell lysates of SH-EP, WAC (2), and SH-SY5Y cells. FAK, MDM2, p53 (Fig. 1 A), and p21 (denoting functioning p53) (Fig. 1 B) were all expressed by these cell lines. Previous publications have documented that FAK and p53 interact in cancer cell lines [17,28] . We have shown that FAK was differentially expressed in neuroblastoma cell lines and provided a survival advantage in these cell lines [11] . Because both FAK and p53 were present in neuroblastoma cell lines (Fig. 1 A), we hypothesized that they may also interact in neuroblastoma. Coimmunoprecipitations in both directions (FAK and p53 antibodies) were used to determine whether a FAK and p53 interaction was present. Immunoprecipitation with p53 antibody followed by immunoblotting for FAK showed coprecipitation of p53 protein with FAK, indicating that an association between these two proteins was present in all three cell lines (Fig. 1 C, left panel). This association was also detected by immunoprecipitation with FAK antibody followed by immunoblotting for p53 (Fig. 1 C, right panel). Immunoblotting of the membranes with their respective immunoprecipitation antibody confirmed the immunoprecipitation of the correct protein (Fig. 1 C, left lower and right upper panels). Furthermore, because the immunoglobulin band for MOPC was located near the band for p53, immunoprecipitation experiments were also completed with rabbit IgG as the control (Fig. 1 D, right and left panels). These coimmunoprecipitation data confirmed the previous findings of an association between FAK and p53 in neuroblastoma cell lines. Next, dual immunofluorescence staining and confocal microscopy were used to further examine the potential association of FAK and p53 (Fig. 2 A–D). In the SH-SY5Y cell line, FAK and p53 were noted to colocalize in both the cytoplasm (Fig. 2 D, white closed arrow right panel) primarily in the perinuclear area and in the nucleus (Fig. 2 D, white open arrow right panel). The same findings were noted for the SH-EP (Supplemental Data Fig. 1A–D ) and WAC (2) cell lines (Supplemental Data Fig. 2A–D ). Manders overlap coefficients were calculated for each cell line, with values of 0 indicating no overlap and 1 indicating complete overlap [27] . The overlap coefficients for the FAK and p53 staining indicated a significant amount of overlap, or colocalization of FAK and p53, in all three cell lines (Fig. 2 E). These confocal microscopy results further demonstrated that FAK and p53 associate in human neuroblastoma cell lines. 3.2 Expression of p53 in the SH-SY5Y cell line was inversely correlated to FAK Next, we wished to demonstrate that p53 expression was inversely related to FAK expression. SH-SY5Y cells were treated with transfection agent alone (control), with FAK plasmid, or with empty vector (EV). Cell lysates were evaluated with immunoblotting for FAK and p53. When FAK expression increased after transfection, the p53 diminished (Fig. 3 A). Densitometry was performed and confirmed decreased p53 in the FAK transfected cells (Fig. 3 A). Next, SH-SY5Y cells were transfected with either Lipofectamine alone, negative control siRNA (siNeg), or siRNA to FAK (siFAK) for 48 h. Cell lysates were examined with immunoblotting. FAK abrogation was confirmed (Fig. 3 B), and as FAK decreased, p53 expression increased; a finding verified with densitometry (Fig. 3 B). 3.3 Expression of FAK in neuroblastoma cell lines was inversely correlated to p53 Cellular stressors such as irradiation, hypoxia, or chemotherapy (5-FU) [29] upregulate p53 activity. Additionally, the small molecule MDM2 antagonist, nutlin-3 [30] , increases the activity of wt p53, whereas pifithrin-α decreases activity of p53 [31] . To examine the effects of increased p53 on FAK, we first treated SH-SY5Y cells with irradiation. Cells were irradiated (2 Gy, XRT), collected at increasing times after XRT, and whole cell lysates examined with immunoblotting. A significant increase in p53 was noted as early as 1 h after XRT (Fig. 4 A). Inversely, FAK expression decreased after exposure to XRT (Fig. 4 A). Increased p21 after XRT further showed that p53 was functioning (Fig. 4 A). We next evaluated pharmacologic manipulation of p53 with 5-FU. SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) neuroblastoma cell lines were treated for 24 h with increasing concentrations of 5-FU. Cell lysates were examined with immunoblotting. Treatment with 5-FU resulted in a consistent increase in p53 and a decrease in FAK in all three cell lines (Fig. 4 B). Next, these same cell lines were treated with increasing concentrations of nutlin-3, a p53 activator, for 48 h, and immunoblotting was performed on cell lysates. The nutlin-3 treatment led to a significant increase in p53 (Fig. 4 C), and there was a concomitant decrease in FAK expression with increasing concentrations of nutlin-3 (Fig. 4 C). To inhibit p53, we used pifithrin-α [31] in the SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cell lines. These cell lines were treated with pifithrin-α for 48 h, and cell lysates examined for FAK and p53. In all three cell lines, there was a decrease in p53 expression after pifithrin-α treatment (Fig. 4 D). There was also an increase in expression of FAK after pifithrin-α treatment in all three cell lines (Fig. 4 D). All these results demonstrated that FAK and p53 coordinately affect each other's expression. 3.4 Inhibition of FAK and activation of p53 act synergistically to decrease neuroblastoma cell survival In preparation of pharmacologic dual inhibition studies to follow, we used a small molecule FAK inhibitor, PF-573,228 [32] . This small molecule was designed to inhibit FAK phosphorylation but has been noted to inhibit total FAK expression [33] . This inhibitor decreased FAK expression in the SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) neuroblastoma cell lines (Fig. 5 A), and p53 was also increased in all three cell lines as FAK diminished, after PF-573,228 treatment (Fig. 5 A). These results were consistent with those seen previously with FAK inhibition. Since there was evidence that p53 and FAK coordinately regulated each of the other's expression, we wished to determine if FAK inhibition coupled with activation of p53 would lead to increased neuroblastoma cell killing in a synergistic fashion or if it simply occurred as an additive event. After 24-h treatment with the FAK inhibitor, PF-573,228 (PF), there was a significant decrease in neuroblastoma cell survival as measured by alamarBlue assay in SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cell lines (Fig. 5 B). In addition, 24-h treatment with nutlin-3 also resulted in increased cell death in all three cell lines (Fig. 5 C and D). Next, combined treatments with PF and nutlin-3 were used for 24 h for the inhibition of FAK and upregulation of p53, respectively, in SH-SY5Y, SH-EP, and WAC (2) cell lines. AlamarBlue assay was used to measure cell viability. Using the method of Chou [34] , the combination indices (CIs) were calculated and isobolograms constructed. The straight line connects the LD50 of each treatment when administered alone. CI values (calculated using the LD50 of the molecules when used together) falling above this line suggest an antagonistic effect, those below the line a synergistic effect, and those on the line are thought to represent an additive effect. In all three cell lines, the CI values were less than one (Fig. 6 A–C) suggesting that there was a synergistic effect on cell death in neuroblastoma cell lines when FAK inhibition was combined with increases in p53. 4 Discussion Here, we showed in multiple neuroblastoma cell lines that the two proteins, FAK and p53, interact. In addition, we demonstrated that these two proteins coordinately regulate each other's expression. These data are of major importance in neuroblastoma. Children with this tumor have few treatment options and virtually none that result in long-term survival, so there is a clear need for novel therapies. FAK overexpression has been described in neuroblastoma and has been shown to affect cellular survival and metastasis [10,13] . In addition, although p53 is wild type in most human neuroblastoma tumors [35] , it lacks proper function as a tumor suppressor. The reasons for this apparent lack of tumor suppressor function have not been fully explained in neuroblastoma and are partly the stimulus for the present study. In this study, it was demonstrated with both coimmunoprecipitation experiments and dual immunofluorescence staining and confocal microscopy that FAK and p53 proteins interacted in neuroblastoma cell lines. The idea of FAK interacting with another protein in cancer is not new. FAK has been shown to bind to growth factors, tumor suppressors, and other proteins. Sieg et al. [36] showed that FAK associated with activated platelet derived growth factor- and epidermal growth factor-receptors, linking integrin signaling pathways with growth factor receptors. FAK has also been shown to associate with IGF-1R in both pancreatic cancer cell lines MiaPaca-2 and Panc-1, providing a mechanism for increased cellular survival [37] . Previously, our laboratory found that FAK had a direct association with vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-3 in human neuroblastoma cell lines, and that interruption of that association with peptides or small molecules resulted in decreased cellular survival in vitro and decreased tumor growth in vivo [38] . In addition to binding to the oncogene p53 [17,18] , FAK has also been shown to bind to the tumor suppressor, neurofibromin [39] . FAK inhibition and disruption of the FAK-neurofibromin interaction resulted in significant cellular detachment and apoptosis, theoretically by increasing expression of neurofibromin tumor suppressor [39] . Finally, Kurenova et al. found that FAK directly interacted with the death domain receptor protein, receptor-interacting protein kinase. When this interaction was diminished through decreased FAK expression, there was a significant increase in cellular apoptosis, showing that the FAK-receptor-interacting protein kinase interaction offered a survival advantage to the cancer cell [40] . Reviewing these studies, it follows that we would find FAK associated with p53 in neuroblastoma cell lines, and that this association may prove to offer a survival advantage to the cells. The current experiments demonstrated that FAK and p53 coordinately affect the expression of one another. The mechanisms of these findings are the subject of ongoing investigations. Some authors have speculated that the function of p53 as a transcription factor may influence expression of FAK protein. Golubovskaya et al. [41] reported that p53 binds directly to the FAK promoter, functioning to directly inhibit the transcription of FAK. In addition, they demonstrated that FAK was more likely to be overexpressed in breast cancers that had p53 mutations [42] . Similarly, Rosado et al. [43] found that FAK expression as detected by immunohistochemistry staining in human oral squamous cell carcinoma was inversely correlated with p53 expression in these tumor specimens. Lim et al. [17] found that FAK facilitated p53 turnover in fibroblasts through enhanced ubiquitination. FAK expression also inhibited p-53–mediated transcriptional upregulation of p21 in mouse squamous cell carcinoma cells undergoing irradiation by an undescribed mechanism [44] . Our findings cannot be completely explained by any of these mechanisms because we have noted changes in the p53 expression that inversely follow changes in FAK expression induced via numerous methods, and vice versa. Therefore, the mechanism for increased or decreased p53 expression in the face of FAK inhibition or overexpression, respectively, is not yet clear and will remain the subject of further investigations. Amplification of the MYCN oncogene is the most prognostic negative predictor of survival in neuroblastoma [15] . MYCN has been shown to bind to the p53 promoter and positively regulate its expression [14] , but whether a significant change in cellular phenotypes results is questionable. For instance, He et al. [45] have demonstrated that silencing Mdm2 in MYCN -positive cell lines inhibited cell growth in a p53-independent manner, whereas silencing Mdm2 in non–MYCN cell lines triggered p53-dependent apoptosis, suggesting the role for other cell survival proteins in the MYCN -positive cells with relation to p53. Additionally, Tweddle, in 2001, published neuroblastoma cell lines without MYCN amplification, but not those that were MYCN amplified, entered G1 arrest after induction of p53 activity with irradiation. These authors suggested a potential abnormality downstream from p53 leading to their findings [20] . These findings could be explained by the association of p53 with other proteins, such as FAK as demonstrated in the present study. Of note, our findings did not suggest a dependence on MYCN . Treatment of isogenic MYCN cell lines, SH-EP (MYCN negative) and WAC (2) (MYCN positive) (Supplemental Data Fig. 3A .) with nutlin-3, an MDM2 antagonist, had similar effects on both cell lines; and in fact, the LD50 for nutlin-3 was nearly identical for the two cell lines (Fig. 6 B and C). In the present study, we demonstrated that in neuroblastoma cell lines, increasing p53 activity in conjunction with FAK inhibition resulted in a decrease in cell survival that was synergistic. This finding is novel in that two small molecules were used to determine the effect. A similar result was seen by Kornberg et al. who used adenoviral dominant-negative inhibitors of FAK and adenoviral vector for overexpression of p53. They reported that coinfection of RPMI 2650 human squamous carcinoma cells with Ad-p53 in conjunction with Ad-FRNK, a dominant-negative FAK inhibitor, resulted in more cellular apoptosis than when this cell line was infected with either agent alone [46] . Recent gene expression profiling showed that disruption of FAK and p53 proteins leads to decreased clonogenicity of colon cancer p53+/+ cell line [47] . On a general level, investigators have suggested that proteins such as FAK may bind to p53, sequestering it in the cytoplasm of the cell, thus preventing it from entering the nucleus and functioning as a transcription factor for cell survival proteins [16] . The variable that remains unknown is whether it is the disruption of the FAK and p53 interaction or the sheer act of combining FAK inhibition with p53 overexpression that were important in neuroblastoma cell killing in our study. Preliminary studies of proliferation in the isogenic MYCN SH-EP and WAC (2) neuroblastoma cell lines using a peptide designed to disrupt the FAK-p53 interaction [18] showed a significant decrease in proliferation in both cell lines treated with the peptide, but the difference was more marked in the MYCN + WAC (2) cells (Supplemental Data Fig. 3B ). This subject will be the focus of future experiments. We believe that the data from this present study indicate that upregulation of the p53 pathway coupled with inhibition of the FAK pathway would result in a synergistic response and have potential for novel combinatorial therapies. Numerous small molecules and novel compounds are currently under investigation. For example, 5-(1H-benzoimidazol-2-yl)-1H-pyridin-2-one 5-(1H-benzoimidazol-2-yl)-1H-pyridin-2-one (CR389) has recently been shown to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in human ovarian cancer cells by upregulating p53 [48] . There have been a number of inhibitors directed toward FAK including those mentioned. Even more exciting are the significant advances in tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including those not specifically designed to target FAK, but found to have action against FAK, such as tivantinib (ARQ-197) [49] . Obviously, combining these compounds would require validation, but realizing the interactions between oncogenes and kinases may prove to be a source of heretofore unrealized therapeutic targets, and may prove to be a potential therapeutic option for neuroblastoma. title: Ribosome biogenesis is a therapeutic vulnerability in pediatric neuroblastoma
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a heterogeneous malignant pediatric tumor, the prognosis of which depends on patient age and disease stage. Current treatment strategies rely on four key diagnostic criteria: age, histological stage, genomic profile, and MYCN gene status. The oncogenic activity of MYC depends on ribosome biogenesis, which is hyperactivated in cancer cells to support their high proliferative capacity, and which may thus represent a vulnerability in neuroblastoma and constitute a therapeutic target. Here, using the well-established IMR-32 cell line along with a previously established panel of patient-derived neuroblastoma cell lines with varying MYCN status, we show that RNA polymerase I inhibition following exposure to CX-5461 and BMH-21 suppressed cell proliferation at nanomolar concentrations and induced ribosomal stress, leading to the activation of apoptosis and the p21 pathway. Furthermore, analysis of expression of ribosome biogenesis factors using publicly available datasets and RT-qPCR data from an in-house neuroblastoma cohort, we identified FBL as a marker of poor prognosis in neuroblastoma. Consistently, FBL knockdown reduced neuroblastoma cell proliferation, supporting its relevance as a therapeutic target. In conclusion, our study reinforces the therapeutic potential of ribosome biogenesis inhibition in neuroblastoma and expands the list of potential targets to include rRNA maturation factors. These findings highlight the relevance of targeting ribosome biogenesis as a novel approach for neuroblastoma treatment.

Fig. 1 Fig. 2 p21 mRNA levels in response to RNA Pol I inhibitors. p21 mRNA levels were quantified by RT-qPCR on cells treated with CX-5461 and BMH-21 (final concentrations: 250 nM and 750 nM) for 96 h in the IMR32 cell line (A) and in neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines, with either no MYCN -amplification (B) or MYCN -amplification (C). Actinomycin D (ActD) was used at 0.05 μg/mL. Data are mean values from 2 independent biological replicates. Fig. 2 Fig. 3 Caspase 3/7 activation in response to RNA Pol I inhibitors. Caspase 3/7 activation was assessed in response to CX-5461 and BMH-21 treatment at 500 nM in the IMR32 cell line (A) and in neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines, with either no MYCN-amplification (B) or MYCN-amplification (C). Fig. 3 Fig. 4 Prognostic value of FBL mRNA levels in neuroblastoma patients. (A –B) Test cohort. Association between FBL mRNA levels determined by microarray (R2 database) and overall survival (A) or relapse-free survival (B) was evaluated in 52 samples using Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank Cox regression based on median as cut-off value. (C –G) Validation cohort. Association between FBL mRNA levels determined by medium-throughput RT-qPCR and overall survival (C) or progression-free survival (D) was evaluated in 26 samples using Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank Cox regression based on median as cut-off value. FBL mRNA levels were compared in the validation cohort between 4S and 4 stage (E), early and late diagnosis (F), and MYC amplification status (G).
