Graphical abstract Image 1 Keywords Ribosome biogenesis Fibrillarin RNA polymerase I inhibitor Cancer Targeted therapy Neuroblastoma MYC 1 Introduction Neuroblastoma is a malignant pediatric tumor of the peripheral sympathetic nervous system, originating from immature fetal nerve cells. Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children, making it the third most prevalent pediatric cancer [1 ], with 90 % of cases diagnosed before the age of 5 [2 ]. Neuroblastoma accounts for 7 % of malignancies in patients under 15 and approximately 15 % of all cancer-related deaths in pediatric populations [3 ]. Despite recent therapeutic advances, the 5-year survival rate for high-risk pediatric neuroblastoma has remained close to 50 % over the past two decades [4 ], emphasizing the need for continued research on this pediatric cancer. Neuroblastoma is a clinically heterogeneous disease requiring treatments adapted to the risk factors of an individual. Indeed, prognosis mainly relies on patient age and disease stage at diagnosis [1 ,5 ]. Poorest survival is observed for children diagnosed with advanced stage 4 disease at > 18 months. In 2015, Pinto et al. described a classification system, known as the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG), which uses combinations of prognostic risk factors to define distinct groups. Based on 5-year event-free survival (EFS) rates, patients are categorized into very low, low, intermediate, or high-risk groups. The INRG classification relies on imaging criteria, the extent of locoregional disease, and the presence of disseminated metastases (skin, liver, and bone marrow) [5 ]. The outcome for neuroblastoma patients in the low or intermediate-risk groups is excellent, with long-term survival rates exceeding 90 % [6 ]. In low-risk cases, surgery alone, even if incomplete, has proven curative for nearly all patients. Patients in some subgroups even display spontaneous tumor regression without treatment [6 ]. For high-risk patients, the current indication involves intensive multimodal therapy: five to six cycles of induction chemotherapy and surgery, consolidation therapy with a high-dose of chemotherapy and radiation, and post-consolidation therapy targeting residual cells. These high-risk neuroblastoma patients have a 5-year overall survival of only 40–50 % [3 ,6 ]. Therefore, new therapeutic advances, such as CAR T-cell therapy, are also being explored to meet the urgent need for novel treatments in these challenging pediatric cancer subtypes [5 ]. In parallel, early detection of the most aggressive neuroblastoma tumors, is also required to improve patient outcome. In addition to the INGR classification, genetic features such as ploidy, MYCN copy number, and 1p or 11q deletions distinguish aggressive tumors from those likely to regress. For example, the identification of MYCN amplification, observed in approximately 25 % of cases [2 ], serves as an independent predictive marker of poor prognosis, associated with an invasive and metastatic behavior. Thus, in addition to age and histological stage, MYCN gene status and genomic profile are now evaluated at diagnosis to assess cure prospects and guide treatment decision [3 ]. Unfortunately, MYC targeting remains challenging, necessitating the exploration of alternative approaches, such as targeting MYC-driven pathways [2 ,5 ]. MYC is a major activator of ribosome biogenesis, by increasing the activity of the RNA polymerase I (RNA Pol I), and regulating the expression of a large set of ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis factors. Consequently, MYC protein overexpression increases ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis [7 ]. Neuroblastoma tumors with an unfavorable clinical outcome overexpress genes driving ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis, supporting the notion than MYCN -driven neuroblastoma may be strongly dependent on ribosome biogenesis [1 ]. More importantly, it has been shown that the oncogenic activity of MYC relies on ribosome biogenesis, and that impeding MYC-driven ribosome biogenesis overactivation is sufficient to reduce MYC-driven leukemogenesis [8 ]. Thus, inhibiting ribosome biogenesis may represent a novel strategy to treat MYC-driven tumors. The first evaluations of ribosome biogenesis inhibition were conducted in neuroblastoma using RNA Pol I inhibitors including Actinomycin D (ActD), and CX-5461 and CX-3543. ActD is a DNA intercalating compound binding to GpC, thereby inhibiting RNA polymerase activity [9 ]. It is commonly used to inhibit RNA Pol I, given the approximatively tenfold greater sensitivity of Pol I compared to Pol II. In contrast, CX-5461 acts by binding to and stabilizing G-quadruplex (G4) structures, which are present in various regions of the human genome and enriched in the promoter region of rRNA genes [10 ]. This stabilization prevents the recruitment of the essential Pol I transcription factor SL1, thereby blocking transcription initiation [11 ]. ActD and CX-5461 were reported to induce cell death in vitro and reduce tumor progression in vivo [4 ,12 ,13 ], indicating that RNA Pol I inhibitors are promising targeted therapies in neuroblastoma, including MYC-driven tumors. However, the two most characterized inhibitors, actinomycin D and CX-5461, were shown to induce DNA damage, an activity that induces non-selective toxicity, requiring the development of new Pol I inhibitors or the identification of novel targets in the ribosome biogenesis pathway. Moreover, there are currently conflicting results on the contribution of the MYCN status to the response to ribosome biogenesis in neuroblastoma [4 ,6 ]. Here, we evaluate BMH-21, another RNA Pol I inhibitor, for the first time in neuroblastoma using patient-derived cell lines with varying MYCN statuses. BMH-21 was identified through a screen for non-genotoxic inducer of TP53 [14 ]. Unlike conventional DNA intercalator, BMH-21 does not induce DNA damage [14 ]. Its binding to rDNA promoter region disrupts the interaction of upstream binding factor (UBF) to the RNA Pol I promoter, leading to proteasome-dependent degradation of the RPA194 subunit of RNA Pol I [15 ]. In addition, we assessed the relevance of Fibrillarin (FBL) as a novel target to inhibit ribosome biogenesis at the rRNA maturation step. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Cellular models and treatments The five patient-derived neuroblastoma cell lines, along with information on the MYCN amplification status, were generated and maintained by the V. Combaret's group from pediatric neuroblastoma patients of the Centre Léon Bérard (Table S1 ) [16 ]. The IMR32 cells and the five patient-derived cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (LIFE TECHNOLOGIES) supplemented with 10 % Fetal Bovine Serum (CLINISCIENCES) and 1 % penicillin-streptomycin (LIFE TECHNOLOGIES). All cells were maintained at 37 °C with 5 % (v/v) CO2 in a humidified incubator. Stable IMR-32 cell lines expressing inducible shRNAs were generated via lentiviral infection as described previously (Erales PNAS 2017). Briefly, lentiviral particles were produced using pTRIPZ-shRNA-NS and pTRIPZ-shRNA-FBL vectors (Open Biosystems, Horizon Discovery) (Table S2 ). Following lentiviral infection, cell populations were selected for 14 days with 1 μg/mL puromycin. shRNA expression was induced using 1 μg/mL doxycycline. CX-5461 (orb251392, Biorbyt) was dissolved in a 25 mM NaH2 PO4 - Na2 HPO4 buffer as previously described [17 ]. BMH-21 (orb304073, Biorbyt) was dissolved in a 25 mM phosphate-citrate buffer as previously described [18 ]. 2.2 Neuroblastoma cohorts The test cohort of advanced neuroblastoma corresponds to the Versteeg dataset publicly available on the R2 database (http://r2.amc.nl ). It is composed of 52 samples and both transcriptomic and clinical data are available. The validation cohort of advanced neuroblastoma is composed of 26 samples (PGEB platform, Cancer Research Centre of Lyon/Centre Léon Bérard, Lyon, FRANCE). The material used in the study was collected in agreement with all applicable laws, rules, and requests of French and European government authorities. Informed consent was taken from patients, or in the case of patients under 16 from either the parents or legal guardians. Ethics approval of the study was taken from the Ethical Review Board of the Centre Léon Bérard (CMT n° 2018–019). 2.3 Cellular based assay Cell proliferation was assessed using the CellTiter 96® AQueousOne Solution Cell Proliferation Assay kit (Promega, G3580) following the manufacturer's instructions. Cell apoptosis was measured using the caspase-Glo® 3/7 reagent (Caspase-Glo® 3/7 Assay, Promega, G8091) following the manufacturer's instructions. Absorbance values at 490 nm and luminescence were measured using a Tecan® Infinite 200 Pro plate reader. Cell proliferation was monitored using a real-time imaging system (Sartorius, Incucyte™ S3) on the Cell Imaging Platform (PIC, Cancer Research Center of Lyon). Cellular confluence was measured using the Incucyte software (Sartorius). 2.4 RNA extraction and RTqPCR Total RNA was extracted using the TRIzol-Chloroform method and quantified with the NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Reverse transcription was performed on 200 ng of purified RNA using the PrimeScript RT kit (Takara, RR037B) with a mix of oligo dT primers and random 6-mer primers. Low-throughput real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) was carried out using the Light Cycler 480 SYBRGreen Master Mix (Roche, ) with the appropriate primer pairs (Table S3 ) on the LightCycler® 96 instrument. Medium-throughput RT-qPCR was performed as previously described using the BiomarkHD system [19 ]. Each biological sample was analyzed in triplicate. Relative fold-changes were calculated using the 2-ΔΔCT method [20 ]. 2.5 Western blot Proteins were extracted in Laemmli buffer and denatured for 10 min at 95 °C. Protein quantification was performed using a TCA assay. Proteins were separated on a 4–20 % SDS-PAGE gradient gel and transferred onto a nitrocellulose membrane. Membranes were saturated in Tris Borate Saline buffer containing 0.05 % Tween-20 and 5 % skim milk and incubated with the primary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature (H3, 1/5000, ab1791; Fibrillarin, 1/1000, ab166630). Secondary antibodies conjugated to horseradish peroxidase (Cell Signaling 1:5000) were used for chemiluminescence detection on a ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad) after incubation with Clarity ™ ECL ( , Bio-Rad), and signals were quantified using ImageLab software (Bio-Rad). 2.6 Statistical analysis and graphical visualization Mean comparison was performed using the non-parametric Mann-Whitney test. Survival curves with associated log-rank tests were generated using the Kaplan-Meier method for overall survival (OS: from diagnosis to death), relapse-free survival (RFS: from diagnosis to either death or local recurrence) or progression-free survival (PFS: from diagnosis to either death or local/distant recurrence). Statistical analyses and graphical visualizations were performed using the R2 database (http://r2.amc.nl ) and GraphPad Prism v7.0a (GraphPad Software, Inc). 3 Results 3.1 Neuroblastoma cell lines are sensitive to RNA polymerase I inhibitors The effect of RNA Pol I inhibitors on neuroblastoma was first evaluated in the commonly used MYCN -amplified neuroblastoma cell line IMR-32, (Table S1 , Fig. 1 A). IMR-32 cells were treated for 96 h with RNA Pol I inhibitors, CX-5461 or BMH-21, using concentrations ranging from 1 to 1000 nM, and cell proliferation was assessed by MTS assay. The IC50 values for CX-5461 and were 173.6 nM (SD ± 61) and 202.3 nM (SD ± 30.6), respectively. As for CX-5461 [13 ], nanomolar concentrations of BMH-21 impaired IMR-32 cell viability. No significant difference was observed between CX-5461 and BMH-21 in this cell line, indicating that the two RNA Pol I inhibitors display the same activity in IMR-32. We then compared the effects of these two RNA Pol I inhibitors in more relevant cancer models, using a panel of five neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines [16 ]. Among these neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines, two are MYCN -amplified (CLB-BA and CLB-LEC) (Table S1 ). A comparison of the response to RNA Pol I inhibitors using MTS assay 96 h post-treatment showed that IC50 values varied across different neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines for both CX-5461 and BMH-21 (Fig. 1 B–C). For each neuroblastoma patient-derived cell line, no significant difference in sensitivity was observed between CX-5461 and BMH-21 (Fig. 1 B–C), as observed for IMR-32. Of note, IC50 values were similar for both RNA Pol I inhibitors across the neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines (Fig. 1 D–E), indicating that in this panel of neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines, MYCN status did not modulate cell sensitivity to ribosome inhibition, in contrast to previous findings on CX-5461 in neuroblastoma [13 ]. Our data support previous observations that neuroblastoma cell lines, including patient-derived cell lines, are sensitive to the CX-5461 RNA Pol I inhibitor at nanomolar concentrations. Moreover, patient-derived neuroblastoma cell lines display a similar sensitivity to the RNA Pol I inhibitor, BMH-21, independently of MYCN status. 3.2 RNA polymerase I inhibitors induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis In cancer cells, inhibition of ribosome biogenesis has been shown to promote a stress response termed ribosomal stress [21 ]. This stress response triggers cell cycle arrest and/or cell death. We recently reported that CX-5461 and BMH-21 promote cell cycle arrest but no cell death in triple-negative breast cancer [22 ]. To determine whether RNA Pol I inhibitors promote similar cellular ribosomal stress in neuroblastoma, we evaluated cell cycle arrest (cytostatic effect) and apoptosis (cytotoxic effect). We first analyzed cell cycle inhibition by quantifying the mRNA levels of p21, a key cell cycle regulator and p53 effector, by RT-qPCR (Fig. 2 ). IMR-32 and our panel of five neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines were treated with 250 and 750 nM of CX-5461 and BMH-21 for 96 h. Actinomycin D (ActD) was used as a reference. In IMR-32, CX-5461 and BMH-21 treatment induced a 40 to 258-fold increase in p21 mRNA levels (Fig. 2 A). In our panel of neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines, a 4 to 87-fold in p21 mRNA level was observed (Fig. 2 B-C). Interestingly, a dose-dependent induction of p21 mRNA levels was observed only in response to BMH-21 treatment. In addition, BMH-21 at 750 nM induced higher p21 mRNA levels than CX-5461 at 750 nM. Of note, a similar increase in p21 mRNA levels was observed in non-amplified MYCN and MYCN -amplified cell lines (Fig. 2 B vs 2A-2C). These results suggest that in neuroblastoma cell lines, cell cycle arrest occurs in response to the two RNA Pol I inhibitors independently of MYCN status, BMH-21 triggering the strongest response. Next, apoptosis was evaluated using a caspase 3/7 activity assay in our panel of neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines in response to 96 h of treatment with CX-5461 and BMH-21 (Fig. 3 ). In response to CX-5461 and BMH-21 treatment, a significant increase in caspase 3/7 activity was observed in IMR-32 (Fig. 3 A) and the 5 neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines, although this activation was limited in the CLB-BOULT cell line (Fig. 3 B). In addition, CX-5461 promoted a higher induction of caspase 3/7 activity than BMH-21 in IMR-32, CLB-SEDP, CLB-BA and CLB-LEC lines, suggesting no correlation between CX-5421-induced caspase 3/7 activation and the MYCN amplification status. Thus, in neuroblastoma cell lines, the apoptotic pathway is induced by both RNA Pol I inhibitors independently of MYCN status. These findings demonstrate that RNA Pol I inhibitors promote both cell cycle arrest and cell death in neuroblastoma independently of MYCN amplification. Overall, these data support the efficacy of RNA Pol I inhibitors in neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines. 3.3 rRNA maturation factors are prognostic markers in neuroblastoma In breast cancer, we recently provided a proof-of-concept that inhibiting the rRNA maturation process is as efficient as inhibiting rRNA synthesis to induce an antitumoral effect [22 ]. To determine whether rRNA maturation can be of therapeutic interest in neuroblastoma, we focused on neuroblastoma with unfavorable clinical outcome. In particular, we analyzed the association between stage 4/4S neuroblastoma patient outcome and expression of two factors involved in rRNA maturation, fibrillarin (FBL) and WDR12. We first focused on a test cohort using the Versteeg transcriptomic dataset (n = 52) of the R2 database, using the median as a cut-off value. A significant association was observed between FBL mRNA levels and both overall survival (OS) and relapse-free survival (RFS) in neuroblastoma patients (Fig. 4 A–B). Indeed, high FBL mRNA levels were associated with poor OS and RFS. A similar significant association was observed for WDR12 (Sup. Fig. 1 A). These data suggested that FBL and WDR12, two rRNA maturation factors, are prognostic markers in neuroblastoma. A validation cohort was then build using samples from the Centre Léon Bérard (CLB) (n = 26). Patients in the validation cohort displayed clinical characteristics of advanced neuroblastoma, including a poor outcome for patients with stage 4, diagnosed after 18 months of age and with tumors displaying MYCN -amplification (Sup. Fig. 2 ). Using medium-throughput RT-qPCR and median as a cut-off value, we observed that high FBL mRNA levels were significantly associated with poor overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) (Fig. 4 C–D). A similar significant association was observed for WDR12 (Sup. Fig. 1 A). Thus, test and validation cohorts demonstrated that high expression levels of factors involved in rRNA maturation are associated with poor outcome in neuroblastoma, supporting their relevance as therapeutic target. Interestingly, a significant correlation was observed between FBL and WDR1 2 mRNA levels in the test cohort (Sup. Fig. 1 B). In addition, high levels of FBL and WDR12 expression were observed in neuroblastoma patients of the test cohort diagnosed at a late stage and with tumors displaying MYCN -amplification (Sup. Fig. 1 B). Similar tendencies were observed in the validation cohort (Fig. 4 E–G and Sup. Fig. 1 C–E). In the validation cohort, FBL mRNA levels were significantly higher in stage 4 than stage 4S (Fig. 4 E), a non-significant tendency was also observed for WDR1 2 mRNA (Sup. Fig. 1 C). When focusing on the age of neuroblastoma patients at diagnosis, similar mRNA levels of FBL and WDR12 were observed before or after 18 months (Fig. 4 F and Sup. Fig. 1 D), despite the predominance of stage 4 in older patients (Sup. Fig. 2 A). Interestingly, both FBL and WDR1 2 mRNA levels were higher in MYCN -amplified tumors compared to non-amplified MYCN tumors, an observation consistent with the ribosome biogenesis promoting activity of MYC (Fig. 4 G and Sup. Fig. 1 E). These findings suggest that factors involved in rRNA maturation are markers of poor prognosis. Compared to WDR12 , FBL is over-expressed in tumors with the poorest outcome (i.e., stage 4, diagnosis >18 months, MYCN -amplification), highlighting the clinical relevance of targeting FBL in neuroblastoma. 3.4 FBL knock-down reduces cell proliferation in neuroblastoma Given that FBL overexpression is associated with poor neuroblastoma patient outcome, we evaluated the impact of inhibiting FBL on neuroblastoma cell proliferation. A stable IMR-32 cell line expressing an inducible shRNA targeting FBL was generated. FBL knock-down was validated by analyzing FBL expression by Western blot in response to exposure to doxycycline for a week (Fig. 5 A–B). In response to doxycycline, FBL protein levels were reduced by 95 % in the shFBL cell line, while no change in FBL protein levels was observed in the shNS control cell line. Growth of shRNA-expressing IMR32 cell lines was monitored in real time for six days (Fig. 5 C). No significant difference in cell proliferation was observed between non-induced and doxycycline-induced shNS control cells (Fig. 5 C, left panel). Conversely, in the shFBL cell line, FBL knock-down reduced cell proliferation as early as 36 h post-induction. At the end-point (i.e., 144 h), shFBL-expressing cells reached only 30 % confluence compared to 90 % for the shNS-expressing cells (Fig. 5 C, right panel). These data indicate that FBL inhibition reduces cell proliferation, supporting its value as a therapeutic target in neuroblastoma. 4 Discussion Neuroblastoma, a prevalent pediatric cancer, presents significant clinical challenges, particularly in the case of high-grade tumors bearing MYCN amplification, where innovative therapeutic approaches are still needed. This study demonstrates the value of targeting ribosome biogenesis pathways, including the rRNA maturation process, as a therapeutic approach in neuroblastoma with unfavorable clinical outcome. Conflicting data have been published on the impact of MYCN on neuroblastoma cell sensitivity. While MYCN was found to sensitize cell lines to CX-5461 and CX-3543 [13 ], several studies reported that the RNA Pol I inhibitor, CX-5461, reduces neuroblastoma growth in vitro and in vivo , independently of MYCN amplification status [4 ,6 ,23 ]. Our data confirm the latter observations in a panel of neuroblastoma patient-derived cell lines established in our laboratory. The use of patient-derived cell lines adds clinical relevance to the efficacy of RNA Pol I inhibitors in neuroblastoma. In addition to CX-5461, we report that the BMH-21 RNA Pol I inhibitor also reduces neuroblastoma cell proliferation. Importantly, we and others reported that CX-5461 induces DNA damage and also acts as a topoisomerase 2 inhibitor [22 ,24 ]. In contrast, BMH-21 did not induce any DNA damage, supporting that the overall vulnerability of neuroblastoma to BMH-21 relies solely on ribosome biogenesis inhibition. This study is also the first to demonstrate the efficacy of BMH-21 in neuroblastoma, supporting the relevance of inhibiting ribosome biogenesis as an anti-tumoral strategy. Both CX-5461 and BMH-21 induce a ribosomal stress response in neuroblastoma cell lines, as evidenced by the increased p21 expression and activation of the caspase 3/7 pathway. Our data support that RNA Pol I inhibitors promote both cytostatic and cytotoxic effects, and further substantiates the role of ribosome biogenesis inhibition in curbing neuroblastoma proliferation [6 ,13 ]. Interestingly, we recently reported that these two RNA Pol I inhibitors promote cell cycle arrest but not cell death in triple-negative breast cancer, suggesting that RNA Pol I inhibitors display distinct cellular responses depending on the cancer type [22 ]. More importantly, these two RNA Pol I inhibitors show efficacy at nanomolar concentrations, indicating a high affinity of these compounds for their targets, thus reducing the risk of side effects in neuroblastoma patients. Our data also demonstrate that other steps of ribosome biogenesis, precisely the rRNA maturation process, may be inhibited to exert an antitumoral effect on neuroblastoma cells. Among the factors involved in rRNA maturation, early pioneering studies revealed the role of FBL in pre-rRNA maturation [25–27 ]. Using two independent cohorts of advanced neuroblastoma, we reveal that FBL is a prognostic marker in neuroblastoma, reporting a significant association between high FBL expression levels and poor overall and relapse-free survivals. The association of FBL with prognosis has also been reported in other cancers such as breast cancer [19 ,28 ]. However, the limited sample sizes of both the test (n = 52) and validation (n = 26) cohorts prevent the conducting of multivariate analyses, which are necessary to evaluate whether FBL is a prognostic marker that is independent of currently used markers (i.e. , age at diagnosis, stage, MYCN amplification). Future studies including larger cohort will be required to determine whether FBL itself might improve the current prognostic stratification. Importantly, we demonstrated that prolonged FBL knockdown drastically reduced neuroblastoma cell proliferation, as we recently reported in triple-negative breast cancer [22 ]. In vivo , FBL inhibition induced a reduction in mammary tumor frequency and suppressing tumorigenesis [22 ,28 ]. FBL is not only involved in rRNA-precursor processing but also in the catalysis of rRNA 2′O-ribose methylation, two maturation processes critical for proper ribosome assembly and function [27 ,29 ,30 ]. Consequently, inhibiting FBL impairs 18S pre-rRNA maturation and 40S subunit production, and thus cell survival [27 ,29 ,30 ]. As demonstrated for rRNA synthesis inhibition by targeting RNA Pol I, we anticipate that inhibiting rRNA maturation by targeting FBL will exert a selective therapeutic effect toward cancer cells due to the differential need of cancer cells to produce high quantities of ribosomes compared to healthy cells [15 ,17 ]. Overall, these findings support the value of FBL as a therapeutic target in neuroblastoma. Altogether, this study presents new opportunities for the management of pediatric neuroblastoma patients. Ribosome biogenesis inhibitors, whether through RNA Pol I or rRNA maturation factors inhibitors, emerge as a promising strategy to exploit the dependency of MYCN -amplified neuroblastoma cells on this process. title: Immunotherapeutic advances in pediatric neuroblastoma: Overcoming resistance through biomarker-guided combinations
abstract: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. It remains a major therapeutic challenge, particularly in high-risk cases where long-term survival rates remain below 50 % despite intensive multimodal treatment. The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), marked by low MHC class I expression and infiltration of regulatory immune cells, has historically limited the efficacy of immune-based therapies. Recent advances in immunotherapy have reshaped the treatment landscape, with anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies such as dinutuximab and naxitamab demonstrating significant clinical benefit, especially when combined with granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). Beyond antibody-based therapies, new modalities are advancing. CAR T-cell platforms targeting GD2, B7-H3, and L1CAM, along with checkpoint inhibitors, cytokine therapies, cancer vaccines, and oncolytic viruses, are showing early promise. However, resistance mechanisms, such as antigen loss, T-cell exhaustion, and suppressive myeloid populations, continue to hinder durable responses. Biomarkers such as Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) mutation status, immune infiltration profiles, and cytokine signatures are increasingly guiding patient stratification and therapeutic personalization. Combination strategies integrating immunotherapy with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents have demonstrated synergistic potential, and recent clinical trials reflect a shift toward multi-agent regimens. Novel platforms such as armored CARs, bispecific antibodies, and metabolic modulators are expanding the therapeutic horizon. This review synthesizes current evidence on immunotherapeutic strategies in neuroblastoma, highlighting resistance pathways, biomarker-driven approaches, and the evolving clinical trial landscape. Future directions emphasize personalized, biomarker-guided immunotherapy to improve efficacy, reduce toxicity, and establish durable, curative outcomes for children with neuroblastoma.

Gastroenterology and Liver Diseases Research Center, Research Institute for Gastroenterology and Liver Diseases, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences Tehran Iran 1 Co-first authors 2 Contributed equally Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. It remains a major therapeutic challenge, particularly in high-risk cases where long-term survival rates remain below 50 % despite intensive multimodal treatment. The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), marked by low MHC class I expression and infiltration of regulatory immune cells, has historically limited the efficacy of immune-based therapies. Recent advances in immunotherapy have reshaped the treatment landscape, with anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies such as dinutuximab and naxitamab demonstrating significant clinical benefit, especially when combined with granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). Beyond antibody-based therapies, new modalities are advancing. CAR T-cell platforms targeting GD2, B7-H3, and L1CAM, along with checkpoint inhibitors, cytokine therapies, cancer vaccines, and oncolytic viruses, are showing early promise. However, resistance mechanisms, such as antigen loss, T-cell exhaustion, and suppressive myeloid populations, continue to hinder durable responses. Biomarkers such as Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) mutation status, immune infiltration profiles, and cytokine signatures are increasingly guiding patient stratification and therapeutic personalization. Combination strategies integrating immunotherapy with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents have demonstrated synergistic potential, and recent clinical trials reflect a shift toward multi-agent regimens. Novel platforms such as armored CARs, bispecific antibodies, and metabolic modulators are expanding the therapeutic horizon. This review synthesizes current evidence on immunotherapeutic strategies in neuroblastoma, highlighting resistance pathways, biomarker-driven approaches, and the evolving clinical trial landscape. Future directions emphasize personalized, biomarker-guided immunotherapy to improve efficacy, reduce toxicity, and establish durable, curative outcomes for children with neuroblastoma.
