Notably, epoxomicin has markedly prevented the down-regulation of N-Myc protein with Dp44mT and DpC in all cell-types (Fig. 8 A-C). This is despite the marked down-regulation of N-Myc mRNA levels induced by these ligands (Fig. 5 A, E, I) and is because epoxomicin inhibits proteasomal activity [84] . This inhibition prevents the decrease in N-Myc protein irrespective of the pronounced decrease of its mRNA levels (Fig. 5 A, E, I). This response has also been observed by others using different models and molecules [86] , and is expected, since mRNA and protein levels are regulated separately [87,88] . 2.12 Silencing the ubiquitin-activating enzyme, UBA1, does not fully rescue N-Myc or cyclin D1 down-regulation induced by DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC The results in Fig. 8 indicate the proteasome could play a role in the decrease in N-Myc protein after incubation with DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC. Previous studies demonstrated N-Myc degradation is regulated by a ubiquitin-dependent mechanism via the proteasome [89] . For other proteins, both ubiquitin-dependent and/or ubiquitin-independent mechanisms of degradation are known [90,91] . Our laboratory reported that cyclin D1 and p21CIP1/WAF1 were degraded in iron-replete cells via a ubiquitin-dependent process, while after iron depletion, ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation occurred [85,92] . Inhibiting the 20S proteasome using epoxomicin [84] in Fig. 8 prevented the ability of DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC, to decrease N-Myc. Considering this, inhibition of the 20S subunit by epoxomicin will also result in inhibition of 26S proteasomal activity [93] required for ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation [93] . As such, this does not differentiate between the ubiquitin-dependent and -independent mechanisms of proteasomal degradation. To suppress ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation of N-Myc, NB cells were preincubated for 24 h/37 °C with an siRNA targeting ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1 ) or a non-targeting siRNA (siControl). UBA1 is an E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme that catalyzes the first critical step in ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation [94] . It is well known that inhibiting UBA1 with either chemical inhibitors or UBA1 silencing essentially abolishes new ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation [95,96] . Herein, silencing was the preferred option, as chemical inhibitors suffer more off-target effects [97] . Complete UBA1 silencing is lethal, and experimentally, it is not possible to completely inhibit ubiquitination, as a small amount of turnover occurs via UBA6-mediated pathways, residual UBA1 activity, or ubiquitin-independent pathways [98,99] . As such, relative controls are required to demonstrate pronounced inhibition of ubiquitination and are included herein. After UBA1 silencing, the media was then removed, and the NB cells incubated for 24 h/37 °C with control medium, or this medium containing Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM) and western analysis performed. Again, TfR1 expression was implemented as a positive control for iron depletion mediated by the ligands after incubation with siControl or siUBA1 ( Fig. 9 A-C). Under both conditions there was a significant (p < 0.05–0.0001) up-regulation of the TfR1 relative to the control or Bp2mT after incubation of DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 9 A-C), as shown previously (Figs. 4 A, 5 B, F, J, 8 A-C). Silencing of UBA1 in all three NB cell-types resulted in a marked and significant (p < 0.05–0.001) decrease in UBA1 expression versus the siControl (Fig. 9 A-C). As implemented in Fig. 8 A-C, cyclin D1 was used as a positive control for inhibition of proteasomal activity [85] mediated by silencing UBA1 , with its levels being significantly (p < 0.01–0.001) decreased by DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC under siControl conditions versus the respective control and Bp2mT in all three NB cell-types (Fig. 9 A-C). Upon silencing UBA1 , cyclin D1 was significantly (p < 0.05–0.01) increased in the control and Bp2mT treatment groups relative to the analogous treatments in the siControl, due to inhibition of ubiquitination. These results were comparable to those observed with epoxomicin treatment (Fig. 8 A-C). However, as observed for the siControl, upon incubation with DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC, cyclin D1 protein was significantly (p < 0.01–0.001) decreased after UBA1 silencing versus the respective control or Bp2mT (Fig. 9 A-C). This response was different to the effect mediated by epoxomicin, which successfully prevented this decrease in cyclin D1 protein (Fig. 8 A-C). N-Myc responded similarly as cyclin D1 to the drug treatment under siControl and siUBA1 treatment (Fig. 9 A-C). This observation indicated the significantly (p < 0.01–0.001) decreased N-Myc observed using DFO, Dp44mT, and DpC versus the respective control or Bp2mT after UBA1 silencing could be due to ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation. 3 Discussion N-Myc is a dominant oncogenic driver of NB [3] . Cellular iron depletion with clinically used DFO suppresses NB growth in vitro and in vivo [11–13] and decreases N-Myc mRNA and protein expression [11] . However, DFO’s limited anti-tumor efficacy, short half-life, and inability to be orally administered and requirement for long subcutaneous or intravenous infusions (12–24 h/day, 5–6 days/week) limits its clinical impact [17] . The thiosemicarbazone, DpC, whose primary targets are cellular iron and copper [29,30] , was specifically designed by structure-activity optimization, displays favorable pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and anti-tumor potency [22,31] . In fact, DpC when administered orally has demonstrated marked anti-cancer activity and good tolerability, with toxicology being examined in a variety of tumor models in vivo , including neuroblastoma [33] , prostate cancer [100] , lung cancer [22] , breast cancer [42] , and pancreatic cancer [41] . The high anti-cancer activity of DpC, tolerability, and appropriate pharmacokinetics led to multi-centre Phase I clinical trials (NCT02688101) in patients with advanced and resistant cancer [32] . Herein, we compare and mechanistically dissect how these ligands regulate N-Myc expression and its downstream networks in NB cells with and without N-Myc amplification. The ligands demonstrate multi-modal mechanisms of action that are illustrated in Fig. 10 and are discussed further in the sections below. These multiple mechanisms of activity guard against the development of resistance mechanisms that often occur when using anti-cancer drugs with a single mechanism of action [101,102] . 3.1 Transcriptomic response to iron depletion: Targeting of p53 and HIF-1 signaling RNAseq demonstrated broadly overlapping transcriptional changes with either DFO or DpC after a 24 h incubation of all three NB cell-types. Despite this, some distinct differences in the cellular response between DFO and DpC were identified. For instance, DFO significantly up-regulated seventeen ribosome protein mRNA levels in only Kelly NB cells, with this not being observed with DpC in any cell-type. On the other hand, only DpC up-regulated metallothionein gene family members and also the Zn transporter solute carrier family 30 member 2 (SLC30A2 ), likely due to the known ability of thiosemicarbazones to avidly bind cellular copper and zinc [22,30,58,59] . This difference in activity between DFO and DpC is probably related to distinct structural design features and different mechanisms of action. That is, DFO is a hydroxamate-based ligand with hard oxygen donors that results in a strong preference for iron and does not redox cycle to generate ROS [17,103] . This is why DFO is specifically used for the treatment of iron overload disease to target iron. In contrast, through a series of structure-activity relationship studies [32,101,102] , DpC was specifically designed as an anti-cancer drug, a DpT ligand that utilizes soft nitrogen and sulphur donor atoms as its metal ligating sites [22,30] . This leads to different metal-binding interactions, redox potentials, and the different responses relative to DFO observed herein, as DpT thiosemicarbazones effectively bind iron, copper, and zinc. The formation of redox-active copper complexes, and less so, iron complexes of the DpT ligands is particularly critical, as it leads to lysosomal membrane permeabilization, which is key for inducing tumor cell death [104] and overcoming P-glycoprotein-mediated resistance [19,105] Data enrichment analyses highlighted “cell-cycle”, “apoptosis”, “cell division”, and “neurogenesis”, which is consistent with the anti-proliferative activity of these ligands [22,30] . The down-regulation of genes involved in the cell cycle by DpC relative to DFO in all three NB cell-types agreed with the greater anti-proliferative efficacy of DpC [106] . This activity is consistent with the ability of iron-binding ligands to decrease the mRNA and protein levels of molecules involved in cell cycle progression, e.g. , cyclin D1 [58,107] . KEGG analysis demonstrated that the p53 signaling pathway was only increased by DFO and DpC in SH-SY5Y NB cells with wild-type p53 (Fig. 10 ), but not Kelly or BE(2)-C NB cells with mutant p53 [77] , supporting previous protein-level observations [79] . Conversely, the HIF-1 signaling pathway was significantly up-regulated by DFO across all three NB cell-types (Fig. 10 ), in line with findings in MCF-7 breast cancer cells [42,53] . Six HIF-1-responsive N-Myc targets [43,108–112] , ALDOA , CDKN1A , HES1 , HK2 , PDK1 , and NDRG1 , were uniformly induced by both DFO and DpC in all NB cell-types. 3.2 Metabolic alterations and reprogramming after ligand treatment Considering the functions of these latter six N-Myc downstream targets, ALDOA and HK2 encode core glycolytic enzymes [113,114] . Their induction probably reflects HIF-1 binding to hypoxia-responsive elements in their promoters after iron depletion [115,116] , a stress that perturbs many iron-dependent metabolic processes, including ATP production [17,103] . It has been reported that cellular iron depletion by ligands transiently depresses ATP levels, activates adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), and provokes a compensatory surge in glycolytic and mitochondrial flux [103] . The up-regulation of HK2 and ALDOA probably forms part of this metabolic compensation to iron stress [103] . HIF-1 also elevates PDK1 expression [117] , which phosphorylates and inactivates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that acts as a “gatekeeper” between glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle [118,119] . This latter effect diverts pyruvate from the TCA cycle into aerobic glycolysis as a part of the Warburg effect [118] . Together, the up-regulation of HK2 , ALDOA, and PDK1 after iron depletion probably accelerates the glycolytic flux that has been observed previously [103] , contributing to an archetypal Warburg-like response (Fig. 10 ). This initial compensatory response to iron depletion mediated by the ligands, is overcome by the induction of tumor killing by multiple mechanisms [18,21,22,30,32] . The other HIF-1 targets identified after cellular iron depletion include both CDKN1A (p21 ) and NDRG1 , which act in concert and enforce growth arrest and the inhibition of metastasis [43,92,104,120,121] (Fig. 10 ). NDRG1 is an iron-regulated metastasis suppressor [43,122] that up-regulates p21 by blocking its NEDD4-dependent ubiquitylation [120] . Furthermore, thiosemicarbazone ligands that up-regulate NDRG1 [123] are known to inhibit tumor cell proliferation and metastasis in vivo [23,40] . These observations demonstrate that the latter alterations in gene expression could have important functional and clinical consequences. Cellular iron depletion also up-regulates the HIF-1 target, HES1 , which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor [124] , that promotes the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) via E-cadherin suppression [125,126] . Intriguingly, and in contrast, cellular iron deletion also up-regulates NDRG1 that increases E-cadherin and suppresses the EMT [123] . Hence, a complex regulatory network exists in terms of the regulation of metastasis after cellular iron depletion. This is further supported by the fact that DFO and DpC increase the expression of the metastasis suppressor, KAI1 [127] , in all three NB cell-types and in SH-SY5Y cells, respectively (GEO accession no. GSE291132). These studies reinforce the anti-metastatic profile of these ligands and the clinical significance of their activity, as metastasis is the major killer in cancer, leading to 90 % of cancer deaths [44,128] , and there are no clinically used drugs specifically designed to target or treat it [45,129] . 3.3 Ligand-induced post-translational regulation of N-Myc protein This study demonstrated the proteasome inhibitor, epoxomicin, generally prevented ligand-induced N-Myc protein down-regulation across all NB cell-types, consistent with the known rapid proteasomal turnover of N-Myc [10] . However, silencing UBA1 , the E1 enzyme initiating ubiquitination, did not prevent N-Myc loss following treatment with DFO, Dp44mT, or DpC [130] . These findings suggest that N-Myc degradation may be mediated via a ubiquitin-independent proteasomal pathway (Fig. 10 ), a mechanism previously reported for other proteins [131] . Oxidatively damaged proteins are known to undergo degradation via the 20S proteasome in a ubiquitin-independent manner [132] . As part of their mechanism of anti-cancer activity, both Dp44mT and DpC become highly redox-active upon chelating iron or copper in cells, generating ROS that contributes to oxidative damage [29,30] .The observed reduction in N-Myc protein levels induced by these latter agents may therefore result from both transcriptional down-regulation of N-Myc mRNA and oxidative stress-induced protein degradation in all three NB cell-types. Notably, UBA1 silencing also failed to prevent the down-regulation of cyclin D1 by these ligands. This effect is consistent with ubiquitin-independent degradation of cyclin D1 that was identified following iron chelation in other cell-types [85,92] . Further studies are required to confirm the mechanism of ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation observed following ligand treatment. This could involve assessing non-canonical SUMO-dependent proteasomal degradation through the 20S subunit, which is ubiquitin-independent [133] . However, considering the apparent rare substrate-specific nature of the latter process and the redox nature of our compounds, it is known that oxidatively damaged proteins undergo ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation [134] . Hence, it could be important to determine whether scavenging ROS prevents N-Myc loss. This may be achieved by pre-treating cells with permeable pegylated catalase (PEG-Catalase) and pegylated superoxide dismutase (PEG-SOD), which neutralize intracellular hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, respectively [135] . Additionally, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which increases glutathione (GSH) and antagonizes thiosemicarbazone-induced oxidative and anti-proliferative effects [30,136,137] , may attenuate N-Myc down-regulation if oxidative stress is involved. Conversely, depletion of GSH using buthionine sulfoximine (BSO), which enhances oxidative activity and efficacy of thiosemicarbazones [104] , is expected to further promote N-Myc degradation. Collectively, these redox-based strategies can help determine the role of oxidative stress in mediating this proteasomal degradation mechanism. 3.4 Advantages of DpC relative to clinically used DFO N-Myc, the major driver of NB pathogenesis, was markedly down-regulated at both mRNA and protein levels by DpC in all three NB cell types, consistent with prior findings using DFO [11] . While these data demonstrate the marked activity of DpC, a limitation to the generalizability of our study is that it did not consider gender/sex issues. However, this was because the current investigation implemented cells in culture to dissect molecular pharmacological mechanisms. Of note, Dp44mT and DpC were more effective than DFO in reducing N-Myc expression across both N-Myc -amplified and non-amplified cells (Fig. 5 A-L). This difference was most evident in SH-SY5Y cells, where DFO failed to decrease N-Myc mRNA and protein levels, while the thiosemicarbazones demonstrated pronounced efficacy (Fig. 5 A, B). Considering the failure of DFO to decrease N-Myc mRNA and protein in SH-SY5Y NB cells, it is known these cells do not possess N-Myc amplification and express wild-type p53 relative to the Kelly and BE(2)-C cells [77] . For the first time, this investigation demonstrated the downstream target of wild-type p53, namely MDM2, played a role in the inability of DFO to decrease N-Myc mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells. A previous study indicated MDM2 stabilized N-Myc mRNA in other NB cell-types by its direct interaction with the 3ꞌ untranslated region, although the effect of drugs on this mechanism had not been investigated [76] . This response was not observed examining DpC-treated SH-SY5Y cells and was probably not due to differential regulation of the p53-MDM2 axis by DFO and DpC. This latter deduction is suggested as both DFO and DpC acted similarly to up-regulate MDM2 mRNA levels in SH-SY5Y cells (p53 wild-type) and not BE(2)-C or Kelly cells (p53 mutant). In fact, in SH-SY5Y cells, the log2 fold-change in MDM2 mRNA levels after incubation with DFO or DpC was 2.17 and 2.32, and the p.adj. was 1.25E-52 and 3.52E-56, respectively. This conclusion is in line with KEGG pathway analysis, demonstrating p53 signaling was affected similarly by both agents in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 2 A). It can be speculated the differential ligand activity in terms of MDM2-mediated stabilization of N-Myc mRNA is due to the rapid ability of DpC to down-regulate N-Myc mRNA versus that observed with DFO (Fig. S-4 ). The pronounced and rapid decrease in N-Myc mRNA levels by DpC may prevent binding by MDM2, effectively countering is ability to rescue the loss. This enhanced efficacy of DpC is likely due to its superior lipophilicity and membrane permeability of the DpT class of thiosemicarbazones relative to DFO [18] . This effect is highlighted by the greater activity of DpC at decreasing N-Myc mRNA than DFO as a function of time (Fig. S-4 ), and is in direct accordance with the markedly more potent anti-proliferative efficacy of the thiosemicarbazones against tumor cells, including multiple NB cell-types [33] . 3.5 Clinical perspectives: advantages of thiosemicarbazones At present, there are no clinically approved, specifically designed drugs that inhibit N-Myc activity [136] . The sole directly acting agent against N-Myc, BGA002, is in an early phase-I trial [138] , while several indirect modulators (e.g. , targeting Aurora-A, BET, Pol-I inhibitors, etc .) have reached phase I/II, with limited but encouraging results. True clinical effectiveness awaits results from these ongoing and future trials [136] . Given that DpC has already advanced to Phase I clinical evaluation with favorable adsorption from the gut and pharmacokinetics [32] , these findings position DpC as a promising chemically tractable platform capable of potently down-regulating a major oncogenic driver in NB, namely N-Myc. Furthermore, DpC has been demonstrated in multiple tumor cell-types to lead to synergistic anti-proliferative activity with a variety of standard chemotherapeutics including doxorubicin, celecoxib, gemcitabine, cisplatin, etc. [139,140] . The potential of DpC is confirmed by studies in vivo in mice against a human NB xenograft where it demonstrated effective activity and tolerability after oral administration in mice [33] and also against multiple other tumor xenografts [22,41,100] . The fact that DpC is relatively simple and economical to synthesize [32] , indicates marked advantages over many chemotherapies (e.g ., immunotherapies) that are highly expensive and require intravenous administration. While DpC demonstrated reversible muscle pain in its clinical trial [32] , recent studies led to DpC analogues, namely the PPP4pSe series, which totally prevent the oxidation of oxy-myoglobin, which was thought to be responsible for the DpC-induced muscle pain [141] . These new PPP4pSe analogues have been specifically designed to prevent this off-target effect and represent a significant advance over DpC, with demonstrated 3-fold greater selectivity against cancer cells relative to their normal counterparts in preclinical models [141] . 4 s In summary, this study demonstrates the anti-cancer agent, DpC, effectively suppresses N-Myc expression at both mRNA and protein levels across three NB cell-types, regardless of N-Myc amplification status. In wild-type p53-expressing SH-SY5Y cells, DFO fails to down-regulate N-Myc due to MDM2-mediated N-Myc mRNA stabilization (Fig. 10 ). In contrast, DpC overcomes this resistance, highlighting its superior therapeutic potential. Compared to DFO, DpC induces a more rapid reduction in N-Myc transcript levels as well as a more pronounced decrease in N-Myc protein levels, further supporting its superiority. While the down-regulation of N-Myc mRNA by the ligands was ATF3-independent, additional studies are required to deduce the precise molecular mechanisms involved. Importantly, both DFO and DpC induce broad gene expression changes, but DpC exhibits potent activity at concentrations 20-fold lower than those of clinically used DFO. Mechanistically, DFO and DpC promote ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation of N-Myc and facilitate nuclear translocation of the metastasis suppressor NDRG1, which interacts with N-Myc following treatment (Fig. 10 ). These findings elucidate the mechanism of action of DpC and underscore its significant advantages over DFO in targeting the central NB oncogenic driver, N-Myc. This study provides a strong rationale for the further development of DpC and its analogues as therapeutic agents for NB. 5 Experimental procedures 5.1 Cell culture The well-characterized human NB cell-types, SH-SY5Y, Kelly, and BE(2)-C were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA, USA). The SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Park Institute-1640 (RPMI-1640) medium supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, Bovogen, Victoria, Australia), 1 % penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich, Missouri, USA), 1 % sodium pyruvate solution (Sigma-Aldrich), and 1 % non-essential amino acid solution (Sigma-Aldrich). The BE(2)-C cells were cultured in Ham’s F12/MEM (50 % Ham’s F12 and 50 % MEM medium) with the same supplements required for RPMI above. 5.2 Compounds DFO was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. The negative control thiosemicarbazone, Bp2mT [19,20] , and the ligands, Dp44mT and DpC, were synthesized and characterized by established methods [19,20,37,41,142] . 5.3 RNA isolation, sequencing, and analysis NB cells were seeded in a 60 × 15 mm petri dish and allowed to attach overnight. The cells were then incubated for 24 h/37 °C with either control medium or this medium containing Bp2mT (5 µM), DFO (100 µM), Dp44mT (5 µM), or DpC (5 µM). The cells were collected in 1 mL of TRI reagent (Sigma-Aldrich), and RNA was extracted as per the manufacturer’s instructions. RNAseq was performed using next-generation sequencing (NGS) with Illumina TruSeq technology (Novogene, Hong Kong, China). The raw data (raw readings from the instrument) were first processed using FASTP software to ensure data quality for further analysis. The differential expression analysis was then performed in R (version 4.3.0; Lucent Technologies, USA) using the DESeq2 package. Genes with an adjusted p -value (p. adj. ) ≤ 0.05 found by DESeq2 were assigned as significantly differentially expressed. The KEGG enrichment analysis was performed through R using clusterProfiler package (version 4.3.0; Lucent Technologies, USA) [51] , while the functional annotation tool was implemented from the database, DAVID (davidbioinformatics.nih.gov; accessed November 2024). Data for generating Sankey diagrams were processed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) [52] . The complete dataset can be accessed from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (accession number GSE291132; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ). Three separate biological replicates were performed and analyzed. 5.4 Western analysis Cell lysate preparation, protein estimation, and western blotting were performed using standard protocols [39] . The primary antibodies used in this project included those against: N-Myc (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA; Cat. #: s), LSD1 (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. #: 2139 s), cyclin D1 (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. #: 2978 s), MDM2 (1/1000; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. #: s); NDRG1 (1/2500; Abcam, Cambridge, UK: Cat. #: ab37897), p53 (1/500; Abcam, Cat. #: ab26), ATF3 (1/1000; Abcam, Cat#: ab207434); β-actin (1/5000; Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. #: A5441); and TfR1 (1/2500; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, Cat. #: 13–6800). The secondary antibodies utilized were from Sigma-Aldrich: anti-goat (1/5000, Cat.#: A8919), anti-mouse (1/5000, Cat. #: A9044), and anti-rabbit (1/5000, Cat.#: A0545). Blots were imaged using an Azure Sapphire Biomolecular Imager (Azure Biosystems, California, United States). Densitometry of the images was collected using Image Lab (Bio-Rad, California, United States) and analyzed using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad, Inc, California, United States). 5.5 Confocal microscopy A 22 × 22 mm cover slip was added into a 6-well plate (Corning) and coated with poly-D -lysine solution (Sigma-Aldrich). Then, 100,000 cells were seeded onto the coverslip and incubated for 24 h/37 °C. The medium was subsequently removed, and the cells fixed by a 10 min incubation with ice-cold 4 % paraformaldehyde followed by 10 min permeabilization using 0.1 % Triton-X 100 in PBS. After permeabilization, the cells were blocked by a 1 h/20 °C incubation with 5 % BSA in PBS/0.3 M glycine and then incubated overnight with primary antibody diluted in 1 % BSA/PBS on an orbital shaker at 200 rpm/4 °C. The primary antibodies used include anti-LSD1 (1/200; Cell Signaling Technology, Cat#: 2139 s), anti-N-Myc (1/400, Cell Signaling Technology, Cat#: s), and anti-NDRG1 (1/200, Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: WH0010397M3). Before the 1 h/20 °C incubation with secondary antibody in 1 % BSA/PBS on an orbital shaker at 200 rpm, the cells were washed using ice-cold 1 % BSA in PBS, 3 times for 10 min each. Then, the secondary antibody was removed by aspiration and washed using ice-cold 1 % BSA in PBS for 4 times for 10 min each. The secondary antibodies used were from Cell Signaling Technology and included anti-rabbit (1/2000, Cat#: 4413 s) and anti-mouse (1/2000, Cat#: 4408 s). Coverslips were subsequently washed 3 times with 1 % BSA/PBS solution and mounted onto a slide using ProLong Gold DAPI mounting solution (Cat. # P36935; Invitrogen, Waltham, MA). The slides were left to dry in a dark room overnight. Confocal/immunofluorescence images were obtained using an Olympus FV3000 confocal microscope (Evident Scientific) with a 100 × objective. Fluorescence intensities and co-localization analysis were quantified using ImageJ software (NIHD). The Pearson correlation coefficient (r ) was calculated using the Image J plugin, JACoP. Further statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad. To maintain uniform samples for the accurate assessment of co-localization, the following measures were implemented during sample preparation and the image acquisition process. These included the use of a consistent number of cells that were seeded on each coverslip per sample to minimize variation in sample thickness. Additionally, only a cell monolayer was implemented, and within each experiment, all microscope acquisition parameters remained constant. 5.6 Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) Whole cell lysates were prepared using lysis buffer (Pierce IP Lysis Buffer, Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat#: ) containing protease inhibitor (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: ) and Phospho-STOP (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat#: ). A well-established co-IP procedure was performed in this study to determine the interactions between target proteins [39] . Briefly, 400 µg of protein from cell lysates was incubated with an antibody against NDRG1 (Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. #: 9485 s), while the respective isotype control antibody (Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. #: 3900 s) was utilized to determine the non-specific binding of immunoglobulins to the protein of interest. Then, the magnetic bead solution (30 mg/mL; Pierce Protein A/G Magnetic Beads; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat#: 10002D) was incubated with the antibody:lysate solution for 1.5 h/4 °C after overnight blocking in 5 % BSA/PBS. The supernatant was removed from the sample after incubation with the magnetic beads followed by five washes using ice-cold PBS. The magnetic beads were then resuspended using 5x loading dye containing 10 % β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich) and the protein was denatured by boiling for 5 min/95 °C. This sample was then used for SDS-PAGE and western blotting as described above. Ten percent (40 µg) of the amount of the proteins used for co-IP was used as the input samples for direct comparison. For subsequent western blotting, the primary antibodies used were anti-LSD1 (1/1000, Cell Signaling Technology; Cat. #: 4218 s), anti-N-Myc (1/1000, Abcam; Cat. #: AB16898). 5.7 cDNA synthesis and qPCR After the extraction of mRNA, as described in 5.3 , the cDNA was synthesized using a cDNA synthesis kit (Promega, Wisconsin). Briefly, 4 µL of DEPC-treated water, 4 µL of reaction buffer with random primer, and 2 µL of enzyme mix were added to prepare a transcription reaction solution. Then, 1 µg of mRNA was added to 10 µL transcription reaction solution, and DEPC-treated water was used to make up the final volume to 20 µL. The cDNA was then synthesized using a PCR machine through a reverse transcription cycle, which included 5 min primer annealing at 25 °C, 60 min extension at 42 °C, and 15 min inactivation at 70 °C. The synthesized cDNA was stored for 24 h/4 °C and then used to perform qPCR to determine the expression level of target genes, including the housekeeping gene, GAPDH . The cDNA was first diluted 1:20 and 2 µL of diluted cDNA was added into the reaction mix, which contained 1x SensiFAST SYBR (Meridian Bioscience, OH), 250 nM forward and reverse primer (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 U/µL RiboSafe RNase inhibitor, and DEPC-treated water to make up the final volume to 20 µL. The system was set at 1 cycle of 10 min for polymerase activation at 95 °C, 40 cycles of 15 s/95 °C for denaturation, 15 s/60 °C for annealing and 15 s/72 °C for extension. During the 40 cycles, the fluorescence reading was recorded at the end of each amplification cycle. The expression level of genes was calculated using the ΔΔCq method. The following primers were utilized: TfR1 : (FW: 5ꞌ-GCTGTTTGGGAATATGGAAGGA-3ꞌ; RV: 5ꞌ-TGCCTACACCGGATTTTGCA-3ꞌ); N-Myc : (FW: 5ꞌ-GGACACCCTGAGCGATTCA-3ꞌ; RV: 5ꞌ-GGGAAGGCATCGTTTGAGGA-3ꞌ); and GAPDH : (FW: 5ꞌ-ACCATCTTCCAGGAGCGAGA-3ꞌ; RV: 5ꞌ-TGCTGATGATCTTGAGGCTGT-3ꞌ). 5.8 Gene knockdown using small interfering RNA (siRNA) A non-targeting negative control siRNA (siControl; Cat.#: , Thermo Fisher Scientific) was implemented along with a specific siRNA (all at 75 µM) against ATF3 (siATF3; Invitrogen; Cat.#: , assay ID: s224089), MDM2 (siMDM2; Invitrogen; Cat. #: AM51331, assay ID: Hs00540450), NDRG1 (siNDRG1; Invitrogen; Cat.#: AM16706, assay ID: ), and UBA1 (siUBA1; Cat.#: , assay ID: Hs01031318). The related sequencing and silencing sites of these siRNAs are available from the supplier’s websites. The siRNAs were transfected into NB cells using Lipofectamine RNAiMAXR (Invitrogen; Cat.#: ), with incubation with siRNA/lipofectamine complex in Opti-MEM medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat. #: ) for 24 h/37 °C. Then, the cell lysates were collected, and western blotting was performed as described above. 5.9 Data analysis Statistical analyses of RNAseq data was performed as described above in 5.3 . All other data analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software, San Diego). The two-sample Student’s t- test (independent/unpaired) was performed using at least 3 independent experiments. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. title: ALK regulates macrophage polarization via the USP7/SOX9/MFAP2-mediated glycolytic pathway to promote neuroblastoma progression
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is a common pediatric malignancy in which activating mutations of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) drive tumor progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that ALK signaling promotes glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis. Using qRT-PCR, western blot, and co-culture systems, we found that ALK inhibition with lorlatinib reduces lactate production, downregulates M2 markers, and upregulates M1 markers in NB cells and NB mouse models. Mechanistically, Co-IP and ubiquitination assays revealed that ALK recruits and activates the deubiquitinase USP7, which deubiquitinates and stabilizes SOX9. Dual-luciferase reporter and ChIP-qPCR analyses further demonstrated that SOX9 directly binds to the MFAP2 promoter to activate its transcription. Functional assays showed that elevated MFAP2 enhances glycolysis, leading to increased lactate and immunosuppressive factor secretion, which in turn polarizes tumor-associated macrophages toward the pro-tumor M2 phenotype. Importantly, in vivo experiments confirmed that MFAP2 overexpression partially reverses the anti-tumor effects of lorlatinib. These findings identify the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 cascade as a critical regulator of metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion in NB, and suggest that targeting this axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for high-risk NB.

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a common pediatric malignancy in which activating mutations of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) drive tumor progression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that ALK signaling promotes glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis. Using qRT-PCR, western blot, and co-culture systems, we found that ALK inhibition with lorlatinib reduces lactate production, downregulates M2 markers, and upregulates M1 markers in NB cells and NB mouse models. Mechanistically, Co-IP and ubiquitination assays revealed that ALK recruits and activates the deubiquitinase USP7, which deubiquitinates and stabilizes SOX9. Dual-luciferase reporter and ChIP-qPCR analyses further demonstrated that SOX9 directly binds to the MFAP2 promoter to activate its transcription. Functional assays showed that elevated MFAP2 enhances glycolysis, leading to increased lactate and immunosuppressive factor secretion, which in turn polarizes tumor-associated macrophages toward the pro-tumor M2 phenotype. Importantly, in vivo experiments confirmed that MFAP2 overexpression partially reverses the anti-tumor effects of lorlatinib. These findings identify the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 cascade as a critical regulator of metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion in NB, and suggest that targeting this axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for high-risk NB. It accounts for more than 7% of malignancies in patients under 15 years of age and is responsible for approximately 15% of pediatric cancer-related deaths [2] . ALK is one of the most frequently mutated genes in NB [3,4] , and activating mutations, such as ALK-F1174L, have been established as a critical risk factor driving NB progression [5] . Particularly when ALK mutation coexists with MYCN amplification, patients often present with relapsed/refractory disease, rendering clinical treatment exceedingly challenging [6] . Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which ALK drives NB progression is of great significance for identifying novel therapeutic targets. Tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in NB progression [7] . Macrophages in the TME, exhibit high plasticity and can be polarized into two distinct states: the M1 phenotype (anti-tumor) and the M2 phenotype (pro-tumor). In NB, tumor-associated macrophages predominantly display an M2-like phenotype, thereby promoting tumor immune evasion, angiogenesis, and metastasis [8] . However, the precise molecular mechanisms by which NB cells regulate macrophage M2 polarization remain largely unclear. Recent studies have revealed that lactate generated from glycolysis can induce macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype [9] . In various tumors, including lung cancer and lymphoma, ALK activation has been demonstrated to significantly enhance glycolytic levels in tumor cells, thereby supporting their malignant phenotypes [10,11] . However, whether ALK regulates macrophage polarization through modulating glycolysis in NB remains unreported. Of note, a recent study has shown that ALK mutation drives NB progression by activating the WNT signaling pathway, and inhibition of the WNT pathway markedly attenuates ALK mutation-induced tumor growth [5] . Moreover, WNT signaling activation has been extensively documented to promote aerobic glycolysis through multiple mechanisms [12] . Based on these findings, we hypothesize that in NB, ALK activation may enhance the glycolytic capacity of tumor cells, and the resulting lactate subsequently induces macrophage M2 polarization. To investigate the upstream molecular mechanisms by which ALK enhance the glycolytic capacity, the transcriptomic dataset GSE228194 (ALK-mutant vs. ALK-wild-type) was analyzed. Differential expression analysis identified a total of 1917 differentially expressed genes, among which microfibril-associated protein 2 (MFAP2) was one of the most significantly downregulated genes and was further identified as an upstream regulator of glycolysis and macrophage M2 polarization. Moreover, analysis using the GeneMANIA database revealed a co-expression relationship between ALK and MFAP2. Previous studies have reported that MFAP2 is upregulated in various tumors and promotes tumor progression through the WNT signaling-mediated glycolytic pathway [13,14] . However, the role of MFAP2 in NB and its upstream regulatory mechanisms have not yet been reported. To further identify the upstream transcription factors regulating MFAP2, we predicted potential transcription factors of MFAP2 using the hTFtarget database and intersected them with significantly upregulated differentially expressed genes from GSE228194 , as well as the top 1000 glycolysis-related genes from GeneCards, leading to the identification of SRY-box transcription factor 9 (SOX9). In addition, JASPAR database analysis predicted that SOX9 binds to the GCATTGTT sequence within the promoter region of MFAP2. Previous studies have shown that SOX9 expression in NB cells is associated with multiple key biological processes, including migration, invasion, and differentiation [15] . However, the specific function of SOX9 in NB and the mechanisms underlying its upregulation remain unreported. Ubiquitination and deubiquitination of proteins are key mechanisms regulating their stability and activity [16] . Using the Ubibrowser database, we identified the deubiquitinating enzyme USP7 as a potential key regulator of SOX9 stability. Ubiquitin-Specific Protease 7 (USP7) plays important roles in tumorigenesis and immune regulation [17] , and can influence the activity of transcription factors (such as REST and cMyc) through deubiquitination [18] . Previous studies have shown that USP7 promotes glycolysis in tumor cells [19] and drives NB progression through multiple pathways [20] . Moreover, various USP7 inhibitors have been demonstrated to suppress NB growth [21,22] . Of note, the activity of USP7 is regulated by phosphorylation, which converts USP7 from an inactive to an active state [23] . However, whether ALK activation promotes USP7 phosphorylation, thereby activating its deubiquitinase activity, subsequently enhancing SOX9 protein stability, and ultimately increasing MFAP2 transcription in NB remains to be experimentally validated. Based on the above findings, this study aims to investigate whether ALK activation in NB enhances the deubiquitinating activity of USP7 via phosphorylation modification, thereby increasing the protein stability of the transcription factor SOX9 and subsequently upregulating MFAP2 transcription. Furthermore, we seek to explore whether MFAP2-mediated glycolysis promotes macrophage M2 polarization, thereby facilitating tumor progression in NB. By elucidating this novel regulatory axis, we hope to provide a theoretical foundation for identifying new therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers for NB. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Animal model establishment and treatment Female BALB/c-nu nude mice (6–8 weeks old, n = 48) were purchased from Beijing SPF Biotechnology Co., Ltd. All mice were maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle at 21–26 °C and 40–70% humidity, with free access to food and water. After one week of acclimatization, a Kelly cell line stably overexpressing MFAP2 was constructed using a lentiviral vector, and 3 × 106 cells were subcutaneously injected into the right posterior flank of each mouse to establish a NB model. Mice were orally administered lorlatinib at 60 mg/kg/day. Tumor sizes were measured every 3 days using a caliper, and tumor volumes were calculated using the formula: V = length × width2 / 2. After 4 weeks, mice were euthanized, and tumors were harvested, weighed, and photographed. Each group consisted of 6 mice. All experimental protocols have been reviewed and approved by Fujian Medical University (IACUC FJMU 2024-Y-0068). 2.2 Cell culture Human neuroblastoma cell lines SH-SY5Y and Kelly were purchased from Xiamen Yimo Biotechnology Co., Ltd. SH-SY5Y cells were cultured in proprietary medium (IM-H227-1, Yimo). Kelly cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (ZB000BF, Sangon) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (10099141C, Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (P1400, Solarbio). Both cell lines were maintained at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator (311, Thermo Scientific). For drug treatment, cells were treated with 10 μmol/L lorlatinib (HY- , MCE) for 24 h. 2.3 Lactate level measurement For cell samples, cells from each group were collected, lysed by ultrasonic disruption in distilled water, and centrifuged at 8000 ×g for 10 min at room temperature. The supernatant was collected for analysis. For tissue samples, tumor tissues were accurately weighed and homogenized in 9 volumes of normal saline (weight: volume = 1:9) on ice using a mechanical homogenizer. The homogenate was centrifuged at rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected. Reagents were added according to the manufacturer's instructions of the Lactate Assay Kit (A019-2-1, Nanjing Jiancheng). After thorough mixing, the absorbance was measured at 530 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher Scientific). 2.4 Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level measurement For cell samples, cells from each group were collected and processed according to the manufacturer's instructions of the L-Lactate Dehydrogenase Assay Kit (P0393S, Beyotime). For tissue samples, tumor tissues were accurately weighed and homogenized in 9 volumes of normal saline (weight: volume = 1:9) on ice using a mechanical homogenizer. The homogenate was centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected. The assay was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions of the Lactate Dehydrogenase Assay Kit (A020–2, Nanjing Jiancheng). Absorbance was measured at 440 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher) for both sample types. 2.5 Flow cytometry analysis of M1 and M2 macrophage polarization THP-1-derived macrophages were used to assess M1 and M2 polarization following co-culture with Kelly cells. Briefly, THP-1 cells were differentiated into M0 macrophages by treatment with 150 nM phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) for 24 h. Differentiated M0 macrophages were then co-cultured with Kelly cells in Transwell chambers for 24 h. After co-culture, macrophages were harvested and centrifuged. Subsequently, cells were resuspended in 1× Binding Buffer to a density of 1 × 106 cells/mL. The cells were then incubated with 2 μL of PE anti-human CD163 antibody (326,505, Biolegend) and 2 μL of APC anti-human CD86 antibody (374,207, Biolegend) for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. After incubation, the stained cells were analyzed using a flow cytometer (RMNNC-3000, Agilent). 2.6 Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay Cell viability was assessed using the CCK-8 assay. Briefly, cells were adjusted to a density of 1 × 106 cells/mL and seeded into 96-well plates with three replicate wells per group. Cells were cultured at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator until reaching confluence. Then, 10 μL of CCK-8 solution (C0037, Beyotime) was added to each well, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 2 h in the dark. The optical density was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher Scientific). 2.7 Wound healing assay Cell migration was evaluated by a wound healing assay. Briefly, cells were seeded into 6-well plates and cultured to confluence. A linear scratch was created using a 200 μL pipette tip. After washing with PBS to remove detached cells, the medium was replaced with serum-free medium. Wound closure was observed and photographed at 0, 24, and 48 h. Migration distance was measured using ImageJ software. 2.8 Transwell invasion assay Cell invasion was assessed using Matrigel-coated Transwell chambers (356,234, BD Biosciences). Cells were resuspended in serum-free medium (2 × 105 cells/mL) and 100 μL was added to the upper chamber, with 600 μL of 10% FBS-containing medium in the lower chamber. After 24 h of incubation, non-invading cells were removed, and invading cells were fixed, stained with crystal violet, and counted under a microscope. Invasion ability was quantified using ImageJ software. 2.9 Immunofluorescence staining of Ki-67 Ki-67 expression in tumor tissues was detected by immunofluorescence. Briefly, paraffin-embedded tumor sections were dewaxed, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval by microwave heating in antigen retrieval buffer (G1203, Solarbio). After blocking with 3% BSA, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-Ki-67 antibody (ab15580, Abcam; diluted 1:200). Subsequently, sections were incubated with CY3-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (A0516, Beyotime) for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (G1012-100 L, Servicebio). Fluorescence images were captured under a microscope. 2.10 Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) Total RNA was extracted from cells or tissues by RNA extraction solution (G3013, Servicebio), and cDNA was synthesized using PrimeScript RT reagent Kit (RR037Q, Takara). qRT-PCR was performed using TB Green Premix Ex Taq II (RR820Q, Takara) to amplify and measure the relative mRNA expression levels of ALK, iNOS, CD86, Arg1, CD206, HK2, PKM2, MFAP2, TGFBI, ALDH1A3, TCF7L2, SMAD3, SOX9, ETS1, STAT3 and USP7. The 2−ΔΔCT method was used for data analysis, with β-actin as the reference gene. All primer oligonucleotides were custom-synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. Primer sequences are listed in Table 1 . 2.11 Western blot Total proteins were extracted from cells or tissues using RIPA lysis buffer (BL504A, Bio Sharp), and concentrations were determined with a BCA protein assay kit (BL521A, Bio Sharp). Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking with 5% skim milk (D8340, Solarbio) for 2 h at ambient temperature, the membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies targeting the following proteins: SOX9 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), Arg1 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), CD206 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), ETS1 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), STAT3 (1:1000, -2-AP, Proteintech), TCF7L2 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), SMAD3 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), MFAP2 (1:1000, ab231344, Abcam), UB (1:1000, -2-AP, Proteintech), ALK (1:1000, , Biolegend), iNOS (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), CD86 (1:1000, -4-RR, Proteintech), HK2 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), PKM2 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), USP7 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), TGFBI (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), ALDH1A3 (1:1000, -1-AP, Proteintech), and pALK (1:1000, bs-3022P, Bioss). β-actin (1:1000, -1-Ig, Proteintech) served as an internal reference. Subsequently, macrophages in the lower chambers were collected for further detection of macrophage polarization markers. 2.15 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) The levels of IL-10 (E-EL-M0046, Elabscience), TGF-β1 (E-EL-0162, Elabscience), and TNF-α (E-EL-H0109, Elabscience) were measured using commercial ELISA kits. All procedures were performed as per the kit protocols. Absorbance was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Multiskan FC, Thermo Fisher), and cytokine concentrations were calculated from standard curves. 2.16 Dual-luciferase reporter assay The MFAP2 promoter dual-luciferase reporter plasmid was constructed by Tsingke Biotechnology. Cells were seeded in 6-well plates and co-transfected with the reporter plasmid together with either SOX9 overexpression plasmid (OE-SOX9) or negative control (OE-NC) using Lipo8000™ transfection reagent (C0533, Beyotime) when cell density reached 70%–80%. Firefly luciferase detection reagent (100 μL, measured at 560 nm) and Renilla luciferase detection working solution (100 μL, measured at 465 nm) were added sequentially, and chemiluminescence was measured using a multimode microplate reader (Spark, TECAN) according to the manufacturer's instructions of the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit (RG027, Beyotime). The ratio of firefly luciferase activity to Renilla luciferase activity was calculated to normalize MFAP2 promoter activity across groups. 2.17 ChIP-qPCR detection of SOX9 binding to the MFAP2 promoter ChIP assay was performed using a Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Kit (P2078, Beyotime) according to the manufacturer's instructions. OE-NC and OE-SOX9 cells were crosslinked with formaldehyde, harvested, lysed, and sonicated. After washing, the complexes were eluted. Following decrosslinking, the samples were digested with Proteinase K, extracted with phenol-chloroform, and precipitated with glycogen to purify the DNA. The purified DNA was used as a template for qPCR with TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ II (RR820Q, Takara). Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA kit (BL521A, Bio Sharp). For immunoprecipitation, lysates were incubated overnight at 4 °C with Protein A + G magnetic beads pre-coupled with specific antibodies (anti-ALK, anti-SOX9, anti-USP7, or control IgG) using an immunoprecipitation kit (P2179S, Beyotime). After washing, bound proteins were eluted by boiling in 1× SDS loading buffer. For ubiquitination detection, cells were treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 prior to lysis. Immunoprecipitated samples and inputs were analyzed by western blot with indicated antibodies. 2.19 Cycloheximide (CHX) assay for SOX9 protein stability Cells were treated with cycloheximide (CHX, HY- , MCE) at a final concentration of 2–3 μg/mL to block de novo protein synthesis. Cells were harvested at 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 h after CHX treatment, and SOX9 protein expression level was detected by western blot. A protein degradation curve was plotted accordingly. 2.20 Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 statistical software, with standard deviation used to estimate intra-group variability. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A two-tailed, unpaired Student's t -test was used to compare data between two groups, while one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed for comparing data among multiple groups. Tukey's post-hoc multiple comparisons test was conducted. 3 Results 3.1 ALK inhibition by lorlatinib suppresses glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization in vivo To characterize the expression pattern of ALK in NB, the expression level of ALK was examined in ALK-positive NB cell lines (CLB-GE, Kelly, and SH-SY5Y). Kelly and SH-SY5Y cells exhibited higher level of ALK mRNA and protein and were therefore selected for subsequent experiments (Fig. 1 A–B ). To investigate the effect of ALK on NB progression in vivo , a nude mouse NB model was established by injection of Kelly cells, and mice were treated with the ALK inhibitor lorlatinib. Lorlatinib treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth rate (Fig. 1 C), reduced tumor volume and weight at the endpoint (Fig. 1 D–E), indicating that ALK inhibition effectively suppresses the tumor progression of NB in vivo . Furthermore, ALK inhibition reduced glycolysis in NB, as evidenced by significantly decreased lactate content (Fig. 1 F) and LDH activity (Fig. 1 G) in tumor tissues following lorlatinib treatment. Given that glycolysis can promote macrophage M2 polarization in the TME [24] , we further examined the expression of immunosuppressive factors and macrophage polarization markers in tumor tissues. Lorlatinib treatment significantly reduced the secretion levels of immunosuppressive factors IL-10 (Fig. 1 H) and TGF-β1 (Fig. 1 I), decreased the mRNA (Fig. 1 J) and protein (Fig. 1 L) expression levels of M2 macrophage markers (Arg1, CD206), and increased the mRNA (Fig. 1 J) and protein (Fig. 1 K) expression levels of M1 macrophage markers (iNOS, CD86) in tumor tissues. These results suggest that ALK inhibition reduces glycolysis and reverses M2 polarization of macrophages in NB progression. 3.2 ALK mediates glycolysis to induce M2 macrophage polarization in vitro To investigate the regulatory role of ALK inhibition on glycolysis and macrophage polarization in vitro , SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells were treated with lorlatinib. Lorlatinib treatment did not significantly alter ALK mRNA expression level in either cell line (Fig. 2 A ), which is expected as lorlatinib inhibits ALK kinase activity rather than its transcription, but effectively reduced ALK phosphorylation level in both SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells (Fig. 2 B–D). Furthermore, lorlatinib treatment significantly decreased lactate production (Fig. 2 E), LDH activity (Fig. 2 F), and the mRNA and protein expression levels of the glycolytic key enzymes HK2 and PKM2 (Fig. 2 G–L) in both cell lines, indicating that inhibition of ALK activity markedly impairs the glycolytic capacity of NB cells. To explore the effect of ALK-inhibited NB cells on macrophage polarization, lorlatinib-treated NB cells were indirectly co-cultured with PMA-differentiated THP-1-derived macrophages (M0 macrophages). Macrophages co-cultured with lorlatinib-treated NB cells exhibited significantly reduced levels of the immunosuppressive factors IL-10 and TGF-β1, as well as decreased protein expression of M2 polarization markers Arg1 and CD206. In contrast, the levels of the pro-inflammatory factor TNF-α and the protein expression of M1 polarization markers iNOS and CD86 were upregulated (Fig. 2 M-P). Consistently, lorlatinib treatment significantly reduced the percentage of M2 (CD163-positive) macrophages (Fig. S1A). To confirm that glycolytic lactate serves as the causal factor for NB cell-triggered M2 macrophage polarization, we performed lactate rescue experiments using lorlatinib-exposed Kelly cells (Fig. S1B-E). Supplementation with exogenous L-lactate (Nala) restored lorlatinib-suppressed IL-10 and TGF-β1 secretion while dampening lorlatinib-upregulated TNF-α release (Fig. S1B–C). Consistently, Nala partially rescued lorlatinib-triggered M1 marker upregulation (iNOS, CD86) and recovered the lorlatinib-reduced expression of M2 markers (Arg1, CD206) (Fig. S1D-E). These results verify glycolytic lactate as the key metabolite mediating ALK-driven M2 macrophage polarization. Taken together, ALK activation enhances glycolysis and lactate production in NB cells to induce M2 macrophage polarization, while ALK inhibition reverses this process. 3.3 ALK upregulates MFAP2 expression to promote glycolysis To explore the key downstream mediators of ALK signaling in NB, we analyzed differentially expressed genes based on the GEO dataset GSE228194 . Volcano plot analysis revealed that MFAP2, TGFBI and ALDH1A3 were significantly downregulated in the ALK MUT (ALK-mutant) group (Fig. S2A). Genemania database further confirmed a strong co-expression relationship between ALK and MFAP2 (Fig. S2B). Notably, analysis of the TARGET Neuroblastoma (NBL) dataset identified a robust positive correlation between MFAP2 expression and glycolysis GSVA score in NB clinical tumor samples (Fig. S2C). To validate whether MFAP2 expression is regulated by ALK activity, we examined MFAP2 level in both in vivo and in vitro models after lorlatinib treatment. Lorlatinib treatment remarkably reduced the mRNA and protein levels of MFAP2, TGFBI and ALDH1A3 both in tumor tissues of NB model mice and Kelly cells, with MFAP2 showing the most pronounced alteration. Of note, TGFBI mRNA expression exhibited no significant difference in Kelly cells following lorlatinib intervention (Fig. 3 A–D ). Collectively, these data identify MFAP2 as a direct downstream target of ALK signaling in NB. To explore the biological function of MFAP2 in NB, MFAP2 overexpression (OE-MFAP2) and knockdown (si-MFAP2) were performed in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, respectively. The efficiency of MFAP2 overexpression (Fig. S2D–G) and knockdown (Fig. S2H–K) was validated in each cell line. Compared with the overexpression (OE)-negative control (NC) or siRNA negative control (si-NC) groups, MFAP2 overexpression significantly upregulated both the mRNA and protein levels of the key glycolytic enzymes HK2 and PKM2, whereas MFAP2 knockdown exerted the inhibitory effects (Fig. 3 E–I). Consistently, MFAP2 overexpression significantly increased lactate production and LDH activity, while MFAP2 knockdown markedly suppressed these glycolytic parameters (Fig. 3 J–K). Furthermore, MFAP2 overexpression significantly enhanced NB cell viability (Fig. 3 L), as well as cell invasion (Fig. 3 M–O) and migration (Fig. S2L), whereas MFAP2 knockdown led to significant inhibition of these capacities. Collectively, these results indicate that MFAP2, which is regulated by ALK, potently promotes glycolysis, invasion, and migration in NB cells. 3.4 ALK promotes MFAP2 transcription by upregulating SOX9 To investigate the molecular mechanism by which ALK regulates MFAP2 expression, potential transcription factors mediating this process were screened. A total of 90 putative transcription factors of MFAP2 were retrieved from the hTFtarget database. These were intersected with the significantly upregulated differentially expressed genes (840 genes) from the GEO dataset GSE228194 and the top 1000 glycolysis-related genes obtained from GeneCards, yielding five candidate transcription factors: TCF7L2, SMAD3, SOX9, ETS1, and STAT3 (Fig. S3A). Further bioinformatic analysis based on the TARGET-NBL dataset uncovered a moderate positive correlation between SOX9 expression and M2-type tumor-associated macrophage infiltration (Fig. S3B). The JASPAR database predicted that SOX9 could specifically bind to the GCATTGTT sequence within the MFAP2 promoter region (Fig. S3C–D). Western blot analysis revealed that lorlatinib treatment significantly downregulated the protein levels of STAT3, SOX9, TCF7L2, SMAD3, and ETS1 in Kelly cells, among which SOX9 exhibited the most pronounced reduction (Fig. 4 A–B ). To validate the transcriptional regulation of MFAP2 by SOX9, MFAP2 expression was examined in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells overexpressing SOX9 (the overexpression efficiency was validated in Fig. S3E–H). The results demonstrated that SOX9 overexpression significantly upregulated both the mRNA and protein level of MFAP2 (Fig. 4 C–G). Dual-luciferase reporter assays further confirmed that SOX9 overexpression significantly enhanced the transcriptional activity of the wild-type MFAP2 promoter (PGL3-MFAP2 WT) in both SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, whereas no significant activation was observed with the mutant promoter (PGL3-MFAP2 MUT) (Fig. 4 H). ChIP-qPCR assays also showed that SOX9 directly bound to the MFAP2 promoter region in both NB cell lines, and this binding was significantly enhanced upon SOX9 overexpression (Fig. 4 I). Together, these results indicate that SOX9, as a transcription factor, directly binds to and activates MFAP2 transcription, thereby mediating the regulation of MFAP2 expression by ALK signaling. 3.5 ALK inhibition promotes proteasome-dependent degradation of SOX9 To further investigate the regulatory mechanism of ALK on SOX9, a series of experiments were performed. Co-IP assays showed that there was no direct protein–protein interaction between ALK and SOX9 in SH-SY5Y or Kelly cells (Fig. 5 A ). The effect of lorlatinib treatment on SOX9 protein stability was then assessed using the protein synthesis inhibitor CHX. In SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells, SOX9 protein exhibited a relatively slow degradation rate and a long half-life. In contrast, lorlatinib treatment significantly accelerated the degradation of SOX9 and markedly shortened its half-life, indicating that inhibition of ALK activity reduces SOX9 protein stability (Fig. 5 B–D). To determine whether this degradation process is mediated by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, the ubiquitination level of SOX9 was examined, and the proteasome inhibitor MG132 was employed for validation. Co-IP assays revealed that lorlatinib treatment significantly increased the ubiquitination level of SOX9 (Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, MG132 treatment effectively rescued the lorlatinib-induced downregulation of SOX9 protein (Fig. 5 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that inhibition of ALK activity promotes ubiquitination and proteasome-dependent degradation of SOX9, thereby reducing its protein stability. However, the absence of a direct protein interaction between ALK and SOX9 suggests that other intermediary molecules may mediate this regulatory process. 3.6 ALK stabilizes SOX9 through USP7-mediated deubiquitination to promote MFAP2 expression To identify the intermediary molecules mediating the regulatory relationship between ALK and SOX9, the UbiBrowser database was employed to predict potential upstream deubiquitinases of SOX9 (Fig. S4A). Given that USP7 has been reported to promote glycolysis in tumor cells [19] , USP7 was selected as the core candidate molecule. We further used PhosphoSitePlus database to predict multiple phosphorylation modification sites on USP7 (Fig. S4B). Moreover, we assessed the impact of ALK inhibition on total USP7 and phosphorylated USP7 (p-USP7). Western blot results showed that lorlatinib treatment reduced the abundance of both USP7 and p-USP7 in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells (Fig. 6 A ), indicating that ALK kinase activity supports USP7 expression and its phosphorylation modification. Co-IP results confirmed that ALK and USP7 reciprocally formed endogenous protein complexes, and lorlatinib treatment drastically weakened their mutual binding (Fig. 6 B). To verify that this interaction is direct rather than mediated by other intracellular factors, we conducted GST pull-down assays with recombinant proteins, which validated the direct physical binding between ALK and USP7 in vitro (Fig. 6 B). The endogenous interaction between USP7 and SOX9 was also validated by Co-IP results (Fig. 6 C). To further validate the regulatory effect of USP7 on SOX9, USP7 overexpression was performed in SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells. Both the mRNA and protein expression level of USP7 was significantly increased in the OE-USP7 groups, confirming the overexpression efficiency (Fig. 6 D–G). The effect of USP7 overexpression on SOX9 protein stability was then assessed using a CHX chase assay. The results demonstrated that USP7 overexpression significantly slowed the degradation rate of SOX9 and prolonged its protein half-life (Fig. 6 H–I). Furthermore, ubiquitination assays revealed that USP7 overexpression markedly reduced the ubiquitination level of SOX9 (Fig. 6 J–K), indicating that USP7 stabilizes SOX9 protein through deubiquitination. On this basis, the effects of USP7 overexpression on the expression of SOX9 and its downstream target gene MFAP2 were examined. The results showed that USP7 overexpression significantly upregulated both the mRNA and protein levels of SOX9 and MFAP2 (Fig. 6 L–O). To genetically validate the hierarchical ALK-USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 cascade, we performed two sets of rescue/blocking assays presented in Fig. S4C–P. First, SH-SY5Y and Kelly cells were treated with lorlatinib alone or lorlatinib combined with USP7 overexpression. USP7 overexpression rescued lorlatinib-triggered downregulation of SOX9 and MFAP2 at both mRNA and protein levels (Fig. S4C–K). We further performed CHX chase assays to evaluate SOX9 protein stability under the same treatment conditions. Lorlatinib notably accelerated SOX9 degradation and shortened its half-life, whereas co-overexpression of USP7 effectively rescued SOX9 protein stability impaired by ALK inhibition (Fig. S4L). These rescue data confirm that USP7 acts downstream of ALK to maintain SOX9 and MFAP2 expression. Next, we carried out epistasis blocking assays in Kelly cells to validate SOX9 as the indispensable downstream effector of USP7. The knockdown efficiency of SOX9 shRNA constructs was verified by qRT-PCR and western blot (Fig. S4Q–S). Compared with OE-NC control, USP7 overexpression significantly elevated intracellular lactate production, upregulated glycolytic genes HK2, PKM2 as well as MFAP2 at both mRNA and protein levels, and increased β-catenin protein expression; however, simultaneous knockdown of SOX9 partially abolished these phenotypes (Fig. S4M–P). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that USP7, as a key intermediary molecule between ALK and SOX9, binds to both proteins, stabilizes SOX9 through deubiquitination, and consequently upregulates MFAP2 expression. 3.7 MFAP2 mediates ALK-induced tumor growth, glycolysis, and M2 polarization in vivo To investigate whether MFAP2 functions as a key downstream effector of ALK signaling in vivo , a Kelly cell line stably overexpressing MFAP2 was established, and a subcutaneous nude mouse model was generated with or without lorlatinib intervention. Compared with the LV-OE-NC group, MFAP2 overexpression (LV-OE-MFAP2 group) significantly accelerated tumor growth (Fig. 7 A ), increased tumor volume and weight (Fig. 7 B–C), and elevated the proportion of Ki-67-positive proliferative cells (Fig. 7 D–E). Moreover, lactate content (Fig. 7 F), the secretion levels of the immunosuppressive factors IL-10 and TGF-β1 (Fig. 7 G–H), as well as the mRNA and protein expression levels of the M2 macrophage markers Arg1 and CD206 (Fig. 7 I–K), were all significantly increased. In contrast, lorlatinib treatment (LV-OE-NC + lorlatinib group) markedly suppressed the above tumor-promoting, glycolysis-promoting, and M2-polarizing effects. Notably, compared with the LV-OE-NC + lorlatinib group, the LV-OE-MFAP2 + lorlatinib group exhibited a partial reversal of these inhibitory effects, as evidenced by significant recoveries in tumor growth, lactate production, immunosuppressive factor secretion, and M2 polarization levels, indicating that MFAP2 overexpression could partially antagonize the anti-tumor effects of ALK inhibition. Conversely, the expression levels of the M1 macrophage markers iNOS and CD86 showed opposite trends (Fig. 7 I–K). In summary, these in vivo findings demonstrate that MFAP2 significantly promotes NB tumor growth, glycolysis, and M2 macrophage polarization. Furthermore, overexpression of MFAP2 partially counteracts the anti-tumor effects of the ALK inhibitor lorlatinib, further confirming that MFAP2 acts as a key downstream effector of ALK signaling and mediates ALK-induced promotion of tumor growth, glycolysis, and M2 macrophage polarization in NB. 4 Discussion NB is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children, and patients with refractory or relapsed NB have dismal survival rates [25] . Despite recent advances in comprehensive treatment strategies, including targeted therapies, the prognosis for patients with high-risk NB remains poor, particularly for those harboring ALK gene mutations [26] . Targeting the ALK receptor has emerged as one of the most promising and specific therapeutic approaches for NB [27,28] . Therefore, elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which ALK drives NB progression is of great significance for the identification of novel therapeutic targets. In this study, we unveil a previously unrecognized mechanism by which ALK drives NB progression through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 signaling axis, which regulates glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization. Specifically, ALK recruits and activates the deubiquitinase USP7, thereby enhancing the protein stability of SOX9. SOX9, acting as a transcription factor, directly binds to the promoter region of MFAP2 and upregulates its expression. In turn, MFAP2 potentiates the glycolytic capacity of NB cells, leading to increased lactate production and immunosuppressive factor secretion, which induces the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward the M2 phenotype and ultimately accelerates tumor growth. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of ALK with lorlatinib effectively disrupts this signaling cascade, suppresses glycolysis, reverses M2 polarization, and impedes NB progression. ALK is one of the most frequently mutated oncogenes in NB, and its activating mutations serve as critical drivers of NB progression [29] . Multiple studies have elucidated the molecular mechanisms by which ALK promotes NB progression from distinct perspectives. For instance, ALK upregulates POSTN and activates WNT signaling to drive NB progression [5] , and super-enhancer-driven IRF2BP2 regulates the chromatin accessibility of ALK and cooperates with AP-1 to maintain NB cell survival [30] . Clinically, lorlatinib has demonstrated favorable efficacy and safety in patients with ALK-driven relapsed or refractory NB, with a modified response rate of 30% as a single agent in pediatric patients and 63% when combined with chemotherapy [31] . Consistent with these reports, the present study shows that ALK is highly expressed in human NB cells and a nude mouse NB model, and that lorlatinib treatment significantly suppresses the proliferation, migration, and invasion of NB tumor cells. More importantly, we reveal for the first time that ALK regulates glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis, thereby expanding the current understanding of ALK signaling pathways. USP7, a widely expressed deubiquitinating enzyme, exerts pro-tumorigenic effects across multiple cancer types, including breast, pancreatic, gastric, ovarian, and lung cancers [17,32–34] . Previous studies have demonstrated that USP7 stabilizes various substrate proteins, such as c-Myc, p53, and PTEN [35–37] , through deubiquitination, thereby contributing to tumor progression. In NB, high USP7 expression is associated with poor prognosis, and pharmacological inhibition of USP7 effectively suppresses NB cell growth [20] . In the present study, we observed that inhibition of ALK activity markedly reduces the interaction between USP7 and ALK. Furthermore, USP7 overexpression significantly prolongs the half-life of SOX9 protein and decreases its ubiquitination level. Collectively, these findings suggest that ALK stabilizes SOX9 by activating the deubiquitinase activity of USP7, thereby providing novel mechanistic insight into the role of USP7 in NB pathogenesis. SOX9 is a pivotal transcription factor of the SOX family, playing critical roles in various malignancies [38] . In NB, SOX9 has been reported to be associated with cell differentiation, migration, and invasion [15] ; however, its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain largely undefined. In this study, we identified SOX9 as a key transcription factor downstream of the ALK signaling pathway, and demonstrated that its protein stability is regulated by USP7-mediated deubiquitination. Furthermore, using dual-luciferase reporter assays and ChIP-qPCR, we provide the first evidence that SOX9 directly binds to the MFAP2 promoter and activates its transcription. These findings not only link SOX9 to glycolytic metabolism in NB but also offer novel insights into the functional role of SOX9 in tumors. MFAP2 is an essential component of extracellular matrix microfibrils [39] and has recently garnered increasing attention in cancer research. Previous studies have reported that MFAP2 is upregulated in various malignancies, including oral squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma, where it promotes glycolysis and tumor progression by activating the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway [13,40] . Consistent with these published findings, our western blot data in Kelly cells revealed that β-catenin protein levels fluctuated synchronously with glycolytic enzymes HK2, PKM2 and MFAP2 upon USP7 overexpression and SOX9 knockdown (Fig. S4O–P), indirectly supporting that MFAP2 may drive glycolysis via WNT/β-catenin signaling. However, the expression and function of MFAP2 in NB have not been previously characterized. In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that MFAP2 is a key downstream effector molecule of the ALK signaling pathway, and its expression is positively regulated by the ALK-USP7-SOX9 axis. Functional assays revealed that MFAP2 overexpression significantly enhances glycolytic capacity, proliferative activity, and invasive and migratory abilities of NB cells. More importantly, in vivo experiments showed that MFAP2 overexpression partially reverses the anti-tumor effect of lorlatinib, further confirming that MFAP2 serves as a critical mediator of the pro-tumorigenic function of the ALK signaling pathway. The interplay between tumor cell metabolic reprogramming and immune microenvironment remodeling is a current hotspot in cancer research. Studies have shown that lactate produced by tumor cells can act as a signaling molecule to induce the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward the M2 phenotype, thereby promoting immune evasion [41,42] . In the present study, we validated this mechanism in NB: following lorlatinib-mediated inhibition of ALK activity, lactate production in NB cells was reduced, accompanied by downregulated expression of M2 macrophage markers and upregulated expression of M1 markers in tumor tissues. Furthermore, in vitro co-culture experiments confirmed that NB cells with suppressed ALK activity induced macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype. Notably, we further performed lactate rescue co-culture assays to provide direct causal evidence: exogenous lactate supplementation largely reversed lorlatinib-triggered M1 shift and restored M2 polarization, verifying glycolytic lactate as the key metabolite mediating ALK-MFAP2 axis-driven macrophage phenotypic remodeling. These findings suggest that ALK not only promotes NB progression through cell-autonomous mechanisms but also reshapes the immune microenvironment via metabolic reprogramming. From a translational perspective, our results offer insights for improving targeted therapy for ALK-positive high-risk NB. Considering the unsatisfactory sustained efficacy of single-agent lorlatinib in clinics, combinatorial treatment with lorlatinib plus USP7 inhibitors or glycolysis inhibitors may concurrently suppress oncogenic signaling, restrain tumor glycolysis and reverse M2 macrophage-mediated immunosuppression. Such combination strategies are expected to improve therapeutic responses and overcome drug resistance, and warrant further preclinical and clinical investigation. The present study has several limitations. First, only female mice were used for in vivo assays, and sex-based differences in metabolism and immune response remain unexamined, which will be addressed in future work. Second, we have not conducted dedicated functional experiments to dissect how extracellular MFAP2 triggers Wnt/β-catenin-dependent glycolysis, which requires further investigation in future work. Third, Correlative analyses based on the TARGET-NBL dataset provide preliminary clinical evidence, yet survival analysis of the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 signature awaits validation in future cohorts. In summary, this study reveals for the first time a novel mechanism by which ALK promotes glycolysis and M2 macrophage polarization in neuroblastoma through the USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 signaling axis. This finding not only deepens our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying ALK-driven NB progression but also provides a new theoretical basis for targeted therapy of NB. Targeting the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 axis, particularly the combination of ALK inhibitors with glycolysis or USP7 inhibitors, may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for high-risk NB patients. Future studies should further explore the role of this signaling axis in NB resistance and relapse, as well as evaluate its value in clinical prognosis prediction. 5 Conclusion In summary, this study elucidates a previously unrecognized mechanism by which ALK drives NB progression. Mechanistically, ALK signaling stabilizes SOX9 via USP7-mediated deubiquitination, which transcriptionally upregulates MFAP2. Elevated MFAP2 promotes glycolysis in NB cells and induces M2 macrophage polarization, thereby facilitating tumor growth. Pharmacological inhibition of ALK using lorlatinib disrupts this USP7-SOX9-MFAP2 axis, suppresses glycolysis, reverses M2 polarization, and attenuates tumorigenesis. Collectively, these findings identify MFAP2 as a critical downstream effector of ALK signaling and establish the ALK/USP7/SOX9/MFAP2 cascade as a promising therapeutic target for NB. title: Chromosomal instability degrades developmental phenotypes essential for anti-GD2 immunotherapy outcomes in high-risk neuroblastoma
abstract: High-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NBL) is a pediatric malignancy that arises during sympathoadrenal development and expresses the surface disialoganglioside GD2. Monoclonal anti-GD2 immunotherapy is a mainstay of HR-NBL treatment; however, it is associated with severe toxicities. Genomic correlates of outcomes following multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy are limited. We profile 840 tumors and identify actionable ALK gene fusions in HR-NBL. We leverage fetal sympathoadrenal single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize patients with improved post-multimodality outcomes. We demonstrate that patients with improved outcomes have tumors that upregulate noradrenergic and metabolic phenotypes characteristic of mature sympathoblasts—a fetal sympathoadrenal cell population. We show that loss of these developmental phenotypes is mediated by chromosome 11q loss. Targeted analysis of 19 biopsy pairs identifies significant clonal evolution and accumulation of cell-cycle mutations following multimodality treatment. Collectively, we identify chromosomal instability—specifically 11q loss—as key in degrading developmental phenotypes critical for outcomes following multimodality therapy containing anti-GD2 immunotherapy.
