Heidelberglaan 25 Utrecht CS 3584 Germany Background Neuroblastoma is among the most fatal pediatric solid tumors and high-risk patients face poor survival despite intensive treatment. Genomic profiling alone has not translated into effective treatment stratification for all neuroblastoma patients. Drug screening offers a complementary strategy, but conventional preclinical models are constrained by limited establishment success from low-input material and by timelines often incompatible with diagnostic decision-making. Here, we evaluated MicroOrganoSphere™ (MOS™) technology, in which tumor cells are encapsulated in Matrigel droplets generated by microfluidic droplet formation, by a head-to-head comparison with the conventional suspension cultures to improve growth and drug testing in neuroblastoma. Methods MOS™ were established from patient-derived tumoroids, freshly dissociated patient-derived xenograft (PDX) tumors, PDX-derived tumoroids, and a freshly dissociated patient tumor to compare growth and drug responses with suspension. Results Tumor cell growth in MOS™ was comparable or superior to suspension cultures. MOS™ drug screens were performed at a 2.5-fold lower seeding density compared to suspension, whilst maintaining reliable results with consistent drug sensitivity profiles and screen quality to suspension. Promisingly, drug testing in MOS™ was feasible within 9 days of receiving fresh PDX tumor tissue. Conclusion These results demonstrate in a proof-of-concept setting how MOS™ technology could support the establishment and drug screening of neuroblastoma cultures from low-input samples within clinically relevant timelines. MOS™ technology provides a promising functional platform to accelerate preclinical drug testing in neuroblastoma precision medicine. Keywords Precision medicine 3D cancer models Pediatric oncology Neuroblastoma Data Availability Supporting imaging and drug screening data is available upon request. 1 Introduction Neuroblastoma, the most prevalent pediatric extra-cranial solid tumor, poses a therapeutic challenge [1] . Current treatment for high-risk patients includes induction chemotherapy, surgery, high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplantation and radiation therapy followed by consolidation therapy with anti-GD2 antibody treatment and retinoic acid [2] . Despite their rigorous treatment regimen, high risk patients face a 5-year overall survival of 50% [3] . The heterogeneity in clinical response highlights the urgent need for a more effective and targeted approach. Median progression-free survival across high-risk pediatric cancers, including neuroblastoma, has been reported as 116 days [4] with ranges from 1 to 65 months reported for neuroblastoma patients [5] . This emphasizes the limited clinical window for identification of effective therapeutic strategies. Currently, pediatric precision oncology trials use genome sequencing to identify patient-specific targetable driver mutations to guide clinical decisions [4,6] . Such actionable driver genes are detected in 37–94% of patients, and the clinical benefit from matched targeted therapies remains limited for many patients. This can partly be explained as genetic characterization does not fully capture the disease’s complexity, and epigenetic and microenvironmental factors should also be considered [7,8] . As an alternative screening approach that could overcome these limitations, functional drug testing is increasingly considered to guide treatment [8–14] . In vivo patient derived xenograft (PDX) models are representative and have been used extensively to study tumor response [15] . However, they are low-throughput, time-consuming and expensive to develop and maintain, as engraftment and stable expansion require approximately 1–11 months, followed by several weeks to assess drug response [9,16–18] . While 2D cell lines are easy to culture, they fail to mimic the tumor's complex architecture [16] . 3D patient-derived tumoroids, that have been established for neuroblastoma [10,18,19] , offer a more promising middle ground with better scalability and lower costs compared to PDX. They more accurately mimic the architecture and physiological responses of solid tumors compared to 2D models [20] . However, tumoroid establishment has several limitations that hinder its clinical implementation for precision medicine: the required large amount of input material, limited success rate, loss of the tumor microenvironment and extended establishment time, typically requiring 3–12 months, after which drug testing typically lasts 5 days [4,9,10,12–14,16,18,20,21] . This often exceeds patients’ progression-free survival [4] . Patients are treated during these extended establishment periods of PDX and tumoroid models, which may limit the representation of the current state of the patient’s tumor. Additionally, in precision oncology programs, treatment strategies are typically discussed in a Molecular Tumor Board, where molecular profiling results become available after a mean turnaround time of 25.4 days. To allow integrated discussion alongside molecular profiling, preclinical models used to guide treatment decisions should ideally provide drug response predictions within a similar timeframe. To shorten establishment timelines, ex vivo short-term drug screening can be performed on freshly dissociated tumor tissue cultured in suspension. This method has been successfully explored in novel pediatric precision medicine studies [8,9,11,22] , but is limited by the low quantity of available tumor material from minimally invasive procedures used in children, variable viability after dissociation, and the time required to expand sufficient biomass prior to screening. Further optimization is therefore required to improve success rates and reduce the time to screen. MicroOrganoSphere™ (MOS™) technology can be used to overcome the previously mentioned limitations of ex vivo screens. MOS™ are droplets generated by microfluidic droplet formation that encapsulate patient-derived tumor cells in Matrigel. MOS™ are automatically and rapidly generated from minimal patient tissue (i.e. low input samples with limited cell numbers) in a high-throughput fashion [23] . Compared to conventional tumoroids, MOS™ require lower input tissue and can be rapidly used for drug screening for personalized medicine. In colorectal cancer, MOS™ responses to chemotherapeutics correlated with clinical outcome [24,25] and Ding et al . demonstrated that drug sensitivities could be obtained within ∼10 days from small, 18-gauge, biopsies. In addition, MOS™ accurately recapitulate patient samples and their microenvironment [24] , recapitulate the heterogeneity within tumors [25] and facilitate the testing of immuno-oncology therapies [26] . The feasibility of MOS™ in pediatric solid tumors, with a different developmental origin and tumor biology than adult colorectal cancer, and its performance relative to suspension cultures have not yet been evaluated. If using MOS™ technology in neuroblastoma could reduce the number of cells required per well, it would allow testing of a broader array of therapeutic agents, increasing the throughput of drug screening processes with the same biomass input. In this study, we explore the potential of the MOS™ platform as an alternative to previously optimized suspension cultures for neuroblastoma patient-derived models: patient-derived tumoroids, PDX-derived fresh tumor and tumoroid models, and a fresh patient tumor. We directly compare MOS™ and suspension cultures to assess viability, proliferation and drug sensitivity testing of tumoroids and freshly dissociated samples. Our findings demonstrate how MOS™ technology can support short-term culture and functional drug testing, providing a framework for integrating MOS™ into preclinical testing pipelines for neuroblastoma to overcome some of the key limitations of currently available technologies. 2 Methods Detailed experimental procedures, including model generation, culture conditions, imaging settings and data processing pipelines, are provided in the Supplementary Methods . 2.1 Model generation and culture All cultures were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO2 . Tumoroid cultures were passaged twice per week, routinely tested for Mycoplasma and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling. 2.1.1 Patient derived tumoroid cultures In brief, three patient-derived tumoroids with distinct molecular s were selected for outgrowth experiments (Suppl. Table 1 ) and cultured in neuroblastoma organoid medium (NBOM) [10,19] . 2.1.2 PDX-derived fresh and tumoroid cultures Neuroblastoma PDX models were previously established and genetically profiled in the ITCC-P4 consortium [27] . Previously reported comprehensive molecular profiling was used in this study: low coverage whole genome sequencing, whole exome sequencing, DNA methylation profiling and RNA sequencing [22,27] . The dissociation method for the PDX samples and the established PDX tumoroids are previously described [18,22] . In brief, fresh PDX tumors were mechanically dissociated, followed by a two-step enzymatic digestion. Fresh PDX cultures were resuspended and cultured in NBOM, with the exception of NB0026, that was cultured in suspension in TSM for 8 days prior to drug screening. For tumoroid establishment, freshly dissociated cells were cultured until stable growth was observed and human tumor cultures were confirmed by SNP analysis and, subsequently, tumoroids were molecularly profiled [18] . 2.1.3 Patient-derived fresh primary culture A fresh neuroblastoma tumor sample was obtained during surgical resection of a refractory patient through an institutionally approved biobank study at the Princess Máxima Center (PMCLAB2025.660). All procedures were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, with age-appropriate written informed consent from patients and/or parents. Preparation of the tumor pieces was started within 2 h after surgery. The primary tumor sample was dissociated via the Liberase protocol, as described in the Supplementary Methods , and immediately MOS™ were generated, and MOS™ and suspension cultures were plated in NBOM. 2.2 Generation and plating of MicroOrganoSpheres™ MOS™ were generated as previously described [24] . Briefly, dissociated tumor cells from patient-derived tumoroids, PDX and human primary tissue digest were resuspended in ice-cold, growth factor–reduced Matrigel (Corning) at a defined density corresponding to 50 viable tumor cells per MOS™. The cell–Matrigel mixture was kept on ice to prevent premature polymerization. MOS™ were generated using a proprietary droplet-based microfluidic generator, which produces highly uniform Matrigel droplets encapsulating tumor cells. Briefly, the cell–Matrigel suspension was loaded into a temperature-controlled microfluidic system in which pressure-driven flow generates monodisperse droplets in an immiscible oil phase. Generation was performed under cooled conditions to maintain Matrigel in liquid state during droplet formation. Droplet size is defined by the microfluidic geometry and pressure settings, resulting in reproducible MOS™ diameters of 230–250 µm. Following droplet generation, MOS™ were collected and incubated at 37°C for 30 min to allow Matrigel polymerization. After gelation, solidified MOS™ were demulsified by transfer onto a hydrophobic PVDF membrane to separate the oil phase from the aqueous droplets. After 2–3 min, polymerized MOS™ were recovered using pre-warmed NBOM. Recovered MOS™ were counted, centrifuged at 150xg for 5 min and subsequently resuspended at the appropriate density for plating for downstream applications. 2.3 Plating of MOS™ and suspension cultures For MOS™ cultures, MOS™ were dispensed in a 384-well flat bottom plate ( , Perkin Elmer) at a density of 40 MOS™ per well, final cell density: 2000 cells per well in 40 µL. For suspension cultures, 40 µL of single cell suspensions were plated in a flat bottom 384-well tissue culture treated microplate (#3764, Corning). For cell growth experiments ( Fig. 1 ), 2000 cells per well were plated, matching MOS™ conditions. For drug screening ( Fig. 2 ), the suspension cultures were seeded at 5000 cells per well, based on previously optimized conditions for neuroblastoma drug screening [10,18] . 2.4 Microscopy-based cell viability readout and analyses In brief, cell viability was assessed by microscopy using Calcein AM viability dye (Calcein; 0.625 µM; #65–0853–78, ThermoFisher) and Ethidium-Homodimer−2 (EthD; 2.5 µM; #E3599, ThermoFisher). The readout was performed with either ImageXpress® Micro Confocal High-Content Imaging system (IXM, Molecular Devices) or the Thunder Widefield Fluorescence microscope (Thunder, Leica™; Suppl. Table 1 ). Wells without any detected viability ( 0.05). No individual compound showed a significantly different response between MOS™ and suspension cultures. Inclusion of the freshly dissociated PDX sample NB0026 indicated the ability to rapidly screen low biomass samples. This sample was briefly cultured in suspension prior to drug screening, which was performed 9 days after tissue receipt in MOS™ and suspension, with a 2.5-fold lower seeding density in MOS™. These results indicate that, under the conditions tested here, MOS™ enables drug screening with comparable drug responses and screening quality compared to suspension cultures at a 2.5-fold lower seeding density. Next to microscopy-based readouts, we used CellTiter-Glo (CTG) luminescent cell viability assay to determine cell viability and subsequent drug response as this is the conventional readout for suspension cultures [18,22] . CTG was performed as a second readout for MOS™ conditions, on the same wells as the microscopy-based readout, to assess drug screen quality using CTG as a readout of MOS™ cultures. Due to low cell numbers in MOS™, CTG readouts were less reliable compared to a microscopy-based readout. The variability in vehicle-treated control wells was too high in the CTG-based readout (CV = 0.35, compared to CV = 0.09 in the microscopy-based readout) and inter-replicate correlation was poor (r = 0.54, compared to r = 0.83 in the microscopy-based readout; Suppl. Fig. 3D ). These results show that for drug screening in MOS™, the microscopy-based readout is a more reproducible and reliable approach compared to CTG. The microscopy-based workflow was fully automated and required comparable time to CTG-based workflows, enabling high-throughput screening. Taken together, these results show that MOS™ technology, combined with a microscopy-based readout, enables reliable drug screening with drug sensitivities and screen quality consistent with conventional suspension cultures, while using a 2.5-fold lower seeding density. 4 Discussion High-risk neuroblastoma remains associated with poor survival despite intense multimodal treatment, and robust biomarkers for treatment stratification are lacking in a substantial subset of patients [1,3] . Functional approaches such as in vitro drug testing have shown promise in guiding treatment in pediatric cancers [8,9,12,14] , but broader implementation is limited by the large amount of required input material, long turnaround times and low establishment success [10,12–14,16,21,36] . MicroOrganoSphere™ (MOS™) technology allows for rapid automated ex vivo testing, with responses to chemotherapy reflecting clinical outcome [24] . Here, we evaluated the potential of MOS™ as an alternative for conventional suspension cultures in neuroblastoma to enable drug screening from limited cell numbers. By this novel direct comparison, we demonstrate that MOS™ technology supports short-term tumor cell growth at least as well as suspension cultures and that drug screening can be performed using fewer cells while maintaining reproducibility and drug sensitivity profiles compared to suspension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MOS™ technology is suitable for standardized drug screening in the rare and understudied pediatric cancer neuroblastoma. Across multiple patient-derived sources, including patient-derived tumoroids, PDX-derived fresh and tumoroid cultures and one freshly dissociated patient tumor, MOS™ supported short-term outgrowth that was comparable or superior to suspension culture. This data demonstrates that MOS™ can maintain neuroblastoma tumor viability even from low-input samples, consistent with previous work showing successful establishment of MOS™ cultures from small 18-gauge biopsies [24] . Although only a single primary patient sample could be included here, this proof-of-concept study supports feasibility for future expansion to larger patient cohorts. As expected, variability in growth of the models was observed, especially for the PDX-derived and freshly dissociated patient tumor. Such variability in growth rates has been previously described and has been associated with partial failure of model development [18,22] . Drug screening in MOS™ was performed at 2000 cells per well compared with 5000 cells per well in suspension cultures, while maintaining comparable reproducibility and consistent drug response profiles. The suspension condition reflected the established neuroblastoma drug screening conditions using 5000 cells per well and a CTG-based viability assessment [18] , whereas MOS™ screening was optimized for lower-input screening combined with a microscopy-based viability readout. Potentially a microscopy-based readout could also improve the quality of suspension drug screens at lower densities. A lower seeding density allows the same number of compounds to be tested with less material, which is particularly relevant for fresh patient samples where material is often limited. While reproducibility of MOS™ drug screens was comparable to suspension and below the preferred acceptance threshold of 10% [31,37] , well-to-well variability could be further reduced by quantifying cell viability at the level of individual MOS™ rather than at the whole-well level, as applied in this study. Recent work has demonstrated that single-MOS™ analyses are feasible and result in high reproducibility (CV ≤ 2.5; [25] ). MOS™ cultures showed a tendency toward slightly reduced drug sensitivity compared to suspension, which might be due to reduced drug penetration into the tumoroids because of the different 3D structure or the presence of Matrigel. Only for the freshly dissociated PDX sample NB0026 the effect could be due to presence of TME, although the trend in this sample is less obvious. Interestingly, the freshly dissociated patient tumor showed rapid growth in MOS™ compared to suspension, where it even decreased in biomass. By testing more samples in the future, it needs to be investigated whether this large advantage of the MOS™ technology is consistent across neuroblastoma subtypes. In a freshly dissociated PDX sample, MOS™ drug screening could be successfully completed within nine days of tissue receipt. Likewise, a fresh patient tumor expanded biomass in the first three days after MOS™ generation, comparable with patient-derived tumoroids and fresh PDX samples that increased biomass. These proof-of-concept experiments in one fresh patient tumor and one fresh PDX drug screen provide initial evidence that MOS™ can support ex vivo testing of fresh material within a short time frame. This is important, as the long turnaround times that often exceed the median time to progression [4] , have limited the clinical use of patient-derived tumoroids [9,10,12] . Ex vivo drug screening of fresh tumor tissue shortens turnaround times [11,22] , and the reduced cell input required by MOS™ could further improve feasibility of screening low-input samples. We could not compare drug response in MOS™ with patient response, as this data was not available for these samples. However, previous studies have shown that MOS™ responses correlated with clinical outcome [24,25] , and that drug sensitivities could be obtained within ∼10 days of sample receipt in adult cancers. Although future studies should expand this work, as larger pediatric cohorts will be essential to validate clinical applicability and to correlate drug response with patient outcomes, these findings suggest that MOS™ is suited for drug screening within a clinically relevant time frame, especially for low-input material. Next to MOS™, many complementary 3D ex vivo modelling approaches are being developed to improve the physiological relevance of in vitro drug testing [38] . Whole-tissue platforms such as ALTEN preserve intact tumor tissue architecture and multicellular niches by encapsulating primary tissue fragments in alginate hydrogels [39] . These approaches are well suited for studying the native tissue niche and interactions with the tumor micro-environment (TME) but are generally less scalable and allow testing of fewer compounds. In contrast to whole-tissue platforms, patient-derived tumoroids provide high scalability and long-term expansion, making them suitable for compound discovery and biomarker research. However, patient-derived tumoroids require longer establishment times. MOS™, in contrast, is optimized for the rapid generation and short-term expansion of tumor cells from freshly dissociated low-input samples, enabling reproducible and scalable drug sensitivity testing within clinically relevant timelines which is especially useful for guiding clinical decision-making. Successful MOS™ generation depends on the quality and viability of the starting material after mechanical and enzymatic dissociation, which may vary between samples. In addition, MOS™ cultures rely on Matrigel, which introduces an extracellular matrix environment that must be tolerated by tumor cells. In our study, using MOS™ allowed parallel testing up to 90 compounds while maintaining 3D growth conditions. As such, MOS™ is particularly suited for precision medicine applications, where speed is crucial. This study did not investigate tumor TME retention, although previous work has shown that MOS™ can preserve stromal components [24] . Exploring if neuroblastoma MOS™ retain elements of the TME will be an important next step for assessing compound activity in a more patient representative setting. In patient samples where other cell types are present, tumor-specific markers, such as NCAM, B7H3 and L1CAM, could be used to distinguish tumor from non-tumor responses. In addition, MOS™ have been shown to support efficient CAR-T cell infiltration and killing, indicating their potential for immunotherapy testing [26] . In addition, culture conditions such as hypoxia have been proposed to better recapitulate aspects of the neuroblastoma tumor niche [40,41] . While hypoxia was not investigated in the present study, MOS™ cultures can be maintained under controlled oxygen conditions after generation. Finally, it should be noted that ex vivo drug screening does not capture in vivo pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic processes. Factors such as plasma protein binding, drug lipophilicity and tissue distribution can influence effective drug exposure at the tumor site and should be considered when translating ex vivo drug sensitivity results to clinical applications [42–44] . Future studies of neuroblastoma MOS™ screening could include evaluation of TME preservation, testing of immunotherapies, hypoxia culture, and better representing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic processes. 5 Conclusion This proof-of-concept demonstrates that MOS™ technology supports the ex vivo growth and drug screening of neuroblastoma cells, including low-input samples, within clinically relevant time frames. Future studies should focus on expanding pediatric patient cohorts, assessing clinical applicability and comparing drug response to clinical outcome, to validate MOS™ as a functional precision medicine platform for preclinical drug testing. title: mRNA vaccination using peptide nanoparticles triggers a strong immune response against endogenous GPC2 in a murine neuroblastoma model
abstract: Neuroblastoma is an aggressive pediatric solid tumor that arises during embryonic development and contributes to 15% of cancer-related deaths in children. To date, neither experimental nor clinical trial data on an mRNA vaccine for neuroblastoma have been published, highlighting a significant gap in the anticancer vaccine development pipeline. This study presents the first mRNA vaccine for the treatment of neuroblastoma. We explored the self-assembling peptide RALA for delivering mRNA encoding glypican 2 (GPC2), a potent tumor-associated antigen in neuroblastoma. These data outline rigorous in vitro characterization of vaccine nanoparticle formulations, cellular uptake, and functionality. Immunization of mice with RALA/mGPC2 generated an antigen-specific cellular immune response against GPC2, with significant increases in IFN-γ and IL-2 expression by splenocytes and TNF-α expression by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Immunization delayed tumor development by 10–11 days and reduced tumor volume by 70% compared with unvaccinated controls in a subcutaneous murine model of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma. This work demonstrates the therapeutic potential of the RALA/mGPC2 vaccine for treating neuroblastoma. Additionally, GPC2 is upregulated across multiple adult and pediatric cancer subtypes, establishing this vaccine as an attractive immunotherapy with far-reaching potential.

Design and synthesis of the DNA and mRNA The Human GPC2 (Clone i.d.: ) cDNA construct was purchased from Horizon Discovery Ltd (#MHS6278- ). The full GPC2 protein-coding region was subcloned from the original vector into pcDNA3.1(−) plasmid (InvitrogenTM #V79520) using HindIII (NEB #R0104) and EcoRI (NEB #R0101). DNA sequence was verified using Eurofins Genomics TubeSeq Sanger sequencing and aligned to Human GPC2 NCBI gene sequence (Gene ID: ) using the BLAST alignment tool. Custom GPC2 codon-optimized mRNA was ordered from TebuBio covering the full protein-coding region. The modified mRNA transcript was ordered with full substitution of N1-methyl-Pseudo-U, capped (Cap 1) using CleanCap AG, polyadenylated with 120A, DNase I-treated, and silica membrane-purified. NPs formulation pGPC2/mGPC2 was encapsulated with RALA at various N:P ratios. The N:P ratio was calculated based on peptide and nucleic acid mass, considering RALA’s positive amino acid content. For an N:P ratio of 1, 1 μg of pDNA required 1.46 μg of RALA, and 1 μg of mRNA required 1.40 μg of RALA, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The plasmid or mRNA was diluted to 0.1 μg/μL using UltraPure DNase/RNase-free distilled water (Invitrogen, # ), mixed gently, and combined with RALA (1 μg/μL). After 30 min of incubation at room temperature, NPs formed spontaneously and were immediately used for downstream applications. Lyophilization of RALA/mRNA NPs RALA/pGPC2 and RALA/mGPC2 NPs were prepared as previously described.23 Freshly prepared 24% w/v trehalose (Pfanstiehl, USA) in UltraPure DNase/RNase-free water (Invitrogen) was added to NPs to achieve a final concentration of 12%. The NPs were transferred to 2 mL glass vials, loosely capped, and lyophilized using an SP Scientific AdVantage Pro freeze dryer according to the recipe outlined in Table 1 . NP characterization NP size, zeta potential, and PDI were measured using a Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern Instruments, UK). Freshly prepared NPs or lyophilized NPs resuspended in UltraPure DNase/RNase-free water were incubated at room temperature for 30 min before analysis. Hydrodynamic size and PDI were measured at 20°C in a microcuvette (Malvern, UK), while zeta potential was determined in a folded capillary zeta cell via Laser Doppler Velocimetry. NP morphology and size were further characterized by TEM. RALA-encapsulated NPs (0.1 μg/μL) were deposited onto carbon-coated copper grids (TAAB Laboratories, UK) and dried for 24 h. Grids were stained with Uranyless EM stain (EMS, USA) and imaged with a JEOL JEM-1000 TEM at 80 kV. Encapsulation efficiency and free nucleic acid analysis Encapsulation efficiency was assessed using ion-exchange chromatography, gel shift assay, and Pico-/RiboGreen fluorescence assays. Ion-exchange chromatography Free nucleic acid content was quantified using SP-Sephadex resin (Sigma-Aldrich, GER) hydrated in 1M NaCl and washed with UltraPure DNase/RNase-free water (Invitrogen, # ). Nucleic acid or RALA-encapsulated NPs (20 μL; ≥20 mg/mL) were loaded into a packed frit column, eluted with UltraPure water, and analyzed via UV-Vis spectroscopy. Gel shift assay Visual assessment of encapsulation efficiency was performed by loading NPs (0.01 μg/μL) mixed with 10X Blue Juice loading buffer (Invitrogen, # ) onto a 1% SYBR Safe-stained agarose gel (Invitrogen, #S33102). Electrophoresis was conducted at 100 V for 1 h, and the gel was imaged using an Amersham Imager 600. Pico-/RiboGreen assay Quantitative fluorescence-based encapsulation efficiency was evaluated using PicoGreen or RiboGreen reagents (Invitrogen, #P11495/#R11491). NPs (0.01 μg/μL) were plated in triplicate in a black 96-well plate with 50 μL of dye solution prepared per the manufacturer’s instructions. After 5 min of dark incubation at room temperature, fluorescence was measured (excitation ∼480 nm, emission ∼520 nm) using a Victor3 plate reader. Encapsulation efficiency was calculated by normalizing fluorescence values to free nucleic acid controls. Cell transfection HEK293 and DC2.4 cells were seeded in 6-well plates with complete growth media. The next day, the media was replaced with Opti-MEM™ Reduced Serum Medium (Gibco, # –070), and cells were incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 2 h. NPs, freshly prepared or reconstituted from lyophilized stock, were added at 4 μg per well in 200 μL. Plates were gently rotated for even NP distribution and incubated for 5 h at 37°C with 5% CO2 . The media was then replaced with complete growth media, and the cells were incubated until the desired endpoint was reached. Cell viability assessment Cell viability was determined using the Cell Titer-Glo 3D assay (Invitrogen, UK). The reagent was thawed overnight at 4°C and then equilibrated to room temperature by placing the bottle in a 22°C water bath for approximately 30 min. Following equilibration, 100 μL of the Cell Titer-Glo 3D reagent was added to each well, and the contents were mixed thoroughly by shaking for 5 min to promote cell lysis or were left to rock for 25 min. Afterward, the plate was incubated at room temperature for an additional 25 min to stabilize the luminescent signal. Subsequently, 100 μL from each well was transferred to an opaque-walled (black) plate. Luminescence was measured using the Victor3 V Plate Reader (PerkinElmer, #1420), and the average luminescence for each condition was calculated using Microsoft Excel. Data were visualized using GraphPad Prism 10. Protein isolation & western blot Total protein was isolated from transfected cells by washing with pre-warmed PBS. Cells were lyzed with RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, # ) containing Halt protease inhibitor cocktail (100X ) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, # ) on ice for 30 min. The lysates were centrifuged at 13,200 rpm for 30 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were carefully collected. Subcellular fractionation of transfected cells in 6-well plates was performed using the Subcellular Protein Fractionation Kit for Cultured Cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific, # ) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, buffers were thawed in a water bath at room temperature and kept on ice until needed. To initiate fractionation, 200 μL of ice-cold cytoplasmic extraction buffer (CEB) was added to each well, and the plates were incubated on ice for 10 min with gentle mixing. The resulting lysates were collected into 1.5 mL tubes and centrifuged at 500 × g for 5 min at 4°C. The supernatant, which contained the cytoplasmic fraction, was transferred to pre-chilled tubes. Next, 200 μL of ice-cold membrane extraction buffer (MEB) was added to the cell pellets, followed by vortexing at high speed for 5 s and incubation at 4°C for 10 min with gentle mixing. The samples were centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 5 min at 4°C, and the supernatant, representing the membrane fraction, was transferred to pre-chilled tubes. For nuclear fractionation, 100 μL of ice-cold nuclear extraction buffer (NEB) was added to the remaining cell pellet, vortexed for 15 s at maximum speed, and incubated at 4°C for 30 min with gentle mixing. The samples were then centrifuged at 5,000 × g for 5 min at 4°C, and the supernatant (soluble nuclear fraction) was collected. The remaining pellet was treated with 100 μL of room temperature NEB+ buffer, vortexed for 15 s at high speed, and incubated at room temperature for 15 min with gentle vortexing. After a final centrifugation at 16,000 × g for 5 min, the supernatant, containing the chromatin-bound nuclear extract, was collected. The two nuclear fractions were then combined. To isolate the cytoskeleton fraction, 100 μL of room temperature protein extraction buffer (PEB) was added to the remaining cell pellet, vortexed at high speed for 15 s, and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. The samples were centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 5 min, and the supernatant (cytoskeleton fraction) was transferred to a fresh tube. Finally, the cytoplasmic and cytoskeleton fractions were combined, and all fractions were stored at −20°C until further protein analysis. Protein concentrations were quantified using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, # ) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Samples were diluted in 4X Bol LDS sample buffer (Invitrogen, #B0007) with the appropriate amount of 10X Bolt™ Sample Reducing Agent (Invitrogen, #B0009) and denatured at 95°C for 5 min. Equal protein amounts (10 μg) were loaded onto Bolt 4%–12% bis-tris plus gels (Invitrogen, #NW04120, #NW04122, #NW04125), and SDS-PAGE was performed at 190 volts for 45 min. Proteins were transferred to nitrocellulose or PVDF membranes at 20 volts for 1 h. The transfer was confirmed by Ponceau S staining (Merck, #6226-79-5), and membranes were blocked with 5% BSA in TBS-T. Their incubations were performed overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Cell Signaling Technology) at room temperature. Animals and& ethics 8-week-old C57BL/6 female mice (Charles River Laboratories, UK) were used for all in vivo studies. The in vivo experiments were undertaken at Queen’s University Belfast’s Biological Services Unit, located in the Medical Biology Center (MBC) building. All experimental protocols complied with the Animal (Scientific Procedures) Act of 1986 and were carried out under project license PPL 2903. In vivo immune response study Immunocompetent female C57BL/6 mice were administered a 3-dose vaccine regimen (20 μg) via intravenous injection on days 0, 7, and 11 followed by a 21-days incubation period. On day 32, mice were euthanized via Schedule 1. Cardiac bleeds were taken, and spleens were harvested and processed for subsequent analyses. Due to the novelty of RALA/mGPC2 , two positive control vaccination groups were included in this study. Mice were vaccinated with recombinant GPC2 (R&D Systems Catalog #: 2304-GP) or a previously verified mRNA vaccine from the McCarthy group. Animals were randomly assigned into 4 groups: naive (n = 5), positive control mRNA vaccine (n = 5), recombinant GPC2 (n = 5), and RALA/mGPC2 (n = 6). Splenocyte isolation At the study endpoint, spleens were processed into single-cell suspensions and seeded with the corresponding media master mixes: unstimulated media only, Con A + LPS positive stimulation, and GPC2 overlapping peptides. For intracellular cytokine staining, Brefeldin A 1000X (Invitrogen, UK) was diluted 1:5 and 10 μL was added to each well and mixed. Plates were incubated for 6 h in an incubator at 37°C, 5% CO2 . The cells were then collected in an Eppendorf tube and centrifuged at 350 g for 5 min at 4°C to pellet cells. Each cell pellet was resuspended in 100 μL of viability stain, then 50 μL of Fc block, and finally 50 μL of an extracellular antibody cocktail (CD4, CD8), incubated on ice for 30 min. After the incubation period, 1 mL of PBS media (PBS +5% FBS +2 mM EDTA) was added, and the mixture was centrifuged at 350 g for 5 min at 4°C. 100 μL of IC Fixation buffer (Life Technologies, UK) was added to each well, and the plate was incubated overnight at 4°C in the dark. The following day, 50 μL of intracellular antibody cocktail (IFN-γ, IL-2, and TNF-α) was added to the samples and incubated at room temperature for 30 min 1 mL of 1X permeabilization buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, UK) was added to each well, and the samples were centrifuged at 550 g for 5 min at room temperature. Samples were resuspended in 500 μL FACS staining buffer (Invitrogen, UK) and analyzed on Attune NxT flow cytometer (Figures S9 A and S9B). ELISpot analysis ELISpot plates for IFN-γ and IL-2 were prepared as per the manufacturer’s instructions. 100 μL of splenocyte cell suspension was added to each well, along with 100 μL of the respective 2X master mix, and incubated for 48 h in a humidified incubator at 37°C, 5% CO2 . Post-stimulation ELISpot plates were washed according to the manufacturer’s protocol, ensuring the membrane was not touched. Detection antibody (5H4-biotin, provided with the Mabtech kit) was diluted to 1 μg/mL in PBS-0.5% FCS and added at 100 μL/well. Secondary streptavidin-ALP antibodies were diluted (1:1,000) in PBS-0.5% FCS, and 100 μL was added to each well. 100 μL/well of the substrate solution was added to each well and incubated, followed by washing with H2 O. The underdrain tray was removed, and the plates were dried for a minimum of 24 h and analyzed using the Mabtech IRIS ELISpot plate reader (Mabtech Inc., US). The data of technical triplicates were averaged and normalized to unstimulated controls. These values were then plotted as a single data point on each graph. Negative values are set to zero, and outliers have been removed via ROUT analysis (Q = 5%, N ≥ 3 per group). Tumor growth kinetics study The growth kinetics of 9464D mouse neuroblastoma cells in mice were analyzed. Tumors were implanted subcutaneously in immune-competent C57BL/6 mice, under isoflurane anesthesia, in the right flank (total volume of 100 μL PBS cell suspension). Tumor mouse weight, and the general health of the mice were monitored three times weekly. Mice were sacrificed using a schedule 1 method when the tumor volume reached 12 GMD (geometric mean diameter). In vivo tumor regression study On day 0, mice were weighed and implanted subcutaneously with 5 × 10ˆ6 9464D cells in 100 μL PBS under anesthesia (isoflurane, <5%). Animals were randomly assigned to 2 groups: control (unvaccinated; n = 6) and RALA/mGPC2 (n = 8). Mice were then immunized with NPs (20 μg) intravenously (100 μL lateral tail vein) in a 3-dose regimen on days 11, 15, and 18 with RALA/mGPC2 NPs. Tumor mouse weight, and general health were monitored three times weekly. Mice were sacrificed when tumor volume reached a maximum of 12 GMD via schedule 1 methods. Serum toxicity biomarker analysis Circulating biomarkers that might indicate toxicity in the heart, liver, kidney, muscles, bone, and brain were assessed in the sera from vaccinated C57BL/6 mice. The following assays were utilized: creatinine kinase (Abcam UK, cat. no. ab155901), creatinine (Assay Genie, cat. no. MOEB2563), lactate dehydrogenase (Assay Genie, cat. no. MOES00965), and alkaline phosphatase (Assay Genie, cat. no. MOFI00633). All assays were performed following the manufacturer’s instructions. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software, USA). To compare (1) the means of two groups, an unpaired two-tailed t test with the Mann-Whitney correction, and (2) the means of multiple groups, an ordinary one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons of mean test were performed, with a p value output indicating statistical significance. These tests were performed on all data that showed statistical significance, as highlighted, unless otherwise noted in the figure legends. For all data analyses, statistical significance was reported as p ≤ 0.05, ∗p ≤ 0.05, ∗∗p ≤ 0.01, ∗∗∗p ≤ 0.001, and ∗∗∗∗p ≤ 0.0001. title: The presence of Y674/Y675 phosphorylated NTRK1 via TP53 repression of PTPN6 expression as a potential prognostic marker in neuroblastoma
abstract: The tumor suppressor TP53 promotes nerve growth factor receptor (NTRK1) -Y674/Y675 phosphorylation (NTRK1-pY674/pY675) via repression of the NTRK1 phosphatase PTPN6 in a ligand-independent manner, resulting in suppression of breast cancer cell proliferation. Moreover, NTRK1-pY674/pY675 together with low levels of PTPN6 and TP53 expression is associated with favorable disease-free survival of breast cancer patients. We determined whether in neuroblastoma this protein expression pattern impacts relapse-free survival (RFS). NTRK1-pY674/pY675, PTPN6, and TP53 expression was assessed in 98 neuroblastoma samples by immunohistochemistry. Association between expression levels and RFS was investigated by multivariate and Kaplan-Meier analysis. Mutant or wild-type TP53 was identified by sequencing tumor DNA. Tumors expressing NTRK1-pY674/pY675 and low or undetectable levels of PTPN6 and TP53 were significantly associated with 5-year RFS (P = .014) when the dataset was stratified by MYCN amplification, segmental chromosomal abnormalities and histology. Similar results were observed with tumors expressing wild-type TP53, NTRK1-pY674/pY675 and low or undetectable levels of PTPN6. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated a significant correlation (P = .004), with a 50% probability of RFS (median survival 4.73 years) when present compared with 19.51% (median survival 11.63 months) when absent. Similar results were seen with non-amplified MYCN or unfavorable/undifferentiating samples and tumors from patients aged 18 months or less. Importantly, NTRK1-pY674/pY675 is an independent predictor of improved RFS. These results strongly suggest that NTRK1-pY674/pY675 together with wild-type TP53 and undetectable or low levels of PTPN6 expression is a potential biomarker of improved RFS of neuroblastoma patients. The predictive value of NTRK1-pY674/pY675 together with wild-type TP53 and low PTPN6 expression could contribute to neuroblastoma patient prognosis.
