title: Novel anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5- a ]pyrimidine conjugates modulate the expression of p53-MYCN associated micro RNAs in neuroblastoma cells and cause cell cycle arrest and apoptosis
abstract: It has previously been shown that anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine conjugates activate p53 and cause apoptosis in cervical cancer cells such as HeLa and SiHa. Here we establish the role of these conjugates in activating p53 pathway by phosphorylation at Ser15, 20 and 46 residues and downregulate key oncogenic proteins such as MYCN and Mdm2 in IMR-32 neuroblastoma cells. Compounds decreased the proliferation rate of neuroblastoma cells such as IMR-32, Neuro-2a, SK-N-SH. Compound treatment resulted in G2/M cell cycle arrest. The expression of p53 dependent genes such as p21, Bax, caspases was increased with concomitant decrease of the survival proteins as well as anti-apoptotic proteins such as Akt1, E2F1 and Bcl2. In addition the expression of important microRNAs such as miR-34a, c, miR-200b, miR-107, miR-542-5p and miR-605 were significantly increased that eventually lead to the activation of apoptotic pathway. Our data revealed that conjugates of this nature cause cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in IMR-32 cells [MYCN (+) with intact wild-type p53] by activating p53 signalling and provides a lead for the development of anti-cancer therapeutics.

Graphical abstract Compounds activate p53 dependent tumor suppressor pathway. In this study anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidine conjugates activates tumor suppressors (p53, p21) and down regulation of oncogenic activity (Mdm2, MYCN) that lead to cell death in IMR-32 cells. In neuronal cancers p53 is tightly regulated by oncogenes such as Mdm2 and MYCN. P53 transcriptionally regulate genes such as p21, Bax, miR-34a and miR-605 and control the cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. It has previously been shown that anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidine conjugates activate p53 and cause apoptosis in cervical cancer cells such as HeLa and SiHa. Here we establish the role of these conjugates in activating p53 pathway by phosphorylation at Ser15, 20 and 46 residues and downregulate key oncogenic proteins such as MYCN and Mdm2 in IMR-32 neuroblastoma cells. Compounds decreased the proliferation rate of neuroblastoma cells such as IMR-32, Neuro-2a, SK-N-SH. Compound treatment resulted in G2/M cell cycle arrest. The expression of p53 dependent genes such as p21, Bax, caspases was increased with concomitant decrease of the survival proteins as well as anti-apoptotic proteins such as Akt1, E2F1 and Bcl2. In addition the expression of important microRNAs such as miR-34a, c, miR-200b, miR-107, miR-542-5p and miR-605 were significantly increased that eventually lead to the activation of apoptotic pathway. Our data revealed that conjugates of this nature cause cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in IMR-32 cells [MYCN (+) with intact wild-type p53] by activating p53 signalling and provides a lead for the development of anti-cancer therapeutics. Abbreviations MYCN N-MYC MTT 3-(4,5-dimethyl thiazol-2-yl)-2,5 diphenyl tetrazolium bromide RT-PCR reverse transcription PCR miRNA microRNA Keywords p53 miR-34 IMR-32 cells Neuroblastoma Apoptosis Neuroblastoma is one of the most common extra-cranial solid tumor of childhood and accounts for 8–10% of all paediatric cancers and 15% of childhood cancer mortality.1 Despite significant advances, it still remains one of the most difficult cancers to cure. Thus there lies an urgent need for identification of novel therapies along with a better understanding of the molecular basis of neuroblastoma. Researchers have identified the role of MYCN, a proto-oncogene in the development of neuroblastoma that encodes a nuclear phosphoprotein member of the c-myc family of helix–loop–helix transcription factors.2,3 Amplification of MYCN is the most powerful prognostic factor in the children affected with the disease. Thereby, tumors having MYCN amplification are refractory to any therapy. Recent studies have indicated that MDM2, a primary inhibitor of p53 tumor suppressor as a direct transcriptional target of MYCN by which MYCN amplified neuroblastomas (MNA) acquire an aggressive phenotype through inactivation of p53-dependent apoptotic pathway.4–6 In this context MYCN, MDM2 and p53 proteins were considered as regulatory factors that balance the cell proliferation and apoptotic events in neuroblastoma. Programmed cell death or apoptosis is an important process under normal physiological condition characterised by distinct morphological characters; which, when deregulated, can lead to cancer. P53 is the guardian of the genome that maintains cellular genomic stability and cell growth on oncogenic challenges by inducing cell cycle arrest, apoptosis or senescence. Understanding the mechanism underlying p53’s ability to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis is critical to treat human gliomas. It is known that N-terminal phosphorylation of p53 particularly at ser15 and 20 cause increased p53 stability and its responsive gene expression that results in apoptosis.7,8 MicroRNAs are a family of small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression both in plants and animals and play important regulatory roles in their normal development and physiology.9,10 MicroRNAs play key role in diverse biological proceses including development, cell proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis. An increasing number of studies have demonstrated perturbation of the normal expression pattern of microRNAs in many human cancers.11 Our recent study have clearly indicated that anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidine conjugates activate p53 in cervical cancer cells and cause apoptosis.12 Although the effects of these conjugates on anti-proliferative and apoptotic activity has been documented in various cancer cells, its therapeutic efficacy and mechanism involved in neuroblastoma is still largely unknown.12 In the present study we identified two anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidine compounds (C-2 and C-8) that activate p53 and down regulate the expression of MYCN and Mdm2 by modulating the expression of microRNAs that have tumor suppressor activity such as miR-34 family, miR-605 etc.13–15 We have also shown its activity in vivo model system Drosophila . Drosophila is considered as an excellent model system for screening of small molecules in anti-cancer therapy. In recent years Drosophila larval brain neuroblast has emerged as a novel model for the study of stem cell self-renewal and tumorigenesis. In addition there exist an evolutionarily conserved molecular mechanism in insects and vertebrates in the process of neurogenesis.16,17 Several studies in Drosophila have clearly indicated that asymmetric division can lead to the formation of tumours. In addition under expression of tumor suppressor genes such as Prospero, Miranda, Numb, Partner of Inscuteable (Pins), Brat and Lethal giant larvae result in massive overgrowth and tumorigenesis further supporting the link between asymmetric cell division and tumor formation.18–20 To understand the potential cytotoxic effect of anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidine conjugates on cancerous cells, cell lines such as IMR-32, SK-N-SH, Neuro-2a (Neuroblastoma), MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 (Breast cancer), A549 (Lung cancer), K562 (Leukemia) were used for MTT assay with Roscovitine as positive control. All compounds of this series (Fig. 1 A and B, Fig. S1, Table S1 ) have shown cytotoxicity in all the cell lines tested. Interestingly neuronal cancer cell lines such as IMR-32, SK-N-SH have shown significant cytotoxicity in comparison to other cell lines analysed. The IC50 values derived from this study are 0.9–1.8 μM (IMR-32), 2–4 μM (SK-N-SH), 3.78–7.7 μM (Neuro-2a), 4–8 μM (MDA-MB-231& MCF-7), 3–6 μM (K562), 5–10 μM (A549) (Table S2). Interestingly in HEK normal non-cancerous cells compounds cause negligible cytotoxicity even at very high concentrations (i.e., 16 μM). The IC50 of these conjugates deduced from MTT assay are 28, 28.2 and 26.66 μM for Roscovitine, C-2 and C-8, respectively (Fig. S2 ). Among the series of compounds tested we observed only compounds C-2 (Tri-methoxy at R1, R2, R3 positions with 2-furfuryl at R′) and C-8 (Tri-methoxy at R1, R2, R3 positions with 3-piperanyl at R′) have shown profound cytotoxicity. This data reveals that trimethoxy group substitution in combination with 2-furfuryl or 3-pipernyl moieties is crucial in causing cytotoxicity in neuronal cancer cells.12 Hence the mechanism of action of these compounds was further investigated. Cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage is an important anti-tumorigenic mechanism.21 It is well known that the progression of cell cycle halts during DNA damage to allow for the repair of damaged DNA and thus preserves the genomic integrity. Multiple pathways lead to cell cycle arrest. Interestingly p53 activation was found to cause both G1 and G2/M arrest.22 Thus we focused our attention on regulation of these conjugates on cell cycle progression. Flowcytometric analysis was conducted using compounds C-2 and C-8 at 0.5 and 1 μM concentrations in IMR-32 (MNA and wt-p53) cell line. At lower concentration (0.5 μM), both C-2 & C-8 conjugates have shown lesser number of apoptotic cells while increase in concentration (1 μM) led to increased apoptosis (19% & 18%) with a clear G2/M cell cycle arrest (42% & 56%, respectively). Further study was conducted for an extended period of 72 h to see the changes in cell cycle. Interestingly we have noticed an increased apoptotic percentage at both the concentrations tested23 (Fig. S3 ). G2/M cell cycle arrest was observed with these conjugates at higher concentration (i.e., 8 μM) in all other cell lines studied (MDA-MB-231, MCF-7, K562 and A549) (Fig. 1 C & Fig. S4 ). A similar observation was seen in cells treated with p53 activator drugs such as Nutlin-3 and MI-63 drugs with G1 cell cycle arrest in MYCN (+), MYCN (−) cells at low concentration (2.5 μM) and G2/M cell cycle arrest at high concentration (10 μM).24–27 Therefore our data clearly showed that these molecules were highly effective in causing cell cycle arrest in MYCN positive neuroblastoma cells (IMR-32) even at lower concentration (1 μM).28 Tumor suppressor p53 is a transcription factor that has the ability to respond to stress and maintain cellular control by deregulating stress response and thereby maintaining cell and tissue integrity.23,29 In addition response to stress, p53 is activated through post translational modifications such as phosphorylation, acetylation etc.30 Phosphorylation varies between cell types and previous studies have indicated that p53 can be phosphorylated on multiple serine/threonine residues at both N and C terminal ends. In particular N-terminal phosphorylation (i.e., Ser15, Ser 20 and Ser 46) of p53 leads to activation of the p53 responsive genes such as Bax and p21 that results in apoptotic event.8,31,32 Thus we were interested to examine the level of p53 and its phosphorylated forms in conjugate treated IMR-32 cells. Here IMR-32 cells were treated with Roscovitine, C-2 and C-8 at 1 μM concentration for 24 h and the lysates were subjected to western blot analysis. We observed an increase in the level of p53 in conjugate treated cells. Surprisingly conjugate treated cells have exhibited pronounced increase in phosphorylation at p53 ser 15 (ninefolds) than others [ p53 ser 20 (twofolds) and p53 ser 46 (twofolds)], thus revealing p53 activating nature of these molecules. Similarly treatment of prostate cancer (PC-3) cells with EGCG cause an increase in p53 ser15 phosphorylation that results in increase the transcriptional activity as well as protein expression of p53 by disrupting the interaction between p53 and its antagonist Mdm233 (Fig. 2 A). It was known that p53 responsive protein coding genes such as p21 and Bax are induced as function of DNA damage induced post translational modifications such as p53 ser 15, 20 and 46.34 Thus we were interested to examine the level of p53 dependent genes such as p21 and bax in conjugate treated (C-2 & C-8) IMR-32 cells (1 μM for 24 h). Western blot analysis has shown an increase in expression level of p21 and Bax by 3 and twofolds, respectively, in compound treated IMR-32cells when compared to untreated control cells, thus revealing the specificity of action of these compounds on p53 (Fig. 2 B). Similar to these conjugates a set of drugs such as Tenovin, Leptomycin B, nutlin-3a, Actinomycin-D were also found to cause increase in p53 protein level as well as its target gene (p21 and Bax) expression by up regulating the transcriptional activity of p53.35,36 Recent studies on animal models have clearly indicated that p53 phosphorylation at ser15 has a profound impact on tumor suppression.37 Nuclear accumulation of p53 was accompanied by phosphorylation of N-terminus at ser15 and disruption of interaction between p53 and Mdm2.38–40 P53, the master tumor suppressor protein exerts many of its effects by transcriptional regulation41 and its translocation from cytoplasmic site of synthesis to nuclear target genes is critical to elicit biological response.42 More over it was interesting to observe that P53 is cytosolic in Neuroblastoma and is non-functional.43 Thus we were interested to examine p53 localization by treating IMR-32 cells with compounds Ros, C-2, C-8 by indirect immunofluorescence experiment. Here Roscovitine32 was used as positive control. As expected, in untreated cells we observed that most of the p53 protein was cytoplasmic where as in treated cells nuclear accumulation of p53 protein was increased (Fig. 2 D). To further confirm the increased nuclear p53 accumulation in conjugate treated cells Western blot analysis was conducted using nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions. We observed an increase in nuclear p53 protein level with concomitant decrease in cytoplasmic p53 in IMR-32 cells treated with Ros, C-2 and C-8 rather than control untreated cells (Fig. 2 E). Thus our data revealed that compounds caused nuclear accumulation leading to activation of p53. Similar to these conjugates, drugs such as Leptomycin B and Adriamycin stabilise p53 protein by phosphorylating p53 leading to retention of the protein in the nucleus.44 To further confirm the active role of p53 in causing cytotoxicity and apoptosis we have knocked down endogenous p53 gene by transfecting IMR-32 cells with p53 gene specific siRNA for 24 h followed by conjugate treatment at 1 μM for 24 h in three neuronal cancer cells lines such as IMR-32, SK-N-SH and NGP that have endogenous wild-type p53 (Fig. S5 ). Our results indicated that knock down of p53 resulted in drastic decrease in induction of cytotoxicity by these conjugates (Ros, C-2 and C-8). Thus the crucial role of p53 in cytoxicity is highly elucidated. In neuroblastomas MYCN and MDM2 are mutually regulated and reciprocally control p53 to inhibit apoptosis.4,6,45 In addition, MYCN also inhibits p53 through direct up-regulation of MDM2 that encodes for ubiquitin ligase and degrade p53 by proteasomal mediated degradation.46 Earlier reports have shown that Nutlin-3a, RITA, MI-63, MI-219 cells have shown disruption of the interaction between p53 and Mdm2 upon treatment of compounds4,6,47–49 and can activate p53 leading to tumor suppression. We were therefore interested in finding the expression level of oncogenes such as MYCN and MDM2 in the case of C2 and C8 compound treated cells. Western blot analysis using anti MYCN and anti MDM2 antibodies, revealed drastic down regulation of Mdm2 and MYCN protein expression (two and threefolds, respectively) when compared to untreated controls (Fig. 3 A) showing a possibility that the compounds act by disturbing the interaction between MDM2 and p53. To further confirm the specificity of the compounds towards MYCN positive rather than MYCN negative cancerous cells, we treated MYCN negative SK-N-SH cells with compounds Ros, C-2 and C-8. Surprisingly we noticed only moderate activation of p53 (1.5-folds) in MYCN negative SK-N-SH cells than MYCN positive IMR-32 cells (2.5-folds) (Fig. 2 C) indicating that oncogenic presence might dictates tumor suppressor function. MicroRNAs are important components of p53 transcriptional network that determine the biological response.13 Tumor suppressor p53 is a transcription factor that induces or represses a large set of genes and microRNAs.13,32–36 Thus it is worth identifying and understanding the microRNAs that are regulated through known tumor suppressor pathway. MicroRNA-34a is a p53 regulated microRNA and appears as a p53 target gene and direct transcriptional activity of p53 target genes such as p21 and Bax.50,51 In addition, miR-605 is a new entry in the p53 gene network, being transcriptionally activated by p53 and post-transcriptionally repressing Mdm2 by binding to 3′-UTR (2329-5677nt) at 12 different potential sites.14 Interestingly, P53 binds to promoters of miR-34a, miR-605, p21 and Bax and regulate their gene expression. Computational analysis predicted that three microRNAs (miR-200b, 429 and 34a) target the MYCN gene. Among these micro RNAs miR-34a and miR-34c play a major role as tumour suppressors in neuroblastoma to inhibit cell growth by targeting MYCN, p53 and Bcl2.51–56 Therefore we carried out RT-PCR analysis specific to miRNAs and checked the level of expression of miR-34a, 34b, 34c, miR-605 and other important microRNAs such as miR-107, 200b, 542-5p53,15 that play a prominent role in neuroblastoma in the compound treated cells and compared them with untreated control. Treatment of IMR-32 cells with compounds caused increase in the expression of miR-34a (fivefolds), miR-34c (sixfolds), miR-200b and miR-107 (twofolds), miR-542-5p and miR-605 (3.5-folds) revealing a direct role of these micro RNAs in regulating p53 activity in MYCN positive cells in response to chemical treatment (Fig. 4 A). In addition it might also be possible that high levels of miR-605 observed in compound treated cells indirectly enhanced the transcriptional activity of p53 on miR-34a via downregulating Mdm2.14 Cellular apoptosis induced by stress is a complex process in which several signalling pathways are involved. P53 stimulates a wide range of signals that act through two major apoptotic pathways. Extrinsic death receptor pathway triggers the caspase cascade and intrinsic mitochondrial pathway shifts the balance between Bcl-2 to Bax (pro-apoptotic) and promote apoptosis.57 P53 responsive genes includes p21, Bax, puma, miR-34.34 P53 up-regulated modulator of apoptosis (PUMA) and Bcl-2 associated X protein (Bax) are considered as key downstream targets of p53 in response to DNA damage and stress.58–61 In addition nuclear p53 activates the expression of puma62,63 and can displace cytoplasmic p53 from Bcl-X(L) and allow p53 to directly activate Bax to induce mitochondrial permeabilization.60 Since we observed p53 activation (nuclear accumulation) in compound treated cells we were interested in investigating the downstream signalling event of apoptosis by measuring expression of Bax, puma, Bcl-2, caspase proteins as well as survival protein Akt1, E2F1.64,65 Thus IMR-32 cells were treated with Ros, C-2 and C-8 at 1 μM concentration for 24 h and Western blot analysis was performed to measure the level of the proteins in comparison to the untreated controls. We observed an increase in level of pro-apoptotic proteins (Bax, Puma) and active caspase-3 with concomitant decrease in the level of survival proteins (Akt1 and E2F1), anti-apoptotic protein (Bcl-2) and pro-caspases 9,12 [Fig. 3 A and B]. In General p53 activation involves stabilization of protein and enhancement of DNA binding as well as transcriptional activity.57 P53 target genes are divided into high promoter occupancy such as p21, Mdm2, Puma and low promoter occupancy (i.e., weak p53 binding) such as Bax, AIP1 and PIG3.31,66,67 To better understand p53 dependent transcriptional regulation of these compounds, p21 and Bax promoter constructs containing p53 binding sites were transfected into IMR-32 cells followed by compound treatment (Ros, C-2 and C-8) at 1 μM concentration for 24 h. The results have indicated transcriptional activation up to fourfolds in case of p21 and only twofolds in case of Bax promoter revealing the ability of the compounds to induce p53 target gene expression (p21 and Bax). To further confirm the importance of p53 in the transcriptional activation of p21 promoter we carried out transfection studies using minimal promoter (−142/+7) lacking p53 binding sites. We observed only 2.0-fold up regulation of p21 promoter activation68 (Fig. 4 C–F). Our results are in coincidence with studies on Saso2 and MDA-MB-453 cells wherein p53 strongly activates p21 having higher promoter occupancy and moderately activates Bax due to weak binding and lower promoter occupancy.66 Thus small molecules of anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidines having tri-methoxy moiety and 2-furfuryl, 3-pipernyl substitutions strongly activates p53 while selectively inhibits the growth of transformed cells, indicating its potential as a drug lead for p53 targeted therapy. Apart from in vitro experiments we tried to focus our attention on in vivo studies using Drosophila melanogaster as a model system to understand the apoptotic mechanism in the neuroblast cells. In the Drosophila larval brain, stem cell-derived tumors are induced by altered stem cell division and/or by impairment of progenitor cell differentiation due to mutations in the genes that are key regulators of NB asymmetric division. Studies have emphasised that many of these identified components act to regulate the self renewal versus differentiation decision and appear to function as tumor suppressors during larval nervous system development.69 To study the effect of anthranilamide pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidines on the key regulators of NB asymmetric division, we treated wild type Drosophila embryos with compounds Ros, C-2 and C-8 and RT-PCR was carried out using primers against tumor suppressor genes such as Brat, Prospero, Pins, Lgl, Miranda and Numb. We found enhanced transcript levels of Brat, Prospero and Pins in the compound treated embryos compared to untreated control, while the expression of Miranda, Numb and Lgl were unaffected (data not shown) (Fig. 4 H). The apoptotic pathway and activation of caspases is highly conserved between Drosophila and mammalian systems70–72 The activation of proapoptotic genes in Drosophila such as Hid , Reaper and Grim down regulate the inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) and results in the activaton of caspases (initiator caspases such as Dronc, Dredd and Strica and effector caspases such as DrICE , Dcp-1 , Decay and Damm ).73,74 More over it is well established that Drosophila p53 is required for damage-induced apoptosis but not for cell-cycle arrest.75 Thus to study the role of these analogues on apoptotic pathway, wild type embryos were treated with compounds Ros, C-2 and C-8. RT-PCR analysis has clearly demonstrated increase in the levels of p53 which activates the apoptotic machinery. We also observed increase of pro-apoptotic genes hid, reaper, initiator caspase dronc and activator caspases drice and decay along with decrease in the levels of diap1 (Drosophila inhibitor of apoptosis 1) upon compound treatment (Fig. 4 I). In the present study we have investigated a series of 24 compounds [anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidines] for their cytotoxic nature in various cancerous cell lines such as IMR-32, SK-N-SH, Neuro-2a (Neuroblastoma), MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 (Breast cancer), A549 (Lung cancer), K562 (Leukemia) by MTT assay with Roscovitine as positive control. The IC50 values derived from MTT assay are in the range of 0.9–1.8 μM (IMR-32), 2–4 μM (SK-N-SH), 3.78–7.7 μM (Neuro-2a), 4–8 μM (MDA-MB-231 & MCF-7), 3–6 μM (K562), 5–10 μM (A549). Among all the compounds studied we observed that C-2 (Tri-methoxy at R1, R2, R3 positions with 2-furfuryl at R′) and C-8 (Tri-methoxy at R1, R2, R3 positions with 3-piperanyl at R′) have shown profound cytotoxicity. Interestingly neuronal cancer cell lines have exhibited significant cytotoxicity when compared to breast cancer, leukemia, lung cancer cell lines. At lower concentrations (0.5 μM) compounds did not induce any cell cycle arrest and upon increased concentration led to G2/M cell cycle arrest. IMR-32 cells treated with compounds caused increase in p53 phosphorylation status particularly at Ser15 (ninefolds) and cause nuclear accumulation of p53. Apart from p53 activation compounds also enhanced the transcriptional activation of p21 and bax. Western blot analysis revealed drastic down regulation of oncogenes such as Mdm2 and MYCN by two and threefolds, respectively. Interestingly compounds also upregulated the tumor suppressor miRNAs such as miR-34a and miR-34c that leads to p53 activation and targets MYCN and Bcl2 thereby preventing cell proliferation. These compounds also disrupted the p53–Hdm2 interaction by modulating miR-605 and decrease Hdm2 protein levels by binding to 3′UTR. The levels of p53 dependent apoptotic proteins such as Bax and PUMA were up regulated with concomitant down regulation of anti-apoptotic proteins (Bcl2) and survival proteins (Akt1 and E2F1). The Drosophila neuroblast specific tumor suppressor gene expression (Brat, Prospero and Pins) was highly increased in compound treated wild-type embryos. Also the proapoptotic genes such as hid and reaper were upregulated with downregulation of inhibitor of apoptotic protein1 (diap1). Further compound treatment also led to the activation of capases (dronc, decay and drice). Our studies revealed the p53 activation as well as apoptotic inducing nature of these series of anthranilamide-pyrazolo[1,5-a ]pyrimidines compounds in IMR-32 neuroblastoma cells and have the potential to be used for further studies. title: MDM2 as MYCN transcriptional target: Implications for neuroblastoma pathogenesis
abstract: MYCN amplification is associated with an exceptionally poor prognosis in neuroblastoma. Furthermore, the crucial effectors of MYCN responsible for this aggressive subset of neuroblastoma await characterization. A critical negative regulator of the p53 tumor suppressor, MDM2, has been recently characterized in neuroblastoma cell lines as a transcriptional target of MYCN. Targeted inhibition of MYCN results in reduced MDM2 expression levels, with concomitant stabilization of p53 and stimulation of apoptosis in MYCN amplified neuroblastoma cell lines. These data suggest the possibility that MYCN-driven expression of MDM2 might play a role in counterbalancing the p53-dependent apoptotic pathways concurrently stimulated by over expression of MYC proteins. Mouse models of lymphoma have demonstrated that MDM2 expression, with decreased p53 activity, is critical for complete MYCC driven tumorigenesis. Our data suggest that a similar situation may apply for MYCN in neuroblastoma. Strategies for pharmacologic and genetic inhibition of MDM2 may prove to be an important new therapeutic approach in neuroblastoma.

Tel.: +31 20 . MYCN amplification is associated with an exceptionally poor prognosis in neuroblastoma. Furthermore, the crucial effectors of MYCN responsible for this aggressive subset of neuroblastoma await characterization. A critical negative regulator of the p53 tumor suppressor, MDM2 , has been recently characterized in neuroblastoma cell lines as a transcriptional target of MYCN. Targeted inhibition of MYCN results in reduced MDM2 expression levels, with concomitant stabilization of p53 and stimulation of apoptosis in MYCN amplified neuroblastoma cell lines. These data suggest the possibility that MYCN-driven expression of MDM2 might play a role in counterbalancing the p53-dependent apoptotic pathways concurrently stimulated by over expression of MYC proteins. Mouse models of lymphoma have demonstrated that MDM2 expression, with decreased p53 activity, is critical for complete MYCC driven tumorigenesis. Our data suggest that a similar situation may apply for MYCN in neuroblastoma. Strategies for pharmacologic and genetic inhibition of MDM2 may prove to be an important new therapeutic approach in neuroblastoma. Keywords MYCN MDM2 Apoptosis Neuroblastoma p53 1 Introduction and background Major improvements in outcome for neuroblastoma are most likely to result from targeted molecular therapies, derived from an advanced understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of the disease. MYCN amplification is the strongest adverse prognostic factor in neuroblastoma treatment [1] and transgenic models of neuroblastoma have revealed that MYCN is also a transforming oncogene responsible for de novo tumor formation [2] . MYCN is involved in many aspects of normal and oncogenic cellular physiology via activation of various transcriptional targets. These target genes encode proteins with roles in proliferation, cell cycle regulation, apoptosis and genomic stability [3,4] . In vitro studies demonstrate that MYCN overexpression induces an aggressive metastatic phenotype with decreased contact inhibition, decreased growth factor dependence and increased proliferation rate [5–7] . Paradoxically, MYCN also suppresses Bcl-2, activates Bax, and sensitizes cells to genotoxicity-mediated apoptosis through intrinsic apoptosis pathways [8] . MYCC (a MYC family member) has also been shown to activate the ARF tumor suppressor leading to p53 activation and apoptosis through Bcl-x and Bcl-2-dependent and independent pathways [9] . Thus MYCN expression induces the apparently contradictory cellular processes of rapid proliferation and apoptotic cell death. Obligate defects in the apoptotic pathways accompanying MYCN amplification have been proposed to circumvent MYCN-stimulated cell death in neuroblastoma [10] . Characterization of the key downstream transcriptional targets of MYCN involved in these conflicting pathways will yield important insight into the pathogenesis of and novel therapeutic approaches to neuroblastoma. 2 MDM2 is a MYCN target Using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) cloning [11] , we recently characterized MDM2 , the essential negative regulator of the p53 tumor suppressor, as a transcriptional target of the MYCN oncogene in neuroblastoma [12] . Real time PCR, Western blots and luciferase reporter assays demonstrate MYCN dependent regulation of MDM2 in MYCN-inducible neuroblastoma cell lines. ChIP and promoter pull-down assays demonstrate that this transcriptional regulation was through a direct interaction with a canonical E-box in the MDM2 promoter. This study also shows that targeted inhibition of MYCN leads to decreased MDM2 and consequently increased p53 mediated apoptosis. In contrast to many tumors, less than 2% of neuroblastomas have mutated p53 and the p53 pathways are functionally active in the majority of de novo tumors [13,14] . The characterization of MDM2 as a direct transcriptional target of MYCN suggests a mechanism by which MYCN over-expression might destabilize p53, thereby raising the threshold for stimulation of growth arrest and apoptosis. As detailed below, inhibition of the MDM2 /p53 pathway in vivo may tip the balance between MYCN driven proliferation and apoptosis in favor of apoptosis through activation of p53. 3 MDM2 expression as a critical determinant in cancer Originally identified as an amplified gene located on a double minute chromosome in a transformed mouse cell line [15] , Mdm2 was later shown to have a critical role in the process of cellular transformation [16] . Amplification and overexpression of MDM2 is found in about 10% of all human tumors [17] . In gliomas, for example, MDM2 amplification identifies a subset of high-risk patients that do not have p53 mutations [18] . In many soft tissue sarcomas, MDM2 amplification and overexpression correlates with poor prognosis [19–21] . Studies of acute lymphoblastic leukemia and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma also demonstrate that MDM2 over expression is associated with poor survival and aggressive disease [22–24] . Validating animal studies (described below) demonstrate that Mdm2 gene dosage is critical for oncogene driven lymphomagenesis. Thus deregulation of MDM2 gene expression likely contributes to the pathogenesis of a wide range of human tumors. 4 MDM2 functions in normal and malignant cells Upon genotoxic or cellular stress, increased p53 activity transactivates numerous genes encoding effectors critical in apoptosis and cell cycle arrest [25] . Additionally, p53 activates the MDM2 gene that encodes a p53 inhibitor forming an autoregulatory feedback loop that tightly controls expression of both p53 and MDM2 [26] . Multiple MDM2 activities inhibit p53 function. MDM2 binds to p53 via an N-terminal domain and directly inhibits the ability of that protein to transactivate its target genes [27] . MDM2 also directs the export of p53 away from its site of action in the nucleus to the cytoplasm, thanks to a central nuclear export signal [28,29] . Finally, MDM2 helps to target p53 for degradation through its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity [30–32] . MDM2 also possesses p53 independent, cell-cycle specific functions relevant to tumorigenesis. These include regulation of p21WAF1/CIP1 protein stability [33] , stimulation of E2F1/DP1 transcriptional activity [34] , inhibition of RB function in the regulation of E2F1 [35] , and blockade of p300/CBP acetylation of p53 [36] . Mouse models demonstrate a role for Mdm2 in developmental regulation and differentiation [37] . Overall, MDM2 permits proliferation through inhibition of p53-mediated arrest and apoptosis, as well through multiple p53-independent mechanisms pertinent to the process of tumorigenesis (see [17] for review). 5 MDM2 functions in neuroblastoma Less than 2% of de novo neuroblastomas harbor mutations in p53 [38] . Recent literature demonstrates that p53 is generally functional, accumulates in the nucleus in response to DNA damage and is efficiently degraded by MDM2 in neuroblastoma [39–41] . There are reports that p53 function may be compromised as a consequence of aberrant MDM2 expression levels in neuroblastoma. For instance, a study examining etoposide-induced p53 activity in a neuroblastoma cell lines suggested an important role for elevated MDM2 expression levels in the regulation of p53 translocation. In SH-EP cells, p53 accumulates in the cytoplasm upon exposure to etoposide. Antisense inhibition of MDM2 can then restore predicted nuclear localization and apoptotic activation, suggesting that increased MDM2 expression levels can play a role in the inappropriate modulation of p53 function [42] . Additionally, elevated MDM2 expression, and accompanying loss of p53 function is associated with multidrug resistance in some neuroblastoma cell lines [43] . The activity of MDM2 is critical in neuroblastoma, as recent work demonstrates that MDM2 ubiquitin ligase activity is rate-limiting for p53 degradation in neuroblastoma [44] . Taken together, these data demonstrate that the MDM2 /p53 pathway is intact in neuroblastoma and suggest that deficiencies in p53 functions may be a consequence of aberrant MDM2 expression. Deregulation of MDM2 as an effector of MYCN could therefore significantly diminish the activity of p53 during neuroblastoma development, resulting in failure to undergo appropriate cell cycle arrest and apoptosis (see below). 6 Transgenic mouse models demonstrate a role for MDM2 in cancer The importance of MDM2 as a negative regulator of p53 is exemplified in a mouse model. Loss of Mdm2 in mice leads to cell death (apoptosis) at the blastocyst stage and embryonic lethality [45–47] . This phenotype is completely p53-dependent as mice lacking both Mdm2 and p53 are viable [45,46] . As adults, Mdm2/p53 double null mice have the same tumor phenotype as p53 null mice [48] . Thus, the most important in vivo function of Mdm2 seems to be to inhibit p53 activity, which is detrimental to cell viability. The availability of an Mdm2 null allele allowed a direct assessment of the importance of mdm2 in tumor development in another mouse model. Mice expressing the Eμ-myc transgene develop B- cell lymphomas and as such, represent a model for Burkitt's lymphoma [49] . Mdm2 haploinsufficiency in Eμ-myc mice profoundly delayed tumorigenesis [50] . Mice expressing Eμ-myc develop B-cell lymphomas with a median age of 20.6 weeks while mice expressing Eμ-myc and inheriting an Mdm2 null allele developed tumors much later with a median age of 44.3 weeks. These data suggest that decreased levels of MDM2 lead to increased p53 activity which delays susceptibility to Eμ-myc lymphomas. Indeed, the increased apoptosis in Eμ-myc Mdm2 +/− pre-B cells is completely rescued by deletion of p53. The ability of MDM2 levels to alter tumor susceptibility has also been observed in human cancers. A polymorphism in the human MDM2 promoter was recently identified that modulates expression of MDM2 via binding of the transcription factor Sp1 [51] . This polymorphism results in increased MDM2 levels with a concomitant attenuation of p53 levels, and its presence correlates with increased susceptibility to tumor incidence in hereditary as well as sporadic cancers. Thus, minor differences in the expression of MDM2 alter tumorigenesis in animal and human cancers. 7 MDM2 as an effector of the MYCN oncogene A longstanding paradox regarding the MYC family of oncogenes is their propensity to activate apoptotic pathways stimulating cell death and to simultaneously promote cell cycle progression. Induction of MYCN in neuroblastoma cell lines, for instance, promotes enhanced sensitivity to apoptotic stimuli [52] , yet stimulates accelerated G1-S progression [5] . Deficiencies in various components of apoptotic pathways, including caspase 8 inactivation and enhanced Bcl-2 and survivin expression levels accompany MYCN amplification in neuroblastoma [53–56] and ensure continued proliferation. We now propose a model whereby MYCN transactivation of MDM2 may also, in be responsible for offsetting the multiple apoptotic pathways stimulated by MYC. As shown in Fig. 1 , MYC promotes apoptosis by inhibiting functions of Bcl-2/Bcl-XL , which protect the cell from the proapototic activity of Bax [57] . MYC also enhances expression of the p19ARF (ARF) tumor suppressor [58] that sequesters MDM2 in the nucleolus [59,60] . This prevents MDM2 -p53 binding and shuttling of p53 from the nucleus for degradation, thereby promoting apoptosis and growth arrest stimulated by p53. Our data supports the hypothesis that MDM2 overexpression in response to MYCN shortens the p53 half-life and/or raises the threshold for activation of p53 by cellular stress, counteracting the opposing effects MYCN on ARF and Bcl-2/BclxL pathways. This novel molecular link between MYCN and MDM2 /p53 pathway suggests an important new layer of regulation promoting growth and proliferation in response to MYCN amplification. Additional evidence implicating MYCN driven aberrant gene expression in the pathogenesis of neuroblastoma comes from the recent work describing hyperproliferation of the sympathetic ganglia of the PTH-MYCN neuroblastoma mouse model [2] . These mice have MYCN expression targeted to neural crest derived tissues under the control of the tyrosine hydroxylase promoter [2] . Ganglia isolated from homozygous mice exhibit persistence of hyperproliferative islands of cells thought to be pre-malignant neuroblasts. The ganglia neuroblasts undergo rapid differentiation with high apoptosis rates under the direction of local trophic factors. Persistence of the hyperproliferative clusters beyond 1wk of age correlates with high rates of neuroblastoma development [61] . It is likely that MYCN is disrupting the normal differentiation response in these cells. MYCN driven elevation in MDM2 levels could well contribute to this phenomenon since high MDM2 levels should alter the cellular response to stress, promoting cell cycle progression at this critical stage of neuroblast development. 8 Implications for novel therapies The biological characteristics of neuroblastoma suggest that targeting the molecular interaction of MDM2 and p53 may be an effective therapeutic strategy. As noted, the majority of neuroblastomas are p53 wild type and therefore dependent on MDM2 regulation of p53 to prevent apoptotic cell death. In several other tumor models inhibition of MDM2 leads to increased p53 activity and triggers an apoptotic stress response [62–64] . In neuroblastoma cell lines, we recently demonstrated that down regulation of MYCN leads to decreased MDM2 expression, p53 stabilization and subsequent rapid cell death [12] . Since MYCN also sensitizes cells to apoptotic stress, neuroblastoma should be particularly sensitive to targeted disruption of the MDM2 /p53 interaction in vivo. MDM2 as a drug target is the topic of extensive reviews and is an active area of research. Small molecule inhibitors that specifically interfere with the binding of MDM2 to p53 have been shown to induce apoptosis and regression of osteosarcoma xenografts [62] . The unique developmental biology of neuroblastoma suggests to us that targeting MDM2 could be effective therapy, especially in the context of MYCN driven tumors. The future evaluation of such approaches will advance our understanding of neuroblastoma pathogenesis and hopefully lead to important clinical advances for this highly fatal pediatric malignancy. title: Pracinostat inhibits the nefarious biological behavior of pancreatic cancer by targeting the miR-381–3p/MDM2 axis to activate the p53 signaling pathway
abstract: Objective Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive malignant tumors in humans, with poor prognosis. The acetylase tumor inhibitor (Pracinostat) has been shown to suppress the growth of various tumors. This study aimed to investigate the effects of Pracinostat on the pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 and to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms through both in vivo and in vitro experiments. Methods BxPC3 cells were treated with Pracinostat, and cell viability was assessed by CCK-8 assay; the differentially expressed miRNAs in cells before and after pracinostat treatment were screened by high-throughput sequencing, and miR-381–3p was selected as the target gene; the targeting relationship between miR-381–3p and MDM2 was verified by double luciferase reporter gene; the relationship between miR-381–3p, MDM2 and P53 signaling pathways was verified by immunoprecipitation, Western blot and other experiments. Pancreatic tumor models were established in BALB/c nude mice to study the role of pracinostat in vivo. Results Pracinostat upregulated the expression of miR-381–3p and p53, while downregulating MDM2 expression. It also inhibited the proliferation and migration of pancreatic cancer cells and promoted apoptosis. Treatment with a miR-381–3p inhibitor reversed the effects of Pracinostat. In addition, MDM2 was found to promote the ubiquitination and degradation of p53 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. In vivo experiments confirmed that Pracinostat inhibited tumor growth in nude mice. Conclusion pracinostat activates the p53 signaling pathway by targeting the miR-381–3p/MDM2 axis, thereby inhibiting the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells. These findings provide novel insights and potential therapeutic strategies for pancreatic cancer, and may also provide a reference for the treatment of other malignancies.

Objective Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive malignant tumors in humans, with poor prognosis. The acetylase tumor inhibitor (Pracinostat) has been shown to suppress the growth of various tumors. This study aimed to investigate the effects of Pracinostat on the pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 and to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms through both in vivo and in vitro experiments. Methods BxPC3 cells were treated with Pracinostat, and cell viability was assessed by CCK-8 assay; the differentially expressed miRNAs in cells before and after pracinostat treatment were screened by high-throughput sequencing, and miR-381–3p was selected as the target gene; the targeting relationship between miR-381–3p and MDM2 was verified by double luciferase reporter gene; the relationship between miR-381–3p, MDM2 and P53 signaling pathways was verified by immunoprecipitation, Western blot and other experiments. Pancreatic tumor models were established in BALB/c nude mice to study the role of pracinostat in vivo. Results Pracinostat upregulated the expression of miR-381–3p and p53, while downregulating MDM2 expression. It also inhibited the proliferation and migration of pancreatic cancer cells and promoted apoptosis. Treatment with a miR-381–3p inhibitor reversed the effects of Pracinostat. In addition, MDM2 was found to promote the ubiquitination and degradation of p53 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. In vivo experiments confirmed that Pracinostat inhibited tumor growth in nude mice. Conclusion pracinostat activates the p53 signaling pathway by targeting the miR-381–3p/MDM2 axis, thereby inhibiting the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells. These findings provide novel insights and potential therapeutic strategies for pancreatic cancer, and may also provide a reference for the treatment of other malignancies. Keywords Pancreatic cancer Pracinostat MiR-381–3p MDM2 Degradation of p53 ubiquitination Data availability The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. 1 Introduction Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a tumor of the digestive system with high malignancy and poor prognosis for survival[1] . Risk factors include smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, and dietary habits[2] .It is expected that by 2025, PC will surpass breast cancer to become the third leading cause of cancer death[3] . Due to the fact that the early clinical symptoms of PC patients are relatively cryptic, the disease course is already in the middle and late stages when local invasion, invasion of adjacent organs or distant tumor metastasis are detected[4] , which leads to a low resectable rate of PC surgery. At the same time, comprehensive treatment measures such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy are not very satisfactory for the treatment of PC[5] . Therefore, it is urgent to find new drugs for PC. Pracinostat (Pralistat, SB939) is a histone deacetylase inhibitor and an anticancer drug with good pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties[6] . It can inhibit the growth and proliferation of tumor cells, and at the same time has the effect of strengthening the immune system, thus achieving the effect of treating cancer. Pracinostat has been shown to have therapeutic effects on a variety of cancers, including lymphoma[7] , leukemia[8] , breast cancer[9] , lung cancer[10] , etc. However, there are no studies reported on pracinostat in the treatment of PC, so this study will explore the effect of pracinostat on PC progression. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of non-coding single-stranded RNA small molecules cut from precursor single-stranded RNA molecules, which can regulate the translation and stability of specific genes [11] . miRNAs can specifically inhibit or target specific mRNAs and participate in the regulation of important cell signaling pathways such as cell development, proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis[12] . In recent years, significant changes in a variety of miRNAs have been found in PC tissues, indicating that miRNAs can directly or indirectly affect PC [13] . In this study, after treating pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 with pracinostat, miRNA sequencing was performed on the samples in an attempt to find non-coding RNA targets for clinical treatment and blocking pancreatic cancer, providing a theoretical basis for the treatment of pancreatic cancer. miR-381–3p has been found to be involved in the occurrence and development of a variety of diseases and to regulate the biological processes of cells, including cell proliferation, apoptosis, migration, invasion and differentiation[14–16] . However, the specific molecular mechanisms by which miR-381–3p regulates pancreatic cell proliferation, apoptosis and migration in PC remain to be studied. Among the downstream regulatory mechanisms of miR-381–3p, it has been found that miR-381–3p can regulate the expression of the downstream molecule p53 by inhibiting its target gene to promote apoptosis of endothelial cells and inhibit proliferation [17] . As a tumor suppressor, p53 is an important regulator of cancer cell homeostasis. It plays a key role in the process of DNA damage, which can block the cell cycle, promote apoptosis, and affect DNA repair[18] . Usually, p53 has low activity, which is due to its interacting protein mouse bi-minute 2 homolog (MDM2) having E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, which can degrade p53 through the proteasome system. MDM2 is a key regulator of proliferation-related pathways and can regulate cell proliferation, apoptosis, and cell cycle by interacting with p53[19] . Studies such as Wang have found that Holliday ligation recognition protein inhibits the expression of p53 by promoting MDM2, which in turn promotes the proliferation, migration, and invasion of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells[20] . Therefore, based on the above research, this study will explore the impact of pracinostat on PC processes by modulating the miR-381–3p/MDM2/p53 axis. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials The BxPC3 cell line was purchased from Punocell Cell Bank. Nude mouse without thymus was purchased from the Animal Experimental Center of Medical University. The Animal Experimental Ethics Committee of Kunming Medical University (Kmmu2020414) provided all necessary approval for these experiments. Clinical samples Adjacent tissue and Pancreatic cancer tissue were obtained from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University. All experiments involving these materials were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University (FEY-BG-39–2.0). Each patient gave written consent for the research. 2.2 Reagent The following materials were utilized for this study: Pracinostat (SB939) from Selleck, mimic of miR-381–3p (miR-381–3p mimic) and its negative control (NC mimic), miR-381–3p inhibitor (NC inhibitor) and its negative control (NC inhibitor), MDM2 overexpression plasmid (Guangzhou Borui Bio), LV-miR-381–3p lentivirus (Shanghai Jikai Bio), DMEM medium (Dalian Meilun, MA0212–2), fetal bovine serum (Punocell, ), Cell Counting Kit-8 (Dongren Chemical Technology (Shanghai, CK04) one-step TUNEL cell apoptosis in situ detection kit (Shanghai Kaiji, KGA7062), FITC-coupled Annexin-V apoptosis detection kit (BD, ), cell cycle detection reagent Kit (biosharp, BL114A), 0.1 % crystal violet aqueous solution (Solarbio, G1064), UltraSensitive SP mouse/rabbit (Fuzhou Maixin, KIT-9720), DAB color development kit (Beijing Zhongshan Bio, ZLI-9019), miRcute miRNA extraction and isolation kit (TIANGEN, DP501), Lipofectamine 3000 transfection kit (Therom, MAN0009872), HA-ub antibody (CST #3936), dual luciferase reporter gene detection kit (MCE, HY-K1013), antibody MDM2 (proteintech, –1-Ig), P53 (proteintech, –2-Ig), CyclinA2 (proteintech, –1-AP), CyclinB1 (proteintech, –1-AP), CyclinD1 (proteintech, –1-Ig), CyclinE1 (proteintech, –1-AP). 2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Cell culture Human pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC3 was cultured using DMEM (Meilunbio, MA0212–2), adding 10 % fetal bovine serum and 1 % penicillin/streptomycin, and cultured in an incubator at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. The cell morphology was observed using a microscope, and the fluid was changed and passaged routinely. Subsequent transfection cell experiments transfected NC mimic, miR-381–3p mimic, NC inhibitor and miR-381–3p inhibitor with Lipofectamine 3000 to BxPC3. The transfection method was carried out according to the reagent instructions, and the transfection efficiency was detected after transfection 48 h. 2.3.2 Animal experimentation Thirty male BALB/c nude mice aged 6–8 weeks were randomly divided into Control group, pracinostat group, Pracinostat+LV-sh-miR-381–3P group, 10 mice in each group. Bxpc3 cells were injected subcutaneously into the left armpit of nude mice at a dose of 1 × 105 . When the tumor diameter was 0.5 cm, Control group was given normal saline as a control. pracinostat group was administered for 15 days, Pracinostat+LV-sh-miR-381–3P group was administered for 15 days and LV-sh-miR-381–3P lentivirus (1 × 108 UT/50 μL) was injected into nude mice through the tail vein (injected every 3 days). The nude mice were euthanized at 21 days of injection of Bxpc3 cells, and the tumors were weighed and photographed for follow-up experiments. 2.3.3 Tumor tissues collection This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University (FEY-BG-39–2.0) and is in line with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments for ethical research involving human subjects. Fifteen pairs of pancreatic cancer and adjacent non-tumor tissues were collected from patients of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University. In addition, written informed consent was obtained from patients for this study. 2.3.4 CCK-8 BxPC3 cells were adjusted to a concentration of 3 × 103 cells/mL and aseptically plated into 96-well plates with 100 μL per well. After 24 h of incubation in a cell culture incubator, the cells were exposed to different doses of pracinostat for 24 and 48 h. Subsequently, 10 μL of CCK-8 solution(Dongren Chemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was added to each well and the plates were further incubated for 2 h. Absorbance was then measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader（BioTek，0284）. 2.3.5 Cell sequencing BxPC3 cells were made into 1 × 105 cells/mL cell suspension and inoculated into 6-well plates, 2 mL per well. The plates were incubated in an incubator for 24 h, and the cells were treated with 0uM and 1uM pracinostat for 24 h the next day. Collected cells were commissioned to Lianchuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd. for cell sequencing to analyze differentially expressed miRNAs. 2.3.6 RT-qPCR Extract miRNAs from cell samples, clinical samples, and animal samples using the miRcute miRNA Isolation Kit ((TIANGEN, DP501)), and determine miRNA concentration and purity. Reverse transcription of miRNAs into cDNA using miRNA reverse transcription reagents and qRT-PCR using SYBR Green Master (Roche, Mannheim, Germany). Fluorescence quantitative PCR was performed with U6 or β-actin as an internal reference, and the experiment was repeated at least 3 times. See Table 1 for primer sequences. 2.3.7 Western blot Cell samples, clinical samples, and animal samples of different groups were treated with RIPA lysate and then the supernatant was centrifuged. The protein concentration was determined by BCA method, and the loading amount was calculated according to the protein concentration. The protein was heat-denatured for 15 min, 10 % SDS-PAGE separator was configured, and 5 % SDS-PAGE concentrate was added to the upper layer. The sample was loaded. After the initial voltage of SDS-PAGE electrophoresis was turned on for 90 v for 20 min, the voltage was adjusted to 110 v and the bottom of the glue was run for 45 min to end the electrophoresis. The electrophoretic gel was neatly cut and gently slowly spread onto the PDVF membrane with a power supply of 250 mA for 65 min and the improved PDVF membrane was taken out with 5 % skim milk and sealed for 2 h. The primary antibody was incubated in the incubation box at 4 °C overnight, and the antibody dilution ratio was 1:2000. The next day, the TBST membrane was washed 3 times, and the corresponding secondary antibody was incubated for 2 h. Imaging was taken with a chemiluminescence instrument imaging system. 2.3.8 Apoptosis and cell cycle were detected by flow cytometry Apoptosis rate was determined using the FITC-conjugated Annexin-V Apoptosis Detection Kit (BD, ). Briefly, the digestive juices of the cells after administration were collected to make a cell suspension. Add 1 mL PBS 1000 rpm/min and centrifuge for 5 min, discard the supernatant and add 500uL 1× buffer to resuspend the cells. Add 5 μL FITC and 5 μL PI according to the kit instructions and stain in the dark for 30 min. Apoptosis rate was detected using flow cytometry（BD, FACSCalibur). The cell cycle was determined using the Cell Cycle Detection Kit (biosharp, BL114A). Briefly, the digestive fluid of the cells after administration was collected to make a cell suspension. After collecting the cells, add 1 mL 70 % ethanol to fix the cells overnight. Wash the cells with PBS the next day. Add 500 μL 1X buffer to resuspend the cells. Add 5 μL PI dye for 30 min. Detect the cell cycle with flow cytometry（BD,FACSCalibur). 2.3.9 Transwell detects cell invasion After diluting Matrigel gel with serum-free medium 1:3, add it evenly and slowly to the upper chamber at the bottom of the Transwell chamber, and air dry at 4 ℃. Aspirate the excess liquid from the upper chamber, place the chamber in a 24-well culture plate, and add 500 µL of serum-free medium. After standing for 15 min, aspirate the medium, add 200 µl of cell suspension to the upper chamber, and add 500 µL of complete medium to the lower chamber. Incubate in an incubator at 37 ℃ for 24 h, and remove the cell culture plate. Fix with 4 % paraformaldehyde for 30 min, add crystal violet stain (Solarbio, G1064), and take pictures with a microscope. 2.3.10 Colony formation assay Spread the cell suspension into a petri dish of about 200 cells/mL medium, culture at 37 ℃, 5 % CO2 for 2 weeks, and replace the fresh culture solution every 2 days. When visible clones appear in the petri dish, terminate the culture and discard the culture solution. Fix with 4 % paraformaldehyde for 30 min and add crystal violet dye, wash off the violet dye with running water, and air dry. Calculate the cell clone formation rate. 2.3.11 Cell scratch experiment The cells were cultured into the 6-well plate by drawing a 1 cm straight line across the hole with a marker pen on the back of the 6-well plate with a sterilized ruler. The cells were treated with medicine the next day and scratched with a horizontal line perpendicular to the back of the 6-well plate. The scratched cells were washed with PBS and photographed under the microscope for 0 h. The 6-well plate was placed in a 37 ℃ CO2 incubator for 24 h and photographed under the microscope for 24 h. 2.3.12 Immunohistochemistry The collected animal samples and clinical samples were fixed using 4 % paraformaldehyde, followed by the steps of dehydration, embedding, sectioning, baking, dewaxing, hydration, antigen repair, etc. Next, use 10 % goat serum to seal for 2 h. Incubate the primary antibody at 4 °C overnight, and wash the tablets with PBST 3 times the next day. Incubate the secondary antibody dropwise for 2 h, and color with DAB. Stain the nucleus with hematoxylin, differentiate with 1 % alcohol hydrochloride, dehydrate, seal, and take pictures under a microscope. 2.3.13 Co-immunoprecipitation Collect the cells and purify the protein, dividing the protein into two parts. Add one part of the protein to the 4X loading buffer and boil for 15 min for denaturation as input. Add 1 μg of MDM2 antibody to the other part of the protein and slowly shake and incubate overnight at room temperature. The next day, add the pretreated 10 μL protein A agarose beads to the protein that was incubated overnight with the antibody and slowly shake and incubate for 4 h at room temperature. Centrifuge and retain the pellet and repeat three times. Add the pellet to the 4X loading buffer and boil for 15 min. Detect the MDM2 and P53 proteins with Western blot. The control antibody is IgG. 2.3.14 Double luciferase reporting experiment The possible binding check point on miR-381–3p and MDM2 3 '-UTR was predicted by Starbase website (https://rnasysu.com/encori/ ). Then, the 3′ -UTR sequence containing the binding check point was amplified by PCR and cloned onto the luciferase-expressed reporter gene vector to construct the wild-type (WT) -MDM2 vector and the mutant (Mut) -MDM2 vector. Next, according to the instructions for use of the Lipofectamine TM3000 (Therom, MAN0009872) kit, miR-381–3pmimic, mimic NC and WT-MDM2, Mutu-MDM2 were co-transfected into Bxpc3 cells and cultured for 48 h. Finally, measure luciferase activity according to the instructions for use of the dual luciferase reporter gene detection kit (MCE, HY-K1013). 2.3.15 Tunel Mouse tumor tissue was fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde and washed with PBS, then stained with tunel using Tunel Apoptosis Detection Kit (Shanghai Kaiji, KGA7062) according to the manufacturer's procedure. Then the nucleus was stained with DAPI, and the slides were rinsed and imaged using fluorescence microscopy. Finally, the apoptosis was analyzed using an image analyzer. 2.3.16 Statistical analysis All data were analyzed on GraphPad Prism version 8 software (GraphPad, USA), and the data were repeated 3 times. Multiple comparisons were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance, and pair comparisons were statistically analyzed using T-test. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 Results 3.1 Pracinostat can inhibit the malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 cells First, Bxpc3 cells were treated with 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2.0 μM pracinostat for 24 h and 48 h, respectively. The results showed that pracinostat had a significant inhibitory effect on the viability of Bxpc3 cells ( Fig. 1 A). Subsequent experiments selected 1 μM pracinostat as the experimental conditions (Fig. 1 B). Then, the apoptosis experiment, cell cycle assay, colony formation assay, cell scratch experiment, and Transwell experiment find that compared with the control group, the apoptosis rate of Bxpc3 cells treated with pracinostat was significantly increased, and the cell proliferation and migration ability were significantly weakened, the proportion of cell arrested in the G2/M phase was significantly increased (Fig. 1 C-G). Western blot results showed that compared with the control group, the protein expression levels of P53, P21, and CyclinA1 in Bxpc3 cells treated with pracinostat were significantly increased, while the protein expression levels of CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1 were significantly reduced (Fig. 1 H). In summary, pracinostat can inhibit the proliferation and invasion of Bxpc3 cells and promote apoptosis. 3.2 miRNA differential analysis and verification After treatment of Bxpc3 with pracinostat, differential expression analysis of miRNA was performed ( Fig. 2 A-B). Sequencing results showed that, compared with the normal group, there were 1102 differentially expressed miRNAs in the dosing group, of which 566 were up-regulated and 536 were down-regulated. Among them, miR-381–3p was significantly overexpressed. RT-qPCR detected the expression of miR-383–3p in the cell samples and found that the expression of miR-383–3p was consistent with the sequencing results (Fig. 2 C). The expression of miR-383–3p in the clinical samples (n = 15) was detected and it was found that the expression of miR-383–3p was significantly reduced in the cancerous tissue compared to the adjacent tissue (Fig. 2 D). 3.3 Pracinostat can inhibit the vicious biological behavior of Bxpc3 by promoting miR-381–3p After transfection with miR-381–3P inhibitor, Bxpc3 cells were treated with pracinostat. CCK-8 results showed that compared with pracinostat, the miR-381–3P inhibitor group promoted cell proliferation ( Fig. 3 A). Flow cytometry detection of cell apoptosis found that miR-381–3P inhibitor reversed the promoting effect of pracinostat on cell apoptosis (Fig. 3 B). Cell cycle assays also found that compared with pracinostat, the proportion of cell cycle arrest in the G2/M phase was reduced in the miR-381–3P inhibitor group (Fig. 3 C). The results of clone formation, Transwell and scratch experiments showed that miR-381–3P inhibitor reversed the inhibitory effects of pracinostat on clone formation ability, invasion and migration (Fig. 3 D-F). In summary, pracinostat may inhibit the malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 by promoting miR-381–3p. 3.4 MiR-381–3p can target MDM2 As a negative regulator of P53, MDM2 plays a regulatory role in many tumors. One of the interesting phenomena is the discovery on the starbase bioinformatics website that miR-381–3p may have the possibility of targeted binding to MDM2. Through dual luciferase reporting experiments, we found that overexpression of miR-381–3p significantly inhibited luciferase activity of the Wt-MDM2 3 'UTR reporter gene vector (P < 0.001), but had no effect on luciferase activity of the Muti-MDM2 3′ UTR reporter gene vector ( Fig. 4 A-B). Further studies found that both interference and overexpression of miR-381–3p affected the mRNA expression level and protein expression level of MDM2 in BxPC3 cells (Fig. 4 C-D). 3.5 MiR-381–3p inhibits pancreatic carcinogenesis by binding to MDM2 This study confirmed that miR-381–3p can bind to MDM2. Subsequently, CCK-8 assay, apoptosis assay, cell cycle analysis, colony formation assay, cell scratch assay, and Transwell assay were performed. The results showed that compared with the control group, transfection with miR-381–3p mimics promoted cell apoptosis and inhibited cell proliferation, colony formation, and invasion. Meanwhile, the proportion of cell arrested in the G2/M phase was significantly increased in the miR-381–3p mimic group. Furthermore, transfection with OE-MDM2 reversed the effects induced by miR-381–3p mimics ( Fig. 5 A-F). Western blot results showed that compared with the Control group, the miR-381–3p minic group upregulated the protein expression levels of P53, P21, and CyclinA. At the same time, miR-381–3p minic reduced the ubiquitination level of P53. Similarly, transfection of OE-MDM2 reversed the effect of miR-381–3p mimics (Fig. 5 G). In conclusion, miR-381–3p inhibits the occurrence of pancreatic cancer through MDM2 binding. 3.6 MDM2 promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of P53 via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway In order to further determine whether P53 is regulated by MDM2, co-immunoprecipitation was used to determine the ubiquitination of P53 by MDM2 in BxPC3 cells. The results showed that in the presence of MG132, the interaction between exogenous MDM2 and P53 was significantly enhanced ( Fig. 6 A), and in the presence of MG132, knocking down MDM2 resulted in increased levels of P53 ubiquitination (Fig. 6 B). This result suggests that MDM2 promotes P53 ubiquitination, thereby mediating P53 degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. 3.7 Animal experiments demonstrate that pracinostat affects the progression of pancreatic cancer through miR-381–3p The pancreatic cancer model was established by tumorigenesis in nude mice, and the results of tumor mass and volume detection showed that the administration of pracinostat could significantly inhibit tumor growth compared with the DMSO group; the administration of pracinostat at the same time as the tail vein injection of LV-sh-miR-381–3P chronic disease into the nude mice, the tumor growth increased faster than that of the administration group alone ( Fig. 7 A-C). It is indicated that the inhibition of tumor growth by pracinostat is achieved by promoting the expression level of miR-381–3p. Immunohistochemical results showed that Ki67 expression levels decreased in the pracinostat group, and LV-sh-miR-381–3P could reverse the effect of pracinostat ( Fig. 8 D); Tunel test results showed that compared with the Control group, the tumor tissue apoptosis in the pracinostat group increased, while LV-sh-miR-381–3P was able to inhibit the effect of pracinostat (Fig. 7 E); Western blot test results showed that compared with the Control group, pracinostat upregulated the expression of P53, P21, CyclinA1, and P53, and reduced the expression levels of CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1, At the same time, Western blot showed that pracinostat reduced the ubiquitination level of P53 (Fig. 7 F). Compared with the pracinostat group, transfection of LV-sh-miR-381–3P reversed the effect of pracinostat (Fig. 7 F). 4 Discussion PC tumor is a very lethal and aggressive malignancy, ranked first among asymptomatic cancers, accounting for 5 % of cancer-related deaths[21] . The factors that cause PC include hereditary oncogene variants, age, blood type, microbiota, obesity, etc[22] . Therefore, exploring the mechanism of PC occurrence and development can help to find effective therapeutic drugs and provide targets for early diagnosis of PC. Pracinostat is an effective anti-cancer drug that has been revealed to have therapeutic effects in a variety of cancers. For example, Lian et al. found that Pracinostat can slow down the progression of breast cancer and improve the immunotherapy effect of breast cancer[23] . The study by Chen et al. also shows that Pracinostat can promote apoptosis by inhibiting the proliferation, migration and invasion of glioma cells, thereby alleviating the progression of glioma[24] . However, there is no research report on the treatment of PC by Pracinostat. In this study, we explore the effect of Pracinostat on the progression of PC. We found that Pracinostat treatment can promote the expression of CyclinA1, a cell cycle-related protein, and inhibit the expression of CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1, while reducing the proliferation, migration and invasion ability of BxPC3 cells, and improving apoptosis. In addition, Pracinostat treatment can also promote the apoptosis of tumor tissues in vivo and inhibit the growth of tumors. This suggests that Pracinostat has the effect of inhibiting the malignant biological behavior of BxPC3 cells, and Pracinostat treatment may be a new method to alleviate the progression of PC. Pracinostat can inhibit the malignant biological behavior of BxPC3 cells, but the specific mechanism by which it alleviates PC progression is not yet clear. In recent years, studies have found that many miRNAs are involved in the process of PC occurrence and affect various stages of pancreatic injury. For example, the study of Jingyang et al. showed that miR-320b can inhibit the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells by targeting negative regulation of FOXM1[25] ; while the study of Zhang et al. found that miR-132 can promote the proliferation, invasion and migration of pancreatic cancer cells by inhibiting the expression of the tumor suppressor gene PTEN, thereby exacerbating the development of PC[26] . In this study, we first found that miR-381–3p was less expressed in PC and Bxpc3 cells through bioletter analysis and miRNA expression differentiation analysis of Bxpc3 cells. In addition, miR-381–3p has been widely studied in a variety of cancers. For example, the study of Shang et al. found that miR-381–3p can inhibit the proliferation and metastasis of cervical cancer cells by down-regulating FGF7, and induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, thereby alleviating the progression of cervical cancer[27] . The study of Sun et al. showed that miR-381–3p can reduce the proliferation level of bladder cancer cells by inhibiting RAB2A, activate apoptosis, and then inhibit the development of bladder cancer[28] . However, the specific link between miR-381–3p and PC is unclear. Therefore, our study mainly focused on miR-381–3p. We also found that the expression of miR-381–3p was highest in Bxpc3 cells after administration of pracinostat. MiR-381–3p inhibitors can partially reverse the effect of pracinostat, promote the proliferation, migration and invasion of BxPC3 cells, and reduce apoptosis. This suggests that the inhibitory effect of pracinostat on pancreatic cancer cells is achieved by upregulating miR-381–3p. This experiment demonstrates that miR-381–3p can target and negatively regulate the expression of MDM2, which is likely to be an important mechanism for miR-381–3p to interfere with the malignant biological behavior of BxPC3 cells. MDM2, a ubiquitin ligase, mainly regulates cell cycle, apoptosis, proliferation, differentiation and transformation functions[29] . MDM2 is highly expressed in many tumors, such as retinoblastoma, as well as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and is considered to be one of the important factors in the occurrence and development of tumors. Previous studies have shown that overexpression of MDM2 can promote the proliferation of retinoblastoma cells, inhibit apoptosis, and then promote the development of retinoblastoma[30] . At the same time, inhibition of MDM2 can effectively inhibit the proliferation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells, promote apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and inhibit the growth of nasopharyngeal carcinoma[31] . In our study, overexpression of miR-381–3p can inhibit the expression of MDM2, while overexpression of MDM2 can effectively up-regulate the expression of cycle-related proteins CyclinB1, CyclinD1, and CyclinE1, and down-regulate the expression of CyclinA1, thereby promoting the proliferation, migration and invasion of Bxpc3 cells, and inhibiting apoptosis. Therefore, the malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 cells is positively correlated with the expression of MDM2, and inhibiting MDM2 expression by up-regulating miR-381–3p may be one of the ways to alleviate the process of PC. It is well known that MDM2 is a major negative regulator of p53 and can interact with p53 to form a stable complex. When MDM2 binds to p53, MDM2 not only prevents the transcriptional activation of p53, but also promotes the degradation of p53 through ubiquitination[32] . Mutations and/or inactivation of p53, a major regulator of anti-proliferative function, are critical for tumorigenesis[33] . External stimulation-induced p53 activation inhibits the proliferation of cancer cells because it promotes the expression of a range of related proteins, thereby inducing apoptosis and cell cycle arrest[34,35] . MDM2/p53 axis has been widely studied in the regulation of cancer process. For example, oryzine activates p53 by inhibiting MDM2, thereby inducing neuroblastoma cell apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and inhibiting the progression of neuroblastoma[36] . Knockdown of RPS27a can inhibit MDM2-mediated p53 ubiquitination and degradation, promote apoptosis and G1 phase arrest of lung adenocarcinoma cells, inhibit cell proliferation, and alleviate the process of lung adenocarcinoma[29] . This study also found that MDM2 can promote P53 ubiquitination and mediate p53 degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. The above results suggest that the inhibitory effect of miR-381–3p on malignant biological behavior of Bxpc3 cells and PC is achieved by mediating the MDM2/p53 axis. Overall, our study found that Pracinostat can increase the targeted binding effect of miR-381–3p to MDM2 by upregulating the expression of miR-381–3p, thereby inhibiting the binding of MDM2 to P53, thereby inhibiting the ubiquitination degradation of P53, further activating p53, thereby inhibiting the proliferation, migration and invasion of Bxpc3 cells, promoting apoptosis and cycle arrest, thereby alleviating the process of PC(Fig. 8 ). Our results suggest that Pracinostat may be an effective therapeutic agent for PC. title: The key vulnerabilities and therapeutic opportunities in the USP7-p53/MDM2 axis in cancer
abstract: The MDM2/MDMX-p53 circuitry is essential for controlling the development, apoptosis, immune response, angiogenesis, senescence, cell cycle progression, and proliferation of cancer cells. Research has demonstrated that USP7 exerts strong control over p53, MDM2, and MDMX stability, with multiple mediator proteins influencing the USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX axis to modify p53 expression level and function. In cases where p53 is of the wild type (Wt-p53) in tumors, inhibiting USP7 promotes the degradation of MDM2/MDMX, leading to the activation of p53 signaling. This, in turn, results in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Hence, targeting USP7 presents a promising avenue for cancer therapy. Targeting USP7 in tumors that harbor mutant p53 (Mut-p53) is unlikely and remains largely unexplored due to the existence of numerous USP7 targets that function independently of p53. Considering that Mut-p53 exhibits resistance to degradation by MDM2 and other E3 ligases and also shares the same signaling pathways as Wt-p53, it is reasonable to suggest that USP7 may play a role in stabilizing Mut-p53. However, there is still much to be done in this area. If the hypothesis is correct, USP7 may be a potent target in cancers containing both Wt-p53 and Mut-p53.
