The MDM2/MDMX-p53 circuitry is essential for controlling the development, apoptosis, immune response, angiogenesis, senescence, cell cycle progression, and proliferation of cancer cells. Research has demonstrated that USP7 exerts strong control over p53, MDM2, and MDMX stability, with multiple mediator proteins influencing the USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX axis to modify p53 expression level and function. In cases where p53 is of the wild type (Wt-p53) in tumors, inhibiting USP7 promotes the degradation of MDM2/MDMX, leading to the activation of p53 signaling. This, in turn, results in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Hence, targeting USP7 presents a promising avenue for cancer therapy. Targeting USP7 in tumors that harbor mutant p53 (Mut-p53) is unlikely and remains largely unexplored due to the existence of numerous USP7 targets that function independently of p53. Considering that Mut-p53 exhibits resistance to degradation by MDM2 and other E3 ligases and also shares the same signaling pathways as Wt-p53, it is reasonable to suggest that USP7 may play a role in stabilizing Mut-p53. However, there is still much to be done in this area. If the hypothesis is correct, USP7 may be a potent target in cancers containing both Wt-p53 and Mut-p53. Graphical abstract Unlabelled Image Keywords Deubiquitinase USP7 (HAUSP) MDM2 p53 E3 ubiquitin ligase Data availability Data will be made available on request. 1 Introduction DNA damage poses a significant threat to the cellular microenvironment and can arise from various internal and external factors. Consequently, the cell must continually engage in DNA repair processes to uphold genomic stability and ensure a mutation-free state [1 ]. The tumor suppressor protein p53 is a vital component of the DNA damage response pathway, responsible for regulating the initiation of programmed cell death in cases where cells gather irreparable DNA damage. USP7 (HAUSP), a notable deubiquitinase (DUB), has garnered significant interest due to its critical role in cancer development and progression by modulating the MDM2-p53 axis. The formation of the USP7-MDM2 complex plays a crucial role in stabilizing MDM2, preventing its auto-ubiquitination. Consequently, this stabilization of MDM2 facilitates the subsequent ubiquitination and degradation of p53 [2 ]. Decades of research have uncovered USP7's diverse array of targets, including both tumor suppressor and oncogenic proteins. These targets play crucial roles in shaping various cancer hallmark abilities, thus influencing cancer evolution and progression. Notably, proteins such as PTEN, FOXO4, RNF168, DNMT1, and LSD1 are among the targets, and they are closely associated with cell cycle regulation, DNA repair, and immune response mechanisms [3–6 ]. USP7-mediated regulation of the tumor suppressor p53 is a highly investigated area, given its impact on controlling crucial aspects of cancer cell behavior. Through its influence on cell cycle progression, apoptosis, immune response, growth, proliferation, and senescence in cancer cells, p53 emerges as a pivotal target in cancer research, recognizing USP7 as a potential therapeutic target in the realm of cancer treatment [7–10 ]. In this review, our primary focus lies on the USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX axis and its regulation by diverse factors in human cancers. Notably, we delve into the intriguing prospect of USP7's involvement in regulating Mut-p53, as it has been observed that Mut-p53 undergoes regulatory mechanisms akin to those observed in Wt-p53. Understanding the therapeutic potential of targeting USP7 in cancers with Mut-p53 could offer valuable insights into novel treatment strategies and potentially pave the way for developing more effective therapeutic interventions for these challenging cancers with p53 mutation. 2 Competitive association of USP7 with p53 and MDM2/MDMX In 1997, the discovery of USP7 marked a distinctive finding in the field of deubiquitinating enzymes. It was recognized as a fresh addition to the ubiquitin-specific protease (USP) family, having been identified as an interacting partner of Vmw110, a regulatory protein of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) [11 ]. The USP7 protein consists of three primary domains, encompassing a total of 1102 amino acids. These regions encompass an N-terminal domain associated with tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factors (TRAF, spanning amino acids 53–206), a central catalytic domain (Cat, covering amino acids 208–560), and a C-terminal arrangement of tandem ubiquitin-like domains (UBL1–5, spanning amino acids 560–1102). TRAF plays a vital role in facilitating the interaction of USP7 with its substrates, such as MDM2/MDMX and p53, through the recognition of P/AxxS motifs [8 ,12 ,13 ]. The Thumb, Palm, and Finger regions within the catalytic core of USP7 form a unique binding pocket for ubiquitin, catalysis, and efficient ubiquitin removal. Through the utilization of molecular dynamics simulations, it has been observed that the transformation of USP7 from its inactive state to its active state is only observable when H294 is rendered neutral with a deprotonated C223 and a charged H464. In the inactive apo state, the positively charged H294 establishes an electrostatic network with W285, E298, and Y224. However, when H294 becomes neutral in the active state, it loses its ability to engage in charge interactions, leading to the disruption of the electrostatic network. As a consequence, this disruption prompts unfavorable changes in the backbone angles of C223, which are subsequently rectified through helical refolding, ultimately resulting in the formation of the active site. Mutations in the catalytic core result in decreased USP7 activation [14–16 ]. The C-terminal Ubl domains arranged as UBL1/2, UBL3, and UBL4/5 contribute to substrate binding and deubiquitination. Deleting the C-terminal domain significantly diminishes deubiquitination activity but including UBL4/5 and the C-terminal tail helps to restore catalytic function. UBL4/5 directly interacts with the switch circuit in the catalytic field, inducing conformational changes that enhance USP7's affinity for ubiquitin [16 ,17 ]. Thus, all three domains are crucial for recognizing substrates and removing ubiquitin by USP7. p53, a protein consisting of 393 amino acids, features five primary domains: the N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD), responsible for interacting with p53-binding sites on MDM2 and MDMX; the proline-rich region (PP) containing five PxxP motifs, playing a pivotal role in apoptosis initiation; the DNA-binding domain (DBD); the tetramerization domain (TET); and a C-terminal domain (CTD), essential for its binding to the TRAF domain of USP7 [18–20 ]. The two USP7-binding sites found in the p53 CTD, located at 359-PGGS RAHSS -367 stretch, where Ser362 and Ser367 are critical for USP7-p53 interaction [21 ]. Biochemical tests reveal discernible resemblances between the binding of p53 and EBNA1 to the TRAF-like domain. The surface of USP7 features a shallow depression where EBNA1 binds, and this same site is also utilized for p53 binding. However, in contrast to EBNA1, p53 interacts with a smaller region of USP7. This distinction in binding explains the comparatively lower intensity of the p53 interaction [13 ]. There are potential binding sites predicted for the USP7 at specific regions of p53, including 12-PPLS-15, 34-PLPS-37, 87-PAPS-90, 92-PLSS-95, and 300-PPGS-303. However, the likelihood of these sequences forming interactions with USP7 depends on their accessibility and their capability to establish hydrogen bonds with USP7's β strand-7. Further comprehensive research is needed to fully explore and understand these potential interactions [22 ] ( Fig. 1 A ) . In a pioneering study, Li et al. utilized mass spectrometry to unveil the USP7-p53 association, marking the first discovery of this interaction. Notably, the overexpression of USP7 exhibited a tumor suppressive effect by stabilizing p53, even in the presence of an abundance of MDM2, the primary E3 ubiquitin ligase known for its antagonistic role in p53 stability [7 ]. Follow-up investigations have demonstrated that nearly complete genetic disruption or ablation of USP7 expression leads to elevated p53 levels, while its normal or intermediate expression facilitates p53 degradation [8 ,23 ]. Mechanistically, USP7 plays a role in stabilizing MDM2. Crystal structure studies have revealed that, despite MDM2 and p53 competing for binding to the shallow groove in the TRAF-like domain of USP7, MDM2 exhibits a significantly higher affinity for USP7 than p53 [19 ,22 ]. Moreover, additional p53 and MDM2 interaction motifs were identified at the C-terminal Ubl domain of USP7 [24 ]. Subsequently, researchers uncovered a direct interaction between USP7 and MDMX, the antagonist of p53 and the homolog of MDM2. MDMX was observed to bind to the TRAF-like domain of USP7, akin to p53 and MDM2. Interestingly, USP7 partially rescued MDMX from MDM2-mediated degradation, suggesting its role in stabilizing MDMX as well. Furthermore, the loss of USP7 resulted in the degradation of MDMX and indirect activation of p53 [2 ]. MDM2 and MDMX proteins display a striking structural resemblance, characterized by the presence of an N-terminal p53-binding domain, a central acidic domain that facilitates p53 ubiquitination, a zinc finger domain, and a crucial C-terminal RING domain responsible for their E3 ligase activity. Several potential USP7-binding sites on MDM2, including 147-PSSSHLVSRPSTS-159, 226-AGVS-229, and 397-PSTS-400, have been identified. Notably, Ser150 and Ser229 are crucial residues for facilitating the MDM2-USP7 binding. Similarly, the P/AxxS motifs 8-AQCS-11 and 398-AHSS-401 of MDMX have been verified as the USP7-binding sites [2 ,12 ,22 ] ( Fig. 1 A) . 3 USP7-MDM2/MDMX-DAXX complex controls p53 fate DAXX is a highly conserved and developmentally essential nuclear protein involved in transcriptional regulation, apoptosis, and carcinogenesis. Under stressful circumstances, the “USP7-MDM2/MDMX-DAXX” complex is short-lived, leading to rapid degradation of MDM2/MDMX through MDM2 autoubiquitination and increased MDMX degradation, even in the presence of USP7 overexpression. ATM-dependent phosphorylation of MDM2/MDMX hinders USP7 binding after DNA damage. The level of p53 protein and its transactivation capacity determine the fate of cells with mutated DNA, influencing whether they continue dividing, undergo senescence, or initiate the apoptotic pathway. This highlights the intricate connection of multiple signaling pathways with the “USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX-DAXX” axis [12 ] [25 ]. Additionally, the DNA damage response and rapid phosphorylation of p53 result in cellular accumulation of p53, making it resistant to MDM2-mediated degradation [26–29 ]. MDM2's auto-ubiquitination activity subjects it to proteasomal degradation, but USP7 can stabilize MDM2 by removing its poly-Ub chains [8 ,30 ]. Moreover, the interaction between MDM2 and MDMX enhances MDM2's autoubiquitination activity towards MDMX, increasing MDM2 stability [31 ,32 ]. While MDMX's interaction with p53 does not impact the overall protein levels of p53, it does disrupt p53's ability to bind to DNA and its transcriptional activity [33 ,34 ]. DAXX contains two distinct regions interacting with USP7: the acid-rich region, spanning amino acids 347–570, and the N-terminal 160 amino acids, housing the PAH1 domain. These regions differ from the primary interacting region of MDM2. The association of DAXX with both MDM2 and USP7 through non-overlapping regions suggests the intriguing possibility that DAXX may facilitate the USP7-MDM2 interaction, leading to MDM2 stabilization, which gains support from the similar effects of DAXX and USP7 on MDM2 stability. However, ATM-dependent phosphorylation of DAXX at Ser-564 can negate this complex's activity in response to DNA damage. Consequently, MDM2 undergoes degradation through auto-ubiquitination activity, restoring p53 protein levels [35 ,36 ] ( Fig. 1 B) . DAXX plays a crucial role in activating USP7, facilitating its mitotic function and Taxol response through stabilizing CHFR and promoting the ubiquitination and degradation of Aurora-A. High USP7 and low DAXX levels are associated with Taxol resistance in certain cell lines. On the other hand, sensitive cells with low USP7 levels can partly compensate through increased DAXX expression. However, the exact effects of DAXX-dependent activation of USP7 and its implications for p53 regulation are still subject to ongoing debate [37 ]. Recent advancements in the USP7 field indicate that cofactor binding can significantly enhance USP7 activity. For instance, GMPS attaches to a “switching” loop near the catalytic domain, substantially increasing USP7's deubiquitinating activity [16 ,38 ]. It is possible that DAXX may similarly bind to USP7 to boost its activity and potentially search for its substrates. However, the precise mechanism of DAXX-dependent activation of USP7 requires further investigation. According to Tang J et al., there is a regulatory interplay between MDM2 and USP7 concerning the protein level of DAXX. USP7 acts as a deubiquitinase, preserving DAXX, while MDM2 acts as a ubiquitinase, promoting proteasomal degradation. In normal cells, USP7 and DAXX work together to regulate MDM2. However, in pathological conditions such as certain cancers where MDM2 is upregulated (found in 7 % of human cancers), MDM2 could potentially inhibit DAXX-mediated apoptosis, leading to tumor growth. Nonetheless, the exact role of USP7 and MDM2 in regulating DAXX-dependent apoptosis (connecting the death receptor Fas to c-Jun N-terminal kinase) requires further investigation beyond the well-established USP7-p53-MDM2-DAXX pathway. As of now, this area lacks sufficient research and clear understanding [39 ]. It has been demonstrated that p53 phosphorylation and acetylation are essential for association with DAXX. Interestingly, MDM2 enhances the DAXX-p53 interaction, resulting in repression of p53 target genes. Further research is needed to determine whether DAXX prefers interacting with p53 after DNA damage and whether USP7 might be involved in this process. Alternatively, it can also be possible that various complexes involving MDM2-USP7-DAXX, MDMX-USP7, or p53-USP7-DAXX might serve distinct functions [40 ,41 ]. Altogether, the N-terminal TRAF-like domain of USP7 is recognized by both p53 and MDM2, but it prefers to bind with MDM2 even in the presence of excessive p53. This leads to MDM2 stabilization and subsequent p53 degradation in healthy cells [14 ,17 ]. However, under genotoxic stress, the p53 degradation is reversed, as USP7 rescues p53. DNA damage induces phosphorylation of p53, MDM2/MDMX, and DAXX by ATM and Chk2, disrupting the USP7-MDM2/MDMX-DAXX complex and triggering p53 deubiquitination by USP7 [19 ,22 ,36 ,42–47 ]. 4 Effector molecules in the USP7-p53-MDM2/MDMX axis The dynamic nature of the USP7-MDM2-p53 axis involves numerous regulators and co-factors that can have favorable and unfavorable effects in controlling the level of p53. These regulators and co-factors can be categorized into three groups. Firstly, there are proteins that positively influence the USP7-p53 interaction, leading to p53 stabilization. Secondly, there are proteins that negatively regulate p53 expression and its transactivation abilities by favorably affecting the USP7-MDM2/MDMX interaction. Lastly, there is a counterbalancing mechanism involving USP7-MDM2/MDMX that differentially regulates the turnover of p53 ( Table 1 ) . Numerous mediators hinder the interaction between USP7 and p53, resulting in a low level of p53 that supports cancer development by reducing the impact of genotoxic stress. For example, TSPYL5 binds to the TRAF-like domain (amino-acid residues 1–208) of USP7, preventing additional substrates from binding and limiting the p53-USP7 interaction, leading to breast oncogenesis. TSPYL5 operates in a manner akin to the viral Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) protein. Both TSPYL5 and EBNA1 interact with USP7 to inhibit p53 function by displacing p53 from its association with USP7 [13 ,21 ]. However, the USP7-TSPYL5 interaction might also interfere with the USP7-MDM2 interaction, causing rapid MDM2 degradation through autoubiquitination. As a result, the p53 stabilization from MDM2 mediated degradation may outweigh the p53 degradation dependent on the TSPYL5-USP7 complex. To resolve this puzzle, determining which interaction is stronger, USP7-MDM2 or USP7-TSPYL5, becomes essential in a cancer-specific context. Further research explores TSPY1, a partner of TSPYL5, which interacts with USP7 to inhibit p53 function and suppress p53-dependent cell cycle arrest. TSPY1 promotes spermatogonial proliferation by reducing the p53 level and enhancing the competitive binding of TSPYL5 to USP7 along with p53 [48 ,49 ] ( Fig. 2 A i) . Unlike TSPYL5-TSPY1, the CSA-CSB complex functions differently but achieves a similar goal. CSA and CSB proteins form a stable complex with p53 and MDM2, leading to rapid degradation of p53. However, in Cockayne Syndrome, non-functional CSA and CSB proteins fail to adequately ubiquitinate and degrade p53, resulting in an enhanced apoptotic response. In this context, it is intriguing to explore the role of USP7 in regulating p53 and MDM2 in the presence of CSA/CSB proteins [50 ] ( Fig. 2 A ii) . The counterbalancing mechanisms involve pairs of acetylases and deacetylases or kinases and phosphatases that regulate p53 degradation and stabilization. In healthy, non-stressed cells, these mechanisms direct the MDM2/MDMX-USP7-DAXX complex towards p53 degradation, maintaining a low level of p53. Conversely, in stressed cells, the scenario is reversed. For instance, SIRT1 disrupts the USP7-MDM2 complex by reversing p300-mediated acetylation on Lys182 and Lys185, leading to MDM2 autoubiquitination [51 ] ( Fig. 2 B i) . Additionally, in non-stressed cells, casein kinase 2 (CK2) phosphorylates the specific isoform of USP7 (USP7S) at serine 18, promoting the formation of the USP7-MDM2 complex and p53 degradation. However, after exposure to infrared radiation (IR), ATM-dependent protein phosphatase PPM1G dephosphorylates USP7S, leading to USP7S degradation and downregulation of MDM2, resulting in p53 accumulation [52 ] ( Fig. 2 B ii) . Moreover, the inhibitor of growth 1 (ING1), a type-II tumor suppressor protein, influences p53 stabilization by opposing p300/E4 ligase-mediated p53 proteasomal degradation. UV and other stresses cause mono-Ub p53 (by MDM2 at several lysine residues) to interact with ING1b. The ubiquitin-binding domain (UBD) of ING1b identifies mono-Ub on p53 and enables USP7 binding for deubiquitination and stability. Furthermore, ING1 promotes p53 acetylation at Lysine 382, enhancing its transcriptional activity. ING-bound mono-Ub p53 then moves into the cytoplasm to initiate mitochondria-dependent apoptosis [53 ,54 ] ( Fig. 2 B iii) . Numerous cofactors in the USP7-p53 axis, categorized as tumor suppressors, are crucial in influencing the interaction between USP7 and p53. Their presence leads to an enhanced expression and accumulation of the p53 protein. Among these cofactors, ABRO1 is a positive regulator of p53 stability by facilitating the association between USP7 and p53, ultimately promoting p53 stabilization. In non-stressed conditions, ABRO1 is primarily localized in the cytoplasm and expressed at a consistently low level. This characteristic proves advantageous for targeting MDM2 by USP7, as it helps to maintain low levels of p53 expression. However, in the presence of genotoxic stress and DNA damage, cells swiftly upregulate the production of ABRO1 and facilitate its translocation into the nucleus. This process amplifies the activity of USP7 in targeting p53. Nevertheless, the precise mechanism underlying the upregulation and nuclear translocation of ABRO1 in response to DNA damage remains insufficiently explained in the study conducted by Zhang, Jianhong et al. [55 ] ( Fig. 2 C i) . HLA-B associated transcript-3 (Bat3), an additional protein, plays a crucial role in the USP7-mediated stabilization of p53, irrespective of its catalytic activity. Notably, USP7-cs (conserved Cys residue at the core domain replaced with the Ser residue) still could interact with Bat3 and assist Bat3 for p53 stabilization. The underlying mechanism involves the preference of the USP7-p53 complex for Bat3 binding, leading to the formation of a ternary complex. This complex effectively stabilizes p53 by impeding its interaction with the proteasome receptor S5a, facilitating the nuclear accumulation of p53. Interestingly, the Bat3-USP7 complex has shown its capability to directly regulate MDM2 stability as well. This suggests that the Bat3-USP7 mediated protein stabilization may extend beyond p53 alone. It is important to highlight that USP7 selectively strengthens the interaction between p53 and Bat3; however, it does not have a similar enhancing effect on the interaction between MDM2 and Bat3 [56 ] ( Fig. 2 C ii) . Moreover, RASSF1A, a candidate tumor suppressor involved in apoptosis triggered by death receptors, plays a vital role in safeguarding p53 from MDM2-mediated ubiquitination and the subsequent degradation of p53 by the proteasome. Additionally, RASSF1A initiates the activation of the p53-dependent checkpoint early stages of DNA damage response. Notably, RASSF1A interacts with MDM2/DAXX, preventing the interaction between MDM2 and USP7. This disruption leads to the autoubiquitination of MDM2 within the nucleus. However, there is a need for further research to understand two key aspects. Firstly, the activation mechanism of RASSF1A, which allows it to disrupt the USP7-DAXX-MDM2 complex, suggests that RASSF1A may act as a cofactor for DNA damage-induced kinases. These kinases could potentially modulate the interaction between RASSF1A and MDM2. Secondly, it is necessary to investigate how the DNA damage-induced ATM-dependent phosphorylation and dissociation of the USP7-MDM2 interaction align with the RASSF1A dependent destabilization of MDM2 during the initial stages of the p53 response [57 ] ( Fig. 2 C iii) . A successful strategy to control the expression of p53 target genes is to restrict their transcription, and cancer cells expressing wild type p53 are more likely to employ this approach. One notable example is the activation of the USP7-MDM2-SIRT1-SUV39H1 complex at the promoters of p53 target genes, resulting in chromatin compaction. Within this complex, the SUV39H1 methyltransferase, which is another substrate of MDM2, is deubiquitinated and stabilized by USP7. SUV39H1 then trimethylates the lysine 9 residue of histone H3, forming transcriptionally inactive higher-order heterochromatin [58 ,59 ]. SUV39H1 is further regulated by Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), an NAD+ dependent deacetylase that primarily targets histone H4 at the lysine 16 residue. Specifically, SIRT1 deacetylates lysine 266 within the catalytic SET domain of SUV39H1, leading to increased SUV39H1 activity at the promoters of p53 target genes [60 ]. The presence of SIRT1 is crucial for SUV39H1-mediated localization of heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) and trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 (H3-K9me3), which are essential for gene silencing. Notably, recent studies have revealed that the deubiquitinase activity of USP7 plays a role in stabilizing SIRT1, adding an additional layer to the regulatory axis of SUV39H1 mediated regulation and maintenance of p53's transcriptional activity. Furthermore, it has been observed that decreased USP7 activity enhances chemotherapy induced p53 dependent apoptosis, underscoring the significance of the USP7-MDM2-SIRT1-SUV39H1 axis in modulating p53 function [61 ]. However, some crucial rational gaps still need to be explored. For instance, after being recruited by MDM2, SUV39H1 and EHMT1 work concertedly to promote the tri-methylation of histone H3 at the K9 position, suppressing transcription at p53 target promoters [62 ]. Unfortunately, Mungamuri et al. did not continue to establish any relationship between USP7 and EHMT1 in controlling the expression of the p53 gene. The dynamics of MDM2 stabilization by USP7 shifting to SUV39H1 protection from MDM2's E3 ligase activity in unstressed cells was also not adequately examined by Mungamuri et al. What is the sequence of events in stress cells or pathological conditions like cancer that could dissociate the USP7-MDM2-SUV39H1 complex and restore regular p53 transcriptional activities? Does MDMX play any alternative undefined roles in this scenario? [34 ,58 ,63 ] ( Fig. 2 D) . 5 How is mutant p53 stability regulated in cancer? The inactivation of p53 is a frequent occurrence in tumorigenesis, with mutations observed in over 50 % of primary human tumors [64 ] ( Fig. 3 A, B ) . Mut-p53 can develop new functions that support tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, and chemoresistance or inhibit any remaining Wt-p53 in a dominant-negative manner [65 ,66 ]. Studies have demonstrated the enhanced tumorigenic potential of p53 mutants such as R248W, D281G, R273H, R175H, and V143A, which were introduced into p53-deficient fibroblasts [67 ]. Likewise, in knock-in mice, the K117R mutant of p53 completely eliminated p53-mediated apoptosis [68 ]. Tumors harboring mutant p53 demonstrate greater aggressiveness and metastatic potential compared to both p53-deficient and wild-type tumors [69 ,70 ]. Somatic TP53 (p53) mutations are found in breast cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer, and head and neck cancer. Crucially, TP53 mutations are associated with an unfavorable outlook in cases of breast cancer, bladder cancer, and hematopoietic system malignancies. Furthermore, the range of TP53 mutations differs across various tumor types [71 ]. 5.1 Differential regulation of mutant p53 degradation in cancer In normal cellular conditions, Wt-p53 is present at low cellular level, while Mut-p53 tends to accumulate at high level in tumors. This accumulation of Mut-p53 implies the involvement of selective mechanisms that stabilize it, although the precise understanding of these mechanisms remains elusive. Like Wt-p53, Mut-p53 can be influenced by post-transcriptional modifications such as ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and acetylation, which regulate its levels and activity. Studies have highlighted specific phosphorylation sites on Mut-p53, including Ser15, Thr81, and Ser392. Significantly, in ovarian cancer, DNA-PK-mediated phosphorylation at Ser15/Ser37 promotes the stabilization of Mut-p53 and amplifies its gain-of-function activity. Conversely, in prostate cancer, the inhibition of NF-κB results in the phosphorylation of Mut-p53 at Ser15, thereby reinstating its ability to bind to DNA [71–73 ]. The regulation of Mut-p53 also involves ubiquitination; for instance, Mut-p53 fails to effectively activate MDM2, leading to the loss of MDM2's negative regulatory function [74 ]. However, it was observed that loss of MDM2 stabilizes the p53 R172H mutant [75 ]. Due to the significant role of Mut-p53 in cancer progression and its association with chemo/radio- resistance, extensive research efforts have been devoted to investigating the potential of targeted therapy, gene therapy, immunotherapy, and combination therapies as treatment options for Mut-p53-associated cancers [76–78 ]. Under stress conditions, both wild-type p53 (Wt-p53) and mutant p53 (Mut-p53) can accumulate within cells. However, a notable distinction is observed in their stability following stress recovery. Mut-p53 remains stable at elevated levels, whereas Wt-p53 returns to its basal level. This differential behavior can be attributed, at least in to the absence of an auto-regulatory loop involving MDM2 and other negative regulators that typically regulate Wt-p53 levels [79 ,80 ]. In addition to the defective auto-regulatory loop involving MDM2, Mut-p53 acquires additional protective mechanisms, primarily through the involvement of co-chaperones and stress-induced heat shock proteins. These mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of Mut-p53 in cancer cells, which is crucial for developing its oncogenic gain-of-function (GoF) activities. Upon DNA damage, both Wt-p53 and Mut-p53 undergo phosphorylation at specific sites, such as serine 20 and threonine 18, protecting both forms of p53 from MDM2-mediated degradation, stabilizing and initiating subsequent activation [81 ]. Furthermore, Mut-p53 receives additional protection from MDM2 through the constitutive phosphorylation of ERK [82 ]. However, a contrasting observation is found with active SIRT1, which can deacetylate Mut-p53. In triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), the presence of active SIRT1 results in the reduction of Mut-p53 levels [83 ]. Besides MDM2, there are multiple E3 ligases involved in the degradation of Wt-p53, including TOPORS, Carps, Cop1, ARF-BP1, Synoviolin, Pirh2, and CHIP. Among these, MDM2 and CHIP have been pinpointed as the main E3 ubiquitin ligases accountable for the degradation of Mut-p53. This is supported by evidence demonstrating that the knockdown of MDM2 and/or CHIP leads to partial inhibition of Mut-p53 destabilization [84 ] [75 ,85 ]., Furthermore, Mut-p53 binds tightly to the acidic domain of MDM2, blocking its E3 ligase activity, leading to the accumulation of Mut-p53. Additionally, the Mut-p53-MDM2 complex lacks efficient ubiquitin release from the activated E2 conjugating enzyme, reducing ubiquitination and further enhancing the buildup of Mut-p53 [86 ,87 ]. Heat shock protein machinery can identify Mut-p53 as a misfolded protein, and it has been demonstrated that Hsp70 and Hsp90, which are connected through the co-chaperone HOP, can form complexes with Mut-p53 (contact and confirmational mutants) and stop MDM2 and CHIP from degrading Mut-p53. Treating cancer cells with Hsp90 inhibitors, such as 17AAG, or with siRNA against HSF1, a transcription factor that regulates Hsp90 expression, can increase the ubiquitination and degradation of mutant p53 [88 ,89 ]. Certainly, the inhibition of Hsp90 was observed to reduce the viability of cancer cells expressing Mut-p53, which includes breast cancer cells (T47D, MDA-MB-231, MBA-MB-468), colon cancer cells (SW480), and prostate cancer cells (DU145) [90 ]. Mut-p53 proteins that are well-folded (p53R273H) and mimic the native conformation of Wt-p53 are more resistant to degradation by CHIP [88 ]. Additionally, conformational p53 mutants (p53R156P, p53V157F, p53R175H, and p53Y220C) can be protected from CHIP-mediated degradation with the aid of the Hsp40 isoform DNAJA1 [91 ,92 ] ( Fig. 3 C) . Moreover, Pirh2, an E3 ligase characterized by the presence of a RING domain, is recognized for its ability to ubiquitinate Wt-p53. It also forms interactions with Mut-p53, thereby facilitating its ubiquitination. However, mutations in p53 disrupt the negative feedback regulatory loop involving Pirh2, as Pirh2 is a target gene of p53. Interestingly, treatment of cells expressing Mut-p53 with Arsenic trioxide has been shown to induce Pirh2-mediated proteasomal degradation of Mut-p53 [93 ,94 ]. 5.2 Role of deubiquitinases on mutant p53 stability - is there any involvement of USP7? There is little information available on how deubiquitinases stabilize Mut-p53. For instance, the Mut-p53 level decreases under the glucose-restricted condition when the protein spautin-1 inhibits USP10 [95 ]. Another deubiquitinating enzyme, UCHL1, plays a role in stabilizing both wild-type p53 and mutant p53 in breast cancer cell lines. However, its influence on cell viability operates through a yet-to-be-identified mechanism [96 ]. Furthermore, in response to oxidative stress, USP29 can deubiquitinate p53 [97 ]. As previously mentioned, USP7 plays a pivotal role in controlling the MDM2-p53 pathway. Nevertheless, there is currently no evidence supporting a direct link between USP7 and the p53 status in cancer. In cell lines carrying Wt-p53, the inhibition of USP7 results in the stabilization of p53, promoting apoptosis. Interestingly, when USP7 is inhibited using P22077, at least one cell line expressing Mut-p53 (SK-N-AS, neuroblastoma) exhibited elevated p53 expression [98 ]. Moreover, ABRO1 has been shown to enhance the interaction between Mut-p53 and USP7, thereby affecting the stabilization of Mut-p53 in HT29 and BT474 cells [55 ]. Furthermore, in a study by Schauer et al., the impact of TP53 on the response to USP7 modulation was investigated. Cell lines were classified as either TP53-functional-Wt and nonfunctional-Mut group, and a comparison was made. The results revealed a significant influence of TP53 functional status on the response to USP7 genetic modulation, as observed in the DEMETER2 and CERES datasets. These findings provide genetic evidence supporting the association between TP53 status and the response to USP7 modulation across various cancer cell lines [99 ]. In a separate study focusing on the radio-sensitivity of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) cells, the role of USP7 was investigated. The researchers observed that downregulating USP7 enhanced radio-sensitivity in LSCC cells with Mut-p53, while it attenuated radio-sensitivity in cells with Wt-p53. These findings suggest that targeting USP7 could potentially enhance the efficacy of radiotherapy in LSCC cases with p53 mutations while minimizing adverse effects on adjacent normal tissues lacking p53 mutations [100 ]. Deletions in TP53 can lead to the loss of critical domains necessary for its tumor suppressor functions. For example, deletions affecting the C-terminal region of p53, which contains nuclear localization signals and regulatory domains, can impede its proper localization and interaction with other proteins. The prevalence of p53 deletion mutations varies in different cancers. For instance, approximately 30 % of breast cancers harbor somatic TP53 mutations, with a significant portion being truncation mutations specifically in BRCA1-related breast cancer [101 ]. p53 truncation mutations are sometimes associated with distinct clinical outcomes; for example, in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), truncation mutations in p53 have been linked to worse overall survival (HR = 2.54, P = 0.008) and progression-free survival (HR = 2.65, P = 0.002) compared to missense mutations [102 ]. Additionally, TP53 exon-6 truncation mutations (R213 and R196), which resemble the naturally occurring alternative p53 splice variant, p53-psi, produce proteins lacking tumor suppressor activity, promoting cancer cell's proliferation, survival and metastasis [103 ]. Regarding the interaction between truncated p53 proteins and USP7, the association remains unexplored. However, we hypothesize that the interaction between USP7 and truncated p53 depends on the available portion of the p53 protein. The USP7 binding site on the C-terminal domain (CTD) of p53, located at the 359–98 PGGSRAHSS-367 stretch, includes Ser362 and Ser367, which are critical for the USP7-p53 interaction. Loss of the p53 CTD, along with these critical amino acids, may result in the complete abrogation of the USP7-p53 interaction, leading to rapid p53 degradation via MDM2 and other E3 ligases, thereby promoting tumor progression. Conversely, if truncated p53 loses the MDM2 interaction, it may become stabilized; however, the loss of canonical tumor suppressive function and the acquisition of oncogenic properties could further contribute to tumor progression. To summarize, the exact role of USP7 in the deubiquitination of Mut-p53 is not fully understood. However, various pieces of evidence suggest the involvement of USP7 in this process. Furthermore, the shared pathway of stabilization between Mut-p53 and Wt-p53 indicates the existence of an undiscovered relationship between these two proteins, which could have a substantial impact on the role of USP7 in tumor progression. Further research is required to delve into the underlying mechanisms and unveil the possible implications of this association. 6 Targeting USP7-MDM2/MDMX-p53 axis in cancer Over the course of the past decade, extensive efforts have been directed towards the exploration and development of small molecule inhibitors, with the specific aim of targeting USP7 (commonly referred to as USP7i) ( Fig. 4 ) . USP7, as a pivotal player in the intricate regulatory network involving MDM2/MDMX-p53 in cancer cells, has garnered significant attention from the scientific community. However, despite the diligent research undertaken in this area, it is noteworthy that as of now, there has not been a specific inhibitor identified that can directly target the interaction between USP7 and MDM2/MDMX [104–106 ]. P5091 is a highly specific USP7/47 inhibitor that was identified through a rigorous process of high-throughput screening. This compound demonstrates remarkable potency and selectivity in inhibiting the deubiquitinating activity of USP7/47, with an impressive IC50 value of 4.2 μM. Notably, P5091 exhibits no discernible impact on other deubiquitinating enzymes even at a relatively high concentration of 100 μM [107 ]. Extensive studies have revealed its in vivo antitumor activity, inhibiting the growth of multiple myeloma (MM) and GBM xenografts [107 ,108 ]. In addition, P5091 has demonstrated its ability to induce cell cycle arrest, inhibit cell proliferation, and promote apoptosis in colorectal cancer [109 ], ovarian cancer [110 ], and Ewing sarcoma [111 ], in vitro and in vivo . P5091 achieves its effects by triggering the polyubiquitination of MDM2 and MDMX, subsequently resulting in their degradation and the activation of downstream targets such as p53 and p21. Additionally, P5091 has the added benefit of enhancing the antitumor immune response by diminishing the immunosuppressive activity of regulatory T cells. In a xenograft model of colon cancer, it exhibits a level of effectiveness in suppressing tumor growth that is on par with the efficacy of anti-PD-1 antibodies. Mechanistic studies indicate that P5091 treatment boosts the antitumor immune response by altering cytokine expression in the tumor microenvironment and reducing immune tolerance [112 ,113 ]. Through optimizing P5091 structure, researchers identified P22077, a dual inhibitor of USP7 and USP47. P22077 facilitates the degradation of MDM2, triggering the activation of p53 and p21, prompting apoptosis, and amplifying the sensitivity of neuroblastoma cells to chemotherapy in vitro . Its effectiveness was validated in mice harboring orthotopic xenograft tumors in vivo . Furthermore, P22077 also plays a role in the ubiquitination and degradation of Tip60, thereby contributing to its cytotoxic effects. However, both P5091 and P22077 exhibit similar selectivity against USP47, leading to questions about their sole dependency on USP7 [98 ,114 ,115 ]. Exploring different structural scaffolds starting from P5091 and P22077 led to the identification of thiazole derivatives, specifically C7 and C19. These compounds exhibit notable inhibitory activity with IC50 values of 0.67 μM and 1.35 μM, respectively. Their discovery was made through the utilization of Ub-Rho screening [116 ]. Additionally, a distinct class of P5091 derivative, known as Compound 14, demonstrates the ability to inhibit the catalytic activity of both USP7 and USP47, with IC50 values of 0.42 μM and 1.0 μM, respectively [117 ]. Reverdy et al. developed a high-throughput screening assay to identify specific USP7 inhibitors, HBX and HBX , from a diverse small molecule library of amido-tetrahydro acridine derivatives. These lead compounds selectively inhibit USP7 with IC50 values of 28.1 and 22.6 μM, respectively, through covalent bonding with Cys223 in USP7's catalytic core, resulting in inactivation, MDM2 degradation and p53 stabilization. However, their efficacy and safety in animal models require further investigation [118 ]. More potent and specific USP7 inhibitors, HBX41108 was developed through further optimization. It inhibits USP7 with an IC50 of 424 nM and effectively reverses USP7-mediated MDM2 stabilization while increasing p53 and p21 expression. Molecular modeling indicates that Compound 14 may form a covalent bond with the ubiquitin-binding sites on USP7, thereby inducing an allosteric inhibition of its catalytic activity. However, it's important to note that HBX41108 exhibits greater potency in inhibiting USP8, with an IC50 value of 96 nM, compared to its inhibition of USP7 [119 ]. Kategaya et al. utilized structure-based designing and nuclear magnetic resonance-based screening to develop two selective USP7 inhibitors, GNE-6640 and GNE-6776, containing 2-Amino-4-ethylpyridine as a core group. These compounds engage in non-covalent interactions with and cleave ubiquitin moieties with free K48 side chains. This competitive interaction inhibits the binding of ubiquitin to USP7, resulting in the destabilization of its substrates, with a particular impact on MDM2. Both GNE-6640 and GNE-6776 demonstrate robust inhibition of cancer cell viability, augment the effectiveness of chemotherapy in vitro , and prolong the delay in the growth of EOL-1 xenograft tumors in vivo [120 ]. Lamberto et al. introduced XL188, a derivative of quinazolin-4-one with a tertiary hydroxypiperidine moiety, as non-covalent inhibitors of USP7, with a selective binding affinity to the S4-S5 pocket of USP7 (KD = 104 nM). Additionally, they exhibit a potent inhibitory effect on its enzymatic activity, with an IC50 value of 90 nM, promoting MDM2 degradation leading to elevated levels of p53 and p21. Continued development of XL compounds resulted in the identification of XL177A, an exceptionally potent and irreversible inhibitor of USP7. It shares a binding mode and functional characteristics similar to XL188 [121 ]. Continuing the research on USP7 inhibitors, FORMA Therapeutics employed a high-throughput screening approach with ubiquitin-rhodamine assay, leading to the discovery of two types of inhibitors. The covalent USP7 inhibitor, FT827, was identified to bind to the catalytic domain of USP7 and effectively inhibiting its enzymatic activity with a KD of 7.8 μM [122 ]. A potent non-covalent inhibitor, FT671, was also developed, which binds to the USP7 catalytic domain with a KD of 65 nM. FT671 has been shown to reduce MDM2 levels and increase p53 levels in a concentration-dependent manner, effectively inhibiting MM.1S cell proliferation (IC50 = 33 nM) in vitro and MM.1S xenograft tumor growth in vivo [122 ]. In addition to the previous discoveries, Gavory et al. made a significant breakthrough by identifying a novel class of non-covalent and reversible USP7 inhibitors. In their initial synthesis, compound 1 (IC50 = 13.1 μM), showed enough promise. Further optimization involving the introduction of a chiral methyl group (R stereochemistry) at the benzylic position of the phenethylamide chain led to the development of Compound 2, a potent USP7 inhibitor (IC50 = 0.3 μM). The researchers continued their efforts, resulted in the identification of potent and selective allosteric USP7 inhibitors, like compound 4 and compound 5 with IC50 value of 6.0 nM and 22.0 nM respectively [123 ]. Furthermore, compound 4 demonstrated the ability to reduce MDM2 levels and increase p53 and p21 levels in vitro . Notably, Compound 4 exhibited superior anticancer activity compared to clinically relevant MDM2 inhibitors, especially in the case of LNCaP (prostate cancer) and RS4;11 (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) cell lines, both of which displayed heightened sensitivity to USP7 inhibition [123 ]. Moreover, in the pursuit of targeting USP7 for MDM2 degradation, researchers have explored the application of Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras (PROTACs). CST967, a notable example, selectively degrades USP7 and induces apoptosis in USP7-dependent cancer cells. It is worth noting that USP7 inhibitors FT671 and XL188 served as initial compounds for the synthesis of CST967 [124 ]. Likewise, U7D-1, which is derived from the highly potent non-competitive USP7 inhibitor Compound 4 (IC50: 6 nM), has emerged as a PROTAC designed to degrade USP7. It demonstrated effective inhibition of cell growth in p53-mutated cancer cells, a context where conventional USP7 inhibitors exhibited no activity [125 ]. Recent studies have also unveiled other potent USP7 inhibitors, such as L55, a piperidinol derivative displaying remarkable nanomolar-level inhibitory activity against USP7 [126 ]. Furthermore, certain naturally-isolated compounds from marine sponges, including Sulawesin A (IC50 2.8 μM), Pyrrole alkaloid (IC50 3.8 μM), and Xestoquinone (IC50 0.13 μM), have been developed and demonstrated promising USP7 inhibitory activity [127–129 ]. Despite significant progress in developing USP7 inhibitors, several challenges remain. Many of these inhibitors lack selectivity and are only potent at low micromolar levels, with only a few reaching the nanomolar range. Even in selective USP7 inhibitors, cross-reactivity with other DUBs is common, complicating substrate identification and specificity. Furthermore, their limited solubility and metabolic properties restrict their assessment to cell-level experiments, with only a limited number undergoing in vivo testing. The accuracy of evaluation results is also hindered by the constrained screening techniques available. Future endeavors should prioritize the improvement of selectivity and potency through the design of novel compounds that target fresh allosteric binding sites to tackle these challenges. The establishment of co-crystal structures involving small molecules and the USP7 catalytic domain would be invaluable for the development of potent compounds. Additionally, the development of an accurate, highly efficient screening method is indispensable for the evaluation and advancement of novel USP7 inhibitors. 7 s and future perspectives The role of USP7 in regulating the p53 protein is complex and involves multiple variables, making it challenging to interpret. Initially, USP7 was identified for its tumor-suppressive role, particularly in relation to p53. In Small Cell Lung Carcinoma (SCLC), low levels of USP7 mRNA expression were correlated with reduced p53 immunostaining and increased cancer aggressiveness [130 ]. In vitro studies have shown that partial depletion of USP7 leads to decreased p53 levels [8 ]. Conversely, USP7 protein and mRNA levels are often elevated in multiple myeloma (MM) and other cancers, such as glioma, neuroblastoma, and ovarian cancer, associated with poor patient survival [98 ,107 ,131 ,132 ]. Following cancers, a higher level of USP7 may contribute to the stability of MDM2/MDMX, resulting in p53 degradation and promoting cancer progression. Therefore, it can be concluded that USP7-mediated regulation of p53 is highly dependent on the context and varies across different cancer types. Based on recent findings, it has been observed that mut-p53 follows similar signaling pathways as wt-p53, indicating that the factors responsible for maintaining the stability of wt-p53 may also contribute to the stability of mut-p53. Multiple factors, encompassing the loss of wild-type p53 (wt-p53) function, the acquired functions of mutant p53 (mut-p53), and the unique microenvironment within cancer cells, collectively exert a substantial influence on the stability and oncogenic potential of mut-p53. Nevertheless, inherent attributes of mut-p53, such as its distinctive conformation and its restricted capacity to activate p53 target genes, additionally contribute to its persistence within cancer cells. In this context, it is intriguing to consider the involvement of USP7 in regulating mut-p53. Therefore, it may be a fascinating, unresolved avenue in the p53-USP7 saga. title: Targeting the MYCN-MDM2 pathways for cancer therapy: Are they druggable?
abstract: Targeting oncogenes and their interactive partners is an effective approach to developing novel targeted therapies for cancer and other chronic diseases. We and others have long suggested the MDM2 oncogene being an excellent target for cancer therapy, based on its p53-dependent and -independent oncogenic activities in a variety of cancers. The MYC family proteins are transcription factors that also regulate diverse biological functions. Dysregulation of MYC, such as amplification of MYCN, is associated with tumorigenesis, especially for neuroblastoma. Although the general survival rate of neuroblastoma patients has significantly improved over the past few decades, high-risk neuroblastoma still presents a poor prognosis. Therefore, innovative and more potent therapeutic strategies are needed to eradicate these aggressive neoplasms. This review focuses on the oncogenic properties of MYCN and its molecular regulation and summarizes the major therapeutic strategies being developed based on preclinical findings. We also highlight the potential benefits of targeting both the MYCN and MDM2 oncogenes, providing preclinical evidence of the efficacy and safety of this approach. In conclusion, the development of effective small molecules that inhibit both MYCN and MDM2 represents a promising new strategy for the treatment of neuroblastoma and other cancers.
