HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 suppresses miR-22 to induce growth inhibition and apoptosis via p53-independent PTEN activation in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells Hui Jin a c Lifeng Liu a Weiping Deng a Yanhua Lu a Jianhui Tian b Hegeng Li b ⁎⁎ Jianwen Liu a ⁎ a State Key Laboratory of Bioreactor Engineering, Shanghai Key Laboratory of Chemical Biology, School of pharmacy, East China University of Science and Technology, Shanghai , China State Key Laboratory of Bioreactor Engineering, Shanghai Key Laboratory of Chemical Biology, School of pharmacy, East China University of Science and Technology Shanghai China b Department of Oncology, Longhua Hospital, Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, National Clinical Research Centre for Traditional Chinese Medicine and Oncology, Shanghai , China Department of Oncology, Longhua Hospital, Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, National Clinical Research Centre for Traditional Chinese Medicine and Oncology Shanghai China c School of Life Sciences and Technology, Tongji University, Shanghai , China School of Life Sciences and Technology, Tongji University Shanghai China ⁎ Corresponding author at: East China University of Science and Technology, #268, 130 Meilong Road, Shanghai , China. Tel.: +86 21 ; fax: +86 21 . ⁎⁎ Corresponding author. Here we report a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor named DWP0016, which exhibits anti-neuroblastoma potential in vitro . DWP0016 effectively inhibited proliferation of neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells at submicromolar levels but did not affect the growth of normal cells. Flowcytometry analysis showed DWP0016 arrested cell cycle at G1 phase and induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently. Western-blotting results showed DWP0016 induced significant increase of histone H3 acetylation in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. Molecular mechanistic studies suggested that DWP0016 activated p21Cip/WAF1 , p27/KIP1 and caspase-3, -9 which facilitated to contribute the cell cycle and apoptosis. Besides, DWP0016 activated tumor suppressor PTEN to inhibit the PI3K/Akt cell signal pathway. Intensive investigations showed down-regulation of miR-22 by DWP0016 stimulated the activity of PTEN promoter and then enhanced PTEN at both transcription and protein expression level. SiRNA silencing results suggested knockdown of PTEN sufficiently blocked cell growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells. Conclusively, our results showed DWP0016 was a promising candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with its PTEN and microRNA regulations mechanisms. Keywords HDAC inhibitor Apoptosis miR-22 PTEN PI3K/Akt pathway 1 Introduction Neuroblastomas are the most common solid brain tumor occurring in children, which accounts for 8–10% of all pediatric malignancies [1] . For more than 30 years, neuroblastoma has remained one of the most challenging malignant tumors for both clinicians and basic scientists though novel gene-regulation therapeutic approaches emerging [2] . Most neuroblastomas are initially chemo- and radiosensitive, but when recurrent, are resistant with 25% of stage 4 patients over 1 year of age being long term survivors. An important mechanism of intrinsic chemoresistance in many tumor cells is an abnormality in the p53 tumor suppressor gene pathway [3,4] . Previously several studies screening for p53 mutations have shown that p53 mutations in neuroblastoma tumors and cell lines are rare. Acquired p53 mutations in the treatment progress possibly determine multidrug sensitivity in neuroblastoma [5–9] . These studies suggest that targeting other genes beyond p53 maybe a novel therapeutic approach for effective neuroblastoma treatment. The tumor suppressor gene phosphatase and tensin homolog deleted on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is regarded as the most potential target for cancer treatment besides p53. Previous work has demonstrated several layers of crosstalk between p53 and PTEN, which twisted the PTEN-p53 tumor suppressor network [10–12] . PTEN plays a role not only in inducing cell cycle arrest and programming apoptosis, but also in other aspects of cell physiology, including the regulation of cell adhesion, for highly acidic substrates, migration, and differentiation. PTEN is down-regulated in many poorly differentiated cancers, including neuroblastoma [13] . Besides, PTEN inhibits PI3K/Akt cell signal pathway by counteracting with the action of PI3K through dephosphorylating the D-3 position of polyphosphoinositides [14] . PI3K/Akt pathway is commonly overactive reducing apoptosis and allowing proliferation in many cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as brain cancers [15] . Previous reports showed PI3K/Akt pathway involved in the biology of neuroblastoma and the chemotherapy-induced apoptosis in neuroblastoma [16,17] . However, the understanding about the regulations balance between p53, PTEN and PI3K/Akt pathway in the biology of neuroblastoma remained largely unknown. MicroRNAs are small 19–24 bp long non-coding RNAs which function primarily to down-regulate gene expression in all metazoan eukaryotes. The microRNAs specifically interact with target mRNAs through base pairing, which made miRNAs play important roles in the pathogenesis of different human diseases [18–20] . Increasing work reported regulations on microRNA to targets tumor genes were reasonable and practicable for carcinoma treatment, including lung cancer, colon cancer, and neuroblastoma [21–25] . A new microRNA-22 (miR-22) is screened out to directly bind to a specific site on PTEN 3′UTR, which resulting in PTEN down-regulation while suppression of miR-22 led to PTEN activation. Interestingly, other reports showed reverse s that over-expression of miR-22 was able to activate PTEN [26,27,28,29] . These debates suggest the complicated interactions between miR-22 and PTEN, which may facilitate to shed a light for PTEN regulations and thus cancer treatment. Histone deacetylases inhibitors (HDACi) emerge as the most potent anti-cancer agents in recent years. HDACi are a class of compounds that interfered with the function of histone deacetylases (HDACs) [30–32] . Inhibition of HDACs by HDACi results in histone hyper-acetylation, which lead to growth inhibition of carcinoma cells, cell cycle block, apoptosis in vitro and in vivo [33] . A variety of HDACis as potent cancer therapeutic agents have entered preclinical and clinical trials aimed at both solid and liquid tumors [34–36] . Companied with the prominent anti-tumor effects of HDACi, more and more new HDAC inhibitors are synthetized for better performance and more applications. Besides, detailed knowledge of mechanisms controlling proliferation and differentiation on HDAC regulations with HDAC inhibitor may lead to a better understanding for the treatment especially for malignancy such as neuroblastoma. In this study, we evaluated the antitumor potential in neuroblastoma of a synthesized HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 (Patent No. ). DWP0016 effectively inhibited the cell proliferation in neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y and other carcinoma cell lines. DWP0016 arrested cell cycle at G1 phase and induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells. Regulations on p21Cip/WAF1 , p27/KIP1 and caspase-3 and -9 are associated with the cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016. DWP0016 up-regulated the activity of PTEN promoter, transcription and protein expression level of PTEN in SH-SY5Y cells. The activation of PTEN by DWP0016 was attributed to the suppression of miR-22 and thus led to inhibition on PI3K/Akt pathway. These findings suggest that DWP0016 down-regulates miR-22 to activate PTEN, which contributes to the antitumor efficacy in neuroblastoma. Conclusively, DWP0016 is a potent candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with its PTEN activation mechanism. 2 Methods and materials 2.1 Chemicals DWP0016, {(E )-3-(2-benzyl-5-(2-(piperidin-1-yl) ethyl)-2,3,4,5-tetrahydro-1H -pyrido [4,3-b]indol-8-yl)-N -hydroxyacrylamide}, was shown in Fig. 1 . These results showed that both the activity of caspase-3 and caspase-9 were activated with DWP0016. Caspase-3 and caspase-9 activation involved in the apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells. 3.5 DWP0016 induce histone H3 hyper-acetylation in SH-SY5Y cells dose-dependently The protein expression of total histone H3 and acetylated-H3 in SH-SY5Y cells were investigated by performing Western blotting. As shown in Fig. 5 A , neither DWP0016 nor SAHA affected the expression of total histone H3. Noticeably, an ascending protein expression of acetylated-histone H3 were both observed in DWP0016 and SAHA-treated samples dose-dependently, which confirmed hyper-acetylation induction efficacy of DWP0016 and SAHA. The protein expression was more pronounced in DWP0016-treated samples. The densitometry results were consistent to the protein expression (Fig. 5 B). These results suggested that DWP0016 induced more remarkable histone-H3 acetylation in neuroblastoma cells than SAHA, which was consistent to the better proliferation inhibition in SH-SY5Y cells than SAHA. 3.6 DWP0016 activated PTEN to inhibit PI3K/Akt pathway in SH-SY5Y cells To assess whether DWP0016 affected the mRNA level and expression of PTEN and PI3K/Akt pathway, real-time PCR assay was performed to detect the mRNA level of PI3K, Akt and PTEN. The results suggested that DWP0016 did not affect the mRNA level of PI3K nor that of Akt, but significantly up regulated the mRNA level of PTEN in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 6 A) . At concentration of 1.0 μM, DWP0016 elevated the mRNA level of PTEN to18.38 fold to the untreated (P 0.05). In contrast, the cell viability without siRNA by the DWP0016 treated was 24.91% (P 0.05) (Fig. 7 C). Moreover, the total apoptosis was 5.02% with PTEN siRNA whereas the value was 48.49% (P < 0.001) without siRNA (Fig. 7 D). As the results shown (Fig. 7 E), at concentration of DWP0016 in 1.0 μM, the cell viability in SHSY5Y cells with p53 siRNA was 56.31% which made statistical difference to the control (P < 0.05). Meanwhile, the total apoptosis was 22.46% with p53 siRNA which also made statistical difference to the control (P < 0.001). These results exhibited that knock-down of p53 did not sufficiently block effects induced by DWP0016 treatment. Instead, knock-down of PTEN sufficiently blocked the cell growth inhibition, cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 treatment. In other words, p53-independent PTEN was required for the efficacy of DWP0016 and PTEN was a crucial target gene for DWP0016. 4 Discussion In this study, we evaluated a HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 inhibited the tumor growth of neuroblastoma in vitro . DWP0016 induced G1 phase cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in SH-SYS5Y cells, which were associated to regulations on p21Cip/WAF1 and p27kip1 and caspases-3 and -9. Down-regulation of miR-22 by DWP0016 activated PTEN in promoter, mRNA and protein expression level. As shown in Fig. 8 , DWP0016 up regulated PTEN to inhibit PI3K/Akt pathway and finally induced the growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells. Neuroblastomas are the most common brain tumor and characterized as a fatal malignancy tumor for children. Its clinical heterogeneity, from spontaneous regression in infants to relentless progression in older children, makes the effects of traditional chemotherapies are limited. Focusing on novel targets and approach enhanced the therapeutic effects for the treatments [2] while required chemo-resistant risk exists. Explorations on more safe and potent approaches make epigenetic regulation agents such as HDAC inhibitor be regarded as promising candidates for neuroblastoma treatments. Their efficacy has been widely recognized as Vorinostat (SAHA) in 2006 and Romidepsin (FK228) in 2009 which were separately licensed to treat CTCL [44] . Guided by the antitumor efficacy of HDAC inhibitor, different HDAC inhibitors are used to treat neuroblastoma [45,46] . However, the effects and involved molecular mechanisms remained largely unknown. The results (Fig. 2 A–E) showed HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 effectively inhibited the cell growth in 3 neuroblastoma cell lines (SK-N-SH, SH-SY5Y and IMR-32) and another 2 carcinoma cell lines (MKN-45 and HCT-8) dose dependently. The lowest IC50 was against SH-SY5Y cells which suggested the potential of DWP0016 in neuroblastoma treatments (Table 1 ). Importantly, the results indicated that DWP0016 did not induce significant cytotoxicity in normal cells (Fig. 2 F). The flow cytometry analysis suggested DWP0016 induced G1 cell cycle arrest and apoptosis dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 3 A–D). Molecular mechanisms studies showed DWP0016 up regulated the mRNA level and expressions level of p21Cip/WAF1 and p27kip1 dose-dependently, which contributed to G1 cell cycle arrest (Fig. 4 A and B). Caspases activity (Fig. 4 C) and cleaved PARP protein expression (Fig. 4 D) suggested the activation of caspase-3 and caspase-9 involved in the apoptosis caused with DWP0016 treatment. Both cell cycle arrest and apoptosis contributed the growth inhibition caused by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells, which made DWP0016 more potent. As HDAC inhibitor induced histone hyper-acetylation to exhibit anti-tumor efficacy and less side-effects, we detected the acetylation of histone H3 in SH-SY5Y cells. Previous reported showed DWP0016 was more effective to inhibit HDAC enzyme activity than SAHA in U251 glioblastoma cells [47] , which led the more obvious acetylated-H3 in DWP0016 treated groups than that of SAHA. Expectedly, the results showed DWP0016 induced much more remarkable acetylated-histone H3 in SH-SY5Y cells than SAHA (Fig. 5 A and B) as in U251 cells. These results are also consistent to previous reports about other HDAC inhibitors [37,48] . We notice that the viability of cells with DWP0016 at the concentration of 1.0 μM was not lower than that of cells with SAHA at the concentration of 5.0 μM though the expression of acetylated-H3 with DWP0016 was more makeable. In our conditions, it was enough for DWP0016 to induce hyper-acetylation of histone H3 in SH-SY5Y cells at the concentrations as indicated, which facilitated the growth inhibition. As doses became higher, other mechanisms might involve in the effects of HDAC inhibitors such as cell cycle arrest, apoptosis and other regulations beyond hyper-acetylation of histone H3. These need further investigations and the explorations were on our agenda. After all, all these results suggest HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 is a potent HDAC inhibitor to treat neuroblastoma with its proliferation inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induction efficacy. One paper examined the gene status of tumor suppressor PTEN in 106 tumors from patients with neuroblastoma and found PTEN was rarely mutated but 100% of tumors expressed PTEN protein [49] . Interestingly, we found both the mRNA level and protein expression of PTEN are up-regulated dose-dependently with DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 6 A and B). As activation of PTEN inhibited PI3K/Akt pathway, we found DWP0016 significantly down regulated the protein expression of p-PI3K and p-Akt. These results were consistent to studies with certain HDAC inhibitors about the regulations on PTEN and PI3K/Akt pathway in other carcinoma cells [50–52] . Previous reports showed promotion of PTEN-p53 physical association and the recruitment of the PTEN-p53 complex to the p53 binding sites in the PTEN promoter, leading to PTEN transcriptional activation [53,54] . Effective acetylation of histone H3 makes the structure of chromatin relatively loose and then facilitates gene transcription and expression [30,31] , which contributes to the molecular regulations of most HDAC inhibitor. Further investigations showed the protein expression of p53 was not affected with DWP0016 (Fig. 6 B), regardless of the wild-type p53 status in SH-SY5Y cells. The effects on p53 were consistent to the effects with DWP0016 in another wild-type p53 harboring glioblastoma cell line U-87 reported but not U251 cells by us [37,47] . However, DWP0016 induced apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells but not in U-87 cells. Considering the PTEN mutant status in U-87 cells [55] but PTEN wild-type status in SH-SY5Y cells, the differences might due to PTEN status between cell lines. Besides, p53-independent PTEN activation induced by DWP0016 attenuated the required chemo-resistant possibility due to effects on p53. Our novel findings suggest that activating PTEN is practicable to exhibit antitumor potential in neuroblastoma with a HDAC inhibitor such as DWP0016. Intensive investigations suggested DWP0016 activated the activity of PTEN promoter dose-dependently (Fig. 6 C) by performing a dual-luciferases report assay. Interestingly, the activity of PTEN promoter with DWP0016 treatment of 4 μM was lower than that of 2 μM though still higher than the control (Fig. 6 C). In our conditions, DWP0016 activated PTEN expression at certain concentrations (<2 μM) which was enough sensitive to SH-SY5Y cells and other tumor cell lines listed in this research. These observations indicated the possibility that higher concentration of DWP0016 might exhibit different effects on PTEN which remained another issue. Previous studies reported the activity of PTEN promoter could be regulated by multiple factors besides p53 such as Egr-1 [56] , Tat [57] , and CBF-1 [58] etc . Recent reports show epigenetic regulations such as methylation and microRNAs also play important roles in the regulations on PTEN promoter. Accumulating evidence reveals that microRNAs involved in the regulations of PTEN, which shed a light in PTEN regulations. According to the studies, PTEN was found to be regulated by multiple miRs including miR-21 [59] , miR-494 [60] , miR-222 [61] , miR-214 [62] and 26a [63] in different reports. Though multiple miRNAs could regulate PTEN expression, the regulations between gene-miRNA may be specific and depend on diverse upstream signaling pathways. miR-22 is a novel micro-oncogene and downregulates PTEN levels acting directly through a specific site on PTEN 3′UTR, which facilitated to associate with tumor suppression function of PTEN. The reason why PTEN was affected by miR-22 was due to an important regulatory element in their promoters. Reversely, one paper showed miR-22 is a tumor-suppressing microRNA and overexpression of miR-22 activated PTEN signaling [26–29] . The controversial reports about PTEN and miR-22 need more identification, especially for cancer treatments. We investigated miR-22 level in DWP0016-treated SH-SY5Y cells and found DWP0016 down-regulated the level of miR-22 dose-dependently (Fig. 6 E). As shown in Fig. 6 F and G, pre-miR-22 down-regulated the mRNA level and protein expression of PTEN. Regardless the down-regulation of PTEN with pre-miR-22, DWP0016 up-regulated the mRNA level and protein expression of PTEN (Fig. 6 F and G). Then we performed a siRNA assay to identify the role of PTEN in DWP0016-treated SH-SY5Y cells. As the siRNA results shown in Fig. 7 A–F, silencing PTEN but not p53 sufficiently blocked the cell growth inhibition, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis induced by DWP0016 in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings suggested that PTEN was required for the antitumor efficacy of DWP0016. There are reports about other HDAC inhibitors such as trichostatin A (TSA) affected microRNA expression to facilitate apoptosis in different carcinoma cells especially in chemoresistant tumor cells [64–66] . Our studies first report that HDAC inhibitor DWP0016 was able to down-regulate miR-22 in neuroblastoma. In this study, our novel findings identified miR-22 suppressed PTEN in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. Besides, associated to the suppression of miR-22 with PTEN, our studies suggested that DWP0016 suppressed miR-22 to activate PTEN in SH-SY5Y cells, which highlighted the unique mechanisms of DWP0016. How DWP0016 down-regulated miR-22 remained unknown. Further studies about DWP0016 may shed more light on these subjects. In conclusion, we reported that DWP0016 induced tumor growth inhibition in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. DWP0016 arrested cell cycle, induced apoptosis dose-dependently in SH-SY5Y cells. Suppression of miR-22 by DWP0016 activated PTEN promoter activity, transcription and protein expression, which inhibited PI3K/Akt pathway. Our findings suggest DWP0016 is a promising antitumor candidate for neuroblastoma treatment with PTEN and microRNA regulations. title: Chemotherapy-Induced Apoptosis in a Transgenic Model of Neuroblastoma Proceeds Through p53 Induction
abstract: Chemoresistance in neuroblastoma is a significant issue complicating treatment of this common pediatric solid tumor. MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas are infrequently mutated at p53 and are chemosensitive at diagnosis but acquire p53 mutations and chemoresistance with relapse. Paradoxically, Myc-driven transformation is thought to require apoptotic blockade. We used the TH-MYCN transgenic murine model to examine the role of p53-driven apoptosis on neuroblastoma tumorigenesis and the response to chemotherapy. Tumors formed with high penetrance and low latency in p53-haploinsufficient TH-MYCN mice. Cyclophosphamide (CPM) induced a complete remission in p53 wild type TH-MYCN tumors, mirroring the sensitivity of childhood neuroblastoma to this agent. Treated tumors showed a prominent proliferation block, induction of p53 protein, and massive apoptosis proceeding through induction of the Bcl-2 homology domain-3-only proteins PUMA and Bim, leading to the activation of Bax and cleavage of caspase-3 and -9. Apoptosis induced by CPM was reduced in p53-haploinsufficient tumors. Treatment of MYCN-expressing human neuroblastoma cell lines with CPM induced apoptosis that was suppressible by siRNA to p53. Taken together, the results indicate that the p53 pathway plays a significant role in opposing MYCN-driven oncogenesis in a mouse model of neuroblastoma and that basal inactivation of the pathway is achieved in progressing tumors. This, in explains the striking sensitivity of such tumors to chemotoxic agents that induce p53-dependent apoptosis and is consistent with clinical observations that therapy-associated mutations in p53 are a likely contributor to the biology of tumors at relapse and secondarily mediate resistance to therapy.

Weiss*,†,§,# *Department of Pediatrics, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA , USA; †Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA , USA; ‡Paediatric Oncology Group, The Institute of Cancer Research, Sutton, Surrey, SM2 5NG, UK; §Department of Neurology, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA , USA; ¶Department of Pathology, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA , USA; #Department of Neurological Surgery and The Brain Tumor Research Center, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA , USA Abstract Chemoresistance in neuroblastoma is a significant issue complicating treatment of this common pediatric solid tumor. MYCN-amplified neuroblastomas are infrequently mutated at p53 and are chemosensitive at diagnosis but acquire p53 mutations and chemoresistance with relapse. Paradoxically, Myc-driven transformation is thought to require apoptotic blockade. We used the TH-MYCN transgenic murine model to examine the role of p53-driven apop­tosis on neuroblastoma tumorigenesis and the response to chemotherapy. Tumors formed with high penetrance and low latency in p53-haploinsufficient TH-MYCN mice. Cyclophosphamide (CPM) induced a complete remission in p53 wild type TH-MYCN tumors, mirroring the sensitivity of childhood neuroblastoma to this agent. Treated tumors showed a prominent proliferation block, induction of p53 protein, and massive apoptosis proceeding through induc­tion of the Bcl-2 homology domain-3–only proteins PUMA and Bim, leading to the activation of Bax and cleavage of caspase-3 and -9. Apoptosis induced by CPM was reduced in p53-haploinsufficient tumors. Treatment of MYCN­expressing human neuroblastoma cell lines with CPM induced apoptosis that was suppressible by siRNA to p53. Taken together, the results indicate that the p53 pathway plays a significant role in opposing MYCN-driven oncogene­sis in a mouse model of neuroblastoma and that basal inactivation of the pathway is achieved in progressing tumors. This, in explains the striking sensitivity of such tumors to chemotoxic agents that induce p53-dependent apop­tosis and is consistent with clinical observations that therapy-associated mutations in p53 are a likely contributor to the biology of tumors at relapse and secondarily mediate resistance to therapy. Received 11 July 2008; Revised 13 August 2008; Accepted 14 August 2008 Copyright 00 DOI Introduction Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of child­hood [1]. The proto-oncogene MYCN is amplified in one third of neuroblastomas and is associated with high-risk disease and poor sur­vival [1–5]. The ability of Myc proteins to induce malignant transfor­mation is limited by coordinate induction of both proliferation and apoptosis [6–8]. Consequently, mutations of p53 are common in sev­eral Myc-driven malignancies at diagnosis and enhance oncogenesis. In neuroblastoma, genetic defects in the p53 pathway function (mutation in p53 or p14ARF, amplification of MDM2) are rare at di­agnosis but are present in cell lines established from patients treated with prolonged therapy [9–12]. In the absence of such mutations, am­plification of MYCN in newly diagnosed neuroblastomas is typically associated with epigenetic abnormalities that impair apoptosis: silenc­ing of caspase-8 or overexpression of the antiapoptotic proteins Bcl-2 and survivin [13–15]. These events are independently associated with poor outcome in neuroblastoma and represent potential mechanisms contributing to malignant progression [13,15,16]. Despite such defects in apoptotic signaling, newly diagnosed neuro­blastoma tumors typically respond to chemotherapeutics such as cyclo­phosphamide (CPM) irrespective of risk group, suggesting that epigenetic regulation of apoptotic pathways is either insufficient to block apoptosis in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy or is not initially present at diagnosis [17,18]. Because virtually all patients respond to initial therapy, outcome in this disease is mainly determined by the like­lihood of relapse, with high-risk patients (including tumors that show amplification of MYCN ) frequently relapsing with drug-resistant tu­mors [10,19]. The TH-MYCN model shows that coordinate mutation of p53 is not required for MYCN-driven oncogenesis in neuroblastoma, mirroring the situation in human high-risk tumors. It follows that apoptosis is functionally suppressed by other means. However, this presents a paradox in that MYCN-driven murine neuroblastomas retain exquisite sensitivity to chemotherapeutics, which exert their effects through induction of apoptosis. To examine this question, we sought to determine whether the p53 pathway was active or in­active in TH-MYCN and whether induction of the pathway occurred in response to chemotherapy. TH-MYCN is a native neuroblastoma model in which tumorigene­sis is driven by targeted expression of a TH-MYCN transgene in the neural crest of transgenic mice [20]. These animals develop an aggres­sive malignancy that is morphologically, genetically, and clinically sim­ilar to human high-risk MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma [21,22]. We show that p53 haploinsufficiency enhances the effect of MYCN-driven transformation in neuroblastoma, that basal p53 pathway function and apoptosis are suppressed in such tumors (in contrast to in vitro observations), that haploinsufficiency amplifies the effect of MYCN on transformation in neuroblastoma, and that the chemoresponse of effective agents such as CPM requires intact p53-driven apopto­sis. Mechanistically, CPM induces p53 and activates a variety of p53 targets critical to apoptosis, including PUMA, Bim, Bax, caspase-3, caspase-9, and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP). The in vivo re­sponse of TH-MYCN–driven tumors to CPM is similar to that ob­served in cultured human cell lines treated with CPM. In three cell lines with equivalent levels of p53 protein but increasing levels of Mycn, the apoptotic response to CPM correlated with the induction of p53 and could be blocked by siRNA to p53. Taken together, these data document the activity in murine tu­mors of a frontline chemotherapeutic agent used in children with newly diagnosed neuroblastoma and add to evidence validating mice transgenic for TH-MYCN as a preclinical platform for developmental therapeutics. Furthermore, these observations highlight the utility of mice transgenic for TH-MYCN as a preclinical model in which to delineate the kinetics and details of apoptotic signaling in response to CPM. The induction and functional activation of p53 in these tumors reinforce the importance of p53 signaling in the therapeutic response to cytotoxic chemotherapy. These observations are also con­sistent with clinical data that cytotoxic chemotherapy selects for loss of p53 function, that recurrence in neuroblastoma is subsequently driven by p53 mutation, and that p53 mutation in relapsed tumors contributes secondarily to therapeutic resistance [10,23,24]. Materials and Methods Cell Culture and Treatments SHEP, SK-N-SH, SH-SY5Y, and Kelly neuroblastoma cell lines were obtained from the University of California at San Francisco. Cells were grown in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium with 10% FBS at 37°C. 4-Hydroxyperocyclophosphamide (4OH-CPM) was obtained from Susan Ludeman (University of North Carolina) and was dissolved at 20 mg/ml in water. For in vivo therapy, CPM from the University of California at San Francisco Clinical Pharmacy was dissolved at 1 mg/ml. Proliferation and Apoptosis Assays Cell growth and proliferation were assessed by soluble tetrazolium (WST-1; Roche, Indianapolis, IN). Necrosis and apoptosis were assessed using a Cell Death Detection ELISA (Roche) that detects intracellular or released nucleosomal H2b DNA. Values were cor­rected for vehicle (DMSO). Cells were plated and assayed at 6 to 24 hours using a Synergy HT-1 spectrophotometer (Biotek, Winooski, VT). Percent toxicity was standardized using Triton X-100 as a positive control (0-100 mM). Immunoblot Analysis and Antibodies Cells were suspended in nondenaturing lysis buffer (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA) with 0.5% SDS. Lysates were sonicated and cleared at 14,000g at 4°C. Protein content was assayed by the BCA method (Pierce, Rockford, IL), and 20 to 40 µgofprotein was analyzed on 4% to 12% gradient denaturing gels (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). Membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with pri­mary antibodies [cleaved caspase-3 (9664; Cell Signaling Technology), caspase-9 (9508; Cell Signaling Technology), p53 (9282; Cell Signal­ing Technology), Bim (4582; Cell Signaling Technology), Bax (2772; Cell Signaling Technology), PARP (9542; Cell Signaling Technology), PUMA (4976; Cell Signaling Technology), and ß-tubulin (05-661; Upstate, Billerica, MA)] and visualized using HRP-conjugated second­ary antibodies (Calbiochem, Gibbstown, NJ) and ECL-Plus reagents. Immunohistochemistry For frozen sections, mice were killed after therapy, and tumors were embedded in Tissue-Tex O.C.T. compound (Sakura, Torrance, CA), cooled at -80°C (24 hours), sectioned at 4-µmthickness, mounted on Superfrost slides (Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA), and placed in 70% ethanol (1 hour at 4°C). Slides were washed three times with wash buffer (Dako, Carpinteria, CA), treated with 3% hydrogen peroxide (for 10 minutes), rewashed, blocked with casein (for 10 minutes), and incubated with caspase-3 antibody (CST 9664) at a dilution of 1:100 at room temperature in a humidi­fied chamber (for 2 hours). Slides were rewashed three times and in­cubated with rabbit Envision+ secondary antibody (Dako) at room temperature in a humidified chamber (for 30 minutes) treated with Dako DAB+ complex (for 4 minutes), rinsed with water, counter­stained with Gills modified hematoxylin (American Master Tech, Lodi, CA), dehydrated, and mounted for analysis. Paraffin-embedded tissues were cut and mounted, deparaffinized with xylene through graded alcohol to water, and then placed in PBS. Heat-induced epi­tope retrieval was performed at 120°C in citrate buffer at pH 6.0, fol­lowed by treatment in 3% peroxide (for 20 minutes). Washing and antibody incubations were as previously mentioned. Ki-67 staining in paraffinized sections was performed using a Ki-67 rat primary anti­body (M7249; Dako) in a 3-hour incubation followed by process­ing as previously mentioned. Development was with streptavidin HRP (Amersham, Piscataway, NJ) at a dilution of 1:100 for 1 hour at room temperature. In Vivo Therapy in TH-MYCN Transgenic Mice TH-MYCN mice were maintained in hemizygotic matings as pre­viously described [20]. Hemizygous TH-MYCN were serially crossed to p53+/- mice (FVBN) [25] and E2F1-luciferase mice (FVBN) [26] for more than four generations to re-establish tumor penetrance in the 129X1/SvJ strain. A similar approach was used in luciferase crosses. For the analysis of the in vivo effects of CPM on tumor growth in mice transgenic for TH-MYCN (in strain 129X1/SvJ), a tumor intervention design was implemented. The assay end point was tumor mass. In par­allel experiments, tumor response and progression were confirmed using luciferase bioimaging of TH-MYCN/E2F1-Luc doubly trans­genic animals, in which a luciferase signal is emitted from proliferating tumor tissue and is a surrogate indicator of Mycn activity. Animals (seven per arm) with palpable tumors (approximately 60 days of life) were treated three times per week with intraperitoneal injections of CPM (150 mg/kg in 100 µl of saline) or vehicle (saline) and were then killed. In parallel, animals (three per arm) were followed by noninvasive imaging, using the Xenogen IVIS Lumina system (Caliper Life Sciences, Hopkinton, MA) with a background bioluminescence setting of 38,000 photons/sec per square centimeters. At sacrifice, tumors were imaged, excised, measured, weighed, and snap-frozen for further analysis. Lysates were prepared for immunoblot analysis as pre­viously mentioned, except that tumors were initially homogenized in TBS with protease inhibitors (Compleat; Roche, Inc.) before lysis. Significance analysis was performed using the Student’s t test. All ani­mals were handled in accordance with institutional guidelines for safe and ethical treatment of mice. Results Effect of p53 Heterozygosity on Neuroblastoma Tumor Formation in Mice Transgenic for TH-MYCN Given the critical role of p53 in regulating myc-driven onco­genesis, we sought to evaluate induction of apoptosis by p53 in spontaneously growing neuroblastoma tumors originating within a native murine background. We therefore used the well-characterized TH-MYCN neuroblastoma model in which tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)–mediated overexpression of MYCN is targeted to the periph­eral neural crest [20]. This model faithfully recapitulates high-risk human neuroblastoma tumorigenesis by all major clinicopathologic criteria. To evaluate the effect of p53 dysfunction on TH-MYCN– driven neuroblastoma tumor formation, we introduced TH-MYCN into a p53-deficient background by serial crosses against animals with an inactivated germ line p53 allele [25]. Tumors arose in doubly transgenic animals with higher penetrance and reduced latency (Figure 1A). The initial anatomic appearance of these tumors was similar to that of p53 wild type TH-MYCN tumors (Figure 1B), but end-stage tumors were larger and were characterized by a higher density of proliferating neuroblasts and lower levels of apoptosis and necrosis on histologic analysis (Figure 1, C and D). Taken together, the data imply that, in neuroblastoma tumor progression, inactiva­tion of p53 could enhance MYCN oncogenicity, at least in part by decoupling the growth-stimulatory activity of MYCN from its ability to concurrently drive apoptosis. Cyclophosphamide Inhibits Tumor Proliferation and Stimulates Apoptosis In Vivo To analyze the effect of CPM on apoptosis, necrosis, and prolifera­tion, we treated a cohort of transgenic animals with early, established tumors, sacrificing animals at several time points within 24 hours of CPM treatment. Tumors showed no changes in vascularity (data not shown) and exhibited no obvious cellular or structural changes (observable apoptosis or necrosis) in response to CPM treatment (Fig­ure W1, A–C). In vehicle-treated tumors, immunoreactivity for the proliferation marker Ki-67 was positive in most nuclei (Figure 3, A and B). In response to CPM, Ki-67 labeling decreased dramatically even by 24 hours (Figure 3C). Whereas control tumors had negligible staining for the apoptosis marker cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 3D), high levels of cleaved caspase-3 were observed 3 and 6 hours after treatment with CPM (Figure 3, E and F ). A wave of apoptosis throughout the tumor was demonstrated at low power (Figure 3, H–J ), with maximal staining visible at 6 hours after treatment. At 24 hours, apoptotic stain­ing was associated with foci of necrosis (Figure 3J, inset). Significantly, levels of apoptosis induced by similar treatment of p53-haplodeficient tumors with CPM were minimal, as assessed by immunostaining for cleaved caspase-3 (Figure W2). No significant differences in apoptosis were seen by immunohistologic analysis in vehicle-treated p53+/- versus p53+/+ tumors (data not shown). Apoptosis in Tumors Treated with Cytotoxic Chemotherapy Is Driven by p53 To evaluate apoptotic signaling in response to CPM, we treated a cohort of early tumor-bearing transgenic animals and assessed levels of key apoptotic proteins by immunoblot (Figure 4A). In contrast to basal apoptotic activity detectable by immunoblot analysis of cul­tured neuroblastoma cell lines, activation of the p53 pathway and caspase-3 cleavage were minimal in vehicle-treated tumors, consistent with the low-level caspase-3 staining seen in Figure 4. Rapid induc­tion of p53 was observed at 3 hours after treatment with CPM, with a peak at 6 hours after treatment (Figure 4A). Cleaved caspase-3 and -9 were maximal at 6 hours after treatment and were sustained dur­ing a 12-hour period. These data indicate that basal apoptotic activity in spontaneously progressing TH-MYCN neuroblastomas is minimal but that p53-driven apoptosis is intact and can be strongly induced in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy. CPM Treatment of Murine Neuroblastoma Activates Apoptosis PUMA and Bim are Bcl-2 homology 3 (BH3)–only proteins, proapoptotic components of the mitochondrial cell death pathway, and are critical effectors of p53-induced apoptosis in Myc protein– driven tumors [27]. In response to CPM treatment, PUMA was strongly induced in vivo, peaking at 3 hours and dissipating by 12 hours (Figure 4A). Bax, a downstream target of PUMA and a criti­cal effector of myc-induced mitochondrial apoptosis, was strongly expressed (Figure 4B). Bim, a BH3-only protein necessary for apop­tosis in myc-driven lymphoma, was induced prominently. Cleavage of caspases-3 and -9 (Figure 4A)and PARP (Figure4B) occurred concurrently, indicating high levels of apoptosis. Taken together, these findings indicate that the proapoptotic effect of CPM proceeds through the intrinsic p53 regulatory pathway of BH3 proteins, im­plicating PUMA, Bax, and Bim as key effectors of p53 function in primary murine neuroblastoma tumors. Discussion To our knowledge, this study is the first in vivo demonstration of the importance of intact p53 function to neuroblastoma tumor pro­gression and chemoresponsiveness. In this MYCN-driven malignancy, the proliferative and apoptotic functions of MYCN are effectively uncoupled by functional suppression of p53-induced apoptosis (in the absence of p53 mutation). Furthermore, any coexistent apoptotic defects required for transformation by MYCN are insufficient to block the apoptotic effect induced by cytotoxic chemotherapy. Mu­tation at p53 is not generally observed in neuroblastoma tumors at diagnosis; however, epigenetic alterations (including silencing of caspase-8, increased levels of survivin and Bcl2, and cytoplasmic sequestration of p53) likely contribute to malignant progression [13,15,29]. Although these epigenetic abnormalities may underlie some relative chemoresistance, our data are consistent with observa­tions in other tumor types suggesting that these abnormalities spare intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic signaling, which can drive apopto­sis in response to cytotoxic chemotherapy. Cyclophosphamide, a first-line agent in children with newly di­agnosed neuroblastoma, is active in murine neuroblastoma. Baseline apoptosis in spontaneously progressing TH-MYCN tumors is sup­pressed, and activation of such proteins is not detectable by immuno­blot analysis, in contrast to observations in cultured neuroblastoma tumor cell lines in vitro. Cyclophosphamide treatment induces mas­sive apoptosis proceeding through activation of p53 and the down­stream Bcl-2-homology domain-3 (BH3) proteins, PUMA and Bim, indicating that apoptosis proceeds through mitochondrial-dependent pathways. Bax, a known effector of apoptosis in murine lymphoma, is also strongly induced [30]. PUMA, Bim, and Bax are all key effec­tors of p53-induced apoptosis, and alterations in PUMA expression modulate the phenotype of c-myc–driven tumors in genetically engi­neered mouse models of hematopoietic malignances [31]. PUMA complexes directly with p53, linking nuclear and cytosolic p53 frac­tions, and is required for induction of apoptosis by nuclear p53 [32]. Impaired p53 signaling likely enhances the oncogenic activity of MYCN in neuroblastoma [10–12,33,34] and probably contributes to relapse as additional (mutational) defects in this pathway are ac­quired with genotoxic therapy. These studies help to clarify observa­tions in cell lines from human neuroblastoma, in which acquisition of mutations in p53 occurred in cell lines established from relapsed tumors [11,24,33]. Collectively, our murine data are in agreement with human cell line data generated here and published by others, suggesting that cytotoxic drugs drive relapse by selecting for muta­tions in p53 or in the p53 pathway. We are currently generating mice transgenic for TH-MYCN that are inducibly dysfunctional at p53 and are backcrossing them into the penetrant 129/SvJ strain to de­termine the utility of these animals as a model for drug-resistant high-risk neuroblastoma at relapse. Belmont, Sutton, Surrey, SM2 5NG, UK. Chemoresistance in neuroblastoma is a significant issue complicating treatment of this common pediatric solid tumor. MYCN -amplified neuroblastomas are infrequently mutated at p53 and are chemosensitive at diagnosis but acquire p53 mutations and chemoresistance with relapse. Paradoxically, Myc-driven transformation is thought to require apoptotic blockade. We used the TH-MYCN transgenic murine model to examine the role of p53-driven apoptosis on neuroblastoma tumorigenesis and the response to chemotherapy. Tumors formed with high penetrance and low latency in p53 -haploinsufficient TH-MYCN mice. Cyclophosphamide (CPM) induced a complete remission in p53 wild type TH-MYCN tumors, mirroring the sensitivity of childhood neuroblastoma to this agent. Treated tumors showed a prominent proliferation block, induction of p53 protein, and massive apoptosis proceeding through induction of the Bcl-2 homology domain-3-only proteins PUMA and Bim, leading to the activation of Bax and cleavage of caspase-3 and -9. Apoptosis induced by CPM was reduced in p53 -haploinsufficient tumors. Treatment of MYCN-expressing human neuroblastoma cell lines with CPM induced apoptosis that was suppressible by siRNA to p53. Taken together, the results indicate that the p53 pathway plays a significant role in opposing MYCN -driven oncogenesis in a mouse model of neuroblastoma and that basal inactivation of the pathway is achieved in progressing tumors. This, in explains the striking sensitivity of such tumors to chemotoxic agents that induce p53-dependent apoptosis and is consistent with clinical observations that therapy-associated mutations in p53 are a likely contributor to the biology of tumors at relapse and secondarily mediate resistance to therapy. title: Streptococcus pneumoniae ClpP protease induces apoptosis via caspase-independent pathway in human neuroblastoma cells: Cytoplasmic relocalization of p53
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes the most severe form of the bacterial meningitis which is the major cause of bacterial meningitis. Virulence factors produced by S. pneumoniae have been known to contribute significantly to the disease process. ClpP protease (ClpP) which is essential for virulence and survival under stress conditions in S. pneumoniae was examined for the ability to induce apoptosis and the mechanism of the induction of apoptosis in human neuron-like cells, SK-N-SH neuroblastoma cells. ClpP inhibited cell growth and induced apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells. Treatment with ClpP resulted in hypodiploid DNA contents, increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The release of cytochrome c from mitochondria into the cytosol, which is an initiator of the activation of caspase cascades, was not observed in ClpP-treated cells. In addition, pretreatment with Z-Val–Ala–Asp–fluoromethylketone (Z-VAD-fmk), a broad spectrum caspase inhibitor, could not rescue apoptotic cells from ClpP toxicity. Coincidently, caspase-3 and -8 activation and cleavage of PARP were not detected. Moreover, caspase independent apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) was released from mitochondria and translocated to the nucleus in response to ClpP. We also found that ClpP treatment resulted in the increase of p53 activity and cytoplasmic p53 levels were increased by ClpP, suggesting that functional activation of p53 is intact despite increased cytoplasmic accumulation. Taken together, these data suggest that ClpP contributes to neuronal damage in meningitis and provide further insight into the mechanisms underlying action of pneumococcal virulence factors during bacterial pathogenesis.

Data are the means ± SEM from three separate experiments with quintuplicate cultures. *p 95% pure by SDS-PAGE and staining with Coomassie brilliant blue R-250 (data not shown). 2.3 Cell proliferation assay SK-N-SH human neuroblastoma cells were seeded at a concentration of 5 × 104 cells/well in 96-well tissue culture plates (Nunc, Denmark) and incubated with different concentrations of ClpP (1–6 μg/ml) for different time period. After treatment, cell viability was assessed by incubating the cells with 25 μg/ml of MTT (Sigma, St. Louis, MO) for another 4 h. Then, the MTT-formazan produced by viable cells was dissolved in Dimethyl sulfoxide and a Molecular device microplate reader (Menlo Park, CA) was used to measure absorbance at 560 nm and IC50 value was assessed by Bliss method. The blank control contained cell culture medium only and the absorbance of untreated cultures was set at 100%. At least three independent experiments were performed. 2.4 Determination of apoptosis by annexin V/PI staining analysis Quantitative analysis of apoptotic cells with or without treatment of ClpP was done by using the annexin V-FITC/propidium iodine (PI) apoptosis detection kit (BD Pharmingen™, San Diego, CA, USA) following the manufacturer's protocol. After treatment, the cells were harvested by trypsinization, washed with ice-cold PBS, and suspended in binding buffer at a density of 1 × 106 cells/ml. Next, the cell suspension was stained with Annexin V and PI and analyzed by flow cytometry (Becton–Dickinson Biosciences, Drive Franklin Lakes, USA). Alternatively, PI staining of DNA was used to analyze the sub-G1 region by flow cytometry. For PI staining, cells were washed twice with PBS and fixed with 70% ethanol for at least 30 min at 4 °C. Cells were then washed twice with PBS and resuspended in 50 μl of a 100 U/mL RNAse-A solution (Boehringer Mannheim) and 20 μl PI (0.1 mg/ml) per 1 × 105 cells for 30 min at room temperature in the dark and kept at 4 °C until flow cytometry acquisition. In some experiments, inhibitor of caspase (Z-VAD-fmk) was included along with ClpP. 2.5 Caspase assays Cells were cultured in the presence or absence of ClpP, then harvested at 16 h. ClpP-treated and nontreated control cells were lysed and their caspase-3 and caspase-8 activities were determined using the BIOMOL Quantizyme Assay kit (Plymouth Meeting, PA) according to the manufacture's instructions. 2.6 Measurement of the mitochondrial membrane potential The mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) was determined using MitoTracker Red (Molecular Probes, Eugene, Oregon). The SK-N-SH cells (5 × 105 cells) were seeded overnight in 6-well tissue culture plates and treated with various concentrations of ClpP for 16 h. The MitoTracker Red CMXRos was added to cells at 100 nM final concentration. The cells were incubated for 15 min at 37 °C, washed with PBS, and fixed in 3% paraformaldehyde. After washing and centrifuging, the cell pellets were suspended with D-PBS buffer. The changes in MMP, as an intracellular red fluorescent intensity, were analyzed by flow cytometry. 2.7 Measurement of reactive oxygen species Endogenous amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were measured by a fluorometric assay with CMH2 -DCFDA, ROS sensitive dye, was used to evaluate the intracellular ROS level. The SK-N-SH cells were treated with various concentrations of ClpP for 16 h to determine the ROS level before severe cell death. The cells were then stained with 5 μM CMH2 -DCFDA for 15 min. After collecting the cells, the intracellular ROS level was measured by flow cytometry. At least 10,000 cells were analyzed. The level of intracellular ROS is expressed as a percentage of the untreated control. 2.8 Western blot analysis Control and ClpP-treated cells were harvested and lysed with cold lysis buffer. In some experiments, inhibitor of caspase (Z-VAD-fmk) was included along with ClpP. The cells were washed twice in PBS and suspended in 70 μl of Buffer A [10 mM HEPES (pH 7.9), 1.5 mM MgCl2 , 10 mM KCl, 0.5 mM DTT, 0.5 mM PMSF and Protease Inhibitor Cocktail] and incubated on ice. After 15 min, 0.5% Nonidet P-40 was added to lyse the cells, which were vortexed for 10 s. Then, the nuclear pellet was obtained after centrifuging twice at 500 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. The nuclear pellet was resuspended in Buffer A, sonicated 2 × 10 s, and stored at −70 °C until used. The supernatants were combined and further centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 30 min at 4 °C, and the resultant mitochondrial pellets were suspended in Buffer A, sonicated, and stored at −70 °C until used. The supernatant from the previous step was further centrifuged at 100,000 × g for 1 h at 4 °C to obtain cytoplasmic S100 fraction. S100 fraction was stored at −70 °C until used. Protein concentration was determined by using the Bio-Rad protein assay (Bio-Rad Lab, Hercules, CA) with BSA as the standard. Subcellular fractions were solubilized in Laemmli sample buffer and separated by SDS-polyacrylamide gel. The fractionated proteins were electrophoretically transferred to an immobilon polyvinylidene difuride membrane (Amersham, Arlington heights, IL) and probed with the appropriate antibodies. The blots were developed using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit (Amersham). In all immunoblotting experiments, the blots were reprobed with an anti-β-actin, lamin A or cox-VI antibodies as controls for the protein loading. 2.9 Immunofluorescence The translocation of AIF or p53 proteins in ClpP-treated SK-N-SH cells was determined by immunofluorescence microscopy. SK-N-SH cells, which were grown on 22-mm diameter glass coverslips, were treated with ClpP. Cells were washed in PBS and fixed with 3.7% formaldehyde in PBS for 15 min at room temperature, and washed in PBS. The ice-cold methanol was added to the cells and cells were incubated at −20 °C for 10 min, and washed in PBS. They were permeabilized with 1% BSA/0.2% Triton X-100/PBS for 1 h before incubation with rabbit anti-AIF antibody (1:50 dilution) for 16 h at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. After three washes in PBS, cells were incubated with FITC-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Nuclei stain was then done with 10 mM Hoechst for 10 min at room temperature. Cells were washed thoroughly, and samples were mounted with glycerol/PBS (4:1) and observed under a fluorescence microscope (BX51-Olympus Optical). 2.10 Statistical analysis Each result is reported as means ± S.E.M. One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance among groups, after which the modified t test with the Bonferroni correction was used for comparison between individual groups. The significant values are represented by an asterisk (*p < 0.05). 3 Results 3.1 Effects of ClpP on cell growth We examined the anti-proliferative effect of ClpP on human neuroblastoma cell line, SK-N-SH cells, by exposing them to different concentrations of ClpP for 0–16 h. Cell viability was determined by MTT assay. When neuroblastoma cells were exposed to ClpP (1–6 μg/ml), the growth of cell was inhibited in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Fig. 1 ). The dose selection for the present experiments was based on the results of preliminary experiment (data not shown). The IC50 at 16 h exposure of ClpP were 6.34 μg/ml. In subsequent experiments cells were treated at 6 μg/ml for 16 h. 3.2 Flow cytometric quantification of apoptosis Flow cytometric measurement was used to quantify the extent of apoptosis. Annexin-V staining combined with PI staining was performed in control cells and cells treated with indicated concentrations of ClpP for 16 h and then analyzed by flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. 2 A, there was significant difference between untreated control group and ClpP–treated groups in apoptosis rate (%) of SK-N-SH cells. Treatment with ClpP (6 μg/ml) for 16 h significantly increased this apoptotic cell population to 10.58%. Additionally, there is an increase in the sub-G1 DNA content and decrease in the proportion in cells of S phase (Fig. 2 B). These results indicate that ClpP induces apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells. 3.3 Lack of caspase activation in ClpP-induced apoptosis Since caspase cascade has been well documented to play an important role in apoptosis, we examined whether ClpP induced a caspase-dependent or –independent apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells. Cells were treated with ClpP for 16 h. Caspase-3 protease activity was assessed in cell lysates by measuring hydrolysis of colorimetric caspase-3 substrate DEVD-pNA. As shown in Fig. 3 A, the lysate from cells treated with ClpP featured levels of caspase-3 like activity similar to those detected in cell lysates from control cells. Western blot analysis also showed that ClpP had no significant effect on caspase-3 activation (Fig. 3 B). Additionally, the activity of caspase-8 which is the initiator caspase of the death receptor pathway of apoptosis was not increased in ClpP-treated cells (Fig. 3 B). Cleavage of the p116/PARP to its characteristic p85/PARP fragments is considered as a marker of apoptosis and a substrate for caspase-3. To further corroborate the colorimetric assay results, cells were treated with ClpP, and the cell lysates were analyzed by Western blot assay using a specific PARP antibody. As shown in Fig. 3 C, ClpP treatment did not lead to PARP cleavage. In addition, at 16 h after treatment, cells exposed to ClpP had a similar percentage of apoptotic cells as cell pretreated with a broad spectrum of caspase inhibitor, Z-VAD-fmk (Fig. 3 D). It was also found that pretreatment with a specific inhibitor of caspase-3, Z-DEVD-FMK, was not able to reduce the number of apoptotic cells (data not shown). Taken together, these results suggest that ClpP induced apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells through a caspase-independent pathway and does not act through the extrinsic apoptotic pathway. 3.4 Effect of ClpP on mitochondrial depolarization, ROS production and AIF translocation, without loss of cytochrome c Mitochondria play an important role in commitment of cells to apoptosis through increase of mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), release of cytochrome c (Cyt C), production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) translocation (Green and Reed, 1998 ). To better understand how ClpP induces apoptosis, we examined its effects on biochemical events leading to apoptosis. The change in the MMP level after ClpP treatment was quantified by measuring the MMP level by flow cytometry after MitoTracker Red CMXRos staining. The ClpP-exposed cells showed a significant decrease in the MMP level at 3 and 6 ug/ml (Fig. 4 A). Release of Cyt C from the intermembrane spaces of the mitochondria into the cytosol is a key event in apoptosis via a mitochondria-dependent pathway. In addition, upon an apoptotic stimulus tAIF (truncated AIF) translocates from mitochondria to cytosol and further to the nucleus where it triggers caspase-independent programmed cell death. We sought to determine the effect of ClpP on these processes. The SK-N-SH cells were treated with various doses of ClpP and the release of Cyt C was examined. As shown in Fig. 4 B, Cyt C was present in mitochondria at all concentrations of ClpP, but interestingly, Cyt C was not detected in the cytosol of cells. In contrast, treatment with ClpP at 6 μg/ml for 12 h resulted in the release of mitochondrial AIF into both the cytosol and nucleus (Fig. 4 C). Moreover, from the double-immunofluorescence labeling it was clearly confirmed by means of immunofluorescence microscopy that AIF is released from mitochondrial then primarily redistributed to perinuclear region (Fig. 4 D). These data further demonstrate that ClpP induces a caspase-independent apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells. Next, in order to determine the effect of ClpP on the intracellular ROS level, the SK-N-SH cells were exposed to ClpP and the intracellular ROS level was measured by flow cytometry after staining with CMH2 -DCFDA. Exposure of SK-N-SH cells to ClpP led to a significant increase in intracellular ROS level (Fig. 5 ). 3.5 Effects of ClpP on Bax, Bcl-xL and Bcl-2 protein levels To further clarify the mechanism of ClpP-induced apoptosis in neuroblastoma cell, we examined the changes in protein expression of apoptosis-related genes, including Bax, Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL by Western blot analysis using antibodies directed against the respective proteins. As shown in Fig. 6 A, treatment of SK-N-SH cells with ClpP resulted in a concentration-dependent decrease in the levels of antiapoptotic Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL proteins expression compared with untreated cells. In contrast, the level of proapoptotic Bax protein expression was increased. Our data also showed that the ratio of Bax/Bcl-2 level is significantly increased in the ClpP-treated cells (Fig. 6 B), indicating the susceptibility of neuron-like cells towards apoptosis. The aforementioned results showed that ClpP induces ROS production. Moreover, it has been suggested that an increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio induced by enhanced ROS production is responsible for the apoptotic death (Basile et al., 1997 ; Li et al., 2004 ). Therefore, to determine if ROS is involved in the regulation of bcl-2 family gene expression, cells were pretreated with the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) followed by ClpP. As shown in Fig. 6 C, the increased ratio of Bax/Bcl-2 protein expression was counter-regulated by NAC, indicating that bcl-2 family gene expression requires ROS production in ClpP-treated cells. 3.6 Effects of ClpP on p53 protein levels and location It has been shown that p53 directly activates the pro-apoptotic protein Bax resulting in mitochondrial membrane permeabilization and Cyt C release which in turn lead to either cell cycle or apoptosis (Leu et al., 2004 ). Treatment with ClpP did not induce the expression levels of total p53 protein, but a significant and time-dependent increase of p53 Ser20P was detected in SK-N-SH cells exposed to ClpP (Fig. 7 A). The phospho-p53 protein level began to rise 4 h after treatment. These results indicate that ClpP increased p53 activity. Next, we examined the cellular localization of p53, because p53 function has been known to be dependent on the subcellular localization in neuroblastoma cells (Tweddle et al., 2001 ). To observe the location of p53 in ClpP-treated cells, we used a primary p53 (DO-1) antibodies. Interestingly, the immunofluorescence studies revealed the cellular localization of p53 in untreated cells to be mostly nuclear, whereas p53 levels were increased in the cytoplasm of ClpP-treated cells (Fig. 7 B). By Western blot analysis, we also observed a significant reduction in nuclear p53 expression with increased cytoplasmic accumulation of p53 as compared to untreated cells (Fig. 7 C), which is consistent with the immunofluorescence staining results These results suggest that ClpP exposure results in relocalization of p53 from the cytoplasm to the nucleus and functional activation of p53 is intact despite increased cytoplasmic accumulation. 4 Discussion There is increasing evidence to suggest that exposure to S. pneumoniae or cytotoxic factors produced by S. pneumoniae lead to neural cell damage, which results in growth inhibition and may lead to apoptosis. Among these bacterial cytotoxic products, ClpP has been interested as a virulence factor evoking cell death. However, the precise mechanism by which this molecule triggers apoptosis remains unclear. In the present study, ClpP inhibited growth and induced apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells, neuroblastoma cells bearing wild-type p53 gene through a caspase-independent pathway and ClpP-induced apoptosis appears to be mediated via p53 activation. As analyzed by annexin V/PI dual staining flow cytometry, ClpP treatment resulted in the increase of early (annexin V+/PI−) or late (annexin V+/PI+) apoptotic cells. Our data also indicate that cells appear to initiate apoptosis following ClpP treatment, but fail to complete apoptosis and enhance a necrotic population of cells at 6 μg/ml. However, present study demonstrated that ClpP treatment caused an increase in the sub-G1 DNA content that is an indicator of the occurrence of cellular apoptosis. Thus, these data suggest that ClpP induces apoptosis of neuroblastoma cells in concentration-dependent manner. Apoptosis can be initiated by extracellular and intracellular signals that trigger a complex machinery of pro-apoptotic proteases and mitochondrial functions. Concerning the potential chemical mediators of apoptosis signaling induced by ClpP, experiments with antioxidant NAC indicated that the ClpP induced increased apoptosis was attenuated by the addition of NAC (data not shown). Our data also show that ClpP treatment results in increase in ROS production. Therefore, the present data suggest that ClpP action is at least partially mediated through ROS production. It is well known that ROS generation is intimately associated with certain functions in the early stages of apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction (Herrera et al., 2001 ). In addition, generation of ROS, together with the release of Cyt C and pro-apoptotic proteins from mitochondria, triggers caspase activation and apoptosis (Hatano et al., 2000 ). Moreover, mitochondria play a central role in commitment of cells to apoptosis via increased permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane, decreased transmembrane potential, release of Cyt C and AIF, and production of ROS (Green and Reed, 1998 ; Susin et al., 1998 ). A change in MMP is essential for apoptosis, leading to translocation of apoptogenic Cyt C and AIF into the cytoplasm. The Bcl-2 gene family members have been known to play an important role in regulating the changes in MMP. Anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) can block these mitochondrial events, whereas pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family members (Bax, Bak, Bad) can trigger these changes. Importantly, the ratio of Bax/Bcl-2 is critical for the induction of apoptosis, and the ratio of Bax/Bcl-2 decides a cell's susceptibility to undergo apoptosis. Change in the ratio of Bax/Bcl-2 stimulates the release of Cyt C from mitochondria into cytosol. In our experiments, mitochondrial changes were observed in ClpP-treated neuroblastoma cells. The ClpP-exposed cells showed a significant decrease in the MMP level. ClpP treatment also resulted in elevated level of Cyt C release from the mitochondria to the cytosol. These findings suggest that ClpP induces mitochondria-dependent apoptosis in SK-N-SH cells. Furthermore, our results showed that proapoptotic protein Bax was highly activated by ClpP treatment, while Bcl-xL and Bcl-2 expression were decreased. In addition, the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio was increased when cells were treated with ClpP. These findings are in accordance with subsequent studies, which demonstrate that the ClpP-induced increased expression of Bax protein and decreased expression of Bcl-2 was attenuated by NAC pretreatment, suggesting that bcl-2 family gene expression requires ROS production in ClpP-treated cells. Cyt C release from mitochondria that occurs after ClpP treatment is possibly controlled by Bax. Previous studies have shown that the translocation of Bax to mitochondria can alter the outer mitochondrial membrane permeability that leads to the release of Cyt C to cytosol (Goping et al., 1998 ) and then activates caspase cascade from apical caspases to effector caspases leading to apoptotic celldeath. The present results that Bax protein level is increased in the mitochondria after ClpP treatment, which was subsequent to Cyt C release. Based on these finding, it is conceivable that sufficient Bax appears to reside at the mitochondrial membrane to induce Cyt C release after ClpP treatment. In this study, the activity of casapse-3 was measured in order to determine if the ClpP treatment induces the activation of caspase-3. We observed that ClpP-induced apoptosis was not inhibited by the broad-spectrum caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-fmk, with no activation of caspase-3. In addition, there was no significant change in caspase-8 activity after the ClpP treatment, indicating that ClpP did not activate plasma membrane death receptor. These findings suggest that the activation of caspases is not involved in this experiment model, pathways other than the death receptor-mediate pathways might be involved, or the toxicity of ClpP at given dose can kill the cells before initiating the caspase-cascade. AIF, which translocates via the cytosol to nuclei, is a hallmark of caspase-independent apoptosis (Daugas et al., 2000 ). In this report, our data demonstrate that ClpP treatment induces AIF release from mitochondria, which provides obvious support for the contention that ClpP is able to induce caspase-independent apoptosis. To gather further information on the pathway of apoptosis, the expression of p53 which plays a central role in the induction of apoptosis by various cellular insults was investigated. It has been known that p53 is predominantly a nuclear protein that acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional regulator for apoptosis-related genes and interacts with Bak, Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL, resulting in mitochondrial membrane permeabilization and release of cytochrome c, which in turn lead to caspase activation and apoptosis (Leu et al., 2004 ). However, there is an emerging evidence supporting that p53 has an extranuclear role in the cytoplasm for the induction of apoptosis (Chipuk and Green, 2004 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that posttranslational covalent modifications, such as phosphorylation and acetylation of specific amino acids of the p53 protein, have been known to affect p53 activity (el-Deiry, 1998 ). In the present study, treatment with ClpP failed to induce the expression levels of total p53 protein, whereas a significant and time-dependent increase of p53 Ser20P was detected in SK-N-SH cells exposed to ClpP, suggesting that ClpP increases p53 activity. The present data also showing that ClpP induced a significant reduction in nuclear p53 expression with increased cytoplasmic accumulation of p53 as compared to untreated cells is keeping with previous notion that cytoplasmic localization of p53 correlates with DNA damage-induced apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells (Goldman et al., 1996 ). Thus, our data suggest that ClpP exposure might result in relocalization from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and functional activation of p53 is intact despite increased cytoplasmic accumulation. There is controversy regarding accumulation and functional inactivation of p53 in neuroblastoma research (Tweddle et al., 2003 ). It has been reported that nuclear accumulation of p53 is triggered by cellular stress in various neuroblastoma cells including SK-N-SH cells. In contrast, Goldman et al. (1996) demonstrated that cytoplasmic p53 levels were increased by ionizing radiation and p53 pathway is intact after DNA damage in neuroblastoma cells. Based on these findings it is conceivable that the cytoplasmic localization in the ClpP-treated cells is largely because of excessive nuclear export rather than complete blockage of nuclear import. In addition, it is likely due to the induction of p53-associated Parkin-like cytoplasmic protein (PARC) by ClpP, since it has been suggested that PARC directly interacts with p53 in the cytoplasm and prevents transport of p53 into the nucleus in neuroblastoma cells (Nikolaev et al., 2003 ). It will be interesting to determine whether these same results are seen in other cell types, especially glial cells. Studies are currently underway to address this possibility. In conclusion, the data in these studies show that ClpP conducts a caspase-independent pathway through the collapse of the membrane potential of mitochondria, the mitochondrial release of AIF and ROS production. Thus, ClpP is significantly neurotoxic and contribute to neuronal injury in bacterial meningitis. Additionally, our data suggest new neuroprotective strategies to reduce neuronal cell death in pneumococcal meningitis. title: N-Myc down regulation induced differentiation, early cell cycle exit, and apoptosis in human malignant neuroblastoma cells having wild type or mutant p53
abstract: Neuroblastomas, which mostly occur in children, are aggressive metastatic tumors of the sympathetic nervous system. The failure of the previous therapeutic regimens to target multiple components of N-Myc pathway resulted in poor prognosis. The present study investigated the efficacy of the combination of N-(4-hydroxyphenyl) retinamide (4-HPR, 0.5μM) and genistein (GST, 25μM) to control the growth of human neuroblastoma cells (SH-SY5Y and SK-N-BE2) harboring divergent molecular attributes. Combination of 4-HPR and GST down regulated N-Myc, Notch-1, and Id2 to induce neuronal differentiation. Transition to neuronal phenotype was accompanied by increase in expression of e-cadherin. Induction of neuronal differentiation was associated with decreased expression of hTERT, PCNA, survivin, and fibronectin. This is the first report that combination of 4-HPR and GST mediated reactivation of multiple tumor suppressors (p53, p21, Rb, and PTEN) for early cell cycle exit (due to G1/S phase arrest) in neuroblastoma cells. Reactivation of tumor suppressor(s) repressed N-Myc driven growth factor mediated angiogenic and invasive pathways (VEGF, b-FGF, MMP-2, and MMP-9) in neuroblastoma. Repression of angiogenic factors led to the blockade of components of mitogenic pathways [phospho-Akt (Thr 308), p65 NF-κB, and p42/44 Erk 1/2]. Taken together, the combination of 4-HPR and GST effectively blocked survival, mitogenic, and angiogenic pathways and activated proteases for apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells. These results suggested that combination of 4-HPR and GST could be effective for controlling the growth of heterogeneous human neuroblastoma cell populations.

S0006-2952(09) -8 Fig. 1 Treatment with 4-HPR decreased cell proliferation and induced morphological and biochemical features of neuronal differentiation. (A) Decrease in cell proliferation and increase in morphological features of neuronal differentiation. Cells were treated with 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 72 h. Appearance of morphological features of neuronal differentiation included small, thin, and retracted cell bodies with elongated and branched processes. (B) Measurement of dimensions of neuronal differentiation (width of cell, length of cell, and length of neurite extension). Treatment of cells with 4-HPR produced significant differences in all these attributes measured. The length of cell and the neurite extensions were significantly increased due to neuronal differentiation, when compared with control cells. A concomitant decrease in the width of cell was observed following treatment with 4-HPR. (C) Representative Western blots to show changes in biochemical markers of neuronal differentiation and cell proliferation. Treatments: control, 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 72 h, 25 μM GST for 24 h, and 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 48 h (pretreatment) + 25 μM GST for 24 h. Expression of β-actin was used as a loading control. All experiments were conducted in triplicates. Fig. 2 Changes in residual cell viability following the treatments. Cells were treated with 4-HPR for 72 h, GST for 24 h, and also pretreated with 4-HPR for 48 h and then treated with GST for 24 h. After the treatments, changes in cell viability were determined by the MTT assay. All experiments were conducted in triplicates and the results were analyzed for statistical significance. Fig. 3 Cell cycle analysis and changes in levels of molecules governing the cell cycle. Treatments: control, 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 72 h, 25 μM GST for 24 h, and 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 48 h (pretreatment) + 25 μM GST for 24 h. (A) Flow cytometric analysis of cell cycle. Distributions of cells in the G0/G1, G2/M, S, and sub-G1 phases were analyzed. (B) Representative Western blots to show changes in cytosolic levels of molecular markers associated with cell cycle arrest at G1/S phase. Expression of β-actin was used as a loading control. All experiments were conducted in triplicates. Fig. 4 Determination of apoptosis in cells after the treatments. Treatments: control, 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 72 h, 25 μM GST for 24 h, and 0.5 μM 4-HPR for 48 h (pretreatment) + 25 μM GST for 24 h. (A) In situ Wright staining to examine morphological features of apoptosis. (B) Determination of percentages of apoptosis based on morphological features revealed by Wright staining. (C) Annexin V staining and flow cytometric analysis of apoptotic populations after the treatments. Flow cytometric data presented here show only one of the three independent experiments in both SH-SY5Y and SK-N-BE2 cell lines. Combination of 4-HPR and GST accumulated significant population of cells in A4 area, indicating apoptotic death. (D) Determination of percentages of apoptosis based on accumulation of Annexin V positive cells in A4 area. Fig. 5 Changes in the levels of molecules regulating angiogenic and mitogenic cascades.
