Overcoming therapeutic resistance mediated by apoptosis evasion represents a critical challenge in cancer treatment. Pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of regulated cell death, provides a promising alternative approach capable of stimulating robust anti-tumor immunity and converting immunologically inert ("cold") tumors into immunologically active ("hot") microenvironments. Importantly, these cell death pathways are not isolated but are interconnected through dynamic molecular switches that determine cellular fate. This review systematically examines the intricate molecular crosstalk between cell death modalities, with particular emphasis on the regulatory roles of the caspase-3/GSDME and caspase-8/GSDMD axes. Current evidence demonstrates that caspase family members, primarily associated with apoptosis, can selectively cleave gasdermin proteins, facilitating a transition from non-inflammatory apoptotic signaling to inflammatory pyroptotic events. We further analyze how inflammasomes, post-translational modifications, and the STING–NF–κB pathway precisely regulate this transition. Through integrated bioinformatic analysis, we identified novel hub genes (e.g., PRKAR1A, PPP2CA, FOSL2) and microRNA networks at the apoptosis-pyroptosis interface, providing novel insights and potential therapeutic targets. Exploiting this 'death switch' offers a novel therapeutic framework through three principal strategies: (1) inducing pyroptosis to eliminate apoptosis-resistant cells, (2) utilizing pyroptosis-induced inflammation to enhance immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy, and (3) developing targeted therapeutics that directly modulate these switch molecules. Although controlling pyroptosis-associated inflammation remains challenging, understanding and manipulating the apoptosis-to-pyroptosis transition provides an innovative approach to overcome drug resistance and develop more effective cancer treatments. Keywords Apoptosis Pyroptosis Molecular switch Cancer therapy Immunotherapy Drug resistance Data availability Data will be made available on request. 1 Introduction Cancer pathogenesis is fundamentally characterized by dysregulated cell proliferation and evasion of programmed cell death (PCD) [1 ]. Research advances over recent decades have substantially expanded our understanding of PCD mechanisms in tumor development and progression, facilitating the development of numerous targeted therapies [2–4 ]. Among PCD modalities, apoptosis represents the most extensively characterized form, distinguished by cellular shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and non-inflammatory clearance [5 ,6 ]. This process plays a crucial role in eliminating senescent, damaged, or potentially malignant cells [7 ]. Consequently, therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring apoptotic pathways in tumor cells - exemplified by the clinical success of the BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax - have become a cornerstone of cancer treatment [8–10 ]. Tumor cells demonstrate remarkable plasticity, frequently developing resistance to apoptosis through genetic mutations or aberrant protein expression, representing a major obstacle for chemotherapy and targeted therapies [11–13 ]. This therapeutic challenge has stimulated investigation into alternative cell death mechanisms independent of apoptotic pathways [14 ]. Among these, pyroptosis has emerged as a focus of intensive research. Morphologically characterized by cellular swelling, membrane pore formation, and pro-inflammatory mediator release [15 ,16 ], pyroptosis was initially identified as a host defense mechanism against pathogenic infections [17 ]. Emerging evidence now indicates its dual role in tumor biology, influencing both cancer progression and treatment outcomes [18–20 ]. A defining feature of pyroptosis is its potent immunogenicity [21 ]. Unlike apoptotic cells that undergo silent phagocytosis and may promote immune tolerance, pyroptotic cells rupture and release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including ATP and HMGB1 [22 ,23 ], along with inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 [24 ,25 ]. These mediators recruit and activate natural killer (NK) cells [26 ] and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) [27 ], initiating robust anti-tumor immune responses. This property creates new opportunities for immunotherapy, particularly in transforming immunologically quiescent ("cold") tumors into responsive ("hot") microenvironments - a central objective in contemporary oncology [28 ,29 ]. Notably, apoptosis and pyroptosis do not function as independent parallel pathways but exhibit complex, multi-level interactions [30 ,31 ]. Under specific conditions, apoptotic stimuli may subsequently induce pyroptosis, and vice versa. This cell fate determination is governed by critical "molecular switches" [32 ,33 ]. Elucidating the mechanisms of these switches and developing methods to modulate them may provide solutions to apoptosis resistance and enable more effective combination therapies for cancer treatment. Compared to other emerging cell death modalities, pyroptosis offers distinct advantages for cancer therapy. In contrast to ferroptosis, which relies on iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and can be counteracted by antioxidant systems, pyroptosis is executed through well-defined caspase-gasdermin signaling that is less susceptible to metabolic bypass [34 ]. Unlike cuproptosis, which is triggered by copper ion accumulation and may be challenging to target with small molecules, pyroptosis is mediated by druggable caspases and gasdermins, providing clear therapeutic targets. Most importantly, pyroptosis is inherently immunogenic, releasing inflammatory cytokines and DAMPs that activate anti-tumor immunity, a feature that is less pronounced in ferroptosis and cuproptosis [35 ]. These comparative advantages render pyroptosis as a particularly promising strategy to overcome apoptosis resistance. Although previous reviews have elegantly introduced the concept of apoptosis-pyroptosis switch [36 ,37 ], this review provides a more granular and forward-looking perspective. We place particular emphasis on the underappreciated role of the caspase-8/GSDMD axis and the non-classical STING–NF–κB pathway as critical regulatory nodes. Moreover, we integrate an original bioinformatic analysis to identify hub genes and regulatory networks, offering a systems-level view. Finally, we expand the discussion beyond mechanistic insights to critically evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies, including nanotechnology-based approaches, and their associated challenges for clinical translation, thereby providing a roadmap for future research and drug development in this field. In this review, we first revisit the core molecular mechanisms underlying apoptosis and pyroptosis and their current therapeutic applications in oncology. We then examine the interaction networks and key transition nodes between these pathways, with the goal of revealing how this regulatory interface can be leveraged to develop innovative anticancer strategies. 2 Apoptosis: the classic paradigm of programmed cell death and its applications in cancer therapy 2.1 Morphological and biological characteristics of apoptosis Apoptosis is a genetically regulated process with evolutionarily conserved morphological features [5 ]. Characteristic changes include cellular shrinkage, detachment from neighboring cells, chromatin condensation and marginalization beneath the nuclear membrane, nuclear fragmentation, and formation of membrane-enclosed apoptotic bodies [38 ,39 ]. Significantly, apoptosis typically does not elicit inflammatory responses because cellular contents remain contained within membranes [40 ], and the resulting apoptotic bodies are efficiently cleared by phagocytes [41 ]. This controlled process progresses through three principal phases: initiation, execution, and termination, ensuring rapid yet orderly completion [39 ,42 ]. 2.2 Key pathways of apoptosis 2.2.1 The intrinsic pathway The intrinsic pathway comprises two distinct mechanisms: the mitochondrial pathway and the endoplasmic reticulum pathway [43 ,44 ] (Fig. 1 ). The mitochondrial pathway represents the predominant intrinsic apoptotic mechanism [45 ]. In this pathway, intracellular stressors such as DNA damage activate BH3-only proteins [45 ], which subsequently inhibit anti-apoptotic proteins including BCL-2, leading to liberation of pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and BAK [46 ,47 ]. Upon activation, BAX and BAK oligomerize to form pores in the outer mitochondrial membrane [48–50 ], facilitating release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c into the cytoplasm [51 ]. Cytosolic cytochrome c binds Apaf-1, promoting recruitment and activation of caspase-9 [52 ,53 ]. This interaction generates the apoptosome complex, which activates downstream effector caspase-3 to initiate apoptotic execution [54 ]. The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) pathway represents an alternative intrinsic mechanism. ER stress disrupts calcium homeostasis and triggers the unfolded protein response (UPR) [55 ,56 ], ultimately activating ER-associated caspase-12 in murine models [57 ,58 ] or caspase-4 in humans [59 ], which subsequently activates caspase-3 to execute apoptosis [60 ]. 2.2.2 Death receptor (extrinsic) pathway The extrinsic pathway initiates when extracellular signaling molecules such as Fas ligand (FasL) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) bind their cognate death receptors (Fas and TNFR1, respectively) [61 ]. This interaction recruits the adaptor protein FADD to the receptor's intracellular domain (Fig. 1 ) [62 ]. FADD then recruits and activates pro-caspase-8 through its death effector domain (DED), forming the death-inducing signaling complex (DISC) [63 ,64 ]. Inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) serve as key apoptotic suppressors. XIAP, the most potent endogenous inhibitor, directly binds and inhibits caspases-3, -7, and -9 [65 ]. As E3 ubiquitin ligases, cIAPs mediate caspase ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby inhibiting TNFα-induced apoptosis [65 ]. IAP depletion or inhibition (e.g., by IAP antagonists) enhances caspase-8-dependent apoptosis, particularly during death receptor activation [66 ,67 ]. Activated caspase-8 either directly activates caspase-3 or amplifies apoptotic signaling through BID cleavage to generate truncated BID (tBID), thereby linking to the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway [68 ,69 ]. 2.3 Apoptosis-targeted cancer therapy and its limitations Restoring apoptotic capacity in cancer cells represents a fundamental strategy employed by numerous anticancer agents [70 ,71 ]. BH3 mimetics constitute a leading approach in this paradigm, functioning as synthetic analogs of intrinsic pro-apoptotic proteins that inhibit anti-apoptotic proteins including BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 [72 ,73 ]. The selective BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax (ABT-199) has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in hematologic malignancies, validating this therapeutic strategy [74 ,75 ]. Current investigations focus on developing broad-spectrum inhibitors such as navitoclax (ABT-263) [76 ], along with agents targeting MCL-1 (e.g., AMG 176) [77 ] or BCL-XL [78 ]. For example, ABBV-155 [79 ], delivered via antibody-drug conjugate technology, is designed to circumvent multiple resistance mechanisms (Table 1 ). Additionally, IAP inhibitors including SMAC mimetics (e.g., LCL161) [80 ] and TRAIL agonists (e.g., dulanermin) [81 ] promote apoptosis through alternative pathways and are undergoing clinical evaluation (Table 1 ). Despite these advances, tumor cells employ diverse strategies to develop primary or secondary resistance to apoptosis-inducing therapies, ultimately leading to treatment failure [82 ,83 ]. Key resistance mechanisms include (1) Mutations in BCL-2 functional domains (e.g., G101V mutation): that reduce venetoclax binding affinity [84 ]; (2) Compensatory upregulation of non-targeted anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., MCL-1 and BCL-XL) conferring resistance to venetoclax, navitoclax, and ABT-737 [85–87 ] (3) Downregulation of pro-apoptotic effectors (e.g., BIM and NOXA); [88 ,89 ] leading to resistance against BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibitors (e.g., APG-1252, S44563) and MCL-1 inhibitors (e.g., S63845, AMG-176); (4) TP53 tumor suppressor pathway disruption via mutations or deletions compromising apoptotic networks [90 ,91 ], resulting in resistance to BCL-2 inhibitors (e.g., Lacutoclax) [92 ]; (5) Tumor microenvironment-mediated protection through physical drug delivery barriers and cytokines (e.g., CD40L, IL-10) promoting anti-apoptotic protein expression [93 ,94 ], conferring resistance to BCL-2 inhibitors (e.g., S55746, sonrotoclax) and MCL-1 inhibitors (e.g., AMG 176, MIK665) [93 ,95 ,96 ]; (6) Mitochondrial metabolic adaptations including enhanced oxidative phosphorylation and biogenesis [97 ,98 ], driving resistance to BCL-2 inhibitors (e.g., venetoclax, lisaftoclax); and (7) Genomic instability-driven clonal evolution selecting resistant clones through novel mutations [99 ], leading to resistance against BCL-2 inhibitors (e.g., ABBV-623, ABBV-453) and MCL-1 inhibitors (e.g., AZD5991, PRT1419) [100 ,101 ]. These multifaceted resistance mechanisms pose substantial challenges for apoptosis-targeted therapies, significantly limiting clinical application of anti-apoptotic agents. Consequently, innovative strategies to overcome resistance are urgently needed. 3 Pyroptosis: an inflammatory programmed cell death and its dual role in cancer 3.1 Pyroptosis exhibits distinct morphological features compared to apoptosis Pyroptosis is primarily characterized by membrane pore formation, cellular swelling, membrane perforation, and release of intracellular contents [102–104 ]. Key distinctions from apoptosis include: (1) Pyroptotic cells undergo membrane swelling followed by rupture and pro-inflammatory content release [105 ], whereas apoptotic cells maintain membrane integrity during controlled shrinkage [106 ,107 ]; (2) Pyroptosis preserves nuclear structure with characteristic DNA fragmentation patterns [108 ], while apoptosis features nuclear condensation and fragmentation into apoptotic bodies with loss of nuclear integrity [109 ]; and (3) Pyroptosis initiates robust inflammation via IL-18 and IL-1β release [110 ], contrasting with apoptosis' typically non-inflammatory clearance by phagocytes [111 ,112 ]. Pyroptosis proceeds through two principal phases: preparation and activation (Fig. 2 ). 3.2 Key pathways of pyroptosis Pyroptosis is closely associated with the gasdermin (GSDM) protein family. Different GSDM proteins activate pyroptosis through distinct mechanisms. GSDMD acts as the "gatekeeper" controlling inflammatory responses. When cells sense pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) or damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), they assemble inflammasomes that subsequently activate caspase-1, caspase-1 specifically cleaves GSDMD to release its N-terminal fragment (GSDMD-N), which triggers pyroptosis and causes the release of mature IL-1β and IL-18 [113 ]. Additionally, intracellular LPS can directly activate caspase-4/5 in humans or caspase-11 in mice [114 ,115 ], these caspases also cleave GSDMD, which is called the “non-canonical inflammasome pathway”. In cells with high GSDME expression, activated caspase-3 cleaves GSDME, once GSDME is cleaved, the mode of cell death shifts from "silent" apoptosis to pyroptosis [116 ]. While cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) or natural killer (NK) cells recognize and attack target cells (e.g., virus-infected cells or cancer cells), they release granzyme A into the cytoplasm of target cells, where this serine protease directly cleaves and activates GSDMB, thereby triggering pyroptosis [117 ]. Under specific conditions, such as in some cancer cells, tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα) binds to its receptor and activates caspase-8, which cleaves GSDMC and switches the classical TNF apoptotic pathway to pyroptosis [118 ]. Additionally, Group A Streptococcus (e.g., bacteria that cause scarlet fever) secretes a protease called SpeB, which specifically cleaves human GSDMA, hijacking the host's pyroptosis mechanism and facilitating bacterial dissemination and infection [119 ]. 3.2.1 The preparation phase of pyroptosis This phase involves recognition of two molecular pattern classes: pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs; e.g., gram-negative bacterial LPS) [111 ] and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs; e.g., TNF-α, IL-1) [120 ,121 ]. Membrane-localized pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) including TNFR, TLR, and IL-1R detect these signals [122 ,123 ]. Receptor activation engages adaptor proteins (e.g., MyD88, TRIF) to stimulate NF-κB signaling [124 ,125 ]. Nuclear NF-κB then transactivates genes encoding essential pyroptosis components, including inflammasome sensors (e.g., NLRP3) [126 ] and pro-inflammatory cytokine precursors (Pro-IL-1β, Pro-IL-18) [127–129 ]. Notably, this phase does not directly induce cell death but prepares the cellular apparatus through NF-κB-mediated accumulation of pyroptosis execution proteins (NLRP3, Pro-IL-1β, Pro-IL-18) [130 ]. 3.2.2 The activation phase of pyroptosis This execution phase initiates when secondary danger signals trigger inflammasome assembly and subsequent reactions [131 ]. Four principal activation mechanisms exist [132 ]: (1) The canonical pathway where PAMPs/DAMPs promote inflammasome (e.g., NLRP3, AIM2) assembly via PRRs and ASC [133 ]; (2) The non-canonical pathway involving direct LPS recognition by caspase-11 (murine) or caspase-4/5 (human), which cleave GSDMD independent of inflammasomes [134 ,135 ], subsequently activating NLRP3 to enhance pyroptosis and IL-1β secretion [136 ]; (3) The apoptosis-associated caspase pathway where apoptotic caspases (caspase-3, -8) cleave gasdermins (GSDME, GSDMC, GSDMB) under chemotherapy or hypoxia [137–140 ], converting apoptotic signals to pyroptosis; and (4) The granzyme pathway where cytotoxic lymphocyte-derived granzymes (A/B) directly cleave gasdermins (e.g., GSDMB) or activate downstream effectors [141 ,142 ], mediating targeted cell destruction. 3.3 Pyroptosis: a complementary pathway for inducing cell apoptosis Pyroptosis exhibits paradoxical roles in cancer biology, functioning as a "double-edged sword" with both tumor-promoting and therapeutic potential [20 ]. While chronic pyroptosis-associated inflammation may fuel tumor progression, its immunogenic properties offer promising immunotherapeutic strategies [143 ,144 ]. Specifically, pyroptosis induction in tumor cells directly eliminates malignant cells while reprogramming immunosuppressive ("cold") microenvironments into immunologically active ("hot") states, enhancing immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy [145 ,146 ]. Pyroptosis-inducing agents (e.g., Paclitaxel, CBL0137; Table 2 ) activate caspase-3/GSDME pathways [147 ,148 ], where caspase-3-cleaved GSDME forms membrane pores causing osmotic lysis. This mechanism operates independently of BCL-2 family regulation, bypassing resistance from BCL-2 mutations (e.g., G101V) or overexpression. Alternative initiation through non-canonical caspase-4/5/11 pathways or inflammasome activation circumvents compensatory upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., MCL-1, BCL-XL) [149 ]. The NLRP3 agonist BMS- (Table 2 ) activates NLRP3 to release IL-8, stimulating NK cells [150 ] while remaining independent of BCL-2 family proteins and TP53 pathways, overcoming resistance from BCL-2 mutations, MCL-1/BCL-XL upregulation, or TP53 mutations [151 ]. At the microenvironment level, pyroptosis-released DAMPs disrupt extracellular matrix barriers (facilitating drug penetration) and counteract immunosuppressive factors (e.g., CD40L, IL-10). Combined with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, pyroptosis synergistically enhances antitumor immunity [152 ,153 ]. Additionally, pyroptosis-induced mitochondrial dysfunction (characterized by ATP leakage and iron-sulfur cluster inactivation) exacerbates metabolic stress [24 ,154 ]. Combining pyroptosis inducers with BCL-2 antagonists creates dual metabolic-apoptotic attacks that improve drug-resistant clone eradication [155 ,156 ]. Notably, pharmacological agents (e.g., metformin, DHA) activate caspase-1/GSDMD pathways [157 ,158 ], completely bypassing apoptotic pathway-dependent resistance mechanisms. Emerging therapeutics targeting downstream components (e.g., canakinumab against IL-1β) [159 ] are under clinical evaluation (Table 2 ), highlighting pyroptosis as a pivotal advancement in overcoming apoptotic resistance and accelerating novel antineoplastic therapy development. 4 Molecular switch of apoptosis and pyroptosis Apoptosis and pyroptosis share common upstream pathways and interact at critical regulatory nodes [160 ], enabling dynamic interconversion that determines cellular responses to diverse stimuli [161 ]. 4.1 Caspase-3/GSDME axis GSDME serves as a crucial apoptosis-pyroptosis switch [162 ]. While expressed in normal tissues, GSDME is frequently silenced in tumors via promoter methylation [163 ]. Chemotherapeutic agents activating classical apoptotic pathways ultimately stimulate caspase-3 [164 ]. In GSDME-low cells, caspase-3 cleaves conventional substrates, executing non-inflammatory apoptosis [165 ]. Conversely, in GSDME-high cells, activated caspase-3 preferentially cleaves GSDME (Fig. 3 ), generating GSDME-N fragments that form membrane pores, converting "silent" apoptosis into inflammatory pyroptosis [166 ]. This discovery redefines mechanisms of many chemotherapeutics, revealing pyroptosis induction as a key efficacy determinant [167 ,168 ]. Corey Rogers et al. [169 ] demonstrated apoptosis preceding pyroptosis, where caspase-3 cleaves DFNA5 (GSDME), converting apoptosis to inflammatory pyroptosis ("secondary necrosis/pyroptosis"). Similarly, Zhang et al. [170 ] showed bee venom peptides (α-MEL) and resveratrol (RES) activating caspase-3-mediated apoptosis while cleaving GSDME to induce concurrent apoptosis/pyroptosis in glioblastoma through three stages: (1) drug combination upregulating p53/PUMA/BAX, increasing mitochondrial permeability and caspase activation; (2) activated caspase-3 cleaving GSDME while upregulating NLRP3/caspase-1/GSDMD; and (3) GSDMD/GSDME-N pore formation causing pyroptosis. Li Baohong et al. [171 ] demonstrated fig latex extract (AFFL) simultaneously activating caspase-9/caspase-3 apoptosis and caspase-1/GSDMD pyroptosis in NSCLC cells (A549, H460), with synergistic antitumor effects. AFFL activated the classical caspase-9/caspase-3 apoptotic pathway, while also upregulating the expression of caspase-1 to activate the gasdermin D-mediated pyroptotic pathway. The synergy between these two modes of cell death constituted a crucial mechanism for AFFL's anti-cancer effects against non-small cell lung cancer. Paclitaxel and cisplatin are two representative chemotherapeutic agents for lung cancer, inducing apoptosis through different mechanisms [172 ,173 ]. Comparing lung cancer chemotherapeutics, Zhang et al. [174 ] showed both paclitaxel and cisplatin activating caspase-3/GSDME-NT in A549 cells. Cisplatin-induced pyroptosis was suppressed by caspase-3 inhibition (Ac-DEVD-CHO) or GSDME knockdown, while paclitaxel-induced pyroptosis was GSDME-independent [166 ], suggesting cisplatin advantages in GSDME-high tumors. In leukemia models, Dong et al. [175 ] found ferroptosis inhibitor Liproxstatin-1 inhibiting K562 proliferation via extrinsic/intrinsic apoptotic pathways (BAX/TNF-α induction → caspase-3/PARP cleavage → caspase-3/GSDME-dependent pyroptosis), suggesting strategies to overcome chemoresistance. Yang Liu et al. [176 ] developed a hGLuc-hGSDME-PCA system identifying FDA-approved pyroptosis inducers (ponatinib, perifosine) from 106 compounds for pancreatic cancer. Additional studies revealed: HMGB1 knockdown sensitizing neuroblastoma cells to cisplatin while converting pyroptosis to apoptosis via ROS/ERK1/2/caspase-3/GSDME pathways [177 ]; cisplatin/doxorubicin inducing renal tubular pyroptosis via ROS-JNK-caspase-3-GSDME [164 ]; colchicine triggering NQO1-mediated ROS accumulation causing concurrent apoptosis/pyroptosis in HeLa cells [178 ]; and gambogic acid inducing ovarian cancer pyroptosis via caspase-3/GSDME, reversible to apoptosis by GSDME knockout/caspase-3 inhibition through ROS/p53/mitochondrial pathways [179 ]. Collectively, these findings establish GSDME as a critical apoptosis-pyroptosis switch, with caspase-3-cleaved GSDME converting non-inflammatory apoptosis to immunogenic pyroptosis, offering novel therapeutic targets to overcome resistance and manage chemotherapy side effects. Therefore, the caspase-3/GSDME axis acts as a fundamental molecular switch that converts the immunologically silent apoptosis into potent and immunogenic pyroptosis. 4.2 Caspase-8’ double-edged sword Caspase-8, an extrinsic apoptosis initiator, also critically regulates cell death modality [138 ]. While typically activating caspase-3 to initiate apoptosis, caspase-8 can directly cleave gasdermins under specific conditions (Fig. 4 A), functioning as an apoptosis-pyroptosis switch [180 ]. Angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4), involved in lipid metabolism [181 ,182 ] and cancer progression [183 ], was shown by Fang et al. [184 ] to inhibit NLRP3/ASC/caspase-8-mediated pyroptosis/apoptosis in lung adenocarcinoma, promoting gefitinib resistance. Zi et al. [185 ] demonstrated hyperthermia/cisplatin combination increasing caspase-8 accumulation with K63-linked polyubiquitination in HepG2 cells, enhancing p62 interaction to activate caspase-3 (apoptosis) while caspase-8 precursors promoted IL-1β/IL-18/TNFα release and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis. Wu et al. [186 ] showed TLR-primed myeloid cells undergoing caspase-8 inhibition (IETD)-induced inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-18 release (pyroptosis) via caspase-8/-1 cooperation. Wang et al. [187 ] found BRD2 inhibiting FOXO4-caspase-8 axis in gastric cancer, with fluorouracil/epigenetic modulation reactivating caspase-8 to induce dual death. IAPs and FLIP critically regulate apoptosis-pyroptosis switching. Targeting death receptors/IAPs/c-FLIP may overcome solid tumor apoptosis resistance [188 ]. Microbial infection or inflammasome activation with IAP inhibition (e.g., Smac mimetics) may promote caspase-1/GSDMD or caspase-3/GSDME pathways by relieving caspase-8 inhibition [189 ,190 ]. FLIP, a caspase-8 inhibitor that competitively binds FADD via DED domains [191 ], is often overexpressed in apoptosis-resistant tumors [192 ]. Moderate FLIP downregulation generates caspase-8/FLIP heterodimers that cannot activate caspase-3/-7 but can cleave GSDMD (especially with low caspase-3 activity) [193 ,194 ], switching cells from apoptosis resistance to pyroptosis activation. Hou et al. [195 ] revealed a non-canonical caspase-8/GSDMC pyroptosis pathway in hypoxic breast cancer, where p-STAT3/PD-L1 interaction promoted GSDMC transcription. TNFα treatment led to caspase-8 cleavage of GSDMC, generating pore-forming GSDMC-N fragments that converted TNFα-induced apoptosis to pyroptosis, causing tumor necrosis. In summary, caspase-8 differentially initiates apoptosis or pyroptosis, depending on cellular context, and acts either through classical caspase-3 activation or through direct gasdermin cleavage. The activation state of caspase-8 critically influences therapeutic efficacy and resistance, making it a promising target for overcoming chemotherapy resistance. 4.3 Post-translational modifications Post-translational modifications (PTMs) critically regulate apoptosis-pyroptosis balance in cancer therapy [196 ] (Fig. 4 B). The linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC) mediates linear ubiquitination [197 ]. Gao et al. [198 ] showed LUBAC linearly ubiquitinating NEMO to activate NF-κB, promoting anti-apoptotic gene expression while SHARPIN (a LUBAC component) regulated NLRP3 inflammasome transcription - a key pyroptosis preparation step. LUBAC thus serves as a shared upstream regulator of both pathways, with dysregulation causing inflammatory diseases [199 ], suggesting therapeutic potential. Chen et al. [200 ] demonstrated PTEN inhibitor bpV(phen) enhancing p62 ubiquitination while reducing stability and disrupting p62-HDAC6 interaction. By activating HDAC6-mediated α-tubulin deacetylation, bpV(phen) caused microtubule instability, impairing autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Subsequent autophagic defect led to oxidative stress/lysosomal rupture, triggering both apoptosis and pyroptosis. Collectively, these findings position mitochondria as a central hub integrating upstream signals to determine the fate of the cell death switch, thereby orchestrating the delicate balance between apoptosis and pyroptosis. Beyond post-translational modifications, the switch is also regulated by metabolic states, such as ROS levels and mitochondrial integrity, as well as by epigenetic mechanisms like GSDME promoter methylation. This creates a multi-layered control network. 4.4 Inflammasomes are innate immune multiprotein complexes recognizing PAMPs and DAMPs [201 ], typically comprising: (1) a pattern recognition receptor (PRR) (e.g., NLRP3, NLRC4, AIM2); (2) ASC adaptors [202 ]; and (3) pro-caspase-1 effectors [201 ,203 ] (Fig. 4 C). Their tumor roles depend on cell type, molecular context, and cancer type [20 ]. For example, Dai et al. [204 ] showed NLRP3 activation inhibiting hepatocellular carcinoma (Bel-7402, SMMC-7721) proliferation via G1 arrest, while FNDC5 promoted M2 macrophage polarization through PPARγ/NF-κB/NLRP3, creating pro-tumor microenvironments [205 ]. Dal et al. [206 ] found curcumin increasing Sub-G1 populations (apoptosis) in colorectal cancer cells (SW480, HCT116) with concurrent NLRP3 upregulation (pyroptosis), demonstrating coexisting death mechanisms. Thus, these inflammatory pathways function as critical amplifiers that both reinforce the pyroptotic decision and create a positive feedback loop propagating the death signal to neighboring cells, highlighting the interconnected nature of the death switch network. 4.5 Non-classical STING–NF–κB pathway This pathway centrally regulates tumor cell apoptosis/pyroptosis [207 ] (Fig. 4 D). p53-STING interaction activates NF-κB to directly bind promoters of apoptosis (BAX), pyroptosis (GSDME), and immunogenic cell death (CCL5, CXCL10, HLAs) genes [207–209 ]. This dual mechanism kills tumor cells while recruiting CD8+ T cells via chemokines, generating systemic anti-tumor immunity. Clofarabine (FDA-approved) triggered this pathway in melanoma/lung cancer models, suggesting clinical potential [208 ]. Unique features include interferon response independence and direct NF-κB-mediated death gene regulation. STING-TBK1 interaction promotes IRF3 phosphorylation and NF-κB nuclear translocation, activating NLRP3 inflammasomes to enhance pyroptosis [210 ]. However, excessive activation may enable immune evasion (e.g., renal cancer suppressing ER stress-mediated pyroptosis via STING) [211 ], necessitating precise regulation for pyroptosis-based immunotherapies [212 ]. Together, these metabolic checkpoints demonstrate that cellular energy status and redox balance are integral components of the death switch machinery. These components offer novel therapeutic opportunities to regulate cell fate through metabolic intervention. 4.6 Pontential molecular targets involved in the mutual regulation between pyroptosis and apoptosis Due to the limited number of reported targets, we performed bioinformatics analysis using STRING 12.0. For apoptosis, we identified 166 human proteins (experimental evidence, medium confidence 0.400); for pyroptosis, we identified 74 proteins. As shown in Fig. 5 A, Venn diagram analysis revealed 21 overlapping genes. The CytoHubba plugin in Cytoscape, incorporating 12 algorithms including MCC, identified the top 10 hub genes (Fig. 5 B). Cross-validation with TargetScan, miRDB, and miRBase identified 82 microRNAs, among which 18 were common to all databases (Fig. 5 C). Subsequently, ENCORI analysis showed that PRKAR1A, PPP2CA, and FOSL2 each interacted with three microRNAs (Fig. 5 D), suggesting promising targets. These findings suggest that these hub genes may play critical roles in the crosstalk between apoptosis and pyroptosis pathways. Building on these results, we subsequently explored the functional implications of these key regulators. PRKAR1A exhibits apoptosis-regulating duality: its deficiency upregulates pro-apoptotic BIM, PUMA or NOXA, triggering caspase-3-dependent apoptosis [213 ], However, it inhibits TGF-β-mediated apoptosis in adrenocortical cells by downregulating SMAD3 and blocking cleavage of caspase-3 and PARP [214 ]. B lymphocytes lacking PRKAR1A show resistance to apoptosis through ERK/BRAF activation and cell cycle progression [215 ], suggesting that inducing pyroptosis may overcome resistance caused by PRKAR1A deficiency in adrenocortical tumors and B-cell lymphomas. PPP2CA promotes apoptosis resistance by (1) mitochondrial remodeling [216 ]; (2) inhibiting death receptor signaling [217 ], and (3) epigenetic silencing [218 ]. Activated caspase-8 interacts with Src to modulate TRAIL sensitivity, while PPP2CA facilitates NLRP3 inflammasome assembly by dephosphorylating PYD domains [219 ], indicating that PPP2CA may play a role in apoptosis-pyroptosis switching, although the mechanisms require further clarification. FOSL2 mediates early apoptosis during radiotherapy/chemotherapy via DNA damage responses [220 ] Meanwhile, accumulating mitochondrial damage increases ROS, promoting inflammasome assembly and NF-κB activation for cytokine release [221 ]. In NSCLC, activation of the FOSL2/NAMPT axis confers cisplatin resistance [222 ]. Additionally, in colon cancer, KLF6-recruited p300 complexes enhance H3K23 succinylation with FOSL2 to upregulate SEMA3C, promoting 5-FU resistance [223 ]. Consistent with our bioinformatics analysis, Li et al. [224 ] demonstrated that dual inhibition of FOSL2 and caspase-1 enhances ovarian cancer apoptosis. They further suggested that co-activation of FOSL2 and caspase-1 might induce pyroptosis to overcome resistance, a hypothesis that needs validation. In summary, our integrated analysis of hub genes and the functional implications of these genes provides a framework for understanding the molecular crosstalk between apoptosis and pyroptosis, with potential therapeutic implications for overcoming treatment resistance. 5 New strategies for cancer treatment based on the interaction between apoptosis and pyroptosis Understanding the inter-regulatory network between apoptosis and pyroptosis provides valuable insights and tools for designing more effective cancer treatment strategies. Consequently, we have outlined strategies for tumor therapy based on the interaction of apoptosis and pyroptosis. A systematic summary of therapeutic strategies targeting the apoptosis-pyroptosis switch in cancer is shown in Table 3 . 5.1 Inducing pyroptosis to overcome apoptosis resistance Many apoptosis-resistant tumors retain functional downstream pathways (e.g., caspase-3) [225 ]. Exploiting "apoptosis-pyroptosis conversion" can bypass upstream inhibitors (e.g., BCL-2 overexpression) [226 ]. For GSDME-expressing (or drug-restorable) tumors, caspase-3-activating chemotherapeutics can induce pyroptosis rather than apoptosis [227–229 ], making GSDME expression/methylation status a potential predictive biomarker. Yu et al.l [230 ] developed neutrophil-mimicking stealth nanoparticles (ANPs; anti-CD11b antibody-modified albumin nanoparticles loaded with decitabine/IR820) for photothermal-enhanced pyroptosis immunotherapy. Systemic administration targeted activated neutrophils to deliver drugs to tumors, with laser irradiation upregulating GSDME and activating caspase-3 to induce pyroptosis and reverse resistance (Fig. 6 A). Nanomaterials exhibit unique advantages in the co-regulation of pyroptosis and apoptosis. One important mechanism is dual-pathway regulation: mitochondria serve as the core hub for controlling these two types of cell death. Through mitochondrial signals such as ROS generation and mtDNA release, nanomaterials can simultaneously activate caspase-1/GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis and caspase-3-dependent apoptosis [231 ,232 ]. For instance, cobalt-based nanomaterials (CoF) induce caspase-1/GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis by releasing Co^2+ ions and ROS, while triggering mtDNA release to activate apoptotic pathways [232 ]. Gasdermin E (GSDME) is a key protein linking apoptosis and pyroptosis. Certain nanomaterials, such as osthole-loaded nanoparticles, activate caspase-3 to cleave GSDME. This process converts apoptotic signals into pyroptosis, which is marked by LDH release and secretion of inflammatory cytokines [178 ]. Another mechanism involves a synergistic induction strategy using nanomaterials. For example, citrate-modified nanomaterials inhibit the tricarboxylic acid cycle, reducing α-KG levels, which activates the HIF-1α-dependent pyroptosis pathway, they also enhance pyroptosis through the caspase-8/GSDMC pathway [233 ]. Moreover, metabolic disorders can indirectly promote apoptosis. Pyroptosis induced by nanomaterials releases IL-1β and IL-18, which recruit immune cells (e.g., dendritic cells) to enhance antitumor immunity, thereby synergizing with immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., PD-1 antibodies) to promote tumor cell apoptosis [234 ,235 ]. The third strategy is achieved through the design of nanomaterials. The multifunctional nano-platform tetrahedral framework nucleic acids (tFNAs) specifically inhibit inflammation and fibrosis through their spatial structure, they also downregulate the activities of caspase-1 and caspase-3, thereby achieving dual inhibition of pyroptosis and apoptosis [236 ]. Cobalt-based nanozymes (CoF) not only directly induce pyroptosis but also act as STING agonists to activate apoptosis-related immune responses, significantly suppressing tumor growth in animal models [232 ]. In summary, nanomaterials have achieved the synergistic regulation of pyroptosis and apoptosis through dual-pathway regulation, synergistic induction, and material design. Future research should focus on clarifying the crosstalk mechanisms between the dual pathways and on developing intelligent nanosystems with spatiotemporal control [237 ]. 5.2 Transforming “cold tumors” into “hot tumors” While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) revolutionized cancer therapy [238 ], their efficacy remains limited in immunologically "cold" tumors [239 ]. Pyroptosis' immunogenicity offers solutions: pyroptosis inducers [240 ] can transform immunosuppressive microenvironments by releasing DAMPs/cytokines that recruit immune cells and present tumor antigens via APCs, activating T cell responses [241 ]. Current pyroptosis inducers include: (1) gasdermin activators [242 ]; (2) pyroptosis-inducing nanoparticles [242–244 ]; (3) chemotherapeutics (cisplatin, doxorubicin, paclitaxel) [245–247 ]; (4) herbal compounds [248 ]; (5) photothermal agents [246 ,247 ,249 ]; and (6) sonodynamic therapies [245 ,246 ]. For example, Hou et al. [250 ] showed doxorubicin upregulating GSDME in 4T1 cells, increasing CD3+/CD4+/CD8+ T cells and TNF-α/IFN-γ to reverse immunosuppression (Fig. 6 B). Wu et al. [251 ] developed tungsten@iron-folic acid composites (WO@Fe-FA) combining photothermal therapy (PTT) and chemodynamic therapy (CDT) to induce immunogenic cell death. Fenton reaction-generated oxygen alleviated hypoxia-induced PD-L1 upregulation, converting "cold" to "hot" tumors (Fig. 6 C). Silin Du et al. [252 ] have developed a novel bionic nanoplatform (CVOVM) that synergistically induces PANoptosis through ROS amplification and glutamine metabolism inhibition. This platform has been demonstrated to effectively remodel the tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment and enhance immunotherapy, representing a cutting-edge strategy to ignite cold tumors. Combining pyroptosis inducers with ICIs may synergistically "ignite" tumors and "release" immune brakes. 5.3 Precision therapy targeting “switches” Caspase-8/-3 constitute attractive drug targets as death modality switches [138 ]. Developing allosteric modulators favoring GSDMD cleavage over pro-caspase-3 activation could force pyroptosis in specific tumors (Fig. 6 C). Molecular dynamics platforms [253 ] combined with drug screening [254 ] and druggability analysis [255 ] may enable precision switch-targeted therapies. Furthermore, emerging drug design strategies such as PROTACs (Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras) could be employed to degrade negative regulators of pyroptosis (e.g., IAPs) [256 ], moreover, structure-based drug design can identify small molecules that stabilize the active conformation of pore-forming gasdermins. 5.4 Potential risks and challenges: managing the “firepower” of pyroptosis Despite promise, pyroptosis' inflammatory nature poses challenges: (1) Systemic cytokine release syndrome (CRS) risks [257 ], resembling CAR-T therapy complications (40–50 % incidence) [258 ] with potential multi-organ failure [259–261 ]; (2) Spatiotemporal control difficulties - current technologies cannot restrict pyroptosis to tumors [262 ], which risks damage to normal tissues [263 ], such as lung inflammation in NSCLC models [264 ,265 ]; and (3) individual variability in inflammatory tolerance (e.g., 7–10 % severe CRS in CAR-T) [266 ,267 ], influenced by factors like HBV status [268 ], necessitates personalized approaches [269 ]. Potential solutions include: (1) Spatiotemporal strategies using tumor-targeted nanoparticles [270–272 ], inflammation modulation with concurrent anti-inflammatories, such as Anakinra, which reduced CAR-T CRS hospitalization by 50 % [273 ]; and (3) immunopotentiation combining pyroptosis inducers with PD-1 inhibitors (Fig. 6 D), which improved efficacy without increasing clinical inflammation [269 ]. Balancing treatment efficacy and safety remains crucial for successful clinical translation. 5.5 Clinical translation The compelling preclinical evidence for targeting the apoptosis-pyroptosis switch is now paves the way for clinical translation, with several strategic paths emerging. The repurposing of conventional chemotherapeutics such as cisplatin and doxorubicin, along with existing drugs like disulfiram, particularly when combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., trials NCT03546829, NCT04303988), represents a near-term strategy to harness pyroptosis for immunotherapy [274 ,275 ]. The development of predictive biomarkers, such as GSDME expression and the hub genes identified in our analysis, is critical to the success of patient stratification. This biomarker-driven approach will identify patients most likely to benefit from death switch-targeting therapies, potentially through companion diagnostics, such as immunohistochemistry assays and circulating tumor DNA analysis. Going forward, the clinical pipeline must expand to include novel agents specifically designed to modulate key switch molecules (e.g., caspase-8/GSDMD), while concurrently addressing the challenge of managing pyroptosis-associated inflammation through targeted delivery systems and combination regimens. Emerging approaches, such as copper-based nanoinducers, disrupt intracellular ion homeostasis to simultaneously induce cuproptosis and disulfidptosis [276 ], highlighting the potential of precisely targeting cell death pathways beyond traditional apoptosis and pyroptosis. Beyond oncology, the death switch concept may find applications in other disease contexts, such as autoimmune diseases by promoting apoptosis of autoreactive cells, infectious diseases by enhancing pyroptosis of infected cells, and neurodegenerative disorders by preventing excessive cell death. The development of real-time monitoring tools, such as non-invasive imaging techniques for caspase activation and circulating biomarkers such as gasdermin fragments, will enable early intervention and dynamic treatment adjustments in non-responders. 5.6 Comparative analysis of therapeutic strategies Each therapeutic category offers distinct advantages and faces unique challenges. Small molecules provide the advantage of oral administration and established manufacturing processes, but their limited specificity may lead to off-target effects. Biologics offer high specificity and durable responses, but their high cost and limited tumor penetration remain barriers to widespread use. Combination therapies leverage the strengths of multiple approaches but are often associated with increased toxicity and complex dosing schedules. Novel approaches, such as nanomedicine and gene therapy, hold promise for targeted delivery and high potency, but they are still in early stages of development and face significant regulatory hurdles. The choice of therapeutic strategy should be guided by several factors, including the patient's biomarker profile, tumor type, tumor stage, prior treatments, and comorbidities. For example, patients with high GSDME expression may benefit from small molecule inducers that specifically target this axis, whereas those with immune-infiltrated tumors may be better candidates for biologics or combination therapies (Table 2 ). For chemotherapeutic agents like oxaliplatin that activate dual pathways, clinical administration should be guided by GSDME methylation status. Patients with silenced GSDME may benefit from sequential therapy: first, treatment with demethylating agents (e.g., decitabine) to restore GSDME expression, followed by chemotherapy to induce the transition from apoptosis to immunogenic pyroptosis. Future research should focus on developing predictive biomarkers to guide the rational selection of the optimal therapeutic strategy for each patient. 6 s and future perspectives The intricate interplay between apoptosis and pyroptosis represents a sophisticated regulatory network that extends far beyond simple binary cell fate decisions. Our comprehensive analysis reveals that the caspase-3/GSDME and caspase-8/GSDMD axes serve as critical molecular switches that determine cellular responses to therapeutic interventions (Fig. 7 ). However, the clinical translation of these fundamental discoveries faces several significant challenges that must be systematically addressed. Foremost among clinical challenges is the precise spatiotemporal control of pyroptosis induction. However, although pyroptosis shows potent anti-tumor effects in preclinical models, its inflammatory nature poses substantial risks of cytokine release syndrome and off-target tissue damage. Current delivery systems lack the sophistication to restrict pyroptosis activation exclusively to tumor sites, necessitating the development of smarter nanoplatforms with tumor-microenvironment responsive elements. Recent advancements in tumor-targeting nanoparticles, such as those responsive to specific proteases or acidic pH in the tumor microenvironment [277 ,278 ], offer promising avenues for inducing localized pyroptosis. Patient stratification is another critical hurdle because the efficacy of pyroptosis-targeting therapies depends heavily on the molecular profile of individual tumors, especially the expression levels of key gasdermin family members and inflammasome components. The development of reliable biomarkers—whether through immunohistochemical assessment of GSDME expression, circulating tumor DNA analysis of gasdermin mutations, or functional imaging of caspase activation—will be essential for identifying patients most likely to benefit from these approaches. Our bioinformatic analysis identifying hub genes such as PRKAR1A, PPP2CA, and FOSL2, providing a starting point for developing such stratification strategies. Managing therapy-induced inflammation requires careful consideration. Although the immunogenic nature of pyroptosis provides its therapeutic advantage, excessive inflammation may lead to detrimental side effects. Combination strategies incorporating anti-inflammatory agents, such as IL-1 receptor antagonists or corticosteroids, require careful timing and dosing to mitigate toxicity without blunting the anti-tumor immune response. The clinical experience from CAR-T cell therapy, where tocilizumab [279 ] (NCT02767557) effectively manages cytokine release syndrome without compromising efficacy, provides valuable lessons for pyroptosis-based therapies. Looking forward, several promising directions emerge. First, the development of novel therapeutic agents specifically designed to modulate the key switches—such as small molecules that bias caspase-8 activity toward GSDMD cleavage rather than promoting apoptotic signaling—represents an exciting frontier. Second, combination strategies that integrate pyroptosis inducers with immune checkpoint inhibitors, cancer vaccines, or adoptive cell therapies may create synergistic anti-tumor immunity. Notably, the recent success of combining disulfiram with anti-PD-1 antibodies in clinical trials (NCT04353999) underscores the potential of such approaches. Third, expanding the therapeutic paradigm beyond oncology to autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders—where the modulation of cell death may restore homeostasis—represents an intriguing future direction. In conclusion, despite significant challenges, strategically manipulating the apoptosis-pyroptosis switch holds tremendous promise for revolutionizing cancer therapy. By addressing these translational challenges through collaboration among basic scientists, clinical investigators, and bioengineers, we can expect groundbreaking advances that ultimately improve outcomes for cancer patients. Abbreviations and glossary ASC Apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD, it serves as the "alarm call to assemble" in the cellular inflammatory response, when intracellular danger sensors such as NLRP3 are activated, ASC assembles into a large "signal station" called the ASC speck. It recruits and activates a large number of inflammatory "executors" (caspase-1), which then release strong inflammatory signals and potentially lead to pyroptosis CRS Cytokine Release Syndrome, it is commonly known as "cytokine storm", a condition where the immune system becomes excessively activated. When a large number of immune cells (e.g., CAR-T cells) are activated, they release an excessive amount of inflammatory signals (cytokines), which not only attack the invaders but also damage the body's own tissues and organs, leading to systemic severe reactions such as high fever, hypotension, and organ failure DAMPs Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns, the "alarm signal" is sent out when a cell is in distress, indicating cellular injury. When a cell dies from injury, hypoxia, or other causes, its contents leak out and are detected as danger signals by the immune system, which initiates inflammation to clear the area and starts the repair process DED Death Effector Domain, this molecular hook, present on proteins such as FADD and caspase-8, allows FADD to recruit caspase-8 to the vicinity of death receptors and assemble them into a complex, thereby initiating apoptosis DISC Death-Inducing Signaling Complex, it is an urgently assembled "execution command post" beneath the cell membrane after the cell receives a "death order". It recruits the command-receiving "receptor" (Fas), the command-transmitting "messenger" (FADD), and the command-executing "executioner" (caspase-8), then activates the execution program immediately FADD Fas-associated protein with death domain, it acts as the messenger for the cell's ‘death order’. When death receptors on the cell membrane receive the ‘suicide’ signal, FADD relays this signal into the cell interior and activates the actual executioner protein, caspase-8, thereby triggering apoptosis FLIP FLICE (FADD-like IL-1β-converting enzyme)-inhibitory protein, it acts as a pressure regulator in the cell apoptosis pathway. Although it is structurally similar to the executioner caspase-8, it lacks enzymatic activity and prevents full activation of caspase-8 by competing for binding sites, thus avoiding excessive cell death. Moreover, under certain conditions, its weak interaction with caspase-8 can instead transmit a survival-maintaining signal GSDMD Gasdermin D,a protein activated upon cellular infection or damage that can form pores in the cell membrane, inducing a type of inflammatory cell death known as pyroptosis, thereby releasing alarm signals and initiating immune responses GSDME Gasdermin E,a protein activated by apoptotic signals that acts like a "switch," converting the cell's "silent self-elimination" (apoptosis) into "alarm-sounding" (pyroptosis), thereby helping to awaken the immune system in cancer therapy IAPs Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins, they are a class of proteins that inhibit cellular activities. These proteins mainly function by inhibiting the executioner proteins (caspases) involved in the cellular "suicide program" (apoptosis), while also transmitting "survival signals" by activating NF-κB, thereby helping cells survive under stress IETD It is a "molecular key" specifically recognized by caspase-8, the executioner protein in cell apoptosis. Scientists attach a "fluorescent tag" to it, and by detecting the intensity of the fluorescence, they determine the activity level of caspase-8 in the cell and thus infer whether apoptosis has occurred LUBAC Linear Ubiquitin Chain Assembly Complex, an enzyme complex attaching "linear ubiquitin chains" to specific proteins. This type of tag functions as a precise signal that primarily initiates cellular survival and inflammatory signaling (the NF-κB pathway), while helping cells avoid inappropriate death under stress PAMPs Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns, they shared "molecular IDs" on pathogens, such as bacteria and viruses. Once the immune system detects these foreign IDs, it immediately sounds the alarm and triggers an inflammatory response to eliminate the invaders PCD Programmed Cell Death, the collective term refers to multiple pathways of programmed cell death, all of which are genetically controlled, follow a fixed sequence of steps, and are crucial for the organism to eliminate unnecessary, damaged, or dangerous cells PRRs Pattern Recognition Receptors, these proteins are known as the "sentinel proteins" of the immune system. They stand guard on duty, and once they identify invading pathogens (PAMPs) or internal cellular damage (DAMPs) via "molecular fingerprints," they immediately sound the alarm and trigger an inflammatory response STING–NF–κB pathway Stimulator of Interferon Genes – Nuclear Factor-kappa B pathway,the DNA alarm system inside a cell detects foreign DNA (such as viral DNA) that shouldn't be present, it activates a signaling cascade that ultimately turns on the "master regulator" NF-κB, which then increases the production of inflammatory signaling proteins and mobilizes the immune system References [1] K. title: Based on network pharmacology and molecular docking to explore the mechanism that Naringin alleviates neuronal injury after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion by inhibiting ferroptosis via TP53/SLC7A11
abstract: Background Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is a global cerebrovascular disease with high disability and mortality. Previous studies have revealed the protection of Naringin against ischemia in the nervous system. This study is designed to explore the role and mechanism of Naringin in oxygen-glucose deprivation/recovery (OGD/R)-induced ischemic neuronal injury. Methods The OGD/R model was built using SK-N-SH cells, followed by exposure to Naringin. CCK-8 and flow cytometry analyzed cell viability and apoptosis. ELISA determined TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β levels. Special kits detected GSH, ROS, and MDA levels. Fe+ levels were determined using Iron assay kit. Western blot determined Solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and tumor protein p53 (TP53) protein levels. Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD), SwissTargetPrediction Database, and GeneCards Database provided targets of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis. PPI networks for intersected targets were constructed. KEGG enrichment analyses assessed the function of intersection targets. Molecular docking recognized the association between Naringin and core targets. Results Naringin relieved OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell apoptosis, inflammatory response, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis. From 64 targets of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis, PPI network identified ten hub genes. Among them, TP53 was mostly enriched in ferroptosis. Furthermore, Naringin had good binding affinity with TP53. Naringin could mitigate OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell damage by regulating TP53. Conclusion Naringin could attenuate OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell injury by regulating TP53/SLC7A11, providing a new idea for AIS treatment.

Dongliang Liu, Department of Neurology, the First Affiliated Hospital of Bengbu Medical University Changhuai Road, Longzihu District Bengbu City Anhui Province China Background Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is a global cerebrovascular disease with high disability and mortality. Previous studies have revealed the protection of Naringin against ischemia in the nervous system. This study is designed to explore the role and mechanism of Naringin in oxygen-glucose deprivation/recovery (OGD/R)-induced ischemic neuronal injury. Methods The OGD/R model was built using SK-N-SH cells, followed by exposure to Naringin. CCK-8 and flow cytometry analyzed cell viability and apoptosis. ELISA determined TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β levels. Special kits detected GSH, ROS, and MDA levels. Fe+ levels were determined using Iron assay kit. Western blot determined Solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and tumor protein p53 (TP53) protein levels. Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD), SwissTargetPrediction Database, and GeneCards Database provided targets of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis. PPI networks for intersected targets were constructed. KEGG enrichment analyses assessed the function of intersection targets. Molecular docking recognized the association between Naringin and core targets. Results Naringin relieved OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell apoptosis, inflammatory response, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis. From 64 targets of Naringin, AIS, and ferroptosis, PPI network identified ten hub genes. Among them, TP53 was mostly enriched in ferroptosis. Furthermore, Naringin had good binding affinity with TP53. Naringin could mitigate OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell damage by regulating TP53. Conclusion Naringin could attenuate OGD/R-induced SK-N-SH cell injury by regulating TP53/SLC7A11, providing a new idea for AIS treatment.
