Results XPO1 is highly expressed in patients who have the poorest outcomes Primary tumor samples from patients with high-risk neuroblastoma were used to perform top-down proteomics to compare profiles of patients who were long-term survivors (controls: >3-year survival) with patients who died rapidly of disease progression (cases <18-month survival). These data demonstrate that XPO1 is one of the most highly abundant proteins in patients who have the most aggressive disease (Fig. 1 a and b, Supplemental Table 1). XPO1 was of interest to our group because of the increased recognition of its key role in cellular homeostasis, the correlation of high protein expression with inferior outcome in multiple cancer types, and the availability of a pharmacologic agent to target it [5 ,34–36 ]. We then utilized an independent publicly available dataset from R2: Neuroblastoma Genomics Analysis and Visualization Platform (https://hgserver1.amc.nl/cgi-bin/r2/main.cgi ) to create a Kaplan-Meier survival curve of the Kocak data set, comparing survival between patients with neuroblastoma whose tumors had low versus high levels of XPO1 . Unlike the proteomics data set that analyzed tumors from patients with high-risk neuroblastoma, the Kocak data set includes patients with neuroblastoma across all risk groups, excluding patients with stage 4S disease. The event-free survival probability of patients with high XPO1 expression was inferior to those with low XPO1 expression (raw p -value of 2.5e-05 and Bonferroni correction of 9.9e-03) (Fig. 1 c), demonstrating that high XPO1 expression consistently correlates with inferior survival. We next surveyed an independent neuroblastoma tumor microarray to assess XPO1 immunohistochemical staining and verify transcriptomic data. Eighty-nine percent of samples stained positive, with a range of intensity from 1+ to 3+ (Fig. 1 d). Tumor cores scored as 0+ (no staining) were primarily ganglioneuromas or poor quality specimens. These data demonstrate that high XPO1 protein expression and high gene expression, regardless of neuroblastoma risk grouping, correlate with inferior outcome, and that XPO1 is nearly universally present in tumor tissue. Selinexor reduces cell viability in a heterogeneous panel of neuroblastoma cell lines with a range of XPO1 expression A panel of nine neuroblastoma cell lines with molecular diversity were analyzed for XPO1 expression by immunoblotting. With the exception of SKNSH, XPO1 expression was substantially greater in neuroblastoma cell lines than in immortalized, nontransformed retinal pigmented epithelial (RPE1) cells (Fig. 2 a). We then generated selinexor dose response curves. The IC50 range for the neuroblastoma cell lines ranged from 4 to 312 nM, whereas RPE1 was relatively insensitive, with an IC50 of 41 µM (Fig. 2 b, Supplemental Fig. 1). Sensitivity to selinexor was independent of cell line biologic features that are relevant in human disease, including MYCN copy number status (IMR5, LAN5, NLF and NB1643 are MYCN amplified). Recognizing that nuclear export of IkB is mediated by XPO1, we analyzed changes in nuclear and cytoplasmic localization of IkB with selinexor. Using immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy, we found that selinexor treatment results in a statistically significant increase of IkB in the nucleus (p -value <0.05, Fig. 2 c and d), while no change in IkB abundance was appreciated in the cytoplasm. The increased nuclear retention of IkB caused by selinexor was confirmed by immunoblotting of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins (Fig. 2 e). We did not identify a correlation between IkB abundance or localization and sensitivity to selinexor. The combination of selinexor and bortezomib is synergistic in neuroblastoma cell lines Selinexor has a fairly favorable toxicity profile when used clinically in adult patients [37] , though children may be more prone to dose-limiting toxicities. We therefore considered combinatorial treatment strategies to augment selinexor activity without the need for dose escalation. Bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor, has been evaluated in neuroblastoma with single agent in vitro IC50s also in the nanomolar range [25] , though results from clinical studies have shown less promising results [38] . Since bortezomib inhibits NF-kB signaling in a distinct manner from selinexor, we hypothesized that the combination of selinexor and bortezomib would more effectively diminish NF-kB-related pro-survival signaling in neuroblastoma. IMR5, NLF and SKNSH neuroblastoma cell lines were selected for their diversity of molecular features, including MYCN amplification (IMR5 and NLF), wild type TP 53 (IMR5 and SKNSH), and differential abundance of XPO1 (Fig. 2 a). To assay for synergy between bortezomib and selinexor, we used combination index (CI) and isobologram analyses. CI values less than 1 indicate synergy, which is present across multiple dose ranges and cell lines (Fig. 3 a–c) and suggests that lower doses of both drugs, compared to single agent concentrations, can achieve high anti-tumor activity and potentially reduce toxicity. We then applied isobologram analyses at effect levels of 0.5, 0.75, and 0.9 growth inhibition (Fig. 3 d–f). The isobole of the combination was below the line of additivity at all effect levels and across all cell lines, confirming the synergy of bortezomib and selinexor regardless of underlying cell line biology. Selinexor and bortezomib promote cell cycle arrest and apoptosis We next investigated the effects of selinexor and bortezomib on cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Using BrdU labeling we found that selinexor monotherapy contributed to an increase in G1-0 arrest (p -value <0.05) and a corresponding decrease in cells in S phase (p -value <0.05). Combination treatment with selinexor and bortezomib enhanced G1-0 arrest in all cell lines, though this was statistically significant only in the MYCN non-amplified cell line, SKNSH (p -value <0.05) (Fig. 4 a). We then proceeded to assess for apoptosis using Annexin-V labeling. Comparing the viable population between treatment conditions, we saw a significant decrease from single drug to combination (p -value <0.001 for selinexor or bortezomib vs. combination in IMR5; p -value <0.01 for selinexor vs. combination and p -value <0.05 for bortezomib vs. combination in NLF). We saw a statistically significant increase in total apoptotic cells with combination treatment compared with selinexor (p -value <0.001 in IMR5 and NLF, p -value <0.05 in SKNSH) and also compared with bortezomib (p -value <0.001 in IMR5, p -value <0.05 in NLF) (Fig. 4 b). To support these findings, we utilized Western blotting to assess protein levels of the cleaved form of PARP (c-PARP), an early marker in the signal cascade for apoptosis. c-PARP was greatest in cells treated with the combination of selinexor and bortezomib, suggesting that they work cooperatively to induce apoptosis (Fig. 4 c). Mechanistic assessment of selinexor-bortezomib combination therapy demonstrates the crucial role of IkB in diminishing Nf-kB activity and cellular proliferation Finally, we directly tested our hypothesis that IkB is critical to the synergy seen between selinexor and bortezomib. Nuclear retention of IkB is a key step in the inhibitory regulation of NF-kB signaling pathway and one that is most pronounced with combination treatment [39 ,40 ]. Using an NF-kB luciferase assay in two cell lines that were amenable to transfection, we first demonstrated that selinexor and bortezomib as single agents led to decreased NF-kB signaling compared to vehicle when stimulated with TNFa, a known activator of NF-kB activity [41] . We then showed that combination treatment resulted in the lowest amount of NF-kB activity (Fig. 5 a). Next, we sought to determine if IkB was necessary for this effect. We found that siRNA knockdown of IkB, using 2 distinct siRNA constructs, eliminated the treatment effect in IMR5 and NLF cell lines, while a nontargeting siRNA had no effect. Specifically, selinexor treatment with siRNA knockdown was similar to vehicle without IkB knockdown (IMR5 – SEL non-targeting vs siRNA1: p -value <0.01, non-targeting vs siRNA2 p -value <0.05; NLF – SEL non-targeting vs siRNA1: p -value <0.05, non-targeting vs siRNA2 <0.01), bortezomib and combination treatment with siRNA knockdown of IkB demonstrated relative increased proliferation activity (IMR5- BTZ/CO non-targeting vs siRNA1: p -value <0.01, non-targeting vs siRNA2 <0.05; NLF- BTZ non-targeting vs siRNA1: p -value <0.001, CO non-targeting vs siRNA1:p -value <0.05, non-targeting vs siRNA2: p -value<0.05) (Fig. 5 b and c). These results reflect the key regulatory role of IkB in the NF-kB signaling pathway and suggest one mechanistic explanation of the synergy between selinexor and bortezomib. Discussion Patients with the most highly aggressive neuroblastoma, often referred to as those with ultra-high-risk neuroblastoma, have dismal outcomes. Up to 15% of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma will die from disease progression within 18 months from diagnosis, and there is a clear imperative to better understand drivers of disease and develop novel approaches to management. We have demonstrated that XPO1 expression correlates with highly aggressive neuroblastoma and that patients with this form of the disease may benefit from a novel combinatorial treatment approach with selinexor and bortezomib. The synergistic effect of these agents addresses concerns about dose-limiting toxicities of selinexor [42] , and accordingly, similar combination strategies have recently led to FDA approval of selinexor in multiple myeloma which may support its use in the pediatric patient population. XPO1 is nearly universally expressed in neuroblastoma, including in the panel of cell lines used in our studies, though we did not identify a correlation between expression level and sensitivity to selinexor. In addition, in one representative cell line pair, CHLA15 and CHLA20 derived from the same patient before and after treatment, respectively, the selinexor IC50 values were comparable. These results suggests that drug sensitivity in patients would be independent of XPO1 expression even though expression can serve as a prognostic biomarker. Retrospective studies of XPO1 expression show how critical XPO1 is to the oncogenic process but with the lack of knowledge on how overexpression occurs, it is the cargo proteins and pathways thereof that remain the most promising for a therapeutic marker of response [43 ,44 ]. In neuroblastoma and other cancers, high transcriptional activity of NF-kB can be inhibited through IkB nuclear localization and stabilization [45–47] . Proteasome inhibitors, such as bortezomib, achieve this through preventing degradation of IkB, thereby maintaining IkB function in the NF-kB inhibitory complex in the cytoplasmic compartment [39 ,48 ]. Bortezomib is now integrated into standard of care across a range of adult malignancies yet it has underperformed in neuroblastoma studies. With the knowledge that IkB is a cargo protein of selinexor, we investigated the use of selinexor and bortezomib in combination, building on prior work in multiple myeloma [39 ,40 ,49 ]. IkB in the nucleus would be expected to inhibit the transcription factor NF-kB and thereby change the dynamics of downstream targets that promote cancer survival in neuroblastoma. We demonstrated that IkB is a key mediator of the synergistic effect of combination therapy on NF-kB activity in neuroblastoma. Although siRNA knockdown of IkB ablated the effect of selinexor, knockdown of IkB promoted the proliferation of cells treated with bortezomib, possibly because stabilization by bortezomib of other proteins that are degraded by the proteasome, results in stimulation of NF-kB activity in the absence of IkB, as NF-kB transcription factor signaling networks can both promote or suppress growth [50 ,51 ]. Understanding these complexities will be crucial for the development of this treatment for patients with neuroblastoma, in particular because resistance to selinexor in multiple myeloma, for example, is associated with increased NF-KB activity [45] . An important finding from this work is that the synergy between selinexor and bortezomib is independent of TP53 mutation status or MYCN amplification status. These two molecular aberrations are associated with aggressive disease and relative chemoresistance. TP 53 is typically wild type in newly diagnosed neuroblastoma, but in relapsed disease can mutate (e.g., NLF cell line is a representation of this phenomenon), and hamper therapeutic responses [52 ,53 ]. TP 53 is also a cargo protein of XPO1 and diminished nuclear abundance correlates with diminished tumor suppression in patients [54–56] . MYCN is similarly an elusive target in neuroblastoma, with the oncogene amplified in about half of patients with high-risk neuroblastoma. MYCN is known to activate numerous genes involved in the promotion and maintenance of cancer and stemness [57] . While cell lines responded to combination therapy regardless of MYCN status, the MYCN non-amplified cell line, SKNSH, demonstrated an inclination towards an increase in cell cycle arrest in response to selinexor and bortezomib. Interestingly, SKNSH has increased levels of Cyclin D1, a protein involved in cell cycle regulation, and the expression of this protein changes as the cell proceeds through G1/S phase transition [58 ,59 ]. Increased levels and activity of Cyclin D1 contribute to a less differentiated phenotype, and loss of Cyclin D1 expression leads to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [60 ,61 ]. The different mechanisms affecting cellular processes in response to combination therapy, including determinants of cell cycle inhibition, in MYCN amplified versus non-amplified lines is a focus of ongoing investigation. In summary, we have demonstrated that high XPO1 protein expression correlates with an inferior outcome in neuroblastoma. In patient-derived neuroblastoma cells that represent the heterogeneous nature of this cancer, there is synergistic inhibition of cellular proliferation with the use of selinexor and bortezomib. This is mediated, at least in by IkB regulation of the NF-kB signaling pathway. Our findings demonstrate that XPO1 is a potential prognostic biomarker and reveal a targeted therapeutic approach, that can be integrated into the next generation of clinical trials. Ongoing work is focused on patient-derived xenograft in vivo testing of selinexor/bortezomib combinatorial strategies, as well as studies to understand how XPO1 overexpression promotes aggressive neuroblastoma. We will also assess dose reduction of bortezomib and/or selinexor when used in combination, similar to approaches used in multiple myeloma to increase tolerability [62] .Results from this work, combined with exploration of gene expression changes in response to single agents and combination therapy, will provide additional insight about our therapeutic strategy that addresses current challenges in treating highly aggressive neuroblastoma. title: Receptor based virtual screening of potential novel inhibitors of tigar [TP53 (tumour protein 53)-induced glycolysis and apoptosis regulator
abstract: TP53 (tumor protein 53)-induced glycolysis and apoptosis regulator (TIGAR) belongs to the phosphatases family of proteins that modulates the level of reactive oxygen species in tumor cells. This protein plays a vital role as a negative regulator of glycolysis, thus lowering ROS levels in the cells, which helps the cancerous cells to resist programmed cell death. Besides, TIGAR also mediates the DNA damage repair in cancer cells by increasing tumor cell survival. In the current study, we have screened natural products that compete with the substrate to bind to the active site of TIGAR. Extra precision and MMGBSA scoring function were used to screen the lead molecules. Five compounds were considered as lead molecules with 2-(2-(3,4-dihydroxy phenyl)-3,5-dihydroxy-8-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-4-oxo-4H-furo[2,3-h]chromen-9-yl) acetic acid(DDFA) as a top lead with a docking score of −9.428, and −53.16 MMGBSA, bind to the positively charged amino acids present in the active site. Further, the molecular dynamics simulation studies indicated the structural stability attained by TIGAR protein upon the binding of DDFA, suggesting it to be a potent inhibitor of TIGAR, and could be employed as an anticancer drug during combinational therapy.

TP53 (tumor protein 53)-induced glycolysis and apoptosis regulator (TIGAR) belongs to the phosphatases family of proteins that modulates the level of reactive oxygen species in tumor cells. This protein plays a vital role as a negative regulator of glycolysis, thus lowering ROS levels in the cells, which helps the cancerous cells to resist programmed cell death. Besides, TIGAR also mediates the DNA damage repair in cancer cells by increasing tumor cell survival. In the current study, we have screened natural products that compete with the substrate to bind to the active site of TIGAR. Extra precision and MMGBSA scoring function were used to screen the lead molecules. Five compounds were considered as lead molecules with 2-(2-(3,4-dihydroxy phenyl)-3,5-dihydroxy-8-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-4-oxo-4H-furo[2,3-h]chromen-9-yl) acetic acid(DDFA) as a top lead with a docking score of −9.428, and −53.16 MMGBSA, bind to the positively charged amino acids present in the active site. Further, the molecular dynamics simulation studies indicated the structural stability attained by TIGAR protein upon the binding of DDFA, suggesting it to be a potent inhibitor of TIGAR, and could be employed as an anticancer drug during combinational therapy. Keywords TIGAR Reactive oxygen species Phosphatase Cancer Apoptosis Introduction Cancer development is suppressed by the tumor suppressor gene p53 by induction of genome stability, apoptosis, and cell cycle arrest. Stress-activated p53 regulates cell survival and death by controlling reactive oxygen (ROS) species levels [1] .ROS level and antioxidant activity of p53 play a significant role in tumor development and DNA damage. The response to ROS by P53 induced proteins depends on the type of ROS generated in the tissue. The level of ROS contributes to the induction of apoptosis. Recent studies proved that p53 family proteins are involved in lowering the level of ROS in the cells. The p53induced proteins like sestrins [2] and Aldehyde Dehydrogenase 4 (ALDH4) [3] reduce the level of hydrogen peroxide and ROS, respectively, in cancer cells. Also, p53 induces target genes such as sestrins, ALDH4, phosphoglyceratemutase [4] , and TP53 (tumor protein 53)-induced glycolysis and apoptosis regulator (TIGAR) in response to ROS stress. Recent studies reported TIGAR regulates the ROS level and protects the tumor cells from apoptosis. TIGAR protein is well-known for its ability to switch the glycolysis pathway into the pentose phosphate pathway to promote antioxidant protection of cancer cells [5] . In hypoxic conditions, TIGAR translocates into the inner membrane of mitochondria. Wherein it interacts with membrane-bound hexokinase 2(HK2) and increases its activity (Fig. 1 ). HK2 helps in the maintenance of the membrane potential of mitochondria by increasing the level of ADP. This event in mitochondria reduces the ROS and prevents the assembling of Bax at voltage-dependent anionic channels. Consequently, the release of cytochrome C into the cytoplasm, caspase cascade, and apoptosis is prevented. Studies on TIGAR have demonstrated that it is a prospective drug target in many cancers. Recent studies by Chu et al. [6] ascertained that TIGAR plays a vital role in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) progression and chemoresistance. Overexpression of TIGAR was correlated with the growth of Hodgkin Lymphoma, Ovarian Epithelial Tumor, Neuroblastoma, Non-Seminomatous Germ Cell Tumor, Seminoma, Kidney Cancer, and breast carcinoma [2,3,7,8] . TIGAR is a potent target for breast and gastric cancers [9] . Inhibition of TIGAR also helps in the radiosensitization of glioblastoma cells [10,11] . Hence inhibiting TIGAR will help combat the cancer chemoresistance. Most of the solid tumors are hypoxic, where TIGAR is level is high. So, the small molecules that are capable of inhibiting the TIGAR could be effective in combinational chemotherapy. Studies proved that TIGAR inhibitors would increase the efficacy of the cancer treatment in combination with anticancer drugs [8] .In this study, we have screened the curate natural products library for TIGAR inhibitors. Our study showed the possibility of using few compounds against cancer prevention mediated through TIGAR regulation. Hypothesis TIGAR can influence cancer progression by showing an effect on apoptosis, cell division, and altered metabolism. This protein is functionally a fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase [6] that degrades the fructose-2,6-bisphosphate(F26BP) in the glucose metabolism resulting in a shift from glycolysis to pentose pathway wherein net ROS generation was lowered. The entire phenomenon allows the cancer cells to survive in low oxygen levels and extensively utilize the metabolic intermediates from the pentose pathway to synthesize amino acids and nucleic acids to maintain the rapid growth of cancerous cells. So we hypothesize that the TIGAR is a key regulator of cancer progression, and targeting this protein with natural products will aid in the prevention of various types of solid tumors with minor or no side effects. Validation of hypothesis Protein Preparation The crystal structure of TIGAR (PDB ID: 3DCY) was retrieved from Protein Data Bank (http://www.rcsb.org/pdb/home/home.do ) [12] . Phosphate was removed from the active site for docking various compounds of interest. The optimization and minimization of protein were then carried out using the Protein Preparation Wizard tool in Schrodinger and Optimized Potentials for Liquid Simulations (OPLS3) [13] . The Protein Preparation Wizard fixes the protein and makes it suitable for docking. It corrects the incorrect bond orders, charge states, orientations of different amide and hydroxyl and aromatic groups within a protein structure. The X-ray structure cannot determine due to limited resolution. Energy minimization was done by molecular mechanics calculation using OPLS3 available in the Protein Preparation tool to minimize the strains and steric collisions in protein. Ligand Preparation Lipinski's rule of five applied for sorting the natural products and their derivatives library. Compounds were prepared using the LigPrep tool for Glide [14-16] and in open babel for AutodockVina, which generates accurate and energy minimized 3-dimensional structures and applied sophisticated rules to correct the Lewis structure and eliminates mistakes in the ligand structures. Active site and grid generation A grid was defined around the active residues using “Receptor Grid Generation” in the Glide module of the Schrodinger suite. The grid enclosing the active site was defined based on literature. TIGAR is a bisphosphatase, having two positively charged open pockets. These pockets can bind to the phosphate group of the substrate during dephosphorylation. Out of two pockets, one was found near the histidine residue at the core composed of HIS11, HIS183, ARG10, ARG61, and GLU89. The second pocket is located at the C terminal end with ARG10 and ASN217.[17] . GLU89, ARG10, HIS183, ARG61, HIS11, ASN17, ASN217, LYS20 residues were found in the active site of Zibra fish active site [17] as human TIGAR protein structure was not available in PDB. These residues are selected for defining an active site. Grid was generated with an internal size of 14 × 14 × 14 Å (x × y × z) and was large enough to accommodate the active site of the protein to allow each ligand to search for the potential binding site. The molecules docked in both AutoDockvina and Glide to compare the results. Molecular Docking/Virtual Screening. Protein-ligand docking studies were carried out based on the optimized structures of TIGAR. Modeled structures were used for docking purposes. A total of 67,823 molecules have been docked against TIGAR. Virtual Screening Workflow performs docking of an extensive collection of compounds against one target. The docking interactions were compared with the standard drug, Trabectedin [18] . Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations MD simulation studies detail the physical movement of atoms and molecules, providing critical information on the overall structural stability of the macromolecules [19,20] . MD simulations of native and ligand-bound TIGAR complexes were studied by applying GROMOS96 54a7 force field [21] employing Gromacs package, version 2018 [22] . Briefly, the SPC water model [23] was used to solvate the system, and sodium and chloride ions were used for neutralization. Energy minimization was done using the steepest descent method. V-rescale thermostat [24] and Parrinello Rahman barostat [25] were used in the NVT and NPT ensembles, respectively, to maintain a constant temperature (300 K) and pressure (1 bar). LINCS algorithm [26] and Particle mesh Ewald (PME) method [27] were applied to constrain the bond length and calculated electrostatic interactions, respectively. Finally, in the periodic boundary conditions (PBC), the production MD trajectories were created for a duration of 3000 ps (30 ns) and analyzed using gmx energy, gmx RMS, gmxrmsf, gmx gyrate, gmxsasa, and gmxh bond modules of GROMACS to examine the overall structural stability of each structure. The binding free energy calculations were done by employing the g_mmpbsa package [28] . For the Molecular mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann surface area (MMPBSA) calculations, new trajectories consisting of the final ten ns trajectories of the production trajectory were created using the gmxtrjconv module with frames generating at every 200 ps. Results and discussion Virtual screening and molecular docking TIGAR is a dynamic protein involved in ROS-mediated cancer progression [9,29,30] . To find the suitable lead molecule, TIGAR was docked with a natural product library. Docking studies were performed with both Glide and AutoDockVina to validate the hypothesis. The binding site of its substrate F26BP was previously solved in zebrafish [17] . GLU89, ARG10, HIS183, ARG61, HIS11, ASN17, ASN217, LYS20 were found in the substrate-binding site of TIGAR in Zebrafish. We chose these residues while defining the binding site as these amino acids were actively involved in substrate binding. ARG10 and ASN17 are present in the active site of TIGAR hydrogen-bonded with F26BP. A hydrogen bond was formed between amide groups of ASN17 of TIGAR with acceptor oxygen of F26BP. We found five lead natural products that have a high affinity towards TIGAR protein. Molecular Mechanics-Generalized Born Surface Area (MMGBSA) and docking score were considered during the lead selection. We observed most of the phosphate-binding residues involved in interaction with docked compounds. ARG10 is most often involved in hydrogen bonding with lead molecules (Table 1 ). ARG10, being a positively charged amino acid, is involved in interaction with the phosphate group in pocket one of TIGAR. Compound 1 is 2-(2-(3,4-dihydroxy phenyl)-3,5-dihydroxy-8-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-4-oxo-4H-furo[2,3-h]chromen-9-yl) acetic acid(DDFA), a derivative of natural product. DDFA was showing interaction with two arginines (10 and 203) and one GLN23 residue. This is a typical example of an electronegative compound interacting with positively charged amino acids (Fig. 2 (a)). The carboxylate group of DDFA forms two hydrogen bonds with a distance of 2.28 Å and 2.07 Å with 141 and 143rd H-atom of ARG10, respectively. The salt bridge was formed between ARG10 and the carboxylate group of DDFA. The oxygen atom of the furo[2,3-h]chromen-4-one ring of DDFA accepts the hydrogen bond (2.54 Å). The affinity of ligand–protein interaction was increased by electrostatic interaction – Cation by catechol ring of DDFAand ARG10. The non-polar GLN23 forms a hydrogen bond (1.85 Å) with the hydroxyl group of the phenyl ring. In the same way, we had tested the interactions of other lead molecules. Tetrahydropyran ring from compound 2 (3-(((2S, 3R, 4R, 5R)-3, 4, 5-trihydroxytetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-yl) amino) benzoic acid) was involved in a hydrogen bond with ARG10. And Pi-cation interaction stabilizes the compound 2 and TIGAR interactions. This compound is also electron-rich and forms hydrogen bonds with the amide group of ARG10. The hydrogen bond distance is about 2.117 Å (Fig. 2 (b)). In compound 3 (N-(4-Carboxyphenyl)-6-deoxyhexopyranosylamine) weak electrophile carboxylate group forms a bond (2.55 Å) with ARG3. The non-polar amino acid GLY173 forms a hydrogen bond (2.122 Å) with an amino group of compound 3(Fig. 2 (c)). The compound 4 ((2R, 3S, 4S, 5R, 6R)-2-(hydroxymethyl)-6-(p-tolylamino) tetrahydro-2H-pyran-3, 4, 5-triol) interacts with ARG10 via Cation-Pi bonding. This compound was patented for fat metabolism modulation (Fig. 2 (d)). Compound 5 ((2S, 3S, 4S, 5R, 6S)-3, 4, 5-trihydroxy-6-(4-nitrophenoxy) tetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-carboxylic acid) forms two hydrogen bonds with ARG10 and ILE21 of TIGAR. The amide group of ARG10 forms a salt bridge with the oxygen atom carboxylate group of compound 5. At 2.30 Å, ILE21 forms a hydrogen bond with the hydroxyoxane ring of compound 5(Fig. 2 (e)). In this study, the ARG10 most often interacts with the carboxylate group of lead molecules. This due to the electronegative oxygen atom of the carboxylate group accepts the hydrogen bond from positively charged amino acids. This kind of interaction may compete with the electronegative phosphate group of TIGAR substrate. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations Based on the best and effective ligand binding, the MD simulations for native and DDFA-bound TIGAR receptors were performed to support the accuracy of binding. The structural variations imposed by the binding of the DDFA molecule and the standard drug Trabectedin were compared with the unbound TIGAR receptor. The MD simulation results displayed stable conformational changes acquired by the target proteins upon ligand binding (Fig. 3 ). The structural stability of the unbound and bound structures was assessed based on root mean square deviations (RMSD) of Cα atoms of the protein from their back-bone and root mean square fluctuations describing the fluctuations associated with the amino acid residues during the simulation [31] . The MD trajectory analysis for RMSD and RMSF revealed that DDFA molecule imposed fewer RMS deviations (0.2024 nm) and RMS fluctuations (0.1019 nm) compared to standard drug, Trabectedin (0.2248 & 0.1309) (Fig. 3 A, 3B & Table 2 ). The packagibility of the target proteins after the binding of ligand molecules, described by the radius of gyration (Rg), indicated that the macromolecule folded itself into stable confirmation as the simulations advanced (Fig. 3 C & Table 2 ). This was supported by the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) analysis detailing the conformational changes displayed by the surface residues of the macromolecule (Fig. 3 D & Table 2 ). The SASA analysis describes the contribution of hydrophobic interactions of non-polar amino acids in attaining structural stability of the overall protein in the solvent environment [19,32] . Further, the structural stability is largely decided by inter and intra H-bond interactions. In inter H-bonds formed between the ligand and the target protein play a critical role in explaining the structural stability imposed by the ligand molecule [33] . The continuous formation of hydrogen bonds throughout the simulation upon the binding of DDFA (fig E) and Trabectedin (fig F)indicated the firm binding of the docked molecules to the binding site of the TIGAR receptor (fig E & F). The binding free energy calculations indicated that the molecule DDFA had interacted significantly with the TIGAR receptor with a binding free energy of −130.755 kJ/mol, whereas the standard drug Trabectedin showed better binding in terms of binding free energy(-144.961 kJ/mol). The terms associated with binding free energy calculations are detailed in Table 2 . A decrease in cancer cells' ROS level is one reason behind their resistance to radiotherapy [34,35] . The continuous expression of TIGAR in solid tumors inhibits ROS production. Besides, metabolic reprogramming, such as a shift in glycolysis and elevated pentose pathway, diminishes the chances of programmed cell death [6] and ROS level in cancer cells. TIGAR lowers the level of F26BP by dephosphorylation, meanwhile blocks the Fructose-bisphosphatase activity [5] . In addition, TIGAR is also induced by HIF-1α, where it triggers the inhibition of apoptosis. Hence, inhibition of the TIGAR by small molecules can decrease cancer progression. In this study, the selected lead molecules competitively bind to the substrate binding of TIGAR. Inhibition of TIGAR activity increases the level of F26BP in cells. An elevated level of F26BP allosterically blocks the Fructose 6-phosphatase-1(FBP1) and induces the Phosphofructokinase1(PFK1). These biochemical changes prevent the pentose pathway [30] . The modulation in the pentose pathway decreases the production of reductive species and intermediates that are involved in the DNA repair mechanism. In addition to this, TIGAR inhibition also increases the incidence of programmed cell death. As mentioned earlier, TIGAR increases the ADP level in the outer membrane of mitochondria by inducing HK2 activity [36] . ADP level maintains the anionic channel Voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC) in an inactive state, which prevents the release of cytochrome C into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome C is required to form apoptosomes during apoptosis [37] . Hindrance of apoptosis helps the tumor cells survive during immunity response, chemo, and radiation therapy. The mitochondrial translocation of TIGAR takes place under the influence of HIF-1α. HIF-1α is a critical transcription factor that facilitates the cells to adapt to solid tumors' hypoxic nature. HIF-1α expressions were high in solid tumors, which in turn can increase the translocation of TIGAR in cells. In solid tumors, the expression of HIF-1α was correlated with a lowered level of ROS and resistance to radiation. TIGAR being the downstream target of HIF-1α, which can able to reduces the ROS level in cells. (23) Hence, targeting TIGAR is relatively novel in combination cancer therapy. Along with radiotherapy, TIGAR inhibitors can increase the efficacy of the treatment. Our virtual screening and molecular docking studies showed that five compounds could able to compete with the substrate as it binds to the substrate-binding site residues. Molecular docking studies are a powerful technique in the prediction of ligand and protein interaction [38] . The binding affinity of a ligand provides the clue as an inhibitor of the target protein [39,40] . The pre-docking ADME prediction reveals the drug-like characteristics of the compounds. Entire studies proved that compounds 1 to 5 could effectively inhibit the TIGAR activity. Conclusion We have investigated the TIGAR inhibitors via virtual screening of 67,823 compounds. We selected the five top-scored compounds for further analysis, and our study showed that the DDFA possess the highest binding affinity towards TIGAR active site. This compound interacts with histidine resides in TIGAR pocket 1. This binding mimics the interaction of the phosphate group of the TIGAR substrate. So with this, we are proposing that DDFA could become a potent competitive inhibitor for the TIGAR. In combination with other anticancer compounds, this compound could be a promising lead to control the growth of cancer cells. The in vitro and in vivo studies on DDFA are underway in our laboratory to validate the findings of in silico studies. The clinical studies will be carried out to test the analysis of efficacy and safety of DDFA, which may benefit the development of a novel drugs against solid tumors. title: Arsenic trioxide triggers ferroptosis in neuroblastoma via USF1/GPX4 axis
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB) is an extracranial solid tumor arising from impaired differentiation of primitive neural crest cells. High-risk NB (HR-NB), which comprises roughly 40% of cases, has a dismal prognosis. Considering the high iron demand of NB cells and the vulnerability of therapy-resistant cells to ferroptosis, ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic strategy. Arsenic trioxide(ATO), a clinically approved anti-tumor agent, has shown efficacy across various malignancies. Our previous clinical study provided preliminary evidence of ATO's therapeutic efficacy in high-risk NB, particularly in relapsed and refractory cases. In this study, we confirmed that ATO induces ferroptosis in NB cells and elucidated the underlying molecular mechanism. ATO significantly reduced NB cell viability, and only the ferroptosis inhibitor deferoxamine specifically reversed this cytotoxicity. Proteomic analysis revealed significant enrichment in the ferroptosis-related pathway. Consistently, ATO increased intracellular levels of ROS, Fe2+, and malondialdehyde while reducing glutathione levels in NB cells. Mechanistically, ATO downregulated GPX4 expression by suppressing its upstream transcription factor USF1, rather than by enhancing ubiquitin-mediated degradation. USF1 knockdown decreased GPX4 expression and enhanced ferroptosis, whereas USF1 overexpression partially rescued the ferroptosis phenotypes induced by ATO. ChIP-PCR further confirmed the direct binding of USF1 to the GPX4 promoter. Moreover, ATO combined with GSTP1 inhibitor TLK199 exhibited synergistic cytotoxicity against MYCN-amplified SK-N-BE(2) cells. This study demonstrates that ATO triggers ferroptosis in NB cells via the USF1/GPX4 axis, providing a mechanistic rationale for the broader therapeutic application of ATO in HR-NB treatment.

author 2 https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1756-5847 Neuroblastoma (NB) is an extracranial solid tumor arising from impaired differentiation of primitive neural crest cells. High-risk NB (HR-NB), which comprises roughly 40% of cases, has a dismal prognosis. Considering the high iron demand of NB cells and the vulnerability of therapy-resistant cells to ferroptosis, ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic strategy. Arsenic trioxide(ATO), a clinically approved anti-tumor agent, has shown efficacy across various malignancies. Our previous clinical study provided preliminary evidence of ATO's therapeutic efficacy in high-risk NB, particularly in relapsed and refractory cases. In this study, we confirmed that ATO induces ferroptosis in NB cells and elucidated the underlying molecular mechanism. ATO significantly reduced NB cell viability, and only the ferroptosis inhibitor deferoxamine specifically reversed this cytotoxicity. Proteomic analysis revealed significant enrichment in the ferroptosis-related pathway. Consistently, ATO increased intracellular levels of ROS, Fe2+ , and malondialdehyde while reducing glutathione levels in NB cells. Mechanistically, ATO downregulated GPX4 expression by suppressing its upstream transcription factor USF1, rather than by enhancing ubiquitin-mediated degradation. USF1 knockdown decreased GPX4 expression and enhanced ferroptosis, whereas USF1 overexpression partially rescued the ferroptosis phenotypes induced by ATO. ChIP-PCR further confirmed the direct binding of USF1 to the GPX4 promoter. Moreover, ATO combined with GSTP1 inhibitor TLK199 exhibited synergistic cytotoxicity against MYCN-amplified SK-N-BE(2) cells. This study demonstrates that ATO triggers ferroptosis in NB cells via the USF1/GPX4 axis, providing a mechanistic rationale for the broader therapeutic application of ATO in HR-NB treatment. Approximately 15% of childhood cancer-related deaths are due to NB [3] . High-risk NB (HR-NB) constitutes nearly 40% of all cases. Despite comprehensive treatment, the five-year overall survival rate for HR-NB remains under 50% [4] . Critically, even with anti-GD2 immunotherapy, nearly half of treated patients still relapse [5] , and it remains prohibitive for most families in China [6] . Induction chemotherapy plays a pivotal role in reducing tumor burden and enabling subsequent treatments, with patient response during this phase closely correlating with prognosis in HR-NB [7,8] . However, most current chemotherapeutic agents for NB primarily exert their anti-tumor effects through apoptosis, which may promote the development of chemotherapeutic drug resistance, leading to minimal residual disease(MRD) and increasing the risk of relapse [9] . Therefore, there is an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies that can overcome resistance and enhance treatment efficacy in HR-NB. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, non-apoptotic form of cell death characterized by lipid peroxidation [10] . Increasing evidence has demonstrated that ferroptosis has emerged as a promising strategy for the treatment of drug-resistant tumors [11] . During NB treatment, spontaneous phenotypic transition toward a mesenchymal-like state has been observed. These mesenchymal cells exhibit strong drug resistance and are considered a major source of MRD and tumor recurrence [12] . Drug-resistant tumor cells across multiple cancer types converge toward a similar mesenchymal phenotype and rely on GPX4 to maintain redox homeostasis. Inhibition of GPX4 effectively triggers ferroptosis and prevents tumor regeneration [13,14] . Moreover, MYCN amplification, a hallmark high-risk feature of NB, has been reported to confer ferroptosis vulnerability. MYCN-amplified NB cells exhibit iron-dependent features, including upregulation of TFRC, increased labile iron pool, and heightened sensitivity to ferroptosis inducers [15,16] . Besides, MYCN-amplified NB cells show a strong dependence on cysteine, and its rapid consumption during tumor proliferation promotes lipid peroxidation, further enhancing ferroptosis sensitivity [16] . Additionally, over 50% of HR-NB patients present with bone marrow metastasis at diagnosis [17] . Conventional induction chemotherapeutic agents, such as cisplatin, vincristine, and etoposide, exert minimal effects on NB-derived bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), leaving metastatic lesions largely unaffected and ultimately contributing to tumor relapse. Conversely, ferroptosis inducers selectively eliminate NB-BMSCs while sparing normal BMSCs [18] . Collectively, these findings suggest ferroptosis could be a promising therapeutic avenue for NB. However, most ferroptosis inducers(such as Erastin, RSL3) are still in preclinical stage [19] . Identifying clinically available ferroptosis inducers may offer a cost-effective strategy to improve HR-NB outcomes. Arsenic trioxide (ATO), the main active component of traditional Chinese medicinal preparations “Pi-shuang”, exhibits broad antitumor activity, including DNA demethylation, cell-cycle arrest, and restoring the function of TP53 harboring structural mutations [20–22] . Clinically, ATO is widely used in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) by targeting the disease-causing promyelocytic leukemia-retinoic acid receptor alpha (PML-RARα) oncoprotein. However, resistance to ATO can develop in some APL patients, often due to mutations in the PML B-box-2 structure or in the unrearranged PML allele [23,24] . Beyond APL, ATO has also been investigated in other malignancies. In our previous clinical trial, we was the first to demonstrate that combining ATO with conventional chemotherapy significantly improved the complete remission rate in patients with HR-NB [25] . Furthermore, we administered ATO in combination with a cyclophosphamide/topotecan-based salvage chemotherapy regimen to patients with relapsed/refractory HR-NB, achieving favorable efficacy and tolerability [26] . Building on these encouraging clinical outcomes, we aimed to further investigate the mechanisms underlying ATO's anti-NB effects. In our previous studies, we found ATO could trigger ferroptosis in NB cells [27,28] . Nevertheless, the precise molecular mechanism of ATO-induced ferroptosis in NB still remains unclear. In this study, utilizing three NB cell lines (SK-N-AS, SK-N-BE(2), and SH-SY5Y), we demonstrate that ATO exerts antitumor activity by inducing ferroptosis through suppressing the transcription factor USF1, thereby disrupting the transcriptional regulation of GPX4. This is accompanied by the accumulation of ROS, Fe2+ , and malondialdehyde, and a marked decrease in glutathione levels. Hence, our findings provide a mechanistic rationale for the broader application of ATO in the treatment of HR-NB. 2 Methods 2.1 Cells culture and reagents The NB cell lines SK-N-AS, SK-N-BE(2) and SH-SY5Y were obtained from the Sun Yat-sen University(Guangzhou, China). Cells were cultured with DMEM (Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Wuhan Pu-nuo-sai Life Technology Co. Ltd., China) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco, USA) at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2 . ATO(Cat# , 99.995% purity) was purchased from Sigma(St. Louis, MA, USA). Deferoxamine(DFO)(S5742, 99.91% purity), ferrostatin-1(Fer-1)(S7243 99.98% purity), MG132(S2619 99.52% purity) and TLK199(S9698, 99.10% purity) were obtained from Selleck (Texas, USA). 2.2 Cell viability assay We carried out the CCK8 assay and cell flow cytometry for the NB cell viability assay. For CCK8 assay, cells were plated into 96-well plates and grew overnight. NB cells were then exposed to different concentrations of ATO for 24 h. After drug administration, 100 μL of medium containing 10% CCK-8 reagent (APExBIO, Houston, TX, USA) was added to each well and incubated for 2 h in the dark, and plates were read at 450 nm. Besides, the combination index (CI) was calculated according to the Chou-Talalay method [29] and CalcuSyn software. For flow cytometry, cells were incubated with different concentrations of ATO for 24 h. After treatment, live/dead staining was performed using Fixable Viability Stain 780 (BD Pharmingen) and the cells were incubated in the dark for 15 min. Cell viability was determined using flow cytometry. 2.3 Colony formation assay Approximately 1000 cells per well were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight. Cells were cultured for 12 days with medium refreshed every three days, followed by exposure to the indicated concentrations of ATO for an additional 2 days. Cells were rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, and incubated with crystal violet solution (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for 10 min. Colonies were photographed and quantified using ImageJ software. 2.4 Wound healing assays Cells were plated in 6-well plates and cultured until confluent monolayers formed. A scratch was created using a 1-ml pipette tip, and cells were plated with PBS to remove debris. Cells were subsequently exposed to different concentrations of ATO, and images were acquired at 0 and 48 h using the microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan). Cell migration into the wound area was quantified using ImageJ software. 2.5 Reactive oxygen species measurement Cells were seeded in 6-well plates and grew overnight. The next day, the cells were incubated with ATO for 16 h, collected, resuspended in serum-free medium containing 10 μM DCFH-DA(Beyotime, Shanghai, China), and incubated for 30 min. Following staining, the cells were washed and the fluorescence intensity was evaluated with flow cytometry. Additionally, Reactive oxygen species(ROS) levels in lentivirus-infected cells were assessed using the dihydroethidium fluorescent probe(Beyotime, Shanghai, China) as the lentiviral vectors expressed green fluorescent protein. 2.6 Cellular iron measurement Cellular iron levels were assessed using FerroOrange(Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan). Cells were seeded in a 6-well plate and grew overnight, followed by ATO treatment for 16 h. Subsequently, cells were cultured with 0.5 μM FerroOrange for 30 min. After staining, the cells were washed and was analyzed by flow cytometry. 2.7 Glutathione assay Cellular Glutathione(GSH) concentration was measured using the GSH assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng, Nanjing, China). After ATO treatment, the cells were lysed, and the supernatants were incubated with dithiodinitrobenzoic acid to generate a yellow chromophore. Absorbance was read at 405 nm. GSH content was normalized to protein concentration (μg/mg protein). 2.8 Malondialdehyde assay Malondialdehyde (MDA) were measured using the MDA assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). After ATO treatment, cells seeded in 6-cm dishes were collected and lysed by sonication. The supernatant was mixed with thiobarbituric acid, and plates were read at 532 nm. MDA content was standardized based on protein concentration (μmol/mg protein). 2.9 Bioinformatics analysis Proteomics analyses were performed by the Jingjie PTM BioLab (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd. The data were deposited in the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB)(OMIX011827). Different expressed proteins(DEPs) were defined as those with a P value 0.585. Protein-Protein interaction (PPI) network were obtained from STRING database(https://string-db.org ) and computed for hub genes using the maximal clique centrality (MCC) method in CytoHubba. Cellular dependency data was obtained from the DepMap Public 22Q4 and Achilled DRIVE Marcotte datasetes using the DepMap (https://depmap.org/portal/ ). Cistrome DB (http://cistrome.org/db/# ) utilized to predict potential transcription factors and ChIP-Seq data acquisition. Correlations between genes was analyzed using data from TARGET-NB cohort accessed through cBioportal (http://www.cbioportal.org ). 2.10 Cell transfection For siRNA transfection, siRNAs were purchased from Gentlegen Biotechnology (Suzhou, China). When the cell reached 30–50% confluence, transfection was conducted wtih CALNP™ RNAi in vitro reagent (D-Nano Therapeutics, Beijing, China) according to the instruction manuals. The siRNA sequences are provided in Supplementary Table S1. For lentiviral infection, USF1-overexpressing lentivirus or negative control vectors (Hanheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) were supplemented into the medium in the presence of polybrene to improve infection efficiency. The cells were selected in medium containing puromycin to obtain stably transduced populations. 2.11 Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction(qRT-PCR) Total RNA was isolated using the RNA-Quick Purification Kit (GOONIE, Guangzhou, China). cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Novizan Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Nanjing, China). qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (Novizan Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Nanjing, China) on a Roche LightCycler system (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). GAPDH was used as the internal control, and relative gene expression was calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCT method. The primers are listed in the Supplementary Table S2. 2.12 Western blotting NB cells were collected, and total proteins were extracted using lysis buffer (CoWin Bioscience, Beijing, China). Protein concentrations were quantified with the Bicinchoninic Acid Assay kit (CoWin Bioscience). Equivalent protein quantities were separated and subsequently transferred onto PVDF membranes, trimmed based on the molecular weights of the target proteins. The PVDF Membrane was blocked for 30 min with rapid blocking buffer (Epizyme, Shanghai, China), incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, and subsequently with secondary antibodies. The primary antibodies used were as follows: β-tubulin (11,400, GB152667–100, Servicebio), GAPDH (11,000, GB12002, Servicebio), GPX4 (11,000, # , Cell Signaling Technology), and USF1 (11,000, A20903, Abclonal). 2.13 Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by PCR (ChIP-PCR) ChIP assays was performed using the SimpleChIP® Enzymatic Chromatin IP Kit(MagneticBeads) (Cell Signaling Technology). Cells were cultured in 15 cm dishes grown to approximately 70–80% confluence and fixed with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature, and subjected to glycine. After washing with cold PBS, the cells were scrapedin PBS containing protease inhibitors on ice and then pelleted by centrifugation. Chromatin was digested with micrococcal nuclease to yield fragments of approximately 150–900 bp. The lysates were incubated separately with specific antibodies (negative control: normal rabbit IgG; USF1 antibody: sc-101,197, Santa Cruz) and immunocomplexes were captured using magnetic beads. Cross-links were reversed, and DNA was purified for subsequent PCR analysis. Primer sequences are provided in the Supplementary Table S3. Thermocycling conditions were as follows: 95 °C for 30 s, 65 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s for 40 cycles. PCR products were resolved on agarose gels, and bands were visualized using a gel documentation system. 2.14 Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism. Data are expressed as mean ± SD from independent experiments(n =3). Comparisons between two groups were performed using a two-tailed independent t -test, while multiple-group comparisons were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. 3 Results 3.1 ATO inhibits cell viability, proliferation, and migration while promotes ferroptosis of NB cells To evaluate the cytotoxic effects of ATO on NB cells, we assessed cell viability using the CCK-8 assay and flow cytometry (FVS780 staining). Three NB cell lines with distinct characteristics were used in this study: SK-N-AS (retinoic acid-resistant, non-MYCN-amplified, MES subtype), SK-N-BE(2) (MYCN-amplified, ADRN subtype), and SH-SY5Y (non-MYCN-amplified, ADRN subtype) [30,31] .We found that ATO could exert killing effect on NB cells in a dose-dependent manner(Fig. 1 A-1 B ). The 24 h IC50 of ATO were 48.51 μM for SK-N-AS, 12.39 μM for SK-N-BE(2), and 10.53 μM for SH-SY5Y. In addition, ATO significantly inhibited cell migration and colony-forming ability, as shown in Fig. 1 C and Fig. 1 D. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ATO exhibits remarkable antitumor activity in NB cells. To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying ATO-induced cell death, rescue experiments were conducted using various regulated cell death (RCD) inhibitors. ATO-induced cell death was partially reversed by DFO (a ferroptosis inhibior), but not by necrostatin-1 (Nec-1, necroptosis inhibitor)and Z -VAD-FMK (Z-VAD, pan-caspase inhibitor). Notably, Fer-1, another ferroptosis inhibitor, also failed to alleviate the reduction in cell viability(Fig. 1 E). Ferroptosis is primarily characterized by intracellular iron overload, elevated ROS and increased lipid peroxidation [11,32] . To further verify that ATO induces ferroptosis in NB cells, we assessed several ferroptosis related markers, including intracellular ROS, Fe2+ , GSH and MDA. ATO promoted the accumulation of total ROS(Fig. 1 F) in NB cells. Using the FerroOrange fluorescent probe, we further confirmed a marked elevation of intracellular Fe2+ in ATO-treated cells (Fig. 1 G). Consistent with ferroptotic processes, GSH levels were substantially reduced in NB cells following ATO treatment (Fig. 1 H). Additionally, ATO increased MDA level in NB cells(Fig. 1 I), indicating enhanced lipid peroxidation. Taken together, these results demonstrate ATO promotes ferroptosis in NB cells. 3.2 ATO induced ferroptosis by modulating GPX4 transcription To further explore the mechanism underlying the anti-NB effect of ATO, we performed proteomic analyses on ATO-treated SK-N-AS cells. A total of 501 proteins were up-regulated and 767 proteins was down-regulated in the ATO-treated group compared with the control group. KEGG analysis showed enrichment of the ferroptosis pathway. In addition, we observed enrichment of the PI3K-AKT and cell cycle pathways, both of which have been implicated in the antitumor effects of ATO in previous studies (Fig. 2 A ). GO analysis revealed the top-ranked terms within each category, among which the biological process “iron-sulfur cluster assembly” was notably enriched, a process closely associated with ferroptosis [33,34] (Fig. 2 B). Furthermore, GSEA demonstrated activation of the ferroptosis in ATO-treated cells(Fig. 2 C). To further pinpoint key ferroptosis-related targets of ATO, the PPI network was constructed to evaluate ferroptosis-related DEPs. Eight ferroptosis-related DEPs showed differential expression after ATO treatment, with GPX4 was identified as the central node(Fig. 2 D), consistent with its established role in ferroptosis. Proteomic analysis revealed that the GPX4, a key anti-ferroptotic protein, was significantly downregulated following ATO treatment(log2 FC =−0.88). We next sought to elucidate the mechanism by which ATO regulates GPX4 expression. As illustrated in Fig. 2 E, ATO dose-dependently inhibited GPX4 mRNA level. We next assessed GPX4 expression in the presence of MG132, a proteasome inhibitor. Western blotting analysis showed that ATO reduced GPX4 protein levels, and this reduction was not rescued by MG132(Fig. 2 F), indicating that ATO regulates GPX4 primarily at the transcriptional level rather than through post-translational mechanisms. The dependence of NB cell lines on GPX4 ranked among the highest across pan-cancer analyses, placing sixth in CRISPR/Cas9 screening data and first in RNAi data in the DepMap database (Fig. 3 A )This confirms that GPX4 is indispensable for NB cell survival and further reveals that NB is among the tumor types showing the highest GPX4 dependency in pan-cancer analyses, supporting the rationale for targeting GPX4 in NB. To further evaluate the role of GPX4 in NB cells, we established GPX4 knockdown cell lines using siRNA. qPCR and western blot analyses confirmed GPX4 inhibition(Fig. 3 B-3 C). The data showed that GPX4 knockdown significantly increased intracellular ROS, Fe2+ , MDA while reducing GSH levels(Fig. 3 D-G) in NB cell. Moreover, the siGPX4+ATO group did not showed statistically significant differences in these ferroptosis-related indicators compared with the siGPX4 group. Taken together, these findings indicated GPX4 is a key mediator of ATO-induced ferroptosis in NB cells. 3.3 ATO triggers ferroptosis via targeting the USF1/GPX4 axis in NB cells In our previous experiments, we demonstrated that ATO suppresses GPX4 expression at the transcription level rather than through ubiquitin-mediated degradation, thereby triggering ferroptosis in NB cells. To further identify transcription factors involved in ATO-mediated regulation of GPX4, we first predicted potential upstream transcription factors using multiple transcription factor databases and selected those present in at least two databases. These candidates were then intersected with DEPs identified by proteomic profiling of ATO-treated NB cells(Fig. 4 A). Overlapping factors were further screened by manual evaluation of expression patterns together with supporting evidence from the literature. Three transcription factors were ultimately selected for siRNA knockdown in NB cell lines. As shown in Fig. 4 B, NFIC knockdown did not alter GPX4 mRNA levels in any of the three cell lines. ZNF148 silencing upregulated GPX4 mRNA in SK-N-AS cells but decreased it in the other cell lines, suggesting that the regulatory relationship between ZNF148 and GPX4 might be cell line–specific. Notably, USF1 knockdown consistently reduced GPX4 mRNA levels across all three NB cell lines. This experimental evidence is in line with our earlier transcription factor prediction analysis, in which Cistrome DB identified USF1 as one of the putative upstream regulators of GPX4 (Fig. 4 C). In addition, JASPAR motif analysis revealed predicted USF1 binding sites within the GPX4 promoter region (Fig. 4 D). To further substantiate the potential regulatory relationship between USF1 and GPX4, we next performed co-expression analysis of the candidate transcription factors and GPX4 using the TARGET-NB dataset. This analysis revealed a positive correlation between USF1 and GPX4 expression (Fig. 4 E). Moreover, proteomic profiling of ATO-treated SK-N-AS cells demonstrated that both USF1 and GPX4 were downregulated after treatment (Fig. 4 F), providing additional support for a functional association between USF1 and GPX4. Given these findings, we next examined whether ATO directly regulates USF1 expression. To validate the proteomic findings, we examined USF1 expression following ATO treatment. As shown in Fig. 4 G–4H, ATO markedly reduced USF1 mRNA and protein levels in NB cells. We next investigated whether USF1 directly contributes to GPX4 regulation and ferroptosis. In NB cells, USF1 silencing reduced GPX4 protein expression (Fig. 4 I). In addition, USF1 knockdown significantly increased intracellular ROS (Fig. 4 J), Fe2+ (Fig. 4 K), and MDA (Fig. 4 M) levels, while reducing GSH levels (Fig. 4 L). These results demonstrated that USF1 is closely associated with ferroptosis and that USF1 silencing promotes ferroptotic phenotypes in NB cells. GPX4 expression was substantially higher in OUSF1 cells than in ONC cells(Fig. 5 A), consistent with the regulatory relationship observed in USF1-knockdown experiments. Notably, although ATO treatment reduced GPX4 expression in both groups, the extent of reduction was substantially smaller in OUSF1 cells than in ONC cells(Fig. 5 A), indicating that USF1 overexpression confers resistance to ATO-induced GPX4 downregulation. We next examined ferroptosis-related markers in USF1-overexpressing cells. Under basal conditions, USF1 overexpression reduced intracellular Fe2+ and MDA levels while increasing GSH levels (Fig. 5 C–5E), consistent with an attenuation of ferroptotic stress. The effects on ROS varied across cell lines: in SH-SY5Y cell line, OUSF1 cells did not show significantly lower basal ROS compared with ONC cells, however, the ATO-induced increase in ROS was markedly blunted in OUSF1 cells across all NB lines (Fig. 5 B). Similarly, the ATO-induced changes in Fe2+ , MDA, and GSH were also substantially mitigated in OUSF1 cells relative to ONC cells (Fig. 5 C–5E). Collectively, these results indicate that USF1 overexpression partially protects NB cells from ATO-induced ferroptosis. Given the consistent regulatory relationship between USF1 and GPX4 at both the transcriptional and functional levels, we subsequently investigated whether USF1 directly binds to GPX4 promoter. Public ChIP-seq data from Cistrome DB revealed a prominent USF1-binding peak in the GPX4 promoter region in SK-N-SH, a non–MYCN-amplified NB cell line (Fig. 5 F). Consistent with this observation, ChIP-PCR analysis performed in the MYCN-amplified SK-N-BE(2) cell line experimentally validated this interaction by confirming the direct binding of USF1 to the GPX4 promoter(Fig. 5 G). Overall, our data demonstrate that ATO drives ferroptosis in NB cells via the USF1/GPX4 axis. 3.4 ATO and TLK-199 synergistically enhance Ferroptosis in NB cells In GPX4-independent ferroptosis pathways, targeting the SMURF2/GSTP1 regulatory axis or inhibiting GSTP1 enzymatic activity has been reported to markedly enhance tumor cell sensitivity to ferroptosis inducers [35] . TLK199, also known as Ezatiostat, is an oral GSTP1 inhibitor, has previously entered phase II clinical trials for myelodysplastic syndrome [36] . Because MYCN amplification is a well-recognized high-risk factor in HR-NB and has been reported to sensitize NB cell to ferroptosis [16] , we selected SK-N-BE(2), a MYCN-amplified cell line, for further investigation. We first evaluated whether ATO and TLK199 exerted synergistic antitumor effects using the Chou–Talalay method. The CI values were <1 across all three concentration combinations, indicating synergistic cytotoxicity between ATO and TLK199(Fig. 6 A-B ). Further analysis confirmed that the combination treatment induced stronger ferroptotic responses than either agent alone, characterized by greater increases in intracellular ROS(Fig. 6 C), Fe2+ (Fig. 6 D), and MDA levels(Fig. 6 F), together with more pronounced reduction in GSH levels(Fig. 6 E). Notably, TLK199 alone exhibied minimal cytotoxicity, whereas its combination with ATO significantly enhanced NB cell death. These findings suggest that ATO may potentiate the antitumor efficacy of low-toxicity ferroptosis inducers such as TLK199 by the amplifying the ferroptotic process. 4 Discussion Despite advances in therapeutic strategies, the clinical management of HR-NB remains challenging, with limited survival benefits and high rates of long-term relapse [4] . The survival rate of patients with relapsed HR-NB is unsatisfactory [37] , highlighting an urgent need for novel therapeutic approaches. Ferroptosis is emerging as an attractive therapeutic strategy for drug-resistant tumors [13] . However, the development of effective ferroptosis inducers has been impeded by unfavorable pharmacokinetic properties, limiting their clinical translation [19] . Although some drug components or drug derivatives have also been shown to induce ferroptosis in other tumor cells, their transition to mature clinical practice remains distant [38–40] . Moreover, pediatric medication requires even greater caution. Therefore, identifying clinically approved agents capable of inducing ferroptosis may provide an opportunity to accelerate clinical implementation in NB treatment. ATO not only possesses antitumor activity but also has extensive clinical application experience in pediatric patients, along with favorable safety and cost-effectiveness [21] . Moreover, the exploration of its integration with emerging technologies such as nanomedicine has opened up broad prospects for its potential application across multiple malignancies [41] . In our previous multicenter clinical trials, the combination of ATO and chemotherapy significantly improved treatment outcomes in HR-NB and demonstrated encouraging efficacy in relapsed or refractory cases, with a favorable safety profile [26,42] . However, the precise molecular mechanisms through which ATO exerts its effects in NB remain incompletely understood. Omics analyses of SK-N-BE(2) cells [28] and SK-N-AS cells in this study revealed that DEPs following ATO treatment were enriched in ferroptosis pathways. In addition, rescue experiments using multiple RCD inhibitors showed that only the ferroptosis inhibitor DFO was able to restore the viability of NB cells after ATO treatment, suggesting that ferroptosis constitutes one of the major cell death mechanisms underlying the antitumor effects of ATO in NB cells. Consistently, we observed that ATO increased intracellular ROS while decreasing GSH levels. These findings were in agreement with previous observations in other cell types, including human pulmonary fibroblasts and spermatogenic cells [43,44] . Additionally, ATO elevated intracellular Fe2+ levels and increased the accumulation of the MDA, further supporting ferroptosis as a key mechanism underlying its antitumor activity. As a key regulator of ferroptosis, GPX4 inactivation leads to lipid peroxide accumulation [45] . Data from the DEPMAP database confirmed that NB cells exhibit high GPX4 dependency across cancers. Cross-validation using both CRISPR/Cas9 and RNAi approaches minimized potential false-positive results from single-platform analyses, further underscoring the critical role of GPX4 in NB cell survival. In this study, we demonstrated that ATO suppresses GPX4 at both the transcriptional and protein levels. Moreover, GPX4 knockdown induced ferroptosis in NB cells, and its combination with ATO did not further enhance ferroptosis-associated biochemical changes. These results further established GPX4 as a key intermediary in ATO-induced ferroptosis in NB cells, providing a possible explanation for why Fer-1 cannot rescue ATO-induced cell death. Although radical trapping antioxidants (RTAs) such as Fer-1 can quench lipid radicals in the downstream autoxidation phase, their late-stage action may be inadequate to counter lipid damage under the persistent upstream oxidative pressure, such as GPX4 or GSH insufficiency [46] . Iron chelators such as DFO reduce the labile iron pool and suppress iron-driven oxidative processes, including the Fenton reaction and the activity of iron-dependent enzymes, thereby preventing the initiation and amplification of lipid peroxidation [47] . These mechanistic distinctions may explain the differential rescue effects observed in our study. USF1, the member of the bHLH-Zip transcription factor family, participates in various cellular processes. Elevated expression of USF1 correlates with unfavorable prognosis [48–52] and has been implicated in drug resistance and immune evasion in multiple cancers [50] . Beyond oncology, USF1 is also involved in non-cancerous diseases, including nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, where it activates CYBA transcription and subsequently promotes NADPH-derived ROS production and lipid accumulation [53] . However, the relationship between USF1 and ferroptosis remains poorly understood. To date, only one study in prostate cancer has reported that USF1 binds to the BEX1 promoter to enhance its transcription, thereby increasing ferroptosis resistance and promoting tumor progression, although no direct association between USF1 and GPX4 was discussed [54] . In this study, co-expression analysis using the publicly available TARGET-NB microarray dataset revealed a positive correlation between USF1 and GPX4 expression. We further demonstrated that ATO downregulated USF1, whereas siRNA-mediated USF1 silencing induced ferroptosis in NB cell lines. Conversely, USF1 overexpression upregulated GPX4 expression and rescued ATO-induced ferroptotic phenotypes, supporting a regulatory role for ATO in modulating the USF1/GPX4 axis. Finally, evidence from public ChIP-Seq datasets together with our ChIP-PCR experiments further substantiated the direct regulatory relationship between USF1 and GPX4: the Cistrome database revealed USF1 binding peaks within the GPX4 promoter region in SK-N-SH cells, and our ChIP-PCR assays confirmed direct binding of USF1 to the GPX4 promoter in SK-N-BE(2) cells. Technical constraints related to transfection and cell viability under our experimental conditions prevented us from obtaining reliable luciferase reporter assay results. Nevertheless, gene expression analyses, gain- and loss-of-function studies, rescue experiments, and ChIP-based validation together provide strong evidence supporting ATO's regulatory effect on the USF1/GPX4 signaling axis in NB cells. In 2017, Van Groningen et al. defined two NB cell states, adrenergic (ADRN) and MES cells, which differ in morphology, biology, and treatment response, yet remain interconvertible [55–57] . MES cells display greater chemoresistance and are enriched in relapsed and refractory NB [12] , and MES-associated transcripts are more frequently detected in patients with poor outcomes [58] . These observations indicate that NB cell plasticity may allow tumor cells to evade therapeutic pressure, as ADRN cells can transition toward a MES, drug-resistant phenotype under genetic alterations(e.g., ARID1A mutations) or treatment stress [59–61] . Notably, across multiple tumor types, mesenchymal and therapy-resistant cancer cells exhibit a marked dependence on GPX4 to eliminate lipid peroxides, rendering them vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition [13,62] . In this study, we demonstrated that ATO triggers ferroptosis in NB cells via USF1/GPX4 axis, thereby mediating its antitumor effects. This mechanism may help explain the clinical benefits of ATO observed in our previous study, particularly in relapsed or refractory NB, and supports its potential application to target MES-like, therapy-resistant NB cells. Further investigation of this therapeutic strategy is warranted. Retinoic acid(RA)–mediated differentiation is a conventional component of consolidation therapy for HR-NB. However, Cardona et al. demonstrated that differentiated NB cell lines acquire resistance to ferroptosis following RA-induced differentiation. This resistance is attributed to increased cystine uptake and the resulting elevation of intracellular cysteine levels, which collectively strengthen the ferroptosis-resistant phenotype of differentiated NB cells. Therefore, ferroptosis-inducing agents may be more effective when administered prior to the RA-induced differentiation phase, consistent with the potential application of ATO during the induction chemotherapy stage in patients with HR-NB. This study preliminarily explored the potential of ATO combined with other drugs to induce ferroptosis. TLK199 alone exhibited minimal cytotoxicity to NB cells, but when combined with ATO, the two drugs synergistically enhanced cell death and related ferroptosis phenotypes, suggesting the potential of ATO in combination with other drugs to induce ferroptosis in NB cells. However, the mechanism underlying the observed synergy remains to be fully explored. Future studies will systematically screen ATO combination drugs, explore the molecular mechanisms, and assess their in vivo effects. Besides, our previously conducted clinical studies have confirmed the clinical potential of ATO for NB treatment. In a non-randomized, multicenter clinical trial, ATO combined with chemotherapy showed a significantly higher objective response rate (86.36% vs. 46.16%, p = 0.020) compared to traditional chemotherapy in children with stage 4/M NB [25] . Additionally, in a study on relapsed/refractory high-risk NB patients, ATO combined with cyclophosphamide/ topotecan (CT regimen) demonstrated an objective response rate of 54.5% and a disease control rate of 63.6%, with minimal systemic toxicity [26] . These results further support ATO's potential for improving outcomes in both newly diagnosed and relapsed/refractory NB patients. So, due to the clinical data already available and in line with the 3Rs principle (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement), we did not conduct animal experiments in this study. Moving forward, in future studies focused on ATO in NB, we plan to further investigate its mechanisms and therapeutic efficacy, particularly in combination with other ferroptosis inducers or nanomaterial-based approaches, and explore the specific mechanisms in clinical samples from relapsed and drug-resistant patients, using animal and PDX models. In summary, our findings demonstrated that ATO triggers ferroptosis in NB cells via USF1/GPX4 axis, thereby exerting a potent antitumor effect (Fig. 7 ). Considering ATO's established clinical application and the emerging relevance of ferroptosis in NB therapy, our study provides a strong rationale for further assessment of ATO for HR-NB treatment. title: Investigation of anticancer mechanism of oleuropein via cell cycle and apoptotic pathways in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells
abstract: Neuroblastoma is one of the most common types of pediatric tumors that can spread quickly in neuronal tissues. Oleuropein which is active compound of olive leaves, belongs to polyphenols group and has antioxidant, anti-microbial, anti-inflammatory, anti-hypertensive and anti-carcinogenic effects. The aim of the study is to determine the therapeutic effects of oleuropein on cell proliferation, invasion, colony formation, cell cycle and apoptotic mechanisms in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line under in vitro conditions. The effect of oleuropein on cell viability was determined by XTT method. 84 cell cycle control and 84 apoptosis related genes were evaluated by RT-PCR. Effects of oleuropein on apoptosis were researched by TUNEL assay. Protein expressions were determined by western blot analysis. Effects of oleuropein on cell invasion, colony formation and migration were detected by matrigel-chamber, colony formation assay and wound-healing assay, respectively. IC50 value of oleuropein in SH-SY5Y cells was detected as 350μM at 48th hours. It is determined that oleuropein causes cell cycle arrest by down-regulating of CylinD1,CylinD2,CyclinD3,CDK4,CDK6 and up-regulating of p53 and CDKN2A, CDKN2B, CDKN1A gene expressions. Oleuropein also induces apoptosis by inhibiting of Bcl-2 and activating of Bax,caspase-9 and caspase-3 gene expressions. Apoptotic cell ratio was found 36.4±3.27% in oleuropein dose group. Oleuropein decreased invasion in SH-SY5Y cells and suppressed colony numbers in ratio of 53.6±4.71%.Our results demonstrated that oleuropein can be a therapeutic agent in the treatment of neuroblastoma.
